Uniform Title: Śrīvidyārṇavatantra Author: Śrīvidyāraṇyayati Editor: Ram Chandra Kak
Editor: Harabhatta Śāstrī Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: September 18, 2010. Chapters 45 to the end added.
Publisher: Varanasi Tantrika Text Series Publication Year: 1947 Publication City: Varanasi
Publication country: India p.
1) Now, atha.
The Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
composed by the ascetic Śrīvidyāraṇya.
The first breath:
her body radiant like a thousand rising suns, subtler than the subtlest,
resembling a mass of lightning and like ten million moons, she dwells within the threefold light.

May that Śrī Madhumatī Śakti, who consists of the threefold fire, who is endowed with the three *kūṭas* known as Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti, and who is transformed by the [digits] four, five, and six, protecting you— she who is eternal in nature and whose form is the consciousness of the universe.
May she, Mālinī, whose form is the universe, always stand before me.
Having thoroughly examined the two systems, I shall separately elucidate the *Paratantra*—titled the *Vidyārṇava*—out of fear that they might otherwise become confused. (1.3)
The Tantrikas know that the identity with the Great Goddess Madhumatī is designated as the *Kādi* [system], whereas the identity with Mālinī is the *Kālīmata*. (1–4)

By means of the thirty-six consonants, which are the fundamental constituents consisting of the nature of Śiva, each separately conjoined with the sixteen vowels and designated as the "Full Mandala. || 1-5 ||
[The deities] consist of the nature of the Siddhas, Kālas, and Nityās multiplied thirty-six times;
they possess bodies doubled through the distinctions of pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the ninefold [mantras]. || 1.6 ||
Through principles consisting of that twofold nature, and through yantras doubled by those,
her form is said to be divided into various distinctions according to the method of the Vedas.
The Goddess Madhumatī, who is complete with the thirty-six principles and bestows the fruit of all mantras—that identity with her which is designated as "Kādi" (the K-group) [is the goal]. 1-8.

She is praised through the traditions, the conventions, the five pentads, the sacred seats, and the visions, by means of the divisions of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, which consist of the multitude [of deities].
That which is called Mālinī is the identity with that [reality], according to the Kālikāmata;
by thorough knowledge of these two systems, a man becomes equal to Śiva. (1.10)

The reality of time, the philosophical views, the pervasiveness, the traditions, the meditations on the limbs, the gross, subtle, and supreme secondary limbs, the seed-syllables, the powers, and the sprouts of the phonemes. (1.11)

Having learned from the guru and from the scriptures the respective sequence, the respective conduct, the respective origin, and the respective worship, one should be untiring in those respective rites.
Devoid of beginning, end, and middle, yet endowed with beginning, middle, and end;
the purifier of the beginningless reality, he is the knower of both the dependent and the independent natures.
One should perform the worship of the Goddess; otherwise, the fruit will be different. He who worships the supreme Śivā without knowing the lineage of the gurus [will suffer]. (1.14)
That worship should be known as fruitless, like an oblation cast into ashes;
therefore, one should diligently ascertain the lineage of gurus from its very root. 1.15
Having constantly learned the tradition from the mouth of the Guru without sloth, one should perform daily recollection for the sake of attaining the potency of the mantra. (1.16)
According to the sequence of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), as well as in the sequence of Kāmarāja, in the sequence of Lopāmudrā, and indeed in the General Sequence (sāmānyakrama). || 1-17 ||
[One should contemplate] the lineage of gurus for those belonging to the families of the Vidyāvatāra and Vidyāpta [Tantras],
as well as for the five Āmnāyas within the initiation of the Five Abodes (Pañcāyatana). (1-18)
Having understood the two systems of doctrine and their mutual interrelation with great effort,
he who performs the worship of the Goddess attains his desired fruit.
If one performs worship otherwise, it leads to malevolent magic (abhicāra).
Furthermore, the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā is a mantra that bestows grace upon others.
Kālikā, Dakṣiṇā, Mālinī, the mantra of the Śrīguru, the [mantra of] Caraṇa, the nine Nāthas, and the sixteen Mūlavidyās. (1–21)
The six supports, the sciences, and likewise the goddesses of consciousness,
as well as the sixty-four great mantras, are established in the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya).
By remembering these, a mortal becomes equal to Śiva in an instant.
Furthermore, the lineage of gurus must be known by those desiring the perfection of mantra. (1.23)
The one named Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora after that;
the fourth is Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta is the fifth. (1.24)
These are the five divine lineages (divyaughas), and after them comes Ādinātha;
after that comes Annadinātha, and after that Anāmaya.
Anantānandanātha and likewise Cidābhāsa—these are the five lineages of Siddhas; the first, however, is the Supreme Lord.
Viśveśvara is the second, and after that is another, Haṃseśvara;
then the one known as Saṃvarteśvara, and after that Dvīpeśvara. || 1-27 ||
The Navātman, the Īśvara, and the six classes of Mānavas are proclaimed;
these are to be known as the gurus designated by the term *kula*, who follow the path of *kula*. (1–28)
They are disciples born of noble lineage, who understand the meaning of the family mantras;
they are seated upon the family seat and are devoted to the family tantras.
Those who have abandoned all darkness through the union with the Kula, who are immersed in the exuberance of the essence of the Great Rasa, and who are joined with the Kula; || 1.30 ||
Ten cubits tall, five-faced, and adorned with garlands of severed heads,
they possess the splendor of a thousand rising suns and are intent upon fulfilling the inner heart.
They hold a sword, a shield, a skull-cup, a trident, and likewise a mallet;
they also carry a khaṭvāṅga staff, an arrow, and a bow, while displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In the fourth watch of the night, within the Kuṇḍalinī of great power,
they are situated below the point of emission (visarga), possessing a luster like liquid lac.
These family preceptors should be honored with effort for the sake of attaining perfection in knowledge;
yet the practitioner does not honor these family preceptors with such effort. (1.34)
For such a person, worship, recitation, bathing, giving gifts, and so forth are in vain;
one should meditate upon these family preceptors who are proclaimed in the Urdhvāmnāya.
Prajñā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; as well as Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kuṇḍalī, Mātṛkā, and Parā. (1.36)
These eleven are the divine currents; after them are Ādinātha, then Parā, Acintyanātha and Acintyā, and then Avyakta and Avyaktikā. (1–37)
Kuleśvara and Kuleśī, the Siddhaughas numbering eight, Tūṣṇīśa and his Siddhā, then Mitra and Kubjā. (1–38)
Gagana, Cāṭulī, and then Candragarbha; Vālibhāgin, Mukta, Mahilā, and then Lalita. || 1.39 ||
Śaṅkha, the one named Śrīkaṇṭha, Śrīkaṇṭhā, the Supreme Lord (Pareśvara), the Supreme Goddess (Pareśvarī), Kumāra, Sahajā, and Ratna. (1.40)
Then Jñānadevī, Brahmā, Nādinī, Ajeśvara, Mahilā, Pratiṣṭhā, Sahajā, and Śiva. (1–41)
The image (pratimā) is consciousness-bliss (cidānanda), and likewise the innate (sahajā);
then Śrīkaṇṭha, bliss, and knowledge (vidyā), and thereafter Śiva and the innate (sahajā). || 1-42 ||
Soma and Sahajā, and then Saṃvit and Sahajā;
Vibudha and Vibudhā, as well as Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 1.43 ||
Ānanda and Nandinī, then the one named Kāmeśvara;
Kāmeśvara and Kamala, along with Sahaja—these are the pairs of Jinas. (1.44)
These multitudes of human beings are traditionally remembered as having lotus-hands that grant boons and fearlessness;
they, the teachers who are the incarnations of Vidyā, should be placed within the lotus of the sky.
These are declared to be the gurus of the Vidyā in the Śāmbhava-krama:
Vyomātītā, Vyomeśī, Vyomagā, and Vyomacāriṇī.
The five Mothers residing in the sky are proclaimed as the Divine Currents (divyaugha):
Unmanā, Samanā, and Vyāpikā Śakti.

Sound (dhvani) and mere sound (dhvanimātra), the unstruck sound (anāhata), and beyond that the point (bindu); the point ends with the word "space" (ākāśa), and the ninefold assembly of the perfected ones (siddhaugha) follows. || 1.48 ||
The Supreme Self (Paramātman), Śāmbhava, Cinmudra, Vāgbhava, Līla, Sambhrama, and likewise Citprasanna. (1-49)
And these eleven groups of men are proclaimed as the nine teachers of the Vidyā and of the lineage of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya).
The practitioner of the Ṣoḍaśī should worship these in the sequence of nine rows;
however, at the end of the Viśva [row], he should place the lineage of his own Guru behind the Goddess.
Kapila, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Sanandana, Bhṛgu, Sanatsujāta, Vāmadeva, and Nārada. || 1.52 ||
Gautama, Śunaka, Śakti, Mārkaṇḍeya, Kauśika, Parāśara, Śuka, Aṅgiras, and likewise Kaṇva.
Jābāli, Bharadvāja, and likewise Vedavyāsa; then Īśāna, Ramaṇa, Kapardī, and Bhūdhara. (1.54)
Subhaṭa and Jalaja, then Bhūteśa, the Supreme;
Vijaya and Bharata, then Padmeśa and Subhaga. || 1.55 ||
Viśuddha, Samara, Kaivalya, Gaṇeśvara, Supādya, Vibudha, Yoga, Vijñāna, Anaṅga, and Vibhrama. (1.56)
Dāmodara, Citābhāsa, Cinmaya, Kalādhara, Vīreśvara, Mandāra, Tridaśa, Sāgara, and Mṛḍa. || 1-57 ||
Harṣa, Siṃha, Gauḍa, Vīra, Aghora, Dhruva, Divākara, Cakradhara, Pramatheśa, and Caturbhuja. (1–58)
Ānandabhairava, Dhīra, Gauḍa, and Pāvaka; Parāśarya, Satyanidhi, and after that Rāmacandra. (1–59)
Govinda Śaṅkarācārya was the seventy-first;
and there were fourteen disciples of Śaṅkarācārya who were firm in their vows. (1.60)
The disciples of the Goddess were firm-souled and capable of both restraint and grace:
Śaṅkara, the one named Padmapāda, Bodha, and Gīrvāṇa. (1.61)
And Ānandatīrtha by name—these five are remembered as the monks:
Sundara, Viṣṇuśarman, Lakṣmaṇa, and Mallikārjuna. (1.62)
Trivikrama, Śrīdhara, Kapardī, Keśava,
and Dāmodara— these are the renowned householders, numbering five.

She is endowed with sovereignty over the monasteries, seats, and secondary seats; she is initiated at the very end; she performs the funeral rites; she is known as Śaṅkarā, and she is joined with [the syllable] *masa*.
The lineage of disciples of the divine Śaṅkara himself is renowned;
among them were Padmapāda, Ṣaḍguruśiṣya, and Paripāvaka.
Nirvāṇa, Gīrdhana, Cidānanda, and Śivottama—these wise ones, dwelling in solitary hermitages, observe silence and have abandoned all envy. || 1.66 ||
In that manner, the various lineages of his disciples wander throughout the world;
many diverse disciples of Bodha exist on earth in Kerala. (1.67)
The disciple of Gīrvāṇendra was indeed Vidvadgīrvāṇa;
his disciple was Vibudhendra, and the disciple of Vibudha was Sudhīndra.
His disciple was Mantragīrvāṇa; from him there would arise various men.
And on earth, there would be householders who were disciples of the one named Ānandatīrtha.

On this earth, there were various leaders of the seats (pīṭhanāyakas) who were disciples of Sundarācārya and who were knowers of the tradition concerning the seat of the sandals of the one to be propitiated. || 1.70 ||
All the lay devotees were seated upon beautiful seats;
there was the disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarman, the learned and eloquent teacher Pragalbha. (1.71)
When this treatise, spoken by me, his disciple, had reached completion,
the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the sustainer of the world, appeared before me.
Thus he spoke: "O child, choose a desired boon.
Then I said, "O Mother, [grant that] my excellent composition may [attain fame]."
Having perceived the lineage of the gurus and having visualized me as the Guru, those practitioners who recite the mantras with devotion—even without formal initiation—[attain success]. (1.74)
"It is my desire that they attain supreme success.
Then the God, being well-pleased, replied, "So shall it be."
Having joyfully granted the boon, she vanished from the lineage of the Guru;
for it is certain that the Goddess is satisfied by mere knowledge alone. (1.76)
The disciple of Śaṅkara, the teacher of the world, was Lakṣmaṇadeśika;
he attained great renown in the world through his asceticism, learning, and splendor.
Having attained the fourth state on this earth, free from passion,
he wandered about, taking refuge in the capital city of the mature deity.
The mature king gave him a residence, ornaments, food, and attendants.
Once, while Lakṣmaṇa was standing in the midst of his assembly hall—
Those who were engaged in trade, having brought various goods and garments from other islands, presented them as gifts to the king. (1.80)
The king gave those many garments to Lakṣmaṇa;
taking them, Lakṣmaṇa, the best of preceptors, went to his own abode.
Having carefully established the fire in the sacrificial pit according to the path prescribed by the Vedas,
he whose self was the Goddess offered those garments as oblations with a spirit of devotion.
Having heard that, even though the mature deity remembered the contrary situation in his heart, he thought:
"I shall give the garments again today, having made an effort to pay their price."
Having spoken thus, the messenger was sent into the presence of Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of clothing;
then, his mind filled with anger, he uttered a curse upon the king.
"May he who steals the sister of a Brahmin become childless even when grown up," saying this, the Goddess caused garments to be begged for and gave them back again. (1.85)
Then, having abandoned that city, he went to the southern region;
at that time, the mature Lakṣmaṇa was deeply distressed in mind regarding that country.
Having reached him, he entreated him, saying, "O Lord, show me mercy.
With a pleased mind, the brahmin spoke these excellent words: (1.87)
O King, know that my word is unfailing even in this world;
nevertheless, being satisfied by your devotion, I speak to you.
"Your offspring shall come to be, but there will be no happiness for it. Having heard that, the king was dejected in mind and departed toward his own city.
Then, after some time had passed, King Prauḍhadeva met his death while his wife was pregnant. (1.90)
Then, at the request of the subjects, I was made to accept the burden of that kingdom;
it was a great wonder, with wealth [offered] equal to ten billion suns.
Having constructed the city named Śrīvidyānagara, radiant with the essence of the Śrīcakra, and having established the fitness for sovereignty in the son of the mature deity; || 1.92 ||
Having seated that king, Ambadeva, upon the royal throne,
by his command, learned men seeking pure truth [proceeded] in his assembly.
Having been entreated by my mother and having diligently received her command,
I have thoroughly examined various tantras and yāmalas in their entirety.
Having thoroughly blended these two systems, I have joyfully composed this work titled *Vidyārṇava* for the benefit of the world. (1.95)
The disciples of the one known as Mallikārjuna are in the Vindhya region;
the disciples of Trivikrama are indeed in the land of Śrī Jagannātha.
In the lands of Gauḍa, Mithilā, and Vaṅgāla, as well as in the regions of Kāśī and Ayodhyā, the disciples of Śrīdhara were indeed renowned as Kapardins.

Indeed, there is no other tradition in the world besides that of the illustrious Śaṅkara; the Tantra known as the Tantrarāja, according to the Kādi-Śakti system, is extremely difficult to obtain. (1.98)
The four texts known as the Mātṛkārnava, the Tripurārṇava, and the Yoginīhṛdaya are thus renowned. (1.99)
Other texts concerning the Kālīśakti doctrine are also renowned on the surface of the earth;
through the thorough knowledge of these two systems, a human being becomes Śiva himself. (1.100)
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment should strive to understand and protect [the teachings];
the establishment in the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) is according to the consensus of the two systems. (1.101)
Whatever has been shown by the Guru with the approval of whichever philosophical system, that the best of practitioners should accomplish; it is in accord with that very system. (1.102)
One should not create a confusion of systems, for otherwise it would obstruct success;
[this applies] to the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja due to its various divisions within the Kālī system.
A man who is a devotee of that doctrine should know the lineage of the gurus:
Prahlādānandanātha and Sanakānanda. (1.104)
Vasiṣṭhānandanātha, Kumārānanda, Krodhānanda, Śukānanda, and thereafter Dhyānānanda. (1–105)
Bodhānanda, Surānanda, and the nine gurus known as the Kulas—
all have two eyes, two arms, and lotus hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

At the previously mentioned time and place, they should be meditated upon by those most skilled in mantras as the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), consisting of consciousness (*cin-maya*), and the divine power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*). (1.107)
Prabodha, Subodha, Ananta, and those known as Siddhas; Sudhāman, Trimūrti, and Jhiṇṭīśa are remembered as the Mānavas. (1.108)
The mantras ending with the word "Ānandanātha" and beginning with the three fixed vowels (dhruvatāra) and so forth— "I worship the pādukā"— consist of seventeen syllables.
The Śaivī [power] consists of seventeen forms; the eternal [mantras] consist of seventeen syllables.
The first is Paraprakāśa, and the other is Paraśiva. (1.110)
Paraśakti and Kauleśa, Śukradevī and Kuleśvara,
and Kāmeśvarī as the seventh— these are the seven [deities] of the Divine Current (divyaugha), numbering as many as the sages (seven).
Bhoga, Klinna, Samaya, Sahaja, and Vedasaṃkhya—these are the Siddhas; then Gaganaviśva and Vimala. (1.112)
Madana, Bhuvana, Nīla, Svātmā, and Priya—these are said to be the eight human beings (mānava) remembered as having the universe as their body. 1-113.
One should worship these nine [deities] in sequence behind the Goddess;
at the end of that, the wise one should worship his beloved lineage of gurus.
From Kapila up to Vyāsa, there are twenty-one in number:
Karuṇa, Varuṇa, Vijaya, Samara, and Guṇa.
Bala, Viśvaṃbhara, Satya, Priya, Śrīdhara, Śārada, Sakaleśa, Vilāsa, Nityeśa, and Viśvapuruṣa. (1-116)
Govinda, the enlightened one, the lion, the hero, the moon, the sun, the immovable, the source of speech, the sound, the deluder, the easily attained, and Śiva.
Mṛtyuñjaya, Vāsudeva, Śaraṇa, Sanandana, Ākāśa, Gopriya, Harṣa, Bharga, Kāma, and Mahīdhara. || 1-118 ||
Īśāna, Gaṇapa, Śrīmān, Kapāla, Bhairava, Diva, and those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara are declared to be seven in number. (1–119)
And there are seventy-one gurus who are the very form of Śiva;
having understood the lineage of their disciples according to the procedure taught by one's own guru, [one should worship them].
In worship, libation, fire-offering, recitation, and especially in ritual placement, the practitioner attains success through mere remembrance; of this there is no doubt.
The lineage of gurus for both the Kālīmata and the Lopāmudrā [traditions] must be known by those desiring spiritual accomplishment as well as by their respective practitioners. (1.122)
Śrīvidyānandanātha, as well as Paraśambhu, Paramātman, Svaprakāśa, and Bhagīratha—these are the divine lineages (divyaugha). || 1-123 ||
Virūpākṣa and the hosts of Siddhas, then Jñānānanda; thereafter Acalānandanātha and Yogānanda are the Mānavas.
One should contemplate these family preceptors in the previously mentioned place:
Kumuda, Kamala, Subhoja, and those known as the Divine (Divya). (1.125)
Ātreya, Bhārgava, and Gautama are known as the Siddhas;
Śaunaka, Vasu, and Suratha are the Mānavas. (1-126)

Preceded by the triad of *tāra* mantras, [the names] ending with the word *Ānandanātha*, one should employ the word "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) at the end of the *pādukā* mantra, and then the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*). (1.127)
All nineteen syllables are indeed Vaiṣṇavas in their essential form;
they are the gurus who manifest as Vidyās and are of the nature of Śiva, without a doubt.
The first is said to be Paramaśiva, and from him Kāmeśvarī;
the Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha)—all of which illuminate wisdom.
These indeed are the seven divine currents (divyaugha); after that comes the divine Citra;
then Kaivalya, Anudevi, and then Mahodaya.
These are the five streams of the Siddhas; beyond them is Citānanda, then Viśvaśaktyānandanātha, and after that Ramānanda.
Kamalānandanātha, and thereafter Manohara, Svātmānanda, and Pratibha—these are the seven human [incarnations]. (1.132)
And one should worship these nine initiation-gurus (dīkṣāguru) according to the sequence of the rows;
at the end of each row, Kapila and then Agastya [are to be worshipped].
Then Anasūyā, then Atri, then Lopāmudrā;
from Vasiṣṭha down to Vyāsa, there are nineteen in number. (1.134)
Āditya, Mahādeva, Vāgānanda, and beyond that Vāmadeva, Ratīdeva, Ananta, Yoga, and Dharādhava. || 1-135 ||
Suhasta, Satyasaṅgha, Brahmānanda, Bhairava, Dattānanda, Kuntīśa, Citghana, Soma, and Gaurava. (1–136)
Tripureśa, Mahābāhu, Akrodhana, Śiva, Ambikā, Vidyānanda, Guṇānanda, Gaurīśa, Vibudha, and Hara. (1–137)
Bhūteśa, Somanātha, Sarvajña, Sarasahari, and those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara are declared to be seven in number. (1-138)
The number of gurus is recorded as sixty-four by the most excellent of teachers;
by the remembrance of these, the Goddess will certainly become well-pleased. (1.139)
Having understood the lineage of gurus for the vidyās worshipped by Manu and others,
those who worship them should mutter their respective great vidyās.
Mahādeva, Parāmbā, and Kūrmeśa possess divine forms; Sadyojāta, Kumāra, and Bhūteśa are known as the Siddhas.
Priyānanda, Līna, and Aghora—these are the men who follow the path of the Kula; they should be remembered at the previously mentioned time and place. (1.142)
Pūrṇeśa and Śaṅkara are known as the "Divine" (divya); Pragalbha, Bhautika, and Tridaśa are known as the "Supreme Accomplished" (paramasiddha). || 1.143 ||
Vidyeśa, Vāsava, and Yatīśa—these are the human gurus who are the incarnations of knowledge; they should be remembered within the lotus of the sky.
The first is the illumination of the other; from that comes the reflective awareness of the other.
Then there is Kāmeśvarī, liberation, and the immortal Puruṣa.
Aghora—these seven are the divine currents (divyaugha), whose nature is Śiva.
Then there is Prakāma and Sadānanda; thereafter follows the supreme current of the Siddhas (siddhaugha).
And there are the four lineages of Siddhas; then the Uttara and the Parama;
then Sarvajña and Sarvasiddha; and then Govinda and Śaṅkara.
The flood of human beings—these seven constitute the lineage of gurus in initiation;
one should worship nine [gurus] on the rear side of the Goddess according to the sequence of rows.
At the conclusion of the worship of Śaṅkara, one should devotedly worship the maṇḍala of the lineage of one’s own gurus,
numbering twenty-one, beginning with Kapila and ending with Vyāsa.
Then there is the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Knowledge, the Conqueror of the Three Cities,
Hara, Kāmeśa, the Destroyer of Tripura, Puruṣa, and the Supreme Hari.
Gālava, Mudgara, Śauri, Paramātman, Dhaneśvara,
Dhanañjaya, Bhāskara, Bhallāṭa, and Vibhāvasu.
Jīvanātha, Gorakṣa, Matsyanātha, Sadāśiva, Gurubhakta, Jitakrodha, Bodhānanda, and Sureśvara. || 1-152 ||
Bhairava is existence-consciousness-bliss, the accomplished Lord, the mine of compassion,
the bestower of prosperity, the embodiment of the Vedas, the Lord of all, difficult to attain, and self-controlled.
Nāgadeva, Kṣamānātha, Bhāveśa, Keśava, Nandīśa, Gaṇapa, Vīra, Durjñeya, Mihira, and Priya. (1–154)
These seven, beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara, who were previously mentioned, together with the seventy-four others, are the gurus who bestow spiritual perfection. (1.155)
Through recollection and worship, there is no doubt for the practitioners;
this is indeed the view regarding the threefold vidyās known as the Kādi and others.

Having understood the three lineages of gurus within the succession of teachers for the descent of the family lore and the ocean of initiations, the wise man should worship them for the sake of attaining the perfection of the Vidyā. (1.157)
Sarvajña, then Īśāna, Bhūteśa, and those designated as Divya; Divya, Sarva, and Bhavya—these are the Siddhas preceded by Śrī. (1.158)
The Mānavas are remembered as Praśasta, Prakāma, and Sudhāma;
they have four arms and three eyes, and are clothed in red garlands and garments. || 1.159 ||
Furthermore, those gurus known as the Kulas, whose lotus-hands are raised holding a rosary, a book, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, should likewise be remembered there.
Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Jñāna, Satya, and Pūrṇa—these are the Siddhas of divine form, preceded by the word "Śrī. (1-161)
O Mānava, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), intuition (*pratibhā*), and the fortunate one (*subhaga*) are considered [the deities];
they are to be meditated upon and worshipped as the masters who bring about the descent of knowledge (*vidyāvatāra-guru*) for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*). (1-162)
Uddyota, Prabhāva, Kuleśa, Divyarūpin, Bhairava, Gaṇapa, and Kumāra are known as the Siddhas. (1–163)
Udbhaṭa, Vāgbhaṭa, and Kamana are remembered as the [three] Mānavas;
all are pervaded by three sets of three syllables and preceded by the seeds of Māyā and Śrī. || 1-164 ||
I worship the *pādukā* ending with the word Ānandanātha;
and in both worship and libation, I satisfy the *pādukā*.
In the act of purification, one should employ the respective words: "I purify" (*mārjayāmi*) here; and likewise, in the oblation that is a limb of worship, one says, "I worship Agnisundarī. (1-166)
In the same way, at the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), one says, "I satisfy Agnivallabhā";
during the ritual purification (mārjana), one says, "I purify Agnidayitā"—such is the sequence.
One should worship these nine gurus of initiation according to the sequence of the rows; there are twenty-one [gurus] from Kamanānta to Vyāsānta, beginning with Kapila.
Avyaya, Viśeṣa, Saṃgraha, Devala, as well as Prakāṇḍa, Gahana, Durlabha, and Durjaya. (1-169)
Viśveśa, Udaya, Tvarita, and then Sundara; Bharata and Dhiṣaṇa, and then Śrīkaṇṭha and Śaṅkara. || 1-170 ||
Anala, Vāsava, Sunetra, and then Subhaga; Vīreśa, Viraha, Klinneśa, and then Vijaya. || 1-171 ||
Karṣaka, Pragalbha, Vinaya, Varada, Śāntana, Citraka, Adbhuta, and Nipuṇa. (1.172)
Vipula and Vimala, then Someśa and Kuśala;
Sumantra and Sutantra, as well as Vidyeśa and Vinata.
Vibhava, Vardhana, Anindya, Supriya, Sāraṅga, Vāruṇa, Satyecchu, and likewise Aribha. || 1-174 ||
Then Vāgyata, Kāmana, Vāṅmaya, Sukṛta, Viśākha, Mañjula, Kāmeśa, and then Vāgbhava. || 1-175 ||
Those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara are declared to be seven in number;
these gurus together amount to eighty-four.
By remembering these, a mortal becomes equal to Śiva in an instant.
Even in the Kādiśakti system, these are remembered as gurus everywhere.
In the Kālīmata, due to the diversity of mantras, there are many varieties of gurus;
they are established upon the eastern, southern, western, and central thrones.
The divisions of Bālādibhairavī are recorded as being thirty-two in number;
there are the sixteen Nityās, the six Darśanas, and the five Pañcikas. (1.179)
The Vidyās of the four Samayas and the Śaktis of the nine enclosures are declared in the Mantrapārāyaṇa as the Vidyās that are the Śaktis of the Śrīcakra.
Having entered the lineage of the gurus with diligent effort, one should venerate the nine noble gurus, beginning with Prahlāda, Ānandanātha, and the others. (1.181)
Samaya and Kakkuṭa are indeed the primary ones known as divine;
Budheśa and Kuthara are likewise Bhārgava, whose forms are perfected.
Kandala, Tapana, and Adīna—these nine are the gurus known as the incarnations of Vidyā. (1.183)
The Supreme Lord is the light of others; from Him comes Paraśiva, Kāmeśvarī, liberation, desire, and that which is known as nectar. || 1-184 ||
These are the seven divine [faces]; beyond them is Īśāna, and Tatpuruṣa should be known as well, followed immediately after by Aghora. (1.185)
Vāmadeva, then Sadyojāta, and the Siddhas are remembered as the Abhīs;
and the Pañcottara, the Parama, the Sarvajña, and the Sarva. (1.186)
The Siddha named Govinda, Śaṅkara, and the seven Mānavas—
these are the gurus of initiation and should be especially worshipped.
From Kapila up to Vyāsa, there are twenty-one in number;
then Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Vikrama, and Vijaya.
Rantideva, Sudeva, Bhoja, Rāma, Guṇa, Bhairava, Bhramaṇa, Ramaṇa, and then Vimala. || 1.189 ||
Vainateya, Vāsava, Anala, Saṅgharṣaṇa,
Vīrabhadra, and Viśāla— these two are experts among the Vidyādharas.
Vaiśvānara, Yajñeśa, Mahīdhara, Kulāntaka, Ananta, Varada, Kāma, and then Jālandhara.
Śaiva, Sadāśiva, Bhadra, Rudra, Kandarpa, Suvrata, Satyavrata, Satyanidhi, Bodha, and Maudgalya. (1.192)
Īśāna, Gauḍapāda, and the others—these seven up to Śaṅkara, along with sixty-eight more, are traditionally remembered as the [gurus] to be honored until the end of the Manvantara. (1.193)
Then, having understood the lineage of gurus (gurukrama), one should worship it with a spirit of devotion;
this indeed is the lineage of gurus for the goddesses of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) and the others.

In the same way, those who worship the deities of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) must know the lineage of their respective mantras and gurus for the sake of attaining those specific accomplishments.
Tāraka, Rucaka, Bhadraka, Divyarūpin, Amara, Satyaga, Bhāsvara, and Siddha—these are their names. || 1.196 ||
The humans, immortal and full of awakening, possess the forms of their [respective] clans;
one should contemplate them within the splendor of those respective pledges and those respective locations. (1-197)
Pradīpa, Prabhāsa, and Pragalbha are those known as the Divine (divya); Prabhāva, Vinaya, and Kumuda are those known as the Accomplished (siddha). (1-198)
The manifestation of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and the one whose form is consciousness (cidrūpa), as well as Prakāma—these are remembered as Mānavas;
these are called the incarnations of Vidyā, teachers difficult to find on earth. (1-199)
Prabhāva, Ādinātha, Vimala, Samaya, and Śiva—these five alone are the divine lineages (divyaugha); then Nirvāṇa, Gaṇapa, and Hara. (1–200)
Paraśambhu, Cidaṃśa—these five are known as the Siddhas;
[then] Kurunātha, Viśuddhi, Kuśala, and Kuntaśekhara. (1–201)
Suḍimbha, Sundara, and Keśa—these seven are remembered as the Mānavas.
The lineage of the initiating gurus (dīkṣāgurukrama) of the Goddess is diligently [to be worshipped] on the back part [of the body]. 1-202.
For the sake of one's own accomplishment, these nine should be especially worshipped in nine rows;
they begin with Vāk, Māyā, Kamalā, Siddha, Guru, and Śabda. (1.203)
From Kapila down to Vyāsa, there are twenty-one in number:
Vīrabhadra, Mahāsena, Girīśa, and Guṇavardhana.
Vāṅmaya, Varada, Vīra, Subhavya, Nandināyaka, Vijaya, Viśvavinata, Vīreśa, and Girinandana. || 1-205 ||
He is beyond negligence and the conjunction of expenditure; he is eternal bliss, transcending the qualities (guṇas);
he is the bliss of the qualities, delighting in the qualities, unobstructed, stainless, and all-pervading.
He is the fortunate one, free from conceptual construction, the great form, immovable, and ruddy;
he is the master of the quiver, the swift, the Dharma, formless, and devoid of sense organs.
Haṃseśvara, Rucigrīva, Droṇa, Viśvaṃbhara, Bala, Sudakṣiṇa, Virūpākṣa, Gurubhakta, and Gurupriya. || 1-208 ||
Those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara are proclaimed to be seven in number;
these constitute the seventy-three lineages of men for the purpose of worship.
By worshipping these, the goddesses renowned in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya will become pleased; therefore, for the sake of attaining the Vidyā-siddhi, the supreme gurus should be worshipped. 1-210.
Having received the lineage of the gurus for the goddesses of the Western Tradition, one should perform worship for the sake of accomplishment, either from the guru or from the scriptures. (1.211)
Bhairava and Bhairavī, Mahādeva and Gaṇeśvara, Virūpākṣa and Mahāsena, Vīrabhadra and Dhanādhipa. || 1-212 ||
The gurus ending with Ānandanātha are designated as Kula;
likewise are Aghora, Ghorasaṃjña, and Ghoraghoratara. (1.213)
Divyaugha, Tatpara Śarva, Sarva, and Rudra are those who have attained perfection;
likewise, Hāṃkāra, Hīṃkāra, and Hūṃkāra are the Mānava [lineages].
These are the gurus known as the introductions to knowledge (vidyāvatāra), who bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi): Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and thereafter [Sadyojāta]. (1.215)
Sadyojāta—these five are the divine currents (divyaugha), along with Samārasa;
Bhūteśa, Lalita, Svastha, Kauleśa, and those known as the Siddhas. (1–216)
Ālasya, Prabhānanda, Rāgiṇī, Vaktrarāgiṇī, Atīta, the one named Kubja, and thereafter Kulakauleśvara. (1–217)
These seven groups of human beings are traditionally taught to be the gurus of initiation;
one should worship them on the back of the Goddess in nine rows according to their sequence.
At the end of the Kulakauleśvara, one should worship the succession of one's own gurus,
numbering twenty-one, beginning with Kapila and ending with Vyāsa.
Ananta, Śaṅkara, Piṅgala, Karālaka, Siddha, Ratna, Śiva, Mehī, Samaya, and Khageśvara. || 1-220 ||
Bhadra, Kūrma, Ghora, Gopa, Mīna, Kaulika,
Tīvra, Ḍāmara, Rāma, Kāma, and Śākinī.
Mahāmāya, Mahānanda, Ādhāreśa, Cakraka, Kurura, Samaya, Śrīśa, Kubjikā, and Kuladīpikā. (1–222)
Śiveśa, Śarvarī, Dharmī, Kāmī, Kāmakalā, Śiva, and those beginning with Gīḍā and ending with Śaṅkara are declared to be seven in number. (1–223)
Sixty-four gurus are indeed remembered as bestowers of accomplishment;
therefore, having recognized one's own lineage of gurus, one should worship them with devotion. (1.224)
One should perform the worship of the goddesses of the Northern Tradition with devotion;
specifically, having recognized one's gurus, one should do so with diligent effort for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of the Vidyā.
Prahlāda, Ānandanātha, and others previously mentioned are the gurus in Kula;
Uḍḍīśa, Kuleśa, and Pūrṇeśa are known as the divine ones.
Kāmeśvara, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śaṅkara are known as the Siddhas;
Ananta, Piṅgala, and Nāda—these are remembered as the Mānavaughas.
Those who are gurus for the descent of knowledge and bestowers of accomplishment are to be worshipped;
they are Mahādeva, Mahādeva, Tripura, and Bhairava.
The gurus of the divine current (divyaugha) have been proclaimed; beyond that is Brahmānanda, then Pūrṇadeva, Advitīya, Calacitta, and Calācala. (1.229)
Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana; Māyā and Māyāvatī—these are proclaimed as the hosts of Siddhas. || 1-230 ||
Vimala, Kuśala, Bhīmasena, Sudhākara, Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, and Prajāpati. || 1-231 ||
Mūladeva, Ratīdeva, Vighneśvara, Hutāśana, Samaya, Ānanda, and Santoṣa—these are remembered as the lineages of men (mānavaughāḥ). (1-232)
On the back of the Goddess, one should worship in the sequence of nine rows;
beyond Santoṣa and Ānanda, one should worship the lineage of gurus.
From Kapila up to Vyāsa, there are twenty-one [teachers] in number:
Śambara, Hṛdaya, Bhoga, Nābhasa, Kaulika, and Dhara. (1.234)
Abhaya, Śambara, Bhadra, Mahāghora, Manomaya, Bhairava, Śavara, Kāla, Brahmā, and Mahākula are thus considered. (1.235)
Vāhana, Khecara, Vyoma, Śvasana, Jvalana, Aja, Īśa, Tāta, Kulātīta, Vāyu, Saṃhāraka, and Kauṭila. (1–236)
The supreme protector of opposition, the six-chakras, the highest beyond the high;
liberated, wise, of noble lineage, true, born of the classes, the embodiment of mantra. || 1-237 ||
Svacchanda, Bhairava, Bhīma, Varṇāḍhya, Śabda, Śabdaja, and those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara—these seven are proclaimed as the number [of the schools]. (1.238)
For these seventy-six gurus are indeed bestowers of spiritual accomplishment;
by remembering them, a mortal becomes equal to Śiva, without a doubt. (1.239)
Having recognized Śaṅkara and the other gurus, one should worship them with a spirit of devotion,
whether in the worship of the five abodes (pañcāyatana) or in individual worship.
The lineage of the respective gurus for the mantras of Gaṇeśa and the others must be known;
without knowing the family of the gurus, one will become lost to the path.
For those who have lost their way, there is no such scope for the fruit of mantra and vidyā if there is no lineage succession among gurus and their disciples. (1.242)
In that case, the mantras and vidyās are fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Whether it be twenty men, or nine, seven, or even three. (1–243)
If a disciple does not know the lineages of his gurus, his own lineage is lost;
therefore, one should know that the lineage of gurus, which is exceedingly auspicious, is superior to one's own lineage. (1.244)
The giver of the mantra is to be known as even greater than Janaka;
therefore, the lineage of gurus is to be understood and honored in every respect. (1.245)
In all cases, it should first be understood that the giver of mantra is the supreme guru;
the supreme and subordinate gurus are Śakti, the Parameṣṭhī, and Śiva. (1.246)
Among all mantras and vidyās, she herself is the embodiment of primordial nature (prakṛti);
from her arises the form of Puruṣa, and from him the lineage of gurus.
For by that very [power], those who possess a portion of Śiva— especially the devotees of Śiva—
are gurus in all mantras, omniscient, and bestowers of spiritual accomplishments.
He is the teacher everywhere of those Śiva-related sciences known as the Śaivya;
Gaṇeśa is considered the master of the Gāṇapatya teachings and the authority over initiation into the Gaṇas.
For the Vaiṣṇavas, he himself is Viṣṇu; for the Sauras, he is indeed Sūrya.
Likewise, there are the Gurus of the divine lineage (divyaugha) and the Gurus of the perfected lineage (siddhaugha).
Human multitudes are to be known everywhere by the teachers as gurus;
[so too are] Gaṇeśvara, Gaṇakrīḍa, Vikaṭa, and Vighnanāyaka. (1-251)
Durmukha, Sumukha, Buddha, Vighnarāja, and Gaṇādhipa—these are the gurus known by their families; one should contemplate them within his splendor.
Surānanda, Pramoda, Heramba, Mahotkaṭa, Śaṅkara, Lambakarṇa, Meghanāda, and Mahābala.
These nine are Gaṇañjaya, the introducers of those sciences:
Vināyaka, Virūpākṣa, Buddha, Śūra, and Varaprada. (1–254)
These are the five divine lineages: Vijaya, Durjaya, Jaya, Kavīśvara, and Brahmaṇya; they are known as the Nidhīśas and the Siddhas.
The sovereign of elephants, the enemy of suffering, the newly born, the bringer of joy;
the Supreme Self, the self of all beings, the great sound, the one with an auspicious countenance. (1.256)
Bālacandra and these nine groups of men are proclaimed;
they are declared to be the gurus for initiation, and when worshipped, they bestow accomplishment.
Then, at the end of Bālacandra, one should worship the lineage of gurus,
numbering twenty-one, beginning with Kapila and ending with Vyāsa.
The calculator, the fortunate one, the eternal, the one whose support is eternal, the everlasting;
full bliss, supreme bliss, the true devotee, the lotus-eyed one. || 1-259 ||
Kāmapāla, the wise one, the most excellent, Gajavaktra, beloved of the Gaṇas, Bhūteśa, the one who plays like a child, Kumāra, the awakener, and Hara. || 1-260 ||
Satyalīla, Sulīla, Vikaṭa, Dhūmravarṇaka, Nandipriya, Nandihāsa, Devīputra, and Dhaneśvara. || 1-261 ||
Viśvaṃbhara, Viśālākṣa, Vighnahartā, Vināyaka, Kūṣmāṇḍeśa, Kapardin, Śiva, Kāla, and Mahīdhara. || 1-262 ||
From Gauḍa to Śaṅkara, these seven who were previously mentioned—these sixty-three gurus indeed bestow spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 1.263 ||
When worshipped and constantly remembered, these mantras— beginning with the seeds of Śrī, Māyā, and Smara, and ending with "Namaḥ Siddhācāryebhyaḥ"— bestow all desired fruits.
Likewise, among the Vaiṣṇavas, these gurus are to be known for the sake of attaining success in mantra:
Prahlāda, Vasiṣṭha, Puṇḍarīka, and Parāśara.
Śuka, Śaunaka, Nārada, Dālbhya, and Vyāsa—these nine are declared to be the gurus who embody the lineage. (1-266)
Then Sarasvatī is to be known, followed by Vināyaka and Śuka;
then Sumantu, Jaimini, and Vaiśampāyana. (1.267)
Nārada, Puṇḍarīka, and Sucela—these nine are the gurus who have manifested as the sciences; they should be meditated upon and worshipped for the attainment of perfection.
Mahādeva, Mahādevī, Parameṣṭhin, Samīraṇa, Varuṇa, Vāmadeva, Kaśyapa, Aṅgiras, and Ṛtu. (1-269)
One should worship these nine gurus of initiation according to the sequence of the rows; numbering twenty-one in total, they begin with Kapila and end with Vyāsa.
Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Satya, Bala, Bāla,
Dhanurdhara, Śaṅkhin, Cakrin, Halin, Khaḍgin, Musalin, Ramaṇa, and Ajita.
Puruṣa, Bhūdhara, Viśva, Govinda, Govivardhana, Gopīśvara, Jitakrodha, Mīna, and Mīnaketana. || 1-272 ||
Manohara, Sātvata, Keśava, Acyuta, Vāmana, Narasiṃha, Avyaya, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Mahīdhara. (1–273)
The portion of consciousness and the light of consciousness, Mādhava and Madhusūdana;
Puruṣottama and Padmākṣa, Ghaṇaśyāma and Dharādhava. (1.274)
Those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara, as well as those previously mentioned—
these sixty-eight gurus are indeed bestowers of spiritual perfection.
Indeed, by the recollection of these, the mantras are accomplished at that very moment;
these [mantras] beginning with the seed-syllable of Manmatha end with "namas" to the Śrīpādas.

Alternatively, for the sake of attaining the success of the mantras and vidyās of the Śaivas, the lineage of respective gurus is proclaimed, ending with "namas" directed toward the feet of the Ācāryas.
Having understood this, one should perform its worship; otherwise, it does not yield fruit.
The Lord Viśveśvara, Mahādeva, the Three-eyed One (Trilocana), is [the deity]. 1-278.
Tripurānta, Kālāgnirudra, and beyond that Kāla;
then Sarveśvara, Nīlakaṇṭha, Dikpati, and Sadāśiva.
Indeed, these eleven are remembered as the gurus who possess the form of the Kula:
Vīrabhadra, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and then Śiva, whose weapon is the trident.
Īśāna, the lord of the Pramathas, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Pracaṇḍaka, Mahiṣa, and Madanārāti [are present] in the incarnation of the Vidyās. (1–281)
The Gurus are remembered as being eleven in number, bestowers of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
They are Aghora, Athaghora, and then Ghoraghoratara. (1-282)
Sarva, Sarvaśa, Rudra, then Tatpuruṣa, then Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, Sadyojāta, and likewise Bhava. (1.283)
These eleven are the divine streams: Bhavodbhava, Vināyaka, Caṇḍīśa, Vāmadeva, Śaṅkara, and Viśvanāyaka. (1-284)
Jyeṣṭha, Śreṣṭha, Kāla, Bhūteśa, and Pramatheśvara—these are the eleven Siddhaughas; after them comes Kalavikaraṇa.
Balavikaraṇa, and likewise Balapramathana; then Sarvabhūtāntaka, Damana, and Manonmana. (1.286)
Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Nīlagrīva, Trilocana, and Vīreśvara are proclaimed as the human [incarnations] who are equal to Rudra. (1–287)
These gurus of initiation must be honored with effort by the teachers for the sake of attaining the perfection of knowledge;
this is the lineage of gurus ending with Vīreśa. (1.288)
It should be known that there are twenty-one [incarnations] from Kapila down to Vyāsa:
Kāmeśa, Kālakaṇṭha, Kālaghna, and Kālarūpadhṛk. (1.289)
The ender of desire, the large-eyed one, Vīrabhadra, the leader, the trident-armed one, the lord of the mountain, Kailāsa, the embodiment of speech, and Hara. || 1-290 ||
Budheśa and Āmareśa, Caṇḍīśvara and Kumāraka, Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Viśvanātha, and Prajāpati. || 1-291 ||
Ātmeśvara, Saṃvarta, Krameśa, Prakāśana, Lalita, Sparśa, Bhūteśa, Ānanda, and Prabheśvara. || 1-292 ||
Rāgeśa, Karāleśa, Siddheśa, Samayeśvara, Jñānānanda, Priyānanda, Kalānanda, and Amṛteśvara. || 1-293 ||
Guhyeśvara, Cidānanda, Kuleśa, and Caṇḍakaulika, as well as those seven beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara who were previously mentioned; [these are the twenty-eight]. (1.294)
And there are seventy-one gurus who bestow accomplishment; beginning with Prāsāda and ending with Namaḥ, they are those whose feet are to be worshipped. (1.295)
When worshipped and constantly remembered, they bestow the perfection of mantras; likewise, having received the lineage of the gurus, the solar deities should be sacrificed to.
Mihira, Sugupta, and Prabheśa are known as the Divine (divya);
Aruṇa, Marīci, and Mayūkha are known as the Perfected (siddha).
Kātyāyana, Ghṛṇīśa, Mārtaṇḍa, and the Mānavas are remembered; these highly powerful preceptors, known by their lineages, are to be meditated upon. || 1-298 ||
The soul of the Vedas, Bhāskara, Bradhna, the divine Bhāsvat, Prabhākara,
Nārāyaṇa, Kapardin, the Siddhas, Arka, and the embodiment of the three Vedas.
Īśāna is declared to be the progenitor of the Mānavas and the source of the sciences; he is Ānanda, Samaya, Vimala, and Jñānadīpana. (1.300)
Cidghana, Somanātha, Savitṛ, Poṣaṇa, Aruṇa,
Maheśa, Vijaya, Bhūteśa, and Devabhāgaka.
These thirteen, including the initiation and the guru, are proclaimed;
they should be worshipped with effort by the wise in nine rows according to their sequence. (1.302)
Then, after Devabhāga, there were twenty-one [generations] from Kapila;
after Vyāsa, there were Jaimini and Sumantu, the increaser of knowledge.
(10) Cidānanda, Cidābhāsa, Cinmaya, the Guru who knows Yoga;
Satyavrata, the embodiment of consciousness (cidrūpa), Bhairava, and Ambaranāyaka. || 1-304 ||
Viśveśvara, Mitrakara, Śubhaṃkara, Divākara, Gaṇeśvara, Mārtaṇḍabhairava, Dyumaṇi, and Ravi. (1–305)
Trivikrama, Vāsudeva, Śaṅkara, Ravilocana, Puṇḍarīka, Rameśa, Guṇārāma, and Dhaneśvara.
Devendra, Gopanātha, and the noble-souled Puruṣa;
Ācāryasiṃha, Govinda, Vedajña, and Mitravindaka. || 1-307 ||
Those beginning with Gauḍa and ending with Śaṅkara are recorded as being sixty-four in number;
by the mere remembrance of these, the solar mantras are mastered instantly.
Having recognized one's own gurus as emanations from Śaṅkara, one should worship them with a spirit of devotion.
All these, beginning with Māyā, [are worshipped] with the formula "Obeisance" (namaḥ) at the end of their names, followed by the word *pādukā*. (1.309)

Those gurus who have been declared in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) as bestowers of accomplishment (siddhi) are to be known as ending with Bhairava in the tradition designated as "Below" (adhaḥ).
Śrīvidyā together with her divisions, Bālā, and Tripurā;
likewise Bhagamālā, Nityaklinnā, and Svayaṃvarā. (1–311)
Madhumaty, Unmanī, Bheḍā, Śārikā, Surasundarī, Aśvāruḍhā, Mahāmāyā, Kurukullā, and Sureśvarī. (1.312)
Bhuvaneśī, Annapūrṇā, and the presiding deities of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya);
likewise Bagalā, the various forms of Vaśinī, and the fruit-bestowing Aruṇā.
Vārāhī together with Bheda, Bhoginī conjoined with Bheda,
Kāmeśvarī, Bheruṇḍā, Vajreśī, and Vahnivāsinī.
Śivadūtī, Vicitrā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Mahiṣārdī, and Mahālakṣmī are the deities of the Dakṣiṇa Āmnāya.
The goddess Mahāsarasvatī is likewise considered to be Vāgvādinī;
and there is Nīlapatākā, as well as Bhairavī, each associated with her respective division.
Cāmuṇḍā, Raktacāmuṇḍā, and the ten deities beginning with Brāhmī;
Pratyaṅgirā and Bhavānī are the deities of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya). || 1-317 ||
Kālikā is considered together with her divisions, Tārā joined with her divisions, as well as Mātaṅgī, Bhairavī, Chinnā, and Dhūmāvatī. (1.318)
The Vidyās taught in the Uttarāmnāya, such as Nāgaśakti and others, bestow their fruits in a swift time; these are now the deities of the Āmnāya.

Having thus understood those various distinctions, one should devotedly follow the respective lineages of gurus with reverence on the correctly proclaimed festival days according to the Kālīśakti-mata.
Having fashioned a mandala of the gurus upon the ground, one should worship the lineage of gurus with supreme devotion for the sake of the flourishing of the tradition. (1.321)
For deities do not bestow their fruits if there is no lineage transmission;
indeed, they do not do so if one fails to understand the lineage transmission, whether through delusion or even ignorance. (1.322)
One who bestows the mantra with diligence, or worships the deity,
should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the fire-oblation (homa), and the ritual procedure for the preliminary course (pauraścaraṇaka).
Whatever that may be, it would be eternal because of the certainty of its non-transgression;
first is the wheel of Gaṇapati, and outside of that is Bhairava.
Outside of that is the circle of Vaṭuka, and outside of that is the circle of the Siddhas;
above that is the one called Caraṇa, and immediately after that is the Śāmbhava circle.
Above that, the Mālinī-cakra consists of seven wheels;
having first laid out a triangle, one should draw a triangle outside of it.
One should project a triangle outside that, and a nine-cornered figure outside that;
outside that, an eight-petalled lotus, and outside that, three concentric circles.
Having projected three squares, the wise one should worship outside of them:
the Praṇava, Vāgbhava, Māyā, Kamalā, and Khecarī.
Having extracted the secondary seed-syllables of that temple for Śiva and Śakti, [one should place] Saṃvarta, Mahākāla, Indra, Water, Fire, and Wind. (1.329)
One should extract the final phoneme, conjoined with Arghīśa and the half-moon;
thereafter, one should extract the name of the venerable Guru, ending with Ānandanātha.
Having uttered the word *śrīpādukā*, one should say "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and "salutation" (*namaḥ*).
With this king of mantras, one should worship the venerable Guru in the center. (1.331)
In this mantra, the preceptor should place the word "parādyam" (beginning with Parā) everywhere;
then, having applied the name of his wife in the place designated for the preceptor, [he should proceed].
Having uttered "Devī Ambā Śrīpāda," one should worship the Pādukā with the mantra ending in "Namaḥ. To the left of the Nātha, one should worship that Sundarī with the same Vidyā.
The triad of gurus beginning with Śrīnātha is to be worshipped in the three triangles at the front;
however, by the side of Śrīcakranātha is the deity who presides over the wheel.
Having thoroughly worshipped Gaṇanātha, one should worship the second enclosure:
first that called Kāmarūpa, and after that Jālandhara.
One should worship the third [seat], named Pūrṇagiri, at the three corners starting from the eastern point;
however, one should worship the distinguished Coḍyāṇa, which will be described later, in the center.
The best of practitioners should worship Bhairava with her mantra,
since he is the presiding deity of the second cakra, located to the south of Kāmākhya.
The wise practitioner, having worshipped Vaṭuka, Yoginī, and Kṣetrapāla with their respective mantras within a triangle starting from his own front, [should proceed]. (1.338)
On the right side of the first [deity], one should worship Vaṭuka, the leader of the wheel;
then, in the nine corners, starting from one's own front and proceeding clockwise. (1.339)
For the sake of one's own accomplishment, those who are gurus in the introduction to knowledge should be worshipped;
then, on the right of the first [deity], while uttering "Salutation to the Siddhas."
One should worship with devotion the Siddhas and the deities presiding over the wheels (cakras).
Then, the wise practitioner should worship the eight messengers (dūtīs) on the eight petals, beginning from the eastern petal.
On the left side of the first [deity], one should worship the two feet, red and white,
with their respective mantras, and then worship within the three circles.
For the sake of one's own accomplishment, the mandala of the five hundred and seventy-six Vīreśvaras is arranged in a circular form by proceeding counter-clockwise. (1.343)
One should utter twice the previously mentioned group of six seed-syllables and the first letter;
then, having pronounced "Rūpavīreśa," one says, "I worship the pādukā. (1.344)
Thus, the mantras for worship have been described in that same number;
the vowels are in the first verse, and the consonants in the second.
On the third [circle], the pervasive syllables are at the tip of its own center;
there, one should worship Śāmbhava with devotion and effort by means of His mantra.
In the seventh [cakra], the Mālinīcakra, which consists of three squares,
one should worship the eight Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, on the first line.
Then, when the second line has been drawn and divided into five parts,
the practitioner should worship the five elements with their respective mantras.
It is surrounded by the twenty-four deities of the letters;
then, on the third line, are the weapons of Indra and the others, outside of that.
In front of himself, the lord of practitioners should worship with devotion Mālinī, whose body is the universe, by means of her vidyā; and outside of that, the pedestal (pīṭhikā).
In this way, the Goddess certainly becomes pleased with the worshiper,
especially on an even lunar day when the asterisms are even, or on a Friday or a Tuesday.
In yoga, one should worship the circle of gurus with devotion at night for the sake of one's own accomplishment;
whoever worships the circle of gurus with devotion among the Kula lineages, [attains success]. (1.352)
He is declared the best of guides; therefore, initiation from him is indeed unsurpassed.
He is the one who holds the tradition, he is the Guru, and he is the very embodiment of the Goddess.
Therefore, initiation is declared to be auspicious; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
On the contrary, the guru would surely destroy the disciple, and not otherwise.
Therefore, on the appropriate lunar days within the [proper] families, she should be worshipped by excellent practitioners:
Sundarī, Sumukhī, Virūpā, and likewise Vimalā. (1-355)
Antarī, Badarī, Dūtarī, and Puṣpabhadrikā—
this is declared to be the group of eight messengers (dūtī) for the worship of the circle of gurus.

The powers of the sacred seats (pīṭhaśaktis) mentioned therein are the Great Vidyās to be worshipped; these powers of the seat are to be known in the worship of the circle of gurus (gurumaṇḍala). || 1.357 ||
Vāṅmāyā, Kamalā, and Khecarī, devoid of supernatural power (ṛddhi);
then, having drawn a preta, one should indeed place the seed-syllable joined with Nādi and the Moon.
Raudrī is conjoined with Ananta; Ananta is joined with Indu (the Moon), Anala (Fire), and Candra (the Moon).
Then Nakulīśa and Māyā—this is declared to be the supreme Vidyā, Mālinī. (1.359)
One should place the first group of six seed-syllables from the previously mentioned Guru-vidyā at the end in reverse order; this is declared to be the supreme Śāmbhava [mantra]. (1.360)
The network of mantras is to be known by means of the path that is about to be described;
now, according to the Kādimata, the worship of the circle of gurus is to be understood.
On a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood, or on a wooden plank, or even on the bare ground—provided that the ground is level, pure, firm, and very beautiful. (1.362)
One should lay down ten threads— eastward, westward, southward, and northward—
and therein a mandala consisting of eighty-one squares is produced.
On the delightful equilateral grid, with squares five finger-breadths apart,
by laying down two threads— one running east-west and one running north-south— (1.364).
Nine squares arise together at every step; in the center of the nine central squares, there is a middle square. (1.365)
One should write the letters starting from the east and so forth, nine in each square;
preceded by the *māyā* and *śrī* seed-syllables, they are designated as *prakāśa* and *ānanda*.
Having clearly awakened the Lord there within the nine syllables in the nine compartments,
one should likewise place the second name of the Lord in the first set of nine.
One should draw them in groups of nine, following the sequence of circumambulation;
thus, there are indeed nine mandalas for the nine lords.
They arise from the arrangement of syllables; there, one should perform worship according to the sequence of the Lords' cycles, on the day that bears the name of a Lord.
From that time forward, the wise man should worship on that day and in those various places with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
With composed mind, having repeatedly satisfied the Lords with betel-leaves, prostrations, and hymns of praise, through the contemplation of their essential unity; || 1.371 ||
The wise one should worship the venerable Guru in front of the Central Lord;
the learned one should worship the nine [deities] in the nine directions according to the sequence beginning with their names.
Outside of that, the wise one should worship the mandala of the lineage of gurus, beginning with Śiva, in a clockwise sequence and with a spirit of devotion. (1.373)
Thus, being attentive during the festival days, one should perform worship at night, having recited with a well-composed mind: "I worship the sandals. (1.374)
On those very full joints, one should indeed construct sixteen squares by drawing the lines of the qualities (guṇasūtra) through those positions.
One should draw the sixteen syllables as before and perform the worship as before;
in this manner, the worship must be performed by practitioners while the Guru is alive.
When the Lord has passed away, one should set aside the word "Nātha" and raise up the word "Śiva.
He who thus worships daily, and especially on special festival days, [attains the goal]. (1.377)
Therefore, initiation is declared to be auspicious; otherwise, it would be inauspicious.
Indeed, for those endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), there are lotuses in the various stations (padas).
Having performed the worship, it should be concluded on the days following the full-moon and new-moon festivals;
on those very full-moon and new-moon festivals, one should perform the sixteen-fold rite as before.
One should prepare the guru-maṇḍala with the five fragrant substances: camphor, sandalwood, saffron, uśīra, and musk.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should apply that paste upon the forehead with a spirit of devotion,
for the sake of attaining prosperity, victory, and success, and for the attainment of long life and health.

At the beginning and at the end of worship, the wise one should recite the hymn to the Guru during the three junctions of the day for the sake of perfect accomplishment, and likewise at night with a concentrated mind.
Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, the auspicious one in the form of the Guru;
you who have assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the descent of knowledge.
Salutations to you, who are ever-new and of ever-new form, whose singular nature is the ultimate reality,
who dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and who are a mass of pure consciousness.

To the independent one, whose form is fashioned by compassion, the supreme self; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in auspicious forms for those who are destined for liberation.
Salutations to the one who is the discernment for the discerning, the reflection for those who reflect,
the illumination for the luminous, and the very form of knowledge for the wise.
In front, on both sides, behind, above, and below,
may you always provide a seat for me by means of your form as my own mind.
One should recite this hymn daily with diligence for the sake of attaining the perfection of knowledge (vidyāsiddhi).
Within the circle of gurus (gurumaṇḍala), the deities of the wheel [should be worshipped], ending with Śakti and ending with Nātha.
When the guru has passed away, the lineage of gurus extends up to Śiva; this threefold status of the gurus is indeed remembered as the *gurumaṇḍala*, known as the *pāraṃparya*.
Through the thorough knowledge of the lineage, the tradition shall become stable; when the tradition has become stable, it shall possess its true character. || 1.390 ||
By that, the deities, vidyās, and mantras are accomplished instantly;
for during the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), one should constantly worship the maṇḍala of the Guru.
Thorough knowledge of the tradition and the recollection of the potency of the mantra—how can a practitioner be [successful] if he does not know these two? (1.392)

The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and that twofold [category] consisting of the primordial (ādya) and the optional (kāmya)—these three are established in their respective order according to time and succession. (1.393)
The names of the lord of practitioners should be known with effort from the venerable guru as well, for the sake of establishing the tradition. (1.394)
Having thus understood this lineage, one should impart it to one's own disciples,
always contemplating the identity of the Guru, the Self, and the Deity-mantras.
And one who is diligent in obeying his commands is called the best disciple.
Regarding the specific days for the worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru, the *Tantrarāja* states:
"The day of the Guru’s birth, likewise the day he obtained his mantra-knowledge, the day of one’s own birth, and the day of the Guru’s pervasive manifestation. (1.1)
The day of the conjunction of the three syllables, as well as the full-moon day—
these six distinguished parvan days, together with the new moon, constitute the seven parvans.
One should perform worship during these [periods], whether for a month or even for a year. || 1 ||
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall declare the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple as taught in the Kādimata, according to that tantra. 1-3.
Handsome, pleasant-faced, pure, easy to approach, and a knower of many mantras; free from doubt, a cutter of doubts, and without expectations—such a one is considered a guru. (1.4)
Beauty is faultlessness; furthermore, in physical form it is pleasantness; in speech, it is addressing others with a smile; and its clarity is the state of having a mind free from crookedness. (1.5)

Ease of access, freedom from pride, contentment, mastery over many branches of knowledge, and lack of doubt regarding the realization of reality—these qualities arise from his teaching them to a disciple. (1.6)
Freedom from expectations, lack of greed, gravity, and the speaking of what is beneficial—one who possesses such qualities should be known as a guru; any other brings suffering to the disciple. (1.7)
Endowed with the first four [qualities], he is possessed of faith, firm in his resolve, free from greed, steady of limb, observant, and has conquered his senses. (1.8)
A disciple should be one who has faith and firm conviction in the guru, the mantra, and the deity;
such a person should be a disciple, for any other causes suffering to the guru.
When the guru speaks these words, he should then address him with these words, showing due respect: "Be gracious, O Lord, O God; so be it. (1.10)

Having prostrated, he should sit at the side; likewise, he should move about with permission. He should serve while looking toward the [teacher's] face and perform whatever is commanded with reverence. (1-11)
One should not speak untruth in his presence, nor should one engage in excessive chatter;
likewise, one should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, laughter, and flattery. (1.12)
Fickleness, crookedness, lamentation, the non-payment of debts, as well as the giving away and the buying and selling of goods. || 1-13 ||
A disciple who desires prosperity should never act in opposition to his teacher;
for the teacher is Śiva himself in visible form—he should worship him by praising and bowing down to him. (1.14)
"As it is with the deity, so it is with the mantra; as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru;
as it is with the guru, so it is with one's own self—such is the sequence of devotion, O Dear One. (1.15)
On the birthday of the Guru, one should perform a festival with devotion:
special worship, feeding the yogins, and the adoration of his feet.
When [the deity] has pervaded, passed away, or gone far, one should perform worship among the elder siblings and others;
when [the deity] is in one place, there is constant worship, and when [the deity] is at a distance, it proceeds according to the number of *yojanas*.
Starting from one [yojana] and increasing by seasons, at a distance of six yojanas within a year; then, when he has gone further, there is service and the fulfillment of his commands. (1-18)
One should likewise worship the seat, the bed, the garment, the ornament, the sandals, the shadow, the wife, and whatever else has been touched by him. (1.19)
In a single village, one should not perform a separate worship without permission.
When the object of worship arrives during the course of a worship, one should bow and announce one's presence.
Having been told, "Perform the remainder," if he does not do so by his own command, he should nevertheless perform that remainder with an unwavering mind. || 1-21 ||
If the Guru, who is to be worshipped, arrives either during the worship, in its midst, or at its conclusion,
one should say, "It has already been performed," and should not maintain silence with them.
One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; for if one should so perceive him, there will never be accomplishment through mantras or through the worship of deities.
One should perform his worship according to the prescribed rite with the mantra, having correctly understood it from that chapter, being entirely devoted to faith. (1.24)
Thus has been declared in the Kālamata the characteristics of both teacher and disciple, according to the procedure taught in that tantra, for the benefit of practitioners. 1.25.
In that *Kulārṇava-tantra*, [it is said]:
"O Supreme Goddess, the venerable Guru is of pure appearance and captivating;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with all beautiful limbs. (1.1)
He knows the true meaning of all scriptures and is conversant with the procedures of all mantras;
his appearance deludes the world, yet he is as pleasing to behold as a god.

He was pleasant-faced, easy to approach, clear-minded, pure in his inner being, and free from doubt; he understood gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and had long since kept wicked people at a distance.
Inward-turned yet looking outward, omniscient, and knowing time and place; perfected through command, knowing the three times, and capable of both restraint and grace. (1-4)
One who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, tranquil, devoted to compassion for all living beings,
has mastery over the movement of his senses, and is capable of conquering the group of six internal enemies.
Foremost among the assembly, exceedingly profound, discerning between those who are worthy vessels and those who are not,
free from the sense of "mine," eternally contented, beyond the pairs of opposites, and possessed of infinite power.
Affectionate toward his true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is preceded by a smile;
dear to his devotees, impartial toward all, merciful, and the instructor of disciples. (1.7)
The wise preceptor is devoted to the highest excellence, eager to honor women, and intent upon blameless rites— whether daily, occasional, or optional.
One who is free from greed, non-violent, impartial, and discerning;
one who is complete in wealth, learning, and other such qualities, and who has mastered mantras, yantras, and the like.
Free from conceptualization and discursive thought, he establishes the determined meaning;
equal toward blame and praise, silent, indifferent, and self-restraining.
O Dear One, the Śrī Guru is said to be endowed with such characteristics as these.
Thus end the characteristics of the venerable Guru. Now, the characteristics of the true disciple:
O Mistress of the Kula, that true disciple is endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of the means such as tranquility (śama), and gifted with virtue and good character. (1.1)
One whose body is pure, who is devoted to righteousness, whose mind is pure, firm in his vows, of good conduct, and endowed with faith and devotion. || 1-2 ||
One who is grateful, fearful of sin, esteemed by the virtuous and the good, a believer in the afterlife, generous by nature, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings. || 1-3 ||
Endowed with trustworthiness and humility, free from stinginess regarding wealth, a accomplisher of the impossible, heroic, and possessed of strength and splendor. || 1-4 ||
One who acts in a favorable manner, is vigilant, and discerning;
who speaks words that are beneficial, truthful, moderate, and affectionate, and is free from fault-finding. (1.5)
One who grasps the meaning upon hearing it once, possesses an expansive and clever intellect;
one who remains free from agitation when raised up from the ground, bed, or seat, and who does not require a servant. (1.6)
One who acts with deliberation, a hero, free from the poverty of mind, highly skilled in all undertakings, steadfast, and helpful to all. || 1-7 ||
O beloved, [one should honor] one who is averse to praising himself or disparaging others, who has a pleasant countenance,
who has conquered the senses, who is well-contented, wise, and a celibate practitioner.
Having abandoned the instability of mental and physical ailments, and being free from the distress of ill-founded suspicions,
one is eager to practice the service, devotion, and recitation of the praises and meditations upon the Guru. (1.9)
One who is devoted to the guru and the deity, eager to serve women,
always remaining in the presence of the guru, and bringing satisfaction to the guru.
O Goddess, he is constantly intent on the service of his guru through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
he is an observer of the guru’s commands and one who illuminates the guru’s fame.
One who knows the authority of the guru’s words, who delights in service to the guru, who follows the guru’s mind, and who acts with circumspection—such a one, O Mistress of the Clan! (1.12)
Free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like in the presence of the guru, indifferent toward the guru's property, and desiring only his grace and so forth. (1.13)
[He is] one who delights in the discourse on the family-dharma (kuladharma), in the yoga of yogins and yoginīs, and in the Kaulika [tradition];
he is devoted to the worship of the Kula and so forth, and follows the path to liberation.
The Guru should accept as a disciple one who is endowed with such characteristics as these.

Now, regarding the characteristics of unworthy disciples, it is said in the Kulārṇava: "One born of a wicked lineage, wicked, devoid of virtues, and lacking beauty; one who was a disciple of another, like a stone egg, a rogue, and one who fancies himself a scholar. (1.1)
With limbs deformed by deficiency or excess, possessed of defective members, lame, blind, deaf, filthy, and afflicted by disease. (1–2)
He was a lecher with a foul mouth who wore whatever attire he pleased at will;
he was a witless fool of wicked conduct, crooked and possessing a terrifying gaze.
Constantly possessed by sleep and laziness, afflicted by lethargy and vices such as gambling, and always concealing its body behind doors, walls, pillars, and the like.
One who is devoid of devotion to the Guru, who is petty, engaged in empty talk, a speaker of contradictions, stubborn, a messenger, fickle, and deceitful—[what use is such a person]? (1.5)
It is devoid of purity regarding wealth and women, lacking both prohibitions and injunctions, revealing secrets, and destroying the purpose of the Goddess's work. || 1-6 ||
One who behaves like a cat or a heron, being intent on seeking out faults;
one who is full of deceit, ungrateful, and who gives while concealing his inner motives. (1.7)

One who betrays trust, a hater of the gods, a doer of evil, one who is untrustworthy, one with defective limbs, and one who desires the accomplishment of misfortune—[these should not be initiated]. (1.8)
O Goddess, [one should avoid] one who seeks to kill, one who desires to seize, one who is contemptible, a false witness, a beggar everywhere, and one who goes to all women by attraction.

One who is devoted to what is untrue, unattached [to virtue], a speaker of many vulgar and such words, an originator of evil reflections and fallacious reasoning, and one fond of quarreling; || 1-10 ||
One who causes vain distractions, who is deluded, who leads others astray, who mocks with words, who finds fault behind one's back, yet speaks pleasantly in one's presence. (1.11)
One should know him to be a thief of knowledge who speaks harsh words, praises himself, cannot endure the virtues of others, is fearful of the virtuous, and is possessed by distress and anger. (1.12)
The Cārvāka system is the friend of the wicked, despised by all the world;
it is malicious, causing distress to others, and terrifying to all living beings.

O Goddess, one who speaks of his own afflictions, a betrayer of friends, a deceiver of his brother, one devoted to the tongue and the genitals, a thief, and one whose conduct is like that of a beast—[such a person is not to be honored]. (1.14)
One who acts out of causeless hatred, derision, affliction, anger, and so forth;
one who performs excessive laughter and improper deeds; and one who mocks others to their very vitals. (1.15)
He was lustful, shameless, indicative of false and wicked conduct, and possessed of envy, intoxication, malice, hypocrisy, and egoism. (1.16)
One who is envious, slanderous, harsh, miserly, angry, and arrogant;
who is lacking in fortitude, miserable, hateful, incompetent, and devoid of the truth. (1.17)
One whose mind is not serene, who is deluded, whose heart is agitated by anxiety,
possessed by craving and greed, wretched, discontented, and a beggar for everything— (1.18)
O beloved, [one who is] a glutton, a hypocrite, a deceiver, and crooked,
and who is devoid of devotion, faith, compassion, tranquility, and righteous conduct.
One who causes laughter among parents, gurus, the wise, and great men; one who is loathsome regarding family property and such things; and one who is arrogant toward the service of the guru. (1-20)

O Mistress of the Family, the Guru should abandon a disciple who is hateful toward women, who has violated his commitments, who has been cursed by his teacher, or who is possessed of such other defects.
If, out of affection or even greed, one should accept [a disciple] or initiate him,
then a curse from the deity will fall upon that guru along with his disciples.
Therefore, one should never accept such a disciple under any circumstances;
if one accepts him out of delusion, the preceptor becomes tainted by that person's sins.
Just as the sin of a minister affects the king, or the sin committed by a wife affects the husband, so too does the sin committed by a disciple generally affect the teacher as well. (1.24)
The conduct of all the castes and stages of life bestows a happy destiny;
O Mistress of the Family, the Guru should instruct one in this conduct three times. (1.25)
For if the disciple does not accept it, then there is no sin for the teacher.
Thus end the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple. Now, regarding the majesty of the venerable Guru’s sandals (*pādukā*) in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Just as the threads and other materials are swallowed up within the primary circle of the snare, so too is the knowledge of the *Kula* tradition established within the sandals. (1.1)

(15) Recollection of the venerable *śrīpādukā* is superior to ten million times ten million great gifts, to ten million times ten million great vows, and to ten million times ten million great sacrifices. (1–2)
O Goddess, the remembrance of the supreme Śrīpādukā is superior to ten million recitations of mantras, to bathing at ten million sacred fords, and to the worship of ten million deities.
In great disease, in great calamity, in great suffering, in great fear,
in great adversity, and in great sin— the sandalwood sandals provide protection when remembered.
By him has been studied, heard, known, given, sacrificed, and honored—
by whom, O Beloved, the sacred sandals of Śrī always abide upon the tip of the tongue.
O Goddess, whoever recites the Śrīpādukā mantra even once with devotion becomes free from all sins and attains the supreme goal. || 1.6 ||
Whether pure or impure, whoever remembers the sandals with devotion shall effortlessly obtain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (1.7)
O beloved, one should daily offer salutations with devotion toward that direction in which the lotus feet of Śrīnātha shine.
There is no mantra superior to the Pādukā-mantra, nor is there a deity higher than the Śrī-guru;
indeed, there is no path higher than the Śākta, and no merit greater than the worship of the Kula.
The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of the scriptures is the word of the Guru; the root of liberation is the grace of the Guru.
O Mistress of the Kula, all ritual actions in this world have their root in the Guru;
therefore, for the sake of attaining perfection, the Guru should be constantly served by those endowed with devotion. (1.11)
Affliction, fear, suffering, delusion, grief, confusion, and the like persist only so long as one does not seek refuge in the glorious Guru, who is compassionate toward his devotees. (1.12)
One wanders in saṃsāra, stained by all manner of suffering, for as long as one does not worship with devotion the glorious Guru, who is the very form of Śiva. (1-13)
This most beautiful collection of mantras, endowed with the fruit of all accomplishments, is the great tree of the supreme reality, rooted in the grace of the guru. (1.14)
Just as the Guru, being satisfied, pleased, and ready to grant boons, bestows the mantra, so too should one diligently please the Guru with devotion, wealth, and even one's own life. 1-15.
When the supreme teacher offers his own self to Śiva, then the disciple becomes liberated; there is no further rebirth after that.
The disciple should propitiate [the guru] until he becomes well-pleased;
when the guru is pleased, the disciple’s sins are immediately destroyed. (1.17)
Even in their minds, those devotees who live by their honor do not harbor any longing; being affectionate toward their master, they bring everything into harmony with his will. 1-18.
When the Guru is satisfied, there is no doubt that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśāna, the deities, sages, and yogis will bestow their grace. 1-19.
The disciple who is instructed by a compassionate Guru satisfied by his devotion shall be liberated from karma and become a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 1-20.
The disciple, too, should receive [the teaching] only when the guru has been satisfied; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (1.21)
Or if, being fully satisfied, the Guru has commanded him at any time, "You are liberated," then he too shall be liberated, O beloved. (1.22)
Or else, O Sovereign Lady, by means of some state free from conceptual proliferation,
I effect the liberation of bound souls from their fetters in the form of the Guru.
