One who is devoted to me is dear to me, even if he is an outcaste, whereas one learned in the four Vedas is not.
To him [the devotee] gifts should be given and from him they should be accepted; for he is indeed to be honored just as I am.
Even a Brahmin endowed with virtues is not praised if he lacks devotion;
even a Mleccha devoid of virtues is distinguished if he possesses devotion. (1.25)
O Mistress of the Family, for one devoid of devotion to the Guru, austerity, knowledge, vows, and noble lineage are indeed fruitless; they serve merely to please the world. (1.26)

One whose evil-natured impurities have been burnt away by the fire known as devotion to the guru is worthy of worship even by the gods, even if he be an outcaste; but one who is an atheist is not worthy of honor, even if he be a scholar.
O Goddess, what need has he for virtue, wealth, or pleasure? Liberation stands in his very hand—he whose devotion to the venerable Guru is always firm through all his goals. (1.28)

Thus [ends the work] composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the great Mahāmahopādhyāya and worshipful teacher.
The first breath (śvāsa) in the tantra named Vidyārṇava. || 1 ||
(p. 16) Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra:
The Second Chapter on Breathing.
Likewise:
"That Śiva, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, exists to me in the form of the Guru"—for him who remembers this with devotion, spiritual perfection is not far off. (2-1)
O Kuleśvarī, for one who possesses supreme devotion toward the God and likewise toward the Guru, these meanings explained here truly shine forth. (2-2)
O Goddess, just as devotion is to be shown toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, one’s parents, and the king, so too should it be directed toward one’s own guru.
One should contemplate Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, Girijā and Śiva, as well as the venerable Guru, the wife of the Guru, and one's parents. (2–4)
O Goddess, O beloved, all perfections are attained through devotion to the Guru in a manner that cannot be achieved through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, pilgrimages, vows, and the like. (2-5)
O Mistress of the Kula, just as unwavering devotion toward the venerable Guru increases, so too does his higher knowledge increase. (2.6)
What is the use of visiting sacred fords and other such great hardships, or what is the use of vows that wither the body?
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who possess sincere service and devotion toward the true Guru, [all else is unnecessary].
O Goddess, whatever fruit is obtained through great physical hardship or even through asceticism, that same fruit one attains with ease by serving the guru. (2.8)

O Goddess, for those seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation, and for those desiring the stations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, devotion to the Guru alone is the path; there is no other—so says the Śruti. (2.9)
Devotion instantly consumes all impurities and even the most heinous sins, just as fire burns a heap of cotton. (2.10)
Salutations to that one who inspires confidence and bestows all accomplishments,
by whom clay, wood, and stone yield their fruit in its entirety.
In this illusion-free Kulamārga, no yoga, austerity, or ritual procedure is prescribed; devotion alone is held to be supreme. (2-12)
O Goddess, within this entire world which is directly composed of the Guru, what place is not a field for those possessed of devotion? For them, what mantra would not be accomplished? (2.13)
One who perceives the teacher as a mere human being, the mantra as a mere collection of syllables, and the images as mere stone shall go to hell. (2.14)
One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; for if one were to perceive him so, there would never be accomplishment through mantras or through the worship of deities. (2.15)
O beloved, for those who remember or speak of the glorious Guru together with common worldly people, all their merit becomes sin.
For parents, the causes of one's birth, are to be honored with great effort;
but the teacher, who reveals what is dharma and what is adharma, is to be honored especially. (2.17)
The guru is the father, the guru is the mother, the guru is the deity, and the guru is the refuge.
When Śiva is angry, the guru is the protector; when the guru is angry, there is no one at all [to save].
Indeed, one must act for the benefit of the guru through speech, mind, and physical deeds;
O Goddess, by practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement. (2-19)
Those lowest of men who deceive the venerable Guru by means of their body, wealth, or life-breaths, attain the state of worms, insects, and moths. (2.20)
From abandoning the guru, death occurs; from abandoning the mantra, poverty results.
By abandoning both the guru and the mantra, one goes to the Raurava hell. (2.21)
One should sustain the body for the sake of the guru; one should acquire wealth for his sake. Having even sacrificed one's own life, one should carry out the guru’s work. (2.22)
O beloved, one should consider the harsh words spoken by the guru as a blessing;
even when struck by him, one should remember it as his grace. (2.23)
One should offer all objects fit for enjoyment to the Guru;
then, O Mistress of the Kula, one should experience them, reflecting that they are the remainder of that [offering]. (2.24)
In the presence of the Guru, one should not perform austerity, nor vows such as fasting;
one should not undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites, nor bathe for the sake of personal purification. (2.25)

One should not issue a command on behalf of one's teacher, nor should one speak for him; likewise, one should not engage in the lending or receiving of debts, nor in the giving away, buying, or selling of goods. (2.26)
A disciple desiring prosperity should never act in opposition to his gurus;
nor, O Goddess, should he engage in debate or even conversation with atheists.
Having observed [this], one should go far away and never sit together with them.
O Ambikā, he who, while the Guru is present, should honor another [person]... (2.28)
He goes to a terrible hell, and that worship becomes fruitless;
one who bears the lotus-feet of the Guru should not carry a burden upon his head.
That which is to be done must be performed by his command; the Guru is traditionally remembered as being the very form of the command.
Whatever has been heard elsewhere regarding mantras, āgamas, and so forth, one should report that to him. (2-30)
One should accept that [instruction] by the command of the guru and avoid what is not desired by him; one should not speak of the secret meaning taught in one's own scriptures to just anyone. (2-31)
If he should say this, he has undoubtedly fallen from his commitment;
one should constantly contemplate non-duality, but not non-duality with respect to the Guru. (2.32)
O Mistress of the Kula, one should act for the benefit of all beings as one does for oneself;
service is fourfold, consisting of [offering] one's own presence, limbs, and true being. (2-33)
O Goddess, by that service a disciple should satisfy the guru;
at every step he undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. (2-34)
But he who is intent on serving his gurus, gods, and great-souled ones—for him, O dear one, it is solely service to the guru that brings about their grace. (2.35)
If that [worship] is accompanied by devotion, it bestows the fruits of all desires;
all sins are destroyed and heaps of merit increase. (2.36)
O beloved, all undertakings are accomplished through service to the guru;
whatever is beneficial to oneself, one should not deceive in regard to that benefit. (2.37)
The merit of one who worships the Guru as a deity cannot be calculated;
for whatever is performed with devotion according to one's means, directed toward the Guru, [its fruit is immeasurable]. (2-38)
Whether the merit be small or great, it is equal for both the wealthy and the poor;
yet he who gives even his entire possessions to the Guru while devoid of devotion [attains nothing]. (2.39)
A disciple does not attain the fruit; indeed, devotion alone is the cause. Whatever substance the Guru desires, the disciple should not consume it. (2.40)
If there should be a necessity, one may experience it by his command;
however, he who lives off even half a sesame seed or half of that as the property of his guru [is lost].
Out of greed or delusion, he who takes for himself even a small amount of another's property that has not been given shall be cooked in the twenty-one hells. (2.42)
O beloved, having entered the womb of an animal, one is devoured by carnivorous beasts;
likewise, one who covets the property of a guru and is eager to approach the wife of a guru [suffers the same]. (2.43)
For one who has fallen [from his vows], there is no atonement for a minor offense:
disobeying the teacher's command, taking his property, and acting disagreeably toward him. (2.44)
They declare this to be an offense against the guru; he who does so is a sinner.
Furthermore, one should not employ one's own property without having first informed the guru. (2.45)
But he who performs [the rite] without having offered it [to the teacher] would be a slayer of a Brahmin;
so too one who destroys the status of the guru, the tradition, or its dharma. (2.46)
Such a sinner should be expelled by his teachers, and he should be punished or even executed.
There is no destruction greater than the anger of a guru, and no sin greater than treachery toward a guru. (2.47)
Death does not come from reviling the guru, nor from the misfortunes caused by the guru's displeasure;
a man might even live after entering fire or drinking poison. (2.48)
Even one who has fallen into the hands of death must not commit an offense against the Guru;
wherever there is censure of the venerable Guru, one should cover one's own ears.
One should immediately depart from that place to a distance so as not to hear [the name];
if one has already heard it, one should subsequently recite the Guru’s name—that is the remedy. (2.50)

One should not insult one's teachers, friends, companions, female servants, male servants, and so forth; nor should one revile the visible commitments, such as the Vedas, the Shastras, the Agamas, and the like. (2.51)
Wearing the sandals of the glorious Guru, recollecting the name of the Guru, and performing japa;
carrying out the Guru’s command is one's duty, as is service and devotion to the Guru. (2.52)
Desiring to enter the abode of the Teacher, with a tranquil mind and exceeding devotion,
[he offered] a fan, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a vehicle, and so forth.
Having discarded one's betel, excessive dress, vehicle, sandals, umbrella, seat, bedding, and so forth, one should enter slowly. (2.54)
Having seen [the teacher], one should pay homage; one should not perform the washing of feet, bathing, anointing, or brushing the teeth for one's own enjoyment. (2.55)
Urine, spittle, shaving, lying down, consorting with women, the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), harsh speech, sitting [inappropriately], and laughing or weeping; 2-56.
O beloved, [one should avoid] loosening the hair, wearing a turban, a bodice, or nakedness; likewise, stretching out the feet, debate, quarrel, and finding fault.
O Ambikā, [these include] the breaking of limbs, playing musical instruments with the body, clapping the hands, shaking [the head], and fighting with dice, cocks, wrestlers, and so forth. (2.58)

One should not practice [prohibited acts] in the presence of the Guru, the Yoginīs, the great Siddhas, or in sacred seats (pīṭha), fields (kṣetra), and hermitages (āśrama); by practicing them out of delusion, one incurs the curse of the deity.
One should remain in the presence of the guru without resorting to mere formal courtesy; one should not enter [the guru's presence] against his will.
One should serve while keeping one's gaze fixed upon the guru's face and should practice exactly what he has instructed. (2.60)

O beloved, one should not show indifference toward tasks whether they have been explicitly commanded by the guru or left unsaid; whatever the guru declares, whether it be good or bad, that should be carried out without hesitation.
In both punishment and favor, the Guru is the cause of everything;
whatever has issued from the mouth of the Guru is called the entire scripture. (2.62)
O beloved, one who is himself capable of serving the Guru should not send another;
even if there are many servants devoted to that task, he should remain personally and exceedingly devoted. (2.63)
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, speaking, or performing oblations and worship, one should carry out only the command of the Guru with an inner self absorbed in him. (2.64)
One should not harbor pride on account of one's birth, learning, wealth, or other such factors;
a disciple should always and constantly serve in the presence of the venerable guru. (2.65)
Avoiding the shadows and the ground [where the teacher stands], disciplined and exceedingly devoted, O Goddess, he should stand before the guru, eager to perform the guru's work. (2.66)

Whether it be his own business or that of another, a disciple who knows the mind of the venerable guru, having approached the guru’s presence, should remain humble, with face lowered and speech measured. (2.67)
If there is a general prohibition, yet one remains in the presence of a true guru, and if that deluded soul acts contrary to proper conduct, the fault shall be ten millionfold. (2.68)
He who, turning his face away, does not listen to the words of his guru without having first received them,
shall go to the Raurava hell, whether those words be harmful or beneficial.
Whatever sin one may incur by killing a cow or a Brahmin,
that same sin one incurs by speaking untruth in the presence of a guru.

O Dear One, one should never abandon the illustrious Guru even when he has gone to another place, is in financial distress, or is situated in a difficult situation; rather, commanded by him, one should proceed. (2.71)
When the guru is seated below, one should never remain above him;
one should not walk in front of him, nor enter a place while the guru has risen.
One should not step over the shadow of the *śakti*, the shadow of the Guru, or the shadow of the deity;
one should not cast one's own shadow upon them, nor should one sleep in the presence of the Guru. (2.73)
One should not engage in speaking, reciting, singing, eating, sleeping, and so forth, unless instructed to do so, nor without first performing a salutation. (2.74)
One who fulfills the command of the guru may commit even a hundred murders of Brahmins;
yet, without the guru’s command, a disciple should not even breathe, for he is beyond all instruction. (2.75)
One should perform everything according to the guru’s command; one should not embrace a woman, O beloved.
Having bowed with devotion, one should rise with palms joined in reverence, O beloved. (2.76)
One should exit from the teacher's house with the right foot first after having paid obeisance;
one should not sit on the same seat as the teacher or those who are his equals. (2.77)
O Goddess, one should not sit upon a seat in the presence of a deity or a guru;
a lion-throne should be offered to the guru, and the best seat to those who are senior.
The lowest-ranking students should use a low seat, while others may use a level seat;
however, one who is superior by birth, learning, or wealth should always rise from afar upon seeing the teacher. (2.79)
One should perform a prostration like a staff and circumambulate three times;
then, one should perform [prostrations] three, six, or twelve times, or even just one for the elders and others. (2.80)
In the case of a conjunction with one's own teacher or his teacher, however, one should salute the supreme teacher;
thereafter, one should bow to one's own teacher, even if that [supreme teacher] should prevent it in the presence of the [other] teacher. (2.81)
In the presence of his preceptor, a disciple should mentally bow to his own teacher;
with the understanding that he is the Guru, he should bow to everything—be it a deity or even a blade of grass. (2.82)
One should not bow to an image made of metal or clay with the thought that it is a deity;
however, one should perform three prostrations to the guru and only one to those who are senior.
Likewise, one should offer a salutation with joined palms to those worthy of worship, and verbal reverence to others;
[one should honor] the gods, gurus, family preceptors, those advanced in knowledge, and those whose wealth is asceticism. (2.84)

O Mistress of the Clan, one should bow to those who are superior in knowledge and established in their own duties; however, one should not bow to those who hate women, those cursed by gurus, heretics, the fallen, or the deceitful. (2.85)

One should not bow down to one who follows forbidden occupations, to an ungrateful person, or to one who does not belong to any stage of life (āśrama). Furthermore, he who eats while staying in the same house without first informing his teacher [is likewise censured].
By that [act], he would have consumed impurity and, upon death, is born as a pig.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to his guru at the three junctions of the day. (2.87)
Standing at a distance of one *krośa*, a disciple should bow to the guru daily with devotion;
from a distance of half a *yojana*, he should prostrate on the five festival days (*parvan*).
Starting from one yojana up to twelve yojanas,
having traveled for as many months as there are yojanas, one should bow to the Guru.
A disciple situated in a distant land, having gone into his presence out of devotion, may go whenever he wishes, even if he remains at a great distance. (2.90)
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth, according to one's ability. (2.91)
O Goddess, he who does not practice in this way shall become a brahmarākṣasa.
The Guru’s Śakti, his son, and his elder brother are equal to the Guru. (2.92)

O Goddess of the gods, toward the younger [disciples] he behaves as toward himself, and toward those who protect the lineage he behaves as toward his own sons; such is the conduct of the Teacher of the World toward both elder and younger gurus. (2.93)
One should perform a prostration to the head of the lineage (gurukulya) just as one does to one's own guru;
these are: one's own elder, the elder by seniority of initiation (kramajyeṣṭha), and the third is the elder by birth (kulajyeṣṭha). (2.94)

"O Goddess of the Gods, [the disciple says] 'The elder of the guru'; thus is the group of four elders. As for the salutation to the elders, it is taught that the order of seniority is determined by the lineage. (2.95)
One should perform prostrations and other rites according to the prescribed rules toward the guru, the elders of the family,
and all those who belong to the category of venerable ones, such as parents and kinsmen.
When he reveals his own self in the form of the Teacher, the faults of the unmanifest [individual soul] become slight through acts such as rising to meet him and prostrating before him. (2.97)
O beloved, if he who has become a husband should perform prostrations to animals, he would incur fault through such acts as rising to greet them and offering salutations. (2-98)
(19) He who has attained the status of a Guru by means of the counting of sandals is called a "great beast" and shall incur the curse of the deity. (2.99)
"But he must be regarded as a son to the Guru; he is to be saluted by the elders, O Dear One, and not [otherwise].
Thus concludes the procedure for the worship of the sandals (*pādukā*) and its greatness. Now follows the conduct of the observances (*samayācāra*). Regarding this, in the *Śrīkulārṇava*:
O Goddess, having bowed with devotion to the venerable Guru, the Kula scriptures, and whatever places of worship there may be, one should recite their names preceded by the word "Śrī. (2-1)
For me, whose lineage of gurus extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, who on this earth would not be worthy of worship, I who am a disciple of all? (2.2)
O Dear One, one should not address the Guru by name except at the time of recitation; in debate or when giving instruction, one should say, "The venerable Lord Śrīnātha. (2–3)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should not speak of the sandals of the glorious Guru, the mudrā, the root mantra, or one's own sandals to anyone other than a disciple. (2-4)
O Dear One, the lineage, the oral tradition, the mantras, the ritual conduct, and so forth—
all these become fruitful only when received from the mouth of the Guru, and not otherwise.

O beloved, one should always worship with devotion the book produced from the refuge of the venerable scripture as if it were a deity, and should never place it into the hands of an uninitiated person (paśu).
O Pārvatī, one should treat the Kula scriptures as one's own wife;
one should avoid all Paśu scriptures as if they were the wives of others. (2.7)
Just as milk from a dog's hide would be undrinkable for the best of the twice-born, so too should the Dharma not be heard from the mouth of a beast by the Kaulikas. (2.8)
He who hears the family tradition and he who explains it according to the scriptures—both of them go directly to the assembly of Yoginīs and Vīras. (2.9)
O Mistress of the Family, those who lack faith here regarding the family traditions do not return from hell until the dissolution of all beings.

The wife of a guru is of five kinds: one who has been married, one who has been supported, one who is as dear as a mother, one who has been brought from her home, and one who has gone to him out of desire. (2-11)
The wives of the gurus are as inviolable and worthy of worship as the gurus themselves.
[One should honor] a young girl who is dark-complexioned, dressed in black garments, and slender-waisted.

One should worship a beautiful woman in the prime of youth with the thought that she is a deity; likewise, one should worship raw meat, a jar of liquor, an intoxicated elephant, and a perfected ascetic.
The mango tree, the *aśoka* tree, a young girl restless with play, a solitary tree, a cremation ground, and even a multitude of women. (2.14)
And having seen a woman dressed in red garments, one should salute her with devotion; likewise, one should salute the Guru, the Śakti, the son, the elder, the younger, and the family preceptor.
The scriptures that reveal the Kula, the Kula substances, the Kaulikas, as well as those who incite, those who indicate, those who recite, and those who show [the way]. (2.16)
[One should not look at] students, those seeking enlightenment, yogins and yoginīs, perfected beings (siddhas), boys and girls, the naked, nor even a woman who is insane. (2-17)
One should not criticize, nor loathe, nor laugh at, nor insult any true yogi of noble family; one should speak neither what is unpleasant nor what is untrue to anyone. (2.18)
One should not say of a woman of noble family, "She is ugly" or "She is too dark.
One should not examine the deeds or omissions of devoted ones or heroes. (2.19)
One should not look upon a naked woman, nor one who is insane or whose breasts are exposed;
one should not consort with a woman during the day, nor gaze at her private parts. (2-20)
Whatever woman there may be in the world, she is born from the lineage of the Mothers;
the Kula-yoginīs become enraged by the transgression against women. (2.21)
One should not strike a woman, even with a flower, for a hundred offenses;
one should not count the faults of women, but rather manifest their virtues alone. (2.22)
The Kula-yoginīs always reside within the Kula-trees; one should not eat from their leaves, and especially not from the leaves of the Arka tree. (2.23)
One should not sleep at the foot of a family tree (kulavṛkṣa), nor should one cause it harm;
having seen it, one should bow with devotion, and never cut it down.
Śleṣmāntaka, Karañja, Akṣa, Nimba, Aśvattha, Kadambaka, Bilva, Vaṭa, and Udumbara are remembered as the nine family trees. (2.25)
One who mocks the established conduct toward deities, gurus, scriptures, and so forth;
a thief of knowledge; and a traitor to the guru, shall become a *brahmarākṣasa*. (2.26)
Those who, out of delusion, fail to serve their guru, who revile heroic men, and who disparage the Kula scriptures, become Brahma-rākṣasas. (2.27)
He who does not respect the guru who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable will, after passing through a hundred births as a dog, attain the state of a caṇḍāla. (2-28)
The wise one should reveal the Guru, but never reveal the mantra;
through revealing what should not be revealed, both prosperity and lifespan are diminished. (2.29)
O beloved, for that great sinner who, relying on the family traditions, does not maintain proper conduct, and who acts according to his own whims— (2-30)
Calamities, misfortune, diseases, poverty, strife, loss of fortune, the wrath of the Yoginīs, and stumbling at every step—[these are the results]. (2.31)
His pride shattered and utterly ruined, deprived of luster and exceedingly miserable, censured by all and hated by everyone, he was distraught and abandoned by his companions. (2-32)
He wanders from country to country and his undertakings are always ruined; even there, the Śākinīs who abide on the path of the Kula and protect the Kula [will obstruct him]. (2–33)
(20) "In former times they devoured [him], but a boon was granted to them by me alone.
Therefore, O Goddess, one who possesses proper conduct shall become dear to the Yoginīs. (2.34)
Through right conduct, the Kaulikas attain divinity and union with the Yoginīs and Vīras; through its opposite, they attain the state of animals. (2.35)
O Goddess, due to being devoid of ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), by transgressing the words of the guru, and by violating proper conduct (*ācāra*), the Kaulika becomes fallen. (2-36)
[The sins] arising from the omission of daily, occasional, and optional rites, as well as those born from the neglect of mantras and tantras;
and those resulting from improper contact with unworthy persons, evil company, and the confusion of mantras. (2–37)
O Dear One, regarding such faults as those arising secretly or openly, or committed through knowledge or ignorance, there is a variation in the gravity or lightness of the sin. (2.38)
Having correctly ascertained the place, time, age, and wealth according to the rule, the preceptor shall prescribe the penance for the purification of all sins. (2.39)
The disciple, too, should perform the expiation as thus prescribed;
or else, for all sins, there is the recollection and chanting of the Guru’s name.
Just as the impurity of Jāmbūnada gold is purified by fire, one should burn away the defilement of improper conduct with the fire of expiation. (2.41)
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to the secret, O Pārvatī:
for all those belonging to the castes and stages of life, right conduct bestows the state of ultimate felicity.
O Mistress of the Kula, the Guru should explain the conduct three times;
if the disciple does not accept it, then no sin accrues to the Guru. (2.43)
Just as the fault of a minister reaches the king and the fault of a wife reaches her husband, so too, O beloved, the teacher undoubtedly incurs the sin of his disciple. (2.44)
Thus, in the *Prayogasāra*:
"In the place of the deity, in the place of the guru, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads, one should avoid sandals, seats, excrement, urine, sexual intercourse, and so forth. (2.1)

One should utter the words "Śrī" before the names of the deity, the guru, those in the position of a guru, the sacred field (kṣetra), the presiding deities of the field, the perfected ones (siddha), and those who dwell with the perfected ones. || 2-2 ||

One should not revile a woman who is intoxicated, one who has recently given birth, one who is menstruating, one whose breasts have fallen away, one who is deformed, one with disheveled hair, or one afflicted by passion. (2-3)
One should not look at a maiden’s private parts, animal play, a woman with disheveled garments and exposed breasts; one should avoid the property of others and the wives of others.
One should never extend one's feet toward grain, cattle, teachers, Brahmins, fire, knowledge, a treasury, or a house; nor should one step over them.
One should avoid laziness, intoxication, delusion, deceit, malice, strife, envy, self-adulation, and the censuring of others. (2.6)

One should not find fault with a Brahmin who bears the marks [of his order] and observes his vows, nor with the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Saṃhitās, the Purāṇas, the Āgama scriptures, or the Kalpas. (2.7)
A pair [of tongs], a pestle, a stone, a rope, a hearth, a mortar, a winnowing basket,
a broom, a staff, a banner, and a beryl weapon.
The water-pot, the chowrie, the parasol, the mirror, and likewise ornaments,
as well as other articles suitable for enjoyment and whatever substances are required for yoga.
Objects located in great sacred places or in temples, as well as those divine substances mentioned in the scriptures, or indeed those possessed by spirits; || 2-10 ||
One should never leap over these, nor should one touch them with the feet:
that social gathering which is despised by the world, and that which spreads according to its own whims. (2.11)
One should never engage in that which consists of harming others;
nor should one accept gifts out of a desire for personal enjoyment. (2-12)
One should acquire wealth with effort for the sake of worshipping the deities and the guru;
one should maintain straightforwardness, truthfulness, good character, equanimity, and fortitude. (2.13)
One should always cultivate patience, compassion, detachment, and divine power;
one should never take shelter in the shade of the *vibhītaka*, *arka*, *kārañja*, or *snuhī* trees.
[One should avoid] the water from pillars, lamps, humans, and other living beings, as well as water from the tips of nails, hair, dust, bathing water, and water from a water-pot. (2.15)
One should avoid from afar contact with this [dust], as well as the dust raised by donkeys and goats;
one should not revile the Lord who is the cause, nor the scripture composed by the Lord. (2-16)

One should not step over the shadow of the Guru or the practitioner, nor over the shadow of the Liṅga. One should not eat the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor step over them; however, one who has been initiated by Śiva may consume them.
One should not disobey the command of the guru, nor speak back to him;
day and night, one should carry out his instructions like a servant. (2-18)
In the same way, one should abandon what is untrue, what is unwholesome, excessive talk, that which is unpleasant, as well as laziness, and especially desire and anger. (2.19)
One should never speak with an uncovered face in the presence of a guru;
nor should one harbor pride on account of wealth, grain, hermitage, and so forth. (2.20)
The property of the guru must never be consumed by him if it has not been given;
if it is given, it should be accepted with humility, and never out of greed. (2-21)
One should respectfully set aside non-duality, the worship of deities, and the emblems of the guru—such as the sandals and the meditation-band—in the presence of the guru. (2.22)
One should never leap over it, nor touch it with one's feet; one should always bow down before it. Likewise, one should not lie upon it in bed, nor stretch out one's feet upon it. (2.23)
One should not engage in stretching the limbs or playful gestures in the presence of the guru;
when going out or returning, one should do so after bowing to the guru’s sandals.

One should not step over the teacher’s shadow, nor should one walk ahead of him; one should depart from the teacher’s house by stepping out with the right foot after having prostrated before him. (2.25)
One should not exercise authority or gather disciples in the presence of the guru;
one should not harbor egoism, nor should one assume an arrogant physical bearing. (2.26)
A wise person should never prostrate to his own guru in the presence of a superior guru;
if the superior guru sees him intent on performing a salutation, he should restrain him. (2.27)
One should not offer opposition to the Guru, nor should one speak of [the teachings] with you, even if they have already been utilized by another or by one who has received initiation. (2.28)
One should never use [another's] parasols, shoes, garments, and so forth;
however, there is no fault in doing so when these are unavailable, in times of distress, or after they have been washed. (2.29)
And likewise for the teachers who have been initiated within their own lineage, there shall be no fault in what is consumed, even if it is brought from what has been given by them. (2–30)

Food and other edibles that have been enjoyed by the mantra, as well as that which has been consecrated by the mantra, one should carry on one's head with bowed head once they have been received from the abode of the Goddess. (2.31)
One should cast [the matter] into the water so that it does not fall upon the earth;
likewise, when misfortune arises or one falls from grace, one should utter an oath known as "heavy" (guru).

One should not allow the perception of the Blessed One to be lost through negligence; if it should be so lost, one must strive to accomplish its purpose by means of worship, recitation, and fire-oblations at the conclusion.
But if the task is not accomplished for the sake of which the oath was taken,
O Goddess, one must then perform a thousand recitations of the *prāyaścitta* mantra of one's own choice.
One should never utter speech that causes distress to the world, that cuts into one's vital points, or that causes agitation regarding one's stability. (2-35)
One should never, under any circumstances, adopt a dress that, though beautiful, brilliant, and even desirable to the mind, is loathed by the world. 36.
He who always respects these aforementioned practices, which are appropriate for both this world and the next, attains peace once he has been initiated. (2.37)
One of pure intention should especially bestow the pledges upon women;
for by observing the pledges, accomplishment arises without delay. (2.38)
The mantra always becomes manifest to one who abides by the *samaya*;
for one who abides by the *samaya*, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) shall arise, with liberation as the final one. (2.39)
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the sun and moon,
on the eighth lunar day, and on the full moon— on these occasions, there is occasional (naimittika) recitation.

Then, having multiplied that [number] by three for the daily [practice], he should perform worship as well—namely, giving, fire-offerings, and ritual adoration—with means acquired through righteous means. (2.41)
"O Goddess, if one does not perform [the rite], one goes downward; even if one performs it with devotion, [the result is the same].
This is the rule of conduct (*samayācāra*). In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
'A Brāhmaṇa, knowing all times, should bestow grace upon all.'"
Due to the absence of that [duality], O best of the twice-born, he is one whose self is peaceful and who is identical with the Blessed One.
One whose self is cultivated, who is omniscient, learned in the scriptures, devoted to right action, endowed with the threefold accomplishment, and consecrated for the office of an Ācārya. (2-2)
Among those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, the Kṣatriya is capable of bestowing favor;
and even for a Kṣatriya, such a person [is acceptable] in the absence of a Guru. (2–3)

A Vaiśya should not be made [to do so] by them; rather, there should always be favor toward both [the Śūdra and the Vaiśya] by a Śūdra of the same caste who is of such [virtuous] character, O Great-minded One. (2.4)
The *anugraha* and *abhiṣeka* initiations should always be performed for a Śūdra, provided that the Guru is either of a superior caste or is renowned. (2.5)
Whether in one's own place or elsewhere, this rite should not be performed by one who desires auspiciousness;
for he who performs it where [the deity] is already present brings about the opposite result.
In this world and the next, there would be ruin for him; therefore, one should practice what is declared in the scriptures.
One born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes may be initiated in the reverse order [of the classes].
One who eats excessively, procrastinates, and is greedy for sense objects;
one who delights in sophistry, is wicked, a mere talker, and a reviler of virtues. (2.8)
Aroma, Bahuroma, Nindita, Āśramasevaka, Kāladanta, Asitoṣṭha, and Durgandhiśvāsavāhaka. || 2-9 ||
Even if he is himself a lord endowed with the characteristics of a wicked man, a teacher who is addicted to accepting many gifts brings about the destruction of prosperity. (2-10)
Thus, in the *Jñānonnayana*:
"The mantra of one's father is devoid of power, as is that of one's maternal grandfather, of a younger brother, and of one who has taken the side of an enemy. (2.1)

O Maheśvarī, a householder seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation should not perform the initiation into the mantra for those who dwell in the forest as monks or for those who follow the stages of life (varṇa).

For those who have abandoned the sacred fires, who are devoid of ritual acts, who are ascetics without possessions, and likewise forest-dwellers— these are inferior to the student (brahmacārī), because they are deficient in comparison.
"Therefore, O Maheśvarī, they have no authority for the bestowal of initiation.
Thus it is said in the Bhairavītantra:
"An ascetic, one who speaks the truth, a householder with a stable mind,"
O beloved, during initiation, one should not regard ascetics (yatīs) or forest-dwellers (vaikhānasas) as one's gurus.
"A householder seeking enjoyment and liberation should likewise choose a *varṇin* [initiate].
Regarding the examination of the teacher and the disciple, it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
With both wisdom and compassion, the teacher should diligently examine the disciple for one year, or half of that, or even half of that again. (2.1)
In matters of high or low importance, one should employ those of low status in high tasks and those of high status in low tasks,
through the granting of life or wealth, and by means of commands that are either equal or unequal [to their rank].
By means of words that pierce his vital spots, through deceptions and cruel actions, and by various displays of partiality and indifference, [he assailed him] again and again. (2-3)
Even when dragged about or beaten, he who does not fall into despondency should always reflect with joy: "The Guru is showing me compassion. (2.4)

Whether in the remembrance of the glorious Guru, or in his glorification, or even in seeing him; or in saluting him, in service, in summoning him, in sending him forth, or in what is dear to him; || 2-5 ||
Those who experience transformations such as bliss, trembling, horripilation, and changes in voice or eyes are fit for the rites of initiation and consecration in this context.

The disciple, moreover, should examine the guru by these characteristics, through recitations beginning with Ānanda, through hymns of praise, and through meditation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth. (2.7)
O Goddess, having recognized the capacity for imparting knowledge, the accomplishment of mantras, and the power of awakening [others], the disciple shall become [a teacher], and not otherwise. (2.8)

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the inferior, middling, and superior nature of disciples, it is stated in that very same work: "By virtue of the descent of devotion at the beginning, middle, and end, disciples are likewise proclaimed as inferior, middling, and excellent. (2.9)
O Goddess, those who say that devotion must first exist for initiation are themselves proclaimed as "original devotees" (ādibhakta), even though their devotion has been subsequently destroyed. (2.10)

Those who have received initiation and the observance of its rules, yet are devoid of theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna), but whose dullness has been destroyed by devotion—they are proclaimed to be of middling capacity. (2-11)
Those who are devoid of devotion at the beginning, or whether they possess devotion in the middle or not, yet become intensely devoted at the end—they are the ones fit for the final goal. (2.12)

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the specific time for fitness according to the division of castes, it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "A Brāhmaṇa becomes fit in one year; a Kṣatriya (*nṛpa*) in two of those; a Vaiśya in three years; and a Śūdra in four years under a Guru. (2.1)
"One who is desirous of serving is to be accepted for the initiatory rites, sacrifices, vows, and so forth.
In this regard, it is heard that Śūdras have no entitlement to mantras; as stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra:
A mantra originating from the Veda does not exist apart from the Veda and the Praṇava;
therefore, the Veda is the supreme mantra, and the Āgama is considered a limb of the Veda.
In the Kali age, all rites such as subjugation and attraction, which bestow both visible and invisible fruits, are accomplished through the Veda by means of planetary sacrifices and other rituals.
There are no sacrifices without the Veda, nor are there Vedas devoid of sacrifice;
therefore, the mantra is supreme only when it is the Veda, and the Veda is not that which is abandoned by the mantra. || 2-3 ||
Śūdras have no authority over mantras; this is the supreme rule.
Indeed, because of the absence of mantras, every ritual act is performed without mantra, as has been declared.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Śātātapa-saṃhitā:
"As many syllables as one might impart of the mantras to a Śūdra, so many instances of Brahman-murder shall he incur; so Prajāpati himself has declared. (2-1)
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in some places even a non-prohibition is heard in the *Bhaviṣya*:
"The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure and stainless—to them indeed the mantras should be given, but not to those whose dharma is mixed. (2-1)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who possess pure intellects are qualified for the worship [of images], provided they are devoted to the worship of their guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
Thus, from the statement of the Yoginītantra.
The Vaidika or the Miśrika path is prescribed for the Brahmins and other [twice-born] castes;
the Tāntrika path is proclaimed even for a Śūdra who is devoted to the Brahmins. (2-1)
Even Śūdras should perform the worship of Viṣṇu with faith according to the procedure taught in their own scriptures, keeping their husband in their hearts.
Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other such rites, provided they are devoted to pleasing their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.

Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*. It should be understood that the phrase "beloved by her husband" refers to a woman whose husband is living, while the phrase "having reflected" refers to a woman whose husband is deceased. Accordingly, it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The sacrament for the twice-born is declared to be as prescribed in the Vedas."
And for those [mantras], one should perform the ritual procedure with the vidyā in each respective case.
One should perform the recollection of the vidyā and the rite enjoined for every occasion;
by that, the accomplishment of identity with that [deity] occurs everywhere with certainty. (2-2)
"One should also attend to other castes with [proper] knowledge.
Thus it is said. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"A woman who is separated from her husband, yet auspicious and possessed of independence..."
And let her, as his consort, receive the mantras by his permission at that time. || 2-1 ||
Without one’s own dharma, whatever [practice] such as the propitiation of deities may be performed will crumble in an instant, like a palace built of sand. (2-2)
Thus, in the Kulārṇava:

"A widow has no authority [to perform rites] except by the command of her son; a maiden, by the command of her father; and a woman, by her own accord, has no authority except by the command of her husband. (2.1)
For women and Śūdras, this mantra ending with "Namaḥ" brings auspiciousness;
knowing this, O Mahāsena, one may initiate even Caṇḍālas. (2.2)
Thus, from the Rudrayāmala: This is the Prāsāda mantra. And likewise:
"Śūdras who are most pure in their vows, righteous, and servants of the twice-born; women devoted to their husbands; and others born of inverse or direct unions. (2-1)
All people, even down to the outcaste Caṇḍālas, are qualified for this [practice], provided they are devoted to the Lord of All and remain intent upon the duties of their own caste. (2-2)
Instruction for all [others] is according to their respective castes;
however, a Śūdra and women should never recite Vedic mantras under any circumstances. (2–3)
"The wise declare that either the Śiva-mantra ending with *namaḥ* or the Vaiṣṇava-mantra [is used].
Yājñavalkya also says:
"A twice-born man giving a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra..."
A Śūdra would go to hell, and a Brāhmaṇa would attain the state of a Śūdra. || 2-1 ||
Thus, in the *Yāmala*:

"Having considered the suitability [of the disciple] for one, two, three, four, or five years, as well as their devotion and qualities, according to the order of the castes and the mixed castes. (2.1)
Thus it is said. Now, regarding the classification of mantras as Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, the *Kulārṇava* states:
"A mantra becomes a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra; it should be given in the direct order (*anuloma*), and only occasionally in the reverse order (*pratiloma*). (2.1)
Thus it is said in the Vāmakeśvara:
"The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the fourfold classes of men belonging to the eastern lineages, according to their respective castes and in cases of intermixture. (2-1)

Thus, in the Sautrāmaṇī Tantra: "The seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) is for the Brāhmaṇa; the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrīṃ) is remembered for the Kṣatriya; the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīṃ) shall be for the Vaiśya; and Vāgbhava (Aiṃ) is declared for the Śūdra. (2.1)
A mantra devoid of four seed-syllables is designated as belonging to the easterners;
for Brahmins it consists of four seed-syllables, and for Kṣatriyas, three seed-syllables. (2-2)
"The Vaiśyas have two seed-syllables (bīja), while the Śūdras have only one.
Thus it is said. In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*, the Goddess said:
"Regarding the Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Saura [traditions], as well as those of Gaṇeśa and Viṣṇu..."
Especially for those of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes, and for those of mixed castes.
I wish to hear about the ritual procedure for the benefit of practitioners; O Śaṅkara, tell me that clearly, as to which mantras belong to which [deities].
Īśvara said:
[One should worship] Umāmaheśvara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Aghoraka, Hayagrīva, Vārāha, and thereafter the eight-syllabled [mantra]. (2–3)
Vāsudeva preceded by the Praṇava, as well as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
should be given to those of the three [twice-born] castes, but never to any other caste.
The Pāśupata, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise the Sudarśana [mantras] should be given to those of two castes, and never to any others.
Whatever fire-mantras there may be, as well as sun-mantras,
and the mantras beginning with *tārā* and ending with *ghṛṇi*, should be bestowed upon the Trivarṇaka.
The Anuṣṭubh meter, the Śakti-mantras, as well as Vindhyavāsinī and Nīlasarasvatī, should also be assigned to the first letter. (2.7)
Mātaṅgī, Ugratārā, Kālikā, Śyāmalā, as well as Chinnamastā and Bālā—these should be assigned to all the colors. (2.8)
Tārādi, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the one named Haridrā—these should be bestowed only upon those of the three castes; they are said to grant all perfections.
(24) Those mantras of Tripurā, as well as the mantras of Vaṭuka and the others,
should be given to all castes, and especially to women. 2-10.
The syllable *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, the *praṇava*, the *vāgbhava*, and other seed-syllables—joined with these seeds, they should be placed at the beginning of the letters. (2-11)
Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava should be given even to Kṣatriyas;
Lakṣmī and Vāgbhava alone are prescribed for the Vaiśya caste.

The Vāgbhava seed-syllable and other seed-syllables are declared for Śūdras; for those of mixed caste (saṃkara), the use of the heart-mantra and so forth, along with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, is recommended. (2.13)
Thus, it is said in the Kulaprakāśatantra:
"All humans who have been born are divided according to the fifty letters;
they are declared to be of two kinds, through the distinction between mantra and vidyā. (2.1)
Feminine mantras end with *vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., *svāhā*); neuter mantras end with *hṛdaya*;
the remaining are said to be masculine. Furthermore, feminine mantras are also used in rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
Mantras are traditionally considered neuter when used for inciting enmity and malevolent rites;
they are all traditionally considered masculine in rites of subjugation and eradication.
Indeed, all the Manus have the nature of Agni and Soma;
those consisting primarily of the letter *ra*, the syllable *oṃ*, and the ether (*viyat*) belong to Agni and are used for cruel rites.
"Those mantras which consist mostly of gentle [vowels] and the nectar of the moon are remembered as being for gentle rites.
Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"A mantra consisting mostly of the letters *ta*, *ra*, *a*, *na*, *ga*, *i*, and *vi* (the sky) is desired as being fiery (*āgneya*)."
One who is disciplined and gentle is praised in both cruel and gentle actions. (2-1)
An Āgneya mantra should generally be gentle (saumya) and endowed with "namaḥ" at the end;
likewise, a Saumya mantra should be known as being endowed with the syllable "phaṭ. (2-2)
When the vital air has entered Piṅgalā, those whose form is fire indeed awaken;
but when the wind has entered Iḍā, those whose form is the moon awaken. (2–3)
O Umā, when the vital wind has entered Piṅgalā and Iḍā, indeed all [the channels] become awakened;
all the mantras become awakened and bear fruit for practitioners.
Thus it is also stated in the *Bṛhannārāyaṇīya*:

"A mantra does not grant success if one is asleep or has only just awakened; the time of sleep is when the breath flows through the left [nāḍī], and the waking state is when it flows through the right. (2-1)
The opposite of this for the Saumya mantra of the Āgneya Manu—
one should know that it brings about both [results] during the time of awakening for both.
"However, at the time of sleep, the recitation of the mantra yields no fruit.
Thus it is said in the *Śivayāmala*:
"Having carefully encapsulated the letters beginning with 'la' along with the nasal bindu..."
Furthermore, one should recite those [syllables] with the visarga, and then the letter *kṣa* alone. (2-1)
Thus, when the mantra is recited in this manner, it becomes awakened and bestows swift accomplishment.
Now, in the tradition of Kālī, the collection of defects of mantras has been declared, along with their remedies, categorized according to external and internal divisions. (2-1)
"I shall explain that which is taught in various tantras for the benefit of practitioners.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Śāradā*:
"Mantras that are defective due to being cut [or otherwise corrupted] do not protect the practitioner."
He is described as "cut," "obstructed," "devoid of power," and "turned away. || 2-1 ||
Deaf, blind, pinned down, and likewise paralyzed;
burnt, terrified, frightened, soiled, and insulted. (2-2)

One who is pierced, one who is fast asleep, and one who is intoxicated with passion are thus described; likewise, one who is fainted, one whose vigor is stolen, one who is deficient, and those who are ruined or like children. (2-3)
Furthermore, [the types of mantras are]: the youth, the adolescent, the mature, the aged, the merciless, the seedless, the devoid of accomplishment, the cruel, and again the deceptive. (2–4)
One who is partless, devoid of essence, squint-eyed, and seedless;
one who is smoky, embraced by smoke, deluded, and afflicted by hunger. (2.5)
One who is excessively arrogant, one who is physically impaired, one who is provoked to extreme anger, one who is exceedingly cruel, one who is full of shame, and one whose mind is tranquil; (2-6)
One who has fallen from his position, one who is incapacitated, and one who is very old are thus proclaimed;
likewise, one who is devoid of affection and one who is afflicted—I shall now describe their characteristics. (2.7)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the definitions of these defects, it is stated in that very same work:
"That mantra in whose beginning, middle, and end the seed-syllable of Vāyu (ya) is said to occur—whether conjoined or uncombined, and again, whether governed by a vowel—in those three ways... (2.8).
That mantra is designated as "broken" (chinna) when it is divided into four or five parts,
marked by the pair of earth-seeds (la-la) at its beginning, middle, and end.
That mantra which is devoid of the three principles of Māyā, the Śrī-bīja, and Rāva, should be known as "obstructed" (ruddha), being bereft of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (2-10)

But that which is said to be "devoid of power" (śaktihīna) is that in which the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) is not found in the middle, the syllable of illusion (māyā) is not at the beginning, and the goad (aṅkuśa) is not at the end.
That [syllable] with the letter *ha* joined by the *bindu* is said to be "turned away" (*parāṅmukha*).
If the *bindu* is absent at the beginning, end, or middle, it is known as "deaf" (*badhira*). (2-12)
A mantra that possesses five vowels but is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (*repha*), and the moon (*indubindu*), should be known as "eyeless"; it bestows suffering, grief, and disease. (2-13)
At the beginning, middle, and end [of the mantra] are Haṃsa, Prāsāda, and Vāgbhava;
the letter Ha with the Bindu, Jīva, Rāva, and also the four-part [syllable]. (2.14)
I bow to Māyā, in whom there is no state that is not fixed;
in whom there is one in the center and two at the head, [namely] the weapon and Purandara.
That mantra, however, exists as paralyzed and obstructed from success, for which fire is joined with wind at its head. (2.16)
When that [mantra] is seen as sevenfold, the knower of mantras should consider it burnt;
[likewise], a weapon-mantra is seen when it consists of two, three, six, or eight syllables.
He in whose mouth the Praṇava does not reside is addressed as "terrified";
whether he be Śiva or Śakti, he is proclaimed as one named "afraid. (2-18)
That mantra in which there are four instances of the letter *ma* at the beginning, middle, and end is considered impure; a knower of mantras should avoid it.

That mantra in the middle of which there is either the letter *da* or the *krodha* (the seed-syllable of wrath) twice at the head, and in which the *astra* (weapon-mantra) resides, is said to be "obstructive" (*tiraskṛta*).

If the mantra has "Oṃ" at both the beginning and the head (the end), and "Vaṣaṭ" as the weapon-syllable in the middle, it is corrupted; such a mantra should be abandoned by the wise when seeking spiritual accomplishments.
That which consists of three phonemes but lacks the *haṃsa* is declared to be deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Furthermore, a mantra or a *vidyā* consisting of seventeen syllables [is likewise so described]. (2-22)

That mantra which begins with the five *phaṭ* syllables and so forth, and is described as "slow" or "intoxicated," has its weapon (*astra*) situated in the middle; such a mantra is "fainted" (*mūrchita*). (2.23)
He whose mantra reaches the place of rest (virāma) is said to have its vitality stolen.
A mantra endowed with four *caturas* at the beginning, middle, and likewise at the head [is effective]. (2.24)
It should be known that this [mantra] which consists of eighteen syllables, or one of nineteen syllables joined with the *tāra*, is inferior. (2.25)
They declare that mantra enriched with the *hṛllekhā* and *aṅkuśa* seed-syllables to be *pradhvastra*.
The seven-syllable mantra is known as *bāla*, while the eight-syllable one is remembered as *kumāra*. (2.26)
A mantra of sixteen syllables is a youth; one of forty syllables is mature; a mantra of thirty syllables, sixty-four syllables, or one hundred syllables is likewise [mature]. (2.27)
Furthermore, that which consists of four hundred syllables is called "Vṛddha" (the aged).
A mantra of nine syllables joined with the *dhruva* is declared to be "Nistriṃśa" (the sword). || 2-28 ||
That mantra at the end of which there is no *hṛdaya* (heart), nor a *śiras* (head) in the middle, nor a *śikhā* (crest), *varma* (armor), *vauṣaṭ*, or *phaṭ*—[is not to be used]. (2.29)
Or, when it is devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti, it is called "seedless" (nirbīja).
In this [mantra], the syllable *phaṭ* is seen six times in these aforementioned positions.
That mantra would be devoid of success; a mantra of ten syllables is called "dull.
A mantra of a single syllable is said to be "cryptic" (kūṭa) and likewise "partless" (niraṃśaka). (2–31)
A mantra of two syllables is devoid of power; one of four syllables is squint-eyed;
and a mantra of six and a half syllables is devoid of seed-syllables. (2–32)
Or, one consisting of twelve and a half syllables that is smoky is censured;
likewise, one of three and a half seed-syllables or one of twenty-one syllables [is similarly condemned]. (2.33)
That mantra which consists of twenty syllables or thirty syllables is said to be "embraced" (āliṅgita);
a mantra of twenty-two syllables is proclaimed to be "deluded" (mohita). (2.34)
That which consists of twenty-four syllables and that which consists of twenty-seven syllables should be known as afflicted by hunger; [likewise] that which consists of twenty-four syllables. (2.35)
A mantra consisting of eleven syllables, or twenty-five letters, or twenty-three letters, is declared to be "haughty" (dṛpta). || 2-36 ||
A mantra of twenty-six syllables, as well as one of thirty-six letters,
or even one of twenty-nine letters, is said to be deficient in its limbs (aṅga-hīna).
One who has twenty-eight syllables or even thirty-one is said to be excessively wrathful; he is censured in all ritual actions.
A mantra consisting of thirty syllables, or even thirty-three, is declared to be excessively cruel; it is censured for all ritual actions.
Beginning from forty and extending up to sixty-three syllables, that number of mantras is declared to be designated as "with shame" (savrīḍa). (2.40)
Those mantras which consist of sixty-five syllables are peaceful in nature;
[this continues] from sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine. (2.41)
Those mantras which consist of thirteen or fifteen syllables are designated by the wise as "fallen from their place" (sthānabhraṣṭa). || 2-42 ||
They are said to be deficient by one hundred, or likewise one hundred and fifty, or two hundred, or ninety-two, or even that [number] minus one. (2.43)
Those [mantras] are said to be unctuous when their number is three hundred;
then, starting from four hundred up to a thousand syllables, they are so designated.
(26) Those who are excessively advanced in their ritual applications should always be avoided by the wise.
Mantras consisting of more than a thousand syllables are called *daṇḍakas* and are known as "afflictions. (2-45)
Mantras consisting of two thousand syllables have been divided into a hundred fragments;
these mantras should be understood as being in the form of hymns, exactly as they exist.
In the same way, the mantras should be understood by practitioners in rites for specific desires.
That fool who pursues a mantra without recognizing these defects [will fail]. (2.47)
"Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the meaning of these verses as understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher (ārādhya) is written here: regarding the word "of Manu"—the term "at the beginning, middle, and end" refers to a collection [of syllables]. According to the oral tradition (sampradāya), "Anila" is the seed-syllable *ya*, and [the following] is the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*).

The names of the *māyābīja* are *mālinī*, *śivavallarī*, *vātāvartiphalā*, *vāṇībīja*, *śakti*, and *kuṇḍalī*, according to the teachings of the Śaiva Āgamas. The *vāyubīja* (the seed-syllable of air) may be conjoined with other intervening syllables or unjoined, being devoid of them; however, the *māyābīja* is pervaded by a long vowel. And it is said in the *Lakṣasāgara*:

"That mantra in which, at its beginning, middle, and end, the seed-syllable of Vāyu is seen fourfold, fivefold, twofold, and as the Single Hero (ekavīra) endowed with vowels—this is proclaimed as the 'divided' mantra. Thus, the seed-syllable of Vāyu is the letter *ya*;
the Single Hero is *hraḥ*, which is conjoined with vowels and possessed of long vowels: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*.
The illustration of that is: *aghorebhyo'tha hrāṃ ghorebhyo hrīṃ ghoraghoratarebhyo hrūṃ sarvataḥ sarvaśarvebhyo hraiṃ namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ hrauṃ*.
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning, middle, and end": the seed-syllable of the earth is the letter *la*; however, here, at each of the three locations, [the mantra is applied].
It has been stated that there are two *la*s; because they are seen within [the mantra], it should be understood that there are two at the beginning and the end, and three in the middle.

As it is said in the *Lakṣasāgara*: "O Dear One, when there are two at the beginning, three in the middle, and again two at the end, the mantra joined with the *vajrī* is proclaimed to be 'obstructed' (*niruddha*). The *vajrī* is the letter *la*. According to the *Piṅgalāmata*:

"In the beginning there are two, three in the middle, and again two at the end; this mantra, having the seed-syllable of Indra, is called 'obstructed' (ruddha). Here, "māyā" refers to the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, which consists of the three principles (tritattva), or the syllable *praṇava*, or *huṃ*, or the sound *phreṃ*; in this context, all of these are not required.
That mantra in which the seed-syllable of Māyā is not present, nor the three principles (tritattva), nor the sound RĀVA,
nor even the Śrīgṛha, is proclaimed to be devoid of power (śaktihīna).
Thus, from the statement of another tantra:

"If the seed-syllable of Māyā, or the three principles (tritattva), which constitute the 'Abode of Glory' (śrīgṛha), are not present, he is known as one devoid of power; such a person destroys the efficacy of the practitioners."

Thus, according to the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Of whom"—that is, at the beginning (mukhe) in the mouth, and at the end (śirasi) in the head. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. And it is said in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"He in whose middle position the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā is not found..."
It should be known that this [mantra] is turned away (parāṃmukha), having the Māyā-aṅkuśa at the beginning and at the end.
Thus it is said. Also in the Piṅgalāmata:

"That [mantra] in which the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) is not in the middle, and the goad (AṂ) is at the end of Māyā (Hrīṃ), is called 'turned away' (parāṃmukha); it is censured in all ritual acts."

Thus: "The letter *ha*."—The letter *sa*, which is the moon (*indu*), its state of being joined with the *bindu* is not required in the three positions of beginning, end, and middle. And it is said in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"Joined with the void (*śūnya*) and the *bindu* at the beginning, the end, and also in the middle."
Or if there should be no seed of life, he is known as deaf.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding "five-colored" (*pañcavarṇa*): *arka* is the letter *ha*; *indu* is the letter *sa*. Because fire, sun, and moon are the deities of the eyes, the mantras also possess eyes. As stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"That five-syllabled mantra which is devoid of fire, moon, and sun..."
He should be known as one deprived of sight, bringing with him suffering, grief, and fear.
Thus: "Ādi" refers to Haṃsa as one's own essential nature (svarūpa), Prāsāda as HAUṂ, Vāgbhava as AIṂ, and Jīva as the letter SA.
Of what kind is that [Jīva]? It is the letter HA endowed with a bindu; the meaning is that it is joined with the letter HA, the vowel Ū, and a bindu. By means of that, the seed-syllable is SHAUṂ.
And so it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
Joined with the eighth vowel, mounted upon Jīva (the letter *j*), and accompanied by the bindu—
whose self is not seen at all, what indeed would be the fruit of these four?
Wherever the *prāsāda*, the *vāgbhava*, the *haṃsa*, or the *māyā* is seen at the beginning, middle, and end, that [mantra] is declared to be "staked" (*kīlita*).

Thus: the *ātman* is the letter *ha*, the eighth vowel; the letter *o* is the eighth vowel because short and long vowels are considered one, as in the *akaḍama-cakra*. *Rāva* is *phreṃ*, consisting of four *kalās*; *hūṃ*. "One" means at the head and at the end. Here, the meaning is not according to the literal hearing [of the text], but rather there is one *la* in the middle and two *las* at the end; or else, one in the middle.
The meaning is that where the syllable *phaṭ* is seen at the end twice or thrice, that [mantra] is "paralyzed" (*stambhita*). And so it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* (p.
"If the seed-syllable of Śakti occurs twice in the middle of the excrement [the *kṣakāra*] and at the end..."
"The wise who know mantras declare that such a mantra is 'paralyzed' (stambhita).
Furthermore, it is said elsewhere:
'Where [the word *stambhita*] is seen at the end of a mantra, divided into two, three, or six parts.'"

"The great weapon, the mantra proclaimed by Śrī Śiva, is paralyzed. Here, it should be understood that the word "even in the middle" (*madhye'pi*) is derived from the root verse itself. Regarding the term "fire" (*vahni*): fire is the letter *ra*, and wind is the letter *ya*; these are joined at the head—that is, at the beginning. And it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
When that mantra is ignited by the seven seed-syllables situated at the beginning and by the fire-syllable (RAṂ) accompanied by the winds (YA), it is declared to be "burnt by Māyā" (HRĪṂ).

Thus. Regarding "the weapon" (*astra*): the meaning is that the syllable *phaṭ* is seen separated by the aforementioned number of syllables. Regarding "of which": at the beginning, in the mouth [of the mantra], *Śiva* is the letter *ha*, and *Śakti* is the letter *sa*. They say that for one possessed of such defects, there is another name: "devoid of the *mātṛkā*. And so it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
They say that a mantra which lacks Śiva, Śakti, and likewise the syllable Oṃ at its beginning is deficient in the Mātṛkās and bestows inferior accomplishments.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the word "ādi" (beginning): the meaning is that where four instances of the letter *ma* are seen combined across all three positions.
And where the letter *ma* is seen four times at the beginning, middle, and end, that mantra is declared by Maheśa to be "malina" (defiled).
Thus, from the statement in another tantra; and also in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"Wherever the letter 'Ma' is seen in three places—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end—the knower of mantras should always know that mantra to be impure."
Thus [it is said]. There is an option between these two. Regarding "yasya" (of whom): the seed-syllable *huṃ* is for Krodha; at the end, there is an option between the letter *da* and Krodha.

The connection is that the weapon (*astra*) is twofold at the head. The meaning is that between the letter *da* and the syllable *huṃ* in the middle, there is one, and at the end, there are two *phaṭ*s. And so it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
That syllable in whose middle the seed-syllable of Krodha (the letter *da*) is situated,
and at the end of which two *phaṭ*s are placed— that syllable is disregarded.
Thus it is said. Also elsewhere:

"He in whose [mantra] the letter *da* is in the middle, the seed-syllable of Wrath (*krodhabīja*) resides in the heart, and the syllable *phaṭ* occurs twice at the end—he is one who is held in contempt."

Thus [it is said]. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). "Omit" refers to the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning; "śīrṣa" means at the end; "vaṣaṭ" is in the middle; and "astra" refers to the two [mantras] from the wheel-spokes—this also applies here. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"The two Astra-mantras are in the middle, with *vaṣaṭ* at the end and likewise at the beginning."
This mantra, with its vowels [a, u, māḥ] separated, is proclaimed as "bhedita" (the divided).

Thus: the weapon is *hraḥ*, *a*, *umāḥ*, and the *oṃkāra*. Regarding the phrase "consisting of three syllables," it means that the mantra consists of exactly three syllables, being devoid of the two syllables *haṃsa*.
And so it is stated in the Bhairavītantra:
"The mantra which consists of three syllables is indeed that which is devoid of *haṃsa*."
But he who is thus in deep sleep should be known as one who robs others of the fruits of all accomplishments.
Thus: "of that which has seventeen and ten syllables" means "of that which has eighteen syllables."
"Phaṭkāreti" means that which begins with five *phaṭ* syllables. And it is said in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"Whether it be a *vidyā* or a *mantra*, if it consists of eighteen syllables preceded by five *phaṭ*s, it is called 'Madonmatta'."
Thus it is also stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"Whether it be a Vidyā or a King of Mantras, if it consists of seventeen syllables more [than that],
and is preceded by five *phaṭ* syllables, it is proclaimed as 'Unmatta' (the Madman)."

Thus [it is said]. Here, that which is qualified by these two attributes alone is defective. "In the same way" refers to [the case] when there is a pause (*virāma*); and "at the place of the pause" means situated within the mantra. "Five" applies to both cases. And it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"If the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) is present both in the middle and at the end [of the mantra] by Śambhu..."
That mantra is known as "of inferior energy" and does not grant accomplishment at all.

Thus. Regarding the phrase "at the beginning": the meaning is that the four weapons (astras) are combined across the three positions. The term "consisting of eighteen syllables" is understood to carry over from the previous context.
In another tantra as well, such a mantra is called by the name *Bhīta*. For example:
"At the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle, it is joined with the weapon four times."
Bhairava spoke to that mantra of eighteen syllables which was afraid.
Thus: "That which would be"—some say *tāra* is the *praṇava*, while others say *tāra* is *phreṃ*; however, in that regard, there is a contradiction with other texts.
And so it is stated in the *Bhairavītantra* (p.

Any mantra consisting of nineteen syllables that is endowed with the *praṇava* (OM) and joined with the *mahāmāyā-aṅkuśa* (the hook of great illusion), they declare that [mantra] to be utterly destroyed.
Thus, in the *Piṅgalāmata* as well: "If that [mantra] consists of eighteen syllables,
or twenty-nine syllables, and is endowed with the *māyā*, the *oṃkāra*, and the *aṅkuśa*,
this mantra is proclaimed by Lord Śambhu as 'Pradhvasta' (the Destroyer)."
Thus [it is said]. Here there are two qualifiers. Regarding "seven-syllabled": forty scripts consist of forty syllables. In the Bhairavītantra it is said:
"A child [mantra] consists of seven syllables, and a youth consists of eight syllables."
One with forty syllables is mature; one with sixteen syllables is young.
Thus: "thirty syllables" refers to [mantras] of four hundred syllables or one hundred and four syllables. And it is said in the Bhairavītantra:
"Whether thirty syllables, a hundred syllables, or likewise sixty-four syllables."
Or, one who has four hundred syllables [of learning] above is called "vṛddha" (an elder).

Thus: "The nine-syllabled" means the nine-syllabled [mantra] joined with the *dhruva* (the *praṇava*), that is, joined with the *oṃ*; for it is stated in the *Bhairavī-tantra*: "Furthermore, the nine-syllabled *nistriṃśa* joined with the *dhruva* bestows death. Regarding the phrase "of which": that at the end of which these two—the heart (*namaḥ*) and the head-mantra (*svāhākāra*)—are absent, [but] the *śikhā* (*vaṣaṭ*) [is present].

The two syllables *varma* and *huṃ*, as well as *vauṣaṭ* and *phaṭ*, or else the syllable *ha* which is Śiva and the syllable *sa* which is Śakti—where these two do not exist in the middle, that is "lifeless" (*nirjīva*); this is the meaning. As it is said in the *Bhairavītantra*:
"Whether at the end of the heart and head, or the crest and armor in the middle, or the eye and weapon—at those places, the two syllables whose nature is Śiva and Śakti do not exist."
He who possesses that king of mantras is proclaimed to be "seedless" (nirbīja) and is censured in all ritual acts.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the word "in these" (*eṣu*): if it is asked how the plural form is used here when only two locations were mentioned in the preceding verse, the answer is as follows.

It is true; however, the author of the work employed the plural form with the intention that even at the beginning of the description of the "seedless" (*nirbīja*) characteristic in another tantra, there exists a syllable that indicates that same defect.

And likewise, in the *Lakṣasāgara*: "That which is devoid of seed-syllables is declared to be at the beginning, [specifically] excluding the syllable *oṃ*. This refers to these [syllables] at the beginning, middle, and end. Here too, in all three places, the six *phaṭ*-syllables should be understood as combined together.
"Manda" consists of five letters; it is ten letters long. And it is said in the *Bhairavītantra*: "It shall be ten letters long."

Regarding "dull" (*manda*): regarding "peak" (*kūṭa*)—a seed-mantra (*bīja*) consisting of many syllables is a *kūṭa*. Although it has many syllables, it should be understood as being essentially a single syllable, being indivisible. A two-syllabled mantra is devoid of essence and lacking in power. A four-syllabled mantra is "squint-eyed" (*kekara*). Also, in the *Piṅgalāmata*, a specific distinction is stated: "A [mantra] devoid of the *dhruva* [syllable], whether with four or six seed-mantras, is considered 'squint-eyed'. Thus the distinction is declared.

"Six-syllabled" means devoid of seed-syllables (*bīja*), being bereft of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth. Here, one should understand that there are either six and a half syllables or twelve and a half syllables due to the addition of a consonant at the end; furthermore, there is the state of having three and a half seed-syllables. These are "smoky" (*dhūmita*)—this is the meaning. [As stated] in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
A mantra of six and a half syllables, or one of twelve and a half syllables,
or alternatively one of three and a half syllables, is declared to be "smoky" (dhūmita).

Thus: "twenty-one" has a clear meaning; "twenty-two" also has a clear meaning; "twenty-four"—the phrase "afflicted by hunger" has a clear meaning; again, "twenty-four" clearly indicates one who is arrogant;
"consisting of twenty-six syllables" also [has a clear meaning]; or "thirty less nine," that is, twenty-nine syllables.

"Furthermore, one with twenty-nine syllables is declared to be deficient in limbs. Thus [it is stated] in the Bhairavītantra. In the Lakṣasāgara, however, a fourth type is also mentioned, namely one with thirty-eight syllables, as well as one with twenty-eight syllables, and so forth.

"Forty" means that starting from forty syllables up to sixty-three syllables, the mantras—increasing by one syllable at a time—are of twenty-four kinds; these are "with modesty" (*savrīḍā*). "Sixty-five syllables" is clear.
"Lacking one" means those beginning with sixty-five syllables, i.e., those starting from sixty-five syllables, are "fallen from their place."

"Thirteen" has a clear meaning. "A hundred" refers to two hundred; if it is "ninety-two," it is a single category, meaning two hundred and ninety-two. "Two hundred and a half" means ninety-two less one, which is the meaning of two hundred and ninety-one. By that, the number of syllables is a hundred, or two hundred and a half syllables.

The meaning is that five types—consisting of one hundred and ninety-two syllables, two hundred and ninety-one syllables, and three hundred syllables—are clearly manifest among those defects characterized by a lack of oiliness (*niḥsneha*). Regarding this, some say that "two hundred" constitutes one type, while "ninety-two" is another and "ninety-one" is yet another; however, that is incorrect.

It is stated that those [mantras] beginning with sixty-six syllables and ending with ninety-nine letters are "fallen from their place" (*sthānabhraṣṭa*). Therefore, regarding the phrase "of whatever number," the grammatical connection is as follows: those mantras whose number of syllables exceeds one hundred are "without affection" (*niḥsneha*). The expression "four hundred" is easy to understand. As for "those of a thousand syllables," these are the *daṇḍaka* verses in the form of hymns.

They are to be known as "afflicted" (pīḍita). Thus—it is to be understood that just as these mantras have defects, so too the vidyās are likewise possessed of defects. And it is said in the Bhairavītantra:
"Just as the mantras are, so are the vidyās; they are thereafter divided by their various distinctions."
These should be understood by the lords of teachers as they have been expounded in various tantras.
29) Since it is stated "in the case of optional rites" (kāmyakarman), it appears that for those free from desire, these defects do not constitute obstacles to the recitation of mantras.
Now, regarding the means for removing the defects of those mantras corrupted by the aforementioned flaws, the *Śāradātilaka* states:
"One should apply those mantras corrupted by such defects as these to one's own self;
having restrained the breath, one should purify them by means of the bound *yonimudrā*."
Thus it is said. The definition of the *yonimudrā* is stated in the *Bhairavī-paṭala* of the *Rudrayāmala*:
"The *liṅga* facing west is proclaimed to be situated in the *yoni*. The *hṛdgranthi* is the abode of Brahmā; the *svayambhū* is the designator of the left."
Furthermore, that which is the intermediate space situated within the knot of consciousness,
as well as the Great Lotus Forest— that is proclaimed to be the Yoga-pīṭha.
With a face like a *kadamba* bud, he is that one whose form is the *bindu*;
indeed, the sphere that is the support of the *suṣumnā* is the very form of Brahman located right there.
The principles (tattvas) beginning with earth are the denoters of the mantras;
however, the principle called Pūrṇa, which is of the nature of the bindu, resides between the two bows.
Above that, there is indeed that which is called Nāda, and from that arises Uḍḍiyāna;
Kāmarūpa is Śakti, and what is named Śiva is Akula, O beloved.
A great thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with red filaments;
situated therein, one correctly obtains raining drops of blood.
By means of the yoga of vyāvaka, one should join the mind to its own substrate;
contracting the yoni located between the anus and the genitals, one should restrain it.
