Having meditated upon Kāma, who has entered a revolving womb, resembling a bandhūka flower,
like the blazing fire of time (kālānala), and possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), the supreme digit (kalā) situated in the point (bindu);
one should contemplate that self as having become one with it.
Moving along the path of Brahman by means of the sequence of piercing the *liṅgas*,
one reaches the nectar situated in the *visarga*, which is characterized by supreme bliss.
Red rays arise for him, raining down in torrents;
having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, he enters the *kula* once again.
One should proceed again to the Ākula [state] through the application of the measure (mātrā), and not otherwise;
and that, O Supreme Goddess, is declared in this Tantra to be Prāṇa.
Indeed, that is called "the upward stroke" (uddhāta) when the vital breath enters within;
for him who practices thus with certainty day after day.

They are liberated from the bondage of existence through [the cessation of] the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth; and whatever creation proceeds within this womb, beginning with those born from sprouts, [is likewise freed].
Furthermore, everything from the fire of time (kālāgni) up to Śiva dissolves back into that [source];
through the practice of the yonimudrā, your bondage is proclaimed to be severed.
Thus [is the instruction]. Its meaning is as follows: there, the Guru, seated in the Siddhāsana, presses the space between the anus and the genitals with the left heel;
then, pressing the base of the penis with the right heel such that the tips of the toes of both feet are pressed against each other above it, he sits with the body held steady.
Contracting the anus, one should raise the downward-moving breath (apāna-vāyu) and effect the union of the restrained prāṇa and apāna;

then, with a one-pointed mind, having contemplated one's own mantra— whose defects have been known— within the Supreme Self in the form of Kuṇḍalinī situated at the Mūlādhāra, one should [contemplate] the syllables of that mantra one by one.

Having reached the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) by means of the *suṣumṇā* path through the sequence of piercing the six chakras known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā,
[he then returns] to the Mūlādhāra by the sequence of piercing the Ājñā, Viśuddha, Anāhata, Maṇipūraka, and Svādhiṣṭhāna chakras.

"One should cause [the mantra] to reach [its goal]" means that one should recite the respective mantra one thousand and eight times, preceded by the nyāsa of its ṛṣi and other components, according to the prescribed visualization; this is the internal purification (*saṃskāra*) of the mantra. Now, for the removal of defects in the mantra, there are ten types of external ritual purifications (*saṃskāra*). Regarding this, it is said in the *Śāradā*:
Ten consecrations (saṃskāra) of mantras are said to bestow accomplishment:
birth, life-giving, striking, and likewise awakening;
Now, consecration, purification, nourishment,
gratification, illumination, and concealment— these ten are the ritual refinements of mantra.
The extraction of mantras from within the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth.
A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra, placing the Praṇava (Oṃ) between each one.
Those proficient in the true nature of mantras declare this to be "living" [mantra]:
having written the syllables of the mantra upon birch bark, one should sprinkle them with sandalwood water.
The practitioner of mantras should strike each [syllable] with the wind [vowel *i*]; that is declared to be "striking" (*tāḍana*).
Having written that mantra, the practitioner [should strike it] with flowers born from the *karavīra*.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the awakening by striking with the number of syllables of that mantra, ending with the letter *ya*,
according to the procedure taught in the *Svatantra*.
One should consecrate the mantra with the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree for the sake of purification;
having contemplated the mantra mentally, one should burn it away with the *jyotis* mantra.
The practitioner of mantra should purify the three impurities within the mantra; this is the purification.
The "Jyotirmanu" is considered to consist of the Tāra (Om), followed by the syllables of space (ha), fire (ra), and mind (kṣa), ending with the staff (phaṭ).
The sprinkling of each syllable of the mantra with water consecrated by recitation using *kuśa* grass is considered,
according to the rule, to be the "nourishment" (*āpyāyana*) of that mantra.
(30) Libation with water while reciting the mantra is known as *tarpaṇa*. The conjunction of the *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* [syllables] is called the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the mantra.
The concealment and non-disclosure of the mantra being recited—
these ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are proclaimed in all tantras as being kept secret.
By performing these according to the tradition, the practitioner of mantra attains his desired object.

Thus [ends the citation]. Now, the meaning of these eight verses is as follows: regarding the phrase "of the mantras," in that context, one should at some point—on a seat made of *śrīparṇī*, sandalwood, or the like—draw the wheel consisting of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika-cakra*) with saffron and other substances as will be described;
having drawn there the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa' according to the sequence of the drawing, therein...

Having invoked and worshipped Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī and recited the Mātṛkā-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should extract from its midst the desired mantra—consisting of vowels, consonants, *bindu*, *visarga*, and conjunct letters—individually and then unify them; thus, according to the instruction of one's own guru, one should produce the mantra. This is "generation" (*janana*). 2.

"Oṃ, etc."—having interspersed each individual syllable of the previously extracted mantra with the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should recite it one hundred and eight times; the meaning is that one should recite it by joining [the *praṇava*] to every syllable, as in "namaḥ śivāya," for example: *oṃ naṃ*, *oṃ maṃ*, *oṃ m* (*oṃ yaṃ*), and so forth. This is the "living" [mantra]. Regarding "on birch bark"—that is, on a leaf of the *bhūrja* tree.

Having written that mantra with substances such as saffron and the like, one should strike it one hundred times while reciting the wind-bīja *yam* and water mixed with sandalwood; this is "striking" (*tāḍana*). Regarding the word "having written": there, having written the mantra on the pedestal as before, one should take karavīra flowers equal in number to the syllables of that mantra while reciting the fire-bīja *ram*.

The instruction is that one should strike [the target] one hundred times with those flowers, syllable by syllable. Regarding the term *svatantra*: there, as before, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) using saffron, *gorocanā*, and other substances, one should fill its pericarp (*karṇikā*) with saffron and other materials, using jasmine buds (*mālatī-kalikā*) equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, or else with a single bud.

"I consecrate such-and-such a mantra; *namaḥ*. Thus, one should perform the consecration one hundred and eight times with fragrant water using each leaf individually; these are the consecrations. "Having meditated" means:
there, having meditated upon the light-mantra to be described later within the fire-maṇḍala at one's own *mūlādhāra*, [one should meditate] above that.

Having visualized the mantra to be refined, one should mentally burn away—repeatedly and one by one—the three impurities of the mantra, namely the *māṇava*, *kārmika*, and *māyīya* stains (known as innate, adventitious, and illusory), through the splendor of the *jyotir-mantra*; one should then meditate upon that mantra as being free from the three impurities. This is the purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*).
He states the *jyotirmantra*: "The *tāra*," and so forth. *Tāra* is the *praṇava* (oṃ); *vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; *manu* is the vowel *au*;

and *daṇḍin* is the *anusvāra*. Regarding "with *kuśa*-water": there, as before, having written that mantra with saffron and other substances upon the *pīṭha* and so forth, one should fill a vessel made of copper or another material with pure water scented with camphor and the like.

Having consecrated [the manuscript] one hundred and eight times with the very mantra written upon it, one should sprinkle each syllable three times with drops of that water using *kuśa* grass while reciting that same mantra; this is the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*). Regarding the phrase "with the mantra": there, having written the mantra as before in a vessel of copper or similar material, one should bring pure water scented with camphor and other fragrances into another vessel, and then [proceed with that].

Reciting the mantra, at the end one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) by offering water with joined palms (*añjali*) over the written mantra one hundred and eight times, saying: "I satisfy [the deity of] such-and-such a mantra; *namaḥ*. Regarding the term *tāra*: *tāra* is the *praṇava*; *māyā* is Bhuvaneśvarī; and *ramā* is the seed-syllable of Śrī. As for the definition of *yoga*, it has been stated that "in the beginning, there must be *yoga*."

The meaning is this: having placed the mantra of the object to be accomplished at the end of the *praṇava*, *Bhuvaneśvarī*, and *Śrī* seed-syllables, one should recite it one hundred and eight times; this is the "kindling" (*dīpana*). The meaning of the subsequent verse is clear. Thus are the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*).
Now, I shall describe the collection of defects of mantras as taught in the Kādimata, for the purpose of their removal and for the benefit of practitioners.
In that regard, the Śrītantrarāja states:
"Having recognized the defects of the mantra, the guru should eliminate them in due order;
otherwise, that guru will certainly destroy the disciple before long."
Therefore, O Goddess, listen with a concentrated mind to that refutation;
I shall explain the manner of the refutation according to the reality of the yogas.
A mantra with six ears is burnt; it becomes terrified by excessive recitation;
it is "roared at" when obtained through improper rites; and its enemies reside in the storehouse of the adversary.
The young are mostly composed of light syllables, while the old are endowed with heavy syllables;
they are overcome by the abundance of karma, incapable, and devoid of essential strength.
Through recitation while asleep, the mantras become incomplete in form, severed, paralyzed,
nasalized, and fail to awaken due to being employed at the wrong time.
Mantras that are recited word by word are pinned down by other syllables;
they are obstructed, disjointed, beset by suffering, and accompanied by enemies.
Those who have become fragmented, who lack the limbs of the mantra-parts, who are unrestrained,
and who have been instructed by one who is incomplete— these are considered to be of deficient power.
Through constant practice, there is dullness; through affliction, excessive delay;
through anger, chatter during recitation; and through other mantras, impurity.
The twenty-five defects that arise from the recitation being deficient due to indifference toward the state [of the mantra] should be pacified by the Guru.
The binding of the *yonimudrā* and the application of the potency of the mantras—
awakening the disciple to both of these, the self-possessed guru should provide protection.
The characteristics of the Guru are as follows: he should cause one to realize the beginning and the end. For syllables devoid of their beginning and end would be like autumn clouds.
Therefore, from the very beginning, he should declare whatever was done out of egoism,
for through the realization of that egoism, a man is born equal to me.

Know that the accomplishment of identity arises from the application of the beginning and end of the *mātṛkā*, which is established through the sequence of no beginning; it is the embodiment of the meaning of all mantras.
"Burnt" (dagdha) is the explicit meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is that a mantra in which the six *kūrca* seeds are seen at the beginning, middle, and end is "burnt."

As it is said in the Tripurārṇava: "In that king of mantras, two *kūrca* syllables are seen at the beginning, likewise two *kūrca* seed-syllables in the middle, and two *kūrca* syllables at the end. (2-1)
But that mantra with six ears is said to be "burnt"; it causes an obstruction to the success of those who recite it, and should always be avoided by all wise men. (2.2)

In this context, *karṇa* is the seed-syllable *kūrca*. As it is stated in that very same source: "O Maheśvarī, the names of the syllable *hūṃ* alone are *kūrca*, *māyā*, *sarasvatī*, *jala*, *nīra*, as well as *karṇa*, *taṭa*, and *kūla*."

Thus [it is said]: "Frightened by the addition of more [syllables]. The meaning is that a mantra in which the addition of extra syllables has been made is called "frightened" (*trasta*). As it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Whether at the beginning, the end, or in the middle, due to the addition of extra syllables, that mantra is declared to be 'frightened'."
For those who recite [it], it bestows inauspiciousness. || 2-1 ||
Thus it is said: "Even though—having recited [the mantra] for three years, [one should then recite] Lopāmudrā, the source of auspiciousness;
thereafter, having joined the Haṃsa, the wise one should recite it at the beginning of the mantra. (2-2)
Then, when three years have passed, one should join [the practice] even in the middle and at the beginning;
then, when another three years have passed, one should join it even at the beginning of the *śakti*. || 2-3 ||
Thus, he who practices the vidyā in this manner becomes a partaker of increasingly superior fruits; otherwise, that vidyā destroys the practitioner—of this there is no doubt. (2.4)

Thus, although this contradicts what is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*, nevertheless, it should be understood that at the very outset, the addition of extra syllables (*adhikākṣara*) is prohibited. Regarding the term "garjita": the meaning is that a mantra which has been obtained without following the specific injunction prescribed for its instruction in the scripture is called "garjita. This is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
But that mantra which is given by the dull-witted, having abandoned the prescribed rule out of delusion or even greed, is always proclaimed to be censurable.

Thus: "enemies" means those residing in the storehouse of enmity; this is the clear meaning. "Children" and "elders"—the meaning is that those consisting mostly of short syllables are children, while those consisting mostly of long syllables are elders. The definitions of short syllables and long syllables are to be known from the *Mātṛkāśvāsa*. "Conquered" means conquered due to the abundance of karma.
This is the meaning. As it has been stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:

"Whether by abandoning what is taught in one's own [tradition’s] tantra, or out of a lack of satisfaction even after having learned [it], or even from the mantras taught by one's own guru, or due to delusion regarding success (siddhi)... (2.1)
For one who repeatedly performs recitation, libation, fire-offerings, worship, and purification, the King of Mantras will always remain conquered and censured. (2.2)
It does not yield its fruit to him even in hundreds of millions of eons;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice that which is taught in the *Svatantra* [Tantras]. (2–3)
Thus: "asaha" means that a mantra chanted without fixed rules is "asaha. As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"By the violation of the rules, the mantra shall always be 'asaha'. "Devoid of sattva" means devoid of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
Just as a living being devoid of vigor is incapable of performing any action, so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). (2-1)
Through the performance of daily and occasional rites, as well as preparatory rituals (puraścaryā) and the like,
the mantra becomes endowed with the quality of sattva, just as a king is served [and thus strengthened] by his subjects.
A mantra that has attained the quality of sattva is equal to a wish-fulfilling creeper.
Thus [it is said]. "Incomplete in form" means devoid of vowels, consonants, and *pallavas*. As it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Due to the omission of *pallavas* and so forth, and through the loss of vowels and consonants, that mantra which has become incomplete is designated as 'broken' (*chinna*). (2-1)
Thus it is said in the Trailokyadāmaratantra:
"The pallava is the placement (nyāsa) of mantras; the praṇava is the head (śiras) of mantras.
A mantra joined with both the head and the pallava yields the fruit of all desires. (2.1)
Without the ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes mute; without the seat (āsana), one is as if asleep;
and without the "sprout" (pallava), the mantra is naked—thus it is proclaimed. (2-2)
A mantra is said to be headless when it lacks its opening syllables, and dead when it is devoid of a guru.
It is slain when given to a wicked person, and it is powerless when it contains an extra syllable. (2-3)
(32) One who is pervaded and pinned down by another seed-mantra is said to be "pinned" (kīlita).
He whose recitation another person hears is called "void" (śūnya), [and such a mantra] is called "dead" (manta). || 2-4 ||
A serpent that is devoid of seers, deities, and meters is mute, asleep, dead, naked, powerless, and slain in vain. (2.5)
A serpent that is pinned down is powerless; likewise, a mantra that is void [of its proper application] is fruitless.
One who desires success in that [mantra] should avoid such a mantra with great effort. (2-6)
The mantra ending in *namaḥ* is proclaimed for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and prostration;
that ending in *svāhā* bestows success in rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and fire-offerings (*homa*). (2.7)
A mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* syllable as its sprout accomplishes nourishment and other such aims;
one joined with the *huṃ* syllable as its sprout is used for killing, except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa. (2-8)
And in the rite of partaking the mantra, which destroys most terrible fear,
[the mantra] ending in *vaṣaṭ* is the destroyer of the great Kāla and the host of seizing spirits.
For the rites of shattering, eradication, and piercing, the mantra is accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*;
the two mantras originating from the Vedas and Āgamas have the syllable *oṃ* at their beginning. (2.10)
The *pallava* exists in the Āgama, but the *pallava* does not exist in the Vedic mantra;
a mantra originating from the Veda should be recited without the *pallava*. (2-11)
"He is not called naked because he is clothed in sovereignty.

Regarding the term "stambhitāḥ" (the immobilized ones), it means they are accompanied by nasalized vowels (*anunāsika*). The definition of nasalized and non-nasalized [consonants] should be understood from the *Mātṛkāśvāsa*. It is also stated in the *Tripurārṇava*: "That which is joined with a nasalized syllable is 'stambhitā'."
[They] are considered [to be so]. Thus, [the phrase] "by application at the wrong time" [is used]; "negligent" is what should be supplied [as the subject]. As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"It is applied at times when the vowel-sound (*svara*) has arrived or when the debt (*ṛṇa*) has arrived."
If a mantra has been recited by me on another occasion when it was prescribed for a different purpose, [it is not effective]. || 2-1 ||
Thus, the definition of time is to be understood from the *Kāmyāśvāsa*. "Non-awakening" means the recitation performed during the time of sleep.
As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"The time of sleep is when the breath flows through the left [nāḍī], and waking is when it flows through the right."
A mantra chanted during the time of sleep, being unawakened, destroys the practitioner. (2-1)
Thus: regarding the phrase "the mantras," it should be completed as "they become enraged" due to reciting or muttering them upon [inscribed] leaves. As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"The lowest of practitioners who mutters [mantras] after seeing them written in a book—four things perish for him: life-span, fame, glory, and prosperity. (2-1)
If the mantra is recited upon leaves, it becomes enraged and destroys the practitioner.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: having omitted that syllable which is intended as the *kīlaka* (stake) within the mantra. This has been stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"The seed-syllable (*bīja*) shall be the beginning of the mantra, while the middle of the mantra is the *kīlaka*."
At the end of the mantra, Śakti is indicated; [these are] the seed-syllables, the kīlakas, and the Śaktis. || 2-1 ||
And setting aside that which has been prescribed as the color of the stake, either the one preceding it or the one following it may be established as the stake. (2-2)
"But one accompanied by another vowel, being 'pinned' (kīlita), causes the obstruction of success.

Regarding the term "obstructed" (ruddhā): the meaning is that they are "obstructed" when devoid of euphonic conjunction (*saṃdhi*). This is because of the statement in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "That which lacks euphonic conjunction is obstructed and is censured in all ritual acts. Regarding the term "painful" (*duḥkhā*): the meaning is that they are "suffering" when endowed with harsh consonantal syllables (*vairya*).
This is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*: "Those who are joined with the letters of the enemy are declared to be afflicted.

Regarding the term "fragmented" (*khaṇḍībhūta*): the meaning is that they have become fragmented due to the omission of parts. This is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*: "They are broken by the omission of letters. Regarding the term "limb-deficient" (*aṅgahīna*): the meaning is that they are incomplete, being devoid of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and so forth. This is stated [in the same source].
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Without the recitation of the hymn of armor for the limbs and sub-limbs, the mantra is declared to be unshielded; it does not bestow accomplishment at all."
Thus [it is said]. "By the incomplete" means that those taught by one who is incomplete are of inferior vigor (*hīnavīrya*). And so it is stated:
"Through the second consecration (*abhiṣeka*), that mantra attains fullness;
otherwise, it would be of inferior vigor and excluded from all ritual actions."

Thus, from the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "From constant application" means that by constantly performing rites for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*), the mantra becomes dulled (*kuṇṭhatā*). This is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"If mantras are employed by men at all times without the respective pacification [rites], [they become ineffective]."

"Those mantras become blunted; therefore, one should perform propitiation (*śānti*). Here, "propitiation" consists of the recitation of ten thousand repetitions of the *mūlamantra* accompanied by ten thousand recitations of the *sāvitrī*. We shall explain its ritual procedure in the chapter on practical applications (*prayogapaṭala*). Regarding "affliction": it refers to [the defect] of a short vowel being pronounced with a protracted (*pluta*) utterance.
The meaning is that there is difficulty in reciting the mantra due to its length. And so it is stated in another tantra (p.
"That which has one mora is called short, and that which has two moras is called long."
The protracted vowel (*pluta*) should be known as having three morae (*mātra*); this is the definition of the vowels. (2.1)
And by means of shortness [the cognition] of the long, by means of length [the cognition] of the protracted, and by means of protraction [the cognition] of the long;
and again, within the short, by means of lengthiness [the cognition] of the long. (2.2)
A mantra becomes defiled by the power of its pronunciation, and not otherwise.
That mantra which has reached a state of defilement acts as an obstacle to accomplishment. (2–3)
"Enraged" means that they become enraged by reciting [the mantra] without silence. As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"If one recites the mantra without silence, the recitation is seized by Rākṣasas;
the mantra also becomes enraged and does not bestow accomplishment at all."
Thus [it is said]. "With other mantras" means by means of the recitation of the root mantra together with the mantras of other deities. As it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"One should not take up another mantra; one should avoid other deities."
One should likewise avoid any other purpose and any other means of accomplishment.
Then the mantra will certainly and swiftly yield the fruit of the wish-fulfilling cow;
when joined with four [defects], the mantra is designated as "impure" (malina).
Thus: "Equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Equanimity is the state of remaining indifferent toward any one among the deity, the guru, or the mantra.

It means that if, after receiving the mantra, some suffering is encountered due to the power of past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), and one performs recitation while keeping in mind the thought, "For what purpose was this mantra received?", that itself is called "recitation with indifference. This is the meaning.
As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"If indifference is shown toward the mantra, the guru, or the deity— whether due to one's state of being or through partiality— the mantra becomes insulted."
Thus: "the binding. The meaning is that by means of the binding of the *yonimudrā*, all defects depart.

That which was previously mentioned is common to both systems (*ubhayamata*). There is a distinction, however, regarding the external consecration (*bāhyasaṃskāra*). "Beginningless," etc.: this refers to the joining of the beginning and end of the *mātṛkā* with each individual syllable.
Now follows the method for the blending of mantras. As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"For the Nityās and the deities of the Tripurā [cycle], the [astrological] divisions such as the *aṃśaka* and so forth need not be considered.
Nevertheless, something is said here for the sake of accomplishing rites such as *ābhicāra* (sorcery) and the like. (2.1)
In the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, one should join the first four letters, excluding the bindu and visarga; however, the bindu and visarga are present in all [the others].
By means of that syllable from the mantra and the first letter of the name, one should count the sixth, the eighth, or the twelfth [syllable]. (2–3)
If the letter of the enemy's mantra occurs [in the query], one should not speak what is beneficial for him;
this applies when [the planets] occupy the seventh, fifth, or third houses from the other zodiac signs and asterisms.
In the rite of grace, the name of the person to be initiated should also be understood as being preceded by the [relevant] lunar mansion and so forth;
for it has been stated that they are devoid of the knowledge of reality. (2.5)

Thus [it is said]: "Of the eternal ones. This means that for as many eternal mantras as there are, and for as many Tripurā mantras as there are, their constituent parts (*aṃśaka*) and other methods of mantra-combination need not be observed. "Nevertheless"—referring to "black magic" (*ābhicāra*) and so forth—the meaning is this: they need not be observed in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites; however, they must be observed in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites. "In Aśvinī and the other [asterisms]"—[this refers to the same].
The meaning is that, having excluded the *bindu* and the *visarga* from the constellations (*ṛkṣa*) and the zodiacal signs (*rāśicakra*), one should write four letters each;

whereas in the constellational wheels (*nakṣatracakra*) beginning with Aśvinī, having included the *bindu* and the *visarga* everywhere, one should write three letters each. This has been stated in the *Mātṛkārṇava*:
One should draw four lines toward the east, west, south, and north;
one should then place four lines in each of the corner regions.
By that [process], segments numbering twelve (the number of the sun) arise, and not otherwise;
upon them, one should write starting from the east in a clockwise sequence. (2-2)
O Supreme Goddess, having excluded the four letters— the *bindu*, the *sarga*, and the letter *sa*—
from among the forty-eight letters, [the remainder is as follows].
In that sequence, one should likewise determine the zodiac signs beginning with Aries; for thus the wheel of signs arises, which the practitioner should here investigate. (2–4)

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the wheel of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatracakra*) as well, it is stated in that very same place: "One should draw the wheel consisting of solar segments according to the method previously described.
Within those segments, starting from the east, one should assign the letters in groups of three in sequence. (2–5)
The goddess named Madhumatī, consisting of thirty-six consonants, likewise joined with the bindu and likewise joined with the visarga. (2.6)
And in each and every segment, nine new castes arise in succession within the one hundred and eight feet of the twenty-seven constellations. (2.7)
In the great wheel known as the *ṛkṣa*, the practitioner should examine each individual group according to the ninefold division of the *navāṃśas*. (2–8)
Thus [it is said]. In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"And that Madhumatī is said to have the form of the thirty-six consonants."
In the Kādimate, Mālinī is produced from fifty phonemes beginning with 'ka'. (2.1)
In the Kālīmata, however, both of these [mantras] consist of fifty syllables;
O Sovereign of the Gods, in each respective system, it is taught that the first syllable of each corresponds to its own specific tradition.
Thus it is said. "By that" means: one should count in a clockwise direction within the wheel consisting of twelve segments, which is composed of zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and constellations (*ṛkṣa*).

Starting from whichever segment the first letter of the mantra resides, one counts up to the segment where the first letter of the name resides; or alternatively, starting from the letter of the name, one counts up to the first letter of the mantra.

One should count them. Then, if the sixth, eighth, or twelfth [syllable] from the beginning of the mantra corresponds to the first syllable of the name, or if the first syllable of the name corresponds to a syllable at the beginning of the mantra, that mantra is "devoid of enemies" (riporahita); this means it is recommended for malevolent rites (abhicāra). Regarding the signs (rāśi): likewise, if it falls on the seventh, fifth, or third [sign], it is for favoring (anugraha).
The meaning is "praiseworthy. He describes the *siddhāricakra*:
"By the conjunction of five lines drawn east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east, sixteen squares are formed here; one should write the letters in them in sequence. (2-1)
One should indeed arrange those [sections] in sequence by dividing them into four groups of four;
the first [syllable] is in the first of the first [group], and likewise in the first of the second.
One should conceive of a second [syllable] as different from the other, and likewise imagine yet another;
one should write each respective fifth syllable in those various cells.
In this manner, one should fill in the four squares up to the point of *kṣānti*;
from whichever square one's own initial letter is seen, [that is the starting point]. (2–4)
One should count from the *siddha* [category] onwards until the first syllable of the mantra is seen:
through recitation, a *siddha-siddha* mantra is accomplished; a *siddha-sādhya* is accomplished by double that amount. (2.5)
Through the attainment of *siddha*, *susiddha*, or *siddhāri*, one destroys those born of one's own lineage;
through *sādhyasiddha*, there is extreme affliction; and *sādhyāsādhya* causes intense suffering. (2.6)
O Śāṅkarī, one who is *sādhyasusiddha* becomes accomplished through worship;
however, a *sādhyāri* kills one's daughter, therefore one should avoid him. (2-7)

A *susiddhasiddha* mantra bestows the desired fruit through study; a *susiddhasiddha* becomes effective for accomplishment (*siddhi*) through recitation and other means, whereas otherwise it would not. (2.8)
But one who is already well-perfected is indeed a Susiddha, having exerted effort in previous births;
therefore, one should employ that person in the mantra for the accomplishment of all siddhis.
If such [a rite] for the destruction of an enemy is performed when it results in one's own ruin, then that well-accomplished enemy will certainly destroy his entire family without exception. (2.10)

A mantra that is easily accomplished (susiddha) by an enemy destroys one’s son; one that is to be accomplished with difficulty (sādhya) by an enemy destroys one’s wife; and a mantra that is well-accomplished (susiddha) by an enemy brings about the destruction of one’s entire lineage. (2.11)
The noble enemy is the mantra that destroys one's own self; this is a firm certainty established by its very attainment.
The meaning is clear. Regarding the method for clearing debts and assets, the *Śrītantrarāja* states:
"Beginning from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra..."
Having divided [the first] threefold, one should split it according to one's own will; the other is the reverse.
One who has performed the ritual service (kṛtya) should be known as superior to a debtor; if the mantra is the creditor, it is excellent.
However, if one is oneself a debtor, one should abandon that mantra, because one is first and foremost a debtor. (2-2)
Thus, in this context, one should investigate [the matter] beginning with the first letter of the name within the *mātṛkā* consisting of fifty phonemes;
or [within] the thirty-six consonants, or within the *mātṛkā* whose form is the full mandala. As it has been said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
In the Madhumatī, the great goddess, the clearing of debt is preeminent;
however, in the Kālīmata, the beginning of the portions and so forth is praised in the Mālinī.
Thus it is said. Here, *Madhumatī* consists of thirty-six consonants; *Mahāmadhumatī* has the form of the colors of the full mandala; and *Mālinī* has the form of the fifty letters.
And so it is asked: "Tell me, how is there a state of debt for the mantras and for the practitioners?"
Due to practice performed in previous births, this [person] does not obtain the fruit from sin. (2.1)
When evil has been destroyed, there is the attainment of fruit upon the dissolution of the body in due time;
by the mere acquisition of the mantra, the previous one becomes perfected.

That man who has obtained a perfected mantra from a guru and attained spiritual accomplishment should not disregard the enjoyment of the mantra due to the intoxication of wealth, but should instead attain its full power.
He should be known as a debtor to the mantra; its worship is the prerequisite.
Therefore, the purification of that debt must be performed by everyone, in every way. (2.4)
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the method for the blending of mantras (*mantramelana*) according to the *Kālīmata*. Regarding that, first is the *nakṣatracakra*;
concerning this, it is stated in the *Śrīrudrayāmala*:
"For the sake of assisting in the attainment of sovereignty, [the sage] Avikhaṛa began [this work] from the land of the Kurus."
The script called Phullā is said to consist mostly of the letters gopālān and kukkuṭī.

Now, this is the method for constructing the wheel (*cakra*): there, having drawn four lines extending north-south and ten lines extending east-west, one forms twenty-seven squares. Then, according to the numerical system of the designations of the consonant groups—namely, the nine beginning with *ka*, the nine beginning with *ṭa*, the five beginning with *pa*, and the eight beginning with *ya*—[the letters are to be placed].

Starting from the first square of the topmost row, one should write the letters in successive rows and likewise write the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, and then investigate. In that regard, in whichever square...
Having understood the first letter of the practitioner’s name and the numerical letter situated there,

one should determine the practitioner’s birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) as whichever asterism falls in that position; then, counting from that point up to the square where the first letter of the mantra resides, that asterism is the "mantra asterism" (*mantranakṣatra*).
Having ascertained [the proper time], starting from the asterism of the practitioner up to the asterism of the mantra.
Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, there are the [six stages]:
birth, prosperity, adversity, security, attainment, and destruction.
Loving-kindness and supreme loving-kindness, as well as birth and so forth, again and again.

Thus, having understood the nine [periods] beginning with birth in their respective order according to the method stated in the Kulārṇava, one should indicate the results. Regarding this, the Kulārṇava states:
"Death occurs through the *tārā* [star] of birth; the destruction of lifespan occurs through the third."
Death is considered to occur on the fifth lunar mansion (tārā), and the seventh is regarded as the killer. (2-1)
Stars situated in the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, and ninth houses are considered auspicious; having understood these results of the stars, one of vast intelligence should bestow the mantra. (2.2)
Now, regarding the classification of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) according to the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
Aśvinī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, as well as Puṣya and Punarvasū, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, and Revatī have Viṣṇu as their presiding deity. (2.1)
Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Pūrvā and Uttarā [Phalgunī], Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvābhādrapadā and Uttarābhādrapadā are the asterisms belonging to men. (2.2)
Kṛttikā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Citrā, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, as well as Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣā— these, O beloved, belong to the host of Rākṣasas.
Viṣṇu is the deity of the Śravaṇa asterism, belonging to the class of gods; here, the elision of the visarga is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. In the Rudrayāmala:
"Affection is highest toward one's own group, and middling toward gods and humans."
Death by a Rakshasa in a rite for the gods is the lowest; death by a human or a Rakshasa is [better].
Now, regarding the wheel of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*). In that regard, the *Śrīkulārṇava* states:

"In the [twelve] signs, the letters are divided in order as follows: *vā* (white), *laṃ* (fair), *kha* (red), *raṃ* (crimson), *śa* (the beauty of the *śamī* tree). In the sign of Virgo (*kanyā*), the letters beginning with *śa* are traditionally taught. (2.1)

The convention regarding the syllables has already been stated. As for the *cakra*: having drawn two lines extending from east to west such that a square is formed in the middle, one should draw a line in each of the four outer corners to produce twelve compartments; then, having written [the syllables] in those compartments starting from the east and proceeding clockwise according to the sequence of the letters—

In the case of a female, one should write the syllables *aṃ, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, la, kṣa*. Then, having written the numbers one through twelve in those twelve sections starting from the east, and having assigned the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries (*meṣa*) to them, one should perform the analysis.
Starting from the first letter of one's name up to the letters of the mantra and so forth,
[the results for] the ascendant, wealth, brothers, kinsmen, sons, enemies, and wife [are determined].
Death, dharma, karma, income, and expenditure are the twelve zodiac signs.

Now, their results in the ocean of one hundred thousand [verses]: The first, the fifth, and the ninth are the zodiac signs that are good friends; the tenth, together with the second, and the sixth shall be the servant signs.
If a mantra is considered to have the inherent tone of Rudra-Agni, it would be nourishing;
a mantra measured by twelve or eight syllables is traditionally known as destructive.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the classification of the colors of the zodiac signs:
Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces are Brāhmaṇas; Leo, Sagittarius, and Aries are Kṣatriyas;
Libra, Aquarius, and Gemini are Vaiśyas; and Virgo, Taurus, Capricorn, and Makara are Śūdras.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the wheel of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika-cakra*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "U, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, and the vowels a, ba, la, and la are the letters of earth.
Ṛ, ṝ, au, gha, jha, ḍha, and the vowels dha, bha, va, and sa are those of water. (2-1)
The letters i, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, and kṣa are the fiery (vahnika) syllables;
the letters a, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and ya are born from the element of air (vāyuja). (2-2)
The letters ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, ṅa, ña, and ṇa—these syllables are salutations belonging to the ether.

Thus it is said in the Śrīkulārṇava: "There is friendship between earth and water, and also between wind and wind; likewise there is a commonality between fire and earth, as well as between water and wind. (2.1)
An enemy becomes a friend through reversal, and elsewhere, the opposite occurs;
where there is a conjunction of mutually contradictory counsels.
One should avoid such a mantra, O Mistress of the Kula, for it causes destruction.
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the method for purifying the *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth. Regarding that, first is the twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāracakra*).
In that regard, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"In the twelve-spoked wheel, [one should place] those [syllables] excluding the *kūṭas* and the *ṣaṇḍas*."
One should write the letters from the beginning to the end starting from the east up to the northeast (Īśvara).
One should write down the numbers starting from one and ending with twelve in order, beginning from the east;
thus the fourfold classification of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* will become clearly manifest. (2-2)
The results of these are stated in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
Nine, one, and five are established (*siddha*); six, ten, and two are to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
seven, eleven, and three are well-accomplished (*susiddha*); and four, eight, and twelve are enemies (*ripu*).
Having understood this, O lady of excellent limbs, the one of vast intellect should impart the mantra.
Their fruits are to be understood as those described in the *Siddhāricakra*.

Thus, in the Tantra known as the Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Govindācārya— the venerable and worshipful supreme Great Preceptor (Mahāmahopādhyāya).
The Second Chapter. || 2 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the third breath (śvāsa).
Now, the sixteen-spoked wheel. Regarding that, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"Having divided the square ground, one should draw sixteen squares.
One should also arrange the *mātṛkā* [alphabet] beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. (3.1)
The wise one should write [the syllables] starting from the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa) and ending at the northwest (vāyavya), following the clockwise order (prādakṣiṇyakrama).
Regarding the method of that writing, the Lakṣmīkulārṇava states:
"In the groups of one, three, eleven, nine, two, twelve, five, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, and five..."
One should write the letters of Ambikā, numbering thirty-three, in order within the grid at the seventh and fifteenth squares, as well as in the remaining spaces.
3-1 || Thus it is said:
The *siddha* [mantra] succeeds in due time; the *sādhya* may succeed or it may not.
The *susiddha* succeeds in that very instant, while the *ari* cuts away one's very root. 3-2 ||
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra:
"A wise person, having carefully and thoroughly examined a mantra that abounds in syllables corresponding to malefic asterisms, zodiac signs, spirits, and so forth, should avoid it with effort. (3-1)
In the conjunctions of the Siddha, Sādhya, and other yogas, and especially when imparting a mantra,
one should employ a well-known name by which [the disciple], though fast asleep, may be awakened.

If it is established at the beginning and at the end, it bestows the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhis). If it occurs at the beginning and at the end, it is "to be accomplished" (sādhya) and is declared to be accomplished with difficulty.
That which is well-established at the beginning and the end succeeds very quickly;
however, that which is an enemy at the beginning and the end will cut the practitioner to pieces.
That which is established at the beginning and difficult to achieve at the end is accomplished by doubling [the effort];
that which is difficult to achieve at the beginning and well-established at the end is accomplished by the aforementioned method.
That which begins with the "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and ends with the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) requires fourfold [repetition];
when that which is accomplished is at the beginning and end, and that which is to be accomplished arises in the middle. (3.6)
When that which is to be accomplished at the beginning and end becomes established in the middle,
both the goal to be achieved and the means of achievement are indeed perfected through the abundance of recitation.
Joined with a *siddha* at the beginning and likewise with a *susiddha* at the end, the practitioner will attain success merely by hearing [this], without a doubt. (3.8)

A mantra whose objective is encompassed by one's own established tenets, or even better, one that is perfectly aligned with those tenets, indeed attains success quickly; this is what has been stated by the foremost among those who know mantras.

If an enemy is intercepted by one who has attained success, even if that [interceptor] is well-perfected, he shall not become an enemy to the mantra; rather, it will succeed only with great difficulty.
If a perfected mantra (siddha) is separated by the one to be accomplished (sādhya), or even a well-perfected one (susiddha) is likewise so separated,
it will be accomplished by the practitioner with extreme difficulty, and not otherwise.
One should likewise abandon that which is obstructed by an enemy, as well as the *siddha* and *susiddha* [mantras].
A mantra defiled by an enemy must never be accepted under any circumstances. (3-12)
Mantras that have few defects and many virtues should be bestowed by the wise;
having understood the "Siddha" and other categories of the table, success is then produced. (3-13)

In the case of a single-syllable mantra, a *kūṭa* mantra, or a *mantranāyaka* of the *traipura* class—whether it was given by a woman or received in a dream—one should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories of] mantras at all. (3.14)

One need not examine the Siddha and other [categories] of the mantras consisting of syllables along with their seed-syllables (piṇḍa) belonging to Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, the temples, and the Praṇava. (3-15)
The three-syllabled mantra beginning with *pāśa*, the Traipura, Caṇḍanāyaka,
Saura, Mṛtyuñjaya, Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Vinatāsuta.
Furthermore, those mantras of the Sun, as well as those of Viṣṇu and Nṛsiṃha,
are devoid of any consideration regarding the categories of Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, or Arī.
One should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] in the case of the three-syllabled *praṇava*, the *māyā* [bīja], the six-syllabled *vyomavyāpin*, or in all *mālā-mantras*. (3-18)
Thus, in the Ratnasāgara:

"One should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] of mantras consisting of eight syllables, such as the *haṃsa*, nor those of five syllables, nor those with one, two, three, or more seed-syllables. (3-1)
(38) [The forms] of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha; Kālikā, Siddhakālikā, Śyāmalā, and likewise Caṇḍī; and the exclusion of the Siddhas and so forth. (3-2)

Thus, in the Rudrayāmala: "O Goddess of gods, O Pārvatī, in the case of the Aghora mantra, the Mālā mantra, and the neuter mantra, one should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories of efficacy]. (3.1)
Thus, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"For one who has been instructed in a mantra in a dream, there is neither formal rite nor ritual action;
having meditated upon the indicated deity, one should recite [the mantra], and it will become auspicious. (3-1)
Thus it is said in the Agastyasaṃhitā:
"O bull among sages, listen regarding all the mantras of Rāma:
because of its status as the *tāraka*, one need not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] in this king of mantras. (3-1)
Thus, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"In a mantra consisting of one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven, or thirty-two syllables, one need not examine the *siddha* and other [categories]. (3-1)
And those who are Buddhists and Jains, cowherds and Vaiṣṇavas—those who are free from deliberation regarding the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Susiddhas, and Aris. || 3-2 ||
The Vyomavyāpin with six syllables, the Mātṛkā, the Haravallabhā, and the Bahurūpa—these five mantras are considered common [to all]. (3-3)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the six-petaled wheel (*ṣaḍdalacakra*): therein, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*, it is stated:
"Having drawn a six-petaled lotus, one should write the letters beginning with 'A'—one by one—in the petals starting from the east; these are the single-syllable *kūṭas*. (3.1)
One should investigate starting from the first letter of one's own name;
in the first [case], prosperity is indicated, while in the second, there is the loss of prosperity.
In the third [period], one should know there is steadfastness; in the fourth, conflict with kinsmen;
in the fifth, one should know there is doubt; and in the sixth, the destruction of everything.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the wheel for the calculation of debts and assets (*ṛṇadhanaśodhanacakra*). Regarding that, in the *Kulāmūlāvatāra*:
"The [debts] to be calculated are multiplied by fourteen, three, two, twelve, fifteen, six, four, three, five, eight, and nine."
Then, multiply the letters of the practitioner by ten, one, seven, eight, eight, six, four, and six respectively.
Having understood the remainder of the name-letters and the remainder of the Kaṭhavaḍaga, the greater of the two remainders shall be the debt or the wealth.

Now, the method for the *cakra-nirvāṇa*: having drawn seven lines extending north-south and twelve lines extending east-west, one forms sixty-six squares. Therein, in the first row consisting of eleven squares located at the very top, starting from one's own left and ending at the right—

Having written the eleven distinct numbers— 14 in the first square, 27 in the second, 2 in the third, 12 in the fourth, 15 in the fifth, 6 in the sixth, 4 in the seventh, 3 in the eighth, 5 in the ninth, 8 in the tenth, and 9 in the eleventh— in the first row,
one should write below them, in the second row from left to right, the eleven vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ.

Having written the vowels in eleven squares, one should write the letters from *ka* to *ṭa* in the row below that; in the row below that, the letters from *u* to *pha*; in the row below that, the letters from *va* to *ha*; and in the row below that, the numbers 10, 1, 7, 4, 8, 3, 7, 5, 4, 6, 3.

Having written the eleven types of numbers in eleven compartments, one should construct the *akaṭhava-cakra* and perform the investigation. Therein, having separated the letters of one's chosen mantra— vowels, consonants, *bindu*, and *visarga*— one should take whichever number corresponds to whichever letter situated at the very top, and [calculate] that respective letter by means of that number.
Having multiplied those figures by that [same] figure, one should divide the resulting total by eight; setting aside the remainder as a separate figure,
among the remaining figures of both the mantra and the practitioner, whichever has the higher number is to be known as the debtor.
If a mantra is a debtor, then that mantra should be accepted; however, that mantra which makes its practitioner a debtor should be abandoned.
Now, concerning the Śrīvidyā, follows the exposition of the Mātṛkā.
Next, I shall describe the Mātṛkā, the sustainer of the universe, whose very form is mantra, for the sake of facilitating the placement (nyāsa), worship, and recitation (japa) of mantras. (3.1)

And for the sake of the upliftment of practitioners, especially according to the Kālikāmata, there are fifty digits (kalās) residing in the fifty phonemes, derived from the five divisions of the Tāra mantra. (3-2)
Expansion and foundation, knowledge and peace immediately follow; then the kindler, the illuminator, the purifier, and the supreme liberator. (3-3)
*Sūkṣmā*, *asūkṣmā*, *amṛtā*, *jñānā*, *amṛtā*, *cāpyāyinī*, as well as *vyāpinī* and *vyomarūpā*— these are the infinite *kalās* born from the vowels. (3-4)
Creation, prosperity, memory, intelligence, beauty, fortune, radiance, stability,
persistence, and accomplishment— these are said to arise respectively from the letters of the *ka*-group.
And from that [source] also came Jarā (Old Age), Pālinī, Śānti (Peace),
Aiśvaryā, Rati, Kāmikā, and likewise Varadā.
Hlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā arise respectively from the consonant groups beginning with ṭa, ta, and ta;
[the remaining powers] are Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrī, Kṣut, Krodhinī, and Kriyā. (3.7)
Utkārī and Mṛtyu are these [deities] born from the *pa*-group in sequence;
the digits (*kalā*) arising from the *ṣa*-group are said to be yellow, white, reddish, and black.
And thus, the fifty [energies] arising from the letters are said to be infinite:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti. || 3-9 ||
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Jyotsnā, Kānti, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā—these are the digits born of the vowels that bestow all desires. (3.10)
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Śuci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 3-11 ||
The twelve [calamities] beginning with *kabhā* and ending with *saurāṣṭhaḍa* are proclaimed;
[the six flames are] Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī. || 3-12 ||
Suśrī, Surūpā, and Kapilā, who carry the oblations to the gods and ancestors—
these are the ten forms of the Yādīs, each a digit (kalā) that bestows dharma.
They take the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, bestowing fruits upon practitioners. Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara—|| 3.14 ||
Arghīśa, Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, Hara, Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara. || 3-15 ||
Akrūra, Mahāsena, and the sixteen forms of the [sixteen] vowels;
followed by Krodhīśa, Caṇḍīśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama.
Then there were Ekavīra, Rudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Caru, Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, Īśa, Sarpa, Someśa, Lāṅgalin, and Dāruka. (3.17)
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍha, Daṇḍin, Adri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohitāśva, and likewise Śikhin. (3-18)
Chagalāṇḍa and Dviraṇḍa, Mahākāla and Kapālī, Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākī, the one named Khaḍgīśa, and likewise Baka. (3.19)
Śveta, Bhṛgu, Nakulī, Śiva, and Samvartaka are recorded;
then there is Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and immediately after that, Śālmalī.
Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and thereafter Dīrghaghoṇā;
then Sudīrghamukhī and Gomukhī, and after that Dīrghajihvā. (3.21)
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and likewise Vikṛtamukhī;
then Jvālāmukhī, Ulkāmukhī, and Śrīmukhī as well.
And Vidyāmukhī is said to be the power of sound (svaraśakti) of the Rudras;
then follow Mahākālī, Sarasvatī, and Sarvasiddhi.
Gaurī shall be the lore of the three worlds; beyond that is Mantraśakti;
then Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Lambodarī.
Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, and furthermore Khecarī and Mañjarī; then Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, as well as Kākodaryā and Pūtanā.
There may be the yoginīs Bhadrakālī and Śaṅkhinī, as well as Garjinī, Kālarātri, Kurdinī, Kapardinī, and Vajrikā. (3.26)
Jayā, Sumukhī, Revatī, and likewise Mādhavī;
Vāruṇī, Vāyavī, and likewise Rakṣovidāriṇī.
Then Sahajā-lakṣmī, and after that the all-pervasive [Vyāpinī],
and Mahāmāyā— these are declared to be the Rudra-śaktis in their respective order.
Herein, the Rudras are remembered as being red in color, bearing tridents and skull-cups;
the Śaktis, stationed upon the seat of Rudra, possess bodies as crimson as vermilion.
Their lotus-like hands are adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups;
[these are] Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu.
Another is named Madhusūdana; then there are Trivikrama and Vāmana;
and after that, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Padmanābha. (3.31)
Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are said to be the forms [of the self] corresponding to the vowels in their respective order. (3.32)
Afterwards, he holds the discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, sword, conch, and plow; then again, the club, the trident, the noose, and the goad.
Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandin, Nara, the conqueror of Naraka,
Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Satya, he who is called Sāttvata, Śauri, Śūra, and Janārdana.
Bhūdharo, Viśvamūrti, Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama, Balī, Bālānuja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and likewise Vṛṣabha.
Haṃsa, Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha are the forms of Halā;
then follow Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Dhṛti. (3.36)
Peace, Action, Compassion, Intelligence, Joy, Faith, and beyond that, Modesty, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Affection, and Delight—these follow in sequence. (3.37)
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī,
Vilāsinī, Vijayā, Virajā, Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunadā, and Smṛti.

She is supernatural power (ṛddhi), prosperity (samṛddhi), and purity (śuddhi); she is enjoyment (bhukti), awakening (buddhi), and intellect (mati); she is forbearance (kṣamā), delight (ramā), Umā, the moistening one (kledinī), the drenched one (klinnā), the giver of wealth (vasudā), the earth (vasudhā), and the supreme (parā).
Pārāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Niśā, Amoghā, and Vidyutā— these are the forms of Hari corresponding to the letters beginning with *ka*. (3.40)
These [deities] beginning with Keśava are dark-complexioned, their hands resplendent with conchs and discs;
their Śaktis, however, rest upon their beloveds' laps, their faces graced with smiles. (3–41)
Their limbs are like streaks of lightning, and their arms hold lotuses and the gesture of fearlessness;
[the names of the sun are] Ravi, Prabhākara, Bhāsvat, Dyumaṇi, Pūṣan, and Bhaga.
Āditya, Arka, Vedamūrti, Karmasākṣin, Divākara, Mitra, Aryaman, Uṣṇaraśmi, Dvādaśātmā, and Vibhākara—[these are the twelve names]. (3-43)
These are the personifications of the vowels: Sūra, Sūrya, Vibhāvasu, Ahaskara, Aruṇa, Vradhna, Bhāsvat, and Saptaturaṅgama. (3.44)
The one with bay horses, the lord of the planets, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhānu, the imperishable Avyaya;
Vikartana, the thousand-rayed one, Mihira, Mitra, and Āṭhara. (3-45)
The witness of karma, the eye of the world, the sun, the lover of the lotus, the fierce-rayed one, the tawny one, the staff-bearer, the rayed one, the glowing one, and the possessor of rays.
The Illuminator, the Eye of the World, the Heater, the Kinsman of the World, the Swan, the Destroyer of Darkness, and the Embodiment of the Three Vedas— these are his forms.
Vidyā, Aho, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū; then Rudravīryā, Prabhā, Ānandā, Poṣaṇī, Ṛddhidā, and Śubhā. (3-48)
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Sendukhaṇḍā, and Śikhaṇḍinī. || 3-49 ||
She is the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
Indrāṇī herself, and she whose body is half that of Śaṅkara.
Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Triśūlinī, Pālinī, Ambikā, Hāriṇī, Samṛddhi, and Vṛddhi. || 3.51 ||
Piṅgalākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Māyā, Saṃjñā, Vasundharā, Śraddhā, Svāhā, Sudhā, Bhikṣā, Devakī, and Kamalāsanā.
Trilokadhātrī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Tridaśeśvarī, Surūpā, and Bahurūpā— these are the fifty powers (śaktis) of the Sun.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the Kāmamātṛkā: Kāmeśa, Kāmada, Kānta, Kāntimān, and likewise Kāmagama; Kāmācāra, Kāmī, Kāmuka, and Kāmavardhana. (3–54)
Vāmorāma, Ramaṇa, Ratinātha, Ratipriya, Rātrinātha, Ramākānta, Ramamāṇa, and Niśācara. (3-55)
Nandaka, Nandana, Nandi, and then Nandayitṛ; Pañcabāṇa, Ratisakha, Puṣpadhanvan, and Mahādhanus. || 3.56 ||
Bhrāmaṇa, Bhramaṇa, Bhramamāṇa, and likewise Bhrama; Bhrānta, Bhrāmaka, Bhṛṅga, Bhrāntacāra, and Bhramāvaha. || 3-57 ||
Mohana, Mohaka, Moha, and Mohavardhana; Madana, Manmatha, Mātaṅga, and Bhṛṅganāyaka. || 3-58 ||
The singer and the songstress, the dancer and the jester, the madman and the intoxicated one, the dandy and the one who increases greed. (3.59)
The forms of Kāma are said to reside within the collection of letters beginning with 'a':
Rati, Prīti, then Kāminī, and thereafter Mohinī. (3.60)
Then there were Kamalā and Suvilāsinī, as well as Kalpalatā, Śyāmā, Śucismitā, and after her, Vismitā.
Viśālākṣī, Lelihānā, and likewise Digambarā; Vāmā, Kubjikā, Kāntā, Nityā, Kulyā, and Bhoginī. (3.62)
Then after that, Kāmadā is mentioned, and Sulocanā;
then Sulāpinī, Mardinī, and thereafter Kalahapriyā.
Varākṣī, Sumukhī, Nalinī, and likewise Jaṭinī;
Pālinī, Śivā, Mugdhā, and then Ramā and Bhramā. (3.64)
Lolā, Cañcalā, Dīrghajihvā, Ratipriyā, Lolākṣī, Bhaṅginī, Pāṭalā, and likewise Madanā. || 3-65 ||
Then there shall be Mālā, Haṃsinī, Viśvatomukhī, Jagadānandinī, Ramaṇī, and Kānti. (3.66)
From that [source] there arose Kalaṅkadhnī, and likewise Vṛkodaryā; also Meghaśyāmā, Lobhavarddhanī, and other such Śaktis.
Then the mortal should meditate upon the objects of desire, resembling pomegranate flowers,
accompanied by the Śakti on his left lap, and bearing flower-arrows and sugarcane bows.
The Śaktis, resembling saffron in hue and adorned with all ornaments, should be meditated upon with blue lotuses in their hands, capable of attracting the three worlds. (3.69)
Thus it is said. Now, the Tripurāmātṛkā:
Kāminī, Modinī, and then Madanonmādinī;
Drāviṇī, Khecarī, Ghaṇṭikā, and Kalāvatī. (3-1)
Kledinī, Śivadūtī, and then Subhagā, Bhagā, Vidyeśī, Mahālakṣmī, Kaulinī, and Sureśvarī. (3.2)
The powers of the vowels have been declared; thereafter [come] Kulamālinī, Vyāpinī, Bhagā, and immediately after that, Vāgīśī.
Then follow Vaṣaṭkārī and Piṅgalā, who moves toward the vulva (bhaga);
after that, Sundarī, then Nīlapatākā, and then Tripurā. (3–4)
Siddheśvarī, Hyamoghā, and Ratnamālinī; after that, Maṅgalā, Bhagamālā, Nityā, and then Raudrī. (3–5)
Vyomeśvarī, Ambikā, and then Aṭṭahāsā; furthermore, Āpyāyinī, Vajreśī, Kṣobhiṇī, and likewise Śāmbhavī. (3–6)
Stambhinī, Anāmā, Raktā, Śuklā, Aparājitā, Saṃvartikā, Vimalā, Aghorā, and she who is joined with Ghorā. || 3-7 ||
Bimbādibhairavī and likewise Sarvākarṣiṇikā—
these fifty have been declared, having the fifty phonemes as their bodies.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the *Gaṇeśamātṛkā*:
Vighneśvara, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama, Vighnakṛt, Vighnahartṛ, Vighnarāj, and Gaṇanāyaka. (3-1)
Ekadanta, Dvidanta, Gajavaktra, Nirañjana, Kapardin, Dīrghavaktra, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Vṛṣadhvaja. (3.2)
Gaṇanātha, Gajendra, Śūrpakarṇa, Trilocana,
Lambodara, Mahānāda— these are the four forms of Sadāśiva.
Āmoda, Durmukha, Sumukha, and Pramodaka;
Ekapāda, Dvijihva, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha. || 3-4 ||
The Bestower of Boons, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍaka, Senānī, Grāmaṇī, Matta, Vimatta, and Mattavāhana. || 3-5 ||
He who has matted hair, he who is shaven-headed, he who bears a sword, the most excellent one, whose banner is the bull,
who is fond of food, the roarer like a cloud, the leader of the hosts, and the lord of the hosts.
These fifty forms of Gaṇapa have been described;
they are Śrī, Hrī, Tuṣṭi, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Sarasvatī.
Rati, Medhā, Kānti, Kāminī, Mohinī, Jaṭā, Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Surasā, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
Ugrā, Jayinī, Satyā, Vighneśī, Svarūpiṇī, Kāmadā, and likewise Madvihvalā are proclaimed [as the goddesses] thereafter. (3.9)
Then Vikaṭā, Dhūmrā, Bhūti, Bhūmi, Satī, Ramā, then Mānuṣī, and then Makaradhvajā.
Vikarṇā, Bhrukuṭī, Lajjā, Ghoṇā, and Dhanurdharā; and then Yāminī, Rātri, Candrikā, and Śaśiprabhā. (3.11)
Lolā, Cañcalākṣī, Ṛddhi, Durbhagā, Subhagā, Śivā, Durgā, Kālikā, and Alakajihvikā. (3.12)
And Vighnahāriṇikā—these are the Śaktis of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Now, for the Yoginīmātṛkās:
Amṛtākarṣiṇī, Indrāṇī, Īśānī, Umā, and Ūrdhvakeśinī.
And likewise Ṛddhidā, as well as Ṛṣā, Ḷkārā, and likewise ḹṣikā. || 3-1 ||
Ekapādā, likewise Aiśvaryā, Okārā who is of the nature of medicinal herbs, Ambikā, and Akṣarātmā— these are the powers (śaktis) of the gods in sequence.
Then Kālarātri, Khātītā, and Gāyatrī immediately after her; then likewise Ghaṇṭādhāriṇikā and the one whose nature consists of the syllable Ṅa.
Cāmuṇḍā, Chāyā, Jayā, and likewise Jhaṅkāriṇī;
Ñārṇātmikā with a chisel in hand, and then Ṭhaṅkāriṇī. (3–4)
Then there are Ḍāmarī, Ḍhaṅkārī, Ṇaṅkārī, and Tāmasī;
followed by Sthānadevī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Dhātrī, and Nandikā.
Pārvatī, Phaṭkārī, Bandhinī, Bhadrakālikā, Mahāmāyā, Yaśasvinī, Ramā, and then Lamboṣṭhikā. (3–6)
Varadā, Śaśinī, Ṣaṇḍā, and likewise Sarasvatī;
then Haṃsavatī, and thereafter Kṣamāvatī is proclaimed. (3.7)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the *pīṭhamātṛkā*:
Kāmarūpa, Kāśīka, Nepāla, Pauṇḍravardhana, Purasthira, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇagiri, and Arbuda. (3.1)
Āmrātakeśvara, and immediately after that Ekāmra;
Trisrotas, Kāmakoṭa, Kailāsa, and Bhṛgupattana. (3.2)
Then Kedāra, Candranagara, Śrīpura, Oṃkāra, Jālandhara, Mālava, Kulānta, and Devikoṭaka. (3-3)
Gokarṇa and Māruteśa, and after that Aṭṭahāsa;
Viraja and Rājageha, and beyond that Mahāpatha.
Kolhamelāpura, and after that Kauleśvara; Jayantikā, Uñjayinī, Caritra, and then Kṣīraka.
Hastināpura, Uḍḍīśa, and thereafter Prayāga; Paṣṭhīśa in Māyāpura, and after that Jaleśvara.
Malaya and the surface of the earth, Śrīśaila and Merupīṭhaka;
then Girivara and Mahendra, and after that Vāmana.
Hiraṇyaka, Mahālakṣmīpura, and Uḍyāna, as well as Chāyācchatra and Mahāpīṭha—these are the fifty syllables. (3-8)
...so it is said.
Now, regarding the Mātṛkās beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī:
"Kāmākarṣiṇī indeed, and likewise Buddhyākarṣiṇī."
And Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī, as well as Śabdākarṣiṇikā. || 3-1 ||
And likewise Sparśākarṣiṇikā, as well as Rūpākarṣiṇikā;
then Rasākarṣiṇikā and Gandhākarṣiṇikā. || 3-2 ||
The attractor of mental stability, likewise the attractor of mindfulness, the attractor of names, and then the attractor of seed-syllables. (3-3)
The Atmākarṣiṇī, the Amṛtākarṣiṇī, and the Śarīrākarṣiṇī likewise; these correspond respectively to the sixteen vowels.
The power that agitates all, then the one that subdues all;
likewise the one that attracts all, and then the one that gladdens all.
She who deludes all, she who paralyzes all, she who causes all to yawn;
then she who brings all under control, and likewise she who delights all.
She who causes universal intoxication, then she who accomplishes all aims,
she who fulfills all prosperity, and likewise she who consists of all mantras.
Then [she is] the destroyer of all dualities, the bestower of all accomplishments;
then indeed the bestower of all prosperity and the maker of all things dear. || 3-8 ||
Then she is proclaimed as the performer of all auspiciousness and the bestower of all desires;
immediately after that, she is declared to be the liberator from all suffering.
She is the pacifier of all death, the warder-off of all obstacles,
beautiful in every limb, and likewise the bestower of all prosperity.
She is omniscient, omnipotent, and the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty;
she consists of all knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases.
She is the essential nature of all supports, likewise the remover of all sins;
she consists entirely of bliss and has the nature of universal protection.
Then it is proclaimed: "She indeed bestows all desired fruits.
Now, regarding the *triśakti-prapañca-mātṛkā*, there are two names for each syllable:
she who is Śrī in the form of the *prapañca*, she who is Māyā in the form of the island, and she who is the ocean.
Kamalā is of the form of the mountain, and she is indeed the beloved of Viṣṇu.

Then she is the form of the city (Pattana), and then indeed she is Padmadhāriṇī; she is the form of the sacred seat (Pīṭha), the daughter of the Ocean and others, and the form of the field (Kṣetra). || 3.2 ||
Then she is the Mother of the World in the form of the forest, then the dweller in the lotus; thereafter she is in the form of the hermitage, and after that, Indrīrā.
Then Māyā has the form of a cave, and thereafter Ramā has the form of a river;
likewise, she has the form of the four [elements] and the nature of that which is born from a lotus.
Then she appeared in the form of one born from sweat, beloved by Nārāyaṇa;
she was likewise called Siddhalakṣmī, and thereafter she appeared in the form of one born from an egg.
Beyond that is Mahālakṣmī, whose nature is the cleansing of old age;
then there is Āryā in the form of *lava*, and likewise Umā in the form of *truṭi*.
Caṇḍikā is the form of the *kalā* (unit of time), Durgikā is the form of the *kāṣṭhā*;
Śivā is the form of the *nimeṣa*, and thereafter she is the form of the *śvāsa* (breath). (3.7)
Aparṇā is indeed in the form of a ghaṭikā, and Ambikā follows after that;
Satī is in the form of a muhūrta, and thereafter she takes the form of a prahara.
Īśvarī is the form of day, and Śāmbhavī follows after that;
likewise, Īśānī is the form of twilight, and Pārvatī is the form of night.
Maṅgalā is the form of the lunar day (tithi), and after that, she is the form of the day of the week (vāra);
Dākṣāyaṇī is the form of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and after that, Haimavatī.
Mahāmāyā is of the nature of yoga; thereafter she is of the nature of the instrument (karaṇa).
Māheśvarī is of the nature of the fortnight (pakṣa), and Mṛḍānī is of the nature of the month (māsa).
Rudrāṇī is the form of the moon, Śarvāṇī is the form of the seasons;
Parameśvarī is the form of the year, and Kālī is the form of the year.
Kātyāyanī, Yugādi, Rūpā, Gaurī, and likewise Pralayarūpā, followed by Bhavānī thereafter. (3.13)
And immediately after that is Brāhmī, whose nature consists of the five elements;
likewise, thereafter is Vāgīśvarī, whose form consists of the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
And thereafter, Vāṇī is the very nature of the organs of action;
and Sāvitrī, whose form is the vital breath, is the very nature of the organs of knowledge.
And after her is Sarasvatī, who embodies the three qualities (guṇas);
she is Gāyatrī in the form of the internal organ (antahkarana), and thereafter she is the bestower of speech.
And thereafter Śāradā, who consists of the three states;
and immediately after that, Bhāratī, whose nature is the seven constituent elements (dhātus).
Furthermore, she is the very nature of the three defects, and likewise consists of knowledge (vidyā);
she is known as the Mother of the Universe (prapañcamātṛkā) and is remembered as the bestower of all accomplishments.
Thus ends the *Prapañcamātṛkā*. Now follows the *Kālīmātṛkā*:
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, as well as Ugrograprabhā, and likewise Dīptā. (3.1)
Nīlā, Ghanā, Balākā, Mātrā, Mudrā, and likewise Mitā;
Brāhmī is proclaimed in the same way—these are the sixteen powers of the vowels. (3.2)
Nārāyaṇī, Māheśī, and Cāmuṇḍā after that;
likewise Kaumārī is mentioned, and Aparājitā as the fifth.
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and Bhairavī immediately after that;
she who is the Bhairavī of Mahat and the rest is declared to be Siṃhabhairavī. (3–4)
Likewise, Dhūmrabhairavī is proclaimed, as well as Bhīmabhairavī, Unmattabhairavī, and Vaśīkaraṇabhairavī. (3–5)
Mohanā and the others, Bhairavī, then Aindrī and Āgneyī, followed by Yāmyā, Rākṣasī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vāyavī. || 3-6 ||
Likewise Kauverī and Īśānī, as well as Brahmāṇī and Vaiṣṇavī;
Vajriṇī, Śaktinī, Daṇḍinī, and Khaḍginī.
Pāśinī, Aṅkuśinī, Gadinī, Śūlinī,
as well as Mālinī and Cakriṇī— these are declared to be the Vyañjana-śaktis.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the sixty-three syllables of the *Tārāmātṛkā*:
Kuleśī, Kulanandā, Vāgīśī, and likewise Bhairavī;
Umā, Śrī, Śāntikā, Caṇḍā, Dhūmrā, Kālī, and Kapālinī. (3.1)
Vāgvādinī, Nakulī, Bhadrakālī, and Śaśiprabhā. || 3-2 ||
Pratyaṅgirā, Siddhalakṣmī, Amṛteśī, Caṇḍikā, Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Siddhā, Kāmākṣī, Hiṅgulā, and Vasā. (3-3)
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Nityāparājitā,
Vilāsinī, Ghorā, Citrā, Mugdhā, and Dhaneśvarī.
Someśvarī, Mahācaṇḍā, Vidyā, Haṃsī, Vināyikā, Vedagarbhā, as well as Bhīmā, Ugrā, Vaidyā, and Sadgati.
Ugrefvarī, Candragarbhā, Jyotsnā, Satyā, Yaśovatī, Kulikā, Kāminī, Kāmyā, Jñānavatī, and then Ḍākinī. (3–6)
Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī,
and Hākinī— these sixty-four Śaktis are the bestowers of supernatural powers (siddhi).
Thus ends the Tārāmātṛkā. Now follows the Ṣoḍaśīmātṛkā:
Kāmeśī, Bhagamālā, and after that Nityaklinnā;
then Bheruṇḍā and Vahnivāsinī, and immediately thereafter Vajreśī. (3.1)
Śivādūtī, Tvaritā, and then Kulasundarī;
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā. (3-2)
Jvālāmālinī is in the painting, and Mahātripurasundarī is [the deity] of the sixteen Mātṛkās; these are declared to be the powers of the vowels.
Grasini, Priyavadini, Karali, Kapalini,
Shiva, Ghosha, Damshtra, Viroma, and likewise Vakprada.
Nārāyaṇī, Mohinī, Prajñā, Śikhivāhinī, Bhīṣaṇā, Vāyuvegā, Bhīmā, and Vināyikā. || 3-5 ||
Pūrṇā, Śakti, Kaṅkālī, Kurdinī, and likewise Kālikā; Dīpanī, Jayantī, Pāvinī, and Lambinī. (3–6)
Saṃhāriṇī, Chāgalī, Pūtanā, and likewise Modikā;
then Paraśakti, Ambā, and thereafter Icchāśakti.
And Mahākālī is proclaimed as the powers (*śakti*) of the consonants;
thus ends the sixteen *mātṛkās*. Now, for the *bhuvaneśī-mātṛkā*:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and likewise Maṅgalā. || 3-1 ||
Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, and likewise Kākinī;
Śākinī, Hākinī, and Yākinī are the powers of the vowels. (3.2)
Maṅgalā, Mahākālī, Kuṇḍalī, Kulasundarī, Kapālī, Kamalāvatī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Meruvāsinī. (3-3)
Bhuvaneśī, Sarasvatī, Kapilā, Kulamālinī, Vināyikā, Jayā, Nandā, Mahālakṣmī, and Bhairavī. (3–4)
Brahmāṇī, as well as Jvālāvalī, Liṅgaprabhā, Muṇḍinī, Mahāvegā, Udbhavā, Vaiṣṇavī, and Śivā. (3–5)
Mahāmāyā, Cakrāṅgī, Ekapadā, Sureśvarī, Kauverī, Maṇḍalī, Vārāhī, and Jalandharī. (3–6)
Kāmākhyā, situated in the midst of desire, is the power (*śakti*) of the consonants;
thus is the *Mātṛkā* of Bhuvaneśī. Now, the *Mātṛkā* of Bhairavī:
Tripurā, Tripureśī, and likewise Tripurasundarī.
Tripurādyā, Vāsinī, and Tripurāśrī after that. || 3-1 ||
Tripurāmālinī, and then Tripurasiddhā;
after that, Tripurāmbā, and then Mahātripurabhairavī.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the powers of the vowels. (3-3)
Viśālā, Viśālākṣī, Nirmalā, Malavarjitā, Kālī, Kālakalpā, Kālarātri, and Niśācarī. || 3-4 ||
Ūrdhvakeśī, Muktakeśī, Vīrā, Mahābhayā, Jayadā, Māninī, Māyā, Pracaṇḍā, and Bindumālinī. (3–5)
Virūpā, Virūpākṣī, Khaṭvāṅgī, Viśvarūpiṇī, Raudrī, Māyā, Pretākṣī, Phetkārī, and Bhayanādinī. (3–6)
Dhūmrākṣī, Yoginī, Ghorā, Viśvarūpā, Bhayaṅkarī, Bhairavī, Bhīṣaṇīyā, Lamboṣṭhī, and Mahābalā. (3-7)
The powers (śaktis) of the consonants have been specifically proclaimed in their sequence.
Thus ends the Bhairavī-mātṛkā. Now, the Chinnamastā-mātṛkā:
Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Śivā, Māyā, Vāṇī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Raudrīśvarī, Jayā, Padmā, Varṇinī, and likewise Ḍākinī. || 3-1 ||
Karālī, Vikarālī, and Ghorā are the powers of sound (svaraśakti);
likewise Kālī, Khaḍginī, Caṇḍā, Bhairavī, and Piṅgalā.
Indrāṇī, Phaṭkārī, Hāriṇī, and likewise Yoginī;
Prakāśinī, Vajriṇī, Sitā, Pītā, and Ramā as well. || 3-3 ||
Naked, most terrible, with disheveled hair, she has consciousness as her refuge;
she is Cāmuṇḍā, Chinnamastā, Bhīmā, Hūṃkāriṇī, and Sitā.
Padmānanā, Padmagarbhā, Puṣpaṇī, Cāruhāsinī, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Kānti, Mālinī, and likewise Tāriṇī. || 3-5 ||
Mahodarī, Asthimālā, and Nāgayajñopavītinī are declared to be the Śaktis of the condiments, granting all desires. (3-6)
Thus ends the *Mātṛkā* of Chinnamastā. Now follows the *Mātṛkā* of Dhūmāvatī:
Dhūmāvatī, Dhūmanetrā, Dharmaṭī, Markaṭī, as well as Ghorarūpā, Lamboṣṭhī, Śyāmā, Śyāmamukhī, and Śivā. (3-1)
Kākadhvajā, Koṭarākṣī, Dhūmā, Dhūmāndhakāriṇī, Muktakeśī, Mahāghorā, and likewise Lambapayodharā. (3.2)
The powers of the vowels are proclaimed as bestowers of all accomplishments:
Koṭarā, Koṭarākṣī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and Digambarī.
She was dark as the night, fierce, discolored, and clad in soiled garments;
she had pendulous breasts, sparse teeth, a long body, and a thin waist.
A widow, with a winnowing basket in her hand, coarse, with a coarse neck, with trembling hands and restless eyes, matted-haired, and with crooked vision. (3-5)
Afflicted by hunger, pained by thirst, sharp, fierce, and terrifying;
belching, wrathful, death itself, the performer of rites, and the crusher of enemies. (3-6)
Satvarā, Kākajaṅghā, Śmaśānālayavāsinī, and Mahākālī are declared to be the accomplished ones (siddhās), the powers of the consonants. || 3-7 ||
Thus end the *Mātṛkās* of Dhūmāvatī. Now, the *Mātṛkās* of Bagalā:
Bagalā, Stambhinī, Jambhinī, Mohinī, Vaśyā, Calācalā, Durdharā, and likewise Kalmagā. (3-1)
The wise one, the one who draws out time, the deluder, and likewise the slow-moving, the enjoyer, and the yoginī. (3-2)
These sixteen forms of the vowels are indeed bestowers of perfection:
Bhagāmbā, Bhagamālā, Bhagavāhā, and Bhagodarī. (3.3)
Bhaginī, Bhagajihvā, Bhagasthā, Bhagasarpiṇī, Bhagalolā, Bhagākṣī, Śivā, and Bhaganipātinī. || 3-4 ||
Jayā, Vijayā, Dhātrī, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Jambhinī, Stambhinī, Mohinī, Ākarṣiṇī, and Umā.
Rambhiṇī, Jṛmbhaṇī, Kīlinī, and likewise Vaśinī;
Rambhā, Māheśvarī, Maṅgalā, and likewise Rūpiṇī. || 3-6 ||
Yellow, clad in yellow garments, auspicious, beautiful, and eloquent—these are declared to be the Śaktis who bestow success upon consonants. (3.7)
Thus ends the Bagalāmātṛkā. Now, the Mātaṅgīmātṛkā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, and likewise Śraddhā;
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, and Mohinī. (3.1)
The first is Bhāvinī, who is indeed the lightning-creeper and the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
then there are Sundarānandā and likewise Nāgabuddhi. (3.2)
These sixteen vowel-energies (svara-śaktis) bestow complete perfection:
Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, and likewise Kānti; || 3-3 ||
Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Ramā, Manmathā, Makaradhvajā, Madanā, Puṣpacāpā, Drāviṇī, and likewise Śoṣiṇī. || 3-4 ||
Bandhinī, Mohinī, Vaśyā, and then Ākarṣiṇī; likewise Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, Mahocchuṣmā, and Karālikā. (3–5)
Then follow Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā,
Anaṅgamadanā, and Anaṅgamadanāturā.
Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgavegā, and Anaṅgādisaṃbhavā; Anaṅgabhuvanapālā and Anaṅgaśaśirekhikā. (3-7)
Manobhavā, Mātaṅgī, and Kāmā are the powers of the manifesting syllables (*vyañjana-śakti*).
Thus ends the *Mātaṅgīmātṛkā*. Now, the *Lakṣmīmātṛkā*:
Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Vidyā, and the contemplation on all beings and so forth.
She is faith, sovereign power, the fragrant one, the bestower of speech, and whose essence is the lotus. || 3-1 ||
Padmālayā, Śacī, Padmā, Śuddhi, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Dhanyā—these are declared to be the sixteen powers of the vowels. || 3.2 ||
And likewise Hiraṇyā, Lakṣmī, Nityapuṣṭā, Vibhāvarī, Aditi, Diti, Dīptā, and Vasudhā. (3-3)
Karuṇā, Dharmanilayā, Padmākṣī, Bhūtadhāriṇī, Padmaprabhā, Vedamātā, and thereafter Padmahastā. (3-4)
Padmodbhavā, Padmamukhī, Padmasundarikā,
as well as Padmanābhapriyā, Padmagandhinī, Padminī, and Ramā.
