Padmamālādharā, Padmā, Suprasannā, and likewise Priyā; Kānti, Priyā, Kamalā, Anaghā, and Harivallabhā. || 3-6 ||
Amoghā, Amṛtā, Divyā, Aśokā, and Vyañjanaśakti—these are the Lakṣmīmātṛkā. Now, the Kāmeśvarīmātṛkā:
Kāmeśvarī, Mahāmāyā, Vāgīśī, and she who is designated as Brahman.
She consists of the syllable, has three measures, three feet, and is composed of the three qualities. || 3-1 ||
She is the presiding leader of the hosts of gods and Siddhas, the Mother of the Gaṇas, and the Sovereign of the Gaṇas;
she is Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍamuṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍī, and the fang-bearing bestower of desired boons.
The powers of the vowels have been declared to bestow all accomplishments:
Viśvambharā, Viśvayoni, Viśvamātā, and Vasupradā. (3-3)
Svāhā, Svadhā, Tuṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Gāyatrī, Gogaṇā, Khagā, Vedamātā, Variṣṭhā, Suprabhā, and Siddhavāhinī. || 3-4 ||
She is the heart of the sun, she is the moon, she is the lunar orb;
she is the golden moonlight, auspicious, and the remover of the fear of the suffering of existence. (3.5)
She is the essence of Śiva, auspicious, peaceful, the giver of peace, and whose form is peace;
she is the bestower of good fortune, the auspicious Gaurī, Umā, Haimavatī, and the beloved.
"The powers of the consonants have been declared in their proper order as Dakṣā.
Thus ends the Kāmeśvarīmātṛkā. Now, the Bhagamālinīmātṛkā:
Bhagamālī, Bhagā, Bhāgyā, Bhaginī, and Bhagodarī.
The secret maiden Dākṣāyaṇī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Sudīptā, Lelihānā, and Karālā are the powers of sound (svaraśaktayaḥ). || 3.2 ||
Dwelling in space, she is Brāhmī, the youthful, and the observer of celibacy;
she delights in the mouth of Brahmā, she is humble, Sāvitrī, and honored by Brahmā.
She is Wisdom, the Supreme Intellect, the Mother of the Universe, and the Eternal;
she is Maitrī, Kātyāyanī, Durgā, and the supreme savior from all difficulties.
She is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the sovereign, the mistress of the Puruṣa, the Pradhāna, and the lords;
she is the nourisher, the purifier, the pure, the auspicious, and the restrainer.
Jyotiṣmatī, Saṃharinī, Sṛṣṭisthityantakarī, Aghorā, and Ghorarūpā are the powers (śaktis) of the consonants. (3.6)
Thus ends the Bhagamālāmātṛkā. Now follows the Nityaklinnāmātṛkā:
Nityaklinnā, Nityamadadravomā, Viśvarūpiṇī, Yogeśvarī, Yogagamyā, Yogamātā, and Vasundharā. (3-1)
Dhanyā, Dhaneśvarī, Dhānyā, Ratnadā, Paśuvardhinī, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Dāruṇī, and Caṇḍī are, in order, the Śaktis of the vowels. (3.2)
Ghora, Ghorasvarūpā, Mātṛkā, Mādhavī, Daśā, Ekākṣarā, Viśvamūrti, Viśvā, Viśveśvarī, and Dhruvā. (3-3)
Śarvā, Kṣamā, Ādi, Bhūtātmā, Bhūtidā, Bhūtivardhinī, Bhūteśvarapriyā, Bhūti, Bhūtamālā, and Yauvanī. || 3-4 ||

Vaidehī, Sītā, the honored one, the illusory power, the bearer of worldly existence; she who abides in goodness, the abode of goodness, and the one who effects both the existence and non-existence of beings.
She who dwells in the universe, whose abode is the night, who possesses the bilva fruit, whose home is Śrī;
she is Śrī, the bearer of the moon, Nandā, and the powers (śaktis) of the consonants. || 3-6 ||
Thus ends the Nityaklinnā-mātṛkā. Now, the Bheruṇḍā-mātṛkā:
Bheruṇḍā, Bhairavī, Sādhvī, Natā, Anantasaṃbhavā, Triguṇī, Ghoṣiṇī, Ghoṣā, Lakṣmī, Puṣṭā, and Śubhālayā. (3-1)
She is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), the intellect of phenomena (dharmabuddhi), and the pair of the sheaths of dharma and adharma;
she is Jyeṣṭhā, the sister of Yama, Cailā, and she who dwells in silk (kauśeya). (3-2)
Bhramaṇā, Bhrāmiṇī, Bhrāmyā, Bhramā, Jñānāpahāriṇī, Māhendrī, Vāruṇī, Saumyā, Kauverī, and Havyavāhinī. (3-3)
She is of the nature of Vāyu, Nairṛti, and Īśāna, possessing the singular form of the world-protectors;
she is the deluder, the generator of delusion, and the subverter of the course of memory. (3-4)
The Yakṣiṇī Siddhi is the mother of the Yakṣas and dwells in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa;
she is Wisdom, Faith, Fortitude, and Insight, saluted by all the gods. (3.5)
Āśā, vāñchā, nirīhecchā, and likewise bhūtānuvartinī—
these are declared to be the fifty-one powers (śaktis) corresponding to the letters in their respective order.
Thus ends the *Bheruṇḍāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Vahnivāsinīmātṛkā*:
Vahnivāsinī, whose abode is fire, whose form is fire;
she is the knowledge of sacrifice, the great knowledge, the knowledge of Brahman, and she whose dwelling is the cave. (3.1)
Bhūteśvarī, Brahmadhātrī, Vimalā, Kanakaprabhā, Virūpākṣā, Viśālākṣī, Hiraṇyākṣī, and Śatānanā. (3.2)
Tryakṣā, Kāmalā, Vidyā, Siddhavidyā, Dharādhipā, the meritorious Devamātā Diti, Danu, Kadrū, and Suparṇikā. || 3-3 ||
The ocean, the repository of waters, possessing great velocity and mighty waves, the abode of Varuṇa;
it is beloved, providing satisfaction, a beautiful shade, and the supreme refuge for those who chant the Sāman hymns.

She is the source of the Vedas, wherein the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman dissolve; she is fond of praise, the chaste beloved of Pradyumna, and the bestower of happiness, good fortune, and spiritual accomplishment.
She is the bestower of all desires, the auspicious one, the most auspicious, and the source of all blessings;
she is the radiant one, the channel of life, the sweet honey-like goddess, and the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The arrows are said to be the striking shafts, which are the expressive powers (*vyañjana-śakti*).
Thus ends the *Vahnivāsinī-mātṛkā*. Now, the *Vajreśvarī-mātṛkā*:
Mahāvajreśvarī, Nityā, Vidhisthā, and Cāruhāsinī.
And Uṣā and Aniruddha’s two wives were Revatī and Raivatātmajā.
The beloved of Halāyudha, Māyā, Gokulā, Gokulālayā, the younger sister of Kṛṣṇa, the dust of Kṛṣṇa, the daughter and offspring of Nanda. (3-2)
She who puts Kaṃsa to flight, the enraged one served by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
whose limbs are the color of cow’s milk, the sustainer, the auspicious one, beloved by the cowherd folk.
Śākambharī, Siddhavidyā, Vṛddhā, Siddhakarī, Kriyā, Dāvāgni, Viśvarūpā, Viśveśī, and Ditisaṃbhavā.
Residing in the foundational wheel (ādhāracakra), she enters the hall of the gateway;
she is subtle, subtler, and gross, possessed of manifold expansion, yet free from all affliction.

She is free from conceptual proliferation, beyond action, yet the embodiment of action; she bestows the fruit, is known as Prāṇa, the Mother of Mantras, and the giver of the nectar of the Moon and Sun. (3-6)

The fifty powers of the wheel are traditionally taught in sequence as being known as *chanda*, having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), bestowing supreme bliss, and being devoid of [worldly] bliss (*nirānandā*).
Thus ends the *Vajreśvarīmātṛkā*. Now, the *Śivādūtīmātṛkā*:
Śivādūtī, Sunandā, Ānandinī, Viṣapadminī, Hṛllekhā—who dwells in the midst of the Pātāla section—and Vanakhecarī. (3.1)
The seventeenth digit is pure, her face resembling the full moon;
she is the light of the Self, self-luminous, the light of fire, and the unstruck sound (anāhatā).
The power of vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) is the power of action (kriyā-śakti); the power of will (icchā-śakti) brings happiness;
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is blissful joy, consciousness, majesty, and splendor. 3-3.
She is the straight path of sacrifice, the essence of the sacrificial chants, and that which delights with the tones of the Sāman;
she is the melody, the sound of the Sāman, the flowing stream, the utterance of "Hum," and the knower of the Sāmaveda.
She is the essence of the sacrifice, born of the mountain, the subtle one, whose nature consists of both restraint and grace;
she is the ancient mother of artisans and the awakener of the understanding of history.
The sacrificial altar, the mother of sacrifice, the great altar accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
and the sciences of logic, the three Vedas, commerce, and cattle-rearing are declared in their respective order.
And there are fifty-one Śaktis who bestow all desires;
thus ends the Śivādūtīmātṛkā. Now, the Tvaritāmātṛkā:
Tvaritā, Totulā, Dhātrī, Kirātī, Kṛṣi, and Vāṇijī.
She is the sovereign of all, eternal, all-pervading, and the source of all knowledge. || 3-1 ||

The three measures (trimātrī), Tripurā, and Sarvākārā are to be known as the objects of measurement; beyond that, Brahmāṇī, who brings about peace, is proclaimed as the powers of the vowels (svaraśakti). || 3-2 ||
Kaumārī, the mother of the universe, the great goddess with a trident in her hand;
Kiṅkarī, who holds a spear in her hand and is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
She who possesses excellent weapons, whose sound is like a conch, and whose form is the unmanifest Vaiṣṇavī;
she who has the form of a boar, Vārāhī; and she who is Nṛsiṃhā, possessing the prowess of a lion.
She has a thousand eyes, is rich in divine power, the auspicious remover of all sins;
she is the messenger of Śiva, possessing a terrible roar, and bears a sickle, a noose, and a sword.
Vikarālī, Mahākālī, Kāpālī, Pāpahāriṇī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahākukṣi, Yoginī, and Vṛndavandinī.
The six wheels, the controller of the wheels, that which moves within the wheels, and she whose form is the womb—these are declared to be the powers (śaktis) of the consonants. (3.7)
Thus ends the *Tvaritāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Kulasundarīmātṛkā*:
Bālomā, Bhairavī, Śāntā, Tripurā, and Tripureśvarī.
Non-violence is the destroyer of darkness, radiant, and like the orb of the sun.
She who possesses excellent weapons, who has beautiful limbs, who is most worthy of choice, and who is the beloved of Viṣṇu;
she who is the Veda, the uninterrupted, the one to be known, the perfection that accomplishes all goals. (3.2)
The secret one consists of five fives; she dwells in the cow-pen and possesses the wealth of cows.
She is the power (śakti) arising from the yoga of twilight, whose nature consists of the measures (mātrā), the moments (kāṣṭhā), and the divisions of time (kalā).
Pīyūṣā, Vājijihvā, Rasādhārā, Iraṃmadā,
Vidyucchataghnī, Siṃhākṣī, and Ekapiṅgāṅkitā are always present.
She is Kapālī, Vedyā, Vetālī, and she who is saluted by the hosts of spirits (bhūtas);
she is the one touched, the one whose feet are touched, existence, manifestation, and she who speaks the languages of all lands.
All undertakings are without undertaking; undertakings flow from existence.
Speech is indeed luminous; these are declared to be the powers of manifestation. (3-6)
Thus ends the *Kulasundarīmātṛkā*. Now, the *Nityāmātṛkā*:
Nityā, Bhairavī, Sūkṣmā, Pracaṇḍā, Sadgatipradā, Priyā, Śuddhā, Śuṣkā, Raktāṅgī, and Raktalocanā. (3–1)
Khaṭvāṅgadhāriṇī, Śaṅkhā, Kaṅkālā, Kālavarhiṇī, Himaghnayanā, and Vṛttā are declared to be the Svara-śaktis. (3.2)
She is the mistress of beings, sustained by beings of the past and future; she is the prosperity of those of wicked conduct;
she is a festival of merit, fragrant with virtue, and the discernor of merit and sin.
She is naked, clothed in linen, or clad in a single garment;
she wears matted hair, bears a garland of skulls, carries a bell, and holds a bow.
Holding a coin in her hand, she is the moving Brāhmī, Hākinī, Śākinī, and Ramā;
she has the face of the protector of the universe, is the illusory power of Viṣṇu, and possesses four arms. (3–5)
She has eighteen arms, she is formidable, variegated, and possesses diverse forms;
seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus, she is radiant with splendor and brings about auspiciousness.
She is silent, crowned with a diadem, venerable, the giver of honor, and the increaser of honor;
she is beloved by the world, containing Viṣṇu within her womb, auspicious, and fond of auspiciousness.

She is prosperity, the bringer of prosperity, the fortunate one, the consort of the lord of serpents, the measured one, the one who purifies with heat, the magical power (kṛtyā), the noble one, and the increaser of the lineage. || 3.8 ||
These powers—Aghaughaśoṣaṇī, Śrāvī, and Kṛttāntā—are the bestowers of all accomplishments for those [mantras] consisting of fifteen syllables. (3.9)
Thus ends the Nityāmātṛkā. Now, the Nīlapatākāmātṛkā:
Now, Nīlapatākā is blue, the illusion (māyā) beloved by the world;
she possesses a thousand vajras, has lotus-eyes, is the lotus-lady (padminī), and is the unsurpassed Śrī. (3.1)
Possessing divine gait, divine enjoyments, and divine garlands and ointments;
clad in white, pure garments, she is gentle and adorned with flowers appropriate for all seasons. (3-2)
These are the powers of the vowels, which grant the desires of the practitioner;
they are endowed with all sovereign qualities and arise from the very tip of the Praṇava.
The manifestor, the revealer, the manifest, following all phonemes;
she is the Mother of the World, the bestower of fearlessness, the sustainer of beings, and exceedingly difficult to attain. (3-4)
She is the passionate woman, the bearer of the staff, she who is to be disciplined; she holds a sword and a mallet in her hands;
she displays weapons and missiles; she is the seed, the seedless, and the supreme possessor of seeds.
The initiation dear to Vācaspati is the examination arising from Śiva;
it is passionate, dark, true, characterized by an abundance of goodness, and delusive. (3.6)
Knowing the past and the future, she teaches the present;
she is the authoritative teaching, consciousness, the awakening of beings, and the upholder of the earth. (3.7)
Gangā is both primordial nature and its transformation; she is Dhūrjaṭi (Śiva) with a distorted face;
she is beloved by yogis, accessible to yogis, the object of meditation for yogis, and both supreme and non-supreme.
Vaiṣṇavī, Tripadī, Dṛṣṭarakṣā, and the Kādi-śaktis—thus ends the Nīlapatākā-mātṛkā. Now, the Vijayā-mātṛkā:
Vijayā, Jayadā, Jaitrī, Ajitā, and Vāmalocanā.
The Mother, born of the family of Māyā, is the Victorious One who abides within as the foundation.
Kṛśāṅgī, Vāyavī, Kṣāmā, Kṣāmakhaṇḍā, Trilocanā—these are the Śaktis of the vowels; [and] Kāmā, Kāmeśvarī, and Ramā.
She who is desirable, who loves desire, who is the embodiment of desire, and who moves and dwells according to her will;
she whose limbs are delicate, who is free from indolence, who is free from disease, and who destroys all ailments.

She is the supreme remover of the arrowhead (viśalyakaraṇī), the ultimate reviver of the dead (mṛtasañjīvanī), the uniter (sandhinī), she who bends the discus (cakranamitā), the crescent moon (candrekhā), and the golden one (suvarṇikā). || 3-4 ||
Standing at the peak of the garland of jewels in the world, marked by the portions of the moon,
she transcends the stars, delivering [beings], abundant, possessing manifold radiance, and the primordial sound (Svarā).
She is the knower of the field (kṣetrajñā), exceedingly pure, and has the form of the mantra *huṃ*.
She is the knowledge of light, the movement of the planets, and the most excellent among all living beings. (3-6)
"The powers of the letters beginning with *ka* are proclaimed as bestowing the accomplishment of the practitioner's desires.
(p. 48) Thus ends the *Vijayāmātṛkā*. Now follows the *Sarvamaṅgalāmātṛkā*:
Sarvamaṅgalikā, Bhavyā, Maṅgalā, Maṅgalaprabhā, Kānti, Śrī, Prīti, Acalā, Jyotsnā, and Vilāsinī. (3.1)
Varadā, Vārijā, Vyagrā, Cāravī, and Vāstudevatā are proclaimed as the powers (śaktis) of the vowels in their respective order; they possess infinite power. || 3-2 ||
The power of desire is incomparable, all-knowing, and the bestower of knowledge;
she is logic, sound reasoning, the observer of others, the awakening within the womb, and languid with passion.

She is the radiance of the knowledge of Brahman, the courtesan, the great machine, and the flowing river; she is meditation itself, the object of meditation, and accessible through meditation; she is the Yoginī who bestows the perfection of yoga.
The knowledge of Brahman, consisting of the stream of the imperishable and the perishable, bestows auspiciousness;
it is the Rudra-knowledge whose essence is the five Brahmans and whose nature is that which is to be known. (3–5)
The Vidyā Tripurā consists of the five principles (pañcatattva) and resides within the principle of the seed-syllable (bījatattva).
She is the perfection (siddhi) whose essence is all seed-syllables, and she approaches through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance.

These are the powers (śaktis) beginning with *kā*, whose conduct is like the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon and who are adorned by serpents; they grant the desires of the practitioner. (3.7)
Thus ends the *Sarvamaṅgalāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Jvālāmālinīmātṛkā*:
Jvālinī, Mahājvālā, Jvālāmālā, and Mahojjvalā—she has two arms, a gentle countenance, and holds the book of knowledge. (3.1)
Kapardinī, Kṛtābhāsā, Brahmāṇī, Svātmavedinī, Ātmajñānāmṛtā, Nandā, Nandinī, and Romaharṣiṇī. (3.2)
These are the powers of the vowels: Kānti, Kālī, Dyuti, Mati, Viṣayecchā, Viśvagarbhā, Ādhārī, and Sarvabhāvinī. (3-3)
Kātyāyanī, Kālayātā, Kuṭilā, Animeṣikī, Nāḍī, Muhūrta, Ahorātra, and Tuṭi are the divisions of time. (3-4)
Abiding in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire, she transcends Māyā and is perfectly pure;
she is absolute, partless, stainless, all-pervasive, and has the sky as her form.
Svacchandabhairavī, Vyomā, she who transcends the void, established beyond the supreme;
she is the praise, the object of praise, the hymn, the one worthy of worship, the sacrifice, and the beloved of the worshipper. (3–6)
"These are the powers (śaktis) declared for the consonants beginning with 'ka'.
Thus ends the Jvālāmālinī-mātṛkā. Now, the Vicitrā-mātṛkā:
Vicitrā, Citravasanā, Citriṇī, Citrabhūṣaṇā.
And the *anuloma-apasandhi* consists of the middle and ring fingers. (3-1)
Tejovatī, Padmagarbhā, Mandarekhā, Ghṛṇāvalī, Viduṣī, Maulinī, Vyaktā, and Sukeśī are the powers of sound (svaraśaktayaḥ). || 3-2 ||
Somapā, Somasaṅkāśā, Vetālī known as Tālā, Somapriyā, Somavatī, Mantrapūtā, and Yajikriyā. || 3-3 ||
Mṛṇālī, Ṛkpradā, Śukti, she who dwells on the peak of the Vindhya mountain, Gadinī, Cakriṇī, Bimbā, Raktoṣṭhī, and Cāruhāsinī. || 3-4 ||
Vāgbhavā, Cārujā, Raktā, Suprasādā, Sulocanā, Kauśikī, Kandarā, Ghoṇā, Kakudmī, and Kāmalocanā. (3–5)
Kāmotsavā, Kāmacārā, Akāmā, Pūjitā, Parā, Tattvāvalokā, Purajit, and Rājñī are the powers (śaktis) beginning with the letter 'ka'. (3-6)
Thus ends the *Vicitrāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Durgāmātṛkā*:
Durgā, Kauśikī, Ugrā, Caṇḍā, Māheśvarī, Śivā, Viśveśvarī, Jagaddhātrī, and she who effects maintenance and destruction. (3-1)
The divine goddess Yoganidrā, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Sudhā are said to be, in sequence, the powers (śaktis) of the vowels, as well as creation, the oblation, and the sacrificial offering itself. 3-2.
Kalā, Māyā, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Stuti, Puṣṭi, Sthiti, Gati, Rati, Prīti, Dhṛti, Nīti, Vibhūti, Bhṛti, and Unnati. (3-3)
She is the earth, forbearance, destruction, splendor, peace, and exhaustion;
she is hunger, thirst, desire, modesty, sleep, and the seal whose essence is consciousness. (3-4)
Girijā, Bhāratī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Saṃjñā, and Vibhāvarī are declared to be the Śaktis of the letters beginning with 'ka', bestowing all perfections.
Thus ends the Durgāmātṛkā. Now, the Sarasvatīmātṛkā:
Sarasvatī is the power of mantra, the mother of the Vedas, and identical with the universe;
she is the mental one, the swan-rider, the female swan, the passionate one, and the bestower of welfare. (3.1)
Akṣayā, Vijayā, Prīti, Lomaśā, Lomahāriṇī, Vijñānadehā, and Saṃmūḍhā are the powers (śaktis) of the vowels respectively. 3-2.
She is the bestower of desires, the passionate one, the beloved, the supreme deity, and the most fearless;
she is bound by merit, the bringer of welfare, whose essence is compassion, and who is full of pity.
She has four udders, performs the five sacrifices, is fragrant, and is worshipped by the gods;
she lives upon trust, is the universe itself, the wish-fulfilling cow, and the granter of one's own desires.

Avidyā is his beloved daughter, tawny-hued and free from impurity; she is well-behaved, has the individual soul as her calf, possesses excellent conduct, and is most affectionate toward her offspring. 3-5.
Nandinī, the giver of victory, the unconquerable, the invincible, the remover of suffering;
the bestower of well-being, the creator of well-being, whose very nature is well-being, and who is the sacrificial fee of well-being. (3-6)
The Śaktis are white in color and bestow auspiciousness upon the consonants.
Thus ends the Sarasvatī-mātṛkā. Now, the Vārāhī-mātṛkā:
Vārāhī, Bhadriṇī, Bhadrā, Vātālī, and Kolavaktrā.
Jṛmbhiṇī, Stambhinī, Viśvā, Jambhinī, Mohinī, and Śubhā. || 3-1 ||
Rundhinī, Vaśinī, Śaktī, Ramā, and Umā are the powers of the vowels;
likewise, Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Śaṅkhinī, and Gadinī. (3.2)
She who holds the discus, she who holds the thunderbolt, she who holds the noose, she who holds the goad, the auspicious one;
she who holds the bow, the destroyer of the bonds of existence, the giver of victory, the bestower of victory.
Mahāghorā, Mahābhīmā, Bhairavī, Cāruhāsinī, Padminī, Bāṇinī, Ugrā, Musalinī, and Aparājitā.
Bestower of victory, Jaya, the victorious, slayer of enemies, free from fear;
Fearless, the proud one, the one with a snout, the destroyer of worms, the fanged one, and Ramā.
"The powers of the letters beginning with 'A' are inexhaustible and bestow spiritual accomplishments.
Thus ends the Vārāhī-mātṛkā. Now, the Trimūrti-mātṛkā:
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu.
Another shall be named Madhusūdana, and there shall be Trivikrama and Vāmana. (3-1)
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, as well as Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, and he who is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇa. (3.2)
Pradyumna and Aniruddha are, in sequence, the embodiments of the vowels;
thereafter follows the power of the Imperishable (Akṣara-śakti), who is primordial and the bestower of desired boons.
Īśānā, Ugrā, Ūrdhvanayanā, Ṛddhi, Rūpiṇī, as well as Luptā, Lūnadoṣā, and then Ekakalāpikā. (3–4)
Aiṃ: Kāriṇī, Oghavatī, Caurvakanyā, Añjanaprabhā, and Asthitālādharā are the powers (śaktis) of the vowels in their respective order. (3–5)
Bhava, Śarva, Caru, and Rudra, and likewise Paśupati; Ugra, Mahādeva, Bhīma, and Īśāna as well. (3–6)
Then the Puruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and beyond that Vāmadeva are to be known as the forms of the letters beginning with *ka*. (3.7)
Karabhadrā possesses the strength of birds and bestows fruits such as heaviness;
she has formidable feet, consists of ten months, and thereafter bears the crescent moon.
Chandomayī, Jagatsthānā (Jhām), Kṛti, Jñānaprabhā, as well as Ṭaṅkaḍhakkadharā, and thereafter Kṛtiḍāmarī (Ṣṭham). || 3-9 ||
And twelve Śaktis are declared for the letters beginning with Ka;
[the lords of these letters are] Brahmā, Yajñapati, Vedhā, Parameṣṭhin, and Pitāmaha.
Vidhātṛ, Viriñci, Sraṣṭṛ, Caturānana, and Hiraṇyagarbha are to be known as the ten forms beginning with Yā. (3.11)
The Yakṣiṇī Rañjinī, Lakṣmī, Vajriṇī, and Śaśidhāriṇī;
she whose abode is the six supports, the leader of all, with a smiling countenance. (3.12)
Lalitā, Kṣamā, and the ten powers beginning with Yā are declared to be the Trimūrtimātṛkā; she is considered the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus ends the Trimūrti-mātṛkā. Now follows the Kāmakalā-mātṛkā, consisting solely of the vowels: Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, Manoramā, Manoharā, and then Mano-rathā is declared here. (3-1)
Then Madanonmādinī, Mohinī, and likewise Śaṅkhinī;
then Śoṣiṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Śiñjinī, and thereafter Subhagā. (3.2)
"These are declared to be the sixteen digits (kalās) of Kāma, the vowels that bestow one's desires.
Thus ends the *Kāmakalāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Somakalāmātṛkā*:
Pūpā, Ceddhā, Sumanasā, Rati, Prīti, and likewise Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and beyond that Aṃśumālinī. || 3-1 ||

From Aṅgiras, Śaśinī was born, and from her, Chāyā; from her, Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā. For the sake of satisfaction, she is called Amṛtā. These are said to be the digits (kalās) of the Moon, together with their vowels.
Thus ends the *Somakalāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Aparājitāmātṛkā*:
Pratyaṅgirā, Siṃhamukhī, likewise Jvālāmukhī, Śivā, Vaiṣṇavī, Nārasiṃhī, Trimātrā, and the supreme Śāṅkarī. (3.1)
The venerable Arddhamātrā, Śūlinī, Śumbhamardinī, as well as Śaśāṅkadhāriṇī, Bhīṣikā, and Kapālinī. (3.2)
The powers of the vowels are proclaimed as Ugrā, Vīrā, Mahājvālā, Hākinī, and Viśvarūpiṇī, who hold tridents and skull-cups. (3.3)
Stuti, Jvalinī, Lakṣmī, Tamisrā, Sarvatomukhī, Vareṇyā, Totilā, Mukhyā, and Vātītā after that. (3–4)
Nṛmuṇḍamālā, Siṃhī, Hantrī, Bhīmā, Khaṇḍinī, Tāriṇī, Bhayadā, Drāviṇī, and Mṛtyurūpiṇī. (3–5)
She is Tyutkārī, the remover of death, the exalted one, and she who is fond of bowing;
she is Mālinī, whose form consists of the letter Ña, the female swan, and the peahen.

Kuṇḍinī, Kṣāntirūpā, and the Śaktis of the letters beginning with *ka* follow in sequence. Thus ends the *Pratyaṅgirāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Bhavānīmātṛkā*: Bhavānī, Anantā, Śarabhī, Cakriṇī, and Karuṇākarā.
One measure, two measures, and another, three measures, is Jaya. (3.1)
The half-mora, the supreme, the subtle, the six-footed, and the wise—
these are declared to be the partless powers (niṣkalāḥ śaktayaḥ) of the vowels, which bestow the wealth of the eightfold dharma.
It is described as a mass of spontaneous bliss, having the form of space, consisting of both prose and verse, and endowed with all poetic ornaments. (3.3)
The series of all her utterances has its steps set upon the feet of the virtuous;
though her form is as hard as the six systems of logic, she is herself devoid of all logical reasoning. (3.4)
She is sun-colored and colorless, characterized by darkness (tamas) and possessing a supreme form;
she is Brahmāṇī, born of the lineage of Brahmā, the sovereign goddess who speaks the speech of the Vedas.
She is the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras along with the Vedāṅgas;
she is all the Vedas, possesses the Vedas, and is the presiding deity of the Haṃsa-vidyā. (3.6)
The sovereign of all, the sustainer of the world, the creator of the universe;
she who is the altar and the form of the Vedas, Kālikā, whose very nature is Time.
The Great Goddess Nārāyaṇī is the one who sets all beings in motion;
she possesses a golden-colored form, and the powers (śaktis) beginning with *kā* follow in sequence.
Thus ends the Mātṛkā of Durgā (Bhavānī). Now, the Khecarī-mātṛkā:
Khecarī is the incomparable Śakti, the Mother of Space (Vyomāmbā), whose form is space;
she resides in space, her nature is space, she transcends space, and she is identical with the universe. 3-1.
Śāmbhavī, the consort of Śambhu, the destroyer of the distress of those seeking refuge, the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, the Supreme Knowledge, and the Auspicious One. (3-2)
These are the powers of the vowels, which liberate one from the bonds of worldly existence:
Parā, Parāyaṇā, Bhavyā, Mālinī, and Madavihvalā. (3-3)
She is subtle knowledge, radiance, twilight, the illusion of the world, and the activity of the world;
she is the night-walker, victory, illusion, the immeasurable, and the increaser of delusion.
She who deludes, she who delights, she who subdues, the inferior one, she whose nature is that of the Mothers;
she who is the knowledge of the Vedas, the Great Knowledge, the knowledge of sacrifice, and the destroyer of Yama.
She is blissful, the giver of bliss, the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, the wielder of the staff, and the goddess Ramā;
she is confident, large-eyed, the source of delight, and likewise imperishable.
The powers (*śakti*) of the letters beginning with *ka* have been declared to bestow the desired fruits upon practitioners.
Thus ends the *Khecarīmātṛkā*. Now follows the *Cāmuṇḍāmātṛkā*:
Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍā, and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Nārāyaṇī, Bhadrakālī, Virajā, and Viśvamātṛkā. || 3-1 ||
Ajitā, Bhārgavī, Saumyā, Durgā, Durgatināśinī, Āpyāyanī, and Caṇḍaghaṇṭā—these are declared to be the Māyā-svaraśaktis. (3-2)
Kamalā, Khaḍginī, Gadinī, the supreme Ghaṇṭikā, Caritrā, Chattriṇī, Jaṅghā, Jhaṅkārī, and thereafter Jayadā. (3-3)
She holds a chisel in her hand, she is the maker of the sound "ṭhaṅ", the wielder of the ḍāmara drum, and the one with the ḍhakkā drum;
she is the auspicious Śivā, the destroyer of darkness, the mistress of the sacred sites, the embodiment of compassion, and the bestower of wealth.
Navyā, Parā, Phaṭkārī, Bandhinī, Bhayavarjitā, Mahāmāyā, Yogīṣī, Raṅkiṇī, and Lambakeśinī. (3–5)
Varadā, Śākinī, Ṣaṇḍā, Sarveśī, Halinī, as well as Lalitā and Kṣāmodarī— these are the powers (śaktis) beginning with the letter Ka.
If one is a devotee of Caṇḍā, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the *mātṛkā* alone,
the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* together with the power (śakti) of Cāmuṇḍā.
Thus ends the *Cāmuṇḍāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Parāmātṛkā*:
Parā, Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Viśvā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Jayā, Vijayā, Mānadā, Dakṣā, Yoginī, Mānadā, and Rati. (3.1)
Kaumārī, Pārvatī, Durgā, Māninī, Svaraśakti, Kalāvatī, Karuṇā, Kāminī, and Kāntidāyinī. || 3-2 ||
Khātītā, Khecarī, Gamyā, Gāruḍī, Ghanagarjinī, Cāruhāsā, Capalā, Jagaddhātrī, Jayā, and Ramā. (3-3)
The savior of the universe, composed of the universe, large-eyed, free from sorrow;
the giver of boons, Vāsukī, the youthful maiden, praised by the Supreme Lord, and steadfastness. || 3-4 ||
Bhāsvarā, Bhāvagamyā, Āryā, Bhānumaṇḍalavartinī, Phaṭkārī, Lāsinī, Tārā, Hāriṇī, and Havyavāhinī—
these are declared to be the *kādi* powers, namely Hlādinī, Kledinī, and Klinnā. (3–5)
Thus ends the *Parāmātṛkā*. Now, the *Kurukullāmātṛkā*:
Kurukullā, whose eyes are like those of a deer, is the destroyer of poison and the remover of venom.
The Sovereign of All, the Large-Eyed One, the Daughter of Garuḍa, she who moves with the gait of an elephant. || 3-1 ||
Vinatā, the mother of the universe, known as Viśvā, the universal mother;
she who consists of passion, darkness, and goodness, adorned with tinkling golden girdles.
These are the powers of the vowels, bestowing wealth, merit, and happiness:
Kalyāṇī, Kamalā, Kāntā, Sauparṇī, and Tārkṣyaśaktinī.
The slayer of serpents, the mother of serpents, the female serpent, the beloved born of the mountain;
the lotus-like one, the joyful one, the auspicious one, she who is ever-flowered, the propitious one.
She who flows with intoxication, who possesses intoxication, who is the delighter, and who is languid with passion;
she who deludes, who is fond of the drum, and who dwells in the minds of sages. || 3-5 ||
She who dwells in the boat, the beloved of the Conqueror of Cities, the power of the boat, the one dear to the City;
she who is sky-clad, Diti, the gentle one, the mistress of the day, and the beloved of the distressed. || 3-6 ||
Dayāvatī, Damaprītā, Dāruṇī, and Lokadhāriṇī—
these are declared to be the Śaktis of the letters beginning with *ka*, bestowing the desired fruits upon practitioners.
Thus ends the Kurukullāmātṛkā. Now, the fifteenth Mātṛkā:
Sundarī, Subhagā, Bhavyā, Mahāmāyā, Manonmanī, Tripurā, Vaśinī, Bālā, and Mahātripurasundarī. (3-1)
Mahākāmakalā, Śreṣṭhā, Nīlā, Nīlasarasvatī, Viśveśī, Vijayā, and Saumyā are proclaimed as the powers of the vowels (svaraśaktis). || 3-2 ||
She is Kaulinī, established on the path of Kula, dwelling at the end of Kula;
she is the sovereign of all vidyās and likewise the sovereign of all mantras.
She is the perfected mistress of all speech, the victorious sovereign of all accomplishments,
the heroine who is the mistress of all heroes, and the auspicious one who is the mistress of all sacred seats.
Bhairavī, beyond conceptualization, accessible through contemplation, the Great Sovereign;
the Great Vidyā, the Great Conqueror, the Great Tripurasundarī. (3–5)
Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Durgā, Vaiṣṇavī, the beloved of Viṣṇu;
the Yoginī established on the path of Yoga, who dwells in the city of the six cakras.
She is Vimalā, the abode of the universe, named the universe, and whose form is the universe;
she is Śaśinī and Śāradā, situated in the center of the lunar orb.
"These are declared to be the powers (śaktis) of the letters beginning with *ka*, which bestow success.
Thus ends the Mātṛkā of Sundarī. Now, the Mātṛkās beginning with Mālinī: Mālinī, Nādinī, Grasini, and Priyadarśinī."
Nivṛtti, Supratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti beyond that. (3-1)
Cāmuṇḍā, Guhyaśakti, Vajriṇī, Karālinī, Kapālinī, and Śivā, as well as Jñānaśakti and Kriyā. (3.2)
These are the powers of the vowels, which bestow the fruits of knowledge and liberation:
Gāyatrī, Chāndasī, Sāvitrī, Dehinī, and Muṇḍamālinī. (3-3)
She who utters *phaṭ* and she who utters *vaṣaṭ*; she who is fond of the oblations of *svadhā* and *svāhā*;
she who is Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī; she who is Brahmāṇī and the expounder of Brahman.
Jayā is the embodiment of the Vedas, Durgā, Jayantī, and Raktadantikā;
she is the conqueror of the world, composed of pure consciousness, and the awakener of the universe.
She is patience, tranquility, compassion, sleep, and the supreme power of Rudra;
she is the utterer of "Huṃ," the sky-walker, illusion, the womb of the universe, and composed of the three Vedas.
These Kādi-śaktis are proclaimed as the destroyers of the fear of saṃsāra;
these Mātṛkās should be installed by those initiated into the atomic [initiation] of the Ūrdhvāmnāya. (3-7)
Thus ends the *mātṛkā* beginning with Mālinī. Now, the *mātṛkā* of the five elements. Regarding this, the *Śāradātilaka* states:
"Wind, fire, earth, water, and space correspond respectively to the fifty letters.
Five are short, five are long, ending in the *bindu*, and produced by [vowel] conjunction. (3.1)
"The five groups beginning with *ka*, accompanied by *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha*. Thus it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The five rows consisting of wind (*prāṇa*), fire (*agni*), air (*anila*), water (*ambu*), and earth (*khātman*) have been proclaimed."
The Lord is the creation designated as the power of illusion (māyāśakti), consisting of the five elements. || 3-1 ||
Therefore, its placement here is not merely in one part of the Śiva-self;
it is the wind, the moving air, the vital breath, the wind-element, the sound, the speed, and the swift motion. (3-2)
Pervasion, touch, and the names of the syllables of the winds in sequence:
Agni, Vahni, Śuci, Tejas, Prabhā, Dāva, Śikhin, and Dyuti. (3-3)
Dāha, grāsa, and nāman are names for both colors and splendors.
Dharā, kṣmā, bhū, sthirā, jyā, ku, gotrā, bhūmi, rasā, and ilā are names for the earth. 3–4.
These indeed are the names of the letters belonging to the earth, in their respective order.
Jalam, vāri, vanam, vāḥ, kam, pāthaḥ, toyam, rasaḥ, ambu, and hṛt [are synonyms for water]. (3-5)
These are the names of the vowels in their respective order:
Vibhu, Kha, Kha, Dyu, Abhra, Vyoman, Śūnya, Nabhas, and Viyat. (3.6)
"Haṃsa" and these other names [are] in sequence for those whose form is space.
52) Thus ends the Mātṛkā of the Five Elements. Now, the Mātṛkā of the Earth-Syllables (*bhūtalipi*). Regarding that, in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
Now I shall proclaim the great mantras of Sarasvatī that grant all desires;
among them, O beloved, the mantra known as Bhūtalipi is first declared.
In the great tantra of Sārasvata, this [teaching] is concealed and extremely rare;
having received it from the presence of Viṣṇu, the sages attained their desired fruit.
O Goddess, they always obtained everything; what is the use of saying more?
The group of five short vowels is proclaimed first. (3.3)
O Goddess, the second [group] is said to be the four syllables beginning with Śiva;
the third is proclaimed to be space, wind, fire, water, and earth.

These five classes [of consonants] are formed respectively by the last letter of each class, the first, the second, the penultimate, and the third; the ninth is considered to be formed by the letters *va*, *śa*, and *bhṛgu* (the letter *u*).
The mantra consists of nine groups and comprises forty-two syllables.
The first group among these groups is composed of the letters Śrīkaṇṭha, Ūrdhvoṣṭha, and Kha. (3–6)
These aforementioned [elements] are said to be joined with the final letters of their respective groups and the letter *va*;
they are considered to be space, air, fire, water, and earth, corresponding respectively to the letters of the [five] groups.
The second group is devoid of earth; the last is joined with water and earth.
Thus, the deities of all nine groups have been stated in order. (3–8)
Those called Viriñci, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the two Aśvins; Prajāpati;
the world-protectors (lokapālas); and the powers of action and so forth are thus proclaimed. (3.9)
Thus ends the *bhūtalipimātṛkā*. Now, regarding the *triṣaṣṭyakṣaramātṛkā*, it is stated in the *Mātṛkārṇava*:
"Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are considered [to exist] according to the doctrine of Śambhu;
they were proclaimed by Svayambhū himself, whether in Prakrit or in Saṃskṛta. (3-1)
There are twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants;
the letters beginning with *ya* are recorded as eight, and four are recorded as the *yamas*.

The anusvāra, the visarga, and also the letters *ca* and *pa* when dependent on another [consonant], as well as the *duḥspṛṣṭa* (the letter *la*) and the protracted (*pluta*) vowel, should be known [as having no place of articulation]. (3-3)
Thus ends the sixty-three-syllable Mātṛkā. Now follows the Śāmbhavī Mātṛkā: the installation (nyāsa) must be performed by those initiated into the Ūrdhvāmnāya.
Śāmbhavī, Tāmasī, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, and Śivottamā.
She with upward-pointing hair, the one with deformed eyes, the sky-walker, the beloved of Śiva. || 3-1 ||
Kuṇḍodarī, Lolākṣī, Viṣṇumāyā, Mahodarī,
Lamboṣṭhī, Vyomarūpā, and Vibhvī are the powers of sound (svaraśakti).
Kānti, Śraddhā, Rati, Prīti, Ambarā, Prāṇarūpiṇī, Śuci, Kṣiti, Bhuvanā, Dyuti, Śrī, and the supreme Ramā. (3-3)
She is the passionate one (rājasī), the devourer (grasinī), the fierce one (caṇḍā), the ogress (rākṣasī), and the confident one (viśāradā);
she is the speaker of words (vāgvādinī), the victorious one (jayā), the formidable one (bhīmā), the auspicious one (śivā), and the beloved of Śaṅkara.
She is the twilight, wisdom, radiance, moonlight, the roaring one, and she who possesses universal form;
she wears a garland of bones, has five fierce faces, is the agitator, and is the intellect. (3-5)
O Maheśvarī, the powers of the letters beginning with 'ka' are traditionally held to be all-pervasive, according to their sequence,
for practitioners engaged in the initiation of the Śāmbhava-krama.
The Śāmbhavī Mātṛkā is proclaimed as the bestower of all desired fruits;
having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of this, one should then perform the sequence of the rays.
Thus ends the Śāmbhavī Mātṛkā. Now, the Kālarātri Mātṛkā:
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Kaṭukā, Subhagā, Śivā, Mohinī, Moharātri, Vidyā, and Kaṭukapatrikā. (3-1)
The daughter of Atharvan, Rañjinī, who deludes the universe;
she who possesses the weapon of enchantment, whose form is enchantment, the embodiment of good fortune, and the increaser of delusion. (3.2)
These are the powers of the vowels, which serve as the means for the desired goals of the practitioner:
Kāminī, who is delighted by desire; Kamanaprītā; Drāviṇī; Kṣobhiṇī; and the supreme Parā.
Madanonmādinī, Manmathā, Manonmanī, Manasvinī, Manovāsinī, Aruṇā, and Madanotsavā. || 3-4 ||

She is the intoxicating one, the continuity of intoxication, the sweet-voiced, the heart-stealing, the delightful, the beloved, the lovely, the one with melodious sound, and the one fond of intoxication. 3-5.
Kāmavardhanikā, Dāruṇā, Damanapriyā, Daṇḍinī, Viśvanaṭinī, Nalinī, and Viśvamālinī. || 3-6 ||

Hāva, bhāva, that which is accessible through emotion (bhāva), that which transcends emotion, the dispeller [of sorrow], the five-arrowed one, and the one who inspires others—these are the powers (śaktis) of the letters beginning with 'ka', in their respective order. (3.7)
Thus ends the Kālarātrimātṛkā.

Thus ends the third [chapter] in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the Great Mahopādhyāya.
Breathing || 3 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the fourth breath (śvāsa).
Now, in the Kālīmata, concerning the sequence of the rays of Tripura with reference to Tripurā:
I shall declare the majesty of the Mātṛkās, which is concealed in all the tantras;
by understanding this through the oral tradition, the practitioner becomes free from doubt. (4.1)
One should personally perform the extraction of the mantra through the awakening of the rays of the Mātṛkā;
first, the sequence of the rays of the Mātṛkā must always be known by the wise. (4.2)
He who performs the extraction of mantras without understanding the sequence of rays is like one who seeks to see an object situated in darkness. (4.3)
Therefore, with every effort, having correctly understood [the truth] from either the guru or the scriptures according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner becomes free from doubt.
One should know the true nature of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing the mantra's potency;
through the awakening of the mantra's potency, accomplishment will come without effort. (4-5)
The person who practices a mantra without understanding the potency of the mantra will not achieve success in the mantra even in thousands of millions of eons. (4.6)
The rays of the phonemes (varṇas) are to be known as being in the form of breaths, without a doubt;
those breaths, moreover, consist of more than six hundred full forms.
Indeed, seven thousand qualities, doubled when not yet complete, constitute those two types of breaths, categorized according to their external and internal application. (4.8)
By the distinction between sun and moon, by the division into the cruel and the gentle,
and by the distinction between Piṅgalā and Iḍā, there are those breaths which possess the form of half-moons.
They are established in the six cakras: at the mūlādhāra, in the navel lotus (svādhiṣṭhāna), in the anāhata, in the viśuddhi, and between the eyebrows. 4-10.
Each wheel consists of three thousand and six hundred [spokes].
The *mūlādhāra* is the locus of earth, while the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is that of fire. (4.11)
Maṇipūra is the seat of water; Anāhata is the seat of air;
Viśuddha is the seat of ether; and Ājñācakra is the seat of the mind. (4.12)
In the *mūlādhāra* is a great lotus endowed with four petals, joined in the centers of its petals with the four letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*. (4.13)
For each individual color, there are nine hundred rays;
furthermore, there are fourteen earthly rays for each.
Each syllable, however, should be understood in sequence from *va* to *sa*:
[the vowels] in the ten-petaled Maṇipūra, which is endowed with the consonants from *ḍa* to *pha*.
There too, the rays should be known as divided into fifty-two parts,
within the self-consecrated [cakra] which has six petals and is endowed with the letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*.
Sixty-two rays are to be known here as belonging to the portion of fire,
within the unstruck solar petal endowed with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*.
In this regard, the fifty-four rays of the northwest direction are to be known;
they reside in the pure sixteen-petaled [lotus] which is conjoined with the sixteen vowels. (4.18)
The seventy-two ethereal rays should be known according to their divisions;
however, in the supreme two-petalled Ājñā-cakra, they are joined with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.
The mental rays are to be known as sixty-four in their respective order;
having arisen in the six supports, the rays amount to three hundred and sixty.
Regarding each individual color, there are rays upon which [the qualities] depend; within those rays, the sixfold [qualities], beginning with the earthly (pārthiva), are said to reside. (4.21)
I shall now state their names as "intermingled rays," located within the support consisting of four petals and within the fifty-six petals.
The rays beginning with the eastern direction are to be known as belonging to the Earth element and are bestowers of auspiciousness;
Sundarī is Tripurā and so forth, and Sundara is Tripura and so forth. (4-23)
Then there is the Heart Goddess and the Heart God;
thereafter the Head Goddess and the Head God, and after that the Crest Goddess.

The deity of the crest and so forth, the goddess of the armor and the male deity of the armor; the goddess of the eyes and the male deity of the eyes, the goddess of the weapons and the male deity of the weapons and so forth.
Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśa, then Bhagamālinī and Bhagamālin; then Nityaklinnā and the eternally moist Nityādiklinnaka.
Bheruṇḍā and Bheruṇḍa, followed by Vahnivāsinī; then Vahnivāsī, Mahāvajreśvarī, and likewise Vajreśvara. (4-27)
Śivādūtī and Śivādūta, Tvaritā and Tvarita, and then Kulādisundarī and Kulasundara. (4.28)
Then Nityā and Nitya; after that, Nīlapatākā;
then Nīlādikapatāka, Vijayā, and Vijaya. (4.29)
And Sarvamaṅgalanāmī, and he who is named Sarvamaṅgalanāmaka; Jvālāmālinikā, and after her, Jvālāmālī.
Citrā and Citra are said to follow, and after that, Mahānityā;
after Mahānityā, Parameśī follows.
The Supreme Lord, however, consists of Mitreśa and is known as Mitreśa;
thereafter, he consists of Ṣaṣṭhīśa and is likewise known as Ṣaṣṭhīśa.
Then Uḍḍīśamayī and likewise Uḍḍīśa; after that, Caryānāthamayī and also Caryānāthamaya.
The terrestrial rays are said to bestow the desired objects of the practitioner;
they are located in the region of the navel within a lotus consisting of ten petals and fifty-two petals.
In that [system] as well, the rays should be known to be fifty-two in sequence:
Lopāmudrāmayī and then Lopāmudrāmaya.
Likewise, there is one consisting of Agastya and one who consists of Agastya;
one consisting of the word Kālatāpana and so forth, and one who is Kālāditāpana.
The sixth is to be known as consisting of Maya; likewise, there is that consisting of the Teacher of Dharma (Dharmācāryamaya);
and thereafter, that consisting of Muktakeśvara and others.

The one consisting of Muktakeśvara and the rest is composed of the digits (kalās) beginning with Dīpa; likewise, that which consists of the Nāthas is composed of the digits beginning with Dīpa and ending with Nātha. || 4-38 ||
Then there is Viṣṇudevamayī and Viṣṇudevamaya;
from Prabhākara onwards, there is Devamaya and Tejomayī.
Thus, he consists of the divine mind, and likewise she consists of the divine mind;
and he indeed consists of the divine mind, preceded by the state of auspiciousness.
Then there was Kalyāṇadeva and others consisting of Devas; likewise, Ratnadeva and others consisting of Devas, and then Ratnadeva and others consisting of jewels.
She is composed of Vāsudeva, and he likewise is composed of Vāsudeva;
she is composed of Rāmānanda, and he likewise is composed of Rāmānanda.

The perfection of atomization (aṇimā-siddhi) and the one perfected in atomization, as well as the perfections beginning with lightness (laghimā), the perfection of lightness, and furthermore the perfection of magnitude (mahimā). || 4-43 ||
First is the perfection known as "mastery" (mahimā); beyond that comes sovereignty (īśitva) and the rest.
From the perfection of sovereignty comes the perfection of control (vaśitva) and the rest. (4.44)

The perfection of mastery (vaśitva) is accomplished; after that, the perfection beginning with the power of irresistible will (prākāmya). Then there is the perfection of irresistible will, and after that, the perfection of enjoyment (bhukti).
From that, there is the perfection of enjoyment (bhukti-siddhi); from that, the perfection of will (icchā-siddhi), which brings about the perfection of will and so forth;
the perfection of attainment (prāpti-siddhi), which is the one perfected in attainment, bringing about the perfection of all desires and so forth.
And one who has accomplished all desires and so forth is Brāhmī; beyond that is Brahmā.
Māheśvarī and Maheśa are to be known as the rays of water. (4-47)
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], which consists of six flavors and possesses sixty-two petals, the fiery rays are to be known starting from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise. (4.48)
Kaumārī and Kumāra, Vaiṣṇavī and Viṣṇu, Vārāhī and Varāha, and Māhendrī and Mahendraka.
Cāmuṇḍā and indeed Cāmuṇḍa, and after that Mahālakṣmī; then Mahālakṣmī and thereafter Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī.
Then there is Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇā, and after that Sarvavidrāvaṇī;
then Sarvavidrāvaṇā and Sarvākarṣaṇikā. || 4-51 ||
Then there is Sarvākarṣaṇakā, followed by Sarvavaśaṃkarī;
then Sarvavaśaṃkara, and after that Sarvonmādanikā. || 4-52 ||
And likewise Sarvonmādanaka, Sarvādikamahāṅkuśā, as well as Mahāṅkuśa, Sarvakhecarī, and Sarvakhecara.
Sarvabījā, Sarvabīja, and thereafter Sarvayoni; then Sarvayoni, Trikhaṇḍā, and immediately after that, Trikhaṇḍa.
Then there is Trailokyamohanā and the others, as well as Cakrasvāminikā;
likewise Cakrasvāmī and Prakaṭayoginī. (4–55)
Then there is Prakaṭayogin, and after that Kāmākarṣaṇikā;
then Kāmākarṣaṇaka, and after that Buddhyākarṣaṇikā.
The one who attracts the intellect, likewise the attractor of ego;
the attractor of ego, and thereafter the attractor of sound.
Then there is the one who attracts sound, and after that the one who attracts touch;
then the one who attracts touch, and after that the one who attracts form. || 4-58 ||
Then there is the Attractor of Form, and after that the Attractor of Taste;
then the Attractor of Taste, and after that the Attractor of Fragrance. || 4-59 ||
Then there is Gandhākarṣaṇaka, and after that Cittākarṣaṇikā;
then Cittākarṣaṇaka, and after that Dhairyākarṣaṇikā. || 4-60 ||
Then there is Dhairyākarṣaṇaka, and after that Smṛtyākarṣaṇikā;
then Smṛtyākarṣaṇaka, and after that Nāmākarṣaṇikā. || 4-61 ||
Then there is the attraction of names, followed by the attraction of seed-syllables;
then the attraction of seed-syllables itself, and likewise in the Anāhata [cakra]. (4-62)
On the fifty-four petals consisting of solar petals,
the rays of Vāyu are to be known, starting from the eastern petal in successive order. (4.63)
Ātmākarṣaṇikā and likewise Ātmākarṣaṇaka;
Amṛtākarṣaṇī the Śakti and likewise Amṛtākarṣaṇa. || 4-64 ||
Then there is Śarīrākarṣaṇī, and from that, Śarīrākarṣaṇa;
thereafter follows Sarvāśāparipūra, the lord of the wheels (cakras). || 4-65 ||
In the same way, after this come Cakrasvāmī, then Guptayoginī,
then Guptayogī, and after that Anaṅgādikusumā.
Anaṅgakusuma, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamekhala;
Anaṅgamadana, Anaṅgamadana, and from the word Anaṅga;
Madanātura, Āta, Anaṅgamadanātura, and indeed [the rest].
Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgādirekhā, and Anaṅgādiveginī.
Anaṅgavega, Anaṅgāṅkuśa, and Anaṅgāṅkuśa;
then Anaṅgamālinī and, after that, Anaṅgādimālin.
Then there is Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī and the others, who are the mistresses of the wheels (cakrasvāminikās); likewise, Cakrasvāmī is the Yoginī belonging to the Guptatarā [class].
In the same way, the yogin [should worship] Sarvādisaṃkṣobhaṇī, and after that, Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī, and then Sarvavidrāvaṇī. (4.71)
Then there is Sarvavidrāvaṇa, and after that Sarvākarṣaṇikā; then Sarvākarṣaṇaka, and after that Sarvāhlādanikā. || 4-72 ||
Then there is Sarvāhlādanakā (the Delighter of All), followed by Sarvasaṃmohanī (the Enchantress of All);
after that, Sarvasaṃmohana (the Enchanter of All), and then Sarvastambhanī (the Paralyzer of All). || 4.73 ||
Then there is Sarvastambhanaka, and after that Sarvajṛmbhaṇikā; then Sarvajṛmbhaṇaka, and after that Sarvavaśaṃkarī. || 4-74 ||
The one who brings all under control, the one who delights all, the one who is the delighter of all;
then follows the one who intoxicates all, and the one who is the intoxicator of all. (4.75)

And because she accomplishes all aims, she is Sarvārthasādhanī; and because he accomplishes all aims, he is Sarvārthasādhana. Because she fulfills all prosperity, she is Sarvasampattipūraṇī; and because he fulfills all prosperity, he is Sarvasampattipūraṇa. || 4-76 ||
In the throat, within the lotus consisting of seventy-two petals— specifically that which has sixteen petals—
the rays of the etheric element are to be known, proceeding in order from the eastern petal onwards.
She is composed of all mantras, and he is likewise composed of all mantras;
she brings about the destruction of all dualities, and he is the one who effects the destruction of all dualities.
Then [comes] Sarvasaubhāgyadāyikā, the Mistress of the Cakra;
likewise, there is the Yoginī Saṃpradāyā and others, who are the Mistress of the Cakra.
And likewise, there is Saṃpradāyādiyoginī, who bestows all siddhis;
then Sarvasiddhiprada, and thereafter Sarvasaṃpatpradā.
She is the bestower of all prosperity and the performer of all that is dear;
she is indeed the maker of all beloved things and the bringer of all auspiciousness.
She is the performer of all auspiciousness and the bestower of all desires;
she is indeed the granter of every wish and the liberator from all suffering.
Likewise, she is the liberator; thereafter, she is the pacifier of all death, the pacifier of all death, and the warder-off of all obstacles.
Likewise Nivāraṇā, and likewise Sarvāṅgasundarī;
and likewise Sarvāṅgasundara, and Sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī.
In the same way, there is the donor, beginning with the Accomplisher of All Aims (Sarvārthasādhaka);
then the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakrasvāminī), and thereafter the Lord of the Kula and so forth.
Then there is the Utterly Transcended Yoginī, and likewise the Yogin beyond that;
then the All-Knowing One, and the All-Knowing One, and the Supreme Bestower of All Powers.
Then she is the bestower of all powers, and thereafter the bestower of all sovereignty;
she is the bestower of all sovereignty and is composed of all knowledge. || 4.87 ||
She consists of all-knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases;
she is the destruction of all diseases and has the nature of the support of all.
She is the nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is indeed the remover of all sins, and likewise she consists of all bliss.
She who consists of all bliss and whose nature is all protection;
he whose nature is all protection and who bestows the fruits of all desires. (4.90)
Likewise, [the deity] who bestows the fruit, starting from Sarvarakṣākara;
then Cakrasvāminikā, and after that, the Lord (Svāmī).
Then Nigarbhayoginī, and likewise the Yogī thereafter;
then Vaśinī and Vaśī, and after that Kāmeśvarī. || 4.92 ||
Kāmeśvara and Modinī, then Modin and Vimalā; likewise Vimala and Aruṇā, Aruṇa, Jayinī, and Jayī.
Then Sarveśvarī and Sarveśa, Kaulinī and Kaulika [reside] in the Ājñācakra,
within the lotus of sixty-four petals consisting of two leaves.
The mental rays are to be known as beginning with the remover of all passion;
then Cakrasvāminikā, and after that, the Lord (Svāmī).
Then there is Rahasyayoginī, as well as Yogī, Bāṇinī, Bāṇī,
Cāpinī, Cāpī, Pāśinī, and thereafter Pāśika.
Aṅkuśinī and Aṅkuśī, then Mahākāmeśvarī;
likewise Mahākāmeśvara and Mahāvajreśvarī. || 4.97 ||
Mahāvajreśvara and likewise Bhagamālinī;
and similarly, Mahātripurasundarī is here [as] Bhagamālī. (4.98)
In the same way, Sundara is the bestower of all accomplishments and so forth;
then Cakrasvāmin, and likewise Svāmī, who is preceded by Ati. (4.99)
The Yoginī of Secrets (Rahasyayoginī) and likewise the Yogi beyond that,
known by the name Śrībhaṭṭāraka and designated as Śrībhaṭṭāraka.
Beyond this is the Lord of the Cakra (cakrasvāmin), beginning with Sarvānandamaya and so forth;
likewise, he is the Lord of the Cakra according to the supreme and inferior secret. || 4-101 ||
Likewise, the Yoginī and the Yogin; Tripurā and Tripura;
(Tripurādīśvarī and then Tripureśvara). || 4-102 ||
Then there is Tripurādisundarī and Tripurasundara;
likewise Tripurādirvāsinī and Tripuravāsaka.
Tripurāśrī, as well as Śrī, then Tripuramālinī, Mālī, Tripurasiddhā, and thereafter Siddha. (4.104)
Tripurāmbā, likewise Ambā, Mahātripurasundarī;
likewise Sundara, and then Mahāmāheśvarī. (4.105)
Likewise, there is Māheśvara, and after that Mahārājñī;
then Mahārāja, Mahāśakti, and after that Mahāśakta. || 4-106 ||
Mahāguptā, Mahāgupta, and beyond that Mahājñaptā; then Mahājñapta, Mahādiś, Mahānandā, and Mahādika.
Likewise, there is Mahānanda here, and beyond that, Mahāspanda;
likewise, there is Mahāmahāspanda, and similarly, Anumahāśaya.
And here, the rays should be known as Mahāmahāśaya;
the sequence of ascent has been declared, now I shall state the sequence of descent.
Following that, there are pairs formed by the elision of fifteen syllables;
then, from the conjunction of the sixteen vowels with the syllables of the Navātman and Īśvara [mantras], there arise further pairs.
Four hundred and forty-four are their pairs;
these are the portions of the five Brahmās, the three forms, and the luminaries.
And there are pairs; indeed, these are the pairs arising from the digits (kalās) of the [deities] beginning with Tva.
Furthermore, there are the digits other than those arising from the syllables of the Navātmeśvara. || 4-112 ||
One should know that there are one hundred and sixty qualities in the joints;
in the movement [of breath] and its return, there are nine pairs arising from the mantras of the Ātman and the Lord.
Likewise, there is the Saptashati (Seven Hundred) and the one exceeding it by twenty; thereafter, there are twenty thousand and seven hundred and thirty-six [verses]. (4.114)
These should be known as the impermanent periods of time; their total count is said to be twenty-one thousand six hundred. (4.115)
In this Kula tradition, the rays are declared to be of the nature of breath;
the sun and moon are to be known from the root syllable doubled. (4.116)
The rays should be known as "intermingled" (saṅkīrṇa) when they are devoid of the bindu from the mark at the base;
this applies both below the mūlādhāra and within the thousand-petaled lotus.
In the same way, thousands of rays shine within the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*);
in the six joints, both below and above, they number thirty and twenty respectively.
The innate rays are to be known as twenty-one thousand four hundred and forty; the mixed rays are two thousand. (4.119)
One hundred and sixty [kalās] are declared; they should be understood therein according to their respective parts.
The divisions of the castes (varṇas) and those belonging to the earth and the waters are to be known in their proper sequence. (4.120)
The Taijasa, Anila, Nābhasa, and Mānasa [elements] belong to the Unmanifest (Avarṇa); their total measure is three and one-half, plus three-quarters. (4.121)
Beyond that, the group of four would be diminished by one-eighth;
beyond that, the group of three and a half would be diminished by one-eighth.
The rays are traditionally said to be one and a half times the number of the Vedas in their respective order;
this is declared to be the sequence of the vowels beginning with *i*. (4.123)
The progression for each individual vowel is twenty-two and a half; for the letter *ka*, it is four and a quarter. (4.124)
Five, four and a half, six, and five and a quarter;
this sequence is to be known for the letter *kha*, which ends in the fifth [vowel]. (4.125)
For the *gha*-vowel syllable, there are four and a quarter *bhūtas* (four), five, four and a half oceans (four), and six and a quarter *bhūtas* (six). 4-126.
And four and a half, four and a quarter, five and a half, four and a half, six, and then five and a quarter. (4.127)
This same sequence applies to the letters ḍa, ca, and cha;
however, for the letter ja, there are exactly five and one-quarter Vedas. (4.128)
The group of five and a half Vedas, the group of six and a quarter;
for the letter Jha, it is four and a half, and likewise four and a quarter.

The group of five and the four-and-a-half [letters], the group of six minus one quarter, the group of six belonging to the letter *ña*, and likewise those of *ṭa* and *ṭha*, are like the letter *ja*. (4.130)
Of the ḍārṇa [mantra], there should be six [syllables] minus one quarter, five and a quarter, six and a half, five, seven, and six and a half. (4.131)
This sequence of the ḍhaṇatāna [mantras] should be known by the best of teachers:
for the thārṇa [mantra], it shall be one and a half bhūtas, and likewise one bhūta plus a quarter. (4.132)
The Rasas (six) should be less by one-quarter; likewise, the groups of six and seven, as well as six and a half, are to be known by the teachers for the various types of curd.
For the letter *pā*, it should be one and a half, five, and six;
for the letter *pha*, it is one and a half, and six elephants—this is the sequence.
(57) Ten [units] for *bārṇa*, ten and a half elephants (*gaja*), nine, and the number of suns (*ravi*)— that is, twelve— along with a row and a half, respectively. (4.135)
The ninefold group of Bhārṇa, the ninefold group with a half, the row itself,
the ninefold group numbering twelve (the sun), and the row with a half, indeed in sequence.
The ninefold [arrangement] of mercury, or eleven including the elephants, or the ninefold [arrangement] numbering twelve, and the row with a half, in sequence. (4.137)
The group of nine for the vowel *ya*, then five and a half elephants (*gaja*), likewise a row;
then a group of nine, numbering twelve (*ravi*), and after that eleven and a half.

The nine syllables of *rārṇa*, then eleven [syllables] equal to half an elephant (*gaja*), then nine [syllables] numbering as the sun (*ravi*), and finally five and a half lines, in due order. (4.139)
The ten [syllables] of *lārṇa*, the ten and a half [syllables] of *gaja*,
the nine [syllables] numbering as the sun (twelve), and likewise the five and a half lines.
For the Vārṇa [mantra], there are as many [syllables] as the number of Manus, and likewise the Viśvedevas;
with half a mora added, there are as many as the number of lunar days (tithis), and the Viśvas likewise with half a mora added.
There are eighteen and sixteen rows of the letters śa, ṣa, and sa;
then twenty-eight rows of the letter ha, and after that, twenty-six.
Thirty-one, thirty-seven, thirty-six, and immediately after that thirty-two; this sequence should be known, and this is also the sequence for the letter *kṣa*. (4.143)
Then, through knowledge, one may fully comprehend the supreme majesty of the entire multitude of phonemes, whose innate rays are intermingled.
There is no doubt in this matter; it is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise.
There are thirty syllables beginning with the letter *ka*, each corresponding to the sun, and likewise thirty more. (4.145)
The sequence of thirty-six for the ten syllables beginning with *ḍa* has been declared;
the number sixty is declared for the ten syllables beginning with *ba*. (4.146)
Thus, ninety syllables of the Vedas for the disputants have been declared;
and for the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, one hundred and eighty are said to be taught.
And for each of the vowels beginning with *a*, two hundred rays are taught;
from the root [vowels], twenty-five rays arise in sequence. (4.148)
The mixed rays should be known as twenty-two and a half individually;
the innate rays are separately two hundred and two and a half each. (4.149)
The rays that constitute the root of the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, numbering one hundred and eighty, should be known individually by the best of teachers. (4.150)
The rays are traditionally said to be mixed in groups of thirty each;
there are two hundred and seventy [rays] that are innate, occurring separately. (4.151)
Of the ten letters beginning with *ḍa*, there are three hundred and sixty;
they are the fundamental mixed [vowels], thirty-six in number, each distinct. (4.152)
The innate rays, which are indeed the fundamental basis for the letters beginning with *ba* and the tastes and colors, number two hundred and sixty-four. (4.153)
The sixty mixed [melodies] should be known by the number sixty;
the fifty-four original ones are separately [listed] in order as five hundred and forty.
The root rays of the nine hundred Vedic syllables of the disputants should be known individually; the mixed ones are ninety, each distinct. (4-155)
Beyond that, there are eight hundred and ten rays belonging to itself;
furthermore, for the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, there are one thousand rays above the eight hundred, which are the root rays.
One hundred and eighty rays are to be known as "mixed";
one thousand six hundred and thirty rays are the "innate" rays, respectively. (4.157)
All the Pārthiva [yantras] are to be known as three hundred and thirty-six;
the Āpya [yantras] are to be known as three hundred and twelve by the best of teachers. (4.158)
It should be known that there are three hundred and seventy-two solar rays;
it should be known that there are three hundred and twenty-four rays of wind. (4.159)
Four hundred and thirty-two rays are considered to be ethereal;
three hundred and eighty-four are recorded as being mental.
Thus, through the knowledge of the sequence of rays, one becomes Paraśiva directly;
there is nothing higher than this in the world for revealing the potency of mantra. (4.161)
This is indeed more secret than the secret; it must not be given to just anyone.
If it were given, there would be a loss of siddhi—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (4.162)

In the rite of immobilization (stambhana), mantras consisting primarily of earth elements should be understood as applicable here; for the rite of pacification (śāntika), mantras consisting primarily of water elements are recommended.
The Taijasa mantras are mostly of the nature of space (ākāśa), as are those for subjugation (vaśyaka) and also for the kārmaṇa rite;
however, for eradication (uccāṭana), Vāyavya mantras are recommended here. (4.164)
Mantras consist primarily of the mind and bestow liberation; of this there is no doubt.
When the Kuṇḍalinī power is awakened, the mantras attain consciousness. (4.165)
Having understood [this] correctly through the prescribed method from either the teacher or the scriptures,
both by way of the ascending sequence and also by way of the descending sequence.
Once the placement of the rays (raśminyāsa) has been performed, the mantras become effective at that very moment.
However, he who exerts effort regarding the potency of the mantras without the placement of the rays [will not succeed].
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of aeons;
however, in the Kālīmata, the rays are taught to be the bestowers of success. (4-168)
Thus, according to the Kālīmata, these are the rays of the Śrīvidyā.
I shall correctly describe the rays in the six wheels according to the Kādima-tantra:
the earth-elements (consonants) devoid of vowels, joined with the seven short vowels. (4.1)
Thirty-five [vowels] have been taught, and when joined with the long [vowels], they become seventy;
furthermore, from the perspective of their purity, there are fifteen [consonants] along with the bindu and the visarga. (4.2)
Three hundred kings have been enumerated, joined with five vowels; they are the udātta, anudātta, and svarita, designated by the number thirty.
Furthermore, those [vowels] are declared to be pure through the emission of the *bindu*;
thus, they number thirty-sixty, which is three hundred and forty-five. (4-4)
The rays are known as "intermingled" (saṅkīrṇa) by the best of teachers at the Mūlādhāra, the seat of the earth; they are known as "abiding in water" (jalāśraya) at the Maṇipūra. (4–5)
The rays are likewise said to reside in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the abode of fire; in the Anāhata, the temple of wind; in the Viśuddha, the dwelling of space; and so forth. (4–6)
In the *ājñācakra*, the location of the mind, there are indeed three syllables—*ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*—joined with the short and long vowels; beyond that, there are five more. (4.7)
These forty are declared; they are further [divided] with nasals, and likewise those without nasals, numbering ninety. (4.8)
Furthermore, these rays, consisting of the pure, the emission of the drop, and both together, are correctly said to be three hundred and sixty in number. (4.9)
The sixfold [elements], beginning with the earthly (pārthiva), have been declared as belonging to the vowels respectively;
for each individual letter, there are separately twenty-two and a half [units].
The sixfold [elements], beginning with the earthy, belong to the letters starting with *ka* and ending with *ra*;
for each single letter, there are thirty distinct [forms] each. (4-11)
The rays beginning with earth and so forth belong to the ten letters starting with *ḍa*;
for each single letter, a sequence of thirty-six is thus declared.
The earthy components and so forth of the six rasas and six colors are stated to be sixty for each individual color, respectively. (4.13)
For each of the disputants and for each of the letters of the Vedas, there are nine times ninety varieties of the sixfold [elements], beginning with earth, according to the stated form. (4-14)
In the two eyes, there are six kinds of rays, beginning with the earthly and so forth, in sequence;
they should be known as one hundred and eighty in each individual color.
In this way, two thousand one hundred and sixty rays expand within each and every wheel; these rays, though intermingled, remain distinct.
All the rays should be known as mixed; they are indeed twelve thousand, increased by ninety-six hundred. (4.17)
O Ambika, in the six joints, there are four hundred and sixty rays above and below;
thus, indeed, eight thousand rays are intermingled.
And having subtracted two thousand from one hundred and sixty more than that, there remain here forty-three thousand and two hundred. (4-19)
For the rays have been fully described as being the fundamental source;
they should be understood as innate, distributed according to their respective parts, and as previously mentioned, intermingled. (4.20)
"Half [of them] have the nature of the Sun, and half have the nature of the Moon. Thus it is said. In another Tantra:
"In the region of the throat, for each triad of the vowels and the three elemental letters..."
The rays of those respective elements are to be known through their division into three hundred parts. || 4-1 ||
For others, there are exactly five each;
for Visarga, however, there are one hundred and three as declared by the mental sons, while for others there are fourteen.
In the [consonant] groups beginning with *ka*, there is a sequence of one hundred and five wind-syllables;
for the other nine groups, there are exactly five wind-rays each.
The three fires belonging to Āgneya have one hundred and five rays each;
the other nine fires have only five rays each.
There are one hundred and twenty-five syllables for Dharā and Ārṇa;
for the other Rudra-syllables, there are ten earthly portions respectively.
There are one hundred and twenty-five [units] for the two, Jala and Arṇa;
for the other Rudra-syllables, there are ten Jala-aṃśus respectively.
Of the two syllables of Ākāśārṇa as well, there are indeed one hundred and twenty-five;
for each of the others, it should be known that there are ten each.
Within the ten-syllable [mantras] beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*, the rays of each respective element should be known separately;
clearly, they amount to one hundred and fifty.
For the other *vasu* (eight) and *varṇa* (sixteen) [elements], there are twelve and a half rays;
separately for the six syllables from *ba* to *la*, and for the two earth-syllables.
Furthermore, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the portions of the earth should be known as one hundred and sixty; the number of rows for the others should also be understood in that same way.
The rays of each of those elements, which illuminate the matrices of their respective elements, are to be well understood by the lords of teachers; there are three hundred for each one.
For the other three castes, however, there is a progression of twenty for each;
for those beginning with the Vārṇas and the four Vedas, the rays of water [are equal to] the waters. (4-12)
One hundred and fifty should be known for others, with a sequence of twenty;
for the second [group], one hundred and fifty, with others following a sequence of three sevens. (4.13)
In this [first group], the ethereal (nābhasa) letters are to be known; likewise for the third [group].
The aerial (vāyavya) letters of the letter *ha* are to be known in sequence as three hundred.
The number of the letter *kṣa* is sixty; there is no doubt that it does not belong to the ether (*nābhasa*).
The fire-portions (*agnyaṃśu*) of the letter *kṣa* should be known as three hundred. (4-15)
The number for Hārṇa shall be sixty; the others are equal [to that], without a doubt.
Thus has the sequence of rays been declared for the benefit of practitioners. (4.16)
O Pārvatī, it should be guarded with great effort like one's own private parts;
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who is not a devotee.
Furthermore, there would be a loss of accomplishment; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having learned [this] from the Guru and from the scriptures, one becomes directly Paraśiva. (4-18)
The vowels are renowned as sixteen; the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five;
and the pervasive letters (vyāpakas) are declared to be ten, having the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
They consist of the three qualities (guṇas) and, respectively, bestow desire, wealth, and dharma;
they consist of the three principles (tattvas) and have the nature of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
They consist of the three forms [of the deity], performing creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
they consist of the three abodes, and indeed possess the nature of the beginning, the middle, and the end.

I shall describe their majesty; listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, [to how it extends] from ascending through the positions situated horizontally, upwards, and downwards, down to descending. (4.22)
In both collective and individual forms, through reverse and direct order, by way of the three states, and through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader. (4.23)
Through the conjunction of the powers of the luminous energies in the form of phonemes,
and by means of the arrangement of Kuṇḍalinī as being essentially like a thread.
The thirty-eight *kalās* should be known as those that effect the potency of the mantra.
Of these, sixteen are declared to be the individual lunar *kalās* of the vowels in their proper sequence. (4.25)
In the absence of *mātrās* for the consonants (*sparśas*), there are six distinct solar *kalās* for each;
likewise, for the pervasive letters (*vyāpakas*), there are ten distinct fiery *kalās* for each. (4-26)
One should know that the number of *arghas* during the ascent is the same as during the descent;
thus, one should understand the digits (*kalās*) of the Sun to remain in their natural state in both cases. (4-27)
The lunar digits are indeed non-material (aprākṛta), and those of fire are likewise; there is no doubt.
It is taught that the digits of the letter *m* are seventy-six in number, according to their sequence in both ways.
Likewise, there are twenty-eight in the ascending order and exactly the same in the descending order;
these are declared to be one's own digits (kalās), whose form is the full mandala.
Through the attainment of the realization of its true nature by means of perfect yoga,
[one should recite] either one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times.
One should recite the mantra twenty-eight times with a concentrated mind;
thus endowed with vigor, the mantra will be accomplished without effort.
Those have been declared to you as the innate arts (nijāḥ kalāḥ); now hear, O beloved, about the mixed ones (saṃkīrṇāḥ).
Thereafter, for the twenty-eight syllables, there are thirty-eight [arts] individually.
The twelve syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ḍha* are remembered as belonging to the Sun;
the sixteen vowels belong to the Moon; and indeed, the ten beginning with *ya* belong to Fire.
There are one hundred and forty-four thousand [verses],
and likewise the *kalās* (phonemes) are mixed, taking on the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Thus they are said to be unmixed, numbering as many as the full mandala;
all those digits (kalās) are declared to be two thousand and twenty.
The mixed kalās of Māraṇa are declared to be one thousand four hundred and forty-four in their entirety.
Short vowels always possess masculine form, while long ones possess feminine form; that which is situated among the vowels, namely the group of four [semi-vowels], is neuter. (4.37)
Some of the letters beginning with *ka* are remembered as having masculine forms, some have feminine natures, some are neuter, and some indeed possess both natures. (4.38)
The letter *ma* alone is declared to be Puruṣa, who is Sadāśiva;
he is the form of the Bindu, the Self of all, the witness everywhere and at all times. (4.39)
And so, O Pārvatī, hear the true nature of the letters of the sky:
the letter *ha* is the supreme sky, and Sadāśiva is the form of the bindu.
The Puruṣa is devoid of qualities, stainless, pure, eternally embodied, and untainted;
yet the Puruṣa who possesses qualities is the letter *M*. (4.41)
The letter Śa is the sky consisting of water, beyond sound and stainless;
the letter Na, O Śivā, is of the nature of emptiness, the sky consisting of air.
The letter ṇa, joined with the earth [vowel], is clearly manifest as the form of space;
the letter ña is likewise described, and the letter ṅa has the nature of the wind.
The letters *ḷ* and *ḹ* are the colors of space, born from earth and fire;
O Supreme Goddess, now hear the nature of the colors of the vowels.
The letter Ya is Śiva, devoid of qualities, having the form of wind and consisting of vital breath;
the letter Ṣa is the living being, the life-force, and the vital air. (4.45)
The letter *pa* is the form of fire; the supreme *va* is the nature of touch.
The letter *ta* is the form of space (*vyoman*); *ya* is the wind that pervades the reality of all objects. (4-46)
The letter *ṭa* is of the nature of a pillar; the subsequent *vāyu* (the letter *ya*) consists of earth.
The letter *ca* is the wind consisting of fire; it is Maheśvara in a gentle form. (4.47)
The letter *ka* is the wind whose nature is space (*khātman*), which deludes all the worlds;
the letter *e* is the form of Rudra, while the supreme [letter *m*] is the wind whose nature is the ether (*vyoman*).
The letter *ā* is the form consisting of sound; the supreme [letter] is wind whose nature is fire. The letter *a* is wind endowed with qualities, the imperishable storehouse of lights. (4-49)
O Pārvatī, listen as I describe the essential nature of the letters of fire-colored [syllables]:
the letter *ra* is the supreme, partless consciousness of all seed-syllables. (4–50)
The syllable of Fire is pure and serves the purpose of purification;
the letter *kṣa* pervades the Wind and is the color of the Wind endowed with qualities.
The letter *pha* is the nature of fire, yet its form is space, being higher than the highest.
The letter *tha* has the form of space, yet it is of the nature of fire with a manifest body. (4-52)
The letter *ṭha* is fire, yet has the form of the moon; it is a syllable whose nature is water.
The letter *cha* consists of both water and fire, and it effects the immobilization of all things. (4.53)
The letter *kha* has the color of wind and pervades the air; the letter *e* has the color of fire and is higher than the highest.
The letter *ai* is fire, possessing the form of wind, and is the life-force of the meaning of all mantras.
The syllable *i* is fire, consisting of the threefold brilliance; it is the syllable of Śakti.
The syllable *ī* is fire in the form of wind, the supreme essence of all seeds. (4–55)
Listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved, to the essential nature of the letters of the earth-element:
