the letter *la* is the color of the earth, devoid of qualities, supreme, and imperishable. (4–56)
The letter *la* is endowed with qualities, has the color of the earth, and is of the nature of air; it is supreme.
The letter *ba* is of the nature of nectar, has the color of the earth, and is the supreme, imperishable one. (4-57)
The letter *da* is of the nature of fire, Śambhu, the great lord, and the phoneme of earth;
the letter *ḍa* shall be the phoneme of the earth... || 4-58 ||

The letter *ja* should be known as having the nature of nectar; the letter *bha* has the color of the earth and bestows nectar. The letter *ga* is of the form of air, while the letter *kṣa* has the color of the earth and acts as a restrainer.
The syllable *o* is of the nature of space (*vyoma*), while the letter *dha* is higher than the highest.
The syllable *ū* is of the nature of fire and is Śambhu; the letter *ra* has the form of the universe. (4.60)
The syllable *ukāra* is of the nature of air, while the letter *ha* is the supreme, all-pervading one. O Maheśvarī, listen as I describe the essential nature of the letters of water. (4–61)
The syllable *va* is the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*), the supreme Śiva devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
The syllable *sa* has the form of the moon; it is the phoneme of Śakti, bearing the form of water. (4.62)
The syllable *bha* is of the nature of the earth; the supreme Śiva is the letter of water (*ja*).
The syllable *dha* is of the nature of space; Maheśvara is the letter of water (*pa*). (4–63)
The syllable *ḍha* is the letter of water, all-pervading, and of the nature of earth;
the syllable *jha* is of the nature of air, the letter of water, and the imperishable Puruṣa. (4.64)
The syllable *gha* is the form of wind, the great lord who is the ocean of water;
the syllable *au* is the form of space, the ocean of water that pervades the sky. (4.65)
The vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* should be known as having the nature of fire, while the vowels *lṛ* and *lṝ* are of the form of water;
thus, O Supreme Goddess, the majesty of the letters of the Mātṛkā has been declared to you. (4.66)

The threefold arrangement of the fires has been explained to you according to their colors and forms; by means of those forms, one should constantly contemplate the mantras through the process of visualization.
Know that the manifestation of the potency of mantra is concealed within all mantras;
recollecting the potency of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should recite it with a concentrated mind. (4.68)
"In a very short time, the accomplishment of mantra arises. Thus, in the *Śrītantrarāja*:
"O wise one, listen to the potency of mantra; I shall describe that which is the abode of happiness."
By which mere consciousness a person becomes liberated while living. || 4-1 ||
It is the cause of the luminaries, of those whose forms are power, and even of the phenomenal world;
and it is declared to be the cause of these three qualities as well. (4.2)
The accomplishment of the contemplation on its true nature is declared to be "perfection" (samyaktva);
that is designated as the potency of the mantra, and it is said to be the very life-force of mantras. (4.3)
The lack of perfection regarding mantras indeed arises from speaking of them to the unworthy, from constant practice at improper times, and from doubt. (4-4)
Due to contempt for the guru, from sins, through engagement in prohibited conduct, by hostility toward the deity, and by the instability of slandering everyone; || 4-5 ||
Due to lack of tradition, ignorance, or even from various types of devotion, that by which rightness (samyaktva) may arise—its vigor has been described first. (4.6)
Thus, in the *Uttaratantra*:
"I shall proclaim the potency of mantra for the benefit of practitioners;
through ignorance of which, mantras certainly become devoid of consciousness. (4.1)
From the root center up to the aperture of Brahmā, one should contemplate the Goddess, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns,
resembling ten million flashes of lightning, and composed of the splendor of ten million moons.

The supreme [goddess], who brings about the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world; who is the digit of consciousness consisting of gnosis; whose form consists of the thirty-eight digits; and who is composed of all mantras.

O Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times according to the various methods such as stringing [the beads];
by thus removing all defects, the mantra becomes potent.
Thus, O Pārvatī, that which has been declared as the fourfold manifestation of the potency of mantra must be guarded with great effort, like one's own private parts.
Listen, O wise one, to the power of the mantra in its various forms, specifically that form which it assumes at the time of initiation during the act of bestowing grace upon oneself. (4.37)
O Supreme Goddess, by means of the Śrī Guru’s attentive [instruction],

The meaning is that the manifestation (*vyakti*) is the "peg" (*kīlaka*) for the consonants (*hal*), which are otherwise inexpressible; through their conjunction with vowels, they become clearly expressible.
For it has been stated in that very same work: "Indeed, the inexpressible consonants become manifested by means of [their] power (*śakti*)."

In the *Siddhasārasvata-tantra*: "On the palm and back of the right hand, on the fingers beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger, and on the left [hand], from the little finger to the palm. (4.1)
O Goddess of gods, O Beloved, one should place the sixteen vowels alone;
their placement up to the palm of the right hand is declared to be *saṃhāra*.
O Goddess, one should place [the syllables] joined with the *visarga* from the palm of the right hand up to the palm of the left hand; this is proclaimed as the "Emission" (*sṛṣṭi*).
One should place [the letters] starting from the little finger of the left hand up to the thumb;
then again, the eight vowels beginning with *ḷ*, joined with the *bindu* and the *sarga*.
O Goddess, O Beloved, from the palm of the right hand up to the little finger,
the placement of the vowels from *a* to *ṝ* is declared to be the *sthiti-nyāsa*.

One should place the letters beginning with *ta* and ending with *śa*, one by one, sequentially upon the five fingers of the left hand, starting from the little finger, across their respective joints.

O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise place [the letters] from *ka* to *ṇa* in the right hand, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger, according to the sequence of maintenance (*sthiti*).
O beautiful one, one should simultaneously place the five syllables beginning with *ha* upon the fingers,
starting from the thumb, as the pervasive [mantra] (*vyāpaka*).
Having thus performed the purification of the hands with the letters of the Mātṛkā, O Maheśvarī,
one should subsequently perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the method that will be described.
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra:
"Then the best of teachers should perform the placement of her six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Between *am* and *ām* shall be the *ka*-group; between *im* and *īm* shall be the *ca*-group. (4.1)
The ṭa-group [of consonants] is situated between *um* and *ūm*; the ta-group is between *em* and *aim*;
the pa-group is between *om* and *aum*, as well as between the anusvāra and the visarga.

One should place these fifty syllables, endowed with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) and auspicious marks (*lakṣa*), along with the two groups of *yaś* vowels. One should meditate on her whose crest is marked by a crescent moon, who has three eyes, whose limbs are pervaded in sequence by the fifty letters,
who possesses the luster of the autumnal moon and the *kunda* flower, and who is burdened by the weight of her breasts.
I worship the Blessed Lady seated upon a lotus throne, who holds in her lotus-like hands a gift, a rosary, a beautiful vessel filled with the essence of nectar, and a sacred book. 4-1.
Having first projected [the letters] within the six supports (ādhāras), the knower of mantras should then project the letters from *a* to *kṣa* upon the body externally.
Thus, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti*: "One should properly place the vowels upon the lotus with six petals at the throat;

"One should place the internal *mātṛkā* [syllables] as 'ha' and 'kṣa' on the two petals in the middle of the eyebrows.

One should place [the mantras] on the nose, cheeks, lips, and teeth, as well as on the head and face.

One should place [the mantras] on the heart, the base of the left arm, the hump [of the back], the base of the right arm, and at the heart and other such locations, as well as on the pair of hands and feet, and on the belly and face.
Having drawn that [lotus] with its pericarp joined by the *vyomānta* (the letter *ha*) and the *saura* (the letter *ra*), and having written the pair of vowels (*e* and *ai*) upon the filaments,

one should then write the eight groups of consonants (*varga-aṣṭaka*) surrounded by the "city of the earth" (*bhūmipura*, the square) in the directions, and joined with the letters *va* and *kṣa* at the corners.
On this pedestal, which is endowed with nine powers (*navaśakti*), one should worship the Goddess.

Then, having worshipped the eight groups, one should worship their powers in sequence.

The practitioner of mantra should then worship Dhāriṇī, Mālinī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Haṃsinī, and likewise Śāntinī; immediately after that, he should worship Brāhmī and the others.
The wise one should worship the world-protectors and their weapons in due order;

One should perform oblations with pure sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets (madhuratra) using one-tenth of that [number]; thereafter, being composed in mind, one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites.

Gold, silver, and likewise copper— these sixteen types of substances, measured according to the directions, when properly fashioned from them, constitute the *rucaka* which grants all desires.

Meditating on her in the form of a lamp-flame, one should drink [the essence] from that [flame], which is the presiding deity of the fire-oblation (*homa*). In the morning, one should meditate on [the deity] residing within the orb of the moon upon the crown of the head for the sake of all prosperity.
Through consecration, through wearing, through worship when fashioned from metal, and through installation in the house or other locations, the yantra bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (4.2)

Thus [it is said]. Now, this is also the meaning of the previously mentioned verse: at the time of dawn, one should visualize the aforementioned yantra, containing the name of the desired object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), within the lunar orb situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus located at the *brahmarandhra*; by that means, the attainment of its fruit occurs. Or else—
Alternatively, having engraved this yantra upon the ground with vermilion or other substances, one should place a water-pot (kumbha) there according to the previously mentioned procedure,

fill it with water infused with colored medicinal herbs, worship the Goddess therein, and through consecration (abhiṣeka), the attainment of one's desired fruit occurs. Or else, by writing [the mantra] on birch bark or similar material and wearing it according to the prescribed rite, [the same result is achieved].

By worshipping the Goddess according to the previously mentioned procedure in a yantra fashioned from gold or other materials, and by installing one fashioned from copper or other metals in a house or similar location according to the prescribed rite down to its placement within the earth, the attainment of one's desired fruit occurs.

The meaning of the second verse is as follows: therein, for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the entire circle of deities (*devatācakra*), one should engrave the *yantra* upon a cloth made from any one of gold, silver, copper, or other materials; having written in the center the name of each respective deity ending in the vocative case followed by the words "be present" (*sannidhehi*), one should perform the ritual of vitalization (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Having prepared that [image] there and worshipped the Goddess with the Mātṛkā-mantra, the knower of reality, being full of the Self, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while touching that yantra. Then, having first firmly established that well-worshipped wheel within the ground, he should install upon it the form of his own chosen deity according to the prescribed rite. When this has been done, in that image... of her—

The presence of the deity becomes especially manifest, and every desired fruit accrues to the one who installs [the image]. Now, whatever specific varieties of nyāsa exist for this Mātṛkā, all their worship, ritual service, and so forth, must be performed according to the very rules already declared. As stated in the Uttaratantra:
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of this [mantra] near the point (bindu) by means of the withdrawal (saṃhāra) visualization;
the sages and so forth previously mentioned, as well as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), should be applied in the same manner. 4-1.
Having reflected, one should place [the letters] according to the path of emanation, conjoined with emanation;

The seer is declared to be Prajāpati; the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed;

The limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the fixed vowels occurring in pairs of short and long;

O Goddess, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is proclaimed as the presiding deity.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed with the groups of consonants as before, joined with the six long vowels and ending with the word Kāma. 4–5.
One should place [the letters] preceded by Rudra, joined with the third vowel (Ū), ending with the Heart (HṚM);
likewise, one should place the letters beginning with YA, conjoined with the elements, together with the Prāṇa, Śakti, and Ātman.
The sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and O Goddess, Ardhanārīśvara is proclaimed as the deity. (4.7)

O Goddess, the most excellent practitioner should install the six-limbed [mantra] using the third consonant of each group joined with the six long vowels, beginning with Māyā (the syllable *Hrīm*) from the Mātṛkā. 4-8.

O lotus-eyed one, one should place the Mātṛkā joined with the seed-syllable of desire; O beloved, the sage is Sammohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is [the one previously mentioned].

the six limbs [of the ritual] are formed by the groups of consonants joined with the long vowel and the letter *ka*.
O Dear One, one should install the Mātṛkā seated upon Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Smara;

First, one should [worship] Mahāgaṇapati, who consists of the five mantras, bestows the attainment of all siddhis, and is accompanied by his ṛṣi, meter, and deity. (4.15) p. 65)

The sage (ṛṣi) of the mantra of the sacrifice of proliferation (prapañcayāga) is declared to be Brahmā; the supreme primordial goddess is proclaimed [as the deity], and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). || 4-21 ||
O beloved, that which is called the Great (Mahas) is the supreme deity consisting of pure consciousness;
it is eternally awakened at the end of the three Vedas, all-pervading, and stainless.
Together with the five mantras recited in reverse order, along with the syllables of Hari and Hara,

The first mantra here is considered to begin with the letter 'A' and end with the letter 'Śa';
the second mantra is desired to begin with the letter 'Ha' and end with the letter 'Kṣa'. (4.26)

The third [vowel] is also declared to consist of the letter *sa*, the letter *a*, and the bindu; and with the addition of the visarga (*sarga*) to the letters *sa* and *a*, it becomes the essence of the six sense organs. (4.27)
And the fourth [syllable] is also formed by the letters *sa*, *ka*, *ra*, *ha*, *a*, *kāra*, and the bindu;
because of its extensive application, Brahmā is here designated as the Sage (*muni*). (4.28)
The wise have declared that the word *parama* expresses the most excellent meaning;
because it protects (*trāyate*) one who sings (*gāyantam*), it is called the *gāyatra* meter.
Since no excellence whatsoever exists among lights, that is called the Supreme State, the Supreme Light, and the Deity. (4.30)

This word *sva* has the meaning of "heaven" (*svarga*), and it may likewise have the meaning of "self" (*ātman*). Furthermore, the prefix *ha-* has the meaning of "loss" (*hāni*) as well as "going" (*gati*); therefore, from every perspective, [the term *svahā*] possesses these meanings. (4-31)
That succession of pervasive light which is the true nature of the heavenly self,
and in which the oblation is declared to be offered with the utterance of "svāhā"— [that is the path].
That which is pervaded by the form of light is designated by the word "with-sound" (saśabda);
the Self is also denoted by the word "I" (ahaṃ). Therefore, the identity of these two comes about. (4.33)
Therefore, according to the rule in the mantra, one should then say "I" (ahaṃ) after the letter *ha*;
by this word "he" (*saḥ*), [one refers to] that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and the illuminator of all objects.
Then one should utter the Haṃsa-mantra, which is true, all-pervading, and untainted;
it is the essence of the moving and unmoving world and consists of the qualities (guṇas).

The progenitor of all worlds is said to be [Māyā] by means of the seed-syllable *māyābīja*, through the three seed-syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *ma*, which consist of the [three] qualities (*guṇas*). (4.36)
That which effects the reality of existence is said to be the meaning of the *praṇava*; the root *hṛ* has the sense of "taking away" that which is undesirable for the practitioner. (4.37)
One should certainly withdraw that aforementioned *mahas* by means of the syllables *ha*, *ri*, *ha*, and *ra*.
This is the mantra of the *prapañca-yāga*, the primordial cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
The sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (prapañcayāga) has been explained; it is that by which the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed.
Here, the oblation (homa) with the limbs [of the mantra] and with substances in the fire is considered to be of two kinds. (4.39)
Having joined [the letters] beginning with 'a' according to the previous procedure,
the knower of the ritual should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the locations mentioned by the Mother using the eight-syllable mantra.
The supreme practitioner, whose self is perfectly purified, [should recite this] fifty times every day;
for all the phonemes are renowned as being of the nature of the external organs of cognition. (4.41)
Therefore, the world is pervaded by those [senses], each of which is perceivable by its respective faculty;
yet, that which is the light of Īśa, which exists in the world as higher than the highest—|| 4-42 ||
That which is performed as an oblation in that fire of Brahman by mantra-knowing priests who are composed of light and are proficient in the mantras, they call [the Brahmahoma]. (4.43)
The offering of sacrificial materials consisting of the Brahman-self to the Brahman-knower as the recipient has thus become lax, differentiated by the distinctions of social classes (varṇas). 4-44.
The body is bound with skin, filled with an abundance of blood, joined with fat, marrow, and bones, and is regarded as being subject to transience. (4.45)

He who, being skillful, a practitioner of mantra, pure in soul, and a treasury of greatness, offers oblations into the fire of Brahman—which is exceedingly clear, all-pervading, and stainless—is truly successful. (4.46)
Only he is authorized for the complete recitation of mantras, for meditation, and for the rite of worship; no other is a partaker of the fruit.

Even when solitary, it ends with the *bindu*; when combined with the principles beginning with *kalā* and the deities beginning with Keśava, it is joined with those beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and endowed with the seed-syllable of *māyā*. (4.48)
The ten nyāsas are proclaimed as follows: those beginning with Lakṣmī, those beginning with the Kāma-bīja, and those joined with the three seed-syllables, all conjoined with the Prapañca-yāga.
All [these rites] are established within all mantras as bestowers of desired objects;
among these, the sacrifice called Prapañca is declared to be the most excellent. (4–50)
"It bestows knowledge, bestows nourishment, and likewise brings about all prosperity;
it specifically effects the destruction of the ignorance arising from the manifold expansion of the planets and minor obstacles.
(4.51) Thus, the fire-oblation is prescribed simply by means of the *prapañca* ritual.
Whatever substances, in whatever manner, and whenever they are obtained by the wise; || 4-52 ||
I shall explain all of this exactly as it is, according to the prescribed ritual,
beginning from the aforementioned procedure and ending with the rite dedicated to Gaṇapati.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with clarified butter; likewise, he should offer a single oblation with ghee using the *prapañcayāga* mantra thereafter.

Fuel-sticks produced from the *vaṭa* and *udumbara* trees, as well as those of *parpaṭī* and *pippala*, along with sesame, white mustard, oblation, and clarified butter, [should be offered] in sequence.
Parpaṭī and Plakṣa—
these eight substances are prescribed; the knower of mantras should offer them according to the rule ten thousand times, or even half of that.
Having enjoyed there the pleasures as he desired, he indeed attains happiness;
then, at the end of the body, he obtains the liberation sought by the sages.
It removes the evils caused by thieves, enemies, malefic planets, diseases, serpents, and rākṣasas;
it is considered that four hundred, or half of that, or half of that again, [of oblations] have been offered. (4.58)
One should increase the number of oblations according to each specific defect;
he who performs the fire-offering with the eight substances for as many thousands as there are suns (twelve thousand) [attains success].
Furthermore, by doubling or even quadrupling this [number],
he shall destroy possession by spirits, possession by grahas, fever, and other such ailments.

For one who performs recitation, worship, and so forth by violating the sequence prescribed in the scriptures, there will be a lapse of memory; he [should perform] a fire-oblation with the eight substances.
One should perform [the rite] a thousand times; one becomes healthy at that very moment.
Furthermore, he who offers oblations with the eight substances two thousand times for each [deity], || 4.62 ||
He shall destroy epilepsy, forgetfulness, and the evil effects of curses;
indeed, he who offers one hundred thousand oblations of the eight substances smeared with the three sweets [will achieve this].
By the manifestation of that great sovereignty at that very moment,
the great fortune of the Lord of Gods would become insignificant compared to it.
He who offers one hundred thousand or fifty thousand oblations of the eight substances soaked in the three sweets within the course of three years, [attains the desired result].
The entire three worlds remain under his control; it is not otherwise.
The accomplishment of subjugation and other rites is proclaimed as that which one should perform by offering the eight substances into the fire.

One should understand the decrease, increase, and so forth in the fire-oblation (homa) according to the gravity of the task. He who performs a hundred thousand oblations with pure sesame seeds according to the prescribed rule— || 4.67 ||
His great sins quickly go to destruction; it is not otherwise.
By offering one hundred thousand lotuses into the fire, great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) arises. (4–68)
An oblation of clarified butter (havis) bestows nourishment; an oblation of barley brings glory;
and an oblation of jasmine flowers (mālatī) shall grant complete subjugation over all.
Having offered sea salt, one should likewise accomplish subjugation (*vaśya*).
Then, one should grind very finely the rice grains produced from *śāli* paddy. (4.70)

The practitioner, having fashioned an image of the person to be acted upon with that very powder mixed with the three sweets, and having worshipped it thoroughly while touching it, [should perform the rite]. (4.71)
The practitioner of mantra should recite the *prāṇasthāpana* mantra one hundred and eight times;
having divided that [number], he should perform oblations at night with a mind not attached to anything else.
Performing this for seven nights, one brings under control instantly either a man or a woman; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (4.73)
Such is the fruit even of a doll made of sea salt,
when it is filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) processed with pigments and medicinal herbs.
Having placed [the vessel] upon the hearth, one should kindle the fire beneath the jar;
once that fire has appeared in the jar, one should offer clarified butter as an oblation into it.

The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over the ashes that have fallen; having consecrated them that many times, he should take them up, for they bestow all accomplishments.
Through consuming it, through smearing it on the body, through making a tilaka mark, and likewise by wearing it upon the head, all calamities are instantly destroyed. (4.77)
It destroys the afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, piśācas, poisons, diseases, and the like;
it brings everything under control for men and bestows fortune, good luck, and victory. (4.78)
At that time, the wise man should perform a fire-oblation numbering one thousand for the guru,
and he should also give a gift of gold, either a full *pala* or half a *pala*.

Just as the gods obtain their desired fruit from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkḥa), even so the practitioner attains his goal through the ritual of the sacrifice of phenomenal expansion (prapañcayāga). || 4.80 ||

Thus [it is said]. Now, in this manner, the procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra has been described for both the worshippers of the Mātṛkā-vidyā and the worshippers of other vidyās; likewise, in the Kālīmata it is stated:
"I shall explain the Prāṇāgnihotra, which bestows all accomplishments."
For the benefit of the entire world, and especially for the sake of the ministers.
Having first assumed the lotus posture on a pure seat in a clean place,
he sits with a serene mind, facing the east, his consciousness steady. (4.2)
The Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa) is marked by the syllable *ha*, which is of the nature of *sattva*;
it is surrounded by the middle [vowel] of that same [syllable], which is the *rajas* of the left eye.
One should contemplate the Mūlādhāra as a triangle enveloped by the syllable *ra* and by darkness (*tamas*), located in the southeast, southwest, and northwest corners.
In the center, as well as in the east, west, north,
and south— one who knows the mantras should visualize five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) within that very level ground.
For the successful accomplishment of his own duties, he must maintain the fires that burn perpetually—
the Gārhapatya, the Sabhya, and likewise the Āhavanīya.
Furthermore, it is declared that the *anvāhārya* fire should become the *gārhapatya*;
thus, by way of the sequence beginning with the middle, these indeed exist according to their names. (4.7)
For [it arises] from the stainless one whose nature is knowledge, which is the cause of the blazing radiance;
and from the stainless Kalpāditya, whose nature is Mūlaprakṛti.

The practitioner of mantra [should contemplate] the Mātṛkā, which has issued forth from the Supreme Self— the Hotṛ of all phonemes— residing within the twelve [spokes], and which consists of the outpouring of nectar.

The preceptor should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in those sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) where the blazing fires are present, using his intellect to divide [the mantra] letter by letter according to the reverse order.
Their *kṣa*-letters and so forth shall resemble emeralds and possess five colors;
likewise, their *śa*-letters and so forth, ending with the five [consonants], shall indeed have the luster of *gomeda* stones.

Those that are blue-colored are to be intoxicated; those resembling coral are not to be eaten; and those with a sound like a thunderbolt are proclaimed to be as [many] as there are [of the former]. || 4-12 ||
Those with edges like rubies and lovely colors like lapis lazuli are the eight *svaras*; beyond that, there are those with the luster of pearls and the luster of rubies.
These nine groups are proclaimed to consist of the nine gems: Ketu, Rāhu (Vidhuntuda), Śani (Manda), Vākpati, and Budha; || 4-14 ||
Bhārgava, Bhauma, Candra, and Bhāskara are proclaimed as the nine;
these are indeed the lords of the nine divisions and the presiding deities of the gems.
Those wise ones who perform the fire sacrifice (homa) daily according to this procedure fifty times shall become honored throughout the three worlds. (4.16)
Those who are rich in gold, garments, and other such things are fortunate and destined for auspicious results; I shall now declare which castes are to be offered as oblations in which [fires].
And that sixth is Samvartaka; likewise, there are those ending with the group of five.
Following that are Ṣoḍaśasvara, Jhiṇṭīśa, and Varghīśa. (4-18)
One should duly offer these ten oblations into the fire-pit called Āvasathya:
the syllable *dharā*, the fourth of the vowels, and the fourth of each of the consonant groups.
Then, the knower of mantras should subsequently offer oblations into the sacrificial pit called Sabhya for these ten [deities], namely Mastaka, Harākhya, and Amareśa.
And Nakulīśa is the sixth; likewise, the third letters of the [five] groups, as well as Sadyojāta and Antasthāṇuka, and Vāmanetra, are to be mastered in sequence. (4.21)
Let him offer oblations according to the prescribed order into the Āhavanīya fire-pit:
the seventh and second [syllables] of each group, as well as the second syllables of the groups.

One should offer oblations of these syllables in sequence into the fire-pit named Anvāhārya, which follows immediately after the one called Sūkṣma, [the syllables] known as Bhautika, Anta, Tithi, and Īśa.
Vāyuṣaṣṭha, Vāyu, the five beginning with the first of the groups (the *varga* letters), the five *pādika*s, Adhara, Kriyā, and Nārāyaṇa— these ten.
The practitioner, composed in mind, should offer oblations into the fire-pit designated as the *gārhapatya*;
thus has the syllable-oblation (*varṇahoma*) been duly proclaimed in its proper sequence. (4.25)
The knower of mantras should then offer all that has arisen as sound, which is equal to space, into the sacrificial pit known as the *āvasathya*. (4.26)
The practitioner of mantras should offer that quality [of sound] into the eastern fire-pit with air, and form into the western one with fire; he should offer the collection of tastes with milk.

Immediately thereafter, the master of mantras who seeks power should offer all types of fragrances into the fire-pit called Uttara in the north, and then into the one in the south, using the Dharā-mantra.
Day and night, one should perform oblations in sacrificial pits resembling the blazing fire of universal dissolution, joined with the phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
The Self, whose nature is eternal purity, supreme bliss, and consciousness, is born.
The fixed [sequence] beginning with *māyā* and ending with *ajapā-homa* is as before. (4.30)
Having performed the placement [of the syllables] fifty times according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner becomes liberated while living and becomes long-lived. (4.31)
"By his splendor he is like the sun; he is the creator and the destroyer, like Śambhu.

This is its meaning: there, having sat down facing east upon a soft seat in the *padmāsana* posture, [one should contemplate] within one's own *mūlādhāra*, which possesses the characteristics previously described, the seed-mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī by means of the quality of *sattva*.

Having contemplated the Mūlādhāra as a triangular fire-mandala, whose central region is occupied by the letter *ha*, which is surrounded by its vowel *ī* (representing the quality of *rajas*), and which is encircled by its consonant *ra* (representing the quality of *tamas*), with its corners situated in the directions of the East, the Southwest, and the Northwest.
In its center, in the east, west, north, and south, there were five sacrificial pits known as the Āvasathya, Sabhya, Āhavanīya, Anvāhārya, and Gārhapatya, filled with blazing flames of fire.
Having contemplated them as bestowers of desired objects,
as the causes of the reflection of the light of all splendors, and as consisting of undivided consciousness;

One should mentally offer the phonemes (*varṇa*)—which consist of the *Mūlaprakṛti*, the *Śabdabrahman* that is the cause of all phonemes, and which reside at the *dvādaśānta*—into the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) whose cavities flash with the flames of the fire at the end of the aeon (*kalpānta*), according to the sequence to be described hereafter. Regarding this, he states that the phonemes possess the colors of jewels: "They would be... and so forth, because they are the presiding deities (*adhidaivata*) of the jewels.

He teaches the planets, beginning with "Ketu" and so forth. He describes the *homa* (fire-offering) for those who have been meditated upon as having the color of jewels due to their nature of being composed of nectar, saying "the *homa*. With the verses beginning with "Saṃvartaka," he shows the letters to be offered into each of the five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) among the fifty letters; "Saṃvartaka" refers to the letter *kṣa*.
The sixth [letter] in reverse order is *śa*; the final letters of the five groups (*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*) in reverse order are *ma*, *ṇa*, *ña*, *ṅa*;
the sixteenth vowel is *aḥ*; *Jhiṇṭīśa* is *e*; and *Arghīśa* is *ha*.
One should offer these ten syllables into the fire-pit named Āvasathya. *Dharā* is *la*; the fourth letter of *Vālī* is *va*.

One should offer these ten syllables into the assembly fire in reverse order: *bha*, *dha*, *ḍha*, *jha*, *gha*; *ma* (the head), *ha* (Hara); *ḷ* (Amareśa); and *u* (Indra). Then: *ha* (Nakulīśa), its sixth [consonant] *la*;
the third letters of the classes, *ba*, *da*, *ḍa*, *ja*, *ga*; *au* (ending with Sadyojāta); and *ḷ* (Sthāṇuka).
The left eye is the syllable *ī*. One should offer these ten syllables into the Āhavanīya fire:

[the seventh and second of the vowels (*ya* and *u*), the letter *sa*, the letter *ra*, the second letters of the five classes (*pha*, *tha*, *ṭha*, *cha*, *kha*), the final letter of the bhūtas (*o*), the Lord of the lunar days (*ṛ*), the subtle (*i*). One should offer these ten syllables into the Anvāhārya fire. The sixth of the winds is the letter *ṣa*.

The letter *ya* is Vāyu; the first letters of the [consonant] groups, *pa*, *ta*, *ṭa*, and *ca*; the vowel *ai*; the action (*kriyā*) which is the vowel *ṛ*; Nārāyaṇa which is the letter *ā*—one should offer these ten syllables into the Gārhapatya fire. This is the ritual of oblation (*homakriyā*). As for the method of oblation: one should offer each syllable individually into each pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the sequence beginning with *oṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā*.

One should offer oblations again and again. The procedure for this is as follows: one should offer the syllable *kṣa* into the *āvasathya*, *la* into the *sabhya*, *ha* into the *āhavanīya*, *sa* into the *anvāhārya*, and *ṣa* into the *gārhapatya*. Then, in that same sequence, one should offer five syllables at a time, beginning with *śa* and ending with *ya*. Now, regarding this, the scripture states: "The syllable *aḥ* is Brahman."
The remaining syllable 'A' should be meditated upon here in every way as the form of Brahman.
Now, regarding those practitioners who act in this manner, the *Uttaratantro* states concerning the *prāṇāgnihotra* to be performed at the time of eating:
"If one takes food every day according to this procedure..."
Then the sacrificial pits, such as the gārhapatya and others, are the vital airs (vāyus), beginning with prāṇa. || 4-1 ||
One should extract the names of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) together with the seventh [case-ending];
likewise, one should extract the names of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, ending in the seventh case.
The colors follow immediately after *hiraṇya*, and likewise after *gagana*;
they occur at the end of *rakta*, at the end of *kṛṣṇa*, and similarly at the end of *suprabha*. (4.3)

Having uttered the words "śucayaḥ padam," one should then recite "pāvakāḥ. Having performed the ritual spreading of the fire (agniviharaṇa), one should then speak of oneself, ending with the word "agni."
One should subsequently extract the syllable to be treated as above, below, and across;
then one should likewise state the syllable above as below, across, and above. (4–5)

One should extract the five mantras ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā). After that, one should utter the word "vaiśvāpada," and then, having become "nara" (man), one should speak the word "pada. (4–6)
"I offer food"—thus one should say; "the foot" (pada), and then one should perform the fourfold foot.
"I cook"—thus one should speak as the foot; according to the rule, one should utter the foot. || 4-7 ||
Having uttered everything ending with "svāhā" with devotion until their satisfaction,
the knower of mantras should first perform a silent oblation (tūṣṇīṃ homa) using consecrated food.

Having drunk a handful of water with the mantra beginning with "amṛta," one should then perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the rules and subsequently carry out the purification sipping.
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending as far as the *dvādaśānta*, one should meditate upon the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as eternally pervading the universe, never departing from it. (4.10)
It is established in its own nature, auspicious, peaceful, devoid of beginning and end, supreme,
and well-satisfied by the offering of pure oblations.
Having thus consumed food dripping with nectar, sprinkled with fifty syllables, and offered as a sacrificial oblation (havis), the practitioner of mantra becomes ablaze with the five fires.
The practitioner who performs the Prāṇāgnihotra rite both morning and evening never experiences the suffering born of dwelling in a womb.
The meaning of this is as follows: first, the five mantras beginning with *prāṇa* are extracted by means of the verses beginning with *gārhapatye*.

This is the sense: in the *gārhapatya* fire, which is the *prāṇa*, may the golden-colored, pure, purifying [flames], having spread out the fire and served the Self, go upward—*svāhā*. In the *anvāhārya* fire, which is the *apāna*, [may] those of the color of the sky...

The pure, purifying [fires], having distributed the fire and attended upon the self, let them go downward; svāhā! In the Āhavanīya, in the Vyāna breath, the red-colored, pure, purifying [fires], having distributed the fire and attended upon the self, let them go crosswise; svāhā! In the Sabhya, in the Udāna breath, the black-colored, pure, purifying [fires] the fire...

"Having spread out [the fire] and served oneself, may they go upward, svāhā! In the domestic fire, being common, possessing excellent luster and color, pure and purifying, having spread out [the fire] and served oneself, may they go downward and across, svāhā!
Having offered five oblations into the five sacrificial pits with these mantras,

In the Gārhapatya, Anvāhārya, Āhavanīya, Sabhya, and Āvasathya fires, and in the prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna breaths, there are [deities] with the colors of gold, sky-blue, red, black, and beautiful luster. (p.

Being pure and purifying, having distributed the fire and worshipped the Self, [one should think]: "Becoming Vaiśvānara, I offer food; I cook the fourfold food. By this procedure, [one should offer] with the mantra: "May they go equally upwards, downwards, and across—Svāhā! [This applies] to the Gārhapatya, Anvāhārya, Āhavanīya, Sabhya, and Āvasathya fires.
Having visualized [the deities] situated in the center between Yama, Śaśin, Varuṇa, and Indra,

and having offered oblations with portions larger than those previously prescribed, one should afterwards eat with the intention that it is a fire-oblation until satiety, and then sip water from the hollowed palms while reciting the mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar."
One should perform the pure ritual sipping of water (*śuddhācamana*). Regarding the fruit obtained by doing so, he says "in the morning and evening," and so forth.

Having meditated upon the *visarga* as two lunar discs emerging from the letter *A*, which are being sprinkled with a stream of nectar flowing from the *bindu* of the *prapañca*, [one should sip] from those two.

By means of the two [bindus] which have first manifested as the splendor of fire and moon, which are sprinkled with drops from the stream of nectar issuing from the *sakāra* filled with nectar, and which remain having filled the entire body of the self through the path of the channels (*nāḍī*), all diseases are suppressed. Now follows the procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra according to the Kādimata. Therein:
In the *Śrītantrarāja*:

"Thereafter, O beloved, hear about the accomplishment [attained] through subtle and supreme oblations (*homa*) performed in the fire located in one's own *mūlādhāra*, which moves at the tip of the *kuṇḍalinī*. (4.1)
In that manner, one should likewise offer as oblation the manifold world consisting of the signified and the signifier,
O Goddess, so that through this sacrifice we may become equal.
O wise Śambhu, tell me now correctly the procedure for that,
as well as the location of the fire in the foundation (ādhāra) and the position of Kuṇḍalinī thereafter.
"O Lord, tell me clearly all about that form and that activity.
Listen, I shall now explain the procedure to you properly and in detail."
Regarding that supreme Prāṇāgnihotra-vidyā which is heard in the three [Vedas], by knowing which a man certainly does not enter the womb of a woman again. (4-5)

That which is free from loss and exertion, which proceeds without dependence on anything else, which is the place of rest for the afflictions of the mind, and which is entirely free from defilement. (4.6)
Heaven, the abode of bliss, consists of the universe through the cognition of consciousness as the object of knowledge;
all that remains to be said here is clearly explained in the thirty-sixth chapter. 4-7.
Therefore, it is demonstrated here, and I shall describe it briefly:
within the center of the *mūlādhāra*, which is said to be both eternal and non-eternal, there is fire.
Likewise, the Sun is situated in the hearts of all living beings,
and the Moon is established at the top of the head, below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
That [reality] should consist of those three alone—the first, the eternal, and the three-partite;
one should likewise contemplate the unity of those three with the mind.

O Śivā, through their mutual arising from the splendors of going and coming, those three splendors were thus kindled; having understood them to be composed of that [single essence], one should then realize them as being identical with it.
One should meditate upon the mind as being free from conceptual construction, as a wondrous oblation,
for those three castes previously mentioned, in their respective order.
Having formed any one [of these] with two [mantras], one should offer oblations with them in a folded manner;
and one should offer the vowels, folded by the syllables of the Sun’s heart-mantra, by means of the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *huṃ* sounds.
With a steady mind, one should offer oblations into the fire at the mouth of the Kuṇḍalī;
likewise, one should offer them in sequence with the lunar [elements] situated within the solar and fiery cavities.
Likewise, one should perform the oblation with the fire-syllables situated within the enclosure of the moon;
likewise, one should perform the oblation with the fire-syllables situated within the enclosure of the sun and the moon.
One should also perform oblations with the letters of the *bhāva* [mantra] situated within the enclosure of the moon and fire;
likewise, one should offer oblations with those same letters situated within the enclosure of fire and the moon.
Likewise, one should also offer oblations for those sixteen [syllables] in reverse order;
thus, the twelvefold oblation should be performed with the syllables as they have been declared.
Having made all that which is expressed and its objective form identical with them,
our own bodies shall likewise consist of the nature of the threefold energy.
Furthermore,
our other forms assumed at will are indeed equal to the bodies of other deities, being subject to our own volition.

Thus [ends] the *Śrīvidyārṇava* Tantra, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the Great Mahāmahopādhyāya.
The Fourth Chapter on Exhalation. || 4 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the fifth breath (śvāsa).
Now follows the extraction of the mantra according to the Kālīmata. First, therein is the Bhūtalipi. Regarding this, it is stated in the Siddhasārasvata-tantra:
"Now I shall describe the Bhūtalipi, which is extremely secret and very difficult to obtain; it is hidden within the great Sārasvata Tantra and bestows supreme accomplishment. (5-1)
O Goddess, having obtained her from the presence of Viṣṇu, the sages always attained their desired fruit in its entirety; what need is there for much speaking? (5.2)
The first group of five short vowels has been proclaimed;
O Goddess, the second is said to consist of the four-syllable [mantras] beginning with Śiva. (5.3)
Space, wind, fire, and water are proclaimed as the third;
these are formed respectively by the final letter of each group, the first, the second, the penultimate, and the third.
The five groups [of consonants], ending with śa, ṣa, and sa, are considered the ninth;
the mantra consisting of nine groups has forty-two syllables. (5.5)

The first letter of each group [of consonants], joined with the letter *śrīkaṇṭha* (the visarga), the upper lip (*ū*), and the void (*kha*), as well as the final letters of each group joined with the letter *va*, are declared in this sequence. (5–6)
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth are considered the letters of the [five] groups in their respective order.
The second group is devoid of earth, while the last is joined with water and earth. (5–7)
The deities of the nine groups are declared in sequence:
Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the two Aśvins, and Prajāpati.
The world-protectors are proclaimed as possessing the powers of action and so forth;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer, and the Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre. (5.9)
Sarasvatī, who is praised by the universe, is declared to be its deity.
The six limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the six groups beginning with Vyoma, joined with their respective *jātis*. (5–10)
Now, the placement of the nine syllables of the first two groups is described:
[they are placed] upon the *ādhāra*, the *adhiṣṭhāna*, the navel, the heart, and the throat, together with the *bindu*. (5.11)

The wise practitioner should correctly place the vowels in the Nāda, Śakti, and Śiva [cakras] in their proper sequence; then, he should place the letters beginning with 'ha' from the third group of consonants in the five [cakras] starting from the top.
One should place the five groups [of letters] in these locations:
in the mouths, at the tips and roots of the arms and feet, and at the root and tip of the bow.
In the middle of the body, on the abdomen, on both sides, and at the navel;
and on the back, one should place the remaining groups of letters on the secret organ, the heart, and the eyebrows.
In the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*, one should place [the letters] ending with the *visarga*; in the *sthitinyāsa*, those ending with the *bindu* and the *visarga*.
One should place them according to the sequence of the first, second, penultimate, final, middle, and intermediate [groups]. (5.15)
One should perform the placement [of the syllables] in their sequential order during emanation, and conjoined with the *bindu* during reabsorption.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now describe its meditation, which is honored by the sages. (5.16)
The wise proclaim that which is eternal and composed of the elements, the seed of consciousness called *bindu* and *nāda*, whose roots are the syllables of the earth-sustainer (*viśvambharā*). (5.17)
It spread extensively in all directions with its multitude of branches, and the three worlds were covered by its mass of leaves the color of water. || 5-18 ||
And the celestial tree was set ablaze by sprouts the color of fire,
as auspicious as if adorned with gem-like sprouts beautified by the syllables of the wind.
O Ambikā, [I salute] him who illuminates the true splendor of his own body with flowers,
and who is bent low by the fruits that are the true forms of the imperishable syllables in the sky.
O Supreme Goddess, he is the eternal refuge of all beings, sprinkling the supreme goddess Vāgīśvarī with the flowing nectar of the highest immortality.
It is beautifully adorned by the exalted heights fashioned by the Nigamas and Āgamas;
it consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti, and the three worlds take refuge in its shade.
At the root of such a tree in the ocean, within the imperishable lotus, the multitudes of lords of sages attained their desired goals by taking refuge there. (5.23)
One should meditate upon the goddess Vāgīśvarī, who bestows all desired fruits;
she has the luster of a kunda flower, possesses large jar-like breasts, and bears the crescent moon upon her head.
With her lotus-hands, she holds the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and the rosary (*japamālā*), as well as a book and a human skull.

One should meditate upon that goddess, who possesses a pair of eyes, whose beauty has reached its full youth, who is composed of the letters of the alphabet, and who is slightly unsteady and languid from the intoxication of honeyed wine. (5.24)
Having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should daily worship the Goddess on the seat (pīṭha) as described by the Mothers in his heart, O Śivā. (5.25)
O Maheśānī, one should fashion the form within the lotus of letters using the root mantra;
having invoked Vāgīśī therein, one should worship her along with the surrounding deities.
The practitioner of mantras should worship the ancillary limbs of the Purāṇa upon the filaments as previously described;
thereafter, he should worship Ambikā and the others, who will be mentioned hereafter, upon the four petals.
Then one should worship Ambikā, Vāgbhavā, Durgā, and Śrī— the Mothers—
on the eight petals, O Maheśānī, and outside of that on the sixteen-petaled [lotus].
One should worship the sixteen Śaktis beginning with Karālī, which will be described hereafter:
Karālī, Vikarālī, the third, Umā, and Sarasvatī.
Śrī, Durgā, and Lakṣmī are declared to be Śruti and Smṛti;
Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, and Kānti are likewise proclaimed. (5.30)
These sixteen noble goddesses are said to hold swords and shields; they are dark-complexioned, have smiling faces, and are adorned with all ornaments. (5.31)
Vidyā, Hī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū;
then Rudravīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Pūṣā, and the auspicious Ṛddhidā. (5.32)
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Sendukhaṇḍā, and Śikhaṇḍinī. (5.33)
The destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the Asura Mahiṣa,
she who is Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī, and the one whose body is half that of Śaṅkara.
Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Triśūlinī, Pālinī, Ambikā, and Hāriṇī— these are the thirty-two white Śaktis.
The Piśācāsīs, with discs in their hands and adorned with beautiful ornaments, are to be worshipped;
they are Piṅgalākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Samṛddhi, and Vṛddhi. (5.36)
Śraddhā, Svāhā, Svadhā, Bhikṣā, Māyā, Saṃjñā, Vasundharā, Trilokadhātrī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Tridaśeśvarī. (5.37)
Surūpā, Bahurūpā, and Skandamātā, who is dear to him;
then Vimalā, Vipulā, Aruṇī, and again Āruṇī. || 5-38 ||
She is primordial nature, transformation, creation, maintenance, and indeed withdrawal;
she is the twilight, the intellect, the existent, the swan-like one, the crusher, and the supreme deity.
The divine mother is the blessed Devakī, whose seat is the lotus;
another is three-faced, while yet another has seven faces and is the crusher of gods and demons.
Long-lipped and with hair standing erect, many-headed and wolf-bellied;
one called Ratharekhā, and another following her called Śaśirekhā.
Gaganarekhā and Pavanavegā follow immediately after that;
then the one named Bhuvanapālā, and thereafter Madanāturā. (5.42)
Anaṅgānaṅgamadanā, likewise Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, and Surabhayaṅkarī. || 5-43 ||
Akṣobhyā, Satyavādinī, Vajrarūpā, Śucivratā, Varadā, and Vāgīśā—these sixty-four are proclaimed. (5.44)
All of them bore bows and arrows, had tongues of flame,
were impelled by fury, possessed fangs and upraised hair, and their minds were intent upon the commencement of battle.
Blazing with all their ornaments, they should be worshipped with great effort;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons outside of them.
Thus, the wise man should properly worship Bhūtalipi, the sustainer of the world;
enriched with the sovereignty of speech, he is honored even by the gods. (5.47)
The practitioner, having received initiation, should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
thereafter, he should offer oblations of pure sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) ten times that number.

Having performed the rites from the libation (tarpaṇa) up to the worship of the twice-born (dvijārcā) as before, the knower of mantras should then perform the rite for specific desires (kāmyakarma) according to the procedure taught by his own guru.
If one performs ten thousand oblations with lotuses, kings shall become submissive;
through oblations of blue lotuses, Mahālakṣmī arises without delay.
O Dear One, the practitioner should offer oblations with the flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa;
within a single year, he shall become a leader among great poets.
By offering oblations of black mustard and salt, the wise one shall bring women under his control;
having encapsulated whichever mantra with this "earth-writing" (bhūtalipi).
By practicing this a hundred times in forward and reverse order, one attains success;
one thoroughly awakens that supreme Kuṇḍalinī, who is beautiful with the poison of sleep. (5.53)
Having united her with the central path, one should flood that supreme station with the supreme nectars, proceeding in sequence from the crown of the head down to the base.
Indeed, this yoga is esteemed by practitioners as the bestower of all perfections;
one whose body is thus established [in this yoga] becomes like the sun in brilliance. (5.55)

Having understood the specific yantras, one should accomplish the rites for desired ends. The mantra "Oṃ, Vyoman (the Sky), Bindu-āḍhya (endowed with the Bindu), Śivayuk (joined with Śiva) [Ha], Hṛt (Hṛdaya) [Namaḥ]"—this is declared for the wise person as being in the pericarp; from here, the letters of the Sky (Vyoman) are to be placed upon the petals.
One should write the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished and the letters of the relative, alternating them with *kha* (the letter *kha*) on the final leaf;
then, this *khayantra*, fashioned from sandalwood and lac, removes poison when placed within a circle.
The two *vāyu* [letters] joined with the two eyes (*netra*) are [the letters *ya* and *ya*]; the word *ṅentakopeśa* joined with cessation (*virati*) and bowing (*nati*) is in the middle;
the letters of the wind-god (*vāyavya*) are doubled by the wind (*pavana*) in the middle of the petals, and the final one is at the very end.

If, during the rising of Saturn in the asterism Svāti, a mechanical device placed on a palm leaf is positioned within its [Saturn's] house of air, it causes the eradication of the enemy; moreover, a trench dug at the very door of that [enemy's] residence yields the fruit of the enemy's death.

The syllables *va*, *hi*, *kramāt*, *śru*, *ti*, *ra*, *da*, *in*, *du*, *yu*, *jau*, followed by one's own name (*svakāntau*), and *ru*, *roḥ*, *sa*, *pha*, *la*, *ṇa*, *tiḥ*—this mantra, placed in the center of a lotus, has the letters of fire (*ra*) enclosed within fire on its petals;

with the final syllable at the edge together with the letters of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) and the nourisher (*supoṣaka*), it is situated in the fire-petals. When drawn on an auspicious day and under a favorable asterism using lac and fine saffron, it provides protection. (5-58)
The pair of vowels *ā* and *ū*, joined with the nasal (*anusvāra*) and the bindu, ending in *ṅe*, [is placed] facing the moon; this is the salutation in the center.
The vowels beginning with *a* are encased within the letters that are the kinsmen of the child (*śiśubandhu*);
and on the petals is the Varuṇa-mantra consisting of the pair of *ca* and *pa*. (5-59)
One should write the syllable *ga* with a bindu at the end of the *gaṇḍa* (the second consonant of the group), and the syllable *ja* situated between the two *gaṇḍas*.

Then, the syllable *l* with *ka* at the end, followed by *ha* in the middle of the heart; thereafter, the letters of the earth (*bha*) ending with the letter of the earth (*dha*), folded in the form of a bud.
Within the petals, it is joined with the letters of the servants and the house of the earth; this occurs at the rising of Indra and Soma (the North-East).
A ground-diagram (bhūmiyantra) drawn on birch bark with red chalk (gairika) upon very fine clay will cause paralysis. || 5-51 ||
Thus ends the section on the *bhūtalipi*. Now begins the section on the *Śrīvidyā* according to the *Kālīmata*:
"Elsewhere there is the *pañcasiṃhāsana*, and from that indeed the *pañcapañcikā*;
likewise the *ṣaḍāyatanavidyā*s and the five *āmnāya*s. (5.1)
The vidyās of the four samayas and the multitude of Śrīvidyās must be known especially for the sake of attaining the state of the deity. (5.2)
Then there is Sampatpradābhairavī, and after that Caitanyabhairavī;
there is another Caitanyabhairavī, the second one, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
Kāmeśvarī, Bhairavī, and the five deities beginning with Bālā, who reside upon the Eastern Lion-Throne, should be remembered for the attainment of all perfections. (5.4)
In the ritual of nyāsa, in the fire sacrifice (homa), and in worship, the practitioner [should employ] Aghorabhairavī and, beyond that, Mahābhairavī in every instance.
Lalitābhairavī, Kāmeśībhairavī,
and Raktanetrābhairavī likewise are seated upon the right-hand lion-throne.
Then indeed there is Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī, followed by Nityabhairavī;
then Mṛtasañjīvanī and thereafter Mṛtyuñjayaparā.
Vajraprastāriṇī herself is seated upon the lion throne facing west;
likewise Bhuvaneśī, Bhairavī, Kamaleśī, and Bhairavī. (5.8)
Kauleśī, Bhairavī, then Ḍāmarabhairavī,
and Kāminībhairavī— these are seated upon the gentle lion-throne.
The first is Sundarī, and likewise the second is Sundarī;
the third is Sundarī, and likewise the fourth is Sundarī.
And Pañcamī and Sundarī are likewise seated upon the upper lion-throne; as are Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī. (5–11)
The three powers, the sovereign Lakṣmīs, and the five [Vidyās] are proclaimed;
namely, Śrīvidyā, Paraṃjyotis, and Paraniṣkalaśāmbhavī. (5.12)
The Ajapā and the Mātṛkā—these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (kośas).
Then there are Śrīvidyā, Tvaritā, and Pārijāteśvarī. (5.13)
Trikūṭā, Pañcabāṇeśī, and the five Kalpalatās are thus remembered;
[she is] Śrīvidyāmṛtapīṭheśī and Sudhāsūramṛteśvarī. (5.14)
The five wish-fulfilling cows, renowned as Annapūrṇā and so forth, are, in order:
Śrīvidyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (5-15)
"She is proclaimed as Vārāhī and is certainly known as the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna).
Now follows the extraction of the mantra: therein, first, the initial syllable is formed by the Guru’s sandals, Śiva, Candra, Anala, Arghīśa, and Bindu.
By means of the sky, the moon, the dissolution, Mahākāla, patience, and water. || 5-1 ||
The second seed-syllable is extracted from the [letters] Vāyu (ya), Agni (ra), Ananta (sa), Bindu (m), and Āta (a).
That same [syllable], with the left ear (ū) added, is extracted as the third seed-syllable. (5.2)
That very same [seed] is declared as the fourth seed by Takṣanetra;
likewise, "Śrīparā" and "Pāvaka," followed by the word "sarva. (5.3)
ĀRĀDHYASARVAGURU, NĀTHASARVAGURUGURU, ŚRĪGURU, and likewise NĀTHA; Vahni is the third seed-syllable.
And having first uttered the four initial seed-syllables from the words "Śrī," "Śambhu," and "Guru" in two ways, the second and following three [syllables] shall arise. (5-5)
The first and the third are declared to be the *sthūlapādukā* (the gross sandals);
preceded by the five *tāra*s, they accomplish all aims. (5–6)
This, when freed from the seed-syllable of Khecarī, is declared to be the Madhyapādukā;
but this, when joined with the three Tāras, is proclaimed as the Laghupādukā.
Then, having uttered the three *tāras*, the name "Śrī-Amukānandanātha," and "I worship the *śrīpādukā*," this is called the *laghutarāparā*.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasakhaphreṃ hasauḥ hasrū& hasakṣamalavayarā& hasakṣamalavayarū& hasakṣamalavaya [riṃ] śrīparapāvaka sarvārādhyasarvagurunātha sarvaguruguruśrīgurunātha raṃhasakṣamalavayarū& | hasrū&.

*Hasakṣamalavayarāṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ hasakṣamalavaya [rīṃ] Śrīśambhuguru hasrūṃ hasrūṃ hasakṣamalavayarāṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ hasakṣamalavaya [rīṃ] hasrūṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ.* Thus is the *sthūlapādukā*.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasauṃ śakṣamalavayarūṃ śakṣamalavayarūṃ hasrauḥ sahakṣamalavayarauḥ hasrauḥ śrīparapāvaka sarvārādhyasarvagurunātha sarvagurusvayaṃguru śrīgurunātha raṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ hasauṃ sahakṣamalavayarīṃ.
*Sahakṣamalavayarūṃ sahalakṣamavayarāṃ śrīśambhuguruhasrauṃ sahakṣamalavayarūṃ śrī-amukānandanāthāmukaśaktidevyambāśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*— thus is the middle *pādukā*.

OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ HASAKHAPHREṂ HASAUḤ HASAKṢAMALAVARAYŪṂ ŚRĪ-AMUKĀNANDANĀTHA OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ SAHAKHAPHREṂ SHAUḤ SAHAKṢAMALAVARAYĪṂ I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of the Mother Goddess Amukadevī Ambā. This is the *laghupādukā*. OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ.

"I worship the *śrīpādukā* of [Name] Ānandanātha and [Name] Śakti Ambā"— this is the *laghutarapādukā*. "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of [Name] Ānandanātha"— this is the *sāmānyapādukā*.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one whose mind is composed, whose body is steady, and who is skilled in the path of yoga, should contemplate the sandals of the Guru. (5.1)
In the *pādukā-mantra* of the venerable Guru, Brahmā is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*);
the meter (*chanda*) is said to be *gāyatrī*, beginning with *nicṛt*, O Maheśvarī. (5.2)
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are likewise at the beginning and the end; the middle shall be the *kīlaka*.
The application for the sake of liberation is declared to be the *ṛṣinyāsa*. (5.3)
In the morning, one should remember the Guru— two-eyed, two-armed, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and peaceful— upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name.
Resembling ten thousand moons and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
he was clad in white garments, glorious, and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
One should meditate upon the Guru, who is embraced by Śakti— red in color, seated upon his left thigh, and holding a lotus in her hand— and who is overflowing with the fragrance of bliss.
Now, the meditation on the Guru who is the threefold flood:
She holds the *cinmudrā* and a skull-cup filled with honey in her two hands; she resembles molten gold and is adorned with red flowers, ointments, and garments.

Let one whose mind is composed worship the lineage of gurus, who possess reddish eyes with compassionate side-glances, who are endowed with variegated matted locks, and who are attended by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas). 5-1.
Now, the salutation to the Guru:
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the applicator of the collyrium of knowledge. (5.1)
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed—the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded. || 5-2 ||
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is the creator and the destroyer—to the Guru, indeed, salutations again and again.
Now, the Kuṇḍalinī mantra:
Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśī, and likewise the Śrībīja;
this three-syllabled mantra is declared to be the bestower of perfect accomplishment for Kuṇḍalinī. (5.1)
The seer is declared to be Śakti; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter;
and the deity here is declared to be the conscious Kuṇḍalinī power. (5-2)
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is proclaimed [as the first], the Śakti is said to be the Śrībīja, and Hṛllekhā is declared to be the Kīlaka for the meditation upon Kuṇḍalinī. (5.3)
The application (viniyoga) has been fully explained by those proficient in all the Agamas;
the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to be performed by repeating the three seed-syllables twice.
I shall describe the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī; listen with attentiveness.
In the Mūlādhāra, within a triangle possessing a luster equal to ten million suns, || 5-5 ||
Having the form of a sleeping serpent, situated in three and a half coils,
slender like the awn of a grain of wild rice, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
The Goddess, who consists of the power of Śiva, is radiant with the brilliance of ten million suns, yet as cool as ten million moons; she abides in the form of a conch-shell spiral.
One should contemplate her, proceeding by way of the central path of the *suṣumnā* as far as the Supreme Śiva, in the form of the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, according to the path of yoga.

Her body is crimson like vermilion, she has three eyes, and her crown shines with a ruby; she wears the leader of the stars (the moon) as her crest-jewel, her face is smiling, and her breasts are full.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is serene, holding in her two hands a jeweled goblet filled with gems and a red lotus, and whose left foot rests upon a jeweled pitcher.
The meditation on the family preceptor has already been explained. Now follows the praise of Kuṇḍalinī from the Śāradā-tantra:

She who resembles the king of serpents awakened at the root, who, having pierced through the interior of the Suṣumnā, quickly traverses the multitude of foundations, and who is like a shimmering flash of lightning—

Having honored her husband with streams of divine nectar flowing from the orb of the moon situated within the sky-lotus, she should again contemplate this Kuṇḍalinī as having returned to her own home. || 5-1 ||

Having grasped by the hand that Haṃsa— who is eternal, infinite, and possessed of non-dual qualities— and having herself experienced his supreme bliss, the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī, the mother of all, emerged from her own support and went to the abode of Śambhu.
She who goes to her own hermitage, radiant as ten million suns, the enchantress of the world, is to be meditated upon. || 5-2 ||
The Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, whose body consists of the three qualities and who resembles a streak of lightning, having led the unmanifest supreme reflection of accumulated luster to the abode of Śiva—
the Destroyer of Cities, who resides in the bulb of the nectar of bliss and possesses the splendor of ten million moons and suns— [unites with Him].
Having looked [upon him], the Blessed One, who is irreproachable in her virtues, went to her own home; she is to be meditated upon. || 5.3 ||

We worship Her as She rises, radiant with the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning within the light that transcends the mass of sounds born from the agitation of the mutual friction of the two winds in the central path— She who is as deep red as fresh saffron and vermilion.
The supreme deity, consisting of the nectar of intense bliss, who has attained Paraśiva. || 5-4 ||
In the processes of going and coming, that Kuṇḍalinī, the swift-footed one, brings about the fruits of yoga;
she is the joyful wish-fulfilling cow of the Kula, a desire-granting creeper for those who worship her. 5-5.

Having duly sprinkled the six lotuses with showers of falling supreme nectar that bestow awakening— [the nectar] which resides in the *bindu* of the power (*śakti*) situated in the *ādhāra*, resembling the awn of a grain of wild rice (*nīvāra*), and consisting of eternal bliss— one [should worship] her who has arisen in the middle of the bow.
One should meditate upon the deity, who consists of pure consciousness and possesses the radiant luster of the bandhujīva flower.
The Goddess, who dwells within the solar orb of the heart-lotus, who is as slow-moving as a flash of lightning,
and who with her splendor, red as the rising sun, utterly outshines the darkness known as Nāda—
she who is curved like the supreme half-moon and consists of pure consciousness, eternal.
One of pure intellect should meditate upon the All-pervading Lord, whose form is imperishable and who is the essence of all splendors.
On his forehead, she resembles the full moon; with the luster of frost and pearls, she drenches the Lord with nectar and delights his immeasurable body.
Having pervaded the universe through his very form, she stands there as the mother of all letters.
One should meditate with a perfectly composed and undisturbed mind upon Ambikā, who consists of pure consciousness.

At the root, on the forehead, and in the heart, the Great Goddess Sāvitrī shines in the form of radiant syllables; she is the Mistress whose waist bends under the weight of her full and lofty breasts.
May the goddess of speech, her limbs today thoroughly sprinkled with nectar dripping from every syllable, bestow upon us complete and perfect prosperity. 5-9.

May Kuṇḍalinī—the consort of Śiva—grant you auspiciousness; she who, arising through the practices beginning with the binding of the foundation (ādhāra-bandha), honors the auspicious seed-syllable of the three abodes (tridhāmabīja) with her nectars. 5-10.

Departing from her own abode with playful graces, casting beautiful smiles upon the lotuses at every step along the way, may that goddess Kuṇḍalinī, possessing the luster of the young sun, illumine her own splendor with the nectars of the temple of Śiva. 5-11.

May the consort of Śambhu bestow immeasurable glory—she who resembles a mass of vermilion, who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, whose face is beautified by three eyes full of bliss, and whose slender body bends under the weight of her full, lofty breasts.
May the Supreme Goddess—who, surrounded by the peaceful deities and others, together with the letters from *kṣa* and the six vowels, resides within the centers of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*);
who is attended by the *ḍākinīs* and others; who is well-known among the deities such as Brahmā and the rest; and who pierces [the veils]—bestow joy upon the minds of the three worlds. (5.13)
[She who] has a body adorned by the qualities arising from her support, who swiftly pierces through the lotuses, who is exalted by the awakening of the dense bliss of pure consciousness,
and [who is nourished] by the nectar flowing from the moon of the agitated Dhruva-maṇḍala—
I meditate upon Śivā, who has sprouted forth from the stream and possesses the form of intense lightning.
In the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*, radiant with the luster of the rising sun, Kāma wanders, possessing the brilliance of ten million rays from the young sun, the black fire, and the aged moon;
he is as beautiful as a lovely bandhujīva flower, shimmering with the splendor of a thousand streaks of lightning.
Having contemplated the Bindu, which is pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas) and is the sole cause for the arising and dissolution of the world. || 5-15 ||

Above that, one should contemplate her who is radiant with limbs shining like a mass of clearly beautiful lightning, ascending along the crest of the path of the *suṣumnā* as far as the orb of the moon upon the forehead;
she is pure consciousness, subtle in form, the cause of the world's arising, and perceivable through meditation alone.
She who is the root of all abodes shines forth incomparably, her chest uplifted by the sound of *hūṃ*.
She was slowly led into the interior of a thousand-petaled red lotus with its face turned downward,
where a stream of nectar flows from the dripping honey of the full moon’s orb;
having drunk that mantra-made essence in the form of a flowing stream of ambrosia, she became intensely red.
Having risen once more from his own abode and having drunk [the nectar], he should enter again. || 5-17 ||
He who practices daily within himself, like a seed, the destruction of evil, old age, death, and disease— he,
having conquered them as if he were the personified God of Love himself, shall live for a long time with his mass of hair exceedingly dark.
Thus ends the hymn to Kuṇḍalinī. Now, the contemplation of the Root Mantra (Mūlavidyā):
The seer (ṛṣi) of the fifteen-syllabled [mantra] is declared to be the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is said to be Paṅkti, and its nature is that of the Supreme Brahman. (5-1)
For the deity is declared to be the glorious Mahātripurasundarī; the seed-syllable Vāgbhava is proclaimed, and the power (śakti) is said to be Tārā. (5.2)
The *kīlaka* (the pinning stake) is the central peak (*madhyakūṭa*) within the four aims of human life;
thus has its application been declared by those proficient in all the scriptures. (5.3)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the three peaks twice.

May the consort of Śambhu, who resembles a mass of vermilion, who is adorned with a digit of the moon, whose face is beautified by three eyes full of bliss, and whose body is bent by her full and lofty breasts, bestow immeasurable splendor! (5.4)
Now, the contemplation of the three *kūṭas*:
The wise man should contemplate the *kūṭa* called *vāgbhava* in the *mūlādhāra*.
For this *kūṭa* called *vāgbhava*, Brahmā is declared to be the *ṛṣi*. (5.1)
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Vāgadhīśvarī;
the first syllable is the seed (bīja), while the last is said to be the power (śakti).
The triad of the middle [syllables] constitutes the *kīlaka* (the pinning), while the *viniyoga* (application) is for the attainment of mastery over speech (*vāksiddhi*).
[The seed-syllables are] "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī" ending in the feminine suffix *ṅe*, and likewise "Viṣṇuvāgrūpiṇī."
She is the embodiment of Rudra’s speech ending in the feminine suffix *ṅi*, likewise the embodiment of supreme speech (*paravāk*);
she is the embodiment of Śiva’s speech ending in *ṅi*, and likewise the embodiment of all speech.
The diligent practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with these [mantras] beginning with *vāgbhava*.
[He should meditate on the Goddess] white, adorned with clear unguents, garlands, and garments, radiant with a crescent moon,
holding in her lotus-hands the gesture of exposition, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the [Goddess] Vidyā.

I bow to the goddess of speech, who sits upon a lotus, whose breasts are slightly bent, who smiles gently; she who bestows the power of eloquence, possesses three eyes, and grants the wealth of good fortune.
The wise one should contemplate the peak-syllable known as Kāmarāja in the heart.
For the peak-syllable named Kāmarāja, Sammohana is recorded as the seer (ṛṣi). || 5-6 ||
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas), and Kāmeśī is remembered as the deity (devatā).
The first syllable is the seed-syllable (bīja), likewise Hṛllekhā is the power (śakti), and it is remembered as the pin (kīlaka). || 5-7 ||
The group of four middle syllables, however, is for the sake of attaining the power of subjugation;
its application here has been proclaimed by those learned in all the Āgamas. (5–8)
To the arrow that agitates, *drāṃ*; likewise, the word for driving away, *drīṃ*;
to the arrow, *klīṃ*; and again, the word for attracting. || 5-9 ||
Then one should again utter the five seed-syllables: *bāṇāya blūṃ* for the arrow of subjugation, and then *unmādanabāṇāya* for the arrow of intoxication. (5-10)
Having said "from all arrows," one should duly install the six limbs with the mantras beginning with the *kāmakūṭa* and ending with *namaḥ*, numbering six.

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, possesses three eyes, and holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal radiant as ten million rising suns, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of Smara, and the Vidyā-mantra.
The foremost of practitioners should contemplate the Śaktikūṭa at the Ājñācakra.
Now, for this Śaktikūṭa, Śiva is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi). (5.13)
The metre is Paṅkti, the presiding deity is Ādiśakti, and the seed-syllable (bīja) here is Saḥ.
Hṛllekhā is declared to be the power (śakti), and the two middle syllables are the peg (kīlaka). (5.14)
The application (viniyoga), however, should be known as certain for the attainment of the four aims of life:
that which ends in the feminine suffix -ī is the power of omniscience, and that which ends in the power (śakti) is eternal contentment.
The fourth [vowel] is designated as Anādibodhinī; likewise, the feminine form in ṅī (ī) is Svatantratāśakti, as well as Nityamaluptatā. (5.16)
The power ending in ṅe, the endlessness and so forth ending in ṅe, and likewise [the others]—
by means of these mantras joined with the *jāti* suffixes and beginning with the *kūṭa* of Śakti, in due order.
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should meditate with undistracted mind upon the Goddess,
who dwells in the midst of a *kadamba* grove, situated within a golden pavilion, residing upon a six-petalled lotus, and appearing like a flash of lightning among the gods and *siddhas*.
I take refuge in Tripurasundarī, the consort of the Three-eyed Lord, who wears the stainless moon as her crest-jewel and whose devotion to the muttering of prayers has blossomed. || 5-18 ||
Now, regarding the contemplation of non-duality:
one should contemplate the Brahma-vidyā from the base [of the spine] up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should then contemplate one's own body as being enveloped by the mass of its radiance. (5-1)
O Goddess, I am not another; I am Brahman itself, free from sorrow.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, possessing the inherent state of eternal liberation. (5.2)
"You alone am I, and I am you; your very body is pure consciousness.
Therefore, O Goddess, may the distinction between us two vanish by the power of your command. (5.3)
"I have crossed over this terrible existence; indeed, I have no further task remaining.
Nevertheless, O Mother, grant me permission to serve you well."
Having performed this reflection— which serves as a new foundation for my dwelling— with a mind established in meditative concentration,
