I shall rise at dawn and continue the journey through saṃsāra for the sake of your welfare. (5.5)
I take refuge in the left half of the Great Goddess, whose anklets produce charming tinkling sounds, who is the root of the world, and who is even the root of all words. 5-6.
Now, the hymn to the Root Deity (Mūladevatā):

O Mother, was service not performed at the root of Your lotus feet by people possessed of devotion—service that is like showers of auspiciousness filled with nectar, and like the auspicious lamps for Lakṣmī’s self-choice marriage? (5-1)

O Mother, this alone is to be desired: that while engaged in worshipping you, my eyes—veiled by water—should behold the presence of your form, which resembles a blossoming red lotus and is drenched in supreme nectar. (5.2)
How many indeed are there, such as Brahmā and others, whose portions of lordship are defiled and who, age after age, are overwhelmed by dissolution?
O Mother, he alone remains with his attainment of stability, who performs a virtuous prostration at your feet. (5.3)
O Tripurasundarī, having once obtained your sidelong glance, which possesses a weight of beauty blossoming from compassion,
those who are devoted to you and made lovely by the state of passion enchant the young women throughout the three worlds.
O Mother Tripurā, dweller in the triangular abode, O three-eyed one, the Vedas proclaim your very name as the syllable *hrīṃ*;
by the mere remembrance of which, casting off fear of the messengers of Yama and others, people sport in the Nandana grove together with the guardians of the world.

O Mother, how could the cruel force of the poison ever reach the throat of the slayer of Pura, when this half of your body is eternally cooled by being bathed in nectar? It is surely for your consolation that this portion of your form remains so.
O Goddess, prostration at your two lotus-feet produces omniscience and eloquence of speech in the assembly;
moreover, it bestows a shimmering, radiant crown, a brilliant parasol, two fly-whisks, and a vast kingdom.
O Mother, your side-glances—oceans of compassion—are like wish-fulfilling trees in granting all desired objects.
O Tripurasundarī, look upon my lord, who is filled with devotion for you alone and whose gaze is fixed upon you.
Alas, others indeed fix their minds upon and bear devotion toward base deities;
O Goddess, I remember you alone with my mind, I bow to you alone, and you alone are my refuge in this world.
O Tripurasundarī, even though there are other objects for your eyes to behold, look upon me somehow;
surely no person has ever been born, nor will one ever be born, who is so worthy of compassion as I am.
For those people who daily chant "hrīṃ hrīṃ" while residing here in Tripura, what indeed is difficult to obtain?
To them—who are honored by garlands, crowns, and rutting elephants—the intoxicating Lakṣmī herself serves.
O lotus-eyed one, these [places] bestow prosperity, delight all the senses, and are skilled in granting imperial sovereignty.
O Mother, may my prostrations, which are intent on removing the flood of misfortunes, attend to you alone incessantly, and not to anyone else.

Victorious is that single form of yours, the witness, which possesses the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows—the form of the Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, the Supreme Bhairava, who performs the cosmic dance at the dissolution of the aeons. (5.13)
O Mother, may this supreme splendor of yours be ever present— red as thick saffron paste,
adorned with a radiant crown and an ornament of a crescent moon, risen in the center of the triangle and moistened by the highest nectar.
The syllable *hrīṃ* alone is your abode; that very form is your name, O beautiful one, whose nature is to dwell in the lotus.
May the union with you—the primordial root of the universe, transformed by your splendor—grant the company of the lotus-dweller.
O Mother, that knower of mantras who daily recites this hymn before you, which is kindled by the great mantra encapsulated by three *hrīṃ*s,
finds kings submissive to him, prosperity long-lasting, and eloquence [attained].
Filled with the weight of stainless eloquent sayings, its long body remains awake.
Thus is the praise.
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
Thus ends the prayer for the ground.

During the twilight prayers, one should face north; during the day and at night, one should face south. One should wear the sacred thread around the neck (nivīta) while performing purification after urination and other acts. Then, outside of water, there should be one application of earth on the penis; five on the anus; ten on the hand; and seven on both hands combined—this is the rule for a householder.
In the case of those who observe that vow, it should be doubled and so forth according to the sequence among the Vaiśyas and others; at night, it shall be half of that.
Thus concludes the section on purification.
Then, for the Śrīkāma mantra, Sammohana is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi);
Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas), and Śrīkāma is remembered as the deity (devatā). (5.1)
The seed-syllable (bīja) is Kāmarāja; "Namaḥ" is declared to be the power (śakti). "Sarvajana-priyāya" is proclaimed as the pin (kīlaka). || 5.2 ||
One should perform the placement of the six limbs with the six-syllable King of Desires (Kāmarāja).

I worship Him who is crimson as a hibiscus flower, richly adorned with jewel ornaments, bearing the fish-banner, with beautiful unguents applied to His limbs, and holding in His lotus-hands the goad, the sugarcane bow, the flower-arrow, and the noose. (5.3)

Having thus meditated upon the seed-syllable of desire and everything pertaining to the god of love, [one recites] "to the one dear to the people"—this is declared to be the heart-mantra of Kāma. || 5-4 ||
Having consecrated the tooth-stick eight times with this [mantra], the wise one should cleanse his teeth and then perform the rinsing of the mouth. (5.5)
Thus concludes the section on the cleaning of the teeth.
Then, having visualized Śrīvidyā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head),
one should thereafter perform the washing of the face with the four Mahāmantras of Lakṣmī.
Thus concludes the rinsing of the mouth.
Having reached the bank and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) with devotion:
"O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon! (5.7)
"Obeisance to you, Bhairava; you should grant me permission.
Having recollected the command of Bhairava, one should perform the Vedic ritual bath. (5-8)
One should perform that Tantric bath according to the path prescribed by mantra;
having visualized the Śrīcakra in the water and drawn in the sacred waters from the mandala.
O Sun, the holy fords within the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
Having drawn in the sacred fords with the mudrā in the form of a hook and having joined them, one should meditate upon the Goddess in the form of the Gaṅgā while reciting the root mantra. (5-11)
Then, one should sprinkle [the disciple] seven times on one's own head with the *jātavedas* and other *ṛc*s together with their root-mantras, using the mudrā known as the *kumbha*.
Having united the Goddess within one's own heart, [one should contemplate] the succession of sacred sites in their respective places:
"Whatever evil deed has been done by me, along with the water and the impurities of the body... (5.13).
"For the sake of purifying that sin, I satisfy Yakṣman";
having thus offered libations on the bank, he should put on two clean garments.
Thus concludes the ritual bath (*snāna*). Next is the application of sacred ash (*vibhūtidhāraṇa*): having placed the sacred ash in the hand, one should consecrate it with the five *tāra*s;
one should also consecrate it with the mantras beginning with "Agni" and with those beginning with "Īśāna. (5–15)
Then the practitioner of mantra should apply [the ashes] using only the root-vidyā.
Thus ends the application of ashes. Now, after the Vedic *saṃdhyā*, one should perform the Tantric *saṃdhyā*:
then, ending with "O Maṇidharinī" and ending with "O Vajrinī, O Mahāprati..."
The mantra is said to end with "sare rakṣa dvayaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 5-1 ||
Having tied his topknot with this very mantra, the wise practitioner,
being composed, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the three peak-syllables ending in the three principles (tattvas).

Then, immediately after that, [one should offer oblations] ending with "svāhā" to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), likewise to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), and to the principle of illusion (māyātattva).

Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should visualize the Śrīcakra in the midst of the water before oneself, and then [invoke] the sacred waters (tīrtha) from the sun by means of the mudrā.
Having invoked [the deity] as before according to the prescribed rite and having displayed the mudrās beginning with the Āvāhanī,
one should carefully take water in the right hand.
Having covered it with the left hand and consecrated the water once with the syllables of the five elements in sequence, he should place it in his left hand.
One should cleanse the head with the vowels using the drops dripping from its back;
then, water should be taken in the right hand together with the root-mantra (5.7).
Having consecrated it with the consonants from *ka* to *ma*, ending with *svāhā*,
one should drink that water and then pour water into the right [hand].
Having consecrated it with mantras as before and placed it in his left hand,
he should likewise sprinkle [the disciple] with the drops streaming forth from its back.

Then, having drawn that water into the interior of the body through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] with care, one should wash away all impurities by means of the pervasive syllables beginning with *ya*, *kṣa*, and *ñ*. (5.10)
Having purged it through the *piṅgalā* channel, one should strike that black-colored water against a blazing diamond-stone while uttering the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Then, having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should take water in his joined palms,
stand up, and, facing the sun, pour it upward while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having thus offered the threefold *arghya* and sat down with diligence,
one should again duly propitiate the goddesses who surround the *śrīcakra*.

Having recited the root mantra twenty-five times for his chosen deity and having offered libations, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Gāyatrī mantra.
The seer of the Gāyatrī is Brahmā; the meter is declared to be Gāyatra;
the deity is said to be Gāyatrī; and it consists of three feet repeated twice. (5-15)
Having duly applied the six limbs [of ritual placement], one should meditate on the Goddess with undistracted mind,
[visualizing her] as wearing a crown of shimmering clusters of radiant jewels and bearing a digit of the moon.

The wise man, meditating upon her who has the luster of freshly smelted gold, whose form is like the orb of the sun, and who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons; 5.17.
Thus, it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"One should perform the morning twilight worship for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha.
In the lotus dwelling at the mūlādhāra, there is the seed-syllable Hrīṃ, resembling blood in color. (5.1)

Having meditated [on her] within the cavity of light and having caused her to emerge externally into the mandala, one should visualize her as belonging to the Sun, with a reddish luster, three eyes, and four arms. (5.2)
She stands in the center of a circle of fire, assuming the form of a young maiden,
and holds a book, a rosary, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Having thus meditated upon the Mother, who is like the rising sun, one should recite the mantra. Then, at midday, during the twilight rite, one should [meditate] upon the unsullied lotus of the heart.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, which resembles white in color, and having emitted it as before,
[one should visualize her] standing in the center of a solar disc, three-eyed and white-bodied.
Having thus meditated upon Jyeṣṭhā, who has attained full youth and bears the discus, conch, lotus, and mace, one should mutter the mantra.

Then, at the evening twilight, having meditated upon the black-colored seed-syllable *hrīṃ* in the *hakṣa*-lotus between the eyebrows and having emitted it as before, [one should perform the ritual]. (5–7)
Seated in the center of a moon mandala, black in color and four-armed,
she bears the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a skull-cup, and likewise the threatening gesture.
Having thus meditated upon her as holding [objects] in her left and right hands, variegated, endowed with three eyes, adorned with diverse ornaments, and fierce, one should recite the mantra.
Having uttered the eight seed-syllables, one should recite the Vāgbhava peak-syllable;
then one should recite "vāgīśvaryai vidmahe," followed by the Kāma peak-syllable.
Then, after "kāmeśvaryai dhīmahi," which is the peak of power (śaktikūṭa), one should utter the word "tannaḥ śaktiḥ" and then recite "pracodayāt. (5.11)
Having uttered the five seed-syllables, this Gāyatrī is proclaimed; then, having recited the root-mantra, one should announce, "It is beyond the secret. || 5-12 ||

Thus concludes the procedure for the Sandhyā. Regarding the abbreviated Sandhyā, however, another Tantra states: "Having meditated upon the Goddess in the evening, morning, and at midday, one should recite the mantra. Thus, the three Sandhyās are mandatory. Likewise, in the Kulārṇava: "The omission of Sandhyā must not be performed; such indeed is the command of Śambhu."
One who is initiated but devoid of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) does not enjoy the fruit of initiation.
If one does not perform that twilight rite (*sandhyā*), one should fall [into penance] by reciting ten times;
at a time equivalent to another *sandhyā*, one should do so with the *sautrakaṇṭakī* mantra.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra, one should meditate upon that Sautrakaṇṭakī—the Supreme Goddess—who has six faces, twelve arms, and three eyes. (5.3)
One should then meditate upon her as being white in color from the neck upwards, yellow from below the base of the neck, and blue-hued from the hips down to the feet.
She is sixteen years of age, red-limbed, adorned with every ornament,
and accompanied by thousands of women who are embellished by the luster of gold and jewels.
She who liberates from all sins, seated upon a red lion-throne;
above that is a white lotus, and above that, a white pericarp.
Seated upon his back is the Goddess, adorned with the three sections and the qualities,
radiant with a jeweled crown, divine, continuous, and filled with sound.
To the smiling-faced Great Goddess, who moves toward the south from her rising, who proceeds to the eternal and partless state for the sake of the Great Pledge Sacrifice (mahāsamayayāga). || 5-8 ||

Having uttered the five *praṇavas*, [one recites] the *vāgbhava* [bīja], which is difficult for others to perform, followed by "the cutter of karma," as well as "O Aghora" and "O Giver of Boons. (5-9)
Having uttered the word *vicce* and the word *māyā*, one should extract the word *trailokya*.
Having uttered the word *rūpa*, she is the one who revolves a thousand times. (5.10)

One should recite this mantra— consisting of the word *mātṛgaṇe*, followed by *padaṃ cānu*, *hasrūṃ*, and the five *praṇavas*— for the purpose of removing the great sin of omitting the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
Then, one should recite the root mantra ten times according to the prescribed rule,
having become self-luminous oneself while remembering the root-vidyā in the heart.
"Taking water for the purpose of worship, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Adorned with all elegant ornaments and attire, [anointed] with camphor, saffron, and other [fragrances]."
His body is smeared with the abundant musk of the great deer, and he is reddened with saffron. || 5-1 ||
Richly adorned with the nine precious gems, resplendent in crimson garments,
his face colored by betel, his mind filled with the bliss of passion.
Having arrived at the sacrificial hall, which was variegated with liquid lac, filled with abundant incense, and strewn with a profusion of flowers. || 5.3 ||
"And smeared with cow dung, adorned with beautiful flowers.
Thus it is said. In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Then one should go to the sacrificial hall, which is decorated and embellished."
Variously adorned and beautiful, the ground was smeared with cow dung.
Above, it was adorned with a canopy of shimmering flowers, perfumed with incense,
and radiant with garlands of lamps and scattered blossoms.
Thus concludes the section on the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
With the mantra *tāraṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, the preceptor (deśika) sprinkles water upon the seat and sits down upon it. (5.3)
One should utter "Tāraṃ," "Māyāviśuddhā," and "Sarvapāpāni," and then say "Śamayāśeṣa" and "Vikalpamapanaya. || 5-4 ||
One should wash one's hands and feet with the mantra *hūṃ*;
then, having sipped water three times in the courtyard with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*.

"Then, having sat down, one should perform the worship of Sūrya according to the prescribed rule. Thus [it is said]. In the *Kularṇava*: "Facing east in the courtyard, one should first worship Mārtaṇḍabhairava. In the *Śambhunirṇaya*:
This worship of the Sun is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold aim;
having reflected upon that, one should perform the worship of the Sun of Consciousness while seated on a comfortable seat.
Facing east and seated facing west upon a smooth, pleasant ground,
one should place the general *arghya* offering on the left and utter the five *praṇavas*.
One should perform the elevation of the mandala; this is the common view.
It consists of a square of five finger-breadths, a hexagon, and an upper line.
Having drawn [the mandala] upon it, one should place the support-vessel (ādhāra-pātra), purified by the weapon-mantra (astra), and fill it with water;
and [one should likewise fill] the waters of the support-vessel.
Likewise, it is manifested by the seeds of Fire, Sun, and Moon;
having thus produced the six long vowels, which constitute the second Praṇava.
Having thus performed the ritual for his body and having established the conch,
the preceptor [visualizes] the solar mandala before him with the tip of his hand from which breath flows.
"With the mantra to be recited hereafter, using musk, sandalwood, and other [substances]...
thus: *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ha sa kha phreṃ ha sauḥ*, O you who contain the moon, sun, and fire within! Flash, flash!
Grant the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa! Reveal, reveal the Great Khecarī Mudrā!
By the command of Śambhu, bestowing the power of accomplishment upon the four lineages: *dadadada kicakica kilakila phreṃ maṇḍalabrahmāṇḍamaṇḍala hasrūṃ mahācaṇḍaśive sahaphreṃ*.
Having worshipped with this mantra an eight-petaled lotus of circular form,
and having constructed a square mandala, one should place it before oneself.
The wise one should draw the general mandala for the special arghya;
on the right, he should draw a square mandala for the purpose of worshipping the arghya of the Sun.
"Having prepared the support and established it, one should worship with this mantra:
*Aiṃ*, obeisance to the placement of the vessel; *Aiṃ*. Therein, the wise should place the vessel, which has been washed with the Astra-mantra and fumigated with incense, saying *Klīṃ*. (5–5)
With this mantra, one should worship the *arghya* with pure water,
using the seed-syllable *Hauṃ* conjoined with the six long vowels.
Having cast eight types of perfumes, one should worship with red flowers;
having performed protection with the Astra-mantra, one should establish oneself [within the deity].
Then, having meditated upon Ananta in the form of a preta in the center of the eight lotuses, one should worship him there as he lies down with this mantra: || 5.11 ||
Aṃ, obeisance to Ananta, Aṃ.
[I bow to him] who has made his own body a couch and whose three hoods have been made into a parasol.
Then, having meditated upon the white Lord of Serpents, one should worship him.
One should worship in the [four] corners—namely, the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest—in sequence:
*hūṃ hūṃ phreṃ* to Prabandhanātha; *hūṃ hūṃ haṃ*; *yaṃ raṃ laṃ* to Trimūrti; *yaṃ* to Ārādhya; *haṃ* to Paramasukha; *haṃ*.

Situated in the center of the small ether (daharākāśa) is the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, resembling blood in color; having drawn forth from the flowing cavity the infinite seat consisting of a corpse, [one should place it there].
Having invoked him, one should meditate upon Mārtaṇḍabhairava, who consists of that seed-syllable. The meditation is as follows:
He is red in color, possesses a massive body, has six faces, and his hair stands erect;
he is endowed with twelve arms and is adorned with serpents, bones, and jewels. (5-14)
He is wrathful, with an erect phallus, and filled with blazing rays;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of severed heads. || 5.15 ||
Uttering the sound "huṃ huṃ," he was devouring the great serpents;
his hands held a trident, a sword, a discus, a scimitar, a goad, and displayed the gesture of granting boons.

The practitioner, having displayed the mudrās of the threatening gesture, the goad, the mace, the bow, the noose, and the granting of fearlessness, and having performed the worship including the invocation and other rites, [should proceed]. (5.17)

Having performed the limb-protection (*aṅga*) for Mārtaṇḍabhairava according to the sequence beginning with *hrām*, one should then present a handful of flowers along with the water offering (*arghya*), accompanied by the mantra. (5.18)
Hrauṃ hasrauḥ, obeisance to Śrī Kulamārtaṇḍa Bhairava; hrauṃ hasrauḥ.
Afterwards, having sprinkled water upon oneself, one should again recite this mantra;
one should properly cast a handful of flowers toward Savitṛ, the witness of all.

*Hasrauḥ kṣrauṃ hasrauḥ phaṭ khphreṃ bhāṃ phaṭ hasrauḥ kṣoṃ hasrauḥ phaṭ khphreṃ bhāṃ*. This is the mantra for the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). As for the mudrās: the trident (*śūla*) and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), as well as the three-fold mark (*tridhākā*) and the deer (*hariṇī*).
Having made a finger-cleft, one should [place them] upon the eight petals starting from the east.
And in the center, one should worship Caṇḍarocis, who holds a trident and the tarjanī gesture;
there, one should sacrifice to the nine Śaktis and also worship the Bhairavas.

JŪṂ Jvālāyai JŪṂ | KṢĀṂ Mitrīśāyai KṢĀṂ | HŪṂ PHAṬ Caṇḍālinyai HŪṂ PHAṬ | SAUḤ Bhīṣaṇāyai SAUḤ | AIṂ Nārasiṃhāyai AIṂ | HRĪṂ Kamalādevyai HRĪṂ | PHREṂ Mārtaṇḍāyai PHREṂ | PHREṂ Kapālinyai PHREṂ | SAUḤ Kaulinyai SAUḤ || 5 || Now.
The Bhairava mantras are: *phreṃ* to Caṇḍa, *phreṃ* to Viśveśa, Mahādeva, Mahākāla, Gabhastīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Taijasa, and Mārtaṇḍa.
Having bound the Khecarī mudrā, one performs the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*) and the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).
Having performed the rites beginning with *hrām* and so forth, [one should worship] with *dūrvā* grass and red flowers.
Having worshipped with incense, lamps, food offerings, and the *arghya* mantra,
one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability, dedicating that recitation with the *arghya* mantra.
And in the previously mentioned *arghya* mantra, one should then extract the self from the heart-lotus of the *cidāditya*, [reciting] "dahadaha kahakahā. (5.24)
Having placed the *arghya* and the food offering (*naivedya*), as well as the radiant *arghya*, outside,
one should draw a square mandala on the left side.
In that common vessel, the preceptor, having worshipped Paśumārtaṇḍabhairava according to the rule by means of His very mantra, [should proceed].
Having offered all the remains of the oblation (*nirmālya*), one should present everything to Him with the mantra:

*hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ paśumārtaṇḍabhairavāya*. This concludes the solar worship (*saurapūjā*). Now follows the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapapūjā*). First, the meditation upon the pavilion (*maṇḍapadhyāna*).
In the ocean of nectar, upon the island of jewels, one should contemplate the Nandana grove,
adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *pāṭala* trees.
With *lavaṅga*, *mālatī*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *nameru* trees, and with the well-flowered *kalpa* trees such as the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*; || 5-28 ||
With sandalwood trees, *karṇikāra*, *mātuluṅga*, and *vañjula*; with pomegranates, *lakuca*, *aṅkola*, betel nuts, and *kurubaka* as well. || 5.29 ||
It was adorned with plantains, kunda, mandāra, and coconut trees,
and embellished by other groves of trees rich in fragrant blossoms.
With *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jātī*, *ketaka*, and *śatapatraka* flowers, as well as with *pārantī*, *tulasī*, *nandyāvarta*, and *damanaka* [leaves]. (5.31)
It was adorned with shimmering trees endowed with the blossoms of all seasons,
while the fragrance of flowers scattered by the gentle breeze filled the quarters of the sky.
In its center stands Mount Meru, whose nature is the supreme light;
in its center [is a lake] always blooming with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses.
With fragrant *kahlāra* lotuses and fresh blue water-lilies, and with *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, bees, and *cakravāka* birds; (5.34)
It was graced by other birds with clamorous cries;
in its midst, upon a most enchanting sandbank in a great lake, [he stood].
One should visualize the great Kalpa-tree, rich with Pārijāta trees on all sides,
situated in the midst of a grove of Nīpa trees and beautifully blossoming with various flowers.
It was strewn with fruits of various jewels, providing shade for the three worlds;
the surface of the earth was turned crimson by the radiance of the emerging gems.
Its horizons were illuminated by the rising sun and moon;
it was constantly attended by the six seasons and increased everyone's delight.
He repeatedly sprinkles the pavilion with honey called *parāmṛta*;
beneath it is a great altar constructed solely of rubies.
A blazing vajra-fence, extending for a hundred yojanas;
in its center, one should visualize a radiant pavilion with a jeweled floor.
Resembling the rising sun, radiant and cool as the moon,
it was provided with four gates and adorned with golden ramparts.
It was adorned with eight doors made beautiful by the arrangement of jewels,
and possessed lofty gate-towers and archways fashioned from the nine precious gems.
It was adorned with rows of banners fastened to golden staffs,
and it shone with rows of pillars set with the nine precious gems.
It was resplendent with a circle of lamps joined by a thousand lights,
and it was enchanting with windows fashioned from refined gold.
It was adorned with hundreds of millions of golden ornaments bound with cloths of various colors,
and with banners provided with rows of tinkling bells.
It was beautified by various wonderful paintings and adorned with rows of golden jars;
it was made of gold, inlaid with jewels, and exceedingly vast.
Adorned with rows of garlands of rubies, gems, lapis lazuli, and gold,
and interspersed at intervals with jewels that captivate the eye.
It was adorned with canopies of various and multicolored patterns,
and possessed a brilliant golden floor inlaid with all kinds of jewels.
With ketakī, mālatī, jātī, campaka, and utpala-kesara; with mallikā, tulasī, yūthī, nandyāvarta, and kadamba.
The surface of the earth was adorned with these and other flowers,
and it was further embellished by ground-levels provided with staircases made of jewels.
The quarters of the sky were illuminated by moonlight, saffron, musk from the navel of the deer, tamālaka, sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Delightful with rows of flower garlands, resplendent with strings of pearls,
radiant with camphor lamps, and adorned with rubies as lamps.
At the edge of the wish-fulfilling trees, amidst jeweled altars,
there was a magnificent throne bound with jewels and adorned with the Śrīcakra.
By the hosts of deities beginning with Indra, by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others,
by numerous groups of yoginīs, and also by the presiding deities of the weapons.
It is presided over by Mahātripurasundarī, whose lotus-feet are being served by her own form, and it grants all desires. (5.55)
The wise practitioner should contemplate the pavilion as being agitated by waves of surging nectar, bestowing the desire for liberation, and filled with manifold incense. (5.56)
One should meditate upon oneself as situated within that pavilion with an undistracted mind, realizing "I am Bhairava," endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the rest. (5.57)
Thus ends the meditation on the glorious pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Now, the worship of the door:

having entered within through the eastern gate of the golden enclosure and proceeding clockwise to the western gate of the jeweled pavilion (*maṇimaṇḍapa*), one begins from there and circumambulates the jeweled pavilion, [entering] through the western gate.

"Having entered the interior of the jeweled pavilion (maṇimaṇḍapa), the practitioner should worship the Goddess"—this is the sequence. By that same sequence, there is the "worship of the door. Therefore, if an enclosure for the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) exists, [the worship] is based on its doors; if that does not exist, it is at the western door of the sacrificial pavilion; and if a pavilion does not exist, it is on the sacrificial ground smeared with cow dung.

Having stood somewhere in the western direction, having prepared the ordinary *arghya* offering, and having thus visualized [the mandala], one should worship it in sequence. Therein is an island made of the nine jewels, extending for ten million *yojanas* and wide for ten million *yojanas*, situated within a great ocean of nectar, most wonderful, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns; in its center, at one-third [of its extent]...

The Nandana garden, named Madanonmādana, was filled with various flowering creepers and situated within a grove of Kadamba trees; in its center was a third part [of the garden] which shone like ten million suns,
surrounded by blazing golden walls, featuring gateways and arches adorned with various fragrant halls and embellished with diverse jewels.
Having meditated upon the glorious pavilion (śrīmaṇḍapa), which is crowded on all sides by the hosts of Indra and other deities who have come for service,

and having sprinkled it with the water of the general arghya, one should worship it in sequence with flowers and water: "Obeisance to the Ocean of Nectar," "Obeisance to the Island consisting of nine jewels," "Obeisance to the Nandana Garden," "Obeisance to the Golden Wall."
One should worship [the deity] above and below the right and left door-panels.
4 Gāṃ, I worship the sandals of Gaṇeśa; 4 Kṣāṃ, I worship the sandals of Kṣetrapāla; 4 Dvāṃ, I worship the sandals of Dvāraśrī; 4 Deṃ, I worship the sandals of Dehalīśrī.

Entering with the right foot foremost, one should worship the guardians of the directions, such as Indra and the others, within the interior in the eight directions starting from the east. Then, in the western part, one should worship the *tiraskaraṇī* (the screen). [One should draw] a circular, triangular, and square maṇḍala.
Having established herself there, mounted upon a beautiful blue horse, adorned with blue garments, ornaments, garlands, and finery,
obscuring the worlds with her veil of sleep, and armed with a sword— may that Blessed Lady protect us.

Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: *Aiṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari paśujanamanuścakṣustiraskaraṇaṃ kurukuru svāhā*. One should worship with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers. Then, having worshipped with "4 kadambavanāya namaḥ" and "4 śrīratnamaṇḍapāya namaḥ," one should worship the deities of its doors with "Sauḥ astrāya."

With "phaṭ," having sprinkled the western door, [one should worship]: on the upper lintel—4 Māṃ Mahālakṣmīpādukāṃ; on the left—4 Sāṃ Sarasvatīpādukāṃ; in the middle—4 Duṃ Durgāśrīpādukāṃ; 4 Dvāṃ Dvāraśrīpādukāṃ. On the right and left lintels: 4 Śaṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi and Vasudhārā. 4.

Salutation to Padmanidhi and Vasumatī. Above, on the right: 4 Gaṃ, salutation to the sandals of Vighneśa; on the left: 4 Kṣaṃ, salutation to the sandals of Kṣetreśa. Above that, on the right: 4 Gāṃ, salutation to the sandals of Gaṅgā; on the left: 4 Yāṃ, salutation to the sandals of Yamunā. Above that, on the right: 4 Dhāṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ; on the left: 4 Viṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Below, at the threshold: 4.

"4 Vāṃ Varuṇapādukābhyāṃ" and "4 Vāṃ Dvārapādukābhyām"—thus is the worship of the western door. Then, having gone to the northern door, on its upper lintel: "4 Vaṃ Vaṭukanāthapādukābhyāṃ" and "4 Dvāṃ Dvāraśrīpādukāyai.
Then, having performed worship as before, starting from Śaṅkhanidhi and Vasudhārā up to the threshold (dehalī), [one worships] in front of the threshold: "4..."
"Oṃ kūṃ Kuberapāda" — thus is the worship of the northern gate. Then, having gone to the eastern gate, on its upper branch: "4 Kṣauṃ Kṣetrapālapāda"; on the right: "4 Viṃ Vighnanāthapāda.
Then, to the left of oneself, at the right, left, and front of Kṣetrapāla:

Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Dvāraśrī, and having worshipped as before starting from the pair of the conch and lotus up to the threshold (dehalī), one performs the worship of the eastern door in front of the threshold with: "4 Lāṃ, to Indranātha-pāda. Then, having gone to the southern door and sprinkled it, [one worships] on its upper lintel: "4..."

*Glauṃ*, worship the sandals of Gaṇanātha (4). *Dvāṃ*, worship the sandals of the Door-Guardian (*dvārapādukā*). One should first worship the couple Kāmadeva and Vasanta on the right and left door-frames.
Above that, having worshipped from the couple Śaṅkha and Padma up to the threshold (*dehalī*), one worships in front of the threshold with: *Yāṃ*, worship the sandals of Yamanātha.

Worship of the Southern Gate. Then, having again gone to the western gate and entered within its archway with the left foot leading, standing facing the jeweled pavilion, one should worship the deities seated upon the dais. Having worshipped the jeweled staircase with "Raṃ, obeisance to the jeweled staircase," [one worships] the deity seated on the dais above it.

Having meditated, one should perform worship. In front of the western door, on the right: *4 Sāṃ Sarasvatī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; on the left: *4 Māṃ Mahālakṣmī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Between them, above, below, and in front, Gaurī and the others, ending with the Mānavaugha, are to be worshipped:
*4 Gauṃ Gaurī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *4 Loṃ Lokadhātrī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *4 Vāṃ Vāgīśvarī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *4 Divyaugha-śrī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

Siddhaugha-Śrīpāda 4; Mānavaugha-Śrīpāda. Then, again at the northern gate, one should worship from Māyādurga up to the end of the Mānavaugha, as before. Then, at the eastern gate, one should worship from Bhadrakālī, Svastīgaurī, and so forth, up to the end of the Mānavaugha, as before. Then, at the southern gate...

"Oṃ svāhā! To the goddess Aśubhaṅkarī; one should worship [the deities] beginning with Gaurī and ending with the multitude of human beings. Then, having again gone to the western door and meditated thus: "I take refuge in the western door, the great temple of Bhavānī, which is protected on the outside by Indra and the other gods and adorned with supreme sovereignty," [one offers] to the western door: 4. *paścimadvārāya*.

Having worshipped the pavilion with "Obeisance to the Jewel Pavilion" (ratnamaṇḍapāya namaḥ), and having opened the door preceded by three claps of the hands (tāla), one should cast white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers using the Nārāca weapon-mantra: "Āṃ! May those beings who dwell upon the earth depart; may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva! 5-Hraḥ! To the Weapon! (astrāya).

Having cast [the offerings] inside the pavilion with the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, one should dispel the threefold obstacles by yielding a path for the multitudes of obstructing spirits departing from there through the contraction of the left limb;
while mentally reciting either the root-vidyā or the armor-mantra (*vāstramantra*) at the threshold itself, one should [ward off] terrestrial obstacles with three strikes of the left heel.
Having dispelled the celestial obstacles (*divyavighnas*) with three claps of the hands (*tāla*) and by gazing with divine vision, he recites: "Oṃ!

May those beings who cause heresy, whether they dwell on the earth, in the intermediate space, or in the celestial realm, perish by the command of Śiva! Having thus recited, he steps across the threshold with his left foot first and enters the interior of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

Then the silent one, pure in soul, perceiving the Supreme Goddess within his heart, the yogi whose mind is not directed toward external objects should enter the sacrificial ground. Thus ends the worship of the doors. Here, if it is impossible to go to each door individually, one should remain at the western door alone, mentally conceive those respective doors, and perform the worship. Some maintain that one should worship the western door alone.
Now, the meditations on the deities of the doors:

One should worship Padmā, who is lotus-colored, who dwells in the lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses, and whose four radiant hands hold two lotuses, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). (5.1)
May the goddess Bhāratī, who holds a rosary and a book, whose splendor is equal to the full moon, and who consists of all knowledge, shine within me. 5-2.
May the goddess Durgā—whose hands are marked with the conch and discus, who is a maiden with curling locks of hair, and whose vehicle is the king of beasts—destroy my difficulties. 5-3.
Resplendent like molten gold, adorned with divine jewels,
the Goddess Door-Splendor (Dvāraśrī) stands upon an upward-facing lotus, her lotus-hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (5.4)
Resembling pearls and rubies, with lotus-faces slightly smiling,
they were intent on embracing one another and held a conch and a lotus.
Their heads are marked by two conchs from which showers of jewels are pouring forth;
seated upon conch-thrones, they are the fulfillers of the world's every resolve.
One should worship him who has a protruding belly and holds the treasure of the conch, who possesses firm breasts like a stream of wealth, and who,
together with his beloved, holds the treasure of the lotus on his left side.
Resembling vermilion, their arms are locked together; they hold red lotuses and blue water-lilies, and are marked on their heads by two lotuses from which showers of jewels are pouring forth.
Seated upon lotus-thrones, they are the fulfillers of the world's every resolve; [they behold] the pot-bellied Lord of the Lotus-Born (Brahmā) and the slender Earth as well.
I bow to the Mind-born God, who possesses the hue of the palāśa and pāṭala flowers, who is delightful and dear to Rati, and who wields the bow of sugarcanes and arrows of flowers. 5-10.
I take refuge in Him who is beloved by His consort, whose radiance is like that of the full moon,
who dwells in the Nandana grove, and who is ever-present with eternal festivity.
I salute the heroic Vighneśvara, who has the face of an elephant and three eyes, whose hands hold a noose, a goad, and a red lotus, and who is pale-red and pot-bellied.
I worship Kṣetreśa, who has a dark form, sharp features, and three eyes; he holds a skull and a trident in his two hands and has destroyed his enemies. 5.13
I worship Gaṅgā, the river of the water from the feet of the Great Goddess, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who is gentle, and whose radiance is equal to ten million moons. 5-14.

I bow to Kālindī, who has the form of Time (Kāla), who arose from half of the left foot of the Supreme Goddess, who is like a surging river, and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I bow to the Lord of the worlds, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus;
who is mounted upon Garuḍa, the Sustainer, whose form is Kṛṣṇa. (5.16)

I salute the Creator, who is red in color, seated upon a red lotus, holding a water-pot along with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, mounted on a swan, and endowed with a rosary of beads. (5.17)
I bow to the protector of the western direction, who is mounted upon a lion, possesses a dark-complexioned body, holds a sword and a shield, and stands beneath the threshold. 5-18.
I salute Varuṇa, who holds a noose and the gesture of fearlessness, whose complexion resembles the full moon,
who is mounted upon a makara, and who is the presiding deity at the door of the venerable feet.
Thus at the western gate.

Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of success upon practitioners, who holds a skull in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff, is dark blue like fresh darkness, and wears a serpent as a sacred thread; he is the cause of the interruption of obstacles during the worship at the time of sacrifice. Kubera is smoke-colored, holds a mace in his hand, and has a man as his vehicle.
May the lord of the northern gate, the lord of wealth of the Supreme Goddess, protect [you]. || 5.21 ||
I bow to the Lord, who bears matted locks entwined with serpents, who has three eyes, and whose luster is like a mountain of blue collyrium;
who holds a skull aloft by his staff-like arms, and is radiant with red garlands, garments, and perfumes;
and who is formidable with the mingling sounds of the jingling bells of his girdle and the *dhāṃkāra* resonance.
I always salute that Kṣetrapāla, who wears white serpent earrings.
White in complexion, with the face of an elephant, he stands upon a mouse, wielding in his four arms a battle-axe, a tusk, a noose, and a trident.
May Śakra, the lord of the eastern gate, who is intensely yellow, the consort of Parā, holding a vajra in his hand, possessing a thousand eyes, and having Airāvata as his emblem, protect [us]. (5.24)
Gaṇeśa is dark-complexioned, four-armed, and clad in the directions (naked);
likewise, he holds a noose and a goad with his left, right, and upper arms respectively.
With his lower right hand he holds a skull-cup filled with honey,
and with his left hand he embraces the temple of the goddess’s love.
Touching with his right hand the red goddess stationed on his left side,
he places his linga in her vulva while holding a lotus with his left hand.
One should meditate upon and worship Yama, who resembles a mass of blue collyrium and rides upon a buffalo, as he smells the vulva with his trunk while she is holding it. 5-28.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Southern Gate, whose powerful arm is adorned with a staff.
Now, the meditation on the deities seated upon the couch:
she who holds a rosary, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness in her arms, and bestows boons.
One should meditate upon the goddess Sarasvatī, who has three eyes and is entirely white.

[She is] Mahālakṣmī, who has four radiant hands displaying the two lotuses, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; her body is as fair as purified gold, and she possesses three eyes.

I bow to the Mother Gaurī, who possesses a reddish luster, who is radiant in red garments, who has three eyes, and who bears the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. (5.3)

I bow to the Mother, the Sustainer of the World, who possesses a golden luster, whose limbs are adorned with divine jewels, and who bears the gestures of dancing, the blue lotus, the boon-granting mudrā, and the gesture of fearlessness. (5.4)
I worship Vāgīśvarī, who is white, clad in white garments, adorned with white ornaments, garlands, and unguents, and who holds two lotuses, a boon-granting gesture, and a mirror in her hands.

I incessantly meditate upon the three-eyed Māyā, who holds in her hands the elephant-goad, the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and the trident— the very root of worldly existence— and whose bodily luster possesses the brilliance of a mass of thick rain clouds.
I bow to Durgā, the remover of misfortune, who holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows, who has three eyes, and whose complexion resembles the blade of a dūrvā grass. 5-7.
I bow to Bhadrakālī, who resembles a mass of crushed collyrium and who holds in her hands a skull, a shield, a sword, and a trident.

One should meditate upon the supreme goddess Svasti, who bestows well-being, who has three eyes, whose splendor is like that of the moon, and whose hands display the gestures of the spear, the svastika, and the protection mudrā.

I worship Svāhā, who is praised by the hosts of gods and sages; she holds a pair of red lotuses along with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands, her face radiant with a smile, red in hue, three-eyed, and adorned with crimson garments.
Holding a grain of rice, a wish-fulfilling creeper, a bow, and an arrow in her four hands, she who possesses the radiant luster of blazing gold—Śubhaṅkarī—shall bestow auspiciousness. (5.11)
Thus are the meditations. Then, having worshipped in the center of the mandala with "Homage to Brahmā; homage to Gṛheśāna;

homage to Vāstupuruṣa in the southwest," and having sprinkled the ground with "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and having consecrated the ground with "Oṃ pavitravajrabhūme rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one recites] "Āḥ Surekhe."
Having inscribed "vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" upon the ground and spread a seat over it,

one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva in the four directions starting from the east and in the center; then, visualizing a triangle above that, one should contemplate the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāna at the three corners and in the center.

Having worshipped with the mantra "4 Hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)," one should worship the seat. Then, sitting upon it facing either east or north, or alternatively, having meditated on the maṇḍala of the Mātṛkās and sat upon it, one should pray to the earth: "Oṃ, O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu."

Supported! O Goddess, you who uphold all, please support me and purify this seat. O Earth, purify me as well; salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Gods! *Oṃ*, for the *āsana-mantra*: the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Meru-pṛṣṭha of the Earth, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Sutala, the deity (*devatā*) is Kṛmoṃ, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the seat. *Oṃ*, for the *praṇava*: the seer is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Paramātman.
The application [of mantras] is in *prāṇāyāma*. Then, having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, one should assign the mantras as follows: "Salutation to Dīpanātha" on the head;

"Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati" and the mantra *gaṇānāṃ tvā* on the right arm; "Duṃ, salutation to Durgā" and the mantra *oṃ jātavedase* on the left arm; "Kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla" and the mantra *oṃ kṣetrasya patinā vayaṃ* on the right knee.

At the left knee: *saṃ*—salutation to Sarasvatī; "May the divine Sarasvatī... [and so forth]. Then, having offered salutations with the words: "Salutation to the Śrī-gurus, salutation to the Parama-gurus, salutation to the Parameṣṭhi-gurus," one should [expel obstructors] by striking the heels, clapping the hands, and opening the mouth wide, [driving away] those who have entered the netherworld, the earth, and the sky.

"The wise one should dispel the obstacles. Thus, having dispelled the obstacles, [he should perform] the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) as follows: with the aforementioned *pāśupatāstra* mantra, he should rub the palm of the left hand twice, starting from the wrist, while it is touched by the right hand; then, having wiped the right hand once according to the stated method, he should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). It is as follows:
Laṃ, obeisance to Indra; I bind the eastern direction with the discus, obeisance to the discus, svāhā!

Oṃ, may we know the Sudarśana, may we meditate upon the Great Flame; may that Discus impel us. 3. Ugra, the Hero, the Great Viṣṇu, blazing with faces on all sides, the Man-lion, the Terrifying, the Auspicious, the Death of Death.

I bow down. Having thus performed the binding of the ten directions: *Raṃ*, obeisance to the fire-wall (*agniprākāra*). *Sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ*, obeisance to the Sudarśana fire-wall. *Oṃ hrīṃ sphura sphura prasphura prasphura ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vama vama bandhaya bandhaya*.

"Kill, kill, hūṃ phaṭ! Salutation to the Aghora Fire-Wall. With these words, one should create a triple fire-wall with water. Having performed the three-fold encirclement by fire, one should then [worship] Gaṇeśa and the fifth [deity].
Durgā, Vighna, Śarabha, Aghora, and Sudarśana. || 5-1 ||
One should recite these samaya-mantras for the pacification of obstacles;
having thus first performed the protection, one should then practice the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
These mantras are to be understood from the Chapter on Extraction (Uddhārapaṭala). In another tantra:
"The preceptor should place the articles of worship on the right side;
on the left, a beautiful jar filled with well-scented water. (5-1)
After washing his hands, he should place the vessel behind him;
he should arrange auspicious lamps, ignited with ghee, all around. || 5-2 ||
"A mirror, a fly-whisk, a parasol, and a beautiful palm-leaf fan.
Thus it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Various kinds of flowers and diverse fragrances, scented with camphor, nutmeg, incense, and the like, as well as perfumed garments. || 5-1 ||
Betel, articles for the deity, incense, lamps, and so forth;
all ornaments, decorations, garments, and the like—O Lord of the Kula, [these are to be offered]. (5.2)
Then, having purified [the area] with water consecrated by reciting the root mantra, one should establish it;
everything should be placed to one's right, and the *arghya* offering should be set down on the left.
And in the west, one should hold the family substances of the deity.

Likewise: Oṃ, to the noble Puṣpaketu, who has gone everywhere and is perfectly awakened; oṃ, flower, flower, great flower, beautiful flower, born from flowers, strewn with the gathering of flowers, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

The purification of flowers and other offerings is performed with the mantra: *oṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having placed one's hand upon the heart with this mantra, one should perform self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*). Then, having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

The purification of the elements that constitute the form of the body, resulting from contact with the imperishable Brahman—this is considered the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 5-4 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should unite the self with the Supreme Self through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, according to the method joined with yoga and by means of the *cinmantra*.

Thus [it is said]. "With the *cinmantra*" means with the mantra of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). With the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā," one should contemplate the six previously mentioned cakras, beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, and then, by means of the mind, [lead] the individual soul (*jīvātman*) residing in the heart-cakra, together with the *kulakuṇḍalinī*, along the path of the *suṣumnā*.
"I unite [the soul] in the state of Paramaśiva situated at the aperture of Brahmā, svāhā! I purify this subtle body (liṅgaśarīra),
svāhā!"— having thus struck with the mind-staff by means of the individual soul,
and having caused that [subtle body] to dissolve through the downward-moving wind constricted by the seed-syllable *huṃ* and the increased heat of the downward fire;

By means of the central path known as the *suṣumnā*, through the sequence of piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) together with the locations, phonemes, and deities, and by way of the yoga of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*),
[one reaches] the Supreme Śiva who resides within the lunar orb situated in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus located at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

One should contemplate the dissolved state. Then, from the feet up to the knees is the locus of earth, yellow in color, square in shape, having Brahmā as its presiding deity, and consisting of the *nivṛtti-kalā*; in its center is the seed-syllable *laṃ*.
By means of the application of the five extractions (*pañcoddhāta*), I dissolve it into water. From the knees up to the genitals is the locus of water.
The white-colored [element], marked by a lotus, shaped like a half-moon, presided over by Viṣṇu,
and consisting of the kalā of Pratiṣṭhā— within that, I dissolve the seed-syllable *vaṃ* into the radiant light through the application of the fourfold *uddhāta*.
From the base of the liṅga up to the navel is the locus of light, red in color, triangular in shape, and presided over by Rudra.
In the center of that [element], I dissolve the seed-syllable *Raṃ*, which consists of the *vidyā-kalā*, into the air by means of the practice of triple suppression (*triruddhāta*).

From the navel up to the heart is the locus of air; it is smoke-colored, hexagonal in shape, marked with six dots, has Īśvara as its presiding deity, and consists of the *śānti-kalā*. In the center of that is the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*.
By means of the application of the double-contradictory breath (*dviruddhāta*), I cause [the deity] to converse in the ether.

From the heart up to the throat is the locus of the ether; it is of clear color, circular in shape, presided over by Sadāśiva as its deity, and consists of the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītā*). In its center—
By means of the practice of the single extraction (*ekoddhāta*), I dissolve the seed-syllable *Haṃ* into the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

The locus of the ego extends from the throat to the space between the eyebrows; it is three-colored, shaped like a staff, presided over by Ādiśiva, and consists of all the *kalās*. In its center is the seed-syllable *Haṃsaḥ*.

By means of the practice of total withdrawal (*sarvoddhāta*), I dissolve [the breath] into the Great Principle (*mahattattva*). The locus of the Great Principle extends from the space between the eyebrows to the forehead; it is white in color, shaped like a half-moon, has Ānandaśiva as its presiding deity, and consists of the nature of the *kalā*s.
Into its center, I dissolve the seed-syllable *so'ham* into primordial nature (*prakṛti*) by means of the practice of partial withdrawal (*ardhoddhāta*).

From the forehead up to the parting of the hair is the natural seat, the color of the rising sun, shaped like a vulva, presided over by the deity Ānandaśiva, and consisting of the nature of the *kalās*. In its center, by means of the application of the initial extraction (*uddhāta*), I dissolve the seed-syllable *haṃ* into the *puruṣa*. From the parting of the hair up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
In the center of that is the station of Puruṣa, brilliant in color, shaped like a liṅga, with consciousness as its deity, partless;

therein I dissolve the seed-syllable of the Nāda, which is the nature of the Supreme Bindu, by means of the practice of restrained breath. The Brahma-randhra is the station of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), white as camphor, possessing a thousand spokes, and having bliss as its deity.

Having contemplated, "In the midst of that [void] which is formless by nature, I meditate upon the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*— which, through the practice of the meditation on withdrawal, is of the essence of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, a mass of consciousness and bliss"— one should recite: *oṃ pṛthivyaptejovāyvākāśagandharasarūpasparśaśabda-*

It consists of the totality of principles known as the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, ears, feet, genitals, anus, hands, speech, movement, pleasure, excretion, grasping, speaking, ego, mind, intellect, consciousness, conceptualization, volition, determination, resolve, the individual self (jīvātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).

I dissolve the two bodies, gross and subtle, which are the very nature of phenomenal expansion, in the order of withdrawal: earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into the ego-principle, the ego-principle into the Great Principle (mahat), the Great Principle into primordial nature (prakṛti), primordial nature into the Puruṣa, and the Puruṣa into the Supreme Śiva; svāhā!

"I purify this gross body, svāhā!"— having thus dissolved all principles (tattvas), both gross and subtle, along with their locations, syllables, effects, causes, presiding deities, limbs, and sub-limbs,
in the order of reabsorption into their respective causes, [one dissolves them] into the Supreme Śiva within the thousand-petaled lotus.

One should contemplate [the elements] as dissolved into the state of seed-syllables. Having established Paramaśiva—who is of the nature of consciousness-power (*cicchakti*), a mass of bliss—the yogi, with a stainless intellect and all senses withdrawn, attains the fruit of the sacrifice: that which is eternally arisen, actionless, and consists of existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*). Thus, in this sequence, one should remain for a moment; this is the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Now...
Contemplation of the Personification of Sin (p.
One should contemplate the personification of sin located in the left side of the abdomen, having the luster of collyrium.
It has the murder of a Brahmin for its head and the theft of gold for its two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the Guru’s bed;
the pair of feet are for those who associate with such sinners—this constitutes the sin of the limbs and their minor parts. (5.2)
One should thus contemplate the wicked one as having body hair like that of a minor offender, with red beard and eyes, cruel, and bearing a sword and shield. (5.3)

Having meditated thus, while reciting sixteen times the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is smoke-colored, one should fill the air through the left nostril with the mantra: *iti dhyātvā yaṃ pāpaśarīraṃ śoṣaya śoṣaya śoṣayāmi svāhā*.
Then, reciting that same syllable sixty-four times through the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), [one should visualize the air] rising from the heart and coming from the six-spoked [lotus].

Having meditated upon the Person of Sin as dried up by the Great Wind, one should exhale the wind through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] while reciting that same seed-syllable (*bīja*) twenty-two times. Reciting the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which is red in color, sixteen times, one should fill the wind through the *piṅgalā* while reciting: "Burn, burn, burn the dried-up body of sin! Svāhā! *Raṃ*. Then, that very [seed-syllable]...

Reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times with the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention), one should visualize the "person of sin" (*pāpapuruṣa*) being consumed by the great fire arising from the navel and coming forth from the triangle; then, reciting that same [mantra] thirty-two times, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā* [nāḍī].
*Ṭaṃ candramaṇḍalaṃ preraya preraya prerayāmi svāhā ṭam*—this is the seed-syllable of the Moon (*candrabīja*).

Reciting [the mantra] sixteen times while filling the breath through the *iḍā* [nāḍī], and reciting it sixty-four times while performing the *kumbhaka* (retention) yoga, one should contemplate the lunar seed-syllable (*candrabīja*)—which delights the universe and is filled with a flood of great nectar—within the center of the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*). Then, reciting it thirty-two times, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā*. *Vaṃ paramāmṛtaṃ varṣaya varṣaya varṣayāmi svāhā.*

Reciting the seed-syllable *vaṃ* of Varuṇa, which is white in color, sixteen times while filling the breath through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], and then reciting it sixty-four times while performing the *kumbhaka* (retention) yoga, one should visualize a great rain consisting of the *mātṛkā* letters produced from that lunar orb, flooding those bones, cremation grounds, and so forth; then, reciting it thirty-two times, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā*. *Laṃ*.

"Śarīram utpādaya utpādaya utpādayāmi svāhā laṃ. Reciting this sixteen times, one should fill the breath with air through the *iḍā* [left nostril]. Then, reciting it sixty-four times while employing the *kumbhaka* (retention) yoga, [one should contemplate]: "Oṃ, the Supreme Self, the Individual Self, consciousness, intellect, mind, and ego..."

It consists of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), comprising all the principles known as determination, resolve, intention, conceptualization, speech, grasping, excretion, pleasure, movement, the organs of speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet, as well as the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; and ether, air, fire, water, and earth.

The two bodies— the gross and the subtle— are produced by the supreme Śiva and his power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) through the process of emanation; from these two distinct principles, the *puruṣa* is produced from *puruṣa*,
*prakṛti* is produced from *prakṛti* by the process of partial production, and the *mahat* is produced from *mahat*.

By the practice of universal origination, I produce space; by the practice of twofold origination from space, wind; by the practice of threefold origination from wind, fire; by the practice of fourfold origination from fire, water; by the practice of fivefold origination from water, earth; and by the practice of sixfold origination from earth, [I produce it]. Svāhā!

Thus, having brought forth all the principles (tattvas)— the six locations, along with the phonemes, their causes, their effects, their presiding deities, and their primary and secondary limbs— both gross and subtle, produced from their respective causes from the presence of the Consciousness-Power (cicchakti) of Paraśiva according to the order of emanation,
[he did so] by means of the great [power] arising from the feet and coming from the square.

Having contemplated that a new, meritorious body fit for the worship of the deity has been produced by being supported by the earth, and having established the *tattvas* in their respective places, one should fill the breath through the *piṅgalā* while reciting that same seed-syllable *laṃ* thirty-two times; then, reciting it sixty-four times, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā*. These constitute six *prāṇāyāmas*.

[The following] come to pass: One should bring the self from the heart-lotus of the Supreme Self; then, with the mantra of the divine Haṃsa, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites. Oṃ haṃsaḥ so’haṃ | Descend, descend from the state of Śiva, by means of the path of the Suṣumṇā through the vehicle of the individual soul (jīva); shine forth, shine forth at the root of the Śṛṅgāṭa; blaze, blaze; burn brightly, burn brightly! Oṃ haṃsaḥ.
Thinking "I am that," the individual soul (jīvātman), together with the power of consciousness (cicchakti) assuming the form of Kuṇḍalinī,

along with the [corresponding] places, phonemes, and deities, should— by means of the yoga of emanation— bring her from the Brahma-randhra down to the Mūlādhāra through the central path of the channel called Citrā within the Suṣumnā, following the sequence of piercing the six cakras, and establish her at the Mūlādhāra.
One should contemplate the individual soul (jīvātman) residing in the heart—this is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now, the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā (Consecration of Life): Oṃ, of this Śrīprāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers;

the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman are the meters; the deity is the Power of Life (Prāṇaśakti) whose form is consciousness; Oṃ is the seed-syllable, Hrīṃ is the power, and Kroṃ is the pin; its application is for the installation of the vital breaths. Having thus performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the appropriate locations, [one recites]: Aṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ...

Ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, to the self of ether, air, fire, water, and earth, [I offer] salutation with the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, to the self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, [I offer] salutation with the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ). Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ Ūṃ, to the self of hearing, skin, sight, tongue, and nose...

Salutation to the two middle fingers. *Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ*, salutation to the two ring fingers, who are the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ. *Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ*, salutation to the two little fingers, who are the self of speaking, grasping, excreting, experiencing bliss, and moving. *Aṃ yaṃ*.

Raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ. To the self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and [subtle] mind, salutation with the palms and backs of the hands. With these very [syllables], joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are formed. Āṃ namaḥ from the navel to the feet; Hrīṃ namaḥ from the heart to the navel; Kroṃ namaḥ.

From the crown of the head down to the heart: *yaṃ* to the self of the skin, *namaḥ*; *raṃ* to the self of the blood, *namaḥ*; *laṃ* to the self of the flesh, *namaḥ*; *vaṃ* to the self of the fat, *namaḥ*; *śaṃ* to the self of the bone, *namaḥ*;

*ṣaṃ* to the self of the marrow, *namaḥ*; *saṃ* to the self of the semen, *namaḥ*; *haṃ* to the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), *namaḥ*; *laṃ* to the self of the individual soul (*jīva*), *namaḥ*.
"Oṃ, salutation to Kṣaṃ, the Supreme Self; salutation. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should meditate upon the power of life-force (*prāṇaśakti*):
"Seated upon a red lotus in a boat upon a red ocean, holding a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, and arrows..."
I bow to the Goddess, who is red in hue, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident and a skull in her lotus-like hands. 5-1.

Having meditated thus: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ so'haṃ haṃsaḥ*. May the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī enter here; thrice [recite]: "the vital breaths"; may the life-force (*jīva*) remain here; thrice [recite]: "all the senses"; may speech, mind, eyes, skin, ears, nose, and breath come here and abide in happiness.

Recite "May they remain for a long time, svāhā! three times while placing the hand upon the heart with the *jñānamudrā*. Then, reciting "Oṃ Āṃ Haṃsaḥ," one should contemplate the body as consisting entirely of bliss, firm [both internally and externally], and as being identical with the principal deity—this is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths).

Thus, in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the illustrious Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of the illustrious Pragalbha Ācārya, a disciple of the illustrious Viṣṇuśarman Ācārya, a disciple of the illustrious Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and a disciple of the illustrious Govinda Ācārya— the venerable and worshipful Great Preceptor.
The Fifth Chapter on Exhalation. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra.
Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: Then one should perform the proper armor-arrangement (saṃnāha) and the thorough placement (nyāsa) upon the body.

There are ten Mātṛkās: those situated internally and externally, endowed with their respective Kalās, accompanied by Śrīkaṇṭha, Viṣṇu, and the others, as well as Lajjā, Ramā, Kāma, Pṛthak, Samoha, and the sacrifice of the universe (prapañcayāga). (6-1)
Two finger-breadths above the anus, situated within the subtle aperture of the suṣumṇā,
is a lotus of golden luster, shining with the fire of the four Vedas.
One should lead the Kulakuṇḍalinī, which resides there, shaped like a flash of lightning, consisting of radiant energy, and exceedingly subtle, upward by means of piercing the six cakras.

Having meditated upon the previously mentioned collection of the Mātṛkā letters, situated in the center of the moon at the *dvādaśānta* and resembling fresh butter, [one should contemplate it] quickly melted by the luster of Kuṇḍalinī.
Having drawn forth the *tejas* (radiant energy) from the hollowed palms, one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
Then, having applied the six vowels beginning with *a* in the sequence of pervading the palms and the backs of the hands,
and having applied the remaining ten vowels upon the ten fingers, while reciting the *mātṛkā* from *a* to *kṣa*.

One should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). As it is said: "The purification of the hands is declared to be performed on the forearm, the wrist, the elbow, the palms of both hands, the backs of those hands, and their tips. This concludes the *mātṛkā-karaśuddhi*. Now follows the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*:

therein, inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed with the vowels, retention (*kumbhaka*) with the consonants (*sparśas*), and exhalation (*recaka*) with the pervasive letters (*vyāpakas*), in this sequence.

Having performed three breath-retentions (prāṇāyāmas), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) while reciting: "For this inner Mātṛkā, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), the venerable Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), the consonants are the seeds (bījas), the vowels are the powers (śaktis), the manifestation of the born is the bolt (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is for the purification of my body. Having thus performed the placement, [one recites]: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ*.
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as before with the mantra "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth, one should meditate. Thus, in the *Saṃhitā*:
"Now I shall describe, O Great Goddess, the Mātṛkā, the mother of the world, whose constituent letters range from 'A' to 'KṢ', and who is the deity of those phonemes. (6.1)
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā; the Gāyatrī is said to be its metre.
O Goddess, Mātṛkā is the deity; the consonants are the seeds and the vowels are the powers. (6.2)
But the vowels, O Supreme Goddess, are the Manifest; the unmanifest is the Kīlaka.
The consonants are indeed inexpressible, yet they become manifest through Śakti. (6.3)

In the subtle Śiva, apart from Śakti, neither name nor abode exists. The consonants (hal), being of the nature of non-existence, are turned away [from manifestation] when they are not in proximity to Śakti.
At that time, the throbbing *mātrās* should be uttered facing [the deity] with their phonemes clearly manifest;
having excluded *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, they are situated between the six pairs of vowels.

The six groups [of consonants] in their proper order, with the seventh joined by the *krodha* [visarga], should be placed at the end; O Goddess of Gods, one should then duly assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
One should properly place the vowels upon the lotus with sixteen petals at the throat;
one should place the letters of that [alphabet] on the twelve-petaled lotus at the heart, and place them on the ten-petaled lotus at the navel.
O Īśvarī, one should place ten syllables within the liṅga, six in the six-petalled [lotus], and likewise four syllables in the four-petalled ādhāra. Then, one should assign the four syllables.
"One should install the internal mātṛkā, ending with *ha* and *kṣa*, in the two petals at the center of the eyebrows.
Thus [it is said]. In another tantra:
"In the *ādhāra*, the *liṅga*, the navel, the heart-lotus, the base of the palate, and the forehead..."

I bow to the form of the letters, which consists of two bowls, sixteen spokes, two sets of ten petals, twelve half-petals, and four [petals]; located at the end of the dwelling, in the midst of the child, joined with the syllables *ḍa-pha-ka-tha-sa*, in the region of the throat, endowed with the meaning of the principles (*tattva*) of the vowels, and pervading all the petals. (6.1)

Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*); this is the internal *mātṛkā*. Now, for the external *mātṛkā*: having performed the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth as before, one should meditate.
One should meditate, in due order, upon her who is enriched by the nature of the letters, whose faces correspond to the vowels,
who is beautiful with the *ka*-group of consonants in her hands and the *ṭa* and *ta* groups at her lotus feet.
She was the supreme woman, whose beautiful sides were like the *pa* class of consonants, possessing slender waists and limbs;
she was lovely with her body like the *ya* class of consonants, and possessed full, high, and firm breasts.
She has deep-set hips, white eyes, and a slender waist;
her body is adorned with white garlands and unguents, and she is beautified by a rosary and a water-pot.
Having thus meditated upon her, who has beautiful hands depicted [upon her body] and who bestows all boons—
[one should place the syllables] at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), as well as on the face, the two eyes, the two ears,
the two nostrils, the two cheeks, and the two lips. (6.1)
One should place sixteen [syllables] on the two rows of teeth and on the two faces at the head;
then one should place them in sequence on the joints of the arms and legs, including the tips, and on the two sides.
Then one should place [the elements] on the back, the navel, and the abdomen;
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituent elements (dhātavaḥ).
O Goddess of the gods, the supreme Prāṇa and Jīva, which reside within the letters beginning with *ya*, should be installed in sequence as being of that very nature.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and the roots of the arms, one should likewise place it on the back of the neck;
then, beginning from the heart, one should place it on the two armpits and likewise on the pair of hands and feet.
"One should place [the syllables] on the belly and the face; thus she is the one whose form is the internal limbs.
By this application of placement (nyāsa), the practitioner of mantra becomes possessed of the very nature of the phonemes."

Thus ends the *bahir-mātṛkā*. Now, the *sṛṣṭi-mātṛkā*: if [the practitioner] is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), he should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* alone; however, if he is wise, he should perform the placement of that same [alphabet] known as *sṛṣṭi*, together with the *visarga*. Thus ends the *sṛṣṭi-mātṛkā*. Now, the *sthiti-mātṛkā*: if the practitioner is a householder (*gṛhastha*), he should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* alone.
One should place the letter *ḍa*, preceded by the nasal bindu and the visarga, as the state of maintenance (*sthiti*). As for the meditation (*dhyāna*):

one should meditate upon the Goddess who possesses the luster of vermilion, adorned with immeasurable ornaments, and three eyes; she holds a rosary of knowledge (*vidyā*), a rosary of rudrākṣa, a deer, and the gesture of granting boons (*vara*); and one should also meditate upon the Blessed Lady standing at her side, possessing a golden radiance.
Holding a book and a rosary of beads in her lotus-like hands.

Having meditated thus, one should place the letters beginning with *ḍaṃ* and *namaḥ*, including the *bindu* and *visarga*, up to the letter *ṭha*, in their respective locations; this is the *sthitimātṛkā*. Now, regarding the *saṃhāramātṛkā*:
having placed the *mātṛkā* alone, a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or an ascetic (*yati*) [should place] it joined with the *bindu* in reverse order.

One should perform the placement of the Saṃhāramātṛkā. As for the meditation: Bow down to the Mistress of the Letters (Varṇeśvarī), who holds in her hands a rosary, a young deer, a lofty axe, and a lore-script; who has three eyes; whose head is adorned with the crescent moon; who is ruddy in hue; who dwells within a red lotus; and who is bent by the weight of her breasts.
Having meditated thus: "KṢAṂ, salutation," and so forth, one should place each respective letter, together with its bindu, in its respective location in reverse order;
this is the *saṃhāramātṛkā*. Now, for the *kalāmātṛkā*:
if one is a devotee of Tāra (*oṃ*), having performed the placement of the pure alphabet (*mātṛkā*), [one should proceed as follows].
The wise one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the portions and digits of the Praṇava.
Prajāpati is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed, and the goddess Kalāsarasvatī is celebrated as the deity. || 6-2 ||
Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), namaḥ is the power (śakti), and the kalās are known as the peg (kīlaka).
These are formed by the long vowels with beautiful resonance, situated between two praṇavas and joined with the viṣaṇḍha syllables. (6.3)
Having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should meditate upon the supreme Goddess Śivā. Now, the meditation:
She holds in Her hands a lotus, a discus, a rosary, a deer, a book, a string of letters, an axe, a skull, a trident, and a golden jar overflowing with nectar.

I bow to that Śāradā, who resembles the full moon, who is bent by her breasts, and who possesses five faces and three eyes—faces as beautiful as pearls, lightning, clouds, crystal, and fresh *japā* flowers. (6.1)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) at the locations of the Mātṛkās with the mantra "Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Kalā Anivṛtti," and so forth; this is the Kalāmātṛkā.
Now, regarding the Śrīkaṇṭha and other Mātṛkās:

if one is a devotee of Śiva, having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā alone, the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā conjoined with the powers (Śaktis) of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others. (6.1)
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara. (6-1)
*Haṃsauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *tuḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*).
One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllables conjoined with the six long vowels. (6.3)

We perpetually take refuge in that form which resembles the Bandhūka flower and gold, which holds a beautiful rosary, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with its own staff-like arms; which bears the crescent moon as an ornament, possesses three eyes, and has the Lord of Ambikā as half of its body.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement [of mantras] with: *hasauṃ aṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya pūrṇodaryai namaḥ*, and so forth; this is the *Śrīkaṇṭhādimātṛkā* placement. Now follows the *Keśavādimātṛkā* placement:
if one is a devotee of Viṣṇu, having performed the placement of the pure *mātṛkā*, [one should proceed as follows].
