The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, which is endowed with the powers (śakti) of Keśava and the others.
Prajāpati is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed, and Lord Hari himself is celebrated as the deity. (6.2)
The seed-syllable of desire (Kāmabīja) is the seed; "Namaḥ" is declared to be the power (śakti); Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī are the peg (kīlaka); and the application (viniyoga) is as before.

One should perform the placement of the six limbs with the six long syllables of the King of Desire (Kāmarāja). He holds in his hands a lotus, a mace, a conch, and a discus; he possesses knowledge, a lotus-mirror, and a golden pitcher, and displays the play of lightning amidst the clouds.

May the bodies of the lotus-eyed Lord and Lakṣmī protect you—bodies that have become one through their longing for embrace, with her left breast high and her ornaments closely pressed against him. 6-1.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with "klīṃ śrīṃ aṃ keśavāya kīrtyai namaḥ" and so forth; this is the Keśava-mātṛkā.
Now, the Nyāsa of the Śakti-Mātṛkā:

If one has performed the Nyāsa of the Mātṛkā alone and wishes to worship Bhuvaneśī, the wise practitioner should perform the Nyāsa of the Mātṛkā preceded by the seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhuvaneśī. (6.1)
The seer is declared to be Śakti; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is Bhuvaneśī Mātṛkā, who is worshipped by the gods. (6.2)
The seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*, while *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*) and the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is the pin (*kīlaka*).
One should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the *māyā* syllable (*hrīṃ*) combined with the six long vowels.
Her lofty, full, and fleshy breasts rival the rising sun with its millions of rays;
she is adorned with a crescent moon on her head, a crown, necklaces, a girdle, and anklets;
and she holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary, a noose, a goad, and a book.
May the three-eyed Mistress of the World, seated comfortably upon a lotus, grant you prosperity.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with "hrīṃ aṃ namaḥ" and so forth; this is the *Mātṛkā* of Bhuvaneśvarī. Now, the *Mātṛkā* of Lakṣmī:
if one is intent on the worship of Lakṣmī, one should perform the placement of the *Mātṛkā* alone.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.
The seer is Bhṛgu, the meter is Gāyatrī, and Lakṣmī is the mother.
Śrīṃ namaḥ is the deity, the seed-syllable, the power, the primordial nature, and the pin.
One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs using the seed-syllable of the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) with its six long vowels.

One should meditate upon her, possessing a radiance equal to a flash of lightning, being sprinkled by four elephants resembling the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), who hold jars of nectar raised aloft on the trunks of their proboscises.

One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, who holds a rosary of *japā* seeds, two lotuses, and a book in her lotus-like hands; she is radiant with shining jewels and possesses breasts that are slightly bent.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement [of mantras] beginning with "Śrīṃ Aṃ Namaḥ"; this is the Lakṣmīmātṛkā. Now, regarding the Kāmeśvarīmātṛkā:
if the worshiper of Kāmeśī performs the placement of the *mātṛkā* alone, [then...]
The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the seed-syllable of desire.
The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is remembered as Kāmeśvarī; *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and the *kīlaka* is [the same]. (6.2)

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the six long seed-syllables of desire. One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has three eyes and holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of Smara, and the Vidyā-mantra, and who is as radiant as ten million rising suns.
She who has the new moon as her crest-ornament.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with "klīṃ aṃ namaḥ" and so forth; this is the *mātṛkā* of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*). Now follows the *sammohanī-mātṛkā*:
if the worshiper of Tripurā performs the placement of the *mātṛkā* alone...
The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma.
The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu.
Sammohanī is the name, *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *śrīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). (6.2)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the three seed-syllables twice.

One should meditate upon [the goddess] Sammohanī, who is ruddy in hue, distressed by her full breasts, and crowned with the crescent moon; she has three eyes and holds in her own hands a rosary, a bow of sugarcane, a noose, two lotuses, a goad, arrows, and a fresh book.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Aṃ Namaḥ" and so forth; this is the Sammohanī Mātṛkā.
The Prapañcayāga has already been explained previously. These are the ten-fold Mātṛkās.
These have been described generally, as it is said that the ten Mātṛkās are to be used everywhere. This is the statement of Durvāsas.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [one should worship] with the six— the Gaṇeśas, Grahas, Bhagaṇas, Mahāyoginīs, Rāśis, and Pīṭhas— along with the many Kalās of the venerable Mātṛkā-syllables, the eight Vāgdevatās, the pairs beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, and the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Keśava within one's own pure body.
O Blessed One, he who remembers you by means of the thirty-six principles beginning with Earth becomes you indeed.

Thus: (The fourfold tradition known as the Varṇamātṛkā-nyāsa, Kalāmātṛkā-nyāsa, Mūrtimātṛkā-nyāsa, and Prapañcayāgamātṛkā-nyāsa). Among these, the Varṇamātṛkā-nyāsa is ten-fold and constitutes an ancillary part of the Śrīvidyā. As it has been said:
He who performs the placement (nyāsa) by ascending and descending [the breath], [placing] the pure [syllable] joined with the bindu, accompanied by the visarga, conjoined with the *hṛllekhā*,
likewise encapsulated by the *bālā* and adorned with the *parā*— that is, the *Śrīvidyā*.
He performs this placement again for the two *haṃsas*.
He alone knows the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all the worlds.
Thus [ends the previous section]. Now follows the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā syllables conjoined with Bālā:
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is cited as the meter (chandas), and likewise the deity is proclaimed to be Bālā composed of the letters (varṇamayī). (6–1)
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is proclaimed, and the third is called Śakti;
Kāmarāja shall be the Kīlaka, as part of the limbs of Śrīvidyā.
For the ritual placement (nyāsa), however, the application (viniyoga) should be performed with the three seed-syllables of Bālā;
one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) by repeating [the mantra] twice in the proper sequence.
Wearing a crest-jewel, earrings, armlets, gems, necklaces, bracelets, rings, and bangles that flash with light; adorned with girdles and shimmering anklets;
bearing a weight of breasts beautiful with their ruby-set bodices; and holding a noose like a digit of the moon—[I bow to her].
A goad, a book, and a rosary [are held] in the upper right arm and the others, starting from the top.

I bow to her whose face is as serene as the full moon, who is illuminated by three eyes, whose limbs shine with a complexion as white as the moon or milk, and who is adorned with garlands, unguents, and garments;
she is the goddess of speech for the entire world, manifested through the fifty letters of the alphabet, and has arisen from the *mūlādhāra*.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady within a lotus of letters.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ aṃ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ, and so forth—one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in this manner; this is the Mātṛkānyāsa encapsulated by Bālā. Now, the Mātṛkānyāsa encapsulated by Parā:
Brahmā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas).
The goddess Sarasvatī Parā is remembered as the deity Mātṛkā. || 6-1 ||
And with the six long vowels as the supreme [mantra], one should perform the six limbs [of worship]:
[the goddess] who has the luster of the stainless moon, who possesses three eyes, and who is endowed with the digit of the moon.
I bow to the Supreme Kalā, whose beautiful arms hold a *mudrā* and a book;
one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with "sau aṃ sauḥ" and so forth—this is the Parā Mātṛkā. Now follows the Śrīvidyā Mātṛkā Nyāsa:
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is declared to be the Seer (*ṛṣi*), and Paṅkti is said to be the meter (*chandas*).
The deity is Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is that of the Mother (Mātṛkā).
One should perform the six-limb ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the three *kūṭas* twice.
[She is] reddish in luster, three-eyed, wearing a jeweled crown, and beautiful with gem-studded earrings; she shines with her lotus-hands holding a noose, a goad, the bow of Madana, and an arrow.

I take refuge in the Goddess who dwells upon a lotus, whose limbs are radiant with a shimmering pearl necklace rolling upon the slopes of her full and lofty breasts, and who wears a crimson garment. 6-1.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting with "mūlam aṃ namāḥ śirasi" and so forth; this is the *Śrīvidyāmātṛkā*. Now follows the *Haṃsamātṛkā*:
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and the goddess Mātṛkā, the Great Goddess Haragaurī, is remembered as the deity. (6.1)

One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the syllable *Ha* joined with the six long vowels. One should meditate upon the Lord of Ambikā, who is as radiant as the rising sun and the flashing of lightning, holding in his lotus-like hands the noose and the gesture of fearlessness, as well as the boon-granting mudrā and the axe.
May the three-eyed one with the moon upon his crest protect you—He who is the root of the universe, whose gentle yet fiery form is adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels. (6.1)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) starting with "Haṃsaḥ aṃ, salutation to the head," and so forth; this is the Haṃsamātṛkā. Now, the Paramahaṃsamātṛkā:
the Seer (ṛṣi) is Paramahaṃsa, and Virāṭ is declared to be the meter (chandas).
The deity is said to be composed of consciousness, having the nature of the Supreme Self.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with the groups of consonants situated between the two *praṇavas*.

One should meditate upon the pure Mother of all beings, whose form consists of the syllables that unfold from the glorious Supreme Self; who is perceived through a path inaccessible to the means of knowledge (*māna*); and who holds the rosary of the Vidyā, the water-pot, and the ritual gesture (*mudrā*).
The three-eyed one. || 6-2 ||
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the respective locations in reverse order, beginning with *so'haṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ* and so forth;

this is the Paramahaṃsa-mātṛkā. Now follows the Kalā-nyāsa, which is fivefold: the Tārotthakalā, the Kāmakalā, the Somakalā, the Trimūrtikalā, and the Aṣṭātriṃśatkalā-nyāsa. As for the Aṣṭātriṃśatkalā-nyāsa:

The [installation of] the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) of light is twofold: the installation of the thirty-eight digits of Śiva and the installation of the digits arising from the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
The installation of the digits arising from the *tāra* has already been explained previously. As for the specific detail:
they should be installed joined with the first letter of the *tāra*, and accompanied by the word "namas."
Then, moreover, one should place the digits (kalās) of the Mātṛkā upon these locations.
From the five divisions of Tāra arise the fifty digits (kalās) residing in the letters. Following the placement of the vowel-digits: these [digits], white in luster, were born from Nāda by Sadāśiva;
their lotus-like hands are enriched with a rosary, a book, a string, and a skull-cup. (6.1)
Thus they are to be meditated upon. Following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits (*kalā*) of the *ka*-group:
Born from the syllable *a* (the letter *a*) as Brahmā, they possess the luster of molten gold;
in their lotus-hands they hold a rosary, a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). (6.1)
Thus they are to be meditated upon. Following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits (*kalā*) of the *ṭa*-group consonants:

"Those born from the syllable *U* by Viṣṇu are proclaimed to resemble the leaves of the *tamāla* tree, with eight arms holding the gestures of fearlessness (*abhīti*), the discus (*cakra*), and the wish-granting jewel (*iṣṭa*). (6.1)
Thus they are to be meditated upon. Following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits (*kalā*) of the *pa*-group:
"Born from the letter *ma* by Rudra, they possess a radiance equal to the autumn moon;
with their arms, they hold the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the trident, the skull-bowl, and the boon-granting gesture (*vara*). (6.1)
Thus they are to be meditated upon. Following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits (*kalā*) of the *ṣa*-group:
"Commanded by Īśvara, [the goddesses] are like the japā flower, resembling the *bindu*.
Holding in their arms the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the deer, and the axe, as well as the boon (*vara*). (6.1)

Thus they are to be meditated upon. The specific worship, however, is to be understood from the section on the arrangement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*). Now follows the placement of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) of Light: one should place the vowel-digits in sequence, beginning with "4 *aṃ* *amṛtāyai namaḥ* on the head," and so forth. Then, on the joints and tips of the right hand, [one places] "4 *kaṃ bhaṃ* to *Tapinī* (the Burning One) *namaḥ*" and so forth, up to *ṅaṃ naṃ*.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) ending with "jvālinyai namaḥ" on the joints and tips of the fingers of the left hand; then, having performed the placement beginning with "caṃ dhaṃ rucyai namaḥ" and ending with "aṃ ṇaṃ bodhinyai namaḥ" on the joints and tips of the fingers of the right hand;
and then, one should perform the placement beginning with "ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ dhāriṇyai namaḥ" and ending with "laṃ jvalinyai namaḥ" on the joints and tips of the toes of the right foot. Then...

Having performed the placement [of mantras] on the joints and tips of the left foot with "4 Vaṃ, salutation to Jvālinī," and so forth, ending with "4 Haṃ, salutation to Kapilā," one should then perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) of the remaining two *kalās* upon the head;
this is the placement of the thirty-eight *tejaḥ-kalās*. Other placements of *kalās* will be described further on. Following this—
The sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (*prapañcayāga*) is the doctrine of the venerable Ācārya; it should be understood according to the manner previously described. Its fruit is as follows:
"Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of these syllables, a person becomes possessed of a divine body.
Then, by reciting all the mantras, one shall attain perfection. (6-1)
That mantra-practitioner who is the ordainer of the rule for the sacrifice of proliferation (prapañca-yāga) is indeed one who has accomplished his purpose;
all radiant mantras become effective for him, and he is called "one who always performs the sacrifice of the Self. (6.2)
(94) The Agnihotra sacrifice is certainly not equal to even a ten-millionth part of this oblation.
Indeed, for one who knows this, there shall be liberation even upon the falling away of the body, wherever that may be. 6-3.
And so it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra* (Paṭala 7,

verse 51): "The pure [syllable], as well as that with the bindu, then joined with the kalās, with Keśava and the others, likewise joined with Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, and with Śakti, Kamalā, and Māra, each one by one."

These ten types of nyāsa have been described separately; they all culminate in the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayāga), and in the ritual procedure for accomplishing the siddhis of the practitioner, they are like wish-fulfilling trees for one's intentions.
The sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-yāga*), however, specifically burns away the particularities of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which is a proliferation of calamities;
and for those who worship the Supreme eternally, it effortlessly and always makes known the meaning of that which is beyond.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his body according to rule, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantras, worship the deities, and offer sacrifice to the fire with undistracted mind, for she is the Mother of the Universe.
"Having become a god, one should sacrifice to the gods; one who is not a god should not worship a god.
Thus says the Śruti directly; therefore, the wise man should first perform the placement [of the deities]. (6.4)
O Dear One, when one who is shielded by the armor of the ritual placement (nyāsa) recites the mantra,
the obstacles flee upon seeing him, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion.
The foolish-souled person who recites the mantra without having performed the various ritual depositions (nyāsa) is afflicted by all obstacles, just as a young deer is by tigers. (6-6)

Thus end all the *mātṛkā*-nyāsas. Now, the nyāsa of the thirty-six *tattvas*: 4. *Kṣaṃ* to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, who pervades the earth-*tattva*, at the feet. In this same manner: *Laṃ* to the water-*tattva* at the *liṅga*; fire at the heart in reverse order; wind at the mouth; ether at the head; smell at the feet; taste [at the feet].

Form is in the *liṅga*; touch is in the heart; sound is in the mouth; the generative organ is in the *liṅga*; the anus is in the anus; the feet are in the two feet; the hands are in the two hands; speech is in the mouth; the sense of smell is in the two nostrils; the tongue is in the tongue; the eyes are in the two eyes;
the skin is in all the limbs; the ears are in the two ears; the mind is in the heart; the ego is in the heart; and the intellect is in the heart.

Prakṛti is in all the limbs; Puruṣa is in all the limbs; Rāga is in the heart; Vidyā is in the heart; Kalā is in the heart; Niyati is in all the limbs; the Kāla-tattva is in all the limbs; Māyā is in the heart; Śuddhavidyā is in the heart; Īśvara is in the heart; Sadāśiva is in the neck; Śakti is in the mūlādhāra; and Śiva is in the sahasrāra. This is the Nyāsa of the thirty-six principles (ṣaṭtriṃśattattva). Now, [the following].
Prāṇāyāma:
Once this has been performed, one certainly becomes authorized for the recitation of the mantra of the supreme deity and other such practices.
By means of this, one should practice the restraint of the vital breath (pavana) for the sake of reciting that mantra which one desires to recite here. (6-1)

Because of the statement, "Having thus performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa* upon the body," and because of the statement, "Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should perform the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*," one should perform the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa* after performing three *prāṇāyāmas* with the root-mantra.
Therein, the procedure for *prāṇāyāma* is explained: therein, [the breath] of the vital airs, even more than the body...

The length [of the breath] is twelve finger-breadths more. *Āyāma* means stretching; its etymological sense is the state of contraction, the calming of the body, or bringing about a state of reduction in the body—this is the meaning of *prāṇāyāma*. For this very reason, it is called "the restraint of the vital air" (*pavanasaṃyamana*). As stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
Now, this body is said by the wise to be ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length when measured by one's own fingers;
however, those who know yoga consider the vital air known as *prāṇa* to be longer than the body by twelve finger-breadths.

Thus, the man who, through constant practice, brings this vital breath (prāṇavāyu) under control so that it does not depart from his limbs, or who attains equilibrium with his body on this earth—he is worthy of worship by the wise among the foremost of those who know yoga. (6.3)

Thus [it is said]. That [prāṇāyāma] consists of the three limbs beginning with *pūraka*. Accordingly, it is stated: "It is declared to consist of three limbs by means of *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka*. Among these, the term *prāṇāyāma* is primarily applied to *kumbhaka* alone, because the other two serve as its auxiliaries. As stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*. (6.1)

Thus it is said. Furthermore, that [prāṇāyāma] is of two kinds: combined (*sahita*) and isolated (*kevala*). Among these, the combined type is also twofold: the sequence beginning with exhalation (*recaka*) and the sequence beginning with inhalation (*pūraka*). Regarding this, the *Yogaśāstra* states concerning the sequence beginning with exhalation: "Prāṇāyāma is declared to be threefold, by means of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)."
Kumbhaka is considered to be of two kinds: sahita (with breath) and kevala (pure).
Having performed purging, inhalation should be practiced slowly along with retention; one should practice with retention until the mastery of kevala-kumbhaka is attained. (6-2)
Thus [it is said]. He states that sequence in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*) is threefold, according to the divisions of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)."

One should release the breath through the right [nostril], draw it in through the left, and stabilize it within the central channel; thus are exhalation (recaka) and the others described. These consist of sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four mātrās respectively.

Thus, the word "by the channel" (*nāḍyā*) is connected with "by the southern one" (*dakṣiṇayā*) and so forth. Accordingly, *iḍā* is on the left of the body, *suṣumnā* is in the middle, and *piṅgalā* is on the other side. The term "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) means twofold among the sixteen [vowels]. Now, he states the sequence of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth in a collective summary:
With reverence, one should slowly fill the abdomen with air through the path of the moon (the left nostril),
free from drowsiness, employing only the necessary measures, while fixing the movement of the mind upon the root of the Kālāgni fire.
Then, with a steady mind, one should retain that breath until it is filled for sixty-four mātrās;
one should slowly exhale it externally through the bright [aperture] for half of those [mātrās], but hold it internally for that same duration.
Likewise, in the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"One should contemplate the inhalation (pūraka), the retention (kumbhaka), and the exhalation (recaka);
having brought about dissolution in the Mūlādhāra, one should slowly drink in the air. (6-1)
The knower of reality who has conquered the senses should expand the body as desired;
thereafter, with the mind fixed upon the light, he should arrest the vital breath.
During the retention of breath (kumbhaka), the wise one should contemplate the auspicious Vidyā that grants liberation;
then, one should exhale the breath as it naturally departs.
The practitioner of mantra should expel the quality of darkness (tamas) residing within his own body;
he should fill the breath through the left nostril and exhale it through the right.
The practitioner of mantra should practice *kumbhaka* (retention) equal to the *māhendra* [breath]; through the constant yoga of *kumbhaka*, one attains the highest perfection.
One who practices should determine the measure according to the desire of those who perceive reality;
one should drink the air according to one's capacity and retain it (kumbhaka) according to one's capacity.
"And the wind should abandon its own nature; from that, accomplishment arises.

Thus, regarding that Vidyā, the sequence beginning with inhalation (pūraka) alone is prescribed in the *Nityātantra*, whereas the sequence beginning with exhalation (recaka) is obtained as the general rule, according to the *Śruti* and works such as the *Prapañcasāra*.

This is because it is taught as being common to the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions. Thus says the Śruti: "Three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) are taught: exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka). Some maintain that the sequence of exhalation and so forth applies only to those who have well-mastered their breaths; however, in either case, its commonality with other systems is established, as even the sequence beginning with inhalation (pūraka) is appropriately applied in the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions as a general rule.

Therefore, in this context as well, although both are obtained as general options, Maheśvara declares that the sequence beginning with inhalation (*pūraka*) holds primacy as the specific rule: "Inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*)," and so forth.
Among these, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) called inhalation occurs at the time of taking in the air; that called retention occurs at the time of holding it.
At the time of exhalation, it is called *recaka*. As it has been said: "The filling of air from the outside into the abdomen is indeed *pūraka*;
the retention of air like a completely filled jar is considered *kumbhaka*; and the expulsion of air from the abdomen to the outside is known as *recaka*. And likewise, Dakṣiṇāmūrti [states]:
O Goddess of the Gods, having filled the abdomen with the left [nostril] using the root mantra,
one should expel it through the right [nostril] by means of retention after three repetitions.

Thus [it is said]. In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Seated properly upon the seat, one should fill the belly with the left [nostril]. Also in the *Tantrarāja*: "One should fill [the body] through the left nasal aperture with that which is of the nature of nectar; while recollecting the water [element], one should afterwards expel the wind through the right.

Regarding this, he states the sequence beginning with "in the *mūlādhāra*," etc. "Dissolution" (*laya*) means the dissolution of the mind; by that very [process], there is also the [dissolution] of the wind.
Because it is cultivated in a state of absorption (*laya*), the *Tantrarāja* states:

"Having fixed the mind in the *mūlādhāra*, having filled [the body] with breath from the base, and having led it through the interior of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), one should cause it to circulate through all the limbs. (6-1)

Thus: "As desired" means that one should draw in the breath according to one's ability, following its natural rhythm of coming and going. "With the mind fixed on the Light" (prakāśagatamānasaḥ) refers to one whose mind has gone to—that is, merged into—the Supreme Self which is Light.
By that [means], being of the very nature of the self-luminous Supreme Self, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, one should perform the retention (kumbhaka).
Now, regarding whether or not there is meditation on the Vidyā during breath control (prāṇāyāma), which consists of three parts, he says:
"One should contemplate [the Vidyā] during the retention (kumbhaka)," and so forth. "Vidyā" refers to the knowledge conducive to liberation;
that is the Śrīvidyā. Therefore, he says: "The auspicious one that grants liberation. Thus, at the time of retention—

It has been stated that "one should contemplate the Root-Vidyā from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)"; thus one should perform the subtle meditation (sūkṣmadhyāna) of Śrīvidyā. However, regarding the "pregnant" (sagarbha) method, it should be understood that this applies either during each stage of inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, or during simple retention (kevalakumbhaka) when one is unable [to do so] individually. He describes the method of exhalation (recaka) with the words beginning with "tadā," etc.; the ellipsis is "it goes outside."

[The result arises] by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), and not from deficiency or excess; otherwise, however, a fault would arise due to improper practice. And so it has been said in the *Gorakṣaśataka* (p.
One should practice inhalation (pūraka) properly, retention (kumbhaka) properly, and exhalation (recaka) properly;
by practicing in this manner, one shall attain perfection.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger must be tamed very gradually, so too must one's own vital wind; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. (6-2)
Through properly applied breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
through improperly practiced yoga, there arises the emergence of all diseases. (6-3)
Hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—various diseases such as these arise from the improper performance of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (6.4)

"Thereafter, one should perform the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) according to the path taught in the scriptures. This means: "one should expel [the breath] from the body. The sense is that one should contemplate that the quality of darkness (tamaḥ-guṇa), residing within the body, has been expelled outward along with the wind of the exhaling yoga (recaka). Now, he states the regulation of the channels for inhalation and so forth, beginning with the words "with the left," etc.

Thus, in the first *prāṇāyāma*, [one should exhale through the left]; however, in the second and subsequent pairs, one should fill [the breath] through the right alone. As it has been said: "One should exhale through that very [nostril] by which one leaves, and then fill and retain; thereafter, one should exhale through the other, slowly, again and again. (Yogaśāstra 6.1). In the Yogaśāstra:
Then, on a firm seat, the self-controlled yogi, eating wholesome and moderate food, should practice breath-control (prāṇāyāma) according to the path taught by the guru. (6.1)
When the breath moves, the mind moves; when it is motionless, it is firmly bound.
The yogi attains stability; therefore, he should restrain the vital air. (6.2)
As long as the vital air remains in the body, so long is it said to be alive;
death is its departure from there, therefore one should bind the vital air. (6.3)

When the channels are congested with impurities, the vital wind does not move through the central channel; how then could the state of *unmanī* arise, and how could the accomplishment of the goal be attained? (6.4)
When the entire network of channels, which was previously clouded by impurities, becomes pure, at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of mastering the vital breath (prāṇa). || 6.5 ||
Thereafter, one should daily practice breath control (prāṇābhyāsa) with a sattvic mind,
so that the impurities situated along the sides of the suṣumnā may be dried up.
The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), should fill the vital breath (prāṇa) with the moon;
having retained it according to his capacity, he should exhale it again through the sun. (6–7)
Having drawn in the breath through the sun (the right nostril), one should slowly fill the abdomen;
having performed the retention (kumbhaka) according to the rule, one should exhale again through the moon (the left nostril).
Having drunk with one [nostril], one should retain [the breath] without cessation;
then one should exhale through the other, very slowly and not with force. (6.9)
If one should drink the breath through the *iḍā* while it is restrained, one should expel it again through the other;
having drunk the air through the *piṅgalā*, one should then bind it and release it through the *vāmā*.
By constantly practicing this method of the sun and the moon, [the yogi attains mastery].
The groups of channels of those who practice self-restraint become purified after three months.
Thus, in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"Therefore, one should perform the reverse again and again, and then once more the reverse of that;
by this method, with a well-disposed mind, one should constantly effect the perfect restraint of the vital winds. (6-1)

Thus [it is said]. Now he states the fruit of *kumbhaka* (retention): "Always," etc., meaning by means of the yoga of pure *kumbhaka*. When the vital air (*vāyu*) has been well-mastered, the counting of measures (*mātrā*) was mentioned for the first practice; regarding that, he states here that there is freedom of choice—"the practitioner," etc. The practitioner is one who is at the stage of initial practice; for those who perceive reality (*tattvadarśin*), the measure is according to desire, that is, as one wishes.

The meaning is that one should cause [the practice] to be performed. He clarifies this very point with the words "according to one's capacity" and so forth. This being the case, a beginner may perform even less than the stated number; a practitioner of intermediate skill should perform exactly the stated number; and a superior practitioner may perform even more than that number.
The meaning of the words is as desired. Now Nārada states the definition of a *mātrā*:
"In the time it takes for one's own hand to circle its own knee-mandala, there shall be a *mātrā*, equal to a single natural breath. (6-1)
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Circumambulating the knee, neither too fast nor too slow, the snapping of the fingers is performed; that is proclaimed as a *mātrā*. (6.1)
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the Kātyāyanītantra:
"When the middle [channel] is pressed from its root to its tip by the thumb, that is declared by the wise to be a *mātrā*; it bestows the desired goal in yoga. (6.1)
p.
97) Thus it is said. In reality, however, the pronunciation of each respective mantra itself constitutes a *mātrā*. Accordingly, in the *Gautamīya*:
"One should exhale the breath through the right [nostril] and then fill [it] from the left."
One should practice the mantra thirty-two times; that is called *prāṇāyāma*.

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, the meaning is that one should practice during the *kumbhaka* (retention) immediately after the *pūraka* (inhalation). This, however, applies to the alternative involving *recaka* (exhalation) and so forth; for this very reason, the recitation (*japa*) and other such acts belong only to the *kumbhaka*, not to the other two. As stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*: "Having made the *prāṇa* and *apāna* equal and having properly performed the *kumbhaka*..."
With a restrained mind, one should meditate upon me seated in the lotus of the heart.

Thus, in the Agastyasaṃhitā: "Restraining the vital breaths as much as possible, the wise person should mutter the mantra with the mind alone, meditating repeatedly on Rāma according to the previously mentioned procedure. (6.1)
Thus: having restrained the vital breaths (asūn) by performing *kumbhaka* and meditating on Rāma, one should mutter the mantra (*manu*) for as long as possible;
this is the connection [of the words]. By this, the Vaiṣṇavas hold that where no specific [duration] is mentioned, one should mutter the mantra according to one's capacity.
In the same manner, by the principle observed in one instance, this method applies everywhere. For this very reason, in the case of the Śrīvidyā—
In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, it is said: "The wise man should contemplate the auspicious Vidyā, which grants liberation, during the *kumbhaka*";

thus they say. However, in reality, whether in the *sagarbha-prāṇāyāma* (retentive breath control), in the *kevala-kumbhaka* (pure retention), or in the *sahita-kumbhaka* (retention with repetition), as well as when one is capable in all three limbs [of breath control] or even when incapable, *japa* (recitation) and *dhyāna* (meditation) are mandatory during the *kumbhaka*.

Now, the distilled meaning of those statements is as follows: it should be performed with the *mūlamantra* or the *bālāmantra*, or, if one is unable to do so, with the *praṇava*. As it is stated in the *Phetkārīya*: "One should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with either the *mūla* or the *praṇava*.

For those for whom the utterance of the *praṇava* is prohibited, it should be understood that in place of the *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ* consisting of three and a half morae (*mātrā*) is to be used.

In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "That which is the fourteenth vowel, known as having three and a half morae (*mātrās*), and joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, is called the 'bridge' (*setu*) for Śūdras. (6.1)

Thus [it is said]. Here, for those who have well-mastered the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) during inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, the number is exactly as stated in the *Tripurāsāra*; however, regarding recitation (*japa*) and the like, it is otherwise in the *Tantrarāja*. As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Once [the breath] has been thus well-mastered, one should then exhale with thirty-two *mātrās*."
One should retain [the breath] for sixty-four [units] and exhale it for one-fourth of that.

Thus is the venerable Kādimata; this is the option between these two systems. In that case, if one is unable, the practice taught in the Phetkārīya-tantra within the General Chapter (Sāmānyapaṭala) should be performed. It is as follows:
likewise, the breath-retention (kumbhaka) is always performed with twelve measures (mātrās).
Therefore, exhalation (recaka) is performed with double that measure. || 6-1 ||

"Thus, each of the three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) consists of a triad. Even if one is unable to do this, that which is stated in the *Subhagodaya* should be performed: "One should perform three breath-controls while again recollecting the Vidyā with the heart. That statement is explained in its own manual (*paddhati*) as referring to the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*).

The meaning is that one should perform three rounds of *prāṇāyāma* as follows: while uttering the root mantra once, fill the breath with air, hold it (*kumbhaka*) four times, and exhale through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) twice. Here, it should be understood that filling [the breath] occurs through the right [nostril] in the case of an even number [of rounds], because in the case of an odd number, the left is specified for the filling and subsequent stages; or else, this may simply be the view of that particular school.

We do not know [the details]. Furthermore, if one is unable even to that extent, the summary is that one should adopt the very practice taught by Jñānārṇava and Dakṣiṇāmūrti: "repeating [the mantra] three times with *kumbhaka*. This is the *sahita-kumbhaka*. Now, as for *kevala-kumbhaka*, it is stated in the *Yogaśāstra*:
Releasing both exhalation and inhalation, the retention of breath within the mouth is called prāṇāyāma; that indeed is the kevala-kumbhaka (pure retention).
When Kumbhaka alone is mastered, devoid of both exhalation (Recaka) and inhalation (Pūraka), there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain. (6.2)
One who is capable of retaining the breath at will by means of the *kevalakumbhaka* alone attains the state of *rājayoga*; of this there is no doubt. (6.3)
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha; therefore, one should practice both together until their perfection. (6.4)
At the end of the exhalation of the breath held in the *kumbhaka*, one should make the mind supportless;
through such practice of yoga, one shall attain the state of *rājayoga*.
From breath-retention (kumbhaka) comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī; from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, the Suṣumnā becomes unobstructed, and the perfection of Haṭha-yoga arises.

Thus: *Ha* is the sun and *Ṭha* is the moon; the union (*yoga*) of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) with those two—the sun and moon—located in the right and left channels, namely the *piṅgalā* and *iḍā*, starting from the *mūlādhāra*, is the meaning of *haṭhayoga*.
That is *prāṇāyāma*, and that is *rājayoga*; and that [occurs] by way of the *suṣumnā* channel through the sequence of piercing the six *cakras*.
The *Tantrarāja* states the characteristics of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti:
"Trembling, horripilation, bliss, purity, stability, lightness, as well as luster and radiance—these are the marks of one perfected in yoga. (6.1)
In the *Yogaśāstra*:
"Emaciation of the body, brightness of the face, clarity of the internal sound (*nāda*), and the eyes being perfectly clear."
Freedom from disease, mastery over the *bindu*, and the stimulation of the digestive fire are the characteristics of success in *haṭha* resulting from the purification of the channels. (6.1)

Thus, the *kevala-kumbhaka* (pure breath-retention) has been described. This *prāṇāyāma* is of two kinds: with seed (*sagarbha*) and without seed (*vigarbha*). And it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Prāṇāyāma is considered to be of two types: with seed and without seed. Likewise, in the *Yoginītantra*:

This breath control (prāṇāyāma) which destroys all evils is said to be "without seed" (vigarbha); when joined with the "seed" (mantra), it is said to yield a hundredfold fruit. That which is devoid of recitation (japa) and meditation (dhyāna) is declared to be "without seed," while that which is endowed with them is "with seed."
By the leaders of sages, devoted to yoga. || 6-1 ||
Thus it is said. Furthermore, that [prāṇāyāma] is threefold, according to the distinction of superior, inferior, and middling. And so it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Prāṇāyāma is declared to be threefold—superior, inferior, and middling. In the superior, there is lightness, the leaving of the ground, and the cessation of the mind. (6.1)

In the inferior stage, there is an increase in perspiration over all the limbs; likewise, in the middling stage, trembling of all the limbs is said to occur through practice performed at the proper time. (6-2)
Even those [lower qualities] shall become supreme virtues through practice and the passage of time;
therefore, one should indeed practice regularly both in the morning and in the evening.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"The self-controlled one, being pure, performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) accompanied by the *praṇava* every day, both at dawn and at dusk."
These months here purify that twice-born man who is burdened by the sin of killing an embryo, burning away the mass of his misdeeds like cotton with fire.
These protect one here from the mass of sins accumulated in other births within even six months;
after a year, they reveal that very state of Brahmā which is known as Acyuta.
Thus it is said. In the Yogaśāstra, however:
"One should practice breath-retentions (kumbhaka) four times a day—in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight—gradually up to eighty [retentions per session]. (6-1)
In the lowest stage there is vibration; in the middle stage there is trembling;
and in the highest stage of the restraint of breath, one repeatedly rises while seated in the lotus posture.
One should perform a massage of the body with water produced from physical exertion;
by this, firmness and lightness of the body arise. (6.3)
At the time of initial practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended;
once the practice has become firm, such strict observance of rules is no longer required.

Thus it is said. The procedure therein is as follows: having assumed the prescribed lotus posture (padmāsana) with both eyes closed and the mental fluctuations fixed upon the *mūlādhāra*, while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and so forth, one should fill the air through the left channel (*iḍā*) for sixteen measures (*mātrā*), [directing it] to the *mūlādhāra*.

Having drawn [the breath] in with the thumb, the little finger, and the ring finger, and having held the two nostrils while steadying that air for sixty-four *mātrās*, one should exhale that air very slowly through the *piṅgalā*, the right channel, for thirty-two *mātrās*; this is one *prāṇāyāma*. Again, that air through the *piṅgalā*—

Having drawn [the breath] in very slowly, one should likewise exhale through the *iḍā*; this is another method. In this manner, by reversing the order, one should perform it twenty times, sixteen times, twelve, six, three, or twice, according to one's capacity;
then one shall attain success. Thus it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*: "By means of the gradual increase of *mātrās*, [one should practice] properly twelve [times]."

Sixteen; such is the summary. In all these cases, everyone has the right to perform rituals only through *prāṇāyāma*, because it is heard in scripture that there is censure for its non-performance. As stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:
"Whatever ritual action is performed without *prāṇāyāmas* is fruitless."
Therefore, those who seek auspiciousness should diligently practice breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 6.1 ||

Thus, for this very reason, it is necessary that this [practice] be performed as part of the worship, just like the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). This concludes the rule for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) common to both systems of thought.

Now, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Yoga-pīṭha: Having meditated upon one’s own body as the Yoga-pīṭha—having its four legs formed by the two shoulders and the two thighs, and its four limbs formed by the face, the navel, and the two sides—[the practitioner] should perform the placement. At the Mūlādhāra: *Oṃ 4 Mahākāyāya raktavarṇāya maṇḍūkāya namaḥ*.
Above that, extending as far as the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, [is] "Homage to Kālāgnirudra, who has five faces and ten arms, with his left and right sides red and black.
Above that, extending as far as the navel, [is] "Homage to Mūlaprakṛti, who is beautiful like a *bandhūka* flower. Above that, extending as far as the heart...
Salutation to Ādharaśakti, who possesses the luster of the autumn moon and holds two lotuses. Above that, at the heart itself:
salutation to Kūrma (4), salutation to Ananta (4), salutation to Varāha (4), salutation to Pṛthivī (4), salutation to Amṛtārṇava (4).
Having recited the entire Mātṛkā, [salutation] to the island consisting of nine jewels, adorned with nine divisions. Right there:
In the nine sections, from Īśāna to the center: 4 AṂ, 16. Homage to the Puṣparāga jewel. 4 KAṂ, 5. Homage to the Nīla jewel. 4 CAṂ (p. 99).
To the Vaiḍūrya jewel, 4 Ṭaṃ; to the Vidruma jewel, 4 Taṃ; to the Muktika jewel, 4 Paṃ;

to the Marakata jewel, 4 Yaṃ; to the Vajra jewel, 4 Śaṃ; to the Gomedaka jewel, 4 Laṃ; to the Padmarāga jewel, kṣaṃ, obeisance! To the Golden Mountain at that very place, obeisance! Above that, to the Nandana garden, 4.

Homage! In the center: *Namaḥ* to the Kalpako garden; *Namaḥ* to the seasons beginning with spring. To the west: *Namaḥ* to the horses of the senses; to the east: *Namaḥ* to the elephants of the objects of the senses; *Namaḥ* to the ground of various jewels. Therein, from west to the middle and end in reverse order: *Namaḥ* to the venerable feet of the Sovereign Lady of Kālacakra.

Mudrācakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Mātṛkācakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Ratnacakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Deśacakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Gurucakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Tattvacakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Grahacakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. Mūrticakreśvarī Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi 4. To the enclosure of the causal waters (kāraṇatoyaparidhi) 4.
To the Maṇikya-maṇḍapa. In its corners, beginning from the southwest (nir-ṛti), and in the center:
4 Deśarūpiṇī-śakti-śrī; 4 Kālarūpiṇī-śakti-śrī; 4 Ākārarūpiṇī-śakti-śrī; 4 Śabdarūpiṇī-śakti-śrī; in the center, Saṃgītayoginīrūpiṇī-śakti-śrī; in the middle of that.

[The worshipper], whose form is the assembly of all the *guṇas* and the manifest circle of *yoginīs*, [worships] the Śakti-Śrī... 4. Then, in the center of that, [he worships] "To the Kalpataru trees" 4;

beneath them, "Salutation to the jeweled altar (*ratnavedikā*)"; above that, "To the white parasol (*śvetacchatra*)"; and below that, "Salutation to the jeweled lion-throne (*ratnasiṃhāsana*)" 4. Having thus placed all of this within the mental lotus (*mānasapaṅkaja*), [he worships] each in its proper place.
Having resolved each of those respective locations as jeweled lion-thrones, one should meditate upon one’s own body [as such].
Therein, one should install the deities of the lion-throne: on the right shoulder—*Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ*, to Dharma, red in color, in the form of a bull;
on the left shoulder—*Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ*, to Jñāna, dark-green in color, in the form of a lion; on the left thigh—*Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ*, to yellow in color...

To Bhūtākāra, for detachment (vairāgya) [at the right knee]. 4. To Indranīlaprabha, who has the form of an elephant, for sovereignty (aiśvarya) [on the left knee]. These are the forms of the legs of the lion-throne. At the mouth [of the face], 4. To Adharma. On the left side, 4. To Ajñāna. At the navel, 4. To Avairāgya. On the right side, 4. To Anaiśvarya. These...
[To the goddesses] having the form of the limbs of the lion-throne: [in the center] 4 to Māyā, 4 to Vidyā. Above that:

4 to the Root of Bliss (Ānandakanda), 4 to the Stem of Consciousness (Saṃvinnāla), 4 to the Petals consisting of Prakṛti, 4 to the Filaments consisting of Vikāra, 4 to the Pericarp (Karṇikā) which is enriched with the fifty seed-syllables of the letters and is the form of all the Tattvas; within it: 4 AṂ.

To the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala) 4; to the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala) 4; to the fiery orb (vahnimaṇḍala) 4; to Sattva 4; to Rajas 4; to Tamas 4; to Ātman 4; to Antarātman 4; to Paramātman 4; to Jñānātman (the self of knowledge) hrīṃ. Above that, in the four directions starting from the east and in the center: 4 obeisance to the self of the principle of knowledge (jñānatattvātmane).

4 To the self of the principle of Māyā (māyātattva), 4 to the self of the principle of Kalā (kalātattva), 4 to the self of the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva), 4 to the self of the supreme principle (paratattva). Then, one should install the nine Śaktis of the pedestal that supports the Śrīcakra upon the filaments, in the eight directions starting from the east and in the center:
4 Dūtī Ambā Śrī, 4 Sundarī Ambā Śrī, 4 Sumukhī Ambā Śrī, 4 Virūpā Ambā Śrī.

Vimalāmbā-śrī 4, Antaryambā-śrī 4, Vadarīmbā-śrī 4, Purandaryambā-śrī; in the center of the pericarp (karṇikā), Puṣpamardanyambā-śrī 4. These [deities] are to be meditated upon as red in color, bearing the gestures of granting boons (vara) and fearlessness (abhaya). Above that, having placed the lion-throne mantra: "Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-throne of all powers," upon that—

Having meditated upon the Śrīcakra, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the root mantra: "Obeisance to the sandals of the Yoginīs of the Śrīcakra, who are the supreme, the non-supreme, and the secret, the most secret, the ultra-secret, the mystery, the greater mystery, the innermost essence (*nigarbha*), the *Kula*, the *Kaula*, and the tradition of the most hidden and the hidden," one should [visualize] a triangle in the heart.

Having visualized that, one should place within it the root mantra: *oṃ hrauṃ klīṃ bhagavati blūṃ nityākāmeśvari strīṃ sarvasattvavaśaṅkari saḥ tripurabhairavi aiṃ vicce hrīṃśrā śrīmahātripurasundaryambāśrī*, and then the root-vidyā beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

Having placed the Śrīcakra consisting of the three cities and meditated upon it, one should utter the *vāgbhava* syllable (*aiṃ*) and perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*), saying: "Obeisance to the first city, which consists of the body and is composed of the square, the sixteen petals, and the eight petals. Then, having uttered the *kāmarāja* syllable (*klīṃ*), [one should place it] upon that which consists of the fourteen spokes and the two ten-spoked wheels.
"Salutation to the second city, whose nature is the intellect (*buddhi*),"— this too is a pervasive [mantra].

Having recited the *Śakti*-syllable (*kūṭa*) and performed the pervasive placement with "Salutation to the third city, whose nature is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the wheel of the eight-spoked, six-cornered,

and bindu [centers]," [one should place it] upon that which is the self of the entire triad beginning with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
"Salutation to the three cities of the Śrīcakra"—this too is the pervasive [mantra].

Then, having meditated upon the three corners of the heart-triangle, beginning from the front corner, as consisting of the three cities and as consisting of the three *kūṭas* beginning with Vāgbhava, one should place there the three *kūṭas* beginning with Vāgbhava, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with "namas. Then...

One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to Nāda, Bindu, Kalā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Vāmā, Viṣaghnī, Dūtī, and Sarvānandā—the nine Śaktis of the wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana located within the Śrīcakra.
Then, one should place the nine Śaktis of the Kāmeśvarī-pīṭha upon the filaments of the heart-lotus: 4. Obeisance to Mohinī. 4. [And so on for the others.]

Having meditated upon Kṣobhiṇī [0 4], Vaśinī [0 4], Stambhinī [0 4], Ākarṣiṇī [0 4], Drāviṇī [0 4], Āhlādinī [0 4], Klinnā [0 4] in the center, and Kledinī [0 4], one should recite the root-mantra of Bālā and the fifteenth [vowel] in the middle of the triangle,
[invoking] Śrī-Ṛddhipīṭha of Uḍḍiyāna, which is red in color; then [recite] 0 4 at the tip of the triangle.

Having uttered the two *vāgbhava* syllables for Bālā and Mūla, [one worships] the venerable Kāmarūpa-pīṭha of yellow color in the form of a square at the southern corner: 4. Having uttered the two *kāmarāja* syllables, [one worships] the venerable Jālandhara-pīṭha of white color resembling a half-moon at the left corner: 4. [One worships] the two *śakti* seed-syllables...

Having performed the placement of the four seats (pīṭhas) as "O Śrī Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha, of smoky color, marked with six dots, and circular," one should again, in the corners starting from the southeast within the central dot (vindu), recite: "4 lāṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the earth; O Śrī [seat] whose throne is the corpse of Brahmā. "4 vāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the waters."
Homage to the glorious Viṣṇu, whose seat is a corpse (pretāsana). Rāṃ Hūṃ! Homage to Rudra, the lord of fire; homage to the glorious Rudra, whose seat is a corpse.
4 Yāṃ Hrīṃ! Homage to Īśvara, the lord of wind; homage to the glorious Īśvara, whose seat is a corpse. 4 Hsauṃ! Homage to Sadāśiva, the five-faced lord of space, whose seat is a corpse-lotus.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five corpse-thrones with the mantra: "Obeisance to the glorious Sadāśiva, the great ghost, seated upon the lotus," one should then place the six thrones upon that, within the red lotus pericarp, on a pedestal consisting of a hexagon containing a square: 4 *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*, obeisance to the throne of Tripurā, the ocean of nectar. 4 *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*... [and so forth for the remaining thrones].

Salutation to the lotus-throne of the boat of Tripureśvarī. 4 Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the self-throne of the goddess Tripurasundarī. 4 Haiṃ Hvalīṃ Hsauḥ, salutation to the universal-cakra throne of Tripuravāsinī. Hsaiṃ Hsaklīṃ Hasauḥ.

"Salutation to Tripurāśrī, the seat of all mantras. Having performed the placement (nyāsa) with "4 hrīṃ klīṃ bleṃ, salutation to the Sādhya-Siddha seat of Tripuramālinī," one should place the four seats of the four thrones (catuṣpīṭha-caturāsana) within the square in the center. In the northeast, having uttered the two Vāgbhava syllables, [one places them] in the Fire-wheel (agnicakra).

In the abode of Kāmagiri, which is the essence of Mitreśanātha and presides over the waking state, is the goddess Kāmeśvarī, whose nature is the power of will (icchā-śakti) and who is identical with Rudra; *hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, salutation to the seat that is the self of the goddess Tripurasundarī. In the northwest corner, on the solar wheel (*sūrya-cakra*), are the two [syllables] of Kāmarāja.

In the Jālandhara-pīṭha, which is of the nature of Ṣaṣṭheśanātha and presides over the state of dreaming, there is the goddess Śrī Vajreśvarī, whose essence is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) and the self-nature of Viṣṇu. *Hraiṃ Hklīṃ Hsauḥ*, obeisance to Tripuravāsinī, who resides upon the seat of all cakras. In the south-west, having uttered the two powers (*śakti*), [one worships] in the lunar wheel (*somacakra*).

In the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri, whose essence is Uḍḍīśanātha and which presides over the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), [I worship] the Goddess Śrī Bhagamālinī, who is the power of the Self of Brahman consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti): *hsaiṃ hsaklīṃ hsauḥ tripurāśrī sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*. In the southeast, having uttered the entire pair four times, [worship] in the Brahma-cakra.

On the great seat of Uḍḍiyāna, to the Goddess Śrī Tripurasundarī—who is of the nature of the power of the Supreme Brahman and presides over the state that is the fourth beyond the fourth, being the essence of the venerable Caryanātha—*hrīṃ klīṃ bleṃ*, obeisance to the Sādhya-Siddha-seat of Tripuramālinī. In the center: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, [the fifteen letters] *ka* etc. (15).
Having performed the placement with "Obeisance to the seat of all mantras of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," [one places] "4 aṃ 51" [representing]:

Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niati, Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṅkāra, Manas, Tvak, Cakṣus, Śrotra, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Upastha, and Śabda.

One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the mantra: "Salutation to the seat of the Yoga-pīṭha belonging to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, whose self consists of touch, form, taste, smell, space, air, fire, water, and earth. Then, having recited the root mantra, [one should say]:
"To the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, O Śrī... [and so on], upon the Great Yoga-pīṭha composed of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) which constitutes the body.
One should place one’s own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the heart; thus, one should contemplate the Supreme Deity upon the seat consisting of the body. This is the *yogapīṭhanyāsa*. In the *Śāradā*:
"Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters upon one's body by way of both dissolution (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*)."
Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
Thus [it is said]. "Then" (tataḥ) means immediately after the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*). *Mantranyāsa* refers to the ritual placement associated with the mantra to be worshipped.
In the *Vaiśampāyanasaṃhitā*:
"Then one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra to be worshipped, including its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components."
Those who are the nose[-like] [elements] of whichever mantra must be employed by one desiring accomplishment.
Even if the recitation, libation, fire-oblation, and worship have been performed with perfected mantras,
these will not yield their fruits if they are devoid of the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other such rites.
For a man who performs all these nyāsas upon his own body, this triple world comes under his control;
his sins are immediately pacified, and the rākṣasas along with the serpents tremble with fear. (6.3)
First, having performed the placement of the Ṛṣis and so forth, then the placement of the hands and limbs;
after that, the placement of the syllables of the mantra, and beyond that, the placement of the words.
One should perform other ritual placements (nyāsa) as specified in various particular kalpas;
then, one should proceed with the letters of the Mātṛkā, enclosed by mantras and accompanied by the bindu.
The knower of mantras should correctly perform the placement [of the syllables] according to the path seen in the scriptures;
then, having performed the assignment of the limbs and the hands, he should display the mudrās.
Such is the sequence. Furthermore, regarding the Śrīvidyā elsewhere:

She is pure within, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution through the digits born of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and through Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, whose bodies are delighted by Viṣṇu, along with Śakti, Lakṣmī, and Manojā.

With the seed-syllables both individually and collectively, there is the excellent arrangement of the letters, the self-sacrifice (ātma-yāga), silence, the sixfold Kāma, the ninefold abode, and all the secret mantras. || 6-7 ||
Thus it is said. Furthermore, this [vidyā] is threefold, being divided into six types such as the Śrīcakra-nyāsa, Karaśuddhi, and so forth.

Among these, the sixfold [nyāsa] is twofold, distinguished as the *pūrva* (prior) and the *uttara* (subsequent). Therein, the *pūrva-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa* pertains to all the *āmnāyas*, while the *uttara-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa* pertains specifically to the *ūrdhvāmnāya*.
The Śrīcakra-nyāsa is threefold, according to the distinctions of withdrawal (saṃhāra), emanation (sṛṣṭi), and maintenance (sthiti). (p.
101) Furthermore, the nyāsa beginning with the purification of the hands (kararaśuddhi) is extensive, as it includes the nyāsas of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, as well as those of Rati, Kāma, and so forth.

Because they are included therein. Among those, the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) consists of the placement of the *saṃhāra*-Śrīcakra, the placement of the *sṛṣṭi*-Śrīcakra, and the placement beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). This is because, at the time of recitation (*japa*), the placement of the *sthiti*-Śrīcakra is included within the purification of the hands and so forth, and at the time of worship, the placement of the *saṃhāra*-Śrīcakra serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
And because it is included within that, the fourfold nyāsa is necessary in brief at this juncture; such is the opinion of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*. In the *Yoginīhṛdaya* it is said:
"O you who are worshipped by heroes, the fourfold nyāsa should be performed in this manner."
O Dear One, there is the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), as well as that beginning with aṇimā and that beginning with the Root Goddess.
Furthermore, for the sake of swift accomplishment, the practitioner must perform the purification of the hands and other preliminary rites at dawn,
or during the time of worship, or while performing the fire sacrifice (homa).
Or else, at the time of recitation, the best of practitioners should perform their application individually; or, at the time of worship, he may perform them all together.
Thus it is said. Regarding that, first is the *pūrva-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa* in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"O Goddess, one should perform the ritual installations preceded by the *ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*.
The first installation is considered to be with the Gaṇeśas, and the second with the planets. (6.1)
The third [placement] is with the constellations (nakṣatras), the fourth with the yoginīs;
the fifth placement is with the zodiac signs (rāśis), and the sixth is said to be with the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
This sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been proclaimed as invincible everywhere;
he whose limbs are thus deposited [with mantras] is to be honored by all yogis.
In this world, he has no person worthy of worship, such as his father or mother;
he alone is to be worshipped by all, for he himself is the Supreme Lord.
O Pārvatī, whoever bows down to one who is devoid of the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), he shall soon meet death and fall into hell. (6.5)
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:

"Thereafter, one should perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), by which Śiva—whose nature is the macrocosm (virāṭ), whose essence is the letters, and who is the form of the cosmic egg—becomes manifest; of this there is no doubt. (6.1)
One should perform the first placement, which destroys all obstacles:
[the deities] who resemble the rising sun, have elephant faces, and possess three eyes.

O Goddess, O Beloved, one should install these [deities]— who hold a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who are endowed with power— in the same manner as the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Thus [it is said]. Here, at the end of "Oṃ, salutations to Śrī and Vighneśvara," others say "salutations to Vighneśvara and Śrī," while some say "salutations to Vighneśvara and Śrī. It should be understood that the Gaṇeśas, the Śaktis, and the Mātṛkās are present in the breath; this is the Gaṇeśa-nyāsa. Now, regarding the Graha-nyāsa, the Jñānārṇava states: "Then, the Graha-nyāsa..."
Thus it is said: "One should contemplate [the colors] as red, white, likewise red, dark-blue, yellow, pale-white, smoke-colored, black, smoky, and smoky-smoky. (6.1)

Having placed the Sun, who is the foremost, capable of assuming any form at will, and adorned with all ornaments, within the heart by means of the vowels; then [one places] the Moon by means of the *ya*-group of consonants.
One should place Mars in the middle of the eyebrows with the *ka*-group;
Mercury in the three eyes with the *ṭa*-group; and Jupiter in the heart with the *ta*-group.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the planet Mercury at the throat with the *ca*-group,
Saturn at the navel with the *pa*-group, and Rāhu in the mouth from the *śa*-group, while [placing the others] above the heart.
O fair-faced one, one should thus place the banner on the two feet with two hundred thousand [repetitions]:
Sūrya and Reṇukā, as well as Soma and Amṛtā.
Maṅgala was joined with Dhāma, Budha with Jñānarūpā, Guru with Yaśasvinī, and Bhṛgu with Śāṅkarī.
Śani is endowed with Śakti, Rāhu is accompanied by Kṛṣṇā, and Ketu is joined with Dhūmrā; these Śaktis are remembered as being near the Mother (Ambā).
Thus is the application as before. Now follows the placement of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*):
"Now one should perform the placement of the host of lunar mansions, which bestows happiness;
[the deities] resemble the blazing fire of time and are adorned with all ornaments. (6.1)
Those beginning with Aśvinī have hands that are not joined; they hold the gestures of granting boons (varada) and fearlessness (abhaya).
Rohiṇī, however, is joined in pairs, pair by pair.
One by one, and likewise in pairs, ending with Puṣya, it is said:
[on] the forehead, the eyes, and then on the left and right ears.

O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise place [the letters] in sequence on the two nostrils and the throat; having duly placed them up to the letter *pu*, one should then place the *sarpa* (the letter *sa*) with the two *kha-gas* (the letters *kha* and *ga*).
With the two syllables *gha* and *ṅa*, one should place Maghā on the right shoulder;
with *ca*, Pūrvaphalgunī on the second shoulder; and those situated as *cha*, *ja*, and *sa* on the right elbow.
O beloved, one should place Uttaraphalgunī on the left elbow;
O beloved, one should place it on the wrist of the hand situated at the syllables *jha* and *ña*.
One should place the variegated Svātī, joined with the syllable *ṭha*, on the left wrist;
one should place Svātī, joined with the syllable *ḍa*, on the right hand.
One should place Viśākhā, conjoined with the syllable *ḍha*, upon the left hand;
likewise, O Pārvatī, one should place Anurādhā, consisting of the syllables *ta-tha-da*, upon the navel. (6–8)
O Dear One, one should place Jyeṣṭhā, joined with the letter *dhakāra*, on the right hip;
likewise, O Dear One, one should place Mūla, situated in *napapha*, on the left hip.
Then one should place Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the right thigh with the syllable *ba*,
and immediately thereafter, Uttarāṣāḍhā on the left thigh with the syllable *bha*.
One should place Śravaṇā, joined with the letter *ma*, on the right knee;
and Dhaniṣṭhā, accompanied by the letters *ya* and *ra*, one should place on the left knee.
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should place Śatabhiṣā joined with the letter *la*;
thereafter, one should place Pūrvabhādrapadā located on the right shank.
One should sequentially assign [the syllables] whose nature consists of the vowels *va* and *śa* to the left calf;
and [the syllable] *ṣa*, which is the last [of the group] beginning with *sa*, to the right foot. 6-13.
Having placed Revatī on the sole of the left foot by means of the letter *kṣa*, as well as the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga, one should begin the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoginīs.
Thus [it is said]. He describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) with the words "blazing," etc., as before. This concludes the *nakṣatra-nyāsa*. Now, the *yoginī-nyāsa*—in another tantra:
"The wise one should meditate upon Ḍākinī in the sixteen-spoked Viśuddha [cakra] at the throat, the deity of the skin-element, for the sake of attaining all desired aims. (6.1)
Red in color, with three red eyes, causing fear to the common folk, holding a trident and a khatvanga in her hands,
and carrying a shield and a chalice filled with wine in her left;
she has one face, is exceedingly fierce with terrible fangs, is the destroyer of the host of enemies, and is intent upon milk-rice offerings.
One should meditate upon that Ḍākinī at the location of the throat, her body surrounded by Amṛtā and the others. (6.2)
Then, having uttered "ḍāṃ ḍiṃ ḍūṃ ḍaiṃ," followed by "ḍoṃ ḍauṃ" and "ḍamale vare," one should state the word "ḍākinī" preceded by "yūṃ," and then say "māṃ rakṣa" twice.
O Goddess Kari, having uttered "sarvasattvavaśam," and then having uttered "āgaccha" twice, as well as "imām pūjām," thereafter—
O Goddess, after that, [there is] the two *gṛ* syllables, then the *vāgbhava*, then the *ghora*,
then the *māyābīja*, then *bhṛgu* with the *sargī*, and after that, *para*.
*Ghore hūṃ ghorarūpe ca ehy ehi iti namaḥ-padam | Cāmuṇḍe ḍa-ra-la-ante ca ka-sa haiṃ śrīmahātri ca || 6-6 ||*

"O Purasundarī, O Goddess!"—thus one should recite the word "Varade" (Bestower of Boons) while [visualizing] the vowels situated upon the Viśuddha-pīṭha; and at the end of the Viśuddha [cakra], [one should recite] "Ḍākinī."
And I worship the sandals of the venerable Lord Viśuddhanātha;
one should place this [mudrā] upon the pericarp with the thumb and the ring finger.
Then, upon the sixteen petals, beginning from the east, one should install the Śaktis, Amṛtā and the others, preceded by their respective initial syllables, in their proper order.
Amṛtākarṣiṇī, Indrāṇī, Śānī, Umā, and Ūrdhvakeśinī; then Ṛddhidā, Ṛṣā, and thereafter the letter Ḷ.

She is the single-syllabled one, the embodiment of sovereignty, the bearer of the syllable *Oṃ*; she is likewise the essence of medicinal herbs, the Mother (*Ambikā*), and the embodiment of the imperishable.
The bodies of the powers (śaktis) beginning with Amṛtā resemble those of the Ḍākinīs;
their weapons and so forth are likewise similar [to theirs] in the visualization for placement and worship. (6.12)
For the sake of all accomplishments, the practitioner should meditate upon Rākiṇī, who resides in the blood-element, within the pericarp of the twelve-spoked Anāhata [cakra]. (6.13)
Dark-complexioned, holding a trident, a lotus, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), and a sharp discus; two-faced, with three red eyes, and with the luster of her bared teeth shining amidst frowns;
blazing, that Goddess of gods, residing in the heart-lotus, the sole mistress of the blood-element.
One should visualize that Rākiṇī as being attached to pure foods and delighted by the intoxication of honey-wine.
Having recited the mantra as before, the wise one should place it upon the pericarp through the conjunction of that syllable, its location, and the word at its end. (6.15)
One should install the Śaktis, beginning with Kālarātri and the others, preceded by their respective colors, upon the twelve petals starting from the east and proceeding in due order.
Then Kālarātri, Khātītā, and Gāyatrī beyond that;
then Ghaṇṭādhāriṇikā, and again the one whose nature consists of the syllable Ṅa.
One should install Cāmuṇḍā, Chāyā, Jayā, Jhaṅkāriṇī, and again Ñārṇātmikā, as well as Ṭaṅkahastā and Ṭhaṅkāriṇī, starting from the east.
The bodies of the powers (śaktis) such as Kālarātri and others are similar to that of Rākiṇī;
their weapons and other attributes are likewise the same in the rites of placement (nyāsa), worship, and meditation.
In Maṇipūra, which has ten petals, the practitioner should meditate upon Lākinī, who resides in the flesh-element, in the center of its pericarp for the sake of attaining all siddhis. (6.20)

One should meditate upon the goddess Kṛṣṇā, who has three faces and is endowed with three eyes; she is fanged and of fierce form, holding a thunderbolt, a spear, a staff, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons in her right and left hands.

Having meditated upon her situated in the lotus at the navel, shining with ten petals and a pericarp, the lord of practitioners should contemplate that Lākinī, who resides in flesh and whose heart yearns for rice cooked in molasses. 6.21.
Having performed the placement of the mantra as before, one should place Ḍāmarī and the others:
Ḍāmarī, Ḍhaṅkāriṇī, Ṇakāriṇī, and then Tāmasī.
Sthānadevī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Dhātrī, Nandā, Pārvatī, and Phaṭkāriṇī— these are the ten who dwell upon the petals.
The bodies of the powers (śaktis) beginning with Ḍāmara are similar to those of the Lākinyas;
their weapons and other attributes are likewise the same in the rites of placement (nyāsa), worship, and meditation.
The wise one should meditate upon Kākinī in the six-petalled lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna,
the Mistress of the Gods residing in the fat-element (medas), accompanied by her retinue.
In the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, beautiful with six petals, she has four faces and three eyes;

she is yellow in luster, holds a trident, a rosary, a skull-cup, and the gesture of fearlessness, and bears the group of consonants [ṭa-va]. She is established in the fat-element (medas), delighted by the intoxication of wine, and is joined with [the seed-syllables] Bandhinī and so forth.
One should meditate upon that Kākinī, whose mind is fixed on curd-rice and who bestows desired fruits. || 6-26 ||
One should install Bandhinī, Bhadrakālī, Mahāmāyā, Yaśasvinī, Ramā, and Lamboṣṭhī in the six petals as before.
The bodies of the powers such as Bandhinī and the others are similar to that of Kākinī;
their weapons and so forth are likewise similar, according to the visualization for placement and worship. (6.28)
One should meditate upon the Goddess Śākinī, who resides in the bone-element within the four-petaled lotus at the Mūlādhāra, together with her retinue, in the pericarp.
I meditate upon the Goddess, whose nature is light, possessing three eyes and five radiant faces with beautiful fangs;
holding in her lotus-like hands a bow, a goad, a book, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā);
who intoxicates all bound souls (paśus) while seated within the lotus at the *mūlādhāra* and resting upon bones.
One should contemplate that Śākinī as being full of affection for food made of mung beans and delighted by the intoxication of honey. (6.30)
The practitioner should place Varadā, Śaśinī, Ṣaṇḍā, and Sarasvatī as the fourth, upon the four petals starting from the east. (6.31)
The bodies of the powers (śaktis) beginning with Varadā resemble those of the Śākinīs;
their weapons and other attributes are similar, as are their placement (nyāsa), worship, and visualization.
Having meditated upon the deity of the marrow element within the two-petalled lotus at the command [center], one should place its mantra there in the middle of the pericarp.

In the center of the brows, upon a two-petaled, beautiful lotus of the *bindu*, she is white in color; with her lotus-hands she holds the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), along with a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a rosary, and a skull-cup.
She has six faces, resides within the marrow, is graced with three eyes, and is joined by Haṃsavatī and the others.
One should meditate upon that Hākinī, who is honored by all the gods and is intent upon food colored with turmeric.
O Goddess, one should also install [the mantra] "Salutation to Haṃsavatī,
the Forgiving One" on two petals in sequence, preceded by their respective syllables.
The forms of the powers Haṃsavatī and the others are like that of Hākinī;
their weapons and other attributes, as well as their placement, worship, and visualization, are likewise similar. (6.36)

One should meditate upon the auspicious goddess Yākinī, together with her retinue, residing within the seed-syllable at the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), situated in the seminal element (śukradhātu).
In the lotus situated within the shaven void, which possesses all its petals, one should meditate upon that Yākinī Bhairavī,
enriched by Yakṣiṇīs, her hands grasping all weapons, possessing all colors, the unified totality,
whose faces begin with the letter Ḍa, who bestows all happiness, and whose nature is that of all the bodily elements.
One should meditate upon her who has a mind attached to all food, who relishes the supreme Śiva, and who possesses every form. (6.38)
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of that mantra as before, one should also [place] Amṛtā and the others all around;
the body of the powers beginning with Amṛtā is similar to that of Yākinī.
In the visualization for the placement and worship, one should employ weapons and other implements identical to those [of the deities].
Thus ends the Yoginī-nyāsa. Now follows the Rāśi-nyāsa:
having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the meditation on the zodiac signs (rāśis) with the root mantra.
One should visualize [the deity] as red, white, yellowish-green, pale, variegated, or white.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should assign the colors tawny, brownish-red, dark, variegated, crimson, and smoky to the four groups beginning with the letter *a*. (6.2)
One should place a ram at the ankle of the right foot; then, by means of pairs, a bull [at the knee];
one should place the Vedas at the shanks, and then a pair upon the testicles.
With two [consonants] one forms Kakaṇṭaka on the belly, with two [more] Siṃhaka on the shoulder;
with the anusvāra and visarga, and with the ś-group [of consonants], one forms Kanyakā.
O you who are honored by heroes, one should place [the letter] with the *ka*-group on the right side of the head,
and likewise on the left side of the head, one should place [the letter] supported by the *ta*-group.
Likewise, O beloved, one should place Scorpio on the shoulder with the *ca*-group;
and likewise, O beloved, one should place Sagittarius on the belly with the *ṭa*-group.
One should place the Makara with the *tavarga* on the left testicle;
likewise, one should place the Jar (*kumbha*) with the *pavarga* on the left knee.
With the *ya*-group and the letter *kṣa*, one should place Pisces at the left ankle. Likewise:
"The five winds—prāṇa, apāna, udāna, vyāna, and samāna—are to be known as the five zodiac signs beginning with Aries and ending with Leo. (6–8)
