Likewise, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadattaka, and Dhanañjaya are declared to be the five signs beginning with Virgo (Kanyā). (6.9)
The individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) are proclaimed as the pitcher (kumbha) and the fish (mīna) [signs].
For the sake of accomplishment, practitioners of mantra should install the zodiacal signs beginning with those two, starting from the Sun's sign. 6–10.
Thus ends the ritual placement of the zodiac signs (*rāśinyāsa*). Now follows the ritual placement of the sacred seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*):
Next, one should place the sacred seats, which indeed consist of all things, according to the prescribed rule;
they are white, black, reddish, dark, green, and yellow, in due order. (6.1)

Furthermore, O Goddess, for the sake of attaining all desires and goals, the wise man should repeatedly and in due order meditate upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas) within the collection of fifty locations. (6.2)

The sequence of the *pīṭhas* as stated in the *Pīṭhamātṛkā*, beginning with "Kāmarūpa is the great *pīṭha*," should be understood; this concludes the *pīṭha-nyāsa*. Thus ends the previous *ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*.
Now, the placement (nyāsa) for the delight of desire (kāmarati):
If one is a devotee of Kāma, having performed the placement of the pure Mātṛkā, the wise one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā conjoined with the power of Kāma. (6.1)
Sammohana is the seer (ṛṣi), and Jagatī is said to be the meter (chanda);
O Goddess, the deities are proclaimed to be the powers (śaktis) who desire prosperity (śrī). || 6-2 ||
The seed-syllable *klīṃ* is the essence (*bīja*), *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and the Mātṛkā is known as the peg (*kīlaka*).
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the six long vowels combined with the Kāma-bīja.
Then, O beautiful lady, the Kāmas, possessing the luster of pomegranate blossoms,
accompanied by the Śaktis on their left sides, held flower-arrows and sugarcane bows.
The Śaktis, resembling saffron in hue and adorned with all ornaments, should be meditated upon with blue lotuses in their hands, capable of attracting the three worlds. (6.5)
Having meditated thus: "4 Aṃ, to Kāma, to Rati," and so forth, one should perform the placement according to the sequence stated for the Kāmaratimātṛkā;
this is the Kāmaratimātṛkā-nyāsa.
Now, regarding the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Śrīcakra, it is stated in another Tantra:

"Having first performed the sixfold [placement] beginning with Kāmarati and the others in this manner, the placement of the Śrīcakra should then be performed for the attainment of the state of Śiva. (6.1)
O beloved, listen to the *cakranyāsa* of the illustrious Tripurasundarī,
which has not been told to anyone and is the supreme purifier of the body.
In the *Śrīrudrayāmala*:

"First, one should contemplate one's own body as having the form of the Śrīcakra, free from the appearance of skin and other [physical constituents], possessing the true radiance of the blazing fire of time (*kālāgni*). (6.1) Thus it is said.

Having recollected the seers (ṛṣi), meters (chandas), and deities (daivata), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). The six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅgaka) should be performed with the Bālā mantra situated in both direct and reverse order.

For the attainment of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should meditate upon the Guru, who consists of Śiva and Śakti, composed of supreme splendor, within the space of consciousness at the dvādaśānta.

I perpetually bow to the glorious Guru, the lord of yogis who is worthy of praise, the physician for the disease of worldly existence—blissful, the source of bliss, serene, whose nature is knowledge, and endowed with his own innate being. (6.3)
One should place Gaṇeśāna on the left knee, Kṣetrapālaka on the left shoulder,
Yoginī on the right knee, and Vaṭukabhairava on the shoulder.
Then the wise practitioner should place Śakra or Hutāśana on the tip of the right foot;
subsequently, he should place Yama on the right knee and [Varuṇa] on the right side.
One should place Nirṛti on the right shoulder, Varuṇa on the left shoulder thereafter,
Samīra on the left side, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) on the left knee.
The practitioner, composed in meditation, should place Īśāna on the tip of the left foot, Brahmā at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
and Ananta at the mūlādhāra.
One should perform the placement [of mantras] starting with "Salutation to the line forming the square" and so forth,
upon the right shoulder, the back, the tips of the hands, the buttocks, and the toes of the feet.

O beautiful one, [the fingers] of the left foot, the buttocks, the tips of the hands, the tops of the shoulders, the crown of the head, and the surface of the back are pervaded [by the deities]. (6.9)
One should place the Siddhis situated between them by way of pervasion, saying, "Obeisance to the central line of the square," O beloved. (6.10)
"Having thus assigned Brahmāṇī and the others to her eight locations.
Thus it is said in the *Śrīrudrayāmala*:
"Pārvatī questioned Śiva as he was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa."
O Lord Śaṅkara, tell me the armor-mantra (kavaca) for the placement (nyāsa) of the Śrīcakra.
Śaṅkara said:
"Well asked by you, O Goddess, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds!
I shall clearly explain to you the armor (kavaca) consisting of the placement of the Śrīcakra."
First, one should contemplate one's own body as having the form of the Śrīcakra,
free from the appearance of skin and other [physical constituents], and possessing the true radiance of the blazing fire of time (Kālāgni).

For the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, one should meditate upon the Guru, who consists of Śiva and Śakti and is composed of supreme splendor, within the space of consciousness at the dvādaśānta.
May Gaṇeśa protect my knee; may Kṣetranāyaka protect my left shoulder;
may the Yoginīs protect [my] right [shoulder]; and may Vaṭukabhairava protect [my] shoulder. (6.5)
May Indra protect the tip of my right foot; may Agni protect my right knee;
may Yama protect my right side; and may Nirṛti protect my right shoulder.
May Varuṇa protect your left shoulder, Samīraṇa your left side,
Dhanādhyakṣa your left knee, and Īśvara the tip of your left foot.

May Brahmā protect the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), and Ananta protect the root-support (mūlādhāra); [one should worship] with the sequence beginning with "Salutation to the line starting from the square" (caturasrādirekhāyai namaḥ) and so forth. || 6-8 ||
O Īśvarī, one should scatter handfuls of flowers as a pervasive offering;
[the goddesses] are mounted upon the vehicle of the treasure (Nidhi), their lotus-hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
May the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, resembling rubies, be gracious;
may *aṇimā* protect the back of the right shoulder, and may *laghimā* protect the tips of the hands.
May Mahiman protect the right buttock; may Īśitva protect the tips of the feet;
may Vaśitva protect the left foot; and may Prākāmya protect the other buttock.

May the fulfillment of desires protect my left shoulder; may the fulfillment of enjoyments protect the tips of my fingers; may the fulfillment of alchemy protect my head; and may the bestower of liberation protect the back of my head. (6.12)
"O Īśvarī, one should perform the placement of the handful of flowers by means of pervasion, in due order, with the mantra 'Salutation to the central line of the square,' and so forth. (6.13)
May Brahmāṇī protect the two big toes, Māheśī the right side, Kaumārī the head, and Vaiṣṇavī the left side. (6.14)
May Vārāhī protect the left knee, Indrāṇī the right knee;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect the right shoulder, and Mahālakṣmī the left.
O Goddess, one should perform the placement with handfuls of flowers by way of pervasion, in sequence, starting with "Salutation to the inner line of the square" and so forth. (6.16)
May the goddesses of the mudrās be gracious, their lotus-hands bestowing boons and fearlessness, for the sake of delighting the deities who are intent upon bestowing grace upon their devotees. (6.17)
The mudrā of my two big toes is the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī;
may the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā protect my right side. (6.18)
Ākarṣiṇī is at the top of the head; Vaśaṅkarī is on the left side;
Unmādinī is on the left knee; and Mahāṅkuśā is on the right knee.
May Khecarī protect the right shoulder, Bījamudrā the left shoulder,
Trikhaṇḍā the limit of the twelve [fingers], and Yoni-mudrā both thumbs at the feet.
May Tripurā, endowed with the Siddhimudrā, protect the center of the heart;
salutations indeed to the sixteen-spoked [wheel], ending in *ṅa*, which fulfills all desires. (6.21)
O Īśvarī, one should offer a handful of flowers as a pervasive placement, [reciting]:
"May the goddesses of Time be gracious, their hands raised holding nooses and goads. (6.22)
May Kāmākarṣiṇī— red-limbed, clad in red garments, and adorned with all ornaments— protect the back of the right ear.
May the eternal Buddhyākarṣiṇikā protect my right shoulder;
may Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī protect my right elbow.
May Śabdākarṣiṇī protect the back of my right hand;
may Sparśākarṣiṇī protect the slope of my right thigh.
May Rūpākarṣiṇikā protect my knees, Rasākarṣiṇī my ankles, and Gandhākarṣiṇikā guard the sole of my right foot. (6.26)
May the goddess Cittākarṣiṇī protect the sole of the left foot;
may Dhairyākarṣaṇikā protect from the base of the foot up to the ankle.
May Smṛtyākarṣiṇī protect the knee, Nāmakarṣiṇī the left thigh, and Bījākarṣiṇī the back of the right hand. (6.28)
May she who draws forth the self protect my left elbow;
may she who draws forth nectar protect my left shoulder; and may she who draws forth the body protect my ear.
Accompanied by the *siddhimudrā*, [the mantra] extends as far as the center of the heart for Tripureśvarī; likewise, "to the wheel, salutation," ending with *ṅe*. (6.30)
O Īśvarī, one should offer a handful of flowers as a pervasive placement;
[these belong to] the goddess Anaṅgakusumā, who is gracious and wears a red bodice. (6.31)
May Anaṅgakusumā, whose hair is the matted locks of the world and who holds a bow of reeds and arrows in her hands, always protect my right temple. (6.32)
May the goddess Anaṅgamekhalā protect my right knee;
may Anaṅgamadanāśakti always protect my thigh. (6.33)
May Anaṅgarekhā, who is afflicted by passion for the bodiless one, protect the space between my two ankles; may she protect my left side and the interior of my ankles.
May Anaṅgaveginī always protect the ends of my thighs;
may Mamānaṅgāṅkuśā guard my left knee.
May Anaṅgamālinī protect my conch-shell on the left incessantly;
may Sundarī protect the interior of my heart with the two mudrās of accomplishment.
O Goddess, one should perform the placement of the handful of flowers as pervading all, using the mantra "to the Cakra, which bestows all good fortune, salutation," ending with the dative case.
May the Śaktidevīs, who hold arrows and bows in their hands,
who are adorned with every ornament, and who possess the luster of lapis lazuli gems, be gracious.
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī protects my right cheek up to the temple, and Sarvadrāviṇī always protects the area beyond that; Sarvākarṣiṇikā likewise protects it. (6.39)
May she who brings delight to all protect my right shoulder forever;
may the power that deludes all protect the right side.
Sarvasaṃstambhinī protects the right thigh and the back; Jṛmbhiṇī protects up to the shanks; Sarvavaśaṅkarī protects the left [thigh].
May Rañjinī protect my left front and my back;
may she who causes universal intoxication protect all my sides.
May she who accomplishes all aims protect my right shoulder;
may she who fulfills all prosperity protect my left cheek.
May she who consists of all mantras protect my forehead and left side;
may she, the destroyer of all dualities, preserve the door and well of my body.
May she who dwells in Tripura protect my heart with the two mudrās of accomplishment;
likewise, [the mantra] "Obeisance to the Cakra" ending in the dative case (ṅe), which accomplishes all aims.
O Īśvarī, one should distribute handfuls of flowers as all-pervading;
may the ten goddesses, who bestow all accomplishments, be pleased.
Possessing the luster of jasmine, mandāra flowers, and pearl necklaces, with lotus hands granting boons and fearlessness, may she who bestows all perfections protect the corner of my right eye.
May she who bestows all prosperity protect the root of my nose;
may she who makes everything dear always guard the corner of my left eye.
May she who brings about all auspiciousness protect my northeast corner;
likewise, may she who grants all desires protect my northwest corner.
May she who liberates from all suffering protect the space between my left knees;
may she who pacifies all death protect the space between my right knees.
May the goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, who wards off all obstacles, always protect my anus; may she protect the western direction of my abdomen.
May she who bestows all good fortune protect my right side;
may Tripurāśrī, accompanied by Siddhimudrā, protect the center of my heart.
O Goddess, one should perform the placement with the mantra "ṅe'ntaṃ cakrāya namaḥ," which bestows all protection, as a pervasive [placement] over the handful of flowers.
May the goddesses dwelling within the inner spokes, who resemble crystal and hold books and rosaries in their hands, be gracious toward me incessantly. (6.54)
The goddess who is omniscient and omnipotent resides in the right nostril;
she bestows all sovereignty and consists of pure knowledge, residing in the breasts and the scrotum.
May she who destroys all diseases protect my perineum;
may she whose nature is the support of all protect my left testicle.
May she who consists of bliss and removes all sins protect my breasts and lips;
may she whose very nature is universal protection protect my left nostril.
May Tripuramālinī, who bestows all desired fruits, protect the region of the nose; may she protect the heart-lotus with the two mudrās of accomplishment. (6.58)
"O Goddess, one should also perform the placement [of mantras] as a pervasive [covering] with a handful of flowers, saying: 'Salutation to the eight-spoked wheel that removes all diseases.'"
May the goddesses of speech be gracious to us— those who are clad in saffron and golden garments, their arms resplendent with a book, a rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
May Vaśinī always protect the right side of the chin;
may Kāmeśvarī protect the throat, and Modinī protect the right heart.
May Vimalā protect the right side from the navel; may Aruṇā protect its left.
May Jayinī protect the left of the heart, and likewise may Sarveśvarī protect the throat.
Kaulinī is the chin, Siddhā is the heart-lotus; [one should also say]: "Salutation to the inner wheel that bestows all perfections. (6.63)
O Īśvarī, one should place a handful of flowers as a pervasive offering;
[one should likewise place] Kāma, Kāmeśvarī, the arrow, the bow, the noose, and the goad in their proper sequence.
May the square [mandala] at the corner of my heart protect me on all sides;
may the womb (yoni), shining above the heart, grant great liberation.
May the sixteen Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, protect me—
she who is the bestower of desires, the power of Rudra, and the dweller in Kāmarūpa.
May Kāmeśvarī protect the upper corner of the Great Yoni for me;
she is the power of Vaiṣṇavī who bestows dharma, whose abode is established at Jālandhara. (6-67)
May Vaiṣṇavī, who resides within the space between the right corner and the yoni, always protect me;
she is the power of Brahmā who bestows wealth and whose abode is made of a full stone.
May Subhagā Bhagamālinī protect the space within the left corner;
may Tripurāmbā protect the center of the yoni, and Siddhimudrā protect me. (6.69)
Dwelling in the sacred seat of Uḍḍiyāna, she is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman;
she is the wish-fulfilling tree and the cow of plenty for the five treasures of the Śrīs, and the presiding deity of the jewels.
Seated upon an adorned throne, she is established within all philosophical systems;
she is praised by the goddesses of the six limbs and worshipped according to the four commitments.
O Mahātripurasundarī, the mother who generates great good fortune and the bestower of great liberation, descend upon my heart and the space between my arms!
May that very goddess Cakreśvarī, endowed with the gesture of accomplishment (siddhimudrā),
protect the goddess Tripurabhairavī from head to foot.
O blessed lady, this armor is a secret that grants all desires;
having uttered the Turīya-vidyā, one becomes the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.

I worship and satiate with offerings the Śrīpādukā of the one who dwells in the supreme Bindu-cakra, who is the power beyond both void and non-void, the Great Tripura, the Unnameable Radiance—*namaḥ*. Therein, one should likewise worship the Nine Mistress of the Cakras (*navacakreśvarī*):
*ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*.

"I worship the venerable Pādukā, which is the abode of the supreme Bindu-wheel, which is both empty and non-empty of Tripura, and which is the manifestation of the Ineffable (Anākhyā); salutations! Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should display one's own mudrā.
That which has not been told to anyone is now made manifest.
The practitioner with a steady mind should place this upon his body. (6.75)
Having abandoned the human state, he shall immediately attain the state of Śiva;
for him who meditates [on this] at the three times of day, it shall be integrated with all his limbs. (6.76)
This host of Yoginīs, whose form is radiant, shines forth;
it cannot be obstructed by ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like. (6.77)
Free from the threefold affliction, the yogi should move about in the world as one who has attained perfection;
wherever the yogi remembers this, he should begin from that point in every direction.
The earth extends to the status of a field for twelve *yojanas*.
Thus ends the *Śrīcakranyāsakavaca* from the *Śrīrudrayāmala*. This concludes the *Saṃhāra-śrīcakranyāsa*.
Now follows the *Sṛṣṭi-cakranyāsa*, which begins with the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*) and ends with *Aṇimā*. Regarding the sequence therein, it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
One should again perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with Mūladevī and ending with Aṇimā;
then, one should place Kāmeśvarī and the others, starting from the east, upon the triangle at the head.

One should then perform the placement (nyāsa) as follows: the two eyes are the arrows, the two eyebrows are the bows, the two ears are the two nooses, and the tip of the nose is the two goads; this sequence begins with the right side.
One should install the eight goddesses of speech according to the sequence of the garland of skulls; O fair-faced one, the wheels beginning with the Bindu should also be installed.
At the root of the eye and at the outer corner, likewise at the front and upper part of the ear, at the lower half of the crest-lock, at the remaining half, and on the back of the ear. (6.4)
One should place [the mantras] at the root of the ears, at the outer corners of the eyes, and at their bases;
one should then place [the mantras] for all attainments and so forth around the neck in a clockwise direction.
In the heart, the powers (śaktis) situated in the corners of the human [figure] are also as before.
In the navel, however, there is an eight-petaled [lotus], with [the petals] in the bamboo-stalk [axis], on the left, and on both sides.
One should place the first four [syllables] on the abdomen and the left side;
one should place the other four beginning from the space between the backbone and the left side.
The best of practitioners should place [the mudrās] in his own Svādhiṣṭhāna, starting from the east and ending with the south;
he should then place the ten mudrās in the Mūlādhāra.
In front, on the left, on the rear, on the left [side], and in the intermediate space, there are ten mudrās—above and below; furthermore, excluding those above and below.
The first group of eight Brahmāṇīs is on the right shank; they are worshipped as before, either beginning from the left shank or following the sequence starting from the left.
One should place the eight Siddhis; the remaining two should be placed on the soles of the feet.
This placement, which has issued forth from the Cause, is manifested like a lamp lit from another lamp.
"Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), O Goddess of Gods, one should contemplate [it] as non-different from oneself.

Having thus explained the placement according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) for the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) in its collective form, he speaks of it according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*):
"beginning with the Root Goddess," and so forth. If it is done in this way, then the placement occurs through the sequence of emanation; that [he now describes].
The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) again. Regarding that, he states the method: "on the head," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should place the triad of seed-syllable goddesses, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, upon the "head-triangle," which is the triangle imagined on the head. To the question of by what sequence this is done, he says: "starting from the east. Here, "east" refers to the front part of the head; [the placement] should proceed starting from that.

From this, it follows that a triangle facing the forehead must be visualized. The sense is that it should be visualized up to the eight spokes in such a way that its lines are appropriately arranged according to the sequence of constructing the Śrīcakra. And that being so, since the triangle has its apex pointing east relative to the head, [the points are located] at the western corner, the south-eastern corner, and the north-eastern corner.
Or it may be thus: in the first case, "from the east" means clockwise; in the latter case, it means counter-clockwise. By that—(p.
"Starting from the west and proceeding clockwise"—this is the view that has come down as the doctrine of the *Tantrarāja*.

On this basis, some maintain that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed exactly in this way, in accordance with the single intent of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*. Others hold that the placement should be performed according to the first two systems of thought, in accordance with the single intent of the *Catuḥśatikā*. In reality, however, this [latter] position is the correct one.

The summary is that this [text] serves as a guide to the purport of the previous *Catuḥśatī*. Regarding the specific locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the weapons, he says "the arrows" and so forth. The "arrows" are the five arrows of Śiva and of Śakti;
thus they are of two kinds. "In the eyes" means having the nature of the two eyes. By the dual number in "eyes," the right eye [is indicated].

The arrows of Kāmeśvara are the right eye; the arrows of Kāmeśvarī are the left eye. Thus, the right eyebrow is the bow of Kāmeśvara; the left eyebrow is the bow of Kāmeśvarī. The right ear is the noose of Kāmeśvara; the left ear is the noose of Kāmeśvarī. The tip of the right nostril is the goad of Kāmeśvara.

"The tip of the left nostril is Kāmeśvarī-Aṅkuśa"; thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon those very locations. Therefore, he says "beginning from the right," and so forth. Although here, as previously stated, the position for the weapons is between the triangle and the eight-spoked wheel, and thus their placement there would also be appropriate, nevertheless, [the placement of] the forms of the vowels follows the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

Due to their proximity, it is appropriate that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the weapons occurs in those very same locations; such is the command of the Lord (*īśvara*). Likewise, since the sixteen *Nityās* are also the embodiments of the vowels, and because they are present in those locations through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), one should consider it the will of the Lord that their placement occurs in those very places. [This is] behind the location for the placement of Śrīvidyā.

The lineages of gurus should be placed in their own respective positions; thereafter follows the mandala of the sixteen Nityās—this is the sequence for the placement according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), whereas in other cases, it is simply the previously mentioned sequence. As stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should place Śrīvidyā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and behind her, the gurus in succession."
Then, O Goddess, the lunar-day goddesses (tithinityās) are joined with the vowels of the Mātṛkā.
O Supreme Goddess, one should install the Śrīvidyā, the Mother of the Universe, within the syllable *aḥ* on the face, like the Mātṛkā, bestowing all prosperity. (6.2)
"O lotus-eyed one with long eyes, one should always perform the placement [of the mantra] according to the musical notes (*svara*).
Thus, this placement should be understood as being included within the *Sṛṣṭi-Śrīcakra-nyāsa*, even though it is performed independently.

Now he describes the sequence of the eight *nyāsas*, beginning with "the garland of skulls" (*muṇḍamālā*). "Skull" (*muṇḍa*) means the head; "garland of skulls" (*muṇḍamālā*) refers to that which is to be established in its proper order. By this, it is meant that starting from the upper corner of the forehead and proceeding clockwise through the east and so forth, one should perform the placement in the eight corners according to the sequence of the garland, following the manner of the ninefold wheel of yoginīs on the head.

The intended meaning is that one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the eight goddesses of speech. Now, one might ask: how should one perform the placement of the *bindu*-wheel? To this he says: "beginning with the *baindava*.
The *baindava* is the great *bindu*-wheel consisting of universal bliss (*sarvānandamaya*). Those [wheels] of which that is the first are the "beginning-with-the-*baindava*" wheels;
having formed them as the wheels such as the triangle (*trikoṇa*) and so forth, they are to be placed—this is the connection. At the beginning...

The meaning is that after placing the *binducakra*, one should subsequently place the triangle (*trikoṇa*) and so forth. If it is asked, "In that case, why was the placement of the *binducakra* not mentioned first?", the answer is no; for it serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Indeed, the *binducakra* is the center of the triangle; how could that [placement of the triangle] be possible without it? Therefore, this is the intended meaning of the specific sequence.

First, having visualized a triangle on the head, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) by saying "Salutation to the wheel consisting of the bliss of Śarva" in its center; having visualized it as a drop (*bindu*), one should install the Root Goddess there according to the prescribed rule.

Then follows the placement on the triangle and so forth. Therefore, the phrase "on the triangle of the head" is an indication using a completed case-ending (*siddhavibhakti*). However, some [teachers] say:

They say that the sequence is as follows: first, one should visualize and place the Bindu-cakra exactly in the center, and then, having visualized it, one should place the Trikoṇa-cakra outside of it; however, this is not approved by the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, so it should be considered [with caution].

Now, he states the locations for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the inner *daśāra-cakra* (ten-spoked wheel), beginning with "at the root of the eye," and so forth. At the root of the right eye—that is, at the front of the throat, which amounts to the vicinity of the nose;
at its outer corner—that is, at the vicinity of the ear; and at the eastern, middle, northern, and rear parts of the right ear, as well as at the crest (*cūlikā*).

Some say that "in the lower half of the *cūlā*" means in the rear half and the remaining half, specifically in the portions of the head and the back; [others say] it refers to the lower half of the *cūlikā*, meaning the depressed area below the *cūlikā* known as the *ghāṭāsīvanī*, in its half—the remaining half—namely, the left half. By that...
Some say that "at the sīvanī of the aggregates" means on the right and left sides; in this regard, there is the possibility of the first case, such is the direction [of the argument].

At the back of the ear—that is, at the back of the left ear—or at the base of the ear, in the middle of the left ear, at the outer corner—that is, at the edge of the left eye—or at its root, and at the front of the throat: in these ten locations, in the sequence of the wheels (*cakrakrama*).
The remaining portion [of the verse] is: "one should place the ten powers beginning with Sarvajñā. Now, he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the outer ten-spoked wheel:

"beginning with Sarvasiddhi," and so forth. The meaning is that one should place the ten goddesses beginning with Sarvasiddhi in the *viśuddha-cakra* at the throat, which has sixteen petals starting with the vowel *a* and ending with the visarga, proceeding clockwise from the eastern petal.

The sense is that this is preceded by the visualization of the lotus as facing upwards. Then, at the very pit of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*), which is the eastern petal, one should perform this placement (*nyāsa*)—which consists essentially of encircling the interior of the throat—as an encircling of the exterior of the throat. Next, he describes the placement of the fourteen spokes, beginning with "In the heart," etc., [referring to] the *Anāhata* wheel.

The meaning is that the fourteen powers, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, who reside in the twelve petals at the end of the throat and in the fourteen spokes, are also to be installed, as before, by proceeding clockwise starting from the eastern petal. Now, he describes the installation on the eight petals, beginning with "In the navel" (*nābhau*), marking a new section.

One should place an eight-petaled lotus at the navel; then, by way of an outer enclosure, as previously mentioned, there is an inner enclosure—this is the meaning. Therefore, he states the specific location for the placement, which consists of eight petals: "on the backbone" means on the left, on the spinal column (merudaṇḍa) covered by that [lotus]. By this, the western petal is on the back and the left side.
The northern petal is in the north, the eastern petal on the right side, and the southern petal [is in the south];
thus, in the four cardinal petals, the four goddesses beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are placed, starting from the west and proceeding counter-clockwise.
The meaning is "one should place. Regarding the petals of the directions, he says: "the bamboo and the left" (*vaṃśa* ityādi). "Bamboo and left" (*vaṃśavāmau*) refers to the bamboo and the left side;

the space between them is the "space between the bamboo and the left" (*vaṃśavāmāntarālam*), which means the space between the bamboo and the left flank. By this, the petal of the northwest (*vāyavyadalam*) is produced, and that itself is the beginning where [the sequence starts].

In the act of placement (*nyāsakriyā*), the phrase "it is so" (*tattathā*) is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is that one should place the other four lines, such as the *anaṅgarekhā*, in such a way that they occupy the space between the lineage-line (*vaṃśa*) and the left [line], and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the space between the left side and the belly, and the space between the belly and the right side, are included.

The space between the right side and the backbone—thus, in sequence, the four petals of the intermediate directions (Vāyavya, Īśāna, Āgneya, and Nairṛta) are produced; such is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the eight petals. Now, he describes the ritual placement of the sixteen-petaled wheel: "In the Svādhiṣṭhāna" means in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, at the base of the genitals, which has six petals.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five powers beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī starting from the eastern petal of one’s own body up to the southeastern petal, one should place the sixteenth power, Śarīrākarṣiṇī, on the sixth petal; such is the sequence of placement as a wrapping around the *liṅga*. Now:
He describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the lines of the square within the *trailokyamohana-cakra* with the words "in the *mūlādhāra*" and so forth.
In the *mūlādhāra*, which has four petals; regarding that, he states the method with the words "in front" (*pura*) and so forth. "In front" means in the east of the body—this is the ellipsis.

The word "one's own" (*svasya*) also follows from the context. "On the left" (*savye*) means on the right; for according to the lexicon, "left" (*savya*) may refer to both the right and the left. [The placement continues] on the backbone (*vaṃśe*).
On the backbone or on the left petal—

having thus placed the four mudrās beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī in these four petals in clockwise order— one should also place the four mudrās beginning with Unmādinī in the four intervals between the petals, namely at the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast.
Having placed [the mudrās] above between Indra and Īśāna, and below between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, one should place the Khecarī and Yoni mudrās respectively;
these are the ten mudrās. Now, he describes the placement on the middle line of the square:
"Again, excluding the top and bottom," and so forth, as before, like the Mūlādhāra.

The meaning is that, having assigned the four Mothers in the four directions starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, one should assign the four Mothers beginning with Vārāhī in the four intermediate directions starting from the southeast; for this very reason, it is said to be "excluding above and below," because there are eight Mothers in total.

6. Now, he describes the placement of the lines of the outer square, beginning with the words "the left shank" (*vāmajaṅghām*) and so forth. This means in a counter-clockwise sequence starting from the left; that is, by proceeding clockwise [from the perspective of the deity]. Thus, having placed four [mantras] on the petals in the directions starting with the East, one should place the remaining eight Siddhis—four on the petals in the intermediate directions starting with the Southeast—and then the two remaining Siddhis on the soles of the feet, specifically on the sole of the left foot.

The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) [of these]. Demonstrating its nature as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), he says: "from the cause," which means from that which consists of universal bliss. "In this way" means one should perform meditation through non-difference from one's own self.
In the middle of the eyebrows, in the heart, in the navel, and then further in the svādhiṣṭhāna;
likewise in the mūlādhāra, as well as in the pair of thighs and also in the two knees.
The best of practitioners, being fully concentrated within Tripurā, should sequentially place the Bindu and the other Īśvarīs upon the calves and the feet. (6.2)
Then, one should perform the pervasive [placement] with the mantra for the offering of each respective wheel.
Thus ends the description of the placement of the Śrīcakra of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Now, the placement of the wheel of persistence (*sthiti*) is described in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Then the wise practitioner should perform the placement beginning with the purification of the hands."
On the crown of the head, in the secret place, in the heart, and also in the three eyes.
O Goddess, having performed the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa) upon the pair of ears, the mouth, the two arms, the back, the two knees, and the navel; || 6-2 ||

Thus, the meaning is that after performing the placement of the Vidyās (*vidyānyāsa*) on the crown of the head and other locations, one should perform the placement of the Vidyās beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). In this context, because of the relationship between the supported and the support, the placement of the wheels (*cakra*) and the Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśvarī*) should also be understood; the meaning is that one should first perform the placement of the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Wheel and so forth. By this, the state of stability is attained. And so it is said:
Creation proceeds from the nine yonis up to the earth, while dissolution proceeds again from the earth up to the nine yonis; such is the certainty of the scripture. (6.1)
Because it is stated right there:
"The first [mudrā] effects the purification of the hands, the second protects the self, and immediately after that, the third is the goddess seated upon the seat of the self. (6.1)
Next is she seated on the wheel-throne, then she established on the throne of all mantras;
the sixth is the supreme one consisting of the illusory Lakṣmī, whose throne is both that of the seeker and the perfected.
And that goddess is proclaimed as the seventh, Mūrtividyā;
the eighth is the Āvāhanī mudrā, and the ninth is the supreme Bhairavī.
The root-vidyā is likewise known as the subduer of the three worlds;
thus, there are nine types [of vidyās] that should be employed with effort at the time of worship.
O Mistress of the Kula, these [syllables] should be deposited in sequence by the practitioner upon the tips of the feet, the shanks, the knees, the thighs, the anus, and the tip of the penis.
One should place the Mūrti-mantra upon the support (ādhāra), and within that, one should place the Āvāhanī-mantra;
O Supreme Goddess, the Vyāpaka-nyāsa must be performed with the Mūla-mantra.
One should contemplate the previously mentioned nine wheels, joined with the Mistress of the Wheels (Cakreśvarī), in the locations such as Akula and the rest that were described before.
I shall state their names according to their sequential order:
among them, the first is the goddess Tripurā, and the second is Tripureśvarī.
And the third is likewise proclaimed as the goddess Tripurasundarī;
and the fourth, O Great Goddess, is the goddess Tripuravāsinī. (6.9)
The fifth is Tripurāśrī, the sixth is Tripuramālinī,
the seventh is Tripurāsiddhi, and the eighth is Tripurāmbikā.
The ninth is the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī;
one should worship these [goddesses] in sequence within the nine cakras previously mentioned.
Thus, at the time of worship, Pārvatī consists of nine aspects;
indeed, she is the primordial Śakti, uniform in form, who brings about freedom from old age and death.

Thus it is said. In that regard, having first meditated upon Akula and the others, one should mentally meditate upon Trailokyamohana and the rest through the recitation of their respective mantras; then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the internal and external contact delimited by those [deities], one should likewise place the nine Cakreśvarīs within that [mandala] of Trailokyamohana and the others. Thereafter, one should again meditate upon each respective wheel (*cakra*) as conjoined with its presiding goddess (*cakreśvarī*). Therefore...
It is said, "joined with the Mistress of the Wheel" (*cakreśvarī*), which means presided over by the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*). For example:

in *Akula*, known as *Viṣu*, the wheel that fascinates the three worlds (*trailokyamohana*) is presided over by Tripurā, located in the thousand-petaled lotus at the base of the *suṣumnā*. In *Vahni*, the *ādhāra*, the [wheel] is presided over by Tripureśvarī, located in the four-petaled lotus.
The wheel that fulfills all desires is located in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, in the six-petalled lotus, presided over by Tripurasundarī;
the wheel that agitates all is located at the navel, in the ten-petalled lotus, presided over by Tripuravāsinī;
and the wheel that bestows all good fortune is in the *anāhata*, in the twelve-petalled [lotus].
The wheel presided over by Tripurāśrayā, which accomplishes all aims, is located in the Viśuddha [cakra] on the sixteen petals;
the wheel that provides all protection, presided over by Tripuramālinī, is at the tip of the uvula on the eight-petaled lotus;
and the wheel that removes all diseases, presided over by Tripurāsiddhā, is between the eyebrows on the two-petaled lotus.
One should meditate upon the wheel presided over by Tripurāmbā, which bestows all accomplishments, located in the moon at the forehead;
and the wheel that produces all bliss, presided over by Mahātripurasundarī, located in the *bindu*. Thus it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
In Akula, in that which is known as Viṣu, in Śākta, and likewise again in Vahni; in Nābha, Anāhata, and Śuddhi; at the tip of the uvula, and within the space between the eyebrows.
Regarding the word *indau*: "Kula" refers to the six-petaled lotus located below the *mūlādhāra*;
one finger-breadth below that is the eight-petaled lotus; and one finger-breadth below that is the red thousand-petaled lotus—this is the sequence.

"Akula" is other than Kula; it means the red thousand-petaled lotus situated at the base of the *suṣumnā*. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...Indeed... [Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly here].
Since the six-petalled lotus is indeed *kula*, the eight-petalled lotus is also *akula* by virtue of following it; therefore, one might ask why [the placement] would not occur there as well.

To this he says: "And in that which is designated as *viṣu*. The meaning is that the placement occurs specifically in that which is designated as *akula* and *viṣu*, and not merely in what is *akula*.
That is to say, in the thousand-petalled lotus, which is named the *vyāpaka* (the pervader), because the *suṣumnā* resides therein.

It pervades the thirty lotuses contained within that; therefore, the meaning is that *akula* is not taken here in the form of the eight-petaled lotus. Regarding the phrase "in the Śākta fire," the construction is inverted as "in the fire of the Śākta" in accordance with the sequence of the wheel (*cakra*).
As for the location of that inversion, it is due to the independent will of Maheśvara. And thus, the fire is the *mūlādhāra*.

Because it is the support for the fire-maṇḍala, the power (śakti) is Hṛllekhā; because it is situated above that, the meaning is that the Svādhiṣṭhāna is "pertaining to power" (śākta). [The centers are located] at the navel in Maṇipūraka, in the unstruck (anāhata) heart-lotus, in the Viśuddhi-throat-lotus, at the tip of the uvula, above the throat at the root of the palate in the eight-petaled lotus, and between the eyebrows.

"In the *ājñā* [cakra], which is a two-petaled lotus, in the moon"—this means in the *bindu* on the forehead. For it has been stated by [the author] himself: "The form of a lamp, consisting of half a *mātrā*, is desired as a circle on the forehead. Regarding "half a *mātrā*": a short vowel's duration of pronunciation is called a *mātrā*;
that whose duration of pronunciation is half of a *mātrā* is "half-a-*mātrā*" (*ardhamātra*). [This is located] on the forehead.
The meaning is that above the eyebrows, the circular shape—the very dot (*bindu*)—is intended as the moon.

By this, the form of the *bindu*, its time of pronunciation, and its location have been stated; the meaning is that the *bindu* is shaped like a lamp, has a duration of half a measure (*ardhamātra*), and is arranged in a circular configuration. He now describes the manifestation (*prapañca*) of the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*) and the others below.
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Below and above the Suṣumnā is [the lotus] endowed with a thousand petals;
it is red and white, and joined with the Śaktis residing upon those thousand petals. (6-1)
O Īśānī, it faces upward and downward, endowed with pericarp and filaments;
O Great Goddess, it is the auspicious form of Śakti, consisting of both Kula and Akula.
O Īśānī, there are two lotuses situated eternally and imperishably;
between them, within the Suṣumnā, is the lotus that is the support of the thirty deities.
Now listen as I describe, in due order, the nature of Śakti, the form of Śiva, the abode of Śarvāṇī’s presence, and the sequence of their forms. 6-4.
O Goddess, the space between the anus and the penis is five finger-breadths in height;
the middle of the anus is one finger-breadth wide and two finger-breadths in expansion.
At its base is the Great Yoni, having the form of a triangle;
Suṣumnā is situated in the middle of that Yoni, O Maheśvarī, at its very root.
Below is a thousand-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments;
it is radiant, glowing red like fire, with the Śaktis stationed upon its petals.
O Dear One, accompanied by the Śaktis arranged like stamens,
the Goddess, the Kula-goddess, is situated in the center of the pericarp.
Above that lotus, in the center of the Suṣumṇā, one finger-breadth higher,
there is a lotus endowed with eight petals and possessed of eight knots.
It is red, endowed with its own pericarp, and adorned with red filaments;
it has three prongs situated at the tip of the knot, and is surrounded by the eight Bhairavas beginning with Brahmāṇī. (6.10)
It is completely surrounded by the powers (śaktis) beginning with the letters of the vargas situated at the knots on the eight petals,
as well as by other powers that are likewise joined together.
Then, one should meditate upon that which is served by the Kaula power in its center;
above that, at a distance of one finger-breadth, is the six-petaled lotus of Kula.
The supporting lotus is yellow, four-petalled, and possesses beautiful filaments;
it is turned downwards, and in its center, O Supreme Goddess, is Kuṇḍalinī.
Situated in the center of the Svayambhū is the inconceivable [deity], surrounded by Varada and the others;
this is indeed the earthen lotus, and beneath it is another, supreme lotus.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon that which is fiery, with the powers situated within it—partless, O Supreme Goddess, resembling a mass of lightning. (6.15)
Above that, in the center of the pericarp, is the orb of fire;
above that is the Pūrṇapīṭha, and above that, O Śivā, Śākinī is established.
Above the supporting lotus, at a height of two and a half finger-breadths,
is a fiery [mandala] with eight petals and a yellow pericarp.
Hṛllekhā resides in the center of the pericarp, served by Anaṅga and others. Two finger-breadths above this is the six-cornered Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Then, having visualized Kākinī— surrounded by the powers beginning with Bandhinīśakti and consisting of the element of water— at the navel, eight finger-breadths above it.
That lotus is Maṇipūra, beautiful with ten petals;
it is situated in the midst of Lākinī and surrounded by Ḍāmari and the others.
Fourteen finger-breadths above the lotus known as Maṇipūra is the twelve-spoked Anāhata lotus, which is the center of Rākiṇī.
It is surrounded by the Śaktis such as Kālarātri and others who reside upon the petals;
in the solar disc situated in the center, however, is the sacred seat (pīṭha) known as Nādoḍyāna.
Therefore, one finger-breadth above that is the pure sixteen-spoked [cakra];
O Supreme Goddess, the Ḍākinī resides in the center, while [the other goddesses] are on the outer petals.
Situated within [the channel] beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Akṣarā is the lunar orb;
above that, O Supreme Goddess, the uvula is four finger-breadths above the throat.
Therefore, the eight-petalled lotus is surrounded by Rasika and the others;
the wheel of command (ājñācakra) is a two-petalled lotus joined with the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
On both sides of the Haṃsavatī and Kṣamā [lines], Hākinī is in the middle;
then, above that, is the circular enclosure of the Bindu located on the forehead.
Resembling ten million suns, exceedingly radiant, and possessing great qualities,
in its center is a lotus measuring ten billion yojanas.
Seated upon its pericarp is the Lord Śāntyatīteśvara,
five-faced, ten-armed, with a form resembling a mass of lightning.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti stand surrounding it in succession, O beautiful one, around that which transcends Śānti.
Seated on the left side is Śāntyatītā Manonmanī;
all [of them] bear five faces, have ten arms, and are adorned with the moon.
The reality of the Bindu (bindutattva) has been fully described as being surrounded by hundreds of billions of [sub-units].
Thus concludes the description of the arrangement of the Śrīcakra for its ritual placement.

Thus [ends the work] composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the great Mahāmahopādhyāya.
The sixth breath (chapter) in the tantra known as the Śrīvidyārṇava. || 6 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇava Tantra,
the seventh breath (śvāsa).

Now, the established conclusion is that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Śrīcakra of Abiding consists of three limbs: the Vidyā-cakra, the Cakra-īśvarī, and the [Vidyā-]aṅga. In this regard, first, according to tradition, one should perform the purification of the hands with the Karaśuddhi-vidyā and perform self-protection with the Ātmarakṣā-vidyā, and then contemplate the Goddess as non-different from one's own self.

Likewise, in the *Śrītantrarāja*: "I meditate upon Bhavānī as being ruddy-hued, her eyes rippling with compassion, holding a noose, a goad, a flower-arrow, and a bow, and surrounded by rays [of light] such as the *aṇimā* powers, [thinking] 'I am she'. (1)
Having thus meditated, one should begin the *śrīcakra-nyāsa*. Regarding that, as for the *vidyā-nyāsa*:

first, one should install the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*)—both in its distributed and undistributed forms according to the divisions of the seed-syllables (*kūṭākṣara*)—in due order upon the head, the secret place, the heart, and the right and left eyes.
One should place [the hands] on the two ears, the two arms, the back, the two knees, and the navel.

Thus ends the *kūṭanyāsa*. Now, the *akṣaranyāsa*: one should place the fifteen [syllables] on the head, the secret place, the heart, the eyes, the two ears, the mouth, the two arms, the back, the two knees, and the navel. Thus ends the *akṣaranyāsa*. Now, the *samastavidyānyāsa*:
In the fifteen locations beginning with the crown of the head,
the wise practitioner should separately place the root-mantra, preceded by the three stars (the *tritārā*), in due order.
Thus ends the placement of the Vidyā (vidyā-nyāsa). Now follows the placement of the Vidyā of the Nine Cakreśvarīs (navacakreśvarī-vidyā-nyāsa):
One should place [the mantras] on the two feet, the two calves, the two knees, the two thighs, the anus and the sides, the two buttocks, the top of the head, the ādhāra, and the mūlādhāra. (1)
This is proclaimed as the Nyāsa of the Navacakreśvarī-vidyā.
Thus ends the Nyāsa of the Navacakreśvarī-vidyā. Now follows the Nyāsa of the Nine Wheels (Navacakra):
[one should perform it] in the Brahmarandhra, the Ādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Navel.
In the Anāhata, the Viśuddha, the Lambikā, and between the two eyebrows; || 1 ||
One should install the nine wheels (cakras) in sequence at the location of the Bindu.

This is the installation of the nine wheels (navacakranyāsa). Now, the installation of the Mistress of the Wheels (cakreśvarīnyāsa): having recited the Vidyās in their respective places—Tripurā, Tripureśvarī...
Sundarī, Tripurā, and likewise Tripuravāsinī. || 1 ||
Tripurāśrī shall be the fifth; the sixth is Tripuramālinī;
the seventh is Tripurāsiddhā, and Tripurāmbā shall be the eighth.
The ninth is the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī;
one should place her in the nine wheels—thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) proclaimed.

Thus ends the installation of Cakreśvarī. Thus concludes the extraction of the installation of the Śrīcakra for the state of maintenance (*sthiti*). Now follows the six-limbed protective installation (*rakṣā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*): [the three *tāras*, then] Bālā, and "Salutation to Tripurasundarī."
Having uttered "Protect me" (māṃ rakṣa) twice, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) therein.
Thus ends the six-limbed protection (*rakṣā-ṣaḍaṅga*).

By repeating the three seed-syllables of Bālā twice, the practitioner should perform the six-limbed rite; this is declared to be the six-limbed placement of the seed-syllables (*bīja-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*). (1)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by repeating the three peaks twice;
this is declared to be the root six-limbed assignment (nyāsa) of the fifteen-syllable Vidyā. || 2 ||
With five, three, one, one, and one [syllables] respectively, these six limbs are formed from the five seed-syllables;
thus is this six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā proclaimed.
Omniscience is eternally satisfied, likewise awakening from the beginningless;
it is independent, and therefore its power is eternally undiminished beyond that.

Those [mantras] of infinite power, preceded by the single seed-syllable of Bālā, constitute the Nyāsa of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) for the young women; this is proclaimed for the attainment of all goals. || 5 ||

At the beginning of each individual peak-syllable (kūṭa), Śrī Mahātripurasundarī is invoked as before with the mantra beginning "to the abode of the power of omniscience" (sarvajñatā-śakti-dhāmne). (6)
"The installation of the Six-Limbed Youthful Goddesses (Ṣaḍaṅgayuvatīnyāsa) is the illuminator of the Root-Mantra (Mūlavidyā).

Thus ends the Root-Six-Limbed Installation of the Youthful Goddesses. "The syllable Māyā (Hrīm), preceded by the six long vowels and the letter Ka, etc., is desired as another method. Now follows the visualization (dhyāna) of the Six-Limbed Youthful Goddesses:

Resplendent with white, blue, black, yellow, and red light, holding the gestures of boon-granting and protection, possessing exquisite limbs, and enriched with all the charms of youth and loveliness—these are the youthful forms of the goddesses of Śrīdevī. (1)
Thus ends the meditation. Now follows the Śrīvidyā-pūrṇanyāsa from the Jñānārṇava:
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme nyāsa of Śrīvidyā.
One should contemplate the complete Vidyā, glowing with a reddish luster, in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head). (1)
One should meditate upon the sixteen-syllable mantra dripping with nectar, which bestows great good fortune;
thereafter, one should rotate the "good fortune-bestowing finger" over the region of the left shoulder.
One should place the *mudrā* called Ripujihvāgrahā at the base of the feet;
then again, O Goddess, one should place it with the *sampūrṇā* [mudrā] above the throat.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should perform the placement with the complete [mantra] by way of pervasion;
at the end of the pervasion, having cast the *yonimudrā* into the mouth and having offered salutation, || 4 ||
This placement (nyāsa), which is the full embodiment of Śrīvidyā, increases good fortune.
O Goddess, one should place it at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and then at the wrist (maṇibandha).
The wise one should place the ring finger on the forehead and meditate upon the sixteen-syllable mantra;
O Goddess of the Gods, this placement is called "Sammohana" (the Enchanter) and it causes agitation.
Meditating on the three worlds as crimson and recollecting Śrīvidyā in his mind,
[he should place the syllables] upon the feet, the calves, the knees, the hips, the navel, and the back.
At the navel, on the two sides, on the breasts, and likewise on the cheeks,
at the two ears, at the aperture of Brahmā, and on the face, O Pārvatī.
Then, in the region of the ear and in the hand,
this great withdrawal (saṃhāra) and placement (nyāsa) is performed in sequence with the sixteen seed-syllables (bījas).
Through the sixteen-syllable nyāsas of the Śrīvidyās, one becomes the Lord of the Universe. O Goddess, O Beloved, for the sake of creation, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as before.

Thus. Here, one who has been initiated by means of the sixteen-syllable mantra through its various divisions and so forth should place only the phonemes [of that mantra]. In this text, there is the sequence of worship prescribed in the *Śrītantrarāja*; therein, the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the fifteen-syllable mantra was performed by the Blessed Lord Śambhu, and therefore, prior to that, [the procedure for] the fifteen-syllable mantra—
The extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) is performed. However, the worship (*pūjā*) of this [mantra] will be written specifically below.

The primary tradition (*mukhyāmnāya*) for this Śrīvidyā is the Ṛgveda. In the fifth maṇḍala (5.47.4), the extraction of the mantra "catvāra īṃ bibhrati kṣemayante" is well-known in the Ṛgveda. [In] the Atharvaveda...

And in the *Upaniṣad* of the Śaunaka recension, the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) is extracted; following that, the sequence for extracting the sixteen syllables is demonstrated. In that regard, it is stated in the *Śrījñānārṇava*:
The Śrī Devī said:
O God, Tripurā has been revealed by you in her various forms;
however, regarding that which was stated as being "threefold," please reveal it, O Śaṅkara.
Īśvara said: O sinless one, I shall describe to you that which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, endowed with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, and consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
O Supreme Goddess, that Śiva indeed abides pervading the entire universe;
having previously described him through his qualities, now hear [the description] of him whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti.
The imperishable power of the *mātṛkā* consists of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'sa';
O Supreme Goddess, the letter 'ha' alone is said to be Śiva. (4)
By virtue of being the first and last syllables, I am the bestower of the entire meaning of that [alphabet];
whatever is expressed by the letters of the Mātṛkā, all that is I, the Lord. (5)
O Supreme Goddess, the letter *ha* is of the nature of emptiness, eternally imperishable;
the letter *sa*, being of the nature of power (*śakti*), expresses the supreme and possesses the quality of emanation.
Since the cause of arising is designated as "power" (śakti),
O beautiful one, that yoga reveals itself by means of the word "I" (ahaṃ).
Through the union of the three points (bindus), she is Mahātripurasundarī;
that Goddess exists in the form of sound (nāda), having the nature of the half-syllable of the letter *ha*.
O Supreme Goddess, since the letter *ha* is the very form of Śiva,
the Great Power (*Mahāśakti*), whose nature is the half-form of the letter *ha*, constitutes his half-body.
Therefore, O Goddess, Mahāvidyā Mahātripurasundarī is called the Eternal One; she is the digit of consciousness (citkalā), the supreme deity. 10.
O auspicious one, O Goddess of gods, by the grace of the glorious Guru, being endowed with the lineage of the tradition,
one should rise in the morning and remember the Guru by his own names.
O Goddess, having performed the twilight ablutions and other rites, the best of mantra-knowers,
adorned with all the finery of ornaments and dressed in fine attire, [anointed himself] with camphor, saffron, and other perfumes.
(Śrīvi. 15, p.
114) His limbs are smeared with the profuse application of great musk, and he is reddened with saffron.
Richly adorned with the nine gems, he shone in crimson garments.
With his face colored by betel-juice and his mind filled with the bliss of passion,
he reached the sacrificial pavilion, which was variegated and adorned with red lac.
Abounding in many kinds of incense, adorned with heaps of flowers,
smeared with cow dung, and covered with beautiful floral canopies.
Having sat upon a seat that is pleasing to the mind, soft, and subtle,
one should perform the extraction of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava [bīja], the Kāmabīja as the second, and the third belonging to Kumārī—this, O Supreme Goddess, is Tripurā. (17)
O Supreme Goddess, the first Vidyā is Karaśuddhikarī;
O Great Goddess, the second is Kumārī, who is Tripureśī. 18.
Having first set aside Tripureśī and the others, one should surround Bhuvaneśī;
by means of this [mantra], one should know the seat (āsana) and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) of Tripureśī.
O Maheśānī, Tripureśī always resides within the three seed-syllables;
know her, O Goddess, as Tripuravāsinī, seated upon the throne of the cakras.
O Maheśānī, Tripureśī is conjoined with Śiva and Candra in the Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja [Kūṭas], while in the third [Kūṭa] she is of the nature of Śiva.
O Dear One, O Daughter of the Mountain, this Tripuraśrī resides upon the seat of all mantras;
however, for her who has taken her seat upon the Self, she remains after abandoning the third [syllable].
Having superimposed the nature of Bala, she stands upon the Sādhyasiddha seat;
know her to be Tripuramālinī, seated upon the Sādhyasiddha throne. 23.
O beautiful goddess, that Bhairavī who bestows prosperity is located in the third seed-syllable; there, having removed the bindu, one should place the visarga.
O mature woman, O Śivā, hear the root-vidyā, which is served by all the Āgamas, which is worshipped by all philosophical systems, and which is the imperishable digit of consciousness.
The syllables Bhū, Mi, Śca, Ndra, Śi, Vo, Mā, Yā, and Śakti—Kṛṣṇa, Adhva, Mādana, Ardhacandra, and Bindu—these nine syllables are said to be Meru. (26)
The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru;
from the letter *la* arises the goddess Earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves. (27)
She is endowed with fifty seats, consisting of all sacred fords, and is supreme;
she possesses the nature of the letter 'Sa', the moon, the stars, the planets, and the zodiac signs.
O Dear One, she who is established in the sphere of space through the union with the letter *ha* and the syllable *śiva*,
and who is the universal form consisting of the Great Fourth (*turya*), arises from the letter *ī*.
From the syllable *eka* arises the power of Viṣṇu, intent upon the protection of the universe;
from the syllable *ra*, she is endowed with splendor, having the nature of the supreme light.
From the letter *ka* arises she who grants desires, who possesses a form at will, and who is the throbbing, imperishable one;
by means of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), O Goddess of Gods, she is declared to be the womb of the universe. (31)
By means of the Bindu, which is the form of Śiva and the form of the Void, she is the Witness;
with this [Bindu], whose nature is immovable, there is pervasion everywhere.
Thus, O lady of excellent vows, by means of this Meru, which is the form of the Supreme Brahman, the mantra of Tripurā is produced with these nine syllables. (33)
Otherwise, O Goddess, there is no accomplishment of the Śrī Tripurā-mantra;
nor, O Queen of the Gods, is the Śrī-cakra anything other than the form of Meru—of this there is no doubt. (34)
The letter *la* is the seed-syllable of the earth; therefore, it is called the earth (*urvī*).
The letter *sa*, O auspicious lady, is the moon, consisting of sixteen digits (*kalā*). (35)
Therefore, O auspicious lady, the letter *ha* is said to be Śiva on the sixteen-petaled [lotus]; since he is eternally eight-formed (*aṣṭamūrti*), there should be eight petals.
The letter *ī* is indeed Mahāmāyā, who protects the fourteen worlds; she is the Supreme (*parā*), therefore, O Dear One, she resides in the northeast corner. (37)
The single Śakti, abiding in ten places, gives birth to the three worlds;
she is renowned as the Source of the Universe (Viśvayoni), the tenfold form of Viṣṇu. (38)
O Supreme Goddess, from the letter *ra*, the Cakra expands, pervading all;
therefore, from that letter *ra* arises the imperishable light of the ten-cornered [Cakra]. (39)
The Fire, endowed with the ten digits (kalās), is the initiator of the ten-cornered [mandala].
From the letter *ka*, O Goddess, arises Mādana and Śiva in his eightfold form.
Then he fashioned its wombs; it should be marked with the womb of the Vasus.
Since the half-measure (ardhamātrā) gives birth to the qualities (guṇas), it therefore exists in the form of differentiation. || 41 ||
The womb (yoni) is triangular in form, and with the bindu it becomes the baindava;
that is the form of Kāmeśvara, whose essential nature is the support of the universe.
"O Varārohā, the Śrīcakra indeed originates from the syllables of the Śrīvidyā.
Thus it is said. In another Tantra:
"Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, and Kāmarāja..."
Agastya, Nandi, and Sūrya, as well as Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Śiva. || 1 ||
Durvāsas and the twelve devotees of the Great Goddess are remembered, as well as Śakra, Utpalī, and likewise Varuṇa. || 2 ||
Dharmarāja, Anala, the Nāga king, Vāyu, Budha,
as well as Īśāna, Rati, and likewise Nārāyaṇa.
Brahmā, Jīva, and Mahādevī are the thirteen worshippers;
O Maheśvarī, the number of worshippers is twenty-five. (4)
"I shall describe to you in brief those varieties of mantras to be worshipped.
Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the seed-syllable (bīja) according to the tradition of Kāmeśvarī."
The entire Bhuvaneśānī is the supreme seed-syllable (bīja) of Kāmeśī. || 1 ||
By means of this, I shall explain all the sciences in detail;
O fair-eyed one, this fourth letter is within Śakti, situated in the midst of the Kalās.
The Vāgbhava [bīja], enriched with five colors, is then called Kāmarāja;
it begins with Śiva and the Moon and ends with Śiva, O fish-eyed one. (3)
The form of four syllables, however, is Tripurā, who is supreme and consists of three syllables.
Here, "the Śakti-kūṭa" means the form of the Kāmeśī-bīja previously extracted. The Goddess embodies all sacred fords and possesses the nature of all the gods.
She consists of all witnesses, she is eternal, she consists of all wombs, and she is supreme.
She is consciousness consisting of all-knowledge, whose form is all wisdom;
she is visibly composed of all the gods, beautiful with every auspicious fortune.
Having worshipped this, O Goddess of gods, Kāma became beautiful in every limb.
This is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Kāmarāja. Thus, the Goddess said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, O handsome one, tell me her divisions; by whom and by what means is she worshipped? Make this clear, O Śaṅkara! (1)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme one named Lopāmudrā,
who is the Śakti and the fourth [state] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, O beautiful one.
Having omitted [the letters] from the beginning, Lopāmudrā is revealed as being enriched by Śiva (H) and Indu (I).
In the Vāgbhava portion of the Kāmarāja-vidyā, having omitted the letter E and the letter I, one should place the letter Ha and the letter Sa at the beginning; the rest is the same. Thus:
This knowledge, worshipped by Agastya, causes the agitation of the three worlds;
this very knowledge is worshipped by Kāmarāja, of this there is no doubt. (3)
*Hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*: this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Lopāmudrā.
We shall explain the distinction between these two later on.
O auspicious one, this pair of Vidyās is difficult to obtain within the three worlds.
O fair-faced one, [this is done] with the Vāgbhava [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja.
I shall now proclaim the extraction of the Vidyā: one should place Śakti and Ādana in the middle;
Śiva should be placed in the Vāgbhava [bīja], while Kāmarāja begins with Śiva. (5)
The third [syllable] begins with *candra* (the moon); this is the Vidyā honored by Manu. *KAHA-E-Ī-LAHRĪṂ*, *HAKA-E-Ī-LAHRĪṂ*, *SAKA-E-Ī-LAHRĪṂ*—thus is the Śrīvidyā worshipped through the mantra.
O Goddess, the first [syllable] is *vāgbhava* (beginning with *sa*), and the one beginning with *candra* (the moon) is situated between the two *śivas*.
Mādana is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), while Śakti-bīja is Hasānana. || 6 ||
This Śrīvidyā, worshipped by the Moon, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is: *sahaka-e-ī-lahrīṃ sahakaha-e-ī-lahrīṃ sahaka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*. Thus:

Know that the first [syllable] is *hasa* (ha-sa), the second is *vāgbhava* (aiṃ) situated between *śiva* (ha) and *sa*, and the third is *mādana* (klim) within the *kāmabīja*; listen to this, O Pārvatī. (7)
She who is worshipped by Kubera has *hasādyam* as her seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The mantra for this Vidyā, worshipped by Kubera, is: *hasaka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *sahakaha-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *sahaka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*.
O Pārvatī, hear now the third [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja;
it is the seed-syllable of Śakti preceded by *sa*, which is worshipped by Agastya.

Thus: *ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *hasasakalahrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Agastya. Likewise, the phrase "by the power of Lopāmudrā, she is manifest as the very nature of Brahman" means that this Vidyā was also worshipped by Lopāmudrā. By this, she is the second [form] worshipped by Lopāmudrā.
Regarding "Śrīvidyā": likewise, in the Vāgbhava [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, abandon Mādana;
having joined Candra to that very place, [place it] thereafter in Kāmarāja. 9.
Having abandoned the *candra* (the nasal bindu), one should place it upon the mouth; this is the Vidyā worshipped by Nandin:
*sa-e-ī-lahrīṃ sahakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ*. Thus is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Nandin. Likewise:
"O auspicious lady, this Kāmarāja [Vidyā] consists of six syllables and is the deluder of all."
O lady of excellent hips, the seed-syllable of Śakti, preceded by the Moon, bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess, having removed [the letter] from the third ground of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, place it there below the moon, situated within the seed-syllable of Śakti.
"This Vidyā, propitiated by Indra, bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, *ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, and *salakahrīṃ* is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Indra. Likewise:
"O Maheśvarī, [this is] the second Vidyā known as Lopāmudrā."
In the Kāmarāja [bīja], one should place that very same [Bhṛgu] in the mouth, omitting Bhṛgu.
With the fourth [syllable] being Śiva, and Śiva residing in the third [syllable] as Indra,
this is the Vidyā known as Tripurā, O lady of beautiful hips, who is worshipped by the Sun.
Thus: *ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *sahakalahrīṃ*, *sahasakahahrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by the Sun. Listen likewise, O Goddess; I shall proclaim the four-peaked Śāṅkarī.
Having written the second [form], Lopāmudrā, O beautiful goddess of the gods... (13)
Having written that same [syllable] again, situated in the fourth and fifth [positions],
one should utter it with a single pronunciation, omitting Bhuvaneśānī.
"The four-peaked Great Vidyā was worshipped by Śaṅkara.
Thus, *ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sahasakalahrīṃ*, *ka-e-ī-la hsakahalasahasakalahrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā practiced by Śiva. Likewise:
O Goddess, one should then write Lopāmudrā again; thereafter, the Nandikeśvara-vidyā becomes the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇavī mantra. (15)

The meaning is that Lopāmudrā is the second [form]. *Ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *Hasakahalahrīṃ*, *Sahasakalahrīṃ*, *Sa-e-ī-lahrīṃ*, *Sahakahalahrīṃ*, *Sakalahrīṃ*—this is the six-peaked Śrīvidyā worshipped by Viṣṇu.
O fair-faced one, [these are] within the three peaks of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja.
She who stands as the Sovereign of the World—divide her into two parts, O Maheśvarī!
Devoid of the *bindu* and devoid of the *nāda*, she was worshipped by Durvāsas;
O Goddess, in former times the supreme, partless (*niṣkalā*) [goddess] was worshipped by Durvāsas. (17)

Thus: *ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ hrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ hrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ hrīṃ*. This is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Durvāsas. These are the twelve divisions. We shall extract the other thirteen Vidyās later. Now, he describes the sequence for extracting the sixteen-syllable Vidyā from the Jñānārṇava:
Listen, O Goddess of Gods, as it is told in fourfold manner: why you are called "Manohāriṇī" (the Enchantress) and why you are said to be difficult to find on earth. (1)

The [syllables] ending in Candra (the Moon) and ending in Varuṇa (Water), each accompanied by Śakra (Indra) and the others, enriched with the left eye (ī), the bindu, and the nāda, and endowed with the kalās of Viśvamātṛ. || 2 ||
O Goddess, one should apply [the mantra] at the beginning of the Vidyā; she is directly the nature of the waking state.
Waking is origination, awakening, and likewise the withdrawal of the mind. (3)
The four *kalās* are established in the waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*). The waking state is said to consist of the quality of *sattva*, and it is purely of the nature of *śakti*. (4)
O auspicious lady, all [the goddesses] have three peaks, for they indeed become five-peaked;
Vaiṣṇavī shall have eight peaks, and Śāṅkarī shall have six peaks.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows:

the letter *ha* is the end of the moon (*candrānta*); the letter *śa* is the end of Varuṇa (*vāruṇānta*); the letter *ra* is the beginning of Śakra (*śakrādi*); and the letter *ī* is the left eye (*vāmākṣi*).
With the *bindu* and *nāda*, the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* are established.
If the previously mentioned vidyās begin with the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), they take the form of "origination" (*utpatti*).

By the addition of the *māyā* seed-syllable to the *kūṭas* and so forth, they take the form of "awakening" (*jāgara*). By the addition of the *śrī* seed-syllable (*śrīṃ*) to the *kūṭas* and so forth, they take the form of "withdrawal of the mind" (*manovyāvṛtti*). By the addition of the *śrī* seed-syllable to the *vidyās* and so forth, they take the form of "enlightenment" (*bodha*).
These divisions consist of the nature of the waking state. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The Vidyās beginning with the seed-syllable of *lajjā* (hrīṃ) are said to be of the nature of origination;
those consisting of the *kūṭas* beginning with the seed-syllable of *lajjā* are said to be of the nature of the waking state. (1)

Thus, through the yoga of the Śrī-bīja, she whose nature consists of the turning away from [ordinary] consciousness is Śrīvidyā; she is proclaimed to be fourfold according to her waking state. || 2 ||
At that time, all the divisions indeed consist of four peaks;
Vaiṣṇavī has seven peaks, while Śāṅkarī has five peaks.
The great vidyās beginning with the two seed-syllables are said to be dream-like in form;
these, such as Māyā, Lakṣmī, and others, have the nature of desire.

If the seed-syllables beginning with the two [seed-mantras] are joined as *kūṭas*, they are proclaimed to be of the nature of delusion (*bhrama*); whereas those beginning with *Ramā* and *Māyā*, when conjoined as *kūṭas*, take the form of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
And these divisions have been described as having the nature of Smṛti, O Maheśvarī;
they consist of five kūṭas, while Vaiṣṇavī consists of eight kūṭas.
The six-peaked Śāṅkarī is proclaimed; she is declared to be the state of dream.
All [the goddesses] are declared through the conjunction of the pair of seed-syllables beginning with "veda" (oṃ).
They arise in the form of deep sleep; deep sleep is the very form of Śiva.
Death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep are all enveloped in darkness (tamas).
(117) O Supreme Goddess, the four digits (kalās) of deep sleep are to be known;
they are Tāra-Māyā and so forth, as well as Māyā-Tāra and so forth. || 9 ||
"O Maheśvarī, there are four varieties of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which take the form of the *kalās*.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: those beginning with *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*; those beginning with *māyā*, *tāra*, and *ramā*; those beginning with *tāra*, *ramā*, and *māyā*; and those beginning with *ramā*, *tāra*, and *māyā*. Thus, in this sequence, there are twelve kinds of *vidyās*."
There are one hundred and forty-four divisions. As stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess, adorned with the Vedas and the like, you are always composed of Śiva and Śakti;
then, O Supreme Goddess, all these divisions consist of six peaks. (1)
Vaiṣṇavī consists of nine peaks, while Śāṅkarī has seven peaks;
by the mere remembrance of this [goddess], the world becomes filled with bliss.
The threefold division has been declared; now listen, O beloved, to the Mahāvidyā, by the mere knowledge of which Brahman is directly realized—of this there is no doubt. (3)
O Supreme Goddess, the fourth state (turyā), characterized by mere radiance from deep sleep to the end of waking, has attained the status of being the culmination of all states.
It is described as being free from existence and non-existence, transcending the qualities (guṇas);
it is dispassion, the desire for liberation, meditative absorption, and a stainless mind. || 5 ||
The determination of existent and non-existent entities are these digits of the Fourth (Turyā);
O auspicious lady, [they are formed] from the first two seed-syllables in reverse order.
Having written [this], O Supreme Goddess, one should then extract the others;
she who faces inward, O fair-limbed one, is the Virgin Tripureśvarī. (7)
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship this sixteen-syllable Vidyā consisting of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā), which is encapsulated by these five seed-syllables. 8.
O auspicious lady, all the Trikūṭas indeed consist of sixteen syllables;
the Vaiṣṇavī consists of nineteen syllables, and the Śaivī consists of seventeen syllables.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: the first two seed-syllables (*bīja*) consist of *māyā* and *ramā*; their reversed order means that *ramā* comes first and *māyā* afterwards. The *kāmabīja* situated within—that is, in the middle—is at the "mouth," which is to say, at the beginning, of the maiden (*kumārī*). By means of these five seed-syllables, [one obtains] the six-peaked and nine-peaked [mantras].
Or "encased" (*sampuṭitāṃ*) means made like a casket; thus, the meaning is that it is encased in both direct and reverse order.
Also in the *Gāndharva*:
"Having extracted the seed-syllable of Ramā, one should apply the seed-syllable of Māyā."
Having written the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), one should write the seed-syllable of speech (VĀG) immediately thereafter. || 1 ||

O Maheśvarī, [the mantra consists of] the Moon (the letter *u*) endowed with the fourteen vowels, joined with a pair of dots (*bindu*), followed by the *praṇava* (oṃ), Bhuvaneśānī (hrīṃ), and Ramā (śrīṃ). 2.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the fifteen-syllable mantra;
and from it, O Supreme Goddess, the previously mentioned five seed-syllables in reverse order.
"Having written [the syllables], one should form a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure); this is the *vidyā* consisting of sixteen *kūṭas*.
And likewise in the *Yoginītantra*:
"The seed-syllable of Śrī, Māyā, Smara, Yoni-Śakti, Tāra, Māyā, Kamalā, and then the *vidyā*."
And by means of the seed-syllables of Śakti and the others in reverse order, she is this venerable Ṣoḍaśī, ordained by Śiva.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Rudrayāmala:
"Śrī, Māyā, Madana, Vāṇī, Parā, Tāra, Śivapriyā, Haripriyā, Trikūṭā, that Parā, Vāṇī, and Manobhava. (1)
"Māyā, Lakṣmī, Mahāvidyā, Śrīvidyā, and the sixteen-syllabled [mantra]. And in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [Tantra]: "The wise one should write the second pair of letters in reverse order."
Having turned the young girl inward, one should then draw [the mandala]. || 1 ||
