O Supreme Goddess, one should then write Tāra, Māyā, and Lakṣmī, as well as the three peaks; one should form the Bālā-mantra and others as an encapsulation (saṃpuṭa) for that which is called Ramā.

Thus: by means of the *kalā*—the aforementioned fivefold *kalā* beginning with *Śakti*—one [attains] the one called *Ramā*, which consists of the six *kūṭas* beginning with the *praṇava*. If the reading is "the one called *Umā*," the meaning is the same. However, some read *bālayā* in place of *kalayā*, and in that case, they read "the Supreme Goddess" (*parameśvarīm*).

The Bālayāntarmukhīs call it *sampuṭa*; they call the Supreme Goddess known as Ramā "Śrīṃ" and "Hrīṃ," and therefore they say on the northern petal: "klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ. This is because they do not understand the meaning of the term *sampuṭa* there. Thus says the Navaranteśvara:
One should first utter the mantra, then immediately follow it with the name of the object to be accomplished (sādhya);
then again, the mantra in reverse order at the end—this is known as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) mantra. || 1 ||

Thus, because it would result in a lack of consistency with the definition of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) and because it contradicts all the Tantras; likewise, in the *Śrīkrama*: "Śrī, Māyā, Madana, and Yoni—place these at the beginning;
the first of the Vedas, Bhuvaneśānī, and the Śrī-bīja, which is the three-peaked (*trikūṭaka*) [mantra]. (1)
"One should make the six-peaked [mantra] encapsulated by the first five syllables. Thus it is said.
In the *Māyātantra*:
"Lakṣmī, Parā, joined with Madana and Yoni, Śakti, Tāra, Parā, and Kamalā—this is the root-vidyā."

And it is taught that the venerable King of Mantras of the Supreme Deity is proclaimed in its reverse order by means of Śakti and the others. By this, the view that [the mantra] is encapsulated by the five seed-syllables in direct order (anuloma) is to be rejected. And in the Śruti: "Ramā, Māyā, Tāra, Parā, Lakṣmī, Kumārikā, Vidyā, Vyastā, Bālā, Śrī, and likewise Parā."
"Separated and inverted" means that they are separated; furthermore, the *kumārī* should be understood as being inward-facing (*antarmukhī*).

Here, following the *kumārikā*, there is a connection with the three seed-syllables beginning with *tārā*, due to the force of syntactic unity and the authority of the *Traipurī-śruti*. Thus, in the *Śrī-māyā*, the *bālikā* is in the middle, followed by *tārā* and *māyā*.

Regarding the phrase "Śrī-vidyā, Parā, and so forth, ending with the five seed-syllables," if the reading is "Śrī-parā," it does not mean that Bālā alone is separated [as Śrī-parā]; rather, this is a statement of the essential nature of the sixteen seed-syllables within the Vidyā, as there is no mention of a sequential order. By this, [the sequence is]: Śrī (Māyā), Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā, Bālā, and the three peaks (Trikūṭa) separately.
The view that Bālā, Ramā, and Māyā are to be abandoned is [the view] to be discarded. In the *Kulāmṛta*: "The Śrībīja, the Śaktibīja, the Kāmabīja, and the Vāgbhava;
the Bīja situated within Bālā, and after that, the Praṇava. (1)
O Supreme Goddess, [one may employ] the seed-syllable of Śakti, as well as Ramā and Vidyā;
or Lopāmudrā, or Kāmarāja, or the supreme Trikūṭā.
O beautiful one, having again deposited the first five seed-syllables,
one should deposit the supreme sixteen-fold [mantra] in reverse order.
Thus it is said; and in the *Yāmala*:
"The seed-syllables of Lakṣmī, Parā, Madana, Vāgbhava, and Śakti, along with the *Tāra* (Om) and the *Bhūti-kamala*, are declared to be the *vidyā*."
And the three peaks (kūṭatraya), joined in reverse order, are here well-known in the tradition as the venerable sixteen-syllable mantra. || 1 ||

One should place *trikūṭa* (the three peaks), beginning with *kāma* (the letter *ka*), for the young girl (*bālā*); and by the word "and" (*ca*), one should include *ramā* (the letter *la*) and *māyā* (the letter *ī*). In the manual (*nibandha*), [one should place] that which ends with the letter *sa*, joined with the seventh letter preceded by *śiva* (the letter *ha*), ending with *sūkṣmā* (the letter *na*), and endowed with the eighth vowel (*au*).
Then [one places] the Goddess (*devī*), the right arm (*dakṣiṇabāhu*), Indra’s eye (*śakranayana*), and *kāma* marked with the digit (*kalā*).

The seed-syllable with its face turned upward between the teeth, possessing living fangs, and joined with the remainder of the mouth—this fivefold [mantra] thus proclaimed bestows the accomplishment of all aims. || 1 ||

One should utter the first of the Vedas (OM), followed by the three qualities (guṇa), then Ramā (LAKṢMĪ), served by Kāma (KĀMA), and again Lopāmudrā; this should be done five times in the reverse order from the beginning.
This is the venerable Supreme Goddess, higher than the highest, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
She is more essential than the essence, the source of origin for all the worlds, and auspicious.
"She is this very one, the form of Śrī-Brahman, consisting of all qualities yet devoid of qualities, beyond the phenomenal world;
she is the direct cow of plenty for desires, saluted by hosts of gods and sages, and whose nature is bliss"— thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava.
Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, I am not at all able to describe the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā. (1)
Vaikharī speech is incapable of describing its qualities because it is the nature of the expressed object;
since the reality is beyond syllables, Parā alone is the cause therein.
For when the Paśyantī becomes silent, it becomes the Madhyamā;
indeed, she is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (3)
O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance [of this mantra], there are ten million Vājapeya sacrifices,
thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, and likewise the merit of circumambulating the entire earth.
O Goddess of gods, the pilgrimages to Kāśī and other sacred sites, numbering three and a half crores, do not equal this; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 5 ||
O Girijā, what need is there to mention the mere Brahman when uttered once?
This sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā must never be revealed.
O auspicious Pārvatī, you must guard this [knowledge] as you would your own womb;
for this Ṣoḍaśī is indeed to be well-concealed, yet it has been revealed out of affection, O Goddess. (7)
Even one's most beloved, children, wife, wealth, and so forth should be given;
a kingdom may be given, one's head may be given, but the sixteen-syllable mantra must never be given away.

Thus, in the *Siddhayāmala*—(it describes the Ṣoḍaśī in another manner): "Kāma, Māyā, Ramā, Bālā, Trikūṭā, Strī, Bhaga, Aṅkuśa, Kālī, Kāmakalā, and Kūrca; O Dear One, the Praṇava comes at the beginning of all. (1)
And this is the venerable Mahāṣoḍhī, who is renowned throughout the three worlds;
she is the knowledge that destroys death through wisdom, and she is saluted by all the Āmnāyas.
O Dear One, seven hundred thousand great vidyās were taught at the beginning of the tantras;
among them, those vidyās which have become the most essential and are well-guarded secrets [are these]. (3)
What is the use of saying more here? O Great Goddess, their essence is indeed the sixteenth, which you have asked about again and again; it has now been revealed.

Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ ka e ī la hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ strīṃ aiṃ kroṃ krīṃ klīṃ hūṃ. (Rudrayāmala, p. 119): If, at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa of Lopāmudrā, it is joined with the Haṃsa-bīja.
Then the seventeenfold Vidyā was directly manifested in the form of knowledge. || 1 ||

*Hasakalahrīṃ sahakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ haṃsaḥ*. In the *Lopāmudrā-vāgbhava*, however, by joining Śiva at the end of the Earth [syllable], and placing the letter *Sa* at the beginning of the *Kāmarāja*, the *Lopāmudrā* mantra consists of sixteen syllables. (1)
By this [mantra], there is no such knowledge within the domain of the ocean of sciences (*vidyārṇava*).
*Hasakalahahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*; *hasakalahrīṃ*, *sahasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*—these are the two *ṣoḍaśī*s. In that very same [source]:

In the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] of the Queen of Wisdom (*vidyārājñī*), who is lovely due to her connection with the infinite, there is this auspicious Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) of sixteen syllables, which consists of the unity of Consciousness and Brahman. (1)
*Hasaka ālahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, and *sakalahrīṃ*. One should apply the seed-syllable of Śiva (*ha*) at the end of Lopāmudrā and Vāgbhava (*ai*).
Likewise, in the seed-syllable of Śakti (*hrīṃ*), one applies Lopāmudrā; this is the seventeen-syllabled mantra. (1)
By the mere remembrance of her, one becomes Śiva; it is not otherwise.
He becomes the lord of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, and an Indra manifest upon the earth. || 2 ||
*Hasakalahahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahahrīṃ*—this is the seventeen-syllable *lopā*.
In that same context, the eighteen-syllable [mantra] is as follows: one should join the lower [vowel] with the *bindu* at the beginning of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable].
O Maheśvarī, [the mantra] beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm) and the first of the third [group] is Mādana. || 1 ||
O Goddess, Bhṛgu, accompanied by Sarga and joined with Manu—this eighteen-syllable Śrīvidyā is indeed difficult to obtain on earth. (2)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, by the grace of the venerable Guru, this [mantra] is eternally bestowing success; indeed, having recited it nine hundred thousand times, one attains Lopāmudrā.
O fair-faced one, this eighteen-syllable vidyā must subsequently be worshipped;
otherwise, one incurs a curse and one's lineage perishes.
The Goddess is the bestower of all auspiciousness, the destroyer of all obstacles, the giver of all good fortune, and the performer of all blessings. || 5 ||
A science such as this is exceedingly rare even throughout the three worlds.
*Aiṃ hasaka-hrīṃ, klīṃ hasaka-halahrīṃ, sauḥ sakala-hrīṃ*—this is the eighteen-syllable *lopāmudrā*.
Likewise:
In the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, [the seed-syllable] Vāgbhava is at the beginning of Vāgbhava; Bhuvaneśī is in Kāmarāja, and the Śrībīja follows Śakti.
This eighteenth [chapter] has also been proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments;
it directly grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and bestows the goals of human existence. || 2 ||
There is no knowledge equal to this within the domain of the ocean of learning;
it does not exist, it does not exist, it truly does not exist—I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Aiṃ ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ, hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ, śrīṃ sakalahrīṃ—this is the eighteen-syllable mantra of Kāmarāja. Likewise:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then [utter] Kulasundarī.
Then [follow] the syllable of desire (KĀM), the letter of power (ŚA), and then Indra (PU) and Hara (HA). || 1 ||
Having extracted Bhuvaneśī in reverse order, then Bālikā, followed by the Praṇava with the Visarga, and again Kulasundarī. (2)
Having extracted the *vāgbhava* [syllable] with its elision, then the *bālikā* in reverse order,
then the *praṇava* with the *visarga*, and then indeed the *kulasundarī*.
O Śivā, one should join the letter *ha* in the middle portion of the *śaktikūṭa*;
there, the syllable of Brahmā (*praṇava*) with the *visarga* follows the reverse-order *bālikā*.
This is the glorious supreme Vidyā, the absolute bestower of liberation;
by merely reciting it one hundred thousand times, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? (5)
By the mere remembrance of this, one becomes Śiva; it is not otherwise.
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ soḥ ka-elaha-hrīṃ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ oṃḥ; aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ ha-saka-la-hrīṃ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ śroṃḥ; aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ oṃḥ.

The Supreme Vidyā. In the *Śrīkrama*: "O Queen of the Gods, hear that Vidyā, which is endowed with Kāma and Indra, joined with the fourth vowel through the differentiation of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. (1)
The Mahāśrīsundarī-vidyā is Mahātripurasundarī;
in the letter Ka, everything has arisen, bestowing both desire and absolute liberation.
The letter *la* bestows all sovereignty, and the letter *ī* grants all happiness;
thus, O Goddess, these three seed-syllables constitute the essential compendium of all vidyās.
One should join Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti;
by means of that, it is declared to be the singular, absolute Brahmavidyā consisting of a single syllable. || 4 ||
*Kala-īṃ* is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Regarding the specific distinction between Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā, the *Kuloḍḍīśa* states:
"Sundarī, who exists with the primordial [syllables] known as Śrī, Parā, Vāgbhava, Īśvarī, Tāra, and Manmatha, is remembered as being sixfold. (1)
p. 120) Of these two, in the first [mantra], there is *kāma*, *māyā*, and the *śrībīja*; then *māyā*, *śrī*, and the *kāmabīja*.

first *kāma*, *māyā*, and *ramā*; then *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, and *smara*.
Likewise, Ramā, Māyā, and Kāma are the threefold syllables of Vasu, Candra, and Akṣi. || 1 ||
"Smara, Yoni, and Lakṣmī— this triad is in your primordial mantra," thus it was propounded by the venerable teacher (Bhagavadācārya). However, in the Śrīkrama, the Śakti, Kāmarāja,
Māyā-bīja, Jhiṇṭhi, Kāma, Śakra, and Viyat follow in sequence.
O Supreme Goddess, it is marked by the moon, the knower of all births.
This is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, and the Kāmarāja-kūṭa is as before;
likewise, the Śakti-bīja is also thus—this is proclaimed as Sundarī.
Sundarī is the vidyā that bestows success and brings the three worlds under control.

Here too, as before, there is the union with the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Māyā* is the vowel *ī*; *jhiṇṭhi* is the vowel *e*. Again, he states the power (*śakti*): "Then this is the *bhaga*; *māyā*, Brahmā, Śakra, Hara, [and] Agni."
Joined with the left eye (the letter *u*) and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*. || 1 ||
This is declared to be the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], with the Kāma-śakti as before.
*Bhaga* is the letter *E*. Here too, the conjunction of seed-syllables is as before. In this regard, there is a distinction:
O fair-faced one, when one should place the Brahma-seed within the three peaks (*trikūṭa*).
The first goddess is Sundarī; the second is Brahmasundarī. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, in the Śaktikūṭa, Anantasundarī is considered [the deity]; this is the sixteenth Vidyā, shown according to different traditions. (2)
Thus he states another mantra:
"At the end of *trikūṭā*, the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, adorned with the *bindu* and the *sarga*;
this, when conjoined with the venerable *prāṇa*, is the destroyer of poverty and suffering. (1)
As for the Śakti-lopāmudrā: Śakti, Maheśa, Kāma, and then the Indrabīja;
after that, Mahāmāyā—this is proclaimed [as such] because of your affection. (1)

As before, the two phonemes known as Kāma and Śakti are of the nature of being "unlocked" (niṣkīlita). Thus are the two Śaktis; this is the Mahāvidyā conjoined with the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya). || 2 ||

Śakti is the syllable *sa*. As before, it is like the Kāmarāja-vidyā; here too, as previously, there is a conjunction of seed-syllables (*bīja*). The seed of Śiva, the moon of Śakti, and Mādana, along with Purandara, joined with ether and fire, and the fourth vowel with the bindu. (1)
As before, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti from Kāmarāja;
O Great Goddess, this Vidyā cannot be fully described.
Śakti is the letter *sa*; Soma is the letter *sa*, as before, like the Kāmarāja-vidyā. Here too, as before, is the union of the seed-syllables (*bīja*):
Śiva-śakti, Bhuvaneśānī, and the supreme Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
O Goddess of gods, [the elements] up to the ether (vyoma) are indeed [composed of] Mahāmāyā, and beyond that is the Supreme.
Soma, Vyoma, and Mahāmāyā are proclaimed as the nine syllables;
O Goddess, this is the power of Rudra, joined indeed with the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya). || 2 ||
Thus, in another Tantra:

"O Supreme Goddess, [the mantra] beginning with Mādana (ma), followed by Gotrabhit (ha) and Sānta (sa), possessing the letter Ra (ra), the left eye (ī), and the Moon (bindu), and joined with Nāda and Bindu, has been declared. (1)
Brahmā, Gaganam, Śakra, Nakulīśa, and likewise Anala—by means of Māyā, Bindu, and Sanāda, one should extract Kāmarāja. (2)
Śakti, Mādana, Śakra, Hara, Vahni, and Indu, joined with Māyā, Bindu, and Nāda, are declared to be the mantra that grants all desires. (3)
O Great Goddess, this eleven-syllabled Vidyā has been declared;
it is the goddess Mahātripurasundarī, the destroyer of enemies and the bestower of spiritual accomplishments. || 4 ||
Mādana and Pañcavaktra; Lohitā and Rudrayoginī; Purandara and Mahāmāyā; and Vāgbhava, the supreme seed-syllable. (5)
As before, O Goddess, one should extract the beautiful Sundarī, known as Kāmaśakti.
Lohitā is the letter *kṣa*; Rudrayoginī is the letter *m*. As before, it is like the Kāmarāja-vidyā. Bhṛgvīśa, Gaganam, Hāntam, Kālam, Indram, and Maheśvaram.
O Supreme Goddess, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is enriched by the left eye, fire, and the moon.
One should recite the Kāmarāja and Śaktikūṭa as before.
Bhṛgvīśa is the letter *sa*; the end of *ha* is the letter *kṣa*; and Kāla is the letter *ma*.
As before, it is like the Kāmarāja-vidyā.
Viṣṇu, Īśa, then [the letters] from ha to kṣa, Kāleśa, then Pṛthivī, and after that Bhuvaneśī—thus the Vāgbhava [bīja] has been declared to you. (1)

O Dear One, the *kāmarāja* and the *śaktikūṭa* have been explained as before. Viṣṇu is the letter *ī*, joined with the letter *a*; Īśa is the letter *ha*; and Kāleśa is the letter *ma*. Regarding the *saubhāgyavidyā*, it is stated in the *Śrīkrama*:
I shall describe her good fortune; listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved!
She is Śakti, Svayambhū, Śambhu, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Śiva, Mādana, Rudra, Indra, and Mahāmāyā; beyond that, Kāma, Śiva, Brahmā, Indra, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (2)
This, however, is the supreme knowledge that brings about the auspicious rise for devotees;
with the seed-syllable *haṃsa* at the end of the three peaks (*trikūṭa*), it then becomes the seventeenth [syllable]. (3)
The seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), Vijayā, Māyā, Brahmā, Śakra, and Pārvatī; the seed-syllable of Love (Mānmatha), Śiva, Śakti, Mādana, Hara, and Indraka. || 4 ||
After that, Mahāmāyā is the power (śakti) pertaining to the creation of men;
then Candra, Prajāpati, and Śakra; and after that, Mahāmāyā again. || 5 ||
The eighteen-syllable mantra is the Vidyā of Mahātripurasundarī;
when joined with the Haṃsa at the very end, it then becomes twenty syllables long.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Speech, creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the inexpressible—these are the five beauties.
O Lord, O God, tell me of them, if it pleases you toward me. (1)
Īśvara said:
Śiva, Mādana, Indra, Śakti, Bhuvaneśvarī, Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, Śakti, Mahāmāyā, and beyond that, the Supreme (Parā). || 1 ||
Mādana and Indra are Śakti and Śiva; Mahāmāyā is at the end of that.
Śakti is the letter *sa*. This is the language (*bhāṣā*): [hakalasahrīṃ kahalasahrīṃ kalasahahrīṃ].
Śiva is the Moon, as well as Kāma, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Śiva, Indra, Kāma, Rudra, Candra, and Parameśvarī. || 1 ||
Śakti, Kāma, Indra, and Mahāmāyā beyond that;
(hasakalahrīṃ halakahasahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ)—this is the creation. Śiva, Indra, Kāma, Śakti, and Mahāmāyā beyond that.
Kāma, Candra, Maheśa, Indra, Śakti, and Pārvatī. || 1 ||
Brahmā, Maheśvara, Śakti, and Śakra are Bhuvaneśvarī;
this is the state [expressed by] *halaka sahrīṃ*, *kasahasa hrīṃ*, *kahasala hrīṃ*. Śiva, Indra, Kāma, and Śakti—beyond them is Bhuvaneśvarī.
Śiva and Śakti, Mādana and Indra; Śiva [is joined] with Vahni, Indu, and Māyā. || 1 ||
Śiva, Śiva, and Kalahā, adorned with Fire, Māyā, and the Moon;
(halakahahrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ hahakalahrīṃ)—this is the withdrawal (saṃhṛti).
Then Śakra, Brahmā, the Moon-seed, Mahāmāyā, and the Supreme (Parā).
This Vāgbhava has been described; now hear the Kāmarāja from here on. || 1 ||
Śakti, Śiva, Mādana, and Indra; beyond them is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī).
Śiva, Śakti, Soma, Śūnya, Brahmā, and Maheśvarī. (2)
The letter *ha* is empty. (*lakasahrīṃ sahakalahrīṃ hasasahakahrīṃ*) This is the Inexpressible. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, tell me of Svapnāvatī and Madhumatī."
Now I wish to hear [this], if you have compassion for me. (1)
Īśvara said:
Śiva, Mādana, and Śakra; Śakti and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Maheśa, Brahmā, and Haṃsa; and Indra as well as Bhuvaneśvarī. (1)
Maheśa, Śakti, Kāma, Purandara, and likewise Viyat; joined with Agni, Māyā, and Kalā, and adorned with Nāda and Bindu. (2)
*Haṃsa* is the letter *ha*; *māyākalā* is the letter *ī*. (*hakalasahrīṃ*, *hakahasahrīṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*) This is known as *Svapnāvatī*, the fifteenth *kalā*, as follows.
Brahmā, Maheśa, Indra, Śakti, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 1 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra; beyond them is Bhuvaneśvarī.
Mādana, Soma, Candra, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (2)
(The letter *ya* is Marut. *Kahala hrīṃ*, *kahayala hrīṃ*, *kasasa la hrīṃ*.
This is known as Madhumatī, concealed in all the scriptures. (Śrīvi. 16, p. 122)
The Vāmakeśvarī-vidyā itself is taught in the sequence of the Trikūṭa.
The five peaks of the fifth [vowel] are formed by the three peaks of the *āśāstrikūṭa* for the sake of good fortune;
the great vidyā of Tripurā is composed of eleven peaks.
The eleven-syllable mantra, the knowledge more essential than the essential, has been declared. Now, the fifth: O Goddess, [the syllables] Kāma, Viṣṇu, Śakti, Māyā, and Indra.
Thereafter, one should extract the seed-syllable Vāgbhava from Mahāmāyā.
Viṣṇu is the letter *a*, Śakti is the letter *e*, and Māyā is the letter *ī*.
Following that is Viyat (the sky), Candra (the moon), and then, in the Kali age, Nakuli (fire).
This is conjoined with the vowel of Māyā and endowed with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. (1)
First is the peak-syllable of Kāmarāja, which is extremely difficult to obtain;
it consists of Viyat (the letter *i*) joined with Viṣṇu (the letter *ū*), followed by Kāma (the letter *e*), Haṃsa (the letter *ha*), and then Śakra (the letter *la*). (2)
After that, Mahāmāyā is called Svapnāvatī.
Haṃsa is the letter *ha*. This is the second peak-syllable (*kūṭaka*) of Kāmarāja. Then follow Mādana, the seed-syllable of Śiva, and the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Thereafter, one should extract the seed-syllable of Indra (HŪṂ) and then Mahāmāyā (HRĪṂ). || 1 ||
Thus is the third [mantra]. This is the Madhumatī.
One should join Śivabīja, as well as Kāma, Indra, and the Goddess;
thereafter, one should extract Mahāmāyā and the Śaktikūṭa. (1)
O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, and the fifth is Śaktikūṭa;
O Goddess, the three middle kūṭas are the enchanting Kāmarāja.
The fifth vidyā, which brings about the auspicious arising in the three worlds, has been declared.
[It is] the Goddess [beginning with] the letter *sa*. The Lord said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, to the Śaktikūṭa, which is very difficult to obtain:
the first peak-syllable is Vāgbhava, and the Kāmarāja is the third peak-syllable. (1)
Out of special affection for you, O Great Goddess, I shall explain the Śaktikūṭa: Jīva and Prāṇa, and immediately after that, Mādana.
Then follows the seed-syllable of Indra (I), and Bhuvaneśī as the fifth;
thus is the Śaktikūṭa. Jīva is the letter *sa*, and Prāṇa is the letter *ha*.
Alternatively, O Goddess of the gods, there is the Vāgbhava of Saubhāgyā.
The three peaks are Kāmarāja and Śaktibīja (the peak), as before. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, this fifth Supreme Sovereign has been declared as Śakti.
Its meaning is as follows: having removed the Vāgbhava-kūṭa of this [mantra], the first kūṭa of Saubhāgyā is to be placed in the position of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa; such is the meaning.
Whether it be the peak-syllable beginning with Vāmanetrā or the peak-syllable beginning with Bhaga,
this Vidyā is the destroyer of enemies, the bestower of success, and entirely free from all defects.
*Bhaga* is the letter *e*. By this, the fifth [syllable] is eightfold through the division of the *vāgbhava-śakti-kūṭa*. In the *Yāmala*:
"The supreme fifth *vidyā* is twofold, consisting of five and five syllables;
in the middle is the six-syllabled [kūṭa], and the *śakti* consists of four syllables. (1)

"Six" means the middle peak (kūṭa) of Kāmarāja-vidyā. "The peak of Śakti" means the peak of Śakti belonging to Kāmarāja. This [Kāmarāja] is fourfold due to the division of the Vāgbhava peak; by this, it becomes twelvefold.
Likewise, of these two [Vidyās], which are established as eightfold and fourfold respectively, the third [peak] of Kāmarāja...
The *kūṭa* is as follows:
O Maheśānī, [one should contemplate] the seed-syllable of Kāma, then the seed-syllable of Śiva, and below that, the seed-syllable of Haṃsa and the seed-syllable of Indra. (1)
After that, one should [place] Mahāmāyā, the peak-syllable which is extremely difficult to attain.
This also, as before, is eightfold; the other is fourfold. And so it is stated in the *Tattvabodha*:
"Kāma, Ākāśa, Parā, and Śakra, whose form is fashioned by the configuration; Parā is the syllable 'Sa'."
Mahāmāyā is embodied by her manifested form. Thus it is said in the Tantra:
"O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable of Kāma, followed by the seed-syllable of Śambhu; below that, the seed-syllable of the Moon, and then the seed-syllable of Earth. (1)
And at its end is the Mahāmāyā-peak, which is extremely difficult to obtain.
(p. 123) This [series] is eightfold as before; the other is fourfold. Thus, the fifth [series] consists of thirty-six forms (in the *Śrīkrama*).
And hear, O fair-faced one, the vital essence of these very vidyās:
one should employ Ramā, Māyā, and the seed-syllable of Haṃsa at the beginning of the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (1)
O Great Goddess, at the end of the Śakti, one should likewise place Haṃsa, Māyā, and Ramā;
O Mistress of the Gods, joined with these, one should perform the recitation of the Vidyā.

And the recitation (*japa*) should be performed exactly seven times, as it is seen [prescribed] for the *Dīpinī*; "of these" refers to the vidyās mentioned previously in the venerable *Śrīkrama*. However, there is a specific distinction regarding the fifth [vidyā], as follows:
one should apply *Ramā*, *Māyā*, and the seed-syllable *Haṃsa* at the beginning of the *Vāgbhava*.
But at the end of the Śakti, O Maheśānī, [one should place] Haṃsa, Māyā, and likewise Ramā. || 1 ||

O Goddess, in the three kings of desire, the letter *ka* is joined with *Śakra* (the vowel *i*), and further endowed with *Māyā* (the vowel *ī*) and the *Bindu* (the nasal *m*); it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns. || 2 ||
First, one should apply this at the beginning of the Kāmakūṭa:
the letter following *va* (i.e., *śa*), joined with fire (*ra*) and adorned with the left eye (*ī*). (3)
The seed-syllable of Śrī, joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, has been proclaimed;
one should then recite the second, the Kāmarāja, after having uttered [the name of] Sundarī.
The sky (ha) conjoined with fire (ra), endowed with the left eye (ī),
and joined with the sound (nāda) and the point (bindu)— this is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīṃ).
O Maheśvarī, one should directly meditate upon the seed-syllable, which resembles a blazing fire and resounds like pure gold, in the center consisting of Kula and Akula.
"One should also recite the Madhumatī mantra, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
Now, the Dīpinī [mantra]:
Tāra, Lakṣmī, Vāgbīja, Mānmatha, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having recited this, one should thereafter extract that which is called the Vāgbhava.
Having first recited the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, Kāma, and Vāgbhava,
one should then chant the Kāmarāja mantra, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, with a concentrated mind, one should also recite the syllable Oṃ, the seed-syllable of speech, Ramā, Manmatha, and Māyā, along with Svapnāvatī. 3.
Having then recited the Praṇava, the syllable Kāma, Ramā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Madhumatī, Māyā, and the Śrī-kūrca-bīja; || 4 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, preceded by the Praṇava and encapsulated by the Haṃsa seed-syllable—
having uttered this seed-syllable, one should then recite the Śakti-kūṭa.
This, however, is the Dīpinī-vidyā, whose form is the breath of Ajapā.
As for the rule of recitation: one should recite at the beginning and recite afterwards, seven times in succession.
And one should likewise cause the illuminator (dīpinī) of the vidyās of Kāmarāja and the others to be made.
O Sovereign of the Gods, regarding the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti-kūṭas:
therein the sequence is as follows— the Dīpinī [mantra] for the Vāgbhava and Śakti-kūṭas should be understood as being like the fifth [vowel],
while for the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, one should employ the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, and Kāma.
The *vāgbhava* [syllable]. The term "the Illuminator" (*dīpinī*) is to be connected with all the *kūṭas*. Likewise, concerning the *vidyā* of Saubhāgya and others, it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"She is divided into thirty-seven parts by means of the distinction between vowels and consonants."
Through thirty-seven divisions, she consists of the nature of the thirty-six principles.
And this Vidyā is always contemplated as having a nature that transcends the [lower] principles;
likewise, the group of ten Śrīkaṇṭhas is indeed the designator of the Unmanifest (avyakta). || 2 ||
O Goddess, the supreme eleventh [letter] stands as the vital breath (prāṇabhūta) in that same manner.

In the first *kūṭa* of the Saubhāgyavidyā, there are five vowels—the four forms of the letter *a* and the letter *i*—and six consonants. In the second *kūṭa*, there are thirteen, distinguished by vowels and consonants.

In the third peak (kūṭa) there are also nine; thus, including those, there are thirty-three syllables. In the three peaks there are three *bindus*, and one as the *nāda*; thus, combined, there are thirty-seven. Therefore, excluding the *nāda*, she consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*); if joined with the *nāda*, she transcends the principles (*tattvātītā*)—this is her eternal designation.
Her nature transcends all reality. Now follows the extraction of the various forms of the Śrīvidyā:
having first written the Vāgbhava-bīja of the Kāmarāja-vidyā, one should then place Śiva, Kāma, Hara, and Indra, followed by Bhuvaneśī. (1)
Omission [of the vowels] is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, while Unmanī bestows all desired things.
Ka-e-ī-lahrīṃ, ha-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ, ha-sa-ka-la-hrīṃ—this is the Śrīvidyā of Unmanī.
Having written the Vāgbhava [kūṭa] of the Kāmarāja-vidyā as well.
The Unmanī is indeed Kāmarāja, while Candra and Haṃsa are Mādana. || 1 ||
Bhūmi is the Mistress of the World (bhuvaneśānī), worshipped by Varuṇa.
Bhūmi is *la*.
*Ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ*, *ha-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ*, *sa-ha-ka-la-hrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Varuṇa.
Between Śakti and Mādana are Indra and Bhuvaneśvarī;
between Śiva and Mādana is Māyā, which is the third [syllable] of Varuṇa.
This [mantra], worshipped by Dharmarāja, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
*ka-ekalahrīṃ*, *hakahahrīṃ*, *sahakalahrīṃ*. This is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Dharmarāja.
Between Candra and Mādana are Indra and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Śiva, Candra, Indra, and Madana, along with Bhūmi and Bhuvaneśvarī. (1)
Candramādana, Śakra, Vahni, Indu, and Bhuvaneśvarī—this Vidyā, worshipped with oblations of fire, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
*ka-sa-ka-la-hrīṃ*, *ha-sa-la-ka-la-hrīṃ*, *sa-ka-la-ra-la-hrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Vahni.
Having uttered the *vāgbhava* [syllable] with the elision [of the nasal], one should indeed utter the *kāmarāja* [syllable] for her;
then, having extracted the entire earth-element and the *bhuvaneśī*, one should raise them up. (1)
This Śrīvidyā, worshipped by the Nāga kings, bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa:
*hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalaralahrīṃ*. This [mantra] is the Nāga-king-worshipped Śrīvidyā, Mādana, Śakti, Vahni, Bhūmi, and Vahni-Sureśvarī.
And Śivamādanabhūmi, Rahalā, and Bhuveneśvarī. || 1 ||
This Vidyā, worshipped by Vāyu, consists of Candra, Anala, Mādana, Indravahni, and Bhuvaneśvarī; it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Ka-era-la-ra-hrīṃ, ha-ka-la-ra-ha-lhrīṃ, sa-ra-ka-la-ra-hrīṃ—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Vāyu;
Mādana, Śakti, Turya, and the two [seeds] of Fire and Indra are Bhuvaneśvarī.
Śiva, Mādana, Sūrya, Indu, and Vahni are Bhuvaneśvarī. (1)
In the Kali age, one should extract the Moon, the Sun, Fire, and Bhuvaneśī;
this is the Vidyā worshipped by Budha, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Ka-e-ī-ra-la-hrīṃ, ha-ka-ha-la-ra-hrīṃ, sa-la-ka-la-ra-hrīṃ—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Bodha.
Mādana, Śiva, and Indra, followed by Bhuvaneśī; then Śiva, Mādana, Bhūmi, and likewise Śiva, Indra, Indra, and Anala. (1)
One should extract the peak-syllable of the power (śakti-kūṭa) of Māyā, the queen of desire;
this is the Vidyā worshipped by Īśāna, which bestows the eight supernatural powers beginning with aṇimā.
*Kahalahrīṃ, hakalahalalarahrīṃ, sakalahrīṃ*—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Īśāna.
*(Ka-e-īlahrīṃ, hasakahalahrīṃ, sakalahrīṃ | This is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Rati.
Through the direct and reverse orders of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja:*
This six-peaked [mantra], worshipped by Nārāyaṇa, is difficult to obtain on earth. || 1 ||
Ka-e-īlahrīṃ, hasakahalahrīṃ, sakalahrīṃ, sakalahrīṃ, hasakahalahrīṃ, ka-e-īlahrīṃ— this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Nārāyaṇa.
One should extract the Vāgbhava syllable from the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja;
then Śiva, Ānanda, Sūrya, Indu, Vahni, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (1)
The Vāgbhava [syllable] belongs to Lopāmudrā, and this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Brahmā:
Ka-E-I-La-Hrīṃ, Ha-Ka-Sa-Ha-Ra-Hrīṃ, Ha-Sa-Ka-La-Hrīṃ; this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by Brahmā.

Having extracted the *vāgbhava* (AIM) with the *lopā* (the nasal bindu), and the *kāmarāja* (KLĪM) of Brahmā with the *lopā*, this [goddess] is indeed worshipped by means of the *jīva* (the vital breath) as the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. || 1 ||
Hasakalahrīṃ, hakahasarahrīṃ, hasakalahrīṃ—this is the Śrīvidyā worshipped by the individual soul (jīva).
In this context, the fifteenfold [system] beginning with Māyā is declared to have the waking state as its essential nature;
however, that which begins with the Śrī-bīja has the dream state as its essential nature. (1)
That which begins with Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is the nature of deep sleep (suṣupti);
however, the venerable sixteen-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the Fourth State (turīya).

Dispassion, the desire for liberation, pure concentration, and a stainless mind—these are the constituent parts of the fourth state (turīyā), which consists in the discernment between the real and the unreal. (3)
The sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with *tārā* and ending with *vairāgya* is proclaimed as the form of dispassion;
whereas the sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with *māyā* is the embodiment of the desire for liberation.
The sixteenth [vowel] beginning with *kāma* (the letter *i*) consists of sixteen syllables; she is the very embodiment of *samādhi*.
The sixteenth [vowel] beginning with *ramā* (the letter *ā*) is the embodiment of the purity of the mind.

The speech beginning with the letter *vā* (Va), which consists of sixteen syllables and whose nature is the determination of existent and non-existent reality, exists in five ways; it is difficult to obtain within the three worlds.

The sixteen-fold knowledge (ṣoḍaśī-vidyā) beginning with *parā* is proclaimed as that which transcends the fourth state (*turyātītā*). Its divisions are to be understood by those learned in the Tantras according to the manner previously described.
They are proclaimed to be of two kinds by way of the distinction between pure and impure;
likewise, there are those characterized by both natures and those that are variegated.
Those sciences which are *anuloma* (in the natural order) should be known as pure, while those born in the *pratiloma* (inverse order),
as well as those of mixed nature (*ubhayātman*), are to be understood as impure.
Pure, impure, variegated, and with inverted or disordered sequence—thus should the fourfold Vidyā be understood by the best of teachers. (10)
"O Śivā, all the varieties of Śrīvidyā have thus been described in their entirety.

This concludes the exposition on the varieties of Śrīvidyā. Now follow the mantras of the Five Lion Thrones (*pañcasiṃhāsanavidyā*). Among them, first is the mantra of the Eastern Lion Throne; therein, the first is Bālā. As stated in the *Śrījñānārṇava*:
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold; hear first of Bālā, by the knowledge of whom, O Goddess, one becomes manifest like the splendor of the Preceptor of the Gods.
Having uttered the solar vowel (*sūryasvara*) which consists of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, one should place the final vowel situated on the earth, conjoined with the fourth vowel. || 2 ||
Overcome by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, the imperishable Bhṛgu, joined with the vowel Śakra (the letter *i*), is considered this three-syllabled Vidyā. (3)
Bestowing words composed of the surging waves of the Gaṅgā,
she generates great good fortune and grants the gift of great eloquence.
Thus: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. Likewise:
"O Maheśānī, the sage of this [mantra] is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
O Dear One, one should place it on the head because of its venerability, and the Paṅkti meter on the mouth. (5)
The deity in the heart is the supreme goddess Bālātripurā;
the seed-syllable (bīja) is Vāgbhava, the power (śakti) is the third syllable, and the pin (kīlaka) is likewise that same syllable.
O Maheśānī, the placement of the *kāmarāja* [mantra] is declared to be the *cchandaḥnyāsa*;
it extends from the navel to the feet, and another from the throat to the navel.
One should place the three syllables in sequence from the crown of the head down to the throat;
likewise, one [syllable] on the palm of the left hand and one on the palm of the right hand.
O Dear One, one should place the three seed-syllables of the Vidyā within the union of both hands;
then, one should place the five arrows in sequence upon the fingers of the hands.
O Supreme Goddess, having written the two groups of letters ending in *tha* in sequence from the thumb to the little finger, they should be placed within the fire [the letter *ra*] in due order.
Adorned on the left by the face and the eye, these two arrows are said to be the "Deluder" (Mādana), situated upon the ground. || 11 ||

O fair-faced one, [the syllable] enriched with the fourth vowel and the bindu, having the form of sound (nāda), is the letter 'pha' joined with Indra (the letter 'i') and adorned with the left ear (the letter 'u'). (12)
O beloved, O Maheśānī, the Moon is joined with the Bindu and Nāda and possesses the vowel 's' (sarga);
O Pārvatī, hear now the names of the five arrows. 13.
O Goddess, [the six acts] are Kṣobhaṇa (agitating), Drāvaṇa (melting), and that which is known as Ākarṣaṇa (attracting);
then Vaśya (subjugating) and Unmāda (maddening) in due order—these are the names, O Supreme Goddess. (14)
The desires therein are to be known; hear their seeds, O Supreme Goddess:
the seed of Parā, the middle Bāṇa, and Vāgbhava.
Then, O beloved, follow the fourth arrow and the seed-syllable of the woman in sequence;
O Goddess, listen to the names of the five Kāmas in order, O dear one. (16)
O Maheśānī, those known as Kāma, Anmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja are proclaimed; Mīnaketu is celebrated as the fifth. || 17 ||
O Goddess of the gods, having performed these placements, thereafter follows the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) by repeating the root mantra twice upon all the surfaces of the fingers.
Then, within the applications of the six-limbed sequence, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā*.

Here, the meaning is that after the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should perform the six-limbed *mātṛkā* placement, namely the internal *mātṛkā* placement and the external *mātṛkā* placement. Likewise—
Having meditated thus, O Goddess of the Gods, one should thereafter perform the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa).
O Dear One, one should effect the armor of the body with the three seed-syllables in their proper sequence.
First, one should place [the syllables] on the hands— at the wrists, the palms, and the tips—
having placed them on the right and the left, as well as on the right elbow and the hands.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should likewise place [the mantras] on the right and left feet;
thereafter, one should place them at the end of the Nāda, in the heart, and in the liṅga.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place [the mantras] upon these limbs according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra);
know this, O Supreme Goddess, to be according to the sequence of the emanation of knowledge (vidyā-sṛṣṭi). 22.
Then, O Great Goddess, one should perform the rite marked by the nine yonis:
on the two ears, the chin, O Goddess, and on the two temples and the circle of the face.
O beloved, one should place [the mantras] on the two nostrils, the pair of arms, the heart, as well as on the two elbows,
the belly, the knees, and the shanks.

O Goddess, one should place the [mantra] consisting of three seed-syllables, known as the nine-yoni, upon the two feet, the secret place, the two sides, the two hands, the two breasts, and the throat. (25)
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, one should perform the six-limbed rite in sequence by repeating it twice,
according to the numbers three, two, one, ten, three, and two.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should place the arrows and the objects of desire upon the fingers;
then, in sequence, upon the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the mūlādhāra.
"Having performed the pervasive [placement] with the root mantra, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Thus it is said. Here, having performed three rounds of breath control and having executed the assignments of the seers and so forth, as well as the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon the hands, one should meditate.
O Maheśānī, one should meditate upon the Goddess as being situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest, within a jeweled pavilion in the interior of a great Kalpa forest. (28)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the shade of a pearl parasol,
she wore a crown fashioned from priceless gems and adorned with jeweled earrings.
Adorned with necklaces, neck-ornaments, and excellent jewels, and radiant with bracelets;
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right hand.
"Devoted to granting boons, divine, and bestowing the great Sarasvatī"—thus [is described] Bālā. Now, Saṃpatpradā Bhairavī. In the Śrījñānārṇava, the Lord said:
Just as the venerable Tripurā Bālā is, so too is Tripurabhairavī;
hear, O pure-minded one, her name which bestows prosperity. 1.
Śiva and Candra situated in Vahni, followed by Vāgbhava;
likewise, O Goddess, Kāmarāja endowed with Śiva and Candra thereafter. (2)
O beautiful one, listen to the third [syllable], which is enriched with the earth-seed (la), the end (ha), and fire (ra).
O Great Goddess, one should join Śiva (ha) and Fire (ra) within the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrīṃ). || 3 ||
O Mistress of Tripura, O Beloved, having abandoned the emission of the Bindu, the Goddess Tripurābhairavī bestows great prosperity. 4.
*Hasraiṃ*, *hasakalarīṃ*, *hassrauṃ*. A vidyā similar to this is difficult to find in the three worlds.
By repeating the root mantra twice, the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is declared. || 5 ||
Meditation:

[One should visualize the Goddess] possessing the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wearing a crimson silken garment and a garland upon her head; her breasts smeared with red pigment, and holding a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

I bow to the Goddess, who possesses the splendor of a lotus-face with three eyes shining, who holds [lotuses] in her lotus-hands, who wears a crown adorned with a crescent moon, and who smiles most gently. 6.
Thus ends Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity. Now, regarding Caitanyabhairavī, in the *Śrījñānārṇava*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim [the mantra] situated on the Eastern Lion-Throne;
having uttered the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, it is endowed with the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (1)"
The second seed-syllable extracted is Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī; it consists of the life-force (Jīva) situated in fire (Ra), adorned with the vowel of Indra (E). (2)
The Great Goddess is the Vidyā who is the Mother of the Three Worlds;
she is the Goddess who fascinates the three worlds, whose essence is the consciousness of the Supreme Brahman. (3)
SHAṂ, SAKALAHRĪṂ, SHRAUḤ—this [mantra] begins with the letter *sa*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent parts] are as before.
The visualization (*dhyāna*): [She who] has the luster of a thousand rising suns and is adorned with various ornaments.
She has a crescent moon shimmering above her crown and is clothed in red garments. || 1 ||
She is the eternal one, holding a noose and a goad, bearing a skull-cup in her left hand;
she is enriched with the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and her breasts are full and elevated like jars.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess seated upon the lion-throne preceded by the *preta*.
This is the Caitanyabhairavī. Now, regarding the second Caitanyabhairavī, it is stated in the Śrījñānārṇava:
"Of this very Vidyā, two seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been proclaimed."
At the end of that, O Supreme Goddess, [is] "nityaklinne madadrave" (O you who are eternally moist, flowing with intoxication).
O Supreme Goddess, the third [mantra] of these Rudras is:
*śaiṃ sakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave śrauḥ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes are as before.
Meditation:

One should meditate upon Caitanyabhairavī, who holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup; she is red in color, wears a garland of severed heads, and is seated upon a lion-throne supported by five corpses. (1)

Thus ends the second [mantra], Caitanyabhairavī. Now, regarding Kāmeśvarī Bhairavī, it is stated in the Śrījñānārṇava: "O Dear One, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] consists of Śiva (Ś), Candra (I), and Mādana (M); it is followed by Pānta (PA) conjoined with Vahni (R), differentiated by Śakti (E), and enriched by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. (1)
Likewise, one should indeed place the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable] of Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity,
as well as the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva and of the Great Lion Throne.
*Hasakhaphreṃ*, *hasakalarīṃ*, *hasauṃ*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before.
I shall now describe her meditation (*dhyāna*), which cuts through the burden of enemies:
she has the luster of a thousand rising suns, bears the moon upon her crest, and possesses three eyes. (1)
She is beautiful with various ornaments, the destroyer of all enemies,
adorned with blood-dripping severed heads, and clad in red garments.
O Goddess, [he holds] the trident, the hand-drum, the sword, and likewise the shield; then the Pināka bow and arrows, and finally a pair of noose and goad, in due order.

Holding a book and a rosary, seated upon a corpse-throne—thus is Kāmeśvarī Bhairavī. These are the deities of the Eastern Lion-Throne. Now, the deities of the Southern Lion-Throne: therein first is Aghorabhairavī.
The form of the Aghora-vidyā, which cuts through great sins, consists of the Vāgbhava-bīja in the Aghora [position], followed by the Bhuvaneśvarī [bīja] in the Ghora [position]. (1)
To Śarva, Sarva, Ghorā, and Ghoratarā from all sides, salutations to you in your Rudra-forms; one should write the pair of seed-syllables of the Goddess. || 2 ||
O Dear One, this Vidyā is said to consist of thirty-three syllables:

*aghore aiṃ ghore hrīṃ sarvataḥ śarva-sarvebhyo ghoraghoratare śrīṃ namaste'stu rudra-rūpebhyaḥ klīṃ sauḥ*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details, as well as the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and meditations (*dhyāna*) for this, are as before.
Thus ends Aghorabhairavī. Now, regarding Mahābhairavī, the Lord said:
"Śiva and Candra (the letter *i*) situated in Fire (*ra*), conjoined with Vāgbhava (*ai*)."
The first seed-syllable, well-conjoined with Nāda and Bindu, has been extracted. || 1 ||
From Lopāmudrā, the second seed-syllable, the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, has been extracted;
it consists of Śiva (H) and Candra (I) situated in Fire (R), conjoined with the vowel of Manu (Ū). || 2 ||
The third seed-syllable is declared to be endowed with *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*:
*hasraiṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, and *hasrauṃ*.
O Supreme Goddess, as before, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the others.
One should fashion the limbs with the middle peak, which is joined with the six long [syllables]. || 1 ||
She possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns; she is radiant with a moon shining amidst her matted locks;
and her crown, adorned with glittering jewels, is beautifully embellished with variegated pearls.
She is adorned with a garland of skulls rich with quivering blood,
enriched by the beauty of three eyes, and endowed with a face like the full moon.
Her full and elevated breasts were like silver jars adorned with strings of pearls;
she was clothed in red garments, her form intoxicated with the vigor of youth.
She holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right;
she is eternally intent on bestowing boons, and is seated upon a great corpse.
Thus ends Mahābhairavī. Now follows Lalitābhairavī:
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should likewise extract Kāmarāja; having extracted the seed-syllable of the Preta, this vidyā becomes three-syllabled. (1)
Hrīṃ Klīṃ Hsrauṃ.
The previously mentioned sages and others are considered the initial ritual of the limbs (aṅgakriyā).
[She who is] resplendent like a thousand rising suns, blazing with a crown of rubies—1.
Adorned with jeweled earrings, pearl necklaces, anklets, and armlets,
she was beautiful with jeweled anklets, wearing red garments and unguents.
Holding a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary, the Goddess,
assuming the form of a young maiden, was intent upon her childhood play.
One should meditate upon her who is beautiful in all her limbs for the sake of attaining all prosperity;
thus ends the Lalitābhairavī. Now, as for Kāmeśvarībhairavī: Kāmeśvarībhairavī is the beautiful one [united] with Kāmarāja; *klīṃ*. Thus.
The seer of this [mantra] is Kāmadeva; Gāyatrī is said to be its meter;
Kāmeśvarī is its deity; and the ritual application of the limbs is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable. (1)
One should meditate upon her who resembles a hibiscus flower, bearing a bow and arrows,
beautiful with various ornaments, and enchanting the three worlds.
Thus ends [the section on] Kāmeśvarībhairavī. Now, regarding Raktanetrābhairavī:
The first seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be joined with the Moon and Vāgbhava; the second seed-syllable is said to be joined with Sakala, Fire, and Māyā. (1)
O Parameśvarī, the third [syllable] of Bālā is extracted as the third seed-syllable:
*saiṃ*, *sakalarīṃ*, and *sauḥ*.
These belong to Kumārī; her seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent parts] are likewise [those of Bālā].
The six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to be performed with the six long lunar seed-syllables. || 1 ||
She possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns and is radiant with a crown of rubies;
she is adorned with jeweled earrings, pearl necklaces, anklets, armlets, and other ornaments.
She is beautiful with jeweled anklets, clad in red garments and anointed with unguents,
and she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary of beads.
She was mature with the intoxication of youth, possessing full and high, firm breasts;
she had broad hips and a slender waist, and her beautiful eyes were reddish at the corners.
Thus ends Raktanetrābhairavī. Thus end the deities of the southern lion-throne.
Now, the deities of the western lion-throne: therein, first is Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī—Śiva, Candra, Mādana, Bhūmi, Vahni, and Ḍāmara.
The three seed-syllables, joined with the mantras for the pacification of speech, have been proclaimed. || 1 ||
hasakalaraḍaiṃ, hasakalaraḍīṃ, hasakalaraḍauḥ—thus.
Having performed the placement of the Ṛṣi and so forth as before, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) by repeating [the mantra] twice.
One should visualize the Goddess, who has the luster of the rising sun and resembles a hibiscus flower.
Delightful with a garland of severed heads, her garment possessing the luster of the rising sun, and her full, elevated breasts shaped like golden jars. (2)
One should meditate upon Bhairavī, seated upon a throne of corpses and lions, holding a noose, a goad, a book, and likewise a rosary for recitation.
Thus ends the Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī. Now, regarding Nityābhairavī:
The goddess Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī exists in reverse order;
she is called Nityābhairavī, the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 1 ||
Ḍara-laka-saha-im, ḍara-laka-saha-īṃ, ḍara-laka-saha-auḥ—thus.
I shall describe to you the meditation upon her, who consists of the very same [deities] previously mentioned, beginning with the Munis;
she is seated upon five severed heads and is adorned with a garland of heads. (1)

One should meditate upon Śivā, who possesses the luster of ten thousand copper-colored suns, is adorned with jewel ornaments, and holds a noose, a goad, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Thus ends the Nityā Bhairavī. Now follows the Mṛtasañjīvanī:
Having uttered Māyā, Haṃsa, and the word *pada*, then the word *sañjīvani*;
then *jūṃ*, *jīvaṃ*, the word *prāṇa*, and then the pair of knots (*granthi*). || 1 ||
This supreme knowledge, the *Mṛtasañjīvanī*, is said to end with *svāhā*.
[The mantra is: *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ saṃjīvani sūṃ jīvaṃ prāṇagranthiṃ kuru kuru svāhā*.
Śukra is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *gāyatrī* is stated to be the meter (*chanda*).
The goddess Mṛtasañjīvanī is proclaimed to be the presiding deity. || 1 ||
The seed-syllable of Māyā is the seed; "svāhā" is declared to be the power (śakti);
and "haṃsa" is proclaimed as the peg (kīlaka) for the purpose of reviving the dead. || 2 ||
The application (viniyoga) is declared to be three, four, and one again;
one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of six, four, and one [syllables] respectively. || 3 ||
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā,
Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, even today I continue to recite [the mantra] with my western face."
The fourfold knowledge is the direct embodiment of immortal bliss. || 1 ||
Listen now to the Sañjīvanī mantra situated upon the great lion-throne there:
having inscribed the seed-syllable of Śakti, one should then inscribe Śiva and Candra. (2)
O Dear One, adorned respectively with the anusvāra and the visarga,
one should write "sañjīvani" and "jūṃ jīvaṃ," situated within the knot of life.
The mantra consists of the word *kuru* three times, followed by *sauḥ sauḥ*, conjoined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*).
It is said to consist of twenty syllables:
*hrīṃ haṃsaḥ saṃjīvani jūṃ haṃsaḥ kuru kuru kuru sauḥ sauḥ svāhā*.
The sage is declared to be Śukra, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī,
the deity is Sañjīvanī, and its power is the primordial seed-syllable (A).
O Goddess, one should duly assign the six limbs in sequence: four, three, five, five, four, and three.

One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who has the luster of camphor, whose garments are adorned with ornaments of diamonds and pearls, and who holds the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and a rosary. 3.
Thus ends the *Mṛtasañjīvanī*. Now follows the supreme *Mṛtyuñjayaparā*:
"Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the supreme *Mṛtyuñjayaparā*.
O Dear One, one should place the pair of words 'vāda' and 'vādanī' in the middle of the word 'vāk'. (1)

O Goddess, one should write the Vāgbhava mantra marked with a hundred thousand [dots], followed by *klinne* and *kledini*, then the pair *mahākṣobhaṃ kuru*, and finally the fire of the digit of the moon of Śiva. (2)

One should then utter the seed-syllable of Tāra, marked with the bindu and nāda of the left eye (vāmākṣi), followed by "mokṣaṃ kuru" twice, and "haṃsaḥ," which possesses the vowel of Indra (the letter 'e') and the visarga. || 3 ||
O you who speak with ever-speaking speech, laugh! O moist one, you who cause moisture, produce great agitation, produce it! Hasrīṃ! Oṃ, produce liberation, produce it! Hasauḥ! Thus.
This is the goddess Sañjīvanī; O beloved, Śiva is her seer (ṛṣi). Gāyatrī is declared to be her meter, and this deity is Bhairavī. (1)
The first peak-syllable (kūṭa) shall be the seed-syllable (bīja), while the middle peak-syllable is the pin (kīlaka);
the final peak-syllable shall be the power (śakti), which is the direct destroyer of death. || 2 ||
One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) with the nine syllables of Śakra and the eight syllables;
then, having meditated upon her, one should invoke the Goddess who dwells in the midst of the Kadamba forest.
One should meditate upon the supreme maiden, white as a jasmine flower, holding a book in her left hand and a rosary of beads in her right.
Thus ends the section on Mṛtyuñjaya-parā. Now, regarding Vajraprastāriṇī, the Lord said:
"The supreme [syllable], *klinne*, and the *vāgbhava* [syllable], and that syllable consisting of *krom*."
Then, one should draw Māyā within the liquid at the edge of the eternal [circle]. || 1 ||
Hrīṃ klinne aiṃ kroṃ nityamadadrave hrīṃ—thus [it is said].
This Vajreśī is sun-colored; Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra of Sanmanu;
the Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), and Vajreśī is proclaimed as the deity (devatā). || 1 ||
The fifth and the fourth [syllables] are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence; the third is the *kīlaka* of the Goddess. Thereafter, one should duly assign the limbs (*aṅga*).
Having abandoned the initial and final seed-syllables, as well as the pair and each single form,
one should fashion the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) consisting of two, two, and three [syllables] respectively.
Having meditated thus, one should invoke the Goddess who dwells in the midst of the Kadamba forest—
she who is red in hue, adorned with a beautiful crown of crescent moons, and graced with excellent ornaments.
Adorned with three eyes rich with the pride of great youth,
she stands upon a great mechanical engine atop a boat floating on the ocean of blood.
She holds a pomegranate, arrows, a noose, and likewise a goad;
she bears a bow and a skull-bowl, and is adorned with red garlands and unguents.
One should remember the goddess as exceedingly red and worship her with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
Thus ends Vajraprastāriṇī. Thus end the deities of the western lion-throne. Now, the deities of the northern lion-throne:
therein, first, Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī—
Having uttered the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] with the elision [of the nasal], one should extract the seed-syllable of the *preta*;
having placed the letter *ra* beneath *śiva*, there is *bhuvaneśī* and *bhairavī*. (1)
*Hrasraiṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *hrasauṃ*.
For one who is not a virgin (*akumāryā*), the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth are considered to be [assigned] by the first [syllable], and the ritual of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) is likewise intended.
[She is] like the *japā* flower, with the luster of the *dāḍima* flower. (2)
She has the crescent moon in her matted locks, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and has full, high, and firm breasts.
I take refuge in Śivā, who is seated upon a corpse-throne, adorned with a garland of severed heads, and who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Thus ends Bhuvaneśī-Bhairavī. Now, Kamaleśvarī-Bhairavī: Bhuvaneśī is preceded by *candra* (the moon) and so forth; likewise, Kamaleśī becomes [accompanied] by *sa-haiṃ*, *sa-ha-kala-hrīṃ*, and *sa-hauṃ*. Everything else is like that of Bhuvaneśī-Bhairavī. Thus ends Kamaleśī-Bhairavī. Now, Siddhakauleśa-Bhairavī:
Hasraiṃ, Hasrīṃ, and Hasrauḥ—these belong to Siddhakauleśabhairavī; she is indeed the Virgin (Kumārī) and the foremost of the sages. I shall now describe her meditation to you. || 1 ||
She has the luster of a thousand rising suns, possesses three eyes, and has a moon as her face;
she wears a crown of jewels sparkling with crescent moons and has a slender waist.
She has shapely hips, wears shimmering garments of jewels and red ornaments;
she is mature with the intoxication of youth, possessing full, high, and firm breasts.
Her limbs are adorned with a garland of heads rich with blood-mud and fine ornaments;
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right.
One should meditate upon her as bestowing boons, seated upon a throne of corpses and lions;
thus [ends the description of] Siddhakauleśabhairavī. Now, regarding Ḍāmarabhairavī, the Lord said:
O Goddess of the gods, even today I recite with my northern face this [mantra] of Bhairavī, the Mistress of the Ḍāmara, who is seated upon the great lion-throne. (1)
Having omitted the supreme Śivā from the Kāmakūṭa of the previously mentioned goddess Bhairavī,
one should then utter the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Great Lion-Throne.
HA-ŚAIṂ, HA-KLĪṂ, HA-SAUḤ—thus [is the mantra].
I shall describe to you the meditation upon her, who is the same as the sages and others mentioned previously:
she has the luster of the Bandhūka flower and dwells upon five severed heads. (1)
She wears a crown of jewels with a throbbing crescent moon and a garland of severed heads;
she has three eyes, is clothed in red garments, and possesses full, high, and firm breasts.
One should constantly meditate upon her, who is honored in the Uttara-āmnāya, holding in sequence a book, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Thus ends the Ḍāmarabhairavī. Now, regarding Kāminībhairavī:
one should extract this Kāminībhairavī by omitting the fire (ra) from the Bhairavī who bestows prosperity (Saṃpatpradā); or she is called Bhayavidhvaṃsinī. || 1 ||
*Hasaiṃ, hasaklīṃ, hasauṃ*—thus [is the mantra]. The sages and other [deities] are exactly as previously mentioned; I shall now describe her meditation (*dhyāna*) to you:
she shines with the luster of ten thousand slightly copper-colored suns and is adorned with ornaments of jewels. (1)

One should meditate upon the supreme Bhairavī, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, who is seated upon a corpse, and who is beautiful with a garland of severed heads.
Thus ends [the section on] Kāminībhairavī. These are the deities of the Northern Siṃhāsana.
Now, regarding the deities of the Upper Siṃhāsana, first is Prathamasundarī. The Lord said:
(Śrīvi. 17, p.
130) Now, O Goddess, this pentad of vidyās, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds, is even today being recited by me with my face as Īśāna. (1)
The Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is conjoined with Śiva; now hear the middle [syllable] within the Vāgbhava.
O Maheśānī, at the end of the letter *ha* and the *kāla*, one should write the seed-syllable of Śiva.

O Dear One, the third [syllable] is composed of the letter *ra*, the left eye (*i*), the bindu, and another bindu; it is enriched with *ha*, *sa*, *anugraha* (*a*), and *sarga* (*visarga*). This is the one beautiful Vidyā.
HAIM, HAKALAHRIṂ, HASAUḤ—this is the First Sundarī. Now, for the Second Sundarī:

the practitioner of mantra should recite it with the letters beginning with A-HA-SA, using the vowels of the Sun (the twelve vowels) and the fourth [vowel] (AU), ending with the final letter [KṢA] joined with the first [A], which consists of the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. (1)
O Goddess of gods, this is proclaimed as the second Sundarī:
*ahasaiṃ*, *ahasīṃ*, *ahasauḥ*—this is the second Sundarī. Now, for the third Sundarī:
O Goddess, [the first part is] the Vāgbhava alone; hear [now] the middle [part] of the Vāgbhava.
And one should join thousands of *hasa* and *ehasa* with the *vāgbhava* [syllable]. || 1 ||
O beloved, listen to the triad of Kalahṛllekhā and the Śaktikūṭa;
[then] the tetrad of the seeds of Śiva, followed by the letter Ra, which possesses the power of grace and creation. (2)
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, the third Sundarī consists of four syllables:
*aiṃ*, *hasa-ehasahasraiṃ*, *hahahakalahrīṃ*, *hahahaharauḥ*. This is the third Sundarī. Now, the fourth Sundarī:

At the end of the *kalā*, one should form the pair of Śivas; likewise, O Śivā, the three *jīvas* should be condensed by means of the *parā* [mantra]. This is the *kūṭa*; one should arrange it in three ways.
One should inscribe [the mantra] in the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Śakti-bīja;
this is known as the fourth Sundarī, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
*Kalahahasasasahrīṃ*, *kalahahasasasahrīṃ*, *kalahahasasasasahrauḥ* (*hrīṃ*)—this is the Fourth Sundarī. Now, the Fifth Sundarī:
*jīvaḥ śivayugaṃ jīvaḥ kṣmākṣakāraśivendumat*.
This [mantra] consists of the first [syllable], the middle [syllable], and [the syllables] *hasa-yuk-kṣmā-akṣa-indu*. (1)
The last [syllable] is adorned with *ha*, *sa*, the *lakṣa* (the moon), the *indu* (the moon), the *indu* (the moon), and space;
this is the fifth beautiful one in the mantra of Tripureśī. || 2 ||
*Saha-hasa-lakṣa-hasaiṃ, saha-hasa-lakṣa-hasīṃ, saha-lakṣa-sahasahauḥ*— thus is the fifth Sundarī.
One should meditate upon this supreme pentad as identical to Sampatpradā Bhairavī.
The worship of the sages and others should be understood as being like that of Tripureśī; it is not otherwise.
Thus end the sciences of the upper lion-thrones. This concludes the exposition of the five lion-throne sciences.
Now, regarding the group of the five pentads (*pañcapañcikāgaṇa*), first are the five Lakṣmīs; therein, first is Śrīvidyālakṣmī:
having uttered the great science (*mahāvidyā*) of sixteen syllables, the knower of the ritual procedure [should proceed].
She is seated upon a throne adorned by a multitude of Mahālakṣmīs and Śrīs.
"I worship the *pādukā* that generates all good fortune.
Thus ends the Śrīvidyā-Lakṣmī. Now, the Ekākṣara-Lakṣmī:
[The syllable] ending with Varuṇa (va), situated upon Fire (ra), adorned with the long Eye (ī).
The Lakṣmī-mantra is declared to be that which is joined with the Bindu and the Nāda. || 1 ||
"Śrīṃ"— thus, O Dear One, the seer is Bhṛgu, the meter is Nicṛt, and the deity is Śrī;
the seed-syllable and power are the fourth vowel (Ī), and the pin is said to be the letter Ra.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with one's own seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the beautiful Śrī, who is saluted by all the gods. (3)
Shining like molten gold, adorned with divine jewels,
she was being sprinkled with nectars and even with the liquid essence of pearls and gems.
O beloved, she who possesses a pair of elephants with the luster of bright clouds, whose crown is bound with a multitude of jewels, and who is adorned with pure silk garments and unguents; (5)
The wise one should meditate upon Padmākṣī, who is to be contemplated in the heart by Padmanābha;
having thus visualized the Goddess, who always holds a pair of lotuses, he should recite her mantra.
[One should meditate on her] with four arms and beautiful eyes, enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
thus is Lakṣmī. Now, Mahālakṣmī:
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), [one recites] the syllable whose essence is Hari.
And then Śrīpuṭa in the lotus; O Kamalā, be gracious! || 1 ||
One should join the ground situated between the *lāya* with the station of Rudra;
one should then join the preceding seed-syllables in the form of an encapsulation (*sampuṭa*). || 2 ||
The *mahālakṣmī-hṛdaya* mantra consists of twenty-eight syllables:
*oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale kamalālaye prasīda prasīda śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*.
Dakṣa Prajāpati is its seer (ṛṣi), and likewise its meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī; the deity is Lakṣmī, and it is proclaimed as the Heart [mantra]. (1)
The second and third are the seed-syllables (bīja) in sequence; O Goddess, the Praṇava is the pin (kīlaka), and then one should duly assign the limbs (aṅgas).
O Goddess, the practitioner, being composed, should assign the limbs as before;
[he should visualize] a vessel of jewels filled with wealth and a pair of lotuses made of gold.
She holds a supreme mirror shining with a row of excellent jewels;
she has four arms, her jeweled anklets sparkle, and she is radiant with a crown.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, and large bracelets, and wearing jeweled earrings,
she is always seated upon a lotus throne and attended by female messengers.
"Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who is adorned with white unguents and garments and possesses the form of a great divine woman, one should worship her.
Thus concludes Mahālakṣmī. Now, the Three-Powered Lakṣmī (Triśakti-lakṣmī):
One should inscribe the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Parā, and the seed-syllable of Kāma;
O Goddess, this Triśakti is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. (1)

"Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ"—thus [is the mantra]. O Dear One, Brahmā is said to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī its metre (chanda). The deity is Triśakti; one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) by repeating [the mantra] twice, O Dear One. (1)
One should meditate [on her], the bestower of all prosperity,
upon a ground shimmering with fresh gold, within a pavilion with a jeweled floor.
Seated upon an excellent jewel-lion throne situated within the forest of the great eon (mahākalpa),
she was enriched with the splendor of a lotus-throne and adorned with jeweled anklets.
Her crown shines with glittering jewels, she is adorned with jeweled earrings,
and she is decorated with various circles fashioned from priceless gems.
Holding a pair of lotuses, a noose, a goad, a bow,
and arrows, she has six arms, a moon-like face, and is surrounded by her female messengers.
With beautiful chowries in their hands, with jewel-mirrors in their excellent palms, with betel-nut cases and golden plates, and with boxes of ornaments in their fair hands; || 6 ||
"Shining like molten gold"—thus ends the description of Triśakti-lakṣmī. Now, the description of Sarvasāmrājya-lakṣmī:
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall speak of the deity of universal sovereignty, by whose worship Viṣṇu himself became the Lord of Lakṣmī. (1)
Adorned with Candra, Īśa, Mādana, Kṣmeśa, Vahni, and Dīrghākṣi, and joined with Vidhu and Krūreśvarī— this, O Dear One, is the Vaiṣṇavī Vidyā.
One should enclose it with the seed-syllable *Śrī*, which bestows universal sovereignty:
*Śrīṃ saha kalahrīṃ Śrīṃ*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Hari, and its meter (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī.
The goddess Lakṣmī is the deluder and the bestower of great sovereignty. || 1 ||
The seed-syllable (bīja) is declared to be the peak-syllable (kūṭa), and the power (śakti) is said to be the syllable Śrī.
Having pierced [the body] with the six initial vowels, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Resembling the flax flower and adorned with jewel ornaments,
she holds in her hands the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrow.
O Goddess of gods, [one should meditate on her] adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness by means of six hands;
thus having meditated upon her as eight-armed.
This is the Lakṣmī of Universal Sovereignty. Thus end the five Lakṣmīs. Now, the Five Sheath-Vidyās—therein:
Śrīvidyākośeśvarī—Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [the root mantra]. Seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly of Mahākośeśvarīs, I worship the sandals of the Mother who generates all auspiciousness. || 1 ||
Thus [ends] the Śrīvidyākośeśvarī.
Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the tetrad of the Śrīkośa vidyās, by the mere knowledge of which there is no further rebirth. (1)
Śrīvidyā, the supreme light, the supreme partless deity (paraniṣkaladevatā), Ajapā, and Mātṛkā—these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (pañcakośa). || 2 ||
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should write the supreme word "Haṃsa"; then "So 'ham" as the head, O Goddess; this is declared to consist of eight syllables.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā. Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and the Gāyatrī meter is declared its meter. The deity is proclaimed to be the Supreme Light itself. || 4 ||
The two syllables at the end of the Praṇava are the Seed (bīja) and the Power (śakti); the remainder is the Pin (kīlaka).
"Svāhā" is the Heart, "So 'ham" is the Head, and "Haṃsaḥ" shall be the Crest-lock (śikhā).
O Goddess of gods, by means of the *māyā* [syllable] one should form the armor (*kavaca*), by the *tāra* seed-syllable the three eyes, and by the *sṛṣṭi* mantra the complete weapon (*astra*).

But as for meditation (*dhyāna*), it has been elaborated upon in the context of performing the sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-yāga*); thus [ends] the section on Kośeśvarī, the Supreme Light.
Now, regarding Kośeśvarī, the Supreme Deity Beyond Parts (*paraniṣkaladevatā*)—(p. 132): "Now, O Great Goddess, I shall explain the Supreme Deity Beyond Parts."
By the mere remembrance of whom, the body becomes the abode of consciousness and bliss. || 1 ||
O Goddess of gods, [this] grace and so forth consists of the bindu, nāda, and kalā;
she is the supreme unmanifest Goddess, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman. || 2 ||
Clad in white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
marked with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), she is served by a multitude of lords among yogins.
The word "to be meditated upon" (dhyeya) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
The seer (ṛṣi) is Brahmā; for this [mantra], the meter (chandas) of Manu is Gāyatrī in sequence;
the deity (devatā) is indeed Brahmā; and the seed-syllable (bīja) and power (śakti) are 'a' and 'ū' respectively.
The letter *ma* is the wedge, bestowing the fruit of liberation and granting knowledge;
having placed it in the middle of the pair of vowels and discarded the four [consonants], [one attains this].

O Goddess of the gods, one should duly assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Thus ends the section on the deity Paraniṣkalā. Now, regarding Ajapākośeśvarī: O sinless goddess, I shall describe to you the worship of Ajapā.
By the mere knowledge of whom, the Supreme Brahman itself becomes the teacher. || 1 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the man who recites the *haṃsapada* mantra every day, yet remains bound by delusion, does not realize it; for him, there is no liberation.
O Goddess, through the grace of the glorious Guru, that [reality] is then known and chanted;
by means of inhalation and exhalation, the destruction of bondage then occurs. (3)
In inhalation and exhalation, there are the two syllables "haṃsa.
Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa), known as Haṃsa, is established in the form of the Self (ātman).
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and sixty of those are considered one *nāḍikā*.
Sixty *nāḍikās* make up a day and night; this is the calculation of recitations for the mind engaged in *japa*.
O Īśvarī, every living being recites daily twenty-one thousand six hundred times the supreme mantra, which consists of vibration and bliss. (6)
Its birth is the commencement, and its death is the offering;
O Goddess of the gods, even without [formal] recitation, the mantra-practitioner's recitation becomes perfected.
Therefore, O Goddess, it is called Ajapeya, which severs the bonds of worldly existence; O Beloved, one attains it through the grace of the venerable Guru, and not otherwise.
O Maheśānī, having thus performed the recitation, one should offer it daily to Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, O Parameśvarī.
To the individual soul (jīvātman) and likewise to the supreme soul (paramātman),
[one should offer] six hundred, six thousand, and again six [hundred oblations] in due order.
Furthermore, one should present six thousand, then another thousand,
and again another thousand to the Guru in due order.
O beloved, having reported that recitation performed during that day and night,
O wise one, perform the innate placement (nyāsa), O Supreme Goddess.
The sage is Haṃsa, preceded by the Unmanifest; it is said that the meter is Gāyatrī.
The deity is the Supreme Beginning, and Haṃsa is said to be the seed-syllable "Haṃ. (13)
He is Śakti, He is the Kīlaka, He is "I" (Aham), and He is indeed the Praṇava, the Tattva itself; likewise, O Supreme Goddess, He is the Nāda, the locus, and the white letter.
The acute accent (udātta) is thus proclaimed to be the essence of the mind;
know this, O Pārvatī, that its application is for the sake of liberation. 15.
Then, for the purification of the body, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa);
O Goddess, [one should meditate on] Sūrya, Soma, and thereafter Nirañjana.
One should sequentially place [the mantras] ending in *svāhā* preceded by *nirābhāsa*,
and having duly placed those ending in *kavaca*, one should then contemplate the word *ananta*.

Having uttered the subtle *tanu* mantras of the four castes ending in the dative case, one should perform the "leading forth" (*nayana*) with the word *svāhā*, preceded by the unmanifested syllable (*avyaktapada*). (18)
The mantra whose nature is awakening, ending with the fourth vowel (ī) and the wife of Agni (svā), is declared to be the Astra-mantra.
O Goddess of the Gods, the two wings of this Haṃsa are the Nigama and Āgama.
Agni and Soma are the two wings, while Tāra becomes the head;
the three Bindus are the tuft of hair (śikhā), and Nāda is established in the eyes and the mouth.
The pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, with the two sides of the fire of time (Kālāgni), is this Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), all-pervading and luminous. || 21 ||
Resembling ten million suns, he shines by his own radiance;
this Haṃsa, whose nature is withdrawal, also reveals discernment.
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
thus [ends] Ajapākośeśvarī. Mātṛkā has already been explained in detail. Thus [end] the five deities of the sheaths (kośa). Now, the five Kalpalatās:
Now, O Maheśānī, O beloved, I shall declare the Vidyās that are like wish-fulfilling creepers; by the mere knowledge of which great calamities flee away. (1)
Śrīvidyā, Pārijāteśī, Pañcakāmeśvarī, the goddess Pañcabāṇeśvarī, and Kumārī—these are proclaimed as the five. || 2 ||

Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mūla-mantra: I worship the sandals of the venerable Śrīvidyā-Kalpalatā, the mother of all good fortune, seated upon a throne adorned by the host of Mahākalpalateśvarīs. Thus ends the section on the venerable Śrīvidyā-Kalpalateśvarī. Now, the section on Pārijāteśvarī:
The knower of mantras should write the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* of Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity;
having encapsulated it with the *tāra* [oṃ] and the supreme goddess [hrīḥ], he should do so. (1)
This mantra for Sarasvatī, ending with *hṛt* (the heart-seed) and consisting of eleven Rudra-syllables (*rudrārṇa*), is proclaimed as:
*oṃ hrīṃ hsraiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (*chanda*).
The goddess Vāṇī is proclaimed as the presiding deity of Pārijāteśvara. || 2 ||
The third and the second [syllables], the seed-power (bīja-śakti), and the savior (tāraka)—these are the pegs (kīlaka), O Supreme Goddess, which bestow great eloquence (mahāsārasvata). || 3 ||
One should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) using the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels.
