[She is] mounted upon a swan, radiant with white pearls, and clad in white garments. (4)
She has a pure smile, wears a moon upon her crest, and is adorned with ornaments of vajras and pearls; she holds the Vidyā-lute, a jar of nectar, and a rosary of beads.
Thus ends [the section on] Pārijāteśvarī. Now, regarding Pañcabāṇeśvarī:
"Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the auspicious Pañcabāṇeśvarī;
O Maheśvarī, the arrows are said to be within the mantra of Tripureśī. (1)
With those same five arrows, the five-syllabled Vidyā becomes:
*drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*. Madana is said to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is its meter (*chanda*).
This Goddess Īśvarī is like Kāmeśvarī, beginning with the seed-syllable and so forth.
One should perform the ritual with five arrows, both individually and collectively, for the various limbs;
[the deity] shining like the rising sun and adorned with various ornaments.
She is clothed in red garments and adorned with red unguents, resembling the blossoms of the Bandhūka flower;
her two arms are resplendent with a sugarcane bow and flowery arrows.
Thus ends [the section on] Pañcabāṇeśvarī. Now, [the section on] Pañcakāmeśvarī:
Now I shall describe Pañcakāmanāyikā, the Mother of the Universe.
By means of the five Kāmas previously mentioned, she becomes Pañcakāmeśvarī. (1)
The seer is named Sammohana; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter.
This deity is the Bestower of Desires (Kāmadā); the seed-syllable, power, and pin are likewise [to be known]. (2)
The practitioner of mantras should place these at the end, both individually and collectively;
the limbs are as before, and there should be two applications of the Kama-bāṇas (Love-arrows).
She is red in color, with red silken garments, red unguents, and red ornaments;
she holds a noose and a goad, a bow and arrows, a book, and a rosary.
Holding the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), she is the one who brings the three worlds under her control.
Thus ends [the description of] Pañcakāmeśvarī. Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe Kumārī, the Mother of the Universe.
The divine Kāmeśvarī, capable of attracting the three worlds. || 1 ||
The wise one, having omitted the Vāgbhava syllable of Tripureśānī, should insert it there;
with the two Kāma-Śakti syllables at its end, this Vidyā becomes three-syllabled. || 2 ||
Klīṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ.
These are the seed-syllables (bījas) and powers (śaktis) of Tripureśī, beginning with the visible [form] and so forth, in their proper sequence;
with the *kīlaka* at the beginning and end, and the middle portion, she becomes the great bringer of subjugation (*vaśya*). || 3 ||
By repeating [the mantra] twice, the six limbs [are established]. Likewise:

She possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with excellent ornaments of rubies, is richly arrayed in shimmering silk garments studded with gems, and is decorated with various ornaments. (4)
One should constantly meditate upon her who holds a sugarcane bow, arrows, a book, and a rosary of beads, and who brings all kings under her control.

Thus end the five Kalpalatā Vidyās. Now, the five Kāmadughās: Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ [Mūla-mantra] Mahākāladugheśvarīvṛndamaṇḍitāsanasaṃsthitā-sarvasaubhāgyajananī-Śrīvidyākāmadughā-Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi. (I worship the Śrīpādukā of Śrīvidyākāmadughā, who dwells upon a seat adorned by the multitude of Mahākāladugheśvarīs and who generates all auspiciousness. Thus.
Śrīvidyākāmadughā: Hrīṃ haṃsaḥ sañjīvani jūṃ jīvaṃ prāṇagranthisthaṃ kurukuru saḥ svāhā. The *ṛṣi*, *nyāsa*, and *dhyāna* have already been stated previously.
Thus [ends] Amṛtapīṭheśvarī. Now, Amṛteśvarī: Aiṃ blūṃ oṃ jūṃ saḥ amṛte.
O source of nectar, O Mistress of nectar, O showerer of nectar, cause the nectar to flow, cause it to flow, svāhā!
The placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and so forth is as before.
[She who] has satiated all moving and non-moving beings with a flood of nectarian rays.
O Bhavānī, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence, I meditate upon you, the Sovereign of Immortality.

Thus is the Sudhāsū mantra. Now, for Annapūrṇā: Having uttered the Śrīkāma-yugala, which consists of Śiva (Ha), Agni (Ra), Vāmanayana (I), Bindu (M), Nāda (H), and Kalā (S), [one says] "O Bhagavatī" at the end of the heart-mantra. || 1 ||

One should likewise write the four syllables of Māheśvarī in the Annapūrṇā [mantra]. This mantra, beginning with the Tārā (Oṃ), followed by the four syllables and the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), has been proclaimed. (2)
"O Maheśānī, it consists of twelve syllables. *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari annapūrṇe svāhā*. This mantra begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā; the meter is declared to be Uṣṇih;
and the goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī is proclaimed as the deity. (3)
The seed-syllable, the power, and the pinning-mantra are said to be *hṛllekhā* and so forth;
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six long vowels combined with the *māyā* syllable.
She has a luster equal to the rising sun, is radiant with variegated garments,
has the moon as her crest-jewel, is intent on the gift of food, and is adorned with jewels.
The Supreme Goddess has two arms; she is bent low by the weight of her breasts which have the shape of golden jars; she finds supreme bliss in the Tandava dance of Rudra.

Abounding in the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, always delighting in the gift of food—thus is Annapūrṇeśvarī. These are the five Vidyās of Kāmadughā. Now, the five Vidyās of Ratneśvarī: therein, first, Śrīvidyāratneśvarī—the root mantra.

I worship the Śrīpādukā of Śrīvidyāratneśvarī, the mother of all auspiciousness, who is seated upon a throne adorned by a multitude of Great Goddesses of Jewels (Mahāratneśvarīs). Thus ends the section on Śrīvidyāratneśvarī.
Now, for Siddhalakṣmīratneśvarī: Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Phreṃ Phreṃ Khphreṃ Aiṃ.

Kṣamarī, O Mahācaṇḍateja-saṅkarṣiṇī, Kālimanthānī, Hrīṃ Saḥ Svāhā! Khphreṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to the Yoginī of all Siddhis, Hasakhphreṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to the eternally arisen Mistress of the entire wheel of the Kula, to the Blessed One, the Protectress of Caṇḍikā, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ!

Khphreṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ haphreṃkṣyai kroṃ klīṃsaḥ khaphavayareṃ! O Supreme Haṃsī, O Goddess who bestows the path of liberation, O pacifier of calamities and misfortunes, O subduer of all evils, enemies, and afflictions, O savior from the ocean of all dangers, O Goddess who crushes all foes: come, come! Laugh, laugh!
O you who devour the blood, entrails, and fat of men, O powerful one, crush, crush my enemies! Eat, eat them!
Pierce, pierce them with the trident! Cut, cut them with the sword! Strike, strike them! Mutilate, mutilate them!
VAḌAKAVALA HRĪṂ HASAKṢAMALAVARAYŪṂ HASAKṢAMALAVARAYĪṂ!

O *sahakṣamalavarayī*, accomplish, accomplish all my desires! O supreme compassionate Goddess, O Blessed One who assumes the form of Mahābhairava, O Mother of the Great Mantra worshipped by the best of the thirty gods, O Goddess who is affectionate toward those who bow before you, O Goddess who destroys the great and terrible Time (*kāla*), *hrīṃ*—be gracious! Render me free from the affliction of passion; act, act!

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kroṃ Phaṭ ṬhaḥṬhaḥ Sahakhaphreṃ Phreṃ Phreṃ! I worship the sandals of the venerable Siddha-Mahālakṣmī, the mother of all auspiciousness, who is seated upon a throne adorned by a multitude of great Ratneśvarīs, and who is the daughter of the Suras and Asuras. Thus ends Siddhalakṣmī. Now:
Mātaṅgī is Ratneśvarī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Mātaṅgī, the deity of jewels:
Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and [the syllable] with the *sarga* (visarga), followed by Bhṛgu in the highest [state]. (1)
Endowed with grace, one should again write the first supreme [syllable], the Śrī-bīja, the Tāraka, and "namo bhagavatyai. (2)
O Mātaṅgīśvarī, at the end of all [mantras], [place] "janādikam" (the beginning of people), which captivates the mind;
and at the end, "sarvarājavaśaṃ" (subjugation of all kings), ending with "kari sarvamukhāntakam" (O performer, the end of all faces).
Then one should utter "rañjini," and after that, the word "sarvastrī.
Having said "vaśam" at the end of "puruṣa," all wicked beings are brought under control. || 4 ||
Having written "vaśam" (subjugation) after "mṛgānte," one should write "sarvalokapadam" (the state of all worlds).
O Daughter of the Mountain, having written "vaśam," one should then utter the word "kari" (elephant).
One should write the supreme Śrī, the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), and Vāgbhava;
these seventy-three syllables, O Dear One, constitute the body of Mātaṅgī.
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ. Salutations, O Blessed One, O Sovereign Mātaṅgī,

who captivates the minds of all people, who brings all kings under control, who delights the faces of all, who subjugates all women and men, who subjugates all wicked beasts, and who subjugates all the worlds.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ.
This is the queen of the Mataṅga-vidyās, which bestows the attainment of the goal of liberation;
the venerable sage Mataṅga is its seer, and Gāyatrī is said to be its metre. (7)
The deity is the Supreme Goddess Mātaṅgī, whose form is sound;
the seed-syllables are Kāma-bīja and Vāgbhava, and the Śakti and Kīlaka are likewise [the same].
Then, O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the third [rite] by placing the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the first three seed-syllables (bīja) repeated twice for each limb.
One should meditate upon Mataṅginī, whose right foot is placed upon a lotus and who wears a silken garment;
her earrings sway with the praise of the languid, resonant sound of her lute.
Delightful with the luster of her rows of teeth, auspicious and beautiful in every limb,
she was adorned with garlands of *kadamba* flowers and intent upon playing the *vīṇā* lute.
One should meditate upon her with a dark body and conch-shell bracelets for the attainment of all goals;
thus ends Mātaṅgīratneśvarī. Now, Bhuvaneśvarīratneśvarī has already been explained previously.
Next, Vārāhīratneśvarī is described in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
(p. 135) O beloved, listen as I describe the fifth [goddess], the Mistress of Jewel-Knowledge (Ratnavidyeshī), by the mere remembrance of whom even this wind becomes still. (1)
Having uttered the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, adorned with the throat, the grace-drop, and the resonance (nāda), one should then utter the Pārthiva seed-syllable. || 2 ||
Furthermore, one should write the first [name] at the end with "namas";
likewise, one should write the pair "Vārtāli" and "Vārāhi" twice. || 3 ||
Then follows the word *vārāhamukhi* as a compound without a hiatus;
thereafter, *andhe* and *cāndhini*, which consist of seven syllables, should be joined with the end of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), O Dear One. (4)
*Rundhe rundhini* [is placed] before *hṛt*; then *jambhe jambhini* and after that *hṛt*;
then *mohe mohini* and also *hṛt*; then *stambhe stambhini* and after that *hṛt*. || 5 ||
Having said this, O Maheśānī, [he addressed] all the wicked and the extremely wicked,
as well as the end of all names, and the mind of all speech.
Having uttered the "eye" (cakṣu), the "face" (mukha), and "gati," one should utter the pair "jihvāstambha.
Then, one should quickly utter the pair "vaśya," followed again by "vāgbhava" and "pārthiva. (7)
At the end of the group of four [letters] beginning with *ṭha*, there is the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and the beloved of Agni;
thus, there are indeed one hundred and fourteen syllables in the mantra.

Aiṃ Glauṃ Aiṃ! Obeisance, O Blessed One, Vārtāli Vārtāli, Vārāhi Vārāhi, O Boar-faced One, O Boar-faced One! Obeisance to Andhā, the Blinding One; obeisance to Rundhā, the Obstructing One; obeisance to Jambhā, the Paralyzing One; obeisance to Mohī, the Deluding One; obeisance to Stambhā, the Immobilizing One—[against] all wicked and malicious beings.

"Paralyze the speech, mind, eyes, face, gait, and tongue of all! Act, act! Quickly bring [them] under control, act, act! Aiṃ glauṃ ṭhaṭhaṭhaṭha huṃ phaṭ svāhā! [This consists of] 114 syllables. The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is proclaimed to be performed with forty-four words.
The knower of mantras should place the ten words upon the face, as in the case of the *mātṛkā*.
One should place twenty syllables of the word *pada* at the joints of the arms and feet, including the tips; then, having assigned them, one should place the final excellent syllable on both sides.
In this very manner, the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters;
thereafter, he should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*) for the purification of the body.
O Goddess, the pair of feet of Vārtālī, followed by her heart, and then the pair of Vārāhī, is declared to be the head-mantra.

One should then place the two Vārāhamukhīs at the crest (śikhā), followed by the seven-syllable mantra; then the armor (kavaca) with seven syllables, and finally the eye (netra), placing them in due order.
She who dwells within a lotus resembling fresh, crimson dawn,
who possesses the brilliance of the great luster of a sapphire, the Mother of the Universe.
Adorned with a garland of *kadamba* flowers and various jewels, she shines with the splendor of a crown fashioned from priceless gems. || 15 ||
She wears a lower garment of silk and is adorned with beautiful coral and gem ornaments;
she holds a plow, a mace, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
She was resplendent with four arms, possessed tawny eyes and a slender waist;
she had shapely hips, the luster of a blue lotus, and firm, excellent breasts.
*Kolānanām* [etc.

... thus ends Vārāhīranteśvarī. Thus concludes the group of the five *pañcikās*. Now follows the exposition of the sixteen *Nityās*: Now, O Great Goddess, I shall proclaim the great exposition of the *Nityās*.
O Pārvatī, there are many great varieties of Kāmeśvarī. || 1 ||
Therein, Kāmeśvarī Nityā is described as difficult to obtain on earth.
Having pronounced Tripureśī, one should then utter the word "Tārā" at the end, followed by the word "Hṛt. (2)
Having uttered the word *Kāmeśvarī*, [and] "O bestower of the fruits of desire and will," having spoken "subjugation of all beings," and the word "O doer, O all-world," || 3 ||
At the end of the *kṣobha* [mantra], one should write "hūṃ hūṃ" in the hand, followed by the arrows and Tripureśvarī in reverse; this is the thirty-six-syllable *vidyā*.

Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Namaḥ (Heart): O bestower of the fruits of desire through the will of Kāmeśvarī, O subduer of all beings, O agitator of the entire world, Hūṃ Hūṃ Drāṃ Drīṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Saḥ Sauḥ Klīṃ Aiṃ.
By repeating the first three parts twice, one performs the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*),
as well as the visualization, the yantra, the worship, and so forth, just like that of Kāmeśvarī.
Thus ends the Nityā Kāmeśvarī. Now, regarding the Nityā Bhagamālinī: Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the Vidyā of Śrī Bhagamālinī:
[The syllable] Vāgbhava, followed by the word *bhaga*, then *bhuge*, and again Vāgbhava. (1)
At the end of *bhagini* is *vāgbhava*, and at *bhagodare* is *vāgbhava*;
at *bhagaklinne* is *vāgbhava*, and at the beginning of *bhagāvahe* is *vāgbhava*.
In the secret place of the vulva is Vāgbhava, and in the womb of the vulva is Vāgbhava;
at the end of the vulva is Pātanī, and [then] Vāgbhava and Bhagasarva.
O Goddess Śaṅkarī, having first written the Vāgbhava [syllable],
one should then place the Vāgbhava within the form of the Bhaga, and the Vāgbhava again within the Bhaganityā.
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of "bhagaklinne," and likewise at the end of "bhagasvānte.
Then [one writes] "rūpe sarvabhagāni" and "me hyānaya," followed by the Vāgbhava syllable. (5)
At the end, one should write *bhagaklinnadrave* and *bhagaṃ kledaya*;
having written *bhagaṃ drāvaya*, [one writes] *bhagāmoghe bhaga*. (6)
"O Mistress of the Yoni (Bhageśvarī), agitate the yoni of all beings here!
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable, then "bhaga blūṃ," and then the Vāgbhava syllable followed by "bhagajaṃ. || 7 ||

One should write the Vāgbhava [syllable] and the Bhagablūṃ [syllable], and the Vāgbhava [syllable] within the Bhaga; one should write the Vāgbhava [syllable] and the Bhagablūṃ [syllable], and the Vāgbhava [syllable] and the Bhagamoṃ [syllable]. || 8 ||
And when [the organ] is moistened by the secretions, one should then write all the *bhagas*;
one should write the *Vāgbhava* (AIM), then *Bhagabhūm* (BLŪM), and then the *Vāgbhava* (*Bhagahem*). || 9 ||
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable, then *bhaga blūṃ*, then the Vāgbhava syllable, and *bhagahaiṃ*;
then one should write *bhagaklinne* and all the *bhagas*, and then *me*. (10)
Having drawn the God of Love with the vulva as the fifth,
one should then draw the essence of Hara and Lakṣmī within the vulva and at the end of the vulva.
At the end of *bhaga*, first recite *kāma*, and then indeed *bhagamālinī*; having uttered [the name] ending in *ṅe*, this is the vidyā that brings the three worlds under control. (12)
Adorned with two hundred and twenty-four syllables,
this Bhagamālā is eternal and bestows the attainment of fruits.
The extraction of the mantra is indeed easy. Its seer is Subhaga, its metre is Gāyatrī, and its deity is this seed-syllable consisting of *ha-ra-bla-m*, O Dear One. (14)
O Supreme Goddess, the Śakti is the female seed-syllable "blūṃ," and the Kīlaka is likewise;
the preceptor should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) by means of the six long vowels.

One should perform the placement of the Kāmas and the placement of the arrows as before, [visualizing the goddess] situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest, possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun. (16)
Adorned with various ornaments and capable of attracting the three worlds,
she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and a stylus for writing on a palm leaf.
"Holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the Mother of the Universe"—thus is Bhagamālinī. Now, for Nityaklinnā:
having uttered Bhuvaneśī, [one says] "O Nityaklinnā, O you whose essence is the flow of intoxication."
This Vidyā, ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā), consists of the color of Rudra and is exceedingly fierce. || 1 ||

"Hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā. O Dear One, the best of teachers should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence: with one [syllable], then two, then two, then two, then two, and then two. || 2 ||
She is red in color, wearing red garments, with the moon as her crest-jewel and three eyes;
her skin is perspiring, her eyes are rolling wildly, and she is adorned with jewels.
One should constantly meditate upon the Eternal One (Nityā), who holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-bowl that likewise removes great fear, and who is resplendent in the lotus posture.
Thus ends the Nityaklinnā-vidyā. Now, regarding Bheruṇḍā:
"Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the supreme goddess Bheruṇḍā.
Having uttered the form 'Bhera', one should encircle it with two goads (aṅkuśas). (1)

The *ca*-group, excluding its final letter (*cha*), adorned with the letter *ra* in four ways and enriched by the *anugraha* (the letter *u*) and the lunar drop (*bindu*), is situated within the belly of the *Tāra* (Om) and the *Svāhā*.
O Goddess, the ten-syllable mantra of Manu becomes a destroyer of great poisons:
*oṃ kroṃ bheḥ kroṃ crauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ jhrauṃ svāhā*.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this is Mahāviṣṇu, and the meter (*chanda*) is said to be Gāyatrī.
This goddess is Parāśakti; she is called the third seed-syllable.
The wife of Vahni (Svāhā) is the Śakti, and Sṛṇi is indeed the Kīlaka;
the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with the seed-syllables (bīja) distinguished by the six long vowels.
Resembling ten million moons, flowing with streams of liquid nectar,
she has a blue throat, three eyes, and is adorned with various ornaments.
She possesses the shimmering luster of sapphire and is graced by the peacock-vehicle;
she holds a noose, a goad, a skull-cup, and a dagger, while displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
"Carrying [the staff] and adorned with golden-linked armlets of emerald—thus is the eternal Bheruṇḍā. Now, regarding the eternal Vahnivāsinī:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the eternal Vahnivāsinī."
Having written "Parā" at the end of the fire-syllable (Ra), one should also write "Vāsinyai namaḥ."
O Great Goddess, this eight-syllabled mantra, "hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ," bestows the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
Vasiṣṭha is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chanda).
The seed-syllable and the power are at the beginning and the end, and the pin is in the middle.
O Goddess, one should perform the placement of the limbs by repeating the three words twice;
and one should meditate upon her, golden-hued and adorned with various ornaments.
She holds a noose, a goad, a svastika, a spear, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she wears a jeweled crown and dispels the darkness of the three worlds.
Thus ends the Nityā Vahnivāsinī. Now, the Nityā Mahāvajreśvarī: Now I shall describe, O Maheśānī, the supreme Mahāvajreśvarī.
Having written Nityaklinnā, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) upon her face. (1)
At the end of *hṛllekhā*, the seed-syllable of the Moon (*ca*) belonging to the self is like the *visarga*;
this is the fourteen-syllabled *vidyā*.
Oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ saḥ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā. Thus it is declared: the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Parameśvarī. || 2 ||
The seed-syllable and the power-syllable are at the beginning and the end, while the *hṛllekhā* is the *kīlaka*;
[the mantra is formed] by means of four, two, and two pairs.
The preceptor should assign the limbs [of the mantra] by means of pairs and couples;
[he should visualize her] resembling a hibiscus flower, radiant with red garments.
She is eternally adorned with rubies and embellished with various ornaments;
she is reeling from drinking the nectar situated within her skull-cup, while holding a noose and a goad.
One should meditate upon her as bestowing fearlessness. Thus ends the eternal [Mahā]Vajreśvarī. Now, the eternal Śivadūtī:
Next, I shall describe the Messenger (Dūtī), who is capable of attracting the three worlds.
Having uttered "Bhuvaneśī," one should write "Śivadūtyai namaḥ. || 1 ||
O Dear One, this Śivadūtī consists of seven syllables and is the mistress of the three worlds. [The mantra is: *hrīṃ śivadūtyai namaḥ*.
Rudra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is its meter (*chandaḥ*), and Śivā is its deity (*devatā*).
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are at the beginning and end, while the middle is called the pillar (*kīlaka*). (2)
One should install the limbs by repeating the three parts of the Vidyā twice;
she is dark-green like dūrvā grass, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a great lion-throne.
One should constantly meditate on her as holding a conch, a discus, arrows, and a bow, as well as a goad, a noose, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus ends the Nityā Śivadūtī. Now follows the Nityā Tvaritā:

Now I shall describe, O Maheśānī, Tvaritā, the bestower of success. One should write the *Tāra* (Oṃ) at the end of *Parā*, followed by the *Kavaca* (Hūṃ), and then the syllables *khe-ca-che-kṣaḥ*. (1)
Having uttered the syllable *strīṃ*, which consists of the essence of *hūṃ*, one should write the supreme weapon-syllable *kṣe*.
This Tvaritā, consisting of twelve syllables, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ khecachekṣaḥ strīhūṃkṣehrīṃ phaṭ. O Pārvatī, Īśa is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chanda), and this goddess is the deity (devatā). The seed-syllables *strī* and *śakti* are proclaimed as the armor (*kavaca*) and the wedge (*kīlaka*). || 3 ||
The pair *ca-ca* is for the heart; *che-kṣaḥ* in pairs is for the head;
then *kṣaḥ-strī* in pairs is the armor (*kavaca*); likewise, *strīṃ-hūṃ* in pairs is the self (*ātman*). || 4 ||
Having assigned the eyes with *hūṃ kṣe*, the weapon-mantra *kṣephaḍ* is proclaimed;
[one should visualize her] with a dark-blue body, adorned by beautiful lotus-like hands and feet that are red.
She had beautiful anklets on her feet like those of a low-born woman, was adorned with hissing snake-fangs,
wore golden garments and golden ornaments, and had a girdle made from a pair of snakes like a Vaiśya woman.
She has a slender waist and a pair of full, rounded breasts;
she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is adorned with bracelets and armlets made of peacock feathers.
Red as the guñjā berry, with armlets of serpent-kings and blood-red ornaments,
her ear-ornaments were shimmering brahmin-serpents, and her eyes were intoxicated and crimson.
She had a dark, curly mass of hair adorned with a cluster of forest flowers;
she was a Kirāti woman, resplendent in a dwelling richly decorated with peacock feathers.
One should meditate upon her who destroys fear, seated firmly upon a shimmering lion-throne.
Thus ends the daily practice of Tvaritā. Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the Śrī Kulasundarī Vidyā.
The one called Bālā, the Mistress of Tripura, is situated on the eastern lion-throne.
That Kulasundarī is to be worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others; thus ends [the section on] Kulasundarī. Now, regarding Nityānityā:
I shall now describe the supreme Nityā, who bestows the goals of human existence.
Having uttered Tripureśī, as well as the Bhairavī named Nityā. || 1 ||
The three *huṃ* syllables are the arrows; this is the nine-syllable Vidyā:
*aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ hasakalaraḍaiḥ hasakalaraḍīṃ hasakalaraḍauḥ huṃ huṃ huṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*. The rest is like that of Tripureśī. This is the Nityā. Now...
Nīlapatākā:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the Vidyā Nīlapatākinī. Having first uttered the Tāra (Om) and the word "hṛt" (heart), one should then utter [the mantra] of Kāmeśvarī. (1)
Having uttered "Kāmāṅkuśe pada" and then "Kāmapatākike," one should then say "Bhagavati" at the end of "Nīla," and "Patāke" near the end of "Bhaga."
(Śrīvi. 18, p. 138) Having written the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) in the middle, one should then write "asviti" and "me.
Likewise, at the end of "para" and in the secret place (guhya), one should write the triad of the syllable *hrīṃ*. || 3 ||
In the *madana* and *madanānta* [sections], one should draw the three worlds upon the body;
likewise, one should cause the armor (*kavaca*), the weapon (*astra*), fire, and the beloved (*vallabhā*) to be inscribed.
O Supreme Goddess, the goddess Nīlapatākinī consists of sixty syllables:
*Oṃ hṛtkāmeśvari kāmāṅkuśe kāmapatākike bhagavati nīlapatāke bhagavati namo'stu me paramaguhye hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ madane madanadehe trailokyam āveśaya*.
Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Red in color, dressed in red garments, and adorned with various jewels;
she stands upon a lotus, bearing a blue banner shimmering with sapphires. (1)
She holds a goad firmly attached to the neck of Kāma, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is the Supreme Sovereign, capable of attracting the three worlds. || 2 ||
Thus ends the eternal Nīlapatākā. Now follows the eternal Vijayā:
Now I shall declare the supreme Vidyā, the ever-victorious Vijayā, which bestows victory;
it is adorned with Śiva, Candra, Kha, Pānta, Agni, Rudra, and the vowels. (1)
One should write: "Obeisance to Vijayā, pervaded by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
That is: *hasakhaphreṃ vijayāyai namaḥ*.
Śiva is her seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and she herself is the deity (*devatā*).
The seed-syllables are the letters in the center of the heart; these are the seed (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka).
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with the seed-syllables interspersed with the six long vowels;
[the deity] has one face, ten arms, and wears a snake as a sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 3 ||
With a face made terrible by fangs, adorned with garlands of human heads,
possessing nothing but bone and skin, she was as radiant as a mass of fire.
Clad in tiger-skin, resplendent upon a fresh and most mature corpse, she bestows victory upon her devotees in battle by her mere remembrance. (5)
One should meditate upon Vijayā, who holds a trident, a serpent, an axe, a sword, a goad, two bells, two thunderbolts, a noose, fire, and the gesture of fearlessness.

Thus ends the eternal Vijayā. Herein follows Sarvamaṅgalā: Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā: [the seed-syllable] Jīva (Sa), enriched by Varuṇa (Va) and Tārā (Ū), with the word "Maṅgalā" at the end. (1)
Having written the heart-mantra at the end, [the mantra] of nine syllables for Sarvamaṅgalā is:
*oṃ sarvamaṅgalāyai namaḥ*.
O Maheśānī, the seer is [the same], and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
by means of the three divisions of the Vidyā, repeated twice, the six limbs [of the ritual] are formed.
Delightful with her seat upon a white lotus, possessing a luster like that of the moon or jasmine, she is exceedingly gracious, moon-faced, and adorned with various jewels.

One should meditate upon her who increases good fortune, who is adorned with infinite ornaments of pearls, from whom flows a stream of the liquid of nectar, and who is enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus ends the Sarvamaṅgalā. Now, regarding Jvālāmālinī:
I shall proclaim the Jvālāmālā [mantra], which always bestows the goals of human existence.
Having uttered the seed-syllable Oṃ, one says "namo bhagavati" (salutation to the Blessed One). || 1 ||
At the end of the goddess Jvālāmālinī, one should write "sarvabhūtāntaṃ saṃlikhet" (one should inscribe the end of all beings),
as well as "hārakāri ca ke jātavedasīti jvalanti ca" (and the harakāri, the fire-born ones, and the blazing ones).
One should cause the pair of flames to blaze forth; the pair consisting of the syllable *hūṃ* is twofold.
One should likewise draw the fire twice, as well as the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*).
One should recite the forty syllables of the formless [mantra] and the syllable *vas* in sequence:
*Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālinī devi sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike jātavedasi jvalanti jvala jvala prajvala prajvala huṃ huṃ ra ra huṃ phaṭ*.
O Dear One, one should place the seed-syllable (bīja) and the power-syllable (śakti) upon the weapon-mantra (repha-astra), and the pin-mantra (kīlaka) and armor-mantra (kavaca);
then, one should assign the spokes of the wheel according to the numbers twelve, twelve, five, three, eight, and four.
O Supreme Goddess, one should encircle her in pairs with the fire-colored [syllable];
she is adorned with golden ornaments and possesses the splendor of a rising creeper of lightning. || 2 ||
Seated majestically upon a great lion-throne, she is formidable with garlands of flames;
she holds a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, a trident, and likewise a hand-drum.
One should meditate upon and worship her as holding a drinking vessel and granting boons.
Thus ends the description of the eternal Jvālāmālinī. Now, regarding the eternal Vicitrā:
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe Vicitrā, the Mother of the Universe."
By the mere remembrance of whom great calamities flee away. || 1 ||

One should write the mantra adorned with the wheel, the favor-bestowing drop (*bindu*), and the nasal dot (*indu*). That is: *cakauṃ*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Brahmā; its meter (*chandas*) is said to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is Vicitrā; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the letter *ka*; and the peg (*kīlaka*) is likewise. (1)
The King of Stars (Tārarāja), however, is Śakti, the bestower of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
The preceptor should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) by means of the six long vowels. (2)
She is of radiant form, eternally bestowing knowledge; she is always clothed in variegated garments, eternally adorned with diverse tilakas, and ever resplendent with various flowers. || 3 ||
Abounding in the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and sometimes bearing various jewels—thus she is the manifold Nityā. Thus end the sixteen Nityās.
[Thus ends the work] by the disciple of the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya, the worshipful Śrī Govindācārya...

Thus ends the seventh breath (śvāsa) in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of the venerable Lord Śaṅkarācārya. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter on Inhalation (Śvāsa)
Now, the science of the abodes (āyatanavidyā):
the systems of the Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Bauddha, and Śaiva [are located] in the east, south, west, north, and above, respectively. (1)
There would be five āyatanas; the Śākta [āyatana] is behind that, and above it.
Therein, the first is the Brāhmya-darśana-brahmagāyatrī, the knowledge of the eastern āyatana:
"Now I shall proclaim the Gāyatrī, whose nature is reality and which consists of the three Vedas."
By which [knowledge] Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, is revealed. || 1 ||
The seven vyāhṛtis begin with the syllable *praṇava*, followed by the words "tat" and so forth;
together with the *śiras*, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables. (2)
"This mantra is proclaimed as the essence extracted from all the Vedas.
Thus ends the Brāhma-darśana. Now follows the Vaiṣṇava-darśana, the Dakṣiṇāyatana-vidyā: Of this Śrī Nārāyaṇa mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is Sādhya-Nārāyaṇa, the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī.
The deity is Śrī Mahāviṣṇu; Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Namaḥ is the power (śakti), and Nārāyaṇāya is the pin (kīlaka);
the application (viniyoga) is as a limb of the Śrīvidyā.
Oṃ, salutation to Kruddholka; to Maholkā; to Vīrolka; to Dyulkā; to Caṇḍolka;
to Sahasrolka—thus is the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). The meditation (dhyāna):
[One should meditate on the deity] who constantly shines with the brilliance of ten million rising suns, and who holds a conch, a mace, and a lotus.

I worship Him who bears the discus, whose two sides are graced by Indirā and Vasumatī; who wears a crown, armlets, necklaces, and earrings; who is clad in yellow garments and illuminated by the Kaustubha gem; who sustains the universe and upon whose chest shines the Śrīvatsa mark. 1.
"Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa"—this is the knowledge of the southern sanctuary of the Vaiṣṇava system.

Now, the knowledge concerning the western abode for the vision of the Sun: for this mantra of the glorious Sūrya, Devabhāga is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), the glorious Āditya is the deity (*devatā*), *Oṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Āditya is the power (*śakti*), *Ghṛṇi* is the pin (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is as a limb of the glorious Vidyā.

Oṃ satyatejojvālāmāline hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, brahmatejojvālāmāline hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, viṣṇutejojvālāmāline hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, rudratejojvālāmāline hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, agnitejojvālāmāline hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, sarvatejojvālāmāline.

*Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—these are the mantras for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). The meditation (*dhyāna*): I praise the Lord of Day (the Sun), who has hands granting boons and fearlessness with a pair of red lotuses; who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings; who wears a crown of rubies; who possesses the luster of the *bandhūka* flower; and whose three eyes shine brightly. (2)

*Oṃ ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityoṃ.* Thus ends the Vidyā of the Western Seat of the Saura-darśana. Now follows the Vidyā of the Northern Seat of the Bauddha-darśana: For this venerable Bauddha mantra, Buddha is the Seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrī-Bauddhī is the Deity (*devatā*), *oṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śaktiḥ*), and *hrīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*).
The application [of the mantra] is as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of Śrīvidyā.
*Oṃ hrīṃ tāraya tāraya svāhā*—this is the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). The meditation (*dhyāna*):

I bow to that Buddha, the root source, who in ancient times, intending to conquer the primordial asuras, assumed the guise of a Pīṭha-marked ascetic and composed this scripture of unfailing efficacy. *Oṃ hrīṃ tāraya tāraya svāhā*—thus ends the mantra for the higher seat (*uttarāyatana*) in the Buddhist system. Now:

The Śaiva Darśana Ūrdhvāyatana-vidyā: for this venerable Śiva-mantra, Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), Paramaśiva is the deity (devatā), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Namaḥ is the power (śakti), Śivāya is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is as a limb of the venerable Vidyā.

To the omniscient one, to the eternally satisfied one, to the beginningless awakened one, to the independent one, to the one whose power is eternally undiminished, to the one whose power is eternally infinite—thus is the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Meditation (*dhyāna*): (p.
141) Homage be to Him who has become the immovable pillar (*sthāṇu*), whose essence is the immortal light-linga (*jyotirliṅga*).
To Śambhu, whose body consists of four forms and whose limbs are radiant. || 1 ||

Thus ends the Vidyā of the Upper Abode in the Śaiva system. Now, as for the Vidyā of the Śakti system, it is indeed the Pradhāna-vidyā; some call it Bhuvaneśvarī, and its ritual procedure has already been explained. These are the Vidyās of the Abodes. Now, the Samaya-vidyās: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Namaḥ (Heart) Kāmeśvari, O bestower of the fruits of desire and will!
O you who bring all beings under control, O you who agitate the entire world! Raṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Drāṃ Drīṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Saḥ Sauḥ Klīṃ Aiṃ. || 1 ||

Aiṃ Hrīṃ! O fulfiller of all desires and aims, O Vajreśvarī, who has entered the center of the vajra-penetrating cage at the vajra-step; Hrīṃ! O moist one, Aiṃ Krom! O you who are eternally flowing with intoxication, Hrīṃ! Salutation to Vajranityā. || 2 ||
Then follows the Bhagamālinī-vidyā. || 3 ||
Klīṃ, O Blessed One! Blūṃ, O Eternal One! Kāmeśvarī! Hrīṃ, O Enchantress of all beings!
Saḥ, O Tripurabhairavī! Aiṃ Vicce! Klīṃ, salutation to Mahātripurasundarī! || 4 ||
Thus end the Vidyās of the Four Samayas. Now follows the Nyāsa of the Vidyās of the Āmnāyas:
"By means of the five faces—east, south, west, north, and upward—in due order, the five deities of the Āmnāyas were proclaimed by Śiva. (1)
"Exalted upon five lion-thrones, they bestow the fruits of all desires.

Regarding that, first is the Vidyā of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), Unmanī: *Oṃ*. Of this venerable Unmanī-mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandas*), the venerable Unmanī is the deity (*devatā*), and *hsrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

*Kalahrīṃ* is the *Śakti*, *Shrīṃ* is the *Kīlaka*, and the application (*viniyoga*) is as a limb of the *Śrīvidyā*. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are performed by repeating [the mantra] twice. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is like that of Saṃpatpradā Bhairavī. *Hsrīṃ Shrīṃ Śrīṃ Kalahrīṃ*—this is the *Iyutmanī* Vidyā of the Eastern Tradition (*Pūrvāmnāya*). Now...
Regarding the *dakṣiṇāmnāyavidyā*: for this *Śrībhoginī-mantra*, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
the *paṅkti* is the meter (*chandas*), Bhoginī is the deity (*devatā*), *aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *sraiṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *klīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*),
and its application (*viniyoga*) is as a limb of the *Śrīvidyā*.

Aiṃ klinne, klīṃ, madadrave kule hsauḥ—these are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*); the visualization (*dhyāna*) is like that of Aghorabhairavī. Aiṃ klinne klīṃ madadrave kule hsauḥ—this is the Vidyā of Dakṣiṇāmnyāyabhoginī.

Now, the Vidyā of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya): for this Śrī Kubjikā mantra, Rudra is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Kubjikā is the deity (devatā), *hasauḥ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hasakhaphreṃ* is the power (śakti), *hasūṃ* is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is as a limb of the Śrīvidyā. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasakhaphreṃ hasauḥ oṃ namaḥ*.

*Bhagavati hasakhaphreṃ kubjikā hasrāṃ hasrūṃ aghore ghore aghoramukhi chrāṃ chrīṃ kiṇikiṇi vicce hasauḥ hasakhaphreṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*—these are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). The visualization (*dhyāna*) is like that of Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī. Thus is the Kubjikā-vidyā of the Western Tradition (*paścimāmnāya*).

Now follows the Kālikā-vidyā of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya): for this Śrī-Kālikā mantra, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī-Kālikā is the deity (devatā), Khaphreṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Īśvarī is the power (śakti), Mahācaṇḍayoga is the pin (kīlaka), and the application (viniyoga) is as a limb of the Śrīvidyā.
The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with *khaphrāṃ* and *khaphrīṃ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is like that of Bhuvaneśvarī and Bhairavī.
*Khphreṃ Mahācaṇḍayogeśvari* is the Kālī-vidyā of the Northern Tradition (*Uttarāmnāya*).

Now follows the sequence of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya): therein, having performed the mantra of Parāprāsāda, one should perform the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa as its ancillary. Within the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa, there is the Kāmarati-nyāsa, the Inner Kāmakalā, and the Outer Kāmakalā-Mahāśakti-nyāsa.

Without performing the installation (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen-syllable root mantra and the installation of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*), one has no authority [to proceed]; we shall describe those installations later. Now, the Great Sixfold Installation (*mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*) will be explained.
First therein is the installation of the thirty-eight digits, as follows:
The preceptor should place Īśāna and the others on the head and on the thumb and other fingers;
first the one named Īśāna, then Tatpuruṣa, and immediately after that Aghora.

They know the sequence of their seed-syllables (*bīja*) as follows: the one called Vāmadeva and Sadyojāta, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and the five short vowels in reverse order, joined with the ether (*viyat*). (2)
Furthermore, with those respective fingers, one should place the respective seed-syllables and so forth upon the regions of the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet, in due order.
Upon the fingers, in their proper order, one should correctly place those *ṛc*s beginning with Īśāna upon the faces directed upwards, eastward, southward, northward, and westward.
The best of teachers should perform the placement [of mantras] starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
or alternatively, upon the head, face, heart-lotus, private parts, and feet.
One should place [the mantras] in the faces starting from the top, and then further arrange the limbs (aṅgas):
having uttered the five *tāras*, "to the All-Knowing" is recited for the heart.
Then the phrase "to Amṛtetejomālinī Tṛptāya," followed by "Brahmaśirase" at its end; then the head limb (śiraḥ-aṅga) ending with "Jvalita. (7)
The crest-lock for Śikhiśikha; the topknot for Anādibodha;
the armor for Vajrin, Vajrahasta, and Svatantra. (8)
Having contemplated "Sauṃ Bauṃ Hauṃ," [one offers] thereafter to the one whose power is undiminished;
the mantra for the eye is "Ślīṃ Paśu Huṃ Phaṭ" ending with "to the one of infinite power."
Having thus discharged the weapon-mantra, one who is composed should perform the six-limbed ritual;
thereafter, the wise one should project the thirty-eight kalās upon the body.
One should sequentially assign the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna to the five faces located in the east, south, west, north, and the center.
Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, is the first digit, Śaśinī;
thereafter is Īśvara, the lord of all beings, who is Aṅgadā. 12.
At the end of the word *brahmādhipati*, [the mantra] "the Lord of Brahmā" (*brahmaṇo'dhipatiḥ*) follows;
then the third [part], "bestower of the desires of Brahmā" (*brahmeṣṭadā*), should be there, followed by "may Śiva be mine" (*śivo me astu*). Thus it ends. (13)
Marīci is declared in the Tantra as the fourth, followed by Sadāśivā;
then Aṃśumālinī is the supreme [mantra], beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ. (14)
Immediately thereafter, the practitioner of mantras should place the four digits (kalās) of Puruṣa in sequence upon the faces facing east, west, south, and north.
"Ādyā tatpuruṣāya" is known as the invocation (vidmahe), and "śāntiḥ" is declared [as the conclusion].
Then, after the word "mahādevāya," "dhīmahi" should follow. (16)
Vidyā is said to be the second; then *tat* and *naḥ*, O Rudra, followed by *padaṃ*; thereafter, Pratiṣṭhā is said to be the third, ending with *pracodayāt*. (17)

All those mantras beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, starting with *nivṛtti*, [should be applied] to the heart, the neck, the two shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest. (18)
These eight are indeed the digits (kalās) of Aghora; the mantra-practitioner [should employ them] according to the rule.
The first digit, beginning with "Aghorebhyaḥ," was previously declared.
Then, at the end of "ghorebhyaḥ," there should be "mohā"; immediately after that, at the end of "ghorān," there should be "kṣamā. This is proclaimed as the third [part]. || 20 ||
From all those most terrible [obstacles], sleep arises, which is intent upon Śarva;
thereafter, the fifth is declared to be disease, more so than all the others. (21)
Death is declared as the sixth; salutations to you who are devoted to her.
Hunger is said to be the seventh; from the forms of Rudra comes thirst. (22)
One should place the digits of Vāmadeva on the secret organ, the pair of thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, the pair of buttocks, the waist, and both sides.
The first [kalā] should end with "namas" for Vāmadeva;
it is proclaimed as the second, Jyeṣṭhā, which is the protection ending with "namas. || 24 ||
"Syādrudrāya namaḥ" at the end is declared the third, Rati;
"Kālāya namaḥ" at the end is proclaimed as Mālinī. || 25 ||
The fifth [digit] should be Kalā Kāmyā;
then, for the sake of the Vikaraṇa, the sixth is said to be Saṃyaminī immediately following that.
The power of action (balakriyā) is prescribed for the transformation of power (balavikaraṇa);
salutation to Vṛddhi, who is the eighth [kalā], and she is the digit situated at the end of power.
After "to Pramathana" at the end, "namo rātri" is uttered;
after "to Sarvabhūtadamana," the syllable "bhrāmiṇī" follows at the end. (28)
The twelfth digit is called Mohinī by those who know the Tantras;
after that, Unmanā is saluted, and the thirteenth is called Jvarā. (29)
It is proclaimed that [the mantras] begin with the syllable Om, end with the dative case, and conclude with "namaḥ";
one should place them on the soles of the feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and the pair of arms.
The mantra-practitioner should correctly [worship] the eight kalās arising from Sadyojāta in their proper sequence:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta"—this is the first kalā, Siddhi. (31)
Furthermore, "sadyojātāya" is indeed the first; "namaḥ" is declared to be "ṛddhi";
"bhave" is the third, which is "dyuti"; and immediately after that is "abhava". || 32 ||
Lakṣmī is said to be the fourth; thereafter, in beginningless existence, she becomes Medhā. She is declared to be the fifth, Kalā; O Bhava, protect me! (33)
The sixth is Prajñā, who is concentrated; at the end of existence is Prabhā, a digit [of light].
After that, "Homage to Udbhavā," and Sudhā shall be the eighth digit.
All the thirty-eight kalās, beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava), ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namaḥ," are said to begin with the words of the five Brahmans.
Having thus disposed his body, he himself becomes Gaṅgādhara (the bearer of the Ganges).
Ananta, Candra, and Bhuvana, followed by the Bindu and joined with a pair of Bindus, [form the mantra]. 36.
The supreme mantra of Śrīprāsāda bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; however, O Mistress of the Kula, the Parāprāsāda mantra is said to begin with the letter 'S'. (37)
"Because it consists of the nature of light and bliss, it bestows the fruit of direct perception.
Thus: Ananta-candra is *nāda* and *bindu*; Bhuvana is the vowel *au*; Bindu is the consonant *ha*; and the pair of *bindus* is the consonant *sa*. By these, *hasauṃ* is established.

If this [seed] begins with *sā*, it is established as *shauṃ*. This pair of seed-syllables (*bīja*) is joined with the *visarga*; such is the extraction [of the mantra] in some traditions. Paraśambhu is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *gāyatrī* is said to be the meter (*chandas*).
The Lord who is half-female is proclaimed as the deity. || 1 ||
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels;
this is the rite called Mahāṣoḍhā, preceded by the Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa of the limbs.
"One who desires accomplishment should perform this as an ancillary part with a concentrated mind" (p.
143). In the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform the sixfold ancillary rite (*aṅga-ṣoḍhā*) by the path previously described."
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Mahāṣoḍhā.
Thus, the placement of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) of the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣoḍhā*), as well as its extraction, has already been explained previously.
Others say it is the "placement of the five Brahmans alone" (*kevala-pañca-brahma-nyāsa*). Of this [practice] called Mahāṣoḍhā, Brahmā is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The Jagatī meter is declared [to be its form], and the Lord Ardhanārīśvara is its presiding deity. || 1 ||
And likewise, the deity has been designated as a constituent part of Śrīvidyā;
thus the application (viniyoga) has been fully declared by those proficient in all the Āgamas. || 2 ||

Now follows the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). Therein: on the two thumbs—*oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasauṃ shauṃ hauṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. On the two index fingers—*heṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*. On the two middle fingers—*huṃ aghorāya namaḥ*. On the two ring fingers—*hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. On the two little fingers—*haṃ*.
"Salutation to Sadyojāta. In this manner, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence upon the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet;
likewise upon the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces. Again, from the thumb to the little finger;
again upon the head, mouth, heart-lotus, secret place, and feet; and again upon the upper face and so forth.

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra beginning "hasāṃhasīṃ," one then performs the six-limbed assignment again with the mantra beginning "shāṃshīm. Then: 5 *sarvajñāya*, 5 *amṛtatejomālinī nityatṛptāya*, 5 *brahmaśirase svāhā jvalitaśikhiśikhāyānādibodhāya*, 5 *vajriṇe*.

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) on the two hands, from the thumbs to the palms, with: *vajrahastāya asvatantrāya* (5), *sauṃ bauṃ hauṃ nityamaluptaśaktaye* (5), *śrīṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ nityamanantaśaktaye*.

One should also perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six limbs, beginning with the heart. Then, having performed the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās* according to the method previously described, one should meditate. The meditation will be explained further on. Now follows the Great Sixfold Placement (*mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*):
the universe (*prapañca*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), the forms (*mūrti*), the mantras, the deities, and the Mothers.
The installation known as Mahāṣoḍhā is the most excellent among all installations. || 1 ||

Therein, first is the *prapañcanyāsa*: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasauḥ shauḥ aṃ, obeisance to Śrī, whose form is the universe (*prapañca*)," and so forth; this application is to be understood according to the method previously described. Thus ends the *prapañcanyāsa*. [From the] *Kulārṇava*:

One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa), saying: "Salutations to the Primordial Mother Goddess (Parāmbādevī), who is by her very nature the root of the threefold entire phenomenal world. 1.

Thus: "Obeisance to the goddess Parāmbā, whose nature is the entire phenomenal universe"—this is the meaning of the instruction that one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the root mantra. Likewise:
"The placement of the phenomenal universe (prapañca-nyāsa) should be thus; now the placement of the worlds (bhuvana-nyāsa) is described."
At the end of the three-syllable root-vidyā, "amām" and "imatalam" should be placed. || 1 ||
Then one should recite "lokaṃ ca nilayaṃ caiva śatakoṭipadaṃ," followed by ten thousand repetitions from the beginning of the Guhyāyoginī up to the end of Mūladeva.
One should recite "vadedādhāraśaktyambādevyai" and place [the mantra] on the heart and the feet.

Thus, the meaning is that one should place it on the feet with the mantra: "aṃ āṃ iṃ, obeisance to the Mother Goddess Ādhāraśakti, who resides in the world of Atala, and who is joined with the hundred million Yoginīs beginning with Guhyā and the Root Deity."

O Dear One, having recited "imamūm" followed by "vitalam," "lokaguhyānte," and the one designated as "śata," and then the remainder as previously stated, one should place [the mantra] upon the two ankles.
"Ṛṃ ṛṃ Ḷṃ, O Dear One, having uttered [these syllables] which denote Sutala— the supreme secret and the inconceivable—
and the remainder as previously stated, one should place them on the two shanks."
Having uttered "ḶṂ EṂ AIṂ" and "Mahātala" along with the *Mahāghyādi-tantra*,
and having stated the remainder as before, O Goddess, one should place [the mantra] upon the knees.
Omauṃ, the supreme secret of Talātala, which is Svādhiṣṭhāna;
and the remainder is declared as before—O Goddess of the Gods, one should place these upon the two thighs.
Having uttered "Aṃ Aḥ," which is the netherworld (rasātala) and the secret known as knowledge (jñāna),
and having spoken the remainder as before, one should place it in the secret region.

Having likewise assigned the guttural class (ka-varga), the netherworld (pātāla), the secret ritual (kriyā), and Śeṣa, in the same manner as previously described, one should place them in the mūlādhāra.
O Dear One, having recited the *ca*-group, the secret of *bhūti*, and ŚrīḌākinī, as well as the remainder as previously stated, one should place them in the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
O Dear One, having uttered the *ṭa*-group of consonants at the end of the word *bhuvar-mahārahasya*, as well as *rākiṇī*,
and having recited the remainder as before, one should place it upon the region of the navel.
O Dear One, having recited the *tavarga*, which is the supreme secret of heaven, as well as Lākinī, and the remainder as previously stated, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart.
O Dear One, having recited the pavarga, the mahāgupta, and also the Kākinī in sequence,
and having uttered the remainder as previously described, one should place [the mantra] at the root of the palate.
O Dear One, having spoken of the group of letters beginning with *ya*, the people who are more secret, and even the illustrious Śākinī,
as well as the remainder as previously described, one should place them within the Command (*ājñā*).
O Dear One, having recited the *śa*-group, *tapas*, *atigupta*, and *śrīhākinī*,
as well as the remainder as previously stated, one should place them on the forehead.
O beloved, having recited "Laṃ Lakṣaḥ," "Satyamahāgupta," and also "Yākinī," and having spoken the remainder as before, one should place [it] in the *brahmarandhra*, O beloved. (15)

At the end of the root mantra consisting of three *tāra*s, one should utter "to the fourteen worlds" (*caturdaśabhuvam*). Then, one should perform the heart-mantra placement (*hṛd-nyāsa*) and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) for the venerable goddess Parāmbā, the Mistress of the [fourteen] worlds (*nādhipāyai śrīparāmbādevyai*). (16)
Having thus performed the assignment of the worlds (bhuvana-nyāsa), one should then perform the assignment of the forms (mūrti-nyāsa):
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu.
He is known as Madhusūdana, as well as Trivikrama and Vāmana;
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara. (18)
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
Akṣara, Ādya, Iṣṭadeśāna, Ugra, and likewise Ūrdhvanayana. (19)

She is supernatural power (ṛddhi) and possesses form; she is the destroyer, the sole leader who has severed all faults; she acts as one and flows like a torrent; she is the radiance of the collyrium that fulfills all desires.
And those wearing garlands of bones are proclaimed as the deities of the vowels:
Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, and Ugra. (21)
Mahādeva, Bhīma, Īśāna, the one called Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva— these are thus proclaimed.
Karabhadrā possesses the strength of birds and bestows fruits such as heaviness;
she is the pacifier of dharma, has a row of noses, and wears the crescent moon.
Consisting of meter, she is the abode of the world; thereafter she is the flowing star.
She bears the chisel and the drum of the sound of knowledge, and she is formidable with the sound of the *ṭhaṅkāra*.
These are the deities of the letters beginning with ka and ending with ṭha:
Brahmā, Prajāpati, Vedhas, Parameṣṭhin, and Pitāmaha. (25)
Vidhātṛ, Viriñca, Sraṣṭṛ, Caturānana,
and Hiraṇyagarbha— these names are said to refer respectively to Brahmā and the others.
The Yakṣiṇī Rañjanīlakṣmī, the wielder of the vajra, the bearer of the spear, whose abode is the six supports, the leader of all, with a smiling countenance. (27)
Lalitā and Kṣamā are declared to be the presiding deities of the *ya*-group;
at the end of the three *tāra*s and the root mantra, one should append the powers (*śakti*) consisting of the vowels and the initial letters [of each group]. (28)
One should place the fourth [syllable] joined with *namaḥ* on the head and the face,
and also on one's own shoulders, sides, belly, thighs, knees, calves, and feet.

O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should place [the syllables] from Dakṣa to Vāma, joined with the letters beginning with Ka and Bha, ending with Ṭha and Ḍa, and conjoined with Śakti. (30)
One should place [the deities] upon the feet, sides, arms, throat, and the five faces;
one should place Brahmā and the others, along with the letters beginning with *ya*, together with their Śaktis, upon the ten supports.
At the end of the three-syllable root mantra, one should place [the mantra] "Śrītrimūrtyātmikāyai Parāmbādevyai namaḥ" and perform its pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa).
The root-mantra of the three stars consists of *aṃ*, *āṃ*, and *iṃ*; there is one hundred thousand [recitations] and ten million [recitations].
Furthermore, there is a division according to all mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and consisting of single syllables. || 33 ||
Then, for the presiding deity (adhidevatā), it shall be complete and bestow all fruits;
likewise, one should utter "Oṃ Āyai Ekakūṭeśvaryambādevyai Namaḥ."

Thus, here the sequence for the extraction of the mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) following the installation of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) has been demonstrated: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ shauḥ aṃ āṃ iṃ*, salutation to the Goddess Ambā, the Sovereign of the Single Peak (Ekakūṭeśvarī), who is the presiding deity of all mantras consisting of single syllables beginning with the Praṇava— comprising one hundred thousand times ten million variations— and who bestows all fruits.

Thus, "one should place [the syllables] in the mūlādhāra"—this is the practical application. Likewise: the two-peaked [mantra] beginning with *ī*, *u*, *mū*, and *mā* etc., and the *haṃsa* etc., as before;
and the three-peaked [mantra] beginning with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *mā* etc., and the *vahni* etc., as before. (35)
And ḶMĒMAIM four hundred thousand times, with the moon and so forth as before;
OṂAUṂMAḤ five hundred thousand times, with the sun and so forth as before. (36)
Kaṃ and Khaṃ are six hundred thousand [syllables] each; Skanda and the others are as before, followed by the supreme.
Ghaṃ and Ṅaṃ are seven hundred thousand [syllables] each; Gaṇeśa and the others are as before, followed by the supreme. (37)
Chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ maṃ [jhaṃ] should be recited eight hundred thousand times for Vaṭuka and the others as before;
likewise, ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ should be recited nine hundred thousand times for Brahmā and the others as before.
Ḍaṃḍhaṃṇaṃ consists of one million and one hundred thousand repetitions, with Viṣṇu and others as before;
taṃthaṃdama consists of eleven million repetitions, with Rudra and others as before. (39)
Dhaṃ, naṃ, paṃ, and dvādaśalakṣaṃ; vāṇī and so forth, as before, followed by paraṃ. (Phaṃ, baṃ, bhaṃ, trayodaśalakṣaṃ; lakṣmī and so forth, as before, followed by paraṃ. || 40 ||

One should perform one million four hundred thousand repetitions of *maṃ yaṃ raṃ*, followed by *gaurī* and so forth as before; and one million five hundred thousand repetitions of *laṃ vaṃ śaṃ*, followed by *durgā* and so forth as before. (41)
One should recite "Ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ" sixteen hundred thousand times, as well as the Tripurā-mantra and others as before;
at the end of the root mantra with three *tāra*s (oṃ), one should utter the entire *mātṛkā*.

O Maheśvarī, during the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), one should perform the "all-pervading heart" (hṛdvyāpaka) for the goddess Parāmbikā, who is the presiding deity of the mantra, beginning with the syllable *saka*.
Beyond the navel, heart, throat, and the *ājñā* [cakra], which are the support (*ādhāra*) and the *liṅga*,
one proceeds to the *nirodhikā*, the half-moon (*ardhendu*), the point (*bindu*), and the stage of the digit (*kalā*).
O Kulanāyikā, one should place [the mantras] upon the faces beginning with Unmanī, as well as upon Nāda and Nādānta, and in the region of the Dhruvamaṇḍala. 45.
At the end of the root mantra consisting of three *tāra*s, one should append the phrase "sarvamantrātmikāyai devyai parā," and as before, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*).

Thus ends the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*). Now, the ritual placement of the deity (*devatānyāsa*): Having performed the ritual placement of the mantra in this manner, one should perform the ritual placement of the deity.
At the end of the root mantra preceded by the three *tāra*s, [one recites] "Amāṃ sahasrakoṭi ca. (47)
p. 145) At the end of the word *yoginīkula*, one should utter the word *sevitāyai*.
O Dear One, one should then pronounce the word *nivṛttyambā* for the Goddess, followed by *namaḥ*. (48)

The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ shauḥ sahasrakoṭiyoginīkulasevitāyai nivṛttyambādevyai namaḥ*, and so forth. One should recite *iṃ īṃ* for the installation of the Yoginīs, and the remainder should be uttered as before.
Uṃ ūṃ, and [one should worship] the knowledge of the ascetics; the remainder should be performed as before. || 49 ||
One should recite *ṛṃ* and *ṝṃ* as Śānta and likewise Śānti; the remainder should be recited as before.
One should recite *ḷṃ* and *ḹṃ* as Muni and likewise Śāntyatītā; the remainder should also be as before. (50)
"Eṃ Aiṃ Devaṃ," followed by "Hṛllekhā" at the end; one should recite the remainder as before.
"Oṃ Auṃ Rakṣaḥkula," and then "Gaganāṃ" as before, O Dear One. (51)
Aṃ aḥ, one should recite the Vidyādhara who is red-colored, with the remainder as before;
kaṃ khaṃ, the Siddha Mahocchuṣma, with the remainder as before. || 52 ||
One should utter "Gaṃ Ghaṃ Sādhyaṃ Karālāṃ," and the remainder as before; likewise, "Ṅaṃ Caṃ Apsarojayāṃ," and the remainder as before. || 53 ||
One should utter Chaṃ Jaṃ Gandharvavijayā and the remainder as before;
then Jhaṃ Ñaṃ at the end of the word "Guhyaka," followed by Ajitā as before. (54)
Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ belongs to Aparājitā Yakṣī; the rest is as before, followed by Para.
Ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ belongs to Kinnaravāmāmbā; the rest is as before, followed by Para. (55)
And [the syllable] ṇaṃtaṃ, the serpent Jyeṣṭhā, and Śeṣa as before;
and thaṃdaṃ, Pitṛraudrī, Ambā, and Śeṣa as before. (56)
Dhaṃ, Gaṇeśa, and Māyā, and Śeṣa as before;
then Paṃ and Pha at the end of the word Bhairava, and Kuṇḍalī as before. (57)
"Brahmā" and "Vaṭukakālī," and the rest as before;
likewise "Maṃyaṃ" at the end of the word "Kṣetra," and "Kālarātrī" as before. (58)
*Raṃ laṃ* for the divine Pramathabhagavatī, and the rest as before;
*vaṃ śaṃ* for Brahmā, and for Sarveśvaryambā, the rest as before. (59)
One should worship Ṣaṃ Saṃ as Viṣṇu, the omniscient, and Śeṣa as before;
likewise, Haṃ Laṃ as Rudra, the creator of all, and the remainder as before.
One should worship Kṣaṃ as the power of the moving and the unmoving, and Śeṣa as before, in the thumbs, ankles, shanks, knees, thighs, hips, and sides. (61)
O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) on the breasts, armpits, shoulders, roots of the ears, and the head, proceeding in order from the right side to the left. 62.
At the end of the three-syllable root mantra, one should utter the entire Mātṛkā,
as well as the presiding deity of all, Śrī Parāmbikā, for the sake of worship.
One should say "Salutation to the Goddess" and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa), O Dear One;
thus the placement of the deities (devatā-nyāsa) is completed, and now the placement of the Mothers (mātṛ-nyāsa) is described.
At the end of the three-syllable root mantra, one should utter the letter 'ka' followed by "anantakoṭi";
then, at the end of the word "bhūcarīkula," one should say the word "sahitāyai. (65)
At the end of "Āṃ," one should utter "namaḥ" followed by "Maṅgalāmbādevyai. At the end of "Āṃ," however, one should speak the word "Brahmāṇyambādevyai."
To Anantakoṭibhūta at the end of the family, and to Sahita; to Akṣa, the Lord of Maṅgala, and to Asitāṅga at the end; to Aṅkṣa. (67)
O Dear One, at the end of Bhairava, one should utter "Namaḥ to the Nātha";
then the cavarga, Khecarī, Mīlā, Carcikā, and Maheśvarī. (68)
O Dear One, one should utter "Namaḥ" to the Lord Vetāla;
having spoken the remainder as previously stated, I shall then explain further, O Maheśvarī. (69)
One should utter the *ṭa*-group, the *pātālacarī* seed-syllable *mūṃ*, and *yogeśvarī*; one should utter *kaumārī*, the *piśāca* seed-syllable *mūṃ*, *yogeśa*, and *caṇḍaka*.
The *tavarga* [is assigned to] Dikcarī, the *ṛ-sāṃ* [to] Harasiddhā, and the Vaiṣṇavī;
Apasmāra, Harasiddhi, and Krodha are likewise as before. (71)
Then [one should worship] the Pavarga [letters], Giricarī, the syllable *aiṃ*, and then *kilikila*; [then] Indrāṇī, the syllable *eṃ*, and Kapālin at the end of *kilikila*. (73)
At the end of the *śa*-group [of consonants], one should worship Vanacarī, Mauṃvā, Kālādirātri, Cāmuṇḍā, Pretamāyā, and the terrifying Kālarātri. (75)
One should likewise utter Saṃhārabhairava and the remainder as before;
at the end of the three *tāra*s and the root mantra, [one should add] the word "Mātṛbhairava. (76)
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) ending with "namas" for Adhipāyī Parādevī;
O Maheśānī, one should perform the Mātṛ-nyāsa upon the eight supports (ādhāras).

Having thus deposited his body [in the sacred sites], O Goddess, he should meditate on the God with undistracted mind upon the delightful Golden Island situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar. (78)
Seated upon a lotus on a glorious lion-throne made of the nine gems, within a pavilion of fresh rubies situated in the midst of a forest of wish-fulfilling trees.
Seated within a triangle, possessing a radiance equal to the moon and the sun, joined with Ambikā as half [of his body], and adorned with distinct ornaments. (80)
(Śrīvi. 19, p.
146) Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, eternally sixteen years of age, with a lotus-face of gentle smiles, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-ornament. (81)
Adorned with celestial garments, garlands, and unguents, and decorated with divine ornaments,
he holds in his hands a drinking vessel, the *cinmudrā*, a trident, and a book.
He bears the perfect accomplishment of knowledge, his face and eyes ever gazing upon bliss,
and he is served by the entire host of deities arisen from the Great Ṣoḍhā.
Thus, one should meditate upon Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara within the lotus of the heart;
O Goddess, one may remember him in male form or contemplate him in female form.
Alternatively, one should meditate on the partless [Brahman], characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
one should meditate on that which consists of all splendor and has the form of both the moving and the unmoving.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, he should display the ten mudrās:
the Yoni, the Liṅga, the Surabhi, and the four Heti-mudrās.
"Vanamālā, Nabhomudrā, and Mahāmudrā, in this order.
Then, one should meditate upon the venerable Guru on the crown of the head, as follows:
"In a thousand-petaled lotus, [he who possesses] the luster of the full moon..."

One should meditate upon the Guru, who bears in his lotus-hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is adorned with pure fragrant flowers and garments, whose face and eyes are serene, who embodies the form of all deities, and who is seated upon a swan at the crown of one's head, preceded by the recitation of his name.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the fruit of the Great Sixfold Deposition (*mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*), it is stated in the *Śrīkulārṇava*:

"O Goddess, when this deposition has been performed in this manner, the practitioner of mantra becomes directly the Supreme Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt, for he is capable of both restraint and grace. (1)
I bow to him who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Mahāṣoḍhā day after day; all the gods pay homage to him—of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Mahāṣoḍhā;
this is declared to be the divine field extending ten yojanas in every direction.
O Goddess, wherever a man goes after performing this nyāsa,
there he shall find prosperity, victory, gain, honor, and prowess, O Beloved.
He who salutes one who has performed the Mahāṣoḍhā ritual placement (nyāsa) without first looking upon them meets with death in an instant, even if Śiva himself were his protector.
Whoever performs this ritual placement (nyāsa) named Vajrapañjara [protects themselves from] those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, on the earth, in mountains, in water, and in forests.
O Dear One, ghosts, vetālas, gods, rākṣasas, grahas, and the like,
with minds seized by fear, do not look upon the practitioner.
The deities beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as all the sages and lords of seers, perform the ritual placement known as Mahāṣoḍhā.
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? One should reveal [this] to a worthy disciple; he attains imperishable perfection and should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in secret.
There is nothing higher than this in the world for the direct attainment of the state of divinity; there is no doubt about this—it is the truth, the truth, without a shadow of a doubt. || 10 ||
Entry into the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya), contemplation upon the Supreme Abode (Parāprāsāda), and thorough knowledge of the Great Ṣoḍhā—these are not the fruit of meager austerity. || 11 ||
Thus ends the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa. Now, the Turīyavidyā—this is indeed the supreme Ṣoḍaśī:
*sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ka-e-ī-la-ha-sa-ka-ha-la-sa-ka-la-hrīṃ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ*. This is the Turīyavidyā. Now, the Caraṇavidyās:
The Praṇava, the three stars (Om Āḥ Hūṃ), the words *haṃsaḥ śivaḥ hsauḥ*, *so'ham*, the Turīya-vidyā, and then the word *cidānanda*. || 12 ||
Likewise, "I am light" is proclaimed first;
then, as before, everything should be recited following the words *saccidānanda*. (13)
Then the second is proclaimed as "I am light" (jyotir aham).
Then, having recited as before, one should utter: "I alone am" (aham evāsmi). || 14 ||
The third, however, is designated as the three-fold movement; the supreme teacher should place it upon the head with the *saṃghaṭṭamudrā*. (15)
Thus ends the three-fold practice. Now follows the *śambhucaraṇa*:
one should utter the *praṇava*, the triple-star (*tritāra*), and the *praṇava* again; then "I am that which I am," "I am Brahman," and "I am He. (16)
At the end of the word *svacchaprakāśa* is *paripūrṇaparāpara*;
at the end of *mahāprakāśa* follows the state of *pūrṇānanda*. (17)

"At the end [of the name] 'the Lord's venerable sandals (nāthaśrīpādukā),' one should worship," with "one should place [this on] the head" being the understood remainder. [This refers to] the feet of Śambhu. The five Mothers have already been explained in detail.
The nine Lords beginning with Unmanākāśa and the nine Lords beginning with Ātmānanda [are also to be worshipped].
The sequence of one's own lineage and so forth has already been explained. Now, the sixteen root-mantras:
(1) One should utter the three *tāras* preceded by the *praṇava*, followed by the word "Svacchā," then "Prakāśaparipūrṇā," and "Parāparamahā. || 1 ||
I worship the Siddhividyākula, the Māyā-bīja, and Kula; and I worship the Śrīpādukā of the root-vidyā of the Yoginīs. || 2 ||
(2) The seed-syllable *parā* of the *Śrīprāsāda*, which awakens one’s own self; and the seed-syllable *parā* of the *Prāsāda*, namely *śrīprāsādaparā*. || 3 ||
"O Mother!"—with these words, I worship the venerable sandals of the Root-Vidyā.
(3) [The mantra consists of] the three Tāras preceded by the Praṇava, followed by Vāgbhava and Makaradhvaja. (4)
At the end of the words *klinne* and *kledini*, [follow] the liquid of the great intoxication-word, two *kāmarāja*s, two *mohaya*s, and the heart of *kāmarāja*. (5)
This Vidyā, ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), is an extremely secret and supreme Yoginī.
One should indeed utter the three Tāras preceded by the Praṇava, followed by "Haṃsaḥ" and "Svacchā. (6)
To the Supreme Self, the state of the Haṃsa, the highest bliss—svāhā hsau hsau. This is the Vidyā preceded by the root-mantra of Śambhu.
(5) One should utter the state of the Great Bindu, which consists of the Praṇava and the three Tārakas, Māyā, Nitya, Sphurattā, and the Self consisting of consciousness and bliss. 8.
At the end of the pervasive [mantra], one should utter the word *mātṛ* and the word *svarūpiṇī*;
preceded by the *praṇava* and the three *tārakas*, this is indeed declared by the wise as *mīmiya*.
The root-vidyā of Hṛllekhā (consisting of the three stars preceded by the *praṇava*), as well as Māyā and the great station of Kula, which are of the nature of pure light. (10)
O Īśvarī, this is the Śrībīja: Mālinī, Vāk, Kulagarbha, Mātṛkā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Samayānta, and Vimalā. 11.
And at the end of the *samaya*, it is called the *vimalamūlavidyā*:
the *tāra* (OM), three *tāras*, the *haṃsa*, and then the *nityaprakāśa*. (12)
Then, from the state of *lini*, there is the command-word (*ājñāpada*): "O Kulakuṇḍā belonging to the Self!
and "O Siddhā Mahābhairavī!"—this is the non-dual awakening of the Self. (13)
O Ambā, O Bhagavatī, at the end [of the mantra] is "māyā" (h), "huṃ", and "iyam īśvarī";
O Parameśvarī, with "parabodhinī" at the end of the root [mantra], it becomes the Vidyā. 14.
One should utter "Tāra," then three "Tāras," and finally "Mokṣa";
this is recited as the root mantra of the five syllables of the Kula. || 15 ||
Having uttered *Tāra* and three *Tāras*, the fifteen-syllable *Lopā* is this root-vidyā of Caitanya Tripurā, O Supreme Goddess. (16)
(10) At the end of the three *tāras*, one should extract the seed-syllable *vāgbhava*;
thereafter [comes] the state that is pure, subtle, formless, and free from conceptual construction. 17.
At the end of the form of the Supreme Brahman (Parabrahma-svarūpī), at the end of Ṇiklīm, and at the end of Parāpada,
one should extract the third seed-syllable of Bālā, which is the word Nanda-śakti.
This, however, is the supreme Kaulinī of Śambhānandanātha;
she is declared by those learned in all the Āgamas to be the Root-Vidyā. (19)
(11) Tāra, three Tāras, Haṃsa, So’haṃ, Svacchāntānanda;
at the end of Parama, Haṃsaparamātmane, followed by Vahnivallabhā. 20.
The *mūlavidyā* is proclaimed as the contemplation of the Supreme Guru.
(12) After the three *tāras*, there should be the word "Aghora. || 21 ||

Then one should extract the state beyond the void (vyomātītapada), the state of the Lord who is both supreme and non-supreme (nāthaparāparapada), the state beyond the void (vyomātītapada), and the state of the Mother, the Sovereign of the Void (vyomeśvaryambāpada). || 22 ||
This supreme goddess, known as Anāmā, is declared to be the root-vidyā.
One should extract the syllable Om, or the three Om-s, Vāṇī, and the seed-syllables Iṃ, Īṃ, and Uṃ. (13, 23)
O Maheśvarī, the root-vidyā called Saṃketasārā has been declared:
[it begins with] Tāra, three Tāras, Māyā, and then the word "Bhagavatī. (14) (24)
One should write "vicce vāgvādinī ca," which is the great lake of Kāmarāja;
then "mahāmātaṅgini vāṇīṃ klinne blūṃ strīṃ"—this is what one should inscribe. (25)
The Vidyā known as Anuttarādivāgvādinī has been fully proclaimed.
[It consists of] the Tāra, three Tāras, the Parā of the Mansion (Prāsāda), and then Khecarī. (15–26)
In the center of the Sampatpradā [cakra], one should write Śrīprāsādaparā;
this indeed is declared to be the unsurpassed Mūlavidyā of Śaṅkara.
(16) Having uttered the Turīyavidyā, O Supreme Goddess, one should extract [the mantra] beginning with "Sarvānandamayī" as Mahātripurasundarī. 28.
“O Īśānī, this root-vidyā has been declared as the bestower of desired fruits.
Thus end the sixteen vidyās. Now, the vidyās of the six ādhāras; therein, the mantra of Parameśvara:
having extracted the five *tāra*s (oṃs), then the *vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*) along with *rahasra* (hrīṃ).
Then the seed-syllable PHREM should be written, followed by the mantra of the Supreme Lord. || 1 ||
One should place the mantra of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) in the center of the pericarp within the command (*ājñā*).
Thus ends the mantra of the Supreme Lord. Now, the mantra of Viśveśvara:
having uttered the five *tāra*s (oṃs), one should extract the *vāgbhava* (*hrīṃ*) along with *hasrūṃ*.
O Kubjikā, "Phreṃ" is for the Viśuddha [cakra], while "Viccīśvara" is the great mantra. || 1 ||
Thus ends the Vicceśvara mantra. Now follows the Haṃseśvara mantra:
having uttered the five *tāras*, one should extract the *vāgbhava* (*hasraiṃ*). Then the word *kubjikāyai*, followed by *hsaphraṃ* and likewise *vicce*. (1)
"The great mantra of Haṃseśvara abides in the state of the Unstruck (anāhata).
Thus ends the mantra of Haṃseśvara. Now, the mantra of Saṃvarteśa:
having extracted five *tāra*s (oṃs), [one adds] hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ in the same manner.
Ha saḥ oṃ kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ, likewise kṣrīṃ, and after that the pair kiṇi. || 1 ||
Hasaphrāṃ hasaphramato hasphrīṃ vicce hrauṃ, and the two *hasat*s;
hasaphreṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ, and the *praṇava* itself. || 2 ||
Having uttered *hasa-kṣama-la-vān*, then *yaraṃ* and likewise *hasa*, then *kṣama-lān* and *vaya-rūṃ*, that seed-syllable is joined with the left eye (*i*). (3)
Then the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], followed by *hasrīṃ*, *hasrūṃ*, and *hasrāṃ*;
then *hrīṃ*, *hraṃ*, *hrāṃ*, and *hlāṃ*, and thereafter the word "Vāṇī," and then "Nitye Bhagavati. (4)
Hasaphraṃ Kuleśvari, followed by Hrāṃ Hrūṃ Hlīṃ Hlāṃ Hvīṃ Huṃ; thereafter Hye Hauṃ Ṅa Ña Ṇa Na Ān Me, and likewise Kṣrāṃ Kṣrīṃ Kṣrūṃ Kṣra. || 5 ||
One should utter *kṣraṃ śrī phaṭ* and *hsrauṃ phreṃ*, followed by *aghoramukhi*.
Then [one says] *kubjikāyai*, and thereafter *chrāṃ chraṃ chrīṃ ghore*. (6)
"Aghore, Vāyu, Vahni, Indra, Vaṃ, Saṃ, Haṃ, two Kiṇis, a pair of Mahākiṇis, and Vicce—this is the great mantra of Saṃvarteśa. (7)
