It should be placed in the great wheel of the Svādhiṣṭhāna by the best of practitioners.
Thus ends the Saṃvarteśvara mantra. Now, the Dvīpeśvara mantra:
having uttered the five *tāra*s, then *hasaphrūṃ*, the *vāgbhava*.
Then the word *rigaṭini* and the word *piṅgaṭini*. || 1 ||
O fair-faced one, this mantra of the Lord of the Island has been declared;
it should be placed in the Maṇipūraka-cakra by the best of practitioners. || 2 ||

Thus ends the mantra of Dvīpeśvara. Now follows the mantra of Navātmeśvara: Having uttered the five *tāra*s (om), and then *sahakṣamalava*, [one says] *rayūṃ namo bhagavati hasphreṃ*; after this comes the seed-syllable (*bīja*). || 1 ||
Then for Kubjikā: *hrāṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ* and *ḍ ña ṇa n me*;
then for Aghoramukhī: *chrāṃ chrūṃ chrīṃ*, followed by two *kiṇi*s and two more *kiṇi*s.
"VICCE" shall be the mantra of Navātmeśvara in the root-lotus.
Thus ends the mantra of Navātmeśvara. Thus end the Śāmbhava mantras of the six lineages (ṣaḍanvaya). Then follows the meditation (dhyāna): The Guru is like a thousand suns, possessing great radiance.
The glorious Paraśambhu, unborn and immutable, is the Lord of the six lineages. || 1 ||
He is endowed with six faces and twelve flashing eyes;
his broad waist is adorned with a tiger skin and a garland of severed heads.
He was completely covered with various garlands of flowers from the pārijāta tree and other firm jewels;
his belly was spread wide by his fangs, and his thumb rested upon the lotus-navel of Brahmā.
Adorned with various ornaments, the all-knowing one who removes the bonds of the individual soul (paśu),
he possesses a massive body and wields a trident, sword, arrow, spear, goad, and an excellent staff.
With hands holding a skull, a fruit, a bow, and a noose, and granting fearlessness,
he is surrounded by deities and sports in the cremation ground on Mount Mānasottara.
Thus one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, resplendent with the weight of her breasts;
having thus meditated and performed worship, one should again [recite] the two root-mantras.
Having practiced thoroughly and then offered [the worship], one should meditate upon the two feet.

The sequence of rays has already been explained previously. Now, the different types of mantras of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) will be described hereafter. Furthermore, in another Tantra, there are the Samaya-vidyās, as follows:
Śrīvidyā, Bagalā, Kālarātri,
Jayadurgā, and Chinnamastā— these are proclaimed as the five Samayas.

The Śrīvidyā has been described previously. Now, regarding Bagalā: for this Śrī-Bagalāmukhī mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī-Bagalāmukhī is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Svāhā is the power (śakti), Kīlaya is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is as a limb of Śrīvidyā. Oṃ Hrīṃ, Bagalāmukhi, [of] all the wicked...
"Paralyze the speech, the mouth, and the feet; pin the tongue; destroy the intellect—hrīṃ oṃ svāhā. These are the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*). The visualization (*dhyāna*):
In the center, upon a jeweled altar within a pavilion of gems in the ocean of nectar...
I worship the Goddess who is seated upon a lion-throne, whose complexion is deep yellow,
whose limbs are adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands,
and who holds a mallet and the tongue of her enemy.
Oṃ hrīṃ, O Bagalāmukhī, paralyze the speech, mouth, and feet of all the wicked;
nail down their tongues and destroy their intellect! Hrīṃ oṃ svāhā. Thus ends [the mantra of] Bagalāmukhī.
Now, Kālarātri: For this venerable Kālarātri mantra, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi) and Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ).
The deity is Śrī Kālarātri; *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*); *hūṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*);

the application (*viniyoga*) is as a limb of the Śrīvidyā; the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the *māyā*-seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
(149) She resembles the reddish sun, her form intoxicated with youth;
she has four arms, three eyes, a terrifying appearance, and the moon as her crest-ornament. || 1 ||
Seated upon a corpse-seat, she grants all desires to those who worship her;
in her right hands she holds the gesture of fearlessness and a noose, and in her left hands the earth itself.
One should meditate upon the goddess Kālarātri, who holds a red staff. [Recite:

Aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ! O Mistress of Time (Kāleśvarī), you who captivate the minds of all people, you who paralyze the mouths of all, you who bring all kings under your control, you who crush all the wicked, and you who attract all women and men!

"Break, break the fetters of bondage! Subdue, subdue all enemies! Destroy, destroy hatred! Crush, crush it! Paralyze, paralyze everything! Expel, expel [them]! Bring everything under control, bring it under control! O Gaṇeśvarī, beloved of the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*! Thus ends Kālarātri. Now, [the mantra of]...

Jayadurgā: For this Jayadurgā mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Jayadurgā is the deity (devatā), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Svāhā is the power (śakti), Rakṣiṇi is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is as a limb of Śrīvidyā. Oṃ, Durge, Durge, Rakṣaṇi, Svāhā; thus: Oṃ Durge Durge Rakṣiṇi Svāhā.
The six-limbed mantras. Meditation:

[One should meditate on her] who has the luster of molten gold, who strikes fear into the hosts of enemies with her sidelong glances, who bears a crescent moon upon her crown, and who, with her hands, holds a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident, and possesses three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, surrounded by the thirty gods, and served by those desiring spiritual perfection. || 1 ||

Thus: *Oṃ durge durge rakṣiṇi svāhā*; this is Jayadurgā. Now, the Chinnamastās: for this Triśakti mantra, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Samrāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), the venerable Vajravairocanīyā is the deity (*devatā*), *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), *phaṭ* is the bolt (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is as a limb of the Śrīvidyā. *Oṃ*.

Oṃ khaḍgāya svāhā, Oṃ īṃ sukhaḍgāya svāhā, Oṃ ūṃ śrīṃ virājāya svāhā, Oṃ aiṃ pāśāya svāhā, Oṃ auṃ aṅkuśāya svāhā, Oṃ aḥ asurāntakāya svāhā— these are the mantras for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-mantraḥ). The meditation (dhyāna):
One should meditate on a pure, blooming, white lotus within one's own navel;
in the center of that lotus calyx is the mandala of the fiercely radiant sun.
Resembling a hibiscus flower and similar to a fresh bandhūka blossom,
it is adorned with the circles of the wombs marked by the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
In the center, however, is that Great Goddess, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
who holds her own severed head in her left hand— Chinnamastā.
With her mouth wide open, she was terrifying, licking her fierce tongue,
and drinking the blood flowing from her own throat onto the earth.
Her mass of hair is disheveled and adorned with various flowers;
in her right hand she holds a razor, and she is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
The goddess is sky-clad, most terrible, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture,
wearing a garland of bones, and having a serpent as her sacred thread.
And some ministers meditate upon her who is seated for the sake of pleasure, always sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts. (7)
When attached to perverse passion, one should meditate upon Rati and Manobhava,
mounted in the yoni-mudrā and seated in a variegated posture.
"Accompanied by Varṇinī and Ḍākinī through the union of the left and right [channels].
Thus: *Śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is Chinnamastā. These are the *samaya* mantras.
Having recited the Gāyatrī, the deities of each respective enclosure (āvṛti) should be worshipped with effort for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
According to this statement, the *gāyatrīs* of the goddesses of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) of the Śrīcakra are proclaimed:
"Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk; may that Tusked One (Dantī) inspire us.
This is the *Gāyatrī* of Gaṇapati.
"May we know the one who rescues from calamity; may we meditate upon Vaṭukeśvara; may that Hero inspire us"—this is the Gāyatrī of Vaṭuka.
"Oṃ, we know the sky-clad one; we meditate upon the one with a skull in hand; may that Kṣetrapāla inspire us. This is the Gāyatrī of Kṣetrapāla.
"Oṃ, we know the all-pervading one; we meditate upon the one of manifold forms; may that Yoginī inspire us. This is [the Gāyatrī of the Yoginī].
The Yoginī-gāyatrī:
*Oṃ devarājāya vidmahe vajrahastāya dhīmahi tannaḥ śakraḥ pracodayāt*.
This is the Indra-gāyatrī.
"May we know Rudranetra; may we meditate upon him who holds a spear in his hand; may that Fire inspire us"—this is the Gāyatrī of Fire.
"Oṃ, may we know Vaivasvata; may we meditate upon him who holds a staff in his hand; may that Yama inspire us"—thus [is the Gāyatrī of Yama].
The Yamagāyatrī:
*Oṃ niśācarāya vidmahe khaḍgahastāya dhīmahi tanno nirṛtiḥ pracodayāt*. This is the Nirṛtigāyatrī.

"May we know the one with pure hands; may we meditate upon the one with noose in hand; may that Varuṇa inspire us"—this is the *gāyatrī* of Varuṇa. "May we know the one who is the life-force of all; may we meditate upon the one with staff in hand; may that Vāyu inspire us"—thus [it is said].
The Gāyatrī of Vāyu:
"We know the Lord of Yakṣas; we meditate upon him who holds a mace in his hand; may that Yakṣa inspire us.
This is the Gāyatrī of Kubera.

Īśvara said: One should fashion a beautiful pedestal with ten parts of gold, sixteen parts of silver, and one part of copper.
Upon that pedestal, one should cause the construction of the Śrīcakra;
it is declared to bestow peace, to nourish, and to utterly destroy all enemies.
It is considered to be the producer of longevity and health, the bestower of luster, and the giver of nourishment.
Listen now to the threefold nature of the Cakra: the Bhūprastāra and the Ardhameruka.
O Goddess, for those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), the arrangement is with downward lines;
for those dwelling in the world of mortals, it is with upward lines, which brings great peace.
O Maheśvarī, among the machines (yantras) that reside in the heavenly worlds and elsewhere, the one named Meru begins from the outer city (bhūpura) and extends to the point of Bindu.
I have described everything as gradually ascending in the form of Mount Meru;
it is proclaimed that there are nine horizontal lines, with the uppermost line being vertical.
The terrestrial expansion resulting from the conjunction of the lower lines has been declared by me;
out of affection, the true nature of the seed of the yantra has been revealed to you by me. (11)
"It must be guarded by you constantly, O auspicious lady, like your own womb.
Thus it is said in the *Śrītantrarāja*:
"Beginning from the square [mandala], one should proceed in sequence through the nine wheels."
From the center of the elevated and non-elevated [points], there shall be the wheel, destruction, and wealth. || 1 ||
(155) By rising three steps at a time, one attains that state of non-procreation and gains prosperity;
rising by the sequence of one, two, or six steps conduces to both fortune and fame.
"Nine [years] of equal form for the accomplishment of all desired aims.
Thus, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"O Goddess, [the result is] elevation in due order, then the acquisition of wealth, and thereafter death."
On the earth-circle, there should be a sixteen-spoked and an eight-spoked wheel, both equal [in size]. || 1 ||
O Īśānī, the remaining [portion] should be raised; it bestows wealth, attainment, and progeny. O Goddess, it should be square and even, with sixteen spokes and so forth, ending in a bindu.
O Goddess, that which is mutually elevated leads to prosperity and fame;
it begins from a square and extends with equal lines to the center-point.
"Likewise, prosperity, fame, and health conduce to immortality.
Thus it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Furthermore, in the case of lead, bell-metal, and so forth, the result is the opposite of what was previously stated."
One should never place [the image] upon a wooden plank, a cloth, or a wall. || 1 ||
If [a debt] has been established through delusion, greed, or even ignorance,
it utterly destroys one's family, wealth, and offspring in every way.
Thus it is said. In the *Lakṣasāgara*: "It should never be done with tin, lead, or iron.
Thus it is stated in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*.
The fire [pit] is one finger-breadth in width, extending east-west and north-south.
A beautiful pedestal for the image should be made measuring one pala.
One should construct a square measuring half a barley-corn on all sides;
upon that pedestal, one should fashion the Śrīcakra.
Thus, in the Sautrāmaṇī-tantra:
"A straight line indicates prosperity; a curved line indicates poverty.
The fire-altar (agni) shall be one finger-breadth in width and half a barley-corn in height. Thus it is said.
The width for gold and likewise for silver is one finger-breadth;
for copper it is the same as the previously mentioned number [one finger]; for rubies and other gems, it is according to one's desire.
A *pala* is measured as three hundred and twenty *guñjās*. Regarding the measurement of a finger (*aṅgula*), the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* states:
"The *mānāntara-aṅgula* is measured by eight barley grains placed side-by-side."
Or, the interval between measures shall be three rice grains placed in a straight line. || 1 ||

Thus [it is said]: "Furthermore, the construction of the altar (vedikā), the pedestal (pīṭha), the palanquin (śivikā), the chariot (ratha), and so forth, must be according to the *mānāṅgula* alone, and not by any other [measure]. Since the Śrīcakra is designated by the word "pedestal" (pīṭha) in this statement, its measurement should be understood as being by the *mānāṅgula* alone. In this regard:

The three wheels ending with the eight-spoked [wheel] from the center are of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); the two ten-spoked wheels and the fourteen-spoked wheel—these three wheels—are of the nature of maintenance (*sthiti*); and above those, the three wheels beginning with the eight-petaled lotus and ending with the outer square (*bhūpura*) are of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Thus it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:

The Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity is said to consist of a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, two sets of ten corners, a sixteen-cornered figure, a twelve-cornered figure, a circle, three circles, and three abodes of the Earth. || 1 ||
Thus, in the *Subhagodaya*:
"By means of the four wheels of Śiva and the five wheels of Śakti, the Śrīcakra—consisting of Śiva and Śakti and known as the body of Śiva and Śivā—is to be understood. (1)
Thus [says] Śrī Bhūtabhairava:
"O Maheśānī, those who arrange the filaments within this mantra—the Bhairavas, together with the Yoginīs, indeed inflict harm upon them. (1)

According to this statement, there are no filaments here. In the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*: "And one should fashion a very beautiful yantra, measuring one cubit, upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).
However, in the *Tantrarāja*:
For the consecration ceremony, the Śrīcakra should be nine cubits or three cubits in size;
for daily worship on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), a space of one cubit is recommended.
"However, in the case of creating [images] out of jewels and such, pride may arise by the power of desire. Likewise:
"Having filled the Śrīcakra with red pigment, one should spread it upon the ground;
all obstacles will perish, and one shall obtain whatever is desired. (1)
One-tenth part [of copper] for gold, likewise one-twentieth for copper, and sixteen parts for silver;
these three metals are auspicious.
Whoever indeed worships in this wheel shall attain good fortune;
he quickly becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
O beloved, [this should be done] on a yantra fashioned from coral,
or else from ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, crystal, or even emerald.
One certainly obtains wealth, sons, as well as a wife and fame;
a copper yantra bestows beauty, while one of gold destroys enemies. (5)
Silver bestows security, and crystal grants all accomplishments;
yet [these qualities are lost] when [the vessel] is chipped, cracked, broken, fallen, or devoid of human care.
When [the fire] has been burnt, touched by an unworthy animal, fallen onto impure grounds, worshipped with another mantra, or defiled by the touch of a fallen person; || 7 ||
Moreover, O beloved, even the gods would not remain present for ten days if the machine were burnt,
shattered, or stolen by a thief.
One should observe a fast for one day without sloth and recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire offerings and libations.
Having gratified the guru with true devotion, one should also feed the brahmins;
some say a hundred thousand or ten thousand.
If a fool ever breaks [an image] that has its marks effaced or is marred by cracks and the like, death will certainly befall him. (1)
Therefore, O Goddess, one should cast it into the king of holy fords, or into the best of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, or into the ocean; otherwise, one shall incur suffering.
Thus, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "Seated upon a red seat, one should perform the drawing of the yantra; one should draw the Śakti seated upon the Śakti, once, in its full extent. (1)
One should enclose it with fire according to the sequence for breaking the joints;
having extended the lines toward the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, one should join them.
O Goddess, in that very same manner, two sets of ten corners arise;
the wise one should draw the lines of the four central corners [toward the center]. (3)
One should effect the piercing of their junction so that the mantra becomes twelve-syllabled,
just as the union of the equilateral triangle and the power (śakti) bestows happiness upon the two eyes.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus without filaments, beautiful in its form, with straight lines manifesting through the division of its joints, extending outward.
In that same manner, O Supreme Goddess, one should indeed draw an excellent sixteen-petaled lotus, perfectly circular; then, one should draw the circle of the earth.
"One should cast a flower there [upon] that which has four doors and is richly adorned. Thus it is said.
A wise man should draw the pedestal for worship (*arcāpīṭha*) upon a Kashmiri mirror or birch bark, using a stylus made of gold mixed with saffron and camphor. (1)
One should draw it on a cloth or a metallic plate mixed with vermilion powder; or else, O Goddess, one may draw it well-lined with saffron upon the ground.
Or one may draw this wheel with vermilion powder for the attainment of all goals, O Maheśānī; it is adorned with a dot (bindu) in its center.
Then, O Maheśānī, there is a triangle, an eight-spoked wheel, a ten-spoked wheel, another ten-spoked wheel, and a sixteen-spoked wheel; this, O beloved, is the central wheel.
O Goddess of the gods, O Pārvatī, the entire center, ending with the Baindava and the eight triangles,
is joined by forty bhagas as well as three bhagas.
O Dear One, it has eight petals, sixteen petals, and is square in sequence;
O Blessed Lady, this Navātman should be marked with nine yonis.
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess of gods, there is no doubt that even the Śrīcakra is in the form of Meru;
the letter *la*, which is the seed-syllable of the Earth, is therein called the city. (1)
O auspicious lady, the letter *sa* is the moon, consisting of sixteen digits (*kalās*). Therefore, the sixteen-petaled lotus is called *ha*, which is Śiva. (2)
Likewise, O auspicious lady, the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti) arises from that; therefore, there shall be an eight-petaled lotus. The letter *ī* is Mahāmāyā, who [presides over] the fourteen worlds.
O Dear One, protecting the northeast from that [direction], she becomes Śakti;
stationed in the tenth place, she alone gives birth to the three worlds.
Known as the source of the universe, she is the tenfold form of Viṣṇu;
from the letter Ra, O Supreme Goddess, she expands, pervading the Cakra.
From that letter *ra*, the imperishable light, the ten-cornered supreme [triangle], arises;
it is the fire endowed with the ten digits (*kalās*), the initiator of the ten-cornered [figure].
O Goddess, from the letter *ka* arises Mādana, who is Śiva in his eightfold form; his source is then the wheel marked with the eight *yoni*s.

Since the half-mora (ardhamātrā) gives birth to the qualities (guṇas) and consists of differentiation, the womb (yoni) takes the form of a triangle; through the point (bindu), it becomes the state of the point (baindava).
O lady of excellent hips, that form of Kāmeśvara, which is the very nature of the support of the universe,
is indeed the Śrīcakra, arising from the syllables of the Śrīvidyā.
There, sitting facing the east on a level and richly prepared patch of ground, one should draw the Cakrarāja with vermilion powder or with colored dust.
One should draw a wheel upon the ground with saffron powder,
with straight lines, pleasing to the eye, with even joints and straight segments.
Alternatively, having fashioned a cloth from gold, silver, copper, or precious minerals,
[one should place it] upon a sacred wooden board made of red sandalwood.

Having prepared the cloth, O beloved, one should write upon it with a golden pen using yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), musk (*kastūrī*), sandalwood (*candana*), and camphor (*indu*). (13)
The preceptor should draw a straight line from Īśāna to Agni;
then, having drawn two lines from the tips of those [lines] at Īśāna and Agni, he should pull them together.
Having unified them within the western [direction], O Dear One, there is one supreme Śakti;
one should draw this in the form of a triangle above her.
The form of a triangle is said to consist of two powers;
one should draw it like a measuring rod from the tip of the eastern power.
O Supreme Goddess, one should then draw a line from the junction of those two powers toward the corner of the wind-demon (the northwest), following the sequence for breaking the joints.
Having drawn lines from the two corners toward its tip, make them extend toward the east;
O Goddess praised by heroes, this is the fire-maṇḍala with its apex pointing east.
And that triad came into being at the end; listen to that, O lady of beautiful countenance, from the two corners formed by Pūrvaśakti and Īśa-vahni, O goddess worshipped by the gods. (19)
Having extended the eastern line from the western fire-corner,
one should likewise draw a western-going line from the wind and rakṣasa corners.
Having expanded it, O Goddess, one should join it according to the sequence of the divisions of power (śaktibheda),
with the tip of the womb [line] in the eastern region, proceeding in order from south to north.
Having joined the two lines situated in the womb (the center) in the western direction in sequence,
extending them to the tips of the corners, there shall then be ten corners.
In the same manner, O Goddess of the gods, the second [line] goes to the ten corners;
from Īśāna to Agni, the lines proceed in sequence to the tips of the eastern yoni.
Having expanded it, one should subsequently join it in the western direction in due order;
O beautiful one, having expanded the lines at the tips of the northwest and southwest corners.
O Goddess, one should likewise join [the line] at the western end, extending toward the direction of Indra (the east),
beautiful and charming, touching the tip of the eastern corner with its single point.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should apply [the lines] according to the capacity that arises;
O Goddess of gods, having omitted four corners among the ten corners.
O Goddess, one should draw the central line between the two ends of the ten corners;
likewise, there are two [lines] in the southern division and similarly in the northern division.
Then, O Goddess, by means of the sequence of dividing the joints of the hexagon,
having joined the *yoni* and the fire (*vahni*), the letter *śa* (Śakra) is thus produced.
One should apply a line situated in the middle of the armpit according to its own form, so that, O Goddess, it becomes straight in shape and exceedingly beautiful. (29)
O fair-faced one, [the mandala] has five points at the top facing forward and four fire-points at the front;
it consists of a dot, a triangle, and eight spokes, according to the different types of wheels.
Know, O Goddess, that the middle wheel likewise consists of two sets of ten spokes; it is marked with the thunderbolt-yoni and is situated between the outer and inner [circles]. (31)
O Great Goddess, this wheel bestows all good fortune;
O Goddess, it grants universal sovereignty and destroys all calamities. || 32 ||
O Goddess, it is filled with many horses, rubies, and gold;
it bestows great liberation and is the great source of the play of speech.
O Maheśānī, this outer circle is round like the full moon;
O lotus-eyed one, make it joined with eight beautiful petals.
Then, O beautiful goddess, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus], and a square provided with four gates, O Supreme Goddess. (35)
Since sixty-four crores of Yoginīs of great splendor reside in this wheel,
they indeed honor the practitioner with special distinction.
It is square, adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining perfection,
and shines brilliantly, set with pearls and rubies.
Named Trailokyamohana, it bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree;
it has sixteen spokes, takes the form of the lunar orb, and is the abode of its own digits.
O Goddess, it fulfills all desires like a shower of flowing nectar;
O Great Mistress, it has eight petals and resembles the hibiscus flower.
Named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, it fulfills all desires;
O lady of excellent hips, these three constitute the Wheel of Emanation (sṛṣṭicakra), which bestows wealth.

O Goddess of the gods, the fourteen-spoked [cakra], which bestows all siddhis, is adorned by the goddesses of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) and others, and has the luster of a pomegranate flower. 41.
O blessed one, it always bestows infinite fruit and grants all prosperity;
O beloved, the ten-spoked [cakra] has the luster of molten gold and resembles vermilion.
The second [wheel] is also five-cornered, resembling a hibiscus flower; it is the wheel that accomplishes all aims and always grants whatever the mind desires. (43)
O Śivā, this wheel which produces all protection consists of great gnosis;
O Maheśānī, these three constitute the wheel of maintenance (sthiticakra), which bestows happiness.
O lady of excellent hips, it is worthy of worship according to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, bestowing desired fruits;
it is eight-cornered and as red as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling the pure luster of a ruby, it always removes all diseases;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the radiance of the bandhūka flower. (46)
O Īśvarī, the wheel that bestows all accomplishments is the abode of one's own creative power;
it is a triangle, the cause of the manifestation of all things, and the eternal bestower of sustenance.
O lady of excellent hips, O beloved, the Bindu-cakra consists of all-bliss;
O Supreme Goddess, it is the leader of the cakras and is composed of Sadāśiva. 48.
(158) This wheel, however, is of the nature of withdrawal, eternally consisting of Brahman;
it is to be served by the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), while the triad [of other wheels] is served by the Northern [Tradition]. || 49 ||
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, within this wheel the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) exist;
O Queen of the Gods, the path of words (padādhvā) is said to reside in the petals of the wheel.
Within the division of the joints of the petals, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is established;
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan), which has the form of the Mātṛkā.
O Dear One, since the eight groups of the Mātṛkā [reside] in the directions as the Siddhis,
know that the sixteen-spoked [wheel] consists of the Earth element and is composed of those [groups], being of the nature of the Kalās.
An eight-petaled [lotus] is formed with the consonant groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa* in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
the letters from *ka* to *ḍha*, numbering thirty-six, are situated in the corners of Indra (the northeast).
The ten syllables beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *bha* are in the first ten-spoked wheel;
those beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa* are in the second ten-spoked wheel.
I shall describe to you the eight groups in the eight corners and the triangle; from the letter 'a' to the end of the triangle, with the pair 'ha' and 'kṣa' in the center.
O Goddess, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been described as having the form of the seat of the Mātṛkās;
it is filled with the thirty-six principles (tattvas) according to the nature of the root wheel (cakramūla).
Bound by five lion-thrones, she is the path of arts (kalādhvan) because she protects the wheels; that young maiden, united with Bhairava, is Mahātripurabhairavī.
O beloved, when [the Goddess] has expanded, pervading the wheel from Tripurā at the beginning to Ambikā at the end, that is definitively declared to be the path of mantra (mantrādhvan). || 58 ||
In this way, one should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which is pure with its six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Thus it is said in the Subhagodaya:
"The ground is a square measuring ninety-six finger-breadths in extent."
Having divided that into four parts at the outset, one should [mark] twenty-four finger-breadths in sequence.
In the [units of] caves (9), mouths (0), tastes (6), limbs (6), fires (3), Vedas (4), fires (3), arrows (5), and seasons (6), one should mark these portions at both ends of those [lines]. (2)

One should assign one *guṇa* (three) to the Sun, one *veda* (four) to the Moon, one *kalā* (sixteen) to Mercury, one *purāṇa* (eighteen) to Jupiter, one *svara* (seven) to Venus, and again one *śara* (five) to Rāhu. || 3 ||
Within the interval of the five powers and the four fires of the ketu-quality,
one should join a pair of lines and Saturn from the sun onto the circle of the earth.
One should bring Ketu from the zenith, the son of Earth (Mars) from Rāhu,
the Sun from the Moon, Ketu from Venus, the Moon from Mercury, Rāhu from Jupiter, and Mars from Saturn.
From Ketu to Budha and from Ravi to Sauri—thus arises the formation of the six wheels.
One should draw three wheels on the outside with a measurement of eight times eight (sixty-four) finger-breadths.
The lotus has eight petals and twenty-four petals; it consists of three enclosures on the ground.
Therein, in sequence, the central womb and the horizontal lines are drawn all around.
The wise one should perform this three times— once, twice, and thrice—
according to the specific tradition, for the sake of forgiveness within the refuge of the universal arts.
In the center, one should draw three circles composed of the three qualities;
this is declared to be the King of Mandalas (Cakrarāja), adorned in the middle with a bindu.
One should worship the wheel after drawing it on the ground with vermilion powder; it generates great good fortune and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Or else, a plate of gold, silver, and so forth, situated upon a pedestal.

This is the extraction (*uddhāra*) according to the sequence of maintenance (*sthitikrama*). In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti* and *Jñānārṇava*, the extraction according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) has been demonstrated. However, the extraction according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) is found in the *Śrītantrarāja*:
Having completed the circle by means of a compass on a perfectly level square surface,
one should erase the line situated in the middle and lay down a cord across it.
There are nine threads among them; having laid down two threads that touch both ends of the circumference, one should then proceed in order from the ends of those two to the end of the middle thread.
When four lines have been drawn, there shall be a hexagon situated at the twenty-first [point], starting from the two eighth-points; it lies between the ninth and the first.
One should draw four lines according to the four vital points (marmans),
from the first and the ninth [points] at the top, extending to the fourth and seventh [points].
One should draw four lines by piercing the eight vital points (marmans);
then, from the commencement of the two ends of the fourth and sixth [lines], one likewise reaches the eighth.
Likewise, one should cast a group of four sūtras reaching to the second [column];
then, in accordance with the four vital points (marmans), [one casts them] from the fifth to the end.
One should draw a pair of third lines resting upon two vital points (marmans);
one should erase the central Brahma-line, and thus there shall be the supreme wheel.
Having fashioned an external eight-petaled lotus as well as one with double that number of petals,
[one should likewise fashion] a circle with six [lines] and a square with eight [lines].
Having laid out its [mandala] with cords, provided with gates to the east and west,
one should likewise mark two positions by means of three lines drawn from south to north.
O Supreme Goddess, one should divide those four squares into two parts each, in sequence, by means of four diagonal lines drawn from the corners.
"This *Lalitārcācakra* is to be obtained sequentially from a true Guru. Thus it is said. The Teachers (*ācāryas*) have also stated:
"By the four Śrīkaṇṭhas, by the five Śivayuvatis who are likewise distinct, and by the nine root-natures (*mūlaprakṛtis*) of Śambhu..."
Together with the forty-four petals of the earth, the digits, the three circles, and the three lines, your corners of refuge have been transformed. || 1 ||

Thus: by the four Śrīkaṇṭhas, who are the objects of the number four; he whose neck bears the poison *śrī* (glory/nectar) is Śrīkaṇṭha, namely Hara; his corners are also Śrīkaṇṭhas—this means "consisting of the nature of Śrīkaṇṭha. By the Śivayuvatis, that is, the Śaktis—this means "consisting of the nature of Śakti."
"By five" means by those numbered as five. The word "api" (also/even) indicates a distinction.

"Distinctly differentiated" (*prabhinnābhiḥ*) means thoroughly differentiated. This excellence, however, exists because of the presence of the *vaidavika* [drop] within the wheel of Śiva and Śakti; and this should be understood according to the system of the *Samaya* school, in the sequence of emanation, when drawing the five wheels.

According to the Kaula doctrine, when drawing the wheel of the nine sources (navayonicakra) by way of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), its state of being "split" (prabhinnatva) should be understood as existing with faces turned upwards and downwards; therefore, both [halves] remain separate.
Regarding the word "of Śambhu," the ablative case indicates that by the term "Śambhu," the four Śrīkaṇṭhas are meant.
"By nine" means by those numbered as nine. The word "api" (also/even) includes the multiplicity that will be mentioned later.

By the "root-natures" (*mūlaprakṛtibhiḥ*), which are the root causes of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), for this very reason they are designated by the term "yoni" (source/origin). The "nine sources" (*navayonayaḥ*) consist of the nine elements (*dhātu*). Thus it has been said:
In the *Kāmikā*: "The elements of skin, blood, flesh, fat, and bone are rooted in Śakti;

the elements of marrow, semen, breath (*prāṇa*), and life-force (*jīva*) are rooted in Śiva. This body consists of nine elements and originates from nine sources. Because it is the substratum for the non-living [elements] within the living elements, it is indeed the element of vitality (*ojas*)."

It is called the *jīvadhātu* (the life-element). As stated by Vāgbhaṭṭa: "Among the elements beginning with *rajas* and ending with *śukra*, the supreme essence (*prasāda*) which serves as the support of life is the element *ojas*. (The tenth) element is the one supreme power, the Mistress of that [element]; she is the tenth source (*yoni*), the station of the *bindu*, the Mistress of *danī*.
The meaning is "of that body.
Thus, the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa) having been produced, the macrocosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) manifested;
and those five [sheaths] belonging to Śiva, beginning with Māyā, are indeed powers (śākta). || 1 ||
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva—these twenty-five principles are included within that very [reality]. || 2 ||
The eleven sense organs and the subtle elements beginning with sound are referred to by that term.

Know this entire world of moving and non-moving things to consist of Śiva and Śakti; "moving" refers to the microcosmic body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), and "non-moving" refers to the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). O Blessed Lady, [this was obtained] from Śambhu through the four Śrīkaṇṭhas.

Together with the five expanded [energies] (*prabhinnā*) and the nine auspicious young women (*śivayuvati*), who are the nine root-natures (*mūlaprakṛti*), they become forty-four when fully transformed. Here, this should be kept in mind:
in this wheel (*cakra*), there are twenty-eight vital points (*marman*) and twenty-four joints (*sandhi*). Now, as for the vital points...
How is it that there are twenty-eight [joints] when there are only twenty-four?
The point where two lines meet is designated as a *sandhi* (joint);
those who know the vital points (*marman*) understand the point where three lines meet to be a *marman*. (1)

Thus, although there is no point of intersection of three lines for the three Śiva-cakras consisting of the eight-petaled lotus, the sixteen-spoked wheel, the triple girdle, and the three outer enclosures, they are nonetheless designated by the technical term *marman* based on scriptural authority. As it is stated in the *Candrajñānavidyā*:
There are twenty-four spokes, two triangles, a dodecagon, an octagon, four circles, twenty-eight vital points (marmas), and twenty-four joints. || 1 ||
Thus it is said in the Rudrayāmala: "The sages and others known as the Pṛśnis are all centered upon the Cakra; they practice the Cakra-rite, which is served by gods and Gandharvas. (1)
The wheel consists of Agni and Soma; the world is composed of Agni and Soma.
The sun shone within Agni; it is remembered as being composed of Agni and Soma.
The wheel of the Mātṛkās consists of three sections and is composed of the Moon, Sun, and Fire;
it is triangular, marked by the Bindu, gentle, and eight-cornered with mixed elements.
The fourteen-spoked [wheel] belongs to Agni, and the radiant square belongs to Bhānu;
by his grace, Indra and the others, the eight Vasus, and the hosts of Maruts [attained their power].
Whosoever in this world were prosperous, they became servants of the wheel of Tripura;
and that triple city of the wheel consisted of the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire.
"The city of Mahālakṣmī is a wheel (cakra), and there Śiva himself resides with her.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Candrajñānavidyā* of the *Bhairavayāmala*, Maheśvara spoke to Gaurī:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Well asked, O beauty of the three worlds!"
This knowledge, more secret than the secret, has not been revealed anywhere.
Kalā-vidyā is the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti), whose form is the shape of the Śrīcakra;
in its center is the station of Bindu, where the Supreme Goddess resides.
O Īśvarī, united with Sadāśiva, she who transcends all beings is the wheel of Tripurasundarī, which has the form of the cosmic egg.
It consists of the five elements, as well as the subtle elements (tanmātras);
likewise, it consists of the sense organs and the principle of the mind.
The form of the principles beginning with Māyā, as well as that which transcends the principles, is the Bindu.
Within the Bindu resides she who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. (5)
O Śivā, Maheśvarī, who is united with Sadāśiva, transcends the principles (tattvas), is the form of light, and possesses a beautiful form; from whose body you were born.
A thousand rays, two thousand, a hundred thousand,
a koṭi, and an arbuda— beyond these, no further number exists.
O Maheśānī, having entered into that very [Light], the world of moving and unmoving beings shines; by the radiance of that Goddess, everything is illumined.
Whatever is devoid of existence, and that which is manifested— there can be no manifestation of that Śiva-śakti, who is of the nature of consciousness, apart from consciousness itself.
O Maheśvarī, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings would surely fall into blindness in the absence of those infinite millions of rays.
O Śivā, in the center there are three hundred and sixty rays of mine;
pervading the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), they consist of the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire.
O Śivā, the rays of the Sun number one hundred and eight,
those of the Moon one hundred and sixteen, and those of the Fire one hundred and thirty-six.
O Consort of Śaṅkara, illuminating both the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and the individual body (piṇḍāṇḍa),
they are like the sun by day, the moon at night, and the fire during the two twilights.
Illuminating time, those three are therefore of the nature of time;
indeed, three hundred and sixty days constitute a year.
Mahādeva, whose self is the year, is heard of as Prajāpati;
Prajāpati, the creator of the worlds, [created] the sages headed by Marīci.
He creates these guardians of the worlds, all of whom are protectors of the world;
dissolution depends on Hara, while origination is fashioned by Bhava.
Protection, however, is centered on Mṛḍa; Śiva is appointed by the Supreme Goddess for creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Thus the world proceeds. (17)
Thus, by the passage beginning with "Having entered into that very [Self]," the meaning of the Śruti—"Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined"—is stated.

Thus [ends the work] of the disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, who was the disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was the disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, who was the disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the illustrious Great Upādhyāya and worshipful teacher.
The eighth breath (chapter) in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya. || 8 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇava Tantra,
the ninth chapter (śvāsa).

Regarding the statement, "In this context, the Meru-prastāraka Yantra is remembered as being eternally identical [to the deity]," the authority for performing worship in the Meru Yantra according to the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi-krama) has been stated. The meaning therein is as follows:
worship beginning from the center and ending with Aṇimā and the other Siddhis is worship by way of emanation; in that context, "beginning from the center" refers to the sixteen Nityās and so forth.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*) is identical with the sixteen *Nityās*, the wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhāracakra*) is identical with the *Mātṛkā*, and the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*) is identical with the *Vaśinī* group and so forth. Having thus extracted the Sovereign Śrīcakra, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the collective mantra (*samaṣṭividyā*). Alternatively—
Having placed [the image] made of iron, jewels, or other materials upon a pedestal fashioned from *śrīparṇī* wood or similar materials in front [of oneself],
one should offer flowers. As for the collective mantra (*samaṣṭividyā*), one should recite the root mantra preceded by the *praṇava* and the three *tāra*s.

"I worship and bow to the Śrīcakra-pādukā, joined with the Yoginīs of the entire collection of the manifest, secret, more secret, Kula, Kaula, Nigarbha, Rahasya, Atirahasya, Parāpara-rahasya, and Sampradāya traditions.
The extraction of the Śrīcakra described above is common to both systems; however, in the Kādima system, it is within the square (caturasra).
The distinction is that the two gates, eastern and western, have been mentioned. Regarding the specific rule for the worshippers of Lopāmudrā, it is stated in the Bhairavayāmala:
"By the worshippers of Lopāmudrā, [the worship] is said to be performed from within the center of the Śrīcakra."
O Supreme Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of the Preta in the center of the Bindu.
Outside of that, in the three triangles located in the east, south, and north,
one should construct three doors, just as the doors are arranged in the outer enclosure (bhūpura).
O Maheśvarī, outside the eight petals at their tips,
one should fashion eight knots as well as eight tridents.
The knots are joined by means of the *praṇava* (Om) as an enclosing frame;
likewise, one should worship the eight Bhairavas in the knots starting from the east.
One should worship the ten Vaṭukas proclaimed for their tips in due order;
O Great Goddess, one should worship the eight Bhairavīs on the tridents.
O Goddess of gods, within the three circles one should worship the Yoginīs who dwell in the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar; O Supreme Goddess, their mantras are as follows.
Salutations again and again to the yoginīs dwelling in the netherworld; salutations again and again to the yoginīs dwelling in the world of the earth. || 7 ||
Homage again and again to the Yoginīs dwelling in the Bhuvarloka; (homage again and again to the Yoginīs dwelling in the Svarloka). || 8 ||

Thus, the distinction is that [the deity] is to be worshipped within these three squares. Here, there are many varieties of the Śrīcakra due to the divisions of creation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra), as well as through different grid-patterns (prastāra); these varieties will be explained further on—this, then, is the summary.
Herein, the procedure for arranging the vessels (pātrāsādana) is written: therein, at the conclusion of the meditation and mental worship, upon a plate made of gold or other materials...

Having drawn the worship diagram with saffron and other substances, having established it before oneself and worshipped it, one should perform the placement of the ritual vessels (*pātrāsādana*). In this worship, the vessels are exceedingly praiseworthy. As it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*:
If one should perform the ritual of consecration for a sacrificial image without a vessel,
the entire rite becomes fruitless, resulting in the loss of wealth such as vehicles and other possessions.
If the bali offering is omitted, there will be famine; if the fragrance is omitted, misfortune;
likewise, if the incense is omitted, there will be agitation; and if the cloth is omitted, the loss of wealth. || 2 ||
If it lacks a canopy, one should remove the canopy; by omitting the canopy, one becomes a crane.

"Canopy" (vitāna) means a celestial chariot (vimāna); if that is omitted, there will be the destruction of both the city and the town. If it lacks an altar (vedi), there will be ruin for the city and the fortress.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by means of water-pots, there shall indeed be the destruction of one's kinsmen. || 3 ||
The phrase "devoid of jars" is to be supplied [to each clause].

In the absence of arches (toraṇas), however, one would destroy kinsmen along with their relatives. If devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), everything would be in vain; there is no doubt in this matter. || 4 ||
But if it is devoid of mantra and vidyā, even if complete, it perishes;
however, when joined with a worthy recipient and the mantra, it becomes the remover of all defects. || 5 ||
Thus it is said elsewhere: "One should not share a single vessel even if it be Maheśvara himself; otherwise, the mantras turn away and calamities arise at every step. (1)
In this world one would be poor, and in the next world one would go to hell; without a support there is ruin, and yet the deities are not satisfied. (2)

Thus, based on the statement from another tantra, the investigation into the vessels, their bases, their measurements, their purification, and so forth, is here demonstrated. Regarding those vessels, the *Tantrarāja* states: "The preparation of the *arghya* [offering water] is done in a vessel made of three metals, glass, or clay. Here, "three metals" refers to gold, silver, and copper.
In the Bhairavītantra:
A vessel made of gold, glass, or silver, one produced from pearl or a skull, one originating from Viśvāmitra, or one made of gold, grants the fruit of desire; a crystal vessel leads to prosperity.

The pearl from the *tāra* (conch) bestows joy and produces desired success; that produced from the auspicious coconut is the *kāpāla*; and here, the *mauktika* (pearl) from the skull clearly produces accomplishment and grants liberation. || 1 ||
Thus, it is said in the Kulārṇava: "Gold, silver, stone, copper, a skull, gourd, earthenware, coconut, conch, and that which originates from a pearl-oyster shell. (1)
"A beautiful and auspicious vessel made from a sacred tree (puṇyavṛkṣa) is well-agitated.
Thus it is said. In the Bhairavayāmala:
"O lady of excellent hips, the vessel [made] from the Tāra-tree is to be known as the most excellent of the excellent."
O Goddess, that which originates from the coconut should be known as superior, middling, and inferior. || 1 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, a glass vessel is to be known as the best of the inferior;
a golden one is the best of the middling, and a silver one is the middling of the middling. (2)
Copper vessels and the like are said to be of medium and inferior quality; those made of bilva wood and from the brahmavṛkṣa tree are of inferior-superior quality.
"The earthen [liṅga] is said to be of inferior-middle quality; that made of clay is of inferior-inferior quality.
Thus it is stated. In the Mahāhāraka Tantra:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious rite for the coconut [liṅga]."
Long ago, indeed, this vessel was fashioned by the wise Viśvāmitra.
The skull of Viśvāmitra, however, is the most excellent of all vessels;
indeed, by worshipping within it, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained. || 2 ||
Merely by the sight of him, O beloved, he will undoubtedly deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage once he becomes a householder.
Upon seeing a coconut vessel, sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as treachery toward a trusted friend, and all other sins are destroyed. || 4 ||
O Maheśānī, he who gives away ten million maidens as well as hundreds of gold pieces when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu— || 5 ||
The fruit of that [offering] is multiplied ten millionfold by the gift of a coconut as an *arghya* offering.
In the absence of that vessel, one should worship with other vessels.
O Goddess of gods, upon seeing the vessel of honor (arghyapātra), the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā,
all the yoginīs, being delighted, dance and bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Thus it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Vessels made of gold and silver, as well as those made of wood, clay, and stone;
and vessels made of gems and the like, marked with auspicious lines. (1)
"One should not employ [the vessel] for the offering of *arghya*, the presentation of food (*naivedya*), worship, or the giving of sacrificial oblations (*bali*).
Thus it is said. In the *Śivarahasya*:
"O Umā, by means of a golden vessel, all desired objectives are accomplished."
Having offered the *arghya* with silver, one shall obtain long life, sovereignty, and sons. || 1 ||
If made of copper, it bestows good fortune; if made of clay, it brings merit;
but when none of these are available, one may use an earthen vessel fashioned by one's own hand.
One should not place a broken seat or an arghya vessel;
however, in all cases, copper is like gold, and for an arghya vessel, it is even more excellent than that.
Likewise, vessel-supports and excellent vessels should be prepared;
for indeed, without a vessel, the performance of the bali-offering and the homa-rite cannot be accomplished.
A bowl of thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed as the best;
the medium is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths.
One should never have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths in size;
its forms should resemble the cavity of the navel and be shaped like a lotus.
One should fashion bowls with the luster of conch shells and blue lotuses;
one should fashion them with the radiance of maṇḍalas that correspond to the respective elements.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause the fruits mentioned therein to be performed here;
whatever the form of the recipient may be, one should bring a support corresponding to that.
Thus it is said in the Devīyāmala:
"O Goddess of the Gods, for rites of subjugation and attraction, one should use a golden vessel; O Beloved, for rites of pacification and nourishment, one should use a silver vessel. (1)

In a vessel made of iron, one should perform killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*); likewise, for all rites of immobilization (*stambha*), a vessel made of clay is especially recommended. (2)
O lady of excellent hips, he who satisfies the deity with that supreme vessel fashioned from the syllables of mantras and medicinal powders— (3)
Within six months, his mantra-attainment (mantrasiddhi) arises;
likewise, an excellent vessel produced from the lunar mansion, tree, or syllable of the mantra [is required]. (4)
With that supreme vessel, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity;
in this way, the accomplishment of the mantra will surely occur—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Goddess, these two vessels must never be disclosed;
they are the most excellent of the excellent, being vessels produced from the mantra and the lunar mansion.
It effects the invocation of another’s success and performs libations with their vessel;
it pacifies the malevolent sorcery of others and bestows the accomplishment of one’s own mantras.
O Maheśvarī, having learned from the mouth of the venerable Guru the vessels arising from syllables, medicinal herbs, lunar mansions, and wombs, one should employ them in the rite of worship.
O lady of excellent vows, in all rites that must be performed, one should employ the Vaiśvāmitra [vessel];
one should know that a wooden vessel is to be used for the practice of mantra worship.
Thus, in the Kulārṇava:

"First the pitcher (kumbha), then the conch (śaṅkha), the vessel of Śrī (śrīpātra), the vessel of Śakti (śaktipātra), the vessel of the Guru (gurupātra), the vessel of enjoyment (bhogapātra), and the vessel of the offering (balipātra) in due order. (1)
These five vessels are to be placed starting from the tip of one's own left [hand]:
the vessel of the limb (aṅga), the vessel of the hero (vīra), the secret vessel (guhya), and the vessel of the Yoginī. || 2 ||
O lady of excellent vows, there should be nine vessels for oneself, for Gaṇanātha, and for Vaṭuka and Kṣetrapāla, together with the sprinkling-vessel (prokṣaṇī).
One should place four vessels for the female messengers behind the Goddess;
these eighteen vessels bring delight to the Goddess.

O Supreme Goddess, the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) and the special water-offering (viśeṣārghya) should be placed according to the rules below the first row, within the center of my venerable mandala.
Thus [it is said]. The definition of the general *arghya* is found in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"With red *bilva*, unbroken rice, flowers, curd, *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds—this is proclaimed as the general *arghya* for all the gods. (1)
The red substance here is saffron.
O Goddess, the conch of the illustrious Tripurasundarī is common [to all]; for other gods, O Īśvarī, the general [conch] is made of silver.
The wise practitioner should place the five vessels, beginning with the *arghya*, beneath that;
the *arghya* vessel in the northwest and the *pādya* vessel in the southwest.
The bathing jar is in the southeast, the water for sipping is in the northeast, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) is in the center; such is the characteristic arrangement of these vessels.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, unbroken rice, curd, grains of rice, sahā, white mustard, dūrvā grass, saffron, gorocanā, and turmeric. || 5 ||
This twelve-ingredient *arghya* is proclaimed for the God and Goddess:
white mustard, saffron, *dūrvā* grass, costus, *lāmajjaka*, and camphor.
"And they declare that there are these six substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*) here.
Thus, in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "The water for the feet is excellent when consisting of water from *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
Likewise:
Phalaka, coraka, karpūra, kuṣṭha, elā, and uśīra—these six substances they declare to be for the water for sipping (ācamanīya). || 1 ||
In the *madhuparka*, clarified butter, honey, and curd are prescribed by the wise;
in the absence of curd, milk should be used, and likewise, in the absence of honey, jaggery.
There is no substitute for ghee; in its place, one should employ water.
Having thoroughly mixed in the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandha), one should properly prepare the bathing water.
There should be five separate vessels for milk, curd, ghee, sugar, and honey respectively, and one vessel for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
There are six distinguished vessels, then the water for sipping;
the seventh is for the water from the stomach, and likewise the eighth and the ninth.
O Goddess of the gods, for the powder used in rubbing the body, there is a tenth vessel of pure water;
these are the ten vessels in the systems of Saura, Śaiva, and Vaiṣṇava.

The wise practitioner should arrange three sets of vessels: the primary vessels for the Gāṇapatya rite, the secondary vessels for the Śākta rite, and the five vessels beginning with the arghya vessel.
Furthermore, two vessels for the water for sipping (ācamanīya) are prescribed;
in the worship of the five deities (pañcāyatana), there are the fivefold offerings beginning with the arghya.
O Goddess, one should satisfy the specific enclosure with the specific *arghya*;
O beautiful Goddess, one should satisfy the general enclosure with the general *arghya*.
The worship of the goddesses should be performed with the nectar contained in the Śrīpātra;
that of the Śaktis with the Śaktipātra; and that of the gurus from the Gurupātra.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should satisfy the sixty-four Yoginīs of the nine enclosures with water from the vessel of the Yoginīs.
The wise one should prepare other objects of enjoyment with the vessel of Bhoga;
and with the vessel of Bhairava, he should satisfy the Bhairavas. || 12 ||
Then, one should satisfy the Vaṭukas with the vessel of the Vaṭuka;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the dismissal of the offering (bali) with the bali-vessel.
One should also satisfy Vārāhī, Kurukullā, and the other offering goddesses (*balidevī*).
Here, by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the offering to the Nine Durgās is intended,
as well as the offering to the five elements (*pañcabhūtabali*) and likewise the offering to all beings (*sarvabhūtabali*).
One should also cause an offering to be made for the Lord of the Kings of Kings by that very same person.
The gratification of heroes with the hero’s vessel has been proclaimed;
one should likewise gratify the secret yoginīs with the nectar of the secret vessel. 15.
The limb of enjoyment through the vessel of enjoyment, and the limb of dissolution through the vessel of the limbs;
likewise, the sequence of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya) and the worship of the assembly of Śrīvidyā.

O Goddess of gods, one should satisfy [the deity] with the special arghya offering through a spirit of devotion; [one should perform] the inner sacrifice, self-worship, and the internal oblation as well. (17)
The most excellent of teachers should perform [the ritual] with water contained in his own vessel;
four vessels for the dūtīs should be employed in the dūtī-yāga.
O beautiful one, for the sake of maintaining the true essence of the lineage, the wise man should establish five, six, seven, eight, or nine vessels worthy of the [divine] power. (19)
One should avoid that which is broken, cracked, burnt, lacking in dignity, unsightly, impure, fallen from the hand, or touched by cattle. (20)
The wise man, having always washed them with pure acidic water, should set them down;
he must not cause a confusion of vessels, especially regarding the ritual substances.
O Goddess, one should satisfy the gurus of the Ūrdhvāmnāya with the special arghya;
and as for the circle of rays, O Mistress of the Gods, one should not satisfy them with any other vessel.
The satisfaction of any other group of gurus is performed with the guru-vessel;
however, for one who is not a [formal] vessel, one should perform it with the water from the sprinkling-vessel (prokṣaṇī).
The collective and individual worship should indeed be performed with water from a conch shell;
the offering to the Kṣetrapāla should be made with the vessel of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa). || 24 ||
The offering for Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the Gaṇas, should be made with the vessel of Gaṇanātha;
O Goddess, one should present the offering for the Central Goddess using the Śrīpātra. (25)
O Great Goddess, regarding the worship of Śrīvidyā, and especially concerning the vessels that serve as the support for the bali offering, listen; I shall describe them in brief. (26)
The offering vessel of the Śrī Guru, the offering vessel of Vārāhī, three for Kurukullā, and the fourfold set for Vaṭuka and the others. (27)
There are indeed five [offerings] for the five elements, one for Bhūtabali,
one for the Lord of the Kings of Kings (Rājarājeśvara), and after that, one for the Goddess.
One [offering] for Navadurgā, accompanied by incense, lamps, and food;
thus there are eighteen vessels, which remove all obstacles.
The five vessels are declared for the purification of the accomplished substance;
one vessel is for the purpose of arranging the substances of worship and the materials for the ritual.
"By means of musk, agallochum, camphor, *kuṇḍagola*, wild meat, molasses, along with sandalwood paste and *svayambhū* flowers"— according to this statement from the *Yoginītantra*.
Other objects of enjoyment, such as perfumes and the like, [should also be offered] specifically.
One should set out beautiful vessels and also worship them. || 31 ||
O Maheśvarī, for the offering of arghya to Mārtaṇḍa, there is a large arghya vessel;
one is a receptacle for a prastha of water, and the other is a vessel for libations (tarpaṇa).
For the worship of the doors and other parts, a single general vessel is recommended; that very same vessel, O Dear One, shall serve as the general *arghya* for the worship of the Sun.
Four jars, provided with covers and lifting-rings, wrapped in fine silk cloths, and joined with a large base; 34.
Filled with pure water, nectar, milk, and ambrosia,
it should then be placed starting from the front of her left side on the right side of the Goddess.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the characteristics of the pitcher of pure water, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: [It should be] provided with curd and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), joined with five jewels (*pañcaratna*), and endowed with the petals of five types of auspicious plants (*bhaṅga*). (1)
The five petals of the [five] branches— namely, the tender shoots of the mango, the holy fig, the banyan, the Plakṣa, and the Udumbara—
one should place there a flawless jar and install the deity Varuṇa within it. || 2 ||
All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans and lakes,
[should be taken] from an elephant, a horse, a chariot-track, an anthill, a confluence, a pool, or a herd of cows.
O Indra among kings, the sacrificer who knows the dharma should bring earth endowed with all medicinal herbs and place it there for the purpose of bathing.
May all the oceans, rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds come to the sacrificer, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes. || 5 ||
Thus, in the Rudrayāmala:
"One who desires prosperity should properly install the auspicious [deity] which brings about wealth and livelihood:
gold, ghee, wheat, along with dūrvā grass and yellow pigment (rocanā). (1)
(165) These five substances [should be placed] in all the jars, and especially in the vessels for the special *arghya* and other offerings, as well as in the *śrīpātra* vessels. || 2 ||
"One should give [this] for the sake of attaining prosperity, fame, health, sons, long life, and victory.
Thus it is said. In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Agni, Brahmā, Bhavānī, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), and the great serpent (Śeṣa)..."
Skanda, Bhānu, the hosts of Mothers, the guardians of the directions, and the nine planets.

Having worshipped each of these in their respective jars according to the prescribed rite— thus it is stated in the Gautamīya: "One should [use] vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's capacity."
The water-pot (kumbha) should be thirty-six finger-breadths in both width and height. || 1 ||
One should perform sixteen or twelve [offerings], but not fewer than that.
There should be three vessels for the *arghya* and likewise three for the *pādya*.
"Likewise, the vessels for the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be arranged separately.
Thus it is said. In the Bhairavītantra:
"He who, having filled the eight-limbed vessel (aṣṭāṅgārghya), offers it upon the head of the Goddess..."
For ten thousand years, he is honored in the world of Durgā. || 1 ||
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, curd, clarified butter,
rice grains, sesame seeds, and white mustard— this is proclaimed as the eightfold arghya offering.
O Great King, by offering the arghya according to the prescribed rite with a wooden vessel to the Goddess, a man shall then obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By offering the respectful water (arghya) in a copper vessel, one obtains the fruit of a white lotus;
by offering it in a silver vessel, one indeed obtains the fruit of a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
By offering the *arghya* with silver, one obtains long life and an auspicious kingdom;
by offering it with a golden vessel, one obtains much gold.
"O Sage, one shall obtain all desired objects by means of a golden vessel.
Thus it is said. In the Bhairavayāmala:
"Two vessels for the goddess Nirmālyavasinī are situated in the direction of Śiva (the north-east)."
In the worship of the five sense-bases (pañcāyatana), one should indeed cast ten vessels.
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra:
"In the offering of a goat and other animals as a *bali*, one should set out nine vessels.
There should be five *bali* vessels and one vessel for the blood. (1)
Furthermore, there was a base for pieces of meat and for heads,
as well as one for cooked meat— [the remainder of the verse].
Thus, in the Rudrayāmala:
"If one desires one's own success, the five vessels beginning with the arghya-vessel must be diligently established separately during the worship of the Kumārī. (1)
Thus, it is stated in the Vārāhī Tantra: "In the sacrifice of a married couple, in the worship of a *suvāsinī*, in the propitiation of the *yoginīs*, and in the worship of the fifty couples... (1)
In the performance of sacrifice, in the worship of the elements and deities performed at fixed times, in the worship of the circle of gurus, and likewise among the lords of the days; || 2 ||

Likewise, in the worship of the lord of the day, the worship of the deity of the lunar mansion, in the worship of the seed-syllables and medicinal herbs, and in the consecration of the rosary for recitation; (3)
In the worship of the book as well as in the ritual for the worship of the fire,
the five vessels beginning with the *arghya* should be prepared separately.

Thus, in the *Kuṇḍaprakāśa*: "For the fire-oblation (*homa*), there are ten vessels, as well as two vessels for clarified butter (*ājya*), two vessels for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and likewise the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* [waters]. (1)
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the full-vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), and another vessel for the oblation materials—these are the primary vessels. || 2 ||
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya:
"In front of the deity, to the left of oneself, one should draw a triangle with sandalwood water, surrounded externally by a circle and indeed by a square. (1)
"Having formed the fish-shaped mudrā on the ground, the practitioner [should proceed]," thus [it is said].
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"A triangle, encircled by a circle and surrounded by a square."
One should apply [the ointment] smeared with fragrance at the tip of one's own left hand using the fish-gesture (matsyamudrā). || 1 ||

Having worshipped with perfumes, one should offer the *arghya* to the deity with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala," and likewise worship the limbs [of the deity] in the corners and in front of the square.
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra in all directions, one should place the conch-stand;
I establish the conch-stand which has been washed with the root-mantra. || 3 ||

Likewise, one should extract the syllable *kā* with its nasal bindu, followed by the Lord of Serpents (*bhujaṅgeśa*), ending with *maṇḍalāya* at the end of the fire-syllable (*ra*), and then *dharmaprada*. (4)
Having uttered "Salutation to the one whose self consists of the ten digits," one should worship with scents and other offerings;
there, one should worship the ten digits of Fire in a clockwise direction.
Thus, in the Kulārṇava:
"Without a support (ādhāra), there is a fall [of the offering], and the Mothers are not satisfied.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should prepare the support according to the prescribed rule. (1)
They say the base should have three feet, or six feet, or four feet;
or else, O Goddess, one should make it circular in shape and pleasing to the mind.
These are the general designations; however, the specific details have already been stated. In the Rudrayāmala:
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Svarūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā. (2)
"And these ten digits of Fire are to be known as bestowers of dharma.
Thus it is said. In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"Having washed the conch with the Astra-mantra, one should place it there and worship it."
The conch-shell measure is one span (prādeśa) and four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) in height. || 1 ||
Having said "This is the vessel for the arghya," one should say with the mantra,
"I establish it," and also say, "For the sake of bestowing the object of purpose," twelve times.
Having uttered the *pada* for the Self of the Kalās, the heart-mantra is for the *arghya* vessel;
having worshipped the conch with this, one should worship the Kalās of the Sun.
Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*: "Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. (1)
"These twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun, which bestow wealth, are to be worshipped.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Then, reciting the Mātṛkā at the end of the root mantra, with waters consisting of nectar..."
There, the worshipper should worship Vilomā with this mantra.
"Having said, 'I shall fill the vessel for the *arghya*,' one should then fill it completely with [water] consisting of nectar flowing from the *bindu*," thus it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*.
One should worship him according to the prescribed rite with waters enriched with fragrant flowers. || 1 ||
The *bindu* is the space between the eyebrows, because the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*) is present there. In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:

"The two ears and the moon joined with the *bindu*, then the word 'bestower of desires' (*kāmaprada*), then the word 'sixteenth' (*ṣoḍaśānte*), then the word 'digit' (*kalā*), and finally 'salutation to the Self' (*ātmane namaḥ*). (1)
"Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should worship the sixteen *kalaśas*.
Thus it is said. *Karṇa* is the letter *U*, *candra* is the letter *Sa*, and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*; therefore, [the seed-syllables are] *uṃ* and *saṃ*. In the *Yāmala*:
"Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti..."
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. || 1 ||
The digits (kalās) residing in the middle of the lunar orb—Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kāmadāyinī, and Svaragā—are bestowers of desires. || 2 ||

Thus, in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having invoked the sacred site (*tīrtha*) as before, and having united it there with the root mantra, one should place a flower upon it with the eye-mantra and [consecrate] it with the crest-mantra. (1)
Having displayed the Gālinī-mudrā and having consecrated [the offering] as nectar according to the rule with the Dhenusaṃjñā-mudrā and the seed-syllable of nectar, the practitioner— || 2 ||
Having meditated upon his chosen deity there and performed the ritual identification (sakalīkaraṇa),
the preceptor should protect the ten directions with the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having gazed [at it] with the Netra-mantra, having secured it with the mudrā known as the conch, and having kindled it with the mudrā in the form of the womb; || 4 ||
There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
having fully worshipped the six limbs, one should consecrate [the object] with the root mantra. (5)
"Then, having offered the *arghya* eight times, one should cover it with the *matsyamudrā*.

Thus [it is said]. In the *Nāradīya*: "The knower of mantras should perform the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) with the eye-mantra; if that is not available, then with the root-mantra (*mūla*). Here, "with the root-mantra" refers to the five-limbed mantra (*pañcāṅga*), because there is no specific eye-mantra in that context. This applies everywhere here as well.
The inclusion of the specific mantras for each limb is by means of the words "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth, which constitute the forms of the limbs.

Regarding the phrase "having enveloped with the armor" (*kavacenāvaguṇṭhya*), the remainder is that it is done with the respective mudrās. As stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "One should pour a little of that water contained in the conch into the water of the jar. And in the *Śāradātilaka*:
To the north of the *arghya* water, one should place the *pādya*, the *ācamanīya*,
and the *madhuparka*, arranging them in order within the three corners.
"One should consecrate each individual vessel eight times with the mantra.
Thus it is said. In the *Uttara-tantra*: "One should give that [gift] in a bell-metal vessel, or one made of gold or silver (*śveta*). Here, *śveta* refers to silver. In the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
That which is the supreme, highest abode is called "Madhu";
when that is attained by him, it is always remembered as *madhuparka*.
Thus it is said in the Śāradā:
"Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the right, one should fill it with water.
Having taken a small amount of the *arghya* water, one should pour it into the *prokṣaṇī* water. (1)
Thus [it is said]. In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Then, one should place a vessel for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamanīya*) again.
In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"Sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds..."
And dūrvā grass—thus the eight substances for the arghya offering have been declared in their proper order. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. "Unbroken" refers to rice grains (*taṇḍula*). In the *Nāradapañcarātra*, the *arghya* for Viṣṇu is described as follows:
"White mustard seeds, sesame, dūrvā grass, barley, sesame, and rice grains—this *arghya* is declared to be provided with water, milk, and ghee."

Thus: "Siddhārtha" refers to mustard seeds; "dūrvā" refers to those possessed of three leaves. As stated in the words of Somaśambhu: "Dūrvā grasses endowed with three leaves are recommended for the rite of *arghya*. And in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The *pādya* (water for the feet) is said to consist of *śyāmāka*, dūrvā, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*."
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is considered to consist of nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola.

"Jātī" refers to nutmeg (*jātīphala*). Likewise, one should offer nutmeg even in the vessel for sipping water (*ācamana*), O Sage, according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*: "Powdered nutmeg and other such items should be offered. Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "Having powdered [the ingredients], one should offer the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) according to the prescribed rule. This is also stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
Kusha grass tips, unbroken rice grains, barley, paddy, sesame seeds, clarified butter, white mustard seeds, flowers, and sacred ash [should be placed] in the arghya vessel.
One should cause kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, and tamālaka,
as well as sacred ash, to be placed in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the *praṇava*.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet with uśīra and sandalwood,
as well as with jasmine, kakkola, camphor, bahumūla, and tamālaka.
Having ground it according to rule, one should pour the water for sipping;
[the herb] dūrvā has many roots.
O Goddess, you are supreme with a thousand roots, possessing a hundred roots and a hundred sprouts.
May the dūrvā grass, which destroys evil dreams, take away all my sin. || 1 ||

Because the word "hundred" (*śata*) denotes plurality. In the *Prapañcasāra*: "The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is prepared with pure waters"; from the statement "with pure [waters]" here, it is understood that caste (*jāti*) and so forth should not be offered.

However, regarding the absence of substances such as the *arghya*, Śaunaka states: "In the absence of these, flowers and so forth [may be used] through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of each respective [substance]."

"One should cast [it]. Thus it is said. In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "In the absence of [the prescribed] substance, auspicious washed rice grains should be offered. However, this has been stated specifically regarding the worship of Śiva. In the case of the *Ādrācāra* (or *Ādyābhāva*), the secondary options (*anukalpa*) and the scriptural authorities for their measurement are demonstrated in the practical application (*tatprayoga*).

Now, the procedure for arranging the vessels (*pātrāsādana*): therein, first, regarding the placement of the jar of pure water (*śuddhodakakalaśa*), according to the *Kālīmata*, one should first perform the placement of the conch (*śaṅkha*) and immediately thereafter perform the placement of the jar. As stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
To the left of the conch, however, there should be the placement of the water-pot;
one should place the jar—either made of gold or likewise of silver—within the mandala.
"Whether it be made of copper, or of earth, or even devoid of any metal.

However, according to the *Kādima-tantra*, the procedure should be performed in the manner beginning with "first the jar, then the conch," and so forth; but in this case, for the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should understand that the order is reversed.

p. 168) Here, one should act according to the teacher’s instruction.
