Thinking "I shall worship," having performed the worship [of the deity], and having worshipped Gaṇapati-Śrī on the right, beginning from the very bottom with the visualization of the seven netherworlds starting from Ātala and so forth, [one offers] upwards: 4 *namaḥ* to Maṇḍūka;
4 *namaḥ* to Kālāgnirudra; 4 *namaḥ* to Mūlaprakṛti; 4 *namaḥ* to Ādhāraśakti.

To Kūrma, 4; to Varāha, 4; to Ananta, 4; to Pṛthivī, 4; to Amṛtāmbhonidhi, 4; to Ratnadvīpa, 4; to Nānāvṛkṣamahodyāna, 4; to Kalpavṛkṣavāṭikā, 4; to Haricandanavāṭikā, 4; to Mandāravāṭikā, 4; to Pārijātavāṭikā, 4.

Having meditated upon [the mandala] as consisting of five pretas, one should visualize Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara as standing in the form of four feet located in the four corners beginning with the northwest.

Having meditated upon Sadāśiva— possessing the radiance of yellow, dark-blue, red, and white suns, four-armed, seated upon their shoulders, firmly attached, lying supine with his head toward the north, and shining like the moon— one should worship him as follows:
in the northwest, 4 *lāṃ* salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth.

*Brahmapretāsanaśrī*, in the Īśāna [direction], *oṃ hūṃ haḥ phreṃ kṣaḥ* (4), obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the left foot; *Viṣṇupretāsanaśrī*. In the Āgneya [direction], *oṃ hūṃ haḥ phreṃ kṣaḥ* (4), *rāṃ*, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of fire; *Rudrapretāsanaśrī*. In the Nairṛta [direction], *oṃ hūṃ haḥ phreṃ kṣaḥ* (4), *yāṃ*, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the wind.

In the center of the venerable seat of the Lord-Preta (īśvarapretāsana), [one should worship] with "4 Hsauḥ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Lord of the Sky; obeisance to the venerable great preta-seat of Sadāśiva. Having thus worshipped the five preta-seats, one should [worship] the fourfold virtues (dharma, etc. in the four corners starting from the northwest of that [seat].

Having worshipped the fourfold [set] beginning with Adharma in the four directions starting from the west in a clockwise direction, and having worshipped Māyā and Vidyā in their center, one should worship above them with the mantra "Obeisance to Ananta, resplendent with five hundred hoods. In his center, upon his crown, is an eight-petaled lotus, the seat of Kāmeśvarī.

Having meditated and performed worship from "Salutation to the Lotus" up to the Supreme Reality (paratattva), one should worship the nine Śaktis— Mohinī and the others— as prescribed in the Nyāsa of the Yogapīṭha, upon the filaments and in the center of the eight-petaled lotus; then,
having worshipped the entire Pīṭha with the Pīṭha-mantra as stated in the Nyāsa, one should [place] the Śrīcakra upon it.
Having meditated [upon her], one should worship the entire *cakra* with the collective mantra of the *yoginīs*, beginning with "samastaprakaṭa... and so forth.
Then, in the *binducakra*, [one recites]: 4 *mūlaṃ oṃ hrauṃ klīṃ aiṃ bhagavati blūṃ nityākāmeśvari strīṃ sarvasattvavaśaṅkari saḥ tripurabhairavi phreṃ vicce hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having worshipped three times with the *pūrṇavidyā*, "Śrī Mahātripurasundaryambā Śrī," and having worshipped again three times with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should meditate upon the *śrīcakra* as consisting of three cities;
then, in the first wheel— which consists of three squares, sixteen petals, and eight petals— one should utter the first *kūṭa*.
"Salutation to the Self of the Body," in the central wheel consisting of two sets of fourteen spokes; 4. Second:
"Salutation to the Self of the Intellect," in the inner wheel consisting of an eight-spoked [wheel], a triangle, and a bindu; 4. Third:
"Salutation to the Self of the Vital Breath"—having thus worshipped, one should again worship in the third outer [circle] according to the divisions of outer, middle, and inner.

Having worshipped with the three *kūṭas* according to the stated sequence, and likewise having worshipped in the three middle wheels and the inner triad, one should worship the four *pīṭhas* in the center and at the three corners of the triangular wheel;
then, in the *bindu*-wheel, the great *Uḍyāna-pīṭha*, one should worship with: "Obeisance to the golden thousand-petaled lotus."

Having worshipped the six seats within the two four-sided lotuses—namely, in the circles of the fourteen-spoked, the ten-spoked, the double eight-spoked, the triangle, and the point—in the four-sided [lotus]: *nādaśaktiśrī*; in the sixteen-petaled [lotus]:

Having worshipped the nine Śaktis— 4 Raudrīśaktiśrī in the inner ten-petalled lotus (antardaśāra), 4 Vāmaśaktiśrī in the eight-cornered figure (aṣṭakoṇa), 4 Vibadhnīśaktiśrī in the triangle (trikoṇa), 4 Dūtarīśaktiśrī in the point (bindu), and 4 Sarvānandāśaktiśrī— and having meditated upon the Śrīcakra as consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), [one recites] 4 Aṃ 50.

Having worshipped the entire seat with a handful of flowers, saying: "Salutation to the Yogapīṭha of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose nature is water and earth," he then places a flower upon it, saying: "In the center above that, I fashion a cushion of flowers. Upon that [he recites]: *4 hrīṃ śrīṃ* [of] Mahātripurasundarī.

Meditating upon the form described in the visualization, thinking "I invoke the form of Oṃ Kāmeśvara-Kāmeśvarī, which consists of the entirety of consciousness and bliss," and having displayed the Śaktyutthāpana mudrā while uttering the root mantra, [one says]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the supreme form of Kāmeśvara-Kāmeśvarī. By casting flowers and other offerings, one should contemplate the form as it has been described.
"One should worship the imagined form"—this is the worship of the yoga-pīṭha.
Now, the worship of the Śrīcakra:

there, first, having meditated upon the Śrīcakra within the lotus of one's own heart, one should meditate upon the Goddess in its center. Next, I shall describe the meditation that is to be practiced by the gods.
Then [he beheld] the goddess, who resembles a lotus and is as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun. || 1 ||
Resembling the hibiscus flower, comparable to the pomegranate blossom,
resembling a ruby, and like the interior of saffron.
Adorned with a network of tiny bells from the rubies of her shimmering crown, she possessed sprout-like, curling locks of hair resembling a swarm of black bees. || 3 ||
Her lotus-like face was like a fresh,
rosy dawn, and her soft forehead-ribbon was curved slightly like a crescent moon.
To the Supreme Goddess, whose creeper-like eyebrows have the form of the Pināka bow, and whose eyes are playfully swaying with waves of joy and bliss; || 5 ||
She whose golden earrings gleamed with a mass of shimmering rays, and whose expansive,
beautiful cheeks surpassed the orb of the nectar-filled moon.
Her nose was perfectly defined by the measuring-line of Viśvakarman’s creation;
her lips were as red as copper, coral, or the bimba fruit; and she possessed a face like nectar.
Her rows of teeth are adorned like pomegranate seeds and diamonds;
her tongue, which speaks sweetly, shines like a lamp of jewels.
She surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of her smile,
and was graced by the region of her chin, endowed with incomparable qualities.
The great goddess Kambugrīvā was resplendent with arms as graceful as lotus stalks,
which were adorned yet weighed down by the burden of jeweled bracelets and armlets.
(182) Her lotus-like hands are delicate, shaped like the petals of a red lotus;
the radiance from the nails of her lotus-hands spreads across the expanse of the sky. || 11 ||
She possessed lofty breasts adorned with strings of pearl necklaces,
and her waist was exquisitely beautiful, encircled by the three folds of skin.
Adorned with a navel shaped like an eddy in the river of loveliness,
she possessed shapely hips encircled by a girdle fashioned from priceless gems.
The Mistress, whose hips were like two elephant globes, whose line of pubic hair was like a beautiful goad,
and whose thighs were as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Adorned with a pair of shanks resembling the plantain tree of loveliness, her two feet with hidden ankles and foreparts surpassed the beauty of tortoises. || 15 ||
Her lotus-feet were exceedingly charming with their tinkling anklets,
and her lotus-pedestals were rubbed by the crest-jewels upon the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
It was adorned with slender, long fingers and shining moon-like nails,
and it laughed with a continuous stream of splendor resembling a hundred moons.
She possesses the hue of the Japā flower, the Aḍima fruit, and red lead surpassed by the Lauhitya river;
she is clothed in red garments and holds a noose and a goad raised in her hands.
Seated upon jeweled flowers, adorned with red ornaments,
she has four arms and three eyes, and she holds five arrows and a bow.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor, and her body was ruddy with the intense saffron and great musk [unguents]. || 20 ||
Richly adorned with every elegant attire and decorated with all ornaments, she is the one who generates delight for the world and causes the world to be enamored. || 21 ||
The Goddess who attracts the world, whose form is the cause of the world, who consists of all mantras, and who is beautiful with all auspiciousness. (22)
One should thus meditate upon the Supreme Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī, who consists of all auspicious fortune, is eternal, and is delighted by supreme bliss. 22.
Having thus meditated on her as one with oneself, and having offered a handful of flowers to the head with the root mantra,

one should again meditate upon the Goddess in the heart-lotus in her previously described form, together with her limbs and her retinue; then, having worshipped the Goddess with mental offerings and presented the food offering (naivedya), [one should proceed].

At the time of eating, one should perform the internal Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. For instance, there, having meditated upon a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the *mūlādhāra*— fashioned from the fourfold [selves] consisting of the *ātman*, *antarātman*, *paramātman*, and *jñānātman*, and blazing with the fire of the *kuṇḍalinī*— and having meditated upon the venerable deity (*śrīdevatā*) therein, [one should offer into] her mouth.

At the end of the root-mantra, one offers the ego-sense with "I sacrifice the ego-sense, svāhā," and so forth; having offered each of these— falsehood, backbiting, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy— one by one with the ladle of Suṣumṇā and the mind as the dipping-spoon, one [offers them] again into the heart-lotus where [the ego-sense] has been consumed.
Having meditated and worshipped with all the services beginning with the *uttarāpośāna* offering, having recited the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*) as much as possible,

having offered the recitation, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should take a handful of flowers with both hands, visualize them as a lotus of the Mother (*mātṛkā*), and [form] the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā.
Having bound [the mudrā] at the heart and meditated upon the Goddess in her aforementioned form together with her retinue within the Sovereign Śrīcakra,
having caused her to assume the nature of radiant energy, one should raise Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra by means of the application of the internal mudrā;
then, together with her, that luminous goddess, throbbing within the heart, [should be led] through the sequence of piercing the six cakras.
Having led [the breath] through the *suṣumnā* path to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
and having rested for a moment in the great ocean of nectar through union with the supreme light,
one experiences the bliss of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti: *hasraiṃ hasakalahrīṃ hasrauḥ namaḥ*.

O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī! O You who dwell within the great forest of lotuses, whose form is the bliss of the primal cause; O Mother, benefactor of all beings, come, come, O Supreme Goddess! Come, come, O Queen of the gods of gods, O Tripurā, worshipped by the deities; O You who are fond of supreme nectar, come quickly!
Be present for the sake of accomplishment! O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible to your devotees and accompanied by your retinue, remain steadfast as long as I worship you.
Having thus recited the invocation mantra, one should bring that radiance through the path of the left nostril into the handful of flowers held in the hand sealed with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā; then,
having placed it upon the crown of the head— the location of the *brahmarandhra*— within the form visualized inside the *śrīpīṭha*.

Meditating upon Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is seated on the lap of Kāmeśvara and accompanied by her retinue, as being present in every limb, one should recite the root mantra and, with the *saṃsthāpinī* mudrā, establish her with the words: "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, stay here, stay here! and likewise: "Be present here, be present here!"

Having caused [the deity] to be present with the *sannidhāpanīya-mudrā*, again restrain [them] in the same manner with "sannirudhyasva 2" using the *sannirodhinī-mudrā*; having made [them] face [you] in the same manner with "sammukhībhava 2" using that mudrā;
and having veiled [them] in the same manner with "avaguṇṭhitā bhava 2" using that mudrā upon the limbs of the Goddess.

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavinyāsa*), likewise having rendered [the deity] nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) through the sprinkling of the stream of nectar with the *dhunī-mudrā*, likewise having rendered [the deity] supreme (*paramīkaraṇa*) with the *mahāmudrā*, and having displayed these nine mudrās beginning with the invocation (*āvāhanī*), one should then [recite] the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).

Having recited the previously mentioned *dīpinī* mantra and the *mātṛkā* from the letter *a* to *kṣa*, one should sprinkle the Goddess three times with the root mantra. Then, [one should perform the placement] in the heart-lotus of the Goddess with the *jīvanyāsa* mantra: *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ haṃ gaṇapakālike sauḥ sakala hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ krīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having established the life-force (*jīva*), one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Therein, touching the Goddess at the heart with the previously mentioned *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, one should recite that mantra three times or once; thus having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, then—

The nine mudrās known as Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Bījā, and Yonī— having displayed each one preceded by the recitation of its respective seed-syllable: *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, *saḥ*, *kroṃ*, *hasakhaphreṃ*, *hsauṃ*, and *aiṃ*— [one should then recite] *āṃ hrīṃ*.
Having displayed the noose mudrā with *kroṃ kroṃ*, the hook mudrā with *ghaṃ ghaṃ*,
the bow mudrā with *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sāṃ*— that is,
the arrow mudrā with these ten seed-syllables— one recites the root mantra four times.

Having worshipped the Goddess with the mantra "I worship the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," one should again recite the root mantra four times and, with the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, [offer libations] with the words "I satiate the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī."

Having offered libations into the lotus-face of the venerable Supreme Deity with drops of special *arghya* water, no fewer than three times and up to one thousand and eight times according to one's capacity, one should perform the sixteen services beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
Then, having recited the root mantra: "O Blessed One, Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, this is your seat."

"I prepare a seat here; please be seated," he says, having prepared any one of the following seats— a wooden, floral, leathern, cloth, or metallic one— and having seated the Goddess on his left side, he displays the lion-throne and lotus mudrās, bows down, and utters "Haṃ Haṃ Haṃ."

Having offered [the deity] with the gesture of supplication (*prārthanā-mudrā*), saying, "Take this, this, and this," one should present a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Then, having recited the root mantra and said, "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, you have arrived," one should inquire after her welfare and display the gestures of welcome and well-being, and offer a handful of flowers with the root mantra.

One should offer [the water]. Then, with the root mantra: *śrīmahātripurasundarīpādukāyai arghyaṃ kalpayāmi svāhā*, one should take a little water from the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and offer it upon the head of the Goddess.
Then, having offered the food (*naivedya*) with the *naivedya* mantra and displayed the *arghyamudrā*, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then...

Having taken water from the vessel for the feet (pādyapātra) with "4 mū0," and having offered the water for the feet to the Goddess's feet with "śrīmahātripurasundarīpādukāyai pādyaṃ parikalpayāmi namaḥ," one should offer it as before, display the mudrā of the water for the feet, and present a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). In the same manner, [one offers] the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Thinking "this is nectar," one prepares the *madhuparka* for the mouth;

having placed it in the mouth and displayed its mudrā, one then again offers water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) from the vessel containing pure water as before, and then brings forward the jeweled sandals.
O Mother, having put on these sandals fashioned from jewels, come to the bathing pavilion situated in the direction of Indra for the purpose of bathing in Tripura.

Having prayed thus, having caused her to put on the jeweled sandals, having led her to the bathing pavilion, having caused her to put on the bathing garment, and having seated her upon a golden throne, one should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya* as before; then, reciting the root mantra four times, one says: "I offer the bath-water to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; obeisance."

Having thus prepared bathing substances such as fragrant oils and *āmalaka* fruits, and having offered them as before, one should perform the anointing, rubbing with unguents, and dressing of the hair according to the *mahārājopacāra* rite; then, having caused [the deity] to bathe with pure water using Vedic and Puranic mantras, [one should bathe him] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having bathed again with pure water, and having bathed with the juices of various fruits such as sugarcane juice, coconut water, jackfruit, and mango— perfumed with camphor and other fragrances— and having sprinkled [him] again with water by means of celestial maidens (devāṅganā),...

Having bathed [the deity] with waters brought from various sacred fords in vessels made of gold and other materials, as before, having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra, having displayed the bathing mudrā, having prepared water for sipping (ācamanīya),
having given a cloth for the purpose of cleansing the hair and limbs, and having caused the removal of the water;
Having sprinkled the pair of garments, inlaid with various jewels, with the syllable *vāṃ*, and having consecrated them with the root mantra, one should worship them with:

"Obeisance to the two garments whose presiding deities are Bṛhaspati. Then, having dressed [the deity] with the words: "Obeisance, I offer these two garments to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," one should recite the root mantra four times.
Having displayed the *vastramudrā*, again offered the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*),

one should offer a neck-thread (*kaṇṭhasūtra*) made of silk thread or fashioned from gold and other materials, consecrated with the mantra "Salutation to the neck-thread whose deity is Viṣṇu," and then display the *upavītamudrā*.
O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī!
"O Mother, having put on these sandals made of jewels from Tripura, come; let us go to the spotless pavilion of ornaments."

Having thus made this request, he should lead [the deity] to the Ornament Pavilion (*alaṅkāramaṇḍapa*), seat her upon the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), and place the ornaments before her. Having sprinkled them with the syllable *vaṃ* and consecrated them with the root mantra, he should worship them with the mantra: "Obeisance to the ornaments whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu. Then [he should recite] the root mantra for the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.
Having offered them in general with "I consecrate the ornaments such as the crown; homage," one should offer them specifically, beginning with "I consecrate the crown;
homage," and so forth: the crown, forehead ornament, ear-pendant, necklace, neck-ornament, ring, long necklace, jewel-thread, string of letters, and ear-tassel.
Side-ornaments, nail-bright rings, necklaces hanging from the throat, half-necklaces, soft-weighted lappets, armlets, bracelets, bangles, arm-wraps,
parting-of-the-hair ornaments, cheek-ornaments, eyebrow-ornaments, navel-ornaments, jeweled garlands, and gem-studded girdles.

There were forty [ornaments], namely: a chain, a tooth-jewel, an ear-ornament, a waist-knot jewel, a knee-ornament, a toe-ring, an anklet-cluster, an ankle-bracelet, a *haṃsaka*, a small bell, and a face-plate; as well as other various kinds such as a crest-jewel and earrings.

Having adorned her with feminine ornaments and offered her as before with the offering mantra (*nivedana-mantra*), having presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and displayed the ornament mudrā (*ābharaṇa-mudrā*), and having brought forward the jeweled sandals (*ratna-pādukā*), [he recites] the root mantra: *Śrī Mahātripurasundarī*.
"Having mounted a pair of sandals, preceded by the five musical instruments, come to the sacrificial pavilion together with your retinue of attendants.
Having thus entreated her, [the officiant] [approaches] her along with the Śaktis, who hold various implements such as the parasol and the fly-whisk in their hands.

Having led [the Goddess] to the sacrificial pavilion, one should seat the Bhagavatī upon the lap of Kāmeśvara and seat the attendant deities in their respective places. Then, having meditated on Tripurasundarī as mounted upon the Śrīcakra according to the previously mentioned method beginning with "one should meditate on Tripurasundarī," one should offer a handful of flowers with the root mantra.

Having offered the fivefold perfumes—namely, sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and so forth; or powder, rubbed [fragrance], that which arises from burning, that produced by crushing, and that derived from the limbs of living beings—or any one of these, having sprinkled it as before, he should worship it with the mantra: "Obeisance to the fragrance whose deity is Viṣṇu."

4. Root Text: Having offered perfume with the mantra, "I offer perfume to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," and having presented it as before, having displayed the perfume-mudrā, and having offered a handful of flowers, one should bring various kinds of fragrant flowers, sprinkle them, [and offer them] to the deities of the forest (vanaspati-devatās).

Having worshipped with "Salutation to the flowers," [reciting] four times the root mantra: "I offer flowers to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, vauṣaṭ," having presented the flowers, displayed the flower-mudrā,
and offered a handful of flowers, one should bring incense in the incense-holder and sprinkle it with water.

Having rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should cast into [the vessel] either ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga*) or guggulu mixed with sugar and clarified butter, using the mantra: *klīṃ surabhitejase svāhā*.
Then, having worshipped the incense with: "Obeisance to the incense whose presiding deity is Gandharva," [one recites] the root mantra four times.
This incense, produced from the essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance, the most excellent scent, fit to be smelled by all the gods— may it be accepted.
Having offered incense with the mantra, "Obeisance, I offer incense to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," and having displayed the incense mudrā, one should place the bell on the left side,
sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra, transform it into nectar with the Dhenu-mudrā, and [worship] again with the Astra-mantra and perfumes and other offerings.
Having worshipped [the bell] and consecrated it with the bell-mantra, *oṃ jagaddhvanimantramātaḥ svāhā*,
while sounding it with the left hand and waving the incense vessel with the right hand, one should present the incense at a low level,
place that vessel on the goddess’s left side, and fill the lamp vessel with cow’s ghee.
Having placed a wick containing camphor into it, having ignited it with the mantra *hrīṃ*,
having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and having worshipped it with "Salutation to the lamp whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu," [recite] four times the root mantra:
"The great lamp, self-luminous, dispelling darkness everywhere, both within and without."

"May this lamp of light be accepted. I offer this lamp to the sandals of Śrī Tripurasundarī; obeisance. Having thus presented the lamp and displayed the lamp-mudrā, having offered it as before, and having held up the lamp loudly while ringing the bell, [place] that vessel before the Goddess.
Having placed [the vessel] on the southern side in front of the Goddess, and having fashioned a square mandala with water,

one should place upon that mandala a vessel made of gold or other materials, filled with various side-dishes, endowed with the six flavors, and accompanied by the fivefold food offering (naivedya), together with its support, while reciting the root mantra.

Having gazed [at the offering], sprinkled it with that same weapon-mantra (*astra*), struck it three times with *kuśa* grass, and sprinkled it again with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should sprinkle it once more with water consecrated seven times with the mantra "Oṃ jūṃ saḥ vauṣaṭ. Then,
displaying the discus-mudrā (*cakramudrā*) with the weapon-mantra while touching the food offering (*naivedya*) with the left hand turned downward, one should touch it with the seed-syllable "Yam."

Having recited [the mantra] seven times, he dries up the defects therein; then, touching it with his right hand turned downward while reciting the fire-seed syllable *ram* seven times, he burns away the defects therein; then, touching it with his left hand turned downward while consecrating it seven times with the seed-syllable *vam*, he transforms it into nectar by means of the root-mantra.

Having sprinkled [the offering] with drops from the special *arghya* vessel, having consecrated it for the food offering (*naivedya*) dedicated to Viṣṇu by saying "Obeisance to the food offering whose deity is Viṣṇu," having protected it with the *astra-mantra*, and having empowered it seven times with the root mantra, one should empower it with the *Kāmadhenu-vidyā*: *oṃ klīṃ kāmadughe amoghe varade vicce sphura sphura śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having rendered [the offering] nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā* (and having rendered it supreme by means of the *mahāmudrā*), having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) to the Goddess as before, having worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*), and having rendered the water in another vessel into nectar, one should take it in the hollow of the cupped hands while touching the food-offering vessel (*naivedyapātra*) with the left thumb.

Having recited the root mantra, one should offer water from the joined palms over the food offering with the words: "I offer the food offering (naivedya) to the venerable Śrī Mahātripurasundarī-pādukā, together with her limbs, weapons, retinue, and all-encompassing self; obeisance. Then, with palms joined, having recited the root mantra, [one addresses] O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī...
O Supreme Goddess, please accept this divine golden vessel containing well-prepared supreme rice, prepared in five ways and endowed with the six flavors.
At the end of this, having offered [the oblation] with the previously mentioned mantra, having consecrated the water in another vessel as *amṛta*,

and having given a little of that water into the right hand of the Goddess, one should cause the Goddess to consume it with the mantra "Kroṃ, thou art the under-layer of nectar, svāhā," while displaying with the left hand the *grāsamudrā* resembling a full-blown blue lotus, with the right hand.

One should display the five mudrās of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as follows: 4 *aiṃ oṃ prāṇāya svāhā*—with the thumb, one should touch the little finger and the ring finger. 4 *klīṃ oṃ apānāya svāhā*—with the thumb, one should touch the index finger and the middle finger. 4 *sauḥ oṃ vyānāya svāhā*...
Thus, one should touch the middle and ring fingers with the thumb, reciting: *4 Aiṃ Klīṃ udānāya svāhā*.
Then, one should touch the ring, middle, and index fingers with the thumb, reciting: *4 Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ samānāya svāhā*.
Finally, one should touch all the fingers with the thumb, reciting: *4 Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ samānāya svāhā*—thus displaying the five mudrās of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

Having caused [the deity] to take five mouthfuls, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite the root-mantra: *aiṃ ātmatattvavyāpikāśrīmahātripurasundarī tṛpyatu*. Again, the root-mantra *klīṃ vidyātattva...*. Three times, the root-mantra *sauḥ śivatattva...*. And the root-mantra *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ sarvatattva...* thus.

Having caused [the deity] to consume four morsels with the *tattvas*, and having uttered the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) with palms joined in reverence, one should display the *naivedya-mudrā* with both hands while reciting: "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, O Goddess, I offer unto You this sacrificial food (*saddhaviḥ*) in the vessel of consciousness (*citpātra*), accompanied by various kinds of delights and many sorts of edible foods. (Mūla, p. 185)
May he accept that [offering] from her together with her followers.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with this mantra, one should present the various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*) as being identical in essence (*tādātmyena*) to the Goddess together with her retinue. Then, having rendered the water—contained in a vessel of gold or other materials and scented with camphor and the like—into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenumudrā*, [one recites] "Oṃ Mūla-mantra Śrī Mahātripurasundari... (4 times).

"Salutations to you, O Goddess of the gods! Accept this supreme, excellent water, which brings all-satisfying fulfillment; it is unoffered to others, pure, in its natural state, and refreshingly cool; it is filled with the bliss of nectar. Having thus offered the water to the Goddess, he should enclose the dining area with a curtain while reciting the Astra-mantra and ringing a bell.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess while she is eating, as follows:
she is surrounded by Brahmā, Īśa, and the other gods seated closely around her,
and she is being fanned by her female companions who are holding a multitude of whirling yak-tail fans.
Devoted to jests, play, and laughter, she who is the sport of consciousness eats the six flavors from a golden vessel while smiling at those who dine in rows.

Having meditated thus, having recited the root mantra ten times, and having offered the recitation while visualizing the Goddess as having eaten and being fully satisfied, one should consecrate water in another vessel with the *dhenumudrā* and, saying "Oṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi svāhā," give the water for the final rinsing (*uttarāpāśāna*) into the hand of the Goddess, and likewise—

Having visualized that [offering] as having been consumed and its essence departed, one should remove the *naivedya* and place it in the southwest direction (*nairṛtyāṃ diśi*). Then, having purified that spot with water from the sprinkling-vessel (*prokṣiṇī*) using the *astra-mantra*,
and having given water to the Goddess for the purpose of washing her hands and face, [one should provide] for the purpose of rubbing the hands...
Having given fragrant powder and caused him to perform mouth-rinses, having caused him to clean his teeth with pieces of camphor, having again caused him to perform mouth-rinses,
and having offered water for washing the feet and water for sipping, [he gave] that which was mixed with fragrance such as camphor.
Having brought betel leaves and sprinkled them with water, worship them with "Obeisance to the betel, whose deity is Vanaspati.
Then, having offered it with "Mūla-mantra: Obeisance, I offer this betel to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," [recite] the Mūla-mantra four times: "Śrī Mahātripurasundarī..."
Please accept this betel, which is scented with tamāla leaves, camphor, and areca nut, made fragrant, and thoroughly refined.

At the end of this, having offered betel-leaf to the Goddess with the mantra: *oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ idaṃ idaṃ idaṃ gṛhāṇa svāhā*, and having prostrated with the *yonimudrā* while worshipping with the root mantra: *I worship the Śrīpādukā of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī*, and having performed the worship according to the method to be described, [he recites] *klīm*.
Having formed the *namaskāra-mudrā* and displayed it with the root mantra, one should prostrate and release [the breath] with "Hūṃ.

If the practitioner is a Śākta, he should worship the Goddess’s body at the locations of the pure *mātṛkā*s using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), employing the letters of the *mātṛkā* encased within the root-vidyā in both direct and reverse order.
One should also perform the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅgapūjā) upon the body of the Goddess— this is the worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅgapūjā).

Having displayed the mudrās such as Saṃkṣobhaṇī and the others for the Vidyā, one should satisfy [the deities] three times with drops from the special arghya using the left hand, and then perform the worship of the surrounding retinue (āvaraṇapūjā).

Now, the worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅgapūjā) is described in another tantra: "With the letters of the Mātṛkā together with their roots, proceeding both in direct and reverse order, one should worship the limbs of the Goddess in their respective locations with flowers moistened by scented water. (1)
Having first performed worship, the wise one should worship with the six limbs;
this is declared to be the limb of dissolution (layāṅga), which bestows the accomplishment of the state of the deity.
One should worship the six-limbed enclosure within the wheel according to the procedure taught in the Kalpa;
that is designated as the limb of enjoyment, which causes the gratification of the deity. (3)

Thus [it is said]. Here, the worship of the *layāṅga* (dissolution limbs) and the *bhogāṅga* (enjoyment limbs) is indeed necessary, because it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Supreme Goddess, one should arrange the *layāṅga* within the body of the Goddess. In this regard, both systems agree on the *layāṅga* and *bhogāṅga*. Regarding the specific procedure for the purification of the deity (*devaśuddhi*), the *Kulārṇava* says:
One should sprinkle [the deity] three times with the root mantra, the Dīpinī, the Mālinī, and water for the arghya offering; this is declared to be the purification of the deity.
This, however, is according to the *Kālīmata*. According to the *Kādimata*, on the other hand:
"One should sprinkle [the deity] three times with the root mantra, with the *Dīpinī*, and with drops of the *madhuparka* *arghya*; thus is the purification of the deity described. (1)

This is because it is stated thus in the *Tripurārṇava*. Here, both collective worship (*samaṣṭipūjā*) and individual worship (*vyaṣṭipūjā*) must be performed. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "Collective worship is at the beginning; individual worship is at the conclusion."
This [rite], which causes gratification to the deity, should be performed by those desiring success. || 1 ||
All the deities of the surrounding enclosure of the Great Goddess are of the nature of rays;
they are reflected within the yantra just as [images are reflected] in a clear mirror. (2)

The worship of the deities reflected [in the mirror] according to the path taught in the scriptures is called collective worship (samaṣṭipūjā); likewise, individual worship (vyaṣṭipūjā) is now described.
(186) Here, in this worship of light-rays by the Great Goddess, may those deities who have been worshipped—merged into the limbs of Śrī Sundarī—be the bringers of all happiness. || 4 ||
Having spoken thus, the deities of the yantra dissolved into the body of the Goddess;
the preceptor, having thus visualized them as having become the very forms [of the Goddess], [placed them] in their respective locations.

"One should worship with flowers upon the limbs of the Goddess; this is declared to be the individual (vyaṣṭi) worship. Thus it is said. At the commencement of the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjā), however, one should recite: "O Supreme Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, who are fond of the sacrificial pap (caru) of supreme nectar;
O Mistress of the Gods, grant me permission for the worship of your retinue. Thus.
Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*); such is the tradition.

*Tāra-trayaṃ dhruvo māyā haṃsaḥ so'haṃ śucipriyā | Sarvasaubhāgyajananīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi ca || 1 ||* [The mantra: The three *Tāras*, the *Dhruva*, *Māyā*, *Haṃsaḥ*, *So'haṃ*, and *Śucipriyā*. I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) of the Mother who generates all auspiciousness.
The wise one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the Goddess with the *anunā* mantra;
then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, he should offer his prayer.
O Goddess, who consists of all mantras, who is saluted by all the gods,
grant me permission, O Queen of the Gods, for the worship of my retinue.
Having thus prayed, all the deities of the coverings emerged from the body of the Goddess like sparks from a fire, appearing in the form of rays of light.
One should contemplate that, by the command of the Goddess, they remain each in their respective places:
Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, and Kāmarāja.
Agastya, Nandin, and Sūrya, as well as Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Śiva;
likewise Dūrvāsas and Śakra, Unmanī and Varuṇa.
Dharmarāja, Anala, the Nāga king, Vāyu, Budha, as well as Īśāna, Rati, and likewise Nārāyaṇa. || 7 ||
Brahmā, Jīva, and Mahādevī—these twenty-five are the worshippers;
by them is this Vidyā worshipped in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
In this binducakra, the Fourth (Turīyā) is to be worshipped with effort using the special arghya-amṛta, encapsulated by the three Tāras in their proper sequence.
Then, having said "I worship the venerable Śrī, the Vidyā worshipped by [Name], the Śrī-pādukā; obeisance," one should perform worship with the five offerings (pañcopacāraka). || 10 ||
Holding nooses, goads, bows, and arrows, and possessing red bodies,
they should be diligently meditated upon by the wise as bestowers of all prosperity.
One should indeed display the Yoni-mudrā, which bestows all prosperity and the power of speech;
by means of this sequential yoga, one should worship the multitude of Vidyās.
One should offer worship consisting of a multitude of vidyās to Mahādevī by means of the rite of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
At this time, O Goddess, one should worship the Tithinityās, having visualized a great triangle in the sequence from the south, to the east, and to the north. (14)
O Goddess, O Adrijā, on the three lines there are five divisions each,
starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī).
One should worship each Nityā daily and shall become a possessor of great good fortune;
indeed, during the dark fortnight, one should worship them starting from Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī.
One should worship sequentially up to the end of the new moon (darśānta) by increasing and decreasing [the offerings] one by one;
one should worship the Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā, in their proper order.
With the fivefold offerings beginning with fragrance, and with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra vessel,
one should recite each respective Vidyā encased within the triple Tāra mantra.
Having uttered "I worship the śrī-pādukā of [Name] Nityā," the word "namaḥ" follows; O Great Goddess, this sequence is prescribed for every instance. (19)
Kāmeśvarī, Mahānityā, then indeed Bhagamālinī, Nityaklinnā, Mahānityā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī. || 20 ||
Mahāvajreśvarī is eternal, and likewise Śivadūtī;
so too is Tvaritā, O Great Goddess, and then indeed Kulasundarī. (21)
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī, and then Citrā Tripurasundarī. (22)
She is red in color, with a red silk garment, smeared with red unguents, and adorned with red ornaments;
she holds a noose and a goad, a bow and arrows, a book, and a rosary.
One should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī in this manner—bestowing boons and fearlessness, bringing the three worlds under her control, and granting subjugation, good fortune, and eloquence. (24)
She stood in the midst of a *kadamba* grove, possessing a splendor like the rising sun, adorned with various ornaments, and capable of attracting the three worlds. (25)
Holding a noose and a goad, a book, and a pen upon a palette,
as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she is the Mother of the Universe.
Thus the wise one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Bhagamālā—red in hue, wearing red garments, with the moon as her crest-jewel, and possessing three eyes. (27)
With a perspiring face and eyes rolling from intoxication, she is adorned with jewels;
she holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-bowl that likewise dispels great fear.
One should constantly meditate upon Nityaklinnā, seated upon a lotus throne,
resembling ten million moons, and flowing with the liquid essence of nectar.
She has a blue throat and three eyes, adorned with various ornaments;
she possesses the radiant luster of a sapphire and is graced by the peacock that serves as her vehicle.
One should meditate upon the goddess Bheruṇḍā, the destroyer of poison, who holds a noose, a goad, a skull-cup, and a knife, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate [on her] possessing the luster of molten gold, adorned with various ornaments,
holding a noose, a goad, a svastika, and a spear, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the Goddess Vahnivāsinī, who wears a jewel-encrusted crown,
who resembles a hibiscus flower, and who is resplendent in red garments.
She is eternally adorned with rubies and embellished with various ornaments;
she is reeling from drinking the nectar situated within her skull-cup, while holding a noose and a goad.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mahāvajreśvarī, who bestows fearlessness, has the color of dūrvā grass, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a great lion-throne. (35)
One should meditate upon the eternal Śivadūtī, the supreme Śivā, who holds a conch, a bow, and arrows, as well as a goad, a noose, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
She has a dark-complexioned body, adorned with beautiful red lotus-like hands and feet;
her beautiful braid is decorated with a vṛṣala-serpent and embellished with jewels on its hood.
Clad in garments of leaves, adorned with ornaments of leaves, with a girdle made of a pair of Vaiśya snakes,
she has a slender waist and a pair of full, rounded breasts, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
She bore the luster of a peacock’s crest, was adorned with bracelets and armlets, was reddish-brown like gunja berries, possessed arm-rings of serpent-kings, and was decorated with jewels. (39)
She whose ear-ornaments were the throbbing ears of a serpent-like twice-born man, whose eyes were intoxicated and reddish,
who wore excellent flowers in her dark, curly braided hair, and who carried a skull.
The wise man should meditate upon Tvaritā, who is adorned with a residence richly furnished with peacock feathers, and who is seated majestically upon a shimmering lion-throne. (41)
One should meditate upon the Goddess Maheśānī, who dwells in the midst of a Kadamba forest,
within a jeweled pavilion in the heart of a great Kalpa forest.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the shade of a pearl parasol,
she wore a crown fashioned from priceless gems and adorned with jeweled earrings.
Adorned with necklaces and neck-ornaments inlaid with excellent jewels, radiant with bracelets, graced with beautiful ornaments of diamonds and pearls, and resplendent in white silken garments; (44)
Her lotus-feet are beautiful with golden anklets and red lotuses;
she is lovely with auspicious unguents on her limbs and radiant with pieces of camphor.
Holding a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right,
she is divine, devoted to granting boons, and bestows the great Sarasvatī.
In this manner, one should meditate upon the Great Nityā, the Goddess of the gods, the Beauty of the Kula;
thus should the best of teachers contemplate the Great Goddess Nityā—resplendent with white garments and a seat, beautiful, and possessing a luster like that of the moon or jasmine. (48)
She is exceedingly serene, moon-faced, and adorned with various jewels;
she wears infinite ornaments of pearls and flows with the liquid essence of nectar. 49.

One should remember the goddess Mahānityā, who is richly adorned with the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who possesses a blue banner, and is decorated with golden ornaments;
she shines with the beauty of a rising streak of lightning and is resplendent in a golden garment. (51)
Seated majestically upon a great lion-throne, she is formidable with garlands of flames;
she holds a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, a trident, and likewise a hand-drum.
She holds a drinking vessel and grants boons, destroying enemies;
she is of radiant form, the eternal giver of knowledge, and always clothed in variegated garments. (53)
She is eternally adorned with various tilakas, radiant with diverse saffron pigments,
enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and in some places bearing various weapons.

For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate on the auspicious Goddess, who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, possesses four arms and three eyes, and holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow.
Thus end the sixteen constant meditations.
At this time, O Goddess, the wise one should worship the gurus;
he should worship the three rows of gurus in the space between the front and the center of the *yoni*. || 1 ||
One should worship one's own guru by means of the guru-mantra or even by name; and with the thumb and middle finger, one should properly satisfy the lineage of gurus.
O Goddess, one should worship the Gurus ending with Ānandanātha, as well as the Śaktis ending with Ambā, in their proper sequence, and likewise the supreme primordial Gurus.
O Goddess, one should worship the lineage gurus— both the higher and the lower— as well as the supreme gurus (parameṣṭhi-gurus), the powers of the gurus, and then the sandals of the venerable guru.
Thus, O Goddess, one should generally worship with the water from the vessel of the Guru;
then [one worships] Ādiśivanātha, Jñānāmbā, and Sadāśiva.
Ichchā, Ambā, and Īśvara; Ambikā and Rudra;
Raudrī, Viṣṇu, Jyeṣṭhā, Brahmā, and Vāmā—these are the designations of the Supreme (Parā).
There are eleven divine lineages, as well as Sanaka, Sanandana,
Sanātana, and likewise Sanatkumāra.
Sanatsujāta, the pervasive Dattātreya, Rocana,
Vāmadeva, Vyāsa, and Śuka are known as the hosts of Siddhas.
The gurus known as Parāpara, Nṛsiṃha, Maheśvara,
and Bhāskara, O Great Goddess, and from him [arose] Mahāśiva.
O Maheśvarī, Sadāśiva, the multitude of human beings, and Aparā—these are the common gurus; thereafter, one should worship Śrīnātha and the others.
Beyond that is Paraśiva, who is self-luminous;
likewise [are] Paraśakti, Kauleśa, Śukladevī, and Kuleśvara. || 11 ||
Kāmeśvarī and the divine lineages (divyaugha) are the gurus known as Parā in sequence;
Bhoga, Klinna, Samaya, and Sahaja are four in number. (12)
The successions of Siddhas known as Parāpara, Gaganau, Viśva, Vimala, Madana, Bhuvana, and Līla; || 13 ||
The multitude of humans known as Ātmapriya and Aparā, as well as those called Nijā,
are proclaimed here as the gurus of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja.
For those who do not know their own gurus and disciples, the gurus are described in succession.
Having said "Salutation to the Gurus," one should say "Salutation to the Pādukās. (15)
In that very same way, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the supreme and the intermediate-supreme [gurus],
the Paramaṣṭhin teachers, and then one's own gurus.
Paramādiśiva and likewise Kāmeśvaryambikā;
then the Divine Current (divyaugha), the Great Current (mahaugha), and immediately after that, the All-named (sarvākhyaugha).
The goddess Prajñā and Prakāśa are proclaimed as the divine currents (divyaugha);
likewise, Lopāmudrā, Prabhā, Māyā, Divya, and Citra. (18)
Kaivalyānandanātha, Devyātmānandanātha, Mahodaya, Siddhaugha, and likewise Citānanda; (19)
Ṛddhyambā, likewise Viśva, Śaktyambā, and Ramā, as well as Kamala, Para, and Manohara, in this order. (20)
Ātman and Pramita are proclaimed as the multitudes of sages (mānavaugha),
and from them came his own gurus of the lore known as Lopāmudrā.
Likewise, there is the illumination by another (paraprakāśa) and the reflective awareness (vimarśa) beginning with the Supreme (parā);
then Kāmeśvarī, liberation (mokṣa), and the immortal Person (puruṣa). || 22 ||
Aghora, Divyaugha, Prakāma, and likewise the true Guru;
Siddhaugha and Uttama—these four are proclaimed. || 23 ||
And the lineages of Siddhas, O Maheśānī, are then known as Uttama, Parama, Sarvajña, Sarva, and Siddhaka. || 24 ||
Govinda and Śaṅkara—these are proclaimed as the multitudes of human [gurus];
they are the gurus solely of the Śrīvidyā, following the sequence of one's own lineage of gurus.
Indeed, all these gurus, in relation to the Fourth State (turīya), have both hands adorned with skull-bowls filled with the nectar of the Wisdom-Seal (jñānamudrā). || 26 ||
The gurus should be red in color, with their heads bearing a mass of matted hair;
one should worship them with the five services using the *saṅghaṭṭa-mudrā*.
Then, having worshipped the lineage of gurus (gurukrama), one should worship the deities of the tradition (āmnāyadevatā) in the eight corners,
starting from the east, with drops of nectar from the śrīpātra vessel.
One should worship the Goddess Unmanī, the Mistress of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), situated in the eastern direction;
and one should worship Bhoginī, the Mistress of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya), in the south.
One should worship Kubjikā, the Mistress of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya), in the west;
and one should worship Kālikā, the Mistress of the Northern Tradition (uttarāmnāya), in the north.

To the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī, the Sovereign of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya), who is red in complexion, auspicious, and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as the noose and the goad. || 31 ||
Having worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) and displayed the yoni-mudrā,
one should then worship the tradition (āmnāya) and duly sacrifice to the sanctuary (āyatana).
In the inner nine-spoked [lotus], starting from the east and so forth, one should worship the Gurus with the nectar from their vessels,
as well as the deity of the eastern abode, Brāhmī, Darśanā, and Gāyatrī.
[Namely] Nārāyaṇa, known as Vaiṣṇava, the deity of the southern sanctuary;
and Sauradarśanasūrya, the presiding lord of the western sanctuary. (34)

One should worship Buddha, the founder of the Buddhist philosophy and lord of the Northern Region (Uttarāyatana), and Śiva, the lord of the philosophy known as the Upper Region (Ūrdhvāyatana-śaiva). || 35 ||
One should worship the Power known as Parā—the mistress of the vision of the Śāktākhya [system] located in the upper abode—within the Bindu-cakra; one should then contemplate the deities.
Red in color, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding their respective weapons in the other two hands;
having worshipped them with the five services (pañcopacāra), one should display the liṅga-mudrā. || 37 ||
After worshipping the sacred site, one should then worship the five jewels with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra, starting from the east on the outer ten-spoked wheel.
Śrīvidyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Vārāhī—O Maheśānī, these are proclaimed as the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna). || 39 ||
O Maheśvarī, in the Cakrarāja, the place of worship for Śrīvidyā,
she is seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly of Mahāratneśvarīs.
Having uttered, "I worship the sandal that generates all auspiciousness," one should perform sacrifice there and display the yoni-mudrā. || 41 ||
Red in color, with nooses and goads in their hands and holding their own weapons in two other hands;
having worshipped the five jewels, one should then worship the five Kalpalatās.
On the fourteen-spoked [wheel], starting from the east and so forth, with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra, one should worship Śrīvidyā, Tvaritā, and likewise Pārijāteśvarī. (43)
Trikūṭā, Pañcabāṇeśī, and the five Kalpalatās are thus remembered;
they are red in color, holding nooses and goads, with their two hands bearing their own respective weapons.
And at the conclusion of the worship of the creepers, one should worship the five lion-thrones on the eight petals, starting from the east, with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra.
Bālā is the bestower of prosperity, and Caitanyā follows immediately after her;
the second is Caitanyarūpā, and Kāmeśī follows immediately after that. || 46 ||
And one should worship these [goddesses] along with Unmanī in due order in the eastern direction;
immediately thereafter, one should worship the throne called Brahmā.
Aghorabhairavī, Mahādikā Bhairavī, Lalitābhairavī, and likewise Kāmeśī Bhairavī. (48)
Then, for the sake of attaining good fortune, one should worship Raktanetrā, Bhoginī, and Viṣṇusiṃhāsana, who are situated on the right side.
Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī, Nityābhairavī immediately after that, as well as Mṛtasañjīvinī and likewise Mṛtyuñjayaparā. || 50 ||
O Goddess, one should worship Vajraprastāriṇī, Kubjikā, and Raudrī, as well as Siṃhāsana, in due order in the western direction.
On the northern lion-throne, however, one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī,
Kamaleśī-Bhairavī, and Siddhakauleśa-Bhairavī.
The wise one should worship the Lion Throne (siṃhāsana), consisting of Bhairavī named Ḍāmara, Kāminībhairavī, and the one called Kālikāmīśvara. 53.
O Maheśānī, situated upon the upper lion-throne in the center of the Bindu are the first Sundarī and likewise the second Sundarī. (54)
The third is indeed Sundarī, the fourth is likewise Sundarī, the fifth is indeed Sundarī, and [the sixth is] Mahātripurasundarī. || 55 ||
Then, O Queen of the Gods, one should worship the Lion Throne known as Sadāśiva;
they are red, auspicious, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding nooses and goads.
After the worship of the lion-throne, there should be the worship of the five vessels;
in the sixteen-spoked [mandala], beginning from the east, one should perform it with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra.
Śrīvidyā, Parajyotis, Paraniṣkalaśāmbhavī, Ajapā, and Mātṛkā—these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (kośas). || 58 ||
One should worship Lakṣmī at the edge of the enclosure for the sake of all prosperity;
in a square [mandala], however, one should worship from the east onwards with drops of nectar from the Śrī-pātra.
Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Triśakti, and Sarvasāmrājyā—these are proclaimed as the five Lakṣmīs. (60)
Having worshipped the five Lakṣmīs, who are red in color, holding nooses and goads, and possessing two hands bearing their own weapons, one should worship the five Kāmadughās.
In the creation wheel (sṛṣṭicakra), starting from the east and so forth, [one should worship] with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra:
Śrīvidyā, Amṛtapīṭheśī, Sudhāsūramṛteśvarī, and [the others]. 62.
The five well-known wish-fulfilling cows, known as Annadā and Pūrṇā, and so forth, appear in sequence;
they hold a noose, a goad, a vessel of nectar, and a jar, and their bodies are red in color. (63)
Having performed worship, one should worship the five *samayas* that grant all desires;
in the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*), however, one should worship them starting from the east with drops of nectar from the *śrīpātra*.
Bagalā, Kālarātri, Jayadurgā, and likewise the goddess Vajravairocanī— these are proclaimed as the five Samayas.
Red in color, with nooses and goads in their hands, and holding their own weapons in the other two hands;
at the conclusion of the worship, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure (ṣaḍaṅgāvaraṇa) along with Samayā.

In the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu within the Saṃhāracakra, and in the center of the Bindu as well as in the four directions, [one should worship] with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra. || 67 ||
One should worship them in sequence in the center and in the directions for the sake of accomplishing all aims:
Sarvajñā, Nityatṛptā, and likewise Anādiprabodhinī. (68)
And the Great Śakti is independent, likewise eternally unimpaired, eternal, and infinite; thus she is described in the six limbs of enjoyment (bhoga-ṣaḍaṅga). 69.
The principal female forms have rays that are white as frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and ruddy; they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
O Great Goddess, these indeed are the specific coverings;
for those who worship the Fourth State (turya), these are truly essential.
In the case of the various secret sciences (kūṭavidyās), there are indeed specific limbs for each respective teacher;
here, O Ambikā, in the center of the arrangement, there is a ninefold repetition.
O Goddess, O beloved, hear now these intermediate arrangements;
indeed, these are necessary for those who worship the Fourth State (turya).
O Goddess, one should then worship Kṣobhaṇa and Drāvaṇa in the north, at the front of the two sides of the eight spokes, with ordinary drops of nectar.
One should worship Ākarṣa and Vaśya-bāṇa on the right side;
having first worshipped Sammohana in front, one should then contemplate the deities of the arrows (bāṇadevatās).

O Goddess, in the inner ten-spoked [lotus], those who are red in color, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing a goad, an arrow, and a bow, are situated on the sides as well as at the front.
O fair-faced one, one should perform the sacrifice with arrows; [the deities] known as Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja are the five desires. (77)
O Great Goddess, those with fish-emblems are proclaimed as the five Kāmas;
they are red in color, holding gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing five arrows and a bow. (78)
O Dear One, one should worship the six Vāc-s on the outer ten-spoked wheel according to the Kāma-vidhi;
merged with the nectar of the common vessel are the lower (aparā), the intermediate (parā), and the supreme (parā) Speech.
They are proclaimed as Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Vaikharī;
they hold the Jñānamudrā and gestures of protection, are white in color, and carry a lute and a book in their hands. 80.
And likewise, upon the fourteen-spoked wheel, on both sides, at the front, and in the center of the *bindu*, [one should worship] with the common nectar-drops. || 81 ||
For the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should worship the numbers of the Vedas and the states;
these are proclaimed as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya). || 82 ||
(190) Red in color, bestowing boons and fearlessness, holding nooses and goads, and auspicious;
then, at the base of the eight petals, O Śivā, there is a circle for the enclosure. 83.
One should worship the deities beginning with Vāmā with the nectar from the common vessel:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and likewise Icchā. (84)
Jñānā, Kriyā, Kubjikā, Bibhvī, Citrā, Viṣaghnikā, Bhūcarī, Khecarī, Jayā, and likewise Vijayā. || 85 ||
Nandā, Sundarī, and Deveśī are proclaimed to be the Śaktis;
they, adorned with divine ornaments, are Vāmā and the others, located upon the circle at the base of the eight petals.
They are red in color, holding nooses and goads, and likewise delighting in the granting of boons;
they hold pearl umbrellas and yak-tail whisks as beautiful as the moonlight of the autumnal moon.
A pedestal adorned with a pair of fans fashioned from moonstones set in uśīra-wood,
and a golden mirror shining with a fringe of pearl necklaces.
A casket made of ornaments, a box filled with moonstones,
one shimmering with the brilliance of the nine gems, and a container for betel-leaf.
A vessel filled with the powder of saffron enriched with camphor and musk,
a goblet fashioned of gold, a jar of nectar, and a water-pot.
A vessel made of jewels, filled with garlands rich with jasmine, *mālatī*, *jātī*, and *śatapatra* flowers, and a comb made of ivory.
Holding a collyrium-stick, they are one's own powers;
then, O Maheśvarī, upon the circle at the base of the sixteen-petaled lotus— (92)
One should perform the worship of the rays as an encircling with the common nectar,
for the sake of the satisfaction and nourishment of Bhāva, Cit, Māyā, Nātha, and Icchā.
Stability, liberation, and enjoyment; existence, non-existence, and that which consists of both existence and non-existence;
as well as action, the self, knowledge, and the worlds, and likewise the gods and the Vedas. (94)
Consciousness, birth, vibration, ideation, and non-vibration, as well as Kuṇḍalinī;
likewise, sounds, phonemes, vowels, and mantras consisting of the conjunction of consonant groups. || 95 ||
Bhairava and Bhūtaraśmi are proclaimed as the multitude of rays;
on the circle at the root of the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the rays beginning with Bhāva are red.
Holding nooses, goads, jars of nectar, and drinking vessels, they are auspicious;
then, on the first circle outside the sixteen-petaled lotus.
One should worship the Yoginīs with the general nectar as an encircling garland:
Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, and likewise Kākinī. (98)
Śākinī, Hākinī, Yākinī, and likewise Yoginī—these Yoginīs, headed by Ḍākinī, reside on the outer circle of the sixteen-spoked wheel. (99)
They carry nooses, goads, skull-bowls, and swords; they ride upon corpses; they are adorned with garlands of severed heads; and their lotus-faces are terrifying with protruding fangs.

O Śivā, [the goddesses] have four faces, are red in color, possess a terrifying form, and are arrogant with intoxication; they serve as the encircling boundary within the middle circle by means of the common nectar.
O Goddess, one should worship the Bhairavīs; immediately after that, Bhairavī, then Mahābhairavī, Siṃhabhairavī, and Dhūmrabhairavī. || 2 ||
Bhīmā, Unmanā-bhairavī, Vaśīkaraṇa-bhairavī,
and the one called Mohanā-bhairavī— these, O beloved, are declared to be the Bhairavīs.
On the outer and inner circles of the sixteen-spoked [wheel], however, are the Bhairavīs, whose faces are terrifying;
they hold nooses and goads in their hands, and carry skull-bowls and tridents.
Wearing garlands of severed heads, red in color, with terrifying fangs, and seated upon corpses—
thereafter, one should worship the ten Bhairavas with the common nectar (sāmānyasudhā).
Heruka, Vetāla, Tripurāntaka, Agnijihva, Kālānta, Karāla, and Ekapādaka. (6)
O Great Goddess, Hāṭakeśvara is of terrifying form and immovable;
on the final circle of the sixteen spokes, the ten [deities] beginning with Heruka are situated. || 7 ||
The Bhairavas have terrifying fangs and faces, and they carry tridents and axes;
dark as clouds, they are mounted upon corpses and bear skull-staffs.
The worship known as the middle arrangement has been described.
Listen, O Great Goddess, as I shall now speak of the worship of the ninefold enclosure (navāvaraṇa).
O Great Goddess, this wheel is adorned with a Bindu in its center;
from that [arise] a triangle, an eight-spoked wheel, and two ten-spoked wheels.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, this is the central wheel, consisting of eight corners;
from the bindu to the end of the eight corners, all of this constitutes the center.
O Pārvatī, it is joined with forty parts and also three parts;
O beloved, it is square, with eight petals and sixteen petals, in sequence.
All this must be marked with the nine yonis, for there are sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great power. (13)
In this wheel, those [powers] indeed honor the practitioner when they possess specific qualities;
however, without the instruction of a guru, they truly devour the practitioner.
In the Trailokyamohana-cakra,
one should worship the deities who bestow accomplishments (siddhidevatās), who reside upon the outermost line, with the nectar from the common vessel.
On the inner lines of the square, starting from the west and proceeding in order, [one should place them] at the gates, at the corners beginning with the northwest, and below and above. || 16 ||
One should worship by means of a clockwise circumambulation for the sake of accomplishing all aims:
namely, *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, and likewise *garimā*. (17)
O Dear One, lordship, mastery, the power to have one's will fulfilled, enjoyment, the attainment of desires, the fulfillment of all wishes, and the perfection of liberation follow in sequence.
Shining like gold recently smelted, auspicious, and bearing nooses and goads, they carry great ornaments and jewels along with gold—these are indeed the treasures (nidhis). (19)
Likewise, those holding a pair of lotuses and bestowing [boons] upon practitioners reside in the Trailokyamohana-cakra, situated along the central line. || 20 ||

The fifty deities of the seats (pīṭhadevatās), possessing the luster of molten gold, have their hands displaying the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; they are manifest in form. || 21 ||
Having worshipped those [goddesses], one should then worship Brāhmī and the others, along with the Siddhis,
in sequence at the eastern gate and the other gates, and in the pure corners and so forth.
O Dear One, they are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī, in due order.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, the one known as Unmatta, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas. (24)
Kāmarūpa, Malaya, the one called Kaula, and Kulāntaka;
O Goddess of Gods, Cauhāra-pīṭha, and after that Jālandhara. (25)
Uḍḍiyāna and Devikoṭṭa are proclaimed as the eight sacred seats (pīṭha).
The Mothers, seated upon the lap of Bhairava, have smiling faces and are languid with passion.
One should meditate in sequence upon the auspicious, manifest, divine Yoginīs, beginning with Brāhmī, all of whom hold a noose and a goad.
Then [he holds] the Vidyā, the trident, the spear, the discus, and the mace;
likewise the diamond-gem and lapis lazuli garland, the lotus, and the boon-granting hand.
The Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, who dwell in the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas),
bear a trident, a skull-cup, a corpse, and a small drum.

The deities of the eight seats (pīṭha) have the appearance of elephants, are formidable, adorned with curved locks of hair, and hold a noose, a goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in their hands.
There, the auspicious Yoginīs, resembling Jāmbūnada gold, are manifest;
O Dear One, one should worship them in this way on the third line as accomplished beings (siddhas).
One should diligently [worship] the goddesses of the mudrās, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī, as well as Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī. || 32 ||
The one who attracts all, likewise the one who brings all under control,
the one who intoxicates all, and then the Great Goad of All.
Then the Sarvakhecarikā, likewise the Sarvabījamudrā, the Sarvayoni, and thereafter the Sarvatrikhaṇḍā are proclaimed. || 34 ||
Those mudrās, headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, possess gentle forms;
they all hold nooses and goads, and likewise bear their respective hand-gestures (mudrās).
The auspicious Yoginīs are manifest, possessing the luster of molten gold;
they have red bodies and hold in their hands a noose, a goad, a blue lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness.
The deities of the four seats (pīṭhas), such as Kāmarūpa and the others, are manifest;
one should worship Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī), in front of the siddhi of aṇimā.
Having propitiated with the five offerings, one should show the primary mudrā;
these manifest yoginīs are established within the square.
In the Trailokyamohinī-cakra, there are likewise the oceans, along with their weapons, vehicles, retinues, and supernatural powers (siddhis). || 39 ||
"May they, together with their limbs and sub-limbs, being worshipped with all ritual services,
be satisfied"— saying this, one should pour water there.
O Tripurā, worshipped by the gods, grant me the fulfillment of my desires;
with devotion, I offer to you this worship of the first enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Having uttered this, one should then offer a handful of flowers to Mahādevī.
Thus, O auspicious lady, the worship of the first enclosure has been described to you.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the worship of the second enclosure;
then, one should worship Kāmākarṣiṇī upon the sixteen petals.
With the nectar from the common vessel, however, in the sequence beginning with the west, [one worships] Kāmākarṣiṇī and likewise Buddhyākarṣiṇī. || 44 ||
The attractor of ego, and likewise the attractor of sound;
the attractor of touch, and likewise the attractor of form. || 45 ||
The attractor of tastes, and likewise the attractor of fragrances;
the attractor of the mind, and likewise the attractor of fortitude. || 46 ||
Smṛtyākarṣiṇikā, likewise Nāmākarṣiṇikā, Bījākarṣiṇikā, and likewise Amṛtākarṣiṇikā. || 47 ||
Ātmākarṣiṇikā and likewise Śarīrākarṣiṇī are stationed upon the sixteen-petaled wheel that fulfills all desires.
And the Yoginīs, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī, who possess secret names,
consist of the sixteen digits (kalās) and abide in the center of the lunar mandala.
Having the color of the sun and being red in hue, their forms stream with nectar;
they hold nooses and goads, and they bestow the joy of jars filled with ambrosia from *kāśmarī* trees.
One should worship Cakreśī and Tripureśī before Kāmākarṣiṇī; one should display the Vidrāviṇī mudrā for the sake of good fortune.
"These are the Guptayoginīs; likewise, [one should offer] a handful of flowers to the Goddess, saying: 'In the Cakra that fulfills all desires, together with the Mudrās,' and so forth. (52)
"O Tripurā, worshipped by the gods, grant me the fulfillment of my desires;
with devotion, I offer to you this worship of the second enclosure. (53)
Having recited this, one should then offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the Mistress of the Gods within the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra, which unfolds with eight petals.
One should worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others with the common sudhā [offering] on the petals in the directions starting from the east, and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
After her was Anaṅgakusumā, then Anaṅgamekhalā;
after that was Anaṅgamadanā, and finally Anaṅgamadanāturā. || 56 ||
Then there were Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgaveginī, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī; these indeed possessed the radiance of the bandhūka flower. || 57 ||
One should worship Tripurasundarī at the tip of Anaṅgakusumā, she who is auspicious and whose hands hold a noose, a goad, and shimmering white and blue lotuses. 58.
Then one should display the Cakreśī mudrā, which attracts all;
these yoginīs are indeed most secret and bring about everything. (59)
Then, the knower of mantras should offer a handful of flowers to the Goddess with the mantra beginning with "kṣobhaṇe ca tathā cakre samudre" and ending with "abhīṣṭhā."
In the fourteen-spoked wheel named Sarvasaubhāgyadā, [one should worship] with ordinary waters, starting from the west and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.
O Dear One, one should indeed worship the Śaktis, of whom Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī is the chief:
the Śakti Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, and likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī; || 62 ||
Then the All-Attracting, followed by the All-Gladdening;
then the All-Enchanting, the All-Stupefying, and the All-Yawning. || 63 ||
The power that brings all under control, likewise the one that delights in all objects;
then the one who intoxicates all, and likewise the one who accomplishes all aims. (64)
From that indeed arises the power that fulfills all perfections;
it is the power consisting of all mantras, which brings about the destruction of all dualities. 65.
In the wheel that bestows all good fortune (sarvasaubhāgyada-cakra), there are the Yoginīs known as the Sampradāya, headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, adorned with all ornaments. 66.
All of them resemble indragopa insects, possessed of proud and intoxicated youth;
they hold a noose, a goad, a mirror, and a vessel for nectar.
Bearing all auspiciousness and bestowing the desired objects of the practitioners, one should worship Tripuravāsinī, preceded by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the others. 68.
Having displayed the mudrā that brings all under control, the wise one [should then invoke] these Yoginīs of the oral tradition in their proper sequence.
Then, O Śivā, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the Goddess Sarvārthasādhakā on the outer ten-spoked wheel with the ordinary nectar (sāmānyasudhā).
O Goddess, one should worship her as before, she who is the foremost bestower of all accomplishments;
likewise, the Goddess is the bestower of all accomplishments and the bestower of all prosperity. (71)
The Goddess who makes everyone dear, the Goddess who brings about all auspiciousness, the Goddess who grants all desires, and the Goddess who liberates from all suffering. (72)
She is the pacifier of all death, the destroyer of all obstacles;
she is the goddess beautiful in every limb, the bestower of all good fortune. (73)
In the wheel that accomplishes all aims, there are the supreme Yoginīs known as Kulakaulā, beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā, who grant all desires. (74)
Resembling hibiscus flowers, adorned with shimmering jewels, they were profound with great beauty, possessing full, rounded, and firm breasts. || 75 ||
With smiles upon their faces, they hold lamps made of various jewels, while the desired ornaments of the practitioner rest within jeweled caskets.
All of them hold nooses and goads and are likewise intent on bestowing jewels;
at the forefront of those who grant all accomplishments, one should worship Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel.
Then the wise one should display the Sarvonmādinī mudrā;
these are the yoginīs known as Kulakaula, as previously described. (78)
One should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the Goddess and then worship the sixth enclosure within the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra, which has ten spokes, O Maheśvarī.
With the nectar from the common vessel, however, in the sequence beginning with the west, [one worships] Sarvajñā, Sarvaśakti, and likewise Sarvaiśvaryapradā. (80)
She consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases, she is the very nature of the support of all, and likewise the remover of all sins. || 81 ||
The Goddess, who consists of all bliss and whose very nature is the protection of all, should be worshipped with diligence; she bestows the fruits of all that is desired. 82.
In the wheel that produces all protection, there are the Yoginīs known as Nigarbhā and others, who bestow auspiciousness;
they are the Sarvajñā and the rest, possessing the blazing splendor of fire. (83)
Possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns and adorned with ornaments of pearls,
they hold in their eight hands the noose, the goad, weapons, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and the gesture of granting boons.
O Goddess, one should worship Tripuramālinī in front of the Omniscient One;
O Goddess, one should show to the Goddess the mudrā known as Sarvamahāṅkuśā. 85.
"These are the Nigarbha Yoginīs in the wheel called Sarvarakṣākara;
together with their mudrās," and so forth—one should then offer a handful of flowers.
In the eight-spoked wheel that removes all diseases,
one should worship Vaśinī and the others in their proper sequence, starting from the west, using ordinary drops (bindu).
Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalāruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī, and Vāgīśvarī. || 88 ||
In the wheel that removes all diseases, there are the Yoginīs known as the Secret Ones, who bestow auspiciousness and grant all desires; they possess the luster of pomegranate flowers. (89)
Clad in red garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
adorned with various ornaments, they carry the five-arrowed bow.
Holding a book and the granting of boons, these bestowers of speech—
one should worship Tripurasiddhā, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī), preceded by Vaśinī.
One should display the mudrā of Sarvakhecarī for the sake of good fortune;
these are the secret yoginīs, O Maheśvarī, and so forth. 92.

And one should cast a handful of flowers for the Goddess with the words, "May there be the attainment of the desired goal," into the intermediate space within the great wheel named Sarvasiddhiprada (Bestower of All Accomplishments).
One should worship the deities of the weapons with the nectar from the common vessel:
the Jṛmbhakas, who are the deities of the arrows of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī.

O Great Goddess, there are the goddesses of delusion, the goddesses of misfortune, the goddesses of the noose who bring others under control, those called the goddesses of paralysis, and likewise the goddesses of the goad.
Then, with the nectar from the Śrīpātra, [one should worship] in one's own front triangle, in the solar wheel called Vāgbhava, and in the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa. 96.
And likewise, Kāmeśī, who is of the nature of Mitreśanātha, presided over by the waking state, and accompanied by the power whose essence is Rudra, bestows all accomplishments. 97.
Then, O Maheśvarī, she is of the nature of Uḍḍīśanātha in the seat known as Kāmarāja, which is the Soma-cakra, and likewise in Pūrṇagiri. || 98 ||
Likewise, the power of Viṣṇu presiding over the dream state is proclaimed as the great goddess Vajreśvarī; she is located in the third corner. 99.
Then, in the Jālandhara seat, within the fire-wheel (vahnicakra) known as Śakti,
she is of the nature of the Lord of the Sixth (Ṣaṣṭheśanātha) and likewise presides over deep sleep (suṣupti).
O Maheśānī, the Goddess Śrī Bhagamālinī, the power of Brahmā and Ātman, has arisen within the center of the Bindu, manifested through the three peaks (kūṭas). 101.
And in the entire wheel of the sky, in the seat known as Uḍḍiyāna, she is the very essence of Caryānātha and is presided over by the Fourth State (turīya). || 102 ||
Śrī Mahātripurasundarī is the power of the Self of the Supreme Brahman;
in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments, the Yoginīs are the givers of success. 103.
These deities of the eight weapons are known by extremely secret names;
the three beginning with Kāmeśvarī shine forth in the three corners. (104)
