Those eight goddesses of the weapons have bodies intoxicated with youth;
they are red, like streaks of lightning, and adorned with profuse flowers. (105)
Richly adorned with the nine gems, they each hold their respective weapons in sequence; bringing happiness, they bear the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as vessels of nectar.
Kāmeśvarī is white in color, adorned with white garlands and unguents; her ornaments sparkle like pearls, and she is embellished with various kinds of jewelry. || 107 ||
Holding a book, a rosary, and likewise the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
she who stands at the foremost corner is celebrated as Rudraśakti.
Vajreśvarī has the luster of saffron, is adorned with shimmering jewel ornaments, wears a garment like the rising sun, and her eyes kiss her dark ears. 109.
Adorned with a sugarcane bow, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
this goddess situated in the southeastern corner is considered to be the Śakti of Viṣṇu.
Resplendent like freshly smelted gold, adorned with a beautiful garland of lotuses, the Mistress of the World wears ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels. 111.
With her lotus-like hands displaying the noose, the goad, the gesture of knowledge, and the granting of boons,
she is the power of Brahmā, the Great Goddess, who cuts asunder the threefold afflictions.
The Goddess situated in the north-eastern corner, who bestows the fruits of all desires, one should worship there as Cakreśī Tripurāmbā, in front of Kāmeśī. 113.
Having propitiated with the five offerings, one should display the seed-syllable mudrā;
these are the yoginīs known as the "Extremely Secret," as previously described. (114)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should indeed offer a handful of flowers to the Goddess in the Bindu-cakra, O Maheśānī, which is named Sarvānandamaya (consisting of all bliss). 115.
O Śivā, in the very sequence beginning from the west, with the nectar of the Śrīpātra and according to the order of the three *kūṭas*, there is at every step a delight born of the mind.
The illustrious Tripurasundarī, the sovereign of all mantras and likewise the sovereign of all cakras, should be worshipped with diligent effort. (117)
She is indeed the sovereign of all tantras, as well as the sovereign of all yogas;
she is the sovereign of all enjoyments, and likewise the sovereign of all heroes. || 118 ||
She is the sovereign of all seats (pīṭha), likewise the sovereign of all speech;
she is the sovereign of all sciences (vidyā), and likewise the sovereign of all accomplishments (siddhi). || 119 ||
She is indeed the sovereign of all worlds, likewise the sovereign of all yogas, and likewise the sovereign of all cakras. || 120 ||
In the supreme wheel consisting of all bliss, which transcends the sphere of sound, the ancient teachers say that the Yoginīs are known as the "Secret of the Higher and Lower. (121)

Possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns and adorned with various ornaments, they all hold a noose and a goad, as well as the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). || 122 ||
One should contemplate all the goddesses as being full of youthful vigor, possessing full, rounded, and firm breasts, and facing toward Śrīvidyā. 123.
One should also visualize Śrīvidyā standing face-to-face with all [the goddesses], or else one should contemplate all the rays as being in the form of goddesses. (124)
O Supreme Goddess, in the Śrīcakra of the Svatantra, [the deities] resemble their respective [consorts];
[one should worship] the Mistress of the Cakra (Cakreśī), Mahātripurabhairavī, preceded by Rati.
Having worshipped [her], one should then display the *sarvayonimudrā* with the words "O Dear One, the Yoginī known as the Supreme and Non-supreme Secret," and so forth. (126)
Having offered a handful of flowers to the Goddess, one should satisfy her three times and again three times.

Thus, in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the illustrious Great Mahopādhyāya and worshipful teacher.
The Tenth Chapter. || 10 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇava Tantra,
the eleventh breath (chapter).
Now, the coverings (*āvaraṇas*) of the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*). Thus, in the *Kulārṇava*:

"Having performed the worship of the nine coverings and having satisfied the Goddess, [one worships] Śiva together with his limbs (*sāṅga*) and coverings (*sāvaraṇa*), by means of the sixteen modes of service (*upacāras*). (1)

O Śāmbhavī, one should worship her along with her entire retinue, who have been awakened by the Great Ṣoḍhā [rite], using the root mantra and offerings such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).

"One should worship each [deity] by its respective name, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*. Thus it is said. In the *Uttaratantro*: "And one should worship the Supreme Śiva, who resides within the *bindu* as the form of the seat (*āsana*)."
Either with the mantra of Parāprāsāda or with the Turīyā-vidyā. || 1 ||
One should worship and satisfy [the deity] thrice with the sixteen services,
using either the nectar from the Guru-vessel or the drops from the Śrī-vessel.
Having uttered the five *praṇavas*, [one recites] "consisting of Śiva and Śakti," and so forth; "I satisfy the *pādukā* of the venerable Supreme Ādiśiva. (3)
One should satisfy [the deities] ten times and display the ten mudrās as prescribed,
in the Bindu-cakra, in the four directions starting from the east, and in the center.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) and the surrounding rites (āvaraṇa) with the nectar from the vessel of the Guru, using the root mantras of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and the others.
Having worshipped the enclosure of the six limbs, as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
one should worship the feet of repose belonging to Rudra, Śambhu, and Parā.

The Ādinātha and other gurus, along with the divine Siddhas, the streams [of teachers], and the human [sages], are to be worshipped with diligent effort for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (7)
Then, by piercing the eight knots situated at the junctions of the eight corners,
[one should worship] with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra, one by one, on each of the two sides.

The sixteen root-mantras (mūlavidyās) beginning with Kulayoginī are red in color; they hold a vessel of ghee, a noose, and a goad, and their hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Then, one should worship and also satisfy [the deities] within the inner ten-cornered [figure],
in the four directions as well as above and below, with drops of nectar from the Śrīpātra vessel.
One should worship the six foundational vidyās in the ten-spoked wheel situated outside that;
having worshipped the kalās of Īśāna, one should then worship those of Puruṣa in the eight-petaled lotus.
One should indeed offer the eight portions (kalās) of Aghora into the knots of the eight petals;
one should worship the portions of Vāmadeva in the sixteen-petaled lotus.
Then, one should worship the Sadyojāta-kalā in the city of Bhūmi;
subsequently, [one should worship] in the intervals and the filaments of the Śrīcakra in due order.
By means of the four-cornered progression with the drops situated in the general *arghya*,
one should worship all the deities invoked in the Great Ṣoḍaśī.
One should perform the worship of the six divine rays of Śambhu within the bindu-cakra;
having thus performed the worship with the sixteen types of offerings (upacāras), [one should proceed]. (15)
"Having worshipped [the deity] who is complete with all [necessary] coverings, immediately thereafter...
Thus it is said in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"The food offering (*naivedya*), endowed with the six flavors and purified by the *Kāmadhenu* [mantra]..."
One should offer betel-leaf together with camphor to the Supreme Śakti. || 1 ||
O Dear One, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) according to the previously mentioned procedure;
O Supreme Goddess, one should also perform recitation (japa) and hymns of praise according to one's capacity.
"By the first two verses [of the text], one should likewise [worship] the deity of good fortune.
As for those first two verses:
"The glorious heart of the Śrīkośa, consisting of the five lion-thrones..."
And it is the fruit of the wish-fulfilling creepers, shimmering with beautiful jewels.
I bow for the attainment of bliss to that which delights in the four sense-bases, which resides within the sheath of the fourfold lineage, the eternally blissful supreme abode of Brahman. (2)
Thus it is said:
"In a vessel made of gold, silver, bronze, or the like, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place a handful of fragrant substances in the center, or indeed, a mudrā there. (3)
One should whirl nine lamps filled with clarified butter upon eight-petaled lotuses,
having placed them three times on the head while reciting the Ratnavidyā mantras.
"One should remember that [mantra] with the root-mantra at the end for the pacification of all obstacles.
Thus it is said. As for the *Ratnavidyā*, however, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Śivā, [the syllables] *ga*, *sau*, *ca*, *pa*, *ma*, and *na* are subsequently situated in the position of Indra (the east) in sequence."
Adorned with the beauty of earrings on their left ears, their heads were embellished with the bindu mark. || 1 ||
This nine-syllabled mantra of Ratneśī is enclosed by the *saṃpuṭa* of Ramā:
*śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ slūṃ plūṃ mlūṃ nlūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, it is stated: "Pradyotana is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (*chanda*)."
Ratneśvarī shall be the deity, and the seed-syllable *māyā* (hīṃ) shall be the seed-mantra. || 1 ||
The syllable Śrī is declared to be the Śakti, and the seed-syllable Glūṃ is remembered as the Kīlaka;
O Queen of Gods, the Viniyoga is proclaimed to be in one's own self-luminous nature. || 2 ||
With the long-enduring power of *māyā*, one should duly install the six limbs.

I meditate with my mind upon Ratneśvarī, whose limbs are adorned with jewels, who wears a crown of rubies, and who possesses the splendor of the rising sun; she holds nine jewel-lamps in her hands and shines brilliantly.
Thus:
"O Goddess Navātmikā, joined with the sovereign of the entire circle of wheels, accept this triple offering (ārārtika), O Goddess, for my spiritual attainment. (1)
The practitioner, kneeling on the ground with his knees touching the earth, should draw the mandala according to his desire;
the characteristic of the drawing of the mandala is performed with both hands joined in the *vahatpuṭa* gesture.
In the square [enclosure], one should worship the wheel of space (vyomacakra) in this sequence:
the syllable Om (tāra), Bhuvaneśvarī, the pervasive [syllables] (vyāpaka), and the mandala.
The mantra beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable and ending with the Heart-mantra consists of twelve syllables;
it should be mixed with food and water in equal parts and worshipped with flowers.
Having placed the vessel right there, one should offer the bali-oblation with the *kalārṇa* mantra;
one should write the *tāra*, the *parā*, and "to all obstacle-makers, sarvabhūtebhyaḥ. (5)
To them, the offering (bali) is made by uttering "huṃ" followed by the fire-seed syllable (raṃ) and the wife of fire (svāhā) three times;
one should perform the previously mentioned offering of bali for the pacification of obstacles.
The fourfold offering of bali is indeed difficult to find in the three worlds;
thereafter, one should satisfy the young maidens with this [offering] dedicated to Tripureśī.
Having honored the rays of the Supreme Sovereign,
that best of men [honored] the supreme consciousness, the mistress of the wheel of power (śakticakra) of the Sky-farer (khecarī).
One should unite [the offering] within oneself through the guru’s compassion in the dense thicket of knowledge;
for the sake of spiritual accomplishment, one should cast the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) at the corner of Śiva for the teachers.
Then, O Goddess, the knower of the guru-mantras should offer the arghya vessel to the guru;
and according to the instruction, he should satisfy himself with his own name-mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, pure and bearing the mudrā of the principles (tattva), one should again perform the practice characterized by the lamp at the ādhāra through the left path.
One should consume [the substance] situated in the center of the *ārātrika* with the root mantra alone;
or else, one should lift up the vessel with the *kapālinī* mantra or with that same [root] mantra.
O Pārvatī, the second [syllable] belongs to the Tattvas;
by means of their conjunction on the right, one should satisfy the Goddess dwelling within one's own heart through the conjunction of the three Tattvas.
The first is the nature of Brahmā, the second is the knower of all mantras, and the third is the form of Īśa; these are to be understood by the best of sages. (14)
O Supreme Goddess, having slightly manifested [herself] through the five mudrās, O Devi, by the command of the venerable Guru, she herself becomes Śrī Tripurā. (15)
One should place all the vessels face down upon the fire; then, withdrawing from the mantras the unbroken rice and other offerings situated therein from the ladles.
Having given it, O Supreme Goddess, one becomes happy; of this there is no doubt.
Know that even that which is priceless has been described by me through these syllables. 17.
O beloved, O auspicious one, you must conceal this by means of the "silence" method and the "moon-lamp" method, just as one would hide the pregnancy resulting from a mother's lover.
Thus [it is said]. Here, we shall explain in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*) the rule for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) in its practical form. Likewise, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind; I shall proclaim the Yantra of Vidyā."
The spiritual teacher destroys, within a single month, the sin accumulated over a thousand births.
O beloved, one should worship with campaka flowers set with jewels or made of gold at all times; one will certainly become a bearer of the supreme command.
It destroys all sins, even those accumulated over ten million lifetimes;
having obtained the earth girt by the oceans, one prospers in happiness. (3)
O Goddess, he who constantly worships the Goddess with silver *campaka* flowers shall become wise and victorious everywhere. (4)
O Maheśvarī, [one should worship] a linga facing west, or one devoid of a bull, or one located in a place of self-manifested (svayambhū) or Bāṇa-liṅgas, or in a shrine of Śiva.
Staying there, one should likewise recite the mantra with a rosary of coral beads,
or with one made of pearls, rudrākṣa, lotus seeds, or crystal.
A wise person should perform the recitation using beads made of rubies, padmarāgas, and other such beautiful gems;
having recited it exactly one hundred thousand times, those earth-dwelling beings who cause obstacles [are subdued].
When even these do not undergo the slightest agitation,
then the wise and pure practitioner should regularly perform three hundred thousand [recitations].
The wise person should recite [the mantra] either mentally, verbally, or in a whisper.
O Goddess, mental utterance yields the fruit of ten million recitations.
O Goddess, whispered recitation (upāṃśu) becomes a hundredfold [more effective] than vocal recitation (vācika);
O Beloved, by the command of the venerable Guru, the "mouth-vessel" (mukhapātra) arises from the vocal recitation.
The fire offering (homa) should be performed with one-tenth of that number using flowers from the brahmavṛkṣa tree;
one should offer safflower blossoms saturated with the three sweets.
O Dear One, this single Vidyā, which embodies the nature of all vidyās,
becomes perfected within the vulva-pit shaped like a bhaga, circular, or crescent-shaped.
In a nine-triangle wheel, or in a square, or in an eight-spoked [wheel], or in a yoni-shaped pit, or in the vulva, there shall be attraction. 13.
O Goddess, there is a circle, a śrīpada, and a half-moon—these three should be present.
By means of the great nine-triangle [yantra], one becomes a possessor of the siddhi of khecarī. || 14 ||
In a square [mandala], every auspicious undertaking shall always be successful;
in an eight-cornered one, there is peace, nourishment, prosperity, and health. (15)
One shall accomplish the ten supernatural powers (siddhis) upon the lotus-mark; of this there is no doubt.
And with jasmine and *mālatī* flowers smeared with the three sweets, one becomes the Lord of Speech (Vacaspati). 16.
By means of *karavīra* flowers with ghee, she becomes the subduer of women throughout the three worlds;
thereafter, [one should offer] camphor, saffron, and wine to the Goddess. (17)
Having mixed it with deer-flesh, one becomes possessed of desire and good fortune;
one should offer oblations of beautiful campaka, pāṭala, mango, and other fruits.
For seven days or for a full month, Lakṣmī attends upon the practitioner;
O Goddess, one should offer oblations of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and guggulu.
Indeed, all the beautiful women of the city become subject to him;
by offering fruit smeared with the three sweets at a crossroads, one attains the power of moving through the sky.
Having offered curd, milk, honey, clarified butter, and parched grain into the fire, one is no longer subject to the constraints of time;
or else, with a concentrated mind, one should recite the vidyā nine hundred thousand times.
One should perform a fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that, according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thus one may accomplish [the mastery over] those dwelling in heaven, the earthly realm, and the depths of Pātāla.
With black mustard seeds and salt, one may agitate this world;
by offering one hundred and eight oblations of curd, one shall destroy untimely death.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of both ghee and milk for the sake of longevity;
with guggulu mixed with honey and ghee, one may bring even a lord of kings under one's control. (24)
Health is attained by performing one hundred and eight oblations with ghee and dūrvā grass,
using red karavīra flowers smeared with honey and clarified butter, along with guggulu resin.
One may bring one hundred thousand enemies under control, or twenty kings; with *karavīra* flowers smeared with honey, one shall bring even a king, together with his retinue, into subjection. (26)
For seven nights, one should sacrifice as before with clarified butter and the moon,
using *pāṭala*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *śatapatra*, and *jāti* flowers.
By worshipping or offering oblations with fresh sprouts of *mālatī*, jasmine, lotus, and *kiṃśuka*— whether used in combination or individually— [one attains the desired fruit].
One obtains all good fortune and is called a lord of speech through wisdom;
[this is achieved] by means of mucukunda flowers, bilva leaves, fruits, and blue lotuses.
Indeed, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained through nagara, rājacampa, coconut, dates, grapes, and the excellent fruits of the mango tree. || 30 ||
Whatever task is mentally conceived by the practitioner is accomplished through the fire oblation (homa);
one should satisfy Śrīvidyā with both worship and the fire oblation. || 31 ||

Having scattered the sacrificial oblation (caru) everywhere through the worship of virgins and other rites, and having gradually gratified the Guru with the offering of the bali as previously described; || 32 ||
Having honored the married women, one should give abundant wealth to the virtuous;
all the flowers should be used in the fire-oblation, and one should offer many *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruits in various ways.
With all the fruits from within a coconut, one should offer what is pleasing to the mind;
likewise, with a single, complete mango fruit, and similarly with a jujube fruit.
One should offer oblations with jackfruit (*panasa*) while observing the embryos within the fruit;
likewise, one should offer the entire *jambū* fruit and also the grape (*drākṣā*).
If the mango fruit were not cut into pieces, its essence would remain light; yet the fruit remains whole and heavy. So too are musk, saffron, and the moon. (36)
O Goddess, one should offer a quantity equal to a guñjā seed; one should offer a hundred rows of sesame seeds;
likewise, the wise one should offer salt and a handful of parched grain.
One should indeed offer food in the measure of a mouthful, and likewise offer cooked foods;
the full offering is made with half a betel nut, and the śrīkhaṇḍa is shaped like a betel nut.
In that manner, one should offer abundant oblations that bring satisfaction to the mind;
one should always offer these with curd and milk, distinguished by a fourfold division. (39)
O Goddess, I shall describe the measurement for all the invocations that is pleasing to the mind, as well as the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which destroys great obstacles. (40)
One should construct a pit for the sacrificial fire (kuṇḍa) that is twenty-four finger-breadths wide and beautiful in every respect.
It should be square, auspicious with all its lines, and then provided with girdles;
having left one finger-breadth everywhere, three very beautiful [lines] should be made.
O Supreme Goddess, all three [lines] are elevated by as many finger-breadths as the number of Ādityas, Vasus, and Vedas, and each has a width of four finger-breadths.
In the western part of the pit, one should fashion a well-characterized *yoni*;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in depth.
In the center, O Goddess, it should be six fingers wide and two fingers high, beautiful to behold;
thus, O lovely one, the characteristics of the square have been described to you. (45)
Whatever measurement is used for this one, or whatever else may be used for others,
with that same measurement the wise man should construct all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
On ground smeared with cow-dung water, one should draw three lines each, extending from east to west and from south to north.
Having sprinkled [the site] with water while reciting the *praṇava*, one should prepare the sacrificial seat (*yāgaviṣṭara*) in the center;
there, one should scatter gravel and draw a triangular enclosure.
Outside of that, one should draw eight petals and then the circle of the earth;
there, one should worship the pedestal (pīṭha) according to its successive divisions.
Then Maṇḍūka and Rudra, followed by Kālāgni and the others;
then Ādhāraśakti and Kūrma, and thereafter Ananta and Varāha. (50)
One should worship the earth, as well as the bulb, the stalk, the lotus, and the pericarp, along with the vessels and the filaments, in their respective places.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the cardinal directions of the seat (pīṭha), and likewise Adharma and the others in the corners of the seat. 52.
Having worshipped again with the *tāra* (the syllable Om), one should place the sacrificial seat;
in the center, [one should place] the mother of the Vedas, who is in her menses and desirous of the Veda.
Having meditated upon [the fire] as presided over by the Puruṣa and situated within the union of their genitals,
one should stir the fire in the sacrificial pit and cast out a few embers.
The wise one should protect all beings with the weapon-mantra;
thereafter, he should kindle the fire through the transition into the fire of knowledge.
One should contract [the breath], which flashes in all directions according to the analogy of one lamp from another, through the path of the nostrils and the path of the source of Manu. 56.
In the middle of the triangular pit (kuṇḍa), one should first wash the pure [implement] with the Vyāhṛtis, and afterwards with the fire-mantra, in due order.
Then one should pray with the mantra: "O Citpiṅgala, strike the pair, burn the pair, cook them in two ways; O Omniscient One, give the command! Svāhā! (58)
I praise Agni, the blazing one, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in all directions. 59.
Having performed the ritual attendance (upasthāna) in this manner, one should arrange the limbs [of the mantra] on the tongue:
the letters *sa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, *va*, *la*, *ra*, *ya*, accompanied by the sixth vowel (*ṛ*) and the vowel *a*. (60)
The seven syllables of the tongues are proclaimed to be marked by the *bindu* and the *nāda*:
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā; || 61 ||
O Supreme Goddess, one should arrange Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā in sequence with their seed-syllables and perform their placement. 62.
In the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, respectively, dwell the Suras, the Pitṛs, the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, and the Pannagas. (63)
The Piśācas and Rākṣasas should also be remembered during those seven [periods]:
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, and likewise Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa. (64)

Then one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantras "dhūmavyāpī," "saptajihvaḥ," and "dhanurdharaḥ," ending with the syllable *ṅa*; thereafter, one should assign the eight forms (*mūrtyaṣṭaka*).
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and Havyavāhana;
the fourth shall be Aśvodaya, and then Vaiśvānara, O Umā. (66)
One should place the sixth, Kaumāratejas, and the two Viśvadevas on the head, the shoulders, the sides, the hips, the buttocks, the flanks, and the thighs. (67)
But all the intermediate [deities] should be known as having the limbs of the forms of Agni in sequence.
Having thus performed the ritual placement upon the body, one should sprinkle it with the water of the *arghya* offering. (68)
Having strewn darbha grass around the directions, he should then perform the sprinkling;
O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here from the west.
And finally, "Lohitākṣa," perform the rites as well; this mantra ends with "svāhā. The syllable "Tāra" (Om) is at the beginning, and "Citpiṅgala" is also in the mouth [of the mantra]. (70)
Having worshipped the Fire with this [mantra], one should then worship the tongues [of fire] in the center and in the six corners; thereafter, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas).
The forms [of the deities] are on the eight petals, and the lords of the directions are on the orb of the earth;
then, having again recited the mantra of Vaiśvānara, who has three eyes and a ruddy luster.
Clad in white garments and adorned with jewel ornaments, he is seated upon a lotus;
he holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons, the spear, the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness.
The wise one should visualize [the deity] adorned with many golden garlands;
thereafter, he should sprinkle the vessels with water for the arghya offering for the sake of purification.
Having turned them all upward, one should pour [the contents] into their respective places:
water into the pair of *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, and likewise ghee into the pot. (75)
One should place all other sacrificial materials into all the vessels;
one should also cast flowers into the *sruk* vessel, the *sruva* ladle, and the vessel of clarified butter. || 76 ||
O Dear One, one should prepare the vessel provided with incense first and fumigate it on all sides;
furthermore, one should encircle all the girdles with rows of lamps.
Then, surrounding the sacrificial pit with three rows [of oblations], one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having worshipped Brahmā to the south, one should indeed offer oblations with the *vaiśvānara* mantra.
One should contemplate the purificatory rites beginning with conception for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
having worshipped the Śrīcakra according to this procedure, one should contemplate it therein.
Then, having invoked Mahātripurasundarī together with all the goddesses who are the mistresses of the wheels (cakreśīs) within that interval, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, with ten oblations of clarified butter, and following the sequence beginning with worship,
[he should offer to] all the mistresses of the wheels (cakreśīs) and the Yoginīs, such as Prakaṭā and the others.
And one should offer oblations with ghee alone, one by one in sequence;
thereafter, one should offer oblations to the supreme Subhagā with the excellent substances previously mentioned.
An oblation offered in a ruby-colored fire shall bestow all spiritual accomplishments;
one that is red like Rudra or golden leads to the attainment of the fruits of all desires. (83)
In Lohitā there shall be pacification (śānti), and in Dhūminī suppression (stambhana) occurs in due order; in Karālinī there is eradication (uccāṭana), and in Māraṇa [there is] killing.

Thus has been described to you the divine and supreme characteristic of the fire-oblation (homa), which, when performed, pacifies the flood of obstacles; it is not otherwise, O lady of excellent complexion.
Relying upon the lamp-stand, one should perform the recitation and the fire-oblation;
one should draw an eight-square grid (vasukoṣṭha) and arrange the tortoise in the central space.
One should write the vowels by dividing them into pairs in the order starting from the east;
likewise, one should write these seven classes of consonants beginning with *ka* in the order starting from the east. (87)
A hundred thousand units should be added in the eighth; this becomes the Kūrma-cakra.
O Goddess, wherever the syllable of the location is found, there success is attained, without a doubt. (88)
The face should be known as the syllable of the position (sthānākṣara), while the two hands are indeed its two sides.
In that [diagram], the pair of middle squares is empty of fruit and bestows death. (89)
This is the belly of the tortoise, while the two hind feet follow in succession;
the tail, situated between those two, brings about the destruction of disease. (90)
It bestows poverty and brings suffering; therefore, one should take refuge in the mouth [of the Guru].
Likewise, O beloved, there is no accomplishment elsewhere than by the command of the venerable Guru.
One may designate a region, a location, a city, or even a village;
one should perform the offering of lamps, how much more so when one performs a sacrifice with oblations? || 92 ||
Thus, in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"O Dear One, having drawn the King of Wheels with vermilion powder, one should worship it with flowers mixed with *svabhaṃbhū* blossoms and with unbroken grains. (1)
Having correctly recited the Gāyatrī mantras of the goddesses of the nine enclosures on all sides, one should then utter [the name] "Amuka" at the end of that.
Bring [her] under my control; at the end, one should utter the name of each respective sprout, and then say: "I worship the śrīpādukā of such-and-such a goddess. (3)
In this manner, through the rites of attraction, delusion, immobilization, and eradication,
the practitioner of mantra shall obtain his desired goal within seven days.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: in some secluded place, having drawn the King of Mandalas (*cakrarāja*) with vermilion or other red substances, and after performing the placement of the *arghya* vessel and the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) as prescribed, and then perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) or flowers smeared with *svayambhū* (autogenous) pollen. In that regard, for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*):

The procedure is as follows: having first uttered the three *tāra*s (oṃ āḥ hūṃ), one should recite the respective *gāyatrī* mantra, followed by "O Goddess [Name], bring [Name] under my control," or "make [Name] submissive, make [Name] submissive, *vauṣaṭ*," and finally, "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Goddess [Name].
In this manner, one should worship each goddess in every enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). For the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should say, "attract [Name], attract [Name]."
The meaning is that this should be applied accordingly in the ritual procedures for immobilization (*stambhana*) and so forth. Likewise:
"Visualizing the Śrīcakra separately within the cakras beginning with the Mūlādhāra, the deities residing in those cakras are surrounded by the rays of the phonemes of the respective elements. (1)
One should perform the immobilization (*stambhana*) by means of earthen substances; such previously mentioned results are to be understood from the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice (*sādhana*) of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*)."
Thus, listen to the sequence for the application of the perfected vidyā. || 1 ||
Having fashioned a wheel with vermilion powder, one should contemplate it there;
then, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) upon a single auspicious leaf.
O Goddess, though she was blazing with flames, she was instantly deluded and, casting aside her fear and shame, she approached; now another thing is told, O beloved. (3)
Seated in the center of that, the practitioner should contemplate himself as having a ruddy luster,
as well as the person to be accomplished, likewise beautiful with good fortune.
One should worship with red offerings while encircled by mudrās;
indeed, he whose name is thus properly invoked shall truly become a servant.
Having written the names of women who have not been seen, along with their complexions, in the center of the wheel,
and assuming the *yonimudrā*, there shall be an instantaneous attraction.
Whether it be a celestial maiden, a princess, or even a daughter of the Nāgas;
[one should prepare] equal parts of gorocanā, saffron, and sandalwood.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, a tilaka-mark becomes all-enchanting;
so too do flowers, fruits, water, food, fragrance, clothing, and ornaments.
O Dear One, he to whom betel-leaf previously consecrated with mantras is sent shall become his slave merely by the woman’s glance.
One should worship with red karavīra flowers smeared with the three sweets,
while meditating for exactly one month upon the name of the woman who is the object of the rite.
Performing thus, one should worship Maheśānī, who possesses a reddish glow;
on a wheel fashioned with vermilion, she will delude the king in an instant.
One may even swiftly summon Rambhā, who is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
for one should indeed draw the wheel with the charcoal of the mind and red liquid.
Having tied it to one's arm, it then destroys fever anywhere in an instant.
With the juices of *arka* and *nimba*, however, one should write [the mantra] using a *likhinī* pen on an *arka* leaf. (13)
One should place that [substance] in cow urine; it will produce hatred in an instant.
One should fumigate with sandalwood at night, or then wear the cloth.
By reciting it one hundred and eight times, one may delude the three worlds.
Then, on ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw [the diagram] with yellow pigment (rocanā).
One should contemplate a beautiful and charming image, richly adorned with ornaments, joined with the circles (maṇḍalas) of its forehead, throat, heart, navel, and private parts. 16.
One should inscribe the Kāmakūṭa, which is interwoven with the Great Vidyā known as Janmanāma and the term ending in Aṅkuśa, so that it is merged into all the joints of the limbs.
Facing the direction of the goal to be accomplished and embodying the installation (*nyāsa*) of the *Śrīvidyā*,
one should recite the mantra eight hundred times while employing the seed-syllable and mudrā of the *Kṣobhiṇī*.
One should unite her in the abode of desire, which consists of the digits of the moon and sun;
she is full of passion, exceedingly pure, and tormented by the arrows of Kama. (19)
One named Trailokyasundarī comes, infatuated, in an instant;
or else, the knower of mantras, having encircled the external wheel of the Mother-syllables (mātṛkācakra). 20.
One should properly worship the wheel and maintain the complete Vidyā;
then one will be invincible to all wicked beings, such as tigers and the like—of this there is no doubt. (21)
One's own name should be written in order using sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron; as before, one should write the Mātṛkā.
By this very method, using rocanā, aguru, and kuṅkuma, there is no doubt that the practitioner attains freedom from old age and death. (23)

Having drawn a wheel [diagram] in which the letters of the target name are interwoven with the letters of the practitioner's name, the mantra-practitioner becomes the enchanter of the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. (24)
O Goddess of the gods, having joined the individual syllables with the *kāmakūṭa*,
one should encircle the Mātṛkā within a triangle formed from the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
It should be worn on the crest-lock or anywhere at all, even amidst gold;
for the world-protectors and kings, as well as the wicked ones residing in the three worlds, [are subdued by it]. (26)
All those fevers, such as the *sannipāta* type and others, come under control;
by this method, having composed the name [of the patient], one should contract [the mantra]. (27)
At a crossroads in the Middle Country, in the directions starting from the east and so forth in sequence, kings will always become his servants, bringing him good fortune. (28)
Then, for six months, that man should constantly meditate on the earth as consisting of throbbing light, blazing with all things moving and unmoving, within the periphery of the wheel.
By this, one certainly becomes as charming as Kandarpa in the world;
by his gaze he attracts people, destroys poison, and cures fevers.
Likewise, it removes poison and causes the entry of a [divine] gaze;
one should worship it at night with a single-minded focus, having written [the mantra] with vermilion.
One performs the summoning from afar, even from a distance of a hundred yojanas;
one should worship it in sequence throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions without interruption.
At that very moment this world becomes submissive, and not otherwise.
One should write the wheel on birch bark with yellow pigment, agallochum, and saffron.
One should name the region or the city after one's own name;
one should cause a mandala, an uneven place, or a wheel to be established upon the ground.
Or, if the mantra-practitioner holds it, he then agitates the city in an instant.
[The substances are: the juice of the *unmatta*, lac, the milky sap of the *arka*, saffron, and yellow orpiment. (35)
Having mixed together musk and lac, one should write the name of that person, O Goddess of Gods; [by this], there shall be no fear arising from thieves or tigers. (36)
Fear born of planets, disease, enemies, or lions; fear from serpents or horses—she deludes them all in an instant. (37)
The wise one should draw the central [syllable] with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma),
situated between two triangles, and marked at the bottom with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
Therefore, one should wear that wheel; within seven days, it will become a servant.
One should write the vidyā beneath the edge of the wheel using yellow substances. (39)
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should project it toward the eastern direction;
by that means, even Brahmā and even a living being, though omniscient, shall fall into muteness.
By this procedure, the mantra-practitioner, facing south, should scratch that [name] with indigo juice; having burned it in the fire, he shall consume his enemies.
One should scrape [the target's name] with buffalo and horse dung and cow urine;
by placing it in fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), enmity shall arise in an instant.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center using a crow’s feather;
having written it with substances such as *rocanā*, one should hold it so that it is visible in the sky.
This is declared to be the "forcible eradication" (haṭhoccāṭa) which quickly eradicates enemies;
[it is performed] with yellow orpiment mixed with the juice of great indigo and milk. || 44 ||
One should draw a wheel with lac-dye; by means of the four syllables, one brings [beings] under control.
According to this procedure, one should place it in water, and indeed with that water... (45)
One attains great good fortune through bathing and drinking [the water]; of this there is no doubt.
If one worships the Cakra while it is being drunk, it shall paralyze all disputants in the east.
A wheel drawn with vermilion in the north brings subjugation of the world;
thereafter, a wheel drawn with red chalk (gairika) is worshipped in the west.
O beloved, if even ministers and deities are brought under control, how much more so women?
In the same manner, one facing south should worship the black discus.
There will be a loss of the mantra for the practitioner, and especially death;
facing the various directions in sequence, starting from the southeast (vahnikoṇa) and so forth. 49.
A man who casts [this mantra] into milk performs paralysis, inciting enmity, causing disease, and expulsion;
yet when written with yellow pigment (rocanā) and forcibly cast into milk, it brings about subjugation.
When burnt while placed in the midst of fire, it destroys all enemies;
and when immersed in cow urine, it effects the eradication of the foe.
O Supreme Goddess, by that very means, there shall be incantation for causing enmity within the wheel;
one should draw the wheel with vermilion at a deserted crossroads.
One should write the Mātṛkā starting from the very outside up to the center;
then, according to the sequence of the Kula practice, one should worship the Krama at night.
O Goddess, the practitioner becomes a sky-walker (khecara); of this there is no doubt.
On the fourteenth day, remaining composed at night, he should worship in the Rudra-ground.
Having been born after a count of six months, like another Rudra manifest before his eyes,
he [attained] collyrium, the power of entering apertures, the accomplishment of the pill, and the magical sandals and ointment.

The practitioner of mantra obtains the sword, the Vetāla, the Saubhāgya, the Yakṣiṇī, the Ceṭaka, and so forth—all of which produce supernatural powers—provided it is done correctly; otherwise, it is not so.
On every fourteenth and eighth day of the lunar fortnight, being composed in mind,
he remained in the water at night for twenty-one nights, stationed among the departed spirits.
In that same manner, the practitioner, who is worthy of worship by the gods, should worship the Śrīcakra with the noose,
goad, bow, and arrows belonging to Puruṣa, O Maheśvarī.

Becoming Kāma, he becomes the lord of all beings, including the women of heaven, earth, and the depths of Pātāla; he himself is both the destroyer and the creator, and his power of attraction is truly great.
By means of the various weapons of Kāmeśvarī, the self of the Goddess effects the attraction of men throughout the three worlds; O Dear One, kings become her servants.
This meditation on the Kāmakalā has been described according to the distinction of its seed-syllables (bīja).
O Goddess, through the worship of the Vāgbhava syllable, the knowledge of Sarasvatī shall arise.
One should worship with white flowers and white ornaments and garments;
O Goddess, by this rite, the propitiation of Vāgbhava is accomplished.
Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the power of that which is called Kāmakalā:
Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja. (63)
And Mahākāma, O Goddess, consists of the five previously mentioned desires in their proper sequence; one should place Kāma in the center of Manmatha, located within the abode of Kandarpa.
With this principle of desire (kāmatattva), one should delude this world by means of the Fish-bannered One (Kāmadeva) situated within that vessel, whose head is the Great Lord of Desire (Mahākāmeśa).
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, the Kuṇḍalinī energy within the Śaktikūṭa is subtler than a thread of spider-silk, [arising] from the root as the creation and dissolution [of all things]. 66.
The goddess Tripurā, who possesses three peaks, shall be the bestower of all siddhis,
since from her [proceed] sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great luster.
"Relying upon this wheel, [the mantras] always bestow success upon the virtuous.
Now, the Śrīvidyā mantras, interspersed with various Vedic mantras, are extracted. In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
The Praṇava, Kamalā, Māyā, the Kāmapiṇḍa, and the Gāṇapa; then the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, and that which slays Vṛtra today. (1)
The great peak of Kāmarāja rose up toward the rising sun;
having drawn the peak of Śakti, all that, O Indra, is under your control. || 2 ||
Next, [one should say] "Gaṇapatim," followed by "Varadānte varada" (at the end of "Varada," [say] "Varada").
Then, at the end of "Sarvajanam me," [say] "Vaśamānaya" and the two "Ṭha"s (i.e., Svāhā). || 3 ||
This mantra is the lord of the lords of hosts; it bestows the fruit of all sovereignty, brings all under control for men, and grants the attainment of longevity and health. || 4 ||
One should write the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati in the Triṣṭubh meter, which is Jātavedasa; then one half of the Saṃvāda-sūkta, and again the other half, in their proper sequence.
The four sections are said to be encapsulated by the three peaks;
for a person who recites them daily according to their capacity, especially so.
"It deludes the world, brings subjugation, and bestows luster, good fortune, and nourishment.
The meaning of this is as follows: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ yad yakac ca vṛtrahan ha-sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ udagā abhi sūryaṃ sa-ka-la-hrīṃ sarvaṃ tad indra te vaśe*.
To Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā! Ka-e-īla-hrīṃ.
Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; he burns up the wealth of the one who acts as an enemy. May he carry us across all difficulties, as if with a boat.

Agni crosses over the Sindhu and all difficulties—*hasakahalahrīṃ*. O Bull, O Agni, you are kindled with every fuel for our purpose. You are kindled in the place of *ilā*; bring us treasures. Come together, speak together;
let your minds be in accord. O Gods, come as of old to your portion.
Perceiving [you], they wait upon the entire *hrīṃ*. The mantra is common, the assembly is common, their mind is common, and their thought is united. I consecrate your common mantra;
with a common oblation I sacrifice for you. Common be your intention, common be your hearts; let your mind be one.
"May it be well with you through good assistance"—thus is the extraction.
One should recite the mantra of Bhadranno Abhimanyu while focusing on Sundarī residing within the womb;
such a person becomes as wealthy as Kubera on this earth. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Its meaning is as follows: "May you cause our mind to attain auspiciousness; *ka-e-īlahrīṃ*, svāhā to the vigor of the Maruts;
*hasakahalahrīṃ*; Indra rules over the universe; *sakalahrīṃ*; be auspicious to us bipeds, be auspicious to us quadrupeds. Thus.
Or else, the goddess of speech, the four [verses], and then the pair of *sasarparī*—this is declared to be the group of five *ṛks*, which bestows the great Sarasvata [attainment]. (1)

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is: "That which the speechless ones utter—Ka-e-īla-hrīṃ; the delightful queen of the gods has sat down—hasaka-hala-hrīṃ; she who has four [breasts] has milked out nourishment and waters—sakala-hrīṃ; indeed, her highest state has gone far away. (1)
The goddesses generated the goddess Speech; the multiform cattle utter her as *ka-e-īlahrīṃ*.
May she, yielding us joy, food, and vigor as *hasakahalahrīṃ*, come to us with excellent praise as the cow of speech, *sakalahrīṃ*. || 2 ||
There are four measured quarters of speech: *ka-e-īlahrīṃ*. Those Brahmins who are wise know them.
*hasakahalahrīṃ*: three are hidden in the cave and do not stir; *sakalahrīṃ*: the fourth quarter of speech is what human beings speak. || 3 ||
Overcoming the creeping intellect, she who was given by Jamadagni has bellowed loudly—*ka-e-īlahrīṃ*;
the daughter of the Sun has spread her light—*hasakahalahrīṃ*; she has extended among the gods fame that is immortal and undecaying—*sakalahrīṃ*. 4.

Let the *sasarparī* bring hither for these [people] this praise, the glory among the five tribes; may she, bestowing new life upon the two wings, be that which Palasti and Jamadagni bestowed upon me. || 5 ||
Thus are the five mantras. Likewise:
"That which by its meter," "My body," and "He who [is the lord] of the gods"—these three;
one should recite them individually and without sloth, as the *Sundarī* residing within the womb. (1)
He was intelligent, possessed a retentive memory, was free from disease, and spoke kindly;
he was deeply learned, an author of treatises, and well-versed even in the Vedas and Āgamas.

"That mortal does not forget; he certainly becomes omniscient. This is its meaning: "He who is the bull among meters, the universal form, *ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ*, who arose from the immortal meters—*ha-sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ*—may that Indra protect me with wisdom (*medhā*)."
O God, may I become the upholder of the entirety of immortality, hrīṃ. || 1 ||
May my body be most excellent; may my tongue be most sweet; may I attain the desire of the mind, the intention, and the truth of speech—Ka-e-īlahrīṃ, Hasakahalahrīṃ, Sakalahrīṃ. || 2 ||
He who is the first among the gods in the east, whom the great seers worship as Rudra, the lord of all;
beholding Hiraṇyagarbha being born—may that god unite us with auspicious mindfulness. 3.

Thus there are three mantras. Likewise: "evā pitre" for the father; "yūyam asmān" for Indra and Agni; "trayambakam" would be the third; "tvaṃ soma pracetaḥ" is the fourth; and "prajāpate" is the fifth. || 1 ||
A man who should separately recite this beautiful [mantra] containing these five verses will certainly be endowed with wealth, grain, land, and sons. (2)
Abounding with cattle, elephants, horses, goats, buffaloes, grain, ornaments, and the like, it brings forth delightful prosperity that extends to one's sons, grandsons, and descendants. (3)

Thus [the verse]. Its meaning is as follows: "To this Father, the All-God (Viśvedeva), the Bull (Vṛṣṇi), we shall offer worship with sacrifices, obeisance, and oblations: *ka-e-īlahrīṃ*. O Bṛhaspati, may we, possessing good offspring and heroic sons, be masters of riches: *hasakahalahrīṃ*... *sakalahrīṃ*. (1)
Lead us toward better fortune, O Maruts, you who are praised for crushing those who offer no oblations;
O worshipful ones, graciously accept our offering of the sacrificial gift, and may we become masters of riches. 2.
Thus, O Indra and Agni, having drunk of the pressed juice—O you who are praised with hymns—conquer all our riches for us! May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant this to us. 3.
O Soma, you are wise through your inspired thought; to whom do you offer this prayer? You lead us along the straightest path.
O Indu, by your guidance, our wise ancestors have obtained their share of treasure among the gods. 4.

O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings—*īlahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ*. May that which we desire as we offer this oblation to you be ours; may we become masters of riches. || 5 ||
Thus are the five mantras. Now:
"Then one should worship Lakṣmī, who dwells in the womb of the horse-giver, as Sundarī, with wealth, grain, riches, and other things such as horses and cattle. (1)
"Ramā, constantly filling [the worlds], delights right there.
The meaning of this is: Lakṣmī, who is born from the ocean, *ka-e-īla-hrīṃ*;
the source of prosperity, the cow, and the supreme light, *hasa-ka-hala-hrīṃ*; Padmā, the goddess Viśvāvasu, *sakala-hrīṃ*, always [delights there].

"May [the goddess] not delight in the house! O giver of horses, giver of cows, Ka-e-īla-hrīṃ, giver of wealth, in great wealth ha-sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ! May the Goddess sakala-hrīṃ delight in my wealth for the sake of accomplishing all rites and purposes!
Thus are the two mantras.
We shall clearly explain the fruits for those who recite [the mantra], having encapsulated it with the four lines of the mantra found in the *Kalātithyūca-sūkta*. (1)

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: the *kalā-ṛcasūkta*, the *puruṣasūkta*, the *sahasraśīrṣa*, and so forth, are well known in the Yajurveda. The *tithyūcasūkta*, the *śrīsūkta*, the *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and so forth, are well known in the Ṛgveda.
As for the "encapsulation" (*sampuṭīkaraṇa*), it is: *sahasraśīrṣaḥ puruṣaḥ ka-e-īlahrīṃ*.

The thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, having covered the earth on all sides, *sakalahrīṃ*, he transcended it by ten fingers' breadth. This Puruṣa alone is all this, *ka-e-īlahrīṃ*, whatever has been and whatever is to be, *hasakahalahrīṃ*; and he is the lord of immortality, *sakalahrīṃ*, that which grows beyond through food.

Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this—*ka-e-īla hrīṃ*. All beings constitute but one quarter of Him—*hasaka hala hrīṃ*; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven—*sakala hrīṃ*. The Puruṣa rose upward with three quarters—*ka-e-īla hrīṃ*; His one quarter, again, became all that exists here below—*hasaka hala hrīṃ*; from that, the universe [was born].
He strode across the whole [world], both with food and without food: *sakalahrīṃ sāśanānaśane abhi*. From him Virāj was born: *ka-e-īlahrīṃ virājo adhi*.
From Virāj the Puruṣa was born: *hasakahalahrīṃ sa jātaḥ*. He was born exceeding [all]: *sakalahrīṃ paścādbhūmimatho puraḥ*. With the Puruṣa as the oblation: *ka-e-īlahrīṃ devāḥ*... [the gods]...
"yajñamatanvata hasakahalahrīṃ, vasanto'syāsīdājyaṃ sakalahrīṃ, grīṣma idhmaḥ śaraddhaviḥ"— having formed a *sampuṭa* (encasement) with these sixteen mantra-padas in this sequence,
one should recite them. One should also form a *sampuṭa* for Lopāmudrā using the mantra-padas of the *Puruṣasūkta*.
It should be understood that this forms an enclosure (*sampuṭa*) for the *Kāmarāja-vidyā* by means of the mantra-foot verses of the *Śrīsūkta*. As it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"The wise one should recite the *Lopāmudrā* [mantra], having enclosed it with the [verses] of Puruṣa."
A wise person should diligently recite the mantra known as Kāmarāja along with the Śrīsūktas.

Thus: with *pauruṣa* [mantras], that is, the mantra-padas found in the *Puruṣasūkta*; and with *Śrīsūktas*, that is, the mantra-padas of the *Śrīsūkta*. Likewise: "O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden-hued, tawny one, who wears a garland of gold and silver—Ka-E-Ila-Hrīṃ; the moon-like, golden Lakṣmī—Ha-Sa-Ka-Ha-La-Hrīṃ; the all-encompassing Hrīṃ. Thus.
One should conquer each one in succession. Thus:
by the first, the attainment of a son; by the second, the birth of a living son;
and by the third and fourth, the destruction of the defect of barrenness. || 2 ||
Then, by the fifth and the sixth [recitation], one shall obtain a long-lived son;
by the seventh, indeed, there is stability of the embryo, and by the eighth.
Easy delivery will destroy defects of the womb from the ninth month onward;
by the tenth or even beyond that, it shall destroy defects of the menses.
But by the twelfth [day], having removed the defect of the girl's [impurity] regarding childbirth,
she will certainly give birth to male offspring through the four subsequent [days].
"All defects born of the womb perish; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now, the fruits of the Śrīsūkta:
through the first [verse], one attains prosperity; by the second, one acquires cattle.
By the third [recitation] there shall be grain, and by the fourth one obtains the earth. || 1 ||
By the fifth mantra one gains servants; by the sixth, great fame;
from the seventh, honor from kings; and by the eighth, firm steadfastness.
By the ninth [day] one obtains horses; by the tenth, one gains elephants;
by the eleventh, garments; and by the twelfth, one obtains sons. || 3 ||
With the thirteenth [gift], he obtained the jewels; with the fourteenth, the great Manu obtained the earth abounding in crops; and with the fifteenth, he obtained prosperity.
Having performed [the rites] with the Rudra-mantras in that manner, one should accomplish those respective actions;
for if the multitude of Śrīvidyā mantras is thus encapsulated (sampuṭita), [the result is achieved].
Fifty thousand and one hundred thousand [mantras] are produced once that sequence has been learned from the guru or even from the scriptures. (6)
One should, being vigilant, employ [the mantras] in their respective applications according to the specific tasks;
the initiation, however, for the sixteen-syllable [mantra], shall consist of six stages.
Therein, first, I shall describe the procedure for the Śākta initiation according to the rule:
a wise man should have a pavilion constructed measuring twenty-four cubits.
One should construct nine pits, which should indeed be square in sequence;
or one may construct them as yoni-shaped or resembling half-moons.
The fire-pits (kuṇḍas) of the preceptor may be triangular, circular, hexagonal, lotus-shaped,
or eight-cornered, situated between the northeast and the east.
Having set aside two and a half cubits, one should fashion the interior of the altar;
having abandoned a space of one cubit, one should fashion the other sacrificial pits.
Thus [ends the section]. We shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) later. In the *Śrīkulārṇava*:

"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain specifically for the Vaiṣṇavas regarding the initiation consisting of sixteen syllables, as well as for the officiating priests during recitations and fire-offerings. (1)
O wise one, listen as I shall declare the mantras for the eight sacrificial pits in their proper order:
Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Varāha, and likewise Vaiṣṇava.
O Pārvatī, having combined Śrīkaṇṭha, Nārasiṃha, Gopāla, and Kārṣṇa on the fifteenth day, one should perform recitation and fire-offerings.
But in the Vedic tradition, one should especially [recite] the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas;
the five verses of Jātavedas; and the two hymns (sūkta) dedicated to the goddess Lakṣmī.
In the Śaiva [tradition], however, there are the five-syllable mantra of Śiva, Aghora, as well as Śarabha,
Prāsāda, Pāśupata, and that known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
O Supreme Goddess, one should [recite] the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra of ten syllables and the Saura mantra of six syllables consisting of the letters of the Vedas, in due order.
The three-syllabled, the sixteen-syllabled, the twelve-syllabled, and the six-syllabled [mantras]—
these are known as Ajapā in the Śākta tradition, as well as the Bālā-mantra and Bhairavī.
Tripurāvāsinī, Siddhā, Mālinī, Tripurādikā, Bhairavī, Tripurāmbā, and likewise Padmāvatī in the Buddhist [tradition]. (8)
Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, Tārā, Nīlasarasvatī, Mātaṅgī, Sumukhī, and likewise Caṇḍamātaṅginī. || 9 ||
According to the sequence of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya), there are likewise two vidyās each;
thus, there are exactly sixteen root-vidyās belonging to the mantra of the venerable Guru for initiation.
The three resting feet are white, mixed, and red;
the two feet of Śambhu are the two vidyās known as Parā and Prasāda.
There are five mantras consisting of Brahman, thirty-eight kalās, and three types [of mantras];
furthermore, there is the single-syllable mantra for Gāṇapatya and likewise Mahāgaṇapati.
And Gaṇeśa known as Kṣipra, likewise Vakratuṇḍa, Lakṣmīgaṇapati, and Herambagaṇapa; || 13 ||
Likewise, [he worshipped] the leader of the host named Vīrya and the lord of the host of Śaktis;
and for Dakṣiṇākālikā, the one-syllable and three-syllable [mantras].
Siddhakālī has six syllables, as do Manu and Vasu; Tārā likewise has two mantras of ten syllables each, and one of sixteen syllables. (15)
The first eight stars are devoid of [the vowel] *ā*; then comes *Bhuvaneśī* and the "Sound-Syllable" (*guṇārṇaka*).
Likewise, there are the threefold *Tripuṭā*, conjoined with Śrī, Vāk, Kāmā, and Parā. (16)
Specifically on the fifteenth day, there are [mantras] consisting of three, four, or five peaks;
the sixth has six peaks, the seventh seven peaks, and the fifth has eight peaks.
The Nityā and Pañcadaśī mantras possess a mutual relationship of primary and auxiliary;
likewise, Pītāmbarā and the eight Vārāhīs have a mutual relationship within the context of initiation.

Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, the wielder of the trident, the one who is difficult to access even for the forest, she who is called Jayā, the nine-syllabled one, and she whose nature consists of peace, fire, and salt. || 19 ||
Immediately after that, the Atidurgā Gāyatrī is proclaimed for the fivefold systems (pañcāyatana), namely those of the Sun, Śakti, and Viṣṇu.
In the Śaiva and Gāṇapatya [traditions], the previously mentioned leaders of mantras [are used];
however, in the midst of the Vaiṣṇava group of eight, one should exclude one's own eighteen-syllable mantra.
O Supreme Goddess, the fourth [syllable] and the Mother of the Vedas are to be joined;
having omitted the Pāśupata [mantra] in the Śaiva [tradition], one should insert the Traiyambaka [mantra] there.
Even in the case of Saura [worship], having omitted the eight-syllable mantra, one should employ the Udyat mantra;
and in the Gāṇapatya [worship], having omitted "gaṇānāṃ tvā," one should employ the Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇeśvara mantra.
In the Śākta [tradition], one should join [the elements] as before during initiation, fire-offerings, recitations, and so forth;
and among these abodes, there is also a mutual relationship of primary and secondary limbs.
I shall correctly explain the Śākta [tradition], wherein the Cakreśvarīs are proclaimed;
indeed, in the teaching of the six Śāmbhavas, there is a mutual relationship of limbs and the possessor of limbs.
Then there is the three-syllabled, the four-syllabled, and beyond that the single-syllabled;
furthermore, there are three other varieties: Siddhalakṣmī, Rājyalakṣmī, and another. (26)

Furthermore, another [aspect] is that here there is a mutual relationship of primary and secondary members (aṅga-aṅgin) among the various sciences and mantras, according to their respective distinctions.

The relationship between the primary and secondary limbs must be established with certainty for each respective rite, especially in the initiation of the five deities (pañcāyatana) and in worship. || 28 ||
I shall explain the relationship of primary and secondary limbs; listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess.
[The mantra] is joined with the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra and the Ghṛṇi mantra.
By joining it with the Parāprāsāda mantra and the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa mantra,
one should perform recitation and worship during initiation using this sixteen-syllable mantra.
The procedure for Dakṣiṇākālikā has been proclaimed in the same manner;
however, the specific distinction regarding Tārā and Chinnamastā is now being stated here.
Mārtaṇḍabhairava, Mañjughoṣa likewise, Ucchiṣṭagaṇanātha, Mukunda, and Bāla as well. || 32 ||
O Dear One, as many Vaiṣṇavas, Gāṇapatyas, Sauras, and especially Śaivas as there are, [they belong] to the Great Goddess Bhuvaneśī. (33)
Bhairavī, Bagalā, Caṇḍā, Mātaṅgī, and Aparājitā—[these are used] especially during initiation, recitation, fire-offerings, and worship. (34)
In the Pañcāyatana tantras, she is celebrated as Tārā, as well as Durgā, Bhuvaneśī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī. (35)
"But other [mantras] should be employed according to tradition by the best of teachers.
And likewise in the *Kādima* and the *Śrītantrarāja*:
"Of all the Vaiṣṇavas [possessing mantras] of six, eight, or twelve syllables..."
Because mantras denote the meaning of the supreme reality through non-difference. || 1 ||
In the same manner, one should [perform it] for the Lalitā-vidyā, for the threefold Prāsāda-mantra,
and likewise for the Parā-gāyatrī according to the form already described.
"Through the union with the nature of those [deities]—the Vyāhṛtis, the Mahāvākyas, the Paramātman, and the Ātmajapa—as well as the Praṇava, one attains identity with each of them. (26.46).
Now, we shall explain the sequence of the traditional transmission (*saṃpradāyāmnāya*) hereafter. Now, [regarding] Śrīvidyā...
Regarding the ṛṣi-nyāsa, dhyāna, and other procedures for the mantras of Nārāyaṇa and others mentioned in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) of the Śrīcakra, as found in other tantras: then,
after performing the morning rites up to the placement of the Yoga-pīṭha (*yogapīṭhanyāsa*), one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra and [place it] upon the head.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by saying, "Salutation to the sage Sādhyānārāyaṇa at the mouth; salutation to the goddess Gāyatrī, the meter, at the heart;

salutation to the deity Śrīparamātman," and having said with palms joined, "The application is for my desired purpose," one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) on the two hands with the root mantra, [ending with] "Kroḍolkāya svāhā."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these mantras upon the fingers and the heart and other limbs—namely: *Hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Maholkāya svāhā*; *Śirase svāhā*, *Vīrolkāya svāhā*; *Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Dyulkāya svāhā*; *Kavacāya huṃ*, *Sahasrolkāya svāhā*; *Astrāya phaṭ*—one should meditate.
Holding a discus, a mace, a club, and a lotus in his hands, possessing a splendor as radiant as the sun, with his shining sides adorned by the goddess Śrī and the Earth, wearing a crown,
marked with the Śrīvatsa sign and the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, and resplendent with armlets and necklaces;
I worship in my heart the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, adorned with shining earrings and clad in yellow garments. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra: *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*.

Then, for the mantra of Vāsudeva, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to Prajāpati, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth;
salutation to the deity Śrī-Vāsudeva on the heart," [one proceeds] for the sake of attaining my desired goal.

Regarding the application (*viniyoga*): having spoken thus with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) upon the two hands with the root mantra, and then recite: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *namo śirase svāhā*, *bhagavate śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *vāsudevāya kavacāya huṃ*, and *namo bhagavate vāsudevāya astrāya phaṭ*.
Then, having become composed, one should remember Vāsudeva in the heart,
[dwelling] on an island in the midst of the milk-ocean, frequented by divine women.
There, having intentionally entered a forest frequented by all seasons,
he beheld in its midst a divine kalpa-tree of wondrous appearance.
Beneath that is a jeweled throne, a lotus of stainless luster,
resplendent with a mass of radiance shining like the full autumn moon.
There, one should contemplate the god Vāsudeva with a smiling face,
possessing the luster of jasmine and the moon, and holding a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch in his hands.
He was enchanting the three worlds with a splendor as radiant as ten thousand moons;
his staff-like arms shone with armlets and bracelets, and he was adorned with jewel ornaments.
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark, wears a glittering jewel-encrusted crown, and is adorned with the Kaustubha gem;
his long eyes are as beautiful and copper-hued as the petals of a lotus.
His cheeks were radiant with earrings, he was clad in yellow garments,
his conch-like neck was beautified by necklaces and strings of pearls, and he wore exquisite bracelets.
His broad chest was adorned with a shining, blossoming forest garland,
while the lords of sages, such as Sanaka and others, were there, desiring a definitive determination of the ultimate truth.
It was frequented by hosts of Gandharvas born of Diti and Aditi,
as well as by exalted Vidyādharas and great serpents.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the recitation and other rites.

Then, following the Varāha-mantra, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (nyāsa), saying: "Salutation to Bhārgava, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Anuṣṭubh, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Varāha, on the heart."

"May this be employed for the accomplishment of all my desired goals"—having said this with palms joined in reverence (p. 206), [he recites]: "Homage to Ekaśṛṅga, the heart; Svāhā to Vyomolkā, the head;
Vaṣaṭ to Tejo'dhipati, the tuft of hair; Hūṃ to Viśvarūpa, the armor."
Having performed the placement of the five limb-mantras with "mahādaṃṣṭrāyāstrāya phaṭ," one should meditate. The meditation is as follows:
from the knees down to the feet it is gold-colored; from the navel to the knees it is white as the moon.
From the throat to the heart, he is like the radiance of fire; from the head to the throat, he is like the moon; and from the crown of the head to the sky, he is lovely, resembling the moon. (1)

I incessantly worship the primordial Boar, who bears upon his palms a discus, conch, sword, shield, mace, as well as a spear, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; whose single tusk shines as he supports the entire earth, which endures all things.
In one's own mind. || 2 ||
Having meditated thus, this mantra should be employed: *Oṃ namo bhagavate varāharūpāya bhūrbhuvaḥsvarpataye bhūpatitvaṃ me dehi dadāpaya svāhā*.

Now, for Viṣṇu: Then, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*), saying: "Salutation to the sage Kapila on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Bhogavāmana in the heart," [one should say] "for me..."

Having said with palms joined, "The application [of this mantra] is for the attainment of all desired goals," one recites: *Oṃ namo hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *bhagavate śirase svāhā*, *viṣṇave śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *surapataye kavacāya huṃ*,
*mahābalāya netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*, *svāhāstrāya phaṭ*.
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should meditate. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Blue in color, four-armed, and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—this Bhogavāmana grants all enjoyments to his devotees. (1)
Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods, the one of great power; svāhā!"

Then, for the Śrīkara mantra, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Having performed the placement (nyāsa), saying: "Obeisance to Vāmadeva, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; obeisance to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas), on the face; obeisance to Śrīkara, the deity (devatā), on the heart," [one should say] "for me..."

Having said, "This is the application for the attainment of all desired objects," with palms joined in reverence, [he recites]: *uṃ bhīṣaya bhīṣaya huṃ*—*namaḥ* to the heart; *ttiṃ trāsaya trāsaya huṃ*—*svāhā* to the head; *ṣṭhaṃ mardaya mardaya huṃ*—*vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; *śrīṃ pradhvaṃsaya huṃ*—*huṃ* to the armor; *kaṃ*.
"Protect, protect! Hūṃ! To the weapon, phaṭ! Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with "Raṃ" on the two eyes, "Svāṃ" on the belly, and "Hāṃ" on the back, one should meditate.
Then, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the bestower of prosperity, within the lotus of the heart,
which is foamy with a mass of restless waves and garlanded with rows of surging billows.
In the midst of the milk-ocean is an auspicious island, white in nature,
filled with golden ground and beautiful with various clusters of jewels.
There, one should contemplate a forest frequented by all the Ṛṣis, excellent, with its heat warded off by groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa). || 3 ||
It was filled with the sweet humming of swarms of bees, its tender leaves were trembling,
it was rising with the pollen of diamond-like flowers, and it was completely covered in frost.
Upon the jewel-like flowers of golden trees, it possesses the luster of Indra’s celestial nymphs,
characterized by the restless movement of swarms of bees.
He accepts even those places where the Apsarases sport with the gods—
those endowed with qualities such as nobility, splendor, sovereignty, and good fortune.
With their tender forms, charming and delightful in appearance, their faces were illuminated by the rays of light from their teeth as they smiled gently. (7)
Delightful, with a luster that surpassed the moon, their eyes shimmering with passion,
they formed a continuous assembly of gods, like a chorus of warbling male cuckoos.
With passion awakened as they awoke, languid with the weight of their full jar-like breasts,
those excellent women moved very slowly due to the burden of their beautiful hips.
Such are the apsarases who sport there with the Cāmaras,
like the commander-in-chief of Māra’s army, as if in the very home of the Goddess of the Forest.
And the birthplace of the seasons was beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) made of the nine precious gems, belonging to the brother of Indirā.
On its auspicious ground, cooled and illuminated by rows of crests,
it was delightful with great jewels and beautified by a golden pavement.
And above the King of Birds, who possesses a mass of renowned prowess and is seated upon a throne radiant with the splendor of the rising sun; (13)
Seated there, he resembled pure, flowing, and brilliant gold,
adorned with beautiful earrings in the shape of makaras that shone with jewels.
His beautiful ornaments were radiant with the circle of directions illuminated by the jewel of his crown;
his spotless tilaka was fashioned from the pure white crescent of the moon. || 15 ||
With a pair of earrings shimmering on his crown and trembling slightly,
his moon-like face was radiant, its surface of cheeks illuminated by a gentle smile.
His beautiful lower lip is resplendent with the flood of light from his rows of teeth;
his ripe bimba-fruit-like lip is like the lovely, red petal of a lotus. (17)
His long, reddish eyes were beautifully adorned with perfectly formed lashes, and his throat shone with the radiance of the multitude of jewels in his broad necklace. 18.
I behold Hari, whose lotus-stalk-like arms shine with celestial jewel armlets,
and who bears a mace, a lotus, a conch, and a discus upon his staff-like limbs.
Then, [he beheld] that chest which was as broad as a door-panel, the abode of Kamalā,
and whose floor was illuminated by the mass of radiance from the shimmering Kaustubha gem.
He shone brilliantly with his chest, which was the abode of the three worlds,
adorned with three folds and graced by a beautiful line of hair possessing a lovely luster.
He shone with a prominent belly and a beautiful waist,
while his jeweled girdle gleamed with the luster of yellow silk garments.
Adorned above with thighs that were plump, lovely, and like autumnal quivers, his pair of shanks was enchanting, possessing a luster as beautiful as a peacock's throat. (23)
His feet moved like red lotuses, with the tips of his toes surpassing tortoises; his soles were marked by a lotus on the banner, possessing a luster resembling the blood of a rabbit.
He is eternally embraced by her who delights in holding a hand-like red lotus,
and he is likewise embraced by Forgiveness, adorned with a fresh ruby.
His entire body was resplendent with the flood of beauty of fresh youth, and he was attended by hosts of Apsarases as well as by the foremost of gods, asuras, and sages. (26)
It was adorned with a canopy resembling the orb of the full moon,
and shone with yak-tail whisks gracefully waved by the lotus-like hands of celestial nymphs.
It was beautifully adorned with victory banners fluttering like streaks of lightning,
and it was frequented by hosts of yakṣas, vidyādharas, cāraṇas, and others.
Having meditated thus, arise, O Śrīkarā, svāhā! This mantra is to be employed [in the sixteen-syllable mantra].

Now, the Nṛsiṃha-mantra: Then, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (nyāsa), saying: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Nṛsiṃha, on the heart."

"For the accomplishment of all my desires, this is the application (*viniyoga*)," having said this with palms joined in reverence, [he recites]: "To the fierce hero, *namaḥ* to the heart; to Mahāviṣṇu, *svāhā* to the head; to the blazing one facing in all directions, *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*);
to the terrifying Nṛsiṃha, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*); to the auspicious one, the death of death..."
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with "To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ; I bow" and "To the weapon, phaṭ," one should meditate:
"I worship Nṛsiṃha, whose arms rest upon his knees, who has three eyes, and whose arms shine with the discus and conch;
who has swallowed the Daitya with a light resembling fire, and whose two tongues are brilliantly illuminated by the fangs adorning his head. (1)

Having meditated thus upon the fierce, heroic, great Viṣṇu, the blazing one whose faces are on all sides, the formidable Nṛsiṃha, the auspicious one, the death of death—I bow to him; this mantra should be employed.

Now, the Gopāla-mantra: Then, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. One should then place the mantras: "Salutation to Nārada, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head"; "Salutation to Virāṭ, the meter (chandas), on the mouth"; "Salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the deity (devatā), on the heart"; and "Salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, on the private parts."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Svāhā to Śakti at the two feet; obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), on all limbs; obeisance to the presiding deity, the illustrious Durgā, in the heart," and having declared with palms joined, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) upon the hands with the root mantra, saying: "Svāhā to the wheel of emanation (*ācakra*)."

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) thus: "Hṛdayāya namaḥ, Vicakrāya svāhā, Śirase svāhā, Sucakrāya svāhā, Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ, Trailokyarakṣaṇacakrāya svāhā, Kavacāya huṃ, Asurāntacakrāya svāhā, Astrāya phaṭ," one should meditate.
With his lotus-like hands holding a flute— whose bowstring was formed by the rays of the moon and whose cloth was the fibers of the reed— he joyfully played it with both hands.
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa situated within the solar disc for the attainment of desired fruits.
Having thus meditated, the mantra "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā" should be employed.
