Now, the mantra of Kṛṣṇa: Then, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, and recite: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ* in the private parts," and so forth.
Having performed the placement [of the mantras] for the sake of attaining my desired goal, one should say with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application (viniyoga)," and then recite:
"Salutation to the Heart, whose nature is perfect knowledge; Svāhā to the Head, whose nature is perfect sovereignty;
Vaṣṭ to the Tuft (śikhā), whose nature is perfect splendor; Huṃ to the Armor (kavaca), whose nature is perfect bliss."

Having performed the placement of the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with "To the Self of Full Radiance, *vauṣaṭ* to the two eyes" and "To the Self of Full Power, *phaṭ* to the weapon," one should meditate:
One should meditate upon [the deity] who resembles an emerald, the sole object of worship for the world... (p. 208)

[I worship] the Lord of Indirā, the essence of beauty, who holds a mirror, a conch, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his arms; who is unconquered, swift, accompanied by Bhaimī and Satyā, and the bestower of all things.
Having meditated thus, the mantra "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ" should be employed. As for the yoga: oṃ hasakalahrīṃ namo hasakahalahrīṃ nārāyaṇāya sakalahrīṃ || 1 ||
Oṃ hasakalahrīṃ, salutation to hasakalahrīṃ; to the Blessed One, the complete Hrīṃ, Vāsudeva. || 2 ||

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, who has the form of a boar; O *hasakalahrīṃ*, O *hasakahalahrīṃ*, Lord of the three worlds (*bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*), O *sakalahrīṃ*, grant me the status of a sovereign of the earth, cause it to be granted! Svāhā! || 3 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods, the one of great power; ha-sa-ka-la-hrīṃ, ha-sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ, sa-ka-la-hrīṃ, svāhā! || 4 ||
Arise! Hasakalahrīṃ! O Glorious One, Hasakalahrīṃ! Svāhā! Sakalahrīṃ! || 5 ||

I bow to the fierce hero Mahāviṣṇu, *hasakalahrīṃ*, blazing with faces on all sides, *hasakahalahrīṃ*; to the auspicious Nṛsiṃha, terrifying and blessed, *sakalahrīṃ*; I bow to the death of Death itself. || 6 ||
klīṃ kṛṣṇāya hasakalahrīṃ govindāya hasakahalahrīṃ gopījanavallabhāya sakalahrīṃ svāhā || 7 ||
klīṃ hasakalahrīṃ kṛṣṇāya hasakahalahrīṃ namaḥ sakalahrīṃ || 8 ||
Thus, the meaning is "yoga."

In the Vedic system, however, he states the mantras: thereafter, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, [one should assign]: "Salutation to the sage Viśvāmitra on the head of this venerable Gāyatrī mantra; salutation to the metre Gāyatrī on the face; salutation to the Supreme Self (Śrīparamātman) in the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Salutation to the Deity," and having spoken with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," he should recite:
"To the Heart, Salutation to the Self of Brahmā, that Savitṛ; to the Head, Svāhā to the Self of Viṣṇu, the Excellent;
to the Tuft, Vaṣaṭ to the Self of Rudra, the Splendor of the God; to the Armor, Huṃ to the Self of Īśvara, we meditate."

Having performed the placement of the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with "dhiyo yo naḥ sadāśivātmane netratrayāya vauṣaṭ" and "pracodayāt paramātmane astrāyaphaṭ," one should meditate [upon the deity] as having three eyes and faces with the lusters of pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white.

I worship Gāyatrī, who is endowed with yoga, whose jeweled crown is bound by the moon, whose nature consists of the letters of the meaning of reality, who grants boons and fearlessness, and who carries in her hands a goad, a trident, a skull-cup, a rosary, a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus: "The most excellent splendor of that Savitṛ—hasakalahrīṃ; we meditate upon the glory of the divine—hasakahalahrīṃ; may he impel our intellects—sakalahrīṃ."

Now, regarding the mantra for Jātavedas: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the Yoga-pīṭha, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, for this Jātavedas mantra: salutation to Mārociputra Kaśyapa, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to the Triṣṭubh meter (chandas), on the mouth; and salutation to the illustrious Jātavedas Agni Durgā, on the heart.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Salutation to the Deity," and having said with palms joined in reverence, "The application is for the attainment of my desired goal," one recites: "We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas" — *namas* to the heart; "He burns up the wealth of the enemy" — *svāhā* to the head;
"He knows the way" — *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair; "May he carry us across all difficulties like a boat" — *huṃ* to the armor.

Having performed the placement of the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with "to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" and "Agni has crossed over the ocean of misfortunes, phaṭ to the weapon," one should meditate [on her] as having a radiance equal to a garland of lightning, seated upon the shoulders of the Lord of Beasts, and terrifying.

One should meditate upon Durgā, whose nature is fire, who wears the crescent moon, who has three eyes, and who is attended by maidens with hands shimmering with swords and shields; she herself holds in her hands a discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow, bowstring, and a raised index finger.
Having meditated thus, [one recites]: "Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas;

*hasakalahrīṃ*, he burns away the wealth of those who act as enemies, *hasakahalahrīṃ*; may he carry us across all difficulties, *sakalahrīṃ*, like a boat across the ocean; Agni carries us beyond misfortunes."

Now, regarding the mantra beginning with "atha tām agnivarṇām": there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having assigned the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other factors as before, one should say with palms joined, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of my desired goal," and [proceed with] "hrāṃ, salutation to the heart."
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hrīṃ, svāhā to the head; Hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; Hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor;

Hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Hraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon," and having meditated upon her as before—her the color of fire, blazing with ascetic heat, [seated] on Hasakalahrīṃ, the Vairocanī among the fruits of karma—
"I take refuge in the Goddess Durgā, who is beloved by *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*; O You who easily carry [us] across, salutations to You who cross over! Thus one should recite.

(p. 209) Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the mantra *athāgne*. Therein, having performed the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*) and so forth, up to the end of the placement on the yoga-pīṭha (*yogapīṭhanyāsa*), one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) along with meditation (*dhyāna*) as previously described. Then [one recites]: *agne tvaṃ pārayā navyo asmān hasakalahrīṃ svastibhirati durgāṇi viśvā hasakahalahrīṃ pūśca pṛthivī*.
"O vast one, be abundant and full of modesty for our offspring and progeny; grant us well-being. Thus one should recite.

Now follows the application of the mantra "viśvāni naḥ. Therein, having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, having performed the *ṛṣi*-assignment and so forth, as well as the *kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* and meditation (*dhyāna*), according to the previous procedure, [one recites]: "O Jātavedas, may all our difficult passages be [crossed] like the ocean by means of a boat—hasakalahrīṃ."
"O Agni, who destroy the sinner and evil deeds, being praised with reverence like Atri, protect our bodies; [sakalahrīṃ]. Thus one should mutter.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the hymn beginning with "pṛtanājitam": having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the visualization (*dhyāna*), one recites:
"We invoke the conqueror of armies, the overcoming, the fierce Agni—*hasakalahrīṃ*—from the highest abode—*hasakahalahrīṃ*;
may he carry us across all difficulties—*sakalahrīṃ*; the god who endures—*kṣāmaddevaḥ*."
"Agni [crosses] over misfortunes. Then follow the Śrīsūkta and Devīsūkta, which are well-known in the Ṛgveda.

Now follows the ritual application for the Śiva [Tantra]: there, having performed the morning duties and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Vāmadeva, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Sadāśiva, on the heart."
Having said with palms joined, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," [one should recite]: "Salutation to the Heart, the Omniscient;

Svāhā to the Head, the Ever-Satisfied; Vaṣaṭ to the Tuft, Beginningless Awareness; Huṃ to the Armor, the Independent; Vauṣaṭ to the Three Eyes, whose power is eternally undiminished; [Salutation] to the Eternally Infinite Power."
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras with the formula "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should meditate [on the deity] as follows:
White as the foam of cow’s milk, with a luster like that of a mountain of silver, adorned with a crown of matted hair graced by the beautiful crescent moon; (1)
Śambhu bears five faces, each with three eyes;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with jewel ornaments. || 2 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *hasakalahrīṃ oṃ hasakahalahrīṃ namaḥ sakalahrīṃ śivāya*.

Now follows the application of the Aghora weapon (*aghorāstra*). Therein, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the *nyāsa*: "Salutation to Aghora, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Triṣṭubh meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī-Aghorarudra, on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, on the private parts."

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) on the two feet with "hrūṃ śaktaye namaḥ," and having said with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application (viniyoga) for the attainment of my desired goal," [one recites]: "hrīṃ sphura-sphura, obeisance to the heart; prasphura-prasphura, svāhā to the head;
ghora-ghoratara-tanūrūpa, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā); caṭa-caṭa pracaṭa-pracaṭa."

Having applied the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) thus: "Kavacāya hūṃ kahakaha vaṃvaṃ for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ; bandhabandha ghātayaghātaya hūṃ phaṭ for the weapon, phaṭ," one should meditate.
With the body thus consecrated by the mantras, the practitioner, with undistracted mind, should meditate upon the God.
The god resembled a dark cloud, with terrifying fangs and three eyes. || 1 ||
Adorned with serpents and endowed with red garments, ointments, and unguents,
he holds an axe, a sword, arrows, and a trident.
O Pārvatī, he holds in his right hands, in ascending order from the lowest,
a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a shield (kheṭaka), a bow, and a human skull-cup (nṛkapāla).

In rites for desired objects, one should meditate on [the deity] as having a reddish luster; in rites of exorcism (abhicāra), as black; in rites of suppression, [one should meditate on him as such]; and for liberation from planets, spirits, and the like, one should meditate on him as resembling a pearl.

Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ sphura-sphura prasphura-prasphura ghora-ghoratara-tanurūpa hasa-kala-hrīṃ caṭa-caṭa pracaṭa-pracaṭa kaha-kaha hasa-kaha-lahrīṃ vama-vama bandha-bandha sakala-hrīṃ ghātaya-ghātaya hūṃ phaṭ*.

Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) of Śarabha: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement of the yogapīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, and then perform the following salutations: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to Śarabha-Śālva, the king of birds, the deity (devatā), on the heart."

Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) for the sake of attaining my desired goal, and having said with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application (*viniyoga*)," [one recites]: *Oṃ namo bhagavate hṛdayāya namaḥ*, "Salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to the heart"; *śarabhaśālvāya śirase svāhā*, "To the Śarabha-Śālva, svāhā to the head"; *pakṣirājāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, "To the King of Birds, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock";
*mama śatrūn nāśaya nāśaya kavacāya huṃ huṃ phaṭ*, "Destroy my enemies, destroy them! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ to the armor"; *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, "Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes."
*Svāhā astrāya phaṭ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):

A golden-peaked mountain with eight facets, its wings and base-kingdom adorned with vajras; its peaks of gold, its body of gold, possessing rubies upon its limbs, and its lotus-face shining from the opening of its beak. (1)
His three eyes, radiant with the splendor of the sun, fire, and moon, illuminate his ruby-like countenance;
the entire mass of his body-hairs shines with the brilliance of sapphires, and his head is made resplendent by the crescent of the cool-rayed moon.

[He is] beautiful with necklaces formed by the clusters of droplets falling in succession from his head, which is occupied by the Ganges flowing through the mass of his excellent matted locks— tawny like Kapila and bound by pairs of Vipra-snakes; [he is] rising with the five-fingered tuft of hair at the tip of his mane, formed by the successive knots of the serpent-bonds rising at the front.
It was beautiful with garlands shimmering upon the pair of arms arising from the chest, the throat, the joints, and the shoulders.

He is the destroyer of the host of enemies at the very moment of their end, who agitates the ten directions with the swelling bells of the playful rays of the moon-like pair of serpents attached to his waist-band;
he is the lord of the venomous serpent-kinghood born from the herd of bulls that move restlessly upon his shoulders in the form of nooses.
He [beheld] that all-enduring earth, made terrible by the bursting hissing sounds and crushed by the multitude of hoof-strikes.
With a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon Śarabha in the form of a bird, devouring the multitudes of enemies of his devotees, and in the form of Śālva. || 5 ||

Having thus meditated upon Śiva in the form of a Śarabha, one should mutter the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate śarabhaśālvāya hasakalahrīṃ pakṣirājāya hasakahalahrīṃ mama śatrūn nāśayanāśaya sakalahrīṃ ghaghahuṃphaṭ svāhā*.

Now follows the application of the Prāsāda mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the Yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the nyāsa: "Salutation to Vāmadeva, the Seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Sadāśiva, the Deity (devatā), on the heart; [salutation] on the secret place (guhya)."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ *haṃ* bīja-āya namaḥ" on the two feet and "Oṃ *śakti*-e namaḥ," and having spoken with palms joined in reverence, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of the accomplishment of all my desired goals," [one should then assign: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the heart;
Hīṃ, svāhā to the head; Hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair; Haiṃ, huṃ to the armor; Hauṃ to the three eyes."
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras with "vauṣaṭ haḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should meditate:
"Then, O child, with a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the God in the heart—His body red like a mass of vermilion, His face smiling, and His three eyes. (1)
His head is adorned by the crescent moon shining upon his jeweled crown;
in his upper right hand he holds a chisel, and below that, the gesture of granting boons (vara).
In her left upper hand she holds a deer, and below it, with devotion, she displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā),
having placed it against the tips of her full, rounded, firm, and lofty breasts.
Seated upon the left lap of his beloved,
who rests upon a red lotus and holds a seated [deity] in her right hand upon a red lotus.

Having meditated thus upon [the deity] blazing with various ornaments and adorned with divine perfumes, garlands, and garments, one should mutter the mantra: *oṃ hauṃ hasakalahrīṃ hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ namaḥ sakalahrīṃ śivāya*.

Now follows the application of the Pāśupata weapon-mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa, one should perform three breath-retentions (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (vinyāsa), saying: "Salutation to Vāmadeva, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīpaśupati, on the heart."
"For the accomplishment of my desired goal, this is the application (*viniyoga*)," having said this with palms joined in reverence, [one recites]: *oṃ huṃ phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ*,
*ślīṃ huṃphaṭ śirase svāhā*, *pa huṃphaṭ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *śu huṃ phaṭ kavacāya huṃ*, *huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *phaṭ huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*.

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the practitioner of mantra, with a one-pointed mind, should meditate: "He should meditate upon Paśupati, who has five faces and ten arms, and possesses three eyes in each face. (1)
He was endowed with a beard resembling flames of fire and possessed terrifying fangs;
he held a sword, arrows, a rosary, a spear, and even an axe.
In his right hands, held in ascending order from below,
he bears a shield, a bow, a water-pot, and a trident, together with the staff of Brahmā.
Holding [objects] with his left hands, possessing a splendor equal to the midday sun, blazing with various ornaments, and adorned by the lords of serpents. || 4 ||
"One should meditate upon [the deity] resembling a mass of crystal, peaceful, and the granter of all protection.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ hasakalahrīṃ paśu hasakahalahrīṃ huṃ sakalahrīṃ phaṭ*.

Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra: there, having performed the morning duties and so forth up to the placement of the Yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, one should place: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śuka, the seer (ṛṣi)," on the head; "obeisance to Gāyatrī, the meter (chandas)," on the mouth; "obeisance to the deity Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti," on the heart; and "Oṃ" on the secret place (guhya).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Bījāya namaḥ" on the two feet and "Hrīṃ Śaktaye namaḥ," and having said with palms joined, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of my desired goal," one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the root mantra. Then:
"Oṃ Hrāṃ Dakṣiṇāmūrtaye Hrāṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ; Oṃ Hrīṃ Tubhyaṃ Hrīṃ Śirase Svāhā."

Oṃ hrīṃ, to the one dwelling at the root of the banyan tree, hrūṃ, to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ; oṃ hrīṃ, to the one whose limbs are solely intent on meditation, hraiṃ, to the armor, huṃ; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Rudra, hrauṃ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ; oṃ hrīṃ, to Śambhu, hraḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ—thus are the six limb-mantras.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should meditate [on Him] seated upon a patch of ground near a banyan tree, the bestower of knowledge from afar to all the hosts of sages.
I bow to the Lord, the teacher of the three worlds, who manifests in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti and is capable of severing the suffering of birth and death. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇāmūrtaye tubhyaṃ hasakalahrīṃ vaṭamūlanivāsine hasakahalahrīṃ dhyānaikaniratāṅgāya sakalahrīṃ namo rudrāya śambhave hrīṃ oṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of Mṛtyuñjaya: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement of the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to the sage Kahola" on the head; "Salutation to the *nicṛdgāyatrī* metre" on the mouth; "Salutation to the deity Śrīmṛtyuñjaya" on the heart; [and] on the secret place...

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Oṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable on the feet; Saḥ, salutation to the power (*śakti*) at the navel; Jūṃ, salutation to the pin (*kīlaka*)," and having said with palms joined, "The application is for the sake of attaining my desired success," one should perform the purification of the hands with the root mantra. Then: "Sāṃ, salutation to the heart; Sīṃ, svāhā to the head; Sūṃ, [salutation] to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras with "Vaṣaṭ! Saiṃ! To the armor, Huṃ! Sauṃ! To the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ! Saḥ! To the weapon, Phaṭ!", one should meditate:
"Then, O child, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the God for a long time."
Resembling pure crystal, he is seated upon a white lotus throne. || 1 ||
His entire body was sprinkled with nectar falling from the crescent moon shimmering upon his matted locks, and his eyes were the sun, the moon, and fire.
In his upper right hand he holds the mudrā called Jñāna, and in the hand below it a rosary;
in his upper left hand a noose, and in the hand below it the Vedas.
One should meditate upon the God who bestows [blessings] and removes the fear of death and disease.
Having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hasakalahrīṃ jūṃ hasakahalahrīṃ saḥ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the application of the ten-syllable mantra: Then, after performing the morning rites up to the placement on the Yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Having performed the placement (nyāsa) thus: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Virāṭ, the meter (chandas), on the mouth;
salutation to Sadāśiva, the deity (devatā), on the heart," [one proceeds] for the attainment of my desired goal.

Having said "This is the application," with palms joined in reverence, one should meditate after having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as follows: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *namaḥ śirase svāhā*, *bhagavate śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *rudrāya kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ namo bhagavate netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *rudrāya astrāya phaṭ*.

I bow to Him who is filled with divine enjoyments, worshipped by the sons of the gods and the daughters of Diti; who bears half the body of the Daughter of the Mountain; who resembles a crystal gem and wears a tiger-skin as an upper garment;
who is clad in the skin of a black antelope and has the crescent moon as His crest-ornament, O Blue-throated One.
I meditate upon Maheśa, who is joyful, pervaded by his powers (kalās), and who bears matted hair of a tawny-brown hue. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *oṃ hasakalahrīṃ namo hasakahalahrīṃ bhagavate sakalahrīṃ rudrāya*.

Now follows the procedure for the visualization of the Sun (Sauradarśana). First, regarding the application of the *ghṛṇi* mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the placement of the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the salutations: "Salutation to the Seer Devabhāga on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter in the mouth; salutation to the auspicious Sun in the heart."

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) with "Salutation to the deity," and having said with palms joined, "The application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of my desired goal during recitation," [one should assign the mantras]: "Satyatejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā, salutation to the heart;
Brahmatejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā, svāhā to the head; Viṣṇutejojvālāmaṇi..."

Having applied the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) as follows: *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* for the crest (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ* for Rudra’s Splendor-Jewel-Flame (*rudratejojvālāmaṇi*) *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* for the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ* for the Fire-Splendor-Jewel-Flame (*agnitejojvālāmaṇi*) *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* for the three eyes (*netratraya*), *vauṣaṭ*, and *sarvatejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā* for the weapon (*astra*) *phaṭ*; one should then meditate.
I praise the Lord of Day, who has two red lotuses and the gestures of granting fearlessness in his hands; who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings;
who wears a crown of rubies; who possesses the splendor of the bandhūka flower; and whose three eyes shine brilliantly. (1)
Having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra: *ghṛṇiḥ hasakalahrīṃ*, *sūrya hasakahalahrīṃ*, *āditya sakalahrīṃ*, *oṃ*.

(p. 212) Now follows the application of the six-syllabled mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement upon the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Savitṛ, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart. Having said, with palms joined in reverence, "The application is for the attainment of my desired goal," [one proceeds].
Svāhā to the subtle form; obeisance to the heart. Svāhā to the subtle radiance; svāhā to the head.

Svāhā to the subtle appearance; vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Svāhā to the subtle hair; huṃ to the armor. Svāhā to the subtle body; vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Having uttered the root mantra, [svāhā] to the weapon.
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras with the syllable *phaṭ*, one should meditate:
"One should meditate upon the Sun-god, who holds two red lotuses in his hands, bestowing boons and fearlessness, possessing the luster of a bandhūka flower, three-eyed, and beautifully adorned. (1)
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *kha ha sa ka la hrīṃ kho ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ lkā ya sa ka la hrīṃ svāhā*.
Now follows the application of the four-syllable [mantra]: therein, after the morning rites and ending with the placement (*nyāsa*) of the yoga-seat (*yogapīṭha*), by means of the root mantra...

Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Bhuvaneśvarī, who is the form of Śrīsūrya, on the heart. Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should say: "The application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of my desired goal," and recite: "Oṃ, salutation to the heart; Hrīṃ..."

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with: "To the head, svāhā! Oṃ, to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ! Hrīṃ, to the armor, huṃ! Oṃ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! Hrīṃ, to the weapon, phaṭ!", one should meditate [upon the deity] as follows:
[The deity] who illuminates the crescent moon shimmering upon a crown adorned with a thousand radiant jewels...

May the body of the Mistress of the Universe protect the world— from the hot season until the cold— with its brilliance as radiant as molten gold, lotuses, hibiscus flowers, and lightning; it holds a goad, a rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in its lotus-like hands, while her breasts are exceedingly high.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hasakalahrīṃ hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ haṃ sakalahrīṃ saḥ*.

Now follows the application of the three-syllable mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows—*namaḥ* to the sage (*ṛṣi*) Aja on the head, *namaḥ* to the Gāyatrī metre (*chandas*) in the mouth, and *namaḥ* to the deity Śrīsūrya in the heart—one should [proceed] for the sake of attaining my desired goal.

Having said "This is the application" (viniyogaḥ) with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the placement (nyāsa): saying "hāṃ namaḥ," one places [the mantra] from the secret parts to the feet;
saying "hīṃ namaḥ," from the throat to the secret parts; and saying "saḥ namaḥ," from the head to the throat.
Then, having performed the six-limbed placement on the hands (kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) with "hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ."
One should meditate [on him] as seated upon a reddish lotus, possessing three eyes and many ornaments,
with hands granting boons and protection while holding a pair of reddish lotuses.
We meditate upon the Sun, whose body is of a rosy hue, who is well-served by his crimson rays, and who is worshipped by the multitude of all the gods. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *hrāṃ hasakalahrīṃ hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ saḥ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the practice of the sixteen-syllable mantra: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *jagatī* meter, on the mouth;
salutation to the deity Śrī Bhāskara, on the heart"—[one should do this] for the sake of attaining my desired goal.

Having said "This is the application" with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the assignment of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as follows: *oṃ aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *saḥ kavacāya huṃ*, *śrībhāskarāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ svāhā*, *astrāya phaṭ*; and then one should meditate.
The Lord is mounted upon a chariot rich with rubies, wears jeweled earrings,
and with his hands bestows desired boons while bearing the conch, the discus, and the lotus.
Wearing a crown, a girdle, and armor,
with a beautiful body, he was endowed with various jewels and adorned by horses as numerous as the sages.
It was frequented by the constellations, planets, zodiac signs, and other celestial bodies, as well as by circles of sages; it was graced by Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon the Sun-god (Bhāskara) accompanied by various deities.
Having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ aiṃ hasakalahrīṃ klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ hasakahalahrīṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ saḥ sakalahrīṃ śrībhāskarāya svāhā*.

Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) of the twelve-syllable mantra: therein, having performed the morning duties up to the placement on the yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, and then perform the placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Obeisance to the Seer (ṛṣi) Devabhāga upon the head; obeisance to the Virāṭ meter (chandas) in the mouth; obeisance to the deity Śrī-Āditya in the heart. Having thus performed the placement, [one proceeds].

Having said, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," and with palms joined in reverence, one should assign the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) as *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hraḥ*. Then, having meditated as before, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ āṃ hasakalahrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ghṛṇiḥ hasakahalahrīṃ sūrya sakalahrīṃ āditya oṃ*.

(p. 213) Now follows the application of the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*): there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), saying "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī-Āditya, on the heart."

Having said, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of my desired goal," and with palms joined in reverence, one should assign the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) as follows: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *klīṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *glauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *hrāṃ astrāya phaṭ*. Then, one should meditate as before: *oṃ*.
One should recite the mantra: *śrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ glauṃ sakalahrīṃ hrāṃ*.

Now follows the application of the eight-syllabled *ātman* mantra. Its ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth have already been explained in detail previously in the section on the procedure for the *mātṛkā*. One should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ haṃsaḥ hasakahalahrīṃ so'haṃ sakalahrīṃ svāhā*.
Now follows the procedure for the Śākta system. First, regarding the application of the Bālā mantra:

there, after performing the morning rites up to the placement of the Yogapīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the nyāsa: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; [salutation] to the heart..."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to the deity Śrībālā at the secret place; salutation to the seed-syllable *aiṃ* at the feet; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *sauḥ* at the navel; salutation to the *kīlaka* *klīṃ*," and having said with palms joined, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of my desired goal," [one should assign: *aiṃ* salutation to the heart, *klīṃ* *svāhā* to the head, *sauḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with: *Vaṣaṭ aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *klīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, and *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should meditate [upon her] as follows:
"Her hair-tresses are dark like wandering bees and adorned with pure flowers."
She was resplendent with a streak of split pearls shimmering from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 1 ||
Her forehead was adorned with a tilaka made of pearls and gems; she wore a crown consisting of a crescent moon enriched with pure pearl drops.
She is adorned with three eyes that shine like wandering bees and are dark blue in hue;
she is the Supreme Goddess, graced by great jeweled earrings as radiant as the sun.
Adorned with ornaments of pearl necklaces shimmering with the luster of semen,
and radiant with the glow emanating from her wrists, which were beautified by bracelets and other glittering jewels.
Adorned with sprout-like hands and feet that resemble coral creepers,
she possesses a girdle of diamonds, lapis lazuli, and pearls, and is of stainless luster.
Adorned with sprouting shoots shaped like the petals of a red lotus,
she was decorated with pearl anklets resembling a garland of stars.
O fair-faced one, she holds a book with one left hand and grants the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā) to the practitioner with the other.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows subjugation, good fortune, and eloquence, holding a rosary and the gesture of granting boons with her two right hands.
"O Beloved, one should meditate upon her who is as white as a jasmine flower, the moon, or milk, and is serene.
Having thus visualized, one should recite the mantra: *aiṃ hasakalahrīṃ klīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of Bhairavī: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the *nyāsa* as follows: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *paṅkti* meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Tripurabhairavī, on the heart; [salutation] on the secret place (*guhya*)."
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) thus: "Salutation to the Vāgbhava-kūṭa seed-syllable on the two feet; salutation to the Śakti-kūṭa power on the navel;

salutation to the Kāmarāja-kūṭa pin on the navel," and having said with palms joined, "The application is for the attainment of my desired goal," one should perform the six-limbed nyāsa by repeating the three seed-syllables twice and then meditate.
Residing in the center of the pericarp of a red lotus situated within the heart,
she resembles a hibiscus flower and is adorned with red garments and ornaments.
She whose great delusion is washed away by her smile, who has three eyes, who bears the moon upon her crest, and who is the embodiment of the ocean of the entire essence of universal beauty. (2)
The Goddess, sweet with bliss, her eyes rolling with intoxication,
was [worshipped] by those known as Brahmā, Abjanetra, Rudreśa, Śiva, and Muṇḍa.
The great goddess, her limbs adorned, wearing a rosary of pearls,
with a book as an ornament in her hand, and bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate upon Tripurabhairavī, who is beautiful with red unguents on her limbs.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *hasakalaraiṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasakalarīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *hasauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.
Now follows the ritual application for Caitanyabhairavī: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the yogapīṭha-nyāsa,

one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, and having executed the nyāsas of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed nyāsa on the hands, according to what was previously stated, one should meditate as follows:
She possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with various ornaments, has a crescent moon shimmering upon her crown, and is arrayed in red garments. || 1 ||
Holding a noose and a goad, with a skull-cup perpetually in her left hand, she is enriched by hands granting boons and fearlessness, and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts. (2)
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess seated upon the eastern lion-throne.
Having meditated in this way, one should recite the mantra: *sahaiṃ hasakalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sahauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application for Kāmeśvarī-Bhairavī: having performed there the rites from the morning duties up to the visualization as previously described, one should recite the mantra: *sahraiṃ hasakalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sakalahrīṃ sahrauḥ*.
Now follows the ritual application for Bhairavī: having performed there the morning rites and so forth, up to the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as previously described,
one should meditate [upon her] as having the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, with the moon as her crest-jewel, and three eyes.
Beautifully adorned with various ornaments, she is the cutter of all enemies.
She is adorned with a garland of heads from which blood flows, clothed in red garments,
and holds a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, and likewise a shield.
O Goddess, she is seated upon a corpse-lion throne, holding in sequence the Pināka bow, arrows, a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary of beads.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *hasakhaphreṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasakalarīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *hsauṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*. This is the Nityābhairavī.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) for Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī:
having performed there the preliminary rites beginning with the morning duties up to the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as previously described, one should meditate—
[one should] meditate upon the four-armed Goddess.
Resembling the hibiscus flower and possessing the luster of the pomegranate blossom. || 1 ||
She has the crescent moon in her matted locks, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and has full, high, and firm breasts. || 2 ||
I take refuge in Śivā, who sits upon a corpse-seat, adorned with a garland of severed heads, and who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *hasraiṃ hasakalahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ hrasauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.
This very [Vidyā], which is to be performed as a whole, is a division of Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī; it bestows prosperity and begins with the letter *sa*.

If she is Kaulīśa-Bhairavī, she bestows prosperity; having omitted the letter *ra* at the beginning and end of the Vidyā that bestows prosperity, she is the Bhairavī who grants all accomplishments (*siddhi*). For these Vidyās, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent parts] are as before.
Now, the mantras of the presiding deities of the Buddhist systems (*bauddhadarśana*). First, the ritual procedure for Padmāvatī:
therein, after performing the morning rites up to the placement of the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra;
then, [one should place]: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation] to Śrī Padmāvatī on the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Salutation to the Deity," and having said with palms joined, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with "hrāṃ hrīm" and so forth, and then meditate.

I bow to Padmāvatī, who sits in the lotus posture, possessing the luster of fresh saffron, holding two red lotuses, endowed with three eyes, wearing crimson ornaments, and having a face as beautiful as a lotus. || 1 ||

Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *hrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ padmāvatī hasakahalahrīṃ svāhā sakalahrīṃ*. Since it is stated that [these deities are] Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, Tārā, and Nīlasarasvatī, their mantras are as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ huṃ ugratāre huṃ phaṭ* is the mantra of Ugratārā.
*Śrīṃ huṃ hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ*—this is Ekajaṭā. *Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is Tārā.

*Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ*—this is Nīlasarasvatī. Regarding the recitation (*japa*) of these four, one should recite each one by joining the three peak-syllables (*kūṭa*) of the Pañcadaśī-mantra, interspersed with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).

The ritual applications (*prayoga*) are as follows: after performing the morning duties and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra.

Then, having performed the assignment (*vinyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to Akṣobhya, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the metre (*chandas*), in the mouth; salutation to the deity Amuka-tārā, in the heart," one should state: "This is the application for the recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of my desired goal."

Having spoken thus with palms joined in reverence, [he recited]: Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the Heart, whose form is the speech of all; Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Head, whose form is indivisible speech; Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the Tuft (śikhā), whose form is the speech of Brahman;
Oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the Armor (kavaca), whose form is the speech of Viṣṇu; Oṃ hrauṃ, [salutation] to the one whose form is the speech of Rudra...

Having performed the placement of the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with "To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" and "Oṃ hraḥ, to the weapon which is the form of all speech, phaṭ," one should meditate [on her] as follows:
seated upon a white lotus blooming in the midst of waters that pervade the universe...
I bow to her who holds a curved knife, a sword, a skull, and a blue lotus in her radiant hands; who possesses a dark-blue luster;
whose body is adorned by excellent serpents serving as her girdle, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and anklets; and who has three blood-red eyes. || 1 ||
She has a single matted lock of tawny hair, a shimmering celestial tongue, and a face made terrifying by her fangs;
her waist is beautified by a garment of tiger skin and she wears a girdle of white bones;
her head is resplendent with Akṣobhya, and her lotus-face is smiling.
One should remember Tārā, the Mother of the three worlds, who wears a corpse-heart as her garment and possesses firm breasts. || 1 ||
Thus one should meditate.

Now follows the practice of Mātaṅgī: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement of the Yoga-pīṭha, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, one should place: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
salutation to Gāyatrī, the metre (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīmātaṅginī, on my heart."

Having said, "The application is for the attainment of all desired goals," with palms joined in reverence, [one recites]: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ namo bhagavati śrīmātaṅgīśvari sarvajanamanohāri hṛdayāya namaḥ;
sarvamukharājisarvamukharañjini śirase svāhā; sarvarājavaśaṅkari.*

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) as follows: "O you who bring all women and men under control, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā); O you who bring all wicked beasts and all sentient beings under control, huṃ to the armor (kavaca); O you who bring such-and-such a person from all worlds under my control, vauṣaṭ svāhā to the three eyes; phaṭ to the weapon (astra)," one should meditate.
Having thus surrendered his body, he should meditate upon the deity of the mantra within a delightful jewel-island situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar.
In a pavilion constructed of jewels and surrounded by a golden wall,
at the entrance of the Kadamba and Bilva trees, it was adorned with the Kalpa-tree.
O Lord, upon a lion-throne of jewels comfortably spread in the center of the altar,
there was a great eight-petaled lotus with filaments and a pericarp.
In the center of that, there should be a triangle; outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus;
again, there should be a sixteen-petaled lotus; and on the outside of that, a four-petaled lotus.
The supreme mandala is said to have four corners and four gates;
in its center sits [the Goddess], dark-complexioned with a pure smile, seated comfortably.
Adorned with garlands of Kadamba flowers and worshipped by gods and asuras,
she has long tresses and is graced by the crescent moon as her ornament.
She has a tilaka-mark upon her forehead, her face is slightly smiling,
and she is radiant with the surface of her forehead shining with a few drops of sweet perspiration.
Adorned with a line of body hair shining from the midst of her wave-like folds,
she was endowed with all ornaments and embellished with a pearl necklace.
She was adorned with waist-bands bound with clusters of various gems,
and with bracelets inlaid with jewels and armlets decorated with precious stones.
Adorned, with two arms, a youthful maiden whose eyes were rolling with intoxication, and whose full, rounded breasts rose high with their expansive circumference. (10)
With her long pendants as ear-ornaments, resplendent with flowers adorning her ears,
dark as a tamāla tree, youthful, and intoxicated by the spring season— such was Mataṅginī.
She has the form of the sixty-four arts on her flanks, is accompanied by parrots and mainas,
resembles ten million rising suns, and is like the color of a hibiscus flower.
Or, one should meditate upon the supreme Mātaṅginī as being yellow in color.
Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo bhagavati śrīmātaṅgīśvari sarvajanamanohāri sarvamukharāji sarvamukharañjini hasakalahrīṃ*.
O subduer of all kings, O subduer of all men and women, *hasakahalahrīṃ*,
O subduer of all wicked beasts, *sakalahrīṃ*, bring such-and-such a person from all the worlds under my control,
*svāhā*. One should recite [the mantra] in this manner.

Now follows the practice of Sumukhī: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Salutation to the sage Tumburu on the head;
salutation to the Gāyatrī meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Sumukhī in the heart. Thus one should place [the mantras].
Having said with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application for the accomplishment of my desired goal," [he recites]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—*namaḥ* to the heart;
*ucchiṣṭa*—*svāhā* to the head; *cāṇḍāli*—*vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; *mātaṅgi*—*huṃ* to the armor; *sarvavaśaṅkari*—*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes; *namaḥ* to the weapon—*phaṭ*.

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras, one should meditate— that is, one should recollect— her as she has reached her first menses, clad in blue garments speckled with drops of blood,
holding a small vessel of honey, and with her three eyes rolling from intoxication.
Sluggish from the weight of her full breasts, with her powdered cosmetics washed away, the young girl held a lute trembling in her hands and wore bright conch-shell earrings. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should mutter: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālimātaṅgi hasakahalahrīṃ sarvavaśaṅkari sakalahrīṃ namaḥ svāhā*.

(p. 216) Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of Caṇḍamātaṅginī: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement (*nyāsa*) on the yoga-throne (*yogapīṭha*), one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, and then recite: "Salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti at the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre at the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīcaṇḍamātaṅginī at the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] for the sake of attaining my desired goal, and having said "This is the application," with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*) using the *māyā* syllable with the six long vowels, and then meditate:
upon Mātaṅgī, whose feet are moist with fresh lac-dye and who wears a shimmering black garment.
One should meditate upon her who is dark as a parrot, whose hands grace the lute, whose breasts are uplifted, who wears strings of pearls and coral,

whose limbs are heart-stealing, who bears white conch-shell earrings, whose lips are like the bimba fruit, who smiles gently, whose braided hair is adorned with curls, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who is dark-complexioned.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *hrīṃ namaḥ hasakalahrīṃ hilihili hasakahalahrīṃ caṇḍamātaṅginī sakalahrīṃ svāhā*.
Now follow the mantras of the presiding deities of the Gāṇapatya system.

First is the application of the single-syllable Gaṇapati mantra: therein, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement of the Yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, and then [place] "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the Seer (ṛṣi)," on the head; in the mouth—

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Salutation to the *nicṛt* meter; salutation to the deity Śrī Vighneśvara in the heart," and having said with palms joined, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of accomplishing all my desires," [he recites]: "Oṃ, svāhā to Gaṇajaya, salutation to the heart;
huṃ phaṭ to Ekadaṃṣṭra, svāhā to the head; salutation to Acalakarṇin."
*Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, salutations again and again to the elephant-faced one; *kavacāya huṃ* to Mahodara;

*netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; *caṇḍāya huṃ phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Alternatively, having performed the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra beginning with "gāṅgī" and so forth, one should meditate.
Resembling blood-red in hue, with the moon upon his crest, holding a goad, a cord, a tusk,
and a boon-granting gesture in his lotus-like hands, the elephant-faced one has three eyes and is smeared with red unguents;
his belly and thighs are large like a citron fruit, and the surface of his cheeks is moist with the flow of ichor.
May Vighneśa, adorned with serpents as his ornaments, the Lord of the Gaṇas, bring about your prosperity. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *gaṃ hasakalahrīṃ*, *gaṃ hasakahalahrīṃ*, *gaṃ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) for Mahāgaṇapati: there, having performed the morning duties and so forth up to the placement of the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the salutations: "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *nicṛdgāyatrī* meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīgaṇapati, on the heart; [salutation to] *gaṃ*, on the secret place."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Bījāya namaḥ" at the two feet and "Hrīṃ Śaktaye namaḥ," and having said with palms joined, "Viniyoga for the attainment of my desired goal," [one recites]: "Oṃ Gāṃ Hṛdayāya namaḥ; Śrīṃ Gīṃ Śirase svāhā;
Hrīṃ Gūṃ Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Klīṃ Gaiṃ Kavacāya huṃ; Glauṃ Gauṃ."
Having applied the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra) with "To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" and "Gaṃ Gaḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ," one should meditate upon [the deity] holding in his hands a discus,
a lotus, a trident, a bow made of sugarcane, a red lotus, a mace,
and a citron with its tip of grain and its seeds, as well as a water-pot.

I worship Mahāgaṇapati, who resembles a hibiscus flower, who is embraced by his own consort whose hands are raised with lotuses, who bears the crescent moon, and who is illuminated by three eyes. || 1 ||

Having meditated thus, one should mutter: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ hasakalahrīṃ gaṇapataye varavarada hasakahalahrīṃ sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya sakalahrīṃ svāhā*. Now follows the practice for the Swift Gaṇapati: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, with the root mantra...

Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to Virāṭ, the meter (chandas), in the mouth; salutation to Gaṇapati, the deity who bestows swift grace, in the heart. Having spoken thus with palms joined, saying, "This is the application (viniyoga) for the attainment of my desired goal," one proceeds with the mantra beginning with "Gāṃ gīṃ... and so forth.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and the six limbs, one should meditate:

"I worship him who has the luster of vermilion, the face of an elephant, and three eyes; who holds a noose and a goad in his hands, a wine-filled skull-cup, and eternally bears the crescent moon upon his crest."

(217) His body is embraced by Puṣṭi, who holds the tip of a banner in one hand and a lotus blooming in the other; her hand is placed upon his hip, while he holds a water-lily shining with a cloth dyed in the earth. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *gaṃ hasakalahrīṃ kṣipraprasādanāya hasakahalahrīṃ namaḥ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) of Vakratuṇḍa: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the placement on the yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the following placements: "Salutation to Bhārgava, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
salutation to Anuṣṭubh, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to Śrīvakratuṇḍa, the deity (devatā), on the heart."

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) for the attainment of my desired goal, and having said with palms joined, "This is the application (viniyoga)," one should perform the six-limbed mantra placement as follows: "Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," "Kra śirase svāhā," "Tu śikhāyai vaṣaṭ," "Ṇḍā kavacāya huṃ," "Ya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ," and "Hūṃ astrāya phaṭ. Having thus performed the placement, one should meditate.
Bearing with his sprout-like hands a noose that possesses a splendor shining like a mass of most beautiful, freshly blossomed, deep-red jewels, as well as a goad,
together with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, joined by the three-eyed Lord, and enriched with jeweled garlands and fine garments—
One should meditate upon this Vakra-tuṇḍa, situated within the opening of a blooming lotus. || 1 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra: *hasakalahrīṃ vakratuṇḍāya hasakahalahrīṃ hūṃ sakalahrīṃ*.

Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) for Lakṣmīgaṇeśa: there, having performed the morning duties up to the placement of the Yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, and then perform the following salutations: "Salutation to the inner controller (antaryāmin) Ṛṣi on the head; salutation to the Nicṛt-Gāyatrī metre on the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī-Lakṣmīgaṇeśa on the heart."

Having performed the placement [of mantras] for the sake of attaining my desired goal, and having said "This is the application (viniyoga)" with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) with "Śrāṃ Gāṃ" and so forth, and then meditate: [He is] golden-hued, wearing yellow garments, holding a discus and a conch with the palms of his lotus-like hands.
May Gaṇeśa— the one with three eyes, holding an elephant tusk and a golden jar upon his trunk, seated upon a lotus,
embraced by Lakṣmī on his left side who holds a lotus and whose right arm shines brilliantly— bestow great prosperity and fortune upon you here. 1.
Having meditated thus, one should recite: *Śrīṃ gaṃ saumyāya hasakalahrīṃ mahāgaṇapataye varavarada hasakahalahrīṃ sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya sakalahrīṃ svāhā*.

Now follows the ritual application for Heramba: there, having performed the morning duties and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra; then, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), saying "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (*ṛṣi*)," on the head; "Salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*)," on the mouth; and "Salutation to Śrī Heramba, the deity (*devatā*)," on the heart.

Having said, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of my desired goal," and having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*) with the mantra beginning with *gāṃgī*, one should meditate [upon the deity] as follows:
"With five serpent-faces resembling pearls, lightning, clouds, nectar, and saffron..."
Rherambo is to be meditated upon, crowned with the moon, mounted upon a proud lion, and possessing the brilliance of a mass of rays.

With his hands he bears a trident, a goad, a lotus, a rosary, a mallet, a male skull, a chisel, and a sweetmeat; he displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and shines with a multitude of rays. || 1 ||

Having meditated thus, one should recite: *oṃ hasakalahrīṃ gūṃ hasakahalahrīṃ namaṃ sakalahrīṃ*. Now follows the application of the mantra of Virigaṇeśa: therein, after performing the morning rites up to the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoga-pīṭha, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, and place [the mantra] on the head with "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the Seer (*ṛṣi*)," and on the mouth...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Salutation to the *gāyatrī* meter; salutation to the deity Viriñci-Vighneśvara in the heart," and having said with palms joined, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of my desired goal," [he continues]: "Viri-viri, salutation to the heart;
Gaṇapati, *svāhā* to the head; Varavarada, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); Sarvalokam, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*) for me."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras with "vaśamānaya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ svāhā" and "astrāya phaṭ," one should meditate [on the deity] as before: "The elephant-faced one, resembling vermilion. Then [recite]: *hrīṃ viriviri hasakalahrīṃ gaṇapativaravarada hasakahalahrīṃ sarvalokaṃ me vaśamānaya sakalahrīṃ*.
One should mutter "svāhā."

(p. 218) Now follows the ritual application for Śaktigaṇeśa: there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the *yogapīṭha*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, and then perform the salutations: "Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *nicṛdgāyatrī* meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to Śaktiśrīgaṇeśa, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart."

Having performed the placement [of the mantras] for the sake of attaining my desired goal, and having said with palms joined in reverence, "This is the application (viniyoga)," one recites: *hrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *gaṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrīṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; to Mahāgaṇapati as the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ svāhā*;
to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; and *hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ* to Mahāgaṇapati, *svāhā*.
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras with "Astrāya Phaṭ," and having meditated as before,
one should recite: *Hrīṃ Gaṃ Hrīṃ Hasakalahrīṃ Mahāgaṇapataye Hasakahalahrīṃ Svāhā Sakalahrīṃ*.

Now, according to the sequence of the Upper Tradition (Urdhvāmnāya), in the instruction of the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā, two mantras for each of the sixteen root-vidyās are to be employed. Those mantras are as follows:
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ saha khaphreṃ sa hauḥ sa hakṣamalavarayīṃ hauṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ.
Therefore, these eleven seed-syllables—so'haṃ svāhā—are to be applied everywhere at the beginning of a vidyā-mantra.
11. *Hrīṃ*, the self-luminous, perfectly full, supreme and non-supreme Great Kula, the Great Kula of the Siddhas and Vidyās, the Yoginī.
Thus is the root-vidyā of the Kula-yoginī. (1)
11. *Hasauḥ* awaken, awaken my own self, *hasauḥ*; *hrīṃ*—this is the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*) of Prāsādaparāyoginī. (2)
11. Aiṃ blūṃ klinne kledini klinnadrave kledaya kledaya klīṃ klīṃ mahāmada mohaya mohaya klīṃ namaḥ svāhā. This is the root mantra of the Rahasyayoginī. || 3 ||
11. *Svacchānanda-paramahaṃsa-paramātmane svāhā* *hasakṣyauṃ*.
This is the root-vidyā of the Śāmbhavī Yoginī. 4.
11. Hrīṃ! She who consists of the bliss of eternal radiance, whose nature is the all-pervading Great Bindu and the Mother-sound, Hrīṃ!
Thus is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī Hṛllekhā. 5.
11. *Hrīṃ* Kulamahāmālinī *hrīṃ*. This is the root-vidyā of the yoginī Samayavimalā, whose nature is pure luminosity. (6)
11. O Haṃsī, whose nature is eternal light, O Kulakuṇḍalinī, O Mahābhairavī who has attained the perfection of the Command!
Awaken, awaken yourself, O Mother, O Blessed One! Hrīṃ Huṃ.
Thus is the root mantra of the Yoginī who brings about supreme awakening. 7.
11. Oṃ mokṣaṃ kuru—this is the five-syllabled root mantra of the Yoginī. (8)
HA-SAIṂ HA-SAKALAHRĪṂ HA-SAḤ | This is the root-mantra of the Yoginī Tripurā, the Consciousness of Lopāmudrā. || 9 ||

11. Aiṃ! O you whose nature is the Supreme Brahman—pure, subtle, formless, and beyond conceptualization; Klīṃ! O Śakti consisting of supreme bliss; Sauḥ! Thus is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī Anuttarakaulinī. || 10 ||
11. *Svacchānandaparamahaṃsaparamātmane svāhā* *hasrūṃ*.
This is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī who contemplates the Supreme Guru. 11.
11. Anābhāsā, who transcends the sky, who transcends the supreme and inferior skies, the Mistress of the Sky (Vyomeśvarī), *hrīṃ*—this is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī Anābhāsā. 12.
11. Aiṃ, iṃ, īṃ, ūṃ—this is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī of the Saṅketasāra-vidyā. 13.
11. Hrīṃ Vicce Bhagavati Vāgvādini Mahāhrade Mahāmāyā Mataṅgini Aiṃ Blūṃ Raṃ Strīṃ—this is the root-vidyā of the Yoginī Anuttaravāgvādinī. 14.
Ha Sa Raṃ Ha Sa Rīṃ Ha Sa Rauḥ—this is the root mantra of the Yoginīs of the Unsurpassed Vidyā. || 15 ||

11. Hīṃ! In the great cakra consisting of universal bliss, in the bindu, you who are the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the power of supreme nectar, the sovereign of all mantras, the sovereign of all tantras, the sovereign of all yogis, the sovereign of all knowledge, the sovereign of all sacred seats, the mother of the origin of the universe—Hrīṃ!
The root-vidyā of Turīyāyoginī. || 16 ||

Likewise, in the *Uttaratantra*: "In the initiation of the fivefold tradition (*pañcamāmnāya*), the deities of the four traditions are declared to be its limbs; one should practice each pair of *vidyās*. (1)
The two Aindrī [weapons] belong to Surendra and Anala; the two Yāmya [weapons] are indeed in the southern and south-eastern corners;
the two Vāruṇī [weapons] are in the western and north-western corners; and those arising in the northern direction are the Saumya [weapons].

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: the "fifth tradition" (pañcamāmnāya) is the "upper tradition" (ūrdhvāmnāya); therein, during initiation, one should worship the deities of the four traditions—the deities of the eastern, southern, western, and northern traditions.
One should practice and unite each pair of *vidyās* belonging to each individual tradition. He describes the division of the directions with the words beginning "Surendra."
In the eastern and southeastern pits, [are] the Eastern and Southern Āmnāya-Vidyās;
in the southern and southwestern corners, [are] the Southern and Western Āmnāya-Vidyās;
in the western and northwestern [corners], [are] the two Western Āmnāya-Vidyās; and in the northern and northeastern pits, [are] those beyond that (the Northern and Central Āmnāya-Vidyās).
When occurring in the northern direction—that is, when produced facing north—it means the knowledge of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
In the *Śrīkulārṇava*:
"Bhairavī is said to be in the eastern pit; Bhuvaneśvarī in the southeast;
or Pītāmbarā, the Bhoginī, is praised in the southern pit. (1)
Vārāhī is in the southwest pit, Aparājitā in the west;
Bhavānī is in the northwest corner, while Śyāmā and Tārā are in the spot beyond that.

Thus it is said: "In the same way, O Supreme Goddess, in the system consisting of five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should employ either the deities of the four Samayas or the Vidyās of the four Āmnāyas. (1)
Thus [it is said]. Now, in the initiation into the Śrī-guru-vidyā, the *caraṇa*-vidyās and others are to be employed as its ancillaries;

however, in the initiation into the Parā-prāsāda, the five Brahma-mantras are used. He explains the division of these five into three groups with the words: "The thirty-eight *kalās* are of three kinds."
The meaning is that the thirty-eight *kalās* of the five Brahma-mantras should be applied in sequence as sixteen, twelve, and ten. (p.
219) In this context, he states the procedure for other *vidyās* during initiation, beginning with "Dakṣiṇā... etc.

"Devoid of the first" is the clear meaning. As for Bhuvaneśvarī, she consists of the Guṇārṇaka [mantra], the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), and Bhuvaneśvarī; Śrī; Śrī consecrated by Śrī and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Vāk; Vāgbhava-conjoined Bhuvaneśvarī; Kāmarāja-conjoined [Bhuvaneśvarī]; and Parābīja-conjoined [Bhuvaneśvarī]. She is thus threefold.
"Triputā" means that which begins with the Śrī-bīja, the Kāma-bīja, or the Māyā-bīja. Regarding "the fifteenfold":

here there are five types, namely waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turīya), and that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta). [This refers to] the knowledge of waking, the knowledge of dreaming, the knowledge of deep sleep, and the knowledge of the fourth state.
The meaning is that for the Turīyavidyā, the Turīyavidyā itself is to be employed; and for the Turīyātītā, the Turīyātītavidyā alone is to be employed. As stated in the Śrīkulārṇava:
"The Parāprāsāda mantra and likewise Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa..."
The great mantra of Cidambaram, which has the form of a bird and the nature of Śarabha. || 1 ||
There are exactly six Śāmbhava mantras, as well as Mahāmṛtyuñjaya;
likewise Lakṣmījanārdana and Lakṣmīvāsudeva. || 2 ||
Rājarājeśvara, Pañcavaktra, Māruti, Mārtaṇḍabhairava, and likewise Mahāgaṇapati. || 3 ||
Ucchiṣṭagaṇanātha and likewise Vakratuṇḍa, the attendants of Gaṇapati endowed with prosperity, as well as Sītā and Rāma; || 4 ||
O Goddess of the gods, there are the Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh, the Pañcabāṇas,
the Pañcakāmas, as well as the Jainas and the Buddhists.
O you who are worshipped by heroes, from the upward-facing mouth of Śambhu alone emerged the various forms of the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva known as Prāsāda, as well as the Śivas.
Likewise, there are the eight-syllabled variations of Viṣṇu called Vāsudeva;
similarly, in the Gāṇapatya [section], there are the one-syllabled variations as well as the Ghṛṇimanu.
The deities of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) are said to be Varāha, Tumburu,
Haridrā, Gaṇapa, the Vaṭukas, and the Kṣetrapālas.
The mantras of the Teacher known as Nṛsiṃha, those consisting of Hari and Hara, the various forms of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa mantra, and those designated as Dadhivāmana; || 9 ||
Those renowned in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya), as well as the various Ucchiṣṭa mantras, those known as Puruṣottama, and likewise the Mālā-mantras; || 10 ||
The divisions of Aghora and Rudra, as well as those various Buddhist sects, the renowned Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), and Dakṣiṇāmūrti itself—[all these are included]. (11)
The mantras of the planets, the world-protectors, and of Caṇḍeśvara, as well as those of the Vetālas and Ceṭakas who are indeed of the nature of Hari and Hara; || 12 ||
Vīrabhadra, Subrahmaṇya, and others, the sons of the Mothers,
are renowned in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) as bestowers of results in a swift time.

Furthermore, for the sake of pleasing one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should also worship the shrines (āyatanas). The shrines refer to the four shrines; these, however, are subsidiary members of one's own chosen deity situated in the center.
Regarding the sequence for their installation, he states in that very same [text]:
Now, I shall describe the installation of the fivefold shrine (pañcāyatana), distinguished by various types of devotion:
the Radiant One (Bhāskara), the Lord of Śrī (Śrīpati), Pārvatīśa, Vighneśvara, Arkādrisutā (Umā), and Hari. (1)
Kṛṣṇā, Ekadanta, Nagendrajā, Īśā, Māyeśvarā, Ibhānanā, Bhāskarā, and Īśā—
along with Vighnādhipa, Śakti, and Kṛṣṇā— are to be worshipped starting from the southeast corner (Agni-kona) in successive order.
Thus it is stated in the Ratnasāgara: "The Sun, Vināyaka, the Goddess, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara are for the worship [of Śiva];
likewise, Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Ambikā, Īśāna, and Nārāyaṇa are for the worship [of Viṣṇu]. (1)
In the worship of the Sun, Śiva, Vighna (Gaṇeśa), Hari, and Kātyāyanī are the deities in sequence;
likewise, in the worship of the Goddess, Śiva, Vighna, Sūrya, and Viṣṇu are the deities.

Śiva, Ravi, Bhavānī, and Viṣṇu are to be established in the worship of Vighneśvara in the corners beginning with the southeast, according to their relationship as limbs and the possessor of limbs (aṅga-aṅgin).
"O Maheśānī, these [deities] are indeed to be worshipped; if they are separated [from one another], they always bestow suffering.

Regarding this, in all worship of the deities, one should extract the respective *cakra* (mandala) for that particular worship and, according to the procedure prescribed in the relevant *kalpa*, worship the deities of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana*) preceded by the worship of their respective seats (*pīṭha*).
Otherwise, the worship would be fruitless. As it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Śāmbhavī, for one who does not know the pervasion of the Yantra of the God whose form is the Yantra, all performed worship and so forth becomes useless. (1)
The yantra is said to consist of mantra, and the deity has the form of mantra;
when the Goddess is worshipped within the yantra, she becomes pleased instantly. || 2 ||
Because it restrains all sufferings arising from defects such as desire and anger, they call this a "yantra"; when worshipped, the Divine is pleased within it.
O beloved, just as the body is to the living soul and as oil is to a lamp, so too is this machine established for all the gods. (4)
Therefore, O Śivā, having either drawn the yantra or meditated upon it,
one who worships Śiva— having learned everything from the mouth of the guru— should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite.
He who performs separate worship on a single seat without [the prescribed] yantra incurs the curse of the deity, even having abandoned the relationship of limb and possessor of limbs (aṅga-aṅgin).

O Goddess of the Suras, one should worship the deities, together with their respective retinues, individually upon their own specific yantras on a single seat, according to their respective injunctions.
If one invokes one deity and then worships another deity,
the practitioner of mantra with a fickle mind incurs curses from both.
Thus, in the Kulaprakāśatantra:
"When [the site] is broken, cracked, burnt, fallen, devoid of humans, deformed, touched by unworthy animals, ruined, or located on wicked ground; || 1 ||"

Furthermore, the gods will not grant their presence in ten kinds of places: those worshipped with other mantras, those defiled by the touch of a fallen person, and the remaining eight [types of impure locations].

Thus: here, even in the worship of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana*), one should worship the deities of the four abodes by designating the eastern direction between the worshipped and the worshipper according to tradition, and then designating the south-eastern direction (*āgneyī*) and so forth accordingly; for this follows the same logic as the previously stated reasoning regarding the worship of Dharma and the others. Here...

Some maintain that immediately after the invocation of the principal deity, one should perform the visualization for the purpose of worshipping its surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-devatās) in front of the deity according to the ancient tradition; however, because the worship of the deities of the four abodes (catur-āyatana) must be performed even prior to that, such a visualization is improper. Therefore, the deities of the four abodes remain as they are in the directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī) and so forth.
They say that [the deity] is to be worshipped [facing east], but that is not so. Regarding optional (kāmya) worship:
one should worship while facing the eastern direction;
O Dear One, for the rite of subjugation (vaśya), one should worship while facing the southern direction. || 1 ||
Facing west, one should worship for the attainment of wealth;
facing north, one should worship for rites of pacification.

This is because of the statement in the *Brahmayāmala*: "One should worship [the goddess] whose face is directed toward the corners of Agni, Rākṣasa, Vāyu, and Śambhu. Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Kulamūlāvatāra* and because it is seen in many other tantras as well, when performing worship according to the established order of directions, [she is to be worshipped] as situated in the northeast corner (Īśānakoṇa).

Because it would follow that there is no fixed rule for the position— sometimes on the left side of the principal deity, sometimes on the right, sometimes in front, and sometimes behind— and because it would be impossible to install [the deities] in their respective fixed positions such as Āgneya and so forth, [the installation must occur] immediately after the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) of the principal deity.

Because the worship of the deities of the four abodes (*caturāyatanadevatā*) is performed even during the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), and because in the worship of the Dharma and so forth one follows the imagined directions starting from the southeast (*āgneya*) according to tradition, and because the deities of the four abodes are subordinate members while the form of the principal deity is the imagined [central] one, it is therefore appropriate that the direction "east" (*prācīna*) be imagined in front of that [principal deity].
Others, however, according to those who possess the tantric initiation, have established [the deities] as follows:
when Śambhu is in the center, Hari, Naha, Hara, Bhū, and Devī are placed; in Hari, Śaṅkara and Āsyā; in Agasuta, Ravi; and in Hara, Gaṇeśa, Ajā, and Ambikā.

When the goddess [is worshipped] through Viṣṇu, Hara, Gaṇeśa, the Sun, the Moon, Lambodara, Brahmā, and Īśvara, she indeed bestows happiness; but when these [deities] are worshipped individually according to the path of Śaṅkara, they cause suffering. || 1 ||

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya* and following the established ancient tradition, the five deities beginning with one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) should be installed in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast. However, for those who lack Tantric initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the procedure should follow] the statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
Considering the necessity of worshipping the deities of the five abodes (pañcāyatana),

those who perform the worship of the five abodes according to any one of the Vedic, Smārta, or Paurāṇika rites should install the deities of the five abodes in their respective positions, starting from the northeast (īśāna) corner and including the center.

Thus they say; however, that is extremely inconsistent, because among those five, since not even one is conceived as the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), there is no status as the principal (*aṅgin*), and thus it is impossible for any one of them to be established in the center. [The five are:
Ravi, Vināyaka, Viṣṇu, Caṇḍikā, and Īśa as the fifth.

"They are to be worshipped in sequence; worshipped out of sequence, they bring fear"—thus it is stated in the *Purāṇasārasamuccaya* regarding the order of worship for those deities of the five-fold abode (*pañcāyatana*). Here, in the worship of the five-fold abode, by those who worship the four deities excluding Gaṇeśa, [the ritual should be performed] according to the stated order.

Having established the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa and having worshipped the four deities obtained through the clockwise order, one should worship one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the center. However,
for those who worship Gaṇeśa, [the sequence] begins with Sūrya in the clockwise direction.

The established doctrine of the Āgamas is that after worshipping the four deities obtained in due order, one should worship Gaṇeśa. Regarding this, some maintain that in the worship of the five abodes (pañcāyatana),
the devotee of the Goddess should worship the Sun, Gaṇeśa, Śiva, and Viṣṇu first, and worship the Goddess at the conclusion.

What is stated in the *Smṛti*—namely, that "they say [this]"—is inconsistent, because it would result in a lack of circumambulation (*aprādakṣiṇya*), and because, since no sequential order is obtained, it would result in a disordered sequence. In reality, however, one should worship after invoking Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā; thus it is said in the *Yoginītantra* regarding the worship of the Goddess.
