Because the sequence for the worship of the five deities (pañcāyatana-pūjā) is observed [in various texts], and because the *Bhairavītantra* also shows the sequence for the worship of the five deities— stating that "first, the wise one should worship the god Gaṇapati, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Umāpati, and Durgā"— this alone is the established Tantric doctrine.
And this is established by the tradition of the masters (*satsampradāya*). Even by the worshippers of other deities, the sequence beginning with Gaṇeśa must be performed in exactly the same way.
(p. 221) According to the principle observed in one case, this worship of the five abodes (*pañcāyatanapūjā*) must necessarily be performed for Śiva.

"He who does not worship Bhāskara, Agni, Keśava, and Kauśikī even with his mind falls from the heavenly world to a lower state. Since this passage from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* declares the sin incurred by failing to perform such worship, the meaning is "not worshipping even mentally. Here, Agni refers to Gaṇeśa. He who is Brahmā is declared to be Hari; he who is Hari...
"He is Maheśvara; Maheśvara is remembered as Sūrya; Sūrya is said to be Pāvaka; Pāvaka is this Kārttikeya; and Kārttikeya is Vināyaka"—thus from the statement in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.

Then, having invoked one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) into the image placed in the center, one should worship it. In that context, the "image" (mūrti) is to be understood as having the form described in its respective meditation (dhyāna); however, this should also be visualized in the case of a Śiva-liṅga, a Śālagrāma stone, and so forth, because Śiva-liṅgas serve as the substratum for the worship of all deities, and thus all deities reside within them.

"They are worthy of worship; their worship should be performed upon their *liṅga*, on a jewel, in a water-pot (*kumbha*), in a mandala, and with the understanding that it is [the Lord] himself, one should worship in a *śālagrāma* stone, on a yantra, and so forth. Because of the statement in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Worship performed upon the ground alone destroys sons, longevity, and wealth," [one should worship] upon the *śālagrāma* stone.

"One should worship with the respective [corresponding] cognition," according to the statement of Somaśambhu. Furthermore, from the *Kulārṇava*: "In the liṅga, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), in the fire, in the sun, in the water-vessel, on the cloth, in the maṇḍala, on the board, on the head, and in the heart—these ten are proclaimed. In these places, O Goddess of Gods, they worship the supreme Śiva."
The term "auspicious" (*śivam*) is an elliptical expression. By the use of the word "of them" (*teṣām*), it refers to those five deities of the *pañcāyatana*;

the phrase "in the yantra and so forth" (*yantrādau*) implies images and other such objects. As it is said: "Worship of Hari should be performed in a *śālagrāma*, a gem, a yantra, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or in images, but never upon the bare ground."

Based on the statement in the *Trailokyasammohana Tantra*, an image should be fashioned according to the forms described in the respective meditations. That image, moreover, should measure between ten and fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size; for it is said in the *Kapila Pañcarātra*: "An image should be worshipped in the home, but one larger than that is not recommended. Thus, an image should be fashioned according to the form described in the *Kapila Pañcarātra*.

The meaning is that it measures either ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) or fifteen finger-breadths. This is because of the statement in the *Hayagrīva-pañcarātra*: "Householders should worship in their homes an image of Viṣṇu measuring ten finger-breadths or fifteen finger-breadths. Here too, by the word "or" (*vā*), [the range] beginning from ten finger-breadths...
The traditionalists state that it has been taught that the image should be made with a height of fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

They further maintain that this is precisely the meaning of the preceding verse as well. The measurement of the *mātrā-aṅgula* (the finger-breadth of the practitioner) is to be understood from the section on the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). As for the method of fashioning the Śiva-liṅga:
In the Śilpiśāstra: "A thread should extend from the center of the top of the liṅga down to the praṇāla;
the thickness of the liṅga and the praṇāla is proclaimed to be exactly that much. (1)
Regarding the height and likewise the pedestal, they prescribe five lines;
one should worship the Śivaliṅga as endowed with these five lines.
"It bestows enjoyment and liberation, and grants wealth, health, and happiness.
As for the method of its construction, it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "A liṅga measuring from one finger-breadth up to a span is worshipped in the home."
But above that, it should be in the temple, where it must be worshipped with great effort.
One should make the width of the top of the *liṅga* equal to the portion to be worshipped;
its circumference should be three times that, and the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be equal to the circumference.
One should make the pedestal twice the size of the portion to be worshipped and well-elevated;
it may be circular or square, and should have a neck in the middle. || 3 ||
One should fashion the circumference of the neck to be twice the circumference of the phallus;
it may have three ridges below and above, or even two ridges, equally spaced.
Then, one should divide the width of the top of the liṅga into six parts;
with one part, one should fashion the girdle (mekhalā), and the excavation (khāta) should be equal to that.
One should construct a water-channel outside of it, equal in length to the height of the liṅga;
its width at the base should be equal to that [height], and its tip should be half of that.
A water channel should be constructed through its center according to the divisions;
one should make the conduit either half the size of the pedestal or as long as desired, as declared by the venerable Śiva.
One should apply this characteristic specifically to all jewel-liṅgas together with their pedestals, as well as to liṅgas made of metal and other materials.

Thus [ends the verse]. Its meaning is as follows: having fashioned the *liṅga* according to one’s own preference, one should bring the width of its head (*mastaka*) to be equal to that part of the worshipful *liṅga* which constitutes its height; that is to say, one should make it so. This is because of the statement in the Śaiva Āgamas: "The width of the *liṅga*-head should be equal to the height of the *liṅga*. Therefore, the width of the *liṅga*-head...

Having made the circumference of the *liṅga* such that it is suitable for being wrapped with a triple-thread, one should fashion a pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the center of the *liṅga*— either circular or square— which is twice as high as the portion of the worshipful *liṅga* measured by the extent of that thread-circumference.
Having made the neck of the *nāha-sūtra* thick enough to allow for the wrapping of a double-strand thread,
and having fashioned three or two girdles (*mekhalā*) above and below the neck in equal proportions,
one should divide the width of the top of the *liṅga* into six parts and [measure] by one part of those.
Having fashioned a molding (*mekhalā*) on the upper portion of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) using its entire outer width,

one should construct a cavity (*khāta*) inside it of the same measurement, joined to it; then, at the base, [one should fashion a projection] with a length equal to the *liṅga* or half the length of the pedestal's measurement, extending outward from the pedestal.
It has a width at its front end equal to one-third of its length, and a width at its middle equal to half of that;
from the base to the tip,
it is provided with a water-channel in the form of a hollow having a width equal to one-third of the width of the spout, and it is furnished with a girdle like that of a pedestal.

"And one should fashion a channel"—this is the general rule for the construction of a Śiva-liṅga, whether it be made from specific gems such as crystal or from stones and the like. Thus ends the method for the construction of the Śiva-liṅga.

Thus [ends] the *Śrīvidyārṇava* Tantra, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable and worshipful Great Preceptor Śrī Govindācārya.
The eleventh breath. || 11 ||
Now,
in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra:
the twelfth breath (chapter).
Now, the method for constructing the Śrīcakra. In the *Śrīrudrayāmala*:
"Then the yogi should prepare the yantra with saffron and vermilion on a plate made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or likewise of wood. (1)
"The Goddess should be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed rite. Thus it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"In a gem, gold, silver, copper, or stone, respectively..."
Having fashioned the image of the wheel, one should install it and also worship it. || 1 ||
For the attainment of fortune, beauty, fame, sons, wealth, health, and so forth;
"on a stone"—specifically on a stone from the Gaṇḍakī river—because of the statement in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā: "On a stone produced by the Gaṇḍakī, or on gold, silver, or copper."
Now, regarding the specific number of years for worship according to the particular metal, it is said in the *Ratnasāgara*:
"O beloved, [the period lasts] for as long as one lives in the case of gold; twenty-two years in silver;
twelve years in copper; and half of that in birch bark. (1)
Thus it is stated in another Tantra:
"In copper, [the practice] lasts for twelve years, but in crystal and other materials, it is always [effective].
Among these, however, that which is made of crystal bestows all accomplishments. (1)
Thus, in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"A yantra fashioned from vermilion powder upon the ground grants all desires; one fashioned from gold brings all kings under one's control. (1)
A yantra fashioned from silver bestows longevity, health, and splendor;
a yantra constructed from copper is considered to grant all forms of sovereignty.
O Goddess, a yantra engraved on crystal indeed bestows the heart's desires;
a yantra inscribed on ruby is considered to grant sovereignty and worldly enjoyment.
A yantra fashioned from gomedaka bestows all sovereignty;
a yantra fashioned from emerald destroys all enemies.
"The yantra produced from the three metals is considered to grant all accomplishments.
Thus [it was said]. The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, how is the yantra produced from the three metals to be made?"
Tell me that out of compassion, if I am dear to you.
Īśvara said: One should fashion a beautiful pedestal using ten parts of gold, sixteen parts of silver, and eleven parts of copper. || 1 ||
Upon that pedestal, one should cause the construction of the Śrīcakra;
it is said to bestow peace, bestow nourishment, and destroy all enemies. || 2 ||
"It is considered to be the producer of longevity and health, the bestower of luster, and the bestower of nourishment.
Now, regarding the threefold nature of the *cakra* according to its different arrangements (*prastāra*), it is stated in that same work:
"The threefold nature of that *cakra* consists of the earth-arrangement (*bhū-prastāra*) and the half-Meru-arrangement (*ardha-meruka*)."
O Goddess, for those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), the layout consists of downward-pointing lines. || 1 ||
O Maheśānī, for those dwelling in the mortal world, the line is upward-pointing;
for those dwelling in the heavenly worlds and so forth, the yantra is known as Meru.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the Bhūpura and ending at the Bindu,
everything has been described by me as being in the form of Meru, gradually increasing in height.
Nine upward lines with a single line above them are proclaimed [as the grid];
through the conjunction of downward lines, the ground-pattern (bhū-prastāra) has been described by me.
(224) O auspicious lady, I have revealed the true nature of the King of Yantras out of affection for you; it must be kept constantly hidden by you, like your own secret.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the fruits of these three arrangements (*prastāra*) and another arrangement, it is stated in the *Śrītantrarāja*:

"Beginning with the square and proceeding through the nine wheels in sequence, from the center upwards, the wheel becomes increasingly elevated; it results in the destruction of wealth or the acquisition of wealth. (1)
If it is elevated by three or two steps, one obtains prosperity and freedom from offspring;
if it is elevated by one, two, or six steps, it conduces to both fortune and fame.
"Nine [lines] of equal form for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Likewise, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"O Goddess, there is elevation followed by gradual [decline], then the attainment of wealth, and thereafter death."
The earth-circle should have sixteen spokes, and it should also be equal with eight spokes. || 1 ||
The remainder, O Īśānī, should be raised; it brings about the attainment of wealth and progeny.
O Goddess, it should be square and even, with sixteen spokes and so forth, ending in a bindu.
O Goddess, that which is mutually elevated leads to prosperity and fame;
it should begin from a square and extend with even lines to the point.
"Likewise, prosperity, fame, and health conduce to immortality.
Now, regarding the substratum of the Śrīcakra, the *Tantrarāja* states the prohibited metals and other prohibited substrata:
Furthermore, in the case of lead, brass, and similar materials, the opposite of what was previously stated applies;
one should never install [the image] upon a wooden plank, a cloth, or a wall.
If it has been established through delusion, greed, or even ignorance,
it utterly destroys one's family, wealth, and offspring in every way.
Thus, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"The beautiful pedestal for the image should be made one finger-breadth wide, extending east-west and north-south, and measuring one *pala* in weight. (1)
One should construct a square measuring half a barley-corn on all sides;
upon that pedestal, one should fashion the Śrīcakra.
Thus, in the Sautrāmaṇī Tantra:
"A straight line indicates prosperity; a curved line indicates poverty.
The fire-altar (agni) should be one finger-breadth in width and half a barley-corn in height. (1)

Thus [it is said]. In the *Lakṣasāgara*, regarding the passage beginning with "the fire of the gold on the finger," the elaboration of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth was not detailed during the previously mentioned discussion on the construction of the *Śrīcakra*. Now, he states the specific details in the *Uttaratantra*:
"Indeed, worship according to the sequence of emanation is prescribed for the Wheel of Emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*)."
O Maheśvarī, worship should be performed according to the sequence of maintenance within the wheel of maintenance.
"By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, worship is performed in the wheel of withdrawal.
Thus it is said. Here, the Śrīcakra is threefold, according to the distinctions of emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra). This has been stated in the Mātṛkāsarvasva:
The Śrīcakra is declared to be threefold, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
each of these should be understood as being further threefold through their diligent application of mutual intermixture.

The fundamental divisions are exactly nine, while their respective subdivisions are manifold. Among these, there are three types: that consisting of emanation-emanation, that consisting of maintenance-maintenance, and that consisting of dissolution-dissolution; as well as [the others]:
that consisting of emanation-maintenance, that consisting of maintenance-emanation, that consisting of emanation-dissolution, and that consisting of dissolution-emanation.
Consisting of stability and dissolution, and consisting of dissolution and stability—these are the nine divisions. Thus, there are twelve divisions in total.
Regarding the distinction here, it is stated in that very [text]:
"The wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra) is fully described as the nine wheels in their proper sequence."
The high, the low, and the middle [of the ground] should be discerned by the most excellent of teachers. || 1 ||
The Śrīcakra, known as the creation of creation, is elevated with each successive line;
it consists of nine equal vertical lines when situated upon a level pedestal.

O Maheśvarī, that very same [wheel] is called the wheel of persistence (sthiticakra), characterized by thick lines; O Śivā, there, the wheel of the persistence of persistence (sthitisthiti) consists of subtle lines.

The meaning is as follows: that which consists of dissolution (*laya*) has a downward line and is gross; that which consists of both dissolution and the state of dissolution (*layalaya*) is subtle and has a netherworld line (*pātālarekhā*). Furthermore, that which consists of creation and maintenance (*sṛṣṭisthiti*) is likewise characterized by creation and maintenance.
This is the meaning:
O Maheśvarī, the yantra consisting of half of Meru is said to be of two kinds;
one half is elevated in sequence from the square and so forth. || 1 ||
Above that, O Śivā, it should be of equal lines and consist of emanation and maintenance;
by the reverse of this, it would consist of maintenance and emanation.
O Īśvarī, beginning from the square, one should draw three circles;
they should rise progressively upward, and above that, there should be a level line with a downward curve.
Its nature consists of creation and withdrawal; however, its state of being both dissolution and creation in reverse order should be understood by the wise as it has been proclaimed.
The lower half is the line of the netherworld (pātāla), while the upper part is the upward line;
this is said to consist of dissolution and persistence, but in reverse order for the other [half].
The forms of maintenance and withdrawal should be understood by the best of teachers;
the wheel whose nature is the maintenance of maintenance is recommended for householders. (6)
It increases longevity, fame, wealth, health, sons, and grandsons;
it is a wheel consisting of creation and maintenance, and through it one attains freedom from childlessness and prosperity.
After the age of fifty, it becomes a bestower of sons and grandsons;
this Yantra, consisting of both maintenance and creation, grants the increase of sons, longevity, and wealth.
Beyond fifty years of age, it causes the destruction of one's offspring;
as for the other varieties of the Śrīcakra that have been described, O Maheśvarī, [they are likewise ineffective].
Regarding the specific distinction for those belonging to the castes among the *yatis* and *vaikhānasas*,
it is stated in the *Uttaratantro*:
"One who desires their own welfare should not worship a yantra upon the back of a tortoise."
Therefore, one should act only after having investigated with every effort. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, in the wheel of emanation, worship culminates in emanation;
in the wheel of maintenance, it culminates in maintenance; and in the wheel of withdrawal, it culminates in dissolution.
Whether obtained through the lineage of gurus, or by the succession of fathers and brothers,
it was received from the venerable Guru and bestowed by the elder and younger gurus.
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune a practitioner should obtain what has been given,
he should perform worship there, O Supreme Goddess, beginning with its establishment and ending with its conclusion.

"O Śivā, even a defective yantra is said to yield results, and not otherwise. Thus, if by the force of time or the power of destiny, one obtains a defective yantra through the lineage of one's father and grandfather or the succession of the gurus, then worship in that yantra should first be performed according to the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
The meaning is that, thereafter, it should be performed according to the sequence of creation and then according to the sequence of maintenance, whereby it becomes a bestower of auspicious results.
Now follows the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), which are ancillary to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the final consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).

Since the knowledge of the eastern direction is indispensable for the construction of the pavilion that constitutes a part of the initiation, the method for determining that direction is demonstrated. Regarding this, the *Divyasārasvata-tantra* states:
On a clear day, in a place free from trees, temples, and the like,
on a level and smooth ground, the wise man should prepare a *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint).
Relying on that [line], the wise one should rotate [the compass] all around to the measure of twelve finger-breadths and place a circle in its center.
The gnomon should have a needle-point, be straight, circular, and twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;
its base, however, should be six finger-breadths in circumference, fashioned by a skilled artisan.
Having carefully marked two points on that ground at the end of the forenoon and afternoon where the shadows from the tips of the gnomon meet, [one should proceed].
Having established two marks, one should draw a cord extending from east to west, and then,
using a cord of either the desired length plus an excess or equal to the diameter of the circle, [mark the center].
Having joined two circles together so that they touch each other in the east and west,
one should extend [the line] from them so as to reach both junctions.
The sūtra whose center is touched by the central mark is the north-south line;
having made marks at the corners using a measurement equal to half of this [sūtra’s length], || 7 ||

"By laying down eight lines upon them, it shall become a square and equal. Now, the method for this construction: here, on a level spot of ground not obscured by trees, temples, or the like, during the day when the sun is not veiled by clouds and the circle of the sky is clear, one should first mark a point.

Using that as a support, one should fashion a circle measuring twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in each direction; therein, one should construct a shape that is straight in form, with a base circumference of six finger-breadths, a circumference at the tip reduced successively until it is like the point of a needle, and possessing a height of twelve finger-breadths.
Having placed a circular gnomon fashioned by a skilled artisan such that its middle circumference at the base of the gnomon coincides with the center of the dot located in the middle of the circle,
one [observes] the tip of the shadow of that gnomon in the forenoon on the western side of the line of that circle.

Having made a mark at the point where [the shadow] meets [the circle], and having likewise made a mark in the afternoon at the point where the tip of the gnomon's shadow meets the eastern part of that circular line,
one should fix a cord reaching both those marks and thereby determine the east-west line.

By means of those two marks as supports, having constructed two circles— one in front and one behind— mutually touching at a measurement equal to half the desired diameter plus the measurement situated between those two marks,
[one should draw] a north-south line passing through the two points where the circle-lines intersect on the south and north, by way of the center of the east-west line.
Having mentally projected a north-south line from that thread which runs transversely,

one should [construct] those pavilions, sacrificial pits, and so forth, at the points where the four ends of the two east-west and two north-south threads meet, using the tips of threads of equal form according to the measurements to be described.

One should conceive of the four directions consisting of east, west, south, and north; thus has the method for establishing the east been shown from a gross perspective. However, the subtle method is stated in another tantra, beginning with "having made the ground perfectly level," after describing the morning ritual according to the aforementioned procedure.
On the following day as well, O Goddess of gods, the wise one, having marked two signs as before upon the circle, [should observe] where the shadow falls, O Supreme Goddess. (1)
When the entry and exit [of the shadow] occur on that same previous day, then the nāḍīs in the middle of that time are the [measure of] the shadow having entered and exited. (2)

Having ascertained [the time] by means of shadows and so forth, one should determine the interval between two days characterized by the disappearance of the shadow, divided into desired parts such as four and so on.
O Goddess of the Gods, having divided that [area] and made marks there with those channels (nāḍīs), the portions fashioned by them should be multiplied with effort.
The result obtained by dividing by sixty should be applied to the eastern line drawn on the previous day;
this is done in the eastern portion during the northern solstice.
O Supreme Goddess, during the southern solstice, the fixed point (dhruva) is certainly situated in the southern direction; if it is moved, then the eastern direction would become clearly manifest.
Having thus performed the procedure for establishing the eastward line,
one should mark this [ground] by making two loops at the ends of a cord twice the length of the diameter;
and for the purpose of drawing [the circle], one should place a peg at the center and another at half the diameter plus a half-measure.

Having fixed two pegs at the eastern ends and having performed the drawing-in and pulling [of the cord], one should mark the hips downward on the peg-marks; likewise, one should transpose the shoulders toward the north.
Thus, according to the method prescribed in the treatises on architecture,
one should prepare the site for the pavilion as a square of equal sides with a width and length greater than the previously indicated measurement.

The meaning of this is as follows: having made a cord twice the length of the desired width of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, with loops at both ends, one should mark a point on the cord at a distance equal to half the width from one loop; then, from that mark on the peg, [one proceeds] forward.
Having laid out the eastward line according to the measurement of the radius of the circle by drawing a mark inward from the center for the pit (kuṇḍa), the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
and so forth, one should drive stakes at its two ends. Then, using a cord,
one should fix its two loops in such a way that the mark made from the radius falls toward the west.

Having drawn the half of the diameter from the mark on the right of the plumb-line mark, one should place a peg at that mark for the southern hip and also place a peg at its northern hip. Then, having crossed the two cords, the two shoulders are thus established. Having thus made the field a perfect square, [one proceeds].

Having marked out a square plot of ground measuring one cubit or more, and having filled it with pure earth free from husks, charcoal, pebbles, and bones— having first dug it to a depth of one cubit and so forth— and having made it firm;
When the base has been made one by means of a peg, and the two staffs have their fine tips separate,
one [staff] is placed near the tip of the other from the mark in the middle of the transverse [line].
When the instrument is to be joined with a peg or similar device, the staff should be held level at both ends;
at the base, a plumb line should hang down without touching the ground, as if it were a weight.
When the two foremost lines are on the ground, starting from the middle mark along the horizontal staff,
one should erase that [mark], fill in another, or otherwise adjust it according to reason.
"As long as the thread reaches the lap, the earth itself will attain equality.
This is the meaning: when two poles of equal thickness and length have their bases fixed by a peg, one should place a horizontal pole near their tips that is half their length.

Having joined it with a peg and made a mark in its center, one should fashion a long triangular shape using three staffs; then, a cord suspended from the bases of the two long staffs, with a small stone or similar weight tied to its end, should be placed so that it does not touch the ground above the central mark of the horizontal staff.

Having touched the ground in that manner, one should hold the base of those two [stakes] at their tips and slowly pull them; wherever the cord moves from the mark in the middle of the horizontal staff, there the ground is low, and one should fill it. Or, having dug elsewhere, one should do so everywhere until the cord reaches the central mark.

One should construct [the pavilion], having leveled the ground according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on architecture (śilpa-śāstra), by building there a pavilion of either the superior, middling, or inferior type as appropriate.
Regarding the characteristics of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), it is stated in another tantra:

"For kings, during fire-offerings (homa) and consecrations (abhiṣeka), initiations (dīkṣā), bestowal of vows (vrata), and so forth, the wise one should determine the directions according to the movement of the sun and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made. (1)
Then, with the sound of five musical instruments, one should construct an auspicious pavilion;
its measurement is considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The supreme measurement here is sixteen or eighteen cubits;
some have stated that twenty cubits is the supreme measurement. (3)
The medium [size] is measured by twelve cubits, and the inferior is measured by fourteen cubits; the wise say it may also be measured by ten cubits.
Some, however, say that it is measured by nine, or likewise by seven, or even by five cubits,
including its width and length.
It is provided with sixteen pillars and four beautiful gates;
the four gates in the cardinal directions are two cubits and eight finger-breadths [in measurement].
From the two hands with fingers extended as prescribed, one should fashion the two hands;
then, one should prepare the thread for the pavilion, which is three times that length.
In the directions starting from the east and so forth, its central portion shall be a pedestal (vedikā);
it should be made of bricks or clay, resembling a mirror in its smoothness.
The pillars, which are of the nature of the Vedas, are to be placed in the corners of the altar;
they should be of the highest height in the best [type of rite], and half that height in the middling and lowest types.
Then, twelve beautiful [pillars] rising eight cubits high, straight and five cubits in width, should be provided with crests on all sides. (10)
In the four corners there are four [threads], and those eight at the ends of the lines;
all sixteen of them, with equal intervals between, should be established by the instructors.
The preceptor should then bury those [pillars] in the ground to the extent of five parts;
furthermore, their tops should be joined together at the top of the four central pillars.
Having fashioned a square of four wooden planks, one should place an auspicious jar upon its center,
adorned with a well-crafted wooden vessel fixed at its mouth.
The supreme instructor should properly position the image fashioned by artisans,
and then cover it with bamboo, mats, and palm leaves.
And outside the door of the pavilion, one should place pairs of arches (toraṇas) in the sequence of the directions,
made from the wood of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
One should bury it in the earth as before, measuring seven, six, or five cubits;
its width, moreover, is considered to be ten finger-breadths.
One should place a horizontal beam across the two arches at their middle portion, measuring five finger-breadths in thickness and having an uneven square shape.
With the mantra "agnimīle," one should install the eastern archway at a height of two and a half cubits, or two, three, or four cubits.
One should install the southern arch with the mantra beginning "iṣe tvā," and the installation of the western [arch] is performed with the mantra "agna āyāhi. (19)
One should offer the northern arch with the mantra "śanno devī" and should fasten a banner upon it, adorned with bells and chowries.
The banner is said to be five cubits long, while the staff is ten cubits;
thereafter, the flags of the world-protectors are measured according to their own arms.
Twelve finger-breadths in width and marked with their respective forms,
they are yellow, red, dark-blue, smoky, white, smoky-black, black, and pale-white.
The banners should bear the marks of weapons and be provided with flowers and perfumes;
equipped with staffs as appropriate, one should install them while reciting their respective mantras.
It was adorned with a canopy as white as the orb of the moon,
its pillars draped in fine silk, and decorated with various lamps and other ornaments.
One should construct an auspicious pavilion with an excellent gate adorned with garlands of mango sprouts and encircled by a rope of *darbha* grass.
Thus, in the Uttaratantra:
"A pavilion of one hundred and twenty cubits is considered the best;
or one of one hundred and eight cubits, or even one of one hundred cubits. (1)
[The measurements are] respectively eighty-one cubits, seventy-two cubits,
sixty cubits, and forty-eight cubits.
A wise man should have the pavilion constructed with thirty-six, thirty, twenty-seven, or twenty-four cubits [in size].
Square, as well as circular, hexagonal, and octagonal;
triangular, resembling an eight-petaled lotus, nine-cornered, and two-cornered. || 4 ||
A five-cornered [mandala], a seven-cornered, and likewise an eleven-cornered;
as well as twelve, sixteen, eighteen, and twenty-cornered. || 5 ||
And [the mandalas] with twenty-four corners, twenty-seven corners, thirty-two corners, and likewise thirty-six corners. (6)
It has forty-eight spokes and takes the form of a fish, a banner, a winnowing basket,
a spear, a sword, a rhombus, a bow, a mallet, and a crow.
Mandalapas should be constructed there, and especially sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
for the full consecration, initiation, consecrations, and rites of pacification.
In the performance of various rites for specific desires, the preceptors, being unwearied, must especially prepare the respective sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) appropriate for each particular rite.
Thus. Here, as many varieties of pavilions (maṇḍapa) as have been mentioned, so many varieties of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) are also to be understood.

Now, the method for constructing this pavilion (*maṇḍapa*): here, in rites such as the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*, those sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and pavilions mentioned as measuring twenty-four cubits (*hasta*) should be constructed.
The excellent pavilion is of four types, measuring twenty-four, twenty, eighteen, or sixteen cubits.
The medium [size] is of two kinds: fourteen cubits or twelve cubits.
The small [size] is of four kinds: ten cubits, nine cubits, seven cubits, and five cubits, with equal length and width. In this case, among these three types, according to the available space—
One should construct a pavilion that facilitates the comfortable seating of the officiating priests, the assembly members, the spectators, and others.
A *hasta* is twenty-four *aṅgulas* in length. Regarding the measurement of an *aṅgula*, the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* states:
"Those rays of the sun which shine, having reached the path of the window, upon them there spread minute particles of dust known as *trasareṇus*. (1)
A mote of dust (trasareṇu) is said to be eight times the size of an atom (paramāṇu);
eight of those are called a hair-tip (keśa), eight of those are a nit (likṣā), and eight of those are a louse-egg (yūkā).
Eight of those [yavas] are declared to be a finger (aṅguli);
that is the "superior" finger, while seven yavas constitute the "middle" finger.
Sixty-four *yavas* are declared to be the *sādhamā*, which is said to be the *mānāṅgula*;
the *mānāntarāṅgula* is formed by eight *yavas* placed crosswise.
Alternatively, the interval between measures may consist of three rice grains placed in a straight line;
this is equivalent to the middle joint of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand.
The long distance between the two joints [of the thumb] is declared to be a *mānāṅgula*;
it is formed by the remaining fingers of the fist, excluding the thumb. (6)
One should divide [the measurement] into four parts; one part is known as a *muṣṭyaṅgula*.
Furthermore, having divided any given human height (*pauruṣāyāma*) into ten parts, [one should proceed].
Having divided one [unit] into twelve parts, one part among those is known as a *dehalabdha-aṅgula*; one should understand that to be its measure. (8)
The height of the image should be based on the *mahāmāna-aṅgula*;
here, the term *mahāmāna-aṅguli* refers to the *mātrā-aṅgula*.
One should indeed construct palaces and other such structures using that same measurement;
furthermore, the procedure for altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and so forth is as follows.
The measurement of the sacrificial implements should indeed be made by the *mānāṅgula* and not by any other;
one should certainly use the *mānāṅgula* for the ritual accessories.
One should fashion the ladles and other implements for the oblation, as well as the sacrificial pit, based on the measurement of the fist and fingers;
likewise, one should determine the limbs of the image using precisely those fingers obtained from the body-proportion.
"The hand shall consist of twenty-four finger-breadths.

Here, the "teacher" refers to the patron (*yajamāna*). It has been stated that the measurement for the patron shall be as such; however, according to the statement in the *Śāradā-tantra*, "in another tantra, it is the right hand of the performer [that is measured]. There is a specific distinction in the *Uttara-tantra*:
One should construct nine or eleven sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the best pavilion;
there should be four pits in the middling one, and even a single pit in the smallest.
Having thus calculated the *hasta* and other units by means of the *mātrā-aṅgula*, *ātmāṅgula*, and so forth as described,
one should construct the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as prescribed. There, on a ground leveled according to the stated rule,
one should have the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions (*svasti-vācana*) preceded by the sounding of five musical instruments.
Having constructed a square measuring one cubit in width as specified,
with four stakes driven into the four corners, and having removed the central lines extending east-west and north-south, that square field—
Furthermore, having divided [the space] into nine parts, there are four pillars situated at the four corners all around,
and eight pillars situated at the eight ends of the four sets of beams extending east-west and north-south across the four cardinal directions; thus, in total, there are twelve.
The pillars should not be too thick nor too thin, nor crooked nor scarred; they should be of a uniform type,

well-rounded, five cubits in height, with each having its own fifth part buried in the pit, being one-third of a cubit in thickness beyond that measurement, and provided with tops rising one thick span in height.

In the four corners of the middle section, there should be four pillars of the same type as the eastern pillars; in the main pavilion (*uttamamaṇḍapa*), they should be slightly thicker than the eastern ones, while in other pavilions their height should be less than that measure, being eight cubits high with a finial (*śikhā*) as before.
Having dug sixteen pillars into the ground by a fifth part of their height, the artisans fixed upon them horizontal beams of the same wood— straight, free from blemishes,
and possessing two ends with perforations suitable for the insertion of the spire.
Having constructed twelve pillars in a square shape on the tops of the four central pillars,
one should join them with a single wooden beam whose ends meet and whose base-penetration enters the tips of the crests of the four central pillars.
It has wooden pillars of the same kind fixed at its four corners, its top adorned with the shape of a lotus,
its base and middle pillars pierced by the tips of twelve columns situated at the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and its four horizontal beams touching the tops of the middle pillars, their ends meeting within the center of those beams, all forming a straight-lined structure.
It is joined with twelve beams extended according to their appropriate length and thickness, reinforced by other beams as required, well-covered with coconut leaves or bamboo mats,
and its four corners completely closed off by those very same materials.

Having constructed a pavilion in the four directions— consisting of superior, middling, and inferior [sizes]— equipped with four doorways having branches, measuring two cubits plus eight finger-breadths, two cubits plus four finger-breadths, and two cubits in width respectively,
one should [proceed] one cubit outside the eastern door of the pavilion.

Having abandoned [the measurements] for the *aśvattha* tree, one should understand that among the superior, middling, and inferior [types], [the sacrificial post] is seven, six, or five cubits high, ten fingers wide, and five fingers thick;
since the width is ten fingers, the thickness is five fingers, and thus a disparity [between width and thickness] is to be understood.
It is an irregular quadrangle with a peak exceeding the standard measure by one span in height;
on both sides of the door, at the upper, middle, and lower sections, there are intervals of two and a half cubits, two and a quarter cubits, and two cubits respectively, as previously described.
Having fixed two wooden planks upon the ground at a depth of one-fifth [of the total height] with the mantra, "I praise Agni, the domestic priest,

the divine ministrant of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of jewels," one should construct a square pillar of irregular shape— equal in width and thickness to those same wooden pieces— at both ends using wood of the same species.

Having fixed the crosswise-measurement result, which is endowed with the piercing suitable for entry into the pinnacle (śikhā), one should tie a garland of *darbha* grass. Likewise, at the southern door, there is an archway (*toraṇa*) made of *udumbara* wood; [one should recite over it]: "For food thee, for strength thee! Ye are winds, ye are approaching winds! May the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent rite."

One should install [the arch] with this mantra. Then, at the western gate, one should install the Plakṣa-wood arch, constructed as before, with the mantra: "O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacrificial grass."
Then, at the northern gate, one should install an archway made of banyan wood, constructed as before, with the mantra:
"śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye āpo bhavanti pītaye | śaṃyorabhisravantu naḥ. Then, having made a hollow in the center of the horizontal cross-beams situated above them, [one should place the items] therein.

Constructed from wood of the same species as the architrave, it measures thirteen, eleven, or nine finger-breadths in length according to the superior, middling, or inferior [categories], with a width equal to one-fourth of that;
it is shaped like a trident for a Śaiva [temple] and shaped like a discus for a Vaiṣṇava [temple], and it is situated upon the horizontal beam above the architrave.

(p. 229) One should install a single kīla at each toraṇa, twelve parts long and marked with a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in the sequence starting from the east. Regarding the method of fashioning the trident there, it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
One should fashion the door-frames at the top using tridents;
the length of the trident should be nine finger-breadths, and its width one-fourth of that.
The central prong should indeed be straight, while those on the two sides should be slightly curved;
this is declared to be the case for the inferior [type], and likewise, one should fix it at a distance of two finger-breadths.

"For the remaining [mandapas], there is an increase of two finger-breadths up to an increase of twenty finger-breadths. Thus it is said. "In the case of a smaller [size], it is the smallest mandapa; for the remaining ones—the middle and the best—there is an entry of twenty [finger-breadths].
So it is stated in the Vāstuśāstra.

On the head, with the twelfth part [of the measurement], one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus according to the sequence starting from the east; these should be made of the same wood as the [main] image.

Thus: the twelve-part horizontal beam (tiryakphalaka) should be made of the same wood as its own [pillar], originating from the same species of wood as the respective archway (toraṇa). By this [proportion], it is four finger-breadths high in the smallest pavilion, four and a half finger-breadths in the middle, and five finger-breadths in the largest. However, some maintain that in those cases, they are measured by one cubit (hasta).

Having established the stakes (kīla) in the Vaiṣṇava [mandala] likewise— [stakes] marked with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, resembling tridents— in the Śaiva [mandala], according to the statement of another Tantra, they say the stake is one cubit (hasta) in length. There, on the horizontal planks, at the front ends of those stakes which are one cubit long, [the measurements are applied] according to the stated dimensions.

It should be made in the shape of a conch or a discus, or in the shape of a trident; the entry into the cave should be performed in the same manner, while the remainder of it appears like a staff. Then, in front of the pavilion, there should be a bamboo pole ten cubits in length, suspended [with a canopy] one cubit in width.
A banner five cubits in length should be provided;

its top should be adorned with a bell marked by the form of the invocation of the mantra-deity, and it should be very white, or else colored in accordance with the specific color of the respective deity. Having thus raised the banner in the ten directions, [one should proceed].

The [staffs] of the world-protectors are twelve finger-breadths in width, suspended by measuring-sticks of appropriate length reaching to the height of the arms, colored according to the respective colors of those world-protectors,
and marked with the forms of the vehicles of those respective world-protectors.

One should fasten the banners with their respective mantras as declared in the Vedas. Among them, Indra’s is yellow, Agni’s is tawny, Yama’s is black, Nirṛti’s is dark, Varuṇa’s is white, Vāyu’s is smoky, Soma’s is pure white, and Īśāna’s is white.
Having adorned [the area] with banners— red-colored for Brahmā and white-colored for Ananta—
and having decorated the interior of the pavilion with very white canopies and flower garlands, [one should prepare] a cord made of darbha grass entwined with mango and aśvattha leaves.

Having surrounded the pavilion both inside and out with a garland of salutations, and having wrapped the pillars with fine silk cloth (*dukūla*), one should construct a square-shaped central section situated within the four middle pillars,
using either unbaked bricks or smooth clay.
Its four sides should resemble the surface of a mirror, and its middle region should be level; it should be raised to a height equal to one-eleventh, one-ninth, one-seventh,
one-fifth, one-fourth, or one-third of the length of the altar-platform (*vedi*).

Or one should construct an altar (vedī) one cubit in height. As it is stated in another Tantra: "Its height [is measured] by parts of one, nine, eleven, seven, four, and three. In the Kapila Pañcarātra:
"Its height may be one-fourth [of its width], or one-third, one-fifth, or one-seventh."
One should construct it with those bricks divided into nine or eleven parts.
Thus it is said in the *Tantrarāja*: "One should construct an altar in the center, one cubit in height. And in the *Śāradā*:
"Then, on an auspicious day favorable to the lunar mansion, the planets, and the day of the week, upon a pure surface of the earth free from husks and charcoal..."
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should construct an auspicious pavilion with an interior space measured by five,
seven, or nine cubits.
It should be provided with sixteen pillars, four of which are to be placed in the center;
they should be eight cubits in height, while twelve are to be arranged on all sides.
Measuring five cubits, they should be without holes, straight, and auspicious;
the best of those skilled in the ritual should bury one-fifth of them in the earth.
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves and bamboo;
at the doors, there should be arches made from milk-bearing trees in due order.
The height of their pillars is recorded as seven cubits each,
and their circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths.
The measurement of the horizontal beam (tiryakphalaka) should be from the middle of the pillars;
one should fashion the spikes (śūla) in the center of the archway (toraṇa) according to the measure of a cubit.
One should fasten banners in the various directions that possess a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors,
and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and other ornaments.
Then, on that field measuring one-third [of the original size],
one should prepare a square altar (vedi) one cubit high for the sake of the mandala.

Thus ends the procedure for the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Here, in the smallest pavilions—even in one measuring ten cubits—the altar (*vedi*) should have a length of three cubits increased by one-third; the space between the altar and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) on both sides should be exactly two paces, and outside of that, on both sides, [the same distance applies].
The ground occupied by the two *kuṇḍas* together with their necks and girdles measures four cubits;
on both sides outside of that, an area of two cubits each is occupied for the purpose of placing the *kumbhas*. Thus, the entire ground of the pavilion is occupied. Beyond this, the master—
Since even a place for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the assembly members (*sadasya*) to sit cannot be found [in that case], this position is not tenable.

Therefore, it should be understood that this position applies to those specific cases where one intends to perform a contraction—such as using only a single *kuṇḍa* or a single *mekhalā*—since the purpose is fulfilled by that much. Having thus constructed the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), therein...

One should construct eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the eight directions starting from the east, known as the square, the womb-shaped (yoni), the half-moon, the triangle, the circle, the hexagon, the lotus, and the eight-spoked [wheel].
Regarding that, first [the author] states the method for constructing the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the *Śāradā*:
"In the previously described pavilion, the wise man, having divided the area outside the altar into three parts, should arrange [the lines] starting from the east in the middle section. (1)
In the eight directions, sacrificial pits of beautiful form should be arranged in sequence:
square, yoni-shaped, half-moon, triangular, and circular.
These [fire-pits] are hexagonal and lotus-shaped, and octagonal by name;
the fire-pit for the Preceptor (ācārya) should be in the center, between Gaurīpati and Mahendra.
One should mark out the ground measuring one cubit as before;
this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square on all sides, bringing auspiciousness. || 4 ||
Those who know the tantras understand a cubit (hasta) to be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long;
a wise person should divide a square field into five parts.
The knower of mantras should place one part in front, according to the measurement of half of a half-corner; then he should draw another [line] with the measure of a corner.
Then one should lay down two cords; the pit (kuṇḍa) should be shaped like a womb (yoni).
Furthermore, the square field should be divided tenfold.
The knower of the tantra should discard one part each from below and above;
he should then drop the cord of the bowstring at the front and rotate it from that measurement.
This beautiful pit should be shaped like a half-moon;
once the field has been divided into four parts, one should place [the markers] on both sides.
One should mark each individual part from the measurement in front;
then, one should draw three lines below, which is declared to be the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The wise one should place one part outside at the eighteenth division of the field;
by that measurement, he should rotate the circle to form an unsurpassed *kuṇḍa*.
One should divide the field into eight parts on both sides of the central line;
by this measurement, one should set aside one part each from the center.
The best of those who know the tantras should fashion four fish-figures on the two sides;
then he should lay down six threads, resulting in an excellent hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having divided the square field into eighteen parts,
one should set aside one part on the outside and draw a circle with that [measure].
One should fashion three [circles] for the petals and so forth, as well as for the pericarp and so forth, on the outside;
this is declared to be the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padmakuṇḍa), which is enchanting to the eyes. || 15 ||
One should divide the previously mentioned field into twenty-four parts;
having set aside one part on the outside, one should fashion a square.
From the two corners of the inner square, one should mark [the points] at a measurement of half of half a corner [of the outer square],
and from the two corners of the outer square, one should likewise mark them.
One should cast eight threads toward each direction according to the rule;
for this is declared by those learned in the tantras to be an eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus, in the *Śrītantrarāja* (Chapter 29, verse 26):
"Having stretched the east-west thread, one should mark the center between them;
then, from that [center], twelve finger-breadths toward the east and west... (1).
Then, taking hold of those tips according to the measurement of the central mark,
one should form the "swan's footprint" (haṃsapada) and cast the squares around it.
Having wiped it thoroughly, one should likewise mark a pair of signs there; using the measurement of the east-west signs, one should hang [the cord] from those two very points.
Having made two *haṃsapada* marks from south to north,
and then having stretched a thread between them, one should erase that [thread] according to the stated measurement.

"The four [sides] of the threads shall form a square and be equal. Now, the method for constructing this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): there, having set aside a portion of ground measuring one cubit by means of the measure of a fist on the eastern side of the altar, according to the previously established sequence of directions—
Having stretched a cord extending from east to west and made a mark at its center,

one should make marks twelve finger-breadths (muṣṭyaṅgula) to the east and west of that central mark; then, having erased the excess portions on either side, [one proceeds] from the midpoint of that cord, using those two marks as supports.

Having constructed two circles, each slightly larger than the other, so that they are slightly intersecting from east to west, one should draw a north-south line through the center of the two "swan's foot" (haṃsapada) marks— which form the southern and northern intersections of those two circles—
and which pierce the "swan's foot" mark located at the intersection of the east-west Brahma-line.

Having stretched the thread there as well, one should mark two points to the south and north at a measurement of twelve finger-breadths from the central mark; then, having erased those respective excess portions,
by means of the four ends of that thread suspended [from the center], one should [mark] at all four corners at a measurement of twelve finger-breadths.

Having made a *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint) mark at each respective end, one should strike four lines— consisting of two lines running east-west to reach those respective *haṃsapada* marks and two lines running north-south— to form a square. Then, within that [square], one should [draw] a regular square whose depth is equal to the measurement of the *brahmasūtra* extending from east to west.

Having dug a pit and set aside a portion of ground measuring one twenty-fourth of the circumference of the *kuṇḍa* all around it, one should construct a *mekhalā* (girdle) outside of that, twelve *aṅgulas* in width and four *aṅgulas* in height;
above that, having again set aside four *aṅgulas* in measurement on the outside all around, [one should construct a girdle] eight *aṅgulas* in width.

Having made a second girdle four finger-breadths high, and having left a space of four finger-breadths on the outside above that, one should make a third girdle measuring four finger-breadths in both width and height.
When this is done, the first girdle is twelve finger-breadths high and four finger-breadths wide.

The second [girdle] is eight finger-breadths high and four finger-breadths wide; the third is four finger-breadths high and four finger-breadths wide. Regarding this, some maintain that the first girdle is four finger-breadths wide and nine finger-breadths high, while the second is three finger-breadths wide and five finger-breadths high, and the third—

They say that the measurement of the girdle (*mekhalā*) is two finger-breadths in width and two finger-breadths in height. This should be understood to apply to the case where the excavation is one cubit deep along with the girdle; for Viśvakarman has prescribed an excavation of exactly fifteen finger-breadths in depth, and it is necessary that its height above that be exactly nine finger-breadths.

Regarding the alternative of digging a pit one cubit deep, the *Tantrarāja* states: "For all [the tiers], one should determine the measurement of the girdles (*mekhalā*) by means of a span (*vitasti*), eight [fingers], and half of that, for both their width and height.
Thus, they are endowed with qualities beginning with *sattva*, and are respectively twelve, eight, and four finger-breadths in height.

"Belts (*mekhalā*) four finger-breadths wide on all sides are considered to grant all perfections (*siddhi*). (Prapañcasāra 5.33). According to this statement from the *Prapañcasāra*, the previously mentioned position alone is correct. Therefore, outside the belt situated at the very outer edge, there is a square [platform] four finger-breadths in length, width, and height.
Having fashioned a pedestal out of clay,
one should place upon it [the vessel] which has a base twelve finger-breadths long, with a circumference that decreases progressively upward, possesses a hollow channel connected to a middle girdle,
and is joined at its base with two jars in the middle.
It is provided with a cavity, situated upon the upper girdle, having a base measuring eight finger-breadths;

it gradually tapers from that region on both sides, having a width of one finger-breadth at its tip, a length of twelve finger-breadths, and is endowed with a girdle one finger-breadth high, resembling an *aśvattha* leaf.
One should fashion the *yoni* from its base, gradually sloping slightly inward so that its tip enters the pit. Then,

by drawing a circle four finger-breadths in measure in each direction, centered on the "swan's footprint" (*haṃsapada*) situated in the middle of the pit, and further drawing another circle outside that one measuring six finger-breadths, [one prepares] that circle.

Having fashioned the pericarp and having made eight petals within the pathway between the two circles, one should construct a navel six finger-breadths high. Thus ends the procedure for the construction of the square sacrificial pit (*caturasrakuṇḍa*).
Now, regarding the *yonikuṇḍa*, the *Tantrarāja* states:
"Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-fifth of its middle portion, [one should do so] from the central point between the two pairs of squares in the east and the west. (1)
O Dear One, one should rotate [the cord] from the western end, using that same measurement for the corner,
up to the northern end and likewise up to the southern end.
By supporting the two tips of the horizontal thread in the middle of that [square], two threads should likewise extend as far as the expanded Brahma-thread. (3)
O auspicious lady, this vulva-shaped pit (yoni-kuṇḍa) occurs in all four types of double-natured [altars].
Within that very [area], I shall describe other pits according to their equal proportions.
That ground which is square on all sides and situated elsewhere [from the center] must be abandoned;
therefore, in all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), all [sides] are [equally] present everywhere.
"Those very same [measures] arise, consisting of ninety-six finger-breadths.

Now, the method for constructing this sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): there, having first constructed a square as before, one should [mark] the eastward direction from the Brahma-thread—which consists of four squares—by means of a fifth part of its measurement.

Having expanded that, by drawing two diagonal lines— one from the southwest to the northeast and the other from the southeast to the northwest— across the southern and northern squares of the square consisting of four squares located in the western portion.
Having established the central region by means of the intersection of two marked lines, and having determined the extent of the corners,
one should [draw] from the western end of the east-west Brahma-line in the northern cell up to the northern end of the north-south horizontal line.

In its southern compartment, starting from the western end of that [central] line and revolving until reaching the southern end of the transverse line, one should produce two half-moons; then, by stretching two lines starting from the eastern end of the transverse line in their center and extending to the eastern end of the previously laid Brahma-line, a yoni-shape is formed.

Having demarcated the sacrificial ground (*kṣetra*) and outside of it, having produced two *yoni*-mandalas according to the stated measurements and methods for the neck (*kaṇṭha*) and the girdle (*mekhalā*), and having dug a pit as before, one should fashion the neck, the girdles, and so forth in the very shape of a *yoni*; such is the form of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and their girdles.
One should perform it in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the statement in the Kulaprakāśa: "In such a manner."
Now, regarding the half-moon-shaped fire-pit (*ardhacandrākārakuṇḍa*), the *Tantrarāja* states:
"Having set aside one-tenth of its center, both below and above, one should likewise rotate [the cord] from its center using the measurement of the remaining portion. (1)

"That by which the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) becomes the shape of a half-moon is so described. (p. 232). Now, the method for constructing this pit: there, having first constructed a square as before, one should divide its diameter into ten parts, and [mark] each single part at the eastern and western [ends].
Having set aside the two marks and drawn a horizontal thread extending from south to north from the western mark,
one should extend it further to the south and north by a measure of three parts outside that square; then,
using the center of the junction with the imagined western Brahma-thread as a pivot, [one should proceed] up to the two tips of that [thread].
Having formed two semicircular mandalas,
starting from the junction of the Brahma-sūtra located in the middle of the eastern line, and by rotating a measuring cord of one-eighth [of the total length],
there shall be a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) in the shape of a half-moon. Thus is the half-moon-shaped fire-pit.

Having emanated that [mandala] and also [the outer one] according to the stated method, having fashioned two mandalas resembling half-moons— one measuring one finger-breadth or twelve finger-breadths— and having made a pit one cubit deep in the center of the first mandala, excluding the area for the rim on the outside;
One should perform the girdle and other rites as previously described.
Now, regarding the triangular pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*), it is said in that very same [text]:
"One should expand the sixth part of that very [square] on both sides; then, using that measurement, one should draw two lines from each [side] toward the western line. (1)
"By laying out [the lines] up to the Brahma-sūtra and by supporting the tips of those two [lines], the triangle pit (kuṇḍa) is declared.
Now, the method for constructing this pit: having first made a square there as before, [one proceeds].

Having extended the eastern end of that Brahma-thread outward and divided its measurement across the square into six parts, one should extend from each of those [six divisions] the two ends of the western horizontal thread outward on both sides; then,
from those two ends, [one should extend] two threads equal in measure to that [original] thread.
Having extended the Brahma-sūtra (the north-south axis) as before, one should strike out from the point where it intersects [the east-west axis] to form a triangular pit (*tri-kona-kuṇḍa*). Then,
by the same method previously described, one should produce two other triangles outside that, measuring one part and twelve parts respectively.
One should fashion the neck, the girdle, and so forth, as previously described.
Now, regarding the circular *kuṇḍa*, it is said in that same [text]:
"One should expand the tip of the eastern thread by one-eighteenth part of its center; then, with that measurement, one should likewise draw a circle outside the transverse thread. (1)
"By relying on the central mark, that circular mandala shall be formed.
Now, the method for constructing this kuṇḍa: having prepared a square plot as before, one should divide the measurement of its diameter into eighteen parts at its center.

From one side of those [four corners], having extended a line from the square outward with its tip pointing east along the Brahma-sūtra, and taking the central mark as a reference, one should produce a circle by rotating around the extent of the extended Brahma-sūtra tip;
outside of that, for the sake of the neck, another circle is made with a measurement of twenty-four units from the square.
Having done that, one should again produce another circle with a measurement of twelve *aṅgulas*; then, having made a pit in the center of the first circle drawn, measuring one cubit in depth,
one should fashion three girdles (*mekhalā*) in the path at a distance of twelve *aṅgulas* outside the neck-circle, as before.

"One should fashion the yoni and so forth. Now, as for the claim of some that there is no yoni in a circular (vṛtta) kuṇḍa—that is not so; for it is the established doctrine of the Tantras that there is no yoni in a yoni-kuṇḍa, and neither a yoni nor a navel in a lotus (padma) kuṇḍa.
Now, regarding the six-thousand-petaled [lotus], it is said in that very same [text]:
"Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-sixteenth part of its center, and having likewise drawn a very clear circle using that measurement... (1)
On that circumference, one should make a mark at the midpoint using half [the length];
there, by the application of six lines, a six-cornered (*ṣaḍasra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is formed.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the method for constructing this *kuṇḍa*: having first fashioned a square as before, one should divide its central measurement into sixteen parts; then, by the measure of one such part, one should extend the eastern end of the *brahmasūtra*, and by that same measure, [marking] from the center of the "swan's foot" situated in the middle of that square—

Having drawn a circle by means of error [of measurement], and having marked six points around the circle starting from the southern end of the transverse line through its center— using half the measure of the diameter across that center—
one should stretch six threads in the form of chords from each mark to the next, and then erase the respective circular segments in the form of those arcs.

Having constructed the area of the hexagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should construct two hexagons outside of it— one part and twelve parts respectively— according to the stated method, and then arrange the excavation and other features as before.
Now, regarding the lotus-pool (*padmakuṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*: "O Ambikā, one should divide the square field into eight parts;
then, with a compass set to the measure of one-eighth part, [one should draw a circle] from the center. (1)
One should rotate it into a circle; this is the pericarp (karṇikā). Furthermore, with two-eighths [of the measurement], there shall be a circle from the center for the filaments (kesarāḥ).
The middle portion of the petals is considered to be one-eighth of the third [measurement];
the fourth field, however, should be produced by a rotation equal to the diameter.
O fair-faced one, having divided the Brahma-thread into twenty-four parts,
take one part and divide it again into sixteen.
O Śivā, having taken one-sixteenth part from each of the five [sides], the fifth maṇḍala outside of that is reduced by eight such parts.
One should rotate [the compass] from the center; the tips of all the petals are considered to be the outer limit.
Then, O Goddess, one should draw the lotus according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (6)

The measurement from the tip of the filaments to the outer edge of the interior— that measurement one should take as the *karkaṭa* (carpenter's square), and having placed it at the tip of the filament.
Having written sixteen half-moons according to the path instructed by the guru, one should draw the tips of the petals with the hand of Kṛti.
Having set aside the height equal to the width of the pericarp,
one should draw the remaining portion as the circle of filaments.
O Supreme Goddess, while digging in that manner, one should dig the leaf-ground so that the leaf-shapes are properly formed.

This is called the *padmakuṇḍa*. Now, the method for constructing this pit (*kuṇḍa*) is as follows: there, having divided the square field—prepared as before—into eight parts, one should, by means of a mark at its center, [draw lines] around it with a measurement of one part for the sake of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Having completed that circle, one should draw another circle outside it with a measurement of two parts for the sake of the filaments (kesara);

then, having fashioned another circle outside that with a measurement of three parts for the sake of its petals (dala), and having rotated a circle outside that with a measurement of four parts; and further outside that as well—

Having drawn five circles— by rotating a single circle outside a square field with a radius of six barleycorns (yava) plus a third (sārgha)— one should, using a compass set to the distance between the second and fifth circles,
draw lines from the tips of the filaments (kesara) to the tips of two horns that touch the outermost circle.

Having fashioned sixteen half-moons and made eight-petaled lotuses with tips, one should leave aside the circle of the pericarp in their center, and having properly excavated the circle of filaments— which illuminates the area around the pericarp— and the circle in the middle of the petals;
In such a way that the petals of the fourth and fifth verses have tips, and so that the area of the square pit is equal to the area of the width and length of the quadrangular *kuṇḍa*,
one should perform the excavation according to the method taught by the Guru; then, outside, the neck, girdle, and other parts should be fashioned in the very shape of a lotus.
One should perform [it].

Now, regarding the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *Tantrarāja* states: "Having constructed a square measuring twenty-four units at its center and likewise on the outside as before, [one should proceed] from the measure of half the eastern corner. (1)
Having indeed made eight marks all around its corners,
O Śivā, one should draw eight threads all around those marks.

"One should construct an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) pit (*kuṇḍa*). Now, the method for constructing this pit is as follows: having first fashioned a square as before, one should divide the measurement of the central cord into twenty-four parts;
then, at the tip of a cord extended outward in each direction from that [center] by the measure of one part, [one should proceed].

Having constructed a square as before according to the prescribed sequence, one should mark two points on each side of the outer square— by supporting them at the reversal of the four corners with a measurement equal to half the diagonal cord situated at the corners of the inner square.

Having sequentially produced the eight marks and, from mark to mark, having struck eight lines as before, an eight-sided sacrificial pit (*aṣṭāsra-kuṇḍa*) is formed by clearing away the corners that extend beyond those lines. Having thus determined the area of the eight-sided pit, [one should fashion] the excavation, the neck, the girdle (*mekhalā*), and so forth.
One should perform it according to the rule; thus, in the initiation ceremony, eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are to be prepared.
Now, as an incidental matter, the characteristics of the five-sided and seven-sided sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) for the sake of optional oblations (*kāmyahoma*) are also stated.
Regarding that, first he describes the five-sided pit in that very same [text]:
"There, having extended the Brahma-thread by one-seventh of its middle [length]..."
Then, having drawn a circle all around with pride and confusion... || 1 ||
Having marked points on that circle according to one-third of its measure, one should drop five lines there; that shall be the five-cornered sacrificial pit (pañcāsrakuṇḍaka).

Thus. Now, the method for constructing this *kuṇḍa*: having first prepared a square field as before, one should extend the eastern end of the *brahmasūtra* outward by one-seventh of the measurement of its middle; then, using that measurement and taking the "swan's footprint" situated in the center of that square as a pivot, one should draw a circle by rotation.
Having completed that square, one should divide the central thread into four parts;

then, using three parts each, one should mark five points around that circle starting from the eastern end of the Brahma-thread. Having struck lines in the form of chords between each point and the next, one should draw five threads.

By smoothing out the segments of the curved [lines] of each respective bow-shape, a five-cornered sacrificial pit (*pañcāsrakuṇḍa*) is formed. Having thus conceived the area of the five-cornered pit, one should likewise conceive two five-cornered figures outside of it for the sake of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) and the girdle (*mekhalā*) according to the stated method, and then perform the excavation and so forth.
Now, regarding the seven-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), it is said in that same [text]:
"Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-tenth of its middle [length], and having then drawn a circle with that measurement by means of rotation... (1)
Having marked seven points on the circle at intervals of one-thirty-third of its sixty-four parts, one should drop seven threads.

p. 234) "That [shape] shall be a seven-sided pit. Now, the method for constructing this pit: having first made a square with equal sides as before, one should divide its central measurement into ten parts;
then, extending the Brahma-thread outward by the measure of one part, and by that same measure—
Having fixed upon the position of the swan in the center of that square and drawn a circle, one should divide the measurement of the cord from the center of that square into sixty-four parts; then,
starting from the eastern end of the Brahma-sūtra, one should mark seven points on the circle at the measure of thirty-three parts each, and [proceed] from point to point.

By stretching seven threads in the form of a bow and erasing the respective circular segments in the shape of a bow, this seven-cornered (*saptāsra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shall be formed. Thus ends the method for constructing the ten types of sacrificial pits. Herein, for the initiation (*dīkṣā*), there are eight pits.

One should construct nine fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in total: eight in the directions starting from the east, and a ninth, square pit for the preceptor (ācārya), situated between Indra (east) and Īśāna (northeast). If one is unable to construct eight pits, then only four should be made in the four cardinal directions starting from the east, known as the square, the half-moon, the circle, and the lotus.

One should perform [the rite]. If one is unable even for this, one should construct only a single square *ācāryakuṇḍa* between Indra and Īśāna. Now, regarding these *kuṇḍas*, there is a difference in the fruits according to the specific type of *kuṇḍa* used in optional (*kāmya*) fire-offerings.
On this point, the *Kulaprakāśatantra* states:
In a quadrangular [pit], there shall be immobilization (stambhana), and it bestows all accomplishments;
in a vulva-shaped pit, there are enjoyments and sons; and the half-moon shape brings auspiciousness.
Some desire a triangle for the purpose of killing, as it produces hatred; others have declared that a circle brings about the destruction of enemies and effects pacification.
The hexagonal [pit] is highly distinguished for rites of eradication and causing death;
the wise know the lotus-shaped pit to bestow rain as well as nourishment. (3)
Some say that an eight-cornered [diagram] is for liberation and also for freedom from disease;
while a five-cornered one is for the pacification of malevolent magic and the destruction of spirits.
"Having understood it as having seven corners, one should accomplish the rites performed for specific desires.
Now, the distinction of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) according to the castes (*varṇa*). In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"O Śivā, the sacrificial pits have been described in sequence, beginning with the names of the castes."
Square, circular, semi-circular, and triangular, in that order. || 1 ||
"O Śivā, for all [initiates], a square [pit] is the best in the case of initiation.
Now, regarding the specific details for constructing the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around the altar, the Tantrarāja states:
"There are eight pits and a group of four; their forms and names [are as follows]."
O sinless one, I shall describe to you the entire process of emanation according to the prescribed rule.
One should construct circular fire-pits (vṛtta-kuṇḍas) according to the location for Libra, Cancer, Aries, and Capricorn— these being the four movable signs (cara-rāśi).
In the fixed signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius,
one should construct square fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in their respective order.
