In Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces— respectively in these pairs—
one should construct Yoni-shaped sacrificial pits for auspicious rites.
In the case of movable signs, one should employ half-moons in the inauspicious houses;
in fixed signs, one should use trine figures; but in dual signs, one should use squares.

"A five-sided, a six-sided, a seven-sided, and an eight-cornered [figure]," it is said. Regarding the placement of the zodiac signs, it is stated in that same work: "In the east are Aries and Taurus; in the southeast is Gemini; likewise in the south..."
Then Cancer and Leo are in that southwest direction, and likewise Virgo. || 1 ||
Libra and Scorpio are situated in the west; Sagittarius is located in the northwest;
Capricorn and Aquarius are in the north; and Pisces is situated in the northeast.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the nature of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and its underlying symbolism (*vāsanā*), it is stated in the *Prathama-tantra*:
"The supreme body of Prakṛti is the form of the pit; the front is the head, the southern and northern hands are the pit, and likewise the west is the belly. (1)
"The womb and the feet are declared [to be the foundation] in all Tantras of Śambhu.
Now, regarding the difference in the measurement of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the difference in the number of oblations, it is stated in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
"In a rite of fifty thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit should be one *ratni* in measure."
But in the case of a thousand-fold oblation, it should be one cubit long for each hundred.
For ten thousand recitations, it is considered to be two cubits plus twenty-four finger-breadths;
for one hundred thousand, it is measured at four cubits; and for ten million, it is six cubits.
"O Maheśvarī, for a *koṭi*-homa, one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring eight cubits.
And another method is stated in that very same place:
"Beginning from one hundred thousand [recitations] up to ten hundred thousand..."
In that manner, one should increase [the measurement] starting from one cubit up to ten cubits. || 1 ||
"O Supreme Goddess, a pit of ten cubits at its corner is recommended. (p.

235) This should be understood to apply to homas performed with leaves, flowers, or [other materials] alone, because there is no purpose for excessive expansion in that case. Now, regarding these specific types of pits measuring two cubits and so forth:

In the ocean of lakhs [of measurements], the area-measures in finger-breadths (mānāṅgula) are as many finger-fruit-measures (phalāṅgula) as there are in the area of one cubit (hasta). For a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of two cubits, double that amount is required. || 1 ||
In this [calculation], there are five hundred and seventy-six cubits, fields, and finger-breadths; the square root of that is the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra).
One should again duly fashion twenty-four finger-breadths,
as well as one thousand one hundred and fifty-two finger-breadths.
That seed-measure (bīja) consists of four *likṣās* plus half one in the middle,
as well as four *yūkās* and likewise seven *yavas*.
The measurement for the middle thread is thirty-three finger-breadths;
it consists of one thousand seven hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths.
This measurement for a field of three cubits has been declared:
its base consists of forty-one finger-breadths and four barley-corns.
A little less than four lice [make one];
there are twenty-three hundred and four finger-breadths (aṅgulas). 7.
Thus is declared the measurement for a pit (kuṇḍa) of four cubits;
its base shall measure forty-eight finger-breadths.
Then, for the Brahma-thread, the measurement is five cubits;
the seed-measure is said to be two thousand eight hundred and eighty finger-breadths.
The base of that [stūpa] is three thousand four hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and it is fifty-eight finger-breadths and six barley-corns (yavas) in thickness.
A certain portion and so forth, two lice,
and twenty-two thousand four hundred [finger-breadths] of seven cubits.
The base [measurement] is sixty-three finger-breadths along with four barley-corns;
from that, the Brahma-thread [extends] for the finger-breadths of an eight-cubit field.
Eight thousand six hundred and sixty-four finger-breadths, and furthermore seventy-seven barley-corns. || 13 ||
Its base is seen to be slightly less than nine cubits;
it measures five hundred and four [units]. (14)
In this case, the measurement of the field shall be eighty finger-breadths;
its base is proclaimed to be seventy-two finger-breadths. (15)
Five finger-breadths [are the measure] of a field measuring ten cubits;
there are thousands numbering as many as arrows (five), and hundreds numbering as many as sages (seven). || 16 ||
And sixty [finger-breadths] are said for this; its root is the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra).
One should increase it by seventy-five [finger-breadths] and likewise by seven barley-corns (yava). 17.
One should calculate in this manner by adding two more *likṣās* to it;
having applied great effort, the wise man should construct the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*).
"And the construction of [liṅgas] measuring two cubits and more is difficult to accomplish, O Śivā.

Regarding "with great effort": here, having correctly understood the ten types of measurements beginning with the *trasareṇu* and ending with the *daśa*, one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) whose width, length, and depth are equal, with a neck and girdles (*mekhalā*) of the dimensions prescribed.

And the meaning is that one should perform [this]; for it is difficult to accomplish because it requires extreme effort. As for the distinctions in the measurement of *trasareṇu* and so forth, they are summarized in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"The subtle dust particle that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice window..."
First, they declare the *trasareṇu* to be the smallest measure of those [units]. || 1 ||
A *trasareṇu* should be known as consisting of eight *paramāṇus*;
a *rathareṇu* is traditionally held to be eight times the size of a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those chariot-dust particles are considered by the wise to be a single hair-tip;
eight hair-tips are a nit, and eight nits are recorded as a louse-egg.
They say eight *yūkās* make one barleycorn (*yava*), and eight barleycorns make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). A *ratni* should be known as twenty-one finger-joints (*parvan*).
A *kara* minus one-sixteenth part is declared to be an *aratni*;
it consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). || 5 ||

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the construction of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) for this [rite], which is equal in width, length, and depth, as well as the measurements for the girdles (*mekhalā*) and so forth, the scriptural statements are as follows:
"Then, having measured out the area of the ground with a cord by means of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)."
And with those [beads], one should strike [the target] as many times as there are; however, one finger and the girdles must be excluded. || 1 ||

Thus, from the *Prapañcasāra*: "The depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit (*kuṇḍa*). From the *Śāradā*: "The depth is like the width of the pit. And from the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "It is as deep as it is wide.
Having first drawn a square divided into four compartments with threads as before...
In the middle of that, one should dig a pit as deep and long as the measurement of a cubit. || 1 ||

This is because of the statement in the *Divyasārasvataprayogasāra*: "It should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length and provided with a corresponding excavation. And because of the statement in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*:
"One should fashion the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with an excavation that is wide by twenty-four finger-breadths."

Furthermore, based on the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, the established conclusion is that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be made with a depth equal to its width and length. On this point, some [hold] that one should dig it to the measure of one cubit, including the horizontal and vertical girdles (*mekhalā*), according to the statement in the *Homasāra*: "Having understood the height of the five triple-girdles, the remainder [is for] below."

One should dig [the pit]. This is because of the statement in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "The depth of the pit is declared by Vyāsa to be one *tithi* (fifteen) finger-breadths lower than the [surrounding] ground. And because of the statement in the *Viśvakarma*: "The *kuṇḍa* [should be measured] in one's own finger-breadths, including the horizontal and vertical girdles (*mekhalā*). And because of the statement in the *Prathama-tantra*: "The pit..."

And from the statement in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, "The measurement of the pit (kuṇḍa) should be [one cubit] including the girdle (mekhalā)," they say that the excavation is one cubit in measure including the girdle.
This is not correct, because it would follow that by the inclusion of the girdle, the excavation itself must also be included. [The excavation...]

"Its status as a subsidiary (aṅga) is declared to be equal to that of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); however, it is distinguished from the girdle (mekhalā) and other elements by way of direct contribution (sannipatyopakāra). From this statement in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, because it is inappropriate for the direct contribution of the excavation to be carried out together with the indirectly contributing (ārādupakāra) girdle, the aforementioned position alone [is correct].
Because it has been so ordained. Furthermore:
"In this tantra, as well as everywhere else, one finger-breadth (aṅgula) shall be understood as one-third of the circumference of the middle joint of the middle finger. (1)
O Śivā, four of those [finger-breadths] make a muṣṭi; three times that [muṣṭi] makes a vitasti; two of those [vitastis] make an aratni; and two of those [aratnis] make a hasta.
Two of those [vyāmas] would constitute one vyāma, and the height of the man should be that measure;
it should be ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and according to those measures, the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is to be performed.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Śrītantrarāja*, since it is necessary for the pit (*kuṇḍa*) to have a length and width of ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), in the case of a pit fifteen finger-breadths deep,
there are twelve, fifteen, and nine [finger-breadths] respectively from the center of the pit up to the top of the girdle (*mekhalā*).

Since it is seen to be only thirty-six finger-breadths [in height], there is a deficiency of two finger-breadths on each of its two sides due to doubling that amount to seventy-two finger-breadths; thus, because it falls short by one-twelfth of twenty-four finger-breadths,
when the pit is one cubit deep along with a girdle twelve finger-breadths high, then on both sides as well—
From Madhyadeśa, by the calculation of twelve, twenty-four, and twelve, there are forty-eight; through doubling that, ninety-six is obtained,
whereby the stated number is fulfilled.
The view that it is better to have a girdle (*mekhalā*) twelve finger-breadths high, situated upon a pit one cubit deep, is indeed superior;
for since there exists a neck (*kaṇṭha*) of one finger-breadth width, by including that on both sides,
there is an increase of two finger-breadths in width, resulting in a total length of ninety-six finger-breadths.

If it is argued that [the mention of] the *kuṇḍa* (pit) is inappropriate, we say no, because the *kaṇṭha* (neck) is not mandatory; for this very reason, the *kaṇṭha* is not mentioned in the *Tantrarāja*. If it is then asked whether a fault is heard of even in the non-creation of the *kaṇṭha*, it is true;

however, precisely because of its contradiction with the *Tantrarāja*, one must understand that [the cited passage] refers to cases where the girdles (*mekhalā*) or the excavations (*khāta*) are deficient.

Therefore, the scriptural statements prescribing the excavation along with the girdles (*mekhalā*) should be understood as pertaining to sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *ratni*, two *ratnis*, and so forth;

for in the case of those where fifty or more oblations (*homa*) are prescribed, there is no purpose for an excessive excavation. Now, in this context, five girdles may be made, measured by five, six, four, three, and two [units].

Thus, according to the statement in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*: "The five girdles should be measured by six, five, four, three, and two [units]," and also according to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, five girdles are to be made.
Likewise, in the Piṅgalāmata: "The two girdles are considered to be [respectively] one-sixth and one-eighth [of the height];
one girdle is considered to have a height and width of six finger-breadths. (1)
Thus [ends the section]. Now, Vasiṣṭha states that faults arise if the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are not constructed according to the rules:
"If a sacrificial pit here is deficient or excessive, it bestows many faults.
Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should construct it only after having examined it thoroughly. (1)
Thus it is said. Regarding this, Viśvakarman states the defects:
"If the pit is deeper than prescribed, there will be disease; if shallower, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
If the fire-pit is crooked, there is suffering; if the boundary-line (mekhalā) is broken, death occurs. (1)

If it lacks a girdle, there is excessive grief; if it is devoid of wealth, there is loss of property. A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) fashioned without a yoni is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.
A *kuṇḍa* that is devoid of a neck is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring.
Thus, it is said in the *Kriyāsāgara*:

"A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that is either deficient or excessive in measurement, one with a cracked girdle (*mekhalā*), or one lacking aesthetic beauty, brings about the destruction of the patron (*yajamāna*). (1)
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Jayadrathayāmala:
"Hatred toward friends occurs when [the thread] exceeds the cord; poverty when it lacks pride;
obstruction of speech when it lacks the throat; and failure results from a pit that is deficient. (1)
If there is an excess [of measurement], there is enjoyment like that of an asura; if the girdle is excessive by measure, diseases arise, and in a low birth, there is epilepsy. (2)
"In the case of a fissure or one crowded with holes, there shall be public censure.

Thus, because of hearing such censure, all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) endowed with the aforementioned characteristics should be constructed. Now, regarding the neck (*kaṇṭha*): on this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "The neck should be the measure of eight barley-corns."
"In the case of a *kuṇḍa*, however, [the depth] should be the measure of one *kara*. Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"The neck (*kaṇṭha*) outside the excavation should be one *aṅgula*; this is the rule for all *kuṇḍas*.
One should calculate twenty-four parts as one *aṅgula*. (1)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the *yoni*, it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"One should fashion a very beautiful *yoni* in the middle of the girdle, either to the west or to the south; it should be slightly depressed and gradually tapering upwards. (1)
With its tip facing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), slightly touching the girdle (mekhalā), joined with two jars, and resembling the leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha). || 2 ||
Thus it is said. And likewise in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
"The yoni is situated in the middle portion, facing east and centered in the middle;
it is eight fingers wide and twelve fingers long. (1)
"Raised at the back, resembling the lip of an elephant, with a cavity and elevated in the middle.

Regarding "with a cavity in the middle," the traditionalists say that a hollow (garta) should be made in the center of the *yoni*, based on the statement from the *Trailokyasāra*: "In the middle, however, it is remembered as the 'holder of clarified butter' (*ājyadhṛti*). Likewise:
In the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:

"O Dear One, the edge [of the altar] should enter slightly into the pit; the girdle is fashioned from a portion of the Jina [the central area]. No separate ground for the purpose of the girdle should be taken from the outside. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Nārada states: "But that [yoni] should be made in the sacrificial field (kṣetra). In the pit (kuṇḍa), the yoni is one-third of the width in height, measuring one finger-breadth (aṅgula); it should be half the length of the pit. Likewise, in the Trailokyasāra:
"The stalk is three suns (twelve) finger-breadths in length, less one-third in width, and it is one finger-breadth in height."
Thus, [the yoni] is three parts less than the width of the *nāla*, which is eight *aṅgulas*, given that the *nāla* is twelve *aṅgulas* in length.
In the *Svāyambhuva* as well, it is stated: "The *yoni* from the middle of the *mekhalā* is half the size of the *kuṇḍa* and three parts wide.
Because its shape at the base is like a *pippala* leaf, the width is determined by this method in *kuṇḍas* of two cubits and so forth.
The *yoni* should be made half as long as that *kuṇḍa*, one-third as wide, and one-twenty-fourth as high.
As it has been stated by Somaśambhu:
"The twenty-fourth part of the fire-pits (kuṇḍa) is designated as an 'aṅgula'.
By dividing [the pit] with that unit, the girdles (mekhalā), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the navel (nābhi) should be constructed. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The twenty-fourth part of the [measurement] is recorded as the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). It is further stated: "The yoni [should be] twelve finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in width; its height should be less by two finger-breadths. Here, there is an option between eight and six finger-breadths, and between one and two finger-breadths [for the respective dimensions].

For it is said in the *Śāradā*: "Thus, their *yoni* is in front of the *hotṛ*, like an *aśvattha* leaf above. According to this statement, the *yoni* should be placed in every case in front of the *hotṛ* according to the prescribed rule. In that regard, in the case of four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), the *yoni* should be placed upon the girdle (*mekhalā*) situated on the southern side of the square and the semi-circular pits.
Because those two *hotṛ* priests face north, the *yoni* should be placed upon the western girdle (*mekhalā*) of the other two *kuṇḍas*,
since those two *hotṛ* priests face east.
The *yoni* of the first [kuṇḍa] is situated in the southeast; that of the second is in the southwest; that of the third is in the northwest;
and the *yoni* of the fifth kuṇḍa is located in the southern direction.
Thus, according to the words of the *Trailokyasāra*:

"The meaning is that this refers to the fifth, the preceptor’s fire-pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*). In this regard, concerning the types of fire-pits: for the pits facing east, southeast, and south, the *yoni* is said to face north; for the remaining [pits], it faces east."

Because of the statement in another tantra, "it is so declared," the yoni should face north in the eastern, southeastern, and southern [sections], while in the others it faces east; however, for the ninth, it is just as before. On this basis, some maintain that a yoni must also be constructed in the yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (*yonikuṇḍa*). That is not so, because of the statement of Viśvakarman: "In the yoni-shaped pit one should avoid the yoni, and in the lotus-shaped pit one should avoid the navel."
Regarding the stalks of these girdles, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Starting from the middle of the outer girdle, its own stalk is one *vitasti* in measure.
This means starting from the center of the outer girdle—that is, from the square pedestal situated therein. The same was explained by the commentator, the author of the *Manoramā*.

Because this has already been explained. However, the venerable teacher [Śaṅkarācārya] stated: "The yoni is in that western direction, with its stalk beginning from a square-shaped base. Regarding this, Padmapādācārya says: "Having made an area four finger-breadths in length and breadth outside the three girdles, the stalk should be placed there."
This has been explained. "A span" (*vitasti*) means twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). However, in the *Prayogasāra* (p. 238):
"The stalk behind the womb (*yoni*) should be four finger-breadths in length;
its width is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively, tapering toward the tip. (1)

Thus, the stalk (nāla) is said to be four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) in measure. This measurement of four or six finger-breadths and so forth should be understood as applying to the case of a small girdle (mekhalā). Regarding the navel (nābhi), the *Tantrarāja* states:
"One should fashion the navel in the center of every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule."
One should fashion an eight-petalled lotus of beautiful form.
One should fashion the pericarp and the petals with four finger-breadths each;
both their width and their height are declared to be six finger-breadths.
Thus it is said in the *Śāradā*:
"One should fashion within the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) a navel resembling a lotus;
its measurement is declared to be either conforming to each respective pit or [according to other specifications]. (1)
The navel of fire-pits measuring one muṣṭi, one aratni, or one hasta should be two, three, or four aṅgulas in height and breadth; in other pits, one should increase these dimensions accordingly.
The one of noble intellect should likewise mark the navel with a distance of two *yava*s;
then, having divided the navel-field into three parts, he should fashion the pericarp.

One should arrange eight petals with two external segments; thus the characteristics of the navel (nābhi) have been stated, and therein it should be understood according to what is appropriate. Since the word *nābhi* occurs in both genders—as in the words "the navel in the sun" (*ātape*), "in a Kṣatriya" (*kṣatriye*), and "also in a limb of a living being" (*prāṇyaṅge*)—the term *nābhi* exists even in the masculine. Now, the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*). Therein:
In the *Śrītantrarāja*:
"In ancient times, there was a certain demon of square form who was the destroyer of all; for his very destruction, all the gods made an effort. (1)
Having done so, they prepared to kill him, but he became invulnerable to them due to a boon;
therefore, in order to repel him, they came to me and spoke thus. || 2 ||
Tell us now about that Vāstupuruṣa;
for if his pride were not quelled, the entire universe would have been overwhelmed by calamity.
When they had spoken thus, I declared that his death would be difficult to achieve;
one should therefore bury him in the earth and place [the weapon] upon his body.
And constantly, for the sake of suppressing those fifty-three [demons], he appointed those who were averse to their worship; however, by those [who were averse], [acts] were performed... || 5 ||
They would accumulate good deeds yet commit evil ones;
therefore, one should always perform their worship every year.
"Only auspicious things arise in these [periods], and never anything inauspicious.
Regarding that, he speaks of the wheel and so forth:
"The procedure for those wheels and so forth is now being described exactly as it is."
Having made the ground clean and auspicious, in a square shape. || 1 ||
The preceptor [should prepare] a grid with sixty-four squares, complete with corner lines, and within that, in the central square surrounded by four squares... (2)
There, one should worship Brahmā again in the square consisting of four parts;
then, by circumambulating from the east onwards, one should worship in the four remaining compartments.
The minister should worship Āryaka, Vivasvat, Mitra, and another Mahīdhara—
one each— in two of the corner half-cells.
From Agni to Īśāna, in the sequence to be described hereafter:
Sāvitra, Savitṛ, Śakra, Indrajit, Rudra, and Tajjit.
Āpa and Apavatsaka—these eight have been declared by name;
one should worship them in the corners, half-corners, and sides, starting from Agni and ending with Īśāna.
Śarva, Guha, Aryaman, Jambhaka, Pilipicchaka,
Caraki, Vidāri, and the guide of the Putanas.
Then, from the east onwards, one should worship the eight [deities] in each direction:
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara; || 8 ||
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are located in the eastern quarter and the [eastern] storehouse respectively; then follow Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Gṛharakṣaka. || 9 ||
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern compartment;
likewise Nirṛti, Dauvārika, and Sugrīvaka. (10)
Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta, and the two Asuras known as Śoṣa and Roga—
these are to be worshipped in due order within the compartments situated in the western direction.
Vāyu, Nāga, and likewise Mukhya; Soma and Bhallāṭaka; Argala and Diti, as well as Aditi, in their respective order. || 12 ||
When the northern squares have been reached, these deities are thus described;
indeed, having filled the positions of the deities with various colored powders.
One should offer oblations of rice, mung beans, and barley, sequentially soaked in honey, ghee, and milk,
either one hundred and eight times or twenty-one times.

One should offer oblations to each of them individually with substances and mantras, and likewise with milk-rice (pāyasa); one should present a bali-offering to them consisting of milk-rice accompanied by various side-dishes.
"With sugar, milk, plantains, cakes, and other offerings," (p.
239). Now, the method for constructing this *cakra* and the procedure for worship will be described:
there, in the southwest corner of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [one should prepare] a space one cubit (*hasta*) in width and length, and one span (*vitasti*) in height.

Having made a very smooth altar (vedikā) that is perfectly square, and having drawn nine lines each extending east-west and north-south, one should form sixty-four squares with equal intervals; therein, starting from the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa) toward the southeast corner (āgneyakoṇa)...
Having struck two diagonal threads— one from the southeast corner to the northeast, and the other from the southwest to the northwest— and having thus constructed the Vāstu-cakra,

one should unify the four central squares; then, outside of that, in the four directions starting from the east, one should unify four squares in each direction, each of which is contiguous with the central squares.
Having visualized the fifty-three stations for the deities and having properly filled those stations with the powders to be described below in such a way that they become beautiful,
one should take a handful of flowers and say: "O Brahmā and the other fifty-three deities, come here, come here!"

Having invoked the fifty-three deities beginning with Brahmā by scattering handfuls of flowers, and having established them in their respective places with the words, "Stay, stay here! one offers a handful of folded flowers to Brahmā and the others, saying, "This seat for Brahmā and the others. Then, in the very center, [one says] "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. In the four directions starting from the east: "Oṃ, obeisance to Aryaka. Oṃ...

Having worshipped in a clockwise direction with "Oṃ, salutation to Vivasvat; Oṃ, salutation to Mitra; Oṃ, salutation to Mahīdhara," one should then worship in a clockwise direction within the eight half-squares located in the four corners starting from the southeast (Āgneya), extending from Āgneya to Īśāna, with: "Oṃ, salutation to Sāvitra; Oṃ, salutation to Savitṛ; Oṃ..."

Having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śukra; Oṃ, obeisance to Śakrajit; Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra; Oṃ, obeisance to Rudrajit; Oṃ, obeisance to Āpa; Oṃ, obeisance to Āpavatsaka," one should [proceed] on the altar situated outside of that, within the four compartments divided by the diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) located in the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya).

In the eight side-compartments, from the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśāna), one should worship them as follows: *Oṃ śarvāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ guhāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ aryamṇe namaḥ*, *Oṃ jambhakāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ pilipicchakāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ carikyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ vidāryai namaḥ*, *Oṃ pūtanāyai namaḥ*. Thus having worshipped them.
Outside of that, in the four avenues, on the avenue facing the east, from the northeast to the southeast: *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, *oṃ parjanyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ jayantāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śakrāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ bhāskarāya namaḥ*, *oṃ satyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ vṛṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ antarikṣāya namaḥ*.

Having thus worshipped these eight deities, one should worship on the southern path from the southeast to the southwest as follows: *oṃ agnaye namaḥ*, *oṃ pūṣṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ vitathāya namaḥ*, *oṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ gṛharakṣakāya namaḥ*, *oṃ gandharvāya namaḥ*, *oṃ bhṛṅgarājāya namaḥ*, *oṃ mṛgāya namaḥ*.
Having performed worship, one should then, in the western row, from the southwest to the northwest, offer salutations with: *Oṃ nir-ṛtaye namaḥ*,
*Oṃ dauvārikāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ sugrīvāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ puṣpadantāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ asurāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ śoṣāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ rogāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped on the northern path from the northwest to the northeast with scents, flowers, and other offerings, [he worships] the fifty-three deities as follows: *oṃ vāyave namaḥ*, *oṃ nāgāya namaḥ*, *oṃ mukhyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ somāya namaḥ*, *oṃ bhallāṭakāya namaḥ*, *oṃ argalāya namaḥ*, *oṃ dityai namaḥ*, *oṃ adityai namaḥ*.

Having performed worship and established the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), on the altar (*sthaṇḍila*), or elsewhere according to the procedure to be described, one should offer oblations individually to each of the deities worshipped with their respective name-mantras ending in *svāhā*, such as: *oṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*, *aryakāya svāhā*, and so forth.

Having offered oblations one hundred and eight or twenty-eight times for each deity by name, using rice, barley, mung beans, ghee, honey, milk, and milk-rice mixed with ghee— each substance individually— with the mantra: "Oṃ, this offering is for Brahmā, obeisance," and so forth.

To the deities who have been worshipped, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) at their respective places with milk-pudding (*pāyasa*) accompanied by sesame seeds, milk, plantains, cakes, and various side dishes, addressing each by its specific name. Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the site (*vāstupūjāvidhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the fruit of the Vāstupūjā and the contrary result of its non-performance, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day every year, one should perform the Vāstupūjā in one's own home within a mandala. (1)
There shall be no untimely deaths, diseases, or afflictions by spirits, ghosts, and the like;
nor shall there be suffering from snakes, mutual quarrels, or other such inauspicious events.
One who possesses sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female slaves;
who is free from disease, victorious, and renowned—such a person lives for a long time in that house. || 3 ||
In all royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens, in the residences of ministers, counselors, and generals, and likewise throughout the city.
The preceptor should perform this every year for the sake of the aforementioned success;
otherwise, there will be constant suffering due to results contrary to what was taught. || 5 ||

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*) is stated in another Tantra: "Seven or nine days prior to the day of initiation, this rite of sowing seeds, which grants all desires, must be performed. (1)
In the northern direction of the pavilion, in another very well-secluded chamber,
one should construct a single mandala, extending from east to west.
Other wise men, however, declare it to be extended from south to north;
there should be twelve squares here, and within them, three positions shall be established.
Then one should fill in the squares, provided with four sets of positions,
using yellow, red, white, and dark-colored powders, starting from the southeast (the fire-quarter).
They say that the vessels, ending with the *īśānta*, are of three kinds;
those belonging to Viṣṇu are called *pālikās*, and they are twenty-four finger-breadths in height.
The five-mouthed vessels of Brahmā (Vairiñcya) should be raised sixteen finger-breadths;
the four Śaiva bowls should be raised twelve finger-breadths.

Having washed [the vessels] and wrapped them with threads, one should place the fires and other elements in their respective locations within [vessels] filled with śāli rice and provided with fragrant substances and bunches of darbha grass.
One should fill those vessels with sand, clay, and dried cow-dung,
accompanied by the sound of conch shells, the five musical notes, and the benedictions of Brahmins.
One should wash [the site] with the seeds of the *dugdhavā* plant and then sow the seeds;
those [seeds] are *priyaṅgu*, *śyāmāka*, sesame, mustard, and rice.
Mudga, āḍhakī, suniṣpāva, khanva, and māṣa are proclaimed [as the grains];
having sprinkled them with turmeric, the Guru should cover them with cloths.
One should offer the supreme bali-oblation at both twilights and during the night,
for all three types of recipients, throughout all seven days.
On the first day, it is prescribed that for the spirits (bhūtas) there should be sesame seeds, parched grain, and turmeric; for the ancestors (pitṛs), curd, barley meal, and rice with sesame seeds.
On the third day, *karambha* mixed with parched grain (*lāja*) is offered to the Yakṣas;
on the fourth day, [an offering] soaked in coconut and ghee is for the Nāgas.
And on the fifth day, an offering of powdered roasted grain (saktupiṣṭa) is prescribed for Brahmā;
and on the sixth day, lotus seeds with unbroken rice (akṣata) along with cakes (apūpa) are offered to Śiva.
On the seventh day, there should be food for Viṣṇu consisting of rice with jaggery;
and if it is a Navarātra, then on both days there should be an offering (bali).
Then, milk-rice and kṛsara should be offered to Viṣṇu in sequence;
these are the bali-mantras, consisting of their respective names preceded by the syllable Om and ending with the heart-mantra (namas).

Thus: *karambha* is curd-mixed barley flour; *padmākṣata* is lotus seeds; *kṛsara* is boiled rice prepared with sesame and mung beans. Now, the method for constructing this mandala: there, prior even to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*), over nine or seven days...
Having constructed a well-enclosed house on the northern side of the previously erected pavilion,
and having prepared a level ground there smeared with cow-dung, one should draw five lines extending eastward and westward,
each five cubits in length, and eleven lines extending southward and northward, with an interval of one span between them.

Having constructed a maṇḍala consisting of forty squares and measuring two and a half cubits in width, one should combine the squares in the northern section to form the pathways (*vīthī*). Then, having cleared away two squares on each side of the central four-square area, there remain three sets of four squares.

Having fashioned a mandala consisting of twelve parts, one should designate four square compartments for each of the positions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, arranged in the order of west, center, and east; therein,
within each of the three groups of four starting from the west, beginning with the southeast compartment (āgneya), one should proceed.

Filling the twelve squares in sequence— starting from the northeast corner up to its limit— with yellow, red, white, and dark-green colored powders, using one powder for each individual square in every set of four, and therein, within the middle set of four, at three locations:
Having placed four *pālikās* dedicated to Viṣṇu— each twenty-four finger-breadths in height and width, shaped like a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*),
and wrapped with white thread together with a *pippala* leaf and a mango sprout— in the center,
one should likewise place five vessels in a single vessel in the western group as follows:
Likewise, having placed four vessels fashioned by a skilled artisan as before, shaped like hand-drums (ḍamaruka), sixteen finger-breadths in height and width, dedicated to Brahmā,
and similarly provided with leaves of the *pippala* tree and other such foliage, one should arrange them in the eastern group of four.

Four seats made of leaves such as those of the *pippala* tree, twelve finger-breadths in height and width, dedicated to the deity Śiva, and arranged as before, should be placed; thus, the twelve vessels, having been washed,
are each placed one by one upon heaps of *śāli* rice within each of the twelve squares.

Having placed those various vessels— equipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and tufts of grass— within a single new vessel made of gold or other materials, or even of clay, and having filled them with sand, earth, and cow-dung,
[one should place therein] the grains known as priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, sesame, mustard, śāli rice, mudga beans, āḍhakī, niṣpāva, and khalva-māṣa.

Having combined the ten grains and washed them with cow’s milk while reciting the *amṛtabīja* "vaṃ," one should sow the seeds into those vessels— first into those dedicated to Brahmā, then into those dedicated to Viṣṇu, and then into those dedicated to Śiva— in that order, preceded by the sound of a conch and the five musical instruments.

Having sprinkled [the image] with water mixed with turmeric and covered it with new cloths, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) every day during all seven days— at both twilights and at midnight. On that first day, having combined sesame seeds, parched grain, flour, and boiled rice with turmeric powder, one should prepare three morsels.

Having prepared all three types of vessels, one should invoke the spirits with the words, "O spirits, come here! Stay here! Having established them, one should worship them with scents and other offerings while reciting, "Oṃ, obeisance to all spirits (sarvabhūtebhyo namaḥ). Then, having worshipped the offering materials for the *bali* with the words, "Obeisance to the materials for the *bali* of all spirits," one should place water in the palm of the hand.

Holding the vessel for the *bali* offering with the left hand and touching it, one should pour water onto the *bali* vessel while reciting "Oṃ, this *bali* is offered to all beings; obeisance! and then cast forth the *bali*. In this manner, one should offer the *bali* near the vessel of Viṣṇu and near the four vessels of Śiva; such is the procedure for offering the *bali* during all three aforementioned times.

Regarding this, some say that an offering (bali) should be given in the four directions of the mandala; in that case, it should be performed according to the instructions of one's guru. Then, on the second day, one should offer the bali to the ancestors with sesame and rice, following the previously mentioned procedure at the three aforementioned times. On the fourth day, [one offers] to the nāgas.
On the fifth day, an offering of flour-cakes soaked in coconut water is made to Brahmā.

On the sixth day, an offering of cooked rice with cakes is made to Śiva. On the seventh day, an offering of rice with jaggery is made to Viṣṇu. In the case of the nine-night rite (navarātra), on the eighth day, [the offering] is likewise for Viṣṇu alone.

p. 241) On the ninth day, an offering (*bali*) of milk-rice (*dugdhaudana*) and an offering of *kṛsara* should be given. In all these cases of offering an oblation, it should be understood that the very procedure prescribed for the first day applies; likewise, the worship and the disposal of the offering should be performed using the respective names of the deities. Here, during all nine days, after the daily offering to each respective deity, [the following should be done].

To the ten guardians of the directions (daśadikpāla) as well, in their respective directions, an offering (bali) consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee and sugar should be given using their respective names, beginning with: "Oṃ, this is my offering for Indra. This concludes the procedure for the sowing of the seed-syllables (bījāropaṇavidhi).
Now, the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*). First, regarding the months. In that regard, the *Manthānabhairavatantra* states:
"Initiation in Caitra leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha it bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*);
in Jyeṣṭha it would bring death; in Āṣāḍha it destroys one's kinsmen. (1)
In Śrāvaṇa, it bestows prosperity upon men; in Nabhasya, it is considered to bring suffering;
in Āśvina, there shall be complete success; and in Kārtika, it grants wisdom.
In Mārgaśīrṣa it bestows auspiciousness; in Pauṣa it destroys the clouds;
in Māgha there shall be the gain of gold; and in Phālguna it grants all accomplishments.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in another tantra:
"In the month of Madhu (Caitra) there will be suffering; in Mādhava (Vaiśākha), an accumulation of jewels;
in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs; and in Āṣāḍha, the destruction of kinsmen. (1)
In the month of Śrāvaṇa there will surely be prosperity, while in Bhādrapada there will be decline;
however, in the month of Āśvina, there shall indeed be auspiciousness for all people in every respect.
In Kārttika there shall be knowledge, and in Mārgaśīrṣa happiness also occurs;
in Pauṣa there is a loss of knowledge, while in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence.

"Prosperity shall also occur in Phālguna; one should avoid the intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Thus, because of the statement in the *Śivayāmala*, "The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) who gives the mantra shall obtain [its fruit] for seven births," the month of Āśvina—though prescribed for initiation (*dīkṣā*)—is nonetheless prohibited.
The fourteenth day of the month of Māgha is Mahābalacaturdaśī, also known as Śivarātri. Likewise, in the *Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā*:
"Initiation during the autumn season or in Vaiśākha yields the most excellent fruit;
it is also excellent in Mārgaśīrṣa and Phālguna, while in Jyeṣṭha it is merely middling. (1)
In the month of Māgha it bestows auspiciousness; in the month of Āṣāḍha it is wicked;
in Śrāvaṇa it grants joy; and in Pauṣa and Bhādrapada it is censured.

Thus it is said. And likewise in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O fair-faced one, on an auspicious day and under an auspicious weekday during the bright fortnight, one should undertake the commencement of the mantra and other rites. Likewise in the *Kālottara*: "O Great Goddess, initiation should be performed by those desiring liberation during the dark fortnight, and likewise by those desiring the spiritual stages (*bhūmi*) during the bright fortnight. And likewise in the *Śaivāgama*:
The best of teachers should perform [the rite] during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight;
in the bright fortnight there shall be all prosperity, while in the dark fortnight it will be middling.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), in the *Cintāmaṇi*:
"Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, as well as Puṣya and the three Uttarās, Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Anurādhā, Viśākhā, and Dhaniṣṭhā. (1)
"Punarvasu and Revatī are considered the best for initiation. Thus [it is said]. Maitra is Anurādhā. Likewise, in the *Kāmadhenu*:
"Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, as well as Puṣya and Hastaka..."
Svāti, Ārdrā, Revatī, and likewise the three Uttarās.
"These are the auspicious lunar mansions for initiation, O fair-faced one.
Now, the prohibited ones according to the *Piṅgalāmata* are:
"In Kṛttikā there is mental distress, and in Bharaṇī there is great calamity."
If it occurs in Pūrvā, the king should inflict punishment; if in Maghā, he should predict death. || 1 ||
One should know that there will be quarrels under Mūla; Jyeṣṭhā brings about loss;
fear is proclaimed for Pūrvāṣāḍhā; and Śravaṇa bestows many diseases.
"Śatabhiṣā brings agitation, while Bhādrapadā causes distress.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the lunar days (tithis):
the full moon, the fifth, the second, and likewise the seventh.
The thirteenth and the tenth lunar days are also praised, for they grant all desires. || 1 ||
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā* (p. 242):
"The second and the seventh [lunar days] are excellent; the sixth is censured in all cases.
It may be performed on the twelfth or even on the thirteenth."
Thus, in the *Vijayamālinītantra*: "The fifth, the eleventh, the seventh, and the thirteenth of the bright fortnight, as well as the tenth and especially the twelfth. (1)
Thus it is stated in the Ratnasāgara:
"The third lunar day is prescribed for daily practice; the sixth is censured in all cases.
On the seventh there shall be the gain of wealth, and on the eighth, the destruction of one's teacher. (1)
On the ninth day there will be loss of wealth; the tenth day bestows happiness;
on the eleventh day there shall be gain of money and cattle.
On the twelfth day there shall be gain of wealth; on the thirteenth, constant prosperity;
on the fourteenth, loss of disciples; but the full moon day bestows success.

"On the new moon day (amāvāsyā) there shall be the loss of a son; the first lunar day (pratipad) destroys prosperity. Thus it is said. Now, regarding specific lunar days for specific deities, the *Kālottara* states: "The full moon day is prescribed for Brahmā, and the twelfth day (dvādaśī) for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu)."
The fourteenth day is said to belong to Śiva, while the thirteenth is said to belong to Speech.
The second, however, is said to belong to Śrī, and the third to Pārvatī;
the fourth belongs to Gaṇanātha, while the seventh is said to belong to Bhānu.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the days for the true essence of the mantra:
"The commencement of the mantra should take place on a Sunday during the bright fortnight, especially on a Wednesday or Thursday;
on a Saturday there is death, on a Tuesday there is decay, and on a Monday it is fruitless in all cases. (1)
Thus it is said in the Uttaratantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, [the initiation] should be performed on a Sunday, Thursday, Wednesday, or Friday;
having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, the wise teacher should bestow the mantra. (1)

Thus, in the *Vijayamālinītantra*: "Under the Sun one obtains intelligence; under Venus, the arrival of wealth; under Mercury, freedom from affliction; and under Jupiter, one shall be endowed with sons. (1)
"Death occurs under Saturn and Mars, while ignorance occurs under the Moon;
having understood this, O lady of beautiful hips, the wise teacher should bestow initiation. (2)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the *yogas*, they are stated in the *Tantraratnāvalī*:
"The *yogas* are Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and likewise Śobhana; Sukarman, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa. (1)
"Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Aindra are the sixteen.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, regarding the yogas therein, Vasiṣṭha states: "Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the first lunar day, Kṛttikā on the fifth," and so forth.
Pūrvābhādrapadā is the sixth, and likewise Rohiṇī is the tenth. || 1 ||
The Sarpa constellation on the twelfth day, and Āryamaṇa on the thirteenth—these are known as Nakṣatralumpas, and they bring destruction even to the gods. (2)

Thus [it is said]. The asterism of the serpent is Āśleṣā; Uttarāphālgunī is Āryamaṇa. Now, regarding the astronomical treatises (jyotiṣaśāstra), they declare the auspicious *karaṇas*, especially for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
One should especially avoid Śakuni and the other [yogas], as well as Viṣṭi. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of Kīṭa, Tughna, Catuṣpada, and Nāga is intended. Now, regarding the ascendants (lagna) in another tantra:
"The commencement of a mantra and so forth in Aries shall bestow wealth and grain."
In Vṛṣa one meets death; in Mithuna there is the loss of offspring. || 1 ||
In Cancer there shall be all success; in Leo, the destruction of clouds;
Virgo constantly bestows fortune; and in Libra, all accomplishments. || 2 ||
In Scorpio there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; Sagittarius brings about the destruction of knowledge;
Capricorn is said to bestow sons; and Aquarius grants the abundance of wealth. (3)
"Pisces always bestows suffering; such is the fruit of the zodiac signs, O beloved.
And likewise in the Rudrayāmala:
"In Pisces, Leo, Sagittarius, and Taurus, loss is produced."
In Aries there shall be all prosperity, and Virgo shall be a bestower of jewels. || 1 ||
In Libra there shall be wealth and grain; in Scorpio, all perfections;
in Capricorn, the gain of sons; and in Aquarius, an abundance of cattle.
In Gemini there shall be the destruction of cattle; Cancer is considered to bestow sovereignty.
Having thus understood the results of the ascendant, the wise teacher should impart the mantra. (3)
One should avoid Taurus, Pisces, Sagittarius, and Leo as ascendants;
however, those beginning with Virgo always bestow happiness, auspiciousness, and grant all accomplishments. (4)
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the auspicious and inauspicious results for planets situated in specific houses from the time of initiation (dīkṣālagna):
Malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses are auspicious, as are benefic planets situated in the angles (kendras) and the trines (trikoṇas).
In the case of initiation (dīkṣā), however, all [planets] situated in the eighth house (randhra) are auspicious, yet they cause total destruction [if otherwise unfavorable]. || 1 ||

Thus: *Āya* is the eleventh house. The ascendant (lagna), fourth, seventh, and tenth houses are designated as *kendras*; the fifth and ninth houses are designated as *trikoṇas*. The Sun, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, Mars, and Mercury joined with malefic planets, as well as the waning Moon (*kṣīṇaśaśī*), are considered malefic (*pāpa*).
Jupiter, Venus, the sinless Mercury, and the full Moon are auspicious; so too are all nine planets when situated in the sixth or eighth house (the *randhra*). Now, the results for the Moon:

the Moon situated in the first, third, sixth, seventh, eleventh, or tenth house is considered to bestow auspicious results. However, the Moon situated in the second, twelfth, eighth, fifth, or fourth house is [inauspicious].
[The day] is considered inauspicious. Now, regarding the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama:

"When the asterism is auspicious and facing downwards, and especially when the moon is pure; during the dark fortnight, one should employ the strength of the lunar mansions (*tārā*) and contemplate the first letter of one's own name. (1)
The morning period (prātaḥkāla) bestows dharma; the saṅgava period is remembered as bestowing sovereignty;
at midday there shall be the attainment of all perfections (sarvasiddhi); and in the evening it shall be beneficial in every respect. || 2 ||
The best of teachers have prohibited the imparting of mantras at night;
one should perform everything during the day, for that is remembered as the supreme bestower of success.
Thus [it is said]. As for the downward-facing constellations:
Mūla, Kṛttikā (Āgneya), Maghā, Pūrvā-phalgunī (Dvidaiva), Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā (Sārpa), and the three Pūrvās—this group of nine stars is indeed proclaimed by the astronomers to be downward-facing.

The excavation of ponds, wells, tanks, pits, and moats; the extraction of hidden treasures; the casting [of spells]; the entry into gambling houses and secret chambers; and the commencement of mathematical calculations—all these are successfully accomplished. || 1 ||

Thus [it is said]. Viśākhā belongs to two deities; the Śruti states that the deities of the Viśākhā nakṣatra are Indra and Agni. Now, regarding the specific time for initiation (dīkṣā), it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should undertake the commencement of mantras and other rites during an eclipse of the moon or the sun."
O Goddess of the gods, from the moment of grasping [the breath], time lasts for a period of seven days. || 1 ||

O Goddess of gods, on the auspicious Pavitra festival day, even if it falls on an inauspicious lunar day, one should not entertain doubts regarding the timing; likewise, [the rite must be performed] during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
"At a holy pilgrimage site, at Kurukṣetra, and at the four seats of the Goddess.
Likewise, in the *Ratnasāgara*:
"At a sacred ford, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, and on the Ananta and Vāmana parvans."
One performing the initiation of mantra (mantradīkṣā) need not purify the month, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and so forth.
Thus it is said: "In this regard, although at the time of a solar eclipse no other [auspicious occasion] need be sought, for there is never another time equal to the time of a solar eclipse. (1)
In that regard, whatever is performed there shall all yield infinite fruit;
on the solar festival (sūryaparvan), there is no need for calculations regarding the month, lunar day, weekday, and so forth.
At that time, a person should give what is desired and receive [it] from the guru;
then the mantra’s accomplishment occurs swiftly, even without practice. || 3 ||

Thus, because we observe scriptural injunctions prescribing only solar eclipses for the *Cintāmaṇi* and *Kālikodbhava* [tantras], [it follows that]: "But the initiation performed during a lunar eclipse, the initiation of forest-dwellers, or the initiation of Janaka—these result in poverty for seven births. (1)
Thus, because of the observation of the prohibition against initiation during a lunar eclipse in the *Yoginītantra*,
and because of the previously cited prohibition regarding mantras at night,
the time of a solar eclipse is also [excluded] by virtue of its commonality with eclipses generally, according to the previously cited statement from the *Śivayāmala*.
It should be understood that because it is prohibited, [the public recitation of mantras] is not entirely commendable; however:
"The mere speaking of a mantra at a lunar or solar eclipse, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva—that is called 'instruction' (upadeśa). (1)

Thus, according to the words of Kālikodbhava, [initiation] is harmful for those who have been duly initiated into other mantras. Now, regarding the ritual initiation (*kriyāvatī dīkṣā*) in the *Uttaratantra*:
"Now I shall explain the procedure for initiations for one desiring the mantras."
Without which indeed the fruits of all mantras cannot be obtained. || 1 ||
These [initiations] bestow self-attainment and also destroy misdeeds; therefore, they are called *dīkṣās* by those who investigate the true nature of reality. (2)

And these four auspicious bestowers of knowledge have been described in sequence: those consisting of ritual action, those consisting of sound, those consisting of the digits (kalās), and those consisting of piercing (vedha). || 3 ||
Thus [it is said] in the *Pañcamīśvarītantra*:

"Having first caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) preceded by the word 'svasti', surrounded by friends and accompanied by the sounds of five musical instruments and the resonance of the Vedas... (1).
Having gone to the teacher’s house, the disciple, having bowed to the teacher’s sandals and presented the materials for the formal request, should make a solemn resolve and choose the teacher.
"Having proclaimed that for the sake of receiving such-and-such a mantra, O best of the twice-born, I choose you as my guru; thus do I appoint you. (3)

Having spoken thus, the disciple should choose [the teacher], saying, "I am chosen. Then the teacher should say, "Perform the duties of a teacher as is appropriate," and the disciple should reply, "I shall do so."
Having uttered "I shall perform [the rite]," preceded by the five musical instruments,
the Guru should then proceed to the sacrificial hall accompanied by the disciple.
Having performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite, the disciple, devoted with supreme faith,
[should honor him] with ornaments such as necklaces, earrings, armlets, rings, bracelets, and other finery.
With golden sacred threads and offerings of honey-mixture according to the prescribed rite, and with costly garments, betel-leaf, fruits, flowers, and fragrant scents; || 7 ||
Having honored one who is free from deceit, he should duly choose him as his preceptor;
likewise, having honored the officiating priests, he should choose them in the number prescribed.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the procedure for the *madhuparka* is stated in the *Ḍāmara*:
"I shall describe to you the procedure for the *madhuparka* exactly as it is: the seats made of *śrīparṇī* wood should be one cubit (*hasta*) in measure. (1)
The braids, consisting of twenty-seven blades of darbha grass, should be equal in length and each eight finger-breadths in height, adorned at their tips with knots.
In all sacrifices, the characteristics for the sacrificial seat have been proclaimed;
there should be copper basins filled with pleasantly warm water for the purpose of washing the feet.
Conch shells, filled with water for the offering of the *arghya* and provided with fragrance, flowers,
and *dūrvā* grass, should be placed separately.
A water-pot of fine copper filled with water for sipping (ācamana), and bronze vessels with joined lids filled with curds and other ingredients for the honey-mixture (madhuparka). || 5 ||
One should collect great and worthy substances, fine ornaments such as rings and the like,
peacock-feather umbrellas, and turbans.
One should bring sandals there, adorned with leather ornaments;
furthermore, whatever else has been prescribed in the Smṛti regarding the worship with Madhuparka should also be performed.
By performing that, one obtains a fruit comparable to the honor paid at a great sacrifice;
it is traditionally taught that the honoring of other Brahmins with madhuparka is likewise meritorious.
One who possesses true devotion should give twice that amount to the preceptor with great devotion;
for in this [rite], the worship of the teacher is equal to that of all other brahmins combined.
In that sacrifice, the fruit was meager, like the earth during a drought;
yet the lord of preceptors, having bathed according to the injunctions, performed his daily rites.
Maintaining silence and adorned with ornaments, he should proceed toward the sacrificial hall;
the preceptor, having seated him on an excellent seat on the preceding day, [should perform the rites]. (11)
Having consecrated the disciple with the root mantra, he should give him a tooth-stick;
having cleansed his teeth, [the disciple] should stand before a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in size.
One should worship in the square and then the Guru should examine it:
at the front of the northeast there is the attainment of knowledge; at the front of the east, excellent prosperity.
In the southeast there is mental anguish; in the south, the loss of kinsmen;
in the southwest, the fear of death; and in the west, mental sorrow. (14)
If it falls toward the northeast, there is agitation; if toward the north, it brings happiness.
If it falls upon an inauspicious spot, one should perform an expiatory rite.
The expiation will be explained later in the section on *puraścaraṇa*.
Then the best of teachers should perform an examination of the dream;
for an initiation following a cruel dream is considered inferior, while one following a non-cruel dream is regarded as middling.

Initiation preceded by an excellent dream is considered the most supreme of all. The characteristics of dreams, the manner of reporting them, and the expiation for bad dreams will be explained later in the section on *puraścaraṇa*.
Having reflected thus, the Guru should perform worship before him;
having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) there and having prepared the general offering of water (sāmānyārghya).
Having sprinkled [the area] with water for the *arghya* offering, one should perform the worship of the door;
thereafter, the preceptor [should dispel] divine obstacles by means of a visual inspection.
Then he should dispel those situated in the intermediate space with missiles and water;
thereafter, having diligently dispelled the terrestrial beings with three kicks of his heels.
Having slightly contracted his limb while touching a branch extending to the left,
he clears the way for the spirits being driven out by moving toward the right.

"Then one should enter the sacrificial pavilion with the right foot. Thus it is said. The worship of the door will now be described. Entry preceded by the right foot pertains to the male deity (puṃdaivata);
however, in the case of the Śākta tradition, it is indeed preceded by the left foot, keeping the left foot foremost.
"One should enter the sacrificial pavilion," according to the statement in the *Tripurārṇava*. Likewise: (p.
245) "One should worship Brahmā and Vāstvadhiśa in the south-western direction, having well-sprinkled the site of sacrifice with water for the *arghya* offering and with products of the cow. (21)
Then, one should perform purification by means of gazing and other rites up to the four doors;
having gazed [at it] with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle it with the weapon mantra.

One should perform the striking with the Astra-mantra and then sprinkle with the Kavaca-mantra; having adorned it with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, one should [sprinkle] seven times with the Astra-mantra.
The mantra-practitioner should scatter sandalwood, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice, and kuśa grass,
along with water, over the mandala, for these indeed destroy all obstacles.
The mantra-practitioner should purify them with a handful of *darbha* grass using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*);
then, for the sake of a seat, he should place them in the northeast with the *vārddhānī* vessel.
Then, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) and having gratified them with effort,
one should subsequently draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala upon the altar.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the *talla* according to all the tantras: the preceptor, having smeared the center of the altar with cow dung... (27)
By means of the sequence of procedure previously described, one should fashion a square,
provided with four compartments and adorned with diagonal lines (karṇasūtra).
Therein, within the four groups of squares, there should be four lines;
in the centers of the corner squares, fish-like figures are seen as follows. (29)
The knower of mantras should lay down four lines for these crocodiles: one pair situated in the directions of Indra and Varuṇa, and two pairs situated in the directions of Soma and Yama.
Likewise, one should draw lines extending east-west and again north-south; there, one should cast the threads as before, starting from the Makara signs.
Just as two hundred and fifty-six beautiful verses appear again, one should likewise cause these very sūtras to be revealed.
One should fashion a lotus in the center using thirty-six squares;
outside of that, one should arrange a pedestal (pīṭha) all around in a single row.
Outside of that, the arrangement of the pathway (vīthī) is said to be by means of two rows;
then, by another pair of rows, the door-ornamentation (dvāraśobhā) is provided according to the rule.
The knower of mantras should also arrange the ornaments and the corners;
now I shall describe, according to the rule, the sequence for drawing the lotus.
One should set aside the twelfth part produced from the location of the lotus;
then, one should properly construct three circles in the center according to the prescribed rule.
One should draw the pericarp with the middle circle, the filaments with the second [circle],
and the petals with the final circle, leaving out one part for the tips of the petals.
Having established the measurement for the center of the final circle upon the tips of the filaments, one should place half-moons on the sides.
Having drawn [the lines] and performed the laying out of the threads connected at the joints,
the wise practitioner should properly draw a circle according to the measurement of the tips of the petals.
The knower of the ritual procedure should, according to the rules, draw the tips of the petals on the outside of the middle line of the circle, using one [unit of measurement] for each side.
The preceptor should place two filaments at the bases of each petal;
for this is declared everywhere in the scriptures to be the "universal lotus. (41)
One should fashion the legs of the pedestal in the corners using three squares each; thereafter, one should construct the body-parts of the pedestal with the remaining squares.
Having properly unified the two rows of paths, one should sweep them;
likewise, each side of the door [should be cleared] with two squares and one square respectively.
From this, beauty arises through three squares on one side;
then, with six squares, one should fashion the secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) and the corners.
One should adorn this mandala with powders of five colors;
the powder of turmeric (niśā) is yellow, while that produced from rice is known to be white.
Red is declared to be saffron-dyed; the wise say black is that produced from the burning of parched grain; and dark-blue is that arising from the leaves of the wood-apple tree.
Five colors are prescribed for the ritual of the initiation maṇḍala;
the lines, one finger-breadth in measurement, are white and as high as a star.
*Tāra* means expansion.
In the rite of the mandala, all the boundary lines should be made white;
then, one should fill the pericarp with yellow-colored powder. (48)
The knower of mantras should fill the filaments with red color, the petals with white color, and the joints with dark-colored pollen.
Alternatively, the practitioner of mantra should fill the pericarp with yellow [pigment],
the filaments with yellow-red, and the parts of the pedestal with white.
In the middle of the four crossroads of the streets, one should fashion wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī),
which are heart-pleasing and adorned with the forms of leaves, roots, and fruits.
The skillful preceptor should then color those [lines] with powders of various colors;
thereafter, he should fill the four doors with white powder.
Its splendor is enhanced by red color, and it is further adorned with yellow;
the corners are black, and beyond that are three lines.
One should decorate it in sequence with white, reddish-brown, and black powders;
this is the universal, most excellent *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Other mandalas will also be described here incidentally;
for now, however, one should cast the lines upon the previously mentioned square.
p. 246) As long as there may be one hundred and forty compartments, in the center of that, a beautiful lotus consisting of thirty-six [squares] should be provided with four [additional squares]. (56)
The pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of a single row; no pathway (vīthī) is seen here.
The beauty of the doors (dvāraśobhā) should be as before, but there is indeed no secondary beauty (upaśobhā) here.
One should likewise form the corners with six squares according to the prescribed method;
all else should be executed auspiciously, as described for the previously mentioned mandala.
This other maṇḍala, moreover, is square and very beautiful;
one should lay down the thread gradually until all the squares are formed on every side. (59)
There should be sixty-four squares in the middle of that;
then one should draw a lotus with four cells, and again surround it.
At the ends of the four pathways within the mandala and in the directions,
the best of mantra-knowers should place lotuses upon the four squares.
The wise one should divide the four sets of four squares located in the intermediate directions;
he should erase them until sixteen squares have been formed.
In this manner, one should fill [the design] with white, yellow, red, and blue powders until the form of the svastikas becomes manifest.
One should likewise arrange another hundred svastikas as before;
this mandala, indeed, is called the "nine-naved" (navanābha) and is most beautiful.
By this very method, there shall be the unsurpassed mandala named Svastika, consisting of five lotuses, which bestows the fruits of all desires. (65)
During initiation, or at a great gift-offering, or during the worship of the gods, vows, and so forth,
a wise person should perform one or another [of these rites] within this very maṇḍala.
Having thus drawn the mandala, the Guru should then sit upon a seat on the altar, facing east, upon one of the aforementioned [seats].
Seated in the bound lotus posture, observing silence, with body erect and senses subdued, the Lord of Guides, having arranged the articles for worship, [should proceed]. (68)
One should place an auspicious water-pot on the right and the left side,
filled with fragrant water for the purpose of washing the hands.
Then, having arranged the vessel, the knower of mantras should light auspicious lamps;
he should place a fan, a mirror, an umbrella, and chowries in the various directions.
One should consecrate all of those according to the procedure to be described hereafter;
then, having performed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the wise practitioner should perform the three claps of the palms (*tālatraya*).
The practitioner, being composed, should perform the binding of the directions with the Śara mantra; he should then protect that [space] on all sides with the Mahas-mantra.

Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should perform the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana) and thereafter carry out the ritual assignments (nyāsa) and other rites.
Then the preceptor should place the Ṛṣi upon the head, place the Chandas within the mouth, and place the Deity of the root mantra in the heart. (74)
The practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of six limbs or five limbs according to the prescribed rule;
for whichever mantra has only five limbs, its "eye" is omitted.
For one whose mind is devoid of limbs, those very [limbs] are fashioned by him;
he should perform the various ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the method prescribed for each respective mantra. (76)
One should conceive of the yoga-pīṭha of one's own mantra within one's body;
then, upon that pīṭha which is identical with the body, one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra. (77)
Then, having displayed the mudrās, one should place the supreme arghya;
thereafter, one should place the prokṣaṇī vessel filled with water on the right.

There, the knower of mantras should place a very small amount of water from a conch shell to the north of that, as well as water for washing the feet, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Then, with a concentrated mind, the practitioner, using water consecrated by the root-mantra,
should sprinkle himself, the mandala, and all other ritual implements and materials.

The best of preceptors, a knower of mantras, having worshipped the seat of yoga according to the method of ritual placement (nyāsa), should sprinkle his own body with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. 81.
Then, having reached the end of the *pīṭha*, one should worship one's chosen deity there;
thereafter, identifying oneself with the deity, one should perform five handfuls of beautiful flowers.
One should worship [the deity] on the head, the heart, the base, the feet, and all the limbs with sandalwood and other offerings, excluding the food offering (naivedya). || 83 ||
One should complete all the remaining services with whatever rites are commanded by the Guru;
one should perform all of this using the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having set aside the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and refilling it as before,
the Guru should worship the maṇḍala with ritual services such as sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should first fill the pericarp with *śāli* rice, then with *taṇḍula* rice;
one should place *darbha* grass upon these, and then a bundle of *kūrca* grass together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Long blades of kuśa grass, twenty-seven in number, with their roots cut off and tied at the tips with a *brahmagranthi* knot, are here called a *kūrca*.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra).
Therein, one should place a pitcher made of gold or other materials, free from any cracks.
It is encircled on all sides externally by a thread consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), and it is thoroughly fumigated in the center with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. || 89 ||
The most excellent preceptor should firmly establish [the vessel] according to the rules for recitation;
having placed nine gems into the jar, he should then place a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) on top.
One should place together dūrvā grass and sandalwood, along with unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as blue flowers, lapis lazuli, coral, and pearls.
Then the preceptor, the most excellent knower of the tantras, [should offer] emeralds, diamonds, hessonite, rubies, and pearls as jewels. (92)

The practitioner of mantra, mentally reciting the Mātṛkā from the sequence beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, and finally reciting the root mantra while contemplating the unity of the self [with it], [should perform the rite]. (93)
The best of practitioners should contemplate the breaking of the jar’s pedestal;
immediately thereafter, he should fill it with the decoction of fifty medicinal herbs.
With decoctions of the bark of milk-exuding trees, or with the bark of the Brahmabhūruṭ (Ficus religiosa), or with auspicious waters scented with fragrant paste, flowers, and the like. || 95 ||
Having filled the conch with water such as decoctions and the like,
the mantra-practitioner should stir within it the auspicious eight fragrances, which bestow all perfections.
Having invoked all the *kalās*, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite;
then, one should pour the water from the conch—which embodies the deities of the *kalās*—into the jar.
With sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and yellow pigment (rocanā), along with hlika, jaṭāmāṃsī, and saṭī, [one should perform] the rite originating from Śakti. 98.
"One should employ this auspicious eightfold perfume for subjugation (*vaśya*) in connection with the *śakti* mantras.
Thus it is said. *Kāśmīra* is saffron (*kuṅkuma*). *Sihlaka* is resin of the *śilā* tree. *Saṭī* is *kacora*.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *cora*, saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *kapī* [are the ingredients].
"The eightfold fragrance of Śakti is considered [to consist of these]," according to the statement in the *Śāradātilaka*.
"Hrīvera, candana, kuṣṭha, aguru, kuṅkuma, mura, sevyaka, and jaṭāmāṃsī—this is declared to be the Vaiṣṇava [fragrance]. (1)
*Hrīvera* is *bālaka*. *Sevya* is *kumudamūla* (lotus root). *Sura* is well known as *moraharī*.
*Murā*, *gandhavatī*, *daityā*, *gandhāḍhyā*, *gandhamādinī*, *surabhi*, *bhūtagandhā*, *kuṭhī*, and *gandhakuṭhī* are recorded as synonyms. (1)
Because the word *ekāṅgī* has various meanings, it is specifically by the word *mura* that it is denoted; for in common worldly usage, *ekāṅgī* is well known as a synonym for *charvū*.
Water, saffron, kuṣṭha, red sandalwood,
sandalwood, tamāla, agallochum, and camphor constitute the eight-fold fragrance (aṣṭagandha) of Śambhu.
Water is the child.
Through the conjunction of the eight perfumes and by the power of the preceptor, the water in the jar becomes endowed with power; of this there is no doubt. (99)
First, one should worship the ten digits (kalās) associated with Fire;
immediately after that, one should worship the twelve solar digits (kalās).
Thereafter, the most excellent guru should worship the sixteen lunar digits (kalās).
These digits, arising from the divisions beginning with the Vedas, are joined with fifty [letters]. || 101 ||

Having brought them near and worshipped them thoroughly, the practitioner of mantra should then worship these five verses as well, in their proper sequence, with one verse placed at intervals between them.
Having uttered the mantra of the self, one should recite the word *śuciṣat*;
then the mantra-word ending in *vasu*, and thereafter the word *ṛkṣasad*. (103)
Having uttered "padaṃ te," "vediṣade," "atithiḥ," and "dupade," one should then say "tataḥ," utter "roṇasatpadam," and then say "nṛṣadvarapade. || 104 ||
One should say "sadṛtasat," "vyomasat," and "abjā"; one should say "gopadam. One should say "jā" and "ṛtajā"; from this, one should utter the word "adrijā. (105)
Having uttered the seventh vowel together with the bindu, one should say "Āṣāḍhin";
having spoken the word "bṛhat" at the end, the first mantra is thus declared. (106)
Thus: the self-mantra is *haṃsa*. The seventh vowel is the letter *ṛ*. *Āṣāḍhī* is the letter *ta*. The other words are their own forms. Likewise:
"The red one (*lohita*) joined with fire (*vahni*), then *pūtanā*, *dvi*, and *antika*."
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu praised him afterwards and spoke words of praise regarding his heroic power.
Then one should recite: "And Bhīma, who wanders on the earth and dwells in the mountains," followed by: "Upon whose three broad strides [the worlds rest] and above whose steps. (108)
One should utter the word *kṣiyanti*, then say *padam*, and thereafter *bhuvanāni*.
After that comes *toyastho mādhavaḥ*, and the end should be joined with *tāyaśānti*. (109)

The second Manu has been declared; now the third is being proclaimed. *Lohita* is the syllable *pa*; *vahni* is the syllable *ra*. By that [is formed] *pra*. *Pūtanā* is the syllable *ta*. *Toya* is the syllable *va*; situated therein is *mādhava*, which is the syllable *i*. By that [is formed] *vi*. *Vāntam* is *śa*. *Toya* is *va*. *Śānti* is *ā*. By that [is formed] *śvā*. The other words are as follows.
Their own essential natures.

The word ending in *ṇa* is *agni*, that ending in *mān* is *upāntyasya*; *kalāyuk* is the third [word], and *caturmukhaḥ* together with the half-moon (*sacandrārdhaḥ*) follows; then there is *yajāmahe*. (110)
Then there arises a supreme fragrance, nourishment, and growth;
thereafter, one should speak of the state as being like a cucumber [freed] from its bond. || 111 ||
One should utter the word *tyormukṣīya* followed by the word *pade*, and then the immortal word *amṛtāt*.
The letter *ta* ends in *ṇa* (i.e., *tṇa*), *agni* is the letter *ra*, and the letter *ma* ends in *ya* (i.e., *mya*). The penultimate digit (*kalā*) is the bindu.
By this [combination], the third part is the letter *va*; the four-faced one is the letter *ka*, and the half-moon is the bindu; by that, it is *kaṃ*. The others [are as follows].
The words are their own forms.
The fourth mantra, known as Gāyatrī-ātmā, is highly renowned in the world;
the Śālmalī tree situated in water is said to be joined with Sahaja, Āḍha, Anta, and Viṣṇu.
"Agni alone is proclaimed; one should utter the word 'yoni' as the kalpa-word.
Then, after the word 'tvaṣṭṛ', [one says] 'may he fashion the forms. (113)
"May Prajāpati sprinkle [the seed]"; "May Dhātṛ speak the word 'after'";
"May he place the embryo"—thus says Āṣāḍhī, joined with Padmanābha. (114)
