These are the five Vedic mantras; one should worship each of them individually. *Toya* is the syllable *va*; *śālmalī* is the syllable *i*. By that [is meant] *vi*. *Sahajā* is the syllable *ṣa*; *ḍhānta* is the syllable *ṇa*, joined with *viṣṇu* (the syllable *u*) and joined with the syllable *u*, thus forming *ṣṇu*. *Agnī* is the letter *ra* alone, without a vowel. *Āṣāḍhī* is the syllable *ta*.
Padmanābha is the letter *e*; by that, they are [so called].
Within the space between the digits (kalās) arising from the fivefold divisions of Tāra, the wise preceptor should first invoke the digits and subsequently cause them to become present.
Having stabilized the vital breaths, the best of practitioners should worship with perfumes and other offerings;
for wherever there is a rite of worship of the Kalās, it is indeed exactly like this.
The wise practitioner should worship the digits (kalās) arising from the five divisions of Tāra; having invoked the ten digits beginning with Sṛṣṭi and caused them to be present, [he should proceed].
Having recited the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," one should perform worship;
having performed the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃsthāpana), one should worship those Kalās.

In this manner, the wise practitioner should worship Jarā and the others, Tīkṣṇā and the others, Pītā and the others, as well as Nivṛtti and the others, according to the prescribed rules and by the stated method.
The letter A is said to be Akāra, and the letter U is Ukāra; the letter Ma consists of Bindu and Nāda.
These seven, including Śakti and Śānta, are declared to be the divisions of Dhruva.
These last two divisions have been described separately:
the letter *sa* with its power (*śakti*), and the letter *ha* ending in *s*.
Then, with the sprouts of the *rasāla*, *panasa*, and *pippala* trees...
[He was] entwined by the creepers of Sutrāman, through the desire for the Kalpa-tree.
The mantra-practitioner, being composed, should perform the installation of the jar;
thereafter, [he should place] an auspicious wheel together with unbroken rice grains and fruit.
The preeminent teacher, possessing clear intelligence, should take the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree and place them upon sprouts, according to his own judgment.
Then, having wrapped the jar with a pair of fine silk cloths,
the most excellent of gurus should likewise place the principal pitcher upon the altar.
Near the archways, starting from the east and proceeding in order,
one should draw a mandala as before and a beautiful eight-petaled lotus.
Having established the jars upon them according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the preceptor should worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vākpati, and Vighneśa within them.
Having established the water-pots (kumbhas) in the corners beginning with the southeast as before—
namely Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala— 127.

Having worshipped [the fire], one should then worship Indra and the other deities starting from the southeast corner; in the eight jars located in the east and the other directions, one should worship them with their respective Vedic mantras.
Furthermore, one should worship the elephants of the directions in the pitchers starting from the east:
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana.
The preceptor, having gone again to the altar and sat upon his own seat, [worships] Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka. (130)
Having intentionally [visualized] the form with the root mantra, the supreme guru, having invoked the chosen deity into that form, should worship it. || 131 ||
Then, having remembered the root mantra, the practitioner should properly draw forth the consciousness through the path of the channels and cause it to emerge from the tip of the nose.
Then the Guru, having raised the light from the lotus of the Mother (mātṛkā) within his joined palms—which is adorned with flowers—up to the top of the head, should invoke it into that [lotus]. 133.

First is the establishment (saṃsthāpana), then the bringing near (sannidhāna); then the complete restraint (sannirodha), as well as the ritual identification (sakalīkaraṇa) and the veiling (avaguṇṭhana). || 134 ||

The nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*) by means of their respective mudrās, and the complete confinement (*sannirodha*); by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it should also be understood that the manifestation before one’s eyes (*sammukhīkaraṇa*) is included.
Then, one should perform the rites in sequence and arrange the ritual services;
having arranged the services beginning with the seat and ending with the flowers. (135)

In the ritual procedures for each respective mantra, one should also perform the worship of the limbs and the enclosures as prescribed, followed at the very end by the worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons.
"Having thus performed the worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings...
(p. 249). In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"When the food offering has been made, then [one should perform] the mandala in due order around [it]."
The officiating priest should place vessels containing auspicious sprouts. || 1 ||
Thus it is said. Likewise:
"Having prepared an excellent sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the right side of the altar, having established and consecrated the fire, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite. (137)
There, having first offered oblations with the *praṇava* and then again with the *vyāhṛtis*,
the wise one should then offer oblations with the root mantra using sacrificial food mixed with clarified butter.
Having subsequently offered oblations twenty-five times with the *vyāhṛtis*,
and having worshipped her with sandalwood and other offerings, one should then unite her with the image on the pedestal.
Having dismissed the fire, one should offer the remaining milk-rice as an oblation (bali) to the attendants,
accompanied by sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Then, having removed that food offering, the wise one should cleanse that place;
he should worship again with the five services and then perform the ritual display.
Afterwards, one should offer an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and excellent betel-leaf;
by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "the umbrella and," both the mirror and the fan are also included.
The practitioner, being composed, should recite the root mantra one thousand times;
then, having offered that recitation to the deity, he should dedicate it for the sake of prosperity.
And here in the northeast direction, that *vikiro* which was previously established, along with a water-filled pitcher joined with gold and cloth; 143.
One should place and worship here the weapon-deity of terrible form,
who stands upon a lion in the western direction, wielding a sword and a shield.
Standing there and having worshipped it, he should then take hold of it and circumambulate it, walking inside while uttering: "Protect [me], O Lords of the World! (145).
Then, one should not meditate upon the deity with water that is not joined with the *nāla*;
rather, one should establish it in its own place and then worship it with the *phaṇa-mantra*.
Having sat down again, the best among those who know mantras should consecrate the weapon with perfumes and other offerings;
then, having properly prepared the fire, he should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with cow’s milk.

In a new vessel made of copper or other metal, having washed it with the *śara* mantra and then consecrated it with the root mantra, one should take grains of rice produced from the *śāli* variety. (148)
Reciting the mantra while counting by the measure of the lunar days (tithi), one should cast the arrow;
then, having covered the mouth of the vessel with a washed vessel.
Then, with the *huṃ* mantra and the root mantra, the supreme teacher, the Guru, facing eastward, should cook it; once it is cooked, he should pour the clarified butter over it.

Then, one should pour [the remainder] with ghee held in the *sruva* ladle while reciting the root mantra; having divided that [ghee] over *kuśa* grass spread out and consecrated by the *astra* mantra with the syllable *huṃ*.
One portion of the offering should be divided into three parts; the supreme part the knower of mantras should present to the deity and offer the next into the fire.
Then, together with his disciple, the guru should consume the remainder. 152.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the knower of mantras, having brought the disciple who has likewise sipped water, [gives him] a tooth-stick of the prescribed length, measuring a span (prādeśa), consecrated with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) as previously described.

Having purified the teeth, the preceptor should give them to the disciple; he should discard the washed [teeth-brush]. Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule, the mantra-practitioner, having secured this [disciple] by binding his topknot, should proceed.
One should lie down upon the sacrificial altar on a bed of kusha grass during the night together with this disciple; thus has the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) been described.

By the phrase "copper and so forth," the inclusion of earthenware is intended. Its characteristics have been stated by Kātyāyana: "A vessel made of clay or even of udumbara wood is recommended as a *caru*-pot, provided it is firm, neither too large nor too small at the mouth, and its height and width are equal to that of a sacrificial twig (*samidh*). (1)
Thus [it is said]: "The *samin* measure is the size of a span (*prādeśa*), neither more nor less than a span," according to the words of Kapila.
The "fifteen handfuls" (*tithiprasṛti*) refers to fifteen *prasṛtis*. The "arrow-sized mantra" (*śarāṇurastramantra*) [is used for] the rice grains that have been washed three times.
This was stated by Govila: "They say that one should wash the rice grains, which have been husked three times, three times for the sake of the gods."

"Skilled" means dexterous; by that [skill], it is as if cooked in a clockwise manner. "Thereafter, it is fit for the act of excision. Regarding "well-steamed": as stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, "Well-steamed, indeed, it is auspicious when not burnt and not hard."
It should not be cooked too loosely, nor should it be devoid of flavor. || 1 ||
The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: "In that which has been thus defined and consecrated with ghee, one should cause [the fire] to descend by means of the *huṃ*-mantra.

Here, in the phrases beginning with "by means of the *huṃ*-mantra," one should understand the armor-mantras (*kavaca-mantra*), weapon-mantras (*astra-mantra*), and so forth, as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*); it does not mean merely the syllable *huṃ* or the syllable *phaṭ*. Now, regarding the installation of the fire (*agnisthāpana*), [it is stated] in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
If, however, at the time of beginning the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have not been performed,
then all of them must indeed be performed in their proper sequence once it has been completed.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Uttaratantro*:

"Next, I shall describe the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*), which is approved by all the Āgamas, performed in a well-consecrated sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of the Guru according to the rules and with the proper purificatory rites. (1)
These eighteen [mudrās] have been proclaimed by those expert in all the Āgamas;
having gazed upon them with the root-mantra (mūlāṇu) and then sprinkled them with the weapon-mantra (astrāṇu).
Having struck it with kusha grass and sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the digging with the Śara-mantra; by that same mantra, the extraction is prescribed.
One should perform the filling with the Heart-mantra and the sprinkling with the Weapon-mantra;
then, the pounding is prescribed with the Armor-mantra and the protection with the Armor-mantra.
Having contemplated the cleansing, the anointing, and its nature as a constituent part,
one should perform the tripling of the thread and fill it with the mantra ending in "namaḥ."
One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa with a blade of śara grass and the clearing of the crossroads with kuśa grass; then one should carry out the opening of the sense organs with the kavaca mantra.
When these purificatory rites have been performed, the preceptor should consecrate the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the oblation,
or alternatively, he should consecrate them with the four rites previously mentioned.
Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed with the arrow-mantra (*śara-mantra*), which has become the respective limb [of the deity], using the tips of the upturned hands.

Sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) is the pouring [of water] with the fist clenched. Filling (*uddhāra*) is with the earth from the excavation; filling (*pūraṇa*) is with other earth. And it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
Then, taking a portion of clay from the middle of the pit with the thumb and ring finger, one should fill it [with water] while reciting the Heart mantra.

"Sprinkling" (secanam) means merely sprinkling with a weapon, a missile-mantra (astramantra), or armor (varman); this term connects with the four [actions] that follow. As it was stated by Somaśambhu:
"Cleaning, smearing, and the visualization of the form of the digits (kalās)."
One should don the three sacred threads and sprinkle the armor with water while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.

Thus: "The conceptualization of the forms of the *kalās* refers to the conceptualization of the forms of the *kalās* of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. The 'making of three threads' (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*) is the fashioning of three threads. The worship with the Heart-mantra, however, pertains specifically to the three girdles. This has been stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
Then, having worshipped [the deity] externally and in the center with the *praṇava*,
one should worship the navel, which resembles the moon, according to that very same procedure.

"In the worship of the three girdles, one should worship the heart-mantra. Thus it is said. "Vajrīkaraṇa" (the making into a vajra) means contemplating [the site] as firm as a vajra. "Catuṣpatha" (the fourfold path) refers to the preparation of four paths in the four directions using kusha grass. However, in the *Śāradātilaka*, it is performed with the armor-mantra (*tanutreṇa*).
It has been stated that one should perform the "cleansing of the dice-board" (*akṣapāṭana*). Regarding the definition of the cleansing of the dice-board, it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:

"With blades of *darbha* grass whose tips are uncut and consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should adorn the entire series of walls of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*). (1)
Thus, this supreme consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) called *akṣapāṭa* should be performed exactly as described.
Regarding what was stated here—that it is "the opening of the senses" (*indriyāṇām udghāṭanam*)—that is precisely how it must be done.
Since the word *akṣa* denotes the sense organs (*indriya*), the meaning of *akṣapāṭana* is the opening of the sense organs.

Some say that the warding off of the *rākṣasas* is by means of the syllable *huṃ*. Others say it is the "piercing" (*pāṭana*) or pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the letters from the beginning to the end [of the alphabet]. He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*atha vā*).
By means of the first-mentioned acts of gazing, sprinkling, striking, and bathing, as well as [the repetition] three times each—
The lines should be drawn from east to north with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. "Northward" (*udagra*) means having their tips pointing toward the north because of their divine nature.
It is traditionally taught that for the lines whose tips face the east, the deities are Viṣṇu, Īśa (Śiva), and Vāsava (Indra) respectively;
and for the lines whose tips face the north, they are Brahmā, Sūrya (the Sun), and Indu (the Moon) in order. (1)
Regarding the inquiry as to where the commencement and where the conclusion lie in the drawing of these lines, it is stated in the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*:
"One should draw [the lines] starting from the south, with their heads directed eastward and extending toward the north."
One should draw it with its tip pointing upward, situated in the east, and beginning from the west.
With its top toward the east and its tip pointing eastward; with its tip toward the north, situated in front, and ending in the east. As stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"One should carefully scratch [the ground] with a blade of *darbha* grass using the king of mantras for weapons (*astrarāja*)."
On the ground, within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), starting from the southern direction, in due order: || 1 ||
One should draw three equal lines reaching as far as the northern limit,
starting from the western side and likewise extending as far as the eastern limit.

Thus [it is said]. Here, there is an option between the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra. Likewise: "Alternatively, one should draw the fire-abode (the corner) situated within a pair of fires in due order; the 'pair of fires' consists of two triangles, forming a hexagon and a fire-corner (triangle). Here, there is an option between the lines and the hexagon. Thus, in the *Yāmala*:

"O Goddess, one should draw a triangle there, surrounded by a hexagon. For this very reason, only a mere line is mentioned in the *Nāradapañcarātra*. In the *Śāradātilaka*: "Having sprinkled [the site] with the *varman* mantra, one should then worship the *yogapīṭha* with the *tāra* mantra. However, in the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*, it says: "One should sprinkle [it] with the *vāgbhava* mantra."

The word "or" (*vā*) mentioned [in the verse] refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). One should sprinkle with water and *kuśa* grass; for it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: "And having sprinkled with water and *kuśa* grass. Furthermore, in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"By means of the ritual of the *prāṇāgnihotra*, [one should perform it] in the place of the fire of the domestic hearth. The ritual of the *prāṇāgnihotra* is also described in that very same [work].

"The fire-pits (kuṇḍas) situated respectively in the directions of Indra, Varuṇa, the Moon, Yama, and the North are the Āvasathya, Sabhya, Āhavanīya, Anvāhārya, and Gārhapatya. Thus it is said. In the *Uttaratantro*: "Then, having sprinkled [the site] with the Praṇava, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha. The worship of the Yoga-pīṭha will be explained in the ritual application (*prayoga*).

There, having recollected Śakti—who is perfectly endowed with the menses, auspicious, beyond the reach of the senses, and whose essential nature is the soul of the entire universe—(he should worship her). || 1 ||
There, one should properly worship her together with Īśāna using perfumes and other offerings;
that Śakti with the Śakti-mantra, and Īśāna with the root-mantra.

Then, having properly worshipped the fire— whether produced from a jewel, from a forest, or born from the house of a noble twice-born man— the knower of the root mantra [should place] the sacrificial fire into the vessel.
Having brought [the portion] with the Astra-mantra, one should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) in the southwest;
the wise practitioner should then establish the portion for the gods in front with the root mantra.
Afterwards, one should consecrate that fire with the purificatory rites beginning with inspection;
having diligently invoked the splendor in the form of a lamp-flame.
Having meditated upon the unification of the earthly element with the fires of the stomach and the drop (bindu),
one should then unite its consciousness by means of the seed-syllable of fire.
Then, having consecrated it with the syllable Oṃ, rendered it into nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā,
protected it with the Śara-mantra, and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Then, having performed worship, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit three times to the right;
thereafter, with the syllable Om (praṇava), [one should place it] facing oneself in one's own pit.
There, at the goddess’s womb, the preceptor, with his knees touching the ground,
should meditate on it as the seed of Śiva and quickly cast the fire.
Then one should prepare water for sipping (ācamanīya) for both the Goddess and the God.
Regarding this, in the *Nāradapañcarātra* concerning the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice:
"In that [sacrifice], the power (*śakti*) of the one named Nārāyaṇa is characterized by lightning."
Having attained a state of form through Lakṣmī, she is the immortal one whose life is nectar.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
"Then one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, intoxicated with passion, and Lakṣmī, in her menses;
by the union of their coming together, the Fire comes into existence. (1)

Thus [it is said]. The Pot-born Sage (Agastya) also said: "One should contemplate there the fire born from the union of Lakṣmī—who is in her menses—and Bhadrā, the splendor of Nārāyaṇa, according to the manner of worldly intercourse. (1)
"In a vessel" means in a vessel made of copper or similar materials. As Atri has said:

"When [the fire] is covered by another vessel, such as one made of copper, one should perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) using a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or even a similar [vessel]. (1)
It is concealed by the *kavaca* mantra. As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

"O Pārvatī, having established the fire with the *astra* mantra and having covered it with the *kavaca*, one should discard the *kravyāda* portion toward the southwest (nairṛtya) with the *astra* mantra. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Likewise, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "In a metallic vessel, or a copper vessel, or even in a new earthen one. By the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*govālīvardanyāya*), the term "metallic" (*taijasa*) refers to anything other than copper. By this [it is meant]:
"In a shallow dish, or a broken vessel, or in a skull, or even on a firebrand..."
One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire, for it brings about the fear of loss of health.
Thus, the ancient statement recorded in the *Sarasvatīsāra* refers specifically to earthen vessels (*mṛtpātra*), because of the mention of the word "new" (*abhinava*).

However, in the *Bhairavītantra*, it is stated: "The practitioner of mantra should thus place his own face upon the womb, and afterwards [place it] with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). In this regard, there is an option between the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the root-mantra. [Regarding] the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*):

Thus: the *bindu* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); because it consists of both fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*), the fire arising from it is *vaidava*. The earthly [fire] is *bhauma*. One should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*. For it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: "Then one should perform the immortalization of the fire with the water-seed-syllable (*sa-binduka-jala-bīja*). With the arrow, which is the weapon-mantra (*astra*). As stated in the *Uttaratantro*:
Having uttered the words *cit piṅgala*, followed by the pair *hana*, the pair *paca*, the pair *daha*, and *sarvajña*, one should then pronounce *ājñāpaya* twice and end with *ṭha*. (1)
"Having recited this mantra, one should then kindle the fire.
Thus [it is said]. *Dviṭha* is the exclamation *svāhā*. In the *Prapañcasāra* (p.
252): "I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations."
Golden-hued, stainless, blazing, and facing in all directions. || 1 ||
"With this mantra, one should attend upon the sacrificial fire while it is ablaze.
Here, the word *sarvajñam* takes the accusative case because it functions as a verbal object within the mantra; however, in the mantra itself, it should be understood as ending in the vocative case.
This is according to the statement of Dakṣiṇāmūrti: "O Omniscient One, give the command, svāhā! One should kindle [the fire] with kuśa grass at its mouth.

Or rather, one should kindle it with *kuśa* grass, according to the statement of Kumbhasambhava (Agastya): "Then one should kindle [it] with *kuśas*"; and also according to the statement of Kātyāyana: "One should blow upon the fire only with the mouth, for this [fire] was born from the mouth.
[Thus it is stated] in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Then one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the tongues of the Fire-god upon the body with mantras,
in sequence upon the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes.
All those [lines] on all the limbs will be described as being of three kinds:
golden, yellow, red, and indeed the very radiant black.
The seven tongues—Bahurūpā, Atiraktā, and Jihvā—are of the nature of sattva;
they are endowed with the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ya', preceded by the syllable 'oṃ' (analer) and followed by the bindu. || 3 ||

Thus: *anala* is the letter *ra*; *īra* is the letter *ya*; *arghi* is the letter *ū*. This sequence is for the purpose of extracting the seed-syllables (*bījoddhāra*). However, in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it is as follows:
[one should place them] in order upon the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes.
One should place her, who possesses many forms and has extremely red extremities, upon all the limbs.
According to this statement from the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, one should install the Bahurūpa-mantra upon all the limbs. In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The practitioner of mantra should again duly install the limbs of Fire in sequence:
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭha, and Puruṣa. (1)
One should duly assign the eight limb-mantras and the eight forms (mūrtis), which are proclaimed as Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara.
The most excellent of teachers should duly place [the mantras] in a clockwise direction upon the head, shoulders, sides, nape, hips, flanks, and shoulders. (3)
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, the one known as Aśvodaraja, and Vaiśvānara; || 4 ||
Kaumāratejas, as well as those called Viśvadevamukha and the rest—these are the eight forms of Fire; [the names] for Agni are preceded by the word "Agni" [as a prefix]. (5)

"Beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*" means that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) by proceeding clockwise, starting from the head, following the sequence beginning with the left shoulder and ending at the right shoulder. Some say "anus" (*andhu*) refers to the "private part" (*liṅga*).
The word "mouth" (*mukha*) is connected to each [term]. It is said: "He shall possess the splendor of youth, be the universal mouth, and likewise the mouth of the deity."
According to the statement in the *Śāradātilaka*: "In the *Uttaratantro*, it is said:
'Having sprinkled [the site] with pure water in a clockwise direction, one should then [place] four blades of *darbha* grass upon the girdle (*mekhalā*). (1)

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] around according to the sequence of the directions, the knower of the Self, excluding the eastern direction, should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) in the cardinal points; there he should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.

"One should surround the fire with four *darbha* blades whose tips point east and north; that is, with *darbha* grasses having their tips pointing east and north," according to the statement in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*. "Then one should surround the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with *darbha* grasses whose tips point east and whose tips point toward the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the north)," according to the statement in the *Bhairavītantra*.

In a pit with three girdles (*trimekhalakuṇḍa*), the scattering of the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be performed upon the middle girdle. As it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"In a pit with a single girdle, one should scatter [the grass] beneath the girdle."
On the second [day] it has two ridges, and on the middle [day] it has three ridges.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the stalk exists by being attached to the western girdle, how can the spreading of grass and the casting of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) take place upon the middle girdle? In response to this doubt, the *Uttaratantra* states:
A wise man should likewise make an opening between the two girdles for the placement of the enclosing ring (paridhi) above the central girdle.

Thus: "One should spread sand upon the ground outside the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Regarding the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), Kātyāyana has stated: "He lays down the enclosing sticks—moist, from a single tree, arm-length in size, such as *palāśa*, *vaikaṅkata*, *kāśmarya*, *vailva*, and so forth. [This refers to] outside the sand on the sacrificial mound. Then...

One should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra "vinyaset paridhīn. The connection is that one should cast the enclosing sticks into the directions, excluding the eastern direction. Regarding the directions—namely the western, southern, and northern—the western one is the thickest and the middle one; the southern one is the smallest and the longest; and the northern one is the smallest and the shortest, according to the rule: "The western is the thickest and the middle; the southern is the smallest and the longest; the northern is the smallest and the shortest. [This applies] in the west.
The tips of the two [ladles] should be turned northward and eastward respectively. As stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"Then, water and likewise ghee [should be placed] in the pair of the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels."
Agastya describes the manner of placing those vessels:

"O Sage, having performed breath control according to the rules and having strewn [the ground] with other *kuśa* grasses, one should then proceed from the direction of the wind (the northwest) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. (1)
Having arranged the vessels according to the rule, the knower of mantras, using the ritual manual, sprinkles the fuel wood with water;
then, having purified them with the *pavitra*, he places them face upwards. (2)
Having sprinkled it again, one should lead the vessel forward, fill it with auspicious water,
offer unbroken grains (akṣata) and a purifier (pavitra), and having purified that [water], one should set it down.
In the northern direction, that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise;
then, having taken a little of the *praṇītā* water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, with those waters—
"One should sprinkle the collection of materials for the sacrificial implements with the root mantra.
Thus it is said. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Then, having prepared a seat for the fire, one should worship it."
The seat and the yoga-pīṭha will be described in the ritual application as follows: one should worship the tongues in the six corners and in the center, the limbs on the filaments,
the eight forms [of Viṣṇu] outside of that, and then the Fire-god in the center.
The wise one [should worship] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, according to the procedure to be described.
Thus, in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"In the six corners, in the center, with the tongues, and upon the filaments."
Then, on the outside, one should [worship] with the limb-mantras and the eight forms (mūrtis) in sequence.
Then, the practitioner of mantras should worship the fire in the center with that mantra, having uttered: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here! (vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha).
One should utter the word "lohitākṣa" followed by "sarvakarmāṇi";
one should say "sādhaya" at the end; this mantra concludes with the wife of Agni (svāhā). (3)
Thus, in the mantra, all words should be understood as being in the vocative case.

Bow down to the three-eyed one, whose crown is bound with the rays of the rising sun, who is clad in pure white garments and adorned with many red ornaments; who stands upon a lotus, holding in his hands the wish-granting jewel, the spear, the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness; and whose shoulders are adorned with a golden garland.
Kṛśānu. || 4 ||

The tongue is said to have the luster of a flame and to be joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; the limbs and the forms possess two upraised arms bearing the Śakti and the Svastika.
The connection is that [this applies] to the six corners and the center.
As it was stated by Somaśambhu:
"In the directions of Rudra, Indra, Agni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara..."
The tongues of Fire, beginning with Hiraṇyā, are situated in sequence as six.
"But in the center, [one should worship] Bahurūpā. In the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*:
"Then one should worship the seven tongues in the center and in the six corners.
Hiraṇyā, having the luster of molten gold, is situated in the direction of Śūlapāṇi (the north-east). (1)
The golden one, with the color of lapis lazuli, is situated in the eastern direction;
the red tongue, resembling the rising sun, is established in the fire.
Resembling a mass of black collyrium, she is situated in the south-western direction;
Suprabhā, possessing the luster of a ruby, is situated in the western direction.
Deeply red and shining like the Japā flower, she is situated in the northern direction;
possessing many forms and appearing according to reality, she resides in the south, the north, and the center.
Thus, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Prabhā, Dīptā, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tāpinī, Karālā, and Lelihā—these are situated pervading the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (1)
In the northeast and southeast directions, the triad beginning with Prabhā is situated;
likewise, in the southwest, west, and northwest, the triad beginning with Marīci is located.
"In the north, the middle, and the south, there is one situated called Lelihā.

Thus [it is said]. These are indeed alternative names for Hiraṇyā and the others, such as Prabhā and so forth. Alternatively, in the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, these are independent [deities]. Likewise, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
Hiraṇyā has a tongue pointing northeast; Kanakā is situated in the east;
Raktā is in the southeast; Kṛṣṇā is in the southwest; and the other is considered to be Suprabhā.
The tongue of the Maruts is intensely red, with a luster corresponding to its own name; another is Aruṇā.
The middle tongue has three points and is called Bahurūpā. Of those points, one blazes toward the right, while the other is on the left.
Thus end the descriptions of the *sāttvika* tongues. The *rājasa* and *tāmasa* tongues will now be described. However, some say:
"Indeed, in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, that tongue known as Hiraṇyā is praised for use on earth in rites such as those pertaining to *kārmika* (worldly) purposes."
For rites such as immobilization (*stambhana*), she is considered golden; for rites such as inciting hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), she is indeed red;
for killing (*māraṇa*), she is declared on earth to be black; and here, for pacification (*śānti*), she is of excellent luster, according to the best of the wise. (1)

Regarding the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), they say that the interior [of the tongue] is intensely red. "Radiant with flames" refers to the visualization of the tongues. This is because of the statement in the *Prayogasāra*: "All tongues are to be fully known as having the appearance of flames by their very nature," and also because of the statement in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*: "These [tongues], radiant with flames, are also endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness."
In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"With clarified butter consecrated by the *saṃskāras*, and with the illuminating and kindling [mantras], one should offer oblations three times with that mantra immediately after the *vyāhṛtis*. (1)
The connection is with the phrase "purified by the two purificatory rites (saṃskāra) known as *abhidyotana* and *uddyotana*.
However, others accept yet another purificatory rite as well. As stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"In the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), eighteen purificatory rites are to be known according to the Śiva scriptures."
"Eight [offerings] in the ghee, the *sruc*, and the *sruva*. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Having taken up the vessel of ghee, one should sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*.
Having filled it there with ghee, well-consecrated by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth..."
Having placed embers outside in the northwest direction, one should deposit [the substances] upon them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
This is designated as "heating" (*tāpana*); thereafter, one should cast two *kuśa* blades [into the fire].
One should place the clarified butter, mixed with ghee, into the blazing fire;
then, one should perform the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*) with two flaming blades of *darbha* grass.
Having consecrated the clarified butter with the *varman* mantra and offered it into the fire, one should cast two blades of *darbha* grass;
this is the *abhidyotana*, and now the *uddyotana* is described.
One should place the blazing *kuśa* grass into the fire, casting it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, having extinguished the ghee in the fire, one should cast the embers back into the fires.
Having touched water, the knower of mantras should then perform the purification;
muttering the Astra-mantra, the practitioner of mantra should take two Kuśa blades, each a span (prādeśa) in length.
Having taken up the clarified butter with the thumb and the ring finger, one should purify it;
then, with two *kuśa* blades held toward oneself, one should stir it while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.

"That [substance] should be clarified butter (*ghṛta*); these are proclaimed as the six purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Regarding 'clarified butter' (*ājya*): cow's ghee is said to be the best, while that from a buffalo is middling."
The goat-milk is the lowest; therefore, cow's milk is praised. || 1 ||

Thus, having filled [the vessel] with ghee well-consecrated by the rites of gazing (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth as taught in the *Piṅgalāmata*, one should consecrate it with the root mantra, transform it into nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*, and subsequently consecrate it with the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). And it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
Having taken cow-derived clarified butter consecrated with the root mantra,
one should contemplate one's own form as consisting of Brahman and heat it thoroughly.

Thus, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "Having placed the mantra [upon the ghee], one should display the mudrā known as the 'Cow' (*dhenu*). The remainder of the sense is: "outside the extent of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The syntactical connection is: "one should cast two blazing blades of *kuśa* grass into the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Having performed the *nīrājana*, one should whirl [the ghee] all around.

The throwing of two *darbha* blades of grass into the fire is a *pratipatti-karma* (a disposal rite); for this very reason, no mantra is prescribed. Consequently, if the *darbha* blades are lost, there is no deficiency even if the throwing is not performed.
The phrase "with the thumb and ring finger" implies that this is done with both hands.
"Utpavet agnisammukham" means [he should purify] facing the fire. As stated in the Śaiva Āgama:

"With two blades of darbha grass, each a span in length, held between the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers and smeared with clarified butter, one should perform the purification (utpavana) facing the fire while reciting the Astra-mantra. (1)
Thus [it is said]. In both cases, the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *kuśa* grasses consists solely in their being cast into the fire. Again, in that same [text]:

"Having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, [holding them] respectively with their openings facing upward and downward, one should heat them three times in the fire and touch them with the roots, middles, and tips of the *darbha* grass. (1)

O Dear One, one should sequentially assign the three principles— consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva— at the base, middle, and upper parts [of the body], using the seed-syllables Hrāṃ, Hrīṃ, and Hrūṃ.
Having placed Śakti in the *sruc* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* spoon with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*),
their necks should be wrapped with three threads and they should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
These two [the *sruk* and *sruva*] should be placed upon the *kuśa* grasses to one's own right;
the touching of the bases of the *sruk* and *sruva* with the roots and other parts of the *darbha* grass is performed.
Having described this touching, it is stated in the *Uttara-tantra*:
Then, taking them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with water using the right hand;
having heated them again over the fire, one should then offer the kuśa grasses into the fire.
"Having heated them thirty times"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. And it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Then, having heated them thirty times, one should cast the *kuśa* grasses face-downward into the fire.
One should place the powers, beginning with *icchā*, in sequence upon the root, middle, and tip. (1)
Thus [it is said]. The powers are will, knowledge, and action. In the *Uttaratantra*:
"Having placed two blades of *kuśa* grass in clarified butter, then measuring them at a span (*prādeśa*), one should make a knot at their tips and contemplate the two as white and black. (1)
The practitioner of mantras should visualize the *iḍā* on the left side, the *piṅgalā* on the right, and the *suṣumnā* in the middle; thereafter, he should perform the fire oblation (*homa*). (2)
The grammatical construction is "two blades of kuśa grass with knots."
Then, taking clarified butter from the right side with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*,
one should offer it into the right eye of the Fire, followed by the mantra "To Agni, Svāhā."
Having taken clarified butter from the left portion, the preceptor should offer it into the left eye of the fire with the heart-mantra, saying: "Svāhā to Soma."

Having taken clarified butter from the middle [of the vessel] with the ring finger and the thumb, the wise one should offer it into the fire with the heart-mantra, saying: "To Agni and Soma, svāhā! (agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā).
Then the wise preceptor, having taken clarified butter from the southern portion with the heart-mantra,
should offer it into the mouth of the fire, saying "Sviṣṭakṛte Svāhā."

In all cases, however, the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) is to be known as the one used for taking the clarified butter (ājya). In the *Śāradātilaka*: "The best of teachers should again offer oblations with the clarified butter accompanied by the *savyāhṛti* [Gāyatrī] mantras; he should offer them three times with the fire-mantra (*agnimantra*). (1)
With the three *vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively— according to the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The rites of the fire, beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *samudvāha*,
one should perform in sequence with eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) using the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*)."
Thus [it is said]. In the *Śāradātilaka*: "The impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), and likewise the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Having meditated upon the newborn as having such a form, one should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarma*)."
Having removed the stalk and then purified the juice from the impurity of birth (sūtaka), [one should proceed].
Having given him the name Śivāgni and preceded by oblations,
he performed the dismissal of the parents, as well as the tonsure, the initiation, and other rites.
"Then, having performed for him the sacrament that concludes with marriage.
Regarding this, in the Śaiva tradition it is called the *śivāgni* (the fire of Śiva); elsewhere, however, it is the *nārāyaṇāgni*, the *durgāgni*, and so forth. In the *Uttaratantre*:
"The *garbhādhāna*, the *puṃsavana*, and likewise the *sīmantonnayana*..."
Then follow the birth-rite, the naming ceremony, and the first outing. || 1 ||
Then follow the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure ceremony, and the initiation;
after that, the Mahānāmnya rite and the Great Vow (mahāvrata). || 2 ||
Then follows the initiation into the Upaniṣads, and immediately after that, the gift of a cow; then the return home and marriage—these are the sacraments ending with death.
"In rites of a cruel nature, [rites] ending in death should be performed by the teachers.
And this mantra is found in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then pronounce the ritual action (*karma*)."
"I accomplish [this], svāhā"—this is the rule for all ritual acts.
Thus, in the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*, it is stated: "Up to the marriage [rite], [the worship] is performed with the *Vāgbhava* [syllable]. This indicates an option between these two [methods].

In the *Uttaratantra*, it is stated: "After the marriage, the knower of mantras, having worshipped the fire and having united the parents within himself... This should be understood according to the specific tradition (*sampradāya*). Likewise:
Then, one should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) smeared with ghee at the beginning and the end;
one should also offer oblations once with ghee using the mantras of the tongue, the limbs, and the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
Thus, in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*:

"Then (one should also) offer oblations once each with the mantras of the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth; the one of sharp intellect [should do so] by appending the name [of the deity] at the end, followed by 'svāhā', in the proper order. (1)
Thus, it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The wise one, meditating upon the deity of the mantra, should offer oblations with the mantra preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, concluding each with *svāhā*. (1)

Thus [it is said]. The Śruti also states: "Whichever deity the oblation has been taken for, one should meditate upon that deity in the mind while about to utter the vaṣaṭ-call. However, the mantra ending with "svāhā" should not be made to end there [with the vaṣaṭ]. In the Uttaratantra:
"Having taken clarified butter four times with the *sruva* ladle, one should pour it into the *sruc*."
Having covered it with that very [vessel], the Guru himself, standing, should offer it into the fire. || 1 ||
"Then, for the sake of prosperity, [one should worship] with the mantra of Agni ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Thus it is said in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The practitioner, whose body is garlanded with flames, [should place the mantra] upon the tongue situated in the center."
With the ten mantras beginning with Tārā, each preceded by the one before it.
One who belongs to the Gāṇapatya lineage should first offer ten oblations with the mantra of Manu;
one should also offer them four times with that same mantra in its entirety.
In all fire-offerings, the wise one should offer clarified butter twenty-five times with the mantra to be accomplished, for the satisfaction of the fire.
p. 256) "This rule has been proclaimed for the Tantrikas regarding those who have offered oblations.
Thus [it is said]. By means of the *Gāṇapatya* [mantra], that is, the *Mahāgaṇeśa* mantra. As stated in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*:
"By means of the *Mahāgaṇeśa* mantra, conjoined with each preceding [mantra] in turn..."
In the six seed-syllables beginning with Tāra, within the Karaṇas, by means of the colors of the mountains. || 1 ||
"O Dear One, one should offer with that [mantra] both divided into ten parts and as a whole.

The mantra for the ritual application will be stated later. "The five arrows," "the five instruments," "the senses," "the five mountains," "the seven," and "the group of six seeds"—this is the division of the words. Regarding the *caru* oblation, one should now cook the *caru*.
The manner of that has already been explained in detail. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Then, having properly worshipped the pedestal of the deity in the fire, the Guru should worship there the chosen deity who bears the form of Agni. (1)

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations twenty-five times with clarified butter while reciting the *sādhya-mantra*; this is considered the "unification of faces" (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) within the mouth of the fire.
Contemplating the oneness of the self, the fire, and the deity,
the knower of the self should then offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
Thus indeed has the joining of the channels been taught by the best of instructors:
one should offer an oblation for each of the enclosures, beginning with the limbs.
In all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the eastern and other directions, the Guru should duly kindle the fire within those consecrated sites according to the prescribed method.

Then, having worshipped all the officiating priests with sandalwood paste and other offerings, they should perform oblations with the root mantra to the aforementioned deity together with all the surrounding retinues.
With milk-rice mixed with twenty-five parts of clarified butter.
Thus, it is said in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
"The clarified butter should be offered with the *sruva* ladle, while holding fuel-sticks in the hand; the remainder [of the offerings] may be offered with the *sruk* ladle or even with the hand.
Each substance should be offered according to its respective rule, and likewise through the proper *tīrtha* (part of the hand) or by means of a *ṛṣi*. (1)

Thus [it is stated]. In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "The oblation is offered with the sacred formula at the 'divine' sacrificial site (tīrtha) into a fire that has bright embers and a bright flame. Thus [it is said].
The man who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or one whose coals are extinguished is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and impoverished.
Thus [it is said]. Likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra*:

"After the oblation has been offered, the preceptor should subsequently present the bali-offering upon the maṇḍala, in due order for the lunar mansions, along with their days of the week and their zodiacal signs. (1)

One should respectfully offer bali, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, to the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī; the zodiac sign (rāśi) consists of two and one-quarter [asterisms]. || 2 ||

Immediately following the names of the constellations joined with Aries and the other signs, one should utter the word "to the deities" (devatābhyaḥ), and likewise say "day and night" (divānaktaṃ). || 3 ||
Then one should indeed utter "namas" to all beings who move;
in this same manner, one should likewise apply it when that heap is complete.
Likewise, one should assign [the results] there and there for the lords of the zodiac signs, for the planets,
for the seven Karaṇas, and for the two signs named Pisces and Aries.
Thus, in the intermediate stage, the powerful one who consists of the kalasha has been fully described;
then, having again lifted up the offering and worshipped it as before, [one should proceed].
Having offered mouth-fresheners and other such items,
the practitioner, endowed with devotion, should then praise [the deity] appropriately with those same offerings and bow down.

Thus [it is said]. Between the signs of Pisces and Aries, in the intermediate direction between the northeast and the east: likewise, in the *Tantrarāja*—Aries and Taurus are in the east; Gemini is in the southeast; Cancer and Leo are likewise in the south; and Virgo is situated in the southwest. (1)
Libra and Scorpio are situated in the west; Sagittarius is located in the northwest;
Capricorn and Aquarius are in the north; and Pisces is situated in the northeast.

Thus [ends] the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, and disciple of the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī Govindācārya.
The twelfth breath. 12.
The Thirteenth Chapter on Inhalation.
In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Having arisen at dawn, they should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, one thousand and eight times, while reciting the mantra of the person to be accomplished. (1)
Or, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the substances prescribed by the ritual injunctions;
then the best of mantra-knowers should make the bathed disciple drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having brought [the disciple] near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should gaze upon him with divine vision;
then, one should unite his consciousness from the lotus of the heart with one's own self.
Then the teacher should gradually purify the sixfold path;
these consist of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), phonemes (arṇa), and words (pada), preceded by the mantras.
Six paths have been proclaimed; their characteristics are now stated.
The kalās beginning with Nivṛtti and the rest—these five are celebrated as that path.
The paths of the principles (tattvādhvan) are divided into many sequences by the Śaiva and other scriptures.
Among them, the Śaiva principles are measured at thirty-six.
Śiva and Śakti shall be described, as well as that which is called Sadāśiva;
these, along with Vidyā, are the seven pure and impure [tattvas].
Māyā, vidyā, kalā, rāga, kāla, and niyati, as well as puruṣa, are impure; so too are prakṛti, buddhi, and ahaṃkṛti.
The mind, the ten sense organs, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements—these thirty-six Śiva-tattvas have been declared by those who know the mantras. (9)
Now, the thirty-two Vaiṣṇava principles will be described; they are the vital breath together with the individual soul (jīva), followed by the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas).
The ten sense organs, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the pentad of gross elements, the heart-lotus, and likewise the triad of fires—these are indeed four [groups]. (11)
Vāsudeva and the others are said to be the solar [deities]; the five elements, the subtle elements (tanmātras), the sense organs, the mind, ego, and intellect [constitute the rest]. || 12 ||
Including Pradhāna, the principles of Śakti are indeed ten;
[they are] the five Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, and then again the Kalā of Bindu. (13)
Nāda, Śakti, and Sadāpūrva, as well as Śiva and Prakṛti—these seven principles (tattvas) are declared by the knowers of Tantra to belong to the threefold nature (tripadātman). (14)
These are the pure sciences of the Self, and they are also the opposites;
the teachers have declared that all these principles constitute the path of the principles (tattvādhvan). || 15 ||
"All worlds here are proclaimed as the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).
Thus [it is said]. "Worlds" (*bhuvanāni*) means the realms (*lokāḥ*). These are described in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Atala, Vitala, Sutala, and Mahātala..."
And following that, Rasātala and Talātala are recorded. || 1 ||
Pātāla, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and those named Mahar, Jana, Tapa— along with Satyaloka— these are declared to be the worlds in their proper order.
The letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' are called the path of letters (varṇādhvan);
the path of words (padādhvan) consists of a collection of letters, and the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) is an accumulation of words.
The Guru should remember those [mantras] at the disciple’s feet, navel, heart, forehead, and crown;
then, touching the disciple with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], he should offer oblations in his own sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
With sesame seeds soaked in ghee, one should offer eight separate oblations with the mantra ending in *svāhā*, beginning with "O Tārā" and including the name of the specific path to be purified here.
Thus, in the Kulārṇava: "For Śūdras and those born of mixed castes, purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi) is not prescribed;
one should effect their liberation from sin by means of offering water for the feet and other such rites. (1)
Thus:
"In this manner, having properly dissolved the six paths in sequence up to Śiva, the supreme Guru should emit those [paths], which were dissolved by the process of emanation, back up to Śiva. (1)
And the lord of teachers, having gazed upon that disciple with his divine vision, should cause that consciousness which resides within him to be fixed in that very [divine state]. || 2 ||
Then the best of preceptors should indeed offer oblations again with ghee, beginning with the limbs [of the deity] up to the enclosures (vṛti), using the *mahāvyāhṛti* mantras.
"Bhūḥ" is joined with the mantra for Agni and subsequently for Pṛthivī;
"Bhuvaḥ" is joined with the mantra for Vāyu and for Antarikṣa. || 4 ||
The mantra "Svar ādityāya ca dive ca" is prescribed for Yama;
and "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ candramase nakṣatrebhyaś ca" is for the eastern direction.
Then one should speak from the directions; this is declared to be the fourth mantra.
And the Great Vyāhṛti mantras should end with the Dviṭha (svāhā).
The word "mahate" (for the great) connects with all four [syllables] beginning with "bhūḥ"; the *svāhā*-utterance occurs twice.
The wise knower of mantras, for the severance of all karma, should offer eight oblations of pure clarified butter with the mantra known as the *brahmārpaṇa*.
From this point forward, one should speak first of the intellect of the vital breath (*prāṇabuddhi*);
thereafter, one should speak of the domain of the body's attributes within the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
One should speak with the mind and voice according to one's own states;
and likewise, one should raise the foot through action by means of the two hands, the two feet, speech, and the belly.
Whatever one speaks, whatever sound one utters, whatever word one recites,
whatever is said, and whatever is done— all that shall become an offering unto Brahman.
Then, the supreme mantra for the offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa), ending with "svāhā," is proclaimed;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantras, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra using the sacrificial ladle (sruva), [should proceed].
Thus [it is said]. The mantra for the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*) is clarified in its practical application in the *Kapilapañcarātra*:
"Having worshipped according to the rule, the wise man should indeed offer oblations again. For the sake of making up for any deficiency or excess, I offer sesame seeds with ghee. (1)
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, together with its limbs, [one says] "kurukuru" and ends with the *ṭha* (svāhā).
This is the eighth letter in the forward order of the alphabet, conjoined with the sixth vowel from the end.
"The seed-mantra of Viṣṇu is proclaimed as being joined with the *praṇava*.
Thus [it is said]. The eighth letter in the forward order is the letter *ha*; the sixth vowel is the letter *ū*; the penultimate vowel is the nasal dot (*bindu*). In the Śaiva Āgama—
Having prepared the fire named Mṛḍa and worshipped it with self-restraint, one should recite:
"O thousand-rayed one, of great splendor, homage to you who assume many forms! (1)
Salutations be to you, the all-consuming, the omnipresent, the purifier!
You are the fierce one and the performer of fierce deeds; you are the slayer of the terrible—I bow to you. || 2 ||
"You are Viṣṇu, the guardian of the world; grant me peace here.
Having filled the sacrificial ladle with clarified butter, one should place a flower upon it with its face turned downwards.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle upon the *sruc* vessel, one should cause a flower to be offered there with the left and right hands joined together like a conch shell.
Having gathered [the materials] and risen, and having placed them crosswise at the navel,
he, being well-restrained, [should perform the rite] with the mantra "pūrṇād arvi" and the root mantra.
"One should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) which fulfill all desires.
Thus [it is said]. The offering of flowers is upon the *sruk* ladle. This is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having filled the *sruk* with the ghee remaining from the *homa*..."
Having placed a flower before it, [he should offer] that [oblation] with the *sruva* ladle turned downwards.
Then, having covered [the vessel] with a bunch of *darbha* grass and [holding] the root-mantra in his joined palms (*añjali*),
he should offer a continuous stream [of oblations] accompanied by recitation, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Thus: "With the *pūrṇādarvi* [mantra] in a specific Vedic branch for the Vedic fire-oblation; with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
and then the utterance of *svāhā* in the oblation—indeed, in the *pūrṇā* [oblation], it is *vauṣaṭ* alone," according to his own statement.
Having offered the oblation, one should present three full-offerings (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the ladle (*sruk*) using the sacrificial food (*havis*).
With the Vaiṣṇava mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ," [he worshipped] the Supreme God. || 1 ||
And from the statement in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "In the absence of ghee, however, one should fill [the vessel] with the substance for the oblation according to the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
'In the absence of ghee itself, one should fill it with the material for the *homa*;
upon that one should place ghee, and above that, flowers and so forth.'"
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the *devīhoma*, however, in the *pūrṇāyāga*:

having filled the *sruva* with clarified butter (*ājya*), and then having filled the *sruc* with it, the knower of mantras, having raised the *sruva* and turned it downward above that [the *sruc*], [should perform the offering]. (1)
Having placed the straight body with its base at the root of the navel,
and having uttered the root mantra ending in "namaḥ," beginning with the left foot— 2.
"Then the mantra-practitioner should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*s with the thought that it is supreme nectar.
Thus [it is said] in the *Gaṇeśvaraparāmarśinī*:
"Oṃ! O Fire, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!"
Even when another task has arisen, please attend to me with respect.
Having thus offered prayer with this mantra, one should also cause the fire to be extinguished.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"The knower of mantras, having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra..."
Having raised the deity from the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), the preceptor should install it in the water-jar (kalaśa).
There, one should worship [the deity] together with the limbs and the enclosures according to the prescribed rule;
and with the seven vyāhṛtis, one should offer a single oblation in sequence to Agnijihvā and the others.
"Having offered [the oblation] and sprinkled [it] with water around the fire," thus [it is said]. In the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
"Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa—a copper vessel fashioned from thirty-two palas of copper. (1)
The wise know that when a vessel is filled with rice, together with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and offered to the chosen preceptor, it is called a *pūrṇapātra*.
Thus, in the *Uttaratantro*:
"The knower of mantras, having united [the elements] within himself, should then cast the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire after performing the ritual strewing (*paristara*). (1)
The best of teachers should cast those [flowers] during both the regular and occasional rites;
having bound the eyes of the disciple with a cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra.
Taking [the water] from the vessel with his hands, he should lead it to the vicinity of the maṇḍala;
having filled his joined palms (añjali) with flowers, he should indeed cast them into the jar.
Preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, the Guru, for the sake of pleasing the deity,
should remove the blindfold and seat [the disciple] upon a bed of kuśa grass.
Then, the supreme guru should cause the disciple to recite this mantra:
"For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the collyrium-stick of knowledge... (5)
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye has been opened;
therefore, through the performance of worship, one should withdraw and then generate it.
One should duly perform all those installations (nyāsa) mentioned by Manu upon the body of the child;
having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra).
There, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti (the infusion of the deity’s limbs) according to the path taught in the Tantras;
then, one should seat the adorned disciple within the maṇḍala.
Then the Guru, having placed the *suradru* (mango) fruits from the *kumbhāsya* [vessel] upon the head of the child,
together with the fivefold sounds and the benedictory words of the Brahmins, [performs the rite].
One should sprinkle the well-established and self-controlled [disciple] with the waters from the ritual jars,
in the same manner as he was previously filled with the essence of nectar.
With waters joined by syllables, one should likewise consecrate this [disciple] by that very same path for the swift attainment of prosperity. (11)
Having first taken up the consecrated water-pot, which is of the nature of the Astra-mantra,
the best of preceptors should sprinkle him with its waters for protection.
Then, with the remaining water, the preceptor should cause the child to sip it;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, identifying the child as the very form of that deity.
Having put on two clean and beautiful garments by the command of his guru,
and having sipped water (performed ācamana), the young disciple should sit near him with speech restrained.

Having worshipped the deity residing within the disciple and contemplating the identity of the two, the Guru [should bestow] the mantra three times upon that humble disciple in the proper manner. (15)
The learned one should speak into the right ear of the Brahmin preceded by water;
for others, however, the wise mantra-master should speak in this very same manner.
Thus said Agastya:
"The Guru should contemplate the Vidyā, consisting of self-luminous light, as she approaches;
the disciple should contemplate her as having arrived, thinking especially, 'I am blessed. (1)
Thus:
"The disciple should recite one hundred and eight times as instructed by the guru;
or the recitation may be performed twenty-eight times, or even eight times. (1)
The disciple should contemplate the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and his own mantra;
the devoted practitioner should repeatedly offer prostrations to the Lord. (2)

Thus, it is recognized in the rites of worship as being either eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) or five-limbed (pañcāṅga); [the former consists of] the two hands, the two feet, the two knees, and likewise the chest. || 3 ||
The eight-limbed [prostration] is said to consist of the head, the gaze, speech, and the mind;
the five-limbed is said to consist of the hands, the knees, the head, the voice, and the intellect.
Then, having contemplated [the deity], the disciple should immediately carry out the preceptor’s command;
he should respectfully present ornaments and garments to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
But with the thought of offering it to the Lord, gladdened by the blessings of the twice-born,
the disciple, having deliberated, should give half to the preceptor and half of that [half] to the other [preceptor].
Or one should give a tenth part [of the merit], free from stinginess regarding wealth,
with a mind always dependent on that, with a heart fixed on that, and devoted solely to that.
"The best of practitioners should be adorned with the dust from the lotus-feet of that [guru].
Thus it is said. In the *Tantrarāja*:
"One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru, who is Śiva himself in visible form."
Or his entire property, or half of that, or half of that again, according to his command. || 1 ||
If there were no transfer of this power, how could he come to possess elephants, horses, female buffalo, rams, cattle, female slaves, and land? (2)
One should give gold, ornaments, clothing, a residence, or whatever else is desired; one may even give one’s own body and one’s own life, according to one’s capacity and with devotion.
Thus it is said:
"Then, with various kinds of foods to be chewed, licked, sucked, and others besides, one should afterwards feed the Brāhmaṇas and bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). (1)

"Thus, the initiation consisting of ritual action (kriyāmayī dīkṣā), as it is connected here, has been described. In this context, by the phrase "preceded by water," the bestowal of the mantra is understood— just like [the giving of] a cow or gold—
as a gift that involves the formal renunciation of one's own ownership according to the prescribed rule.

It takes the form of transferring ownership to another; however, no statement or tradition is observed to the effect that after giving a mantra to a disciple, the guru neither recites nor worships that mantra again, nor does he give it to anyone else.

Therefore, it must be said that the offering of water is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). If so, why would the offering of water not be common to all four castes (*caturṇām api varṇānām*), given that there is no distinction regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) and because [the offering] is figurative? Therefore, the offering of water...

It is indeed of the nature of the gift of a mantra. In that regard, even though the transfer of ownership to another has been effected, the absence of relinquishing one's own ownership must be understood as being like the giving away of a maiden; let this matter rest here.

I shall now describe, according to the prescribed rule, the initiation into the nature of the phonemes (varṇa) as just mentioned; for it has been declared that the phonemes consist of the nature of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti.
And such a nature of the body has indeed been explained here by the teachers;
therefore, the best of teachers should place the phonemes upon the body of the disciple.
By the power and command of the preeminent teacher, who is of the nature of the deity, he should withdraw the phonemes situated in their respective locations in reverse order.
Then the disciple becomes one whose self is the deity and whose true essence is fully absorbed;
thereafter, he should unite the consciousness of the disciple with the Supreme Self.
Having then produced those constituent elements (tattvas), one should place them within the body of the child;
and into that [body], one should again place consciousness (caitanya) according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama).
The disciple shall become one with the deity, a child whose nature is eternal bliss;
this initiation, consisting of the ocean of knowledge, is said to bestow all accomplishments.
Now it is said: that initiation which bestows divinity consists of the *kalās*. The five *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti* are proclaimed as belonging to the elements (*bhūtas*). (7)
The wise one should pierce those [kalās] sequentially within the body of the disciple composed of the elements:
the kalā Nivṛtti is situated from the feet up to the knees.
The portion from the knees up to the navel is known as the kalā called Pratiṣṭhā; the portion from the navel up to the throat is established as the kalā called Vidyā.
Indeed, the portion called Śānti is situated from the throat up to the forehead;
likewise, the portion called Śāntyatītā is said to extend from the forehead to the head.
The wise one should pierce [the disciple] out of sequence or at a location other than the prescribed place;
by the command of the Lord, this is declared to be the initiation of *kalā*.
Now, the initiation consisting of piercing (vedha), which liberates one from worldly existence, is described:
one should visualize [the lotus] with four petals at the mūlādhāra in the body of the disciple.

The wise one [should meditate] upon the Goddess, who consists of three revolutions, whose form is like a mass of lightning, within the cavity described as the triangle, conjoined with the three abodes.
She is the goddess who is the very embodiment of Mahādeva, manifest as the nature of pure knowledge alone; subtler than the subtlest, she pierces through the six wheels.
Traveling by way of the Suṣumṇā toward the divine abode of Śiva,
one should withdraw the vowels and consonants situated on the petals into the lotus-born Brahmā.
Having properly joined that [seed-syllable] *taṃ* with the pair of letters beginning with *la* on the petals of the six-petaled lotus in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Guru should pierce it. (16)
One should bring those letters into Viṣṇu, and that Viṣṇu into the navel-lotus;
one should oneself pierce the lotus petals in the cardinal directions, joined with the letters beginning with Pha and Ḍa.
One should join those phonemes to Rudra, and that Rudra to the heart-lotus;
one should oneself pierce the lotus whose petals consist of the letters beginning with the final *ṭha* into Īśvara.
One should bring those letters into this throat-lotus, and likewise [place] that [syllable] there;
having carefully joined the vowels to the petals consisting of the *kalās* in the lotus.
Having joined them to Sadāśiva in the two-petaled lotus at the center of his eyebrows, which is conjoined with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, the preceptor should then pierce [the path].
One should draw those two Ha-kṣas into the Bindu; one should draw that [Bindu] into Kalā;
having joined Kalā with Nāda, one should then join Nāda into the end of Nāda (Nādānta).
The Guru himself should dissolve the Unstruck Sound (nāda) within the center of the Transmental (unmanī), the Transmental within the mouth of the Equinox (viṣuvaktra),
and the mouth of the Equinox into his own mouth.
Together with his power (śakti), he should thus lead the self up to Paraśiva.
Then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple, with his ignorance burnt away, [remains] upon the earth. (23)
Then, having attained supreme knowledge, he becomes omniscient;
he himself shall become Sadāśiva—this is the truth, there is no doubt. || 24 ||
The auspicious initiation consisting of piercing (vedha), which bestows knowledge, has been described by me. Thus, four initiations have been properly indicated as bringing about welfare. (25)

Thus, in the *Śrīkulārṇava*: "Having visualized the City of Śiva in his hand, the Guru should recite the *Mūlāṅgamālinī*; he should then touch the body of the disciple—this shall be the initiation by touch. (1)
Having fixed the mind on reality, one should utter the combined mantras augmented by the supreme reality; this is called the "initiation of speech" (vāgdīkṣā).
Having closed his eyes and meditated upon the Supreme Reality with a tranquil mind, the Guru should clearly behold the disciple; that, O Dear One, is the initiation through the gaze (dṛgdīkṣā).
Through the mere glance of the Guru, through his speech, or even through touch, knowledge arises immediately; that is considered the Śāmbhavī initiation.

[The nature of] the mantras should be known through the established doctrines, the meaning of the scriptures, the oral tradition, and other such reasons; for those mantras which are taught without [these foundations] would be fruitless. || 5 ||
The gods praise such a person as the one who initiates the lineage—
the guru who is proficient in the mantras and the scriptures, and who observes the rules of conduct and observances.

Even though he is dispassionate, the Guru, by the command of Śiva, should perform this for a certain period of time for the sake of the disciple's qualification and then hand it over to a worthy disciple.
"For one who has thus surrendered his office, yoga leads directly to the supreme Śiva;
from that, eternal liberation follows—so it was spoken by Śaṅkara. (8)
Therefore, O Dear One, with every effort, a guru should always maintain the unbroken tradition directly proclaimed by Paraśiva.

For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Guru, having examined [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule, should thereafter impart the mantra; otherwise, it shall be fruitless. (10)
O Goddess, he who gives by unjust means and he who receives by unjust means— for both the giver and the receiver, there shall be a curse upon their lineage.
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, give or receive instruction without having examined one another, they both go to the state of a piśāca.
But he who accepts or bestows instruction that is contrary to the scriptures—both of them shall experience twenty-one terrible hells. (13)
But he who, being of deluded intellect, gives instruction without performing the consecration and deposits that mantra like sowing rice seeds in sand; (14)
The knowledge of reality does not abide in one who is conceited;
therefore, one must speak only after investigation, otherwise it will be fruitless. 15.
The knowledge that is imparted to a good disciple who is exceedingly devoted leads him to that very reality, just as a cow yields milk from which clarified butter is produced.
One should not initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, greed, or similar motives;
[if one does so], one incurs the curse of the deity, and what has been performed becomes corrupted. || 17 ||
Thus [ends the previous section]. (Now the procedure for the Full Consecration is written: In the *Uttaratantra*:
"I shall explain the Full Consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), which brings auspiciousness to practitioners;
without which consecration, a practitioner cannot attain the state of complete awakening. (1)
One does not attain the status of a teacher nor the desired higher state;
therefore, the Guru, having instructed his beloved disciple, should perform the consecration.
Having fashioned a large wheel within an exceedingly beautiful pavilion,
one should place a pitcher filled with a khārī measure of water in the center of the wheel.
Having duly placed other jars, filled with jewels, cloth, and gold, upon the petals, one should invoke the chosen deity there.
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures in the center and in the other [locations],
he should, as before, consecrate the disciple with them under the birth asterism of the disciple.
"This is the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), which bestows the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the measure of a *khārī*, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"Two *palas* are considered a *prasṛta*; a *kuḍava* is held to be double that."
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*; an *āḍhaka* is made by four times that amount. || 1 ||
Four *droṇas* make one *kumbha*, and two of those are known as a *kumbha*;
eight such *kumbhas* constitute a *khārī*.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-prayoga*): Having deliberated thus, on the day prior to the day of initiation during the prescribed times, the disciple—having bathed in the morning, performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), and being well-adorned—should proceed with the chanting of the *svastivācana* by Brahmins, preceded by the sounding of the five musical instruments.

Having gone to the teacher’s house together with his dear friends, he should bow down to him according to the prescribed rite; then, by the teacher’s command, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), [he should say]: "Oṃ! Today, in such-and-such month, when the sun has entered such-and-such zodiac sign, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, I, a Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage named such-and-such Śarmā..."
