If I am a Kṣatriya, [I am] so-and-so-varman; if a Vaiśya, so-and-so-gupta; if a Śūdra, so-and-so-dāsa;
desiring the accomplishment of the fourfold aims of human life, I shall undertake the reception of such-and-such a mantra.
p. 262) Thus, with *kuśa* grass in hand, facing either east or north, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*),

and having worshipped the venerable Guru with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Vedic branch and using the materials for the honey-mixture as specified by the authoritative texts;

Having placed before the preceptor the materials for the formal offering, which include a pair of washed upper garments as coverings, a golden ring, earrings, a golden sacred thread, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and various other ornaments, as well as an umbrella, chowries, a pair of shoes, a bed, a couch, and a boat for crossing over;

"Today," and so forth, as before; at the conclusion of recording the lunar day (*tithi*), having uttered [his name] according to his caste—such as "I, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named such-and-such Śarman"—[he says]: "Desiring the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), for the purpose of receiving such-and-such mantra, I, of such-and-such lineage..."

Having prostrated at the feet of the Guru with the words, "I choose such-and-such a person, a student of such-and-such a branch within such-and-such a Veda, as my Guru by means of these materials for the formal selection (varaṇa) prepared according to my ability," one should present the collection of items for the selection. Then, when the Guru has given the reply, "I am chosen," [the ritual continues].

The disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should say, "O Guru, perform the rite as prescribed. Then the Guru should reply, "I shall do so. Having thus honored the Guru, and with his permission, [he should invite] eight Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas and are worshippers of their own chosen deity.
In the same manner as previously described for the selection of the preceptor (*guru*), one should choose the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with the requisite materials.

In the case of four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), exactly four priests should be appointed. Then, the preceptor, having been thus chosen by the disciple, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), and being well-adorned, [proceeds] preceded by the sounding of five musical instruments.
Surrounded by Brāhmaṇas and friends, and accompanied by his disciple, he went to the entrance of the pavilion;

having performed the worship of the door there according to the procedure to be described, and likewise having first expelled the obstructing spirits (bhūtas), he entered the interior of the pavilion in the same manner.
Having first sprinkled [the site] with water mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the water of honor (*arghya*),

it is consecrated within the pavilion by the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with "inspection" (*vīkṣaṇa*) to be described hereafter, and is perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.

Having scattered sandalwood, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice, and parched grain— each consecrated seven times with the *astra-mantra*— within the pavilion, and having swept [the area] with a handful of *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra*, he should have the Brahmins establish [these items] in the northeast corner of the pavilion.

Having caused the *puṇyāhavācana* to be performed and having carried out the worship of the *vāstupuruṣa* and other rites, preceded by the command of Bhairava, one should spread [the ritual materials] upon the altar and worship them according to the procedure to be described; then, seated there facing east upon the level ground in front of oneself on top of the altar—
One should construct the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala. For that purpose, having drawn seventeen lines extending east-west and seventeen lines extending north-south,
one should fashion a square maṇḍala consisting of two hundred and fifty-six compartments.
Having unified the thirty-six squares situated in the center, and having cleared and unified a single row surrounding those on all four sides, one should fashion the pedestal (*pīṭha*); then,
having cleared and unified the two rows situated on the four sides outside of that, one should fashion the pathway (*vīthī*).

Having visualized it, one should leave out twelve parts on all sides around the location of the lotus situated in the very center; then, by relying on the absolute center, one should produce three concentric circles with equal intervals between them.
Therein, having fashioned the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in the middle of all the circles, [one should fashion] the path of the circle located outside of that.
Having determined the location for the filaments and divided that space into sixteen parts, one should,
by means of the marks [thereof] and according to the measurement of the cord spanning the interval between the second and third circles,
determine sixteen half-moons using the method taught by the Guru; and by means of those, one should form the eight petals.
Outside the third circle, having omitted one part and established another circle by means of the central mark,

one should fashion the tips of the petals according to the method taught by the Guru; then, having fashioned the lotus so that two filaments are visible at the base of each petal, one should complete it.
Having fashioned the four legs of the pedestal from three squares each at the four corners of the square base— which consists of a single row extending outward from the lotus—
and having formed the body of the pedestal by unifying the remaining squares;
Having thoroughly wiped away the squares of the two rows situated outside that [inner grid],

one should merge two squares with two squares in the middle of each of the four directions of the row situated outside that; likewise, for the row situated on the very outer edge, in each of the four directions—
Having fashioned four doors by clearing away the four central squares,
one should place three squares from the inner row and one square from the outer row on both sides of each of the four doors.
Having combined the four central squares and fashioned the primary ornament (*śobhā*), one should likewise combine another set of four squares—
consisting of one square from the side rows and three squares from the outer rows— and fashion the secondary ornament (*upaśobhā*); with the remaining six squares...

One should fashion the four corners with squares; having thus constructed the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala, one should adorn the locations of the lotus pericarp, filaments, petals, tips, pedestal, path, doors, secondary ornaments, and corners with powders of five colors. As for the five-colored powders: turmeric powder...
Yellow powder is rice flour; white is safflower flower powder; red is burnt rice flour; black is *bilva* leaf powder; and dark green is [the same].
As for the method of arranging the powders: all the lines reaching the boundary are [to be made] with white powder.

They should be made with a height and width of one finger-breadth. Having properly filled the lotus pericarp and the filaments with yellow powder, and having filled the petals with white powder, one should fill the joints of the petals with dark blue powder; or alternatively, the pericarp with yellow [powder] and the filaments...

Having filled the petals with yellow and red [powders], the joints of the petals with red, and the surface with black powder; having filled the interior of the pedestal (pīṭha) with either yellow or black, the legs of the pedestal with red, and the body of the pedestal with white powder; [one should draw] the wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī) in the four pathways.
Adorned with buds, flowers, shoots, and fruits, having fashioned [the mandala] with powders of various colors and having filled the four gates with white powder, the gate-decorations with red powder,
the secondary ornaments with yellow, and the corners with black, [he should do so] outside of that.
One should draw three lines with white, red, and black powders, each separated by an interval of one finger-breadth;
having thus constructed the Sarvatobhadra mandala, one should light lamps around the altar,
arrange the materials for worship according to the procedure to be described, and likewise consecrate them.
Having set aside the parasol, the pair of fly-whisks, the mirror, the fan, and so forth, each in its proper place,
and having performed the salutation to the Guru and others,

[one should proceed with] the purification of the hands, the three *tāla*-claps, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the triple wall of fire (*agniprākāra*), and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having performed the installation of the *mātṛkā*, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the yoga-pīṭha, and the placement of the root mantra (p.

Having performed the formation of mudrās, meditation on one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), mental worship (mānasapūjā), the Vaiśvadeva offering, the recitation of the root mantra (mūlamantra) and its dedication, the placement of the arghya water, self-worship, the internal fire sacrifice (antarhavana), and the recitation of the root mantra with its dedication, [one should say]: "Obeisance to the Śarvatobhadra maṇḍala."
Thus, having worshipped the maṇḍala with the five offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha), and having sprinkled it with arghya water,

one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) therein according to the procedure to be described; then, having filled its pericarp (karṇikā) with śāli rice, [one places] grains of rice, kuśa grass, and dūrvā grass with twenty-seven [mantras].
Having placed there a *kūrca* (grass-bundle) whose tip is unified with *kuśa* grass and fashioned with a *brahmagranthi*,

and having worshipped the fire-mandala and the digits of fire (*vahnikalā*) upon a heap of *śāli* rice according to the procedure to be described, [one should place] therein [the vessel] made of gold or other materials, its entire body wrapped with a triple-stranded thread.
Having fumigated the jar with incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and having placed it there while reciting the *praṇava*,
one should deposit within it the nine gems— namely, topaz, sapphire, lapis lazuli, coral, pearl, emerald, diamond, hessonite, and ruby— along with gold, and [place] them upon the jar.

Having placed there a *kūrca* of the previously described characteristics, accompanied by perfumes, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and *dūrvā* grass, one should recite the root mantra three times at the end of the reverse-order *mātṛkā* beginning with *kṣaṃ laṃ*, while contemplating the identity of oneself, the water-pot, and the *yogapīṭha*.
Having filled a water-pot with the decoctions of the fifty medicinal herbs to be mentioned later, or with the decoctions of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees,
or with the decoction of the bark of the *palāśa* tree,
or with water from sacred fords scented with camphor, sandalwood, musk, and saffron;
Having placed a conch shell before oneself according to the procedure to be described,
having filled it with water of the same kind as that used for filling the ritual jar, and having stirred the eight fragrant substances therein,
one should invoke the fire-energies (*vahnikalā*), solar energies (*sūryakalā*), and lunar energies (*somakalā*) mentioned below, and [worship] them individually.
Having separately performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) and worshiped,
one should worship the fifty-one *kalās* arising from the *praṇava*, as described in the *Kalāmātṛkā-nyāsa*.
Among them, those originating from the letter 'A'— Brahmā— are produced from the *ka*- and *ca*-groups.

Having invoked the ten kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi, and having recollected the seer and other attributes of the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad" as follows: Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is the meter (chandas), and Sūrya is the deity (devatā)—one recites: "Oṃ, haṃsaḥ śuciṣad, vasurantarikṣasad, hotā vediṣad, atithir duroṇasad."

Having recited the mantra: "The one seated on the waters, seated on the earth, seated in the excellent sky, born from the lotus, born from the cow, born from the Ṛta, born from the mountain— the great Ṛta," and having worshipped with "Salutation to Brahman," one should [perform the installation] using the previously mentioned *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, substituting the word "mine" (*mama*) with "of creation and so forth" (*sṛṣṭyādīnām*).

Having placed the foot and performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) for Sṛṣṭi and the others, the ten digits (*kalās*) beginning with "Oṃ Kaṃ Sṛṣṭyai Namaḥ" and so forth should be worshipped.

Then, having invoked the ten digits beginning with Old Age (*jarā*), which arise from the group of eight consonants starting with *ṭa* and are produced from Viṣṇu via the letter *U*, [one should worship them] with "Oṃ... and so forth.

Having recollected the seer and other details of the mantra "pratadviṣṇuḥ"— namely, that Dīrghatamas is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Viṣṇu is the deity (devatā)— one recites: Oṃ pratadviṣṇuḥ stavate vīryeṇa mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro giriṣṭhāḥ | yasyoruṣu triṣu vikramaṇeṣvadhikṣiyanti bhuvanāni viśvā || 1 ||

Having recited "viśvā" and worshipped with "namaḥ to Viṣṇu," one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) for the ten *kalās* beginning with *jarā*, as previously described; then the ten *kalās* are to be worshipped with "oṃ ṭaṃ, obeisance to Jarā," and so forth. These were produced from Rudra, who arose from the letter *ma*.
Having invoked the ten digits (kalās) beginning with Tīkṣṇā, which arise from the *payavarga*, one should remember the seer and other attributes of the mantra "Oṃ Tryambakam":

Vasiṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), and Tryambaka Rudra is the deity (*devatā*). Then [one recites]: "Oṃ, we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity..."

Having recited, "May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, but not from immortality," and having worshipped with "Obeisance to Rudra" (Rudrāya namaḥ), one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breath) for them. Then, the ten *kalās* (energy-forms) beginning with "Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to Tīkṣṇā" (Oṃ paṃ tīkṣṇāyai namaḥ) are to be worshipped; these were produced from the Bindu of Īśvara.
Having invoked the five digits (kalā) beginning with yellow and corresponding to the five colors, starting from the letter *ṣa* and ending with *kṣa*,

and having recited the Gāyatrī preceded by the remembrance of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs], one should worship them with "Oṃ, obeisance to Īśvara," and then perform the ritual installation of their vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with: "Oṃ, ṣaṃ, obeisance to the Yellow One."

Having thus worshipped the five *kalās* beginning with these, one should then invoke the sixteen *kalās*— Nivṛtti and the others— which arise from the *nāda*, are produced from Sadāśiva, and are born of the vowels. For the mantra "Viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu," Tvaṣṭṛ is the *ṛṣi*, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and Viṣṇu is the deity.
Having recollected the Ṛṣis and others, and having recited: "Oṃ, may Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;

may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you," and having worshipped them with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śadāśiva," and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breaths) for them, [one worships] "Aṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti."

The sixteen digits (kalās), beginning with *namaḥ*, are to be worshipped. Having thus worshipped the ninety-four deities within the conch, one should pour the water of the conch—which consists of all the digits—into the pitcher while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Then, having wrapped the sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *āmra* trees with the creeper of *indravāruṇī*.
Having placed [the vessel] in the water-pot with the thought that it is a *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree), and having set upon it a vessel of the same type as the pot,
filled with rice and enriched with coconut fruits with the thought that they are the fruits of the *kalpavṛkṣa*,
one should wrap the jar with a pair of silk cloths on the altar.

Having performed the installation of the principal pitcher (pradhānakumbha), one should install one pitcher at each gateway according to the previously mentioned procedure— either upon eight-petaled lotuses or upon heaps of rice within the previously described mandalas near the eastern and other gateways— and therein:
Having worshipped Dhruva in the pitcher situated in the eastern direction, Dharā in the south, Vākpati in the west,

and Vighneśa in the north— and likewise having established pitchers in the four corners starting from the southeast— one should worship Amṛta in the southeastern pitcher, Durjaya in the southwestern, and [Vijaya] in the northwestern.

Having worshipped Siddhārtha and Maṅgala in the northeast, and having again invoked the world-protectors, Indra and the others, into the jars starting from the east and worshipped them with their respective mantras as prescribed in the Vedas,
one should then [worship] Airāvata and Puṇḍarīka outside the jars in the eight directions starting from the east.
"One should worship Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sarvabhauma, and Supratīka. Having thus worshipped the elephants of the quarters, the Guru again goes to the altar, sits upon his own seat,
performs three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with his chosen mantra, and [proceeds] for that...

Having performed the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), beginning with the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to the hands and preceded by the [assignment of] the *mantra*’s preceptor (*ārṣa*) and so forth, one should [worship] the deity.

Having meditated and worshipped with mental offerings, one should fashion the form within the principal pitcher according to the method to be described; then, having invoked one's chosen deity there, one should perform the worship along with the limbs and the oblation according to the method to be described by means of the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).

Having worshipped according to the procedure prescribed for each respective ritual manual, one should prepare on the southern side of the altar a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of sand, measuring one cubit in length and breadth and one thumb-joint in height, according to the procedure taught for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) that will be described hereafter.
Having established the fire and cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru), having invoked the deity therein and worshipped them,

and having offered oblations with clarified butter and that caru substance according to the procedure prescribed for the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma), one should again worship the deity, merge him into the image contained within the water-pot (kumbha), and likewise worship and dismiss the fire.

Having performed the bali-offering for all beings according to the procedure to be described, as well as the offering of the specific bali prescribed in the respective *kalpa*, and having performed for the deity the rites from the *uttarāpośāna* up to the *nīrājana* according to the method stated for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*),
preceded by three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth upon the hands and the six limbs (*kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*).

Having recited the root mantra one thousand and eight times, and having offered the recitation to the deity according to the procedure to be described, one should place a water-pot filled with water, containing gold within it and wrapped in a pair of cloths, upon a heap of scattered offerings (vikira) previously established in the northeast corner of the pavilion.

There, having meditated upon the weapon-deity in the form of a lion— holding a sword and a shield in her right and left hands, possessing a fierce appearance, and facing westward— one should remain standing,
worship her with the five offerings beginning with perfume, and pay homage to that water-pot.
Having lifted [the vessel] with both hands and circumambulated within the pavilion,

he should place the water-pot (karaka) in its proper place, sit down, and once again worship that deity of the weapon-mantra with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the weapon-mantra; then, in the previously prepared sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas)...
The preceptor should perform the installation of the fire in the sacrificial pit of the Ācārya located between Indra and Īśāna.

Therein, first, having smeared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with cow dung and having spread and worshipped one's own seat near the pit according to the procedure prescribed for daily worship, one should sit there facing either north or east; then,

having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra).

Having meditated upon the deity and worshipped them with mental offerings, having recited the root mantra as much as possible and offered the recitation, and having prostrated before the venerable Guru, one should perform the purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Therein, first, having inspected the pit with the root mantra, sprinkled it with the weapon mantra,
struck it three times with kusha grass using the weapon mantra, and sprinkled it with the armor mantra; having dug slightly in the middle of the pit with the weapon mantra,
one should lift up that earth with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the weapon mantra.
Having cast out [impurities] externally with the Heart-mantra, filled the excavation with pure clay, leveled it with the Astra-mantra,
sprinkled it with water while reciting the Kavaca-mantra, made it firm by pounding it with wood and other materials using the Astra-mantra,
and swept the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with Kuśa grass using the Kavaca-mantra;
Having smeared [the area] with cow-dung water while reciting the *kavaca* mantra,
and having meditated upon the form of the thirty-eight *kalās* of Agni, Sūrya, and Soma while reciting the *kavaca* mantra,
one should [bind] each of the three girdles with a triple-stranded thread three times for each girdle while reciting the *kavaca* mantra.

Having wrapped [the kuṇḍa], one should worship each respective kuṇḍa— beginning with the first square— with offerings starting from the seat (āsana) and ending with the lamp, using the formula "Oṃ, this seat for such-and-such kuṇḍa, obeisance" (*oṃ amukakuṇḍāya etadāsanaṃ namaḥ*) and so forth, employing the name of that specific kuṇḍa in the dative case followed by the word "obeisance" (*namaḥ*). In the same manner, one should likewise worship the navel (*nābhi*).
Having likewise worshipped the three girdles with the heart-mantra,
and having meditated upon the sacrificial pit as firm as a diamond using the weapon-mantra, one should, with the heart-mantra and blades of *kuśa* grass,
arrange four paths in the four directions of the pit to manifest the play of the flames of fire.

One should perform the "cleansing of the eyes" (akṣapāṭana) by covering the entire surface of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with unbroken-tipped kuśa grass consecrated with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra) and the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra); thus one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras). In case of inability, one may perform them with only the first four rites as previously mentioned.

Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should draw three lines each with the root of kuśa grass— oriented eastward in the southern, middle, and northern sections, and oriented northward in the western, middle, and eastern sections— using either the heart-mantra or the weapon-mantra; then, having sprinkled them with water while reciting the *praṇava* (oṃ), [one should proceed] with those lines oriented eastward.
On the lines: on the southern line, salutation to Viṣṇu; on the middle line, salutation to Rudra;
on the northern [line], salutation to Indra. On the lines with their tips pointing north:
on the western [line], salutation to Brahmā; on the middle [line], salutation to Sūrya; on the eastern line...

"Salutation to Soma. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha there—beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Paratattva—according to the sequence of the Yoga-pīṭha to be described hereafter. Then, upon the filaments of the lotus, proceeding clockwise from one's own front (the east) to the center, one should worship with "Oṃ, salutation to Jayā," and likewise to Vijayā.
Homage! Homage to Ajitā! Homage to Aparājitā! Homage to Nityā! Homage to Vilāsinī! Homage to Dogdhrī! Homage to Aghorā! Homage to Maṅgalā!
Having thus worshipped, one should offer a handful of flowers in the center with the mantra: *Hrīṃ, homage to the lotus-throne of all powers*.
Having placed Bhuvaneśvarī there,
having performed the rites from invocation (*āvāhana*) through the final consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) with her respective mantra and the corresponding mudrās,
and having worshipped her with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with the seat (*āsana*), one should meditate upon Śrī Śiva there.

Having likewise worshipped with the root mantra, one should visualize the Goddess as having bathed after her menses and the God as intoxicated with passion; then, using a vessel made of gold or the like, or a new earthen vessel, or one produced from a sun-crystal, or from a fire-drill, or from the house of a Vedic scholar, [one should take] the fire with the Astra mantra.

Having placed [the substance] in a vessel, covered it with another vessel of the same kind while reciting the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), and having received what was brought by a maiden or a well-dressed woman, the Guru takes a single coal from its midst with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*);
he discards the "flesh-eating" portion (*kravyādāṃśa*) toward the southwest corner (*nairṛtakoṇa*) and [retains] the "divine" portion (*devāṃśa*) with the root mantra (*mūla*).
Having sprinkled [the site] with the Astra-mantra, struck it with Kuśa grass using the Astra-mantra, and sprinkled it again with the Kavaca-mantra, [one should contemplate] from the Bindu—
which is of the nature of Agni and Soma and resides within the Fire-mandala at one's own Mūlādhāra—
outward, together with the digestive fire located in the Maṇipūra.
Flowing through the path of the *suṣumnā* and exiting via the nostril, while uttering the seed-syllable of fire, *raṃ*, he casts [the fire] into the fire situated in the vessel before him. (p.

Having united the consciousness of the fire, and contemplating the oneness of the fires of the stomach, the moon, and the earth, one should consecrate it with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), transform it into nectar using the *vam* syllable and the *dhenumudrā*, protect it with the weapon mantra (*astramantra*), and veil it with the armor mantra (*kavaca*). Oṃ.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "Raṃ, obeisance to Vahni," and having knelt upon the ground,
he takes that vessel with both hands, circumambulates it three times over the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and,
meditating on the seed-syllable of Śiva within the womb of the Goddess, [places it] facing himself.
Uttering the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) into the center of the sacrificial pit, he should cast that fire [into it],

offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the God and Goddess with the thought of sexual union, and then, blowing through his mouth while reciting the mantra: *oṃ citpiṅgala hana hana paca paca daha daha sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā*.

Having kindled the fire with *kuśa* grass and built it up with wood, standing with palms joined in reverence, he should worship the blazing fire with this mantra: "Oṃ, I bow to the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations; stainless and golden-hued, well-kindled, facing in all directions. Thus, having approached the flaming fire.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the fire-mantra to be mentioned hereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows: "Salutation to Bhṛgu, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (chandas), on the mouth; salutation to Agni, the deity (devatā), on the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *raṃ*, on the secret place; salutation to the power (śakti) *svāhā*, on the feet. Thus having performed the nyāsa, [one proceeds].
"Viniyoga for the *dīkṣā*-limb-homa"—thus he should say with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*). [He should assign: *sarayūṃ* to the *liṅga*, obeisance to Hiraṇyā;
*ṣarayūṃ* to the anus, obeisance to Kanakā; *śarayūṃ* to the head, obeisance to Raktā;
*varayūṃ* to the mouth, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā; *larayūṃ* to the nose.

Salutation to Suprabhā. For the two eyes: *rarayūṃ* to Raktā, salutation. For all limbs: *yarayūṃ* to Bahurūpā, salutation. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seven tongues of fire, [one recites]: *Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā*. *Uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya*...

To the crest (śikhā), Vaṣaṭ! To the smoke-pervading one (dhūmavyāpin), the armor (kavaca), Huṃ! To the seven-tongued one (saptajihva), the three eyes (netratraya), Vauṣaṭ! To the bow-bearer (dhanurdhara), the weapon (astra), Phaṭ! Having thus performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), [one should assign:
"Obeisance to Agni Jātavedas" on the head; "Obeisance to Agni Saptajihva" on the left shoulder.
On the left side, *namas* to Agni Havyavāhana;
on the left hip, *namas* to Agni Aśvodaraja; at the *liṅga*, *namas* to Agni Vaiśvānara;
on the right hip, *namas* to Agni Kaumāratejas; on the right side, *namas* to Agni Viśvamukha.

Having placed the forms [of the deities] with the mantra "Obeisance to Agni, the mouth of the gods, on the right shoulder," and having meditated upon one's own self as the form of Fire, one should display the *saptajihvā-mudrā*. Then, on a bed of *kuśa* grass to the north of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should place the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*), the vessel for the *caru* oblation (*caru-sthālī*), and the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having placed the fuel-sticks consisting of five pieces of wood that have been trimmed, and a handful of kuśa grass with its roots and tips intact,
one should arrange the vessels face down; likewise, having arranged other sacrificial offerings such as curd, unbroken rice, and so forth,
as well as the materials for worship such as scents and flowers, each in their proper place, they too should be placed face down.
Having first performed the inspection by sprinkling water with the hands turned downward while holding the *pavitra* blades, one should turn the *sruk*, *sruva*, and other implements face upward,
wash the *praṇīta* vessel, and place it upon a bed of *kuśa* grass in front of oneself.

Having filled it with pure water and placed therein scents and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), one should place a *pavitra*— consisting of two *kuśa* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) long with their tips intact and joined by a *brahmagranthi* at the center— with its tips pointing north, upon the surface of the water; then,
with the ring fingers and thumbs of both hands, [one should touch] the root and tip of the *pavitra*.

Reciting the *vidhṛti* weapon-mantra, one should pour water three times from the vessel outside [the pavitra] through the middle of the *pavitra*. Having thus performed the purification (*utpavana*), one should place a small amount of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in its center,
lift that vessel with both hands up to the head, and [place it] upon a bed of *kuśa* grass on the northern side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having placed darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon that [altar], one should set down the *praṇītā* vessel;
then, having washed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and filled it with pure water,
one should pour some of the water from the *praṇītā* vessel into it using another vessel, and with that water—

One should sprinkle all the vessels, the oblation materials, and the worship materials with the root mantra; thus having performed the placement of the materials, one should sprinkle the fire with the *prokṣaṇī* water and,
beginning from the eastern direction, [cover it] with four *darbha* blades that have not yet been used.

Having strewn [the grass] in the east with the tips pointing north, from Īśāna to the southeast; then again in the south with the tips pointing east, covering the roots of the previous eastern strewing with the tips;
and again in the west with the tips pointing north, covering the root of the southern strewing with the root.

Again, in the north, having strewn [the grass] with its tips pointing eastward, so that the tip of the western layer meets the tip of the eastern layer, one takes up the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*):
the thickest one in the west with its tip pointing north, and then the smallest one in the south with its tip pointing east.

One should place the three enclosing sticks (paridhi) upon the middle girdle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) over the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), such that the base of the western stick rests upon the base [of the middle stick], and likewise, from there, the smallest one is placed toward the north with its tip facing east, so that its base rests upon the tip of the western stick. Now:

On the western girdle, the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be performed in the space between the *yoni* and the upper girdle. On the western enclosing stick: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
On the southern enclosing stick: *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. On the northern enclosing stick: *oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*.

Having thus performed the worship, he should invite a Brāhmaṇa initiated by his own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), seat him upon a cushion of *kuśa* grass to the south of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and [address him as follows]: "I, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and named such-and-such Śarman, belonging to such-and-such lineage and such-and-such branch within such-and-such Veda..."

One should choose [the officiant] with garments, ornaments, and so forth, saying: "I choose you, O meditative one named So-and-so Śarman, for the office of Brahman to oversee what has been done and what remains to be done in the fire-rite (*homakarma*) which is an auxiliary part of my desired initiation. Then, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings.
In the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, having worshipped a bundle of Kuśa grass,
one should place the vessels for the Arghya, Pādya, Ācamanīya, and Madhuparka, consecrate them with the fire-mantra (vahnimantra),
and fashion within the center of the sacrificial pit a lotus having a pericarp containing a hexagon and complete with filaments.
Having visualized the fire's seat of worship (*pūjāpīṭha*) as an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three squares provided with four gates, there, according to the previously mentioned procedure—
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha, beginning from the frog and ending with the supreme reality (paratattva), one should worship on the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus,
proceeding clockwise starting from the eastern petal: "Salutation to Pītā," "to Śvetā," "to Aruṇā," "to Kṛṣṇā," "to Dhūmrā," "to Tīvrā," "to Visphuliṅginī," "to Rucirā," and "salutation to Jvālinī."

Having worshipped the nine powers at the center and the end, and having worshipped the entire pedestal with the mantra "Raṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of all powers," one should [visualize] therein the Fire-god, who holds in his hands the gestures of boon, svastika, power, and fearlessness, who is seated upon a lotus, and who has three eyes.
I praise Agni, who is the color of vermilion, adorned with ornaments of refined gold, and whose head is graced by matted locks. || 1 ||

Having meditated thus and displayed the Saptajihvā mudrā, one should worship the fire three times with a handful of flowers while reciting: *oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā agnaye namaḥ*. Then, having again uttered the mantra of the fire, [one offers] this seat to Agni.
"Oblation! Thus, O Agni, this is your portion, svāhā! This is your water for washing the feet, obeisance!
This is your water for sipping, svadhā! This is your honey-mixture, svadhā! This is your water for sipping again, svadhā! This is your bath, obeisance!"
Having conceived the visualization of the fire's respective limbs— beginning with the face, head, and other parts of the body, as well as the outer girdle—

within another vessel outside the girdle, and having performed the rites from the *arghya* and *pādya* up to the bath, one should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and then offer a garment to the fire itself.

Having again offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) and presented the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and having again offered water for sipping outside, one should offer the scents and flowers into the fire itself; thus,
having performed the services beginning with the seat and ending with the flowers using the fire-mantra, [one proceeds] in the six corners.
Beginning from the northeast corner and ending at the center: *sarayūṃ* homage to Hiraṇyā;
*ṣarayūṃ* homage to Kanakā; *śarayūṃ* homage to Raktā; *varayūṃ* homage to Kṛṣṇā; *larayūṃ* homage to Prabhā; *rarayūṃ* homage to Atiraktā.

*Namaḥ*. Having worshipped with "Oṃ *yarayūṃ*, salutation to Bahurūpā," one should worship on the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, at the front of the deity, and in the four cardinal directions starting from that: "Oṃ *sahasrārciṣe*, salutation to the Heart;
*svāhā*. "Oṃ *svastipūrṇāya*, salutation to the Head; *namaḥ*. "Oṃ *uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya*..."
*Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ namaḥ*.

*Saptajihvāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ dhanurdharāyāstrāya phaṭ namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [one should worship] on the eight petals, starting from the front of the deity and proceeding clockwise with *oṃ*:
Salutation to Agni Jātavedas; likewise, salutation to Agni Saptajihva,
to Agni Havyavāhana, to Agni Aśvodaraja, to Agni Vaiśvānara, to Agni Kaumāratejas, to Agni Viśvamukha, and salutation to Agni Devamukha.

Having worshipped the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) in a clockwise direction, and having worshipped Indra and the other deities with their weapons within the square outside of that, one should again worship the fire with the fire-mantra, offer incense, lamps, and so forth, present the food offering (naivedya), cast it into the fire, and then, as before, offer water for sipping (ācamanīya). Thereafter—

Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their openings facing east and their bases downward in the fire, one should cleanse them three times— with the tips [of the *kuśa* blades] for the tips [of the ladles], with the middles for the middles, and with the roots for the roots— and then,
having cast those [blades] into the fire, place the *sruk* and *sruva* upon a bed of *kuśa* grass in one's own southern quarter.
Taking the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) and washing it with the Astra mantra, place it on a bed of Kuśa grass before oneself.

Upon that, place a pair of Kuśa blades serving as a purifier (pavitra), measuring one span (prādeśa) in length, with their tips pointing northward and joined at the middle by a Brahma-granthi. Then [take] pure cow’s ghee from another vessel.

Having placed into the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī) that which is free from defects such as foul odor, purified by the four refinements beginning with inspection, rendered nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā* while reciting "vaṃ," and consecrated eight times with the root mantra;
Having taken embers from the hearth and cast them onto the ground outside the girdle in the northwest corner,

one should place the vessel for clarified butter upon them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Then, having ignited two blades of *kuśa* grass and cast them into the clarified butter with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should throw the remainder into the fire and [place] another two blades of *darbha* [grass].
Having ignited [the fire] with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra) and having circled the vessel of clarified butter (ājya-sthālī) around it,
one should cast the burnt residue into the fire; then, having again ignited the kuśa grass and displayed it over the clarified butter with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra),
one should cast the burnt residue into the fire and lift up the vessel of clarified butter.

Circumambulating the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) clockwise, bringing [the embers] before himself, and placing them upon a bed of *kuśa* grass, he should cast the embers from the outer area into the center of the pit; then, touching water,
he should take the *pavitra* with both hands using the thumb and ring finger at its root and tip.

Holding [the ladle] while reciting the mantra, one should purify the ghee through the middle of the *pavitra*; then, reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should likewise sprinkle the ghee three times toward oneself through the middle of the *pavitra*. Having placed that *pavitra* with its tip pointing eastward in the center of the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), [one prepares] two portions.
Having conceived of the right side as the bright fortnight and the left side as the dark fortnight,
and then likewise visualizing the triad of channels— *iḍā* on the left side, *piṅgalā* on the right side, and *suṣumnā* in the middle— one [should proceed] from the right side with the *sruva* ladle.
Having taken clarified butter with the *hṛdayamantra* and offered it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra "To Agni, svāhā!",

one should perform the ritual renunciation of the offering with the formula "This is for Agni, not mine. Then, again taking clarified butter from the left side with the *hṛdayamantra*, one offers it into the left eye of the fire with the mantra "To Soma, svāhā!"

Having performed the renunciation of the offering with the formula, "This is for Soma, not for me," and having again taken clarified butter from the center with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one offers it into the eye on the forehead of the fire with the mantra, "Oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā," [saying]: "This is for Agni and Soma, not for me."

Having thus performed the renunciation of the offering, one should again take clarified butter from the heart [of the vessel] with the right hand and, having offered it into the mouth of the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," perform the renunciation of the offering with the words "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, this is not mine. Then: "Oṃ Bhūḥ Svāhā; to Agni, this is not mine. Oṃ."
*Bhūr* svāhā! This is for Vāyu, not mine. *Oṃ* *Svaḥ* svāhā!
This is for Sūrya, not mine. *Oṃ* *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* svāhā! This is for Prajāpati, not mine.

Having offered oblations three times with the fire-mantra: *Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*, and having performed the renunciation of the offering for Agni with the words *agnaye idam na mama*, [one should recite]: *Oṃ agner garbhādhānaṃ saṃpādayāmi svāhā*.
Thus, having performed the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana* rites, and having offered eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) for each rite,

one should meditate upon the Fire born from Vāgīśvara in the form previously described; then, having offered eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra "of the fire’s birth-rite" (*agner jātakarma*), and having performed the cutting of the fire’s umbilical cord, one should purify the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*).

Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter with the formula "The naming of Vahni, svāhā," and having given him the name Śivāgni, [he offers] with the formulas: "The departure of Vahni, svāhā; the first feeding of Agni, svāhā; the tonsure of Agni, svāhā; the initiation of Agni, svāhā; the Mahānāmnī ceremony of Agni, svāhā."

Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter for each rite with the formulas: "I accomplish the *Mahāvrata* of Agni, svāhā! I accomplish the *Aupaniṣada* of Agni, svāhā! I accomplish the *Godāna* of Agni, svāhā! I accomplish the *Samāvartana* of Agni, svāhā! I accomplish the *Udvāha* of Agni, svāhā!", [he performs] the rites from the *Garbhādhāna* to the *Udvāha* of Vahni.
Having performed the purificatory rites for the fire and having worshipped and dismissed the Father and Mother— the God and Goddess— as before,
one should silently offer five fuel-sticks soaked in ghee into the fire with a single handful [of sticks] for each deity at the root and the tip,
[reciting]: *oṃ sarayūṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*, and likewise *ṣarayūṃ*.

*kanakāyai* (to Kanakā), *śarayūṃ* (to Śarayū), *raktāyai* (to Raktā), *varayūṃ* (to Varayū), *kṛṣṇāyai* (to Kṛṣṇā), *larayūṃ* (to Larayū), *suprabhāyai* (to Suprabhā), *rarayūṃ* (to Rarayū), *atiraktāyai* (to Atiraktā), *yarayūṃ* (to Yarayū), *bahurūpāyai* (to Bahurūpā). *Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya svāhā*. Likewise, *svastipūrṇāya śirase* (to Svastipūrṇa, the head).

To the Rising One, to the Tuft (śikhā), to the Smoke-Pervading One, to the Armor (kavaca), to the Seven-Tongued One, to the Three-Eyed One, to the Bow-Bearer, to the Weapon (astra). Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Jātavedas; likewise, svāhā to Agni Saptajihva, to Agni Havyavāhana, to Agni Aśvodara, to Agni...

Having offered one oblation each with the mantras of the tongues, limbs, and forms—namely, "To Vaiśvānara Agni," "To Agni of youthful splendor," "To Agni whose face is the universe," and "To Agni whose face is the gods"—one should then offer: "Oṃ Laṃ, to Indra, Svāhā!
This is for Indra, not for me. Likewise for Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.
To Varuṇa, to Vāyu, to Kuvera, to Īśāna, to Brahmā, to Ananta, to the Thunderbolt (Vajra),
to the Spear (Śakti), to the Staff (Daṇḍa), to the Sword (Khaḍga), to the Noose (Pāśa), to the Goad (Aṅkuśa), to the Mace (Gadā),
to the Trident (Śūla), to the Lotus (Padma), and to the Discus (Cakra). Thus, with each respective name, he offers one oblation for each.

Having offered [the oblation], one should perform the renunciation (*tyāga*) by specifying the respective names for each occasion. Then, taking clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon, pouring it four times, and placing the *sruva* face-down upon the mouth of the *sruc* ladle, one should rise;
while standing before the fire, reciting the previously mentioned mantra of Agni, one should substitute "vauṣaṭ" in place of "svāhā" and [offer] with the *sruc*.
Having offered [the oblation] and sat down, [one recites]: Oṃ svāhā; Oṃ śrīṃ svāhā; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā;
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ svāhā;
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ svāhā; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ.
To Gaṇapati, svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, svāhā!

Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, may all people [be favorable] to me, svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, may all people [be favorable] to me...

Having offered ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇapati mantra divided into ten parts as "vaśamānaya svāhā," [he should then offer] four [oblations] with the complete and individual mantra: "oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā."
One should offer oblations of clarified butter. This is the procedure for the installation of the fire.
Having thus performed the installation of the fire, one should wash a new vessel made of copper or other metal with the Astra-mantra;
then, while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should place into that vessel fifteen *prasṛti* measures of rice grains that have been washed three times and consecrated eight times with the Mūla-mantra.
Having poured in fresh milk until it reaches the point where steam arises, one should cook it;
then, covering the mouth of that vessel with a washed bowl while reciting the Kavaca mantra,
when that milk rises upward due to the force of the steam, [one should stir it] with a wooden ladle.
Circumambulating clockwise while stirring [the vessel] upwards and recollecting the root mantra, the Guru, facing east,
cooks the *caru*; when it has boiled, he pours clarified butter (*ājya*) into it with the *sruva* ladle using the root mantra,
removes the vessel from the fire using the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), and places it upon a bed of *kuśa* grass consecrated with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Having set aside the *caru* and divided it into three parts, he should offer one portion to the deity residing in the water-pot (*kumbha*). Then,
having placed around the pavilion the vessels containing the sprouts that were prepared during the previous rite of sowing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*),
and having set down flour-made lamps filled with ghee, he should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having gone and sat down upon his own seat, he should there perform the placement of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings according to the procedure to be described by means of the root mantra; then, having visualized the wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) within the mouth of the fire in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [he should proceed] there according to the procedure to be described.

Having worshipped [the deities] from the Maṇḍūka-pīṭha up to the Manvantara, one should invoke the deity there and worship them with all the ritual offerings (upacāras), along with their limbs (aṅgas) and retinues (āvaraṇas), according to the procedure to be described. Here, the sequence from the arghya offering up to the bath (snāna) is exactly as in the fire-worship (agnipūjā), but outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in a separate vessel.

One should prepare [the offerings] with reference to the deity; all else should be prepared within the center of the *kuṇḍa*. Then, having offered twenty-five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra for the purpose of unifying the mouths of the fire and the deity, one should contemplate the identity of one's own self, the fire, and the deity.
Having offered oblations eleven times with clarified butter using the root mantra for the purpose of joining the channels (*nāḍī*),

and having offered one oblation each to the deities of the six limbs and the surrounding retinue, one should divide the previously prepared *caru* into nine parts and, using one part with the root mantra—

Having become twenty-fivefold, the Guru should repeatedly take fire from his own *kuṇḍa* and deposit it into the *kuṇḍas* situated in the eastern and other directions, which have been consecrated by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to the previously mentioned procedure through the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). The officiating priests likewise [deposit] the fire into their respective *kuṇḍas*.

Having kindled [the fire] according to the previously mentioned procedure and approached it, having properly gratified it with sprinkling, strewing, placing the enclosing sticks, offerings, worship, and so forth, when that [fire] has been well-kindled—
On page 268:

Having invoked the deity according to the prescribed rite for the daily worship of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), and having worshipped him thoroughly with offerings beginning with betel-leaf (tāmbūla) and ending with the fire-oblation (homa) for the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa)— following the sequence of unifying the faces and joining the channels (nāḍīsandhāna)— ...
Having been divided by the Guru and given with the root mantra, they should offer oblations twenty-five times each into their respective fire-pits using milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
Then the Guru, in the four processional paths (vīthī) of the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala starting from the east, places the signs of the zodiac in their respective positions: Aries and Taurus in the east;
Gemini in the southeast; Cancer and Leo in the south; Virgo in the southwest; Libra and Scorpio in the west; and [Sagittarius and Capricorn] in the northwest.

In the north, one should place the bow; in the northeast, Capricorn and Aquarius; and in the northeast, Pisces. Having thus divided the positions of the zodiac signs, one should offer a bali-oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) from the remnants of the fire-offerings to the planets presiding over the signs, as well as to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and the Karaṇas, just as one does for the positions of Aries and Scorpio.
Kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ: to Maṅgala, lord of the signs of Aries and Scorpio, this is the goad of scents and flowers; obeisance to this milk-rice offering (pāyasa-bali). Likewise, Caṃ 5:
to Śukra, lord of the signs of Taurus and Libra, this [is the goad of scents and flowers]; Ṭaṃ 5.

To Mercury, the lord of the signs Gemini and Virgo, this [offering]. Yaṃ 10, to Soma, the lord of the sign Cancer, this [offering]. Aṃ 16, to Sūrya, the lord of the sign Leo, this [offering]. Taṃ 5, to Guru, the lord of the signs Sagittarius and Pisces, this [offering]. Paṃ 5.

To Śanaiścara, the lord of the Makara-kumbha [sign], this milk-rice offering (pāyasa-bali) accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice (akṣata) is offered; salutations! Again, in due order, to the deities of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the quarter of Kṛttikā, who constitute the portion of the Meṣa zodiacal sign located in the station beginning with Meṣa...
"To all beings who roam by day and night, this fragrance... and so forth, as before.
In this manner, [the offering is made] to the three quarters of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and Mṛgaśiras—the lunar mansions that constitute the portion of the zodiac sign Taurus.

To the deities of the constellations: to the deities of the constellations Mṛgaśiras (the latter half), Ārdrā, Punarvasu (three quarters), and Puṣya, which constitute the portion of the sign Gemini. In the same manner, the mantras for the subsequent [signs] should be inferred. Then, for the *vava* karana situated between Pisces and Aries: "To this... and so forth.

Thus, in the interval between Taurus and Gemini, [the offering] is for Bālavāya; in the middle of Gemini and Cancer, for Kaulavāya; in the middle of Leo and Virgo, for Taitilāya; in the middle of Virgo and Libra, for Gara;
in the middle of Scorpio and Sagittarius, for Vaṇija; and in the middle of Sagittarius and Capricorn, this [offering] is for Viṣṭi.
One should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra "Namaḥ," accompanied by fragrant substances, unbroken rice, flowers, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
According to the tradition, the bali for the lords of the two zodiac signs should also be offered in the locations of those two signs.

Then the Guru, having performed for the deity residing in the water-pot (kumbha) the rites beginning with the *uttarāpośāna* and ending with the *nīrājana* according to the procedure to be described hereafter, and having offered praise and prostration, should ask for forgiveness. Then, having eaten the third portion together with the disciple, the Guru himself, having sipped water (*ācānta*), [should do so] for the disciple who has also sipped water.

To the disciple who has been rendered complete (sakalīkṛta) through the application of the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should give a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) measuring a span (*prādeśa*), consecrated eight times with the previously mentioned heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
The disciple, having performed the cleansing of his teeth with it and having washed the tooth-stick, [places it] before him.

Having discarded [the sacrificial grass] and performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should go into the presence of the Guru. Then the Guru, having protected the disciple by binding his topknot with [grass] consecrated by the root mantra, should sleep that night upon a bed of *kuśa* grass on the altar together with him; this is the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).

In this regard, during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the deities of the lineages beginning with the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the respective mantras and the sequence of worship for each deity according to the procedure previously explained.
However, the worship of the nine planets (*navagraha*) should be performed using either the mantras taught in the *Āgamas* or Vedic mantras.
The tradition holds that [the initiation] on the altar in the northeast corner should indeed be performed separately.
"Purified by the two vidyās consisting of five and six kūṭas over many days"— in this manner,
according to the sequence stated, the procedure for the application of initiation is most excellent.
In that regard, because other mantras are not mentioned as being constituent parts [of the rite],
whereas in the procedure for the primary initiation of knowledge (*vidyādīkṣā*), which constitutes a limb of the six systems (*ṣaḍdarśana*),
those various mantras which serve as limbs within the six systems—
In accordance with that same method, the oblations, recitations, worship, and other rites prescribed for the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be performed.
The Guru, likewise, must provide instruction in the form of the complete [tantra] along with its auxiliary branches (saṅgopāṅga).
We shall explain the ritual for the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) later in that specific section.

Wherever instruction is given primarily according to the Vedic systems of philosophy, the specific details therein should be understood as being governed by the rules prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti; otherwise, there is equality [with other systems].

Now, at the beginning of the initiation into the Vedic systems of philosophy, follows the ritual procedure for the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa-pūjā), starting with the worship of Gaṇādhipa. Therein, first is the worship of Gaṇeśa:
the patron (yajamāna), having sat upon his seat, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and completed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Holding *kuśa* grass and unbroken rice grains in his hand, he should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows:
"Today," and so forth, after specifying the month, fortnight, and other details, [he continues]:
"for the pacification of obstacles to the performance of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the mantra of such-and-such a deity which is about to be performed."

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati," and having worshipped Gaṇapati with the sixteen services (upacāras) beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) using the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," one should pray with palms joined in reverence (baddhāñjali).
O curved-tusked one of massive body, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, O God, always grant me freedom from obstacles in all my undertakings. (1)
"May the worship reach completion; having recited [the mantra], one should dismiss [the deities].

Thus it is said. Then, upon heaps of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) on the pedestal, one should worship the sixteen Mothers beginning with Gaurī and the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī. They are as follows:
Gaurī, Padmā, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā—the Mothers, the Mothers of the World. || 1 ||
Fortitude, contentment, and likewise nourishment are the family deities of the self;
as well as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 2 ||
“Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and the Seven Mothers. As for the method of worship: having prepared the articles of worship, one should sit facing the east.
Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)— beginning with "Kuśa grass, barley, sesame seeds, etc., here today... and so forth—

that "I shall perform the worship of the sixteen Mothers, Gaurī and the others, as well as the worship of the seven Mothers, Brāhmī and the others, as auxiliary parts of the mantra-initiation (*mantradīkṣā*) to be performed," [one should worship] with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) while reciting *Oṃ*.
Having invoked [the deity] with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, O Gaurī, come here;

stay here," and having established her with the mantra prescribed in one's own Vedic school (śākhā), one should perform all [the rites] according to the sequence of individual objects (padārthānusamaya) in the manner beginning with "Salutation to Gaurī, this is the seat."
Each of those situated in the north should be worshipped individually. The same applies to Brāhmī and the others as well.

However, when the Mothers possess the status of group deities (*gaṇadevatā*), then one should worship them simultaneously, having uttered each name individually and said "to Gaurī and the others" (*gauryyādibhyaḥ*). The same applies to Brāhmī and the others as well. Then:

According to one's own custom, one should pour five or seven streams of clarified butter while they are attached to the vessel, reciting "Thou art the purifier of Vasu. Some also say that its worship should be performed. Then follows the recitation of the Śānti hymns.
Thereafter, one should perform the Vṛddhi-Śrāddha according to local custom and as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā), preceded by the formal declaration of intent (saṅkalpa).

Then follows the *puṇyāhavācana*: with the words "Having placed the knees upon the ground," and so forth, he should cause three Brāhmaṇas to hear him say, "May you, sirs, declare it to be auspicious (*puṇyāha*). They, in turn, should respond three times, "It is auspicious. [He says] three times, "Oṃ, may you, sirs, declare it to be well-being (*svasti*)," and the response is three times, "Oṃ, well-being."
"Oṃ, may you declare success," [he says] three times. "Oṃ, let there be success," is the response three times.

Then, outside the pavilion in the western direction, on a smeared surface, the patron sits facing east, performs the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), restrains his breath (prāṇāyāma), and begins with "Today here... and so forth.

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the selection of the preceptor (ācārya) and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) in order to carry out the ritual initiation (dīkṣā-karma) for the mantra of such-and-such a deity," one should seat the preceptor facing north and adorn him with white garments, golden earrings, necklaces, armlets, and beautiful throat-ornaments.
With palms joined in *añjali*, having prayed, "May you be my guru in the bestowal of initiation," and being told by him, "So be it," [he should say: "I,
who belong to such-and-such a lineage (*pravara*), such-and-such a clan (*gotra*), and who study such-and-such a branch within such-and-such a Veda..."

"I, [Name] Śarman, belonging to the [Name] lineage and born of the [Name] clan, choose you, [Name] Śarman, endowed with the [Name] Pravara, as my preceptor (*guru*) for the bestowal of initiation into the [Name] mantra, with these perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, betel, golden ornaments, a ring, and garments. He should reply, "I am chosen. Thus...

One should select nine Brahmins— specifically one for the purpose of performing the Gāyatrī-homa in the eastern pit (pūrvakuṇḍa), and seven for the purpose of performing homas in the pits located in the southeast, south, southwest, west, northwest, north, and northeast. Then, [one should select another] for the purpose of guarding the eastern gate.

One should select eight individuals separately: two Rigvedins for the purpose of guarding the southern gate, two Yajurvedins for the purpose of guarding the western gate, two Sāmavedins for the purpose of guarding the northern gate, and two Atharvavedins [for the purpose of guarding the eastern gate]. The formula for the selection is as follows:

It is exactly as before. In this manner, one should choose the book-teacher (*pustakācārya*). Here, however, the door-keepers are common to all systems of philosophy (*sarvadarśana*). Then, wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, accompanied by his wife, disciples, and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*) [should proceed] amidst auspicious sounds.

While [the child] is being born, with a full water-pot in hand, having circumambulated the pavilion while chanting the mantras beginning with "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," having entered through the western door,
and having sat down in the western part inside the pavilion, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), regulate the breath (prāṇāyāma), and recollect the place and time.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "Today, as an ancillary part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) to be performed, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*),
and so forth," and having worshipped Gaṇeśa with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), [he should scatter] white mustard seeds in all directions.
One should scatter [the grains] within the pavilion. There, the mantras for destroying obstructing spirits (*rakṣoghnāḥ*) are as follows:
"Whatever being is here, having always resorted to this place, let all of them leave this spot and go wherever they belong. (1)
May the spirits and piśācas depart in every direction; without causing offense to any of them, I shall commence this rite of Brahman. || 2 ||

Thus, one should sprinkle everywhere and on all sides with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and *kuśa* grass, using the verses "śucī vo havyā" and "āpo hi ṣṭha". Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should mutter the two mantras beginning with "svastyayanaṃ tārkṣyam". Thereafter, at a distance of one cubit outside the door of the pavilion in the eastern direction...
Having placed a *vaṭa* (banyan) or *aśvattha* (peepal) archway— known by such names as "Very Firm" (*sudṛḍha*) or "Very Beautiful" (*suśobhana*),

and marked with the sign of a conch shell— and having consecrated it by name with the mantra "Agnim īḷe purohitam," one should smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and then install Rāhu and Bṛhaspati there. In that regard, there is one [verse]:

The *kalaśa* (water-pot) should be established. Regarding the mantras therein: having touched the ground while reciting "mahī dyauḥ" and made a prayer, and having scattered barley with "oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante," one should place the *kalaśa* down with either "ā kalaśeṣu" or "ājighra kalaśam. Then, having filled it with water using "imaṃ me gaṅge," [one should recite] "gandhadvārām."

With the verse "The fragrance, those herbs... he places all kinds of herbs; with "The herbs have gathered together... he places barley; with "From stalk to stalk... he places *dūrvā* grass; with "In the holy fig tree is your... he places five twigs; with "O Earth, be propitious... he places five types of earth; with "Those that bear fruit... he places fruit; and with "For you are treasures... he places five gems.

Having placed gold—consisting of gems and gold coins—within [the vessel], one should wrap the face with a cloth and a red thread while reciting the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ. Having placed a shallow bowl filled with grain on top with the mantra "pūrṇā darvi," one should invoke Dhruva there and worship him. Then...
To the south, having placed a gateway (toraṇa) made of udumbara wood, or one that is auspicious, formidable, or marked with wheels, while reciting "For food thee!

For strength thee!", he should worship it by name as before, smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and install the deities Sūrya and Aṅgāraka. Then, having established the water-pot (kalaśa) as before—
There, having invoked the Earth (Dharā), one should worship her. Then, in the west, having placed a gateway (toraṇa) made of Plakṣa or Udumbara wood—

possessing a beautiful top-knot (suhotra), radiant (suprabha), and marked with a lotus— while reciting "śanno devīḥ," one should worship it by name as before, smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and [invoke] Śukra and Budha.
There, one should place [the vessel]. Having deposited the water-pot as before, one should invoke and worship Vākpati.

Then, to the north, having placed a palanquin made of *aśvattha* or *pālāśa* wood, marked with a mace, and named Pūrṇasukarman or Subhīma, as a gateway (*toraṇa*), while reciting "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*), one should worship it by name.

Having smeared [the area] with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should place the Moon, Ketu, and Śani there. Then, having placed a water-pot as before, one should invoke and worship Vighneśa therein. After that, again at the eastern door, one should place two water-pots adorned with curd and unbroken rice on the two door-panels.

One should install [the vessels] with the mantras as before; the mantras are to be repeated for each jar. Having placed two Airāvata jars, one should worship them. In that regard, there are two Ṛgvedic officiants (*ṛtvij*).
The Ṛgveda has lotus-petal eyes, its meters are *gāyatrī*, and its presiding deity is Soma.
O best of Brahmins, you who belong to the Atri lineage, perform the recitation for peace during this sacrifice.
Having prayed thus, one should worship each [deity] individually with scents and other offerings while reciting "agnim īle". Then:
"Come, come, O Lord of the immortals who wields the vajra, praised by all the gods, siddhas, and sādhakas;
being fanned by a host of apsarases, protect our sacrifice, O Blessed One! Salutations to you! (1)
Having invoked Indra— along with his limbs (aṅgas), his retinue, his weapons, and his powers— into the door-vessel (dvārakalaśa) with the words, "O Indra, come here,
stay here," and having worshipped Indra there with the mantra "trātāram indram," [he worships] the two yellow banners as well with the mantra "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ."

One should raise a staff five cubits long; or the mantra is "Indraṃ vo viśvataspari. There, having meditated upon Indra—standing upon the intoxicated Airāvaṇa, possessing a thousand eyes, wearing a yellow crown and earrings, and holding a vajra and a lotus in his right and left hands respectively—[one should perform the rite].

Indra, the lord of the gods, the most excellent, wielder of the thunderbolt, possessed of great strength, the deity who presides over a hundred sacrifices—to him, eternal salutations again and again. (1)

Having thus bowed, one should offer the oblation with the words: "I offer this oblation of black gram (or cooked rice) to Indra, together with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his powers. Then, having sipped water for purification, one should go to the southeast, place the water-pot as before, worship the *puṇḍarīka* lotus there, and [worship] Amṛta.
Having been worshipped, come, come, O Vaiśvānara, carrier of oblations, who art attended on all sides by the foremost of sages;
together with the radiant multitude of worlds, protect my sacrifice, O Sage—salutations to you! || 1 ||
Having invoked Agni— along with his limbs, retinue, weapons, and powers— into the pitcher with the mantra "O Agni, come here,
stay here," and having worshipped Agni with scents and other offerings using the mantra "tvanno agne," one should offer a red banner and a red flag with the mantra "agniṃ dūtam."

One should raise a staff five cubits long. Then, having meditated upon Agni—standing upon a goat, red in color, holding a red water-pot in his right and left hands, and wearing a sacred thread—one should recite: "The person of the southeast is red, composed of all the gods, and imperishable."
Salutations again and again forever to him, the presiding lord of the dust of smoke-bannered fire.
Having thus bowed and recited "to Him with His limbs" and so forth, one should offer the oblation (bali) with the words: "I offer this oblation of black gram rice (māṣabhakta) to Agni."

Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and gone to the south, having established two jars at each door-jamb as before, and having placed the dwarf-elephant there, one should worship it. Then, two officiating priests (ṛtvij) learned in the Yajurveda [should be appointed];
the Yajurveda has fearful eyes, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has Viṣṇu as its deity.
O best of brahmins, you who belong to the lineage of Kāśyapa, perform the recitation for peace during the sacrifice.
Having thus prayed to each one individually with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship them with the mantra: *iṣe tvorje tvā*. Then:
"Come, come, O Vaivasvata, O Dharmarāja, worshipped by all the immortals, embodiment of Dharma!
Lord of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, joy, and sorrow; for our welfare, protect the sacrifice; homage to you! (1)
Having invoked Yama with the mantra "O Yama, come here, stay here," which is distinguished by its limbs and other parts,

and having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "To Yama, Soma," one should hoist a black banner and a black flag, raising a staff five cubits long while reciting "The cow came. Then...

Having meditated upon Yama— who is mounted upon a buffalo, whose two right and left hands hold a staff and a noose, who resembles a mass of black collyrium, and whose three eyes are like fire— one should contemplate him as being of great strength, mounted upon a mighty buffalo and holding a staff in his hand.
I invoke you into this sacrifice; may my worship be accepted. || 1 ||
Having thus prostrated with the mantra beginning with "sāṅgāya," one should offer the bali with the words: "I offer this bali of black-gram flour to Yama."
Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and having placed a water-pot (kalaśa) in the southwest as before, and having worshipped Kumudagaja and Durjaya, [he recites]:
"Come, come! You are the leader of the hosts of Rākṣasas, together with the multitudes of Viśāla, Vetālas, and Piśācas."
Protect my sacrifice from the Piśācas; O Blessed One, you are the Lord of the World; homage to you! || 1 ||

"O Nirṛti, come here, stay here!"— having thus invoked her along with her limbs and other attendants, and having worshipped Nirṛti with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "mo ṣu ṇaḥ" or "asunvantam," one should raise a blue banner and a flag on a five-cubit staff while reciting "mā ṣu ṇaḥ. Then, [one should place] a man mounted [upon it].
Having meditated upon Nirṛti, who has a sword in his hand, is blue in color, and wears blue ornaments;
who is mounted on a man, possesses a massive body, holds a sword in his hand, and is endowed with great strength;
who is blue, attended by hosts of Rākṣasas, and adorned with blue ornaments. || 1 ||
I invoke Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand and is the sole leader of all the worlds;
may he accept my worship in this sacrifice. (2)
Having thus prostrated with "To the one with limbs," and so forth, he should offer the bali with the words: "To Nirṛti, I offer this bali of black gram and rice."

Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should place two jars at each branch of the western gate as before, install the collyrium and the world-elephant (diggaja), and worship them. Then,
two officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are learned in the Sāmaveda [should be appointed].
The Sāmaveda, O best of Brahmins, has tawny eyes, is composed in the Jāgata meter, and has Śakra as its deity;
you, belonging to the lineage of Bhāradvāja, perform the recitation for peace at this sacrifice.
Having prayed thus, one should worship [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the mantra "agna āyāhi. Then:
"Come, come, O Lord, together with the hosts of aquatic creatures, the oceans, Parjanya, and the Apsarases;
you who are praised by the lords of the Vidyādharas and the immortals—protect us! Homage to You! (1)

Saying "O Varuṇa, come here! Stay here!", he should invoke Varuṇa along with his limbs and other attributes. Having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "tattvā yāmi," he should raise a white banner and flag while reciting "imaṃ me varuṇa. Then [he should worship] the white-colored [deity] holding a noose in his hand upon a crocodile.
I invoke Varuṇa, the wearer of a crown, who is described as having a noose in his hand and being the lord and repository of the waters; salutations again and again to Varuṇa in this sacrifice. (1)
Having thus bowed down, one should offer the bali with the words: "I offer this bali of black-gram and rice to Varuṇa, together with his limbs and attendants," and so forth.

Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and placed a water-pot in the north-west as before, and having worshipped Puṣpadanta and Siddhārtha, [he should say]: "Come, come! For the protection of my sacrifice, mounted upon a deer, together with the hosts of Siddhas!"
Lord of the vital breath, companion of Kālakavi, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you! || 1 ||

"O Vāyu, come here, stay here! Having thus invoked Vāyu along with his limbs and other attributes, and having worshipped him with scents and other offerings while reciting "tava vāyo ṛtaspate," one should raise the smoky-colored banner and flag while reciting "vāyo śatam. Then [one should worship] the one mounted upon a deer...

Having meditated upon Vāyu, who holds a variegated garment and a banner in his right and left hands, who dwells in space, and whose vehicle is the wind—O Pavana, I invoke you to this sacrifice; please accept this worship. (1)
Formless yet possessed of great power, moving through the sky with the gait of a beast, to that venerable Vāyu, the wind, I bow down. || 2 ||
Having thus prostrated with the mantra beginning with "sāṅgāya" and so forth, one should offer the bali with the words: "I offer this bali of black-gram and rice to Vāyu."
Then, having sipped water (ācamya), one should place two jars on each side of the door-posts at the northern gate as before;
having installed and worshipped the all-pervading world-elephant (sārvabhauma diggaja), one should then [appoint] two officiating priests (ṛtvij) learned in the Atharvaveda, [reciting]:
"Bṛhannetra is the Atharvaveda, of Anuṣṭubh meter, with Guru as its presiding deity."
O Vaiśampāyana, best of brahmins, recite the Śānti at this sacrifice.

Having prayed thus and worshipped with scents and other offerings while reciting the mantra "śanno devīḥ," [he should then say]: "Come, come, O Lord of Yakṣas! Perform the protection of this sacrifice together with the host of stars.
Together with all medicinal herbs and the ancestors, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you! (1)
Having invoked Soma with the mantra "O Soma, come here, stay here," together with his limbs and other attributes,

and having worshipped him with the mantra "Soma, we [worship] thee, O Soma," or with "O Soma, [thou art] a cow," he should place a green and white banner and flag while reciting "Āpyāyasva. Then, [he should visualize Soma] seated in a celestial chariot drawn by men, resplendent with earrings, necklaces, and armlets.
Having meditated upon Kuvera, who holds an excellent mace in his right and left hands, wears a crown, has a large belly, a massive body, and is green in color— (p. 272)
Among all the constellations, King Soma is established;
homage to that divine Soma, the lord of the constellations. || 1 ||
