Having thus prostrated with "sāṅgāya" and so forth, one should offer the oblation (bali) with the words: "I present this oblation of black-gram flour (māṣabhakta) to Soma."
Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and placed a water-pot (kalaśa) in the northeast as before, and having worshipped the auspicious world-elephant Supratīka there,
[he recites]: "Come, come, O Lord of the Universe, wielder of the trident and the khaṭvāṅga staff, together with your own retinue!"
O Lord of the World, Lord of Sacrifice, for the sake of the perfection of the sacrifice, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you! (1)

"O Īśāna, come here! Stay here! Having thus invoked Īśāna together with his limbs and other attendants, and having worshipped that Īśāna with perfumes and other offerings, one should hoist a white banner or a flag of all colors while reciting "abhitvā deva savitar. Then [one should worship] him mounted upon the bull.
Having meditated upon Īśāna— white in complexion, three-eyed, holding an excellent trident in his right and left hands,
mounted upon the shoulders of a bull, with a trident in hand and three eyes;
I invoke you to this sacrifice; may you accept my worship. || 1 ||
To the sovereign of all, the great god, Īśāna, the pure Lord, the wielder of the trident, the three-eyed one—to him, eternal salutations again and again. (2)
Having thus bowed with "to [the deity] together with his limbs" and so forth, one should offer the *bali* with the words: "I offer this *māṣa*-bean-flour *bali* to Īśāna."

Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), [he should offer oblations] below in the space between the northeast and the east, saying: "Come, come, O Lord of the Earth in the Netherworld (Pātāla), whose praises are sung by the wives of the Nāgas and the Kinnaras;
together with the hosts of Yakṣas, lords of serpents, and the immortals, protect our sacrifice, O Ananta! (1)
Saying "O Ananta, come hither, stay! he should invoke Ananta, distinguished by his limbs and other attributes;
having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "āyam gauḥ," he should raise a cloud-colored banner and a white flag while reciting "āyam gauḥ."
Seated upon the bed of Ananta, adorned with seven hoods, his two upper right hands hold a lotus and a conch, one above and one below. || 1 ||
Having meditated upon Ananta, who is blue in color and whose two hands on the upper and lower left sides hold a discus and a mace— one who, in his infinite form,
[pervades] the cosmic egg with all its moving and non-moving beings—
One should bear him upon the head like a flower; to him, eternal salutations, salutations! || 1 ||

Having thus prostrated with "to [the deity] along with his limbs," and so forth, one should offer the oblation (bali) with the words: "I offer this oblation of black gram porridge (māṣabhakta-bali) to Ananta."

Then, having sipped water (ācamana), [he should invoke] in the middle of the west and southwest, facing upwards: "Come, come, O Lord of All, together with the world of the lords of gods and the ancestral deities!
You are the sustainer of all, possessed of immeasurable power; protect our sacrifice for our constant welfare. (1)
Having invoked Brahmā, distinguished by his limbs and other attributes, with the words "O Brahman, come here! Stay here!",
and having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the mantra *brahma jajñānam*, one should raise a red banner and a flag with that same [mantra].

Having meditated upon Brahmā— four-faced, bearded, with matted hair, pot-bellied, and red in color; holding a rosary and a handful of kuśa grass in his two right hands, one raised and one lowered, and holding a sacrificial ladle and a water-pot in his two left hands, one raised and one lowered.

To him who is born from the lotus, who possesses four forms, who is the abode of the Vedas, the grandfather, the presiding deity of sacrifice, and the four-faced one—to him, eternal salutations again and again. (1)
Having thus bowed, saying "to the Brahman together with his limbs," and so forth, he should offer the oblation, saying, "I offer this oblation of black-gram flour to the Brahman."

Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), [one should set up] for Indra a great banner of variegated colors in the middle of the pavilion, possessing a very tall staff equipped with chowries and small bells— either ten or sixteen cubits in length, or five cubits long and three cubits wide, or one cubit long and one cubit wide.

The Vṛṣṇi [image] is to be installed; and at that very spot, the worship of Brahmā should be performed with the mantra "brahma jajñānam. Then, one should offer salutations to all the gods upon the sixteen pillars of the pavilion, and salutations to the Kinnaras upon the rafters. Thereafter, in the eastern direction...
Having smeared a small portion of ground and sat down:
"May all those beings in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, grant me protection. (1)
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas; sages, Manus, cows, and likewise the divine mothers. || 2 ||
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Kṣetrapālas together with their hosts, filled with joy, perform protection for me throughout the entire sacrifice. (3)
May they protect the pavilion and slay the *rakṣasas* on all sides!
Homage to the stationary beings dwelling in the three worlds!
Homage to the moving beings dwelling in the three worlds! Homage to Brahmā! Homage to Viṣṇu!

"Salutation to Śiva, to the gods, to the Dānavas, to the Gandharvas, to the Yakṣas, to the Rākṣasas, to the Pannagas, to the Ṛṣis, to human beings, to cows, and to the Mothers of the Gods. Having thus worshipped each one individually with flowers and other offerings, [one should proceed].
As before, with the same mantras, one should offer a bali of black-gram porridge upon that very ground for these [deities].

Then the teacher, having washed his feet and hands along with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and having sipped water (ācānta), shall enter the pavilion through the eastern door as before; having sat down in the western part of the southern door and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), he should say:
"O Brahmins, perform the rites as prescribed. Then...

The Guru, having scattered flowers upon the great altar (mahāvedi), should fasten a five-colored canopy adorned with fruits and flowers above it, according to the dimensions of the altar. On the planetary altar (grahavedī),
he should likewise fasten one of those dimensions and draw the Sarvatobhadra diagram.

In the initiation of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā*), however, one should construct either the Śrīcakra or the maṇḍala of one's chosen deity upon a central altar measuring nine cubits. One is consecrated with the Śrīcakra measuring either nine cubits or three cubits.
For daily worship on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), a space of one cubit is recommended.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Tantrarāja*: "In that system, the altar for the planets (*grahavedī*) and the altar for the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala are established in the northeast;
the altar for the guru-maṇḍala in the northwest; the altar for the worship of the couple (*mithunapūjāvedī*) in the southeast;
and the altar for the daily worship of the Nityā of that day near the *vāstu*-maṇḍala—such is the tradition."

Likewise, at this juncture, the preceptor (ācārya) shall perform the installation of the fire (agnisthāpana) in his own sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the procedure prescribed for his own home. Following that same sequence, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) shall also perform the installation of the fire in their respective pits according to the procedures prescribed by their own Vedic branches (śākhā). The Guru, as the supervisor of all rites, shall remain present.

When the fires have been thus established, the Guru, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) on the planetary altar (*grahavedī*) and the *sarvatobhadra* mandala—beginning with "Today here... and so forth—"I shall perform the installation of the deities of the pavilion as a subsidiary rite (*karmāṅga*) for the ceremony known as the bestowal of initiation," he should install Brahmā and the other deities. In the center is Brahmā, [with the mantra] "brahma jajñānam."
Gautama is the seer, Vāmadeva is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the metre; its application is in the installation and worship of Brahmā.

Thus, for the subsequent [verses]: "Oṃ, brahma jajñānam" (1); in the north, "somaḥ" (2); "Oṃ, abhitvā deva savitar" (3); in the east, "indram vo madhucchandāḥ," Indra is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre (4).

In the southeast is Agni; "Agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe" (We choose Agni as the messenger), by Kaṇva Medhātithi, addressed to Agni, in the Gāyatrī meter. 5. In the south is Yama; "Yamāya somaṃ" (To Yama the Soma), by Vaivasvata Yama, addressed to Yama, in the Anuṣṭubh meter. 6. In the southwest is Nirṛti; "Mo ṣu ṇaḥ" (Do not seize us), by the terrible Kaṇva, addressed to Nirṛti...

The meter is Gāyatrī. 7. In the west is Varuṇa; [the mantra] "tattvā yāmi" [is from] Śunaḥśepa; [the deity is] Varuṇa; the meter is Triṣṭubh. 8. In the northwest is Vāyu; [the mantra] "vāyo śataṃ" [is from] Gautama Vāmadeva; [the deity is] Vāyu; the meter is Anuṣṭubh. 9. Between Vāyu and Soma are the eight Vasus; [the mantra] "jmayā atra" [is from] Maitrāvaruṇa Vasiṣṭha.

The *vasavas* are in *triṣṭubh* meter. 10. Between Soma and Īśāna are the eleven Rudras; "ā rudrāsaḥ" belongs to Śyāvāśva; the eleven Rudras are in *jagatī* meter; "ā rudrāsaḥ. 11. Between Īśāna and Indra are the twelve Ādityas; "tyān nu kṣatriyān" [is] by Sāṃmada (Matsya); [the hymn is] by Māga.

The twelve Ādityas; Gāyatrī meter. (12) Between Indra and Agni are the two Aśvins; Rāhūgaṇa Gautama [is the seer] for the two Aśvins; Uṣṇih meter. (13) Between Agni and Yama are the Viśvedevas with the Pitṛs;
"omāsaḥ" [is the ṛc]; Madhucchandas [is the seer] for the Viśvedevas; Gāyatrī meter. (14) Between Yama and Nirṛti...
Seven Yakṣas. Vāmadeva [saw] "Abhi tyam" (To that one). Seven Yakṣas are the *prakṛti*. Om!

To that god Savitṛ, the wise in intellect, I sing with hymns—the one of true impulse, the bestower of jewels, the beloved, the inspired sage, the source of thought—whose lofty inspiration has shone forth in his impulse.

Hiraṇyapāṇi, the one of excellent wisdom, measured out the dear worlds. 15. Between Nirṛti and Varuṇa are the Bhūtas and Nāgas; Āyam-gauḥ, Sārparājñī, and the Sarpas [are the meters]; Āyam-gauḥ is the Gāyatrī. 16.
Between Varuṇa and Vāyu are the Gandharvas and Apsarases; of the Apsarases, Etaśa and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga [are the seers].

The Gandharvas and Apsarases are in the Anuṣṭubh meter. Oṃ, [the mantra] of the Apsarases and Gandharvas. 17. Between Brahmā and Soma are Skanda, Nandīśvara, Śūla, and Mahākāla; [the mantra] of Kumāra is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and Kumāra is the deity. 18. [The mantra] of Ṛṣabha is in the Ṛṣabha meter.

Vairāja is the meter; Anuṣṭup is the meter for "Ṛṣabhaṃ mā" (19). Between Brahmā and Īśāna, Dakṣa and the others are in the seven corners, or Aditi; Lokya is Bṛhaspati; Dakṣa is the deity; Anuṣṭup is the meter; "Oṃ aditir hy ajaniṣṭa" (20).
Between Brahmā and Indra are Durgā and Viṣṇu; [the mantra] "tām agnivarṇām" is for Durgā, with Saubhari as the seer.

Triṣṭubh: Oṃ *tām agnivarṇām* || 21 || Gāyatrī: Kaṇva Medhātithi; Oṃ *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ* || 22 || Brahmāgneya: In the center, Svadhā; *udīratām* (Śaṅkha); Svadhā; Triṣṭubh; *udīratām avare* || 23 || Brahma: In the center, Viṣṇu; Death and Diseases.
"O Death, beyond [is] Saṅkasuka; the diseases of death are Triṣṭubh. (24) (p.
274) Between Brahman and Nirṛti is Gaṇapati; "Gaṇānāṃ tvā" is by Gṛtsamada; Gaṇapati is Jagatī.

25. Between Brahmā and Varuṇa: *āpaḥ śaṃ no*, [composed by] Ambarīṣa, [addressed to] Sindhudvīpa, the Waters, in the Gāyatrī meter. 26. Between Brahmā and Vāyu: *maruto yasya*, [composed by] Rāhūgaṇa Gautama, the Maruts, in the Gāyatrī meter. 27. At the base of Brahmā’s feet, below the pericarp: *śyonā*.

Medhātithi, Bhūmi, Gāyatrī. 28. In that very place, the rivers such as the Gaṅgā; "imaṃ me sindhu-kṣit," [the seer] Praiyamedha, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī, Jagatī. 29. In that very place, the seven oceans;
"dhāmno dhāmno rājan ito varuṇa no muñca" and "yad āpo aghnyāḥ."
"By Varuṇa we swear; therefore, O Varuṇa, release us. O Vāyu, do not harm the plants within me;
therefore, becoming all-pervading (viśvavyacāḥ), release us from this, O Varuṇa. (30) Above that, one should worship Meru by name.
On the outside, near Soma and the others, one should worship the weapons in order: the mace (gadā), the trident (triśūla), etc.

The vajra, the śakti, the sword, the noose, and the goad. Outside of that, starting from the north, are Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Arundhatī. (8) Outside of that, starting from the east, are Aindrī, Kaumārī, Brāhmī, and Vārāhī.

Having installed these eight Śaktis— Cāmuṇḍā, Vaiṣṇavī, Māheśvarī, and Vaināyakī— each with their respective mantras, one should worship them either individually or together. Having thus prepared the fire, the installation of the eighty-five deities, beginning with the planets (grahas), takes place upon the altar for the installation of the deities.

One should perform it. The procedure for this is as follows: "Today, here, etc., in the rite called the bestowal of initiation (dīkṣā), I shall perform the installation of the deities of the seats (pīṭha-devatās) beginning with the planets. For the *praṇava*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Supreme Brahman, the deity (*devatā*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the meter (*chandas*) is the Goddess Gāyatrī. For the *vyāhṛtis*, [the seers are] in their respective order...

Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, and Bhṛgu are the sages (*ṛṣis*); Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya are the deities (*devatās*); Devī Gāyatrī, Devī Uṣṇik, and Devī Bṛhatī are the meters (*chandāṃsi*); and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Sūrya and the others. Therein, in the center of the primary seat, within a circular mandala twelve finger-breadths in size—

Facing east, one should invoke the Sun with red flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) using the mantra beginning with *ākṛṣṇena*. Hiraṇyastūpa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Savitṛ is the deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the Sun. *Akṛṣṇena*... *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ*, [O Sun] born in the Kaliṅga country, of the Kāśyapa lineage (*sagotra*).

Having invoked [the deity] with "O Sūrya, come here," one should establish him with "Stay here. 1. Then, in the southeast, upon a square mandala measuring twenty-four finger-breadths, one should place Soma facing east with white flowers and unbroken rice grains, using the mantra "Āpyāyasva" (Gautama). Soma is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is for the invocation of Soma. Oṃ.

"Āpyāyasva... Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ! O you who are born on the banks of the Yamunā, belonging to the Ātreya gotra, O Soma, come here! Having thus invoked him, one should establish him with the words, "Stay here. 2. Then, in the southern triangle, on a three-finger-wide mandala, one should [worship] Bhauma facing south with red flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).

The verse "agnirmūrdhā" is by Virūpa Āṅgirasa; Aṅgāraka is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter, and its application (viniyoga) is in the invocation of Aṅgāraka. Om agnirmūrdhā; Om bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ! O Bhauma, born from Sarasvatī, of the Bhāradvāja gotra, come here—having thus invoked him, one should establish him with the words, "stay here. 3. Then...

In the northeast, upon a four-finger-wide arrow-shaped mandala, one should face north and invoke Budha with yellow flowers and unbroken rice grains. The mantra is: "Obe, awaken! (udbudhyadhvam). Budha is the deity, Saumya is the seer, Triṣṭubh is the meter;
this is the application for the invocation of Budha. Oṃ udbudhyadhvaṃ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ.
Having invoked the preceptor born in the Magadha country, of the Ātreya *gotra*, with the words "O wise one, come here," one should establish him with the words "Stay here.

4. Then, to the north, within a long square measuring six *aṅgulas*, one should worship Bṛhaspati facing north with yellow flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), using the mantra "Bṛhaspate" (RV 2.23.1); its seer is Gṛtsamada, its deity is Bṛhaspati, and its meter is *triṣṭubh*.

The application (viniyoga) is for the invocation of Bṛhaspati. Reciting "O Bṛhaspati, he who... and "Oṃ Bhūrbhuvaḥ Svaḥ," one should invoke him with "O Bṛhaspati, born in the Sindhu region, of the Aṅgiras gotra, come here! and then establish him with "Stay here!
5. Then, in the eastern pentagon, on a nine-finger mandala, [one should place] facing east...
One should worship Śukra with white flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). According to Pārāśara, the mantra is "Śukraḥ"; Śukra is a *dvipadā-virāṭ* meter.

This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of Śukra. *Oṃ śukraḥ śuśukvān oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ, O Śukra born in the region of Bhojarāja, of the Bhārgava lineage, come here! Having thus invoked him, [one says] "Stay here!"*

One should install [the deity]. 6. Then, on a mandala measuring one *dhanus* (bow-length) or one *aṅgula* to the west, one should invoke Śani facing west with black flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), using the mantra "śam agniḥ. The seer is Ir̥mbiṭhi, the meter is Uṣṇik, and the application is for the invocation of Śanaiścara. "śam agniḥ" — Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.

"O Śani, born in the country of Saurāṣṭra, of the Kāśyapa gotra, come here!"—having thus invoked him, one should establish him with the words, "Stay here. 7. Then, upon a black winnowing-basket-shaped mandala, one should invoke Rāhu facing south with smoky-colored flowers and unbroken rice grains, using the mantra "kayā naḥ". Vāmadeva is the seer, Rāhu is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter; this is the application. Oṃ.

"Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Rāhu, born in the eastern region, of the Pāṭala lineage, come here!"—having thus invoked him, one should establish him with the words, "Stay here! (8). Then, in the northwest, upon a banner-shaped maṇḍala, one should worship the comets (ketus) facing south with black flowers and unhusked rice, using the mantra "ketuṃ kṛṇvan... (RV 1.9.3).
The Madhucchandas are the *ketavas* (luminaries); this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of the *ketus*. "Oṃ *ketuṃ kṛṇvan*...
Oṃ *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*, you *ketus* born in the Middle Country and belonging to the Jaimini lineage, come here!"—having thus invoked them, one should establish them with the words, "Stay here! || 9 ||

Now, the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the Sun and others should be installed in order to the right with white flowers and unbroken rice (akṣatas). "Tryambakam" [is the mantra]; Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. The application (viniyoga) is to be assigned everywhere.
Tryambakam: Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Īśvara. 1. "Gaurīrmimāya"; Dīrghatamas is the seer.
"Umā jagatī" (Umā, Jagatī meter), at the Soma-dakṣiṇa [sacrifice]. 2. "Yadakrando dīrghatamāḥ" (Yadakrando by Dīrghatamas), Skanda [is the deity], Triṣṭubh meter.
3. "Viṣṇo dīrghatamāḥ" (Viṣṇo by Dīrghatamas), Viṣṇu [is the deity], Triṣṭubh meter. 4. "Brahma jajñānam" (Brahma jajñānam), Gautama Vāmadeva [is the seer], Brahmā [is the deity], Triṣṭubh meter. 5.
(275) *indraṃ vaḥ*—Madhucchandas; Indra; Gāyatrī. 6. *yamāya somam*—Yama;
Yama; Anuṣṭubh. 7. *mo ṣu ṇaḥ*—Ghora Kaṇva; Gāyatrī. 8. *uṣo vājam*...

Praskaṇva, Citragupta, and Bṛhatī [are the seers]. 9. In this very same manner, having uttered the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of the mantras for the planets with white flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) on the left, and having said, "Come here! Stay here!", one should install the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatās*). Agni, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Agni, Gāyatrī; [the mantra for] Agni...

1. *Dūtam*: Medhātithi; the Waters; Anuṣṭubh meter. 2. *Syonā*: Medhātithi; the Earth; Gāyatrī meter. 3. *Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*: Medhātithi; Viṣṇu; Gāyatrī meter. 4. *Indra śreṣṭhāni*: Gṛtsamada; Indra; Triṣṭubh meter. 5. *Indrāṇīm*: Vṛṣākapi; Indrāṇī.

The *paṅkti* [meter]. 6. "O Prajāpati" (*prajāpate*)—Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. 7. "This bull" (*āyaṃ gauḥ*)—Sārparājñī is a serpent; the meter is *gāyatrī*. 8. "The Brahman born" (*brahma jajñānam*)—Gautama Vāmadeva is the Brahman; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. 9. Then, with white flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), [one should worship] Vināyaka and the others.

Pañcaka: For the Gaṇas, Gṛtsamada; Gaṇapati; Jagatī meter; for Rāhu, on the left, Vināyaka. 1. For Jātavedas, Kaśyapa; Durgā; Triṣṭubh meter; for Śani, to the north, Durgā. 2. For Vāyu, Ṛtaspate; Āṅgirasa; Vāyu; Gāyatrī meter; for the Sun, to the north, Vāyu. These [deities].
The traditionalists recite the mantras: 3. "O Vatsa, [the mantra] 'āditya pratnasya'—Ākāśa is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre;
for Rāhu, [the deity is] Ākāśa. 4. "This Dawn"—Praskaṇva is the ṛṣi, the Aśvins are the deities, Gāyatrī is the metre;
"O Aśvins, come hither, stay here"—for Ketu, [the deity is] the Aśvins. 5.
Then the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*): "Indra, the conqueror of all," by Mādhucchandas; Indra, the *anuṣṭubh* meter;

"O Indra, come here, stay here"—thus for the east. The same applies to the subsequent directions. (1) "Agni," by Medhātithi; Agni, the *gāyatrī* meter. (2) "Soma for Yama," by Yama; Yama, the *anuṣṭubh* meter. (3)
*Mo ṣu naḥ ghoraḥ*: Kaṇva; Nirṛti; Gāyatrī. 4. *Tvanno agne*: Vāmadeva; Varuṇa; Triṣṭubh. 5. *Tava vāyo vyashvyaḥ*: Vyaśvya; Vāyu; Gāyatrī. 6. *Somo dhenum*:
Gautama; Soma; Triṣṭubh. 7. *Tamīśānam*: Gautama; Soma; Īśāna; Gāyatrī. 8.

"Sahasraśīrṣaḥ" (The Thousand-headed), Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Anuṣṭubh meter; [one should worship] Ananta between the northeast and east. 9. "Brahma jajñānam" (Brahmā was born), Gautama Vāmadeva, Brahmā, Triṣṭubh meter; [one should worship] Brahmā between the southwest and west. 10.
12. Beyond that, in the north, Vāmadeva is the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) with the Anuṣṭubh meter;
Vasiṣṭha is the lord of the dwelling (vāstoṣpati) with the Triṣṭubh meter. Then: "You, whose body is the sound of the Sāman, are the vehicle of the Supreme Lord."
It is eternally the remover of poison and sin; therefore, grant me peace. || 1 ||
And with this [mantra], having invoked Garuḍa in the north; one should invoke Śeṣa to the east of Ravi (the Sun),

Vāsuki in front of Soma (the Moon), Takṣaka in front of Bhauma (Mars), Kārkoṭaka to the north of Budha (Mercury), Padmaka in front of Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śaṅkhapāla to the west of Śani (Saturn), Kambala in front of Rāhu, and [Kulika] in front of Ketu.
In front, from the seat of Kulika in the east, [he places] the seven lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī,

the seven yogas beginning with Viṣkambha, the two karaṇas Vava and Bālava, the seven continents, and the Ṛgveda. In the south, [he places] the seven lunar mansions beginning with Puṣya, the seven yogas beginning with Dhṛti, the two karaṇas Kaulava and Taitila, and so forth.

In the west, [he worships] the seven oceans and the Yajurveda; the seven lunar mansions beginning with Svāti, the seven yogas beginning with Vajra, the two karaṇas Garaja and Vaṇija, the seven netherworlds (pātālas), and the Sāmaveda. In the north, [he worships] the seven lunar mansions beginning with Abhijit, the six yogas beginning with Sādhya, and the karaṇa Viṣṭi.
[He should worship] the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr and the Atharvaveda; in the northwest, Dhruva and the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).

Then, according to available space, [he should worship] the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the seven principal mountain ranges (Kulācalas), the eight Vasus, the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the forty-nine Maruts, and the sixteen [Mātṛs].
[He worships] the Mothers, the six seasons, the twelve months, the two solstices, the fifteen lunar days, the sixty years, the Nāgas, Sarpas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Apsarases,
Rakṣasas, Bhūtas, and humans. Then, having placed a water-pot in the northeast of the altar—
There, having invoked Varuṇa and worshipped him, one should honor him. As for the consecration of the water-pot (*kalaśa*): "Viṣṇu is at the mouth of the pot, Rudra is stationed at its neck;
Brahmā is situated at its base, and the hosts of Mothers are remembered to be in the middle. (1)
Within his belly were the seven oceans and the earth with its seven continents;
likewise, the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda.
Together with all their limbs, they are all seated within the water-pot;
here are Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Śānti, and likewise Puṣṭikarī.
May they come, the destroyers of the sacrificer’s misfortunes, when the great ocean was being churned during the conflict between the gods and the dānavas. || 4 ||
Then you were born, O Kumbha, personally sustained by Viṣṇu himself;
all sacred fords are in your water, and all the gods abide in you.
All beings abide in you; the vital breaths are established in you.
You alone are Śiva himself, and you are Viṣṇu and Prajāpati.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and all the Viśvedevas together with the Pitṛs—
all of them abide in you, since you are the bestower of the fruits of their desires.
O Lotus-born One, through your grace I desire to perform this sacrifice;
O God, grant me your presence and be forever gracious to me. (8)

...thus [it is said]. Then, having dedicated the canopy (*vitāna*), which is radiant with garlands of fruits and flowers and has Bṛhaspati as its presiding deity, with the formula "This is for the Sun and the other planets;
it is not mine," one should fasten it above the altar of the planets (*grahavedi*). In this manner...
One should perform the consecration of the pavilion and other rites as prescribed in the Vedas; all else should be carried out according to the previously stated rules.

Then, having risen at dawn and performed his necessary duties, the Guru, together with his disciple, should give the disciple a tooth-stick of the prescribed length, consecrated seven times with the root mantra, and have him clean his teeth. Having purified his teeth, [he should proceed].
Having washed the tooth-stick, one should discard it upon a square altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit on each side in front.

Then the Guru should perform its examination. Regarding that, the auspicious and inauspicious results have already been explained in the determination of the measurements, and the expiation will be stated later. After that, the disciple also—
Having bathed, performed the morning rites, and adorned himself, he should bow to the venerable Guru and,

by his command, sit beside him. Then the Guru and the officiating priests (ṛtvij), having likewise worshipped the Deity along with His limbs and retinue in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍa), [proceed].

They should perform oblations (*homa*) one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, or with the specific substances for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*). Then, the Guru, having made the disciple— who is not a *śūdra*—
drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), leads him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and gazes upon him with divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*).

Having extracted the individual soul (jīvātman) from his heart-lotus through the path of the *brahmarandhra* out of that body according to the procedure described for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and having united it with one's own self by means of the power of yoga through the method taught by the Guru, one should perform the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*) of the disciple. Therein, at the feet of the disciple—

Having contemplated the path of the *kalās*— which consists of the five *kalās* known as *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *śānti*, and *śāntyatītā*— one should then [place] upon the region of its *liṅga* [the principles]:
Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, Kāla, Rāga, and Niyati.

One should meditate upon the path of the Śiva-tattva, which consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas): Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṅkāra, Buddhi, Manas, Śrotra, Tvak, Cakṣus, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Upastha, Śabda, Sparśa, Rūpa, Rasa, Gandha, Ākāśa, Vāyu, Agni, Salila, and Pṛthivī. Thus.
In the Śaiva initiation; however, in the Vaiṣṇava initiation, it is taught that there are the individual soul, vital breath, intellect, mind,
the ten senses, their respective mantras, the pentad of elements, the triad of the heart-lotus, the thread, and likewise the four [deities] headed by Vāsudeva.

The ten faculties previously mentioned are the ears and so forth, as well as the organs of speech and so forth. The subtle elements are sound and the rest. The five gross elements are ether and the rest. The triad of luminaries consists of the moon, the sun, and fire, along with those headed by Vāsudeva.

The four [Vyuhas] are Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. In the initiation of Saura [worship], however, there are the elements, the subtle elements, the senses, the mind, ego, intellect, as well as the faculty of understanding (dhī), and primordial matter (pradhāna). The ten senses are distinguished according to the sequence of their cognitive functions. Ego (garva) is the *ahaṅkāra*. Primordial matter (*pradhāna*)...

The *prakṛti-tattva*. In the initiation of power (*śakti-dīkṣā*), however, there are ten principles (*tattvas*): the five kalās beginning with *nivṛtti*, bindu, nāda, śakti, sadāśiva, and śiva. In the initiation of the three steps (*tripada-dīkṣā*), however, [the principles are]: Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva; these same [principles] in reverse order, and furthermore, the "all-principles" (*sarvatattva*). "In reverse order" means...
"Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman"—in this sequence, these very same [principles] are indeed Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva; thus, there are seven principles (*tattva*).
In this manner, during each respective initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should contemplate the corresponding path (*adhvan*).
In the initiation of the Gāṇapatya [tradition], however, only the Śiva-tattvas are to be known. Then, at the disciple's navel,
[one should contemplate] Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Mahātala, Talātala, Rasātala, Pātāla, Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana—

Having meditated upon the path of the fourteen worlds, consisting of the realms of Tapoloka and Satyaloka, one should then contemplate within the disciple's heart the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), whose nature consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
Then, one should visualize on the disciple's forehead the path of words (*padādhvan*), which is composed of an assembly of phonemes. Then...

One should meditate on the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*), which consists of the collection of syllables in the form of the root-mantra, upon the head of the disciple. Having thus contemplated the six paths within the body of the disciple, the Guru, touching him with the *kūrca* [sacrificial grass], should offer oblation into his own fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, I purify the path of kalās of [Name], svāhā."
Having offered oblations eight times with sesame seeds smeared with ghee, one should contemplate the path of the *kalās* as dissolved into the path of the *tattvas*.

Then, having offered oblations eight times with the mantra "Oṃ, I purify the *tattvādhvan* of [Name], svāhā," one should again contemplate the *tattvādhvan* as dissolved into the path of the *bhuvanas*. Again, Oṃ...

Having offered oblations eight times with the mantra, "I purify the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) of [Name], svāhā," one should contemplate that the path of worlds has dissolved into the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). Then, having again offered oblations eight times with the mantra, "Oṃ, I purify the path of phonemes of [Name], svāhā," one should [contemplate] that [the path of phonemes] into the path of words (*padādhvan*).

Having visualized that [the path] has dissolved, one should offer oblations eight times with the mantra: *oṃ amukasya padādhvānaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. Then, having visualized that it has dissolved into the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), one should again offer oblations eight times with the mantra: *oṃ amukasya mantrādhvānaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. Then that...

Having meditated upon [the soul] as dissolved into Paraśiva situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should again emanate the path of mantras from Paramaśiva by means of the reverse order of reabsorption; then the path of words (padādhvan),
from that the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), from that the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and from that the path of principles (tattvādhvan).
Then, having created the path of the *kalās* and established them in their respective locations,

and having gazed upon the disciple with divine vision, one should project the disciple’s consciousness— which resides within oneself— into the *brahmarandhra* of that [disciple] from the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayāravinda*) by means of the procedure prescribed for invocation. Herein:
For those born of the *śūdra* caste or mixed castes, the purification by fire (*adhva-śodhana*) should not be performed;

for them, one should perform purification by offering water for the feet (*pādodaka*). Then, as before, having offered one oblation each with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and the deities of the limbs and enclosures (*aṅgāvaraṇadevatā*), [one recites]: *oṃ bhūr agnaye ca*.

To Earth and the Great One, Svāhā! Om, to Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) and the Great One, Svāhā! Om, to Āditya and the sky (div) and the Great One, Svāhā! Om, to the Moon, the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), the quarters (diś), and the Great One—Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ—Svāhā!

Having offered four oblations with "Svāhā," [one should recite]: "Whatever [evil] was previously done by me through the authority of my life-force, intellect, body, and sense-objects, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, by means of mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the stomach, and the generative organ— whatever was remembered..."
Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra: "Whatever has been said, whatever has been done—may all that be an offering to Brahman, svāhā," (p.
Oṃ! O you of a thousand rays, of great splendor, homage to you who assume many forms!
O all-consuming, all-pervading purifier, let there be salutation to you. || 1 ||
You are Raudra, you are the performer of terrible deeds, and you are the slayer of the terrible; homage be to you!
You are Viṣṇu, you are the guardian of the world; grant me peace in this matter. || 2 ||

Having thus petitioned Agni and worshipped him with the fire-mantra as before, one should offer an oblation of sesame seeds with clarified butter while reciting: "For the sake of rectifying any deficiency or excess, I give sesame with ghee; Oṃ Hūṃ, perform [the rite] with all its limbs, Svāhā!
Having offered the oblation with sesame seeds, one should fill the *sruk* ladle with clarified butter and, upon that—

Having placed the flower with its face downward into the *sruk* ladle and grasping it with both hands joined like a conch shell, he stands up; placing the bases of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles at his navel,
he offers three oblations with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and worships the deity there as before.
Having withdrawn [the fire] from the presence of the hearth and deposited it into the water-pot (kalaśa),

one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter for each of the mantras of the Vyāhṛtis, Agni-jihvā, Aṅga, and Mūrti, as before; then, having sprinkled around the fire with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, as previously described.
O Agni, O you of great power, who fulfills all desires!
Even when another ritual task has arrived, grant your presence with respect. (1)
Having thus petitioned the fire, he should dismiss it into his own self by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*;

then, having silently cast the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) into the fire, and having dismissed the *praṇītā* vessel, he should place it upon a bed of *kuśa* grass before himself and say: "Oṃ, salutation to the eastern direction," and likewise, "to the southern direction."

Having sprinkled water from the *praṇītā* vessel toward each respective direction with the mantras "Salutation to the western direction," "Salutation to the northern direction," and "Salutation to the upward direction," and having poured water on the ground with "Salutation to the downward direction," he should sprinkle himself and the disciple with the kuśa grass using the water that has fallen upon the ground.
Having performed the dismissal of the excellent [deities] and dismissed Brahmā, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to be given a full vessel (pūrṇapātra) together with gold at the station of Brahmā;
thus ends the rule for the fire-oblation (homa) as a constituent part of initiation. As for the nature of the full vessel:

This has been stated in the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*): Then, having bound the disciple’s eyes with a strip of new cloth using the eye-mantra (*netramantra*), and taking him by the hand, one goes near the water-pot;
together with him, filling his joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers while oneself reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having caused the deity residing in the jar to receive an offering of flowers with both hands (puṣpāñjali), and having released its blindfold, he should seat it upon a bed of kuśa grass; [with the mantra:
"For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the collyrium-stick of knowledge..."
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye was opened. || 1 ||

Having thus caused [the disciple] to recite the mantra, and having worshipped the deity together with his limbs and enclosures (aṅga-āvaraṇa) in the water-pot (kumbha) with all ritual offerings (upacāra), and having visualized the body of the disciple according to the previously mentioned procedure for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), purified it, and generated [the deity within], one should perform the entire network of nyāsas, beginning with the seer (ṛṣi) of the root mantra, upon that disciple's body.

Having again performed the rite for the deity residing in the pitcher and worshipped them with the fivefold offerings beginning with fragrance, one should [place] the deities of the pavilion gates, the deities of the limbs and the surrounding retinue together with the world-protectors,
and the deities of the four sanctuaries beginning with Gaṇeśa, along with their respective limbs and retinues, upon the limbs of the Lord.

Having contemplated that [the disciple] has dissolved away, and having performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the previously mentioned method of applying the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*),

one should transform him into the form of radiant energy (*tejas*). Then, while contemplating that water in the jar— which is in the form of that radiant energy— as being composed of the Supreme Brahman, one should place the well-adorned disciple near the altar.

Having seated [the disciple] on an auspicious throne facing east within a *sarvatobhadra* or similar mandala in one of the directions— east, northeast, or north— the Guru, preceded by the sounding of the five musical instruments,
lifts up the water-pot and regards the mango sprouts and other items within the pot as being the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).

Having placed [the vessel] upon the head of the disciple while the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and other Brahmins chant the resonance of the Vedas, he— standing facing north— should again consecrate him, who is seated facing east, with the root mantra and the reverse-order alphabet (*vilomamātṛkā*).
Having first taken up the form of the weapon (astra) that was previously worshipped and having consecrated [the disciple] with its waters,

he should cause the disciple to sip the water remaining in that vessel; then, having made him complete (sakalīkṛtya) by performing the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) as before while identifying him with the nature of the deity, and having caused him to put on two clean, new garments.

Having had him perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and seated him near himself, one should worship the deity who has been transferred into the disciple’s body with the five offerings beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) within that very body; then, contemplating the identity of the disciple and the deity, one should [impart] the *Śrīmūlamantra* into the right ear of the well-composed disciple.
In the initiation of Gaṇeśa, preceded by the mantras of the four shrines beginning with Gaṇeśa,
one should recite [the mantra] three times according to the sequence of worship for each respective limb, preceded by Sūrya and the others;
if the disciple is a Brāhmaṇa, one should place water in his hand as a form of bestowing the mantra.

But to others, one should speak exactly as follows. Then the disciple, having first performed the nyāsa of the ṛṣis and so forth upon the hands and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) for the mantra taught by his own guru, should recite it one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times, or eight times; then, having offered the recitation (japa), he should contemplate the oneness of the guru, the mantra, and the deity.

Having contemplated [the Guru] and prostrated before him many times with eight limbs, one should again prostrate with five limbs. The definitions of the eight-limbed and five-limbed prostrations have already been stated previously in the section on the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*).
Having thus prostrated to the Guru and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as prescribed by the authoritative texts.
Thus concludes the initiation consisting of ritual action.
Now, if one is unable to perform the initiation through ritual action (*kriyādīkṣā*) in such detail,

then— in the previously mentioned smallest pavilion (*kaniṣṭhamaṇḍapa*)— having constructed a mandala on the altar as before and having likewise performed the installation of the water-pot (*kumbha*) there, the Guru, being unable to select officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [should prepare] a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having performed all the rites there, beginning with the installation of the fire, and having consecrated [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule, he should bestow initiation.

If one is unable to construct a pavilion, one should prepare a maṇḍala— or a circle for the worship of the respective deities— in some auspicious place as previously described; or, if that is impossible, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the aforementioned rule, one should establish the fire there according to the prescribed method.

Having performed the fire-oblation and other rites, and having consecrated [the disciple], one should impart the mantra. Now, regarding those qualities of fire such as color and so forth, it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"The luster, the fragrance, the sounds, and likewise the forms of fire..."
The expansions and the crests must also be perceived for the accomplishment of one's actions. ||1||
The best [ruby] has the luster of a lotus, a radiance equal to liquid lac, the color of the rising sun, or the brilliance of fire and the hibiscus; it is praised by the wise. (2)
Then the fire appears resembling an indragopaka insect, with the luster of blood;
it is excellent when resembling Indra’s bow (a rainbow) and likewise has the hue of safflower.
"Fire is said here by the color of red varieties of flowers. Now, as for the scent:
"The scent of fragrant substances is fire; the scent of ghee is most beautiful."
Āyurda is Padmagandha, and Suvrata is Bilvagandha. || 1 ||
Resembling the *nāga*, *campaka*, *puṃnāga*, *pāṭalī*, and *yūthikā* flowers; resembling the *padma*, *indīvara*, *kahlāra* lotuses, clarified butter, and guggulu resin. (2)

"The fragrance of the fire is auspicious. Now, as for sound: a sound resembling that of clouds, a lute, a peacock, or a mṛdaṅga drum brings success to the sacrificer; otherwise, it would be non-granting of success. (1)
Thus it is said in the Śāradātilaka: "The sound of kettledrums, clouds, and lordly elephants is auspicious for fire."
Now, O best of the twice-born, as for the shape: it is circular, resembling a banner or a chowrie, [belonging] to the celestial chariots, the horses, the palaces, and the bull. (1)
Furthermore, by the form of swans or peacocks, it bestows success;
Agni in that shape is traditionally held to grant immediate accomplishment at all times.
The form of other fanged creatures is not recommended for the rite of fire-offering (homa);
however, if one must wait for that specific form which has been described, [then one should do so]. (3)
"When they attain mutual correspondence, then the fire brings about success.
Now, regarding the flames:
"The odd-numbered flames of the fire, beginning with three, bring about auspiciousness."
Flames that are short, rising from a short base, and long are known to bestow success. || 1 ||
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Flames that are smokeless, free from flickering, and shaped like umbrellas bring auspiciousness to the sacrificer, and especially to his kingdom. (1)
Thus [it is said]. Now, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:

"When the fire is blazing, licking [the offerings], smokeless, and endowed with its qualities (saguṇa), as well as when it is pleasing and bestows satisfaction, one who desires success should offer oblations. (1)
That which is smooth, turning clockwise, and possesses a beautiful sound is always auspicious, provided it is devoid of other defects.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the prohibited [fire] is described:
"A fire that has little luster, is rough, accompanied by sparks, and whose flames are enveloped by smoke—such a fire does not grant success. (1)
That which is foul-smelling, licked by animals, or white and black, as well as that which scratches the ground—such a place also brings about defeat. (2)
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"A black [line], being the color of the path of Kṛṣṇa, destroys the patron;
white [line] quickly destroys the kingdom; and that which resembles the sound of a crow [destroys the lineage]. (1)
A sound from fire resembling a harsh voice brings about total destruction;
if the sacrificial fire has a putrid odor, it will cause suffering for the sacrificer. (2)
A crest that is severed or distorted causes death and the depletion of wealth;
smoke resembling the wings of a parrot or having a luster like that of a pigeon [is likewise inauspicious]. (3)
"It quickly causes the loss of horses and cattle.
Likewise, in the Tantrasāra:
"In this matter, the cries of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and the like do not lead to success."
It is harsh, accompanied by a crackling sound, and likewise moves in a counter-clockwise direction.
O best of sages, one who scratches the earth and one whose hair-tuft points downward are not accepted in this scripture of the Supreme Lord.
Thus [it is said on] p. 279. Regarding such faults as these, the expiation has been stated in the Kulaprakāśatantra:
"In the case of such faults, for the sake of expiation, the Guru..."
One should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
There are twenty-five [varieties] for each defect. Alternatively, regarding the different tongues of the fire according to their *sāttvika* nature and so forth:

therein, the *hiraṇyā* and others have already been mentioned previously in connection with the *sāttvika* *śāntika* homa as part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now, concerning the optional homas for subjugation (*vaśya*) and other such purposes:

In the descent of the Kula-mūla, there are five tongues of fire (jihvās): the first is Rājasyā, the second is Padmarāgā, the third is Suvarṇā, the fourth is Bhadralohitā, the fifth is Lohitā, the sixth is Śvetā, the seventh is Dhūminī, and the eighth is Karālikā.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the tāmasa [powers], it is stated in that very same place:
"The fourth is Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, and Manojavā. (1)
The fifth is named Lohitā, and Karālī is likewise declared;
Kālī is said to be the seventh; these should be understood according to the distinction of their functions. || 2 ||
"In the rites of sacrifice, in optional oblations, and in cruel homas, respectively.
Now, regarding the presiding deities of the tongues, the *Kulaprakāśatantra* states:
"The presiding deities of the tongues are the gods and likewise the ancestors."
And the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Piśācas, and likewise the Rākṣasas. || 2 ||
One should offer oblations into the tongues of the gods and others for the accomplishment of one's purpose;
thus satisfied, the deities will then grant the most excellent desired success.
"The channels (rasanās) are generally considered to bear their own names [as the tongues] of the fire.
Thus it is said. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"The preceptor should meditate upon Vaiśvānara stationed [within] during the oblations of kindled fuel."
He should be lying down during the oblations of clarified butter, and seated during the remaining rites.

Thus. Now, at the time of the fire-oblation (homa) here, having understood the tongues, head, ears, and so forth of the fire, one should offer the oblation specifically upon the tongue. As it is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra and in the Rāhukalpa:
"For the sake of the successful accomplishment of all undertakings, one should offer the oblation upon its tongue."
Having identified the eyes, ears, and other [limbs], the most excellent of teachers should perform the fire oblation (homa).
If one offers an oblation in the ear of Agni, it will cause fear from disease;
if offered in the nose, there will be great suffering; and if in the eyes, blindness shall occur.
It is said that [a flame] on the hair bestows poverty; therefore, one should perform the oblation upon the tongues of the flames.
Where there is wood, there are the ears; where there is smoke, that is the nose.
Where the eye has little flame, there is the head, which is ashes;
where the fire blazes intensely, there the tongues are proclaimed to be.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The wise man should offer oblations into the fire within the mouth for all rites;
[if offered] into the ears, there would be disease, while in the eyes, blindness is declared. (1)
Affliction of the mind occurs in the nose, and loss of wealth in the head;
the head is said to be the smoky fire, and the eyes are the smokeless fire. (2)
When blazing, the ear becomes thin, as does the nose when wood is on fire;
where fire is produced, it resembles pure crystal.
"The root of that [post] should be known there as being four finger-breadths in measure.
Now, regarding the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the *Uttaratantropaniṣad* states:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* are made from *śiṃśapā*, *aśvattha*, *śrīparṇī*, *khadira*, or *āmra* wood."
The two types of sandalwood, devadāru, vikaṅkata, śamī, and bhava. || 1 ||
[It was adorned] with bilva, udumbara, palāśa,
nāgakesara, bakula, aśoka, punnāga, plakṣa, nyagrodha, and campaka trees.
Regarding the phrase "created" (*nirmitā*): In the *Śāradātilaka*, it is said:
"The wise one, having taken one of the following—*śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or a milky tree—and having divided it into thirty-six parts each measuring one cubit (*hasta*)... (1)
The staff (daṇḍa) shall be made with twenty parts, and the altar (vedi) with eight of those parts;
the neck (kaṇṭha) is measured by one part, and the face (mukha) is measured by seven parts.
The width of the neck is proclaimed to be one-third [of the total height];
the top [of the neck] should be equal to the neck, and one should fashion the opening at the mouth.
The pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part in the middle of the altar for the exit of the clarified butter, measured by the width of the little finger.
One should fashion a navel-lotus in one part of its exterior;
its excavation should be circular with three parts, extending outward by half a part.
One should arrange eight petals all around using one part;
the girdle (mekhalā) and the face-altar (mukhavedī) should be on all sides with a measurement of half a part.
At the base and tip of the staff, there should be two bulbous ornaments (kumbhas) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively;
the pair of handles (daṇḍīs) should consist of eight parts, and this is declared to be the circumference of the staff.
The back portion of the altar, consisting of six parts, should be shaped like a tortoise;
one should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a boar.
The back portion of its face is declared to be the characteristic of the *sruva*.
One should fashion the *sruva* with twenty-four parts, just as one would for the *sruk*.
Its measurement by the staff (daṇḍa) is proclaimed to be twenty-two parts;
its circumference is four parts, and its head is that which receives the clarified butter from the *karṣa* measure.
One should bury two parts [of the staff] in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint;
at the root and the tip of the staff, there should be a knob adorned with a bracelet.

Thus [it is said], because it was stated by [the author] himself that "the pair of *gaṇḍīs* is in the shape of bracelets and is adorned with *kaṅkas*," and also because of the statement in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "The *gaṇḍī* should be like a bracelet. In other places, however, the *gaṇḍī* is a water-pot (*kumbha*), since that alone is necessary there. In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*...
"The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles may also be made of metal. Regarding the absence of *sruk* and *sruva*, Agastya said:

"O Sage, in the absence of *sruk* and *sruva*, one should provide two beautiful *sruk* and *sruva* made from flawless *palāśa* leaves, or even from *aśvattha* leaves, for the performance of the *homa* ritual in a concise manner."

Thus [it is said]. Now he describes the manner of its arrangement: therein [are the trees] *śiṃśapā*, *aśvattha*, *śrīparṇī*, *khadira*, *āmra*, *candana*, *raktacandana*, *devadāru*, *vikaṅkata*, *śamī*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *panasa*, *bakula*, *aśoka*, *nāgakesara*, and *punnāga*.

Having taken a piece of wood from among the *campaka* or *vaṭa* trees that is not dried out, free of wounds, undecayed, not damaged by woodworms or the like, larger than the prescribed measurement in thickness and length, and perfectly square, one should [measure] twenty-four finger-breadths there using the fist-finger measure.
Having divided those [dimensions] into thirty-six parts, one should divide twenty parts into half-daṇḍas; then,
having designated eight parts out of the remaining sixteen parts at the front for the sake of the face,
one should construct a square altar (*vedi*) using the remaining eight parts.

Having made a mark in the center of that [square] and taking that mark as a reference, one should produce a circle on all sides with a measurement of half a unit; then, producing another circle outside that one with a measurement of one unit, one should fashion three depressed divisions in the space between the two circles, with a central pericarp (karṇikā) in the shape of a circle.
Having set aside that [portion] and made it go outside, one should produce a circle all around by measuring half a part outside of that; then,
having produced another circle outside of that by measuring one part,
and having fashioned eight petals in the space between the two circles, [one proceeds] at a measurement of half a part outside of that.
One should create a beautiful, well-proportioned, and variegated splendor.

Then, using the remaining portion in front—specifically one-third of the altar (vedi) by carving away portions from both sides—one should fashion the neck (kaṇṭha) with one part in the middle; starting from that neck...
Having made the remaining portion slightly higher, with its top edge measuring seven parts and its width equal to that of the neck,

and having made it so that the width diminishes progressively from bottom to bottom; and having fashioned a molding (mekhalā) at the mouth like an altar (vedī), without interrupting the molding of the mouth below the neck.
Having made a channel-shaped excavation one part deep and sized to admit the little finger,

[one should arrange it] so that the ghee flows from the center of the excavation situated in the middle of the *karṇikā* into the center of the channel-shaped excavation situated in the middle of the mouth.
Likewise, having made a perforation by piercing the neck-ring and the rim with a heated iron rod,
one should similarly make a hole at the front for the passage of clarified butter,
a cavity suitable for the entry of the little finger. Then, on the back part of the ring...
Having made it somewhat level in the middle like the back of a tortoise so that it remains steady on the ground,
one should make a slight depression in the middle of the back part of the mouth,
and below the mouth-opening, a raised portion in the shape of a swan’s beak.

Having caused a beautiful figure in the form of an elephant's face or a boar's face to be made at the tip of the staff, one should fashion three or four ring-shaped ornaments by piercing it with a single part;
then, with four parts equal to half of that [thickness], one should fashion the middle of the neck and the face.
Having fashioned the upper portion beautifully adorned from the base upward with its face turned upwards, one should again fashion bracelets below that by a single part as before; below that,
the middle of the staff is a place suitable for wrapping with thread, measuring nine parts in circumference and six parts in length.

Having done so, one should again fashion bracelets with one part, and with three parts of half that size, a pot facing upward as before; below that, one should again fashion bracelets with one part. Having thus constructed the *sruk*, [one proceeds] with the thirty-six divisions of the *sruk*.

Having fashioned a *sruva* ladle that is twenty-four parts in length, circular in shape at the tip with a measurement of two units, provided with a thick head, and perfectly round; and having made a hollow in its mouth-region, shaped like the footprint of a deer in the mud, with a capacity of one *karṣa*.
Below that, however, one should fashion bracelets according to the same measure as before; then a pitcher (kumbha) using four parts of half that measure;
then again bracelets using one part; and then, having made a space suitable for wrapping with a cord of four-part length using a measurement of eleven parts.

Furthermore, one should fashion the two rings with one part, the bowl with three parts, and again the two rings with one part; such is the method for constructing the *sruva* ladle. In this manner, the *sruk* and *sruva* should be made of gold, silver, or copper; in the absence of a *sruva*, [one may use] that of the *pālāśa* tree.

For the fire-oblation (*homa*), two middle leaves or two *pippala* leaves should be taken; furthermore, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed for the two leaves just as it is for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. Now, regarding the quantity of the oblation materials, it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
One *karṣa* of ghee is prescribed for the oblation, and one *śukti* of milk is likewise recorded;
the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are declared by the sages to be equal in measure to those.
p.
281) That same amount of honey, milk, and rice is declared to be the size of an akṣa;
curd should be the measure of a prasṛti, and parched grains (lājāḥ) should be commensurate with a muṣṭi. || 2 ||
The *pṛthuka* grains should be of that same measure; parched flour (*saktu*) is likewise declared to be so.
Jaggery (*guḍa*) should be half a *pala* in weight, and sugar (*śarkarā*) is traditionally recorded as being the same.

Half a mouthful shall be the measure of the sacrificial oblation (caru); sugarcane is traditionally held to be measured by its joints. One should likewise prepare each leaf, flower, and cake individually.
They know that the fruits of plantains and oranges are each offered individually;
the citron is divided into four pieces, and the jackfruit into ten.
The wise know that coconuts are cut into eight pieces;
the wood-apple fruit is made into three parts, and the wood-sorrel fruit is cut into two.
In the fire-oblation (homa), the fruit of the urvāruka should be cooked and cut into three pieces;
other fruits should remain uncut, and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, along with guḍūcī and caturaṅgulā;
there should be a handful of rice, as well as mudga, māṣa, and barley.
The rice grains should be half that amount; the kodrava grains should be measured by a handful (muṣṭi). The wheat and red kalama rice are prescribed to be measured by a handful.
Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful; mustard seeds are of that same measure.
Salt should be the size of a śukti, and there should also be twenty black peppers.
Pura is known as Varadamāna, and Rāmaṭha is remembered as being equal to that;
likewise are Candana, Aguru, Karpūra, Kastūrī, and Kuṅkuma.
"The teachers have declared them to be the size of tamarind seeds.
Thus it is stated. In the *Uttaratantro*: "And the milk-rice is measured by an *akṣa*. The definition of a *karṣa* is given in that very same work:
"Ten *guñjās* shall be one *māṣa*; sixteen *māṣas* are called a *karṣa*."

The measurement for oil is also the same as this. A *śukti* is two *karṣas*; a *prasṛti* is the measure of one *mātra*; a *muṣṭi* is the measure of two *palas*. A *grāsārdha* is one *pala*, half a *pala*, two *karṣas*, or eighty *raktikās*. (From the *Kulamūlāvatāra*)
Four *guñjās* make one *daṃśa*, four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*,
two *śāṇas* make one *ghaṭaka*, and that [same measure] is also called a *kola*, a *badara*, and an *ikṣaṇa*.
Two of those [tindukas] make one pāṇitala; two pāṇitalas make one karṣa; two karṣas make one suvarṇa; two suvarṇas make one kavalagraha;
two kavalagrahas make one picu; two picus make one biḍālapadaka; and two biḍālapadakas make one tinduka or akṣa. || 2 ||
Eight *śukti*s are one *pala*; two *bilva*s make a *caturthika*; a handful is an *āmra*; likewise, two *praguñja*s are a *prasṛti*. (3)

Thus: *mātuluṅga* is the citron; *urvāruka* is the cucumber. "Half-portion" means measured by a *śukti*. "The size of a handful" means the measure of the palm of the hand, that is, one *karṣa*. "Equal to an *akṣa*" means two *karṣas*. *Pura* is *guggulu* (bdellium).
A *badara* measure consists of eighty *guñjās*. *Rāmaṭha* is asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). In the *Nāradapañcarātra*, the third section states: "The roots should be short, according to their own proportions.
Also, in the *Śaivāgama*: "There should be three pieces of the roots, and they should likewise be very fine."

One should perform the oblation (*homayet*). Thus, it means exclusively unbroken [in its continuity]. "The eighth part of the bulbs (*kanda*) and two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for the creepers (*latā*). So it is said.
Now, regarding the sacrificial fuel (samidh): therein, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*— The fuel should be the size of a span (prādeśa), cut evenly;
likewise, it should not be shattered, split, too short, crooked, too thick, or too thin, nor should it be of two kinds [in its quality]. (1)
Those that are bitten by worms, elongated, skinless, or devoid [of auspicious marks],
as well as those that are split in two and give rise to disease, bring about the exhaustion of one's lifespan.
If it is short, one meets death; if crooked, it is considered to cause obstacles;
if thick, it takes away prosperity; and if thin, emaciation arises. (3)
If there are two [lines], there will be defects of the eyes; if they are bitten by insects, they destroy wealth.
If they are long, they produce hatred; if they are made skinless, they are killers of life.
Fuel-sticks that are accompanied by sap, neither too long nor too short, which grant all desires, possessing moist bark, cut evenly, and rounded like a finger, [are recommended]. (5)
The wise man who performs such an oblation attains vast prosperity;
these are the sacrificial fuels proclaimed for rites prescribed by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Tantras.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:

"Those [sticks] should be made of Palāśa wood, or else of other sacrificial wood, twelve finger-breadths in length; they should be straight, not naturally dried, possessing their bark, free from wounds, and even. (1)
They are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, or equal in size to the little finger;
or, if available, they may be a span in length—all of them may indeed be offered.

Thus [ends the previous section]. Now, the procedure for the initiation by letters (*varṇadīkṣā*) and so forth for those incapable of the initiation by action (*kriyādīkṣā*) in the present context is written: therein, having duly projected the letters of the *mātṛkā*—from *a* to *kṣa*, which consist of the nature of the individual soul (*pums*) and primordial matter (*prakṛti*)—upon the body of the disciple, which likewise consists of the nature of the individual soul and primordial matter, and then again...

By way of the process of withdrawal, I dissolve the letter *kṣa*, located from the head down to the heart, into the letter *la* at the interior of the navel; and I dissolve the letter *la*, located from the heart down to the navel, into the letter *ha* situated from the heart down to the tips of the left foot.
I dissolve the letter *ha*, located from the heart up to the tips of the left feet, into the letter *sa*, located from the heart up to the tips of the right feet.
I dissolve the letter *sa*, located from the heart up to the tip of the right foot,
into the letter *ṣa*, located from the heart up to the tip of the left hand;
[and likewise] the letter *ṣa* located from the heart up to the tip of the left hand.

I dissolve [the letter] Śa, located from the heart up to the tip of the right hand, into the letter Va; thus, by this method, one dissolves the letter Śa into the letter Va, and so forth. Likewise, I dissolve the letter Ā, situated in the mouth, into the letter A located in the head; having thus dissolved the phonemes (varṇas) by this method, that consciousness once again—

Having united the entire collection of principles (tattva-grāma) with the Supreme Self (paramātman), and having meditated upon the disciple as one whose multitude of principles has dissolved, who is free from all impurities, and possesses a divine body; then,
[one should contemplate] from the presence of the Supreme Self the letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa'.

Having generated the phonemes (*varṇa*) and having performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* phonemes upon the body of the disciple according to the sequence of the creation-deposition (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*) to be described, one should again unite that consciousness, together with the aggregate of the principles (*tattva*), within him and perform the instruction according to the stated method; this is the initiation consisting of the phonemes (*varṇātmadīkṣā*).

Now, the initiation of the *kalās*: therein, one should [visualize] the *nivṛtti-kalā* from the soles of the feet up to the knees; the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* from the knees up to the navel; the *vidyā-kalā* from the navel up to the throat;
and the *śānti-kalā* from the throat up to the forehead. From the forehead...
Having visualized the power beyond peace (śāntyatītākalā) extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) within the body of the disciple,

I dissolve the power of withdrawal (nivṛttikalā) into the power of establishment (pratiṣṭhākalā), I dissolve the power of establishment into the power of knowledge (vidyākalā), and [I dissolve] the power of knowledge into the power of peace (śāntikalā).

Thinking "I withdraw [the soul] into the Śāntyatītā-kalā," one withdraws it in due order; having pierced it and withdrawn it into the Supreme Self (paramātman), one purifies and regenerates its body as before.
Then, from the Supreme Self, one [withdraws] the Śāntyatītā-kalā, then Śānti, and then Vidyā.

Then, having joined *pratiṣṭhā* and *nivṛtti* to their respective locations within the body of the disciple according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), one should perform the instruction and so forth. Thus, having purified the disciple through the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) of dissolution (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) by means of the thirty-eight *kalās*, as stated in various ways, one should bestow initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The initiation of art (kalādīkṣā).

Now, the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā): there, the Guru, meditating on his own Guru—who is the very form of Śiva—upon the palm of his own hand, and while reciting the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) and the six-limbed Mātṛkā, shall place his right hand upon the head of the disciple and instruct him; such is the initiation by touch.

Alternatively, there is the initiation by speech (*vāgdīkṣā*): in that regard, the Guru, having fixed his mind upon Śiva whose nature is supreme consciousness, and meditating with a focused mind on all the mantras arising from Him, should himself impart those mantras to the disciple;
this is initiation by speech.

Now, the initiation by sight (*dṛgdīkṣā*): there, the Guru, having closed his own eyes and meditated upon the deity whose nature is the Supreme Self, with a serene mind, should gaze at the disciple with divine vision and impart the instruction of the mantra; this is the initiation by sight. These three types of initiation have been described subsequently.
This is what must be done by a teacher who knows reality for disciples who are dispassionate; however, for women, only the initiation through word is prescribed, and no other.

Now, the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā): there, the Guru, having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī in her aforementioned form within the triangle in the center of the four-petaled lotus at the disciple's *mūlādhāra*,
[should contemplate] the four syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *sa* situated in the midst of those four petals.
Having withdrawn that Brahmā situated in its center into Viṣṇu—

who resides in the middle of the six-petaled lotus called *adhiṣṭhāna* located above it— and having pierced him, one should [dissolve] the group of six letters from *va* to *la* situated in the middle of those petals into Viṣṇu.
Having joined [it], one should join Viṣṇu above that in the navel-center (nābhimaṇḍala), known as Maṇipūra, which consists of ten digits (kalā); there,
one should join Viṣṇu together with the ten consonants from *ḍa* to *pha* situated in the midst of its ten petals.

Having joined and pierced that Rudra situated in the center of that lotus, one should join him to the heart-lotus called *anāhata*, which is endowed with twelve petals and enriched by the twelve syllables from *ka* to *ṭha*; having joined him there,
one should pierce him together with those syllables into the Lord situated in its center.

Having joined that Īśvara with the sixteen vowels in the Viśuddhi-cakra— the sixteen-petaled lotus rich with those sixteen vowels at the region of the throat— and having joined the Īśvara together with those vowels into Sadāśiva who resides in its center, one should pierce through that Sadāśiva.

Having led [the consciousness] to the *ājñā-cakra*, the two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows, one should join Sadāśiva— accompanied by the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* located on its two petals— to the *bindu* situated in its center;
then, having pierced that *bindu*, [one joins it] to the *kalā* situated above it.

Having joined that [Kuṇḍalinī] again to the Nāda, that [Nāda] to the end of the Nāda (nādānta), that [end of the Nāda] to the Unmanī state, and that [Unmanī] to the Viṣu-cakra, and having joined the Viṣu-cakra to the mouth of the Guru— thus joining and piercing it progressively— one should pierce that Kuṇḍalinī together with the individual soul (jīvātman) by uniting it with the Supreme Śiva. When this has been done, the disciple...

By the command of the Guru, the bonds of saṃsāra are severed; rendered unconscious, he immediately falls to the surface of the earth. Then the Guru, having generated Kuṇḍalinī from Paraśiva by means of the reversed order of withdrawal, likewise [generates] the entire heart and all the respective deities within the various cakras in the body of the disciple through the order of emanation.

Having joined the *jīva* in the heart and having joined the *kuṇḍalinī* at the *mūlādhāra*, one should perform the instruction and so forth. Then, possessing divine awakening and knowing the past, future, and present, he becomes Sadāśiva; this is the *vedha-dīkṣā*. Generally, in the Kali age, the one who performs the *vedha-dīkṣā* [is the one who attains this].
The teachers say that such a guru and a worthy disciple are difficult to find; this has been written here as well by way of occasion. May there be auspiciousness.

Then, for those who have been thus initiated, who are endowed with true devotion, and who have acquired the entirety of the secrets and the supreme reality from both the teacher and the scriptures, the teacher [performs] for the disciples that which is called the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).

One should perform the second consecration. Therein, having constructed upon the altar in the previously mentioned pavilion the extensive wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) to be described below, [one should proceed] as before with the five powders (*pañcagavya*).

Having filled the pericarp, petals, filaments, corners, and so forth, one should install in its center a jar filled with a khārī-measure of water according to the previously mentioned procedure; and in the other petals,
corners, squares, and all locations for the worship of the deities of the surrounding enclosures.
Having placed two-prastha water-filled jars there, having invoked the deity into the central jar and worshipped it with the sixteen services according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having likewise worshipped the deities of the limbs and the surrounding retinue in the other jars according to the procedure prescribed for initiation—

On the birth asterism of the disciple, preceded by the sounding of the five musical instruments as before, one should duly consecrate him together with Brahmins devoted to his chosen deity. Then the disciple also, having prostrated before the venerable Guru as before and having offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth, [should proceed].
One should satisfy the Brahmins with abundant sacrificial fees and other offerings; such is the procedure for the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
If a practitioner who is devoid of the full consecration dies, he attains the state of a piśāca and falls into hell. || 1 ||
Thus, according to the statement in the *Kulārṇava*, this consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is indispensable.
Thus [ends the work] by the disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, who was himself the disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the Great Mahopādhyāya and Worshipful Master.

In the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the ascetic Śrīvidyāraṇya— who was a disciple of Śrīpragalbhācārya, who was himself a disciple of the teacher ŚrīViṣṇuśarmācārya— this is the thirteenth chapter (śvāsa).
Now...
In the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the fourteenth breath (chapter).
Now follows the ritual for the full consecration according to the Kādimata.
In the *Śrītantrarāja* (Chapter 2, Verse 52):
"A disciple endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and adorned by proper conduct,
who has been purified for many days by means of the five and six peak-syllable vidyās..."
Having consecrated him with water-pots and seated him within the Śrīcakra,
one should contemplate the wheel in the center of the foundation, the heart, and the head.
Having invoked [the deity] from his own heart, established [him], and worshipped him together with the ritual placement (nyāsa),
he— whose mind is full and who is one with the Goddess— should mutter the Vidyā three times into the ear.

Meditating with joy on the identity of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one's own self, he should recite [the mantra] a hundred times while standing before [the deity]; he should dwell nearby for three days.
If the mobile power (sañcāriṇī śakti) does not come to the Guru, there is no doubt;
therefore, one should dwell near him, performing worship, providing a place for instruction, and so forth.
Since he must attain identity with the Guru who consists of the mantra,
from that time forward he remains dependent upon him for wealth and other necessities.
Then, having obtained the two kinds of consecration by his command, one should perform acts of grace and so forth for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
Having fashioned a wheel in its center and placed a jar within the yoni,
having filled it with decoction water and consecrated [the disciple], one should recite the mantra.
For one who is devoted to the traditional conduct handed down through lineage and is endowed with devotion,
one should perform the second consecration for the sake of the self-perfection of the Goddess.
Having fashioned a large canopy and sixteen [petals] according to their respective origins,
and having constructed triangles here, one should place a water-pot in the center.
[The vessels] made of gold, silver, copper, glass, and even clay,
filled with a khārī measure of water and infused with medicinal herbs that have been boiled [together].
Having placed the nine gems and various grains,
as well as gold and copper, one should wrap them with two pieces of cloth.
It was adorned with red sandalwood, sprouts of the mango, jackfruit, and holy fig tree,
entwined with the Śatakratu creeper, and provided with mātuluṅga fruits.
Having covered the other jars, one should place them one by one upon the others;
they are said to be in the sequence of thirty-six, five, and one thousand and five hundred.
In the center of the wheel, having prepared the excellent water and so forth, and having invoked and worshipped [the deities],
one should recite the mantras of the Kālātmanityās on the previous day.
Having risen early on one's birth-star day, one should worship one's own Nityā there;
thereafter, one should recite the mantra a thousand times and perform oblations on all sides.
With the sounds of musical instruments such as the horn, the kettle-drum, and the conch, accompanied by song and dance, groups of joyful yoginīs, each one embodying a deity, [attended him]. (17)
The Guru himself should perform the consecration together with those who have been well-honored for their conduct;
from that time forward, he too should explain his own tradition to him.
If that [mantra] should fail, one should perform it in an uninterrupted sequence;
one should recite the vidyā a thousand times, accompanied by consecration.
Alternatively, one should place ninety-six pitchers there;
having invoked the Śaktis into them and worshipped them, one should perform the consecration.
