Or, having prepared a single water-pot on one's birthday, one should perform the consecration;
in this manner, one should constantly perform the occasional rite without interruption.
Thus, in the *Mātṛkāraṇava*:
"One should instruct the disciple in the eternal Vidyās consisting of fifteen parts, as well as those of three peaks (*trikuṭa*), four peaks (*catuṣkuṭa*), and likewise five peaks (*pañcakūṭa*). (1)
Those with six peaks, seven peaks, eight peaks, and those consisting of nine;
likewise those with ten, eleven, and twelve peaks. (2)
There are those consisting of thirteen, as well as those designated as fourteen;
likewise those called fifteen, and those with sixteen peaks.
The sciences of the limbs and sub-limbs, as well as the deities of the enclosures, the sciences of the five abodes, and likewise the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa).
One should teach all the vidyās—those that are pure, impure, and variegated—in their proper sequence; the disciple should indeed recite them one by one as they arrive in order.
One should dwell constantly devoted to the service of the guru and obedient to the guru’s command, within that collection of great vidyās obtained through the lineage, which is full of devotion. (6)
One should perform the second consecration for the sake of the self-perfection of the Goddess;
the wise practitioner should properly construct the pavilion according to the procedure previously described.
And on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion, at a propitious moment when a lucky hour was rising, he constructed a pavilion measuring one hundred and twenty-four cubits.
One should first worship Gaṇeśa preceded by the five musical instruments;
then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should properly perform the Puṇyāhavācana rite.
One should perform the worship of the Mātṛkās and likewise the Vṛddhi-śrāddha;
thereafter, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas, preceded by the recitation of the Svasti-vācana.
The wise man should honor the venerable Guru with golden ornaments and garments;
by his command, he should also honor the other Brahmins with gold and clothes.
One book-teacher, eight officiating priests (ṛtvij),
nine Brāhmaṇas, and eight gatekeepers.
With devotion, he honored four other twice-born men of pure vows who were practitioners of their own sacred sciences by offering them rings of gold and jewels for the recitation of peace-mantras.
At the command of the twice-born, the wise preceptor should draw a beautiful wheel upon the center of the altar,
using perfectly aligned lines according to the method taught by the venerable Guru.
One should diligently fill every line with red rice grains,
in each of the seventy-seven triangles and in each of the yonis.
One should fashion a sixteen-spoked [mandala] with three threads, numbering sixteen;
the wise one should place the jars upon all the heaps of śāli rice.
And in the midst of the central womb, one should place a jar filled with a khārī of salt;
in the others, one should place jars capable of holding only a prastha.
For each goddess, beginning with Padeṣukāmeśī and the others, there are sixteen [syllables];
and for each weapon, beginning with Aṣṭāyudha, there are sixteen [syllables] in their respective places.
The foundation consists of exactly sixteen [elements] within the words for the gestures of accomplishment (siddhimudrā);
there is one on each of the two sides and three jars behind the goddess.
Adorned with fruits of gold and gems and beautified by two garments as its sprouts,
one should construct the guru-maṇḍala in the center of a six-cornered figure and an eight-petaled lotus.
Between the lotus and the eight-spoked [wheel] is the mandala of the lords of the lunar days (tithīśas);
in the northeast is the mandala of the planets and the Sarvatobhadra mandala.

One should place the mandala of the Lord of the Week in the center, between the eight-cornered and the preceptor’s fire-pits; however, one should construct the mandala of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) in the southeast, the east, and the middle.
In the center of the half-moon within the womb [of the mandala] is the supreme Nityā-maṇḍala;
it is for the worship of Dadininityā in the middle of the southern and southwestern [sections].
The phrase "one should construct a mandala" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

In the south-west, during the worship of Vāstu, the wise one should construct a mandala; specifically, within a circle and a triangle, there is the mandala of the deities of the elements (dhātudevatā). 24.
Between the hexagon and the circle is the mandala of the couples;
that of Kurukullā is in the southeast, and that of Vārāhī is in the northwest.
"Between the various mandalas of the Śeṣika offering goddesses.
Thus, the sequence for the worship of the Guru-maṇḍala and the Sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala has already been explained.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of the nine planets and others. Regarding this, the *Śrītantrarāja* states (Chapter 28, Verse 72):
"Since the form of the planets is the body of the Mātṛkā-vidyā, I shall describe their abode, the maṇḍala, for the purpose of their worship."
The orb of the moon would consist of the sounds of nectar, while that of the sun would take the form of the consonants of nectar; for the others are composed of those [sounds]. (2)
Therefore, I shall describe their mandalas to you with their respective colors;
in the worship of those nine, the ninth mandala consists of them.
O Goddess of gods, having performed the separate worship of the mandalas of the Moon and the Sun, listen now in due order to that which consists of all that brings about supreme welfare.
By laying down four lines—east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—one should produce nine squares, each measuring exactly three cubits. In those [squares], indeed: || 5 ||
Having clearly drawn three circles in the middle of the two eastern compartments,
one should drop two threads— one horizontal and one vertical— into their center.
Having divided [the space] into nine parts, one should write [the letters] in order starting from the center and the northeast;

[one should place] the eight vowels beginning with *a* (representing air, etc. in the [surrounding] positions, and in the center, the *praṇava* (om) joined with the [vowel] representing space (*nabhas*).
One should write the Mātṛkā along with the vowels within the two circular paths by means of the sky (the void);
there, one should worship the Sun with his twelve names as they have been proclaimed.
In all cases and at all times, one should worship the Sun with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with "Namaḥ";
likewise, having joined the first [syllable] of Soma with its own [name], one should worship with that as well.
There, one should write the eight vowels enriched with dots (bindus) under that name,
as well as the sixteen vowels and the Mātṛkā, according to their respective conjunctions.
One should draw [the design] between the two circles and also write that [syllable] in the central square;
one should worship it there in the mandala, accompanied by the fire of burning and the breath.
p.

286) At all times, according to the aforementioned sequence and at the prescribed moments, one should always present offerings of sugar, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa), along with other articles of worship. || 12 ||
Having likewise drawn three circles within the other seven compartments,
one should place the letters beginning with each respective class-consonant (varga) and also that Mātṛkā composed of vowels.
Having drawn the center and likewise having arranged those [sections] in their proper order,
one should also write the letters of each respective group (varga) together with the three syllables that denote them.
In the center, one should write the first letter of each group of consonants situated within the *praṇava* (oṃ);
when these nine [squares] have been thus prepared, one should worship the nine planets.
One should write the names in order, starting from Agni (the southeast) and ending at Īśāna (the northeast), surrounding [the central deity];
one should worship them with those [names] in the dative case, consisting of three syllables each. || 16 ||
Mars, Mercury, Saturn, Jupiter, Rāhu, Venus, and Ketu—
with these [deities] one should perform worship everywhere, even when no specific mantra is mentioned.
Thus, the mandalas of the nine planets have indeed been declared;
by worshipping them within those very mandalas, one should effect their favor.
O Pārvatī, listen to [the description of] the worship and the mandala on those two days of the Sun and Moon— on the new moon and the full moon— when they are situated in their respective exaltations.
Having drawn two circles, one should write eighty-one squares in their center by means of nine lines drawn horizontally and vertically.
Having entered from all sides starting from the northeast cell (īśakoṣṭha) and so forth,
[one places] the eighty-one syllables ending with *mā* (the letters of the alphabet), and then [places] the *dāva* (the syllable *ha*) in the center.
Having placed the Mātṛkā between the two circles and having woven it with those five [syllables], one should draw it there in the mandala and worship Soma.
Then, one should draw the orb of the moon with camphor and sandalwood;
from among red sandalwood, vermilion, and red ochre, choose one for the sun.
Having fashioned an image there, one should worship it according to the prescribed form.
Having drawn two circles and lines at equal intervals across, upwards, and diagonally, || 24 ||

In the midst of those [squares], one should write the nineteen [syllables] previously mentioned, beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *namaḥ*, each joined with its own [seed-syllable] and conjoined with the vowels. (25)
Between the two verses, with those twenty-five syllables,
one should write the script strung together by vowels joined with *bhānta* and the ten-syllable [mantra] of fire (*vahni*).
Having drawn a clearly defined form measuring three cubits in length and breadth, one should invoke the Sun into its center and worship him as before, O Goddess. (27)
Having prepared a pedestal, or a ground surface smeared with lime, or a level, uncovered area at the top of a temple spire, one should worship the images according to the prescribed rules.

Thus, throughout this entire tantra, the worship of the planets has been proclaimed; in cases where no specific instruction is given, one should perform the worship according to that general sequence.
The meaning of this will be explained in the section on the ritual application (*prayoga*). The worship of the site-mandala (*vāstumaṇḍala*) has already been demonstrated previously.
Now, regarding the deities of the lunar days (tithi), weekdays (vāra), and asterisms (ṛkṣa) according to the Piṅgalāmata:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the deities of the weekdays, lunar days, and asterisms: for Sunday, O Goddess, they are Sūrya and Śiva; for Monday, they are Soma and Ambikā. (1)
On Bhauma, Maṅgala and Guha; then Śuddha (Budha) and Viṣṇu; next, Guru and Caturvaktra; and on Bhṛgu, Śukra and Purandara. || 2 ||
"On Monday, Dhaneśvara; on Tuesday, Kāla—thus the lords of the days are proclaimed. "Pare" means on Wednesday; "pare" means on Thursday. Likewise: "Brahmā, Vidhātṛ, Viṣṇu, Yama, Śītakara, and Guru."
Indra, the Vasus, the Nāgas, Dharma, Śiva, and Divākara. || 1 ||
O Goddess, on the new moon day (darśa), Manmatha, Kali, the Viśvedevas, the lords of the lunar days (tithīśvaras), and the ancestors (pitaraḥ) are to be worshipped with all ritual offerings.
The Aśvins, Yama, Vahni, Brahmā, Indu, Śiva, Aditi, Guru, the Sarpas, the Pitṛs, Bhaga, Aryaman, and the Lord of the Day (Sūrya). (3)
Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, then Indra and Agni, Mitra, and Indra; thereafter, O beloved, Nirṛti, Water, the Viśvedevas, and Prajāpati. || 4 ||
O Goddess, Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād,
Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are declared to be the deities of the lunar mansions.
O Goddess, one should worship these [deities] on those specific days with all ritual services,
using their names preceded by the Praṇava (Om), ending in the dative case, and followed by the word "Hṛt" (Namaḥ).

Thus [it is said]. Here, "Indra and Agni" refers to two deities for a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), because of the Vedic revelation that the *viśākhā* lunar mansion has Indra and Agni as its deities. For the *uttarāṣāḍhā* lunar mansion, the Viśvedevas are the deities; for *śravaṇa*, Viṣṇu; and between these two, Prajāpati is stated [to be the deity].
That *Abhijit* exists; it is to be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Now follows the procedure for the daily worship of the Nityā on that day.
In the *Śrītantrarāja* (Chapter 25, verse 78):
"O Dear One, hear now the ancillary rites (*aṅga*) of these Nityā-vidyās."
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) for both the hands and the limbs using those syllables repeated twice.
Having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā as prescribed, one should likewise recite each of the Vidyās individually.
They are red in color, clad in red garments, and adorned with red ornaments, garlands, and unguents.
One should visualize [the deities] holding a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows;
one should likewise visualize the five Śaktis of their enclosures as being similar to them.
Having drawn two squares adorned with two doors,
one should worship her in the center upon an eight-petaled lotus within the ninefold source (navayoni).

One should place the enclosures of the limbs (*aṅgāvṛti*) within the central womb; the enclosures of the weapons (*āyudhāvṛti*) should be in between; the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*) behind; and [the deities] in the eight corners in due order. (5)
Likewise, one should worship on the outer petals with the syllables in reverse order,
accompanied by the Rūpiṇī Śaktis and joined with the seven-syllabled Māyā mantra.
One should worship the powers beginning with Brāhmī outside that [mandala] in two squares;
and one should perform the offering of oblations for these along with Kurukullā.
"Recalling with the intellect the form as described by means of the seven-syllabled [mantra] alone.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): therein, after the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) for the daily mantra (*nityā-vidyā*) of that day, and [place it] upon the head.

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the face; salutation to the Paṅkti meter, on the mouth; salutation to Kālanityā, the deity, on the heart. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) and having also performed the placement on the six limbs beginning with the heart, one should meditate [on her] as "red, clad in red garments," and so forth.

Having performed the mental worship and other rites, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with filaments using saffron and other pigments upon a gold plate or similar surface in front of oneself; within that, one should construct a nine-yoni cakra,
and outside the eight petals, two squares divided into internal sections.

Having constructed [the mandala] with two doors in the east and west, one should write the three syllables of the *nityā-vidyā* for that specific day within the *yoni* in its center; then, having placed it upon a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood or similar materials before oneself,
one should offer a handful of flowers there with the *nityā-vidyā* for that specific day.
Having placed the vessels for the *tattva-arghya* and other offerings, performed the worship of oneself (*ātmapūjā*),
and performed the worship of the seat of the Śrīcakra, one should serve [the deity] with the ritual services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with flowers;
then, having performed the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga-pūjana*), one should display the Yoni-mudrā and the four mudrās beginning with the Pāśa.
Having worshipped the six limbs as before— within the central yoni in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, in front of the Goddess, and in the four directions starting from that—
the [worshipper] proceeds within the intermediate spaces situated inside the eight corners outside the central yoni.

Having worshipped the four weapons as before, one should visualize three lines in the space between the two yonis at the back of the Goddess, in the place where the three lineages of gurus reside; upon these, on the first line, one should contemplate the triad of gurus beginning with Prakāśānanda, and on the middle line...
One should worship the three lineages of gurus: the triad of gurus beginning with Śrījñānānandanātha on the third line, and the triad of gurus beginning with Svabhāvānanda [on the second].
Then, in the eight triangles, starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding counter-clockwise, [one should worship] the daily *niyā* vidyā.

Having joined the middle syllable with the sixteen vowels and preceded by the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), one should utter their initial syllables and worship the eight powers beginning with: "I worship the sandal of the power Rūpiṇī," and "I worship the sandal of the power Rūpiṇī" [repeated for the others]. Thus, the eight powers.
Having worshipped [the deities] on the eight petals in counter-clockwise order, and having worshipped the remaining syllable-energies (*akṣaraśakti*),
one should worship the eight energies beginning with Brāhmī and preceded by the *māyā* seed-syllable on the outer square-path (*vīthī*) in counter-clockwise order.

After performing the worship of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), the offering of food (*naivedya*), and the presentation of the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, one should conclude everything; this is the procedure for the daily worship of the Nityā on that day.
Now, the procedure for the worship of the six elemental deities, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, is written. Regarding this, it is said in the *Śrītantrarāja*:
(16.72) Having drawn seven hexagons on the ground according to the prescribed sequence of directions,
one should worship that Nityānityā in the center with perfumes and other offerings. 16.
One should worship that group of six in the six corners surrounding it, in their respective order;
and one should also worship those [deities] in the outer [corners] as before, with the previously mentioned syllables.

Likewise, within the six corners of those [six lotuses], there are thirty-six goddesses together with their Śaktis; they are all equal to the principal Goddess in every respect, including their forms, weapons, and so forth.

As before, there should be five vowels; [then] the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, which are not previously mentioned. With those [consonants], excluding the letters *ya*, *va*, *la*, and *kṣa*, one should likewise perform the worship in the subsequent [sections].
Furthermore, the worship of those wheels and their powers in reverse order is known as "suppression" (nigraha); it leads to the ruin of enemies.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): there, on a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) smeared with cow dung, free from the sight of animals, having performed the worship of one's own seat (*svāsanapūjā*) and so forth up to the end of the placement of the *yogapīṭha*, and having completed the rites beginning with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and ending with mental worship (*mānasapūjā*) according to the procedure prescribed for the daily worship of Nityānityā, one should make a dot (*bindu*) somewhere in front of oneself.

Using that as a support, one should produce a circle by drawing a circumference measuring twenty-four finger-breadths all around; then, having fixed a Brahma-thread (the north-south axis) extending east-west through its center,
one should [mark] from the eastern end of that Brahma-thread on the circle at a distance equal to half the measure of that Brahma-thread.

Having made four marks in total— two marks on the southern side starting from the western end and two marks on the northern side— one should stretch two horizontal threads from mark to mark, extending from south to north.

Starting from the two front points of the western transverse line, one should lay down two lines reaching as far as the eastern end of the Brahma-line; then, starting from the two ends of the eastern transverse line,
one should draw two lines reaching as far as the western end of the Brahma-line, thereby forming a hexagon.

It is produced. Then, having drawn two Brahma-lines— one from the southeast corner to the northwest corner, and likewise one from the northeast corner to the southwest corner— and having divided each of those three lines into three parts and marked them with signs;

Having drawn seven circles— one in the center and six in the positions of the third parts of the Brahma-lines located in the western, northwestern, northeastern, eastern, southeastern, and southwestern directions— using as their radius the measurement of half the respective [Brahma-line], one should then lay down three Brahma-lines.
Having divided each [circle] twenty-fourfold, starting from the center-point located in the middle circle,

one should mark the points of the Brahma-thread situated at the center of each respective [division] at every tenth-part position across the six surrounding circles; furthermore, regarding the middle circle...
From the center (p.
having made a mark at the tenth part of the circle located in the southeast corner along the Brahma-line, as before.

In the same manner, having made a mark at the tenth part of the Brahma-sūtra located at the center of the circle in the northwest (vāyavya), starting from the interval between the circles in the southeast (āgneya) and the center,
one should likewise make two marks on each circle using the aforementioned method for the circles situated in the northeast (īśāna) and southwest (nirṛti) corners.

Having likewise laid down the Brahma-sūtra extending from east to west, and having marked two points on each of the seven circles— at the tenth part starting from the western end and starting from the eastern end as before—
one should draw two horizontal lines at each mark within every circle, and then [proceed] with those.
Having produced seven hexagons according to the previously stated method, one should draw circles within each hexagon and in the center of the six triangles, and then erase the Brahma-threads;
thus having extracted the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), one should offer a handful of flowers in its center with the *Nityānityā* mantra.

Having set down [the offerings] with the *Nityāvidyā* mantra, from the installation of the *arghya* vessel up to the end of the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should worship the group of six beginning with *Ḍākinī* according to the prescribed rite therein— starting from the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) and ending with the offering of flowers— in the central hexagon according to the method taught for the worship of *Nityānityā*, and then offer incense and lamps.
Having offered the sixfold food-offering (*naivedya*) to be described hereafter, and having offered everything including betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) and so forth,

one should invoke *Ḍākinī* in the center of the smoke-colored [mandala] in the southwest corner (*nirṛtikoṇa*). Having visualized her as smoke-colored and possessing faces, arms, and other features equal to those of *Nityā*:

Having performed the ritual of "entire-making" (sakalīkaraṇa) by means of the application of the six-limbed nyāsa (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) together with the six-limbed mantras beginning with *Ḍāṃḍī* joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for her. In the same way, in the subsequent cases as well, the entire-making of Rākiṇī and the others is performed using their initial syllables joined with the six long vowels and their respective seed-syllables.

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath). Then, having worshipped [the deity] facing oneself with the services beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with flowers, one should worship the powers (*śakti*) of its enclosure in the southwest corner (*nirṛtikoṇa*) with: "Hrīṃ Āṃ, I worship the sandals of the power Aṃśakti."
Thus, having worshipped: in the northwest corner (2) I worship Kaṃ Śaktipādukā; in the east corner (2) Khaṃ Śaktipādukā;
in the southeast corner (2) Gaṃ Śaktipādukā; in the northeast corner (2) Ghaṃ Śaktipādukā; in the west corner (2) Ṅaṃ Śaktipādukā. Thus, having completed the worship.
Having offered incense and lamps, presented iron-rice (yāyasa-anna),
and satisfied her with the services beginning with betel and ending with prostration, one should invoke Rākiṇī— red as vermilion— into the northwestern hexagon which is colored like vermilion.

Having meditated upon her as possessing a face and arms that are both eternal and non-eternal, and so forth, and having performed the offerings beginning with the seat up to the flowers, [one should worship] in the six corners situated to the left, right, back, left, right, and front of Rākiṇī and the others, with the mantras: *hrīṃ āṃ aṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. Likewise: *caṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ* (twice).
Having worshipped with "chaṃ śaktipāda," "jaṃ śaktipāda," "jhaṃ śaktipādukāṃ," and "ñaṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi," and having offered incense and lamps,
one should present molasses-rice (guḍaudana) and arrange betel leaves and other offerings as before. Then:

In the blue-colored hexagon situated in the eastern direction, one should invoke Lākinī, who is blue in color and possesses [the same] faces, arms, and so forth as before; having meditated upon her, and after the offerings beginning with the seat and ending with flowers,
one should, according to the prescribed method, [place] *hrīṃ āṃ aṃ śaktipādu* in the hexagons, *2 ṭaṃ śaktipā* [in the second], and *2 ṭhaṃ śaktipā* [in the third].

Having worshipped with "2 ḍaṃ śaktipāta," "2 ḍhaṃ śaktipāta," and "2 ṇaṃ śaktipāta," and having offered incense and lamps, one should present mung-bean rice (*mudgaudana*) and perform the remaining rites as before.
Then, having invoked Kākinī— who possesses the color of the rising sun— into the six-cornered figure located in the south-eastern direction;

Having meditated as before, and having performed the offerings from the seat up to the flowers, one should worship as before within the six corners with: *hrīṃ āṃ aṃ śaktipātaḥ*, *taṃ śaktipātaḥ*, *thaṃ śaktipātaḥ*, *daṃ śaktipātaḥ*, *dhaṃ śaktipātaḥ*, *naṃ śaktipātaḥ*. Having thus worshipped and offered the oblation, the remainder is to be treated as before.

One should perform [the rite]. Then, having invoked Śākinī into the golden-colored hexagon situated in the northeast direction and having meditated upon her as being gold-colored, at the conclusion of the offerings beginning with the seat (āsana) and ending with flowers, one recites:
2 aṃ śaktipāta | 2 paṃ śaktipāta | 2 phaṃ śaktipāta | 2 baṃ śaktipāta | 2 bhaṃ śaktipāta.
2. *Maṃ* Śaktipāta. Having thus worshipped and offered food mixed with sesame seeds, one should perform the remaining rites as before.

Then, in the western hexagon, which is white in color, having invoked Hākinī and meditated upon her—endowed with [her] arms and so forth as before and white in color—at the conclusion of the offerings beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with flowers;
Having worshipped with "2 aṃ śaktipātaḥ," "2 raṃ śaktipātaḥ," "2 śaṃ śaktipātaḥ," "2 ṣaṃ śaktipātaḥ," "2 saṃ śaktipātaḥ," and "2 haṃ śaktipātaḥ," and having offered incense and lamps,
one should present pure food (śuddhānna) and arrange betel leaves and other offerings as before. Then, [one should worship] the Nityā.

Having worshipped her with her respective vidyā as before, having offered incense and lamps, and having gratified her with praises, prostrations, and so forth, one should either unite the ḍākinīs and others along with their retinues within her, or dissolve her into one's own heart; then, becoming one with her, one should dwell in happiness.
Now follows the worship of the fifty couples. Regarding this, the *Śrītantrarāja* (Chapter 16, verse 95) states:
"With fifteen-syllable mantras beginning with the two seed-syllables and ending with the seven-syllable [mantra], joined with the forms of the Śaktis from the letter 'A' to 'KṢa' as before..."
The fifty Śaktis are to be worshipped along with the fifty Kṣetrapālas;
their two seed-syllables consist of the phonemes conjoined with the forms and the lords of the fields.
The fifteen-syllable mantras are joined with the seven-syllable [mantra];
in the middle group of four among the sixty-four squares, they are combined with the daily science (dinavidyā).
Having drawn the desired couples upon them,
one should worship them situated in the center of the *hṛt* and *māyā* mantras, according to the sequence of the *ghaṭikās*.
Through the conjunction of the *ghaṭikās* during the days, even fifty pairs [of yogas] are attained; thus, from half a month of the maṇḍala, one surely obtains what is desired. (5)
By constantly invoking them and performing worship upon that wheel,
the attainment of all desired objects occurs perpetually and from every source.
Thus, the meaning of these six verses beginning with "from A to Kṣa" and ending with "on all sides" is as follows:
there, as previously stated, nine threads with equal intervals are [drawn] in an auspicious location.
Having laid out lines toward the east, west, south, and north, one should construct a square grid consisting of sixty-four squares;

then, having combined the four central squares of that grid into one, one should write therein the letters of the daily *nityā* for that day in the center, along with a prayer for one's desired object, and [proceed] immediately thereafter.
Starting from the right cell in the middle pair of the outer bottom row,

proceeding in a clockwise direction according to the previously mentioned sequence, moving outwards until reaching the bottom cell of the left row of the wheel, [the letters are placed] in sixty cells.

Having written the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā— beginning with the letter of sunrise (tad-dinodaya) and including the visarga-svarams— enclosed within the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, one should then again write the ten remaining letters beginning with sunrise (*udaya*) within those [spaces].

In the sequence of writing, among the sixty *ghaṭikās* beginning with the letter *Udaya*, one should worship the pair of *ghaṭikās* there with sixteen offerings and thereby obtain the fruit thereof. Here, the mantra for worship is:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ rūpiṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth; these are the *śakti-vidyās*.
"Pañcāśat Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ, I worship the sandals of Rūpa-kṣetreśa," and so forth;

these are the fifty Kṣetreśas. Thus, one should worship the sixty pairs, beginning with the fifty syllables, one by one in their proper order, without delay. This is for the worship performed every ghaṭikā.
Because that refers to the subject of rites performed for a single desire. Thus ends the worship of the fifty couples.

Now, the procedure for the worship of the fifteen Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, is written. Regarding that, the procedure for the worship of the Nityā Kāmeśvarī is stated in the *Śrītantrarāja* (Chapter 7, Verse 1):
Now, listen to the essential truth concerning Kāmīśvarī, who is proclaimed as the second among the sixteen Nityās and who bestows all desires. || 1 ||
The placement of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*), the varieties of meditation, their powers, and their worship [are described];
the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) is likewise therein: (3.6) "The first [syllable] is *śuci* joined with itself; the second shall be *lalitā*."
Then, Śūnya joined with Agni, followed by Ravi conjoined with Vyāpta. || 1 ||

The vital breath (prāṇa), joined with the fire of essence (rasāgni) and the pair of voids (śūnyayugma) accompanied by the moving [element]; then this sky (nabhaḥ) and the earth (gotrā) are again conjoined with burning (dāha). || 2 ||

The syllable *ambu* (va), conjoined with the mobile (*ca*) and joined with the power of the forest (*na*), and [the syllable] *hṛt* (ha)—this is the eternal Kāmeśvarī, the eleven-syllabled mantra that grants all desires. (3)

Thus: *aiṃ sakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ*. Likewise, in the *Tripurārṇava*: "The seer is declared to be Saṃmohana; Triṣṭubh is cited as the meter; Kāmeśvarī shall be the deity; and the seed-syllable of Brahmā is the seed. (1)
Śakti is said to be Kāmakalā, while the seed-syllable of the Earth is the *kīlaka*.
In the *Tantrarāja* (7.3):
"In this manner, one should perform the six limbs in sequence using the very syllables of the root-vidyā."
With one [finger] the heart, with two the head, and likewise with two [fingers each] for the other two [limbs]. || 1 ||
In the same manner, the weapon is enjoined with four [syllables] for the eyes and with one for the arms;
[the remaining syllables are assigned] to the directions, the two ears, the two nostrils, the tongue, the heart, the navel, and the private parts.
Thereafter, one should install the syllables of the Vidyā upon all limbs, from the head down to the tips of the toes, by means of pervasion in these locations.
One should indeed perform the pervasive [consecration] in its entirety according to the stated sequence.
Now I shall explain the meditation (dhyāna) as prescribed for the daily rituals (nityapūjā).
By whom the Goddess, being well-pleased, grants one's desire without effort—she who resembles ten million rising suns and is radiant with a crown of rubies. || 5 ||
Adorned with necklaces, neck-ornaments, girdles, rings, anklets, and so forth, she wears red garments and is beautified by red ornaments.
She has six arms and three eyes, her head is adorned with a digit of the moon, and she resides within a hexagon,
a square, and [inner figures of] five, eight, sixteen, two, and six [triangles].
Her face radiant with a gentle smile, her glances languid with compassion (or modesty),
she holds a noose and a goad, as well as a bow of sugarcane and flower-arrows.
Visualizing the Goddess in this way— bearing a jewel-bowl filled with nectar and granting boons with her hands— one should worship her during daily rites for the sake of spiritual accomplishment.
In all [stages] beginning with the preparatory practice (prayoga), I shall indeed explain the meditations therein;
namely, Madana, Unmādana, Dīpana, and Mohana.
And Śoṣaṇa—thus the five arrows previously mentioned are declared; followed by Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, and Madanāturā. (11)
Those [mudrās] preceded by the word *anaṅga* are five; the fifth is *madaveginī*.
After that comes *bhuvanapālā*, and immediately following her is *śaśirekhā*.
Another line, preceded by the sky (ākāśa), is to be worshipped on the eight petals:
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, and Manoramā.
The eighth [day] is declared to be Manoharāṣṭamī, and here the goddess is Manorathā;
thereafter follow Madanonmādinī, Mohinī, and Śaṅkhinī.
Śoṣiṇī, Vaśaṅkārī, Śiñjinī, and Subhagā—these sixteen, together with their respective notes (svaras), are declared to be the beloved and charming [mudrās]. || 15 ||
p.
290) They are to be worshipped on each leaf of the sixteen-petaled [lotus], namely:
Pūṣā, Ceddha, Sumanas, Rati, Prīti, and Dhṛti. || 16 ||
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and beyond that Aṃśumālinī; then Śaśinī, Aṅgirā, Chāyā, and finally Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā. (17)
The digits (kalās) of the Moon, known as Tuṣṭi and Amṛtā, together with their vowels,
should be worshipped in due order upon all sixteen petals.
Outside, one should likewise worship the Ḍākinīs and others in the corners of the hexagon;
outside of that, on the square ground, one should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) equal to them.
One should worship Vaṭuka, Gaṇapa, Durgā, and Kṣetreśa on all sides,
using the seven-syllable mantras beginning with Vidyā and others situated within the corners starting from the southeast.
One should offer a bali-oblation to them with their respective names, accompanied by perfumes and other offerings as prescribed;
thereafter, having prepared the arghya-water with the two limb-mantras (aṅgavidyās), one should worship Śivā.
Then, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the previously mentioned ritual services and so forth,
using auspicious red flowers smeared with ghee or honey.
"One should offer oblations with food and drink, and then conclude as before.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Kāmeśvarī-vidyā* and [place the seed-syllable] for the sake of enchantment upon the head.
Salutation to the Seer (Ṛṣi). Salutation to the Triṣṭubh metre (Chandas) in the mouth. Salutation to the deity Kāmeśvarī in the heart.
Salutation to the single seed-syllable (Bīja) in the secret place. Salutation to the power of Ī (Ī-Śakti) in the two feet.
Having performed the ritual placement (Vinyāsa), saying "Salutation to Laṃ, the Kilaka, in the navel," for myself...
"The application [of this mantra] is for the sake of attaining the fruit of the second initiation known as the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* which is to be performed.
Having spoken thus with palms joined in reverence, [he recites]: *aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *sakalahrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*;
*nitya* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *klinne* to the armor, *huṃ*; *madadrave* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*, [one places: *aiṃ namaḥ* on the right eye;
*sakalahrīṃ namaḥ* on the left; *ni namaḥ* on the right ear; *tya namaḥ* on the left; *kli namaḥ* on the right nostril; *nne namaḥ* on the left; *ma namaḥ* on the tongue; and *da* on the heart.

*Namaḥ* at the navel; *dra namaḥ* at the secret place; *ve namaḥ* at the genitals; having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with *sauḥ* over all the limbs and performed the meditation (*dhyāna*), at the conclusion of the mental worship (*mānasapūjā*), one should draw a five-petaled lotus with saffron and other pigments on a plate of gold or similar material, an eight-petaled lotus outside of that, and [another] outside of that.

Having fashioned the worship-circle (pūjācakra) consisting of a sixteen-petalled lotus, outside of which is a hexagon, and outside of that a square provided with four gates, and having placed it upon a pedestal made of sandalwood and other materials in front of oneself, one should offer a handful of flowers there with the Kāmeśvarī-vidyā.
Having set aside the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and so forth, and having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) at the conclusion of the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*),

one should mentally fashion the form (*mūrti*) there using the *Kāmeśvarī* mantra; then, after performing the worship from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of flowers and ending with dissolution (*laya*), [one worships] upon the filaments of the five-petaled lotus.

Having worshipped the six limbs in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, Vāyu, in front of the Goddess, and likewise in the four cardinal directions starting from that point, and having worshipped the three Gurus— as described in the *Viniyoganityāpūjā*— in the space between the five-petaled and eight-petaled lotuses behind the Goddess, [one should worship] upon the five petals.
Having worshipped by proceeding clockwise from the tip of the Goddess [the central point], [one offers] "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Drāṃ, obeisance to the Madana-bāṇa (Intoxicating Arrow)";

twice, "Drīṃ, obeisance to the Unmādana-bāṇa (Deluding Arrow)"; twice, "Klīṃ, obeisance to the Dīpana-bāṇa (Kindling Arrow)"; twice, "Blūṃ, obeisance to the Mohana-bāṇa (Enchanting Arrow)"; and twice, "Saḥ, obeisance to the Śoṣaṇa-bāṇa (Drying Arrow). Thus one should worship.
Outside of that, on the eight petals, starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: 2 Anaṅgakusumāpā0; 2 Anaṅgamekhalāpā0; 2 Anaṅgamadanāpā0; Anaṅgamadanāturāpā0;
2 Anaṅgamadaveginīpā0; 2 Anaṅgabhuvanapālāpā0; 2 Anaṅgaśaśirekhā.
