Thus: Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālini devadevi sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike jātavedasi jvalanti jvala jvala prajvala prajvala hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ ra ra ra ra ra ra ra.
*jvālāmālini huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus [ends the mantra]. In the *Tripurārṇava*:

"O Dear One, Kaśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and this [goddess] is the deity (*devatā*). The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are in the weapon-mantra (*astra*), while the *kīlaka* and armor (*kavaca*) are likewise. (1)
Thus [ends the description of] this Jvālāmālinī. In the *Tantrarāja* (20.3):
"With one, two, four, five, four, and ten syllables, one should perform the limb-projections (*aṅga*) with the root-syllables; first, six [projections] are for the hands and the limbs. (1)
Resembling a blazing fire, radiant with a crown of rubies,
she has six faces and twelve arms, and is adorned with every ornament.
Holding in her lotus-like hands a noose and a goad, a shield and a sword, a bow and arrows, and a mace; she bears a trident and fire, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (3)
She is surrounded on all sides by powers equal to herself;
her lotus-face is graced with a beautiful smile, and she is endowed with three eyes.
Having meditated thus, one should worship her constantly with those ritual offerings;
having constructed two squares provided with four gates.
Then, having constructed an eight-petaled lotus with its branches, followed by an inner group of eight [petals],
and then a hexagon with a triangle in the center, one should worship Śivā there.
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action, located in the three triangles in sequence;
the Ḍākinīs and others in the hexagon, and the Ghasmarīs and others in the octagon.
The voracious one who swallows the universe, with tremulous eyes and a flickering tongue;
she who devours all, the thousand-eyed one, free from attachment, and fond of dissolution.
One should also worship these [goddesses] on the outer eight-petaled lotus, proceeding clockwise:
Acintyā, Aprameyā, Pūrṇarūpā, and Durāsadā.
One should worship, as previously described, those who possess the form of all perfections, who are purifying, and who are of a single form, at the outer doors and in the corners.
Having performed worship as before, one should worship that [wheel] in the manner described within the circle;
this, ending with the offerings and oblations, has been correctly explained. || 11 ||

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): there, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoga-pīṭha as before, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the Jvālāmālinī-vidyā. Then: "Salutation to Kaśyapa, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the eternal deity Jvālāmālinī, on the heart; [salutation] on the secret place..."

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with: "Oṃ *raṃ* to the seed-syllable, obeisance" at the feet; "Phaṭ to the Power (*śakti*), obeisance" at the navel; and "Huṃ to the Pin (*kīlaka*), obeisance" at the navel; and having spoken with palms joined, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of my desired goal," [one recites]: "Oṃ to the heart, obeisance"; "Namaḥ to the head, svāhā"; "Bhagavati to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), vaṣaṭ."
Having performed the assignment of mantras to the hands and limbs (*kara-ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*) with: "O Jvālāmālinī, *huṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*); O Goddess of gods, *vauṣaṭ* for the three eyes;

O you who bring about the destruction of beings, *phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*)," and having performed the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the root mantra and meditated, at the conclusion of the mental worship, [one should draw] before oneself with sandalwood paste and other substances...

Having drawn the worship-diagram (pūjāyantra) and placed it before oneself, having worshipped it and performed the installation of the arghya and other offerings, and having completed the self-worship,
one should worship the pedestal of Bhuvaneśvarī and [install] the form with the root mantra.

Having performed the visualization and the offerings beginning with the invocation up to the flower-offering as before, and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and the three lineages of gurus, one should worship in the space between the triangle and the hexagon with: *oṃ* [2] *abhītyai namaḥ*;
*oṃ* [2] *vahnaye namaḥ*; *oṃ* [2] *śaṅkhāya namaḥ*; *oṃ* [2] *bāṇebhyo namaḥ*. *Oṃ* [2].

Salutation to the sword (khaḍga). Salutation to the goad (aṅkuśa). 2. Salutation to the noose (pāśa). 2. Salutation to the shield (kheṭa). 2. Salutation to the bow (cāpa). 2. Salutation to the mace (gadā). 2. Salutation to the trident (śūla). 2. Salutation to the boon-granting gesture (vara). Having thus worshipped, [worship] within the triangle: 2. Icchā-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi. 2. Jñāna-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi. 2. Kriyā-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi. (Note: The final line is implied by the context of the trikoṇa worship).

Having worshipped with "Kriyāśaktipāda," [one worships] within the six corners: in the corner at the left front of the Goddess, 2 Ḍākinīpāda; in the corner at the right front, 2 Rākiṇīpāda; in the rear corner, 2 Lākinīpāda;
in the rear left corner, 2 Kākinīpāda; in the rear right, 2 Śākinīpāda; and in the front corner, 2 [Hākinīpāda].

Having worshipped with "Hākinīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," [one worships] in the eight corners: 2 Ghasmarāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Viśvakavalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Lolākṣīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Lolajihvikāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Sarvabhakṣāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Sahasrākṣīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Niḥsaṅgāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi; 2 Saṃhṛtipriyāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] in the eight petals: 2...

Having worshipped [the goddesses] as follows: Acintyāpā, Aprameyāpā, Pūrṇarūpāpā, Durāsadāpā, Sarvāpā, Saṃsiddhirūpāpā, Pāvanāpā, and Ekarūpiṇīpā— at the sides of the four doors of the square [mandala], starting from the door facing the Goddess:
Beginning from the right side and extending to the edge of that door, having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī at each door in pairs,
one should again worship her in the center with the Jvālāmālinī-vidyā, and then offer all the [substances] such as incense (dhūpa) and so forth.
Having performed [the rite] as before, one should bring it to completion; thus ends the procedure for the daily worship of Jvālāmālinī Nityā.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Citrānityā. In the *Śrītantrarāja* (21st chapter):
"Now, O Śivā, among the sixteen Nityās, she who is the sixteenth is called Citrā; listen now to her ritual manual (*kalpa*), which grants the accomplishment of all aims. (1)
The Vidyā has already been explained, along with its application of limbs (aṅganyāsa), meditation, the Śaktis, worship, the means of accomplishment, and its fruits. || 2 ||

Thus it is said. In that very same [text] (3.72): "With *vāyu*, *prāṇa*, and *vanasva*, that [mantra] becomes variegated (*citrā*) with two syllables. This refers to *car* and *kau*. In the *Tripurāṇava*, it is stated that Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra, *gāyatrī* is its meter (*chandas*), and *vicitrā* is its deity (*devatā*). This is found in the *Tantrarāja* (21.4).
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence with the Vidyā-mantra joined with the long vowels, as before; then one should install the Mātṛkā using the Vidyā. || 1 ||
She has the splendor of the rising sun’s orb, is adorned with ornaments of gold and jewels,
wears a crown of nine gems, and is radiant in garments of variegated silk.
She has four arms and three eyes, her face radiant with a pure smile;
she is eternally composed of all bliss and bestows every desired object. || 3 ||
Holding a noose and a goad with her four arms, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she dwells within the fresh source of the pericarp of the auspicious lotus.
The worship of that wheel by means of its powers is likewise declared;
one should worship Brāhmī and the others, who are endowed with nine birthplaces and eight groups [of letters]. (5)
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action from the middle corner;
and one should worship the weapon (hetis) all around the Goddess, near her arms.
One should worship all the eternal Lords to the west of the Goddess, each with their respective *akāra* syllables and their respective mantras, according to the prescribed rule.
The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru and other such rites have been declared as common to all the Nityās, since these [Nityās] are born from the outpouring of the Primordial One (Ādyā).

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): therein, at the conclusion of the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the Yoga-pīṭha, having performed three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) with the Citrā-vidyā, one should perform the following depositions: "Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the goddess Citrā, on the heart. Having thus deposited [the mantras], *caḥ*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs on the hands and body with: *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *cīṃ śirase svāhā*, *cūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *caiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *cauṃ netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*, *cāṃ astrāya phaṭ*; [one should then perform the placement of the letters] from *cakauṃ aṃ namaḥ* and so forth, up to *cakauṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ*.

Having thus performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* up to this point, and having completed the meditation and mental worship, one should draw two squares with four gates each upon a plate of gold or other material using saffron and so forth; within those, a thirty-two-petaled lotus, and within that, an eight-petaled lotus.

Having fashioned the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) within that [space] as the nine-fold womb (*navayoni*), and having established it before him and worshipped it, one should perform the rites beginning with the placement of the *arghya* and ending with self-worship;
then, having worshipped the seat (*pīṭha*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, one should [visualize] the form within that by means of the *citrā-vidyā*.

Having performed the visualization, invocation, and so forth, up to the offering of flowers as before, one should worship the three rows of Gurus in the space between the triangle and the octagon. Then,
in the four locations on the right and left within the spaces between the triangle and the octagon, [one should worship] with "Oṃ Abhayāya Namaḥ" and "Oṃ Aṅkuśāya."

Having worshipped with "Oṃ Namaḥ 2 Pāśāya Namaḥ 2 Varāya Namaḥ," one should worship the powers of Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā) in the inner triangle, proceeding clockwise starting from the front of the Goddess. Then, in the eight triangles:
[at the first] "2 Aṃ 16 Brāhmī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi"; [at the second] "2 Kaṃ 5 Māheśvarī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi"; [at the third] "2 Caṃ 5 Kaumārī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi"; [at the fourth] "2..."

Ṭaṃ 5, Vaiṣṇavī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Taṃ 5, Vārāhī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Paṃ 5, Indrāṇī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Yaṃ 5, Cāmuṇḍā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi; Śaṃ 5, Mahālakṣmī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi. Having worshipped these and the other Śaktis mentioned in the Sarvamaṅgalā-pūjā on the eight petals and other locations, one should conclude everything in the same manner. Thus.
The ritual procedure for the multicolored impermanent worship.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Kurukullā. In that regard, the Śrītantrarāja states:
(20th chapter)—"Now, that which was declared as the offering deity (*balidevatā*) among the sixteen *Nityās* is the mantra of Kurukullā, a *vidyā* consisting of twenty-five syllables. (1)
Thus it is said. In that very [work], at 3.89:
"The burning of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is conjoined with earth; then again, the first [vowel] in *rasa* is air (*marut*).
Pervaded [by that] and joined with the power of air is earth; then the triad conjoined with itself. 1.
At the beginning of this [mantra], however, there is a pair of *rasas* (the letters *sa* and *va*) joined with *cara* (the letter *ya*);
then follows *haṃsa* conjoined with *dāha* (the letter *ra*), *vahni* (the letter *ra*), and *śakti* (the letter *ī*). || 2 ||
Nabha (0), twice hṛt (2), sadāha (34), ambu (1), and jyā (2) joined with itself (0); then ambu (1) joined with viyat (0), and nabha (0) joined with marut (2), O Dear One. (3)
The void (śūnya) pervaded by earth (bhū), the *haṃsa*, and the first and last [letters] of the three mantras;
from the five syllables beginning with the sixth of this [mantra], the last two are said to be the first [syllable].
The second [mantra] is declared to have eleven syllables with the last two [being long];
the third has twenty-five syllables; thus the mantras are proclaimed in sequence.
Oṃ kurukulle svāhā; this is the seven-syllable mantra. (1)
The thirteen-syllable mantra of Kurukullā is: Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. (2)
The twenty-five-syllable mantra of Kurukullā is: Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ, bring all people under my control, hrīṃ svāhā. (3)
Thus, in that very same place—(22.2)—it is stated:
"That very [Vidyā] consisting of three parts is proclaimed there by way of its numerical count:
the first is said to consist of seven [syllables], and the other is joined with thirteen. (1)
The third, however, is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five syllables;
thus, through these three forms of vidyā, she bestows all that is desired.
Thus, in the Tripurārṇava: "The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is declared to be Paṅkti, and the deity is Kurukullā."

In the *Tantrarāja* (22.4): "One should worship that Lalitā, who is eternally delighted by amusements, on the island of the nine jewels situated in the midst of the oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, and milk."
On its bank, one should worship the goddess Pañcamī Tīrapālikā;
one should worship Ratnapotacarī all around those oceans.
By his command, one should worship the jewel-boat (ratnapota) under that very name;
and by that same [name], one should worship the wheel of power (balicakra) in its center.
Having constructed a square [mandala] provided with gates in the eastern and western directions,
one should draw within it a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having fashioned a beautiful pericarp, one should worship the nine-yoni diagram;
having performed the six-limbed ritual with the Bālā mantra, one should likewise prepare the arghya offering with it.
One should invoke her with the first root mantra and the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā;
having thus meditated upon that Goddess together with her retinue, one should worship her in due order with perfumes and other offerings.
One should meditate upon her with disheveled hair, naked, red in color, and embodying bliss,
holding in her hands an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad. (7)
The goddesses situated outside possess weapons, forms, and complexions identical to his;
they have bathed after their menses, their wombs quiver with vitality, and their eyes are ever-joyful and reddish-brown.
One should perform the ritual services, such as installation and the rest, with the *hṛllekhā* mantra.
Then, by her command, one should mount the *bhrāmiṇī* [wheel] and worship the *drāviṇī*.
Beginning from the western door, one should worship the right branch and so forth:
Sūrya, Soma, the lunar day (tithi), the day of the week (vāra), as well as the yoga, the asterism (ṛkṣa), and the karaṇa.
And likewise, [one should worship] Yakṣiṇī and Tārā on the two doorposts of the eastern gate;
together with the Śaktis whose forms are space, wind, fire, water, and earth,
as well as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, in the same manner as before.
One should worship Prāṇa, Buddhi, and Śakti upon the eight petals.
One should worship the eight goddesses of speech in the inner and outer corners;
thereafter, one should worship the arrow, the bow, the noose, and the goad on all sides.
In the center, having worshipped the powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action within the corners of the triangle,
one should then worship the seat of consciousness (saṃvidāsana) in its midst.
Then he should worship her with the root mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables.
Then, by her command, he arrived at an island surrounded by a boat.
Having obtained the western [stone], the puṣparāga, one should descend gradually;
while circumambulating, one should indeed worship these [stones] in their respective places throughout the directions.

One should first worship the oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, and milk— starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order— with perfumes and flowers, using their names preceded by "namaḥ."
The island made of the nine gems and so forth was previously described;
thus worshipped, it brings delight to the Goddess Lalitā. (18)
Thus, because the Goddess quickly grants many desired things to her worshipper, she becomes pleased; therefore, O Sovereign Lady, one should worship her in this manner.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Kurukullā among the goddesses above the boat-shaped vessel at the conclusion of the worship with the twenty-five-syllable root mantra.
The offering for the Goddess has been declared through the mantra of Tārāśakti;
listen to it, O beloved! I shall now speak the ten-syllabled Tārā-vidyā.

The syllable *bhūḥ* joined with its own [seed-syllable], followed by *raya* joined with *dāha* (the letter *ra*) accompanied by a vowel; then *raya* joined with *dharā* (the letter *la*), and finally a pair of *rayas* joined with *marut* (the letter *sa*). 22.
O Dear One, this [syllable] is the third; it becomes the sixth when joined with the fourth and the seventh;
one should know that the sixth becomes the eighth when conjoined with the heart (hṛ), water (ambu), and wind (marut). (23)
The ten-syllable Vidyā is said to be *haṃsa* joined with the wind (*marut*):
*oṃ tāretu tāreture svāhā*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer the *bali* oblation to her with this Vidyā.
O wise one, listen to the meditation of the Goddess, which cuts through all afflictions. || 1 ||
In her waters, there is no obstruction anywhere for one who remembers her—
she who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, two-armed, and holds a boon-granting lotus.
She who bears [them], surrounded by powers (śaktis) of many colors and many forms, with a smiling face and adorned with red pearls. || 3 ||
"One should meditate upon her whose pair of lotus-feet are placed upon jeweled sandals.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): there, having drawn upon the ground on top of the altar a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp containing nine *yoni*s using sandalwood paste or vermilion (*sindūra*), outside of that—

Having constructed the worship mandala consisting of two squares joined by two doors, one facing east and one facing west, and having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Kurukullā mantra, [one should assign]: "Obeisance to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti at the head;
obeisance to the Paṅkti meter at the mouth; obeisance to the deity Śrī Kurukullā at the heart."

Having performed the *nyāsa* with "Namas," and having said with palms joined, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the offering of the *bali* to be performed," one should perform the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* on the hands and limbs using the three *bālā* seed-syllables as in the case of the root-vidyā; then,
having performed the pervasive *nyāsa* (*vyāpaka*) with the Kurukullā-vidyā and meditated upon her with the verse beginning "Vikīrṇakuntalām" (She of the Disheveled Tresses).

At the conclusion of the mental worship (mānasapūjā), after performing the placement of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and so forth up to the end of the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should worship [the elements] from Maṇḍūka down to Earth, just as in the Śrīcakra worship; likewise,
worshipping in reverse order starting from the west, one should worship sugarcane, *irā*, ghee, and milk on the shore of the Sugarcane Ocean.

In the southwest corner of the island (dvīpa), having recited the Vidyā of Vārāhī and worshipped Goddess Vārāhī— seated facing the Root Goddess— with the mantra "Vārāhīdevīpādukāṃ," and then, by her permission,
having worshipped the Jewel Boat with "Hrīṃ Ratnapotāya Namaḥ" upon it...
Having worshipped [the deities] according to the sequence of the Śrīcakra worship, beginning with the Jewel Lion Throne (ratnasiṃhāsana) and ending with the Power of Manonmanī (manonmanī-śakti),
one should then, in the center of that, worship the Person who is the consort of the Goddess, saying "Salutation to the Seat of Consciousness" (saṃvidāsanāya namaḥ),
using there the twenty-five-syllable Kurukullā mantra.

Having invoked her with the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*, and having displayed the mudrās beginning with *sthāpana* and ending with *paramīkaraṇa* while reciting "hrīḥ," one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) for her and [display] the four mudrās beginning with *pāśa*.
Having displayed the offerings beginning with the seat and ending with flowers, one should pray, "O Śrī Kurukullā,
grant permission for the worship of the retinue. With that permission,
the practitioner himself boards the jewel-boat, at the eastern and western ends of which—
Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ Bhrāmiṇī Śrīpādukāṃ" and "Hrīṃ Drāviṇīpādukāṃ," one should worship the nine Śaktis in clockwise order, beginning from the southern jamb of the western door. For instance:
on the southern jamb of the western door, "2 Hrīḥ Sūryarūpiṇī Śaktipādukāṃ."
In the northwest corner: 2 Hrīḥ Somarūpiṇī.
310) Worship within that wheel with her powers is likewise prescribed in the same manner.
One should worship the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī, who possess nine wombs and are endowed with eight groups.
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action from the middle corner;
and one should worship the weapon (hetis) all around the Goddess, near her arms.
One should worship all the eternal protectors to the west of the Goddess with their respective *akāra*-syllables and their respective mantras, according to the prescribed ritual.
The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru and other such rites have been declared as common to all the Nityās, since these [Nityās] are born from the outpouring of the Primordial One (Ādyā).

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): therein, after performing the *nyāsa* of the Yoga-pīṭha, one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Citrā-vidyā*. Having performed the *nyāsa*, saying: "Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; salutation to the goddess Citrā, on the heart. And then, *caḥ*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs on the hands and body with: *Hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Cīṃ śirase svāhā*, *Cūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Caiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *Cauṃ netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*, *Cāṃ astrāya phaṭ*; [one then performs the placement of the letters] from *Cakauṃ aṃ namaḥ* and so forth, up to *Cakauṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ*.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* up to this point, and having completed the meditation and mental worship (*dhyāna-mānasa-pūjā*), one should draw two squares with four gates each using saffron and other pigments on a plate of gold or similar material; within that, a thirty-two-petaled lotus, and inside that, an eight-petaled lotus.

Having fashioned the worship-circle (pūjācakra) within that [space] as the ninefold womb (navayoni), having established it before him and worshipped it, and having performed the rites from the placement of the arghya water up to the end of self-worship (ātmapūjā),
he should worship the seat of Bhuvaneśvarī and, upon that, the form by means of the Citrā-vidyā.
Having performed the visualization and the sequence of offerings beginning with invocation and ending with flowers as before,
one should worship the three rows of Gurus in the space between the triangle and the octagon; then,
in the four locations on the right and left within that same space between the triangle and the octagon— (2).

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Abhayā," "Salutation to Aṅkuśa," "Salutation to Pāśa," and "Salutation to Vara," one should then worship the powers of Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā) within the inner triangle, proceeding clockwise starting from the front of the Goddess; then, [one worships] in the eight yonis.
2 aṃ 16, the feet of Brāhmī; 2 kaṃ 5, the feet of Māheśvarī; 2 caṃ 5, the feet of Kaumārī; 2 ṭaṃ 5, the feet of Vaiṣṇavī; 2 taṃ 5, the feet of Vārāhī; 2 paṃ 5, the feet of Indrāṇī;
2 yaṃ 5, the feet of Cāmuṇḍā; 2 śaṃ 5, the feet of Mahālakṣmī—[to be worshipped] on the eight petals and so forth.
Having worshipped the powers (śaktis) mentioned in the rite of worship for Sarvamaṅgalā, one should likewise conclude everything; such is the procedure for the worship of Citrānityā.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Kurukullā. In that regard, the Śrītantrarāja states:
(Chapter 20)—"Now, that which was declared as the deity of the offering for the sixteen Nityās is the mantra of Kurukullā’s Vidyā, consisting of twenty-five syllables. (1)
Thus it is said. In that very same [text] (3.89):
"The burning of the vital breath (prāṇa) is conjoined with Earth; then again, the first [element] in the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is Air.
It is pervaded by Air joined with Power (śakti); then Earth conjoined with itself—thus the triad. 1.
At the beginning of this [mantra], however, there is a pair of *rasas* (the letters *sa* and *va*) conjoined with *cara* (the letter *ya*).
Following that is *haṃsa*, joined with *dāha* (the letter *ra*), *vahni* (the letter *ra*), and *śakti* (the letter *ī*). || 2 ||
Nabhaḥ (0), twice hṛt (2), sadāha (41), ambu (1), and jyā (2) joined with itself (0);
then ambu (1) followed by viyat (0), and nabhaḥ (0) joined with marut (2), O Dear One. (3)
The void (ha), pervaded by the earth (la), is *haṃsa*; the first and last [letters] of the three mantras constitute the [next] three.
From the five letters beginning with the sixth of this [mantra], the last two are said to be the first [of the next]. (4)
The second is declared to have eleven syllables with the last two [long], and the third consists of twenty-five syllables; thus the mantras are stated in sequence.
Oṃ kurukulle svāhā—this is the seven-syllable mantra. (1)
The thirteen-syllable mantra of Kurukullā is: Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. (2)

The mantra of Kurukullā is: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ mama sarvajanaṃ vaśamānaya hrīṃ svāhā*; this is the twenty-five-syllable [mantra]. Thus it is said in that very same work (22.2): "That same [mantra] is declared there as the three-part [vidyā], according to its numerical count."
The first is said to consist of seven [syllables], while the other is joined with thirteen.
The third, however, is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five syllables;
thus, through these three forms of vidyā, she bestows all that is desired.
Thus it is said. In the *Tripurārṇava*: "The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is declared to be Paṅkti, and the deity is Kurukullā. In the *Tantrarāja* (22.4):
"Upon the nine jewels situated in the midst of an ocean of sugarcane juice, molasses, ghee, and milk..."
On that island, one should worship that Lalitā, who is eternally delighted by diversions. || 1 ||
On its bank, one should worship the goddess Pañcamī Tīrapālikā;
one should worship Ratnapotacarī all around those oceans.
By his command, one should worship the jewel-ship (ratnapota) using that very name;
and within it, one should likewise worship the wheel of Bali (balicakra). || 3 ||
Having constructed a square [mandala] provided with gates in the eastern and western directions,
one should place within it a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having fashioned a beautiful lotus with nine birthplaces (navayoni) in the pericarp, one should worship it;
having performed the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) with the Bālā mantra, one should likewise prepare the arghya offering with it.
One should invoke her with the first root mantra using the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā;
having thus meditated upon that Goddess together with her retinue, one should worship her in due order with perfumes and other offerings.
One should meditate upon her with disheveled hair, naked, red in color, and embodying bliss,
holding in her hands an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad. (7)
The goddesses situated outside possess weapons, forms, and complexions identical to those [of the inner deities];
they have bathed after their menses, their wombs quiver with vitality, and their eyes are eternally blissful and reddish-brown.
One should perform the ritual services, beginning with installation, using the *hṛllekhā* mantra;
then, by her command, one should ascend [the wheel] and worship *Bhrāmiṇī* and *Drāviṇī*.
Beginning from the western door, one should worship the right branch and so forth:
Sūrya, Soma, the lunar day (tithi), the day of the week (vāra), as well as the yoga, the asterism (ṛkṣa), and the karaṇa.
And likewise, [one should worship] Yakṣiṇī and Tārā on the two doorposts of the eastern gate;
[and the deities] whose forms are space, wind, fire, water, and earth, conjoined with their Śaktis,
as well as Sound, Touch, Form, Taste, and Smell, in the same manner as before.
One should worship Prāṇa, Buddhi, and Śakti upon the eight petals.
One should worship the eight goddesses of speech (vāgdevyaḥ) in the inner and outer corners;
then, one should worship the arrow, the bow, the noose, and the goad all around.
In the center, having worshipped the powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action within the corners of the triangle,
one should then worship the seat of consciousness (saṃvidāsana) in its midst.
Then he should worship her with the root mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables.
Then, by her command, he arrived at an island surrounded by ships.
Having obtained the western Puṣparāga stone, one should descend in due order;
as one moves around [the site], one should indeed worship these [stones] in their respective locations within the directions.

First, one should worship the oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, and milk, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order, with their respective names ending in "namaḥ," using perfumes and flowers.
The island made of nine gems and so forth has been described previously;
thus worshipped, it brings delight to the Goddess Lalitā. (18)
Thus, because the Goddess quickly grants many desired things to her worshipper, one should therefore worship Her in this manner, O Sovereign Lady. (19)
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Kurukullā among the goddesses above the boat-shaped vessel at the conclusion of the worship with the root mantra of twenty-five syllables.
The offering for the Goddess has been fully described through the mantra of Tārāśakti;
listen to it, O beloved! I shall now speak the ten-syllabled Tārā-vidyā.

The syllable *bhūḥ* joined with its own [seed-syllable] *sva*, followed by *raya* joined with *dāha* and accompanied by *cara*; then *raya* joined with *dharā*, and finally a pair of *raya*s joined with *marut*. (22)
This is the third; the sixth should be the fourth, O beloved, and the seventh;
one should know that the sixth is the eighth, joined with the heart, water, and wind. (23)
The *haṃsa* joined with the wind (*marut*) is declared to be the ten-syllabled *vidyā*:
*oṃ tāretu tāreture svāhā*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to this [deity] with this *vidyā*.
O wise one, hear now of the Goddess’s meditation, which cuts through all afflictions. || 1 ||
In her waters, there is no obstruction anywhere for one who remembers her—
she who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, two-armed, and holds a boon-granting lotus.
She was surrounded by spears of many colors and many forms,
possessed a smiling countenance, and was adorned with red pearls.
"One should meditate upon her whose pair of lotus-feet are placed upon jeweled sandals.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): there, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a ninefold pericarp using sandalwood paste or vermilion upon the ground on top of the altar, outside of that—

Having fashioned the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) as two squares joined by two doors, one facing east and one facing west, and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Kurukullā* mantra, [one should assign]: "Homage to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head;
homage to the Paṅkti meter in the mouth; [homage] to the deity Śrī Kurukullā in the heart."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Namas," and having said with palms joined, "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the offering of the *bali* to be performed," one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) on the hands as in the Root-Vidyā using the three *Bālā* seed-syllables; then,
having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the Kurukullā-vidyā and meditated upon her as "she whose locks of hair are disheveled."

At the conclusion of the mental worship (mānasapūjā), after performing the placement of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and so forth up to the end of the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should worship [the elements] from Maṇḍūka down to the Earth, just as in the worship of the Śrīcakra. Likewise,
worshipping in reverse order starting from the west, one should worship sugarcane, *irā*, ghee, and milk on the shore of the Sugarcane Ocean (*ikṣusāgara*).

In the southwest corner of the island, having recited the Vidyā of Vārāhī and worshipped Goddess Vārāhī with the mantra "vārāhīdevīpādukāṃ," who is seated facing the Root Goddess (Mūladevī), and having received her permission,
one should worship the Jewel Boat with "hrīṃ ratnapotāya namaḥ" and [worship] upon it.
Having worshipped according to the sequence of the Śrīcakra-pūjā from the Jewel Lion Throne (ratnasiṃhāsana) up to the power of Manonmanī,

one should then worship within that [center] the Person who is the consort of the Goddess, saying "Salutation to the Seat of Consciousness" (samvidāsanāya namaḥ), using there the twenty-five-syllable Kurukullā-vidyā.

Having invoked her with the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* and displayed the mudrās beginning with *sthāpana* and ending with *paramīkaraṇa* while reciting "hrīḥ," one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) for her and [display] the four mudrās beginning with *pāśa*.
Having displayed the offerings beginning with the seat and ending with flowers, one should pray, "O Śrī Kurukullā,
grant permission for the worship of the retinue. With that permission,
the practitioner himself mounts the jewel-boat, [standing] at the eastern and western extremities of the jewel-boat.

Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ Bhrāmiṇī Śrīpādukāṃ" and "Hrīṃ Drāviṇī Pādukāṃ," one should worship the nine śaktis in a clockwise direction, beginning from the southern jamb of the western door. For instance: on the southern jamb of the western door, [one worships] "2 Hrīḥ Sūryarūpiṇī Śaktipādukāṃ."
In the northwest corner: 2 hrīḥ, [the goddess] Somarūpiṇī.
(p. 312) In the north: 2 hrīḥ, Tithirūpā. In the northeast: 2 hrīḥ, Vārarūpā. To the north of the eastern gate.

On the branch: 2 Hrīḥ, O you whose form is Yoga (yogarūpa). On the right branch: 2 Hrīḥ, O you whose form is the Constellations (ṛkṣarūpa). In the southeast: 2 Hrīḥ, O you whose form is the Means (karaṇarūpa). On the south: 2 Hrīḥ, O you whose form is the Fortnights (pakṣarūpa). In the southwest: 2 Hrīḥ, O you whose form is the Months (māsarūpa). Having thus worshipped, then on the eight petals, starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise:

Having worshipped [the deities] as the form of space, the form of sound, the form of wind, the form of touch, the form of fire, the form of form, the form of water, the form of taste, the form of earth, the form of smell, the form of vital breath, the form of intellect, and the form of power, [one worships] within the eight triangles, proceeding clockwise starting from the front of the Goddess.
Having worshipped the eight goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī, outside the womb within that [triangle], one should worship them as Bāṇa, Cāpa, Pāśa, and Aṅkuśa. Then, in the central womb,
starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise, one should worship them as Icchā, Jñāna, and Kriyā.

Then, in the center, having worshipped the seat of consciousness as before, one should worship Kurukullā upon it with the twenty-five-syllable mantra using perfumes and other offerings; having offered incense and lamps and completed all else, [one performs this] as an ancillary part of the Kurukullā worship with the mantra: *oṃ tāre tutāre ture svāhā*.
Having offered the bali, one should conclude; such is the ritual procedure for the worship of the Kuru lineage.
Now, the procedure for the worship of Vārāhī. In the *Tantrarāja* (Chapter 23):
"Now, among the sixteen Nityās, the fifth is indeed an ancillary [to them].
She was previously described as being twofold, along with her ancillaries and the method of worship."

I shall describe the means of accomplishment for one whose mantra has been mastered, through ritual applications, meditations, worship, fire-offerings, and yantras, for the sake of attaining all desired goals. (2)
Thus it is said. In that very same [work]—(3.73):
"The pure [ether], then by its own nature, becomes empty; the earth is stable through the ether; water follows; then fire with wind; likewise, water and wind. 1.
The fire conjoined with *ilā* (earth), then water conjoined with *marut* (wind), burning by means of wind, and the *haṃsa* which is fire—these three again [form the next group]. (2)
Water and fire joined with air; then the swan (the letter *ha*) with earth (*dha*), which is the sky (*na*);
fire joined with fire (*ra*); these five [elements] together with air joined with itself (*ya*). || 3 ||
First, water with *cara*; then, water joined with fire;
then, the void with the pervasive and the pure; and the void joined with power and space. (4)
Fire together with Earth, and Water accompanied by Air;
these four mentioned previously are below, and after this [is the next].
The bowstring is conjoined with its own [essence], as is the moving sap; this is the first [group].
The sap is spoken of again by Agni from the group of four as the triad at the end.
The sky [is joined] with the earth, and the swan [is joined] with the mobile;
first, the swan [is joined] with fire—this triad is the heart, conjoined with its own [nature].
First, the *rasa* [tattva] is joined with *cara* and then with fire (*agni*);
afterwards, O Dear One, the previously mentioned triad [is joined] with wind (*vāta*) and space (*nabhas*).
Subsequently, the vital breath (prāṇa) is joined with its own [seat], and the heart is joined with its own [essence] of rasa;
thereafter, these three are pervaded by the burning of the heart conjoined with water.
The *gotra* (ga) is joined with *dharā* (a); *sparśa* (pa) is joined with *nāda* (i); it is joined with *java* (ya).
It is preceded by *dāha* (ra), and each preceding [element] is joined with *marut* (sa). (10)
The void [element], accompanied by wind, is the heart; by burning it becomes water, and by movement it becomes touch.
Touch, accompanied by wind, is the heart; joined with burning it becomes water. (11)
The fire (Ra) joined with its own vowel (Ā), likewise the swan (Ha) with water (U) and wind (Ma);
[these] joined with their own heart (Sva), and the essence (Sa) joined with itself (A). || 12 ||
Life-force (prāṇa) and fire (dāha) joined with earth (dharā); again, those two joined with fire (vahninā) become ether (viyat).
Water (ambu) consists of water (vār) joined with fire (dāha); ether (viyat) is that which is pervaded by its own [element] joined [with the others].
The two syllables previously mentioned twice, Śuci joined with itself, Sthira with Rasa and Vana with itself, Dāva, Haṃsa, and Dhara joined with Sva. (14)
Dyuti, Nādavatī, then Hṛdambu joined with Marut,
and Haṃsa with Marut— this is the Vidyā of one hundred and ten syllables.

Thus: Aiṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Vāttāli, Vāttāli; Vārāhi, Vārāhi; O you whose face is a boar, O you whose face is a boar; homage to Andhā, to Andhinī; homage to Rundhā, to Rundhinī; homage to Jambhā, to Jambhinī; homage to Mohā, to Mohinī; homage to Stambhā, to Stambhinī.

"Paralyze [Name]! Paralyze! Cause the tongues of all those who are wicked and hostile to be paralyzed! Act, act! Quickly bring them under control! Aiṃ ṭhalauṃ ṭhaṭha huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus [ends the mantra]. The syllables are 110. In the *Tripurārṇava*, the seer (ṛṣi) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
"The Gāyatrī metre is declared [to be used]. Thus, in the *Tantrarāja* (23.3):

"Having performed the limb-projections (*aṅga*) with the seven mantra-syllables and with the six [syllables] joined in pairs, [the mantra] is endowed with the classes [of consonants] numbering ten, seven, and seven. (1)
Having constructed a wheel consisting of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and two circles,
one should invoke [the deity] there by means of one's own name and perform worship.
O Dear One, having worshipped with the Vārāhī-vidyā consisting of one hundred and ten syllables in the very center, [one should worship] from the left, the right, and the tip of the corner.
Then one should worship Krodhinī, Stambhinī, Caṇḍā, and Uccaṇḍā with their respective names, joined with the first seed-syllable, the final letter, and the vital breath (ha).
In the six corners, beginning from one's own front [corner], one should worship Brāhmī and the others counter-clockwise;
and likewise, one should worship Mahālakṣmī as the fifth in the circle at the center.

"Having performed the *bali* offering with the sixteen-syllable mantra and having worshipped with the ritual services (*upacāra*s)," so it is said. Now, the procedure: having fashioned a mandala on the altar consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, two circles, and a square, and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, [one should place] upon the head...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrīvārāhī in the heart," and having spoken with palms joined, "This is the application for the attainment of my desired goal," [one recites]: "Aiṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lady, salutation to the heart; Vāttali 2."

*Śirase svāhā*. *Vārāhi vārāhi*, *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Varāhamukhi varāhamukhi*, *kavacāya huṃ*. *Andhe andhini*, *namaḥ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. *Rundhe rundhini*, *namaḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Having thus performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the hands, one should meditate as follows:
And one should meditate upon the goddess Kolāsyā, who resembles molten gold, possessing the form of a woman down to her throat, with blazing tawny hair. (1)
She has three eyes and eight arms, holding a discus, a conch, a goad,
a noose, a mace, a plough, as well as granting protection and bestowing boons.
One should contemplate her seated comfortably upon the shoulder of Garuḍa.
Having meditated thus, at the conclusion of the mental worship (mānasapūjā), having performed the ritual of self-worship beginning with the placement of the *arghya* and other offerings,
and having worshipped the seat (*pīṭha*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, one should fashion the form [of the deity] with the root mantra and [worship it] with that vidyā.

Having performed the rites from invocation (āvāhana) up to the final consecration (paramīkaraṇa) with their respective mudrās, and having completed the offerings beginning with the seat (āsana) and ending with flowers, one should worship as follows: in the left corner of the triangle, *2 kroṃ krodhinyai namaḥ*;
in the right corner, *2 staṃ stambhinyai namaḥ*; and at the front, *2 kṣoṃ kroṃ*.
Salutation to Caṇḍoccaṇḍā. Then, in the corners of the hexagon, beginning from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise: Āṃ, salutation to Brāhmī; Īṃ, salutation to Māheśvarī;
Ūṃ, salutation to Kaumārī; Ṛṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; Ḷṃ, salutation to Vārāhī.
Having worshipped with "Aiṃ, obeisance to Indrāṇī," one should worship outside of that on the two circles with "Oṃ,
obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā" and "Aḥ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī" in front of the Goddess. Then,
having worshipped Indra and the others in the square, and the thunderbolt and the other weapons outside of that, one should again worship the Goddess in the center with her mantra.
Having worshipped with all [substances] such as incense and so forth, one should conclude as before; this is the ritual procedure for the worship of Vārāhī.
Now, the procedure for the worship of the Lords of the Days (vāreśas): Having prepared a hexagonal mandala on that altar, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra,

and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the worship of the Lords of the Days as an ancillary part of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) which is about to be performed," [one proceeds].

Having invoked the lords of the day and that [day’s] weekday into the center of the hexagon and worshipped them with the ritual services beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with flowers (*puṣpa*),
one should then worship two by two the lords of the weekdays starting from the one following that [central pair], in sequence, moving clockwise from one's own front toward the corners of the hexagon.

Having offered all [substances] beginning with incense, one should conclude everything else as previously described. As for the lords of the days: for Sunday, Sūrya and Śiva; for Monday, Soma and Ambikā; for Tuesday, Bhauma and Kumāra; for Wednesday, Brahmā and Budha; for Thursday...
Bṛhaspati and Viṣṇu [are worshipped] on Friday; Bhṛgu and Śukra on Saturday; Kubera and Saura on Sunday. This is the procedure for the worship of the lords of the days.

Now, the procedure for the worship of the Lords of the Lunar Days (Tithīśas): Having drawn a fourteen-spoked maṇḍala upon that altar and performed three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, one should resolve:
"I shall perform the worship of the Tithīśas as an ancillary part of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) to be performed."
Having formed the mental resolve, one should invoke the respective Lord of the lunar day (tithīśa) in the center, worship him with offerings beginning from the seat up to flowers,
and then, proceeding clockwise starting from the front, worship the Lords of the lunar days and others in the fourteen spokes.

Having worshipped them in a clockwise sequence and offered incense and other offerings, one should conclude the rite as before. As for the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśas*): on the first day (*pratipad*) it is Agni; on the second, the two Aśvins; on the third, Umā; on the fourth, Vighnarāja; on the fifth, the Serpent; and on the sixth, Ṣaṇmukha.
On the seventh day is Ravi; on the eighth, the Mothers; on the ninth, Durgā;
on the tenth, the Directions; on the eleventh, Ghanada; on the twelfth, Keśava; on the thirteenth, Yama; on the fourteenth, Hara; and on the fifteenth, Candra.
"The ancestors [are worshipped] on the new moon day"—this is the sequence for the worship of the lords of the lunar days (tithīśa).
Now, the procedure for the worship of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) deities: there,
having fashioned upon that altar a worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) consisting of twenty-seven spokes,
and having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, [one recites] "Today here," and so forth.

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the worship of the lords of the lunar mansions as an ancillary part of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) that is about to be performed," one should worship the respective lord of the lunar mansion and lunar day in the center with offerings beginning with the seat (āsana) and ending with flowers; [then] regarding the twenty-seven constellations:

Having worshipped, starting from the lord of the lunar mansion (nakṣatreśa) mentioned therein, by proceeding clockwise from one’s own front [corner], and having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should conclude the rite as before. As for the lords of the lunar mansions:
in Aśvinī, the two Aśvins; in Bharaṇī, Yama; in Kṛttikā, Agni; in Rohiṇī...
Dhātṛ [presides] over Mṛgaśiras; Candra over Ārdrā; Śiva over Punarvasu; Aditi over Puṣya; Guru over Aśleṣā; the Pitṛs over Maghā; and Aryaman over Pūrvā-phalgunī. (p. 314)
In Uttarāphalgunī is Bhaga; in Hasta, Sūrya; in Citrā, Tvaṣṭṛ; in Svātī, the Maruts; in Viśākhā, Indra and Agni; in Anurādhā, Mitra;
in Jyeṣṭhā, Indra; in Mūla, Nirṛti; and in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Water.
In Uttarāṣāḍhā, the Viśvedevas; in Abhijit, Prajāpati; in Śravaṇa, Hari;
in Dhaniṣṭhā, the Vasus; in Śatabhiṣaj, Varuṇa;
in Pūrvābhādrapadā, Ajaikapād; and in Uttarābhādrapadā, Ahirbudhnya.
The procedure for the worship of the lords of the lunar mansions is thus: "Pūṣan in Revatī."
Now follows the ritual procedure for the worship of the nine planets (*navagrahapūjāvidhi*). The practical application therein is as follows:
having cast four lines—east-west and north-south—upon an altar three cubits in length and breadth, one should produce a wheel consisting of nine squares with equal intervals.

Having drawn three circles within the intervals of all the squares, and having produced nine squares by the intersection of two lines through the center of each, one should place the syllables *aṃ, āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ, ṝṃ* in the central square and in the eight directions,
starting from its own top and proceeding clockwise.
Having written the eight vowels beginning with *a* (the vowel of Vāta) and having written *moṃ* in the central square,
one should write *maṃ māṃ miṃ mīṃ muṃ mūṃ mṛṃ mṝṃ meṃ maiṃ moṃ mauṃ maṃ maḥ* in the two intermediate spaces of the three circles, specifically in the innermost intermediate space.

Having written the Mātṛkā from *aṃ* and *āṃ* up to *kṣaḥ* in the space between the outside and the inside, one should worship the Sun (Bhāskara) there. Then, in the mandala consisting of nine compartments located in the eastern direction, one should write "soṃ somāya namaḥ" in the central compartment and "hrīṃ" in the eight surrounding compartments.

Having written the eight vowels— ḷṃ, ḹṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ, and aḥ— in the directions starting from the east and so forth, one should write the letter *ha* joined with the sixteen vowels beginning with *haṃ* and *hāṃ* in the intervening spaces; outside of that, having written the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) accompanied by the *bindu*, one should place the Moon there.

One should worship. Then, having written the letter *ka* containing the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the central square of the mandala consisting of nine squares located in the southeast direction, and having written the eight syllables *kaṃ 5 maṅgalaḥ* in the eight squares outside of that, [one should place] the sixteen vowels in the intervening space.

Having written the letter *ka*, one should write the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) in the space between it and the outside, and there worship Mars (*mauma*). Then, in the central square of the southern mandala, having written the letter *ca* containing the *praṇava* (oṃ),
and having written "caṃ 5 budhāya" in the eight squares outside of that—
In the inner intermediate space, having written the letter *ca* joined with the sixteen vowels beginning with *caṃ*,

and having written the Mātṛkās outside of that, one should worship Budha there. Then, in the center of the Nirṛti-maṇḍala, having written the letter *ṭa* containing the Praṇava (*oṃ*) within it, and [having written] outside of that in the eight [directions]...
Having written the eight syllables "Ṭaṃ 5 Sauraye" in the compartments starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise,

having written the letter *ṭa* joined with the sixteen vowels in the intermediate space outside of that, and having written the Mātṛkā in the intermediate space outside of that, one should worship Saturn in the center with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Then...
In the central square of the western maṇḍala, having written the letter *ta* containing the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ),
one should write "taṃ 5 gurave" in the eight squares outside of that; then, in the space outside of that,
one should write the letter *ta* joined with the sixteen vowels, and in the space outside of that, one should write the *mātṛkā*, and therein—

One should worship the Guru with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Then, having written the syllable *pa* containing the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the central square of the Vāyavya maṇḍala, one should write the eight syllables— *paṃ 5 śukrāya*— in the eight squares outside of that, starting from the eastern side and proceeding clockwise.

Outside of that, in the intervening space, one should write the letter *pa* joined with the sixteen vowels; then, in the intervening space outside of that, one should write the Mātṛkā. Therein, one should worship Śukra with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
Then, in the central square of the northern mandala, one should write the letter *ya* containing the *praṇava*.

Outside of that, in the eight compartments starting from one's own front and proceeding clockwise, having written the eight syllables "yaṃ 5 rāhave iti," and having written the letter *ya* joined with the sixteen vowels in the intermediate space outside of that, and having written the Mātṛkā in the intermediate space outside of that, [one should place] Rāhu there.

One should worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Then, having written the letter *ṣa* containing the *praṇava* (Oṃ) in the central square of the Īśāna-maṇḍala, one should write the eight syllables *ṣaṃ ketave* in the eight squares outside of that, starting from its own [northeast] corner and proceeding clockwise.

Having written the letter *ṣa* joined with the sixteen vowels in the space between that [circle] and its exterior, and having written the *mātṛkā* in the space between that and its exterior, one should worship Ketu there with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
This is the procedure for the worship of the nine planets.

Thus [ends] the work titled *Śrīvidyārṇava*, composed by the ascetic Śrī Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of Śrī Pragalbhācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was a disciple of Śrī Bhagavat Śaṅkarācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the illustrious Mahāmahopādhyāya and worshipful teacher.
In the Tantra, the fourteenth breath [chapter]. 14.
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the fifteenth chapter.

Then, at the time of awakening in the morning, the best of instructors, contemplating himself as the very self of Tripurā, should rise with his body [mentally] projected, [visualizing] the form of light—the feet of the Lord—situated in the aperture at the crown of the head. Thus [it is said in the *Tantrarāja* 5.17]: "with his body projected."

Having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) upon his body by means of those to be described— namely, the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the four seats (*caturāsana*), and the eight deities of speech (*vāgdevatāṣṭaka*)—
and having offered praise with the verses beginning "Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One" (*namaste nātha bhagavan*).

Having recited the Guru-mantra— *hrīṃ śrīṃ ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rūṃ amukānandanātha hrīṃ śrīṃ sa ha kṣa ma la va ya rīṃ amukadevyambāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*— as many times as possible, [one should contemplate] the Kuṇḍalinī from the base (*mūla*) to the top of the head (*mūrdhan*).
Having meditated upon oneself as identical with Tripurā, preceded by the contemplation of the act of going,
one should recite the hymn spoken in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"In the morning, I bow to the lotus-feet of the Mother of the worlds."
Of the illustrious Tripurasundarī, the eternal mother of the worlds. || 1 ||
I bow to the lotus-feet of Tripurasundarī in the morning— she who is gracious toward her own devotees and who is saluted by Hara and the other gods.
I bow to the lotus feet of Tripurasundarī, by whom Hari, Hara, and Viriñci perform the acts of creation and the rest—at dawn. (3)
I bow to her who, in the morning, holds a noose, a goad, and arrows in her hands— she whose water for the feet shines as the Gaṅgā upon the head of Maheśvara.
In the morning, I bow to the lotus feet of the illustrious Tripurasundarī, who resembles the rising sun and by whom this entire world is illuminated. (5)
By the grace of that Tripurasundarī, whatever [obstacle] might arise,
the man who recites these five verses daily at dawn shall be liberated from it.
"Śrī Tripurasundarī shall grant her own state to him.

Having thus praised [her], [one should contemplate] women of various colors, weapons, forms, vehicles, and ornaments, who are all-pervading, givers of everything, and bestowers of all siddhis through the offering of the bali. (Tantra 5.18) "They shall be so"—thus it is said.

Having placed [the vessel] before oneself upon its base, filled with food, condiments, flowers, and water, one should first strike the palms of both hands three times while reciting the sixteen-syllable mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hrūṃ svāhā*.

The *bali* offering should be presented with a mudrā that consists of two fists held in an upward and downward position, with the two index fingers extended, symbolizing the display of the *bali* substance offered to the deities. Then, having performed the necessary [purifications], [one recites]: *klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajanapriyāya*.

Having cleaned one's teeth with the mantra "namaḥ," and having performed the washing of the face, bathing, and applying the *tilaka* with the *mūlamantra* and the daily *nityā-mantra*, one should complete the Vedic *saṃdhyā* and then perform the Tantric *saṃdhyā*. Then, having sipped water (*ācamana*) three times, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*.

One should contemplate the three sections of Vidyā within the cavity of the heart, which is the support; it is red, and by the penetration of its radiance, one's own body becomes red as well. (Tantrāloka 5.32) Contemplating this, one should fill [the body] with the nature of nectar through the left nostril, while subsequently recollecting water and wind.
One should expel [the breath] through the right [nostril]. When it has been thus well-mastered, one should subsequently inhale for thirty-two *mātrās*.

One should retain it for sixty-four [mātrās] and exhale it for a quarter [of that time]. (Tantra 27.68) Having performed three, six, twelve, sixteen, or twenty such *prāṇāyāmas* in this sequence, [one recites] *aṃ āṃ*...

Having performed the purification of the hands with *sauḥ*: *Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, *namaḥ* to the heart, on the two thumbs; *3*, *svāhā* to the head, on the two index fingers; *3*, *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair, on the two middle fingers; *3*, *huṃ* to the armor, on the two ring fingers; *3*, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes, on the two little fingers; *3*.

*Astrāya phaṭ* for the palms and backs of the hands. *3 Hṛdayāya namaḥ* at the heart; *3 Śirase svāhā* at the head; *3 Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* at the crest-lock; *3 Kavacāya huṃ* at the armor; *3 Netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* at the three eyes; *3 Astrāya phaṭ* with both palms extended.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by placing the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) in the cardinal and intermediate directions, above, below, and in the center— with sound, preceded by three claps of the hands, and through the joining of the index and thumb fingers—
one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*). As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
Kālanityā, however, is [worshipped] through the Lords, the Principles, and the eternal Vidyās,
in the Foundation, the Heart, the Head, Fire, the Sun, and the Moon.
Meditating during the three junctions of the day, one should recite the entire alphabet of consonants and vowels;
and one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the locations of the Mātṛkā for the purification of that body.
Thus [it is said]. However, the specific details are found in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Sandhyā should be known as fourfold: Bālā, Kaumāra, and Yauvanā..."
The goddess Sandhyā is proclaimed to be both mature (prauḍhā) and partless (niṣkalā). || 1 ||
In the morning, the Great Goddess is considered to be Vidyā-Vāgīśvarī;
at midday, she is Kāmeśvarī; and in the evening, she is Purabhairavī. (2)

"At midnight, Mahādevī Tripurasundarī is to be known. Then, having consecrated water before oneself with the *dhenumudrā* and empowered it eight times with the root mantra, one should [sprinkle] with that water using *kuśa* grass while reciting the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa'.

Having sprinkled one's own head letter by letter with the vowels accompanied by the *bindu*, having sprinkled it three times with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), and having meditated upon the Goddess in her described form within the solar orb, one should take water in the right hand and consecrate it seven times with the mantras *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ*.

Having consecrated it three times with the root mantra, one should sprinkle one's own head with drops of that water using the thumb and ring finger while reciting the root-vidyā; then, placing the remaining water in the left hand,
one should draw that water— which has become the form of light— into oneself through the *iḍā* [left nostril], thereby [removing] all impurities situated within one's own body.
Having washed that water and perceiving it as black-colored and emerging through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī],
one should take that water again in the right hand, visualize a blazing vajra-stone in one's left side,
and strike against that stone with the *pāśupatāstra* mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ*.

Having washed both hands and taken water with the root mantra (mūlavidyā), one should visualize it as having become one with the supreme nectar residing in the thousand-petaled lotus via the flowing channel (nāḍī); then,
having caused that water to emerge through the opening between the teeth and out through the path of the eyes, one should place it in the left hand and, with it—

Sprinkling one’s own head three times with water while reciting the mantra *amṛtamālini svāhā*, [one should then recite]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "I purify the first peak-syllable, the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), svāhā"; *2*, "I purify the second peak-syllable, the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), svāhā"; *2*, "the third peak-syllable, the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*)..."

I purify, svāhā! Having recited the entire Vidyā: "I purify all reality, svāhā! Having thus performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and taken water in the hollowed palms: *Uthāra* 2; [we] meditate upon the first peak-syllable for Vāgīśvarī; [we] contemplate the second peak-syllable for Kāmeśvarī; the third peak-syllable...

Having offered the *arghya* three times with "tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt," and having given three *arghya* offerings to the Sun with "hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūrya eṣa te 'rghaḥ svāhā," one should satisfy the Goddess three times with the root mantra,
and then satisfy the Sun three times with "hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ."

Having meditated upon the first *kūṭa* at the *mūlādhāra*, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning, extending from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should cause that light to pierce the *brahmarandhra* via the path of the *suṣumnā* and enter the orb of fire situated in space through the path of the nostrils.
Having invoked her from that splendor, one should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī, who has arisen:
yellow in color, wearing yellow garments, adorned with yellow garlands and unguents, shining like ten million flashes of lightning, youthful, and radiant with a rosary of beads. (1)

One should meditate upon her who holds a book and a lotus in her lotus-like hands, who is seated upon the seat of fire, who is the source of speech, who has arisen from the Vāgbhava syllable, who possesses three eyes, and who is smiling.
Having thus meditated upon the first *kūṭa* within the circle of fire situated in the sky, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings, saying: "I worship the sandals of Tripurā Vāgīśvarī.
Then, having recited the Vāgbhava Gāyatrī, one should offer the *arghya* water, saying: "I prepare this *arghya* for Tripurā Vāgīśvarī."
Having offered the *arghya* with joined palms three times while uttering "Svāhā," and having again satiated the first *kuṭa*,
Tripurāvāgīśvarīpādukā, by reciting "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*) three times, one should bow to the venerable Guru (*śrīguru*),
perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) on the hands as before, and [place them] upon the locations for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *praṇava*, the three *tāra*s, the root-vidyā, the daily *nityā*-vidyā for that day, the *haṃsa* twice, and the *mātṛkā* beginning with "aṃ namaḥ," one should recite the previously mentioned *gāyatrī* as much as possible and then recite the *vāgbhava-gāyatrī*:
*Aiṃ tripurādevyai vidmahe vāgīśvaryai dhīmahi.*
Having recited "tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt," one should recite the root-vidyā in this manner in the morning:
"In the lotus situated at the mūlādhāra, within the circle of fire..."
She is eternal, whose form is the seed-syllable of speech, and who shines like a mass of lightning. || 1 ||
Her hands are radiant, holding a flower-arrow, a sugarcane bow, a noose, and a goad;
she assumes a body by her own will and is composed of the eternal syllables of the Yugas. || 2 ||
Then, [he saw] those on all sides endowed with the Ghaṭikā-enclosure, with palms joined in reverence,
holding the Jñāna-mudrā in their hands, and intent upon the worship of Vāgbhava.

"One should remember the nine Nāthas in the root-lotus within the yoni-maṇḍala. Thus, in the four junctions of the day (sandhyā), [the mantra is]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ* [followed by] the root-mantra, the daily *nityā*-vidyā for that day, *haṃsaḥ*, and *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ hrīṃ*.

*Śrīṃ*, [to] the feet of *Śrī Mahātripurasundarī*, whose nature is light and bliss; having recited as before up to the end of *haṃsaḥ*, [then] *ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [to her] whose nature is reflective awareness and bliss (*vimarśānanda-rūpi*). Again, having recited up to the end of *haṃsaḥ*, [then] *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ*.

Ṅaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, [to the goddess] whose nature is bliss-bliss (ānandānanda-rūpa). Again, reciting in the same manner: Caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, [to the goddess] whose nature is knowledge-bliss (jñānānanda-rūpa). Again, reciting in the same manner: Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, [to the goddess] whose nature is truth-bliss (satyānanda-rūpa). Again, in the same manner: Taṃ thaṃ daṃ...

*Dhaṃ naṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, O you whose form is full bliss (*pūrṇānanda-rūpa*). Again, in the same manner: *Paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, O you whose form is the bliss of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānanda-rūpa*). Again, pronouncing in the same way: *Yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, O you whose form is the bliss of creative intuition (*pratibhānanda-rūpa*). Once again, in the same manner...
*Ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Subhagānandarūpa*.
(Thus, on page 317) one should recite the root-vidyā as being composed of the nine *nāthas*. Then, [one should recite] the daily vidyā of that specific day.

One should recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity; this is the daily recitation for the fixed time. Then, meditating on the root-vidyā—possessing a radiance equal to a thousand rising suns—extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and having recited the root-vidyā one hundred and eight times, [one should visualize it] within the fire-maṇḍala situated in the external space.
Meditating upon Vāgbhaveśvarī in the form previously described, one should recite the Vāgbhava-kūṭa one hundred and eight times in the morning. Then,
having performed the recitation preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, one should offer it to the Goddess, prostrate, and offer praise.

Having projected the Root Goddess and Vāgbhaveśvarī from the solar orb and the fire orb into the heart and the *mūlādhāra*, one should bow to the venerable Guru. Thus ends the procedure for the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*). Now, the meditation on the Guru at the times of ritual action is described in the *Rudrayāmala*:

"At the time of initiation, one should perform the daily rite (āhnika) while meditating with that same disposition by which [the Guru] was seen by him during his own act of grace. The word "of the Guru" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. This meditation on the Guru is to be understood as applying to instances other than the morning recollection (*prātaḥsmaraṇa*).
O Īśānī, this morning twilight rite must always be performed by the practitioner at all times during every ritual for the sake of the complete attainment of mantra-siddhi. || 1 ||
If one performs the worship of the deity while neglecting the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā),
he is impure, of wicked conduct, and excluded from all sacred rites.

O Maheśānī, if a man performs the worship of the deity and other rites while neglecting the morning twilight prayer (prātaḥ-sandhyā), even after performing fire-oblations (homa), he is born as a denizen of hell.
O Śivā, a Brahmin who abandons the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) and performs fire-oblations (homa) or libations (tarpaṇa) without cause will certainly become a dog.
O Goddess, even one who has mastered the Vedāṅgas is born as a Piśāca [if he neglects this];
among all the Sandhyās, the morning Sandhyā is the most important. (5)
"Therefore, a Brahmin should not abandon it; by abandoning it, he would attain hell.

Thus, according to the *Tripurārṇava*, this must necessarily be performed—this is the word of Śiva. Now, one should perform sixty recitations (*japa*) as a *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa*. And that [is as follows]:

In five days, there is the form of six revolutions of the *mātṛkā*. Thus, in the *Tantrarāja*: "Beginning from the rising of the sun, one by one in the sequence of *ghaṭikās*, each of the fifty letters of the *mātṛkā* [is repeated] through the revolution. (1)

Thus: at the time of sunrise, the letter *a* arises. Thereafter, during the moments (*ghaṭikā*) from the second up to the fiftieth, the letters beginning with *ā* and ending with *kṣa*—excluding the *visarga* and the vowels—arise each at the time of their respective moment.

They arise. Then, beginning from the fifty-first ghaṭikā, during the remaining ten ghaṭikās, the ten phonemes starting with *a* and ending with *ḷ* arise at the time of their respective ghaṭikā-occurrences.
In this manner, on the second day, the vowel *e* arises at the time of sunrise; thereafter, [the others arise] at the time of their respective ghaṭikā-occurrences.

Forty-nine letters beginning with *ai* and twenty groups beginning with *a* arise. On the third day, at sunrise, the letter *ca* arises; thereafter, at the time of the rising of their respective *ghaṭikās*, the letters from *cha* to *kṣa* (and from *a* to *ṇa*) emerge.
Fifty-nine phonemes arise. On the fourth day, at the time of sunrise, the letter *ta* arises;

thereafter, at the time of the rising of its own *ghaṭikā*, the fifty-nine phonemes beginning with *tha* and ending with *kṣa*, as well as those beginning with *a* and ending with *ma*, all arise together. On the fifth day...

At the time of sunrise, the letter *ya* arises; thereafter, at the time of the rising of each respective *ghaṭikā*, the forty-nine letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa* (or from *a* to *kṣa*) arise. In this way, within five days, there occurs six revolutions of the Mātṛkā.
In this manner, by means of these syllables in sequence, one should perform sixty recitations known as the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa*.
That method is now demonstrated: therein, the fifty letters from *a* to *kṣa*, excluding the *visarga*, form five groups of ten each; for this very reason, they bear those names.
With these, the sixty-fold recitation (*ṣaṣṭijapa*) should be performed. The procedure for that is as follows: [first] the root mantra, then the daily *nityā-vidyā* of that day, and then *haṃsaḥ*.

Aṃ Namaḥ. (Having thus recited the five groups ending in *kṣa*, one should again repeat the first group beginning with *a* and ending with *ḷ*. Thus is the sixty-fold recitation. On the second day: 2.
The Root Mantra, the daily mantra of that day’s Nityā, *haṃsaḥ*, and *eṃ*. In this manner, [one should recite] the four [groups] ending in *kṣa*.
Having repeated the groups [of consonants], one should repeat the first and second groups again. Thus is the recitation of sixty [syllables].

On the third day: the root mantra, the daily mantra of that day’s Nityā, and *haṃsaścaṃ*. Having thus [recited] the three groups ending with *kṣa*, one should repeat the three groups beginning with *a* and ending with *ṇa*. Thus...

60 | (On the fourth day: 2 repetitions of the root mantra, the daily mantra (*nityā-vidyā*) of that day, and *haṃsaḥ ṭaṃ*. Thus, having recited two groups up to *kṣa*, one should again repeat the four groups beginning with *a* and ending with *ma*. Thus [60]. On the fifth day: 2 repetitions of the root mantra and the daily mantra (*nityā-vidyā*) of that day.)
*Haṃsaḥ yaṃ*. Having thus recited the group ending in *kṣ*, one should again repeat the fifty letters from *a* to *kṣ*.
Thus is the sixty-fold recitation. Thus are the six cycles. Then, on every sixth day...
Furthermore, beginning again from the letter *A* and following the aforementioned method, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa* without interruption.
Now, at this present time,
the practitioners [should calculate] the days elapsed of the Kali Yuga by means of the *ahargaṇa* according to the method stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.
Having understood this and counted up to the day of the commencement of one's own sequence,
one should divide by five; having determined the rising syllable from the remainder, one should begin the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa* on that day when the vowel *a* becomes the rising syllable.
The recitation of the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa* should be performed in the morning alone, according to the prescribed sequence.
p.

318) Now, regarding the midday twilight (*madhyandina-sandhyā*): having performed there everything from the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) up to the libation to the Sun exactly as in the morning twilight, one should perform the seed-syllable twilight (*bīja-sandhyā*). It is as follows: therein—

At midday, one should meditate upon the red-colored Kāmarāja-kūṭa of the Mūlavidyā within the Anāhata-cakra. Visualizing that radiance as it flows through the path of the Suṣumṇā and emerges through the nostrils,
one should invoke it into the solar orb and meditate upon Kāmeśvarī arising from it, as follows:

Meditate upon Kāmeśvarī, who is red in hue, richly adorned with garments and ornaments of deep crimson, holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting; she possesses a pure smile, is endowed with the vigor of exuberant youth, and has three eyes.
Having meditated thus twice, one should worship three times with "Śrī Tripurā Kāmeśvarī-pādukāṃ," and then, having uttered the Gāyatrī of the Kāmarāja-kūṭa,
[one offers] "I offer the arghya to Śrī Tripurā Kāmeśvarī, svāhā."

Having raised the *añjali* of the threefold *arghya*, and having again uttered the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja, one should satisfy [the deity] three times with the mantra: "I satisfy the sandals of Śrī Tripurā Kāmeśvarī.
Then, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* as before.

Having recited the *Gāyatrī* of the Fourth State (*turīyavidyā*), one should recite the *Kāmakūṭa-Gāyatrī*. It is as follows: "We know the Goddess of the Three Cities; we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; may the Wet One (*klinnā*) impel us. Having recited this according to one's capacity, [one should contemplate her] as being composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
One should recite the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*). It is as follows:
At midday, upon the solar disc in the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should visualize the Goddess, whose nature is Kāmarāja, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (1)
She is endowed with a flower-arrow, a sugar-cane bow, a noose, and a goad,
and is surrounded on all sides by her own principal powers, the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
One should meditate upon her who is surrounded by red garlands, garments, unguents, and ornaments,
who consists of the eternal syllables of the Yugas, and who is encircled by the Ghaṭikās.
Bearing flower-arrows and sugarcane bows, and possessing crimson bodies, they are devoted to the worship of Kāmarāja within the lotus of the heart. || 4 ||

Thus, having meditated upon the Goddess [twice], [one offers] the root-mantra, the daily mantra of that day’s Nityā, *haṃsaḥ*, *aṃ* (16 times), "to the Śrīpādukā of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is the embodiment of the Śiva-tattva. [Twice] the root-mantra, the daily mantra of that day’s Nityā, *haṃsaḥ*, *kaṃ*, "to the Śakti-tattva... [Twice] the root-mantra, the daily mantra of that day’s Nityā...
Haṃ is the form of the Khaṃsa-Śiva-tattva; likewise, Gaṃ is the form of the Īśvara-tattva;

Ghaṃ is the form of the Śuddhavidyā-tattva; Ṅaṃ is the form of the Māyā-tattva; Caṃ is the form of the Kalā-tattva; Chaṃ is the form of the Vidya-tattva; Jaṃ is the form of the Rāga-tattva; Jhaṃ is the form of the Kāla-tattva.
Aṃ: the form of the principle of Aniyati (the Unrestricted). Ṭaṃ: the form of the principle of Puruṣa (the Spirit). Ṭhaṃ: the form of the principle of Prakṛti (Primordial Matter).

Ḍaṃ: the form of the principle of Ahaṅkāra (Ego). Ḍhaṃ: the form of the principle of Buddhi (Intellect). Ṇaṃ: the form of the principle of Manas (Mind). Taṃ: the form of the principle of Śrotra (Auditory Organ). Thaṃ: the form of the principle of Tvak (Tactile Organ). Daṃ: the form of the principle of Cakṣus (Visual Organ).

Dhaṃ: the form of the principle of the tongue; naṃ: the form of the principle of the nose; paṃ: the form of the principle of speech; phaṃ: the form of the principle of the hands; baṃ: the form of the principle of the feet; bhaṃ: the form of the principle of the anus; maṃ:
the form of the principle of the generative organ; yaṃ: the form of the principle of sound; raṃ: the form of the principle of touch.
Laṃ—form-tattva; Vaṃ—taste-tattva; Śaṃ—smell-tattva; Ṣaṃ—space-tattva;

Saṃ—wind-tattva; Haṃ—fire-tattva; Laṃ—water-tattva. 2. Mūla—the daily mantra of the Nityā, Haṃsaḥ Kṣaṃ—the earth-tattva-form. Thus, by means of the yoga of the thirty-six tattvas, [one recites] the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Then, having recited the Kālanityā-vidyā one hundred and eight times,

he should meditate upon the Kāmarāja-kūṭa within the center of the heart-lotus— possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns— and its mass of radiating rays pervading from the heart down to the mūlādhāra.

Having recited the *kāmarājakūṭa* one hundred and eight times, and having offered the recitation preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites, and having prostrated, one should dissolve the root goddess Kāmeśvarī into one’s heart. Thus ends the procedure for the midday twilight ritual (*madhyāhna-sandhyā-vidhi*).
