Now, the procedure for the evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā): having performed there the rites beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma) and ending with the libation to the Sun as previously described, one should perform the "seed-sandhyā" (bījasandhyā). At evening, in the Ājñā-cakra, within the lunar disc known as *ha-kṣa*, one should recite the third peak (kūṭa) of the root-mantra and [offer] to Tripurāmṛteśvarī-pāda.
Having thus worshipped three times with perfumes and other offerings, one should recite the Gāyatrī of the third peak (kūṭa) which is to be described hereafter,
and after offering the *arghya* three times with the mantra "I offer *arghya* to Śrī Tripurāmṛteśvarī, svāhā," one should again recite the third peak and say, "I satiate Śrī Tripurāmṛteśvarī."

Having satiated [the breath] three times and having recited the Gāyatrī of the Fourth Vidyā preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before, one should recite the Śaktikūṭa-Gāyatrī as follows: "2 sauḥ! We know the Goddess Tripurā; we meditate upon Śaktikāmeśvarī; may that Immortal One inspire us. Thus.

Having recited the Śakti-Gāyatrī twenty-eight times, one should recite the Root-Vidyā in the evening as being composed of the sixteen Nityās, as follows: [One should meditate upon her] at night as having a splendor equal to the moon, situated upon the moon located in the lotus of the Ājñā-cakra.
She consists of the seed-syllable of Śakti and is endowed with a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, the supreme and eternal one whose syllables are the Yugas, who is surrounded by the Ghaṭikās as her enclosure, the Blessed Lady who is encircled by the Nityās; || 2 ||
One should meditate in the evening upon the sixteen Nityās during the period of command (ājñā), who possess smiling faces and hold a book and a rosary.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, one should recite the root mantra of the daily Nityā, the *haṃsa*, and the mantra of Kāmeśvarī, and then say:
"I worship the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is the very form of the daily Nityā Kāmeśvarī. *Aṃ* [Kāmeśvarī-nityārūpiṇī-śrīmahātripurasundarī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi].
Homage!
319) 2 Having uttered the root mantra of the daily Nityā, *haṃsaḥ*, and the *vidyā* of Bhagamālinī, [one recites] *āṃ*.

Bhagamālinī-nityārūpiṇī-śrīmahā... (3) 2 Root mantra, the *vidyā* of the daily *Nityā*, *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the *vidyā* of Nityaklinnā: *iṃ* Nityaklinnā-nityārūpiṇī-śrī... (4) 2 Root mantra, the *vidyā* of the daily *Nityā*, *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the *vidyā* of Bheruṇḍā: *īṃ*...
*Bheruṇḍā-nityārūpiṇī* || (5) 2 Recite the root mantra, the daily *nityā*-vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*,

then recite the *Vahnivāsinī*-vidyā, [and utter] *uṃ*: *Vahnivāsinī-nityārūpiṇī* || (6) 2 Recite the root mantra, the daily *nityā*-vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*, then recite the *Vajreśvarī*-vidyā, [and utter] *ūṃ*.

Vajreśvarī-nityārūpa... (7) 2 [Recite] the root mantra, the *dinanityā* vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*, then recite the *śivādūtī* vidyā; *ṛṃ*, *śivādūtī-nityārūpa*... (8) 2 [Recite] the root mantra, the *dinanityā* vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*, then recite the *tvaritā* vidyā; *ṝṃ*, *tvaritā-nityārūpa*... (9)
2. The root mantra, the daily *nityā* mantra, and *haṃsaḥ*;

having uttered the *Kulasundarī* mantra, [worship] *ḷṃ*, the form of *Kulasundarī-nityā*. (10) 2. The root mantra, the daily *nityā* mantra, and *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the *Nityānityā* mantra, [worship] *ḹṃ*, the form of *Nityānityā*. (11) 2. The root mantra...
The root mantra, the daily Nityā-vidyā, *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the Vijayā-vidyā, *aiṃ* [Nīlapatākā-nityārūpā]... (12) 2 The root mantra, the daily Nityā-vidyā, *haṃsaḥ*;
having uttered the Vijayā-vidyā, *aiṃ* [Vijayā-nityārūpā]... (13) 2 The root mantra.

Having uttered the *haṃsa* of the daily *Nityā-vidyā*, one recites the *Sarvamaṅgalā-vidyā*: *oṃ sarvamaṅgalānityārūpāyai namaḥ* || (14) 2 Having uttered the *haṃsa* of the daily *Nityā-vidyā*, one recites the *Jvālāmālinī-vidyā*: *oṃ jvālāmālinīnityārūpāyai namaḥ* || (15) 2
The root mantra, the daily *nityā*-vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the *vicitrānityā*-vidyā:

*aṃ* [to] the form of *vicitrānityā*. (16) 2. The root mantra, the daily *nityā*-vidyā, and *haṃsaḥ*; having uttered the fifteenth vidyā: *aḥ* [to] the venerable Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is the eternal (*nityā*).
Having thus recited [the mantra] as consisting of the sixteen Nityās, and having likewise recited the Kālanityā-vidyā as before,

one should meditate on the third *kūṭa*— resembling ten million autumn moons— from the space between the eyebrows up to the *brahmarandhra*, and recite that third *kūṭa* one hundred and eight times. Then:

Having offered the recitation preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having praised and bowed to the Goddess, one should dissolve the root goddess Amṛteśvarī, who resides within the solar orb, into the heart and between the eyebrows.
Thus concludes the procedure for the evening twilight devotion (sāyaṃsandhyā).

Then, at midnight, one should perform the fourth twilight worship (*turīyasandhyā*). As in the evening, having performed everything from breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) to the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) in the solar orb without the meditation on the Goddess,
one should [visualize] the fourth peak-syllable (*turīyakūṭa*), which consists of the thirteen syllables of the root-vidyā, within the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrārakamala*).

Having meditated on [the deity] possessing a radiance equal to a ruby, having invited her from the circle of stars into the supreme space through the flowing nostril, and while meditating on the Blessed Lady arisen therefrom with the form as previously described, one should utter the fourth peak-syllable (turīyakūṭa).

Having offered the *arghya* three times with "śrīmahātripurasundarīpādukāyai arghyaṃ kalpayāmi svāhā," and having again uttered the fourth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), one should satisfy the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī three times with "śrīmahātripurasundarīpādukāṃ santarpayāmi. Then, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the other [preliminaries], [one should perform] that which was previously described...

Having recited the Turīyagāyatrī according to one's capacity, and having recited the Kālanityā-vidyā one hundred and eight times, and having completed the recitation preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, and having praised the Goddess,
one should dissolve her from the supreme ether into the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.
One should meditate upon the Self in the form of Kāmakalā. Thus ends the procedure for the fourth twilight devotion (tūrīyasandhyā).
This worship of the four junctions (*sandhyā*) is mandatory for those who practice this Vidyā.
Even in the event of incapacity, one must perform the twilight worship at midnight in the form of meditation alone.
If it has not been performed, on the following day one should recite the root Vidyā one hundred and eight times as an expiation.
Furthermore, one becomes entitled to perform ritual action; such is the teaching of Śiva.

"Regarding the omission of the ritual bath, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), and worship, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times," according to the statement in the *Tantrarāja*. The remainder of the sentence is "one should recite the root-vidyā. In this matter, the omission of the twilight prayers must not be performed; for such is indeed the command of Śambhu.
One who is initiated but devoid of the twilight prayers does not enjoy the fruit of initiation.
According to this statement, the fourfold twilight ritual (*sandhyācatuṣṭaya*) must necessarily be performed by practitioners.
If, however, a lapse of the twilight ritual occurs here due to negligence, then at the time of the next twilight,
one should perform the rites of the previous twilight preceded by the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
One should perform the twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) at its proper time. And it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:

"If one is devoid of the [proper] twilight rite during another twilight, then, having performed the ritual of the preceding twilight, one should, with a concentrated mind, perform the ritual of the subsequent twilight. (1)
Thus [it is said]. After the Sandhyā-vandana, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors and others.

Therein, preceded by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the ritual placement of the Ṛṣis and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa), one should invoke the Tīrtha as before into the water in front of oneself, and transform it into nectar using the "vam" syllable and the Dhenu-mudrā.

Having consecrated [the water] eight times with the root mantra, one should visualize the Śrīcakra therein; having invoked the Goddess into its center preceded by the worship of the seat (*pīṭhapūjā*) according to the method to be described,
one should fully worship the Goddess in the water with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the enclosure according to the procedure to be described, one should recite the root mantra (mūlavidyā) one hundred and eight times,
or half of that [fifty-four], or twenty-eight times, or as many times as possible, saying: "I satiate the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," using the waters of that sacred site.

Having perceived the supreme nectar in the lotus-face of the Supreme Deity, one should satisfy the deities of the enclosure in their proper order with single handfuls [of water], using the mantras prescribed for worship and substituting "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*) in place of "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*). If one is unable to do that:

One should offer libations to the Root Goddess, who is accompanied by the four [deities] beginning with Vaṭuka, the six limbs, the young maidens, the three lineages of gurus, and the seventeen Nityās; she resides in the center of a triangular maṇḍala endowed with a square and a circle, and is joined by the powers of the weapon-enclosure within the triangle. If one is unable even for that much:

Having meditated upon the Goddess in consecrated water and worshipped her, one should offer libations to the Goddess alone; this is the procedure for the daily libation (*nityatarpaṇavidhi*). Now—[the practitioner] wearing red perfumes and garments, adorned with garlands...
Adorned with red ornaments, with a serene mind, his mouth scented with camphor, and anointed with fragrant unguents;
seated in the lotus posture, facing east, and having restrained his breath, the disciplined one—(Tantrāloka 5.19).
Such is the excellent teacher who, as before, [should perform] for the pacification of obstacles by means of the sixteen-syllable mantra.

Having offered the bali-oblation to all beings, one should worship one's own Lord on the crown of the head with the nine services— namely, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, worship, hymns of praise, and the contemplation of one's own self as identical with Him— and thus become absorbed in that [Lord].
Having meditated upon him as being of that nature, and subsequently, by his command, having performed the three types of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the body of the disciple,

and at the conclusion of the mental worship (*mānasapūjā*), one should meditate upon the fire-mandala consisting of ten digits (*kalā*) within the base of the central pitcher, in the respective locations of those digits.

Having meditated upon the thirty-eight *kalās* of Śiva according to the previously described method, as well as the thirty-eight *kalās* of the Form (*mūrti*) taught in the *Mahāṣoḍha*, and contemplating the unity of them all,
[one should anoint] the vessel of the *kalaśa* with the eight fragrant substances of Śakti.
Having smeared [the vessel] and covered it with a pair of fine cloth garments, having placed upon it a fruit, five sprouts, and so forth,
and having wrapped it with flower garlands, one should visualize the Śrīcakra above that, worship it, and perform self-worship with the eight-syllable mantra of oneself.

One should begin the worship of the seats (*pīṭhapūjā*). Therein, first reaching the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice in the west, and within it, in the western corner, one should propitiate Tīrapālikā—the fifth [seat]—according to the aforementioned method with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Then, by her command, in the north-western corner of the ocean...

Having obtained the jewel-boat, one should perform the worship of Kurukullā, beginning with "Hrīḥ, homage to the Jewel-boat," and so forth. Then, by her command, while circumambulating the Jewel Island in reverse order, one should offer:
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, homage to the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice" in the west; "Homage to the Ocean of Wine" in the south; and in the east—

To the Ocean of Ghee (Ghṛtasāgara) [in the east]... To the Ocean of Milk (Dugdhāsāgara) in the north, obeisance. Having thus worshipped and offered flowers at the western side of the Jewel Island (Ratnadvīpa), and having reached the Flower-Pillar (Puṣpadaṇḍa), one should descend by its command. Then [one beholds] that most wonderful place, ten million yojanas in extent and breadth.

Having meditated thus: "The island consisting of the nine jewels, surrounded by those mountains of measurement, resembling a thousand suns," [one should offer salutation]: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ* (five times) *namaḥ to the island consisting of the nine jewels, resplendent with nine divisions*. To the garden of the Kalpavṛkṣa trees right there, *namaḥ*. Right there...

Having meditated on the six seasons beginning with spring as being gazed upon by the Goddess, [one says]: "Homage to the six seasons beginning with spring. Having meditated on the horses of the senses facing the Goddess in the west, [one says]: "Homage to the horses of the senses. Having meditated on the elephants of the sense-objects facing the Goddess in the east, [one says]: "Homage to the elephants of the sense-objects."
Then, one should worship the nine jewels in reverse order from the west to the beginning, middle, and end:
2 *namaḥ* to Puṣparatna in the southwest; 2 *namaḥ* to Nīlaratna in the south;
2 *namaḥ* to Vaidūryaratna in the southeast; 2 *namaḥ* to Vidrumaratna in the east; 2 [to the next jewel] in the east.

Salutation to the pearl-jewel in the Īśāna [corner]. Salutation to the emerald-jewel in the [Īśāna corner]. Salutation to the diamond-jewel in the North. Salutation to the go-meda-jewel in the Vāyavya [corner]. In the center, *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to the ruby-jewel. Then, in that same sequence:
I worship the sandals of the Śakti, the Mistress of the Nine Wheels who beholds the Goddess; salutations!

Likewise, I worship the sandals of the Śakti whose nature consists of the Kāla-mudrā, the Mātṛkā, the Ratna, the Deśa, the Guru-tattva, the Graha, and the Mūrti; salutations! Then, [offer] "Salutation to the moat of the waters of compassion. Then, in the center of that—

Having meditated upon the ruby pavilion (māṇikyamaṇḍapa), which possesses the brilliance of ten million suns and constitutes the third portion of Ratnadvīpa, one should [worship] outside the pavilion, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order: 2. Kālacakreśvarī-pāda;
2. Mudrācakreśvarī-pāda; 2. Mātṛkācakreśvarī-pāda; 2. Ratnacakreśvarī-pāda.
Having meditated upon the goddesses who gaze [upon the center] as the Śaktis in the corners beginning with the southwest (nir-ṛti) in reverse order:
"2. Obeisance to the Śakti whose nature is space (deśa). 2. Obeisance to the Śakti whose nature is time (kāla).
2. Obeisance to the Śakti whose nature is form (ākāra). 2. Obeisance to the Śakti whose nature is sound (śabda). Then...
Having meditated twice upon the Saṅgītayoginīs seated in rows on both sides within the pavilion,
gazing at the Goddess— [perform] the descent of power (śaktipāta) of the Saṅgītayoginīs. Then,
having meditated twice upon the Śaktis seated around the vicinity of the lion-throne, gazing at the Goddess— [perform the descent of power].
To the feet of the venerable assembly of all secret and manifest *siddha-yoginīs*. Thus ends the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭhapūjā*).
Now, the placement of the *arghya* vessel: there, having placed before oneself a vessel made of the three metals or any one of the earthen vessels along with its base (*ādhāra*),
and having filled it with water, [one should contemplate] within the waters of the base-vessel that which consists of the nature of fire, sun, and moon.

Having reflected upon this and understood that [the mantra] consists of three sections of knowledge (*vidyā*) and thirty-eight *kalās*, and having considered the *rocanā*, *candana*, *kāśmīra*, and *laghukastūrikā* as being respectively of the nature of the elements earth and so forth, you should cast them into the water while performing the *dhenumudrā* with the third [mantra].
Having displayed the *yonimudrā* and meditated upon the *śrīcakra* therein,

one should worship ten times each with the six limb-mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) in the northwest, northeast, southeast, and southwest corners of the *arghya*, as well as in the center and the four directions starting from the west in clockwise order.

Having recited the sixteen *Nityās* once each with the third [mantra], the daily mantra ten times, and the daily mantra of the day three times, and having performed worship, one should sprinkle all the implements for self-worship with that *arghya* water using the *vidyā*. Thus, having prepared the *arghya*, [one should perform] the ritual placements (*nyāsas*).

One should perform [this]. Then, having restrained the breath (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the method previously described, one should effect the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) by wiping the backs of the left and right hands against each other with the mantra *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*.
Then, for the feet: *2 hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ devyātmāsanāya namaḥ*; for the shanks: *2*...

HAIṂ HKLĪṂ HSAUḤ | Cakrāsanāya namaḥ | [At] the two knees: 2 HSAIṂ HSAKLĪṂ HSAUḤ Sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ | [At] the *liṅga*: 2 HRĪṂ KLĪṂ BLEṂ Sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the four seats, [one should perform it] twice with the Kulasundarī-vidyā.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the hands as before, one should perform the ritual placement of the eight goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī. Then, with the root mantra and the [six] limbs, one should perform the placement from the head down to the heart;
with the subsequent [mantra], from the heart down to the tips of the feet; and with the final [mantra], from the feet up to the heart.

One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the hollowed palms (*añjali*), starting from the soles of the feet and ending at the heart. Thus end the ritual placements (*nyāsas*).

Then, having visualized the Śrīyantra as described in one's own specific Tantra above the jar (kalaśa), and having fashioned the form (mūrti) within the bindu using the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ* with the Gesture of Raising the Power (śaktyutthāpanamudrā), [one recites] *hsraiṃ hsakalarīṃ hsrauḥ*.

Saying "namaḥ," having formed the three-segmented *puṣpagarbha* mudrā, one should, by means of the *tripurā-mudrā*— which consists of the contemplation of the nature of Fire, Sun, and Moon at the root, heart, and head [of that mudrā]— [invite] the deity, who is the embodiment of those three splendors, through the nostril.
Having brought [the deity] from one's own heart and invoked her into the visualized form, one should meditate upon her with her attendants:
"One should remember her as red and graceful, holding a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad in her hands; she is joyful and held within the lap of Kāmarāja. (1)
Adorned with necklaces, neck-ornaments, jewels, and the like, as well as rings and anklets,
she was further embellished by variegated clusters made of the nine precious gems.
She was resplendent with bracelets, armlets, and jeweled rings,
that divine lady wearing celestial garments.
She of the pure smile, delighted by listening to the songs sung by the multitude of Śaktis, whose very form was composed of bliss born from the enjoyment of innate nectar. || 4 ||
She bestowed compassion, which protects its practitioners with side-long glances,
and adorned it all around with various ornaments such as black yak-tail fans and the like.
She beheld the resplendent elephants and likewise the horses,
all displayed before her with spears, while she was filled with intense joy.
It is the supreme [state] served by those who are equal to oneself and by those who are expansive and eternal,
because it consists of the intense radiance of the central principal goddess.

By means of the recitation of these [mantras] strung together, the mantras of the student (varṇin) are accomplished;
there are two thousand three hundred repetitions of the Lord within the mass of mantras.
And these four should be known as the proclaimed "repetition of reality" (tattvāvṛtti);
the "constant repetition" (nityāvṛtti) consists of a thousand [recitations] according to the number of the full mandala.
"Two hundred and ninety-six [verses] have been declared in their entirety.
We shall elaborate upon this further below. In the present context, regarding the well-known jar, by means of the *kālanityā* vidyās numbering twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six...

The invocation has been stated; those *Kālanityā* vidyās have been taught in works such as the *Tripurārṇava*, and they are also indicated in the *Śrītantrarāja*. Those [vidyās] mentioned in the *Tantrarāja* are extracted here.

For example, the thirty-six letters representing the principles (tattva), beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', when each is joined individually with the sixteen vowels which constitute the essence of the sixteen Nityās,
become five hundred and seventy-six in number, known as the Full Mandala (pūrṇamaṇḍala).

Each individual phoneme among the previously mentioned thirty-six *kalās*, *nityās*, and *vidyās* is the initial phoneme of the thirty-six *vidyās*; thus, all these phonemes are known as the *vāgbhava*.

The thirty-six phonemes of the principles (tattvas) mentioned previously, joined together by means of the form of all the Vidyās, become the second phonemes, beginning with Kāmarāja, repeated again and again in sequence. The vowel *ī*, however, is the third phoneme for all the Vidyās, known as the Śakti-peak (śaktikūṭa).
They come into being.

Now, these vidyās are presented in sequence through the very procedure of recitation for mastery (*pārāyaṇa*). Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I shall perform the consecration of the full water-jar (*pūrṇakalaśa*) with the *vidyās* of the Kālanityās, numbering twenty-seven hundred and thirty-six," [one should proceed] by [reciting them] at each of the thirty-six locations, beginning from the crown of the head and the root of the right arm.

Having visualized a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should visualize the thirty-six letters of the principles (tattva), from *a* to *kṣa*, each joined with the sixteen vowels; then, having placed the first of those letters in the center, [one places the others] on the petals starting from the east.

One should then place those sixteen syllables, which are modifications of that [seed-syllable], beginning with it. among the colors of the previously mentioned full mandala.

Among the five hundred and seventy-six [syllables], each individual syllable possesses the status of a "yuga-syllable" (yugākṣara) for each respective Yuga. Having fully understood all of this from both the teacher and the scriptures, one should perform the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) and the ritual chanting (*japa*). Thus...

The recitation (*japa*) of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) consists of one thousand one hundred and fifty-two (1,152) repetitions. However, the recitation of the limb-mantras (*aṅgavidyā*) for each individual group (*varga*) consists of ninety-one repetitions;
thus, from the recitation at the beginning of two groups, it amounts to one hundred and eighty-two (182).
Even the recitation of the root-vidyā alone, performed four times with three repetitions each, amounts to twelve;
thus, when combined, the total number of recitations becomes one thousand four hundred and forty-six (1,046).
Having thus performed the recitation of the root-vidyā the stated number of times according to the prescribed method, [one should proceed].
Again, having recited the root-vidyā alone three times,
and having recited the previously mentioned dīpinī-vidyā and the guru-pādukā-vidyā once each,
one should recite the uttīrṇa-vidyā— namely, *ḍa ra la ka sa ha aiṃ ha sa ka la ḍīṃ sa ha ka la ra ḍau namaḥ*— once for me.

With palms joined in reverence, one should recite once the prayer-mantra: "Fulfill all my desires, fulfill them; salutations to you. This should be understood to apply at the end of both sections as well.
Thus, the recitation of the limb-mantras (*aṅgavidyā*) and the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), and so forth, is recommended for the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*).

However, in rites such as the consecration of the *kumbha* (water-pot), only the *Kālanityās* alone should be recited, because it has been stated in that very [text] that they are to be performed "by day, by weekday, by fortnight," and so forth; thus, there is excellence even here when the rite is to be accomplished over many days. But the tradition holds that when the rite is to be accomplished in three or four days, the [Kālanityās] alone are used.
Then, having recited this hymn at the end of the section, the commencement of the second section should be performed,
as it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"By means of the earth, water, fire, ether, sky, sun, moon, eight, six, and the vowels of the ages..."
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, who has become one with Mātṛ and Bhairava. || 1 ||
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, whose form consists of all eight groups of letters beginning with 'ka', who is surrounded by the eight powers.
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, who resides within the thirty-six principles (tattvas), through the thirty-six supreme and non-supreme [manifestations] of the sixteen vowels. (3)

I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, who is established within the thirty-six principles (tattvas), and even within the digits of the moon of Śiva; she who dwells between the letters 'ka' and the end of the principles.
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, who is the supreme soul of all, possessing the various digits of the moon through the manifold limiting conditions of non-duality. 5.
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, who resides within the womb of the six paths and the aggregate, who is the Kuṇḍalinī of the three mandalas, and who transcends the three liṅgas.

I bow to the goddess Tripurabhairavī, who dwells within the heart of the Self-born (Svayambhū), whose eyebrows are like arrows, who stands beyond all else, and who is the consciousness of the West within the East.
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, the supreme power, the sovereign of the universe, whose name and form are the blessings inherent within the syllables, and who is the very action itself. 8.
This hymn should be recited at the end of the section by those who are composed.

Having thus offered praise, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) as before and say: "O Protectress of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us; O Goddess, may success be mine through your grace, for you abide within me."
Thus, having offered the *japa* to the Goddess, one should commence the *japa* of the second group (*varga*). For example: Mūla-di0 ka-ā-ī haṃsaḥ. Thus everywhere: ka-kā-ī; ka-kha-ā-ī;
ka-ga-ā-ī; ka-gha-ā-ī; ka-ṅa-ā-ī; ka-ca-ā-ī; ka-chā-ī; ka-ja-ā-ī; ka-jha-ā-ī; ka-ña-ā-ī; ka-ṭa-ā-ī.

kaṭhā-ī | kaḍā-ī | kaḍhā-ī | kaṇā-ī | katā-ī | kathā-ī | kadā-ī | kadhā-ī | kanā-ī | kapā-ī | kaphā-ī | kabā-ī | kabhā-ī | kamā-ī | kayā-ī | karā-ī | kalā-ī | kavā-ī | kaśā-ī | kaṣā-ī | kasā-ī | kahā-ī | kalā-ī | kakṣā-ī || Thus.
Having recited [the mantra] again— beginning with *kā-ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and ending with *kākṣā-ī haṃsaḥ*— and likewise having recited beginning with *ki-ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and ending with *kikṣā-ī haṃsaḥ*,
and having recited beginning with *kī-ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and ending with *kikṣā-ī*, [one should recite] beginning with *kū-ā-ī haṃsaḥ*.

Having recited up to *kukṣā-ī*, one should again recite from *kū ā-ī haṃsaḥ* up to *kūkṣā-ī*; having recited from *kṛ ā-ī haṃsaḥ* up to *kṛkṣā-ī*; having recited from *kṝ ā-ī haṃsaḥ* up to *kṝkṣā-ī*; and beginning from *kḷ ā-ī haṃsaḥ*...
Having recited up to *kḷkṣā-ī*, one should again begin with *kḷ ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and recite up to *kḹkṣā-ī*; likewise, having begun with *ke ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and recited up to *kekṣā-ī haṃsaḥ*,
one should then begin with *kai-ā-ī haṃsaḥ* and recite up to *kaikṣā-ī haṃsaḥ*.

Having recited from "ko-ā-ī haṃsa" up to "kokṣā-ī," and having recited again from "kau ā-ī haṃsa" up to "kaukṣā-ī," and having recited again from "kaṃ-ā-ī haṃsa" up to "kaṃkṣā-ī," and again from "kaḥ ā-ī haṃsa" up to "kaḥkṣā-ī."
One should recite up to this point. Again, as before: from *kha ā-ī* and so forth, up to *khaḥ kṣā-ī*, [making] 576 [syllables].

From *ga-ā-ī* and so forth, up to *gaḥ-kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *gha-ā-ī* and so forth, up to *ghaḥ-kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *ṅa-ā-ī* and so forth, up to *ṅaḥ-kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *ca-ā-ī* and so forth, up to *caḥ-kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *cha-ā-ī* and so forth, up to *chaḥ-kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *ja-ā-ī*...

From *ī* up to *jaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *jha ā-ī* up to *jhaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *a ā-ī* up to *aḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *ṭa ā-ī* up to *ṭaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *ṭha ā-ī* up to *ṭhaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *ḍa ā-ī* up to... [the end].

From *ḍa ā ī* up to *ḍaḥ kṣā ī*, there are 576 [mantras]. From *ḍha ā ī* up to *ḍhaḥ kṣā ī*, there are 576. From *ṇa ā ī* up to *ṇaḥ kṣā ī*, there are 576. From *ta ā ī* up to *taḥ kṣā ī*, there are 576. From *tha ā ī* up to *thaḥ kṣā ī*, there are 576. From *da ā ī* up to *daḥ kṣā ī*...
From *dha ā-ī* up to *dhaḥ kṣā-ī*, 576; from *na ā-ī* up to *naḥ kṣā-ī*, 576; from *pa ā-ī* up to *paḥ kṣā-ī*, 576;
from *pha ā-ī* up to *phaḥ kṣā-ī*, 576; from *ba ā-ī* up to *baḥ kṣā-ī*, 576.
From *bha ā-ī* up to *bhaḥkṣā-ī*, 576; from *ma ā-ī* up to *maḥkṣā-ī*, 576; from *ya ā-ī* up to *yaḥkṣā-ī*, 576; from *ra ā-ī* up to *raḥkṣā-ī*, 576; from *la ā-ī* up to *laḥkṣā-ī*, 576; *va ā-ī*.
From *ityādi* up to *vaḥ kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations]. From *śa ā-ī* up to *śaḥ kṣā-ī*, there are 576 [combinations].

From *ṣa ā-ī* up to *ṣaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [forms]. From *sa ā-ī* up to *saḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [forms]. From *ha ā-ī* up to *haḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [forms]. From *la ā-ī* up to *laḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [forms]. From *kṣa ā-ī* up to *kṣaḥkṣā-ī*, there are 576 [forms]. Herein...

In the *Pārāyaṇa*, there are five distinct modes of recitation: according to the day, the weekday, the fortnight, the month, and the thirty-six days. It is taught that those whose nature is the eternal Vidyā should perform the recitation for even a single day. (Tantrarāja 25.96) || 1 ||
Longevity, health, sovereignty, victory, and desired objects are obtained in succession by those through whom Lalitā becomes possessed of the tradition. (2)
On a single day, however, for a one-time performance, this is the procedure:
one should begin at midday and conclude at midnight.
And once, during the recitation on the days of the week, on the first day,
Sunday, [one should recite] the first group of Vaśinī and the second of Kāmeśvarī.
Having recited the two groups [of mantras], the wise practitioner should recite one from the Modinī group on each of the six days beginning with Monday. (5)
Furthermore, during the recitation performed once a fortnight on the first lunar day and subsequent days,
one should recite the Vidyās situated in the two rows every single day.
On the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days, respectively,
when they are full, the wise practitioner should recite the vidyās arising from the four rows.
When practiced thus every day for a month, these become perfected;
there is no knowledge in the worlds equal to these.
Therefore, by means of these methods, one should accomplish everything desired;
whatever is one's own desire, that shall become easy to perform, even if it were difficult.
Being steadfast and endowed with devotion, one should accomplish [the goal] through recitation, satiation, fire-offerings, worship, and sprinkling, having repeated the mantra fifty times. || 10 ||
Having recited [this] one hundred times, those possessing the power and majesty of knowledge are liberated from painful shackles and most dreadful enmities with enemies. (11)
Even barren women obtain sons endowed with all virtues by repeating this knowledge one hundred and fifty times with devotion. (12)
They obtain a wife endowed with beauty and other virtues without effort;
likewise, a maiden, after being turned back [in marriage], obtains a husband possessed of all excellent qualities.
They obtain sons, grandsons, and so forth, and they flourish, endowed with prosperity;
by performing these two hundred [revolutions], one is certainly liberated from poverty. 14.
With three hundred [lines], one becomes rich in land and grain; with four hundred, wealthy; with five hundred, a lord of the earth; and with six hundred, a king. (15)
With seven hundred [of them], Ramā does not abandon his lineage;
with eight hundred, all the kings then become her servants.
In this manner, Kandarpa [is invoked] by nine hundred [recitations] among women;
having thus recited nine hundred times, one shall obtain all desires.
"The worship of all of them together is said to grant the accomplishment of all goals.
Regarding these verses, the explanation of the difficult terms is as follows: the two and a half verses beginning with "dinataḥ" are clear. In the case of a single rotation—

The meaning is: when the recitation (*japa*) of the root mantra is performed daily according to the prescribed rule, with a number equal to that of the *Kālanityā-vidyās*—which total twenty-seven hundred and thirty-six—in number; and on the days of the week, from Sunday through Saturday.

The groups of the Seven [Mothers], beginning with Vaśinī, have been previously mentioned; "group," "row," and "womb" are synonyms. "Seka" means consecration (abhiṣeka). "Sthira" means one who possesses unwavering devotion.
The recitation for specific desires (kāmyajapa) has been elaborated upon in the verses beginning with "pañcāśat."

This sequence, pertaining solely to the eternal ignorance (*avidyā*) of time, is to be understood from the Guru and from the scriptures. The method for the arrangement of the *Kālacakra* will be explained further on. In the present context, following the consecration of the water-jars (*kumbha*), in every case, for each of the sixteen jars prepared with the *ṣoḍaśī* [mantra], [the procedure is] performed individually.
Having invoked Lalitā in the center and the fifteen Nityās in the [fifteen] [vessels],

and having worshipped them with the sixteen ancillary offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), one should again approach the central principal vessel, perform the worship of the propitious state (prasannapūjā), present the nocturnal lamp-offering (ārātrikā), and recite the previously mentioned hymn of praise to the Guru beginning with "namaste."
Having recited "O Lord, Blessed One," and so forth, one should recite the twelve verses. They are as follows (*Tantrarāja* 2.88):
[She who] has the form of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs...
I bow to the Goddess, who consists of mantra, the Mother (Mātṛkā), whose form is the sacred seat (pīṭha). || 1 ||
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother, the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings an end to the turbulent agitation of the surging waves of time.
If a man competes with the Sun, Garuḍa, the Moon, Cupid, Śiva, Fire, and Viṣṇu even when only a single syllable has been mastered, [he is a fool]. (3)
I praise the Goddess Mahāśrīsiddhamātṛkā, the Sovereign of All, by whom the three worlds are adorned with the lunar radiance of her syllables. 4.
I bow to that Mother of Siddhis, who threads these three worlds— from the cosmic egg down to its shell— upon the string of the Imperishable Great Sūtra.
That which arises from the three triangles of the seed-syllables of the eleven supports—the universe, from the cosmic egg down to the shell of the world—is visible even today. (6)
She whose syllables consist of the letters beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *na*, *ḍha*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *kṣa*;
she who dwells in the head, the limbs, the arms, the heart, the back, the hips, and the feet.
I bow to that Great Goddess, who is both transcendent and immanent, whose essence is the extraction of the syllable *tām*, and whose form is supreme bliss.
Even today, the gods do not know even slightly her true nature—
what she is, from whence she comes, where she is, by whom she was created, nor her formless state of being.
I bow to that Goddess, whose form consists of imperishable syllables,
who flashes forth from the surging waves of the Kula-stream, and who is born from the supreme *aulija*.
I bow to her, the sovereign of the eight great siddhis arising from the eight groups, in whom the eight measures abide according to the sequence of the classes of consonants.
I bow to the venerable Tripurā, who dwells within the Śrīpīṭha known as Kāmapūrṇaja, and who is the treasury of the four commands (ājñās). 12.
Thus, this hymn consisting of twelve verses brings about all accomplishments;
for it is a hymn to you, the Goddess whose form is indivisible. (13)
Having praised [her] thus, one should recite the *Nityā-kavaca* (as stated in the *Tantrarāja*, chapter 28, verse 52):
"For the sake of liberation from all calamities and for the attainment of all prosperity..."
For the pacification of afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, demons, and the like, and for the attainment of happiness. || 1 ||
For the destruction of all diseases and for victory in battle,
[I offer this] in the midst of fearsome dangers such as thieves, lions, tigers, elephants, gavayas, and the like.
In the forest, in dense mountain thickets, on the road, or likewise during a famine;
when afflicted by water, fire, or wind, or in the perils of ships and the like upon the ocean.
Having recited the Nityā-kavaca once, he crosses over everything;
he lives happily, free from dualities, without rivals, and with his senses conquered. || 4 ||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare to you that ninefold armor (kavaca),
by which even I am always victorious over the gods and asuras in battles.
May Lalitā protect me, her very self, everywhere and at all times;
may Kāmeśī protect me from the front, and Bhagamālā immediately thereafter.
May she protect the [southern] direction, and likewise may Nityaklinnā always protect my right side;
may Bheruṇḍā always protect my direction. || 7 ||
In that same way, Vahnivāsinī shall protect the western quarter,
and Mahāvajreśvarī shall always protect the intermediate direction.
May the messenger Tvaritā always protect my left side;
may she guard the northwestern direction (vātyā), and may Kulasundarī protect me.
May Nityā protect me from above; may Sādho protect me at all times. May Nityā, known as Nīlapatākā, and Vijayā protect me from every side.
May she who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, whose form is garlanded with flames, always bestow blessings upon my body, senses, mind, and vital breaths.
May Citrā protect me incessantly; may she protect my mind at all times from desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and even arrogance.
One should always [protect oneself] from evil, from envy, from grief, from doubt in every respect, from inertia, and from exertion toward unwholesome actions. (13)
May they always protect me from untruth, from cruel thoughts, from violence, and likewise from theft; and may they cause my will to be directed toward auspicious things. (14)
May the sixteen eternal goddesses, mounted upon elephants with their own Śaktis, protect me;
likewise, may those mounted upon horses always protect me from all sides.
May those mounted on lions, as well as those mounted on hyenas, protect me;
and may those mounted on chariots protect me from all sides at all times in battle. || 16 ||
May they, mounted upon Tārkṣya, protect me; likewise may they protect me while moving through the sky.
May they, remaining on the earth, always protect me everywhere and at all times. 17.
May they cause the afflictions of ghosts, spirits, demons, epilepsy, sorcery, and the like to flee from me with their own terrifying weapons, which are manifestations of their powers. 18.
May the countless goddesses Śaktis—who are mounted upon elephants, horses, leopards, lions, and Garuḍas, and who bear all weapons—protect me always from every side. (19)
Chanting daily this all-jeweled armor (*kavaca*) in the evening and the morning, one never sees anything inauspicious, nor does one hear it; such is its power.
Having thus recited the *Nityākavaca* and prayed properly,

one should offer oblations (*bali*) consisting of food, side-dishes, and so forth, along with their respective mantras, to Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, the Kṣetrapālas, Gaṇapati, all spirits (*sarvabhūta*), Kurukullā, and Vārāhī within their respective maṇḍalas.
There, the Guru, together with his disciples, officiating priests, and companions, should spend that night amidst great festivities.
Thus concludes the procedure for the rite of consecration.
The sequence here is as follows: on the first day, having sat upon one's seat in some auspicious place smeared with cow-dung outside the aforementioned pavilion,
one performs the worship of Gaṇeśa, the worship of the Mātṛkās, the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, and the Puṇyāha-vācana.

Having performed the rites ending with the selection of the preceptor and officiating priests according to the previously stated procedure, and having carried out the expulsion of malevolent spirits (*bhūtāpasāraṇa*) within the pavilion, one should fashion a vast and beautiful *śrīcakra* in the center;
then, preceded by the sounding of the five musical instruments, together with the officiating priests and fellow practitioners, [one should enter] into the center.
Having constructed the maṇḍalas prescribed for the guru-maṇḍala and others upon the respective altars (vedikās) all around the enclosure,
and having performed the consecration of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), one should first perform the offering and worship of the Vāstu deity in the Vāstu-maṇḍala,
and then install the deities within the guru-maṇḍala, the Sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala, and other such maṇḍalas.

Having performed worship in the Śrīcakra at the prescribed locations, having established the prescribed jars and also completed the decorations for the jars, one should conclude the ritual up to the installation of the fire in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). Thus ends the duties of the first day.
On the second day, having performed the rites from rising in the morning up to the *nyāsa* on the *yogapīṭha*, and having completed the daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*),
one should again worship the deities of that maṇḍala and invoke the Goddess together with her retinue into the central jar situated within the *śrīcakra*.

Having worshipped with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), one should invoke and worship the sixteen Nityās, beginning with Lalitā, in the other jars as well; then, having completed the ritual actions— including the daily fire-oblation (homa), recitation (japa), and the waving of lights (nīrājana)— within the span of two watches (prahara), one should perform [the remaining rites] from two watches thereafter until midnight.

Having performed the consecration of the water-jars (*kumbha*) with the *Kālanityās*— numbering twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six (20,736)— which are devoid of the root-mantras (*mūlavidyā*), one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) according to the prescribed rite. Thus ends the ritual duties for the second day.

On the third day, having performed the daily rites as before, one should worship the Goddess together with her limbs and retinue in a water-pot under the birth asterism of the disciple, and recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times.
Having recited [the mantra] a hundred times and offered oblations into the fire-pits according to the prescribed rules for the daily *homa*, and having completed the remainder of the worship,

the Guru— preceded by the sounds of various musical instruments such as the horn (*śṛṅga*) and the trumpet (*kāhalā*), and accompanied by the blessings of the Brahmins previously invited— [should proceed] with those who have become the very essence of the deities.

Together with the practitioners of Śakti, the principal officiant himself should lift up the main pitcher and perform the consecration according to the previously mentioned procedure. Thereafter, the Śaktis and the initiates (sāmayikas) should lift up their pitchers and perform the consecration for the disciple who has been adorned with ornaments.

The teacher should explain his own lineage (*svakrama*), beginning with the imperishable (*akṣara*) that arises eternally through the succession of daily rituals. The disciple, for his part, should perform the worship according to the sequence taught by the guru, ensuring that the succession remains uninterrupted from that point forward.
If the succession, as understood through the guru’s command, should be interrupted, the disciple [must receive] the initiation...

One should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For each day that [the practice] was interrupted, one should perform the expiation consisting of sixty recitations for each of the three *sandhyās*, as well as recitations for each *ghaṭikā* and a hundred-fold recitation;
having performed this expiation, one should then resume the sequence of worship from that specific day onward. Then, to the Guru...

Having given away all one's possessions or half of them— according to the manner previously described— along with wealth and other items to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the members of the spiritual community (*sāmayika*), and the poor and helpless, and having ensured their satisfaction through the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), on the fourth day, together with the venerable Guru and the members of the spiritual community in one's own home...

Having performed the great worship (mahāpūjā) and having fed the Brahmins, the poor, the blind, and the wretched, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and so forth; such is the procedure for the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
Now, regarding the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*: if one is unable to elaborate on the previously mentioned construction of the sixteen triangles and so forth,
one should draw out the extensive *śrīcakra* and, as before, place a large jar in the central triangle and other jars in the remaining ninety-six triangles.

Having established the worship of the protective enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) and performed the ritual, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Alternatively, having established and worshipped a jar filled with five *khārī* measures of water at the very location of the drop (*bindu*) situated within the central triangle, one should perform the consecration. In this regard, regarding the procedure for the placement of ninety-six jars (*kalaśasthāpana*):

The worship of each of the deities of the coverings (āvaraṇa-śaktis) for every individual jar, and the worship of the Root Goddess (mūladevī) in the central pitcher—this is the procedure. Herein, the latter alternative pertains to those who are incapable [of performing the full rite].
Thus ends the ritual for the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka). As for the definition of a *khārī*, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
Two *pala*s are considered a *prasṛta*; twice that is a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍava*s make a *prastha*, and four *prastha*s make an *āḍhaka*. (1)
Four of those *āḍhakas* are declared by the wise to be one *droṇa*;
two *droṇas* are a *kumbha*; a *śūrpa* is [the same]; and sixteen *droṇas* are a *khārī*. (2)

Thus. Now, the method for constructing the Kālacakra: first, having placed a dot (*bindu*) somewhere, one draws a circle around it with a measurement of six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Outside of that, drawing circles at intervals of one finger-breadth each inward, there are sixteen circles; together with the first circle drawn, there are seventeen.
Having divided the completed squares by thirty-six lines so as to produce thirty-six paths consisting of sixteen cells each,
one should [place] sixteen [syllables] in those paths, starting from the outermost cell of the path at the front and proceeding in a clockwise direction.

Having written the vowels, one should then, in the second row reached by proceeding clockwise, write the letter *ka* joined with the sixteen vowels starting with *kakā-kikī*, beginning from the outermost square in the same manner;
and in the third row, [one should write the letter *kha*] joined with the sixteen vowels starting with *khakha-khikhī*.
Having written the letter *kha* in the fourth row, one should write the sixteen [vowels] beginning with *ga-gā-gi-gī* and so forth;

having written the sixteen [consonants] beginning with *gha-ghā-ghi-ghī* and so forth in the fifth row; having written the sixteen [consonants] beginning with *ṅa-ṅā-ṅi-ṅī* and so forth in the sixth row; and [having written] the sixteen [consonants] beginning with *ca-cā-ci-cī* and so forth in the seventh row...

Having written sixteen [syllables] in the eighth path, beginning with *cha cha chi chī* and so forth; having written sixteen in the ninth path, beginning with *ja jā ji jī* and so forth; having written sixteen in the tenth path, beginning with *jha jhā jhi jhī* and so forth; and having written sixteen in the eleventh path, beginning with *ña ñā ñi ñī*...
Having written the sixteen [syllables] beginning with *ṭa-ṭā-ṭi-ṭī* in the twelfth path, having written the sixteen [syllables] beginning with *ṭha-ṭhā-ṭhi-ṭhī* in the thirteenth path,
and having written the sixteen [syllables] beginning with *ḍa-ḍā-ḍi-ḍī* in the fourteenth path.
Having written the sixteen syllables beginning with *ḍha-ḍha-ḍhi-ḍhī* in the fifteenth row,

having written the sixteen syllables beginning with *ṇa-ṇa-ṇi-ṇī* in the sixteenth row, having written the sixteen syllables beginning with *ta-ta-ti-tī* in the seventeenth row, [and] in the eighteenth row [the sixteen syllables] beginning with *tha-tha-thi-thī*...

Having written sixteen [syllables] in the nineteenth path, beginning with *da da di* and so forth; having written sixteen in the twentieth path, beginning with *dha dha dhi* and so forth; having written sixteen in the twenty-first path, beginning with *na na ni* and so forth; and having written sixteen in the twenty-second path, beginning with *pa pa pi* and so forth.

Having written sixteen [letters] in the twenty-third path, having written "phaphāphiphī" and so forth, sixteen [letters] in the twenty-fourth path, the *ba*-group in the twenty-fifth path, the *bha*-group in the twenty-sixth path,
the *ma*-group in the twenty-seventh path, the *ya*-group in the twenty-eighth path, and the *ra*-group in the twenty-ninth path.
One should write the *la*-group (30) in a row, the *va*-group (31) in a row, the *śa*-group (32), the *ṣa*-group (33), the *sa*-group (34), the *ha*-group (35) in a row, the *la*-group (36) in a row,
and the *kṣa*-group; thus, in these thirty-six rows, [one writes] five hundred and seventy-six in number.

Having drawn the colors of a full mandala, one should write the four syllables *ā-ī haṃsaḥ* in the pericarp; then, having produced three circles outside the outermost circle and fashioned an eight-petalled lotus with filaments, one should construct a square outside of that. Herein:
By means of the arrangement of the syllables, facing the deity situated in the center, all the syllables should be written in such a way that they are correctly positioned.
Thus is the method for the arrangement of Kālacakra.
There are five hundred and seventy-six varieties of this wheel.
Thus, in the *Tantrarāja* (Paṭala 25, verse 29):
"Now, the yantras shall be described in their prescribed number, in due order."
It is circular, thirty-six-sided, and likewise eighteen-sided.
Twelve-sided, nine-sided, or eight-sided, six-sided, square, or triangular—these are the nine varieties in sequence. (2)
These [mantras] are each eightfold due to the different arrangements of their phonemes;
thus, there are seventy-two varieties among them by virtue of the distinctions of the eternal phonemes (nityārṇa).
Thus, the stated number is proclaimed as eightfold for each;
from the arrangement of the first of these meters, the others should be inferred.
One should draw a single circle by rotating [the compass] six finger-breadths;
in this manner, one should repeat it again and again, increasing outward by one finger-breadth at a time.
When it has become seventeen-fold, one should then divide that by thirty-six spokes; thereafter, one should place the letters within them starting from the beginning.
There are also the forward and reverse orders, the external and internal pairings,
the external and internal reversals, as well as the interspersed order.

Thus: the direct order (*anuloma*), the reverse order (*viloma*), the external enclosure (*bāhyasaṃpuṭa*), the internal enclosure (*ābhyantarasaṃpuṭa*), the external reversal (*bāhyaparāvṛtti*), the internal reversal (*ābhyantaraparāvṛtti*), the external intermingling (*bāhyavyākīrṇa*), and the internal intermingling (*ābhyantaravyākīrṇa*); these are the eight varieties according to the arrangement of syllables.
Regarding the previously mentioned yantras: having written the names of the wind (Marut) and fire (Vahni) everywhere upon the pericarp (karṇikā),
one should join them with those situated in the outer compartments according to the sequence and the method previously described.
The arrangement of petals for others is declared to be thirty-six;
in the eight-sided [figure], there should be sixteen spokes, and the circle of thirty-six is as described before.
Having painted this on a cloth, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus outside;
then, having prepared it, one should inscribe the eight goddesses of speech sequentially upon the petals.
Then, having properly performed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of that [manuscript] as previously described,
one should worship it daily for the sake of attaining the success mentioned in the rules for manuscript worship.
For one who performs both [these duties], Lakṣmī remains firm in his lineage;
never shall there be a loss of fortune in his family.
Having filled a large pitcher with water consisting of decoctions of colored medicinal herbs,
and having invoked the Goddess therein, he should worship her according to the prescribed rites during the night.
Having recited the mantras of the eternal principles (tattvas) on another day while seated upon his seat,
and having worshipped him and established the disciple there, he should consecrate him with devotion.

Thus, it is stated here that the cycles of the principles (*tattva-āvṛtti*)— numbering five hundred and seventy-six— are indeed identical to the number of the Full Mandala, as it has been stated in that very [text].
In this manner, on the full-moon days of birth, subsequent birth, and so forth, the practitioner...
One should fashion a ring of one karṣa of gold, and a cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 15 ||
Thus, the practitioner who has been consecrated for a year without interruption will undoubtedly become either a sovereign lord of the earth or one worthy of being honored by him. || 16 ||
By consecration for two years, the Goddess Ramā shall become firmly established in that house;
by consecration for three years, through spiritual perfection (siddhi), one becomes a Vidyādhara. || 17 ||
Through initiation at four years of age, there shall be union with the Khecarīs;
through initiation at five years of age, one does not undergo death.
By initiation for six years, one becomes equal to a world-protector;
by initiation for seven years, one becomes equal to the sun. || 19 ||
By initiation at eight years of age, one becomes like the moon;
by initiation at nine years of age, one attains the same form as the Goddess.
For the sake of victory, one should properly accomplish the thirty-six or indeed fifty-one vidyās through repetition, fire-oblations, worship, and libations.
Having conquered all enemies by means of that, one prospers like the sun;
likewise in all portents, as well as in afflictions such as disease.
Likewise, for the sake of accomplishing one's desires, for the warding off of magical spells (kṛtyā),
and for the prevention of the arising of such spells, this [mantra] bestows the fulfillment of all aims.
Relying upon this wheel-spoke, the planets, constellations, and so forth proceed;
and the earth is seen as having the form of the arrangement of this wheel-spoke. (24)
Therefore, everything consists of this [Brahman], and by worshipping Him,
all desires are fulfilled through acts of devotion according to the tradition.
Having first performed the sequence appropriate for the time, one should then engage in the other sequences;
this same order applies to recitation, libation, fire-offerings, worship, and ritual bathing.
Having understood this, one should act accordingly; otherwise, it would bring about misfortune.
In the arising of a task, in the defeat of an enemy, and in subjugation, [the application] is contrary [to the usual].
That which is obtained at the proper time is proclaimed to be effective everywhere else;
for subjugation and protection, the two pairs of enclosures (saṃpuṭa) are used in sequence.

When the victory over a royal enemy has been proclaimed, this indeed occurs through the process of reversal; it is also prescribed for the acquisition of cattle, land, gold, vehicles, and so forth. (29)
In rites of eradication, one should employ the scattered [mantras], while for those [same rites] performed for pacification, one should worship according to the sequential order;
gods and demons alike bow down to one who is proficient in this procedure.
In that state, afflictions caused by enemies, such as malevolent spells (kṛtyā) and the like, do not manifest at all;
on the contrary, they turn back and surely destroy the perpetrator himself.
Wherever he dwells, that place is a sacred field, a grove of asceticism;
whether it be a cremation ground, a mountain, a desolate forest, or a place of minor affliction.
When the king of machines is firmly established, that great realm shall become like Amarāvatī,
with its wheel set in place and entirely arrayed.
Furthermore, O Goddess, once [the enemy] has been eradicated, he is not to be protected by me either;
[this should be written] on a stone slab, a copper plate, or one fashioned from silver or gold. (34)
Having drawn it on the ground, one should bury it in villages, kingdoms, cities, and so forth;
having constructed a temple there, one should indeed install the discus within it.
One should place the *vera* (the enemy) in the center of the pericarp for the sake of achieving the presence [of the deity];
likewise, in the protection of a village and so forth, one should place it there in the center and also in the eight directions.
Having dug a pit, one should again firmly compact it with stones;
having invoked and worshipped [the deity], one should establish them within by means of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Having covered it with a stone and made a stable pedestal upon it,
one should worship it daily with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should perform this at the three junctions of the day; otherwise, it does not bestow success.
In all cases, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) prescribed for those specific times are used in the nine types of fire-offerings (homa).

For those who offer oblations, whatever they desire—whether sacrificial fees, clothing, land, ornaments, servants, cattle, or wealth—that very thing, though difficult to achieve, shall become easy to obtain. (40)

And so forth. Here, within the *yuganityās*, there are also *tattvanityās* equal in number to the full mandala; these are likewise situated therein. When this is fully understood, the first syllable of the *vidyā* of the *dinanityā* for that particular day becomes a *yugākṣara* (a syllable of the age), while the second syllable becomes a *tattvākṣara* (a syllable of the principle).
As for the thorough knowledge of the daily mantra (nityā-vidyā) for that specific day,

one should calculate the sum of days (ahargaṇa) since the beginning of the current kalpa according to the method stated in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra); when this is divided by the number of syllables in the full mandala, the remaining syllable is the first syllable of the daily mantra for that day.

(With a division by thirty-six, the second syllable) arises. Thus, the two syllables Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja are produced. The vowel *ī* is to be joined at the end of all *vidyās* in the place of the Śakti-kūṭa.
Thus, when the knowledge of the *vidyā* of that day’s Nityā has been attained.
From the first vowel of the *nityā-vidyā* of that particular day, up to and including that same vowel, [the letters] are joined as syllables in the same manner as before;
thus, 576 *yuga-nityā-vidyās* arise. In this way, from the *nityā-vidyā* of that day...
Taking that which is the second syllable and joining it with the [other] syllables as before, there arise 576 *tattvanityās*. "Tattvanityā" and "dinanityā" are synonyms.
Here, 576 syllables are known as the *vāgbhava*, and 36 syllables are known as the *kāmarāja*.

These are to be understood. As for the sequence of the synonyms of permanence: starting from the day on which the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the venerable teachers took place, when the count of days (*ahargaṇa*) is divided by the number of the full mandala, the first syllable is obtained. In the same way, [when the count of days is divided] by thirty-six...
When divided, the second syllable obtained is the third seed-syllable, *oṃ*.
Thus, the *paryāyanityā-vidyā* consists of three syllables. As before, the first syllable of this [mantra] is a *yuga*-syllable, and its second syllable—
The syllable of reality (*tattvākṣara*) arises. By this, the *yuganityā* and *adinanityā* are obtained. Here, the *kālanityā* vidyās are 20,736; the *yuganityā* are 576; the *tattvanityā* are 576;
the *taddinanityā* vidyās are 576; and the *paryāyanityā* vidyās are 576. Regarding the recitation (*japa*) of the *kālanityā*s:

However, the sequence for the *nātha* [mantras] must be known daily; the sequence for the *nitya* [mantras], however, is 1,296 in number every day. If it is thus, one should understand that the days are accounted for by the *nātha* sequence alone, while the *nitya* sequence accounts for 13 days. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) according to the *Kādimata*.

Now, the occasional worship (*naimittikapūjā*): there, one who has been initiated, who has received the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), who has performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), and who is devoted to the daily worship (*nityārcanā*), should perform the occasional worship.
The procedure for the preparatory rite will be explained further on. (Śrītantrarāja, Chapter 6, Verse 2).
The obligatory, the occasional, and the optional [rites] depend sequentially upon each preceding one;
if one desires to perform them otherwise, one brings about a succession of calamities.
The occasional worship (naimittikārcana) must be performed by the Siddhas who are devoted to the daily worship (nityārcana).
Therefore, I shall describe its procedure, beginning with Caitra and ending with Phālguna.
Thus: the great worship performed on special days is called "special worship" (*viśeṣapūjā*).
The worship to be described from Caitra until Phālguna is, however, "occasional worship" (*naimittikapūjā*).
Some, however, say that special worship is included within the occasional. This—
One should perform the occasional worship (naimittika-pūjā) only at night. As it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:

"One should perform the daily worship during the day and the occasional worship at night; the rites for specific desires (kāmya-karma) pertain to both times—such is the determination of the scripture. (1)
Thus [it is said].
The specific days, however, are those days mentioned in the *Tantrarāja* and other such texts;
they consist of the birth-day, weekday, lunar date (*tithi*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*) of one's Guru, Paramaguru, and Parameṣṭhiguru.

The day of one's own birth, the weekday, lunar date, and asterism; the day of attaining knowledge; the anniversary of the preceptor’s passing; the eighth, fourteenth, full moon, and new moon days; the days of the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti), the beginning of the Yugas, the Puṣya asterism, and Sunday.
The days for visiting sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), the arrival of teachers, the sight of heroes (*vīra*) and great yogins (*mahāyogin*),

journeys to pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), festivals such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, visits to special fields (*viśeṣakṣetra*), the vision of deities, and the days of the conjunction of the three syllables (*akṣaratraya-sampāta*). [The term] *akṣaratraya* [refers to the three syllables].

The "day of conjunction" (*sampātadina*) is that day on which a single syllable is perceived as a syllable of the day, a syllable of the rising, and a syllable of the age (*yuga*); such a day is a special festival (*viśeṣaparvan*). On these days, following the daily worship, one should perform [the rite] according to one's strength, according to one's faith, and at the appropriate time.

According to the location and according to the extent of one's wealth, free from stinginess regarding money, one should perform a special worship with the substances as prescribed and according to the teacher’s instruction, together with those possessing power and the initiates (sāmayika). Then, one should satisfy the teacher and the initiates in accordance with the scriptures. In this regard:

On the days of the Guru’s festivals, having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (sarvopacāra) as many practitioners as there are Gurus in the lineage of the human stream (mānavaugha)— according to the number prescribed for the worship of the Guru-lineage— and having addressed them by their respective names,
one should satisfy them with gifts of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and so forth according to one's capacity. On those festival days...
The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru should also be performed. In the Śrī Tantrarāja (6th Paṭala, verse 4):

"In the month of Caitra, one should perform [the rite] with *damanaka* plants—either with their roots or in clusters—on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, having established them at night with the Vidyā. (3)
On the following day, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform worship with these [mantras];
and on the full moon of this month, the worship for the Spring Festival (Vasantotsava) should be performed.
One should perform a brilliant worship as before, using flowers produced at that time, along with moon-creepers (*candana*), fragrant blossoms (*saugandhika*), and saffron (*kāśmīra*).
Thus it is said. Regarding that, the injunction is as follows: one should worship with *damanaka* flowers on the full moon day of the month of Caitra.

For instance, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the practitioner, having performed his daily obligatory rites, should go to the vicinity of the *damanaka* plant together with other practitioners; then, having invoked the *damanaka* with the root mantra, according to the *Kālīmata*:
Having consecrated the *damana* plant with the previously mentioned four *kalpalatā* vidyās, he addresses the *damana* with: "Oṃ!

Born from the grace of Śiva, be present here! For the sake of Śiva’s work, you are to be uprooted and led away by the command of Śiva. Having thus addressed the *damana*, [he places] Kāmadeva and Rati there.
Having meditated upon the *damana* plant at its root according to the method of that mantra which is about to be described,
and having worshipped it, one should return home. Then, on the fourteenth day, the practitioner, having performed his daily rites,
should go again to the vicinity of the *damana* plant together with other practitioners and [protect] the *damana* with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

Having uprooted the clusters along with their roots using a weapon, and having thrown them into the house and brought them inside, one should sprinkle the *damana* plant at the place of worship with the mantra: "O Aghora, Aiṃ Oṃ! O Ghora, Hrīṃ! O most terrible one, Śrīṃ! Salutations to you, O forms of Rudra, from all sides, to all the Śarvas! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ!"

In a certain vessel, having divided the *damana* [grass] into nine parts and placed them in the center and in the eight directions, one should sprinkle the *damana* with water while reciting the *hṛnmantra*. Then, having smeared the place of worship with a paste of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other substances, one should recite: *haṃ namaḥ*, *saṃ namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the *damana* grass— divided into nine parts with the mantras *kṣaṃ namaḥ*, *maṃ namaḥ*, *laṃ namaḥ*, *vaṃ namaḥ*, *raṃ namaḥ*, *yaṃ namaḥ*, and *oṃ namaḥ*— starting from the center and proceeding clockwise, and having protected it with the *astra-mantra*, one should form the *triśūla-mudrā* with both hands.

One should cause the *damanaka* flower to revolve over [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*kavacamantra*). Then, having covered it with a new cloth, one should place the *damanaka* in a secluded spot;

thus one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the night of the fourteenth day. Thereafter, on the morning of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), having completed the daily obligatory rites such as the ritual bath and worship, together with the initiates (*sāmayika*s)...
Having brought the *damana* plant to the place of worship preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*),

if the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) was performed on the previous day, one should address the *damana* according to the prescribed rite at evening on the fourteenth day; then, having brought the *damana* on the full moon day— or alternatively—
On the full moon day itself, having invited and brought Damana, and having performed the immediate consecration (*adhivāsana*) according to the prescribed rite,

one should draw before it a nine-petaled lotus diagram (*navayonicakra*) surrounded by two squares using vermilion; then, within its nine petals, [one should place] nine jars made of gold or other materials.

Upon a heap of barley, having placed one *kumbha* (water-pot) in the central womb according to the procedure to be described in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*), and having performed the rites from the worship of one's own seat (*svāsana*) up to the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*),
whether elaborately or in brief; and if it is a five-deity (*pañcāyatana*) rite, [one should worship] Gaṇeśa and the others with *damana* flowers.
Having performed worship, one should construct the previously described *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala on one's right side;
or, if unable to do that, having made an eight-petalled lotus with vermilion or other pigments,
one should worship an *aśoka* tree in its center using powders of five colors.

Below that, having meditated upon the youthful Kāmadeva within a triangular maṇḍala— red in color, adorned with red garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents, graced on his left and right by Rati and Prīti, holding flower-arrows and a bow of sugarcane, and accompanied by Vasanta— [recite] *klīṃ*.

Having worshipped Kāmadeva with the mantra "Kāmāya namaḥ" using the five offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha), one should meditate on Rati at his left side— fair-complexioned, adorned with all ornaments,
dressed in red garments, and holding a lotus in her hand— and [worship her] with "4 Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Kroṃ Ratyai."

Having worshipped Rati with the mantra "Namaḥ" and the five types of offerings, one should meditate on Prīti to the right of Kāma— she is dark-complexioned, adorned with all ornaments, dressed in red garments, and holding betel in her hand— (four times).

Having worshipped Prīti with the mantra *śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ kṣauṃ prītyai namaḥ* using the five articles of worship (*pañcopacāra*), one should then [visualize] Kāmadeva dwelling in the midst of a *kadamba* forest before him— fair-complexioned, holding a jar of nectar in his left hand and [a bow in his] right hand.
Having visualized [him] bearing a collection of various flowers, adorned with red garments and ornaments,
and with red garlands and unguents, one should worship Vāsanta with the five offerings using the mantra "Vaṃ, obeisance to Vāsanta," and then [worship] Kāmadeva in the center.

Having worshipped with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)— beginning with "Oṃ *klāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*"— upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus in the four directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu. Then, on the eight petals,
proceeding clockwise starting from the front, one worships with "Oṃ to Kāma, *namaḥ*."

Oṃ, homage to the one whose body is ash. Oṃ, homage to the bodiless one. Oṃ, homage to the one who agitates the mind. Oṃ, homage to the friend of spring. Oṃ, homage to the one who remembers. Oṃ, homage to the bearer of the sugarcane bow.

Oṃ, salutation to Puṣpabāṇa. Having thus worshipped the eight Kāmas, one should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons on the outer square. Again, having worshipped Kāmadeva with his mantra and offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should prostrate and [recite]: Oṃ, we know Kāmadeva...

"Let us meditate upon the one with flower-arrows; may that Anaṅga inspire us. Having thus recited the Kāma-gāyatrī as much as possible and offered it, one should prostrate to Kāmadeva, saying: "Salutations to the one with flower-arrows, the cause of joy for the world, to Manmatha, the conqueror of the world, and the beloved of Rati and Prīti. Thus, having bowed to Kāmadeva.

Having performed the placement of the seers and so forth, as well as the six-limbed nyāsa, with the root-vidyā; having invoked the Goddess into the central jar as before and worshipped her with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra); and having worshipped, according to the previously stated sequence, the deities beginning with the Tithinityā and ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla) using *damana* flowers; [one should say: "You have been invoked."

"O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, everything that was previously to be performed by me at the proper time must now be done immediately at this very moment by your command. Having thus informed the Goddess, and having worshipped her again with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having presented incense, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth as before, [he performs] the occasional fire-sacrifice (naimittika-homa).
Having performed the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) according to the prescribed rules, having offered the royal services (*rājopacāra*), the great waving of lights (*mahādīpārārtika*),

and having conducted the worship of the virgins (*kumārī*), the married women (*suvāsinī*), the *vaṭuka*s, and others, and having satisfied everyone with food, clothing, ornaments, ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), betel, and so forth, [he should also satisfy] his own guru.

Having thus satisfied [the preceptor], or in his absence, having satisfied another person of that same lineage, one should recite the root-mantra three times its usual number through constant recitation; then, having offered the recitation to the Goddess, praised her, and prostrated, [one should pray]:
"O Mother of the World, O bestower of the fruits of desired objects, fulfill my desires, O Goddess! regarding the sixteen-syllable mantra.

"O Goddess, Sovereign of the Lord of Desire! Having thus prayed to the Goddess, one should again worship Kāmadeva with *damanaka* flowers using his mantra, and worship Rati, Prīti, and Vasanta with *damanaka* flowers;
then, having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should bid farewell to Kāmadeva and Vasanta.

Taking a handful of flowers, [he says]: "O Sovereign of all the circles, embodiment of all vidyās, O Goddess, my Mother! By your command, may this desired object of mine be fulfilled. Having thus offered the handful of flowers and performed the dismissal (*visarjana*), he completes everything, including the removal of the *śrīpātra* vessel, and [dismisses] the other Śaktis and initiates (*sāmayikas*).

One should also satisfy the Brahmins with abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), food, and other offerings. Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of *damanaka*. If this worship of *damanaka* cannot be performed on the full moon day of Caitra, then it should be performed on any one of the following lunar days within either fortnight: the eighth, the ninth, or the fourteenth.

If it does not occur in the month of Caitra, then one should perform it on any one of the aforementioned lunar days in the months of Vaiśākha or Jyeṣṭha. Alternatively, if it occurs only on the full moon day in the month of Caitra, [one should use] those materials available at that time.

One should perform the Vasantotsava worship with sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and white water-lilies (*kahlāra*). For this occasional (*naimittika*) worship as well, one should place the articles of worship in a vessel somewhere on the previous day at night,
sprinkle them with the root-vidyā, and [proceed] with the root-mantra and the daily Nityā-mantra.

Having worshipped with offerings of fragrance and so forth, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), on the following day, after completing the daily rites, one should perform special worship with those [offerings] and also worship one's own guru; thus should the preliminary consecration and the worship be understood. Likewise:
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship with cool lotuses,
or else with camphor, musk, sandalwood, and cool water.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform a special worship preceded by the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), using either snow-water or cool water mixed with camphor, musk, and sandalwood, according to the previous procedure. Likewise:
And on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Goddess with fruits produced from plantain, jackfruit, and mango trees, as before, for the attainment of all perfections.

Thus it is said. Therein, on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having performed a special worship and having gratified the Goddess with great offerings of plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes, one should perform the worship of the Guru and the others. Likewise:
