On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Śivā with sandalwood mixed with saffron, along with cardamom, kakkola, and jasmine.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is quite clear. Likewise:
"In the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the full moon day, one should worship Śivā with sacred threads (pavitra).
O auspicious lady, listen to this procedure for it, which bestows good fortune. (9)
With threads made of gold or silver, or those produced from silk, or auspicious red cotton threads, [the cord] should be multiplied ninefold. || 10 ||
One should prepare a purifying thread (pavitra) for all the Śaktis, measuring sixteen finger-breadths or nine finger-breadths, and provided with that same number of knots and other [ornaments].
Alternatively, having determined the respective measurements in finger-breadths and so forth for the powers of the enclosures (āvṛti-śaktis),
one should worship them in their proper sequence, preceded by the preliminary rite of consecration (adhivāsa).
At home, the pavitraka should consist of a single-strand knot;
that which brings down the power (śaktyavatāraka) should be made with one hundred and eight threads.
One should suspend [the canopy] from the ceiling according to the measurement of the worship seat,
as one does for the primary Śakti, so too for the Śaktis such as Vārāhī and Kurukullā.
One should prepare the purifier according to one's own measurement and the prescribed number;
for disciples who know the sequence of the tradition, it is declared to be equal to one's own body.
For other powers of the Yoginīs, there are nine [lines] starting from a single knot;
according to the measurement of the circumference, they are drawn with a single thread around the pavilion.
Having fashioned three sacred threads (*pavitra*) consisting of ninety-six finger-joints, including the knots, he should offer them to the Goddess. (17)
Among the three stated measures, one should accept whichever is available from any source;
however, one should not create a confusion of measures, for if one does so, it leads to ruin.

Thus [ends the citation]. Its meaning is as follows: therein, one should perform the rite of *pavitrāropaṇa* on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. Here, "the month of Śrāvaṇa" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). The time for the *pavitrotsava* begins from the sun’s entry into Gemini (*mithuna-saṃkramaṇa*) and extends until its entry into Libra (*tulā-saṃkramaṇa*). As for the lunar days (*tithi*), they apply to both fortnights.

The fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, and the full moon day— these are the [preferred] times, while those following are secondary times. As for the sacred threads (*pavitra*), they may be made of gold, silver, copper, silk cloth, silk thread, lotus fiber, *darbha* grass, or *śāṇa* (hemp) thread.
One should prepare the thread from one of these: bark-fiber, cotton, or [other] threads.

Having tripled the cotton thread spun by married women, and having formed it into a single strand of nine threads, one should fashion the *pavitra* [sacrificial rings] using the aforementioned number of threads. In that regard:
One should make the purifiers sixteen finger-breadths in length, provided with sixteen knots by means of sixteen threads;

or nine finger-breadths in length, provided with nine knots of the [nine] rasas; or, in whichever enclosure there are as many Śaktis, one should make the purifiers provided with that same number of finger-breadths and knots.

One should perform [the rite]. In that regard, according to the view that the number of fingers for the covering power (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) is sixteen and so forth, one should prepare the purifiers (*pavitra*) for the root goddess with a length of sixteen fingers and so forth, for the fifteen Nityās with a length of fifteen fingers and so forth, and for Vārāhī and Kurukullā likewise, as for the root goddess.

One should prepare the *pavitra* (sacred threads) for the weapons with a length of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and knots, according to the number of fingers prescribed for each respective Guru in the three lineages of Gurus, or starting from nine finger-breadths. In this manner, there should be as many *pavitra* as there are deities in the assembly to be worshipped in the *Śrīcakra*.

Having prepared one large *pavitra* according to any one of the aforementioned positions— provided with one hundred and eight knots and measuring the length of the sacrificial seat (*pūjāviṣṭara*) from the canopy— for himself and for his disciples who know the lineage of the tradition;

One should prepare a *pavitra*— free from knots— that follows the length from the shoulders (*skandha*) to the navel (*nābhi*), possesses knots according to the number of deities accepted by the practitioner, and is provided with nine knots for other general yogic powers; its measurement should be equal to the circumference of the pavilion when wrapped with a single thread.

In this regard, according to the view that the number of finger-breadths corresponds to the number of obscuring powers (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), knots should be made on the purifying threads (*pavitra*) for oneself and for disciples who know the traditional lineage, just as for the Root Goddess;
these knots should be made with either the *mālā-mantra* or the *kavaca-mantra*. Regarding the knots:

The number of thread-wrappings may be according to one's desire. Having thus prepared the purifiers (*pavitra*), on the day before the day of the offering of the purifiers (*pavitrāropaṇa*), the practitioner, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), should bring the purifiers to the place of worship at night together with the initiates (*sāmayika*). Then, in the place of the purifiers...
Having fashioned a nine-yoni wheel (navayonicakra) surrounded by squares and circles using vermilion and other pigments,
one should place within that mandala on some vessel the sacred objects smeared with a paste of gorocana, saffron, red sandalwood, musk, and camphor.

Having placed [the images] decorated at their joints with lac, red ochre, and other pigments, and having established the *pavitra* (sacred threads) fashioned from cotton thread—upon these nine threads [one recites]: *oṃkārāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ candramase namaḥ*; *oṃ vahnaye namaḥ*; *oṃ nāgāya namaḥ*; *oṃ brahmaṇe*.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Ravi; Oṃ, homage to Guru; Oṃ, homage to Sadāśiva;
Oṃ, homage to all the gods. Having thus worshipped one deity for each thread, having consecrated it with the Śiras-mantra, sprinkled it with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and secured it with the Astra-mantra—

Having worshipped the root-vidyā with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) within the *pavitra* vessels, and having worshipped the sixteen *Nityās*, one should place fragrant *kuṅkuma* into them, and then deposit the five jewels and all medicinal herbs. As for the jewels, they are diamond, pearl, sapphire, [ruby, and emerald].

The [gems] known as ruby and emerald; the mustard seed, *kuṣṭha*, turmeric, *dāru*, *lodhra*, *musta*, *uśīra*, *priyaṅgu*, *mura*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and the one called *śilī*—these are all the medicinal herbs.
Then, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) by covering [the image] with a pair of new cloths, one should proceed.

On the following day, the practitioner, having performed his daily obligatory rites, enters the place of worship together with the initiates; having adorned the sacrificial pavilion with canopies and other ornaments,
[he prepares] from above the canopy down to the sacrificial seat.
Having donned the extremely purifying thread called the Śaktyavatāra,

having performed the entire series of ritual placements (nyāsa) beginning with the worship of the seat (āsana-pūjā), and having performed the installation of the water jar (kumbha-sthāpana) as before,
one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) at the conclusion of the self-worship (ātma-pūjā) beginning with the installation of the arghya vessel.

If it is the five-āyatana [rite], one should worship the deities of the five āyatanas, honor them with purificatory offerings (pavitra), invoke the Goddess into that jar, and worship her with all ritual services (upacāra). Then, according to the sequence of daily worship, one should honor the mass of rays with purificatory offerings, perform the ancillary oblation (aṅgahoma), and the occasional rite (naimittika).

Having gratified the Guru and offered him the sacred thread (*pavitra*), having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and made the offering of the sacred thread to the fire, and having himself donned the sacred thread with the Guru’s permission,
[he should likewise honor] the Śaktis and the initiates (*sāmayikas*) as in the worship of *damanaka*.

Having satisfied [the officiants] by the offering of purifiers (*pavitra*) and so forth, as well as by the giving of food, betel, and ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as an occasional rite (*naimittika*), one should dismiss the Goddess and satisfy the Brahmins and others with meals and abundant ritual fees. If one is unable to perform this much:

Having prepared three *pavitra*s, each ninety-six finger-breadths long and provided with knots on the left side, one should perform the ritual as before, beginning with the installation of the *kumbha* vessel; having offered them to the Goddess, one should complete the remainder of the rite.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the *pavitra*. However, in the *Kālīmata*, according to the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
Āṣāḍha is the best month, Śrāvaṇa is middling, O dear one, and Bhādrapada is inferior; [these apply to] both fortnights, the bright and the dark.
First, one should perform it during the bright fortnight; if that is not possible, during the other (the dark fortnight). One should indeed worship on the fourteenth, eighth, and full-moon days.
Thus, in the *Tantrarāja* (Chapter 6,
Verse 20): "Now, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the full moon day, one should worship the Goddess with flowers produced from the *ketakī*, in accordance with the previously mentioned procedure."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is: on the full moon day of Bhādrapada, one should perform a special worship (viśeṣapūjā) with *ketakī* flowers, having first performed the consecration (*sādhivāsa*). Likewise—

In the month of Āśvayuja, however, there is a special rule: beginning from the first day (pratipad) following the new moon (darśānta), one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and offerings.
When the [count] reaches one hundred and increases by that amount until it is full,
one should daily offer one thousand oblations and likewise perform the recitation.
Having invoked the Goddess into a young girl and worshipped her with devotion,
and having offered oblations along with ornaments, garments, and other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should cause her to depart.
In this manner, O Dear One, one should worship up to the full [moon] by increasing the count starting from one;
by that, one becomes pierced through and attains perfection, making even a king a worshiper.

Thus: here, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) in the month of Āśvayuja until the full moon (pūrṇimā), one should worship the Cakra-maṇḍala daily as an occasional rite (naimittika) following the obligatory worship (nitya-pūjā) during the fifteen lunar days (tithis). Starting from the first lunar day, with an increase of one [deity] per day, on the first day...
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) for two hundred on the second lunar day, three hundred on the third, four hundred on the fourth, and so forth,

one should recite sixteen hundred on the full moon day and perform sixteen hundred oblations. On the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*), starting from one and increasing accordingly, there should be sixteen maidens on the full moon day.

One should perform the worship of the maiden (kanyāpūjana) exactly as it is prescribed. Then, having invited the maiden every morning, at the conclusion of the worship, recitation, and fire-offering (homa), one should seat her— who has bathed well and is fully adorned—
upon a soft seat in the place of worship, and [proceed] with her...

Having invoked the Goddess according to the previously mentioned procedure and worshipped her, one should satisfy her with offerings of clothing, ornaments, food, betel, and monetary gifts (dakṣiṇā), and after bowing, bid her farewell. In the same manner, even when worshipping many maidens, one should perform the worship for each individually. In this very [context]...

Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) of the month until the ninth day, one should perform special worship during these nine nights and carry out recitations (japa) and other rites with an increasing number starting from one; likewise, one should perform the worship of young maidens (kumārī-pūjana) with an increasing number starting from one. In this regard, there is a specific rule for the worship during the nine nights (navarātra).

Having performed the worship on the first day, one who is one year old [is worshipped]; on the second, one who is two years old; and so on, until on the ninth day, a girl of nine years is to be worshipped. Furthermore, on that lunar day (tithi), one should worship the nine maidens—ranging from one year old to nine years old—in such a way that those who were worshipped on the preceding days are included among the nine maidens on the ninth day.
Their names are as follows: on the first day, Śuddhā; on the second, Bālā; on the third, Lalitā; on the fourth, Mālinī; on the fifth, Vasundharā;
on the sixth, Sarasvatī; on the seventh, Ramā; on the eighth, Gaurī; and on the ninth, Durgā.
The mantras are as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śuddhāyai namaḥ*; *bālāyai namaḥ*;
*lalitāyai namaḥ*, and so forth; one should worship with these name-mantras (*nāmamantra*). In this regard:
"One should avoid for the purpose of worship any girl who is only one year old."
She finds no pleasure in perfumes, flowers, fruits, and the like. || 1 ||
Therefore, the most excellent of practitioners should worship maidens from the age of two up to ten years old, according to the procedure previously described. || 2 ||

Thus, according to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa, one should worship girls beginning from those two years old up to ten years of age. Alternatively, during the Navarātra festivals, one may worship married women (*suvāsinī*) who possess fresh youth and the aforementioned characteristics. Of these [women]...

The names, however, are: Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, Mahocchuṣmā, Karālikā, Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Durgā. Here too, the mantras end with the three *tārās* (oṃ āḥ hūṃ), such as "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, obeisance to Hṛllekhā," and so forth.
Now, the characteristics of the kumāris who are worthy of worship and those who are not. First, the characteristics of those worthy of worship, as stated in the *Śrīkulārṇava*:
"One who is healthy, with well-nourished limbs, beautiful in form, and free from sores..."
One should properly honor a maiden born of the same lineage. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the characteristics of girls who are not to be worshipped, in that same [text]:
"One who has deficient or extra limbs, one who is wicked, one born of a family lacking good conduct, one whose limbs are knotted, cracked, or withered, and one marked by wounds of blood and pus. (2)
One should avoid a maiden who is blind from birth, squinting, one-eyed, deformed, or has excessive body hair;
likewise, one should reject a girl who is diseased or born of a slave woman's womb.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, regarding specific types of worshipable maidens for specific results, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "In all undertakings, one should worship a Brāhmaṇa girl; for the sake of victory, one born of a royal lineage; for the sake of gain, one born of a Vaiśya lineage; and for the sake of a son, one born of a Śūdra lineage. (1)
"And in the terrible [rite], a man should worship one of the lowest castes according to the prescribed rule.
Now, regarding the characteristics of the *suvāsinī* (married woman) worthy of worship, it is stated in the *Śrīkulārṇava*: "One who is beautiful, youthful, peaceful, compliant, joyful, and pure..."
Free from doubt, endowed with devotion, and useful for the profound scriptures. || 1 ||
Free from greed, virtuous, with a smiling face, speaking kindly, deeply devoted to her gurus, deities, and the virtuous, pure-minded, and beloved by those of the Kaula lineage. || 2 ||
Free from envy, possessing specialized knowledge, and eager to propitiate the deities;
she was fully engaged with mantra and tantra, and a protector of the conduct prescribed by the samaya.
"Manoharā, of virtuous conduct, this Śakti is endowed with auspicious marks.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the characteristics of the venerable married woman (*suvāsinī*), it is stated in that same source:
She is wicked, fierce, harsh, stubborn, contemptible, and a defiler of her family;
she is of evil conduct, dependent on others, devoid of affection, and indolent.
One who is addicted to sleep, extremely dull-witted, deficient in limbs, afflicted by disease, foul-smelling, miserable, foolish, aged, insane, or a betrayer of secrets. (2)
Engaged in fallacious reasoning and base chatter, shameless and fond of quarreling, she was deformed, treading a wrong path, wrathful, crippled, blind, and possessed of a distorted face. (3)
"One should avoid such a power associated with mantras in the sacrifice.
Thus [it is said]. This worship of the Nine Nights (Navarātra-pūjā) takes place during the twelve months beginning with Caitra and ending with Phālguna;
or within the four months of Caitra, Āṣāḍha, Āśvina, and Pauṣa; or else in either of the two months of Caitra or Āśvina.

Or, during the bright fortnights, it should be performed according to one's means and with full elaboration. Even there, if one is unable to perform the nine-night rite (*navarātra*), it may be performed for seven nights starting from the third day up to the ninth,
or for five nights starting from the fifth, or for three nights starting from the seventh, on the aforementioned lunar days.

One should perform the Navarātra festival with the worship of the Kumārīs and other rites. In this way, there are many other specific occasional (naimittika) forms of worship as well; these, however, are to be learned from the Guru and the scriptures. (Śrī Tantrarāja, 6th Paṭala, verse 25).
On the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, one should worship with saffron;
at night, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with lamps fueled by clarified butter.
One should place sixteen lamps before the Goddess in sequence with the Vidyā-mantra;
one should place one lamp for each of the Śaktis in front of them respectively.
Alternatively, having placed one [flower] in the center of the vessel and nine around it,
he should offer them along with flowers while reciting the root mantra.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: there, on the full moon day of Kārttika, having worshipped the Goddess with saffron, one should perform the installation of the fire in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), or elsewhere at night, using offerings made of flour, filled with ghee, and illuminated by camphor wicks.

Having offered oblations according to the sequence of the perpetual fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*) with lamps, one should also perform the offering of lamps to the Goddess together with her limbs (*sāṅgā*) and her retinue (*sāvaraṇā*). Therein, having fashioned a vast *śrīcakra* on a level surface with vermilion (*sindūra*) and other substances, and having invoked and worshipped the Goddess there, [one should worship] in the center, within the *binducakra*.
Having prepared sixteen lamps made from flour of barley, wheat, and other grains mixed with sugar and milk,
containing camphor within their wicks and filled with ghee, and having lit them, one should place them before the Root Goddess while reciting the Root Vidyā and then offer them.

One should place each [offering] individually before each of the deities to be worshipped in the Śrīcakra— beginning with Nityā— in their respective places of worship, using their respective mantras, and then offer them. If one is unable to perform this much,
one should [draw] a nine-yoni cakra or an eight-petaled lotus with saffron and other substances in a single vessel made of gold or similar material.

The meaning is that, having fashioned nine lamps of the form described therein and having placed them upon the eight petals—the [eight] sources—or in the center, one should worship the Goddess, release [the offering], and then present it. Likewise:
"And on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, [an offering] joined with coconut water and the moon..."
Having offered [the oblation], one should worship with cakes made of mung-bean flour according to the prescribed rite.

Thus: On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, having prepared the arghya-vessel with coconut water mixed with camphor, and having worshipped it with fragrant flowers and other offerings, one should present as the food offering (naivedya) apūpas made from mung bean flour. Furthermore:
And on the full moon day of the month of Puṣya,
for the sake of attaining one's desired goals, one should worship with sugar or jaggery and offer cow’s milk as an oblation.

Thus: On the full moon day of Pauṣa, having worshipped with sugar—or in its absence, with jaggery—one should offer cow's milk for the attainment of one's desires. Likewise, on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, [one should worship] with sesame seeds, sour gruel, and other such offerings.
One should always worship with offerings of milk, white cakes, and the like.

Thus: there, on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, having worshipped the Goddess together with her retinue using white or black sesame seeds, one should present an offering of sugar, milk, cakes, and so forth.
Likewise:

On the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship with golden and silver lotuses, as well as with mango blossoms, saugandhika, and madhuka flowers, for the attainment of one's desires.

Thus it is said. Therein, on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Goddess with lotuses and flowers of gold and silver. Likewise: "Worship is to be performed during the equinoxes, the solstices, the new moon days, and the beginnings of the Yugas."
One should indeed perform special meritorious acts even among those prescribed in the scriptures.
Thus concludes the occasional worship (naimittikapūjā).

Now, regarding the ritual for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) according to the *Kālīmata*, one should construct the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedikā*), and so forth, as previously described. Here, however, there is a specific distinction:
having constructed a pavilion measuring twenty-seven cubits, one should fashion sacrificial pits in the eight directions.
Having constructed an altar measuring nine cubits in the center, and having fashioned the Śrīcakra upon that altar,

and having performed all the rites such as the installation of the pitcher (kalaśa) and so forth as previously described, the Guru, having performed the rituals from the morning duties up to the Nyāsa on the pedestal (pīṭha-nyāsa), should perform the Mahāśakti-nyāsa. In that regard:
First, having meditated on the world as being empty in form and without support, [one should recite] "HŪṂ, homage to Earth" and [visualize] the earth beneath one's seat.

Having performed worship, touching one's own seat with the left hand and having recited the *bīja* of Bhuvaneśvarī seven times, [one should offer salutations]: 4 *Oṃ jayāyai namaḥ* | 4 *Oṃ vijayāyai namaḥ* | 4 *Oṃ jayantyai namaḥ* | 4 *Oṃ ajitāyai namaḥ* | 4 *Oṃ aparājitāyai namaḥ* | 4 *Oṃ saṅgamāyai* |
Salutation. 4. With "Oṃ, salutation to Rambhā," one should worship the seven Śaktis on one's own seat.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, of this Great Śakti Nyāsa, Paraśiva is the Seer (ṛṣi), Atijagatī is the meter (chandas), the venerable Parāśakti is the Deity (devatā), Aiṃ is the Seed-syllable (bīja), and Śrīṃ is the Power (śakti)."
*Sauḥ* is the *kīlaka*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the *mahāśaktinyāsa* as a limb of the *Śrīvidyā*.
Having performed the assignment of the *ṛṣi* and other elements, and having performed the *kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* of the three *tāra*s by repeating them twice, one should perform the *nyāsa*:
therein, at the *yoni*, *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ*; at the navel, [the same] four.

*Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ namaḥ*. *Klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ namaḥ* on the tips of the hands. *Hrāṃ hrīṃ hlūṃ namaḥ* in the heart. *Sāṃ sīṃ sūṃ namaḥ* on the forehead. *Hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ namaḥ* on the ears. *Drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ namaḥ* at the base of the arms.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "4 sauḥ śrīṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ" at the tip of the bindu (the palate), and "4 aiṃ āṃ sauḥ aṃ namaḥ" at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should contemplate the letter *a*, which is the root of all letters from *a* to *kṣa*,
as being in a subtle form like clarified butter within milk.

Visualizing it as established, one should place those [syllables] consisting of that [essence] and no other color in the locations to be described: there, on the palate, *4 aiṃ īṃ sauḥ āṃ namaḥ*; at the tip of the nose, *4 iṃ namaḥ*;
on the perineum (*paścimaliṅga*) or on the light-liṅga located in the *mūlādhāra*, *4 īṃ namaḥ*.

In the anus: 4 | 3 uṃ namaḥ | In the back: 4 | 3 ūṃ namaḥ | At the joint of the waist: 4 | 3 ṛṃ namaḥ | At the end of the testicles: oṃ 3 | 3 ṝṃ namaḥ | In the middle of the back: oṃ 3 | 3 ḷṃ namaḥ | At the location of the uvula: 4 | 3 ḹṃ namaḥ | In all limbs: oṃ 3 | 3 eṃ namaḥ |
Furthermore, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation upon the three-lined *yoni* encircled by the *bindu*, reciting "Oṃ 3 | 3 Aiṃ Namaḥ" over all the limbs,
this power (*śakti*) which pierces the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is called the *yoni*.
One should dissolve the ointment upon the body; this is remembered as the *repha* and the *bindu*. || 1 ||
The Great Power (Mahāśakti), pervading the cage-like structure of the seventy-two thousand channels, flows during the menstrual cycle of women.
The blood that has entered the network of channels (nāḍīcakra) is discharged through the path of the womb;
it becomes the menstrual flow (puṣpa) when the female organ (bhaga) has blossomed, occurring in succession during the months, fortnights, and so forth.
The syllable Aiṃ itself is the Yoni; no deliberation is required here.
O Goddess of the gods, the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, are established within it.

Contemplating the meaning of this collection of verses up to that point, one should meditate on dissolution into the Great Kāmakalā situated at the *brahmarandhra*. Then, recite: *oṃ 3 | 3 oṃ namaḥ* at the *brahmarandhra*;
*oṃ 3 | 3 oṃ namaḥ* in the midst of the *nāda*; *oṃ 3 | 3 aṃ namaḥ* at the end of the *nāda*; and *oṃ 3 | 3* at the throat.

Aḥ, salutation! Oṃ thrice, three times, salutation to the heart. Likewise, Khaṃ, salutation to the head; Gaṃ, salutation to the two shanks; Ghaṃ, salutation to the two breasts; Ṅaṃ, salutation to the tip of the nose; Caṃ, salutation to the *ājñā* [cakra]; Chaṃ, salutation to the left side of the abdomen; Jaṃ, salutation to the right side of the abdomen.

*Namaḥ*. *Jhaṃ namaḥ* at the roots of the thighs. *Ñaṃ namaḥ* at the rows of teeth. *Ṭaṃ namaḥ* on the tip of the tongue. *Ṭhaṃ namaḥ* on the mouth. *Ḍaṃ namaḥ* on the armpits. *Ḍhaṃ namaḥ* on the joints of the bones. *Ṇaṃ namaḥ* in the mind. *Taṃ namaḥ* on the navel. [And] *Naṃ namaḥ* on the forehead.

*Thaṃ* namaḥ; to the two ear canals, *daṃ* namaḥ; to the two cheeks, *dhaṃ* namaḥ; to the two eyes, *naṃ* namaḥ; to the white thousand-petaled lotus, *paṃ* namaḥ; to the heart-lotus, *phaṃ* namaḥ; to the two shoulders, *vaṃ* namaḥ; to the middle of the eyebrows, *bhaṃ* namaḥ.

*Namaḥ* to *maṃ* at the root of the throat; *namaḥ* to *yaṃ* at the root of the palate; *namaḥ* to *raṃ* between the genitals and the anus; *namaḥ* to *laṃ* on the tongue; *namaḥ* to *vaṃ* on all limbs;
and *namaḥ* to *śaṃ* as a wrap from the left foot up to the right head.
At the root of the palate: *ṣaṃ* namaḥ. On all limbs: *saṃ* namaḥ. In the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*): *haṃ* namaḥ.
On all fingers and toes of the hands and feet: *kṣaṃ* namaḥ.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with *oṃ* three times, three times upon the Kuṇḍalinī situated in the previously mentioned Mūlādhāra, [one recites] *oṃ* three times, three times.
Uttering the entire Mātṛkā, one leads that Kuṇḍalinī through the path of the Suṣumṇā by means of the sequence of piercing the six cakras, and having brought her to the Brahmarandhra,
[one unites her] with Śiva, the Supreme Self, who resides there in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled A-kula lotus.

Having contemplated her as dissolved: *Oṃ* 3 | 3 *rakṣa rakṣa śūlini trailokyānandadāyini tripure devi rakṣa māṃ tripureśvari rakṣa rakṣa mahādevi asmadīyam idaṃ vapuḥ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ha sa phreṃ hsauḥ 2 ha sa phreṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ*.
O Samayinī, Madirānandasundarī, worshipped by all the gods and asuras,
whose lotus feet are adorned by the garlands of crowns of serpent-kings,
who dispels the arrogance of the rows of formidable fangs— protect, protect my body!
O Supreme Goddess, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Oṃ *bhūḥ* svāhā! Oṃ *bhuvaḥ* svāhā! Oṃ *svaḥ* svāhā!
Oṃ *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* svāhā! O you who are adorned with ornaments of garlands of human entrails, O Great Kaulinī, O Proponent of the Great Brahman, O You who cause the intoxication of great wealth!

O bestower of great wealth, [protect] our body; [make it] adamantine, *krukuru*! Slay, slay the wicked kings! Devour, devour the enemy's army! Shatter, shatter the hostile forces! O bringer of victory, O you who move through the sky, O Mistress of the Three Worlds!
Yamalavarayūṃ bhamalavarayūṃ vamalavarayūṃ śamalavarayūṃ, O Śrī Bhairavī, grant your grace, svāhā!
O Tripureśvarī, may my entire lineage of noble women be [graced].
May the goddess, whose limbs are divine, whose nature is divine, and who bestows enjoyments, protect [us]. || 1 ||
Protect, protect, O Great Goddess, the supreme sovereign, my body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head within the bliss of wine! (2)
Having thus performed the protection of oneself, [one should know] the Great Goddess named Tripurā, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There is no object equal to the Guru; there is no deity comparable to Śaṅkara. (3)
There is no yoga higher than Kaula, nor is there a science equal to Traipura;
there is no knowledge higher than peace, nor is there any happiness greater than forbearance.
There is no ritual placement (nyāsa) equal to Śakti, nor is there a lore (vidyā) equal to Traipurī,
among all philosophical systems and especially among the heretical sects.
"Of divine form is the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign everywhere"—

having thus remembered the majesty of the mantra and the vidyā, she who dwells upon the seats (pīṭhas), the subsidiary seats (upapīṭhas), the head, the mountain of the sky, the mountain of the world, and the cowherd settlement of the world, is victorious.

May she who dwells in the earth and the netherworld (pātāla) through the power of the Kula, who pierces through the Kulakaula, and who brings joy to the minds of all people— may that one hundred Bhairavis, the Supreme Sovereign who rests upon the mandala of passion, purify me and accomplish my intended purpose; [she who is the essence] of the seven thousand million mantras.

Having recited the mantra "Parameśvarī" once, [one should recite]: "Aiṃ! Salutations, O Blessed One, who dwells in the triangle, who possesses three-fold revolutions, who is adorned by the Great Liṅga, who causes the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds, who is accompanied by Hrīṃ, and who bestows the bliss of Kandarpa!"

Saha Hrīṃ, O line of Brahma’s staff! Saha Hrauṃ, O you who are adorned with the noose and goad by means of the nature of consciousness! Speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech! Śrīṃ, O bestower of the kingdom of the great protector of the fist! Aiṃ Vaṃ, O hand of Śiva, the giver of boons!
O you who bring joy to all people! *klīṃ klīṃ*, you who take refuge in the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja!
*drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlūṃ saḥ*, agitate, agitate, O agitator! *hasauḥ hasaḥ hsauḥ*, churn, churn, O bestower of fearlessness! O four-armed one, three-eyed one, you who arise upon a corpse-throne!

O Goddess adorned with a great garland of skulls, O Moon-crested One, O Mistress of the Three Cities, O Bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation: *oṃ aiṃ oṃ namaḥ siddhaṃ* [51 times], from *kṣa* down to *a* in reverse order [51 times], *ddhaṃsimaḥ na oṃ aiṃ oṃ*. O Mother of all seeds, O Śrī Samayinī, [fulfill] my heart's desire.

"Dehi dehi svāhā. Having recited this, one should perform the worship of the Traipura mantra with "Aiṃ īṃ sauḥ śrīmantrarājāya namaḥ," and then worship the thirteen Vidyās by their great names beginning with Tripurā: (1) Oṃ aiṃ sahaḥ sahalahrīṃ saha hrauḥ.

Aiṃ saha hrīṃ saha hūṃ, obeisance to Kāmatripurā. (2) Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hasauḥ, obeisance to Tripurabhairavī. (3) Oṃ 3 aiṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Vāktripurā. (4) Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī Tripurā.

Salutation! (5) Oṃ aiṃ preṃ klīṃ, salutation to Tripurā, the Enchantress. (6) Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ, salutation to Tripurā, the Bee-like One. (7) Oṃ 3 aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ preṃ hasauḥ, salutation to Tripurā, the Mistress of the Three Worlds. (8) Oṃ.
Aiṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ ḍaiṃ ḍauṃ ḍaḥ, salutation to Tripurā, the Haṃsī.
(9) Aiṃ aiṃ aiṃ sauḥ, salutation to Kaulikā Tripurā. (10) Aiṃ aiṃ sauḥ, salutation to Ṣaṇḍikā Tripurā. (11) Aiṃ aiṃ sauḥ, salutation to Tālumadhyamā.
Salutation to Tripurā. (12) Aiṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ, salutation to Tripurā, the dweller in the sprout of the skull.

(13) Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. Having recited this as many times as possible, one should worship with red flowers and with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice (akṣata) seven times on the head, saying: "Aiṃ Īṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the body of the Self."

Having offered incense and lamps, one should meditate upon the Great Kāmakalā, who agitates the woman, within that very body of Tripura using the mantra *aiṃ īṃ sauḥ*. Then, one should recite one hundred verses while maintaining the contemplation of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Therein:
O Tripurā, make my body consist of Śakti and Rudra;
O Goddess of the lords of gods, grant me the eternal boon that I desire. || 1 ||
May Maṅgalādevī protect the head, Kulasundarī the forehead, Mahākālī the pair of eyes, and Kuṇḍalī the ears. || 2 ||
May Kapālī protect the interior of the ears, Kamalāvatī the cheeks, Cāmuṇḍā the teeth, and Meruvāsinī the chin. (3)
May Bhuvaneśvarī protect my brow-center and the region of the throat;
may Sarasvatī protect my tongue, and Tāluvāsinī protect my palate.
May Kapilā abide upon my shoulder, Kulamālinī on my left shoulder;
may Vināyakī abide in my belly, and Jayānandā on both my breasts.
Mahālakṣmī resides in the pit of the throat, Caṇḍabhairavī in the heart,
Brahmāṇī in the region of the navel, and Jvālāvatī stays in the anus.
Liṅgaprabhā is in the Liṅga, Medamaṇḍalā in Muṇḍin,
Mahāyogā in the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), and Udbhaṭā in the right hand.
Mahāmāyā resides in the left hand, along with the Vidyās on the fingers of that hand;
and Vaiṣṇavī, equipped with her discus weapon, dwells in the left foot.
Likewise, at the end of the right foot is Sureśvarī with one foot;
Kauverī is in the toes of the feet, and Mahādbhaṭā is in the pores of the skin.
Maṇḍalī is at the root of the nose, Vārāhī is in the circle of fat,
Jālandharī is in the place of water, and Kāmākṣī resides in the center of desire.
Udbhaṭā is at the end of the navel and the liṅga; Pūrṇapīṭhagā is at the tip of the nose; Jayādevī is on the spinal column; and Carcikā is in the joints of the bones.
May the highly illustrious one always abide in my skin;
and may my auspicious destroyer abide within my blood and at the end of my mind.
Māheśvarī and Kaumārī—these two should be stationed on the shanks;
Vīrālī should be on the left and right hips at the joints.
May the Goddess protect my body, and may the Beloved of the Kula protect my head; likewise, may earth, water, fire, air, and space [protect me]. (14)
May Bhūteśī, who dwells within the five elements, always protect my family;
may Aindrī grant me sovereignty and progeny rich with offspring. || 15 ||
May Māyā always grant me wealth, grain, and likewise fame—in battle, in the royal court, amidst enemies, and in the great forest. || 16 ||
May the Great Goddess with blood-red eyes fulfill my intention;
may she who is the pledge protect the pledge, and the Vidyā protect the Vidyā in the Kula tradition.
O Mistress of the World, bestower of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation upon practitioners, O Prāṇā, O Trailokyavijayā, grant me success and happiness! 18.
May that Ghaṇṭālī, the Great Vidyā, who is the leader of seven thousand million mantras, grant me auspiciousness. (19)
May that goddess Sureśvarī always grant me success;
may Ulkāmukhā abide in my mouth, and Mārjārī in the joints of my body.
May that Vidyā which is Bhadrakālī abide within me as the essence of Śiva;
and may the supreme wheel of Tripura, triangular and revolving in three directions, [abide there].
May that previously mentioned Tripura-śakti, who assumes many forms, abide eternally at the end of that [mantra] upon my head; may she, arisen from the god of love, abide within me.
"O divine Yoginī, who agitates the entire world and is overwhelmed by the bliss of wine, take up residence now within my body. (23)
Come, come, O Great Goddess, Siddhayoginī in my lineage, for the purpose of slaying enemies and bestowing enjoyment upon the victors! (24)
O Mahāyoginī, always make your abode in this body;
O Māhendrī, remain at the crest-lock, and O Gaṇeśvarī, stay in the middle of the womb.
May she who is renowned by the name Pretāśī perform what is auspicious for me;
and may the Ḍākinī in the eastern quarter grant me happiness. (26)
May Śākinī in the western limbs and Rākṣasī (or Kiṇī) in the south, and Mahāmāyā on the left side, grant me well-being. || 27 ||
May that Bhairavī, who is vast, large-eyed, stainless, and free from all impurity, always protect my head and remain there forever. (28)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is fashioned by Time as Kālī and is called Kālarātri, abide upon my head as Śrī. (29)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the night-stalker honored by the princes of the night-dwellers, abide as Śrī upon my head. (30)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is named Ūrdhvakeśikā, whose hair is disheveled, and who is most terrifying, abide as Śrī upon my head. (31)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is celebrated as Vīrā, the bestower of victory upon heroes, abide as Śrī upon my head. (32)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is celebrated as Mālinī and who wears a garment of coral upon the tip of her nose, abide as Śrī upon my head. (33)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, whose body is formidable with skeletons and who wears fierce skeletons as earrings, abide as Śrī upon my head. (34)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, Śrī, Pracaṇḍā, Virūpākṣī, Virūpā, and Viśvarūpiṇī abide upon my head. (35)
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called Khaṭvāṅginī and Raudrī, worshipped by Rudra, may Śrī abide upon my head. (36)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is renowned in the world as Kali-yoginī in this Kali age, remain upon my head as Śrī. (37)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called Pretākṣī and is devoid of the harshness of the Phetkāra sound, abide as Śrī upon my head. (38)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is proclaimed as Dhūmrākṣī in this scripture of the Yoginīmata, abide as Śrī upon my head. (39)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called the Great Goddess of terrible form in the Kula scriptures, abide as Śrī upon my head. (40)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the Śrī who is the universal form, especially manifest throughout the three worlds, abide upon my head. (41)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is declared to be Bhayaṅkarī and described in the Kulāgama, abide as Śrī upon my head.
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called Kapālamālikā and who wears a garland of severed heads, remain as Śrī upon my head. (43)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the goddess named Bhairavī of terrifying prowess, abide as Śrī upon my head. (44)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who dwells in the Nyagrodha tree and is praised by the gods, remain as Śrī upon my head. (45)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is Śrī, Bhairavī, and the terrifying one praised by the eight Bhairavas, abide upon my head. (46)
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the goddess Śrī, shall abide upon my head;
she is called Dīrghalambauṣṭhī, Mahāmāyā, and Mahābalā. 47.
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the great power who wields the skull-topped staff and delivers one from the ocean of worldly existence, abide as Śrī upon my head. (48)
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the Śrī, shall abide upon my head;
she is proclaimed as the Mantravādinī among all mantras. (49)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the supreme goddess who is called Kālaghnī at the end of the age, abide as Śrī upon my head. (50)
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, known as Grāhiṇī by the gods, asuras, and great serpents, shall abide upon my head as Śrī. (51)
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called Cakriṇī, one-footed, and three-eyed—may that Śrī abide upon my head. (52)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the goddess who has arms reaching everywhere and who is ever beloved by Viśvanātha, abide as Śrī upon my head. (53)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the Supreme Goddess known throughout all philosophical systems, abide as Śrī upon my head. (54)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is known in the scripture as Kaṇṭakī for the purpose of uprooting thorns, abide upon my head as Śrī.
That Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is called Kīlikī, seven-cubit tall and possessed of great strength, may Śrī abide upon my head. (56)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who as the Great Goddess is called Mahāmārī in battle, abide upon my head as Śrī. (57)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who is renowned as Yamadūtī and is worshipped by gods and demons, abide as Śrī upon my head. (58)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the goddess Karālinī, who is a great Vidyā of immense power, abide as Śrī upon my head. (59)
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the auspicious one, reside upon my head;
she is Lalitāmbā, the Great Queen, the sole leader of all the cakras. 60.
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, the Śrī, abide upon my head;
may the Kaulikā abide on the tip of my nose, and likewise Madanā on my face.
May that Yoginī Mahāmāyā, who steals away [sins] from the thighs, cheeks, and neck, remain as Śrī upon my head. (52)
Drāviṇī, Kṣobhiṇī, Stambhinī, and Mohinī, as well as Raudrakarmā, Mahāghaṇṭā, Camarī, and Tvaritā— these are the [deities] according to the Mata school.
Raudrī, the Mother of the Kula, with the gaze of a crow and face turned downward;
Kapālakuṇḍalā, the tall one, the bearer of the skull, who moves within the Kula. 64.
May the divine protect my limbs; may Kulamālinī protect my head; and likewise may earth, water, fire, air, and space [protect me]. 65.
May Bhūteśī, who dwells within the five elements, always protect my family;
may Aindrī grant me sovereignty and progeny rich with offspring.
May Māyā always grant me wealth, grain, and likewise fame—in battle, in the royal court, in the midst of enemies, and in the great forest. || 67 ||
May the Great Goddess with blood-red eyes fulfill my intention;
may she protect the pledge through the pledge, and the vidyā through the vidyā in the Kula tradition.
The Lord of the World bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation upon practitioners;
she is called Dvijaṭī and Trijaṭī, and is known as Kandalī and Lalitā in her entirety. 69.
Gāyatrī, Ambikā, Tārā, Pārvatī, Kamalaprabhā, Mādinī, Madanonmādā, Mandārī, and Madanāturā. (70)
Bhīṣaṇā, named Bhīṣaṇī, and Vibhīṣaṇā, who are perfected as pretas;
likewise Kṣudhā, Tṛṣṇā, Nidrā, Kānti, Buddhi, and Dyuti. (71)
Sandhyā, Dhṛti, Rati, and Kṣānti are indeed recited constantly;
she who is renowned as Suranāthā is the deity residing in the city. (72)
The village goddess is indeed the presiding deity; they know her as the Mistress of the Sacred Seats (Pīṭheśvarī).
She is called Kāverī, Narmadā, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā. (73)
The Godāvarī is proclaimed to be of great merit, as is Arundhatī;
she who is revealed by the name of a woman is the Great Goddess even throughout the three worlds. (74)
That goddess, the Fortune (Śrī) who abides within my heart as the hundred-thousandfold form, is indeed said to be the Vidyā known as Suvarṇarekhinī. 75.
May she, who uproots serpents, who is renowned as Kurukullā, and who was born from the mouth of the king of birds, grant me happiness. (76)
That Vidyā, who is of great form, shall always abide on the tip of my tongue;
known as Oṃkāriṇī, she shall always reside within my body. (77)
May she named Vidyāpahāriṇī, who rends asunder the form of Kali, remain in my throat; may Bheruṇḍā remain on my head. (78)
Likewise, may the Śavalarekhā also always remain at my root;
may the Jāṅgalī [mantra] destroy poison and grant me perfection in speech. (79)
This Vidyā brings about all accomplishments and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I am Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, and I am the Lord Maheśvara.
I am the abode of all beings in the world, the contemplator of Śrī-Śakti;
by means of a body purified through the placement of Śakti (śaktinyāsa), [I dwell among] the gods and demons.
O Śaṅkara, by the mere command of the Pradhāna, may they always grant me knowledge; for whatever form of Yoginī exists within the three worlds, [may they grant it]. 82.
All that remains within the body when the *śaktinyāsa* is practiced;
and even a passionate woman who performs this *nyāsa* with devotion [attains the same]. (83)
They know that Goddess, abiding in a divine form within saṃsāra, as Tripurā.
Salutations to you, O Mother of the World; salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Universe. (84)
Homage to the Goddess who bestows enjoyment; (homage be to you), O Maheśvarī!
You are all manifest and concealed, the Nirvāṇā, Bhairavī, and Śivā. 85.
Sambhramā, Vijayā, Haṃsā, Śubhā, Sānaladevatā, Yakṣiṇī, Cūḍakanyā, and likewise Ākāśagāminī. || 86 ||
Bhūcarī has practiced [the path]; Kumbhī dwells within all the scriptures;
the Goddess is the support of the sixty-four [Yoginīs]. By whomsoever these Yoginīs have been meditated upon, [they are attained]. || 87 ||
When they dissolve into the *ādhāra*, that yogi becomes a knower of yoga;
the *maṇḍala* should remain at the forehead, and the *virajā* should remain at the crown of the head.
May Ekākṣī stay on my right shoulder and Trilocanā on my left;
may Jayantī abide in my belly and Kandarpakuṇḍalī on my hip.
Mālinī should reside at the junction of the *liṅga*, and Samādhinī in the heart;
Ambikā should reside in the spinal column, and Medinī on both sides.
Diggajī should be on the tips of the hands, Nāgendrī at the joints of the nails;
Vyāghrī and Cakrī should be on the shanks, and Mahī on the soles of the feet. 91.
May Amṛtā protect the cavity of the conch, Vilāsinī the two eyes,
Kālindī the root of the tongue, and Raktinī the blood.
Lāṅgalī shall protect the bones in the joints of the bones, Jaṅgalī the marrow in the body, and Śukreśvarī likewise the semen in the semen. (93)
May Vetālī, the destroyer of my diseases, protect my skin; may Rudraṭā always bring peace to my body. (94)
May Pādatālā stand upon my feet; may Pathinī protect me on the road; and may Bhairavī protect me from the fear of thieves, fire, kings, and serpents.
May that knowledge called Cāpeṭī, which always binds the vision of the wicked, grant me auspiciousness. (96)
I pay homage to the fourfold group of vidyās: Markaṭī, Ghaṇṭakarṇī, Hanumantī, Rāvaṇī, Ghurghurā, and the one renowned as Kīrti. (97)
Ceṭakā, Jñānadā, Vidyā, Kaumārī, Caraṇāvalī, and Vighnarājī—by these names she was then pleased, she who takes the form of progeny. 98.
The female swan (haṃsī) residing in the mūlādhāra, exalted by the crushing of sins—may these ten mantra-vidyās remain upon my head. (99)
May Śubhā stand before me; may Lohitā stand on my right;
and may Śṛṅkhalā stand at my left side and behind me at the time of sexual union.
Śaṅkhinī shall protect the crest-lock; the auspicious Vastravatī the garment;
Kavacāṅgī the armor; and Netrakṛtotsavā the eyes. (101)
Yoginīs in the form of yoginīs abide throughout the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving;
may all those yoginīs constitute my body. (102)
It should then be given to one's sons, and especially to devoted disciples;
this Śaktinyāsa is to be given, but it must not be given to just anyone.
O Lord, he who performs the great nyāsa, such as the sixteenfold nyāsa (ṣoḍhānyāsa) and others, bestows the fruit of one's desired objects upon men in the world of mortals. (104)
He indeed exists as the very form of life, capable of uprooting the three worlds;
once the ritual placement of power (śaktinyāsa) has been performed, whoever might be a cutter shall live.
"By means of action, mind, or speech, his destruction shall come.

This is the *śaktinyāsa*. Having thus performed the *mahāśaktinyāsa* oneself and having caused it to be performed by the disciple, one should perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). It is as follows: [one should perform] three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra.

Having prepared a square area in front of oneself with the water for the general *arghya* offering, one should place the vessel containing all the water along with its base, reciting the self-mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā*. Then, one should contemplate one's own body and the disciple's body as being in the form of the *Śrīcakra*. (Aṃka 36)
Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara,
Śuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Vidyā, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṃkāra, and the [organs of] hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, mind, intellect, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.

"Salutation to the Śrī Mahātripurasundarī Yoga-pīṭha, which consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), the self of all— sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, water, earth, and the individual soul.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers at the heart with this collective mantra of the Pīṭha.

Having adorned the Goddess with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having meditated upon her facing oneself within the heart, one should display the mudrās of invocation and so forth, present the services beginning with the seat,
and then, preceded by meditation, worship and satisfy her three times within the heart with the mantra "sāṅgām" and so on.

Having offered the services beginning with perfumes and ending with betel leaf using the root mantra, one should perform the purification of the four principles (*tattva*). As follows: *Aiṃ aṃ 16 aḥ bhūmijīvasarvātmane aṃ āṃ aiṃ idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame* (Rig Veda 1.22.17).

I offer this supreme nectar of Greatness (Mahantā), which has arisen from the vessel of "this-ness" (Idantā), into the fire consisting of Supreme I-consciousness (Parāhantā), in the form of Śiva. *Mūla-mantra:* "To the Self of the Principle of the Self, I purify the gross body; Svāhā! Having thus partaken of a small portion with the vessel of the Self, [recite] *klīṃ kaṃ khaṃ*.
And so forth. 25.
To Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Vidyā, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṅkāra, Śrotra, Tvak, Netra, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Manas, Buddhi, Vāk, Pāṇi, and Ātman—Kaṃ. 25.

*Klīṃ!* The mighty ones, with their praises, impel the sacrifice—the one possessing Soma, the seat of *barhis*, the well-purified—while establishing Soma among the divine deities. May we, as sacrificers with beautiful hymns, rejoice in Indra.
Within [the heart], where there is no interval and no fuel, yet which blazes forth, acting as the adversary to the darkness of delusion...

In the fire of consciousness—on a certain ground for the expansion of the rays of the elements—I offer the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva, into the fire of consciousness (samvid-agni), which is the essence of the *vidyā-tattva*.
(Root Text, p.

344) I offer the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva, into the fire of consciousness, on a certain ground for the expansion of the rays of the elements. (Root Text, p. 344) [I offer it] to that which is the self of the *vidyā-tattva*.

"I purify the subtle body, svāhā. Having accepted a small portion as before, [one offers it] with "sauḥ yaṃ raṃ" ten times to the self consisting of the feet, anus, genitals, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, and water.
O Savitṛ, grant us that which is desirable today, and that which is desirable tomorrow, and day after day;

for you, O God, are the master of abundant desirable wealth. Through our prayer, may we be partakers of that desirable wealth. (Yajurveda 8.6) May all the Mothers, the Bhairavas, the Vināyakas, and the Kṣetrapālas be satisfied.

"The Yoginīs are established within my body. To the Self of the Śiva-principle, I purify the causal body, svāhā! Having accepted a small portion as before, [recite] *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ—aṃ 51 bhūmijīvasarvā*.

To Maheśvara, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Vidyā, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṅkāra, and to those whose nature is hearing, touch, sight, taste, mind, intellect, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, sound, touch, ether, air, fire, and water— AṂ 51 AIṂ KLĪṂ SAUḤ.

With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the fire of the Self, kindled by the fuel of dharma and adharma, via the path of the *suṣumṇā*. Root-text: "To the Self of all principles, I purify the body—gross, subtle, causal, and great causal—svāhā."

As before, having accepted a small portion [of the offering], one should again meditate upon the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*)— presided over by Kuṇḍalinī— in the square hearth (*kuṇḍa*), which is ignited by the fuel of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and shaped as a square representing the fourfold self;
then, having mentally worshipped it with the root mantra and "Haṃsaḥ, obeisance to the circle of the fire of consciousness" (*cidagnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*).

With the mind alone, I offer merit; *svāhā*. Likewise, having offered sin, what was done, what was not done, resolve, conceptualization, dharma, and adharma, and having thus sacrificed, holding the vessel of the self in the hand, [recite] the root mantra and *haṃsaḥ* from here until previously.

Whatever has been thought by the mind, spoken by speech, or performed by action— with the hands, feet, stomach, or genitals— throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, by virtue of the functions of the vital breath, intellect, mind, ego, body, and the sense organs; all that.

"May it be offered to the Guru and the Deity; Svāhā! Having thus offered everything, one should place the vessel upon the support (ādhāra) and [visualize] Kuṇḍalinī—extremely subtle like a fiber of lotus-stalk, possessing the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe—who has ascended from the support to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having meditated upon her in the form of the Goddess and having performed recitation as much as possible with the root *mālā* of beads, one should offer the oblation:
"In the principle ending with Māyā, I am Śiva; in the principle ending with Śakti, I am Consciousness-Śiva (*cid-ahaṃ śivo’ham*);
in the principle ending with Śiva, I am Śiva, the giver of bliss; beyond this, I am the Full, the Unsurpassed."
With the body perishing through the instructions of the Guru’s words, and the void consisting of vital breath and mental constructs [dissolved],

one who possesses the bliss of the reflective awareness of non-dual consciousness should contemplate, "Today I am Śiva, I am Śiva, I am Śiva," and having offered salutation, [place] the three *kūṭas* in the place of the three *bālā*-seeds of the disciple as well.

Having joined [the mantras] and purified them, likewise having divided the sixteen-syllable mantra into three parts and purified them, having placed [them] upon a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood and other materials, and having himself lifted up the principal pitcher while the officiating priests and assistants lift up the other pitchers;

The Guru should perform the consecration preceded by the recitation of the respective mantras; others as well should perform the consecrations. Then, having seated [the disciple], adorned with garments, garlands, and so forth, upon the Śrīcakra, [he should empower him] with the Parā-prāsāda, the sixteen-syllable Śrī-vidyā, the various divisions of the Vidya, and the six-fold Śāmbhava-krama-caraṇa-vidyā.

The traditional precepts (*āmnāya-samaya*), the five lion-thrones (*pañca-siṃhāsana*), the six philosophical systems (*ṣaḍ-darśana*), the groups of five pentads (*pañca-pañcikā-gaṇa*), the sciences of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana-vidyā*), the ten great sciences (*daśa-mahāvidyā*) such as the various divisions of the *Śrīvidyā* clusters, and the sciences of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapatya, Saura, and Śākta [traditions], as well as the sciences of the Guru’s sandals (*gurupādukā-vidyā*).

One should teach the complete sequence of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), beginning with the vidyā of the Great Sixfold (mahāṣoḍhā) as taught in the *Ṣoḍaśanityā-vidyā*, and one should also teach one's own lineage (*svakrama*). The disciple, in turn, [should honor] the venerable Guru with cows, land, gold, garments, elephants, horses, buffaloes, female and male servants, houses, and so forth.

Having gratified the officiating priests and those associated with the ritual through the giving of abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings, and having performed the great worship (*mahāpūjā*) at night, on the following day he should feed the Brahmins along with the poor, the blind, and the wretched, satisfy them with the distribution of sacrificial fees, and [receive] grace and so forth by the command of the venerable Guru.
From that time forward, one should perform [the rites]. Thus concludes the procedure for the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) according to the tradition of the *Kālīmata*.

Thus [ends] the work titled *Śrīvidyārṇava*, composed by the venerable ascetic Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of the venerable Pragalbhācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Govindācārya— the worshipful feet of the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya.
In the Tantra, the fifteenth breath. 15.
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the sixteenth chapter.
Now follows the procedure for *puraścaraṇa* according to the tradition of Kālī:
"A mantra that has been perfected through *puraścaraṇa* indeed bestows its fruit;
what is the use of fire-offerings (*homa*), what use of recitations (*japa*), and what use of elaborate mantra-depositions (*nyāsa*)? (1)
For if there were no preliminary rite for secret mantras,
the preliminary rite is indeed said to be the primary seed of mantras.
Just as an embodied being devoid of vigor is incapable of all activities, so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 3 ||

Since Vaiśampāyana has thus stated the necessity of *puraścaraṇa*, and since one hears a censure regarding performance devoid of the prescribed rules— namely, "Nirṛti destroys the fruit of those actions performed without the ritual injunctions"— the procedure for its performance is here written down with careful analysis. In this regard:
The etymological derivation of the term *puraścaraṇa* is given in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"The practice of the root mantra is called *puraścaraṇa*, because it must be performed prior to the ritual acts known as *viniyoga*. (1)
"Or it is stated thus because of its application at the beginning.
Thus, the definition of *viniyoga* (application) is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The application [of means] to virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*) according to the path of the scriptures."
The application of a perfected mantra has been fully explained by the wise. || 1 ||
This application of the mantra for the sake of attaining results is determined to be preceded by *puraścaraṇa*, just as service to a king is [preceded by preliminary efforts]. (2)

"Because it precedes the performance [of the rite], it is called *puraścaraṇa*. By this, it is stated that *puraścaraṇa* is the ritual action that generates the efficacy for the rite known as *viniyoga*, or the action which serves as the cause for the realization of the self as being identical with the mantra, pertaining to both this world and the next. Regarding this, some say:

"Having obtained this [mantra], the procedure for recitation (*japa*) should be performed with diligence by the wise, along with the procedure for oblation (*homa*), for the sake of accomplishing one's own desired goal" (Prapañcasāra 6.123).
Having thus stated this in the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*),
[the author] likewise prescribes worship, recitation, and oblation at various points within that same section, as well as the praise of the deity of the mantra through those very mantras.

This is because it was stated by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, the author of the *Prapañcasāra*, in his concluding summary: "by means of recitation, meditation, fire-oblation, worship, and so forth"; and because the author of the *Śāradātilaka* also, in every instance, prescribes the performance of worship, recitation, and fire-oblation before describing the ritual applications (*prayoga*).
A mantra is not perfected through non-recitation, nor does it bestow fruit without oblations; if unworshipped, it takes away one's desires. Therefore, one should practice these three.
Thus, based on the statement from the *Brahmaprakāśatantra*, they declare that the *puraścaraṇa* consists of three limbs. Others, however, say:
"If one desires one's own welfare in this world which abounds in suffering..."
"By the worship of the five limbs alone, the practitioner of the preliminary rite (puraścārī) shall proceed with ease. Thus [it is said].
O Great Goddess, O Īśvarī, the five limbs are: recitation (japa), fire sacrifice (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), one's own consecration (svābhiṣeka), and the propitiation of Brahmins.

"Preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) is said to consist of one-tenth of each preceding part," according to the statement in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*; thus they speak of the five-limbed [rite]. In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:
"Recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), sprinkling (seka), and the feeding of Brahmins."
In this world, the five-limbed worship is called *puraścaraṇa*.

Thus [it is said]. Others, however, citing the statement of Kapila—"The recitation and so forth of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) should be one-tenth of that of the root-mantra (mūlamantra)"—and the statement of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā—"One desiring success should perform the recitation of the limbs as one-tenth [of the main mantra]," maintain that there are six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Others, however:
Recitation, fire-offerings, libations, self-consecration, the rite for wiping away sins (*aghamarṣaṇa*),
offering water to the Sun, drinking water, prostration, and worship of the deity. (1)
The feeding of Brahmins in proportions of one-tenth for each preceding stage,
and the worship with devotion in one-tenth [of that], is called *puraścaraṇa*.

Thus, based on the statements of other tantras, they say that [the ritual] consists of ten limbs. In some cases, the fire-oblation (homa) is equal in number to the recitation (japa), and the libation (tarpaṇa) is also equal to the oblation; in other cases, all are indeed equal. In yet other applications, one should perform the oblation with even a hundredth part of the number of recitations;
in such instances, one should offer libations for these mantras to that same extent.

Regarding the phrase "according to the number of oblations," in the case of dancers and cowherds, one should perform the homa and other rites as many times as the mantra has been recited; however, since this is not stated anywhere regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) at the time of initiation and because the number of recitations there is smaller, one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
"One thousand of that [with] auspicious sesame seeds"— this refers to the context of Mahiṣamardinī, because there the recitation (*japa*) is more extensive;

or else, according to the statement in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā, "one should utter the mantra ending in *svāhā* as a fourth part of the recitation," one should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand syllables, and one thousand of that.

One should offer oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in ghee, according to the statement in the *Śāradātilaka*: "One should offer oblations with milk-rice drenched in ghee"; and because of the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*: "In another field [of practice], success is achieved through one-eighth of the number of recitations (japa)";
and also because of the statement in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "One should offer oblations with sesame and rice grains mixed with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that [recitation]."
Because the number of oblations (*homa*) is not fixed, one should satisfy [the deity] with milk-rice mixed with ghee in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that [number].
Then, by performing an oblation of one-tenth [of that], the mantra becomes perfected; for there is a statement by Sanatkumāra:
"One should satisfy other mantras according to the number of oblations offered; such satisfaction is prescribed as a daily requirement."

Furthermore, because of the statements in the Śaiva Āgamas and because the number of libations (tarpaṇa) is also not fixed, our established doctrine is that the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should be performed exactly as prescribed in the respective Kalpas. Regarding the specific number of recitations for the Śrīvidyā in this context,
it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
When he has recited the mantra just one hundred thousand times, those two goddesses who cause obstacles [appear];
yet even then, he does not experience even the slightest agitation.
"Then, being pure and wise, one should recite it three hundred thousand times according to the rule.
Thus it is said in the Vāmakeśvara:
"When only one hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the women on the earth become agitated."
For if the mind of the practitioner is not disturbed even slightly in this manner, [then success is attained]. (1)
Then all the Naga maidens in Pātāla were greatly agitated;
yet even they did not cause him the slightest agitation of mind.
Then the celestial damsels dwelling in heaven flee away;
thus, having recited it three hundred thousand times while established in the vow, the most excellent practitioner— || 3 ||
"O Goddess of the Gods, she agitates the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Thus, because the fruit of causing agitation in the world takes the form of an obstacle, the *Jñānārṇava* describes the *puraścaraṇa* for Śrīvidyā on page 17:
In whatever place there may be a linga facing west—whether it be self-manifested (svayambhū), a Bāṇaliṅga, devoid of a bull, or situated in water—[that is the site]. || 1 ||
O you of excellent vows, whether at the western abode or elsewhere,
in fields of power, by the Gaṅgā, at a river, or on a mountain peak— II.2.
In a pure and auspicious place, the goddess, with a serene mind, should recite the vidyā;
staying there, she should recite it one hundred thousand times, becoming manifest in the very form of the goddess.
Then this knowledge, which brings the three worlds under control, becomes effective;
thus, having first performed the recitation according to his capacity, the best of practitioners [proceeds]. (4)
O fair-faced one, one should perform the oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers,
or else with safflower (*kusumbha*) blossoms mixed with the three sweets, using a tenth part [of the total number].
By means of the method prescribed by the ritual injunctions, one shall destroy the multitude of obstacles in an instant;
it bestows all desires and grants the fruits of sovereignty, enjoyment, and liberation.
Thus [ends the section on] the other mountain-linga. In this manner, one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) constitute the *puraścaraṇa* for the Śrīvidyā.
This is because the rule for the ten-part oblation (*daśāṃśahoma*) grants all desires, as its fruit is also explicitly stated;
and according to the maxim "because of the instruction of that duty within," the determination of the reality [is established] at the beginning of the ritual application (*prayoga*).
When there arises the inquiry as to how the accomplishment of those ritual applications (*prayoga*) for which no specific injunctions have been stated is achieved,

it is because of the statement, "This application is ordained as being preceded by *puraścaraṇa*," and because that [method] alone is suitable for description. Likewise, in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, after extracting the *Lopāmudrā-vidyā*, it is said:
"Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times in this manner, one becomes the destroyer of all sins"—thus it is stated that merely one hundred thousand recitations are required.

They say that the same has been stated in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* as well. However, in reality, when the *Jñānārṇava* is considered in its syntactic unity with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, [it is understood differently].
It appears that the *puraścaraṇa* consists precisely of the three hundred thousand recitations mentioned in the section on the practice (*sādhana*) of the Śrīcakra.
As it is said in the Jñānārṇava (p. 14):
"Listen, O lady beautiful in all her limbs, to the supreme procedure for the Śrīcakra."
By whose mere consciousness Sadāśiva is always the agent and the remover. || 1 ||
By this method, wherever the Śrīcakra is worshipped according to the sequence, one shall bring everything under control; of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, the city, the country, and the province come under one's control;
all women become submissive, tormented by the blazing fire of desire. (3)
O Goddess of gods, by the sight of him, all women whose hearts are deluded by worldly knowledge become fixed in mind upon the practitioner. || 4 ||
Resorting to a rosary (akṣamālā) which consists of the forms of the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā), or one made of pearls, which bestows the fruit of liberation of speech. || 5 ||
It constantly bestows all accomplishments and brings all kings under one's control;
it may be made of pearls or likewise fashioned from crystal.
A rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows all prosperity for the sake of liberation;
a coral rosary, however, brings subjugation and accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
A rosary of rubies bestows fruits [of merit] and grants the fruit of sovereignty;
a rosary of putrajīva beads, however, brings about subjugation and yields worldly enjoyments. (8)
Then, having worshipped the rosary and having honored it with sandalwood paste,
one who is pure should take hold of it and recite the vidyā exactly one hundred thousand times.
When women cause his mind, though it be very steady, to waver, then the best of practitioners should recite the second hundred thousand [times]. 10.
The daughters of the great Naga kings from the depths of Pātāla agitate him;
yet, despite the nets of their sidelong glances, the practitioner does not fall into delusion. || 11 ||
Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform three hundred thousand [recitations].
When the third hundred thousand is reached, celestial maidens will speak to him. (12)
Through pride born of the intoxication of beauty and fortune, they surely cause the practitioner to melt away;
therefore, he remains steady-minded.
Then, having recited it three hundred thousand times—this which thoroughly destroys all sins—the virtuous one, established in the vow with a tranquil mind, [attains his goal]. || 14 ||
O Dear One, he agitates the inhabitants of the earth, the atmosphere, and the nether regions; he brings under his control men and women, and even all that is moving and unmoving.

Having thus stated the recitation of three hundred thousand [times], and because the practice of the Śrīcakra has been taught, and because the practice of the Śrīcakra is a rite for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*), and because such a rite for specific desires requires the accomplishment of the *vidyā*, and because the accomplishment of the *vidyā* is rooted in the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), [the author] has not yet described the *puraścaraṇa*.

Because it is inappropriate to discuss the performance of rites for desired objects at this point; because the classification of rosaries must be explained only in the section concerning the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the rosary; and because, by the very mention of the abundance of obstacles, such obstacles—being hindrances to success—are prohibited specifically during the time of the *puraścaraṇa*.

However, in the case of *kāmya* (optional) recitations, since only the aforementioned obstacles are specified as being the results [of their removal], it is appropriate to mention the observances (*niyama*) and mental steadiness (*manaḥsthairya*)— in the words "one established in the vow, with a steady mind"— precisely because these two are absolutely essential at the time of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*). This is also stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice for the realization of the Śrīvidyā mantra.
[One should perform it] with shoots of *śamī* and *dūrvā*, and with sprouts of *aśvattha* and *arka*. (1)
O Goddess, one who is composed should worship the Śrīcakra for just one month;
by doing so, the teacher destroys the sins accumulated over a thousand lifetimes within that month.

Beginning thus, after describing the three types of obstacles according to the previously mentioned method, he speaks of the recitation (*japa*) characterized by [the distinctions of] *sthāna*, *akṣamālā*, *upāṃśu*, and so forth, in the manner taught in the *Jñānārṇava* preceded by expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Having thus described the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras], he prescribes the fire-oblation (*homa*) with one-tenth of that number.

"One may offer oblations with flowers born of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, or with safflower (*kusumbha*) blossoms soaked in the three sweets (*madhuratrika*). From this very statement regarding the *daśāṃśa-homa* (the ten-part oblation), the truth is that this recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] constitutes the *puraścaraṇa*. As for what is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*, beginning with: "In whatever place there is a true *liṅga* facing west... and so forth.
Having first described the place for recitation (*japa*), it is stated that "staying there, one should recite a *lakṣa* [of mantras], thereby becoming the very embodiment of the Goddess in person.

This word *lakṣa*, however, is a reminder of the three *lakṣas* mentioned previously, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*. For this very reason, it belongs to the section concerning the practice of the *Śrīcakra*.

In this context, only the *sthāna-homa* (fire-offering at specific locations) and the *anukta-sthāna-homa* (unspecified location offering) are mentioned; otherwise, it would have been more appropriate to mention the *akṣamālā* (rosary) and other such items here as well. Some authorities state that even for nine hundred thousand recitations (*navalakṣa-japa*), there must be a preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). Regarding this path, it is said: "One should perform nine hundred thousand [recitations] to attain imperishable fruit, and thereafter, one should [perform the fire-sacrifice]."

In some cases, it is for the sake of a greater fruit; and thus, in the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra], there is the traditional teaching that each [mantra] yields a hundred thousand-fold result: "O Goddess, by reciting one hundred thousand times, one is liberated from great sins. (Pañcasāyaka 5)
By two hundred thousand [recitations], the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes are [purified]. || 1 ||

The Goddess Tripurā shall undoubtedly destroy [all obstacles] for the practitioner, provided that the reciter of the mantra, restrained and embodied by the mantra, has performed three hundred thousand recitations. || 2 ||
If one recites this vidyā four hundred thousand times, it shall swiftly destroy even the sins of a thousand births, and one will become a great Lord of Speech.
By reciting five hundred thousand times, even a poor person becomes like Vaiśravaṇa himself;
by reciting six hundred thousand times, one becomes a lord among the great holders of vidyās.
By reciting this mantra seven hundred thousand times, one achieves union with the Khecarī;
and by reciting the Vidyā eight hundred thousand times, O Maheśvarī, [the same result is attained].
Having recited the mantra of Tripurasundarī nine hundred thousand times, one becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, honored by the gods.
When born according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner becomes like another form of Hara;
O Gaurī, he himself is the creator and destroyer, a lord unassailable in the world.
"Serene, joyful, steadfast, moving at his own will, the Lord.
Thus [it is said].
Also elsewhere: "Alternatively, one should recite the vidyā nine hundred thousand times with undistracted mind. One should recite it one hundred thousand times.
In some places, it is also stated as "mantra. Among these three positions, the tradition of the Guru maintains that the former refers to its lack of efficacy.
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* as well:
"Alternatively, with a concentrated mind, one should recite the vidyā nine hundred thousand times."
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that [number], according to the previously mentioned procedure.
"One shall accomplish [the subjugation] of those dwelling in heaven, the earthly realm, and the depths of Pātāla.

However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, a recitation of nine hundred thousand is not mentioned; rather, the specific fruits for each stage—from one hundred thousand up to nine hundred thousand—are described individually, but no fruit is stated specifically for a second hundred thousand.
Regarding the phrase "of the third hundred-thousand": therefore, by combining those, a recitation of four million five hundred thousand arises;

consequently, there is not even a suspicion that this constitutes a *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) there, for it is certain that it is merely a recitation for a specific desire (*kāmyajapa*). Furthermore:
"Because the mantra is already perfected, there is no need for the arduous labor of [reciting] the number of ages here. Now follows the determination of the recitation (*japanirṇaya*).
And in that case where the number of mantras is prescribed by means of the *nigada* itself, there the repetition of all those mantras occurs according to the sequence of the Yugas. (1)
