The number stated for the Kṛta age remains the same; in Tretā it becomes double;
in Dvāpara it is declared to be triple; and in Kali, the number is fourfold.

Thus it is said in the Rudrayāmala: "In the Kali age, one should perform four times the prescribed number of recitations. Regarding this, some maintain that in the Kali age, the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for even the recitation mentioned in the *Prapañcayāga* and the *Śāradātilaka* must be performed by multiplying it fourfold and so on; however, this is not so, as it is seen in the *Nāradapañcarātra* and other such texts.
The recitation (japa) prescribed in the *Prapañcasāra* and other texts is indeed fourfold. Likewise, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Having fasted for three days or even one day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, beginning on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, one should recite the eight-syllabled mantra. (1)
The twice-born practitioner of the *puraścaraṇa* rite should recite [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times without interruption;
he should be of pure conduct, clean, bathed, restrained in speech, and have his senses subdued.
The accomplishment of mantras, which has unseen results, arises from two hundred thousand recitations;
indeed, through twice that amount of practice, it becomes both worldly and otherworldly.
Thus may this purification of the self be accomplished; such was the extent [of the practice] in the first age (Kṛta-yuga).
In the Tretā age it is said to be twofold, and likewise threefold in the Dvāpara age.
"In the Kali age, it is fourfold, possessing thirty-two characteristics.

Thus, [the purification] has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and brings about union with the mantra (*mantrasāyujya*). It is "pertaining to this world" (*aihikī*), bestowing happiness in this life; it is "pertaining to the hereafter" (*āmuṣmikī*), bestowing worlds such as heaven; and it is "purification of the self" (*ātmaśuddhi*), which is the purification that serves as the means for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). In this way...
"For this very reason, one should again recite the mantra thirty-two lakhs of times by that measure";

thus it has also been stated by the venerable Ācārya. Having spoken regarding Bālā in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the section on Bālā: "O Dear One, one should recite the mantra one lakh per syllable and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that."
"One should perform all [rites], such as the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and worship, for this [deity] as before"—thus it is taught in the *Bhairavī-mantra*.

Having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should perform the recitation (*japa*) three hundred thousand times, quadrupled, and then recite the mantra one million times according to the principles (*tattva*); having thus declared this in the *Bhairavī*, she is likewise known as "the Child" (*bālā*) in the *Bālā[-tantra]*.
"She who brings the three worlds under her control. One should perform all rites such as recitation (*japa*) and worship for her as previously described;
this has also been taught by the author of the *Śāradātilaka*. According to the statement in the *Prayogasāra*: "One hundred and fifty thousand [recitations] or one million two hundred thousand;
therefore, some wise ones say there are twelve mantras," [this applies] to the *Prapañcāra*.

In the *Bhairavīprakaraṇa* (9.9), however, it is said: "Having received initiation from a guru who possesses the specific characteristics and belongs to a true lineage, the self-controlled practitioner, having obtained this mantra, should recite it with great restraint for half a million according to the reality (*tattva*).
Thus, twelve hundred thousand recitations are mentioned. Likewise: “One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.”

Regarding the *tripuṭā* mantra mentioned in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it is stated that "one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the Sun" (*ādityalakṣam*), meaning "one should recite this [mantra] one hundred thousand times for the Sun"; however, in the *Prapañcasāra* and *Śāradātilaka*, a fourfold repetition is specifically prescribed. Therefore, what has been determined in one [text] applies [to all].

By this reasoning, it is determined that in all cases, the fourfold [japa] alone is prescribed. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the mention of "half-japa" in the *Prapañcasāra*—on the grounds that even a number half of that would not involve any contradiction.

For, by the aforementioned statement of Nārada himself, [the practice may vary] depending on whether it is intended for success in this world (*aihika-siddhi*) or for success in the hereafter (*āmuṣmika*).

Because there is no contradiction. Thus, a wise man should recite [the mantra] on the banks of rivers flowing to the ocean, or in a secluded place, or in his own home, or in the temple of Viṣṇu. [The term] "flowing to the ocean" is used explicitly; otherwise, since all [rivers] are such by way of succession, the qualification would be redundant. "Wise" means endowed with faith.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, [one should practice] on the bank of a river flowing toward the ocean, or in a cow-pen,
or at the root of an Aśvattha or Bilva tree, or on the shore of the ocean, or by a reservoir of water.

"In a temple facing west, or on a mountain peak. Here, "Deva" refers to Śiva. Furthermore, according to the words of Kumbhasambhava (Agastya): "In a place for Śiva facing west, provided it is devoid of a bull (*vṛṣabha*). This is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*.
Mountains, cow-pens, flowing rivers, forests, hermitages, and lakes—
these are the sacred places for recitation (*japa*), or wherever one feels a natural inclination. (1)

Thus [it is said]. A "flow" (*praviṣyanda*) is a spring. A "river" is the bank of a sacred river. A "forest" is a sacred forest such as Puṣkara, Arbuda, and so forth. "Purifying wealth" is mentioned in the *Śāradātilaka*. In the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*:
"O Dear One, having resorted to the shade of a Bilva tree, or at the root of an Aśvattha tree..."
Or in the presence of the Guru, in a cow-pen, in a place devoid of bulls, or in a temple of Śiva. || 1 ||
On a riverbank, on a mountain peak, or even in a grove of *tulasī* trees,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind in the presence of one's chosen deity.
Thus [it is said]: "On a riverbank, specifically on the bank of a sacred river, because other riverbanks are prohibited. In the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
'Sacred fords (*tīrtha*), holy sites (*kṣetra*), forests, groves, temples, rivers, and lakes—these secluded places of Hari are the ones that grant success in mantra. (1)
Thus it is said. In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Japa is recommended in the presence of the sun, fire, a guru, the moon, or a burning lamp, as well as in the presence of Brahmins and cows. (1)
Alternatively, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Recitation performed at home is said to be standard; in a cow-pen, it is ten times more effective.
In a grove or likewise in a forest, it is said to be a thousandfold;
on a sacred mountain it is ten-thousandfold, but by a river it is a hundred-thousandfold.

"They say that ten million [offerings] are for a temple, while an infinite number are in my presence"—that is, in the presence of me, Śiva. Likewise, Śaṅkha says: "An infinite [number] is in the presence of Viṣṇu. Thus, in the *Yāmala*:
"In a place free from the fear and distress caused by barbarians, wicked people, wild beasts, and hunters..."
In a solitary, pure place, free from censure and filled with devotion. || 1 ||
One should dwell in a beautiful region, in a righteous kingdom, where food is abundant and there is no affliction;
in a delightful place inhabited by devoted people, and not under the patronage of others.
The path upon which kings, ministers, royal officials, and powerful men travel— that path a knower of reality should not dwell upon.
One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, houses, or at the foot of trees; nor on riverbanks, mountain slopes, or in earth-cavities and the like.
Having gone to a field of merit or a similar place, one should perform the consecration of the ground and say: "For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of such-and-such a mantra. (5)
"May this ground be accepted by her; may my mantra be accomplished"—having thus performed the formal acceptance of the ground, he should determine its dimensions on all sides.
In places such as rivers, mountains, and sacred fords, [the area] is delimited by measurement;
in a village, the site is one *krośa*, and in a city, it is remembered as being twice that.
One should drive stakes made of milky trees, consecrated with weapon-mantras,
into the ten directions, and worship the Weapon-deity within them.
A mantra that has been "staked" by the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa) is not overcome by obstacles;
therefore, the one most skilled in the ritual rules should worship the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla) and others there according to the injunctions.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the lords of the directions, one should then take refuge in the sacred field (kṣetra).
He who performs the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) without knowing the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) [acts improperly].
"There is no fruit for one who recites that [mantra]; it leads to all manner of misfortune.
Thus it is said. In another Tantra:
"He who, having fully understood the Kūrma-cakra, abides in the procedure for recitation and so forth..."
One attains all that has been described; otherwise, one meets with destruction. || 1 ||
Therefore, having understood the entire division of the tortoise, one should perform [the rite] in its entirety; it exists in four ways in the world, and that method is now described. (2)
The first is the supreme tortoise (para-kūrma), and then there is that which pertains to the country, the village, and the house; thus it is established as fourfold.
Then, one should divide the region, village, house, or site into nine parts;
from east to west, one should assign the letters from *ka* to *ma*.
One should write the eight syllables beginning with *ya* and *a* in the two feet;
then, one should place two [syllables] in the *īśa* [corner] and the vowels from the east onwards in the center.

Thereafter, one should place the letters ending with *īśa* (Ṣa) in pairs; that from which the first letter of the name originates is the face, and the letters on either side of it are the two hands, the belly, and the feet, respectively.
One [line] is the tail, then the middle, and one is the back, possessing six limbs.
Through the mouth there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; through the two hands, all accomplishments.
In the belly there is constant fruitlessness; in the feet, no accomplishments at all; in the tail, death is certain; [but] in the head, the accomplishment of all goals.
"Therefore, having understood that well, one should perform all [rites] such as *japa*.
Then, concerning the *Śrīvidyā* according to the system of the *Kādimata*, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
Having visualized the letters from *a* to *kṣa* residing within the Brahma-nāḍī,
and having joined each letter with the nasal bindu, the wise practitioner should recite his own chosen mantra.
Having joined [the vowels] beginning with *a* and likewise those beginning with *ka* in their proper order,
one should then conceive of the syllable *kṣa* as Meru there, O Mistress of the World.
Then the script shall consist of a rosary numbering fifty;
by means of this, the recitation of all mantras accomplishes every purpose. (3)

One should recite the mantra starting from the letter *kṣa* located at the summit of Meru and proceeding in reverse order from the letter *la*, skipping one letter at a time; thus it bestows the fruit.

Thus it is said. Here, when the recitation (*japa*) is to be performed one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times, it should be done according to the division into the eight groups (*varga*), so that there are one hundred and eight [recitations]. In this context, the recitation of the eight groups must be performed only until the completion of the prescribed number of one hundred or other such counts. This...
The recitation [prescribed] for the Kṛta Age must be performed with four times that number of recitations and so forth in the Kali Age. As stated in the Śrītantrarāja (Chapter 5, verse 68):
"The means of accomplishing the Vidyā, its success, its observance, and likewise what is to be avoided..."
At that time, the obstacles from previous lives manifest as signs directed toward one's goal. || 1 ||
Listen in due order, O Goddess of gods, to that which always brings delight;
by means of which even a mortal may attain perfection, becoming liberated while living and identical with Bhava.
Having bathed in fragrant waters and assuming the form prescribed for the preliminary worship,
one should satisfy the Guru with wealth and then practice the ritual sequence in a red chamber.
Performing the recitation during all three junctions of the day, remaining silent and observing the vow,
one should offer milk-porridge (pāyasa) prepared with milk, devoid of plantains, jaggery, and sugar.
One should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with camphor during those very twilight periods;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in ten parts [of the recitation] and the libation (tarpaṇa) with water mixed with camphor.
After one's own anniversary (svanityā), one should perform three thousand recitations every day;
by that means, O Īśvarī, the full hundred thousand will be completed by the end of the anniversary.
Thus, three hundred thousand [years] are declared for the first age, the Kṛtayuga;
likewise, it is twice that in the Tretā, and remembered as three times that in the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, it is said that the number of syllables is fourfold;
thus, by multiplying the third [set] by seven, the total becomes twenty-one.
Thus, having separated the vowels, consonants, and bindu of the third peak (kūṭa), there are seven syllables.
For each of these seven letters, three hundred thousand recitations are required;
thus, totaling twenty-one hundred thousand recitations constitutes the *puraścaraṇa* in the Kṛta Yuga. In the Kali age, this is fourfold.

"Japa" refers to what is called *puraścaraṇa*. *Puraścaraṇa*, however, consists of five limbs (*pañcāṅga*), namely: recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), self-consecration (*svābhiṣeka*), and feeding Brahmins (*brāhmaṇabhojana*).
In this context, these five limbs should be performed as ten percent of the [main] recitation, as previously stated (though in the *Tantrarāja* it is said...).

The specific distinction is that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be equal in number to the count of the *homa* offerings. Likewise, in that same [text]: "Therefore, it is declared that in other ages there should be an increase in the number [of offerings], provided that no obstacle arises from the agitation of women or from sensual enjoyments. (9)
When those numbers are completed, having made his request, he should resort to his own practice.
O Goddess of the Gods, hear now what things are always to be avoided on those days.
Conversation with atheists, sexual intercourse, censured acts, anxiety, grief, idle talk, and wandering through foreign lands; (11)
O Śāṅkarī, other things to be avoided on those days have been declared;
listen now to those that are destructive everywhere, for everyone, and at all times. (12)
One should not desire the fields, houses, or wives of others, nor should one engage in their censure; one should not direct anger or blows toward women, even those who are wicked.
The signs of accomplishment have been described by me in the discourse on latent impressions;
now hear, O practitioner, the signs of favorability as they occur during the time of attainment.
For one who is accomplishing the practice and intent upon the *puraścaraṇa*, that is the time for *puraścaraṇa* when there occurs in a dream at night a meeting with groups of women on boats,
or wandering upon the peaks of elephants, mountains, and palaces, or the sight of a king. (15)
The sight of elephants and women, dancing and singing, festivals, as well as the sight and touch of liquor and meat; 16.
O Goddess of gods, hear now of the censurable things that cause obstacles and misfortune:
being struck by dark-complexioned soldiers in a dream, and the smearing of oil. (17)
Sexual union with the wives of others, as well as the loss of semen, leads to the upheaval of the kingdom, fear arising from fire and wind, and the destruction of kinsmen. (18)
Neglect toward the guru, the affliction of objects by disease, faith in the worship of other mantras, and constant obstacles to the daily worship; (19)
Through many merits performed by men over many lifetimes, there arises steadfastness in faith and the attainment of the lineage-succession in the daily worship. (20)
Now, the Tortoise Diagram (*kūrmacakra*). In that very same work—(5th Paṭala, verse 88)—it is said:
"He who performs rituals such as recitation (*japa*) without knowing the configuration of the Tortoise does not obtain the results described; rather, they lead to ruin. (21)
Therefore, having understood the entire division of the tortoise, one should perform [the rite] in its entirety. It exists in four ways in the world; listen, O beloved, to that method.
The first is the supreme tortoise; thereafter, it is established in four ways: as pertaining to the region, the village, and the house. (23)
Then, one should divide the region, village, house, or site into nine parts;
from east to west, one should assign the letters from *ka* to *ma*.
One should place the four identical syllables at the two ends;
then, one should place the two [syllables] of Īśa in the middle, and the vowels from the east onwards.

In the squares ending with Īśa (northeast), starting from two at a time toward the west, wherever the first letter of the name occurs, that is the face; on both sides are the hands, then the belly, and then the feet in successive order.
One [digit] is the tail, one is the middle, and one is the back; thus it possesses six limbs.
Success in all goals is achieved when it is in the mouth, while its presence on the hands brings about only minor success.
In the belly, there is constant fruitlessness; on the two feet, it causes the loss of everything. In the tail, death is certain; on the back, it bestows all desired objects. (28)
Therefore, having thoroughly understood this, one should perform everything with full concentration:
the consonants should be in the Deśakūrma, and likewise the vowels in the Gṛhakūrma. (29)
In a village and such places, there are two tortoises, but not two in a foreign land;
because [the practitioner] must always face the east, the accomplishment of that [practice] is thus declared.
Thus, this fourfold division of the *kūrma* has been described to you,
by which there shall then be the accomplishment of all mantras in every respect.
Having increased the sum by its own extent and divided by eight, one should determine the remainder;
having understood the square root among those [digits], one should assign the first letter of the name to the name.
In those respective locations, there is likewise a fixed absence of misfortune; thus, in the case of dwellings whose forms are unknown, it becomes established by name alone.

Thus it is said. Here, even though the name of the teaching (*deśanā*) is joined with a consonant (*vyañjana*), the predominance of the consonant should be understood in the "teaching-turtle" (*deśakūrma*); likewise, in the "village-turtle" (*grāmakūrma*), the predominance of the vowel (*svara*) should be understood. However, in all cases where it is joined with a vowel alone, the mouth should be known as the outer square (*bahiḥ-koṣṭha*) of the vowel. As stated in the *Devīyāmala*:
One should not contemplate the location of the lamp at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Mahākāla, or Kāśī. || 1 ||

Thus. Regarding that, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: at the seashore, on a riverbank, on a mountain peak, on the bank of a river flowing toward the ocean, in a temple of Viṣṇu, in a secluded private house, in a cow-pen, at the root of an *aśvattha* or *bilva* tree, by a reservoir of water, facing west, under a banyan tree, in a deserted temple of Śiva, in the presence of one's guru, in a grove of *tulasī*, or in the presence of one's chosen deity—

The coming and going of [the king] and his ministers and others to a place of their own choice— a field of merit, a sacred ford, a forest, a grove, a river, a lake, or any other location free from fear of barbarians, wicked beasts, and predators; secluded, devoid of censure, righteous, a refuge for devotees of one’s chosen deity, well-supplied with food, and free from disturbances.

One should select one of these secluded locations—either within a village for a distance of one *krośa*, or within a city for two *krośas*, or in a river, mountain, sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and so forth, where there is no fixed limit—and take possession of this ground with the mantra:
"For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of such-and-such a mantra, I take this earth; may my mantra be accomplished."
Having performed the ritual appropriation of the ground (*bhūmiparigraha*), one should prepare ten stakes made from milky trees that are straight and well-proportioned;
having consecrated each individually eight times with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should drive them into the eight directions starting from the east—
in the space between Indra and Īśāna, and between Nirṛti and Varuṇa— and having fully worshipped the weapon-mantra within them.

In those places, one should offer an oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) to Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions (*daśadikpāla*). Then, having worshipped Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇeśa, and Vāstupuruṣa, and having drawn four lines extending east-west and four lines extending north-south to form nine squares, [one should proceed] within them.
Having written the seven groups known as ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa in the seven squares according to the sequence starting from the east,

and having written the syllables *lakṣau* in the northeast square, one should likewise divide the central square into nine parts and write the sixteen vowels two by two in the eight surrounding squares according to the sequence starting from the east.

Having fashioned the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*), one should worship the nine Kṣetrapālas— the Amṛta, Vṛṣabha, Śailarāja, Vāsuki, Arthakṛt, Śakti, Padmayoni, Mahāśaṅkha, and Chāyācchatra— within the central group of nine, in the eight directions starting from the east, using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), the dative case ending, and followed by *namaḥ*.

Having performed worship, one should construct a house for the purpose of recitation—capable of warding off cold, wind, and heat—in the direction of the square corresponding to the first syllable of the village's name within the mouth of the *kūrma* diagram; or, if that is unavailable, in the middle of the *kūrma*'s back, or in any one of the two squares below the mouth, or in the hand of the *kūrma*. This is according to the *Kālikodbhava*:
Wherever enmity exists between the names of the site and the practitioner, one should understand that from the science of syllables (akṣaśāstra) and properly abandon it. || 1 ||
Thus it is said in the Akṣaśāstra: "The state of being an enemy between two non-duals is expressed by the letter *ga*;
that of two *ṛ*s by the letter *ṭha*, and that of the letter *ṭha* also by that [same letter]. (2)
The two *ḷ* vowels are [substituted] for the letter *pa*, and the letter *pa* is also [substituted] for the two *ḷ* vowels;
the two *o* vowels are [substituted] for the letter *ṣa*, and the letter *ṣa* is [substituted] for the pair of *au* vowels. (2)
The substitution of *ja* by *ṭa*, of *jha* by *kha*,
of *ḍa* by *ta*, and of *pha* by *dha [occurs].* (3)
The letter *bha* is an enemy of *ra*, and *ya* is an enemy of *sa*;
these letters are enemies to one another, while others possess a friendly disposition.
In the Kūrma-cakra, the practitioner should diligently avoid the position of the enemy;
for example, Aṭṭahāsa, the great city, was the enemy of Garga.
In this manner, one should apply [the mudrās] to the forms of Gayā and Māreśvara;
for Ṛjubhaṭṭa, the one called Ṭhakka; and for Ḷtaka, the enemy is Padmaka.
Uḍḍiyāṇa belongs to Ṣaṇmukha, and Raudra to Ṣaḍguṇaka;
Jyanti belongs to Ṭaṅkadhāra, and Khaṃdhāra to Ṛṃṝ(jhaṃjha)ṇa. || 7 ||
From Phaṇḍibhaṭṭa [came] the one named Tārā for Ḍākadeva and the one named Dharma;
for Bhadra, Ramyaka; and for Yajñadatta, Somaka. (8)

"Having thus purified it in sequence, the wise one should abandon the position of the enemy. Now, as for the *mālā* (rosary): it is of two kinds, consisting of the letters of the *mātṛkā* and consisting of beads such as *rudrākṣa*.
Regarding the first of these, the *Uttara-tantra* states:
By means of a garland of letters fashioned from the syllables of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu, and arranged both in direct and reverse order.
Mantras endowed with their respective seed-syllables, when recited, bestow all accomplishments;
this is true even for mantras directed against enemies, let alone those that are already well-accomplished.
Thus it is said in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Because it is joined with the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', it is celebrated as the 'Akṣamālā' (rosary of beads).
One should fashion a rosary for recitation using gems equal in number to those letters. (1)
Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess, the letter 'A' is the first, and the letter 'Kṣa' follows as the last;
this is renowned as the 'Garland of Letters' (*akṣamālā*), consisting of the forms of the *mātṛkā* phonemes."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the recitation of the eight groups (*varga*) should be performed at the conclusion of the prescribed number. As it is stated in the *Mātṛkārṇava*: "Beginning first with the letter 'A', one should mentally recite the Mātṛkā up to its end."
Having held that final [syllable], one should recite it again until the very end during the descent;

then one should mutter the eight letters ending with *la*, and subsequently, at the conclusion, the letter ending with *kṣa* joined with the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). This is the *Mālā* taught by Paśupati in the *Yāmala*. || 1 ||
Thus, having placed [the letters] in the position of Meru, [one places] the letter *kṣa* at the end. [One places] the letters ending in *l*, namely *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa,* and *la*.

Following that, after the completion of the number indicated; "at the end" means at the conclusion of the hundred or other number indicated. The particle *eva* is used for emphasis. However, the second [case-ending] is used in the subsequent tantra.
Now I shall describe the procedure for the rosary for the sake of the practitioner's desire;
it is said that one consisting of twenty-five beads bestows worldly enjoyment.
With thirty [syllables] she is the giver of wealth, and with twenty-seven [syllables] she is always the one who possesses the eyes;
she is conceived as the performer of malevolent rites when consisting of fifteen [syllables].
With fifty-four syllables, she bestows success in rites performed for specific desires;
arranged with one hundred and eight syllables, she is considered the granter of all desired objects.
Jewels originating from conch shells are said to bestow prosperity;
those made of crystal grant liberation; and lotus-seed beads increase nourishment.
Rudrākṣas are said to bestow enjoyment and liberation, granting all spiritual perfections;
those originating from the Putrajīva tree grant abundance of sons, cattle, and grain.
Gems originating from coral bestow wealth, good fortune, and subjugation;
pearls are said to grant liberation and provide the abundance of all prosperity.
"Those made of kuśa grass remove sin, while those made of gold and silver grant desires.
Likewise, in the Śāradātilaka (Chapter 23, verse 118):
"A rosary of rudrākṣa beads brings about the fulfillment of the practitioner's desires during recitation."
A rosary fashioned from lotus seeds is considered to be the destroyer of enemies. || 1 ||
A rosary made of knots of *kuśa* grass instantly destroys sin;
one fashioned from *putrajīva* fruits brings about the attainment of sons.
A rosary fashioned from precious gems and jewels grants one's desires when recited;
a garland crafted from golden beads bestows all longed-for objects.
A garland fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth;
a crystal garland grants good fortune, and one made of pearls confers prosperity.
Fashioned from conch-shells and gems, it produces imperishable fame;
that garland, when composed of all these [materials], leads men to liberation.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding "by all," some say it means by one, five, or five [each]; however, regarding their mixing, the *Uttara-tantra* states the prohibition:
"If one should recite with *indrākṣa* beads, or likewise with *rudrākṣa* or crystal beads..."
Nothing else should be inserted in the middle, such as the *putrajīva* seed and so forth.
Whatever else one might employ in the act of recitation with a rosary,
that which is dear to her bestows neither desire nor liberation.
In another birth, he becomes one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
thereafter, he enters into association with Caṇḍālas of sinful deeds.
Thus, in the Brahmayāmala:
"A rosary made from the horn of a rhinoceros grants liberation to the ancestors;
one made from *niśā* wood is for subjugation, and one made with lac is for rites involving fever. (1)

For the eradication of the sun [deity], it should be made of *śrīphala* wood; for the attainment of knowledge, it should be made of elephant tusk; and for bestowing all goals, one should make it of jewels. (2)
A copper [image] is prescribed for subjugating all kings and for deluding;
an iron one is declared for killing; [images] made of bilva wood or the wood of the śrīphala tree [are used for other purposes]. || 3 ||
Furthermore, she is said to be threefold: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa; among these, the first consists of one hundred and eight auspicious [forms].
With gems produced from conch-shells, those originating from white lotuses, with gems of the *sāttvika* type, *putrajīva* seeds, and those produced from silver; (5)
The *rājasī* [line] is fashioned with four additional [strings] made from white sandalwood, other types of white trees, and knots of *kuśa* grass.
With fifty seeds of the red lotus, red sandalwood, [seeds] from golden trees, and those produced from yellow *sāra* wood; || 7 ||
[The vessels] produced from Padmaka wood, those originating from Rajani wood, those originating from Devadāru wood, and those originating from Kṛṣṇa wood. || 8 ||
It was constructed with twenty-eight dark-colored gems;
it was made of śamī, nimba, and bimba wood, and produced from indra and bhadra.
It was constructed from the bones of monkeys, tigers, and bears, as well as other creatures,
and even bound together with the sinews of men, horses, donkeys, and elephants.

"That specific [rosary] should be prepared by the wise according to the distinction of each respective purpose. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the rosary of *kuśa*-grass knots is for Brahmins alone: "A Brahmin should recite with a *kuśa*-knot rosary; a king (Kṣatriya) with gold beads; a Vaiśya with *putrajīva* seeds; and all [castes] may likewise use lotus seeds. Thus it is stated.

According to the words of Nārada, for the recitation (*japa*) of Gopāla, a rosary of lotus seeds (*padmākṣa-mālā*) is highly recommended, because Gautama prescribes that alone, as follows: "Having become composed in mind, one should recite with a rosary known as the lotus-seed. Also, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "They say [this] is the best among the classes of recitations..."
"With lotus seeds that increase devotion. Even for Vaiṣṇavas, a rosary of rudrākṣas is highly praised;
for it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa, beginning with "He who, having become a devotee of the Bhagavat... and concluding with "...and with rudrākṣas, [attains] the highest."
Now follows the time for the consecration of the rosary (*japamālā*). Regarding this, the *Yoginītantra* states:
"On the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), the best of practitioners who know mantras should diligently fashion a Vaiṣṇava rosary during the divine portion [of the day] using a Viṣṇu mantra. (1)

Thus [it is said]. In the divine portion, during the forenoon; for the Śaktis as well, it should be performed at night after eating, according to the rule. However, the meal itself should be taken only during the day. On the eighth, the ninth, and likewise on the thirteenth [lunar days], it should be done in the same manner.
Likewise, O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform [this] for Śiva on the fourteenth day as well.
On the fourth [lunar day], that of Gaṇanātha; at midday, that of Bhāskara;
and on the seventh, O Goddess, O Sovereign of the World, it should be performed in the forenoon.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the Sūtras on that very same subject:
"A garland made of silk thread always pleases the Goddess;
a Vaiṣṇavī garland is likewise made of cotton or even of lotus fibers. (1)
A rosary for Śiva is proclaimed to be made either of wool or of bark fibers;
for others, one should prepare a prayer-bead string from cotton threads.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the specific details concerning cotton thread, they are found in that very same source. Then, having tripled the thread—which has been fashioned by a meritorious woman of the best of the twice-born and is devoid of knots—one should wash it with care. In the *Kālottara*, Skanda said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of creation, maintenance, and dissolution!"
O Maheśvara, how indeed should a rosary for recitation be made from rudrākṣa beads?
"And how, O dear one, should the consecration be performed, and what is its fruit?
Īśvara said:
"Listen, Ṣaṇmukha, I shall explain how it is performed with rudrākṣas."
By means of the prescribed method for the rosary, it bestows the perfection of recitation.
They should be made with one face, two faces, four faces, five faces, or six faces; however, one should avoid those that are mixed [in number].
One should place face against face, but one must avoid placing the base against the face;
the best Rudrākṣa is said to have its face facing forward and its back sloping downward.
This is declared to be the best when the size of an *āmalaka* fruit;
it is middling when the size of half a *badara* fruit, and inferior when the size of a chickpea.
That which is called Meru should be made with its face turned upward; one must not step over it.
It should be strung together with a new thread without touching it.
p.
354) Thus it is said. "Not touching one another" means that in the *Uttaratantra*, a single Meru should be assigned there for all [the deities], arising from the gross [form].
The first is gross; after that, it is lesser, and likewise still more minute.
Therefore, one should place them in sequence, since it is of the form of a serpent;
one should fashion each seed-syllable according to the rule, joined with a Brahma-knot.
Alternatively, it should be free of knots, provided with a firm cord,
wound three times around the middle, and wound half as many times at the end.
"The knot that winds to the right is designated as the *brahmagranthi*.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "Having first performed a single meal (*ekabhakta*), the practitioner himself should then tie [the knots];
the single meal, however, is on the previous day, not on that [very] day; otherwise, it would contradict [the rule] that [the rite] is to be performed in the forenoon."
Because eating is impossible and improper prior to the consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
one who has performed the daily obligatory rites, being pure and knowing the mantras, should carefully bring the dice as desired and as available upon the aforementioned dice-board. || 1 ||
Effort has been described regarding the avoidance of mixing up the faces.
[The teeth should be] mutually equal in form, neither too thick nor too thin, ungnawed by insects and the like, not decayed, and fresh. (2)

Having washed those [rudrākṣas] individually with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) on the previous day, one should first [use] *akṣa* seeds—that is, *rudrākṣa* seeds—according to one's desire, since it is taught that there is a difference in the fruit according to the difference in the number of faces. It should be understood that a single meal (*ekabhakta*) is prescribed for anyone except those who are physically incapable. As for the *pañcagavya*:
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
the milk of a golden-colored cow, the cow dung of a white one, the cow urine of a copper-colored one, and the curd of a blue-colored cow [are prescribed]. (1)
"Ghee from a black cow"—this refers to the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Furthermore, cows of various colors are easily found in whatever regions they may be.
Therein, one should procure the five products of the cow according to their respective colors;
if the colors cannot be obtained, there is no fault, but one should avoid using them in deficient quantities.
In the *pañcagavya* mixture, cow urine is said to be twice the amount of cow dung, ghee four times as much, milk eight times as much, and curd likewise.
Taking cow's urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with the ṛc "dadhikrāvṇo."

With the mantra "Tejo 'si śukram," one should wash [the image] with clarified butter; with "Devasya tvā," with water infused with Kuśa grass; and with the mantra "Sadyojāta," with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having stated "having washed," he himself explains how that is done: "immediately" with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and with water.
This is because of the statement in the *Tattvasāra*: "One should wash with the five products of the cow using the *sadyojāta* mantra, and with pure water.
One should rub [the object] with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, using the *vāmadeva* mantra.
One should fumigate it with black aloe-wood and suguggulu using the Aghora mantra.

One should smear [the object] with sandalwood and other substances using the mantra known as *tatpuruṣa*. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), camphor, musk, saffron, and so forth are included. One should consecrate each [substance] one hundred times with the fifth [mantra] alone. Furthermore, one should consecrate the *meru* with the fifth [mantra] and likewise with the *aghora* mantra. Thus it is said.
In the Śaiva Āgama: One should fashion a lotus shape with nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
there, one should place the thread and the gems, having washed them with scented water.
Having separately inscribed the Tāra, the Śakti, and the Mātṛkā upon the thread and the rudrākṣa beads,
one should worship them and offer oblations of clarified butter according to one's capacity.
Taking each individual gem, one should join it there upon the thread;
it should be made like a cow’s tail, tapering to a single point, or uniform throughout.
Having displayed the eight mudrās, one should worship each one in succession;
O Sadāśiva, [the rite] is always strung together with five mantras as before.

Thus [it is said]. With the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, the fire-oblation (homa) is also performed with these very same mantras, because it is necessary for the worship (pūjā) and the oblation to share a single mantra. "Ekāgra" means having a uniform form. As for the eight mudrās, they consist of the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, because the procedure for worship is prescribed immediately thereafter. Regarding the point that this consecration (saṃskāra) applies to other gems as well:
[To say otherwise] is merely the manifestation of ignorance. "This consecration (*saṃskāra*) of Rudrākṣas has been declared as enjoined by the Vedas;
however, for others, that prescribed in the Tantras must be performed by the Guru and the practitioner"—this is precisely because of the statement from the *Kālottara*.
Now, [I shall describe] the majesty of the Rudrākṣa, its origin, its various types, and their respective fruits. Regarding this:
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Formerly, there was a Daitya named Tripura who was exceedingly invincible;
by him all the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other deities—were conquered. (1)
For the sake of slaying Tripura, for the protection of the gods, for the destruction of the world's fear, and for the promotion of the laws of the seasons. || 2 ||
O son, that unsurpassed Aghora-weapon which I have meditated upon is composed of all the gods, divine, blazing, and of terrible form.
She remained there until her husband’s wife was finally seen;
by her, the eyes had been opened for thousands of divine years. (4)
From his two eyes, which were agitated and filled with tears, drops of water fell;
those very drops of tears became great rudrākṣa trees.
Having attained the state of immobility for the sake of favoring mortals,
they indeed bear fruit at all times, bestowing their fruits without interruption.

Thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha and the Laiṅga: "In ancient times, during the period when Śambhu was engaged in the task of crushing the Asuras for the sake of protecting Brahmā, Indra, and all the gods,
the water produced from the obstruction of his three eyes became, at that time, the multitude of Rudrākṣa trees."
One should wear ten Rudrākṣas on the neck, twenty-two on the head,
six on each ear, twelve on each of the two hands,
sixteen on each of the two arms according to the digits of the moon, and one on the crest-lock.
He who possesses one hundred and eight marks upon his chest is himself Nīlakaṇṭha. || 2 ||
Those who wear the rudrākṣa seed on the earth— in their hand, on their head, as well as on their chest and on the region of their back— [attain the highest state].
They dwell together as equals in the cities of Yama, Śatapatra, Netra, Padmāsana, Indra, the Suras, and the Kinnaras.
There are thirty-six [beads] for the garland on the head, twelve for the necklace around the neck,
sixteen are prescribed for the elbows, and twelve for the two wrists.
A sacred thread is prescribed as consisting of one hundred and eight strands;
half of that for the chest-garland, and one strand is said for the topknot.
The sequence of concentration (dhāraṇā) for the two ears is also said to be sixfold in number.
One should not perform it with fewer numbers; however, performing it with more does not cause any fault.
I shall now explain the different numbers for the rosary used for recitation:
twenty-five beads are for the purpose of liberation, while twenty-seven are for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
Thirty [verses] are for the attainment of wealth, and fifteen for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
There are four castes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
These [beads] are white, red, golden-hued, and black in sequence;
among these, the white one is most excellent for the purpose of making a rosary for recitation.
In the absence of those belonging to the twice-born, however, even members of their own respective castes may be used;
provided they are neither too thick nor too thin, not cracked, not fragile, and not light.
A Rudrākṣa that is broken, previously worn, or decayed is not considered excellent.
In the case of a bead, the elevated part is the face, while the depressed part is the back.
O child, one should arrange the beads in a single direction like a row of fine teeth;
for by rubbing against one another, the loss of the recitation will certainly occur.
With that firm cord, in the form of three coils, auspicious knots should be made in the middle of each other. (13)
The faces of the rudrākṣas range from four to fourteen in sequence;
their fruits for wearing them shall now be described according to rule and in order. (14)
Śiva with one face directly removes the sin of killing a Brahmin; Śiva and the Goddess with two faces certainly destroy the sin of killing a cow. 15.
The three-faced fire himself instantly removes the sin of killing a woman;
the four-faced Brahmā himself dispels the sin of killing a preceptor.
One who directly bears Śiva with five faces is liberated from all sins;
one who bears Kārttikeya with six faces should wear him on the right hand. (17)
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt about this.
There is a great serpent with seven mouths, known by the name Ananta.
A man is forever liberated from the sins of killing a cow and stealing gold;
he becomes the eight-faced Mahāsena, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God manifest. || 19 ||
His obstacles perish, and at the end he attains the supreme goal;
one should wear Bhairava with nine faces on the left hand.
He is declared to be the bestower of enjoyment and liberation; he shall be as powerful as I am.
O child, he shall have ten faces and is the Lord Janārdana himself in person.
The afflictions arising from piśācas, grahas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and pannagas,
as well as all other possible defects, are swiftly destroyed by its retention.
Eleven Rudrākṣas on the face are considered to be the eleven Rudras;
one should always wear them on the crest-lock—listen now to the fruit of his merit. (23)
Whatever fruit results from a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows; [that fruit one obtains by bathing here]. || 24 ||
One attains that fruit by wearing an eleven-faced rudrākṣa;
the twelve-faced rudrākṣa is identical with the twelve-fold sun.
O child, if one wears a thirteen-faced Rudrākṣa, he obtains the fruit of many gold, horse, and cow sacrifices through its wearing.
If one should wear a fourteen-faced Rudrākṣa, it is constantly worshipped by the gods and the highest merit is attained. (27)

But when that [state] is eternally established upon the crown of the head, the man who dies then becomes himself the one whose face consists of purity and who bears the crescent moon upon his head. (28)
O Six-faced One, listen to the truth: he is constantly worshipped by the gods, he acquires abundant merit, and he becomes a fortunate man. (29)

During bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation; || 30 ||
And whatever Vedic rite a Brahmin who has become a wearer of Rudrākṣa beads should constantly perform, that rite shall become fruitful. || 31 ||
Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"By merely wearing Rudrākṣas on the neck, the head, the hands, the ears, and as a sacred thread, a human being becomes Rudra. (1)
Thus it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"A Brahmin should wear rudrākṣas during the twilight prayers and other rituals;
all that is declared to be fruitful, certainly multiplied a hundred thousand-fold. (1)
The merit from seeing a Rudrākṣa shall be like that from seeing a sacred emblem (liṅga);
furthermore, by wearing it, a person obtains a hundred-fold crore of merit.
By wearing it on the head, one gains ten million [merits]; on the ears, one hundred million;
by tying it around the neck, one billion; and on the crown of the head, ten billion.
Ten thousandfold for wearing it as a sacred thread, and a hundred thousand times ten millionfold for wearing it on both arms;
one who wears excellent rudrākṣas on his hand shall obtain immeasurable fruit.
Thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha-laiṅga:
"Whether eating meat, drinking liquor, or associating with those of the lowest castes, one's soul becomes instantly purified if a rudrākṣa is placed upon the head. (1)
Thus, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"If even a dog dies with a rudrākṣa resting upon its neck, it too attains the state of Rudra; how much more so for humans and others? (1)
Whether one is impure from eating leftovers, engaged in forbidden acts, or burdened by all manner of sins,
a man is liberated from all evils by wearing Rudrākṣa beads.
Even one who is devoid of devotion, yet constantly wears a rosary of rudrākṣas around his neck, is honored in the world of Rudra despite being a performer of sinful deeds. || 3 ||

Thus [it is said]. In the Śaiva Purāṇa: "If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing Rudrākṣa beads, he does not obtain the fruit thereof. In the Vāsiṣṭha and Laiṅga [Purāṇas]:
"O great sage, those who feel shame regarding the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads..."
O Brahman, their lineage succession would become intermixed.

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding other specific types of beads, it is stated in the Yoginītantra: "The most excellent practitioner, having fashioned a rosary strung with the aforementioned threads upon the aforementioned beads, and having placed it in a vessel smeared with perfumes and other substances... (1)
Having completed the worship beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform worship there;
having invoked Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā, one should worship them.
Having cast it into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the *hauṃ* mantra,
the knower of mantras should lift that rosary from there and place it in a golden vessel.
The wise one, having performed the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for those two [deities] in sequence with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, ending with incense; || 4 ||
Having gradually established [the image] right there, one should bathe it with cool waters;
then, with sandalwood, fragrant flowers, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Having smeared it [with unguents], one should recite the *hsauṃ* seed-syllable one hundred and eight times;
upon it, one should also worship the nine planets and the guardians of the directions.
Then, having worshipped the Guru, one should take up the auspicious rosary.
Thus it is said. In the Bhairavītantra:
first [one should worship] the god Gaṇapati, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Umāpati.
And the wise man, being well-composed, should worship Durgā with a garland.
One should cast the rosary, consecrated with the Prāsāda mantra, into the five products of the cow;
then, having lifted it up, one should place that rosary in a golden vessel.
Here, having bathed [the deity] with the *pañcāmṛta* and with cool water, using the *prāsāda-mantra* to be mentioned later,
[one should worship] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Then, having performed the consecration with this mantra,
the knower of mantras [should visualize] the vital breath mounted upon the individual soul (jīva) and adorned with the vowel sound Oṃ.
One should properly install the King of Mantras, joined with the Bindu and Nāda;
then, having worshipped the nine planets, one should perform the worship of the Guardians of the Directions.
Then, one should perform oblations according to one's ability with sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
one should give gold as a sacrificial fee and satisfy the Brahmins.

"By this [mantra] *prāsāda*," means that one should perform the placement (*pravinyaset*) and recite it one hundred and eight times. *Prāṇa* is the syllable *ha*, and *jīva* is the syllable *sa*; thus, it is *hsoṃ*. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the teacher (*ācārya*).
In the absence of a golden vessel, a vessel made of *aśvattha* wood should be taken, according to the statement in the *Uktayoginītantra*. As for another method, the *Kubjikātantra* states:
"One should first worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments."
Being greatly delighted, he should have a pure garland made of gold and silver.
The wise practitioner should fashion the threaded garland according to the appropriate proportions;
it should be made according to the measurement of the [deity's] color and soaked for three days in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

"By the measure of the syllables" means by the measure of the syllables of the *mātṛkā*, that is, by their number. By this it is established that the rosary should be made with beads numbering one hundred.
Furthermore, on the fourth day, one should wash the string as well with the mantras of the *astra*.
One should measure [the ground] with a thread of the same color while reciting the Hṛdayamantra.
Or the most excellent practitioner should tie it with threads of gold and other such qualities;
then he should apply either a Brahma-knot or a Naga-noose.
Then, intent on meditation, one should bind the rosary with the Kavaca mantra;
finally, at the end of all [the beads], one should place the Meru bead provided with two threads.
The supreme practitioner should string [the beads] by means of the *tāra*-yoga and bind them;
having thus completed this, O Goddess of Gods, he should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having drawn a mandala upon the sacrificial ground according to the sequence of the prescribed rules for each portion,
one should worship the chosen deity in due order and according to the proper method.
The *maṇḍala* is the circle for the worship of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Having completed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times,
and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, offering whatever is dear to whichever deity it may be.

By the phrase "that which is dear," it is stated that one should perform the oblation with whichever substance has been prescribed for whichever deity during the preliminary fire-sacrifice (puraścaraṇāṅgahoma).
Then, the wise practitioner should place that rosary in the center of the mandala.
Then, having performed the placement of the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should then perform the placement of the root-mantra (mūlamantra).

Having performed the placement of those limbs, one should contemplate them as being like a deity; having attained a state of non-difference, one should then fashion the rosary as being of that very nature.
Then, having thus established the chosen deity within the rosary, that best of practitioners should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the preceptor and the artisan according to the prescribed rite;
he should not recite another mantra there if he desires his own success.

Thus, the mantra to be recited, such as the weapon-mantra (*astra*), should be taken; the offering (*bali*) for the rosary should be made with those same oblation substances. Likewise, it is stated in the *Uttaratantro*: "One should employ a firm thread for the recitation, according to one's preference."
Furthermore, having tied a new thread onto a worn-out one, one should recite the mantra one hundred times. || 1 ||
Thus it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
"When the rosary has been broken, one should string it again as before;
once it has been consecrated, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. (1)

Thus: "Likewise, one should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should one shake or swing it. One should not touch it with the left hand, nor allow it to fall from the hand. When moving the beads, one should move them with the thumb and not touch another bead. During the time of recitation, the wise person should never [touch] the *meru* bead."

One should not cross over [the thread]; at the time of changing [the thread], one must certainly not make a sound. If there is a sound, a quarrel will arise; if it moves, the mind will waver. If it moves, there is enmity; if it breaks, disease occurs.
If it falls from the hand, there is a great obstacle; if the thread is cut, one perishes. Some, however, maintain that the recitation (japa) should be performed with the fingers alone.
They say it should be performed; in this regard, the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) should be considered, though in reality it should also be understood from the *puraścaraṇa* [sections].

In the absence of a rosary (*japamālā*), the counting of the recitation (*japa*) should be done with the hand alone. And it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Then one may also begin the rite of recitation using the fingers alone. Also in the *Prapañcasāra* (20.40):

Seated in the lotus posture, facing east, refraining from idle chatter, and fixing his mind upon that [deity], he should perform the recitation with his fingers—excluding the thumb—using a rosary, neither too fast nor too slow. || 1 ||
Thus it is said. In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "One should perform the counting of the recitations (*japa*) either by means of the fingers or by the finger-joints.
Regarding that method, the *Śrībhairavītantra* states:
"Starting from the ring finger and the middle finger, proceeding in sequence through the little finger..."
The rosary is proclaimed to extend from the middle finger to the root [of the thumb]. || 1 ||

Thus it is said. Gautama also says: "One should always perform the recitation (*japa*) with the little finger, the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger. When the counting is performed over the nine joints—starting from the base of the ring finger, the middle finger, and the little finger, and proceeding through their middles and tips, as well as the tips and middles of the ring finger, and finally the middle and bases of the middle finger—the recitation is completed nine times.

The recitation (*japa*) takes place. Thus, by repeating [the mantra] twelve times over and over again, the recitation becomes one of one hundred and eight [times]. By repeating it one hundred and twelve times, the recitation becomes one of one thousand and eight. In this manner, it should be inferred for ten thousand (*ayuta*) and other numbers as well; however, in reality, this is based on the observation of other tantras.
The recitation (*japa*) should be performed with the fingers together with the index finger (*tarjanī*). As it is stated in the *Kulamūlāvatāra* (p.
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall explain the fruit of counting in recitation."
The fruit arising from counting on the fingers is traditionally held to be of single-fold merit.
One should know that [the merit] from a line [of beads] is eightfold; with *putrajīva* seeds it is ten times more;
with remaining gems it would be a hundredfold; and with coral it is a thousandfold.
With crystal beads, ten thousand [repetitions] are said [to be achieved]; with pearls, a hundred thousand;
with lotus seeds, ten hundred thousand; and with golden beads, ten million is said [to be achieved]. (3)
With knots of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* beads, the merit becomes infinitely multiplied; with rosaries of white lotus seeds, the fruit of the recitation shall be immeasurable.
Performing the recitation with the fingers, one should recite using all the fingers including the thumb;
O Dear One, that which is recited without the thumb becomes fruitless.
O beloved, one should recite daily using the joints of the fingers;
here, O beloved, it is the two middle joints of the middle and ring fingers.
Performing the visualization of Mount Meru while circumambulating in successive order,
starting from the root joint of the ring finger and proceeding through the sequence ending with the little finger.
O Goddess, one should count in this very sequence from the tip of the index finger to the base of the middle finger, while slightly contracting the palm.
O Maheśvarī, one should not separate the fingers during the time of recitation;
for if the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away through the gaps.
O Goddess, one should never recite a mantra while disregarding the count, for the Rākṣasas forcibly seize that recitation, O Īśānī. (10)
Alternatively, O Dear One, O Goddess, having made the base-joint of the middle finger the Mount Meru, one should recite [the mantra] up to the base-joint of the index finger.
"Indeed, in a clockwise sequence starting from the first joint of the ring finger and the middle finger.
Here, the recitation with the hand (*karamālājapa*) is threefold: recitation on the fingers (*aṅgulījapa*), recitation on the lines (*rekhājapa*), and recitation on the joints (*parvajapa*).
Among these, *aṅgulījapa* consists of counting repeatedly from the little finger up to the thumb.
Japa performed by means of the lines on the fingers beginning with the little finger is *rekhājapa* (line-japa), and that which is performed by means of the joints is *parvajapa* (joint-japa);
these are indeed defined by the characteristics already mentioned. As stated in the *Mātṛkārṇava*: "Those letters of the white mantra, distinguished as vowels and consonants..."
Having separated them from those [other letters], one should specifically form the *varṇamālā* (the garland of phonemes). || 1 ||
The wise one should make Mount Meru the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and perform recitation with that rosary;
success will indeed come quickly—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 2 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, having understood the excess of syllables through the various sequences of the *prastāra*, one should [place] the consonants in the positions of those elemental letters. (3)
Having joined each of those elements with their respective vowels, the wise one should apply three vowels,
making the primary syllable of each element the "Meru" (the central pivot).
One should recite that mantra there with a rosary; success is certain.
[Success is achieved] with a rosary made of pills from the powder of medicinal herbs corresponding to the number of syllables in the mantra.
"One should recite [the mantra]; there will be the accomplishment of all goals; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the practices prescribed for the time of *puraścaraṇa*, Nārada states therein:
"Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra..."
Undistractedness and perseverance are the causes for the successful accomplishment of the recitation. || 1 ||
Thus, in the *Trailokyasammohana-tantra*:
"One who is free from greed and envy, and devoid of desire and anger, attains accomplishment in every way; otherwise, it shall be fruitless. (1)
Thus [spoke] Agastya:

"Whatever duties prescribed for one's caste and stage of life—whether they be obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—one should perform those very actions with the mind fixed upon them and making them one's supreme goal. (1)
Self-controlled, bathing three times a day, observing silence, with his inner self cleansed,
steady-minded in his ritual actions, and with his senses restrained, he should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite.
Thus said Gautama:
"O best of the twice-born, for him who delights in his own duty, success is not far off; for another, however, there would be no success even from afar."

"It is the truth, there is no doubt, that even for a cruel person there would be no success; how much less so for another who is devoted to his own duty, even after a long period of time. From the *Mantrārṇava*:
"Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, and freedom from malice..."
One should bathe daily at the three sessions of the day and avoid minor, trivial activities. || 1 ||
Daily worship, daily charity, the praise and glorification of the deity, occasional rites of adoration, and faith in the Guru and the God. (2)
"These twelve qualities rooted in Japanīṣṭha shall grant the perfection of mantra.
Thus it is said. Celibacy (*brahmacāritva*) is the cessation of the eightfold sexual union. As stated by Gorakṣa:
"Remembering, praising, longing, looking, secret conversation,"
Volition, determination, and the very accomplishment of action. || 1 ||
The wise declare this eightfold sexual union;
celibacy is the opposite of this very same thing, characterized by these eight qualities. (2)

Thus, longing, recollection preceded by longing, verbal proclamation, and gazing are forbidden. *Keli* refers to external activities such as jesting and the like. *Guhyabhāṣaṇa* is secret consultation for the purpose of sexual union.
*Saṃkalpa* is mental action. *Adhyavasāya* is the determination to engage in sexual union. [The rule applies] three times a day.

Bathing is prescribed for those who are capable. It is declared that bathing should be performed at the three junctions of the day; however, due to incapacity, one may perform it twice or even once—thus says the statement of Śaṃpāyana. As for minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*), Nārāyaṇīya quotes another Smṛti: "Deceit, hatred, as well as eradication (*utsāda*), expulsion (*uccāṭa*), delusion, killing, and disease. This concludes the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).

Since the rule for recitation (*japa*) always precedes the libation (*tarpaṇa*), there is a special worship (*viśeṣapūjā*) at the beginning of occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as the *āmayana*. As it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Having performed the libation with devotion one thousand and eight times..."
That which one should mutter every day is known as the daily (nitya) recitation. || 1 ||
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on the twelfth lunar day, and on the full moon—on these occasions, the recitation is occasional (naimittika). || 2 ||
"Then, from the daily [recitation], that [number] is tripled, and likewise the worship of Hari.
Thus it is stated in the *Kapilapañcarātra*: "The mantra should be recited on the lunar days (tithi), stars (nakṣatra), and days of the week (vāra) dedicated to the deity. And likewise, Gautama says:
Then one should worship the lotus-feet of the guru with handfuls of flowers;
from him, blessings should always be received, and thereafter one should practice contentment.
"When the guru is satisfied, O God, the Lord is satisfied; it cannot be otherwise.
Likewise, there is the word of the Blessed One:
"For him whose guru is satisfied, the three worlds are satisfied."
When the Guru, the Sage, is well-pleased, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished.

"One should place the words of the guru in one's heart and never transgress them. Thus [it is said]. Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) states: "One should bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure myrobalan (amalaka) alone."
Immediately thereafter, one should bathe with mantras declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. || 1 ||
"One should constantly perform what is to be performed, being pure and most observant of vows.

Thus it is said. In the *Prapañcasāra* (10.41): "Then, eating only sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) or eating only at night, one should likewise mutter the mantra. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
One's food, consisting of alms and other such restricted items, is prescribed to be taken once at night; or one may take food every day consisting of tubers, roots, and fruits. (1)

Thus it is said in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*: "The mantra-practitioner should possess a pure mind toward his guru, cows, brahmins, children, and those who are distressed, blind, or miserable; he should never commit an act of malice against them. (1)
"Afterwards, having honored the cows, one should give them a very beautiful morsel of food.
Thus [says] Gautama:
"Devotion toward cows should always be practiced, as well as service toward cows."
When the cows are always pleased, even the cowherd becomes pleased. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Now, the forbidden [acts] are stated in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*:
"A wise man should never speak unpleasantly to anyone, nor should he ever speak untruth; he should not step upon the shadow of a *vibhītaka* or a *karañja* tree. (1)
One should not do anything for anyone else, nor should one accept anything during the recitation;
one should not perform an oil massage, and one should avoid honey and meat. || 2 ||
O Goddess, one should not engage in conversation with women while being deluded;
nor should one go naked, nor be heavily perfumed, and one should avoid singing and instrumental music.

Thus [it is said]: "One should not accept [alms]"—this applies when it is possible; however, if it is impossible, one should accept only the alms obtained on that very day, according to the rule regarding the bringing of food (*bhakṣamāna*). "Deluded" means being under the sway of desire. From the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should not take shelter in the shade of the *vibhītaka*, *arka*, *kārañja*, or *snuhī* trees. [This was said by] Agastya (*kumbhasambhava*).

Constantly free from desire for women and other such objects through the actions of speech, mind, and body, [he avoids] speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, atheists, or those who have consumed leftovers. (1)
One should always avoid speaking what is untrue or vulgar;
nor should one speak even with the correct words during the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, worship, and so forth.
One should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music, watching dances, as well as chewing betel, applying perfumes and ointments, and wearing flowers. (3)
One should avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it;
one should strictly avoid improper speech and the worship of others. (4)
One should avoid crookedness, shaving, anointing with oil, eating food that has not been offered, performing actions without prior resolve, and activities such as massaging.
One should abandon bathing with warm water, as well as the use of fragrant *āmalaka* and similar substances.
Regarding what is obtainable, Nārada states the following expiation:
"If a sound is uttered even once, one should utter the *praṇava*."
Even when the word "pāmara" has been uttered, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) once.
After enduring much idle chatter, one should then recite the mantra while placing the limbs [in their respective positions];
likewise after sneezing, and similarly upon touching places that should not be touched.

Thus [it is said]. Yogi-Yājñavalkya states: "If, in any way whatsoever, there should be a lapse of silence during japa and other rites, one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the immutable Viṣṇu. (1)
Thus, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Upon seeing, speaking to, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those of the lowest birth; upon sneezing, passing wind, or yawning—one should cease the recitation. (1)
Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) for these [mantras],
one should properly recite the remainder, or else perform the visualization of the Sun and other deities.
Having seen a cat, a cock, a curlew, a dog, a vulture, a donkey, or a monkey, one should perform ritual sipping (ācamana) and then carry out one's duties; having touched them, bathing is prescribed.
"One who performs the *puraścaraṇa* should observe such rules as these.
Likewise, the venerable word of Śiva states:
"Anger, sneezing, and intoxication—these three, along with spitting and yawning [must be avoided]."
And one should avoid the sight of low-caste dogs during the performance of the recitation of prayers.
Having sipped water, he should, if possible, remember me along with you, or gaze upon the luminaries, or perform the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma). || 2 ||
Thus [it is said]. "Me" refers to Maheśvara. "Together with you" means together with Pārvatī. In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"The sun, fire, the moon, as well as the planets, lunar mansions, and stars—these are called luminaries by the wise, and likewise the Brāhmaṇas. (1)
Thus it is said:
"Anger, pride, hunger, drowsiness, spitting, yawning, looking at a dog, sleep, and idle chatter—these are the enemies of japa. (2)
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having bathed, one should mutter [the name] while seated; in cases such as sneezing or stumbling during worship, one should proclaim the name of Kṛṣṇa seven times. (1)
Thus, in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"When the best of mantra-knowers perceives something impure at the time of recitation, he should then perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and thereafter complete the remainder. (1)
And when the mantra-practitioner himself should likewise become impure,
he should bathe and sip water according to the rule, perform the ritual placements (nyāsa), and recite [the mantra] once more.

Thus [it is said]. Nyāsa (ritual placement) effects the qualification [for the rite]. By this, it is understood according to Vaiśampāyana that in the event of impurity arising from the voiding of urine and so forth, one should bathe; otherwise, having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the six-limbed nyāsa, one should complete the remainder of the rite.
There is no fruit for one who does not bathe, nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors,
nor for one who does not satisfy the gods, nor for one who speaks untruth.
"One should not recite the mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor while distracted by many garments.
Thus it is said in the *Yoginītantra*: "Recitation without resolve is that which is characterized by utter lack of faith in the act of recitation."
Laziness and the inability to cultivate meditative absorption certainly lead to the destruction of spiritual accomplishments. || 1 ||
One should abandon malicious gossip and avoid slander;
one should avoid contact with wicked people and abandon that which arises from suspicion and the like.
Thus it is said in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:

"One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one whose head-ornament is loose, one whose neck is covered, one whose hands lack the purificatory ring (pavitra), one who is impure, or one who is talking idly—such a person should never perform japa. (1)
Having placed his hands uncovered upon his head, or even being covered [by a cloth], or with a mind distracted by anxiety, or angry, or bewildered, or overcome by hunger; || 2 ||
Whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing,
one should recite [the mantra] on a street or in an inauspicious place, but not in a place of darkness.
Nor should one recite with feet covered by sandals, nor while seated on a vehicle or a bed;
one should not recite with the feet stretched out, nor while sitting in the utkaṭāsana posture.
Thus, in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:

"If, due to distraction or laziness, one rises during the intervals of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), or worship (*arcana*), then one should again perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (1)

Thus [it is said]. *Apavitraka* refers to the *pavitra*, which is *kuśa*. For the lexicon (*kośa*) states: "The word *kuśa* is not feminine; it denotes *kuśa* grass and the *darbha-pavitra*. Because the *Kūrma Purāṇa* declares its necessity with the words: "Whatever rite is performed without *darbha* grass, or again without the sacred thread (*sūtra*), all that becomes demonic (*rākṣasa*); it does not yield fruit in this world or the next."

The *sūtra* is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Viṣṇu also says: "Having bathed, with hands and feet well-washed, pure, with his topknot tied, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, having sipped water (*ācamana*), sitting facing either the east or the north, silent and meditative, one should worship the deities. In that rite, there should be many *kuśa* blades on the left and [fewer] on the right.
This is the technical definition of *pavitra* (the purifier). Thus, at the commencement of the *saṃdhyā*, Kātyāyana says:
"Having placed *kuśa* grass in his left hand, one should perform the act of sipping water (*ācamana*).
The *kuśas* used for ritual practice should be short, while those for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should be long. (1)

It is said that *darbha* grass is the purifier; therefore, in rites such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), the left hand should hold the water-vessel (*upagraha*) and the right hand should hold the *pavitra* grass-ring.

Thus [it is said]. "On the left" means on the left side. Now, one might ask: what kind are to be held in the right hand, and what kind are to be held in the left? To this he says: the short ones are for the purpose of performing the *pārvaṇa*, the five great sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*), and so forth; the long ones, known as *barhis*, are for the purpose of spreading out the sacrificial grass (*prastāra-paristaraṇa*). In rites other than these performances, such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and others, many *darbha* blades are required.

Those [objects] devoid of specific distinction are the means for purification in ritual acts, but not a single one alone. For it has been stated by Pāraskara, Gobhila, and others: "The grasping of *kuśa* grass," "with *kuśa* in hand," and "one should keep the hand not empty with gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass. Therefore, due to the absence of a specific rule, the left hand is used in the *saṃdhyā* and other rites.

"A fistful of kuśa grass; the right [hand] [holds] a pavitra made of kuśa, with its tip intact, consisting of two blades, one span in length—this is to be known as the pavitra for any rite whatsoever. Thus equipped with the pavitra of the described characteristics, one should, having set aside the first (which has an internal core), the second (which is split at the core), and the third (which has an internal core within a core), take the fourth.
[The hand] should be held [empty]. Laghuhārīta says:
"During recitation, burnt offerings, giving, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors, one should ensure that the hand is not empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass. (1)

Thus [it is said]. As for the wearing of gold, it is on the right ring finger; for in the section concerning the wearing of gold, there is a statement from the *Devīpurāṇa*: "That [gold] should be worn on the ring finger of the right hand. However, silver is to be worn on the forefinger. Wherever a ritual action is enjoined but the specific limb of the performer is not mentioned, the right [limb] is to be understood therein.

Based on the statement of Kātyāyana, "The other [finger] is to be known as the performer of actions," and because the root of the index finger (*tarjanī*) is the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, it is logical that the wearing of silver for the gods should be done precisely there; this is established as authoritative by the practice of the great people (*mahājana*), and thus silver [is worn] on the index finger.

And because of the statement written in the *Smṛtisamuccaya*: "It should be worn... twisted clockwise and counter-clockwise and provided with a *brahmagranthi*. According to the statement, "One should cross over [the finger] by only one joint, but one should not cross over a second," the *pavitra* should be worn on the joint of the middle finger of the ring finger (*anāmā*) together with the knot. One should perform this at the time of ritual action.

And because of the statement of Śaṅkha: "One should step over the ring-finger together with the pavitra; one may step over its first joint, but one must not step over the second. Furthermore, the use of the plural number in the phrase "with gold and silver" indicates that wearing [the ornaments] in multiple ways is an auxiliary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*). And that...

It is also logically consistent that the universals (jāti) of curd-ness, gold-ness, and silver-ness reside [in their substrates] starting from the dyad (dvyaṇuka) onwards, even when they are apprehended as a single unit. In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
