"A rite performed without water, or a rite performed without *darbha* grass..."
And without clarified butter (ājya), those oblations will not yield any fruit at all.
Thus, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "Kuśa grass, kāśa, barley, dūrvā, uśīra, and śara in equal parts; wheat, rice, muñja, and valvaja—these are the ten types of darbha. (1)
On the new moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one who is pure should gather darbha grass;
these darbhas, being untiring, may be employed again and again.
Born together with Viriñci, O you who are produced from the creation of Parameṣṭhin;
dispel all evils and be the bringer of well-being for me. || 3 ||
Having recited this mantra, then facing either the east or the north,
one should cut [the hair] once with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and remove it.
For rites for the ancestors (pitrya), auspicious green blades that are uncut and have undried tips should be used;
for rites for the gods (daivika) and for activities such as japa, those that are rootless should be employed.
Kuśa grass with seven blades is prescribed for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors;
the two purifiers (pavitraka) should be without internal nodes, possess tips, and be one span in length.
The purifier for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four darbha-blades;
one blade is omitted for each successive social class (varṇa), according to the sequence.
For all [rites], it is auspicious when knotted with two [strings];
however, for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), three should be used, and likewise five for rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*).
In the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), it should be performed four times; in the case of hatred (*dveṣa*), twice; and in other cases, once.
Accompanied by a *pavitra* and *darbha* grass, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) as an auxiliary part of the rite.

That [water] does not become *ucchiṣṭa* (leftover) for him; however, one should avoid water that has been made *ucchiṣṭa* by those who have performed the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*), or the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*).
The discarding of those darbha grasses that have been in contact with feces, urine, and the like is prescribed;
likewise, those situated at the waist-knot and those standing upon the sacrificial ground must be discarded.
While the darbha grass is held in the left hand, one should drink with the right;
however, there is no fault in drinking while holding water from a cloth or other such vessel.
One should never sip water using the *brahmagranthi* (the sacred thread knot) nor with *dūrvā* grass,
during bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, giving gifts, Vedic study, or the libations to the ancestors.
One should perform the rite with hands provided with a pavitra and darbha grass, and not otherwise;
in the absence of kuśa grass, however, kāśa grass may be used, for kāśa is remembered as being equal to kuśa.
In the absence of *kāśa* grass, other suitable *darbha* grasses should be taken.
One should not cut it while wet, nor at night, nor during the two twilights.
"In the absence of *darbha* grass, one may perform the ritual even with gold, silver, or copper.
Let this suffice for the details. In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"One whose hands are not purified, who is naked, or whose head is covered—even if [otherwise prepared]..."
Or if one mutters while talking, it is said to be fruitless for as long as that lasts. || 1 ||
Thus it is said. Ātreya states: "One is naked if one wears dirty clothes; likewise, one is naked with wet garments.
One is naked with double-layered clothes; likewise, one is naked with glossy garments. (1)
"With two folds, without an upper garment, naked, and indeed without clothing.
Thus it is said. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"With two folds, with a remaining fold, and likewise with a fold outside."
Wearing a single loincloth, having no loincloth at all, or being naked—this is remembered as the fivefold [classification]. || 1 ||
Thus says Devala: "One who wears many garments becomes as if naked; one who is naked is [only truly] clothed by a loincloth. Kātyāyana states:
"One should not perform giving, sipping water (ācamana), fire-offerings (homa), eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or the libation (tarpaṇa) with the feet raised off the ground."
He who has placed his feet upon the seat, with his knees and shanks likewise [there], and has performed the *avasakthikā* posture, is called *prauḍhapāda*. (2)

Thus [it is said]. However, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, after stating the aforementioned rules, it is said: "All this applies thus when one is capable; if one is incapable, one should perform the recitation by means of [the power of] Śakti."
Then, regarding recitation (japa) therein, the Pot-born Sage [Agastya] said:

"Recitation is indeed the constant repetition of the mantra obtained from the guru; it is traditionally held that this recitation is preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the internal syllables. (1)
Thus [it is said]. "Aṅga" is an address to Sutīkṣṇa. The connection is that "japa" (recitation) is the internal revolving of syllables. The Vāyavīya-saṃhitā states its varieties:
"Japa may be vocal, whispered, or mental, consisting of the repetition of syllables."
Whoever [recites] with high, low, and circumflex tones, with words and syllables clearly articulated; || 1 ||
One should recite the mantra with the voice; that is known as vocal (vācika) recitation.
One should utter the mantra slowly and move the lips slightly.
That which is audible to some extent is known as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation;
that which is performed with the tongue alone is to be understood as *jihvājapa* (tongue-recitation). || 3 ||

When one utters, through the intellect and with the recollection of the meaning, the sequence of syllables consisting of words, letters, and vowels, that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa). || 4 ||
Muttering aloud (uccairjapa) is superior to sacrifice and other rites by tenfold;
whispered (upāṃśu) it is a hundredfold superior, and mental (mānasa) recitation is declared to be a thousandfold superior. || 5 ||
Thus it is said in the Nāradapañcarātra:
"The verbal [japa] is for all ritual actions; the whispered [japa] is for all spiritual accomplishments;
the mental [japa] is for matters concerning liberation; and one should indeed meditate in every respect. (1)
Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Of all sacrifices, the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) is praised;
for by not harming living beings, a great fruit indeed arises. (1)
"The best of the twice-born who is devoted to Japan obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
And there is the word of the Blessed Lord: "Among sacrifices, I am the knower of Japa. In the *Padma* and *Nāradīya* [Purāṇas]:
"Whatever ritual sacrifices there may be, and whatever blazing austerities,"
All of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). || 1 ||
By constant recitation, the deity, being praised, becomes pleased;
being pleased, she bestows abundant enjoyments and eternal liberation. (2)
Thus, in the Bhṛgusaṃhitā:
"The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña)—all these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). (1)

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the seats, Nārada says therein: "Provided with *kuśa* grass, deerskin, and cloth, measuring four finger-breadths in height, four cubits or two cubits in width, very firm, soft, and pure. (1)
"Having prepared a seat, one should begin the rite of recitation.
Thus said Vaiśampāyana:
"A tiger skin for all accomplishments; a deer skin for the accomplishment of knowledge."
A seat made of cloth removes disease, while one made of cane increases prosperity.
"Silk is to be known as nourishing, and woolen cloth (*kambala*) as the liberator from suffering.

Thus [it is said]. "Woolen cloth" refers to *āvikam* (wool). For, according to the statement of the *Brahmayāmala* to be cited later, a fault is heard regarding sitting on a seat consisting of mere cloth. Among cloths, woolen cloth is the best seat for the satisfaction of the deity.

Thus, from the statement of the *Uttaratantra*: Bhṛgu says— "For the sake of desired objects, a woolen blanket (*kambala*) is indeed the bestower of what is wished for; specifically, a red woolen blanket [is used].
The attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa occurs upon a layer of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass. (1)
Thus, in the Brahmayāmala:
"The two blankets are white and red, variegated, blue and yellow;
there is also a tiger skin and an antelope skin, along with various other types of seats. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding prohibited seats, the *Sārasaṃgraha* states: "A practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, bricks, stone, earth, grass, or leaves, as it bestows poverty, disease, and suffering. (1)

A householder who has not been initiated should never enter [the sacred enclosure] wearing the skin of a black antelope; however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a celibate student, and one who has completed his Vedic studies may enter. (2)
Thus, in the *Brahmayāmala*: "Grass, shoots, wood, stone, as well as earthenware, a bamboo seat, cloth, and a bare ground seat. (1)
O Goddess, one should thus avoid these eight kinds of seats:
on a seat of grass there will be disease, and on a seat of sprouts there is delusion of the mind. (2)
Likewise, on a stone seat there is eradication [of power], and on a clay seat there will be fever;
sitting on the bare earth causes affliction, sin, boils, and suffering. (3)
On a bamboo seat, one becomes poor; on a cloth, there is the destruction of one's position;
there is intense anxiety, loss, various types of fever, and distress. || 4 ||
Diseases such as grief and colic, as well as death, may occur on a wooden seat;
thus, O Goddess, one should avoid these eight seats in all ritual activities.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the preliminary rites for the day preceding the recitation (*japa*). Regarding this, the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra* states:
"On an auspicious moment and under a favorable lunar mansion (at a pure time), one who is firm in his vows, having obtained the permission of the Guru, should then commence the ritual. (1)
Thus [spoke] Sanatkumāra:
"Now I shall describe the supreme preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the mantra.
Having performed the ritual ablution according to rule and having received the mantra from the mouth of the Guru... (1)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule at an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion, and on a propitious day,
one should satisfy the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other such gifts.

Having satisfied the preceptor and himself with land, wealth, garments, ornaments, and other gifts, he should thereafter commence the recitation (japa), preceded by the preceptor’s permission. || 2 ||

Thus, in the *Prathamatantra*: "Having worshipped the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) according to the rule. As for the mantra for the oblation:
first the two words 'ehi' (come), then 'viduṣi', and finally the two words 'muru'."
Furthermore, there are two Mañjaya [mudrās] and likewise two Tarjaya [mudrās]. || 1 ||
Then, [one should worship] the pair of feet of Vighna, which are intent upon Mahābhairava;
[and one should worship] the pair [of feet] of Kṣetrapāla, who accepts the offering (bali), and of Pāvakasundarī. 2.
This is declared to be the bali-mantra, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
likewise, one should offer the bali-oblation to the retinue with this very mantra.

Thus [it is said]. The mantra will be explained in the section on ritual application (*prayoga*). Following that, the fast (*upavāsa*) must be observed. Now, regarding the commencement of the recitation (*japa*), it is stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"In this manner, during the lunar mansion, the lunar day (*tithi*), and so forth, as well as on the day of the yoga-vāra..."
The instruction in mantras by the guru and the practice that brings about auspiciousness. || 1 ||
Thus, one should understand that the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and other such factors are common to both initiation (*dīkṣā*) and preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
Having deliberated thereon according to the previously stated rule and having ascertained an auspicious time, one should commence [the rite].
Thus it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*:

"An eminent and learned man, relying upon the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), should accomplish [the rite] after bathing according to the rules during an auspicious moment, lunar mansion, and lunar day. (1)

"Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśa, and having bowed to Durgā and the Mothers. Likewise, Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) says: "Then, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* with devotion. In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], it is said that the wise man should perform the *saṃkalpa* preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastivācana*). Similarly, Devala says:
Then, having not yet eaten in the morning, one should bathe, sip water, and with a concentrated mind,
perform the vow after making offerings to the deities beginning with the Sun.
The connection is that one should perform the vow in the morning; a "vow" (vrata) is a formal resolve regarding the observance of rules concerning one's own duties.
As it was said by the Pot-born Sage (Agastya):
"The undertaking of a restrictive rule regarding everything that is to be performed is called a *vrata*;
apart from such a restrictive rule, everything becomes fruitless. (1)
Thus [it is said]. By the singular expression "without having eaten the morning meal," it follows by implication that one should observe the *ekabhakta* (single-meal) vow on the preceding day.

Therefore, for one who is unable to fast, the *ekabhakta* is to be understood as the substitute. Regarding the phrase "to the deities beginning with Sūrya," the meaning is that one should offer [the food] according to the sequence mentioned in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, starting with "Sūrya, Soma," and so forth. Those verses, however, are used in the actual ritual practice (*prayoga*).
It will be stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Taking a vessel of udumbara wood filled with water and facing north, the wise man should undertake the fast and likewise make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). (1)

"Facing north" is for the purpose of observing a specific rule (*niyama*). "One should resolve" means one should regulate [the mind] through the intellect. Thus says Gautama: "Having placed the hands between the knees, with water and *kuśa* grass, and having fixed one's intention upon the fruit [of the action].
Likewise, Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) states: "For those free from desire, direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) shall occur by this very means."

"Direct realization" means the vision of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) through this preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). In this regard, although it is stated in the words of Hārīta: "One conceives with the mind, expresses with speech, and accomplishes with action," and likewise:
"Therefore, what a person attains with the mind, that he speaks with speech, and that he performs with action."

Furthermore, when there is the verbal expression of what has been understood by the mind through scripture, it follows that the verbal expression must be made in the very same form in which it was understood by the mind; therefore, one arrives at the understanding that "this must be done by me with such-and-such a desire," wherein the mention of both the result and the action is clearly perceived. Nevertheless...
The mention of the month and so forth must also be made. Thus, it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

"One who does not perform the formal mention (ullekhana) of the month, fortnight, lunar day, and all the specific occasions shall not partake in the fruit [of the rite]. Here, "of the month, fortnight, and lunar day" means in every respect—that is, in every manner.

By way of the relationship between the general and the particular. Therein, [it is specified] generally by the terms *māsa*, *pakṣa*, and *tithi*, and particularly by the terms such as *Kārttika-śukla-pratipad*. Indeed, the usage of the sages is seen in such expressions as "in this month, in the bright fortnight," and so forth. And in every respect regarding the causal factors such as place, time, and so on—
In this context, it is referred to generally by the term *Bhāratavarṣa* because it is the cause of the fruits of all actions. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"From here one attains heaven; from here indeed one proceeds to liberation; and [from here] one attains the state of animals or the state of hell-beings."

"From here, O Sage, the person goes [to the world of Yama]; indeed, no other place than this is ordained as the land of action for mortals. Thus, [the time] is specified by the mention of Kāśī and so forth; it is specified generally by the word "today," and specifically by the mention of a solar eclipse and so forth. And it is not only the months and such that are [specified].

There would be the consequence of two separate mental representations (*ullekha*) regarding the objective cause (*nimitta*), because according to the principle of "separateness despite conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva-nyāya*), a single representation alone serves the purpose of both; furthermore, it has been stated that there is no result for one who does not perform the utterance of the words (*vacana-prayoga*). For this very reason, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, in the section on *śrāddha*: *oṃ*...

The verbal formula begins: "Today, in this place, in such-and-such month, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, when the sun is situated in such-and-such zodiac sign," and so forth. In the *Agni Purāṇa*: "Today, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the time of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and at other such auspicious bathing places (*sutīrtha*). Likewise: "When the sun is in Capricorn (*makara*) in the month of Māgha, at the time of dawn, even in water as small as a cow's footprint, bathing [is meritorious]."
"It bestows heaven even upon sinners. Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* in the injunction regarding the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn (*makara*).

This is likewise heard in other injunctions as well. Furthermore, the fruit here is the attainment of mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*) for those with desires, according to the cited statement. And it should not be asserted that this perfection of mantra pertains only to the present life.

This is because, as stated by the words of Nārada, both [pūjā and japa] are established as being declared to be the fruits of *puraścaraṇa*. Likewise, the one born from a jar (Agastya) has stated that *puraścaraṇa* consists precisely of *japa* and the other rites: "Worship performed at the three times daily, constant *japa*, libations (*tarpaṇa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and the feeding of Brahmins—this is called *puraścaraṇa*. Thus, it is *japa* and the rest that are intended.
Furthermore, because it is designated by the term *puraścaraṇa*, one must declare: "I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa*.

Nor is it improper to say, "On such-and-such a lunar day today, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa*," despite the fact that *puraścaraṇa* requires a long period of time; for the root *kṛ* (to do) signifies merely the act of doing (*kṛti*) at the present moment.

Since an action is associated with the general category of "effort" (*kṛti-sāmānya*), it is established that on the current lunar day (*tithi*), the action can be fulfilled by any effort whatsoever; thus, the performance of the specific rite on that particular day is logically sustained. In this way, once one has resolved, "I shall perform the recitation (*japa*) starting from today," there is no obstruction to the *japa* even during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).
As it was said by Viṣṇu:
"In sacrifices, vows, marriages, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire-offerings (homa), worship, and recitation (japa)..."
There is no birth-impurity (sūtaka) regarding what has already begun, but there is birth-impurity regarding what has not yet begun.
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the selection [of priests]; in the undertaking of vows and recitations, it is the formal resolve;
in marriage and similar rites, it is the *nāndīmukha* ceremony; and in a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), it is the preparation of the food.

Thus it is said. In reality, however, even when impurity (*āśauca*) and the like occur for those who possess Tantric initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is no suspension of their daily worship (*nityārcana*). For the *Devīyāmala* states: "The rite of recitation (*japa*) and the ritual of deity-worship must be performed by men endowed with initiation; for there is no sin nor any birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for those who are self-restrained. This applies during both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*).

"Likewise, one should perform recitation, worship, and so forth, preceded by the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), during the emission of smoke and other such [omens]," according to the statement in the *Mṛḍānītantra*. Furthermore: "For one who has received initiation for the worship of Śiva or Viṣṇu, and for those who have maintained the sacred fire (*agniparigraha*), as well as for celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and ascetics (*yati*), there is no impurity (*sūtaka*) in their bodies."

This is because of the statement in the *Viṣṇuyāmala*: "O best of Brahmins, for one who is always permeated by Viṣṇu and engaged in his practice, immediate purification occurs during both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*). Furthermore, it is because of the statement in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"In the case of worship, however, purification of the body occurs for Brahmins," and the statement of Parāśara: "In that regard..."

From the statement "of the *vipras*," it is understood that there is no entitlement for *kṣatriyas* and others. This is because of the following words of Viṣṇu: "I am to be worshipped by the *brāhmaṇa* alone, whether he be pure or impure; contact with women or *śūdras* is as unbearably painful as a thunderbolt. Furthermore: "But for the *vipra*, I am always [accessible], whether he be pure or impure."
"I accept the worship of a Śūdra who conducts himself according to his own prescribed duties," so says the word of Śiva. Furthermore, from the statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:

"O Maheśvarī, one should never eat without first worshipping the Śivaliṅga; even during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), the worship of Śiva must not be abandoned. Here, the term "of a Śūdra" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Because it is stated [in the scriptures] "of the Brahmin," this [qualification] applies only to Tantric worship; however, there is no entitlement [to it] in the case of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and so forth.

For the *Gautama-smṛti* states: "Purification for the purpose of rites such as the *agnihotra* is considered to be momentary (*tātkālikī*); indeed, one should perform the five great sacrifices even while being impure. "Momentary" means as long as that particular rite is being accomplished.
Furthermore, O Nārada, even those who follow the Tantras have no authority for occasional or optional worship when impurity due to birth or death (sūtaka/mṛtaka) is present;
this applies even when a mantra is worshipped out of desire, or in certain rites such as pacification (śāntika).
The practitioner of mantra should devoutly recite the lion-mantra five hundred times;
furthermore, in accordance with the rules for expiation, one should recite it three hundred times even without specific desire.
Thus it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*. Regarding occasional worship performed without specific desire (*akāmāt*), the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* states:

"For the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) the prescribed number of times according to the rule of a single meal, without delay or haste. (1)
Contemplating with his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite it with a one-pointed mind from the morning until midday.
One should perform that very number [of recitations] every single day as originally undertaken;
if one should make it less or more, that person becomes fallen from his vow.
Thus [it is said]. Here, because the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra* also mentions the word "by day" in the rule for the *puraścaraṇa*—

stating that "one should perform the recitation by day, and avoid it at night"— and because the one born from a jar (Agastya) prohibited recitation during the night, [this applies] when there is a possibility of disturbances such as those caused by place or time.

It should be recited until the end of the fourth *muhūrta*. However, regarding the fifth *muhūrta*: "That time is named Rākṣasī and is censured for all ritual acts," because it is thus condemned in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Here, by the word *muhūrta*, a portion is meant; the meaning is that the fifth portion of the day is prohibited. Likewise:
In the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"A mantra, even if perfectly perfected, does not become gracious if it is neither meditated upon nor worshipped;
it does not desire to grant success if it is not recited, nor does it yield fruit if it is not offered oblations. (1)
Therefore, if the practitioner desires success, he should personally perform these four rites—worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering—every day. (2)
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should meditate upon Śiva; at the conclusion of meditation, one should recite again.
Endowed with both recitation and meditation, the knower of mantras quickly attains perfection.

Nārada said: Upon completing the count, one who is composed should, with his own materials, offer oblations into the sacrificial pit as prescribed, according to the rules, for one-tenth of the number of recitations.
"Alternatively, having recited [the mantra] every day, one should indeed perform the oblation for that same period as before, [specifically] one-tenth of that amount. Vaiśampāyana said:
"The rule of continuity has been declared; one must not let even a single day pass by."
If a day passes by, the accomplishment of the mantra for a person will certainly not occur. || 1 ||
One should recite on the following day exactly as many times as one did on the preceding day;
otherwise, it will act as an obstacle to success.
Gautama says:
For meditation, worship, and recitation, three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) each are prescribed at the beginning and the end, moving through the nostrils. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said].
In the *Uttaratantro*:
"At the beginning of recitation and other rites, one should worship the rosary, having carefully sprinkled it with water."
Having placed it either inside the mandala or in the left hand.
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed:
Oṃ! O Mālā, O Mahāmāyā, whose nature is the embodiment of all powers!
The fourfold aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. (1)
Having performed worship, one should then take the garland in the right hand, first uttering the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati and immediately thereafter [the mantra]. (2)
"O Mālā, grant me freedom from obstacles; may you be taken up"—with these words [he speaks].
The connection is as follows: having placed it inside the mandala, or having sprinkled it with water while it is held in the left hand, one should worship it. Likewise—
Thereafter, one should commence the recitation (japa), remaining established in meditation as before;
taking the rosary in hand, one should contemplate Śivā with the mind. (1)
Having visualized the Guru upon the crown of the head according to his description and so forth,
and having meditated on the mantra at the throat as being yellow in color and golden in nature.
One should place Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru,
and thereafter, in the wheel of command (ājñācakra), the Guru, the mantra, and oneself.
Then, having brought [the breath] into union with the Goddess through the path of the *suṣumṇā*,
one should cause that single wheel, which is the very nature of reality (*tattva*), to be attained.
Having meditated with effort for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within the six cakras,
one should cause [the disciple] to attain the primary sixteen cakras by means of the root mantra.
O Goddess, contemplating her who resides within the sixteen primary cakras and who bestows bliss upon the practitioner, the sādhaka should commence the rite of japa.
Above the eyebrows, at the junction of the three channels, is said to be the location of the triple-path; it is hexagonal and measures four finger-breadths.
And the red [channel] is held by those who know the yoga of the banks to be the *ājñācakra*;
at the throat, there exists an encircling of three channels for human beings. (8)
The hexagon formed by the Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā is six finger-breadths in size;
it is called the "six-chakras" (ṣaṭcakra) and is white, located in the middle of the throat.
The three channels also become one within the heart;
that location is a sixteen-spoked [lotus], measuring seven finger-breadths in extent.
That is said by the knowers of yoga to be the first sixteen cakras, which pertain to the meditation upon the mantras to be meditated upon, as well as to their contemplation and recitation. (11)
"Because it is the primordial heart, it is therefore called 'Ādi' (the Beginning).
Thus, [it is so called] because of the utterance of the *praṇava*. As it is said in that very same place:
"And just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant,"
In the same way, the mantra of sacrificers, being without a bridge, leaks away in an instant.
Therefore, in all mantras, the twice-born of the four castes should commence the rite of recitation (japa), having established a boundary (setu) on both sides.

The meaning is "they should begin. The singular number is used due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). Regarding the mantras, the *praṇava* is the bridge; thus the *praṇava* is remembered as that bridge. That which is the fourteenth vowel, the remainder known as the letter *au*, together with the *anusvāra* and the moon (*candra*), is called the bridge for the *śūdras*. In this regard:
The term "Śivā" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), meaning one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā); for it is stated [in the source] that this applies to all forms of worship:
"Having thus worshipped, one should then take the rosary in the right hand."
In the middle portion of the middle finger, excluding the index finger.
Having placed the rosary there with the ring and little fingers joined in a state of humility, one should hold it with the tip of the thumb.
Taking each seed-syllable one by one above the *aṅka*, O Bhairava,
one should recite the mantra slowly at every turn without moving the lips.
The seed-mantra of the rosary should be recited, but one must not let the beads touch one another;
O Bhairava, they should be moved with the tip of the thumb by the one engaged in the prior recitation.
If one recites the previous seed-syllable while touching the subsequent seed-syllable with the thumb, that recitation will always be fruitless for him.
Holding the rosary near one's own heart with the right hand, one should perform the recitation while meditating upon the Goddess; one should not touch it with the left hand.
Thus [it is said]. "Above the joint" means with the tip of the thumb. "The seed of the garland" refers to the gem associated with it. In the Śaiva Āgama:
"One should not touch the thread with the forefinger; one should neither shake nor swing it."
One should not touch it with the left hand, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand.
While moving the beads, one should not touch another bead with the thumb;
at the time of recitation, the wise man should never cross over the *meru* bead.
And at the time of turning [the bell], one should not cause it to strike;
for when it swings with a clattering sound, the mind becomes agitated by strife.
If it falls, there is enmity; if it cracks, the arising of disease;
if it slips from the hand, a great obstacle; and if the thread breaks, one perishes. || 4 ||

When [the bead] has fallen, when it has gone between the middle fingers, when the gem has cracked, and likewise when the thread is severed— the meaning being that this also applies when the string is broken. Thus:
In the case of coughing, sneezing, or yawning, one should discard one *āvartana*;
if the ring finger is touched through negligence, one should discard an *āvartana*. (1)
"If one has touched something forbidden during the recitation, one should wash [the rosary] and recite again.
This refers to the repetition of the mantra. In the *Yoginītantra*:
"In all rosaries, the Meru bead is prescribed to be on the side."
One should never touch these two; for if they are touched, there is a return [to the beginning] once again.

"One should not touch with the index finger" means that because touching with the index finger is prohibited in all cases, it is impossible for the other fingers not to touch [the rosary]. Likewise, in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"With a single-minded and tranquil self, holding a rosary, pure..."
With his neck slightly bent, he was tranquil and free from the twitching of itching. || 1 ||
The wise man should recite the mantra in sequence—clearly articulated with its visarga, its mātrās, and its bindu, along with its syllables—neither too rapidly nor with excessive pauses. (2)

Thus, it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "From the syllable to the Imperishable, [the recitation] is free from all defects; it is neither too slow nor too fast, and it arises from clearly articulated words. (1)

O Brahmin, having performed the recitation (japa) in this manner— free from mental distraction and endowed with an exceedingly exalted intellect— one should offer it up just as in a sacrificial rite (yāga).
Thus, in the Yoginītantra:
"Or, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should place [the rosary] upon the head a hundred and eight times:
'O Rosary, you are the giver of pleasure to all the gods; grant me auspiciousness. (1)
O auspicious lady, grant me prosperity, fame, and valor at all times;
let the Puṣkara, situated within the seed-syllable of Śikhin, become endowed with the most subtle of the subtle.
Ā, Kha, Śa, Saṃ, and Yu, joined with Siddhyaṃ and Hṛdayaṃ—this five-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as that of the rosary. || 3 ||
One should employ it for seizing, fixing, and worshiping. The form for the sake of accomplishment consists of Puṣkara (the letter *ha*), Śikhī (the letter *ra*), and Sūkṣmasūkṣma (the vowel *ī*),
joined with Ākāśa and Śaśin (the bindu and the half-moon).

"Hṛdaya, obeisance! Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*). From the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the recitation according to one's capacity, such as ten thousand times (*ayuta*) and so forth."
And that [offering] should be presented to the Lord, accompanied by speech, action, and mind.
O lotus-eyed one, soul of the universe, embodiment of mantra, Janārdana!
O Eternal Lord, accept this recitation from me, who am wretched. (2)
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, one should place the water for the arghya offering upon a flower held in the right hand and cast it before Viṣṇu while reciting the root mantra.
"Lord Viṣṇu, whose essence is mantra, shall become a bestower of perfection without delay.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding Śiva and others, Somaśambhu says:
"One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of one among these: mental, whispered, or audible."
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, neither too quickly nor too slowly. || 1 ||
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Lord, may accomplishment be mine through your grace, abiding as it does within you. (2)

Having recited this verse, the enjoyer (the practitioner) should offer it with his right hand, using water for the *arghya* consecrated with the root mantra, into the excellent hand of Śambhu. || 3 ||
Thus, in the Nāradapañcarātra:
"Having performed worship, one should then perform the recitation (japa) for two watches (prahara);
beyond that, having bathed as before, the knower of the ritual rules should perform it with special care. (1)

One should perform all the previously mentioned rites up to the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), including everything from worship to the fire oblation (agnihoma); thereafter, one should begin the recitation (japa). || 2 ||
Then, having bathed again until the end of the day, the twice-born man,
having performed the twilight worship as before, should once more worship the God.
Having finished his meal, he should always perform [the ritual] at the rising of the stars;

the connection is that, having performed the *sandhyā* worship, he should worship the God as before. Now, therefore, the things to be avoided and not avoided are stated in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*.

Subsisting on alms, or eating sacrificial oblations, or consuming vegetables, roots, and fruits, or observing a milk-vow, one who is self-restrained and single-minded should recite [the mantra]. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) describes the true nature of alms-seeking (*bhikṣā*):
"One who subsists on alms from Brahmins born of noble lineages, who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, virtuous, and descended from well-born families. (1)
p.
368) Thus says Nārada:
"Rice-porridge, roots, fruits, milk, curd, alms-food, and barley-meal."
This sevenfold sacred observance of fasting is thus proclaimed. || 1 ||
Thus says Kapila:
"Barley, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, alms-food, and sacrificial oblation—
each preceding one among these is more highly commended as food for the accomplishment of mantras."
Thus it is said by the Pot-born Sage: "The sacrificial oblation (havis) is that which is of a single kind, white, and grown in winter; it is the food of sages (munyanna) prepared by oneself;
it is that which has not been threshed by a Śūdra, nor that which has been threshed by lifting with the feet. (1)
Curd, milk, ghee from a cow, sugarcane products excluding jaggery, sesame seeds, white mung beans, and tubers excluding the kemuka; || 2 ||
The coconut fruit, the plantain, and likewise the lavalī;
the mango, the āmalaka, the jackfruit, and the harītakī. (3)
The wise consider sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be recommended for other vows;
however, that which is not dedicated to Viṣṇu is both unobtainable and improper during such vows.
If one desires one's own success in this matter, all of that must indeed be abandoned;
one should eat light, pleasant, and wholesome food, be humble, and possess a tranquil mind.
*Munyanna* (the food of sages) is *nīvāra* grain. Śātātapa states:
"Winter rice, white rice, steamed rice, *śāli*, mung beans, sesame, barley, peas, millet, *nīvāra*, *vāstūka*, and *hilamocaka* [are pure]."
Sixty-day rice, black pot-herbs, radish, and *kemuka* or other [grains], bulbs, rock salt, sea salt, and the curd and clarified butter of a cow. (2)
Milk from which the cream has been removed, jackfruit, mango, and harītakī;
long pepper, cumin, and likewise orange and tamarind. (3)
Sages declare that plantains, lavalī fruits, and emblic myrobalan, along with honey and molasses, when not fried in oil, constitute *haviṣyānna* (sacrificial food).
Even radish is forbidden for the Vaiṣṇavas. As it is stated in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"Where there is meat, as well as liquor, or eggplant and radish—one should never offer these; therein lies the singular devotion to Hari. (1)
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the things to be avoided: therein, Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) says—salt, meat, alkaline substances, honey, and other savory juices;
black gram, mung bean, lentils, and the like, as well as *kodrava* and chickpeas. (1)
"Alkali" (kṣāra) is connected with "salt" (lavaṇa). White mung beans (mudga) [are prohibited]. In the Uttaratantra:
"Steamed salt, meat, garlic (gṛñjana), eating from bell-metal vessels, black gram (māṣa), pigeon pea (āḍhakī), lentils (masūra), kodrava grain, and chickpeas (caṇaka) as well. (1)

"One should avoid betel, eating twice a day, difficult conversation, and negligence. Thus it is said; for in the *Brahmayāmala*, through certainty, enthusiasm, and fortitude, the vision of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is revealed.
Through eating little and through non-attachment, the mantra is accomplished by means of these six [qualities]. || 1 ||
Through excessive effort, overindulgence in food, idle chatter, obsession with restrictive rules, association with the base, and fickleness— by these six, the mantra is not perfected.
With a mind free from doubt, because she is composed of the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti),
the Goddess should directly meditate upon herself as consisting of mantra within her own self.
If the mind is in one place, Śiva in another, and Śakti in yet another, along with the vital breath (māruta),
O lady of excellent hips, one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Stale food, fermented gruel, food made from *kodrava* grain,
lentils, a bell-metal vessel, and oil— these six are destroyers of the potency of mantras.
One who has been kept overnight destroys both vigor and consciousness and robs one of knowledge;
therefore, with every effort, the practitioner of mantra should discard what has been kept overnight.
The mantra-practitioner, seeing another [impurity] submerged in the āranāla, should discard it;
for there will certainly be a loss of fruit, and it will surely take away the potency of the mantra.
For that reason, the practitioner of mantras should avoid alkaline substances;
for bilious food certainly brings death, as do inferior grains such as kodrava.
Kodrava grain must be avoided in every respect during the practice of recitation;
likewise, lentils, which destroy one's spiritual merit, should always be abandoned.
That pure bell-metal vessel was cursed by Viṣṇu in ancient times;
it swiftly robs away the power of a mantra, even if the reciter were Maheśvara himself.
Therefore, with every effort, practitioners must renounce bell-metal;
however, sesame oil purified by mantras is sanctifying and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (11)
Having rubbed [the body] with effort, one should always perform a bath;
however, during the time for recitation (japa), the wise should always avoid food.
p.
369) "The mantra-practitioner must never eat [at that time]," so it is said.
Now, regarding the sequence of eating therein, Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) states:
Having spread the base layer [of ghee], poured the clarified butter over it, and consecrated it with sprinkling and other rites,
the knower of mantras should cook it with Vedic mantras and again with the root mantra.

The connection is that one should cook [the food] with Vedic rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth; the ellipsis is that one should consecrate it with the root mantra. Likewise, Somaśambhu says: "The practitioner should feed [the guest] with the Hṛdaya-mantra and cause him to rinse his mouth with purified waters.
[This means] he should drink water consecrated with the root mantra while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra. [He should eat] from a Palāśa leaf.
They say that one should eat only from a row of leaves prepared by excluding the middle leaf;

the reality is that this is a restrictive rule [intended] because of the prohibition against using bell-metal vessels. Now, regarding sleeping, the *Vijayamālinītantra* states: "Sleeping on the ground, with a purified soul, having conquered anger and subdued the senses."
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Having eaten, one should sleep on a bed that is very clean and very cool;
having risen at midnight, the twice-born should perform the purification of the feet. (1)
Having sipped water (ācamana), recollected the God, and quickly performed worship as before,
one should perform the recitation (japa) according to one's ability and likewise offer it to the Lord, O Goddess.
Thus says Vaiśampāyana:
"One wearing clean garments should place the bed upon a bed of kuśa grass; one should wash that garment daily, otherwise it will bring about obstacles. (1)
Thus it is said; likewise, in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"Pure, having spread out an unwashed covering and a bed with darbha grass, and meditating on Śiva over the consecrated [bed], one should sleep at night with the head toward the east. (1)
Thus [it is said]. "Consecrated" means with one's own chosen mantra. "Auspiciously" is an elliptical expression. In the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
"Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued, having gone to a bed of *darbha* grass at night, one should report the dream seen. (1)
Thus it is said in the Yoginītantra:

"When the divine [dream] arises far away while one is awake, having restrained these mantras three times with self-restraint, eating lightly, and sleeping on the right side, one should examine the dream according to the instruction. (1)
By the plural form "mantrān," the entire hymn (*sūkta*) is understood. Thus:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull;
O Eternal One, explain to me the auspicious and inauspicious nature of my dream. (1)
Thus, having slept upon a bed strewn with kusha grass with a disciplined mind, he beholds at the end of the night a dream,
whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Thus, in the Piṅgalāmata: "The Tāra (Om), followed by 'hili' twice, then 'śūlapāṇaye', and ending with 'dviṭha' (svāhā)—this is proclaimed by Śambhu as the Svapnamāṇava mantra. (1)
Salutations to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutations to the Left-handed One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams. || 2 ||
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dream regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall bring about the accomplishment of every task. (3)
Thus, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: Oṃ! Salutation to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, the sovereign of all worlds, the universe itself, who possesses universal forms, and the master of dreams. (1)

"This dream-mantra of the Māṇava has been taught by Nārada and others. Now, regarding auspicious dreams, the Yoginītantra states that their perception is of three kinds: that which is true and that which is untrue.
For the sight of those who are not well-established in their own place is indeed devoid of clarity. || 1 ||
That which accords with reality and that which does not accord with reality arises from the disorder of those who are unwell;
mental cognition, being free from physical fire, is said to have results that correspond to reality.

He states their essential nature: "That which" refers to the vision of the gods and others, which is born of transformation; that of the ancestors and others is mental, being born of a modification of the mind.
According to the established doctrine of the Āgama:

in the first year, [the result occurs] in half a year; in the second, in a watch (yāma); in the third, after a quarter of a year; in the fourth month, [the result occurs] in a watch of the night; and that which is seen among the Visargas has its fruition immediately. || 1 ||

The fruition (*pāka*) of a dream seen in the first watch of the night occurs after one year; likewise for the subsequent watches as well. At the end of the night (*visarga*), it is at the conclusion of the night. Thus, in the distant [watch], it is inferior; when seen in the [next] watch, it is middling; and in the [final] watch, it is supreme.
The meaning is that there is no success higher than this; it occurs in the "supreme dream. He explains those very [dreams] in that same place:
"In a dream, one indeed beholds the God, one's own chosen deity, facing in all directions; the Guru, with a face gracious with favor, [like] the stainless lunar orb. (1)

One should recognize the appearance of the Gaṅgā, a cow, the goddess Sarasvatī, the sun, a person wearing a sectarian mark, or the phallic emblem of Īśvara there as a sign of success in the vision of a dream.
Therefore, even that which is already accomplished is [attained] through one's own chosen deity when He is pleased. In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"The acquisition of land, crossing the ocean of calamities, worship of the fire, performing oblations (*homa*) in the blazing fire, and likewise victory in battle. (1)
The mounting of chariots by swans, cuckoos, and peacocks;
the world as a *cakravāka* bird. In the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
"A maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, and a river."
An elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, and a fruit-bearing tree. || 1 ||
Having seen a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, liquor, spirits, and all such things as these, one shall attain perfection.
Thus says the Śruti as well:
"When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for specific desires, one should know that there will be success in accordance with that dream-vision. (1)
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra: "Crossing rivers and oceans, traveling through the sky, as well as the rising of the sun and the blazing fire. (1)
The appearance of the orbs of the moon, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars; the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, and the stars being others;
as well as ascending a palace tower or even the pinnacle of a temple.
Mounting upon elephants, horses, bulls, and lions, as well as climbing trees and mountain peaks.
Traveling by means of celestial chariots, the sight of one who has perfected the mantra, the acquisition of a perfected master, and the vision of goddesses; || 3 ||
Having seen such things as these, a man shall attain success; likewise, in a dream, the drinking of liquor and the eating of raw meat [are auspicious]. (4)
Anointing with worms and excrement, sprinkling with blood, eating curd-rice, and anointing with white garments. (5)
Having seen a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, a royal consecration, jewels, ornaments, and so forth in a dream, one attains success.
Thus, in the Nāradapañcarātra:
"The guru, the deity, the twice-born, a maiden, cows, elephants, horses, and the lion; a mirror, a conch, two drums, stringed instruments, and yellow pigment (rocanā). (1)
The chewing of betel, as well as the enjoyment of curd, cooked food, raw meat, liquor, women, wine, and spirits; || 2 ||
An umbrella, a vehicle, white clothing, as well as other white sandalwood, flower garlands, pearls, necklaces, and the full, risen moon. (3)
The sun with its fierce rays situated in the sky, the river and the great ocean, the tree in full bloom, the rice crop, yellow pigment, saffron, and honey. (4)
Parched grain, white mustard seeds, a new vessel, and milk-rice;
then the preceptor, having arrived, was joined by the excellent Gāyatrī.
Others that bring joy to the mind and have attained a state of praise in the world—
all such auspicious dreams are said to bestow the fruits of spiritual accomplishment and liberation.

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding those indicating inauspiciousness, Nārada says: "Those others which are the opposite, which cause distress to the mind, which are censured and loathed by the world—such dreams indeed bring about inauspicious results. (1)
Therefore, it is said in the *Kapila-pañcarātra* regarding [omens] indicating auspiciousness:
"A Caṇḍāla, a young elephant, a crow, a pit, an empty space, an inauspicious thing, a man smeared with oil, a naked person, a withered tree, and one with thorns. (1)
Upon seeing the top floor of a palace, a person may contract a disease;

"kalabha" refers to a young camel. Regarding the expiation for this, Kapila says: "By performing a fire-oblation (homa) after seeing an evil dream, one shall attain success. Likewise, in the Piṅgalāmata: "If it is auspicious, what is seen will become auspicious for him."

"An expert should perform one hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra in the case of inauspiciousness, following this sequence. Having seen this in the *Nāradapañcarātra*, O Sage, one should perform the homa prescribed for the tooth-stick;
or else, for the sake of pacification, one may do so with clarified butter alone using the Siṃha-mantra.
371) Regarding the section on the tooth-stick, he himself says:
"A twice-born man [should use] a hundred, a thousand, or eight more, according to his ability."
And with their names encased by the weapon-mantra (astra) and accompanied by "svāhā. || 1 ||

"Abandon the defects! Abandon them!"—this phrase, ending with the name [of the deity], is used as an alternative for either the Astra-mantra or the Siṃha-mantra. [This refers] to these causes of defects. Now, regarding the reporting of dreams, it is stated in that same [text]:
The disciple, being pure and having sipped water for purification, with flowers in hand and joyful, should bow his head to the most excellent guru and report his dream to him.
If a wonder that causes great joy should suddenly arise, whether in a dream or before one's very eyes, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru.
O best of Brahmins, one who desires spiritual accomplishment must not reveal to anyone the sign produced by the grace of the mantra, except to a guru. (3)
He who, out of delusion or impatience, reveals the bliss born of mantra,
finds that the accomplishments (siddhis) which were close at hand depart far away from him.
"Sufferings and various sorrows also manifest.
Thus it is said in the *Vakratuṇḍakalpa*: "Clarity of mind, contentment of the intellect, moderation in eating, and turning away from agitation. Likewise, in the *Bhairavītantra*:
One perceives light everywhere, or the body as endowed with radiance;
indeed, one’s own body becomes composed of the deity itself.
Thus, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"O Nārada, for one who is intent on the propitiation of the mantra and established in the observances, many obstacles arise during the first three years."
If the practitioner does not experience agitation through either action or mind,
then after the third year, kings and sovereigns [will come to him].
Even those who are proud and full of self-respect entreat others out of consideration;
therefore, O Lord, grant me your grace for the sake of my deliverance. (3)
And they behold him blazing with splendor and majesty;
therefore, O tiger among sages, they are unable to speak harshly.
After the ninth year, the king of mantras becomes spontaneously perfected;
indeed, various wonders consisting of the accomplishment of the mantra arise within the heart.
Bestowing supreme bliss both immediately and externally through direct perception, even one of dull intellect remains enraptured for a moment, though it may vanish in an instant. (6)
For a moment he hears the resonance of drums from the sky,
and for a moment he hears sweet music accompanied by various songs.
For a moment he smells fragrances born of camphor and musk;
for a moment, indeed, he beholds his own self by means of the self as it arises.
For a moment, the twice-born should gaze at the sky filled with the rays of the moon and sun;
and for a moment, he should listen to the sounds of elephants, cows, and bulls.
For a moment, he even draws toward himself the various stars situated in the sky, along with the agitation of the overflowing clouds, like a yogin.
The observer of the vow always sees for a moment the mantra being recited,
and for a moment the sound of joyful shouting, as well as the cries of swans and peacocks.
For a moment he might see the rising of clouds, and for a moment night while it is day;
and at night he might for a moment behold the light of day together with the sun.
He was filled with strength and like the sun in splendor;
he resembled the full moon in radiance and was like a bird in his gait. || 13 ||
He may be said to be endowed with vigor, serenity, profundity, and happiness;
he does not become emaciated by eating very little, nor does he increase even when eating much. (14)
Furthermore, there will be a reduction in feces and urine, as well as victory over sleep;
the practitioner of mantra engaged in recitation and meditation does not experience exhaustion. (15)
"O Sage, for a fortnight, a month, and so forth, without food or drink"—by such signs as these, which cause great wonder. (16)
"One should be fully awakened regarding the activity [of the mantra], for the King of Mantras is gracious.

Thus says Baudhāyana: "There are three signs of success: the giver, the enjoyer, and the non-seeker. This means one who is both a giver and an enjoyer, yet remains free from seeking. From the *Prapañcasāra* (Chapter 10, Verse 43):
Then, as he recites the mantra, these signs indeed arise for him:
a lamp placed at night becomes such that the house is free from darkness.
O Lotus-born One, he becomes as radiant as the sun; she shall be his constant servant;
diseases perish instantly upon seeing him; and his vicinity becomes filled with wealth and grain.
The gods always offer salutations to him, and serpents do not bite his sons.
May he, whose grandsons and friends have prospered, attain the supreme abode of Viṣṇu even in the face of his own calamity. (10th Paṭala, 47th Śloka, p.
Thus it is said. Even if [the goal] is not accomplished despite performing [the rite] in this manner, then one should perform the preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*) twice or thrice.
As it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Obstruction by a powerful opposing action [occurs] only through [such] ritual effort."
If one does not attain success, one should perform it again two or three times. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Now this sequence of the fire-oblation (*homa*) is considered. Regarding that, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:

"Now I shall describe the ritual of the fire (*agnikārya*), whether in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or on an altar (*vedi*), or in a vessel made of iron, or in a new, auspicious earthenware vessel. (1)
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should perform the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) fire-oblation (homa) either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or upon a well-prepared surface on ground smeared with cow-dung. (1)
One should construct that very beautiful [mound] out of sand, measuring one cubit in size,
square on all sides, and one finger-breadth in height.
Thus, in the *Kriyāsāra*:

"A level area in the eight directions, sloping toward the east, or even sloping toward the northeast; or a region sloping toward the north—this is remembered as the site for the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*). (1)

Thus [it is said]. "Prahva" means inclined. And so says Kapila: "The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) may be made with sand, or even with red earth or dust. Likewise Vasiṣṭha states: "In a concise rite of oblation (homakarma), the sacrificial ground should be one cubit (hasta) in measure. Since he specifies "in a concise [rite]" here, an oblation numbering a thousand or more is performed on a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).

Some say it should not be performed. Regarding that: "The preceptor, who is a knower of all the Vedas, should commence the fire-oblation (homa) in a consecrated pit (kuṇḍa) or on a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila), having performed the bringing forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana). He should perform one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds with the Vyāhṛtis. From this statement in the Vāyu Purāṇa, [it follows that the rite is to be done] either in a pit or on a mound.

Or else, a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed there; for it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "The number of oblations is ten thousand, and likewise the fuel-sticks are of *palāśa* wood. Furthermore, in the event of an inability to perform the oblation, recitation (*japa*) alone must be performed, according to the statement of Nārāyaṇa: "For one who is incapable [of the former], recitation is prescribed in all cases. In that regard, by the Brahmins—

The recitation for the *puraścaraṇa* should be performed four times the prescribed number by Kṣatriyas, six times by Vaiśyas, and eight times by Śūdras. For those three [classes] who are capable of performing the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), the recitation is equal [to the sacrifice]. For those incapable of performing the fire-sacrifice, it is measured by the Vedas (4), the seasons (6), and the Vasus (8). This is according to the statement in the *Uttaratantra*: "For those capable of the act of *homa*, there is equality with the recitation; for those incapable of the act of *homa*, it is measured by the Vedas, the seasons, and the Vasus."

However, in the event of inability, for Brahmins it is double; for Kṣatriyas, triple; and for Vaiśyas, quadruple. According to the statement of Gautama: "For Brahmins who are unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (*homakarman*), the recitation (*japa*) is double; for the other castes, however, triple and so forth is prescribed. Even in that case, if there is inability—

The recitation (japa) should be performed four times the number of the oblations (homa). According to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "In the event of inability to perform the oblation, one should perform a recitation four times the number of the oblations. This [rule] also applies specifically to Brāhmaṇas; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as previously stated, the recitation consists of six or eight times [the number of oblations], based on the aforementioned scriptural authority.

If one is unable even for that, a recitation (japa) twice the number of the burnt offerings (homa) should be performed. Whatever limb [of the ritual] may be omitted, a recitation twice that number must be performed with devotion by one who is incapable [of the full rite], for the sake of accomplishing the rite along with its limbs.
Thus, according to the words of the Pot-born Sage (Agastya):

"By one who is incapable of that"—meaning by one incapable of performing the *puraścaraṇa* with its prescribed number of repetitions multiplied by four and so forth—this [penance] also applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa alone;
for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is a reduction to threefold and fourfold [respectively], precisely because of the previously cited statement of Gautama.

However, for Śūdras who are not devotees of the twice-born, there is a ten-fold recitation in the case of the four-fold rule, but a five-fold recitation in the case of the two-fold rule. For those Śūdras who are devotees of the twice-born, the recitation is that which is prescribed for the specific caste upon which that Śūdra has taken refuge. As it is said in the *Uttaratantra*:

The recitation (japa) which has been prescribed by the wise for the twice-born in the absence of fire-offerings (homa), that same [recitation] is prescribed for their wives, as well as for a Śūdra who has resorted to that [same] caste. || 1 ||
"Therefore, one who is devoted to faith should perform the recitation (jāpa) prescribed for women.
Thus [it is said]. Gautama also says:
"In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), however, that recitation which was previously declared for the twice-born is prescribed."
For that same [state] belongs indeed to women with beautiful brows and to those Śūdras who are his servants.
Thus it is said. Therefore, since women and śūdras lack the qualification for performing fire-offerings (homa), they should perform only the recitation (japa). In the Uttaratantra:
"Then, having worshipped the deity in water with a tenth part of the oblations, one should offer libations upon the head with water, having uttered 'I satisfy' at the end of the mantra. (1)
Thus said Vaiśampāyana:
Reciting the mantra ending with "namaḥ" ten times for every part of the libation (tarpaṇa), one should sprinkle one's own head with water using the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kumbha). || 1 ||
Thus it is said in the *Uttaratantro*:

"At the conclusion of that [rite], one should feed Brahmins of good conduct in the tenth part [of the number of mantras recited], with various kinds of foods—those to be chewed, those to be eaten, those to be licked, those to be sucked, and others as well. (1)
In every way, one should feed the Brahmins for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the rite;
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, even a deficient ritual attains completeness.
If even a single limb were to be missing, one would not obtain the desired result;
for whatever action is deficient in its limbs does not accomplish the intended purpose. (3)
Actions that are deficient or excessive do not bear fruit according to one's desires;
only when they are all complete do they reach fulfillment.
Therefore, in all rites, one should diligently feed the learned;
for whatever actions may be deficient are made complete by the feeding of the twice-born.
Those [teachings] would be as useless as seeds sown in saline soil;
afterwards, one should satisfy the teacher with cows, gold, garments, and other such gifts.
For when the guru is pleased, the mantra becomes satisfied and grants success to the practitioner;
in this way, through the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), the deity becomes propitious.
Thus, in the Śrīkulārṇava:
"If one mutters a mantra heard by chance, or even through deception or fraud, or one imparted by another, or a mere verse, it brings about misfortune. (1)
Those who recite mantras after looking at them written in a book are proclaimed to have a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin. || 2 ||
Numerous millions of mantras are causes for mental agitation;
however, a single mantra received from the mouth of the Guru shall bestow all accomplishments.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): therein, the rosary for recitation (*japamālā*) is of two kinds, consisting of the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) and so forth. Regarding that, the beads (*maṇi*) are specific types of seeds, namely: *putrajīva*, conch, coral, gems, pearls, lotus seeds, gold, silver, *kuśa* grass knots, and *rudrākṣa*. As for the number of beads (*akṣasaṃkhyā*), however—
There are one hundred and eight beads according to the division into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types, as well as fifty-four and twenty-seven.
Now, regarding the time for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the rosary: therein, for Viṣṇu, it is the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) during the forenoon;
for Śakti, the eighth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days at night; for Gaṇeśa, the fourth lunar day at midday; and for Śiva—

The thirteenth day is by day; for the Sun, it is the seventh day during the forenoon. Now, regarding the threads for the rosary: for Viṣṇu, a lotus thread or a cotton thread; for the Goddess, a silk thread; for Śiva, one made of wool or bark-fiber; and for the Sun and Gaṇeśa, a cotton thread.

One should prepare a silk thread or a cotton thread spun by a Brāhmaṇa woman, or spun by a woman of one's own caste; it should be triple-stranded and then twisted into a threefold cord. In the case of other types of threads, the procedure should be performed as appropriate. Now, regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*): therein, with a vessel of the prescribed dimensions...

Having prepared the *pañcagavya*— consisting of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water— the practitioner, who has observed a single meal on the previous day (unless he lacks the capacity), having performed his daily morning rites,
should wash the thread and the beads individually with the *pañcagavya* and with water in nine [vessels].
Having placed the thread and the beads upon betel-leaf plates fashioned in the shape of lotuses,

and having deposited the *praṇava*, the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, and the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet— assigning them to the thread and to each individual bead— and having worshipped the beads and the thread with perfumes and other offerings in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or elsewhere;

Having established the fire according to the rules for the daily *homa*, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with ghee or with pure ghee alone using the five mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta* according to one's capacity; or, if unable to perform the *homa*, having performed recitation (*japa*),
if the beads are made of *rudrākṣa*, *putrajīva*, or *padmākṣa*, one should join mouth to mouth [the beads] upon the thread.

Having fixed another jewel according to its respective face, having fashioned a *brahmagranthi* within each individual jewel according to the method taught by the Guru, and having tied them together in the shape of a cow’s tail, one should join two threads at the top with a single, larger, homogeneous jewel facing downward to form the *meru*, and thus tie it together.

Having washed the completed garland with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and cool water while reciting the mantra: *oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhavasva māṃ bhavodbhavāya namaḥ*, [one should then recite]: *oṃ vāmadevāya namo jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ śreṣṭhāya*.

With the mantra: "Salutation to Rudra, salutation to Kāla, salutation to Kalavikaraṇa, salutation to Balavikaraṇa, salutation to Bala, salutation to Balapramathana, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana, salutation to Manonmana," one should rub [the image] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, and [recite]: "Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ..."
"Obeisance to you who are terrible, more terrible than the most terrible, who are all-encompassing, and who are the lords of all— obeisance to you in your forms as Rudras.
Having thus offered incense made of agallochum, *śīra*, camphor, sugar, *guggulu*, honey, sandalwood, and clarified butter, [he recites] "Oṃ."
"May we know that Tatpuruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us.
With these words, one should smear [the image] with sandalwood paste, musk, saffron, and camphor. Then: "Oṃ, Īśāna is the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings..."

One should consecrate each seed [of the rosary] one hundred times with the mantra: "May Brahmā, the sovereign of Brahmā, the lord of Brahmā, the auspicious Śiva, be ever propitious to me. One should also consecrate the *meru* (the central bead) one hundred times with this [mantra], as well as with "aghorebhyotha... (either once for each or one hundred times for each). Then, there [in that place]...

Having invoked, by means of the previously mentioned distinctions of faces, whichever deity belongs to whichever Rudrākṣa, one should perform the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), bringing near (*saṃnidhāpana*), confinement (*saṃnirodhana*), facing toward [the worshipper] (*saṃmukhīkaraṇa*), making whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*) with their respective mudrās.

Having performed the worship of that deity with the five offerings for each seed-syllable using the five previously mentioned mantras, as one would for one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should perform the recitation (japa) with the rosary thus consecrated.
This is the procedure for the consecration of the rosary.

Thus, while performing recitation with a rosary that has been consecrated, when one perceives that the string has become worn out, at that very moment one should tie a strong new string and likewise recite one's chosen mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of expiation; thereafter, one should perform the recitation with that rosary as before.

This method of consecration applies specifically to the rudrākṣa and not to others. However, the procedure for the consecration of other [beads], such as lotus seeds and the like, is now demonstrated: having placed the strung garland in some vessel, within it—
Having separately invoked and worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Durgā,
and having placed [the offerings] into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the mantra "Hauṃ," one should again take them out from that and place them in a golden vessel.
Or, having placed it in the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) which are contained in a *pippala* leaf and perfumed with incense, one should take it out again, place it in cool water, wash it,
smear it with the paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, saffron, and fragrant lotus, and [recite] "haum" over it.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, having worshipped the nine planets and the ten guardians of the directions,

and having offered oblations according to one's capacity with sesame seeds mixed with ghee using one’s chosen mantra, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor according to one’s means and satisfy the Brahmins with food and other offerings.

Alternatively, having placed the thread and the gems in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three days, one should remove them on the fourth day, wash them with the *astra-mantra*, tie them with a knot using the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
and having prepared a maṇḍala for the worship of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should fully worship that chosen deity therein.

Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and having offered oblations according to one's capacity— either with clarified butter or with the materials for the *puraścaraṇa* fire-sacrifice prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of one’s chosen deity—
one should place the rosary in the center of the mandala and [recite] the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) over it.
Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and visualized her in the form of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā),

one should offer the bali-offering to all beings according to the procedure to be described; then, having worshipped that chosen deity within her [the image] and satisfied the preceptor with ritual fees and other gifts, one should prostrate before him.
One should satisfy the Brahmins with food and other offerings; thus, with a consecrated rosary, one should constantly recite the mantra.
Now, the prescribed requirements for the period of preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) are as follows:

concentration of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, detachment, faith, enthusiasm for the recitation (*japa*), absence of anger, renunciation, contentment with the performance of the duties of one's own caste and stage of life, and control of the senses.
The observance of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), bowing to one's gurus, bathing with pure *āmalaka* fruits, consecration by sprinkling water empowered with mantras,
bathing three times a day, twice if possible, or once if unable,
and the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, ancestors, and one's own chosen deity.
At night, one should eat sparingly and show compassion toward cows, Brahmins, children, and others, while seated upon a row of Palāśa leaves fashioned from leaves stripped of their midribs.
Now, those things prohibited at that time:
stepping on the shadows of the *karaja*, *vibhītaka*, *arka*, and *snuhī* trees;

accepting gifts; conversing with women, *śūdras*, outcasts (*patita*), atheists (*nāstika*), or those who have not rinsed their mouths after eating; and [performing] bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth—[these are forbidden].

Wearing many garments, wearing a single garment, wearing soiled garments; performing rites for specific desires, performing actions prescribed for one’s own caste and stage of life without having formed a formal resolve (asaṃkalpita); eating from bell-metal vessels, eating during the day, speaking what is improper, worshipping what is unworthy, crookedness, and [the consumption of] jaggery...
Oil massage, association with the unwholesome, bathing in hot water, rubbing the body, listening to songs and instrumental music,

watching dances, the eightfold sexual intercourse, conversing about it, minor occupations, touching improper places, injury to living beings, wearing turbans and warm hats, and not covering the hands or head with hair— these [are the causes of the decline of the lifespan].
Momentary head-covering, anxiety, anger, wandering,
haste, longing, lying down, rising, walking, darkness, inauspicious places, wearing sandals, and mounting vehicles or beds.

Spreading out the feet, sitting in a squatting posture, yawning, stretching, hiccuping, mental distraction, sitting with the feet raised high, and the absence of sacrificial grass (kuśa) and other such items [are faults].
Now, the seats there were prepared, consisting of tiger skins, deer hides, mats made of cane, woolen blankets, *kuśa* grass mats, and red cotton cloths.
Now, the prohibited seats: those made of bamboo, wood, stone, grass, cloth, bark, or brick, as well as the bare ground alone.
Now, the preliminary rites for the day preceding the commencement of the *puraścaraṇa*: having bathed in the morning, performed the daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*),

gratified the Brahmins with food and other offerings, and satisfied one's own guru with garments, ornaments, wealth, grain, and so forth, [one should proceed] to the place of recitation (*japasthāna*).
In a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square, [one should say]: "Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla! O Kṣetrapāla, come here, come here!

Having thus invoked Kṣetrapāla and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings using the aforementioned mantra, one should place before him, upon a triangular mandala, a vessel together with its base, filled with rice, side-dishes, and water.

Having placed the offering vessel [before him], one should give the offering while reciting the mantra: "Ehyehi vidvi(du)pi murumuru bhañjaya bhañjaya tarjaya tarjaya vighnavighna mahābhairava kṣetrapāla baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā," and then observe a fast.

Now, the ritual duties for the day of commencing the *japa*: On an auspicious month, under favorable lunar and stellar conditions, on a propitious day determined by the purification of the lunar date, weekday, and asterism, one should bathe in the morning, obtain permission from the Guru and Brahmins, have the Brahmins perform the *svastivācana* rite, and with *kuśa* grass in hand, recite: "Oṃ! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla..."
The twilight beings, day and night, the wind, the lord of the quarters, the earth, space, and the gods who move through the sky.

"Abiding by the teaching of Brahmā, prepare the presence here. Having recited this, and taking kusha grass, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and water in a copper vessel, facing north, [he says]: "Om! Today, in such-and-such month, when the sun is in such-and-such zodiac sign, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, in the region of the earth called Bhāratavarṣa, in a special sacred field..."
In this particular field, [the practitioner], being a Kṣatriya named Amukaśarman, or a Vaiśya named Amukavarman, or a Śūdra named Amukagupta, or [anyone else] named Amukadāsa,
desiring the accomplishment of such-and-such a mantra, performs this preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of this many recitations (*japa*) of such-and-such a mantra.
