Having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as "I shall perform [this] from today for so many days" or "I shall perform it," and having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and the Mothers, and having completed the worship (*pūjā*), one should begin the recitation (*japa*). Therein,
having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), [one should proceed with] the root mantra...

Having performed the *ṛṣi*-vidyā and the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), and meditating on the deity in his heart, he should place the rosary in his left hand or in some vessel, sprinkle it with the water of the *arghya* offering while reciting the root mantra, and [recite]:
"Oṃ, O Mālā, O Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), whose nature is all powers! The four aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, [grant them] to me..."
"Be the bestower of success. Having thus worshipped the rosary with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
one should take the rosary in the right hand while reciting the mantra "Oṃ, O rosary, perform [this] without obstacle," and place it upon one's own head.

Having meditated on the illustrious Guru of yellow complexion at the throat, the root mantra in one's own heart, the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) at the feet of the Guru, and one's own self [at the navel],

and having contemplated the unity of the Guru, the Deity, the Mantra, and the Self within the Ājñā-cakra situated between the eyebrows, [one should contemplate] in the Viśuddhi-cakra located at the throat.
Having brought those four [elements] together as one through the path of the *suṣumṇā* and meditated upon the deity there,
one should bring them by means of the root mantra to the *anāhata-cakra* located in the heart; then, while meditating on the deity there as well,
one should bring the rosary near the heart and place it upon the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand.
Having composed his mind into one-pointedness, with his neck slightly bent and his body held erect, free from scratching or closing his eyes,
and making no sound such as "khaṭ-khaṭ," he should focus his mind on the meaning of the mantra;
reciting the mantra for each individual bead of the rosary, he should not touch the subsequent bead while he is in the process of reciting the previous one.

Having begun the mantra with the utterance of the *praṇava*, one should continue from the morning until midday; or, if there is a possibility of disturbances such as those arising from the location, one should complete it with haste,
or having recited it for up to two and a half *praharas*, one should again utter the *praṇava* at the end of all the remaining repetitions.

"O auspicious garland, having completed my recitation, may you grant pleasure to all the gods and bestow auspiciousness; O blessed one, always grant me welfare, fame, and valor. Having placed the garland upon his own head with this mantra, he should again perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), the assignment of the ṛṣis and other elements, and the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), using the water from the arghya vessel.

Having offered the recitation with the previously mentioned mantra and having fully worshipped the rosary with the previously mentioned rosary-worship mantra, one should place it in a secluded spot. In this regard, the utterance of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) applies only to those of the three [upper] castes;
however, for Śūdras and others, the vowel *au* should be taken as the *praṇava* at the beginning and end. Then—

Having performed the midday bath and other rites, and having again performed the worship in detail, if one follows the daily *homa* practice, one should offer the tenth part of the recitation (*japa*) into the fire consecrated according to the rules with the substances prescribed in the ritual manual; then, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as the tenth part of the *homa*, and the sprinkling (*mārjana*) as the tenth part of the libation.
One should perform the feeding of Brahmins and the offering of a tenth part of the *mārjana* [mantras] every day.

In the case of the method involving one hundred thousand *homa*s, having completed the recitation (*japa*) numbering one hundred thousand, and having performed the *homa* and other rites consisting of a tenth part of that, one should begin the recitation of the fire-mantra (*agnimantra*) for one hundred thousand times.

After completing the recitation (*japa*) according to the number prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), if one intends to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should complete the recitation according to the number stated in the manual and subsequently perform the oblation and other rites numbering one-tenth of that; this is the first of the three possible options.
The procedure for the fire-oblation has already been explained previously in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, if one is unable to perform the oblation, there is only recitation.
It should be performed in this manner. In that regard, for Brāhmaṇas, four times the number of the *puraścaraṇa* should be performed;

for Kṣatriyas, six times; and for Vaiśyas, eight times should be performed. In case of inability in this matter, Brāhmaṇas should perform the recitation (*japa*) twice the number of the *puraścaraṇa*, and Kṣatriyas three times.
Regarding the phrase "fourfold for Vaiśyas": even there, if one is unable, a recitation fourfold the number of oblations (*homa*) should be performed.

This refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as before, the recitation is sixfold and eightfold respectively. Even there, if one is unable, a recitation double the number of oblations may be performed; this also refers solely to Brāhmaṇas.

For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, however, the recitation (japa) is threefold and fourfold [respectively]. For Śūdras other than those devoted to the twice-born (dvija), the recitation is tenfold; but according to the view that it is fourfold or twofold, the recitation is fivefold.
As for Śūdras devoted to the twice-born, a Śūdra who has taken refuge in whichever caste [the twice-born belongs to] must perform the recitation prescribed for that specific caste.
"The same applies even for the wives of the twice-born. Since women and Śūdras lack the qualification for the fire-oblation (*homa*), only the recitation (*japa*) is prescribed for them.
Having thus performed the *homa*, [one should perform the sprinkling] with waters scented with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and so forth, ten times the number of the oblations.

Having meditated upon the deity in the water according to the previously mentioned procedure, having worshipped and offered libations (tarpaṇa), and while meditating on oneself as the form of the deity, one should sprinkle oneself on the crown of one's head with the *kumbha-mudrā* ten times—according to the ratio of one-tenth the number of libations—with the words: "At the end of the root mantra, I sprinkle myself; *namaḥ*."

Having performed the consecration, one should invite in the morning as many well-conducted Brahmins devoted to one’s chosen deity as constitute the tenth part of the number of consecrations; having summoned them, bathed them with oil massages and other rites,
adorned them with garments, perfumes, and so forth, and [provided them] with various foods of the six tastes, consisting of both hard and soft edibles.

Having fed [the guests] with the thought that they are one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), and having satisfied them with betel, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth, one should dismiss them; this should be performed daily, or at the end of one hundred thousand [recitations], or upon the completion of the entire total number, preceded by devotion.
Then, in the present context, after the midday worship, one should perform the daily rites (āhnika) such as the Vaiśvadeva offering.

Having spent the remainder of the day through the recitation, meditation, chanting, listening to the praises, and other such acts concerning the mantra of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should—if capable—perform the evening bath, worship the Deity, and then eat. Regarding the foods to be eaten there: they consist of alms-food, or white, single-grain, non-sweated, autumnal *nīvāra*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *kaṅgu*, barley, or wheat, threshed by a Śūdra woman.

Sugar-cane products excluding jaggery, black sesame, mung beans, and peas; various bulbous roots excluding the *kemuka*; coconut, plantain, *lavalī*, jackfruit, mango, *āmalaka*, *ārdraka*, *harītakī*, *vāstuka*, *kālaśāka*, and *hila* [vegetables]. These were repeatedly crushed with the feet and carried away, devoid of molasses.
Mocaka, rock salt, sea salt, salts from which the essence has not been extracted, products of cow's milk, long pepper, cumin, orange, tamarind, and radish.

Now, the things to be avoided: jaggery, artificial salt, alkaline salts, salted food, steamed food, stale food, food devoid of oil, food defiled by insects and the like, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), *gṛñjana*, *bilva*, *karañja*, garlic, lotus stalks, *kodrava* grain, scum of boiled rice, and anything cooked in oil.
Excessive eating and eating during the day include black gram, lentils, chickpeas, wheat, foxtail millet, and so forth.
Now, the sequence for the meal: there, having placed the food— which is the grace of one’s chosen deity—
upon a row of leaves prepared with *palāśa* leaves from which the middle leaf has been removed,
and having consecrated it with Vedic mantras and sprinkled each substance with the root mantra, [one should proceed].
Having consecrated it seven times, one should eat small portions with the *hṛdayamantra*, and one should drink water consecrated thirty-two times with the *mūlamantra*.
p.

376) Now, regarding the bed: there, having spread upon a bed made of *kuśa* grass that has been washed with alkaline water a garment that has likewise been washed, one should consecrate the bed with the root mantra.

Having consecrated it seven times with the hymn beginning "yajjāgrataḥ," [the following is the application]: Śivasaṃkalpa is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Manas is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation of this hymn.
That divine power which rises far away from the waking state, that very same power likewise departs from the sleeping state;
that one light of all lights, which travels far—that mind of mine may be intent on auspicious resolve. 1.

May that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve—the mind by which the wise and skillful perform their deeds in sacrifice and ritual assemblies, and which, when about to worship, perceives what is unprecedented among living beings. 2.
That which is wisdom, as well as consciousness and fortitude; that which is the inner light, the immortal within living beings;
without which no action whatsoever is performed—may that mind of mine be intent on auspicious resolve. (3)

May that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve—the mind by which all this past, present, and future world is encompassed by the immortal, and by which the sacrifice with its seven priests is extended. 4.
In which the Ṛg-verses, Sāman-chants, and Yajus-formulas are established like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel;
in which the entire consciousness of living beings is woven together—may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve. || 5 ||

Like a skilled charioteer who guides horses with reins, that mind of mine which is led by the objects of sense—firmly established in the heart, agile, and most swift—may it be of auspicious resolve. 6.
Having recited these mantras three times:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull;
O Eternal One, declare to me the auspicious and inauspicious nature of my dream."
Thus: *Oṃ hili hili, svāhā to the wielder of the trident!
Homage to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Self;
homage to the one who is favorable, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams!* (1)
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dream regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall bring about the accomplishment of the task. (2)
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the powerful lord of all the worlds;
salutation to the universe, whose form is the universe, the sovereign of dreams. || 3 ||
Having recited these mantras once, one should examine the dream while lying on the right side with the head toward the east.
Among those dreams seen during the watches of the night: for one seen in the first watch, the fruit is realized in a year;
in the second, in six months; in the third, in three months; and in the fourth, in one month; at the end of the night, the fruit is immediate.
It should be known as follows.

Now, dreams indicating success: seeing one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), the guru, or one's own preceptor with faces bright with grace; seeing the pure orbs of the moon and sun, the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, renunciants (saṃnyāsins), or the Śiva-liṅga; and the acquisition of land.
Crossing a sea of blood, victory in battle, worship of the sacrificial fire, seeing swans, ruddy geese,
peacocks, and cranes, mounting a chariot, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a serpent, a noble family, and a tree.
The sight of mountains, purifying substances, meat, horses, wine, and liquor; the sight of women; crossing rivers; traveling through the sky; the sight of planets and constellations;
ascending the tops of mansions, palaces, elephants, horses, bulls, trees, and mountain peaks; and traveling by celestial chariot (vimāna).
The visions of non-goddesses consist of visions of drinking intoxicants, eating meat, smearing oneself with excrement, being sprinkled with blood, and wearing jewel ornaments and the like.

Now, those indicating inauspiciousness: seeing a Caṇḍāla, a young elephant, a crow, an empty pit, an inauspicious object, a dirty substance, a man smeared with oil, a naked man, a withered tree, the base of a thorny tree, or a ruined palace portends disease. Regarding that, the expiation is as follows:

Having recited the Nṛsiṃha mantra, one should say, "Destroy, destroy the defects indicated by bad dreams," and having again recited the Nṛsiṃha mantra, one should offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the word "Svāhā. Alternatively, the fire sacrifice (homa) may be performed in this very same manner using the Astra mantra. The Nṛsiṃha mantra consists of a single syllable, which is *kṣraum*; the Astra mantra, however, is as follows:
Of one's own root-vidyā which is to be worshipped.

Now, regarding the reporting of the dream: having prostrated before the pair of lotus-like feet of the Guru with flowers in hand, one should report the dream to him; one must not disclose it to anyone other than the Guru.
Now, the signs of accomplishment (*siddhicihna*): clarity of mind, satisfaction of the intellect, eating little, little sleep, seeing light, sudden great joy, hearing the sound of celestial drums,
the hearing of various songs, and the smelling of the fragrant scent of camphor and other perfumes.

The light of the sky is filled with the rays of the moon and sun. Even when this has been performed, if success is not attained, one should perform it again two or three times, repeatedly. Now, there is another method for the attainment of mantra-siddhi; regarding that, in the *Kulaprakāśatantra* (p.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one who is pure and has previously fasted [should perform it]. (1)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind from the time of touch until liberation.
"Having recited [the mantra] in this manner for that duration, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites.

This is the meaning: therein, during a solar eclipse, one who has fasted on the preceding day, or during a lunar eclipse, one who has fasted on that very day, having seen the eclipse and performed the ritual bath, [should recite] "in such-and-such month, when the sun is situated in such-and-such zodiacal sign..."

On such-and-such a day of the fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar date, at such-and-such a sacred ford, during a solar eclipse or a lunar eclipse, I, [Name], belonging to the [Name] lineage and known as [Name],
desiring the perfection of such-and-such a mantra, beginning from the time of this eclipse...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—"I shall perform the recitation of this mantra until liberation"—one should recite it until liberation. The resolve for the fire-oblation (*homa*) is: "I shall perform the oblation consisting of one-tenth of the number of recitations performed at the time of initiation. In the event of inability to perform the oblation, the recitation should be performed as previously stated. However, another [view] says:

The method for the accomplishment of mantras: Regarding that, Agastya [says]: Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should meditate upon the deity and recite the mantra forty thousand times. (1)
Thereafter, one should offer oblations ten times the number [of syllables], perform libations, and carry out the consecration;
then the mantra becomes perfected. || 2 ||

Thus, the meaning is as follows: there, one who desires the accomplishment of a specific mantra—beginning with the words "tatrādya" and so forth—should first perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), saying: "Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until its fourteenth day, I shall perform forty thousand recitations of this specific mantra. Having thus made the resolve, he should divide the forty thousand recitations into seven parts.

Having recited [the mantra] five thousand seven hundred and fourteen times, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites constituting one-tenth of that number. Another method is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra encapsulated by the syllables of the Mātṛkā."
Through the forward and reverse order [of recitation], the accomplishment of the mantra arises. || 1 ||
Encased within the syllables of the Mātṛkā consisting of sixty-three letters,
by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times in direct and reverse order for one month, the mantra becomes perfected.
By the mere recitation of the Mātṛkā, tens of millions upon tens of millions of mantras become perfected;
of this there is no doubt, for everything originates from it.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: one should recite the mantra encased within the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) in both direct and reverse order one hundred times every day for the duration of a month. Here too, one should form the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform the recitation of the mantra encased within the *mātṛkā* in direct and reverse order, one hundred times each day, for the duration of a month."
Having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, one should recite [the mantra]. Here, the word "hundred" (śata) serves to exclude any number lower than that;

therefore, the meaning is that one should recite it one hundred and eight times. As for the method of enclosing [the mantra] with the *mātṛkā* vowels: *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ...*
Ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ | Mūlaṃ kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ ||

Bhaṃ baṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ. Thus [recite] the root mantra one hundred times.

Regarding the instruction "one should recite": it has already been stated (in the third chapter, page 64) that the *Mātṛkā* consisting of sixty-three phonemes is mentioned in the *Bahvṛca-Prātiśākhya*: "Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are considered [to exist] according to the opinion of Śambhu.
Thus, with this sixty-three phoneme *Mātṛkā*, joined with a *bindu* for each individual letter as before, [one should recite] one's own chosen mantra.

Having encapsulated [the mantra] for exactly one month, one should recite it one hundred and eight times every day. The ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is also to be performed as before. Furthermore, another method is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"For one month, one should recite the mantra encapsulated by the *bhūtalipi* [alphabet]."
By reciting [the mantra] a thousand times, both in direct and reverse order, within a month the mantra becomes perfected.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: there, having encapsulated the root mantra with the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) arranged both in direct and reverse order, one should recite it one thousand and eight times every day for the duration of a month. The ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is exactly as before. The *bhūtalipi* has already been explained (3rd Āhnika, p. 64). "One hundred and eight" [is the minimum].

In this recitation, it should be understood that the mantra has been previously mastered through guru-guided repetition (*gurujapta*). However, there is another method stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:

"He who worships the deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings at the three times of day and night, even without performing the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), [the deity] becomes pleased. (1)

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) beginning with "Today, here... and so forth, "Desiring the accomplishment of such-and-such mantra, I shall perform worship three times a night," one should worship the Goddess, together with her limbs and retinues, every day at night for a period of one year, three times a day, with all ritual offerings (*upacāra*). In this manner, for six months or three months.
Or one may worship for only a month; even without the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), the accomplishment of the mantra occurs.
However, according to the Kādima-tantra, there is another method:
pills prepared from medicinal herbs corresponding to the letters of a mantra, in numbers equal to those assigned to each respective letter, grant the accomplishment of that mantra. (1)
Likewise, its consecration, its wearing, its tasting, its smearing, and its worship are undoubtedly bestowers of accomplishment; of this there is no doubt. (2)

378) This is the meaning: therein, one should perform the wearing, the eating, and the smearing of pills made from medicinal substances according to the number of syllables in the mantra, as well as worship with them.
One should perform bathing with the water decocted from that [substance] and wear its ashes; by that, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs.
As for the medicinal herbs of the [four] castes, they are stated in the *Prapañcasāra* (Chapter 3, verse 53):
"Sandalwood, red sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, ushira, roga, jala, and saffron..."
Kakkola, jasmine, māṃsī, murā, coraka, granthi, rocanā, and patrā. || 1 ||
Pippalī, bilvā, guhā, aruṇā, tṛṇakā, lavaṅgāhvā, kumbhī, vandinī, udumbarā, kāśmarī, sthirā, abjā, darapuṣpikā, and mayūraśikhā. || 2 ||
Plakṣa, agnimantha, siṃhī, kuśāhva, darbha, kṛṣṇadarapuṣpī, rohiṇa, ṭuṇṭuka, bṛhatī, pāṭala, citrā, tulasī, and apāmārga. || 3 ||
Śatamūlī, latā, dvirephā, viṣṇukrāntā, muṣalī, añjalinī, dūrvā, śrīdevī, saha, as well as lakṣmī and sadābhadra. (4)

Thus have been declared the medicinal herbs according to the sequence of the letters beginning with 'A', which bestow all accomplishments through their various forms as pills, decoctions, and ashes. (5)

Thus it is said. Now, their names are as follows: sandalwood, red sandalwood, agarwood, camphor, uśīra, kuṣṭha, vāla, saffron, nutmeg, jaṭāmāṃsī, murā, cora, granthi, gorocanā, patrā, pippala, bilva, pṛśniparṇī, citraka, cloves, kattṛṇa, kaṭphala, vandi, and udumbara.
Pāṣāṇabheda, Padma, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Mayūraśikhā, Plakṣa, Agnimantha, Siṃhī, Kuśa, Kṛṣṇaśaṅkhapuṣpī, Rohiṇa, Syonāka, Bṛhatī, Pāṭalā, Mūṣakaparṇī,
Tulasī, Apāmārga, Indravallī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Aparājitā, Tālamūlī, Kṛtāñjali, Dūrvā, and Śrīdevī.
The fifty-one medicinal herbs— kumārī, bhāraṅgī, and bhadramustā—
are for the fifty-one letters in sequence from *a* to *kṣa*. Furthermore, another method is given in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
Having bestowed the consecrated and honored mantra upon the disciple,
the preceptor should then effect the union of the two according to the path seen in the scriptures.
Having interlaced the mantra with the letters of the name in their proper order,
one should then write the entire name at the beginning and the end, followed by the Praṇava.
One should inscribe the vowels upon the petals and meditate on them as being of the nature of nectar,
using yellow pigment, perfumes, and other substances upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf in the center of a lotus.
Having wrapped it with pure clay and then with beeswax,
one should place it in a small earthen vessel filled with honey.
He should place that small vessel into a new jar filled with milk;
the preceptor should hold the jar near the sacrificial fire-pit.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the identity of the mantra and the practitioner,
the knower of mantras should offer oblations a thousand or even a hundred times with the root mantra.
One should pour the three auspicious sweet substances into the pitcher;
having completed the fire-oblation, one should cast that pitcher into a body of water.
One should satisfy one's own guru and the Brahmins with gold, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and other offerings;
he who does not know this is not called a practitioner (sādhaka).
This secret has been told; one should not speak it to just anyone. However, one may speak this to an excellent disciple or to one's own son.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus on birch bark with yellow orpiment, fragrant substances, and so forth, one should write the mantra—interspersed with the letters of the practitioner's name—in its entirety within the pericarp, preceded and followed by the *praṇava* (oṃ).
Then, having written the vowels in pairs in sequence upon the petals, one should roll it into a pill.

Having wrapped it with purifying clay and further encased it with beeswax, one should place it into a small earthen vessel filled with the three sweets (madhuratrika). Then, having placed that earthen vessel— equipped with its mechanical pill (yantragutikā)— into a new pitcher filled with milk,
one should consecrate the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth according to the previously mentioned procedure, and position that pitcher near it.

Having performed the ritual placement (*saṃsthāpana*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows: "Oṃ, beginning with 'today' (*adya*) and so forth, desiring the accomplishment of such-and-such mantra, for the sake of achieving the unity of the Vidyā and the practitioner, I shall perform one thousand and eight or one hundred oblations of the three sweets (*madhuratraya*). Then, [one proceeds] with the mantra to be worshipped.
At each oblation, one should cast into the *kumbha* the residue of the offering clinging to the *sruva* ladle, according to the number previously determined;

having thus offered and cast that *kumbha* into a body of water, one should satisfy the preceptor, the Brahmins, and others with gold and other gifts. Even when this has been done, if success is still not attained, then [one should perform] the "melting" (*drāvaṇa*) and other rites of the mantra.
One should perform [these rites]. As it is stated in the *Mahāhārakatantra*:
"The wise one should perform liquefying, awakening, subduing, pressing, nourishing, drying, and burning; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected. (1)
Having written that mantra upon a yantra using seeds of the Varuṇa plant according to the sequence of stringing, with stone-paste, camphor, and saffron; || 2 ||
One should write the mantra joined with *uśīra* and *rocanā*;
one should place that written [mantra] in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. (3)
Through worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, he becomes melted and yields his fruit;
even if he is melted but not yet perfected, one should cause him to undergo awakening.
One should recite that [mantra] encased within the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī;
thus one becomes an accomplished Buddha, or otherwise, bring him under one's control. || 5 ||
With red sandalwood, as well as with wood, turmeric, madana, and realgar— by these, the mantra should be written upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf.
Madana, kastūrī, śilā, and manaḥśilā—when these are worn around the neck, one becomes a perfected master (siddha); otherwise, they will cause affliction.
Having indeed recited the words in the form of upper and lower [positions], [the mantra is effective].
In that same manner, one should meditate upon the deity who possesses both lower and higher forms;
having written the Vidyā with "milk from the sun" (cow's milk) and having stepped upon it with one’s foot.
With such a mantra, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed day after day;
for if one is afflicted and overcome by shame, the rite will not be perfected if he does not provide sustenance.
One should wear the written mantra encased by the first and third seed-syllables, using honey and milk; or alternatively, one should perform the rite of drying.
One should write the mantra interlaced with two seed-syllables of Vāyu;
one should wear it around the neck with ashes, otherwise one would be burned by the fire-seed syllable.
One should write the syllables of the mantra, surrounded on the four sides by the seed-syllable of fire, using oil from the *pālāśa* tree; one should then wear it around the neck.
"Śaṅkara has said that the mantra will be effective; there is no doubt in this matter.

Now follow the applications of these [mantras]. First, regarding the rite of subduing (*drāvaṇa*): the root mantra is strung together with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, *vaṃ*, using camphor, saffron, *gorocanā*, realgar, and orpiment.

Having drawn the yantra in the form of a circle of worship (pūjācakra) in the center, one should mix milk, honey, ghee, and water together in some vessel, place the yantra therein, and perform worship, recitation (japa), and fire-offerings (homa).
Now, as for awakening (bodhana): that consists of the recitation of the mantra encapsulated by the Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
Now, regarding subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*): in that regard, one should write the root mantra on birch bark with red sandalwood, *dāruharidrā*, musk, and realgar, and wear it around the neck.

Now, regarding *pīḍana* (suppression): having recited the mantra-syllables in an inverted order (*adharottara-bhāvena*), and having meditated upon the deity also in an inverted order, one should write that mantra with the milk of the *arka* plant on an *arka* leaf; then, standing upon it with one foot, one performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) while reciting the mantra in its inverted sequence.
One should perform [it].

Now, regarding nourishment (*poṣaṇa*): in that regard, one should write the mantra—enclosed within the third seed-syllable of the child—and wear it, having inscribed it on birch bark or similar material with cow's milk and honey.
Now, regarding drying: there, one should write the mantra interlaced with the seed-syllable of Vāyu using sacrificial ashes and wear it around the neck.

Now, regarding burning (*dāhana*): having written each individual syllable of the mantra encased within the fire-seed (*vahnibīja*), and having inscribed the fire-seed both below and above each letter using oil from *pālāśa* seeds, one should wear it around the neck. As for the definition of *vidarbha*, [it is stated] in the *Śāradātilaka*:

"One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between pairs of mantra-syllables; this is to be known as *vidarbha*. Thus it is stated in another tantra: "Interlacing with one [mantra-syllable] intervening is *grathana*, while that which has two intervening [mantra-syllables] is *vidarbha*. And in the *Ekavīrākalpa*:
One should perform each of these rites until the completion of the mandala;
the number for the auxiliary components, such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa), is one hundred and eight.
Thus, if [the goal] should not be accomplished, then the wise one should mutter the mantra upon nine leaves of the Aśvattha tree, along with the yantra and the rosary.

Having established the ritual procedure and the manual, and having performed the worship, one should cast [the image] into the water and then quickly take refuge in a guru for the sake of initiation. || 3 ||
Thus [it is said]. All this refers to subjects other than the Mahāvidyās;

however, because the Mahāvidyās have liberation alone as their primary goal and because worldly enjoyments are not to be pursued, according to the maxim of "incidental inclusion" (*ārthasamāja*), if enjoyments should occur, let them be; if they do not, let them not be.
Because it is improper to abandon the great vidyās. Now, incidentally, the characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhi*) are stated in another tantra:
"The effortless fulfillment of one's desires is the supreme characteristic of accomplishment."
In that same way, there is the removal of deaths as well as the vision of the deity. || 1 ||

Likewise, the accomplishment of the applications is the accomplishment of the afflictions; moreover, the characteristics of accomplishment are the entry into another's body and the entry into cities. (2)
For in this way, there is indeed the upward ascent, the movement within the city of the moving and the unmoving, the union with the Khecarīs, and the hearing of their stories, and so forth. (3)
He should perceive the cavities of the earth and the confluence in the subterranean realms (pātāla) and elsewhere;
likewise, he should effect the attraction of celestial women and the women of the nāgas.
Likewise, having attained sandals, pills, collyrium, and the secret entrance, as well as the powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), one shall attain liberation alone.
Thus, O Brahmin, has been described the primary characteristic of success:
renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, and a long life. (6)
It is the supreme means for subjugating kings and women;
it brings wonder to all places and in all worlds, and bestows happiness.
By its mere sight, it removes disease and likewise neutralizes poison;
it bestows scholarship and poetic talent—these four [benefits] effortlessly. (8)
Detachment, the desire for liberation, renunciation, mastery over all things, the practice of the eightfold yoga, and the total abandonment of the desire for enjoyment. (9)
Compassion toward all beings, the arising of qualities such as omniscience,
and the perfection of such virtues— these are the characteristics of middling accomplishment.
Renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, long life, affection from kings and women, and mastery over the world; (11)
Great sovereignty, wealth, and the prosperity of sons, wives, and so forth—
these are declared to be the inferior accomplishments (siddhis) for practitioners on the first stage.
Instruction in the mantra at a sacred ford, faith in the practice of recitation, and the conviction that it will bear fruit— this is the characteristic of true spiritual attainment.
If one should apply seeds—whether they be desire, poison, or other seeds—to those mantras that are seedless, the mantra bestows success upon those who recite it. (14)

Mantras bestow boons when established in their proper place, and they grant fruit when established in meditation; for those devoid of both place and meditation, there is no fruit even from ten million recitations. 15.
The wise practitioner should recite the root mantra encased within the *mātṛkā* [alphabet] one hundred times in both forward and reverse order; at the end of that, he should recite the mantra alone.
One should thus recite it every day until the month is completed;
it has been stated by those who know the tantras that the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur.
One should satisfy the guru with devotion through ornaments, clothing, and other such offerings;
by the mere satisfaction of the guru, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur. (18)
"Those who know the tantras say that all this has its root in the Guru;
O Goddess of the Gods, one who bypasses the Guru has no authority in this scripture. (19)
O Goddess, if the application of these mantras and tantras is performed without the permission of the guru, the loss of accomplishment occurs. (20)
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
For whomsoever [the mind] is unwavering toward these three—the Deity, the Mantra, and the Guru—[he attains liberation]. 21.
For one whose devotion is uninterrupted, accomplishment is not far off;
but for those who lack meditative cultivation, who are petty, and whose minds are base, it is not so.
"Recitation fourfold is prescribed for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it shall not be so.

From this statement in the *Ekavīrākalpa*, it follows that for those who abide in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), the attainment of mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*) results from the fourfold preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). For this very reason, it is said: "The mantra is practiced in four ways."
It was stated previously: "of small animals" is the meaning. "Meditation" refers to the meditation on the divine hero (divyavīra).
Now, regarding the divine preliminary practice (*divyapuraścaraṇa*) in another tantra:
"If a brahmin is of excellent lineage and devoted to the substances of the *kula*, then he should perform the *kulasādhana* according to this procedure. (1)
Liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—these should be known as the constant requirements for one another in the worship of the Kula deity. (2)

Thus: whether it be a Kulottama, a Divya, or a Vīra, by this procedure—that is, by the procedure to be described hereafter—the Pāśava method alone is set aside for the Brahmins by the term "vipra-pradāna" (bestowal upon Brahmins), which refers to the rules for secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Kulārṇava*, having introduced the Kula lineage (*kulakrama*):
This should always be performed by Brāhmaṇas; by Kṣatriyas at the onset of battle;
by Vaiśyas in the application of wealth; but never by Śūdras.

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, statements such as "the secondary alternative (anukalpa) is for Brahmins" refer primarily to animals and Brahmins; for, in abundance, Brahmins are indeed like animals. In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"And at the time of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should worship the Kula-Śakti."
One should honor the initiated woman with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with food items consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa). || 1 ||
At the time of commencement, having personally brought the woman into an empty house with food, snacks, and drinks, one should purify the arghya and other offerings.
Having performed the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should bring the Śakti face-to-face;
first, one should offer a seat and then say "welcome" once more.
Having offered water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water for rinsing,
one should bathe [the image] with scented flowers and water, and then begin the ritual grooming of the hair.
Then, having perfumed the hair, one should offer a silken garment;
thereafter, having spread a seat in another place, one should offer a pair of sandals.
Having given [these] and seated her there, one should adorn her with various ornaments and decorations, and offer unguents, perfumes, and garlands.
One should offer within the center of the maṇḍala, in a beautiful golden vessel, the five types of food: that which is to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, and eaten.
Various kinds of flour-based sweets endowed with diverse flavors,
as well as milk, curd, ghee, buttermilk, and fresh butter with sugar.
It was filled with stones and various kinds of elixirs,
as well as coconuts, wood-apples, oranges, and *sudarśana* fruits.
Limpāka, bījapūra, and the excellent dāḍima fruit;
likewise, various forest fruits and various fragrant ointments. || 10 ||
Sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, fresh sprouts, ṭaṅkaṇa, and likewise lodhra—both that which grows in water and that which grows in the forest. || 11 ||
Produced from various mountains, adorned with various ornaments,
[it is to be used] especially for recitation and worship in the beginning, the end, and the middle. (12)
If one does not honor one's beloved, then one is besmeared by obstacles;
there is no fruit for what was previously acquired—what need is there to speak of the next life? (13)
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, as well as the pacification of my anger and heat and the destruction of obstacles, one should strive with every effort. (14)
"Women of noble families, whether of the *kula* or non-*kula* [lineages], should be honored with effort.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, the rule regarding the beginning, middle, and end [of the ritual] is to be observed even in the absence [of these women]; for it is stated that even in the case of their absolute absence, the essential rite must be performed at the beginning and the end, as well as at the time of commencement, and especially at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*).

Thus, in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the venerable ascetic Vidyāraṇya, who was a disciple of the venerable Pragalbhācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Viṣṇuśarmācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Govindācārya— the worshipful feet of the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya.
The sixteenth breath-exhalation (śvāsa). || 16 ||
Now, in the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra,
the seventeenth chapter.
Now, the secret preliminary practice (*rahasya-puraścaraṇa*). This is stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "Alternatively, the preliminary practice is desired by another method:
on a Tuesday or a Saturday, a human skull is procured. (1)
Having mixed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and especially with sandalwood and other substances,
one should deposit it in the ground at a depth of half a cubit in a grove or forest.
If on that day, during the night, he should recite the mantra alone a thousand times according to the measure, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
having brought a corpse and dug a trench right there at its door with that very [corpse], || 4 ||
From that day until that same day, he shall possess one hundred and eight [of these];
he will become a master of all supernatural powers—of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is said. Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired to be performed in another manner on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
Having recited [the mantra] from sunrise until the next sunrise, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments.
Thus it is said. In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner, specifically during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth lunar day."
Having worshipped with devotion, one should then recite the thousand [names] alone at night in a solitary place, a dwelling solely of darkness.
One should be intent on fasting from the eighth day until the ninth;
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the next eighth day of the dark fortnight. (3)
When the mantra has been recited one thousand times, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is considered complete;
this is done during the great festival beginning from the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight until the ninth.
One should perform worship especially on the eighth and ninth nights;
on the tenth day, one should break the fast with offerings including fish, meat, and so forth.
Devoted to worship, one should daily recite the mantra six thousand times,
beginning from the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] until the next fourteenth day.
O Great Goddess, when this has been recited that many times, it is considered the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
indeed, by mere recitation alone, the mantras become perfected.

Thus, it is said in the *Svatantratantra*: "At night, having worshipped the Goddess with meat and juice according to the ritual injunctions, one who is naked and even moist with [sexual] fluids should then approach a naked woman. (1)
Then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations to the Goddess into the blazing fire;
remaining steady in the *yonikuṇḍa*, one should likewise offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter, meat, fish, and so forth.
The practitioner should satisfy [the deities] with fish mixed with meat ten times [the number of offerings made];
and having performed the consecration of the one who embodies the universe ten times the number of those libations (tarpaṇa), [he should proceed].
One should feed a tenth part [of the offering] as a sweet treat to the practitioner, which is dear to the deity;
one should also present the first portion of meat, fish, and chewed food.
"Then, O Dear One, one should satisfy the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other offerings.

Because the Divine System (Divyamata) is the most excellent, the recitation (*japa*) should be exactly one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*); the daily [recitation] should be only a thousand, precisely because this is consistent with the previously cited statement that "one should recite a *lakṣa*."

In the fire sacrifice and other rites, the first and subsequent ritual items hold primacy; there is a fixed rule regarding the sacrificial pit having the form of a womb. As stated in the *Kulasambhava*:
"At night, one should remain naked with hair loose even during sexual union, according to the true principle."
It should be recited with diligence for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. || 1 ||
Thus it is said in another tantra:
"One should recite the mantra for as long as one does not emit semen;
O Goddess of the gods, once the semen has been emitted, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra again. (1)
"At night, with his mouth full of betel, he should bow down a hundred thousand times upon his bed.
And: "Entering the temple of the *liṅga* yields even greater fruit than sitting upon a corpse."

As with the consecration of the womb (*yony-abhimantraṇa*) and so forth, or the sacrifice to the female messenger (*dūtī-yāga*), it was previously stated that at times other than those for formal practice, the sight of naked women is forbidden. O Goddess, if by the power of fortune the vision of the Kula arises, then at that very moment, one should personally perform mental worship toward them.

"One should arrange [it]"—thus it is stated in some places, even though it has already been enjoined. In this way, when there is a contradiction, the prohibition is that one must not engage in mockery by force of a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*);
rather, the injunction is preceded by the cultivation of the internal state (*bhāva*). And so it is said in another Tantra:
One must never, under any circumstances, inflict blows, verbal abuse, crookedness, or unkindness upon them; otherwise, it will become an obstacle to success.
Women are gods; women are life; indeed, women alone are existence.
One should always remain among groups of women, even in the absence of one's own wife.
One should offer to the deities the flowers gathered by his hand, the water gathered by his hand, and the food gathered by his hand. || 3 ||

Thus [it is said]. Because of the statement, "Whether one is divine (divya) or a hero (vīra), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of a hundred thousand [times] at night," the procedure for both the divine and the heroic is identical. For the divine [practitioner], the practice of the *kula-rūpa* is essential, according to the saying: "By the very sequence of the *gāndharva* [union], the fifth [state] is difficult to attain on earth."

Regarding the Śrīvidyā, the procedure is indeed divine (*divya*), whereas elsewhere both [procedures] are equal. Now, concerning the *vīra-puraścaraṇa* which is of the nature of the *kula*, it is stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"The task of *vīra-sādhana* must be performed by heroic persons (*vīra-puruṣa*)."
It should be performed even by divine beings, but not by common, vulgar people. || 1 ||
"It is certain that whatever action is divine and heroic is not [permitted] for the animal [initiate].

Here, by the phrase "even by the divine [initiates]," it is established that [these actions] are to be performed by the divine [initiates]. This being the case, the heroic rite is secret within the divine [rite], and the divine rite is secret within the heroic [rite]; even so, that [latter] occurs only occasionally.

"O Pārvatī, although they appear in the guise of divine heroes, in reality everything must be concealed and guarded with effort, like one's own birthplace. Through disclosure, there is a loss of accomplishment; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. This is because of such statements from other Tantras, and because it has been said: "One should guard [this] like the lover of one's mother."
During the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and other such practices, heroes should worship another’s wife who has been initiated, according to their capacity. As it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"At the time of the *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship another’s woman."
Having initiated her with garments, ornaments, and the like, he should feed her with foods consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa).
At the time of commencement, he should himself prepare cooked food,
as well as milk, curd, ghee, buttermilk, fresh butter, and sugar.
A moist piece of coral, various kinds of elixirs, a coconut, a wood-apple, an orange, and a *sudarśana* fruit. (3)
Limpāka, bījapūra, and the excellent dāḍimī fruit;
likewise various wild fruits and various fragrant ointments. || 4 ||
Sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, fresh sprouts, ṭaṅkaṇa, and lodhra—both that which grows in water and that which grows in the forest. || 5 ||
Having brought [the image] produced from various stones and adorned with various ornaments into an empty house, it was purified with water for the *arghya* offering.
Having performed the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should bring the Śakti before oneself;
she may be a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, or a Śūdrā who is an ornament to her family.
The courtesan, the barber’s daughter, the washerwoman, and likewise the actress—
all of them were women of noble family, distinguished by their exceptional skill.
Thus, having installed the eight empowered goddesses (*śakti*) in sequence, having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering,

and having sprinkled them with the *arghya* water, one should transform them into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting "Vam," and then effect the differentiation of their forms into the eight *śaktis*.
Having assigned names to them by means of the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī,
one should first offer a seat and welcome them again and again;
then [offer] the arghya, the water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (pānīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water [for rinsing].
One should bathe [the image] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and likewise perform the grooming of the hair;
then, having fumigated the hair, one should offer silk cloth.
Then, having spread a seat in another place and placed a pair of sandals there,
he brought [her] there and adorned her with various ornaments and decorations.
Having fumigated [them] with incense, one should offer perfume and garlands as anointment;
having invoked each respective power, one should bring them together at their heads.
Then, having invoked that Śakti in her successive forms beginning with Brahmāṇī, one should perform the installation of the life-force (jīvanyāsa) and so forth; as follows:
by means of the previously mentioned mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), [one should recite] "the vital breaths of Brahmāṇī are in this place," and so on.

The meaning is that one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) here according to the sequence beginning with "the vital breaths" (*iha prāṇāḥ*). In the same way, the passage beginning with "O Great Sovereign" (*māheśvaryai*) and so forth is to be inferred.
Then, having offered perfume, flowers, lamps, food, condiments, and so on, [one should place them] in order upon their left ears.
One should recite the hymn of praise. It is stated in that very same place:
"In the center of the maṇḍala, one should offer food—namely, what is to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, and eaten—in a beautiful golden vessel. (13)
If there should be any women who have not been initiated, one should then present them with the Māyā-mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the hymn of praise into their left ears.
O Mother Goddess, salutations to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman;
through your grace, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra. (15)
O Great Goddess, bestower of boons, whose form is supreme bliss!
By your grace, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all vidyās, supreme in the play of Kumāra, please remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra. || 17 ||
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O carrier of the son of Vinatā!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacle and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, you who lifted up the earth with your tusk!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Goddess who bears the form of Śakra, worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads and blood, O destroyer of obstacles!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacle and grant me the perfection of mantra.
O Mahālakṣmī, you of great energy, who destroy agitation and torment;
out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra.
O Goddess, who consists of both the measure and the measurer, yet who is beyond the measure and the measurer;
O Goddess, who are one and manifold, whose form is the universe—salutations be unto you!
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of undertakings, or upon seeing a clever woman, for him no obstacle shall arise. (24)
O son, these have been declared to you as the door-deities of one of noble lineage;
if he does not worship them at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [he incurs fault].
O child, the fruit of his worship is carried away by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas;
however, if she is overcome by shame during the meal, [the fruit is taken] from outside her house.
Standing, one should recite or remember the hymn until satisfaction arises;
having sipped water, one should offer mouth-fresheners and the like, as well as betel.
Then one should offer a garland again, as well as sandalwood paste mixed with fragrant unguents;
having performed circumambulation and requested a boon, one should depart in happiness. || 28 ||
If she does not go to another, she may approach her own daughter, her own younger sister, her elder sister, her maternal aunt, or her mother’s co-wife. (29)
In the absence of the former, the latter is to be worshipped, for they are considered to be my own portions;
indeed, in the absence of all, even a single one should be worshipped with great effort.
O Bhairava, if there is even one person there who knows the family scriptures and is worthy of worship, then all the gods—including Brahmā, Śiva, and the others—are truly worshipped. (31)
O Kulabhairava, if even a single young woman there is honored and looked upon,
then all the supreme goddesses are indeed honored.
Thus it is said in the Vīratantra:
"Whoever, being well-composed, performs the heroic practice (vīrasādhana), attains the supreme accomplishment; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (1)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana), which grants the accomplishment of all goals, provided one remains pure and free from fear. (2)
There exists nothing superior to this for bestowing swift accomplishment;
it was proclaimed of old by Bhairava as the granter of the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (3)
Having indeed clothed [the image] with the *mūla-mantra* by means of tying it with a cord,
one should again clothe it with another garment outside that, and anoint its limbs with the *mūla-mantra*.
Having worn the uṣṇīṣa with the root mantra and an upright tilaka mark made of vermilion,
and having bowed to one's chosen deity and the guru, the journey should take place within the middle watch of the day.
And that [practice] should be performed by the practitioners together with their hearts focused on the mantra;
remaining unperturbed after having eaten food, one should perform the ritual means (sādhana) once the meal is finished.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
on Tuesday, and during the dark of night, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
Having undertaken the ritual observance, including the nectar of the family and other substances,
Unmattānandabhairava [dwelt] at night in the marketplace of the dead.
"Clad in the directions, pure, adorned with ashes, with disheveled hair.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, being clothed in the directions (digvāsas) is prescribed in some places; and elsewhere:
"The new moon day joined with Mars (Bhūmiputra) brings about an auspicious rising."
O blessed lady, during that conjunction of Puṣkara, that best of excellent heroes [was present].
Thus, in the Rudrayāmala, in the Satyakrama: "In the Kṛta age, one should worship the Goddess with the four castes using milk, clarified butter, honey, and flour-cakes;
in the Tretā age, one should worship the Goddess with clarified butter by all castes. (1)
In the Dvāpara age, one should worship her with honey and all varieties of colors;
in the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped solely with those fermented liquors (āsava).
Thus, the rule for the secondary rites (*anukalpa*) in other ages is common to all castes; even the primary rite (*pradhānakalpa*) in the Kali age is of that same nature.
Furthermore, liquor made from jaggery and ginger is not permitted for a Brāhmaṇa.
The gauḍī [liquor] is for the kṣatriya, while the mādhvī is indeed for the vaiśya.
All liquor made from plantain, honey, and rice-bark, or even plain liquor, is prescribed for a Śūdra, as is any other substance that serves as an oblation.

Thus [it is said]. In some places, the explanation is as before: in reality, this is a secondary option (*anukalpa*) that occurs when the primary [option] is unavailable, and not intended to refer to the distinction between eras or castes, such as the Gauḍī and Mādhvī [liquors].

The distinction lies in being intent upon desire (*kāmanā*). Alternatively, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "it becomes" (*bhavati*), such that the meaning is: "if it does not become liquor (*surā*). In the term *gauḍī-mādhvī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to *guḍa* and *madhu*. Even for Śūdras, when the primary [liquors] are unavailable, plantains (*kadalī*) and the like are indeed considered liquor (*surā*).

This is a secondary alternative regarding liquor. Or rather, the word "there" (tatra) indicates the meaning "on the funeral pyre," because this is the section concerning the practice of *vīrasādhana*. Since going to the funeral pyre, touching the corpse, and so forth are irreproachable in that context, what inconsistency is there in the primary [practice] being irreproachable? That [word "there"] then signifies the shaking of the head [in assent].

This is because both the primary and secondary options are prescribed. Regarding the phrase "with the juice of jaggery and ginger," as well as "plantain" and so forth, one should offer coconut water in a vessel of bell-metal or copper, and likewise honey;
similarly, curd and milk [should be offered] in copper, as well as curd mixed with jaggery, or else jaggery and ginger for the purpose of worship.

One should arrange [them]. Thus, even that [arrangement] becomes equal to the primary [rite] precisely through the conjunction with such vessels and so forth; yet, because of the prohibition, it remains in that very state. Therefore, these statements refer to secondary alternatives (anukalpa) even when the primary [materials] are available. Furthermore:
"One should worship the Supreme Goddess precisely according to the sequence of the *Kulāgama*," because this is the inherent intent (*svarasa*) of all the Tantras.
And the *Kulāgama* is the *Kulārṇava*. As it says (p. 5):
"In the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, and Buddhist systems..."
In the Buddhist, Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, Māntra, and likewise in the Kālāmukha [traditions]. || 1 ||
O Pārvatī, in the Dakṣiṇa and Vāma Siddhāntas, as well as in the Vedic and other traditions,
worship performed without the two hundred syllables [of the mantra] shall be fruitless.
O Goddess, if one performs recitation, worship, vows, or austerity without the ritual substances,
that becomes fruitless, just like an oblation poured into ashes.
Just as the drinking of soma among the learned at sacrifices is not considered a fault, O Goddess, so too the drinking of wine grants both enjoyment and liberation, like soma. (4)

By such words, occurring by the thousands, [the practice] is prescribed for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; likewise here, because it is prescribed by the Veda inferred from Smṛti, it is not a means for unrighteousness (*adharma*), whereas in the case of what is prohibited, unrighteousness certainly arises. In the *Laghustava* composed by the venerable Dharmācārya: "The Brahmins, the kings..."
"The others [should] dissect [it] with milk, clarified butter, honey, and liquor. In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Indeed, there are distinctions of caste according to the sequence of castes; moreover, a Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with a sattvic liquid alone. Likewise:
In this manner, even a Kṣatriya should never offer an image made of flour;
likewise, he should not offer coconut water in a vessel of bell-metal or copper, nor should he offer honey.
The gift [of a cow] belongs to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, never to the twice-born Brāhmaṇa;
by merely giving it away in this manner, the Brāhmaṇa becomes short-lived.
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra: "In that [rite] where the offering and consumption of wine are necessarily prescribed, a Brāhmaṇa should prepare honey-wine (madhu-madya) in a copper vessel. (1)
By giving liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa;
by giving the blood from his own body, he incurs the sin of self-slaughter.
"Thus, through the investigation of various scriptures, the worship of the Brahmins according to the secondary method (anukalpa) is performed;
with a purely sattvic disposition, the Brāhmaṇa should satisfy Śivā. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
O Goddess of the Gods, those who disregard the dharma appropriate to their caste and stage of life consume meat, blood, or even liquor by us two. (1)

"They become *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, or *brahmarākṣasas*. In reality, however, even in the Vāmāgama, there is no eligibility for a Brahmin, because of the statement: "Wine made from jaggery and ginger is not [permitted] for a Brahmin. And likewise, the Śruti says: "Wine is eternal..."

The statement "a Brahmin should avoid" is a mandatory injunction (*nityapada*). Wherever there is mention of occurrence through desire, it is likewise a mandatory prohibition even in the case of unintentional action; this is because its definitive meaning has been established by the Veda itself. Thus, it should be understood that for a Brahmin, there is indeed a prohibition even regarding the acquisition of wealth through improper means.
Likewise, meaning is also conveyed by words such as "ā" and so forth; for example: "For a Brāhmaṇa, [liquor] is always forbidden to drink;

for a Kṣatriya, when battle approaches; for a Vaiśya, when in possession of wealth; but for a Śūdra, never at all. And in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "The Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk, the [Kṣatriyas] with ghee..."

[It is to be performed] by those born of royal lineages, by Vaiśyas of the honey-making caste (*mākṣika*), by those of the Śūdra caste, and so forth. Indeed, the discernment between the essential and the non-essential is required. Regarding that, the rule is as follows:
one should be free from hesitation, fearless, heroic, shameless, and devoid of curiosity.
Having determined the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, one may drink the Varuni wine that bestows boons.
If there were a lapse in the performance of that rite for men who are engaged in it, how then could the seven crores of lords of sages perform it? (2)
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, there is a censure regarding what is prohibited:

"Even a Vīra, by drinking alcohol in vain here without worshipping the repetition of mantras (āvṛtti), the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti), and Vaṭuka and the others, shall incur the curse of the deity. (1)
Without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation of the mantras, even a hero who drinks according to the rite for drinking the *paśu* will go to hell. (2)
He who engages in this scripture without knowing the Kaulika conduct and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru—you certainly cause him suffering. (3)
But he who, being uninitiated in the Kaula knowledge, desires to consume the substance,
O Goddess, is a great sinner, excluded from all dharma.

For one who has fallen away from the conduct of the samaya, who acts according to his own whims, and who is evil-minded, there are no accomplishments; rather, there is a fall from his lineage, and all of that leads to hell.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains no perfection in this world nor the supreme goal in the hereafter.

For one who lives according to their own whims and is devoid of the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā), there is no attainment of the true goal anywhere, even through asceticism, pilgrimages, vows, and the like.
One who drinks unfermented liquor, engages in sexual intercourse by force,
or eats meat brought for one's own pleasure, shall go to the Raurava hell.

There are hundreds of such statements concerning injunctions and prohibitions. However, there is a counter-exception (pratiprasava) in certain cases: "If, by chance, one obtains the substance *mali*, having taken it with devotion, having recollected the Guru and his *pādukā* with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), [one should consume it] conjoined with the three principles (*tattvatraya*)."
One should take [the substance] while reciting the root mantra. This also refers specifically to the special substances for the consecrated worship (*saṃskṛta-pūjā*).
Regarding the scriptural promise of results (*phala-śruti*):
"That made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*); that made from molasses (*gauḍī*) bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*)."
O Dear One, the three kinds known as Mādhvī, Surā, and that called Muktikarī should be understood.
The Ikṣuvī is said to bestow knowledge, while the Drākṣā grants sovereignty;
the Tālajā is praised for paralyzing, and the Khārjūrī destroys enemies. (10)
That which originates from the coconut bestows prosperity; that known as the breadfruit grants auspiciousness;
and that known as the madhūka produces knowledge and destroys the enemy of poverty.
O Kuleśānī, that which is called maireya destroys all sins;
it is wine produced from milk-trees, originating from their bark.
O Goddess, that substance which possesses unsurpassed bliss, fragrance, and is captivating to the mind—that is the most excellent, bringing delight to the deities. (13)
Merely by the sight of Surā, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy fords (tīrthas);
merely by smelling its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices (śatakratus). || 14 ||
O Goddess, by drinking it, one directly attains the fourfold liberation;
however, the result of seeing meat and so forth is like the result of seeing liquor.
Thus, it appears logical that the very words spoken in the *Kulārṇava* are what should be respected; enough with further chatter. In the *Nīlatantra* (Paṭala 11), the Goddess said:
O God, the sequence of the Mahānīla has been indicated but not fully revealed;
O Mahādeva, please explain this great [teaching] which bestows all accomplishments.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess of noble hips, to the supreme Vīrasādhana, which bestows all accomplishments directly and is saluted by all the gods. (2)
O Goddess, it removes all sins and destroys all diseases;
O beautiful lady, it belongs to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the guardians of the quarters.
O Goddess, it bestows spontaneous accomplishment upon all the Bhairavas, Gandharvas, and Yogins; it is the great abode of them all.
O Goddess, there is nothing else that bestows accomplishment apart from the heroic practice (vīrasādhana);
[only one who is] of great strength, great intelligence, great courage, and pure [attains it]. (5)
O Great Goddess, for their sake— the great pure ones who are compassionate and devoted to the welfare of all beings— this Nīla-sādhana has been told.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights—and especially during the dark fortnight—one should practice according to the prescribed rule. (7)

O beautiful woman, on a Tuesday during the dark fortnight, when one watch of the night has passed, within that half-watch, one should properly prepare the articles for worship and the sacrificial offering (bali).
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of meat with fat, jaggery, goat meat, liquor, flour-cakes,
and various fruits, according to the specific practice prescribed for each respective ritual manual.

Having brought him to the cremation ground, the practitioner himself, free from fear, [should proceed] with friends who hold weapons in their hands and are endowed with qualities equal to his own. (10)
Intent on meditating upon the deity, he should not look toward the four directions;
if the practitioner is afraid there, [he should consider that] there are practitioners in all four directions.
If he is not proclaimed as Bhairava himself alone, then the most excellent practitioner, having gone to a cremation ground that has been cleansed, [should proceed]. (12)
If [the ground] has been washed, one should generally perform the collection of the bones;
[this is done] with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra (*astra*), while sprinkling [water] upon the sacrificial grounds.
Having meditated upon the dust of the Guru’s feet, as well as Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and the Mātṛkās, beginning with the left foot; 14.
And those gods who are stationed here, as well as the terrifying rākṣasas, piśācas, yakṣas, siddhas, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases; || 15 ||
May the yoginīs, the mothers, the spirits, and all the women who move through the sky be the bestowers of siddhis today, and likewise may they be my protectors. (16)
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the Lord of the Cremation Ground,
Bhairava Kālabhairava. (17)
The knower of mantras should diligently worship Mahākāla in the four directions beginning with the east using water for the feet and other offerings, and afterwards present the bali offering.
Then again, after the seed-syllable of the corpse (Śavabīja), [one recites] the mantra of the Lord of the Cremation Ground (Śmaśānādhipati):
"O you who possess meat and food, accept this bali-offering thereafter. (19)
Then, [recite] "gṛhṇa gṛhṇāpaya yugam vighnanivāraṇam"; thereafter, perform "kuru siddhim me," and at the end, provide [the mantra] accompanied by "svāhā. (20)
O Goddess, the first bali offering is said to be with the mantra beginning with Tārā;
at the end of Māyā, one should utter Bhairava, and after that, Bhayānaka. (21)
Having extracted the previous mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation on the right;
at the end of "hūm," one should extract [the mantra] from Mahākāla as before.
In the western direction, one should assign [the deity] to Kāladeva, preceded by the Praṇava;
at the end of "Śabda" (or "Vā") and at the end of the word "Kāla," the word "Bhairava" follows.
Saying "O Lord of the Cremation Ground," one should offer [the oblation] to the north as before;
then, one should present three supreme bali-offerings in the middle of the funeral pyre.
O Kālarātri, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā of terrible roar!
Accept this offering, O Mother, and grant me the unsurpassed siddhi. (25)
Having offered the bali-oblation to Lālikā, one should cause it to be given to Bhūtanātha;
at the end of "Śabda" (or "Vā") and at the end of "Bhūtanātha," one should also say "Śmaśānādhipa."
One should cause the supreme bali offering to be given with a mantra beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ);
[the mantra is] "Hūṃ," followed by "sarvagaṇanāthān," and then again "dhipa. (27)
Having placed [the offering] on the head of the cremation ground, one should recite as before;
O beautiful lady, having offered the bali with the syllable Om (Tāra) at the beginning, [one should purify] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed the sprinkling of the bones, one should then install the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra);
one should install that seat-mantra there upon either birch bark or a leaf of the banyan tree.
Having spread out a seat upon that [altar] and then assumed the vīrāsana posture,
O Goddess of the Gods, one should scatter clods of earth in all directions as part of the vīrārcana rite.
O Goddess, [there are] two *kūrca* seeds, followed by a pair of *māyā*s; then *kālike*, *ghoradaṃṣṭre*, *pracaṇḍe*, and *caṇḍanāyike*. (31)
Having said "dāraya" (tear asunder) for the Dānavas, then "hana" twice;
then the supreme seed (Vīra), and then the pair "chedaya" (cut down) for the great obstacle. || 32 ||
The mantra for the worship of heroes is considered to end with *dviṭha* (svāhā) and end with *varma* (huṃ) and *astra* (phaṭ).
One should cast clods of earth consecrated with this mantra into the ten directions.
In the midst of that, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles;
yet, O Goddess of gods, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear, [then he is overcome].
Then, protected by various groups of friends, he is not overcome;
[he is like a lamp] whose wick is made of cotton and vātī-lata fibers, together with the sun, moon, and white [substances]. 35.
Having placed a lamp there, one should worship the yantra;
if that great lamp is extinguished, one is overcome by obstacles.
And below that, one should bury a "bank-lamp" with the Astra-mantra;
then, according to the specific ritual procedure for each [deity], one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites.
One should again install the sixteenfold vidyā conjoined with the letters of the alphabet, both in direct and reverse order; this is proclaimed as Tārāṣāḍhā. (38)
One who has thus disposed the body in six ways becomes manifestly the Lord of the Universe;
having performed either the sixfold placement or the placement of the *tāraka*, one should then recite the mantra. (39)
Thus it is said in another Tantra:

"O Goddess, if [the deity] says 'Give! Give! at the end of the recitation or even in the midst of the recitation, one should then offer the *bali* offering; otherwise, the *bali* should be offered at the conclusion."
The *bali* consists of goats and the like; however, food mixed with meat and other offerings are for the purpose of the *balipātra* vessels.

Furthermore, it is stated in some places that one should perform the recitation (*japa*) while seated in the western part of the funeral pyre (*citā*). "Whether it be the Guru, a fellow disciple (*satīrthya*), a student (*śiṣya*), or even a practitioner (*sādhaka*), he should be established in the southern direction."
"And the wise one should become the superior practitioner (uttarasādhaka) at a spot some distance away from the place where the arrow was thrown. And in the Rudrayāmala:
"Then, with the fivefold offering (pañcopacāra), one should worship the deity in front."
After closing his eyes and meditating upon the Goddess, he should recite the mantra. || 1 ||
One should recite the single-syllable mantra a thousand times and the three-syllable mantra ten thousand times;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should recite the Gajāntaka mantra one thousand times.
Or, beginning at night, one should perform [the rite] until sunrise;
if there is unbearable fear, one should bind the ears and eyes with a cloth.
Then, if one perceives nothing until midnight,
one should offer arghya and mustard seeds with the mantra known as Jayadurgā.
You are sesame, having Soma as your deity, the giver of satisfaction through the Gosava sacrifice;
you are the bestower of heaven upon the ancestors and capable of granting fearlessness to mortals.
"Bringer of peace against obstacles caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*.
Having thus cast the sesame seeds, O Goddess, in four parts beginning with Śiva; (6)
Having gone seven steps again, he should sit down in that very same place;
having worshipped the deity there as well, he should mutter the supreme mantra.
One should recite the mantra fearlessly until success is attained;
whatever occurs, such as fear, should be understood as being like a dream, and on the following day one should perform the remaining rites.

Thus [it is said]. The "remainder" refers to the feeding of Brahmins and so forth. Having risen with the aforementioned substance, one should mutter the *mantra*; this is the removal of fear and the protective *tilaka*, as mentioned in some places.
Saffron, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, red sandalwood, camphor, ruby, saffron flower, and yellow sandalwood. || 9 ||
Having prepared each [ingredient] individually, the wise man should combine them in one place;
the hero, being composed, should take blood from the tip of his tongue in a cremation ground.
Having fashioned a pill with that very [substance], one should mutter the mantra of Bhadrakālī:
"The blue one, the one with a blue banner, the one with a lolling tongue, and the formidable Karālikā. (11)
Having applied a tilaka on his forehead, the practitioner himself becomes free from fear;
O Goddess, it is endowed with the weapon of space (viyad-astra) and adorned by the moon of the left eye.
O Pārvatī, listen to the seed-syllable of each of those individual entities;
the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra three hundred times along with it. (13)
"O Cāmuṇḍā, you of terrible roar, take the blood from the tip of my tongue;
having consumed this offering, grant me a boon in this dense forest! (14)
