O Kālī, O Kālī, O fierce and terrible one! Then [recite] the weapon-mantra and again the armor-mantra.
She is called Kālī out of a desire for the welfare of living beings. (15)
O Great Goddess, the pair of *kūrca* mantras for Nīlā has been told to you;
O Goddess, [the mantra] joined with *viyat* (ha), *agni* (ra), and *bala* (ba) conjoined with *indra* (la). (16)
Then, joined with the crescent moon (candrakhaṇḍa), there is again the blue syllable (nīlapada);
then follow the banners (patāke) and hūṃ phaṭ—this is considered the mantra of the eastern peak. || 17 ||
The goddess Jayaśrīdharaṇī is on the banner at the boundary of the enclosure;
thus, this blue banner is to be employed, or it is used in the practice of Nīla.
That Vidyā who is Mahātārā is proclaimed as Kālī;
[one should offer] ruby, saffron, and especially fragrant substances. (19)

Thus: *viyat* is the letter *ha*; "endowed with the weapon" means endowed with the letter *ra*; *vāmākṣi* is the letter *ī*; "the moon" is the *anusvāra*. Therefore, the seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*. The sequence [of the mantras] is, respectively, the weapon (*astra*), the armor (*kavaca*), and so forth; however, the sequence of "weapon" and "armor" is [reversed] by that [rule], resulting in *huṃ phaṭ* and the pair of *kūrca* [syllables].

*Hūṃ hūṃ* is the essential form of power (*bala-svarūpa*). *Indra* is the letter *ī*; thus, [the seed-syllable] *harabalīṃ* is the *kūṭa*. *Jaya* is the letter *na*, and *Śrī* is the letter *ī*; *Dharaṇī* is the letter *la*, thus [the seed-syllable] *nīla*. *Varaṇa* is armor (*kavaca*), thus *huṃ*; *skhalana* is the weapon (*astra*), thus *phaṭ*. In some places it is also said: "with eyes anointed with collyrium. Furthermore:
The Lord Bhairava himself is indeed present there, marked by a staff;
seeing him wandering here and there, the hero should recite the mantra.
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune a staff is obtained there,
then that very Bhairava himself becomes the sustainer of the universe.
There, O beautiful lady, having bowed to Mahādeva and Mahākāla and having applied that mark of ashes, one becomes Vīreśvara himself. (3)
Thus, "that ash" refers to the ash of the cremation ground; the meaning is that it is the sectarian mark (tilaka) consisting of the wearing of sacred ash (vibhūti).

As for the ritual application (*prayoga*) therein: first, having identified the lunar festival (*parvan*) such as the new moon day prescribed for that time, when half a watch (*praharārdha*) of the night has passed, one—either fasting or having already eaten—should don a garment secured with a cord (*ghaṭībandha*) while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Above...
Having covered himself with a garment that conceals all [the body], wearing a turban, or with hair loose or naked,
having applied a tilaka previously prepared with the root mantra, having anointed his eyes with collyrium,
smeared his limbs with red sandalwood and other substances, and having made an *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark with vermilion using the root mantra itself—
Having meditated on the Goddess in the heart and the Guru at the crown of the head, and having bowed,
one should take whatever materials for worship and the bali-offering vessel are available— such as *kulāmṛta*, meat, grain-flour, fish, and *vaṭuka*— and a goat or similar animal for the *bali*.

Having taken perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), with friends acting as guards holding swords in their hands, having performed protection rites with the Aghora-weapon mantra and other spells,
having tied his topknot, and remembering the root-mantra in his heart, [he should approach] a funeral pyre that has not been washed and has just been prepared.

One should go to a place that has been washed or to an ancient burial mound. In the case of washing, however, one should perform the collection of the bones. Then, at a distance of only one *kāṇḍa* (the range of an arrow-shot) from there, one should station four friends as observers in the four directions, who are assistants in the northern rite and hold swords in their hands.
If there is someone at a short distance to the south, having supported that northern practitioner with the intervals between the arrows,
he himself should offer the ordinary *arghya* from the west; then,
at the end of the root mantra, having sprinkled the sacrificial ground with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the weapon mantra (*astramantra*).

Having paid homage to Guru, Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, and placing the left foot forward, [he recites]: "Oṃ! And whatever gods, terrifying Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, and hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases are stationed here..."

"May the Yoginīs, the Mothers, the Bhūtas, and all the women who move through the sky grant me success today, and likewise may they be my protectors. Reciting this mantra while prostrating, one should cast three handfuls of flowers and three mouthfuls of food into the center of the cremation ground. Then, [the offering of] the *bali* vessels...
One should place seven four-legged stools in the four directions, or three stools on the funeral pyre in the western, middle, and eastern sections in the shape of a triangle;
and upon the triangle in the eastern direction, [one should place] the cremation-ground lord and the cremation-ground pillar.

Having honored [the deity] with water for the feet and other offerings, one should present the bali offering with: "Oṃ hūṃ! O Lord of the Cremation Ground, accept, accept, cause to accept, cause to accept this bali of food mixed with meat (or nectar); ward off obstacles, ward them off; grant me accomplishment, svāhā! [Then one should offer] milk.

Or, in all cases, the ritual intention (*saṅkalpa*) may be performed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Having thus worshipped Bhairava in the southern direction with [the mantra] "Oṃ, O terrifying Bhairava, Lord of the cremation ground, this... and so forth, one should worship Mahākāla in the western direction.

(389) Oṃ hūṃ, O Mahākāla, Lord of the Cremation Ground, this [offering], and so forth. In the northern direction, Kālabhairava: Oṃ hūṃ, O Kālabhairava, Lord of the Cremation Ground, this [offering], and so forth. Thus.
Having first worshipped Śmaśānakālikā upon the funeral pyre: Oṃ Hūṃ!
O Śmaśānavāsinī, O Mahābhīme, O Kālarātri, O Mahākālī, O Kālike of terrible sound! Accept this offering, O Mother, and grant me the unsurpassed siddhi. (Oṃ Hrīṃ) To Kālikā.

Svāhā! Having thus worshipped Bhūtanātha with "Oṃ hūṃ, O Lord of the Cremation Ground, O Bhūtanātha, this [offering]," and so forth; and having worshipped Gaṇanātha at the head of the cremation ground with "Oṃ hūṃ, O Lord of the Cremation Ground, O Lord of All Gaṇas, this [offering]," and so forth.

Then, having gathered some bones together on either the western or southern side of the funeral pyre, one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting: *oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. Having written the mantras for the seat of the pedestal of the five *pretas* on either birch bark or a *vaṭa* leaf with red sandalwood paste and other substances, [one should proceed].

Having placed bones upon it and spread any one of the seats such as a woolen blanket or a deerskin on top of them, having worshipped [it] and sat there in the *vīrāsana* posture, [one should recite]: "Hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ! O Kālikā, you of terrible fangs, O fierce one, O leader of the fierce ones, tear apart the Dānavas, tear them apart, slay them, slay them!"
Having consecrated ten clods of earth with the mantra for the worship of the Hero, "Paravīraṃ mahāvighnaṃ chedaya chedaya svāhā hūṃ phaṭ," one should throw them in the ten directions.
[One should also prepare] a wick made from *arka* bark, camphor, white *vāṭyālaka*, and *tūla* cotton, along with ghee, oil, and so forth.
For the sake of protection, one should kindle a lamp consecrated with the *aghora-astra-mantra* while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Therein, one should worship the *yantra*. One should exercise such care that it remains burning until the completion of the recitation (*japa*). Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*),...
Having performed the network of the sixfold nyāsa beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as appropriate, having consecrated the arghya and other offerings,
having visualized the Great Wheel (mahācakra) in the midst of the funeral pyre, and having established the deity at the conclusion of the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā),
one should worship [the deity] with the available articles of service (upacāra) and perform the worship of the retinue (āvaraṇapūjā) and so forth.
And one should recite [the mantra] according to the prescribed number, preceded by meditation on the deity.

If, after reciting in this manner, one perceives nothing at all, then one should offer *arghya* to the Goddess with the *Jayadurgā* mantra: "Oṃ Durgā Durgā Rakṣaṇī Svāhā," and [recite]: "Tilo 'si Somadevatyo..."

"You are the provider of satisfaction through the *gosava* sacrifice; you are the giver of heaven to the ancestors and capable of granting fearlessness to mortals; you are the bringer of peace amidst the obstacles caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*. Thus, one should scatter sesame seeds everywhere. With the *jaya-durgā* mantra, one should scatter mustard seeds.

Having scattered [the offerings], stood up, and walked seven steps, one should sit down there again, worship the Goddess, and recite the mantra fearlessly. The performance of the sacrificial offering (*bali*) of goats and other animals should be carried out at the prescribed time according to the stated sequence.
Upon the completion of the recitation, having made the request for boons and performed the rites of dismissal (*visarjana*) and so forth, one should cast the ritual materials into the water.

Having cast it down and bathed, one should return home; if by good fortune a staff is obtained, then one should take it and return. Thus ends the preparation of the funeral pyre. Now, regarding the preparation of the corpse, as previously stated in the *Nīlatantra*: "The practitioner, having taken the offerings and other requisites..."
One should accomplish [the practice] and likewise resort to a place for the means of attaining siddhi.
One should mentally perform everything previously mentioned, beginning with the meditation on the Guru;
for the sake of worshipping the Hero, there is no delusion regarding the illusory nature of the ground.
One should offer three handfuls of flowers with the mantra beginning "ye cātra," and one should present the bali offering to the lords of the cremation grounds as before.
One should perform the binding of the topknot with the mantra known as Aghora;
one may likewise effect self-protection with the Sudarśana mantra, or with both.
Again, "māyāsphuradvayaṃ," and again "prasphuradvitayaṃ";
then, at the end of "ghoraghoratara," the word "tanurūpa" follows. (5)
At the end of that is the pair *ca-ṭa*, then the pair *pra-caṭa*,
then the pair *ka-ha*, then the pair *va-ma*, and then again the pair *baṃ-dha*.
With the two *ghātaya* syllables and the armor (*varma*) ending in *phaṭ*,
this mantra consisting of fifty-one syllables is declared to be composed of the Aghora-weapon (*aghorāstra*).

Having extracted the *hālāhala* [syllable] which has the form of a thousand spokes, this great mantra, ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) syllables, is proclaimed as that of Sudarśana. (8)
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should duly perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla).
With the mantra known as Jayadurgā, one should scatter mustard seeds in all directions.
With the mantra "tilo'si," one should scatter sesame seeds in the directions;
[this applies to one who has been] pierced by a spear, pierced by a stake, pierced by a sword, or one who has died in water. 10.
One bound by a rope, one bitten by a snake, a Cāṇḍāla, and one who is overwhelmed;
one who is young, beautiful, brave, a child, lost, and one who is blazing. (11)
One who stands facing the enemy in battle without fleeing, one who has died by his own will, a two-year-old calf, and likewise one who has protected women, cows, or Brahmins; || 12 ||
One who has died from lack of food, one who is afflicted by disease, and likewise one who has been dead for seven and a half years—
having avoided these eight types [of corpses], one should take any other corpse previously mentioned.
Having taken [the image] with the root mantra, one should bring it to the place of worship;
even a Cāṇḍāla, when thus empowered, bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment. (14)
One should perform the sprinkling of the corpse with the Astra-mantra preceded by the Praṇava:
"Oṃ, Kūrmabīja, obeisance to the dead body, Phaṭ. (15)
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate while touching [the deity], saying:
"O Hero! O Supreme Bliss! O Bliss of Śiva! O Lord of the Kula! (16)
O Śaṅkara, who takes the form of Ānandabhairava and rests upon the lap of the Goddess;
I am a hero, I take refuge in you—arise for the worship of Caṇḍikā! (17)
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should then wash [it];
one should utter the mantra ending with *tāra* (oṃ), *śakti* (hrīḥ), and *mṛtakāya namaḥ*. (18)
This [rite] is taught in all tantras within the mantras for bathing the corpse;
having fumigated it with incense and having anointed (or smeared) it with perfumes and so forth. (19)
O Goddess of the gods, if one with red eyes should consume the Kula-sādhana,
he should go into the presence of a corpse and wear it at his waist.
If it should cause distress, one should offer spittle upon the corpse;
having washed it again, one should bring it back to the place of recitation.
Having prepared a bed of *kuśa* grass, one should place the corpse upon it;
[it should be adorned] with cardamom, cloves, camphor, jasmine, and the heartwood of *khadira*.
Having placed betel-leaf in his mouth, one should turn the corpse face downwards;
having positioned it thus, one should smear its back with sandalwood paste.
Having visualized [the area] from the base of the arms to the hips as a square,
one should imagine in its center a lotus with four doors and endowed with eight petals.
Then, one should place a deer-skin covered by a woolen blanket;
and sacrificial wood pieces measuring twelve finger-breadths should be placed in the cardinal directions.
Having established them there, one should worship the ten deities beginning with Indra;
then, having written "viṣam" for Indra, followed by "surādhipataye" (to the Lord of the Gods).
"O couple, accept this *bali*; O pair, cause it to be accepted. Having warded off obstacles, grant success—*ṭha* twice. (27)
With this mantra, one should first offer a bali-oblation consisting of meat;
having uttered each deity's respective name and so forth, one should present the bali as before. (28)
Then, O Goddess of the Suras, the most excellent practitioner should offer an oblation (bali) to all the world-protectors and to the deities presiding over the corpse.
One should offer the bali-oblation together with liquor to the sixty-four Yoginīs;
the materials for worship should be placed nearby, while the assistant practitioner stands at a distance.
Having prepared a seat and worshipped it, one should then mount the horse there with the mantra "trapāṃ phaṭ" at the end of one's own mantra.
Having placed kusha grass beneath his feet and having spread out the hair of the corpse,
he firmly tied his topknot, thereby accomplishing his resolve.
Having ascended upon the corpse and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should consecrate it with the worship of the Hero (vīrārcana) and cast clods of earth in the directions.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess with extensive ritual services,
O Goddess, one should perform the nourishment of the deities (*devatāpyāyana*) according to the rules within the mouth of the corpse.
Having risen and stood facing [the deity], one devoted to devotion should recite:
"O Lord of Gods, be under my control; [grant] such-and-such a position for me. (35)
"O highly fortunate one, grant me success! O you who have made the cremation ground your garment!"—reciting this root mantra, the practitioner should then [touch] the two feet of the corpse. (36)
One should bind it with silk thread; then one will not be able to rise up.
O Bhīmabhīma, O Great Being, O you of auspicious eyes, O Compassionate One! (37)
"Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the lords of all beings!"—thus one should draw a triangular wheel upon the soles of his feet. (38)
Then he is unable to rise; even a corpse would become motionless.
Sitting down again, one should extend his two arms to both sides. (39)
Having spread kuśa grass upon his hands, he should place his feet there;
with his lips firmly closed, he should remain steady-minded and steady-sensed. (40)
Always meditating on the Goddess in his heart, he should perform the recitation while observing silence;
O Kuleśvarī, he should perform the recitation in a cremation ground for the number of times previously specified.
Alternatively, from the time of commencement until the sun rises—if nothing at all is perceived during the recitation up until midnight—[the rite is successful]. 42.
Then, as before, having performed the offering of water (arghya) and so forth, and having taken seven steps,
one should sit right there and perform the recitation (japa) with undistracted mind.
There is no fear from that which is moving or unmoving; when fear has arisen, one should speak again:
"O Lord of Gods, whatever you desire—a man, an elephant, or the like. (44)
"But on another day I shall give [it]; tell me your own name.
When this was said, he, being fearless, should speak again in Sanskrit alone. (45)
If he speaks sweetly again, then one should speak sweetly in response;
at that time, one should act under the power of truth and then request a boon. (46)
If one does not act truthfully or does not grant the boon, then the wise man should again recite [the mantra], remembering with a one-pointed mind. (47)
Without a human form, even a deity does not approach there;
it should be understood that by means of another mechanism, humans or those of divine origin [may do so]. (48)
Whether it be his mother, or his daughter, or likewise his maternal aunt,
she comes and creates obstacles through her illusory power, possessing a charming form.
"Arise, my child; everything that needed to be done has been accomplished, there is no doubt.
The time of dawn has arrived, and your father is crying out in the house. (50)
For the most part, people are envious, and kings are wielders of the rod;
if they should ever punish someone for some reason, what then will you do? (51)
With such various words as these, one must not abandon the recitation (japa);
for there, the hosts of deceased ancestors who dwell in foreign lands [await]. 52.
Then the kinsmen, assuming divine forms, go there;
and the wife, sons, and servants are seized and led away by others.
All the sons, brothers, younger siblings, and disciples wept,
[clutching] their own beloved’s body-contact, clothing, ornaments, and so forth. (54)
Whatever is seized and led away by the guardians—one should abandon the fear thereof;
if one is not agitated in that situation, then what indeed cannot be obtained? || 55 ||

The Goddess, assuming the form of a woman, and the Man, assuming the form of a twice-born, shall indeed utter the sound "ŪRŪ" (or "Huṃ Huṃ") three times; at the end of those three times, one shall obtain a boon.
Whether by a virtuous man or even by an unvirtuous one, she bestows boons upon womanhood; then, what is there that cannot be accomplished for that heroic husband by means of her? (57)
O Goddess, there is no doubt that she is well-refined when born into a family of a man free from sin, whereas she is even more unrefined when born into one joined with sin.
Whether facing them or not facing them, whoever speaks another [word] in Sanskrit—that person is that very Goddess, there is no doubt; he is Bhairava himself.
If she should not be thus, but rather possess a body crooked with deceit, one should not choose her there, nor should one say anything at all to her. || 60 ||
One such as this explains and speaks the refined (saṃskṛta) language, as well as that which is to be spoken;
however, if one does not do so oneself, it is better to accept the unconfused [meaning] through worldly speech.
Alternatively, some intense benefit for oneself may be obtained;
or else a sound arises perfectly, yet even death is not attained. (62)
Having reflected upon all this, it should be understood that obstacles are proclaimed in this way;
O Goddess, they take the forms of deities, yet their intellects are fixed on Bhairava.
One must certainly be afraid there; one should never have confidence in that place.
Bhairava, Vaṭuka, and the others are devoted to the Kula scriptures.
In connection with this treatise, a Kṛtyā of crooked form may, having become a son, steal one's knowledge, or, having become a woman, delude one. (65)
Therefore, a hero devoted to reality should exert effort in inquiry;
having obtained the boon of truth, he should abandon recitation and the like.
Knowing that the fruit has been produced, one should then loosen the topknot;
having washed and positioned the corpse, one should release the binding of the feet.
Having wiped clean the footprints, one should cast the offering materials into the water;
or, having placed the corpse in the water or in a pit, one should perform the ritual bath.
Then, having gone to his own home and offered the oblation (bali), on the following day at night, he [thought]: "I am the sacrificer for whichever deities [are to be worshipped]. (69)
"May they accept this bali-offering given by me"; thus is this mantra recited.
Now, those by whom [the offering] was requested for horses, men, elephants, and boars—|| 70 ||
Having given [the offerings] made of flour, he should observe a fast,
[using] either barley meal or rice meal.
One should cause [the victim] to be slain with the Candrahāsa sword according to the rule and with its mantra;
on the following day, having performed the daily rites, one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
There, one should feed Brāhmaṇas in the number of twenty-five, or reduced by five at a time, down to ten in sequence. || 73 ||
Then, having bathed and eaten, one should dwell in an excellent place;
if there is no food to be offered to the Brahmins, then one shall fall into poverty.
If, because of that, one should become destitute, then the Lord becomes enraged;
for three nights or six nights, one should conceal the Kula practice.
If he should indeed go to his bed [at that time], one should predict illness;
by hearing music he becomes deaf, and by seeing a dance he becomes blind.
If he speaks a word during the day, then he shall become mute;
for the deity’s residence within the body lasts until the end of fifteen days.
One should never engage in the censure of cows, Brahmins, or deities;
and being pure, one should touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, and others every day.
In the morning, after completing his daily obligatory rites, he should drink the water of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, when the sixteenth day has arrived, he should bathe at a sacred ford or similar site.
Having uttered the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should say the words *tarpayāmi namaḥ*;
in this manner, one should satisfy the deity with water three hundred times or more.
"Without bathing and libations, there can be no propitiation of the deity";
by this injunction, one certainly attains accomplishment. (81)
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures right here in this world, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari;
whether it be incomplete or complete, fruitless or fruitful.
Having performed this very sādhana, one will become most dear to Śakti. In the absence of a corpse, the sādhana of the hero (vīra) should be performed in a cremation ground.
If one does not worship with those very elements that have been declared for a particular [deity], the practitioner becomes fallen through the sequence of the ten-day period. 84.
One should not teach the state of a hero, nor should one prescribe worship there;
rather, having received the mantra from the Kula, [one should practice] until accomplishment arises. 85.
Thus it is said in another tantra:
"In the Vīrasādhana, for all living beings who are devoid of life, one should perform the Vīrasādhana by making a brahmin into cow-dung. (1)
He who worships the auspicious Pārvatī without the Mṛtāsana [posture] shall dwell in a terrible state for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts. || 2 ||
Great corpses are recommended for the accomplishment of deities and heroes;
small ones are recommended for practitioners of rites, as they bestow all siddhis.
(392) Thus, O goddess, O sinless one, the sequence of the Blue [Deity] has been told to you.
It must not be spoken of to anyone; it was uttered by me out of affection for you. 4.

Thus [it is said]. As for the ritual application (*prayoga*): having observed the previously mentioned lunar day (*parvan*), at the time specified, having gathered the aforementioned materials and being accompanied by the subsequent practitioner (*uttarasādhaka*), one should reach the prescribed location, perform the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), and carry out the purification of the site.
Having paid homage to the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and the others, one should write the mantra for the worship of the Vīra on the ground.

Having performed the offering of three handfuls of flowers and so forth with the verse beginning "ye cātra... and having presented the seven previously mentioned *bali* vessels to the lords of the cremation grounds (*śmaśānādhipati*), [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ sphura sphura ghora ghoratara...*

Having bound the topknot with the Aghora-weapon mantra: *tanurūpa caṭacaṭa pracaṭapracaṭa kahakaha vamavama bandhabandha ghātayaghātaya hūṃ phaṭ*, and having performed self-protection with the Sudarśana-weapon mantra: *oṃ sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having performed the entire network of nyāsas, such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as prescribed in one’s own respective ritual manual (kalpa), one should scatter mustard seeds with the Jayadurgā mantra and sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si. Then, having gone near the prepared corpse, one should gaze at it with the root mantra (mūlamantra) and sprinkle the corpse with water while reciting the weapon mantra (astramantra): "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the deceased, phaṭ."

One should cast three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the corpse while touching it with the mantra: "Oṃ hūṃ! O Hero, supreme bliss, bliss of Śiva, Lord of the Kula! O Śaṅkara, who has the form of Ānandabhairava and whose couch is the Goddess!
I am a hero; I take refuge in you; arise for the worship of Caṇḍikā! Thus, preceded by touch.

Having prostrated and bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and fragrant water while reciting the *Pañcabrahma* mantras— beginning with "Oṃ Hrīṃ Mṛtakāya Namaḥ"— and having fumigated it with incense and anointed it with scents and other offerings, one should hold it at the waist while muttering the root mantra.

One should bring him to the place of recitation; having brought him, one should perform the purificatory rites. Having spread a bed of *kuśa* grass upon the ground and placed him thereon, one should give him *tāmbūla* (betel) mixed with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and *khadira* wood into his mouth.
One should place the corpse face down. On its back, one should smear sandalwood paste from the base of the arms to the hips in the shape of a square.
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus together with a *bhūpura* (outer enclosure) consisting of four gates. Therein—
Having spread out a seat made of woolen cloth and other materials, and having driven ten stakes made from sacrificial wood measuring twelve finger-breadths in length into the ten directions,
one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions upon those stakes with the previously mentioned mantras, and offer an oblation of rice mixed with ghee.

One should offer the three oblations at a certain distance, saying: "Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the presiding deities; Oṃ ḍāṃ, salutation to the Ḍākinīs; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the sixty-four crores of Yoginīs. Having placed the materials for the worship and offerings nearby, one should station the assistant practitioner at a distance.
At the end of the root mantra, having worshipped the seat with "Hrīṃ Phaṭ!
Salutation to the corpse-seat," and while recollecting the root mantra, one should sit upon the corpse facing east in the manner of a horse-rider;
then, having placed *kuśa* grass beneath one's own feet, spread out the hair of the corpse, and tied it into a firm topknot.
Having consecrated the *arghya* and other offerings to his left, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),

he should cast clods of earth in the ten directions with the mantra for the worship of the Hero (*vīrārcana*). Having placed the previously mentioned protective lamp to the right, he should contemplate the wheel (*cakra*) of his own deity upon his tied topknot.

At the conclusion of the worship of the *pīṭha*, having invoked the Goddess along with her retinue and worshipped her with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and having performed the rite of the *bali* offering to Vaṭuka and the others, one should stand up, remain facing [the deity], and say: "O Lord of Gods, come under my control; O highly fortunate one, grant me, who have established this hermitage, the success [known as] Ambara."
One should recite with devotion. With the root mantra, one should bind the two feet of the corpse with a silk thread.

One should draw a triangular wheel on the sole of the corpse's foot, reciting: "Oṃ! O Bhīma, O Bhīma, O Great Being, O You of Auspicious Eyes, O Compassionate One! Protect me, O God, Lord of Gods, Sovereign Lord of Corpses!"
Again, sitting upon the corpse in the same manner, having extended the arms of the corpse on both sides and spread *kuśa* grass over the hands, one should place one's own two feet there. Then,
having performed *prāṇāyāma* and other rites, being free from fear, one should meditate upon the deity.
Observing silence and keeping body, speech, and mind steady, one should perform recitation (*japa*) with the secret rosary according to the number prescribed for the cremation ground.

One may recite from the beginning until the dawn. In some traditions, it is heard that the corpse should be placed face-up; in that case, the seat is upon the heart. The worship of the deity is performed at the mouth of the corpse.

During the recitation (*japa*), the offering of water for honor (*arghya*) and other rites should be performed as before. If great fear arises, then an offering (*bali*) of goats and the like should be made—at the beginning, in the middle, or at the conclusion. Having thus averted such fears as mentioned, one should perform the recitation with mindfulness, pray for a boon with truthful words, and then cease the recitation.
Having ascertained that the fruit has been produced, having dismissed the deity, having loosened the corpse-knot (*śavajūṭikā*),
having washed the entire [corpse], having released the foot-bindings, having cleansed the wheel of the feet,
having cast the offering materials into the water, and having placed the corpse in the water or in a pit;

Having bathed, one should go home. On the following day, having fashioned the previously resolved *bali* offering out of flour, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, on the night of the next day, those deities for whom I am the sacrificer—may they accept what has been given by me: the man, the elephant, and the boar. With a sword, [one should cut] the flour effigy.

One should cause [the rite] to be performed. Having performed it daily for another day, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and feed twenty-five, twenty, fifteen, or ten Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having bathed and eaten oneself, one should dwell in an excellent place. Thus is the three-night *kulasādhana*.
Or one may observe it for six nights. For up to fifteen days, one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), maintain silence during the day,
avoid women, dancing, singing, instrumental music, going outside, and so forth, and speak only the truth.

One should possess restraint of the senses and, in particular, devotion to cows, Brahmins, and deities. On the sixteenth day, having bathed at a sacred ford or similar site, one should satisfy the deity three hundred and fifty times;
this is the ritual for the corpse (śavasādhana). This same procedure is prescribed for whichever goddesses are most fierce.
According to the statement, this pertains to the domain of Ugradevatā; furthermore, "the secret" (rahasya) is another name for these two, the Divine (divya) and Heroic (vīra) sequences.
393) Now, regarding the abbreviated preliminary practice (*saṃkṣepapuraścaraṇa*) in another tantra:
At the time of an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, being pure and having previously fasted, [one should perform the rite].
Standing in water reaching up to the navel in a river that flows toward the ocean. || 1 ||
With one-pointed mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of touch until liberation;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, and offer libations (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that.

"One should perform the consecration with a tenth part [of the total], and a tenth part [of that] should be the feeding of Brahmins. Thus it is said. "Having fasted" means having not eaten. "Flowing to the ocean" means either directly or indirectly. In the absence of such a river, in a pond or similar body of water; even if one is unable to stand in the water, one may remain on the bank. "By touch" [refers to the water].

Even if there is a deficiency in the limbs [of the ritual] due to a delay in the touch [of the mantras] during the *prāṇāyāma*, the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*), and so forth, as well as the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the recitation must nevertheless be performed in this very same way, because it yields great fruit. Likewise—
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
Beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise, by reciting [the mantra] during that time, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments. || 2 ||

Thus [it is said]. Here, there is a distinction in the *puraścaraṇa* according to the difference in lunar days (*tithi*). However, the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites are as before. "Free from affliction" (*nirātaṅka*) means devoid of doubt.
Or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner.
Especially during the autumn season, from the fourth day until the ninth.
Having worshipped with devotion, one should then recite it a thousand times at night alone in a secluded place, or solely in a temple of Śiva.

"One should be intent on fasting from the eighth day until the ninth. Thus it is said. Regarding the sequence beginning with the fourth day, there are differences of opinion. In some places, sequences beginning with the ninth day of the dark fortnight, the first day (*pratipad*), or the sixth day are mentioned; however, in reality, the sequence beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) is [the standard].

This is according to the tradition. "At night" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). "Tāvatsahasrakam" means a thousand [recitations] per lunar day (*tithi*), or rather, a thousand every single day. Regarding the sequence of increasing the number, it is with a mantra of few syllables;
elsewhere, it is simply a thousand. In that case, the word "tāvat" is used for metrical completion (*pādapūraṇe*). [This applies to] the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth.
It is exactly as stated before. This is the ritual procedure for those who possess cattle. Likewise:
"Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner;
elsewhere, one must never cause the path of the Guru to be transgressed. (1)

At the junction of the eighth lunar day, the practitioner of mantra, having entered an eightieth-plus-one (eighty-first) bower of creepers, should worship them with effort according to the prescribed rite.
Having adopted the previously mentioned ritual procedure, one should perform the worship and other rites;
one should then recite the mantra of Kāmadeva alone one hundred and eight times.
Having worshipped Ugrā at the base of their leaves and at the node,
the accomplishment of the mantra occurs immediately from seeing and worshipping the creeper.
Thus [it is said]. And the "time of the junction" (*sandhivelā*) refers specifically to the autumnal period; according to the previous sequence, the meaning is one hundred and eight [recitations].

Or, if there are only eight [recitations] as the "excellent" (*uttara*), then that is the best. "Creeper-house" (*latāgṛha*) refers to a meeting place (*saṅketa*) for creepers. Having entered and become united, or being surrounded [by them]. The previously mentioned ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is the ritual procedure for the worship of Śakti.

Having written the fierce goddess at the root of the leaf and the root of the *mudrā*, and the three portions of the *vidyā* at the tip and the three sides—this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Furthermore, one hundred and eight recitations (*japa*) should be performed for each. Kāmadeva is to be depicted wearing divine attire. Likewise—
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
with a state of passionate devotion, one should recite the supreme mantra in the house of a woman who has been attracted [to the practitioner]. || 1 ||
Having inscribed the mantra upon her body, which was like a creeper drawn from her ears, and having performed the consecration there and offered it to her; || 2 ||
Having recited the mantra a few times and led it [into the heart], being intent on the state of the deity,
one should dismiss it, pay homage, and then oneself recite again at ease.

"Having offered the *bali* to women in the morning, there is no doubt that the mantra will be perfected. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the one who has been attracted and enjoyed: in the *kulāgāra*, the visualization of the complete *vidyā* is performed upon the *mudrā*. The drawing of the three parts is done upon the three ears.

Having offered the *saṃskāra*, which is the empowerment (*śakti-saṃskāra*), and having satisfied [the deity], one should perform a recitation (*japa*) preceded by physical contact for one hundred and eight times; the meaning is that one should oneself recite it one thousand and eight times.
Alternatively, staying in a secluded and beautiful place, one should be intent upon the bed or seat.
Having recited it during the day until sunrise, one shall become a master of all accomplishments. || 1 ||
The phrase "on a bed or seat" implies "provided with the necessary power. This is an alternative method according to the divine tradition. Likewise:
"Or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired by another method:
on a Tuesday or a Saturday, a human skull is procured. (1)
Having mixed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and especially with sandalwood and other substances,
one should deposit it in the ground at a depth of half a cubit in a grove or forest.
If a man, alone at night, should recite the mantra a thousand times within that opening there, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
Thus [it is said].
On Tuesday (Kuja), a human skull—either freshly severed or as available—should be used;
even regarding a skull from a corpse, there is both what is prescribed and what is prohibited, measured at half the length of a forearm.

"Measuring twelve finger-breadths [in height] in a forest or a very dense jungle—this is the meaning. Likewise—or else, in another manner, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired: having brought a corpse, one should bury it right there at its door."
From that day until that very day, for as long as one hundred and eight [days], he shall become the lord of all supernatural powers; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.

"Thus" means on the day of Maṅgala (Mars) and so forth; "by that very measure" is the meaning. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times every day, starting from that day, which is the day of commencement."
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
at night, in a cemetery (mṛtahaṭṭa), [one should worship] Unmattānandabhairava. 1.
If one is naked, pure, adorned with ashes, with hair loosened,
and holding a skull and a sword in hand, one should recite the Mātṛkā.

"Then, O Great Goddess, all accomplishments (siddhis) arise for him. Thus [it is said]. At midnight on the two nights [of the dark fortnight], in a cemetery where corpses are sold, there is Unmattānandabhairava, accompanied by intense exultation, naked and sky-clad, [united] with Mātṛkā, the abode of the Mothers.
The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; this is a secondary procedure (*anukalpa*) according to the *Vīramatā*. Likewise:
"Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is desired in another manner:
having brought the Guru and established him there, one should perform the worship of the Guru as if he were the Deity. (1)
And having satisfied the preceptor himself with garments, ornaments, gold, and other gifts,
as well as his son, his daughter, and likewise his wife.
"Having performed worship and recited the mantra, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Here, "having recited the mantra" means having recited it one thousand times. Likewise:
"Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) is described by another method."
Having meditated upon the lotus feet of the Guru within the thousand-petaled [lotus] and having performed the recitation, || 1 ||

"By means of the state of a god alone, one shall become the lord of all siddhis. The remainder [of the instruction] is that this should be recited according to the number prescribed for one's own mantra. This, however, is for when the Guru is not present. This is an alternative procedure (anukalpa) common to all systems (mata). In these cases, there is an absence of fixed rules regarding the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth. Thus it is said.
The abbreviated preliminary practices.

Through the investigation of various tantras and by rejoicing in the manifold states of existence, a person should strive for complete perfection by means of the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 1 ||
Now, regarding the specific applications in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:

"Having thus performed the daily rite (nityakrama), one should then perform the occasional rite (naimittika). O Brahmin, when the occasional rite has been performed, there is the fulfillment of the daily rite. (1)
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times to obtain the qualities of the *aṇimā* and other [siddhis].
With a concentrated mind, subsisting on water from the ocean or cow's urine, one should recite it one hundred thousand times.
When the Sun is situated in the natal sign, by performing ten thousand oblations with lotuses, the sins accumulated over ten million births are certainly destroyed. (3)
One shall destroy all sins and also attain perfection of speech;
one should worship the God on a mountain peak, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should worship the Lord for one month with the finest white lotuses;
indeed, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa will then come into one's very hands.
For him, Lakṣmī shall become stable, following after his sons and grandsons;
likewise, one who drinks milk during the month of Vaiśākha should offer oblations with Śrī flowers.
He who brings about the destruction of all impurities and increases all accomplishments—that bull among men, all the gods worship with devotion. (7)
At the conclusion of the worship, being intent on devotion, one should satisfy the God with one hundred and eight offerings of auspicious water mixed with sugar and camphor.
From the maṇḍala, he shall obtain accomplishment, whether it be difficult or easy;
whatever the mantra-practitioner desires is obtained without effort. (9)
Constantly offering libations with water, perceiving it as milk, one hundred and eight times, one obtains all desires and attains liberation. || 10 ||

Having worshipped with *kuśa* flowers for the duration of one month, remaining established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one becomes free from disease, attains fame, and achieves the increase of dharma. (11)
By means of white *hayāri* flowers, one becomes possessed of wisdom from the maṇḍala;
likewise, by means of red *aśvamāra*, one attains unwavering devotion. || 12 ||
Likewise, by worshipping with both [these], one attains worldly enjoyment and liberation;
[this applies] to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and those of the remaining castes. 13.
And for women especially, this [practice] should be performed on specific occasions;
having performed these for just one month, one may accomplish the desired goals.
Thus, by reciting the mantra encapsulated by the *praṇava* ten thousand times over three nights,
one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati and a commentator on all the scriptures. On Sundays,
one should repeatedly recite it one hundred and eight times using a rosary made from the wood of the *aśvattha* tree.
Śānti [bestows] a lifespan of one hundred and eight years. Through worship for a mere month with fine garments, there is liberation from the most terrible sins, such as the *malinakṛcchra*.
By worshipping with silk threads, there is incomparable prosperity; by worship with coral, there is the subjugation of the three worlds;

by worship with rubies, one attains sovereignty over the entire earth; by worship with rubies (padmarāga), one attains kingship; by worship with emeralds, one attains knowledge; and by worship with diamonds, all perfections (siddhis) are attained.
By worshipping with golden flowers, one attains wealth equal to that of Kubera, and at the end of the body, the state of liberation;

this applies in all cases within the span of a single month. In another Tantra it is stated: "The practitioner who has thus mastered the mantra should then accomplish the ritual applications. As stated in the *Śāradātilaka* (Paṭala 23, Śloka 123):
Now, in accordance with all tantras, I shall correctly explain in this tantra the characteristics of the six rites, which grant the accomplishment of the fruits of their application. (1)

The wise proclaim the six rites (ṣatkarma) to consist of pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), followed by inciting enmity (vidveṣa), expulsion (uccāṭana), and ending with killing (māraṇa). || 2 ||
The removal of diseases, malevolent spells, planetary seizures, and so forth is declared to be *śānti* (pacification).
The bringing under control of all people is declared to be *vaśya* (subjugation). (3)
The obstruction of the activity of all [senses] is declared to be "stambhana" (paralysis);
causing mutual hatred among those who are affectionate is considered "vidveṣaṇa" (inciting enmity). || 4 ||
Uccāṭana is proclaimed as the expulsion from one's own country and so forth;
māraṇa is declared to be the taking away of the life-force of living beings. (5)
Having understood one's own deity, the directions, time, and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual acts;
[the deities are] Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Durgā, and Kālī, in due order.
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship them at the beginning of the ritual.
The directions are considered to belong to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. (7)
Beginning from sunrise, ten successive ghaṭikās constitute the seasons, starting with spring, day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, the early winter (hemanta), and the late winter (śaiśira) are the seasons;
hemanta is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), and spring for rites of subjugation (vaśya).

The cool season (śiśira) is to be known for immobilization (stambhana); the summer (grīṣma) is declared for inciting enmity (vidveṣa); the rainy season (prāvṛṣ) is to be known for eradication (uccāṭana); and autumn (śarat) for the rite of killing (māraṇa).
The wise declare that the postures (āsanas) are called Padma, Svastika, again Vikata, then Kukkuta, Vajra, and Bhadraka.
The six mudrās should be known in sequence as those called the lotus, the noose, the mace,
the pestle, the thunderbolt, and the sword, for the rites of pacification and the others.
Water is recommended for rites of pacification; fire is declared for subjugation;
earth is praised for paralyzing; and space is proclaimed for causing enmity. (13)
Vāyu is traditionally prescribed for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), while Agni is considered suitable for the rite of killing (māraṇa);
these should be properly employed during the rising of their respective elements, conjoined with their corresponding maṇḍalas.
The mantra-practitioner, with a disciplined mind, should perform the respective rites for the moon,
water, earth, sky, wind, and fire.
The seed-syllables of the yantras for the six rites (ṣatkarma) are the phonemes in their respective order:
grathana, vidarbha, sampuṭa, and likewise rodhana.
Yoga and pallava—these six should be applied to the six rites;
one should arrange the letters of the name interspersed with the letters of the mantra according to the rule.
One should know that "grathana" (interlacing) is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika).
One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), situated between pairs of the letters of the mantra. (18)
This is to be known as the *vidarbha* among the secret agents for the rite of subjugation;
it consists of the mantra at the beginning and end of the name, and this is considered the *saṃpuṭa*. (19)
This is declared by those who know the mantras to be recommended for the purpose of paralyzing;
the insertion of the name at the beginning, end, and middle of the mantra is considered "obstructing" (rodhana).
In the procedure for causing enmity, this [mantra] is praised as the most excellent;
for the purpose of eradication, the application of the name at the end of the mantra is prescribed.
Since the mantra is like a sprout before the name [is joined], it is used for the purpose of killing;
[the mantras] are proclaimed as white, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored. (22)
According to the color [of the ritual], the deities mentioned in the Mantra-tantras [are employed] in the six types of rites.
The substances for drawing the yantras are sandalwood, gorocana, and turmeric.
House-soot, charcoal from a funeral pyre, the eight poisons for the purpose of killing, as well as hawk-fire, balls of salt, and the juice of *dhattūra*—these are [the ingredients]. (24)
House-soot, the three pungents, and the eight poisons have been declared;
having correctly understood the deity, time, mudrās, and so forth, the wise practitioner [should proceed]. (25)
One should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described.
Thus, having introduced the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, it is said in that very same work (*Pañcarātra*, p. 23, v. 91):
Thus, when the mantra has been fully accomplished, it shall yield the fruits of the six rites; by means of that mantra, the preceptor should establish the vital breaths everywhere.
At the end of the seed-syllables (bīja), one should employ the female messengers (dūtīs) at the beginning of these words:
Mṛtā, Vaivasvatā, Bhūyojīvahā, and Prāṇahā.
Ākṛṣyā, Grathanī, Pramādā, Visphuliṅginī, and Kṣetrapratiharī—these are remembered as the nine messengers of the vital breath (prāṇadūtīs). || 3 ||
One should extract the life-breaths of the sādhya who has his movements bound by the noose, whose mind is seized by the spear,
and who is even drawn in by the goad.
Having fashioned an effigy of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) measuring twelve finger-breadths,
one should place within its heart the life-force diagram (yantra) together with the insect.
At the time of midnight, while the sādhya is asleep, [one should visualize] in his heart-lotus,
on its petals, [the syllables of] Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa, and after that— (6)
Within the pericarp, one should contemplate the letters beginning with 'ya', joined with the letter 'haṃ', having the form of bees, representing Īśa, Rakṣasa, Śītāṃśu, and Yama.
One should thus mentally visualize [the deities] in the form of bees within the lotus of one's own heart, their bodies bound by threads produced from the head-cloth (the *bindu*).
Having dispatched the female bees residing in the heart-lotus of oneself through the path of the breath,
one should cause each individual bee to bring back [the essence] from the heart-lotus of the person to be acted upon.
The mantra-practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure, should place [the deity] either in the effigy or within his own heart;
then, being self-controlled, he should perform the severing of the thread with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ).
Then, having drawn in the bees that are the hearts of the targets, one should immobilize them with the earth [syllable];
in this manner, one should perform eleven rounds in all rites.
A wise person should visualize the deities as red for the rites of subjugation and attraction;
as smoke-colored for delusion and enmity; and as black for the rite of killing.
One should meditate on [the deity] as yellow for the purpose of paralyzing, and during the rite of drawing in the vital breaths;
having drawn in the life-breaths from the heart of the target, one should establish them within one's own heart.
In rites of a cruel nature, the placement of those [limbs] in an effigy is prescribed;
one should place the vital breaths of the target as frogs and one's own [breaths] as serpents.
An expert should always recollect [the following] in connection with cruel rites:
[the mantras] written on leaves by means of the letters beginning with *ya*, accompanied by Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, Rākṣasa, Indu, and Preteśa.

Then, one should contemplate the *prāṇa*-ātman yantra, which has the *vindvantika* syllables at its center like swans moving through the sky, surrounded by the letters and enriched by the earth element (*dharā*). || 16 ||
Thus, one who knows the mantra and is skilled in this application shall bring all the gods under his control, let alone even earthly kings. (17)

Thus, in another tantra: "Each individual syllable of the name of the one to be accomplished, when joined with a syllable of the mantra, is called 'interwoven' (grathita); it is supremely effective for subjugation and attraction. (1)
One should first utter the mantra, then immediately follow it with the name of the object to be accomplished;
then, by repeating the mantra again at the end in reverse order, that becomes the "enclosed" (sampuṭa) form.
It should be known as effecting peace and nourishment, bestowing sovereignty over the three worlds;
the wise practitioner should place half and half of the mantra at the beginning and the end [of the ritual]. (3)
If the object of the rite (*sādhya*) should appear in the middle of it, it is called "seized" (*grasta*);
one should employ this in all rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), or even in the act of killing (*māraṇa*).
One should first utter the name and then likewise utter the mantra;
this is declared to be the complete procedure for causing the eradication of enemies.
Where two mantra-syllables are interspersed with each syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya),
that is declared to be "vidarbha," which destroys the wicked and possesses the characteristics of subjugation (vaśya).

If the object to be accomplished stands surrounded on all sides, interspersed with the syllables of the mantra, one should know that it is "overpowered" (ākrānta); this immediately accomplishes all aims.
In rites of praise, paralysis, possession, subjugation, and eradication,
one should first recite the mantra once, and likewise again at the end.
And they know that the object to be accomplished should be placed in the middle, with [the name of] the practitioner at the beginning and the end;
this is the supreme method for causing enmity among those who are otherwise bound by mutual affection.

One should employ the mantra twice—at the beginning and likewise at the end—and one should declare that the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), placed once in the middle, is situated within the womb [of the mantra]. || 10 ||

One should employ and cause to be performed upon men the rites of killing, expulsion, and subjugation; likewise, the paralyzing of weapons, ships, armies, intellect, and the womb, as well as the immobilization of movement.
One should utter the mantra three times at the beginning and likewise three times at the end;
the object to be accomplished (sādhya) should be placed once in the middle—thus one should know it to be enclosed on all sides.
It pacifies all calamities, wards off untimely death,
generates all forms of prosperity, and bestows immortality upon the deceased.
First one should utter the mantra, then the name, and again the mantra;
in this very way one should perform it three times, and it becomes "interlaced with logic" (yuktividarbhitam).
It is declared to be the remover of all diseases and the subduer of spirits and epilepsy;
having taken each syllable of the name of the person to be healed and interwoven it with the mantra. (15)
One should arrange another [name] as previously described at the beginning and end of that [mantra];
this is called the "interlaced" (vidarbha) form, the supreme characteristic of a mantra. || 16 ||
It is declared to accomplish all rites and bestow the fruit of all sovereign powers;
thus these applications shall grant success to one whose mantra is perfected. (17)

Thus it is said. It should be understood that these [methods], such as *grathita* (strung together) and so forth, pertain to the drawing of diagrams (*yantra*) and other matters within their respective ritual acts.
In another tantra:
"The *praṇava* is said to be the head of all multitudes of mantras."
Huṃ phaṭ svāhā vaṣaṭ vauṣaṭ namaḥ—these are known as the "sprout" (pallava) suffixes. || 11 ||
In the performance of various rites and in the consideration of their respective mantras, a mantra joined with the head and the sprouts becomes the bestower of success. (2)
Thus, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the means for the Cakrarāja;
likewise, hear the sequence of application for the Vidyā once it has been perfected. (1)
Having made a wheel with vermilion powder, one should visualize it there;
then, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) along with their image, one should contemplate it. || 2 ||
O Goddess, instantly blazing with light, she became deluded yet free from fear;
casting aside her shame, she approached. Now, O beloved, another matter is told.
Standing in their midst, the practitioner should contemplate himself as having a reddish glow,
as well as the person to be accomplished, who is then beautiful through good fortune.
One should worship with red offerings while encircled by mudrās;
indeed, whoever is properly joined with [the mantra] of his name shall truly become a servant.
Having written the names and descriptions of women who have not been seen within the center of the wheel,
and having assumed the yoni-mudrā, there shall be an instantaneous attraction.
Whether it be a celestial maiden, a princess, or even a daughter of the Nāgas,
one should [anoint her] with equal parts of gorocanā, saffron, and sandalwood.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the *tilaka* (forehead mark) brings about the enchantment of all;
so too do flowers, fruits, water, food, fragrance, clothing, and ornaments.
O beloved, whoever— be it a woman or a man— to whom betel previously consecrated with mantras is sent, shall in an instant become his servant.
One should worship with red karavīra flowers smeared with the three sweets,
while meditating for exactly one month upon the name of the woman who is the object of the rite.
Acting thus, O Great Goddess, one should worship her of ruddy luster;
on a wheel fashioned with vermilion, she shall delude even a king in an instant.
Or, one may swiftly summon even Rambhā, who fascinates the three worlds;
for one should indeed draw a wheel with funeral ashes and red liquid.
Or, having tied it somewhere on the arm, it destroys fever in an instant.
Furthermore, one should write [the mantra] with a pen using the juices of arka and nimba.
One should write the names of the two [persons] in the middle and on the outside of the wheel;
having placed it in cow urine, there shall be enmity in an instant.
One should burn sandalwood incense at night or wear [sandalwood] paste;
then, by repeating [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one may enchant the three worlds.
Then, on ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw [the form] with yellow pigment (rocanā);
one should contemplate a beautiful and charming image, richly adorned with ornaments. (16)
One should join the Great Vidyā of one's birth-name with the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the genitals,
interlaced within with the goad-mantra.

Facing the direction of the person for whom the rite is intended, and embodying the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Śrīvidyā, one should inscribe the Kāmakūṭa, which is dissolved into all the joints of the limbs. 18.
One should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times with the seed-syllable and mudrā of agitation;
one should then unite her in the abode of desire, which consists of the digits of the moon and the sun.
Overwhelmed by passion and tormented by the arrows of Kama,
she who is named Trailokyasundarī arrives in an instant, utterly infatuated.
Alternatively, the knower of mantras, having encircled the Mātṛkā outside the wheel, should worship the wheel correctly and maintain the complete Vidyā. || 21 ||
He is undoubtedly invulnerable to all wicked beings, such as tigers and the like;
[he is adorned] with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron.
One's own name should be written in sequence, and one should write the *mātṛkā* as before;
by that, the practitioner attains freedom from old age and death—of this there is no doubt. (23)

In this very manner, having drawn a wheel with yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (agaru), and saffron (kuṅkuma), interspersed with the letters of the person to be accomplished and the letters of the practitioner; 24.
The mantra Trailokyamohana becomes effective without a doubt;
O Goddess of the Gods, it is formed by combining the syllables separately with the Kāmakūṭa.
One should encircle the Mātṛkā letters outside the triangle containing the name of the person for whom the rite is intended;
this, placed within gold, should be worn on the crest-lock or somewhere else.
The world-protectors and kings, as well as the wicked ones residing in the three worlds—all these, along with fevers such as *sannipāta* and others, come under one's control. (27)
Having composed the city of names according to this method, one should contract it at the crossroads in the central region, starting from the east and proceeding in order through the directions.
His good fortune increases such that kings are always his servants;
he beholds the earth, consisting of moving and non-moving beings, as blazing and radiant with splendor. || 29 ||
A man should constantly meditate on the edge of the disc for six months;
by that means, he will certainly become as beautiful as Kandarpa in this world. (30)
By her glance she attracts the worlds, she destroys poison and fevers;
likewise, she removes poison and brings about possession by her glance.
At night, one should worship with single-minded devotion that which is drawn with vermilion;
it effects attraction even from afar, from a distance of hundreds of yojanas.
One should worship [it] unbrokenly, in sequence, in the cardinal directions and corners;
at that very moment this world becomes submissive, and not otherwise.
One should draw the wheel on birch bark with yellow pigment, agallochum, and saffron;
one should inscribe one’s own name upon it, or that of a region or a city. (34)
The practitioner of mantra should cause a mandala or a wheel to be placed upon uneven ground on the earth;
or, having held it, he then causes the city to tremble in an instant.
Having combined madana, lac, the milky sap of arka, saffron, gorocanā, musk, and alaktaka, one should then draw [the design].

O Goddess of gods, by whose name there is fear born of thieves, fear born of tigers, as well as fear born of planets, fear born of diseases, fear born of enemies, and likewise fear born of lions— (37)
There is nothing born of snakes or born of horses; it deludes everyone in an instant.
A wise person should draw [the diagram] with *rocanā* and saffron, placing [the syllables] in the center. (38)
One should wear that wheel, which is marked with the name of the person to be cured and situated within both triangles at the bottom; from that, one shall become free from fever within seven days.
One should draw the wheel within with yellow substances and write the Vidyā below it; having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should cast this into the eastern direction.
Therefore, even Brahmā and even the individual soul (jīva), though omniscient, would fall into muteness;
then, one should write [the mantra] by this method using indigo juice.
Facing south, the practitioner, having burned his enemies in the fire,
should draw [the diagram] with the dung of buffaloes and horses, and with cow urine.
One should place it in fermented rice-water (āranāla), and enmity will arise in an instant;
one should write the name of the person to be targeted in the center and collect [the materials] with a crow’s wing-feather.

Having drawn [the figure] in the sky with yellow pigment (rocanā) so that it is visible to the eye, one may swiftly cause enemies to be eradicated; this is declared to be "forcible eradication" (haṭhoccāṭa).
One should draw a wheel with lac juice mixed with the milk of *rocanā* (yellow orpiment) extracted from the juice of *mahānīlī*; this will bring the four castes under one's control.
By this procedure, one should place it in water;
by that water, through bathing and drinking, one attains great good fortune—of this there is no doubt. (46)
One should worship a yellow wheel in the east to paralyze all disputants;
a wheel drawn with vermilion in the north brings the world under one's control.
Then, in the west, the worshipped wheel should be drawn with red ochre;
by this, even the deities of the mantra-practitioner are brought under control, O beloved, let alone women. 48.
Likewise, one facing south should worship the black discus;
for the practitioner, there will be the loss of the mantra and especially [the victim's] death.
Gradually facing the various directions, starting from the southeast corner and so forth, a man performs, in sequence, the rites of paralyzing, inciting hatred, causing disease, and expulsion. (50)
If written with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) and cast into milk, it quickly brings about subjugation by force;
having burnt it and placed it within fire, one shall destroy all enemies. (51)
O Supreme Goddess, when this [mantra] is placed in the midst of cow urine, it causes the eradication of enemies;
by that same means, O Supreme Goddess, it brings about enmity within the circle.
One should draw a wheel with vermilion at a secluded crossroads;
having commenced all the rites to be accomplished, one should write the Mātṛkā from the center to the end.
Following the very sequence of family tradition, the practitioner should worship the Krama at night;
O Goddess, he becomes a Khecarī, of this there is no doubt.
On the night of the fourteenth day, being established in well-being, one should worship on the ground of Rudra;
through the practice of this sequence for six months, one becomes like another Rudra manifest before one's eyes.
The accomplished collyrium, the opening [of the eye], the pill, the victorious sandals, the sword, the vetāla, good fortune, the yakṣiṇī, the servant, and so forth. || 56 ||
The practitioner of mantra attains everything that produces success, and not otherwise,
provided he is composed on every fourteenth day and on every eighth day.
For twenty-one nights, on the surface of the Preta-śilā at night, one should worship the Śrī-cakra in that same manner; thus the practitioner becomes worthy of worship by the gods.
O Maheśvarī, having become Kāma, by means of his human-like noose, goad, bow, and arrows, he [acted] upon the women of heaven, earth, and the depths of the netherworld.
He himself is the destroyer and the creator; there is a great attraction.
In that same way, through the weapons of Kāmeśvarī, the self of the Goddess [pervades] the three worlds.
O beloved, this attraction of men is like kings to their servants;
this meditation on the Kāmakalā has been described according to the distinctions of its seed-syllables.
O Goddess, through the propitiation of Vāgbhava, the knowledge of Sarasvatī shall arise;
one should worship her, who is white in luster and adorned with white garments, with white flowers. 62.
O Goddess, by this method, the worship of Vāgbhava is accomplished.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear about the power known as Kāmakalā.
Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and Mahākāma—these are indeed the five Kāmas mentioned previously in their respective order. (64)
O Goddess, [one should meditate on] Kāma, situated in the center of Manmatha, who has gone to the abode of Kandarpa;
he is the fish-bannered one residing within that cavity, with the head of Mahākāmeśa. 65.
By means of this reality of desire, one may delude this world;
she whose nature is like a lotus fiber, [presiding over] the emanation and reabsorption beginning from the root. 66.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti resides within the Śaktikūṭa;
O Goddess, she is Tripurā consisting of three peaks (trikūṭā), the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments. || 67 ||
Since sixty-four million yoginīs of great power, residing in this very circle, are always bestowers of accomplishment upon the virtuous. (68)
Thus it is said. And in the Vāmakeśvaratantra (chapter 2):
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the yoga of mantra according to the rule, wherein the practitioner performs worship by means of this procedure. (1)
In a country, a city, or a village, a disturbance of the world arises;
their minds are scorched by the heat and power of the blazing fire of desire. || 2 ||
Women approach from afar like ants carrying grains of rice;
their hearts are bewildered by spells, and the circles of their hips quiver. (3)
O Great Goddess, by the sight of it all women are born;
when even a single hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the women on the surface of the earth become agitated.
(399) If the practitioner’s mind is not disturbed even slightly in this way,
then all the Naga maidens in the underworld become agitated. || 5 ||
When he does not experience even the slightest agitation on their account,
then the celestial women dwelling in heaven flee away.
Having thus recited it three hundred thousand times while established in the vow, the supreme practitioner,
O Queen of the Gods, agitates the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Having drawn a large wheel and placed an image in its center,
one should then write the name joined with it and meditate upon it as blazing.
Even she who may be situated at a distance of a hundred yojanas, though unseen,
comes forth utterly deluded, completely freed from fear and shame.

Or else, when the practitioner, having entered into the midst of that [mantra], contemplates everything as himself, reddish, and the person to be accomplished (sādhya) likewise rendered reddish; || 10 ||
From that, O Goddess, he is born beautiful with all auspiciousness, the beloved of all the world, and a practitioner of spiritual power, O Supreme Sovereign. (11)
One should worship with all red offerings while encircled by mudrās;
whoever is addressed by name shall become submissive like a servant.
But having joined the name of one who is unseen into the center of the wheel and having formed the yoni-mudrā, he draws that person forth in an instant.
Or a yakṣiṇī, or a gandharvī, or a kinnarī, O Mistress of the Gods;
or a daughter of the Siddhas, a daughter of the Nāgas, a daughter of the gods, or a female wanderer of the sky.
A Vidyādharī, an Apsaras, or even the Ṛṣi’s daughter Urvaśī, with the circle of her hips quivering from the agitation born of passion. (15)
Through meditation on the Mahākāmakalā, one may agitate all women.
[One should prepare a paste] with equal parts of gorocanā, saffron, and sandalwood. (16)
A person who has recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and applies the *tilaka* will then see Yama, speak with him, touch him, and fully contemplate him. (17)
And by means of wealth and his very body, he must go [to serve him] like a slave;
likewise, O Maheśvarī, [he offers] flowers, fruits, perfumes, drinks, and garments. (18)
If one recites this one hundred and eight times and sends it forth to a woman,
she, her heart utterly bewildered, will be instantly drawn toward him.
O auspicious lady, this forceful extraction is never obstructed anywhere.
One should draw an image with yellow pigment (rocanā) upon the surface of the earth in a secluded place. (20)
She was beautiful, adorned with charming ornaments and attire,
and joined to his forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the region of his birth.
Having written the syllables of Madana, interlaced with the Great Vidyā of one’s birth-name up to the end of the goad (aṅkuśa), and embedded within all the joints of the limbs; 22.
Then, facing toward that hope, having made his body threefold (tripurīkṛta),
and having bound the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā, he should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times.

By such statements as these, it is made known that internal worship (*āntaropāsanā*) is superior. The mention of "oblation" (*homa*) is illustrative; indeed, the internal nature of recitation (*japa*) and other rites has already been stated in other tantras. Fearing excessive bulk due to the infinity of ritual applications, only a mere indication of the direction has been shown here. Such [texts]...

Since it is heard in the scriptures on expiation that "the best of practitioners who performs [these] rites should perform the recitation of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra for the sake of self-protection," it is determined that these ritual applications (prayoga) produce undesirable results.
Therefore, it is established that the wise should practice meditation free from desire.
Now, regarding the qualified practitioners, the Kulārṇava states:

"Men who have cast off the karma of the body (that which is to be abandoned), who perform meritorious deeds, in whom the knowledge of the Kula has arisen, and who are firm in their vows—they worship me. (1)
