Furthermore, these statements indicate that the qualification for external worship and the like belongs only to one who is established in internal worship, and not to anyone else. It has been shown previously that this qualification is common to all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* (31st Paṭala, verse 35):
O Supreme Goddess, only one who has been initiated has authority here, and no other;
for he who acts after seeing it written in a book and knowing it himself [is not authorized].
He is not tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, or the theft of gold;
of this there is no doubt, yet he dwells in hell. (2)

Thus [it is said]: "Elsewhere also, having bypassed the Guru, there is no authority even among the gods in this scripture. Now follows the procedure for the optional fire-oblation (*kāmyahoma*). Therein, first, one should examine the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) according to the sequence taught in the Tantras, and having understood the entry of the oblations into the mouths of the gentle and cruel planets.

On the day of the entry into the mouth of a benefic planet, one should begin an auspicious *homa*, or on the day of the entry into the mouth of a malefic planet, one should begin an inauspicious *homa*. The method for determining this is as follows: having counted from the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) occupied by the Sun up to the lunar mansion occupied by the Moon.
One should distribute three constellations each from the nine planets beginning with the Sun for the purpose of receiving gifts (*pratigraha*).

In this regard, the sequence of the planets should be known as follows: first the Sun, then Mercury, then Venus, then Saturn, then the Moon, then Mars, then Jupiter, then Rāhu, and finally Ketu. Herein—

The method for thoroughly understanding the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) is as follows: the commencement of the *homa* occurs at its base, while the entry of that oblation occurs at its mouth. In this regard, during a gentle (*saumya*) *homa*, there is sorrow when [the planet] is the Sun, the arrival of wealth when it is Mercury, the attainment of desired fruits when it is Venus, affliction when it is Saturn, and happiness when it is the Moon.
The results of the planets are as follows: with Mars there is imprisonment; with Jupiter, the attainment of wealth; with Rahu, disease; and with Ketu, death.

Then, having understood the abode of the Fire-god in the heavens, on earth, and in the netherworld, and having known their respective fruits, one should undertake the performance of optional (kāmya) oblations. The method for such thorough knowledge is as follows:
having counted from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the specific lunar day of the oblation, and likewise from Sunday onwards.
Counting from the commencement of the *homa* until the end of the week, one should add the numbers obtained for both [the day and the weekday] together with the number twenty-nine;
having divided the resulting sum by three, if the remaining number is one, he dwells in the heavenly realm (*svarga*).

If [the fire] is in the netherworld (pātāla), it is auspicious; if it is in the mortal world, it is empty—having thus understood the condition of the fire, one should indicate its results. In that regard, if the fire is situated in heaven, there is a portent; if in the netherworld, loss of wealth;
if situated in the mortal world, the attainment of all worlds. Having thus understood the wheel of fire, as previously stated...

In the pavilion, having performed the installation of the fire according to the previously stated procedure within the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) situated in the positions of the twelve zodiac signs as mentioned before— which possess the previously described auspicious and inauspicious forms—
and having discerned the distinctions of the tongues of fire as previously stated, one should offer oblations with the prescribed substances according to the ritual rules. Therein:
Regarding the materials for the gentle oblation (*saumyahoma*), the *Jñānārṇava* (17.152) states:
"O Goddess, by offering flowers of *mālatī*, *jātikā*, and *mallikā* mixed with honey and filled with clarified butter, one attains the status of the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśatva*). (1)
For even one who is mute, dull-witted, or like a stone, it is not otherwise;
[one should worship] with hibiscus flowers mixed with clarified butter, and likewise with karavīra flowers of that same kind.
By means of the oblation, the practitioner of mantras shall delude the inhabitants of the three worlds;
O Goddess, camphor and saffron should indeed be mixed with musk.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, through the performance of this oblation, Madana shall be conquered by the practitioner by means of good fortune, charm, and even power.
By offering *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, the practitioner of mantra attains great, radiant prosperity that illuminates the sky, and he may even paralyze this entire world.
Then, one should offer oblations of śrīkhaṇḍa, guggulu, candana, and aguru;
by this, one shall bring under control the wives of kings, great serpents, and gods.
All the worlds come under his control; of this there is no doubt.
One who is afflicted by the fear of poverty shall obtain a kingdom through the oblation of lac.

O Goddess of the gods, the pacification of difficult calamities occurs through the oblation of meat and the three sweets, performed by the preceptor according to the path he has taught for those situated at a distance.
Homa should be performed by those desiring subjugation; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
By performing homa at night with the blood-smeared flesh of a goat, [the goal is attained]. 9.
Combined with the three sweets and prepared according to the instructions given by the Guru,
it brings even an entire great fortress of a foreign kingdom under one's own control.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the *mahāpala* [substance], one shall destroy the enemy's army;
having performed a *homa* at a crossroads at night, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). (11)
O fair-faced one, by offering milk, honey, curd, and clarified butter separately into the fire,
men attain longevity, wealth, great health, and prosperity.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by offering milk and honey in sequence, one destroys death;
by an oblation of curd and honey, one obtains good fortune and wealth.
An oblation with white [sugar] alone causes the paralysis of enemies;
an oblation with red lotuses properly bestows complete prosperity.
With red lotuses, the world is brought under control; kings come under one's power in an instant.
With blue lotuses, even the most wicked are brought into subjection; it cannot be otherwise.
By offering white lotuses in the sacred fire, one obtains prosperity and eloquence;
by performing oblations with white lotuses, one shall attain fortune and good luck.
By offering white water-lilies (kahlāra), the mantra-practitioner shall obtain good fortune and wealth;
and by the homa of ripe jujube fruits (badara), he shall bring the gods upon the earth under his control.
By means of a homa performed with *mātuluṅga* fruits, a Kṣatriya woman comes under one's control;
indeed, by means of a homa performed with *nāraṅga* fruits, Vaiśya women become submissive.
By the oblation of kūṣmāṇḍa fruits, Śūdras and others likewise become submissive;
through one hundred thousand oblations of grape fruits, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained, without a doubt. (19)
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with plantain fruits, ten kings will certainly become subject to one's will; of this there is no doubt.
By means of one hundred thousand oblations of dates, twenty kings shall be brought under control; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
(405) O Dear One, through oblations of coconut fruits, prosperity arises;
by means of just one hundred thousand [recitations], the knower of mantras becomes like another king, O Dear One. (22)
O beautiful one, by offering one hundred thousand oblations of mango fruit,
one may bring the earth, bounded by the four oceans, under one's control.
O Goddess of the gods, by performing one hundred thousand oblations with jackfruit (*panasa*), hundreds of kings become submissive; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (24)
O Goddess, O Beloved, through the oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter, the accomplishment of one's purpose occurs;
furthermore, by means of black mustard and salt, one may bring wicked people under one's control.
O Goddess, by offering oblations of saffron, one may bring the three worlds under one's control;
and by the oblation of guggulu resin, one shall destroy all miseries.
Even enemies quickly come under one's control through the oblation of sandalwood;
indeed, by means of an oblation of red sandalwood, both men and women are brought under subjection. (27)
By the oblation of camphor, the subjugation of the speech of men is achieved;
by the oblation of musk, O Goddess, kings and royal ministers [are won]. (28)
O Dear One, all [the deities], together with their retinues, become submissive;
through an oblation of sesame seeds and rice, peace prevails within the home. (29)
By means of an oblation of sugar and jaggery mixed with white sugar,
the practitioner brings the three worlds under his control and attains success in grain.
Through the homa of various kinds of weapons, the attainment of grain will certainly occur;
and with *vaṭaka* cakes together with their accessories, one shall destroy calamities.
By performing a fire sacrifice with *bandhūka* flowers, one brings all sentient beings under control;
with *japā* flowers, the world is brought under control, and with *bāṇa* flowers, there is enchantment.
By offering flowers of the *vakula* tree, great good fortune arises;
by the homa of ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga-dhūpa*), one obtains incomparable good fortune. (33)
Thus, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:

"Māṃsī, śivā, the pith of *kauśika* and *sarja*, and the barks of trees in equal parts, each subsequent one being half the size; along with *śaileya*, *mustā*, *karaja*, and *kuṣṭha*—this is declared as the ten-fold compound (*daśāṅga*) for all purposes."
Thus it is said:

"O Goddess worshipped by the gods, women are brought under control by *jambū* fruits, the daughters of the Daityas by *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits, and incomparable Lakṣmī by *śrīphala* fruits or their leaves. (34)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of pieces of sugarcane one attains happiness, and by its juice, princesses become submissive; or likewise, by means of coconut water.
"By the mere offering of oblations of clarified butter, all the powers become granters of boons.
Likewise, in the Tantrarāja (32nd chapter):
"Now, O Śivā, I shall explain the fire-offering for the Lalitā-vidyā."
By which even a mortal becomes renowned in the world as equal to a deity. || 1 ||
O wise one, listen to the procedure for that [rite], according to the distinctions of materials, time, and so forth,
as it is enjoined for those rites performed in the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) previously mentioned.
One should perform the oblation according to the prescribed method, preceded by meditation upon the fire therein;
beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, one should offer lotuses.
During those days, one may attain prosperity by offering white water-lilies (kairava) sprinkled with the three sweets, as well as auspicious reddish flowers.
By performing these for an uninterrupted year, a man becomes like a king;
by offering white lotuses and clarified butter during those very days, he attains that same status.
By offering white water-lilies (kahlāra) during those days, one becomes possessed of wealth and grain;
likewise, by the oblation of blue lotuses (utpala), one attains abundant prosperity.
By offering oblations of red lotuses, one shall obtain a maiden;
by offering oblations of ketaka flowers on those same days, one shall obtain prosperity.
By worshipping with those six [substances] soaked in powdered saffron and by performing the fire-oblation on that day, one attains good fortune, fame, and health.
And having attained unshakable prosperity, he lives happily on this earth,
by performing oblations with those [leaves] smeared with sandalwood on those specific days according to the prescribed rite.

A human being endowed with sons, female slaves, and male servants lives for a long time; by performing a fire-oblation (homa) with those very same substances smeared with molten silver, he becomes like Kandarpa himself.
A man who [performs this] together with women lives a long life and survives for many years;
he should offer oblations with them from the beginning of the first lunar day of the dark fortnight until the new moon.
By offering oblations smeared with ghee for one year, one shall obtain prosperity free from rivals;
on those very days, one should offer oblations into the fire with jaggery soaked in honey.
By performing oblations with grapes sprinkled with milk for those same number of days, a man lives on this earth endowed with splendor, fortune, victory, and health. (13)
One who subsists on milk lives for a long time upon this earth with a pure disposition, by means of oblations of dates mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) performed on that very day. (14)
One enjoys prosperity endowed with long life, health, and victory, as well as by means of an oblation of plantain fruits on those specific days. (15)
One who possesses meritorious fame, honored by kings, shall live happily for a hundred years, [having offered] the pulp of coconut fruits combined with sugar and honey. || 16 ||
By performing oblations on those days with [offerings] sprinkled with sugarcane juice, one shall indeed obtain all desired fruits through that very sacrifice on those days. (17)
He shall obtain garments of various colors that are highly precious;
and by offering all of these anointed with the three sweets, he shall attain prosperity.
By offering oblations with those [plants] that have been consumed by a black cow together with her calf,
or even by sprinkling them with buffalo milk during the fire-sacrifices (homa) and other rites, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
One should offer oblations with those [materials] soaked in goat's milk, likewise soaked in sheep's milk,
or even with them mixed with the powder of coconut fruit and milk.
Likewise, by constantly performing oblations with each of the twelve substances combined together, and likewise individually, accompanied by milk, honey, and clarified butter; || 21 ||
(He certainly attains a land with abundant crops,) and he lives on earth enriched with cattle, land, gold, and garments. || 22 ||
Likewise, by offering oblations of white food smeared with milk on Sundays and Saturdays,
or with food smeared with ghee or drenched in honey, there shall be an abundance of food within a year.
By offering coconuts mixed with sugar on Mondays, one certainly attains a earth abundant with crops. (24)
On a Tuesday, by performing a fire-oblation with food smeared with honey, one shall obtain prosperity;
by performing an oblation with those same materials mixed with desired earth, one shall obtain that land.
By performing a fire sacrifice on Wednesdays with sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee for one year,
one obtains Śrī, the abode of all auspiciousness.
On Thursdays, by offering oblations for only one year with the pollen of jackfruit seeds sprinkled with milk, one obtains an excellent house.
On Saturdays, one should offer oblations with coconut kernels mixed with sugar or with jaggery; thus, one prospers with fortune for a very long time.
By performing oblations on Saturdays with pure sesame seeds, some soaked in oil and others not, one obtains exceedingly enchanting prosperity within a year. (29)
One should offer oblations with all of these combined and smeared together, in sequence, over seven days;
through the power of this vidyā-homa, one shall become enriched with fortune (Indirā).
On each of those respective days, out of devotion to him, one should well-entertain two or three guests,
providing them with ghee, milk, sugar, honey, jaggery, and cakes.
One should offer oblations in sequence into all nine lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī,
using śāli rice, husked rice, mung beans, black gram, and sesame seeds other than white.
With such mustard seeds and kodrava grains for the sake of attaining Lakṣmī,
[one should offer] honey, ghee, sesame seeds, milk, and rice soaked in sugarcane juice.

In the nine [asterisms] beginning with Maghā, one should likewise perform the oblation (homa) with those [substances] mixed with the milk of buffalo, goat, and sheep respectively, using nine [offerings] for each of the nine.
With chickpeas and dishes of chickpea flour, with dishes of mung beans and kṛsara, with dishes of black gram and turmeric rice, as well as with molasses-rice and milk-puddings.

For the attainment of fame, prosperity, and victory, one should likewise offer nine oblations with well-prepared food smeared with the three sweets, using the nine [mantras] beginning with the root mantra.
With parched rice, roasted flour, fried grain, and stalks of sugarcane soaked in milk;
with preparations derived from śāli rice, chickpeas, and mung beans, as well as those produced from the flour of black gram and sesame seeds. (37)
With cakes anointed with honey, one shall certainly obtain victory, fame, fortune, health, long life, good luck, and honor. (38)
One who performs oblations with the substances prescribed for the Siddhayogas shall possess prosperity;
likewise, one should perform oblations during the yogas known as Amṛta for the pacification of disease.
One should diligently offer oblations with guḍūcī, sesame, and dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu),
as well as with reddish lotuses, during the ucca-yogas.

In the yoga known as Parvata, one certainly becomes preeminent among all of one's own kinsmen; for by means of whatever substances one offers oblations in that yoga, one indeed makes them into a mountain.
O Supreme Goddess, this shall come to pass in no long time;
now listen to another wonderful oblation which I shall describe to you.

One should offer oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) sprinkled with ghee and mixed with sugar, using the mantra, for the satisfaction of the planets when they are situated in their own signs or in their exaltation.
Whoever should always perform this rite of oblation according to the prescribed rules at the times specified for each, there shall be no affliction from the planets in his family.

One should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule during the three months of one's birth; by doing so constantly with dūrvā grass, amṛtā, and sesame seeds for as long as one lives, one shall become happy.
On those days, one should recite the vidyā a thousand times daily;
for him, no affliction whatsoever shall ever arise anywhere at any time. (46)
On that day, one should perform libations with sweet water scented with camphor,
or otherwise worship [the deity] with flowers rich in fragrance.
Could it ever be that the three births of a practitioner of mantras are not fruitful?
If it were so, he would certainly suffer from diseases and other afflictions. (48)
When the Moon or the Sun is situated in its exaltation or its own sign,
one should recite the mantra of Vidyā a thousand or a hundred times, or worship Śivā.
He for whom no affliction from disease shall ever certainly arise—by acting thus during the times prescribed, he shall become happy. (50)
For a practitioner afflicted by planetary influences, diseases, poverty, and distress, his status as a master of mantras will become an object of sorrow and ridicule in the world. (51)
By offering oblations with palāśa flowers, fruits, leaves, stalks, and roots,
even one who is dull-witted shall become eloquent within a single year.
By means of *arka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one shall obtain the desired result through oblations and other rites;
likewise, by means of its leaves, sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), or even from its root, [the same is achieved] through the mandala. (53)
One should offer oblations with bilva flowers, fruits, leaves, and stalks, as well as roots, for the complete attainment of Lakṣmī; may she never depart from her lineage.
By performing oblations with lotus seeds smeared with honey for that many days,
a man obtains delightful prosperity that causes wonder among all people.
One should offer oblations of *campaka* flowers mixed with honey for as many days as there are [in the vow];
thus, one who is childless shall become wealthy and obtain virtuous sons. (56)

By performing oblations with those very same offerings soaked in clarified butter when a favorable planet is situated in its exaltation, one shall obtain land abundant with all kinds of crops and become an enjoyer thereof. (57)

When the Moon is in its exaltation, by offering oblations of those [seeds] soaked in milk for that many days, the practitioner becomes a master of a hundred [mantras]; likewise, by offering them soaked in the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar), he obtains the triad.
By performing oblations with *pāṭala* flowers sprinkled with honey, one shall obtain a daughter;
likewise with those made from *tagara*, with parched grains (*lāja*), and also with *kuṭaja*.
By performing four oblations with those [offerings] mixed with milk,
one obtains wealth and various costly garments within those same days.
Through oblations of hundred-petaled lotuses smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one shall obtain Lakṣmī;
likewise by means of the filaments of Kadamba, Kunda, and Vicakila flowers.
At the commencement of the rite, one should offer oblations ending with the fifth [day], drenched in honey, using *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *punnāga*, and *nameru* flowers. (62)
By performing the oblation with each of these individually as well as all of them together, one shall attain great prosperity (Mahālakṣmī).
By performing the oblation with those very same substances mixed with milk, one shall obtain gold.
Likewise, by offering oblations with ornaments smeared with clarified butter, one obtains prosperity;
and by offering oblations for several days with *karṇikāra* flowers smeared with honey, one attains the same.
With kahlāras, red kumudas, utpalas, and pairs of kamalas offered at sunrise, one certainly attains immovable prosperity. (65)
By performing oblations as before, starting from Nanda and ending with Pūrṇā— either individually or by groups of five— one obtains fortune along with land, ornaments, and vehicles.

Likewise, the best of practitioners [should perform] oblations with each of the three sweets individually or all together, or by means of *ketakī* flowers soaked in honey; and by such homa for those days, [the goal is attained].
One obtains many variegated garments that are priceless;
by performing a fire-oblation with white flowers soaked in milk, one attains this within those very days.
One should offer white garments, strings of pearls, and silver, along with maruvaka flowers soaked in honey, for the attainment of one's desired goal. (69)
Likewise, by offering oblations with *damanaka* leaves, one attains prosperity;
O Dear One, if one should offer flowers of whatever color while reciting the vidyā, [the same result follows]. 70.
The practitioner certainly obtains garments of that very color;
indeed, by performing oblations at night with black pepper and mustard seeds soaked in oil.
One should bring back the beloved woman, who is trembling with shame and eager to abandon her family, by means of flowers produced from the *pāṭalī*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, and *śephālī*. (72)
By offering auspicious flowers of the campaka, aśoka, puṃnāga, and nameru trees,
mixed with honey, one shall bring all women under one's control.
By offering oblations of those very same flowers soaked in clarified butter, one may bring even men under one's control;
by performing the fire-sacrifice at night with those flowers smeared with ghee, one obtains the fortune of sovereignty.
One should bring the entire world of living beings under one's control with these [seeds] combined with white [sugar];
by daily offering oblations of them soaked in ghee, one shall become possessed of abundant food.
In the same manner, one should constantly offer oblations for the sake of longevity with sesame seeds and rice;
however, at midnight, one should offer salt that has been finely ground and well-blended.
By offering oblations smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one may bring all women under one's control;
likewise, by offering oblations of salt mixed with curd, one may bring even an enemy under subjection through the fire-sacrifice.
Likewise, by offering oblations sprinkled with the juice of red sugarcane, kings shall become submissive.
By performing oblations with clarified butter alone for the number of days specified, one shall become wealthy. || 78 ||
By means of a daily oblation of clarified butter, one becomes endowed with splendor and enjoyment;
he is bathed, anointed, adorned with garlands, and clothed in white garments and white perfumes. (79)
Having worshipped the Goddess with a satisfied mind in the consecrated sacrificial fire,
he should cook [the offering] in twice the amount of milk from a white cow with her calf.
Having prepared a large ball of rice—one *prastha* measure of white *śāli* rice—mixed with white milk and ghee, [he should offer it]. (81)
Having taken hold of the vidyā with his hand and recited it one hundred times,
he said, "O Goddess, grant me prosperity," while [offering it] into a fire blazing with wood.
Having offered oblations, completed the worship, and likewise eaten on that day, one should pass the year in silence;
thus one attains abundant prosperity.
If one should offer oblations continuously and constantly according to this lineage, Ramā never abandons him; such are the wondrous powers of the mantra.
On Sundays, the practitioner should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) during the full-moon days;
and by presenting it in worship, he shall become most wealthy within a year.
Then, one should place fresh butter from the milk of a reddish-brown cow with her calf, along with food from that same day, into a white water-lily flower.
Having extracted that [mantra], one should offer oblations into the fire on a Tuesday when Mars is in its exaltation;
at that time, within those same number of days, one will certainly obtain prosperity enriched with ornaments. (87)
Likewise, having placed fresh butter upon a white lotus of pure form and taking it up in silence, one should offer it into the fire on a Friday.
By performing this practice for seven cycles, one shall obtain great fortune—
honored by kings, pleasing to all, endowed with various enjoyments, and auspicious. (89)
Likewise, on the day of the sun, having placed fresh butter produced at dawn within the pericarp of a full-blown lotus, one should then [proceed] with that.
O Śivā, by performing oblations eight times with karṇikāra flowers as well as those born of the campaka, the practitioner shall become wealthy.
When Jupiter is in its own exaltation, one should offer oblations smeared with fresh butter;
[the practitioner] shall then be free from disease and invincible against kings, thieves, and robbers.
She attains great fortune, which follows her lineage, simply by performing oblations with fresh butter mixed with sugar. (93)
One shall obtain fame, fortune, wealth, health, victory, and long life;
by performing the fire-sacrifice with Bandhūka, Kiṃśuka, and mango flowers smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one attains these.
She brings good fortune, prosperity, victory, splendor, and wisdom.
Through the oblation of curd and rice, the practitioner shall become abundant in food within three months.
Having written one's own desire upon moist pieces of palm leaf and combining them with fresh butter, one should offer them as oblations at night.
Within a month from the mandala, or even within a week, one certainly attains one's own desire;
likewise, having drawn [the mantra] upon Palāśa leaves with vermilion, one should offer oblations.
Or, having written [the mantra] on mango leaves with saffron, one should offer oblations at night;
likewise, having written it on jackfruit leaves with sandalwood paste, one should perform the homa sacrifice.
Having scratched the desired object on betel leaves with the powder of [the bird's] wings, one obtains one's own wish by offering them as oblations at the prescribed time. (99)
Writing with musk on leaves from the campaka tree is desired;
by offering those [leaves] as oblations according to the prescribed rite for those days, one obtains that [result]. 100.
Having written one's desired object upon a lotus-born leaf with white [pigment] mixed with cardamom, cloves, kakkola, and nutmeg; 101.
One should perform oblations for its complete accomplishment; what is the use of speaking much here?
There is nothing in this world that cannot be achieved through the aforementioned oblations of the Vidyā. 102.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the cruel fire-sacrifice (*krūrahoma*). In that regard, the *Tantrarāja* (31st chapter) states:
"O Supreme Goddess, you have been told by me the subtle and supreme fire-sacrifices;
now I shall describe the gross fire-sacrifice which crushes enemies."

In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) prepared for each specific rite, one should perform the oblation (homa) with the prescribed methods for the purposes of inciting hatred, causing death, suppressing disease, or winning over others.
Having ascertained the life-span of the enemy, in accordance with the asterisms mentioned for the ascendant,
one should examine the positions of the planets constituting that [life-span] and their aṣṭakavarga.
One should not perform that malevolent rite (abhicāra) when the three [planets] are in a favorable state;
for otherwise, they surely destroy the one performing cruel deeds.
Then, one should perform those very same actions while avoiding the three [faults],
maintaining devotion to that deity, faith, and conduct toward the guru.
Having consulted with the mantra-experts stationed at his side regarding the suppression of the enemy, he should carry out the action;
otherwise, his power will be rendered fruitless and he himself will meet destruction.

When the eighth house from the ripu [the enemy] is the ascendant and the time is situated in the eighth sign, the practitioner should perform inauspicious rites for the destruction of that [enemy]. || 7 ||
In the east are Aries and Taurus; in the southeast is Gemini; likewise, Cancer and Leo are in the south, and Virgo is situated in the southwest.
Libra and Scorpio are situated in the west; Sagittarius is located in the northwest;
Capricorn and Aquarius are in the north; and Pisces is well-situated in the northeast.
Having thus understood the sequence of the zodiac signs, one who is instructed should perform the rites;
for at that time, five ghaṭikās each shall occur according to the sequential conjunction.
And during all twelve months beginning with Caitra,
the Sun moves through the zodiac signs starting with Aries, as well as through the other planetary spheres.
Likewise, within the bodies of living beings, one should perceive those [channels] extending from the head to the feet through their division into twelve parts, each measuring eight finger-breadths.
One should perform actions in accordance with these three and not otherwise;
for auspicious and inauspicious actions certainly bear fruit when performed in this manner. (13)
Likewise, having identified during the day the locations of poison and the locations of nectar, one should employ the application of the effigy (puttalī) in every respect accordingly.

On the forehead, in the heart, on the breasts, the throat, the nose, the eyes, as well as the ears, on the eyebrows, the base of the temples, and in the middle of the head; therein, from the middle of the eyebrows and the temples.
It resides in the ear, the eye, and the nose of a person;
likewise in the left throat, the slope of the breast, the heart, the navel, and the private parts.
On the joints of the knees, the sides of the feet, and likewise on the right thumb;
on the limbs, the joints, the knee, the private parts, and the navel—these are the locations for the dark [syllables]. (17)
If it remains deficient in the male, the left [channel] and so forth function in the female;
one should pierce with a thorn at the place of poison during the poisonous channel (viṣanāḍī). || 18 ||
Likewise, with that which is called the "contracting" [spear], which is intensely sharp and made of bone, or with iron-core needles produced from jujube wood and the like. || 19 ||
Whichever limb of the effigy is pierced,
that very limb born from the body of the enemy will certainly become afflicted by disease and, in due course, uncontrollable.
There, afflicted by that suffering, he shall go to the city of the Lord of Life.
I shall now describe the method for making a doll for the sake of achieving subjugation; listen! (21)
Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, and Venus;
Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, Jupiter, and the Moon are the lords of the signs beginning with Aries. (22)
The constellations are indeed four-footed, numbering one hundred and eight;
and there are this many effigies (puttalī) according to the sequence of their degrees (aṃśaka).
In the first group of nine, the measurements for the portions of the Moon and the Sun are sixteen and twelve, respectively, in the count of finger-breadths (aṅgula).
In all other divisions (navāṃśas), fourteen [degrees] are prescribed for everyone;
in the second ninth-part (dvitīya-navaka) of others, they would be thirteen and a half. || 25 ||
In the third group of nine, thirteen others are proclaimed;
likewise, the sequence of the stated numbers for the moon and the sun is of one kind.
For the creation of a mechanical doll (puttalī), the substances consist of clay from the hand of a potter,
funeral-ground clay, ashes, salt, ginger, and long pepper.
O Īśvarī, black pepper, soot from a house, garlic, asafoetida, rock salt, and red ochre— these are said to be the materials for the effigy.
An effigy (puttalī) is fashioned using flour mixed with ground mung-bean powder, beeswax, and hair taken from the body of the enemy.
Having determined the height of the doll, one should then divide it into eight parts;
from the top, three parts constitute the head, and from the waist upwards, three parts likewise form the two legs.
Having thus fashioned a doll with a single joint for both the hips and the feet,
one should then perform all the ritual applications according to the Tantra.
In the Pātāla yoga, the one called Nīca, the Viṣa yoga, the Mṛtyuja, the Nāśa yoga, the Dinaja-mṛtyu, and the Krakaca yoga; || 32 ||
In Caṇḍīśa, Caṇḍāyudhaka, Mahāśūla, and Kāṇaka; in Raktasthūṇa, the one named Kaṇṭaka, Sthūṇa, and the one known as Pañcārka. || 33 ||
One should perform ritual applications for the purpose of defeating adversaries or even for causing death; having carefully examined [the situation], one should act and shall attain success. (34)
One should properly fashion four effigies according to the prescribed method for the purposes of subjugation, attraction, creating enmity, paralyzing, causing flight, and killing. (35)
Likewise, they may be made from flour, from clay, or even from the mud from the wheel of a potter;
or from the wood of the tree belonging to the nakṣatra of the person to be subdued (sādhya), provided they possess the characteristics previously described.
The practitioner, having dug up the earth from the seat, the place for the feet, and the middle of the sacrificial pit,
should place beeswax within the vessel.
With her feet raised upward from the middle of the pit and her head bent downward—
having thus prepared the common [foundation], one should perform the rite as prescribed.

Thus [it is said]. Now follows the explanation of the difficult words therein: the term *nigraha* refers to defeat in battles and the like. The meaning of these four verses, beginning with "the lifespan" (*āyurdāya*) and ending with "destruction" (*vināśana*), is as follows: at the time of an enemy's malevolent ritual (*abhicāra*), according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*)...

Having examined the longevity at that specific time according to the methods stated in the *Horā-skandha*, as well as the positions of the planets within the *gocara-aṣṭakavargas*, one should perform the rite of sorcery (*abhicārakarma*) for that person only if these three factors are favorable; however, if they are unfavorable, one should not do so. Rites performed without regard for these [factors]...

Since cruel deeds destroy one who performs them, one should therefore act only after having thoroughly examined [the situation]. Furthermore, having ascertained the enemy's devotion to deities, their faith, conduct, preceptor, and even the mantra-practitioners in his vicinity, as well as their spiritual power and so forth—
Having considered this by those who know it, when that [evil influence] is powerful, one should not perform such acts as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against it.
The meaning of this verse beginning with "ripoḥ" is as follows: therein,
when the ascendant is the eighth house from the enemy's birth asterism and sign, or from the moon sign or the ascendant, at the time of its rising,
[the results are determined] according to the twelve houses to be described hereafter, specifically in the place of the eighth house from the enemy.
One should perform action for the sake of its destruction.
The meaning of these two verses beginning with "In the east" (*prācyām*) is as follows:

therein, within a pavilion or similar structure constructed for the performance of rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery), which has been made square and divided into nine sections, in the eastern section, one proceeds sequentially toward the north and south.
The two positions of Aries and Taurus are in the southeast;
Gemini is in the south, arranged from east to west; Cancer and Leo are in the southwest;
Virgo is in the west, arranged from south to north; Libra and Scorpio are in the northwest; and Sagittarius is in the north.
In the sequence from west to east, [the signs] are Capricorn and Aquarius in the north-east, and Pisces in the north-east;
by the term "well-established," it is stated that it does not rotate like the wheel of zodiac signs situated in the Kālacakra.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "evam" (thus) is as follows: having understood the sequence of the zodiacal signs' positions in the various regions according to the stated order, and having also understood—by means of the rotation of five *ghaṭikās* per sign starting from the sign presided over by the Sun at the time—the sequence of the rising of the twelve signs at the time of their appearance; [then one may proceed].

"One should perform cruel deeds"—as for the deficiency or excess of the zodiacal signs, it is stated in the mathematical treatises (*gaṇitaśāstra*) that this arises from the irregularity of place and time; therefore, it is irrelevant here.

The meaning of this verse beginning with "In Caitra and so forth" is as follows: during the solar months of Caitra and the others, the sun moves together with the orbs of the moon and other planets through the specific durations prescribed in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* for the revolutions of those respective planets, according to the sequence of traversing each successive zodiacal sign starting from Aries.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "deheṣu" (in the bodies) is as follows: one should mark the twelve zodiac signs within the bodies of all living beings in twelve locations, according to the sequence starting from Aries and ending with Pisces, following the progression of eight finger-breadths for each sign.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "of the three" (p. 410) is as follows: actions performed in accordance with the suitability of place, time, and body—as will be described—become fruit-bearing; otherwise, they do not.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "tathā" is as follows: there, on the day of practice (*prayoga-divasa*), the word "tathā" is to be construed with the phrase "the locations of the nectars" (*amṛta-sthānakāni*). These [locations] are:
the big toe, the foot, the ankle, the knee, the penis, the navel, the heart, the breast, the throat, the nose, the eyes, and the ears.
In these locations known as the eyebrows, the conch-shell, and the head, during the bright fortnight,

starting from the big toe of the right foot of the person and ending at the head, [the breath flows] through the fifteen locations— beginning with the first and ending with the full moon— situated on the five right sides as previously described.

On each lunar day (*tithi*), in one specific location, there is one digit (*kalā*) of the nectar-digit (*amṛtakalā*) situated according to the sequential order of ascent. However, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),
[the digits reside] in the fifteen aforementioned locations, beginning from the left side of the head and ending at the big toe of the left foot.

In the [lunar] stations, immediately after the full moon, the presence of the nectar digits occurs in the fifteen lunar days (tithis) starting from the first day (pratipad) until the new moon (amāvāsyā), following the sequence of descending order for each respective day. However, for women, it is as follows:

Starting from the right side of the head and ending at the right thumb, in the fifteen aforementioned locations, following the full moon (pūrṇā), the lunar digits (amṛtakalās) abide in their respective positions according to the descending sequence, one for each lunar day (tithi), beginning with the first day (pratipad) and ending with the new moon (darśā).

In the fifteen aforementioned locations, beginning from the big toe of the right foot and ending at the right side of the head, the nectar-constellation (amṛtakalā) resides sequentially during each lunar day (tithi), starting from the first day after the new moon until the fifteenth day of the full moon, following the order of ascent.
The locations of poison (*viṣasthāna*) will be described below.

The meaning of the three and a half verses beginning with "white" (*sita*) is as follows: therein, during the thirty lunar days (*tithi*) from the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight up to the new moon (*darśa*), on the right side of men—
Furthermore, in the nine locations from the heart to the top of the head; then again, on its left side, in fifteen locations from the top of the head to the big toe of the foot;
and then again, in six locations from the big toe of the right foot to the navel—altogether:

The meaning of the three and a half verses beginning with "viṣanāḍyām" is as follows: in the case of women, a reversal of the poison occurs across thirty locations on the respective lunar days (*tithi*) at those specific places, by means of alternating between the right and left sides. Regarding that:

Among the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), during the four *nāḍīs* of time designated as "poisonous" for each individual mansion according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), one should [strike] the body of an effigy made of an enemy's likeness at the specified poisonous locations with the sharp bone from the body of a specific fish called the *saṅkoca*.

Due to piercing with thorns such as those of the jujube tree, or due to the affliction of diseases in various parts of the enemy's body, death occurs either quickly or after a delay, depending on the gravity or lightness of the ritual application.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "Bhauma" is as follows: therein, "Arki" refers to Śanaiścara (Saturn). The meaning is that the planets, beginning with Mars (Bhauma), are respectively the lords of the twelve signs starting from Aries and of the twelve-twelfth-parts (dvādaśāṃśaka) arising from the three constellations (nakṣatra) starting from Aśvinī.

The meaning of this verse beginning with "nakṣatrāṇi" is as follows: the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras), starting from Aśvinī, consist of one hundred and eight degrees each, by way of four quarters per mansion.
There are one hundred and eight small figurines for them.
The meaning of these three verses beginning with "prathamā" is as follows:
therein, within the portions of the nine constellations from Aśvinī to Āśleṣā,
the twelve-finger [length] [images] of the solar and lunar *puttalīs* are [placed] in sequence.

The measurement is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas). For Mars and the others [of the second group], the measurement is fourteen finger-breadths. For the nine constellations from Maghā to Jyeṣṭhā, as well as for the Moon and Sun, it is as before; for Mars and the others [of the third group], the measurement is thirteen and a half finger-breadths.

The measurement for Mars and the other planets, from the first ninth-part (navāṃśa) beginning with Mūla up to the third ninth-part ending with Revatī, is thirteen finger-breadths; for the Sun and Moon, it is as previously stated.

The meaning of the three verses beginning with "puttalīkaraṇe" is as follows: therein, the clay from the hand of a potter (*cakrihasta-mṛt*), clay from the hand of a wheel-turner (*kulālahasta-mṛt*), salt together with funeral-ground earth and ashes, powdered ginger and other spices, garlic, the juice of *rasona*, and the tree corresponding to the victim's birth-star (*sādhya-nakṣatra-vṛkṣa*)— these are to be sprinkled (*siktaka*).
By the phrase "beeswax, hair from the body of the enemy," and so forth, the word "and so on" includes his nails and foot-dust. Herein is the distilled meaning:
one should fashion an effigy with wood from the tree of the enemy's birth-constellation, and another with clay from a potter's hand.

Four effigies (puttalī) should be prepared for all rites: one with black gram flour (māṣapiṣṭa), another with beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa), and the other two likewise. For those involving cruel rites (krūrakarman), eight substances such as ginger (śuṇṭhī) and others, along with ashes from a funeral pyre and so forth, and hair from the body of the enemy, should be ground into powder as appropriate.
Having mixed clay, flour, and beeswax together, one should subsequently fashion the respective effigies.
This is the meaning of the two verses beginning with "The measurement of the effigy's length," and so forth. In that regard:
Having divided the length of the doll (puttalī) specified for each respective part into eight equal portions,

one should fashion the area above the neck with one portion, the region of the hips with one portion, the area from the heels upward with three portions, and the remaining limbs, beginning with the forefeet (prapada), with half a portion.
One should perform the oblation with a snake-headed ladle in rites of inauspicious action;
likewise, having prepared the blood of an enemy, one should offer it as a libation at a crossroads.
Having turned toward the direction of Yama (the south) at midnight in a triangular sacrificial pit,
one should perform the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra) in a cremation ground or a desolate place.
Wherever on earth a practitioner performs a rite of malevolent incantation (abhicāra-homa),
the king should have protection provided all around that place for the sake of his own success.
If the enemy king, having learned of this through spies, should slay him,
one should form an alliance with his own kingdom, but not within one's own territory. (42)
If a practitioner of mantras, deluded by ignorance, should perform [the rite] through negligence, then enemy kings will gradually afflict that kingdom. (43)
By performing a fire sacrifice (homa) in a fire kindled with Akṣa wood and Karañjaka fruits smeared with the juice of gold leaves, one shall destroy one's enemies. || 44 ||
Or one should likewise offer oblations with its fruits into a fire kindled with *naktamāla* wood;
even a formidable enemy, afflicted by disease, shall go to the abode of Yama.
Having kindled a fire with the wood of the *unmatta* plant, one should offer oblations of its seeds moistened with water from its leaves; within a month, an enemy shall fall into a state of delusion.
In a fire kindled with *āragvadha* fuel and with its fruits,
each measuring a span (*vitasti*) and smeared with *elā*, the death of one's enemies occurs right here on earth.
By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with seeds of *aruṣkara* soaked in its own clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in a fire kindled with *aruṣkara* fuel,
death will certainly occur from a violent fever within seven days.
Furthermore, by performing a fire-oblation with cotton seeds smeared with *sauvīra* from within the mandala, the death of enemies shall come about through mutual strife. (49)

One should offer oblations of mustard seeds soaked in clarified butter, along with ginger, *māgadhī* (long pepper), and black pepper, into a fire made from the wood of the enemy’s birth star (*janmarkṣa*). From that *maṇḍala*, death occurs for him due to fever.
Having fashioned an effigy with the previously mentioned substances according to the prescribed method,
one should offer oblations at night, sprinkling them with mustard seeds, *aruska* seeds, and clarified butter.

Having offered oblations as before with its constituent parts, one who is wrathful in mind and clad in crimson garments shall destroy enemies through the fire-offering (homa) performed with red garlands, perfumes, and flowers.
By performing oblations with three seeds of the *aruṣkara* (marking nut) that have been smeared with ghee and shaped like a serpent’s head,
the enemy will suffer from a burning fever within three days.

By offering oblations of meat arising from the enmity, asterism, and womb-sign [of the victim], drenched in its blood, and also by offering oblations with fuel-sticks produced from that same tree; 54.
Within a few days, the enemy, being tormented, will certainly meet his destruction—
either by the falling of trees or walls, by a thunderbolt, or even by a sword.
[He is protected] from water, from fire, from the bite of snakes, from intoxicated elephants, and from maces;
[he is protected] from Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and Brahmarākṣasas.
Or by other means, the enemy will certainly meet with swift destruction;
[this is achieved] by means of neem leaves, cotton seeds, and pieces of wood produced from those very trees. (57)
From oblation with mustard oil, enmity shall arise;
one should offer into the fire when it is joined with the *nīca* yoga and fueled by wood from an enemy tree. (58)
An enemy struck by the power of the mantra, using pieces of that tree smeared with oil in the middle of the night, will be driven away within days and shall surely depart. (59)
One should offer oblations into the fire with the leaves, wood, and seeds of that [tree] during the Śuci month;
then the enemy's elephants and mounts will certainly perish from disease.

Having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of red chalk when [the enemy] is in the eighth house, one should gradually pierce its limbs with the previously mentioned "thorns" (kaṇṭaka) and other [substances]. (61)
Likewise, in the vein of poison, in the location of poison, or similarly in the "thorn of Yama," at the half-watch,
at the head [of the watch], or during the watch, very slowly.
In the case of an enemy, there may be death through blows and the like to various parts of the body, or by means of knots, thorns, wounds, swellings, and tearing. (63)
Having placed a doll made from the wood of the tree specified for that constellation along with Erakā grass into the urine of a donkey, one should boil it slowly.
An enemy seized by a burning fever slowly departs for the abode of Yama;
having fashioned that [image] with beeswax, one should heat it slowly at night. (65)
Seized by that insanity and fever, he slowly goes to his death.
One should dig up her [image], whose limbs are pierced by those thorns, in the house of the ancestors at night.
In an instant, the enemy, possessed by a piśāca, goes to the abode of Yama;
likewise, one should fashion an effigy using all those very same materials previously mentioned.
Having fashioned that [image] and buried it in the center of the sacrificial pit,
one should offer oblations at night into a well-kindled fire with its fuel-sticks smeared with oil.
Afflicted by a fever born of the humors' imbalance, with a crooked tongue and an extremely deluded mind, he goes to the abode of Yama while muttering softly and casting off his body. (69)
One should bury such an image during the dark fortnight,
on the ninth day of the month of Aṅgāra, in the mother’s house upon the foremost pedestal.
Struck upon his own head by spirits and other such beings, as if by an unobserved thunderbolt, the enemy perishes within seven days at night.
Having ground mustard, powdered mung beans, sesame, and rice from the *śāli* variety, one should also mix them with the bark-shavings of the *sādhyarkṣa* tree.
Then, having fashioned a doll joined with castor seeds and having placed the name of the enemy inside its chest, [one should write it] upon a palm leaf.
Having consecrated it with mantras while touching that [object], one should recite the Vidyā one thousand times in reverse order from the third syllable,
when the victim's natal asterism is situated in the eighth zodiacal sign.
Having bound her feet with a thread made from the *bhānu* tree and grasping her by the "life-hand," he should recite the mantra while casting her into pure ground.

Having offered a thousand oblations into the fire with those [mantras], on that day he was overcome by a fever that was agitated by heat and thirst, as she stood with her feet upward and her face turned downward.
With his body seized, rolling on the ground, unconscious, and muttering repeatedly,
he quickly meets his death through the power of the application, O Śivā.

412) A doll fashioned from the wood of the tree belonging to the [natal] asterism of the person to be accomplished, smeared with the milk of the *arka* plant or with *vajrī* milk, and bound as before with its face turned downwards; (78)
One should suspend [the vessel] above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) together with the name of the person for whom the rite is performed;
then, during the night, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh) soaked in its milk.
Then, after three days, there shall be the affliction of fever for Arāti;
if he has a desire to protect himself, one should bury him within the belly of a pond.
Therefore, for him there is happiness gradually from being in the midst of the mire;
likewise, if he does not act thus, he will remain afflicted by disease for a long time. (81)
Likewise, having placed her in a vessel of bell-metal on a Tuesday,
one should dig her womb in a temple of Caṇḍikā and offer an oblation before it.
Having slain and delivered over the enemy,
one should strike him down with calamities by digging beneath the hearth in one's own house and increasing the fire upon it.
From one whose breath is uninterrupted, there may arise diseases such as fever;
yet, she who is thus fashioned in form, joined with the bone of Ruru’s shank— (84)
Having bound [the mantra] with the previous thread, one should dig it into the house of the enemy at night;
within eight months from that zodiac sign, the person is driven away elsewhere.
Having fashioned a pair of such puppets according to the prescribed method,
they should be bound with the skins of a cat and a mouse and inscribed with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
If one buries [the remains] in the river, in the father's house,
or in the mother's house when the river is full, there will always be enmity between the two.
Having generated those very [mantras] as before, endowed with the name of the one to be accomplished and so forth,
and having perfected their recitation, he should then dig them up in the house of the enemy.
Likewise, in the middle and in the eight directions, there shall be the destruction of that family;
thus has the malevolent rite (abhicāra) against those living nearby been described. (89)
"How can there be a malevolent rite against enemies situated at a distance?
Listen, O wise one, as I tell you how it may be done against an enemy who is very far away. (90)
The ritual application for destruction is indeed swift and malevolent;
by it, an enemy standing nearby shall first of all fall into a pitfall.
Having fashioned eight hundred effigies from the wood of the tree belonging to the constellation of the one to be subdued,
they should be sprinkled with the two types of milk as previously described and provided with their respective names.
Facing each respective direction, one should offer all of those [oblations] without exception— one by one— from midnight onwards, according to the measure of their respective portions.
Or, even if situated at a great distance, one becomes subject to destruction at the time of those respective planetary divisions (aṃśaka);
otherwise, how could one who possesses the power of mantras be capable of being slain? (94)
Listen to that, O Śivā; I shall tell you the method for its suppression.
First, one should cause those practitioners of mantras to create enmity toward him. (95)
Death is easily brought about upon one who hates that [mantra], because of the lack of support;
whereas fortune and the like, when associated with a mantra-practitioner, provide great protection. (96)
"O Lord of Gods, tell me how one might kill a king or a prince through the application of means, if such a method exists. (97)
I shall tell you; listen, O wise one, to this unfailing and terrible form, the supreme sorcery that swiftly brings about the destruction of enemies. (98)

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with mantras that have been mastered, which are not overly oily, and with sixteen [substances] of very stable nature, in an uninterrupted form according to the sequence of the directions and watches of the day.
By that [mantra], there shall be the destruction of that [enemy] even for one who is protected without effort;
thus, by the prescribed method, one should effect the destruction of the foe. (100)

Now, the measurement of the substances for optional oblations (*kāmyahoma*). In the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 17): "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the measurement that grants success in the fire-oblation (*havana*).
One should offer a flower in its entirety, and likewise a lotus in its fullness. (Verse 1)
O beloved, one should offer safflower and bāṇa flowers as desired;
there should be a hundred counts of black mustard seeds and a hundred counts of sesame seeds.
The parched grain should be the size of a handful, the clarified butter the measure of a *gāndhāra*, half a small vessel of curd and milk, and the cooked rice should be the size of a mouthful. (3)
O Maheśānī, the fruit is large—such as the kūṣmāṇḍa and the mātuliṅgaka; indeed, the fruit certainly becomes pleasing to the mind through these pieces. (4)
If the plantain fruit is light, it should be cut into four pieces;
otherwise, one should make the coconut piece large, for that is pleasing to the mind. (5)
At the place of the joints, there should be a sugar-cane stalk that brings satisfaction to the mind;
likewise, there should be a whole grape, as well as an orange and a date.
Guggulu should be half the amount of betel nut, and saffron likewise;
camphor should be equal to a guñjā seed, as should musk and saffron.
O Goddess, O Sulocanā, sandalwood and agallochum should be mixed with betel nut; having made offerings dear to the mind, one should perform the fire sacrifice.
This measure of oblations, which bestows all accomplishments, has been told to you;
O lady of excellent limbs, one should satisfy Śrīvidyā according to one's desire.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Śāradātilaka (5th Paṭala, verse 141):
"In a fire-oblation, one karṣa of ghee is prescribed, and one śukti of milk is likewise recorded;
the wise have declared that the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are equal to those [quantities]. (1)
An equal amount of honey, milk, and cooked rice is declared to be the measure of an akṣa;
curd should be the measure of a prasṛti, and parched grain (lāja) should be commensurate with a muṣṭi. || 2 ||
(413) Pṛthukas should be of that same measure; likewise, roasted barley flour (saktavaḥ) is said to be so.
Jaggery (guḍaḥ) should be half a pala in measure, and sugar (śarkarā) is considered to be the same.
Half a mouthful should be the measure of the sacrificial oblation (caru); sugarcane is prescribed as being the size of a joint;
one should likewise prepare each leaf, flower, and cake [of that same measure].
They know that the fruits of plantains and oranges are each offered individually;
the citron is divided into four parts, and the jackfruit is cut into ten.
The wise know that coconuts are cut into eight pieces;
the wood-apple fruit is divided into two parts, and the wood-sorrel is cut into three.
In the fire sacrifice (homa), the fruit of the urvāruka is said to be cut into three pieces;
other fruits should remain uncut, and the fuel sticks (samidhs) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three stalks of dūrvā grass are prescribed, along with guḍūcī and caturaṅgulā;
there should be one muṣṭi measure of rice, as well as mudga, māṣa, and barley.
The rice grains should be half that amount, and the kodrava grains should be measured by a handful; likewise, the wheat and red lotuses are prescribed at the measure of one handful.
Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful; mustard seeds are of that same measure.
Salt should be the size of a śukti, and there should also be thirty black peppers.
The city should be the size of a jujube fruit, and the rāmaṭha (asafoetida) is remembered as being equal to that;
likewise for sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
"The teachers have declared them to be the size of tamarind seeds.
Thus is the definition of a *karṣa* stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Ten *guñjās* shall be a *māṣa*; sixteen *māṣas* are called a *karṣa*. This same measure applies to oil as well. A *śukti*—

Two *karṣas* (the measure of a *prasṛti*) is two *palas*; a *muṣṭi* is [also] two *palas*; a *pala* is half a *pala*; and half a mouthful (*grāsārdha*) is eighty *raktikās*. Thus it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
Ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*.
Two *śāṇas* make a *ghaṭaka*, which is also called a *kola*, a *badara*, and a *drakṣaṇa*. (1)
Two of those [tindukas] make a pāṇitala; two pāṇitalas make a karṣa; two karṣas make a suvarṇa; two suvarṇas make a kavalagraha;
two kavalagrahas make a picu; two picus make a biṃḍālapadaka; and two biṃḍālapadakas make a tinduka, which is also called an akṣa. || 2 ||
Eight *śukti*s make one *pala*; two *palas* make one *bilva*; four *bilvas* make one *muṣṭi*.
One *muṣṭi* of mangoes makes one *praguñja*; likewise, two *palas* make one *prasṛti*.

Thus [are described] *mātuluṅga* (citron) and *bījapūra* (pomegranate). *Urvāruka* is the cucumber (*karkaṭī*). "Half-parts" means measured in *śukti*s; that is to say, the measure of a handful, the size of the palm of the hand, or one *karṣa*. *Pura* is *guggulu* (bdellium). The measure of a *badara* is eighty *guñjā*s. *Rāmaṭha* is *hiṅgu* (asafetida).
Likewise, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"The third [portion] is for the roots; they should be short according to their own measure. Also in the *Śaivāgama*:
"There should be three portions of the roots; one should likewise offer these subtle [portions] into the fire."
For bulbs, one-eighth part [of the root]; for creepers, two finger-breadths. || 1 ||

Thus [it is said]. These are the fuel sticks (*samidh*). In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "The fuel stick should be the size of a span (*prādeśa*), cut evenly; likewise, it should not be shattered, split, too short, crooked, too thick, or too thin—nor should it be of two kinds. (1)
Those that are worm-eaten, elongated, skinless, or devoid [of luster] cause the destruction of one's lifespan; those that are split in two give rise to disease.
If it is short, one meets with death; if crooked, it is considered a cause of obstacles.
If it is thick, it carries away prosperity; if it is thin, depletion occurs. (3)
If there are two [lines], there will be defects of the eyes; if they are bitten by insects, they destroy one's wealth.
A long line produces hatred; those that are skinless are known to be destroyers of life.

Fuel-sticks that contain sap, which are neither too long nor too short, which grant all desires, which have moist bark, which are cut evenly, and which are as round as the index finger [are recommended]. (5)
A wise person should offer such oblations and thereby attains vast prosperity;
these sacrificial fuels (samidh) have been proclaimed for rites prescribed in the Śruti, the Smṛti, and the Tantras.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
"Those [sticks] should be made of Palāśa wood or other sacrificial woods, twelve finger-breadths in length, straight, not dried up, with their bark intact, free from wounds, and even. (1)

Alternatively, they are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, or equal in size to the little finger; or, in the absence [of these], even all [other types] may be offered when they are merely a span in length.
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the procedure for the optional fire-oblation (*kāmyahoma*) or recitation (*japa*). Regarding this, in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 17):
"O Goddess, one who is firm in his vows should worship the entire wheel (*cakra*), whether it be situated externally within [the body], or he should worship the central wheel alone. (Verse 1)

Having propitiated [the deity] with ritual services, the pure practitioner of mantra, remaining established before it, should recite the mantra a thousand times; thereby he shall obtain infinite fruit.
Alternatively, having meditated upon the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) within, accompanied by worship, the wise one should begin the recitation; this shall become the destroyer of great sins.
One should recite [the mantra] either aloud, in a whisper, or mentally. O Supreme Goddess, "aloud" (nigada) means it is uttered with clear speech. || 4 ||
(414) But that which is unmanifest, with quivering lips, is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*;

O fair-faced one, daughter of the mountain, that which is recited a hundred thousand times in a loud voice (nigada) becomes equal to a single instance of whispered recitation (upāṃśu).
O lotus-eyed one, O Supreme Goddess, even a mere hundred thousand recitations performed in a whisper are equal to a single recitation performed mentally.
One who, being equipped with the yoga of the mudrās through the previously mentioned yoga of meditation,
recites [the mantra] exactly one hundred thousand times, is liberated from all sins.
By two hundred thousand [recitations], one shall destroy even the sins arising from seven lifetimes, including the foremost of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka); of this there is no doubt.
Then, having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one whose body consists of nothing but the yantra shall destroy ten million great sins; of this there is no doubt. (10)
O Goddess, by reciting [the mantra] four hundred thousand times, one becomes a great master of speech;
O Queen of the Gods, by five hundred thousand times, one becomes like Kubera—of this there is no doubt. (11)
By merely reciting [the mantra] six hundred thousand times, one becomes a great Vidyādhara;
by seven hundred thousand recitations, the practitioner of mantras becomes a connoisseur of the Khecarīs.
By reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times, the practitioner becomes worthy of worship by the gods;
O Dear One, he becomes the leader of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
Kings become submissive, and women especially so;
one should indeed recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī nine hundred thousand times.

The form of Rudra himself is the creator and the destroyer; of this there is no doubt. He is always worthy of worship by all, established in his own self, and shall possess all auspicious fortune. || 15 ||
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the procedure for the separate accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) of the three *kūṭas* is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 19, Verse 2):
"O Vārārohā, this *vidyā*, which has come down through the lineage of succession, destroys the bondage of worldly existence when remembered; it is the remover of sins. (1)
Through recitation, she grants victory over death; through meditation, she is the accomplisher of all aims;
when worshipped, she becomes the destroyer of suffering, misfortune, poverty, and fear. (2)
She pacifies the great flood of calamities merely by being remembered; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now describe to you the sādhana for each of the three distinct seed-syllables.

who is white as camphor and adorned with bright flowers and ornaments.

Kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods come under her control;
O Goddess of the Gods, she is like Kandarpa in taking away the pride of women. 17.
The woman conceived in his mind shall become submissive like a maidservant;

One who meditates upon the womb of women shall agitate even the celestial beauties;
how much more so a mortal woman, O Goddess? He would delude even the three worlds. (19)

Having meditated upon a woman of red complexion,
one should then visualize her seed-syllable (bīja) upon her head, raining down a shower of nectar through her splendor.
Meditating thus, O Goddess, one should delude him whose mind is inflamed by passion;
in a mere moment, O Mistress of the Gods, one may bring the three worlds under control.
O fair-faced one, from meditation upon this *kāmakalā*, the five desires delude the entire world; O Pārvatī, listen to the ritual application (*prayoga*). (23)

O Goddess of the gods, the five previously mentioned desires are to be understood; by means of the first desire, beginning with the *vidarbha* [intercalation], place [the name] within the *manmatha* [heart]. (24)
Having formed the *kandarpa-sampuṭa* and then placed it within the interior of the corners—

One should direct it toward the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) to delude this world;
this practice is proclaimed by the name "Deluder of the Three Worlds. || 26 ||
Thus. Herein, the meaning of these two and a quarter verses, beginning with *vidarbhya* and ending with *kuryāt*, is as follows:

first, having written the syllable *klīṃ*, which is the peak of Manmatha; then, having written the syllable *hrīṃ*, which is the peak of Kāmarāja, within the interior of the letter *ka*; and then, within the interior of its letter *ha*, below the letter *ra* of the word *mama*.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)— interlaced with the syllable *hrīṃ*— with the instruction "bring such-and-such a person among those two under control," one should encircle it with two *aiṃ* syllables in the form of a triangle outside the two seed-syllables (forming a hexagon with its interior triangles enclosed), and then [place the mantra] within the six corners of that hexagon.
Having written the fourth seed-syllable, the "peak-syllable" (kūṭākṣara) *blūṃ*, which is the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Makaraketana),
and having encircled it within and without the hexagon with the "peak-syllable" of the fish-bannered one (*strīṃ*),
one should employ it for one's desired aims. Here, by the writing of the fifth peak-syllable...
The secret meaning is that the entire yantra, situated within the fire-place of those syllables, should be drawn exactly according to the sequence taught by the Guru. Likewise:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the seed-syllable of Śakti."
One should contemplate the supreme body as extending from creation to dissolution.
She was raining down streams of flowing nectar, destroying all poison,
shining with a golden luster, and possessing the brilliant splendor of a mass of lightning.
She holds a jar filled with the shimmering crescent moon, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bears the gesture of wisdom— she is the very embodiment of nectar.
Meditating thus, the practitioner of mantra removes poison existing in various forms;
by the mere recollection of this, O Goddess, he attained the state of being Blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭha). || 4 ||
Having become a conqueror of death, I wander upon both water and land;
as a counselor equal to Vainateya, I dispel thousands of loads of poison.
It shall destroy spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, as well as the accumulation of diseases;
it shall eliminate all quartan fevers and epileptic seizures.
Then Mahātripurasundarī, complete with the three peaks,
when meditated upon by the practitioner, swiftly brings the three worlds under her control.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, she is gradually visualized as having a reddish luster situated in the circles of the navel, heart, and face, and as being as transparent as a ruby.
For him, an eightfold sovereignty and good fortune arise;
by remembering her name, the practitioner of mantra becomes beloved by the yoginīs.
The wheel of the Mothers resides within his body; through that, he shall become happy together with them.
O Goddess of the gods, there is no doubt that the practitioner of mantra becomes possessed of sons by means of meditation. 10.
Thus:
"When she is established in the wheel (*cakra*), full and bestowing the siddhi of the *khecarī*, for from her [proceed] sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great splendor. (11)

the word of invocation at the beginning, the eight seed-syllables in the middle, and [the remaining letters] on the outside. (12)

Likewise, with his body composed of those very [deities], he was endowed with the bonds of Śaktis and weapons.

And Hari, O Supreme Goddess, O Beloved, having become the Enchanter of the Three Worlds through the worship of Tripura,
became the eternal sustainer of the universe.
By propitiating her, Brahmā became the creator;
and by her grace, O lady of beautiful hips, the moon and sun became the agents of creation and destruction. (17)
Thus [ends the previous section]. Now follows the procedure for the practice (*sādhana*) of the Śrīcakra. Regarding this, in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 14):
"Listen, O lady beautiful in all her limbs, to the supreme procedure of the Śrīcakra;
by the mere knowledge of which, one becomes Sadāśiva, the agent of creation and destruction. (1)
By this method, wherever the Śrīcakra is worshipped according to the sequence, one shall bring everything under control; of this there is no doubt.
O Adrijā, the entire city within the ten districts comes under one's control; all women become submissive, tormented by the blazing fire of desire.
O Goddess of gods, by the sight of him, all women whose hearts are deluded by worldly knowledge become fixed in mind upon the practitioner. || 4 ||
Thus it is said:
"One should draw the King of Mandalas with substances such as gorocana and the like;

"Blazing, accompanied by the name, and interwoven with the great seed-syllable.

Then, O Goddess, one should contemplate it for thousands of yojanas;

O Daughter of the Mountain, having first established the city according to the previous sequence,

A great agitation arises among women, even among great men, and likewise among all wicked people standing before one. (36)
Within this [egg] is the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, blazing and adorned by all the lords of kings, clothed in the oceans. (37)

One destroys poison by merely looking [at it]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
