"You shall attain universal sovereignty; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.

Thus [it is said]. Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): there, the practitioner, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), should go to the house of a young girl (*kumārī*) on the day prior to the day of worship and so forth, recollecting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) while saying, "O Blessed Goddess Kumārī..."

"Having invited her with coconuts, betel nuts, and other offerings, saying, 'I have invited you for the sake of worship; please make me successful,' one should then, on the day of worship, after the daily ritual,
summon the maiden who has been well-bathed with fragrant oils and adorned."
Having personally and thoroughly washed her feet with warm water upon some maṇḍala outside the shrine room,

and having wiped them dry with a fine cloth, he should lead her to the place of worship and seat her facing westward upon an auspicious pedestal adorned with vermilion and the like, which is provided with a beautiful covering on an eight-petaled lotus.

Having seated [the preceptor] himself opposite her, he sits upon his own seat; having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) beginning with "Today... and stating, "I shall perform the worship of the maiden for the sake of such-and-such a desire," and having first paid obeisance to the Guru and others, he performs three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Having performed the entire collection of nyāsas beginning with the ṛṣi-nyāsa, having conducted the self-worship (ātmapūjā),
and having first performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should invoke the Goddess into that [pedestal], meditate upon Her,
and offer water for sipping (ācamana) with the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
Having offered services beginning with garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps,

and feeding her with various kinds of food and drink such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should recite the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) in silence for as long as she is eating. Then, once she has finished eating—
Having offered water for washing the hands, mouth-rinsing, and sipping, and having presented betel-leaf with camphor, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony;

then, having worshipped with royal honors such as the parasol and fly-whisks, and having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, one should prostrate and bid farewell. Now, in this regard:
The characteristics of worshipable and non-worshipable maidens. Among these, first, the characteristics of worshipable maidens are described in the Skanda Purāṇa (p.
One should properly honor a maiden who is healthy, well-proportioned in her limbs, beautiful, free from blemishes, and born of a single lineage. || 1 ||
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the characteristics of those unworthy of worship, in that same [text]:

"One who has deficient or extra limbs, one whose limbs are afflicted by leprosy, one born of a family lacking moral conduct, one whose limbs are marked by knots, cracked, or decayed, and one whose body is scarred by wounds of blood and pus. (2)
One should avoid a girl who is born blind, squint-eyed, one-eyed, ugly, or excessively hairy; as well as one who is diseased or born from the womb of a female slave.

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the specific fruits and the specific types of women to be worshipped, it is stated in that very same work: "For all undertakings, one should worship a Brāhmaṇī; for the sake of victory, one born of a royal lineage;
for the sake of gain, one born of a Vaiśya family; and for the sake of a son, one born of a Śūdra lineage. (4)
And in the terrible [rite] of the outcaste castes, a man should worship according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the worship of the Kumārī.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the fivefold offering (bali) to Vaṭuka and the others.

In that regard, having fashioned offering-mandalas consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square in each of the four corners of the worship-circle starting from the northeast (īśāna), one should offer into the northeast mandala: *Vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka Bhairava*.

Having thus worshipped Vaṭuka with perfumes and other offerings, and having placed there a copper or similar vessel containing food, side-dishes, water, flowers, and so forth, along with its base (sādhāra), one worships the substance for Vaṭuka’s bali-offering with the mantra: "Obeisance to the substance for Vaṭuka’s bali-offering. Then: "4. Come, come, O Son of the Goddess, Vaṭukanātha!"
"O you who are radiant with a mass of tawny matted hair, three-eyed one, Jvālāmukha! Destroy, destroy all obstacles!
Accept, accept this bali-offering together with all ritual services, svāhā!"—with these words, [one should offer] water drawn from the previously established arghya vessel using another vessel.
One should offer the bali-oblation with the ring finger and thumb.

Thus, having worshipped the Yoginīs in the Āgneya-maṇḍala with the mantra "Yāṃ yoginībhyo namaḥ," [one should contemplate them] above the Brahmāṇḍa, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, or in the formless realm.
Whether in the netherworld or in fire, in wind or water, or wherever they may abide—

in sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats— may those goddesses, who have established their feet there, who are pleased by incense, lamps, and the like, and who are worshipped by the lords of heroes, always protect us with the rite of auspicious offerings. || 1 ||
One should offer the bali with a stream of arghya water using the left thumb, ring finger, and middle finger, reciting: *yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā sarvayoginībhyo huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, in the maṇḍala located in the southwest corner, one should [worship] Kṣetrapāla with: *kṣāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*.
Having performed worship as before and placed the vessel for the *bali* offering, [one should recite]:
*kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣai kṣauṃ kṣaḥ,
sthānakṣetrapāla, gṛhṇa gṛhṇa dhūpadīpādisahitaṃ baliṃ svāhā*.
With the left thumb and forefinger, or with the forefinger alone,
one should offer a stream of *arghya* water into the *bali* vessel as before.
Then, having worshipped Gaṇapati in the northwest mandala with the mantra "Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," [one should proceed].

Having prepared the vessel for the *bali* offering as before and having worshipped it, one should offer the *bali* as before with the left thumb and middle finger, reciting: "Oṃ Gāṃ Gūṃ, O Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, bring all people under my control; accept, accept this *bali*, Svāhā! Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for the fourfold offering of bali to Vaṭuka and the others.

Now, the characteristics of the *kulluka* and so forth. Regarding this, the Lord said in the venerable *Rudrayāmala*: "Having performed the recitation of the *kullukā* upon the head, one should contemplate the *setu* in the heart;
then, one should extract the pure *mahāsetu* in the thousand-petaled lotus. (1)
In Maṇipūra is Nirvāṇa, and Mahākuṇḍalinī is below;
in Svādhiṣṭhāna is Kāmarāja, and Rākiṇī is situated at the head.
O Goddess, O Śivā, having reflected according to the rule, one should meditate upon the Trika from the Mūlādhāra up to the Viśuddha,
[visualizing it] as thinner than a fiber of a lotus stalk.
For the place of the altar is the tip of the tongue, repeatedly encircled by the root mantra;
there, one’s own chosen goddess, who is one's very own form, resides incessantly within the powers of will and action.
"O Supreme Goddess, one should know [this] and recite the unsurpassed mantra.
The Śrī Devī said: "O Lord, what is Kullikā like? And O God, what is the Setu like?"
Or what is the great bridge like, O Lord, and what is nirvāṇa like? || 5 ||
"Or whatever else has been told to me— tell me, O Lord, what is its nature?
The Lord said:
O Goddess, this most secret of secrets is told out of affection for you;
without which, O Maheśānī, O Supreme Sovereign, everything is fruitless.
The goddess Mahānīlasarasvatī is the Kullikā of Tārā;
the five-syllabled [mantra] is declared to be the Kullikā of Kālikā.
O Maheśānī, for Chinnā, the eight-syllable Kullikā mantra consists of Kālī, Kūrca, Vadhū, Māyā, and the syllable Phaṭ, which is Parameśvarī. (8)
And at the end of Vajravairocanī, *huṃ phaṭ* is proclaimed;
she is considered the Kullikā of Bhairavī, the first [of the goddesses] who bestows prosperity.
The twelve-syllable Kullikā of the illustrious Tripurasundarī consists of the Vāgbhava seed-mantra as the first, followed by the Kāmarāja.
After that, the seed-syllable of Lañjā (hrīṃ), then Tripureśī, and thereafter the word "Bhagavatī"; at the end, one should extract the two Ṭha-syllables (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ).
One should employ the own seed-syllable of Kālikā, namely the *kūrca* (hūṃ), for the bride;
at the end, one should give the weapon-mantra of Lajjā (hrīṃ). This is for Tārā and Nīlasarasvatī.
But for others, O Maheśānī, the three-syllabled Kullikā mantra is as follows: having extracted Tāra (Om) and Kūrca (Hūm), one should thereafter extract Aṅkuśa (Aṃ). || 13 ||
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the Kullikā in brief.
O Beloved, that base person who recites [the mantra] without knowing this Kullikā [is lost].
He quickly meets his death, and the loss of his spiritual accomplishment occurs;
all that recitation is in vain and fruitless—of this there is no doubt. (15)
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Kullikā upon the head.
Now, therefore, I shall explain this; listen, O Priyamvadā! (16)
Without knowledge of which, recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites become fruitless;
for Brahmins as well as for Kshatriyas, the Praṇava is the bridge. (17)
O Goddess of the gods, it is said that for one of the Vaiśya caste the mantra ends with *phaṭ*, while for a Śūdra it is *māyā* (hīṃ); having thus recited this [mantra] of Sundarī Bhuvaneśvarī.
The seed-syllable of Kālikā is her own [seed-syllable], while that of Tārā is the *kūrca* seed-syllable;
for the others, however, it is the *vadhū* seed-syllable, O fair-faced one—this is the great bridge. (19)
Having first recited the Mahāsetu, one should then recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
such a person becomes equal to Kubera in wealth and like Brahmā in speech.
In battle he is like the God of Death, yet among women he is like the God of Love;
for him there shall be cries of victory at all times, without a doubt. (21)
Now I shall speak of Nirvāṇa; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should utter the beginning of the Mātṛkā.
Thus, O Īśānī, one should recite the mantra with the root syllable encapsulated during the inhalation;
that fool who does not know this [attainment of] Nirvāṇa is indeed base.
Even in a hundred million years, he shall never attain success.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, with every effort, [one should practice] whatever has been taught.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, the preceptor should recite the supreme mantra;
its seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (devatā), seed-syllable (bīja), power (śakti), and pin (kīlaka) [should also be established].
O Goddess, one should meditate with effort and then recite the *setu* and other [protective formulas].
If the practitioner of mantra recites the unsurpassed king of mantras in this manner, [he shall attain success]. (26)
Within six months one attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He himself is manifest as the sovereign lord of the worlds; of this there is no doubt. (27)
He is indeed worthy of refuge, he is truly a man of knowledge, and he alone is a knower of the reality of mantra;
he alone dances upon the earth and moves about as he pleases.
Merely by the sight of him, enemies flee.
Having thus performed the "entirely folded" (*sakalapuṭita*) [mudrā], one who recites the king of mantras— having recited the *kullīkānta* [mantras] that are the blood of existence— attains nirvāṇa.

In the same way, for them, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are in their hands throughout the entire world; the reality is in their speech, and their word is within every lotus of the lotus-like universe.
Thus: here, *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ* is the *kullikā* of Tārā along with her divisions.
*krīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ* is the five-syllable *kullikā* of Dakṣiṇakālikā along with her divisions. *vajravairocanyai hūṃ phaṭ* is that of Chinnā.

The *kullikā* for [the mantra] with its divisions (*sabhedā*) is as follows: *aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ bhagavati svāhā*. This twelve-syllable [mantra] is the *kullikā* of Śrī Tripurasundarī with her divisions, of Sampatpradā, and of Bhairavī with her divisions. Om.
The meaning is that the three-syllable mantra *hrūṃ kroṃ* serves everywhere as the *kullikā* (the unifying bridge) for other mantras and *vidyās*. For Brahmins, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) is the bridge;
for Kṣatriyas as well, it is that very same one; for Vaiśyas, *phaṭ* is the bridge; but for Śūdras, however—
The seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) is the bridge. *Krīṃ* is the great bridge for the various forms of Kālikā.
*Hūṃ* is the great bridge for Tārā. For others, however, *strīṃ* is the great bridge.
*Oṃ aṃ mūlaṃ aiṃ aṃ oṃ oṃ āṃ mūlaṃ aiṃ āṃ oṃ oṃ iṃ mūlaṃ aiṃ*.

The root mantra encapsulated by each individual syllable, beginning with *iṃ oṃ* and so forth, is called "nirvāṇa. However, some say that one should recite the root mantra *oṃ aṃ*, followed by *aiṃ aṃ* and the entire *mātṛkā*, ending with *oṃ* at the end, seven times in the *maṇipūraka*. In this matter, one should act according to the instruction of one's guru.

Now follows its ritual application: having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* with the root mantra, one should say: "Salutation to the Seer (Ṛṣi), [Name], upon the head of this Śrī Mahātripurasundarī-vidyā.
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) thus: "Salutation to [Name] Chanda in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī in the heart;
salutation to [Name] Bīja in the secret place; salutation to [Name] Śakti in the two feet; salutation to [Name] Kīlaka in the navel"; [one recites]: *aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*.

One should recite "Bhagavati svāhā" over the *kullikā* at the crown of the head seven or three times. Having likewise recollected "Oṃ" as the *setu* (bridge) in the heart; having likewise recollected "Hrīṃ" as the *mahāsetu* (great bridge) in the *sahasrāra*; and having likewise recollected "Oṃ aṃ mūlaṃ... Oṃ aiṃ aṃ 51 Oṃ" as *nirvāṇa* in the *maṇipūraka*.
One should likewise meditate on *klīṃ* in the *liṅga*. One should likewise meditate on the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) on the tongue.

On the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) at the crown of the head, one should recite: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ roṃ rūṃ raiṃ rauṃ raḥ ramalavarayūṃ rākiṇi māṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvasattvaśaṅkari devyāgaccha*.
"Accept, accept this worship! Aiṃ Ghore Devī! Hrīṃ Saḥ Paramaghore! Hrūṃ Ghorarūpe! Ehyehi! Obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā! Ḍalarakasahaiṃ!
O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī Devī, bestower of boons, Vicce! Thus one should meditate upon Rākiṇī at the crown of the head. Thus [it is said].
The Ritual of the Kullukā and Others. Now follows the procedure for the Consecration of Vitality (Prāṇapratiṣṭhā). In the Kulārṇava:
One should extract the Tāra (Om), Nārāyaṇa (Nṛ), with the Moon (I), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and the Aṅkuśa (Kroṃ).
Having extracted the seven syllables beginning with Ya together with the Bindu (Ū), one should join them with Viyat (Ha). (1)
One should utter the mantra of the Supreme Self known as Ajapā, joined with the Bindu; having extracted the word "amuṣya" (of this one), one should then say "prāṇā iha" (the vital breaths here).
One should again utter the letters beginning with *pāśa* (pa), numbering fifteen, which represent the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Then, one should extract [the mantra] with the words: "The life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such a person resides here. (3)
Again, at the end of the fifteen syllables, one should utter the word "amuṣya";
then "sarvendriyāṇi," and again the fifteen syllables.
May the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, feet, and vital breaths of that person come here and remain happily for a long time; [this is] the *dviṭha* [mantra]. (5)
Thus has the mantra known as Prāṇapratiṣṭhā been proclaimed by the wise;
consisting of fourteen syllables, this mantra bestows the accomplishment of all goals.

Thus: *tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); *nārāyaṇa* is the letter *Ā*; *sendu* means with the nasal dot (*anusvāra*), thus forming *Āṃ*; *māyā* is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī; *aṅkuśa* is the seed-syllable *Kroṃ*; *viyat* is the letter *Ha*; *oṃ svarūpa* refers to the nature of Oṃ; and *bindu* is the nasal dot (*anusvāra*). Therefore, it becomes *Hoṃ*. *Ajapā* is *haṃsa*, the mantra of the Supreme Self; and *so'ham* is [the mantra of] the individual self.
The *svāhākāra* is placed twice; in place of the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such), the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should be joined in the genitive case.

If one is performing it for oneself, the word "mama" (mine) should be used. Regarding this, some maintain that the fifteen syllables beginning with the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśabīja*) are to be uttered only at the very beginning, and not in other positions.

They say that at the time of performing rites for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*), there is no utterance of these [mantras] in other locations during recitation, worship, and so forth; for the *Śāradātilaka* states: "At every single word, one should employ the *pāśa* and the others in their entirety. In this matter, the opinion of one's own guru is the authority. Thus:
The seers of this mantra are declared to be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures say that its meters are the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is the deity, residing in the heart of all living beings;
the noose is the seed-syllable, power itself is the pin, and the goad is power.
The application, however, should be understood as being for the rite of establishing the vital breath (prāṇa-sthāpana).
[One should employ] Śrīkaṇṭha joined with the Bindu, and the Ka-group joined with the Bindu.
One should not utter the elements of ether, air, fire, water, earth, and the self.
The heart-mantra is Ananta (Ha) with the Bindu; one should utter the subtle [form] joined with the Bindu.
At the end of the *ca*-group, conjoined with the *bindu*, are sound, touch, and form;
then, at the end of those whose nature is taste and smell, one should place Trimūrtīśa together with the moon (*bīnduka*).
One should utter this "head-mantra" (śiromantra), which consists of the Lord of the Gods (the letter *i*) with the bindu;
then, having likewise extracted the *ṭa*-group [of consonants], one should then utter "ear, skin, eye. (12)

The mantra for the head is *Arghīśa* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*); the mantra for the crest-lock (*śikhā*) is *Jhiṇṭīśa* joined with the nasal drop, followed by the dental class (*tavarga*) in the same manner. (13)
To the self consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, and to the physical bindu;
[the mantra] consists of the armor-syllable (vaṃ) joined with the seed-syllable and bindu, followed by the 'sa' group (sadyaḥ) joined with the labial class (pavarga) and bindu. || 14 ||
Speech, grasping, excretion, movement, and bliss for oneself—this is the favor conjoined with the *bindu*, which is declared to be the Netra-mantra. || 15 ||
Having uttered the ten letters beginning with *ya* adorned with the nasal drop (*bindu*) at the end of the vowels of the lunar days (*tithi*),
one should then utter the word *citātmane*, ending with *manobuddhyahaṅkāra*.
This *visarga* is declared to be the mantra named "Weapon" (*astra*). Thus are the six-limbed mantras, beginning with the three seed-syllables of expansion. (17)

The mantras, joined with their seed-syllables (*jāti*), should be placed by the practitioners upon their own hands and limbs, extending from the tips of the two feet up to the neck, the heart, and the head. 18.
One should install the seed-syllables, beginning with the noose (pāśa), up to the throat;
then, one should meditate upon an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the heart-lotus.
In its [mandala], there are [deities] in the directions of wind, fire, and the east, as well as in the west and northeast;
and in the southwest, north, and south, upon the pericarp and the petals.
One should place the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*), one by one, excluding *la*; thereafter, one should meditate upon the Goddess in the heart.

Thus. As for its ritual application (*prayoga*): for this *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, [one offers salutation] to the sages (*ṛṣi*) Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva on the head; to the meters (*chandas*) Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma on the mouth;
and to the deity (*devatā*), the Supreme Vital Power (*parā-prāṇa-śakti*), in the heart.

*Namaḥ*. *Namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *Āṃ* at the secret place (*guhya*). *Namaḥ* to the power (*śakti*) *Hrīṃ* at the two feet. *Namaḥ* to the pin (*kīlaka*) *Kroṃ* at the navel. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should speak with palms joined: "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of establishing the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of this [deity]. Then: *Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Aṃ Kaṃ* (five times) *Āṃ*.
Oṃ Āṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ to the Self of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Iṃ Caṃ 5 Īṃ to the Self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

*Īṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ uṃ ṭaṃ 5 ūṃ* to the self consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; *ūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ eṃ taṃ 5 aiṃ* to the self consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.

Aiṃ, to the armor, huṃ! Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ oṃ paṃ 5 auṃ, to the three eyes whose essence is speech, grasping, relinquishing, movement, and bliss, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ yaṃ 10 aḥ, to the weapon whose essence is mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness, phaṭ!

*Phaṭ*. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras from the thumbs to the palms of both hands, one should also place them on the six limbs beginning with the heart. Then, from the navel to the tips of the two feet: *Āṃ namaḥ*; from the throat to the navel: *Hrīṃ namaḥ*; from the head to the throat: *Kroṃ*.
*Namaḥ*. Then, in the heart-lotus: *yaṃ namaḥ* on the northwest petal; *raṃ namaḥ* on the southeast; *laṃ namaḥ* in the east; *vaṃ namaḥ* in the west;
*śaṃ namaḥ* in the northeast; *ṣaṃ namaḥ* in the southwest; *saṃ namaḥ* in the north; *haṃ namaḥ* in the south; and *kṣaṃ* in the pericarp.

*Namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), [one recites]: *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ rho haṃśaḥ sohaṃ*. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of such-and-such a person are here; 15. The life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such a person is stationed here; 15. All the sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of such-and-such a person; speech, mind, skin, and eyes (*vāṅ-manas-tvak-cakṣuḥ*).

Having performed the all-pervading placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) three times on all limbs with the mantra *oṃ śrotra-jihvā-ghrāṇa-prāṇā ihāgatya sukhaṃ ciraṃ tiṣṭhantu svāhā*, one should meditate [upon her] as follows:
She stands upon a red lotus, which rests upon a boat in a red ocean; she holds a noose, a goad, a bow made of sugarcane, and arrows.
I bow to the Goddess, who is red in hue, three-eyed, and holding a trident and a skull with the tips of her hands. || 22 ||
Having thus meditated upon the Mother of the World and recited the mantra one hundred thousand times,
he should perform a fire sacrifice with sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee, consisting of one-tenth of that number.
One should worship according to this rite upon the Śaktipīṭha, which is enriched with six corners;
one should honor Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara in the six corners.
One should then worship Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā, followed by the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
On the petals, the Mothers (mātaraḥ) are to be worshipped, and outside of that, the Lokanāyakas.
In this manner, one should worship the Goddess with fragrant flowers and other offerings;
thus accomplished, the mantra shall grant the fruits of the six rites.
"The instructor should fix the vital breaths everywhere with this mantra.

Herein, the procedure for its worship is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement on the yoga-pīṭha (yogapīṭhanyāsa) as before, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, followed by the ṛṣi-nyāsa and the six-limbed nyāsa (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon the hands.

Having performed the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), one should draw the worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*)— consisting of a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure (*bhūpura*)— with vermilion and other substances before oneself; having placed it in front, worshipped it, and completed the rites beginning with the installation of the *arghya* vessel up to the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*).
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha, which extends from Maṇḍūka up to Paratattva, one should worship [the goddesses] upon the filaments: Oṃ, salutation to Jayā;
salutation to Vijayā; salutation to Ajitā; salutation to Aparājitā; salutation to Nityā; salutation to Vilāsinī; salutation to Dogdhrī; salutation to Aghorā.

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Maṅgalā," and having worshipped the entire pedestal with "Hrīṃ, salutation to the lotus-seat of all powers (Sarvaśakti-kamalāsana)," one should conceptualize the form [of the deity] using the root mantra. Then,
after performing the offerings beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with flowers, [one worships] in the six corners in front of the Goddess.

In the right and left corners behind the Goddess: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *oṃ rudrāyai namaḥ*. In the right front, the area behind the Goddess, and the left side: *sarasvatyai namaḥ*, *lakṣmyai namaḥ*, *gaurīṃ namaḥ*. At the junctions of the six corners, the limbs (*aṅga*) as previously described.

Having worshipped [the goddesses] on the eight petals, starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise, one should worship Brāhmī and the others as previously described; then, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons within the square, one should complete everything, including the incense, lamps, and so forth, as before. Likewise—
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru) at one-tenth that number;
thereafter, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
Thus, in the *Śāradā*: (23.62) "At the end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and at the beginning of these words, one should worship the female messengers (*dūtīs*):
Mṛtā, Vaivasvatā, Jīvahā, and again Prāṇahā. (1)
Ākṛṣṭi, Grasanā, Paścādbhramadā, Visphuliṅginī, and Kṣetrapratiharī—these are remembered as the nine messengers of the vital breath (prāṇadūtīs). || 2 ||
One should extract the life-breaths of the sādhya who has his movements bound by the noose (pāśa), whose mind is seized by the power (śakti),
and who is even dragged away by the goad (aṅkuśa).
Having fashioned a doll of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) measuring twelve finger-breadths,
one should place within its heart a life-force yantra together with an insect.
At the time of midnight, while the sādhya is asleep, [one should place the letters] in his heart-lotus;
thereafter, on the petals, those of Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa.
Within the pericarp of the lotus, one should contemplate the letters beginning with *ya*, joined with the *haṃsa*, having the form of bees, belonging to Īśa, Rakṣasa, Śītāṃśu, and Yama.
One should thus mentally contemplate them in the lotus of one's own heart as having the form of bees, their bodies bound by threads arising from the bindu at the crown of the head.
Having dispatched the female bees residing in the heart-lotus of oneself through the path of the breath,
one should cause each individual bee to bring back [the essence] from the heart-lotus of the person to be acted upon.
The mantra-practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure, should place [the effigy] either in a doll or within his own heart;
then he should perform the severing of the threads on all sides by means of the fire-seed syllable.
Then, one should arrest with the earth-mantra the bees that have been drawn from the hearts of the targets;
in this manner, one should perform eleven repetitions in all ritual acts.
The wise practitioner should visualize the [deities] as red for the rites of subjugation and attraction;
as smoke-colored for delusion and hatred; and as black for the rite of killing.
One who knows the rite of drawing in the vital breaths should meditate on them as yellow for the purpose of paralyzing;
having drawn in the vital breaths from the heart of the target, one should establish them within one's own heart.
In cruel rites, the placement of these [limbs] within a doll is prescribed;
one should place the vital breaths of the target as frogs and one's own [breaths] as serpents.
In that regard, one who is skillful should always remember [the following] for cruel rites:
with the letters beginning with *ya* written upon the petals of the deities Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, Rākṣasendra, and Indu.

Then, one should contemplate the Prāṇa-ātman yantra, which is situated on the earth, encircled by the letters, and is to be accomplished by the swan-like breath moving through the sense-faculties. || 14 ||
Thus, one who knows the mantra and is skilled in this application can subjugate all the gods; how much more so, then, earthly people?
Thus, having stated the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the specific detail is given in the *Brahmayāmala*:
"In this practice, the practitioner of mantra should daily offer nine oblations with flowers derived from the *japā* or *akiṃśuka* trees, or else with red lotuses, using the root-mantra. (1)
Having performed the oblation with the three seed-syllables, one should then offer oblations one by one in sequence.
Nine Prāṇadūtīs are traditionally taught, arising from the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *haṃsa*.
Mṛtā, Vaivasvatā, Jīvahā, Prāṇahā, as well as Ākarṣiṇī, Grasanā, Bhramadā, and Visphuliṅginī. (3)
And she is called Kṣetrajñahāriṇī; thus they are proclaimed in their proper order.
One should offer oblations to them in sequence, according to their respective names beginning with their castes and so forth.
The ritual application begins with: *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ mṛtāyai svāhā*, and so forth.
O Maheśvarī, I shall describe the meditation as it is to be performed during these applications:
having gone to the target and bound him firmly with the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśabīja*), O beautiful one... (5)

Having grasped that power by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti and having drawn forth the vital breaths of the sādhya by means of the goad-seed-syllable (aṅkuśa-bīja), one should always meditate upon her as bringing them [to oneself].
O Goddess of the gods, when the sādhya is asleep at the time of midnight, [one should place] Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa upon the petals of his heart-lotus.
In the directions of Īśa, Rakṣasa, and Saumya, and in the south within the pericarp,
one should contemplate the letters beginning with *ya*, joined with the *haṃsa* and having the form of bees.
One should thus mentally contemplate [the deities] in the form of bees within the lotus of one's own heart, their bodies bound by threads originating from the bindu at the crown of the head.
Having dispatched the bees residing in the heart-lotus of oneself through the path of the breath,
one should bring back each bee individually from the heart-lotus of the person to be acted upon.
The mantra-practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure, should place [the deity] either in the effigy or within his own heart;
O Pārvatī, he should perform the severing of the thread with the fire-seed syllable (raṃ).
One should paralyze the bees at the hearts of the targets who have been drawn in by means of the seed-syllable of the earth (laṃ);
in this manner, one should perform eleven rounds in all ritual actions.
O Dear One, one should visualize [the deities] as red for the rites of subjugation and attraction;
as smoke-colored for delusion and hatred; and as black for the rite of killing.
O Goddess, one who knows the rite of drawing in the vital breaths should employ yellow [mantras] for the purpose of immobilization;
having drawn in the vital breaths from the heart of the target, he should establish them within his own heart.
In rites of a cruel nature, it is taught that one should place their [the targets'] vital breaths into a doll;
the breaths of the victim are likened to frogs, while those of oneself are likened to serpents.
O Goddess of the gods, one should always remember [the deity] during cruel rites;
thus, O beautiful one, one skilled in application should act with this mantra. 16.
One shall bring under control all the gods, how much more so mortal men—those belonging to Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Śiva, the Rākṣasas, Soma, and the Earth. 17.

O Pārvatī, one should write the letters beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'da', followed by those from 'ha' to 'ṇa', joined with the *bindu*, upon the eight petals starting from the southern one; the letter 'kṣa' is to be placed within the pericarp.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having drawn [the diagram], one should write the two syllables "haṃsa" in its center, accompanied by the name of the person for whom the rite is intended.
One should enclose this Yantra of the vital breath and mind within a square,
using the eight substances such as poisons and others prescribed for cruel rites.

One should fashion a doll made of clay, twelve finger-breadths in measure, possessing clearly defined limbs and being exceedingly beautiful, and provided with the hair of the person to be subdued (sādhya).
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, one should place the life-force mechanism (prāṇayantra), written upon a cloth from a corpse and containing insects, within her heart.
One should cause the vital breaths of the target to enter into that [image] according to the prescribed form;
having cut it up, one should offer them as oblations at night in the fire of a cremation ground while recollecting the target.
By practicing this for seven nights, one may kill one's own enemy.
442) "With insects" and "with life" means that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the victim (*sādhya*) has been established [within it]. As for the eight poisons:
Hawk-feathers, fire, a lump of salt, the juice of thorn-apple,
house-soot, and the three pungents (trikaṭuka) are declared to be the eight poisons (viṣāṣṭaka).

Thus it has been stated. *Śyena* is a hawk; *śyenaviṣṭā* is [an image] inhabited by a hawk; *agni* is fire; *citraka* is a painting; *loṇapiṇḍa* is artificial salt. The rest is easy to understand. Likewise:
"The knower of mantras should invoke the *kalās* into the water-pot, the images, and so forth."
In the Śaiva and Gāṇapatya systems, ninety-six kalās are traditionally taught.
Eighty-five arts are said to belong to the Saura [tradition], ninety-four to the Vaiṣṇava;
seventy are proclaimed for the Śākta, and some say they belong to the Śaiva as well. (26)
The meaning is that some say that the ninety-six *kalās* of Śaivya should also be applied to the Śākta [system].
He states the *kalās* of Śiva: "In that regard, there are thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), and thirty-two in the systems of Kāma and Soma."
The messengers are nine; the vital breaths are ten; and the colors are nine, beginning with 'ya'. || 27 ||
I shall here describe the Śaiva kalās: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Vidyā, and Kalā. || 28 ||
Passion, time, necessity, the person, as well as primordial nature, ego-sense, intellect, mind, and then the ears and the skin; || 29 ||
The tongue, the nose, speech, the hands, the feet, and thereafter the anus; the generative organ; sound, touch, taste, smell, space, and wind. (30)
Vahni, Salila, Pṛthvī, Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, Manoramā, and then Manoharā. (31)
Manorathā, Madanonmādinī, Mohinī, as well as Śaṅkhinī, Śoṣiṇī, Vaśaṃkarī, and Śiñjinī. || 32 ||
The Sutas and the Sasvaras are proclaimed here as sixteen;
[the latter being] Pūṣā, Idhā, Sumanas, Rati, Prīti, and likewise Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and then Aṃśumālinī; Śaśinī, Chāyā from Aṅgiras, and then Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā. (34)
These digits (kalās) of the Moon, together with their vowels, are said to be Tuṣṭi, Amṛtā, and so forth.
The ten vital breaths beginning with Amṛta and the nine phonemes beginning with ya [are likewise assigned]. (35)
Ninety-six arts have been declared in the Śaiva, Śākta, and Gāṇapa [traditions].
Now I shall describe those called Vaiṣṇava; listen, O fair-faced one! (36)

The individual soul (jīva), the vital breath (prāṇa), the intellect (buddhi), the mind (manas), the twenty [senses] beginning with hearing, as well as the heart-lotus, and those called the sun, moon, fire, and Vāsudeva; thus [are they]. (37)
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and thereafter Aniruddha;
here Śraddhā and the others are to be known as solar—listen, I shall describe them to you. (38)
Space, air, fire, water, and earth;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; and the ear, the skin, and the eye. (39)
The tongue, the nose, speech, the hands, the feet, and likewise the anus; the generative organ, the mind, ego, intellect, and discernment—after that, primordial nature (prakṛti). || 40 ||
O fair-faced one, listen: faith and the others are to be understood here as belonging to Śakti;
these—Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva—are again [assigned] in reverse order. 41.
Furthermore, in direct order, all the principles (tattvas) are likewise [to be understood];
thereafter, faith and the others are proclaimed, and all the constituent parts (kalās) are thus described.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: in rites pertaining to the *saumya* (lunar) category, during the invocation (*āvāhana*) into an image or similar object, the practitioner—having performed his daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*)—should sit upon his seat before an image possessing the prescribed characteristics.
Between himself and the image, he should place a full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*) filled with all the ritual components (*kalā*) that were previously invoked on another day.

Having established the common base and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) at the end of recording the date and other details as follows: "I shall invoke the [specific] number of kalās that effect the presence of the deity [Name] within the image of [Name]"; then, [one should install] the life-force mechanism (prāṇayantra).

Having consecrated it with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra and tied it to the neck of the image, one should perform the invocation. As for the method of constructing the *prāṇayantra*: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus on birch bark or similar material using the eight fragrant substances (*aṣṭagandha*), one should write the letter *kṣa* together with the object of the rite (*sādhya*) in the pericarp, followed by *haṃsa*.
Having encircled the letter *kṣa* with these two syllables,

one should write the eight letters— *yaṃ* in the northwest petal, *raṃ* in the southeast, *laṃ* in the east, *vaṃ* in the west, *śaṃ* in the northeast, *ṣaṃ* in the southwest, *saṃ* in the north, and *haṃ* in the southern petal— and then draw the outer square enclosure (*bhūpura*).
Having encircled [the diagram] with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, one should write the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) in their respective locations;
thus having drawn the *prāṇayantra*, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with the remnants. Then, with the mantra of the deity of the *āhavanīya* fire...
Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the ritual application of the Ṛṣis and so forth, the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), and the meditations (dhyāna);

and having performed for the image the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) up to the assignment of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa); while touching the heart of the image, one should [recite] the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), substituting the name of the deity to be invoked in the place of the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such).
Having established [the deity] with the word ending in the genitive case and having recited the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra one hundred and eight times, one should invoke the *kalās*. For instance,
one should remove the cloth covering the mouth of the full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*) which is filled with fragrant water and flowers.

Having extracted a single flower from the midst of that [offering], [one should recite]: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ yaralavaśaṣasahoṃ*. "The vital-force-portion (*prāṇakalā*) of the deity [named] so-and-so, whose nature is the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*), is established here. 15. The life-force-portion (*jīvakalā*) of the deity [named] so-and-so, whose nature is the Śiva-principle, is established here. 15."
Having uttered: "O all the digits (kalās) of the senses of [Deity X], whose nature is the Śiva-principle, fifteen in number;

O the digits of speech, mind, sight, touch, hearing, taste, smell, and breath of [Deity X], whose nature is the Śiva-principle—come here and remain happily for a long time, svāhā!"—[one should offer this] upon the head of the image.
One should deposit [the deity]. In this manner, the sequence for the form of the Śakti-tattva, the form of the Īśvara-tattva, and so forth, is to be inferred.
Regarding this, the oral tradition (*sampradāya*) is as follows: one should invoke [the deity] by reciting the first *kalā* once.

On the second [lunar day], it is recited twice; on the third, three times; and on the fourth, four times. Thus, the recitation proceeds in sequence with an increase of one each time. As stated in another tantra:
"Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the lunar day becomes full."
The practitioner of mantra should likewise perform the invocation (āvāhana) in an auspicious image or similar object. || 1 ||
The extraction of the digits (kalās) occurs during the dark fortnight, beginning from the first day (pratipad);
it consists of the waning and waxing of the moon's digits, distinguished by the dark and bright phases.
Just as [the lunar day] arises according to the sequence of the lunar days (tithi), so too does the sequence of the days (dinakrama) occur here;
having correctly understood this from the Guru and from the scriptures, the preceptor (deśika) should perform [the rite]. || 3 ||

"He who acts without knowing dies himself, being of deluded intellect. Now follows the procedure for establishing the fire (*agni-sthāpana*) for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*): in the northeast portion of the place of worship, on a surface such as a pit or an altar smeared with cow dung, one should gaze at it with the Root-mantra and purify it with the Weapon-mantra.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, struck it with Kuśa grass, and sprinkled it with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should draw three lines pointing eastward with the Hṛdaya-mantra for the deities Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra,
and three lines pointing northward with the root of a Kuśa blade for the deities Brahmā, Yama, and Candra.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the *kuśa* grass while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should worship the *yogapīṭha* in its center with the mantra: *hrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*. Therein, having visualized the goddess *Buvaneśī* in her state of menstruation, one should contemplate [the seed-syllable] as the seed of Śiva within her womb, in the place of the domestic fire (*āvasathya*).

Having established the fire produced from a sun-crystal or other source with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having kindled the fire by blowing upon its mouth with *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ citpiṅgala, strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! O Omniscient One, give your command! Svāhā! and having made it strong with pieces of wood, [one should worship] Oṃ Agni...

"I bow to the blazing Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations, golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions. Reciting this, with palms joined in reverence, having approached and sat down, [one should worship] at the *liṅga* with "Oṃ *sarayūṃ*, obeisance to Hiraṇyā; at the anus with *ṣarayūṃ*, obeisance to Kanakā; at the head..."

*Śarayūṃ*, salutation to Raktā on the mouth; *Varayūṃ*, salutation to Kṛṣṇā on the nose; *Larayūṃ*, salutation to Suprabhā on the eyes; *Rarayūṃ*, salutation to Atiraktā on the two eyes; *Yarayūṃ*, salutation to Bahurūpā on all the limbs. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seven tongues, [recite] *Oṃ*.
*Oṃ*, salutation to the thousand-rayed heart; *oṃ*, *svasti-pūrṇāya*, *svāhā* to the head; *oṃ*, *uttiṣṭha-puruṣāya*, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; *oṃ*, *dhūmavyāpine*, *huṃ* to the armor;
*oṃ*, *saptajihvāya*, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes; *oṃ*, *dhanurdharāya*, *phaṭ* to the weapon. Thus.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [one should place the mantras]: "Homage to Agni Jātavedas" on the head; "Homage to Agni Saptajihva" on the left shoulder; "Homage to Agni Havyavāhana" on the left side;
"Homage to Agni Aśvodara" on the left hip; and "Homage to Agni Vaiśvānara" on the generative organ (*liṅga*).
Homage! On the right hip, homage to Agni Kaumāratejas; on the right side, homage to Agni Viśvamukha; on the right shoulder, homage to Agni Devamukha.
Having thus assigned these eight forms, [one should worship] the fire with *darbha* grass devoid of inner shoots.

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] starting from the east in sequence, with the tips pointing north and the tips pointing east, one should visualize a hexagon at the mouth of the fire; there, having worshipped the seven tongues previously mentioned in the center and in the six corners, proceeding clockwise from the center, and having visualized an eight-petaled lotus outside of that—

Having worshipped the previously mentioned six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon its filaments— starting from the tip in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Nirṛti, and Vāyu, and starting from the front in the four directions beginning with the East— and having worshipped the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) previously mentioned in the eight petals outside of that, proceeding clockwise starting from the East, [one worships] in the square outside of that.

Having worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons, one should worship the fire in the center with scents and other offerings, reciting: "Oṃ Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā! Then, having poured clarified butter (ājya) into a butter-pot that has been washed with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should place it there.

Having consecrated [the ghee] eight times with the root mantra, having rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while uttering "vaṃ," and having performed the *nīrājana* rite with two blazing *darbha* blades while reciting the *kavaca* mantra, one should cast those two *darbha* blades into the fire. Then, having kindled new *darbha* blades and displayed them over the ghee while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should cast them into the fire, and [then take up] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

In the absence of that, having taken two middle leaves of *palāśa* or two leaves of *aśvattha*, warmed them over the fire, swept them with *darbha* grass while reciting the *Kavaca* mantra, warmed them again, sprinkled them with water while reciting the *Astra* mantra, and placed them upon *darbha* grass, [one should then wash] the sweeping *darbhas* with water.

Having touched the *rāṃsū* and cast it into the fire, and having taken clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* ladle, one offers it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra "To Agni, svāhā! Having performed the renunciation of the offering with the thought, "This is for Agni, not for me," one again takes clarified butter and offers it into the left eye of the fire with the mantra "To Soma, svāhā! [Having performed the renunciation] "This is for Soma..."
Not mine. Again, into the fire’s forehead-eye: *agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*. Into the fire’s mouth:
*agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. Then: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, to Agni this, not mine; *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, to Vāyu this, not mine; *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, to Sūrya this, not mine.
Reciting "Mama | Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā | To Prajāpati, this is not mine," he offers four oblations; then, reciting the mantra "Oṃ vaiśvānara jātavedaḥ," he offers three oblations;
and with "I perform the impregnation of Agni, svāhā," he performs the *garbhādhāna* and *puṃsavana*.

Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter for each of the purificatory rites— namely, the parting of the hair, the birth ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the initiation, the return home from studentship, and marriage— separately;

Having offered one oblation each to the deities from the previously mentioned tongue up to the form [mūrti], using their respective names in the dative case followed by *svāhā*—such as *sarayūṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā* and so forth—one should then offer:
*oṃ svāhā*; *oṃ śrīṃ svāhā*; *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*; *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā*; *oṃ*.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ svāhā | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ svāhā | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye svāhā | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada svāhā |
oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me svāhā | oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me svāhā ||

"Bring [him] under my control, svāhā! Having thus divided the Gaṇapati mantra tenfold and offered oblations, one should again offer oblations four times with the entire Gaṇapati mantra. Then, having meditated upon the deity in the consecrated fire and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra—

Contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity, one should perform the oblation with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, using any one of the following— clarified butter, milk-rice, sesame seeds, rice grains, barley, or cooked grain—
and having performed the threefold application for substances other than clarified butter, as well as the application of clarified butter alone.
Having offered twenty-five oblations with the root mantra,
six oblations with the mantras of the six limbs, and twenty-five oblations again with the root mantra, one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter for each of the deities of the retinue.

Oṃ bhūr! To Agni and to the Earth and to the Great One, Svāhā! Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Intermediate Space and to the Great One, Svāhā! Oṃ svar! To Āditya and to the Sky and to the Great One, Svāhā!
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! To the Moon and to the Constellations and to the Quarters, [Svāhā!]

And "To the Great One, Svāhā!"—having thus offered these four oblations of clarified butter, [he recites]: "Om! Whatever [evil] was done by me previously, during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, while under the authority of the vital breaths, the intellect, and the body, through mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the stomach, or the generative organ; whatever was remembered..."

Having offered eight or one oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) with the mantra, "May all that has been said become an offering to Brahman, svāhā," and having worshipped the fire as before, [one should say]:
"I give sesame seeds with ghee for the sake of rectifying any deficiency or excess; oṃ hvaṃ, make [the rite] complete with its limbs."

Having offered one oblation of sesame seeds with the mantra "Kuru Svāhā," [he recites]: "Oṃ! You of a thousand rays, of great splendor, homage to you who assume many forms! To the purifier who consumes all and pervades all, let there be homage to you!
You are the performer of fierce and terrible deeds, yet you are the destroyer of the terrible; homage to you! You are Viṣṇu, you are the protector of the world."
"Grant me peace here," thus having prayed to the fire, one should fill the *sruk* with clarified butter (*ghṛta*),
place a flower upon it, cover its opening with the *sruva* held face-down,
grasp the two [ladles] together like a conch shell, and rising up, [offer them] with the root mantra.
Having offered three oblations ending with *vauṣaṭ*, having sprinkled the fire with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel,
and having worshipped one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) there with the root mantra, one should dismiss [the deity] into the circle of worship (*pūjācakra*) by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*,
transfer [the deity] into one's own heart, and after worshipping the fire, address it: "O Fire, O you of great wisdom!"

"O accomplisher of all rites, even when other tasks arise, please remain present with reverence. Having thus petitioned the fire, one should dissolve it into one's own heart using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
This is the procedure for the installation of the fire (*agni-sthāpana-vidhi*) in the *niyata-homa* (regular oblation).

The procedure for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) of Śrīvidyā has already been described previously (page 181, section 10). Now, the general procedure for the daily worship of all mantras is presented. Worship is of two kinds: that which is without remains (*anirmālya*) and that which is with remains (*sanirmālya*).
Mental worship is without *nirmālya*, while external worship is with *nirmālya*. As it is stated in the *Tattvasāra*:
"Worship is considered to be of two kinds: that without *nirmālya* and that with *nirmālya*;
[the latter] being performed with divine substances born of the mind, such as perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth. (1)
That worship which is without leftover offerings (nirmālya) bestows divine enjoyments and liberation;
it is performed with delightful sacrificial materials produced from both cultivated and wild sources. || 2 ||
Whatever worship is properly performed by devotees with the remains of offerings (nirmālya),
that very worship consists of flowers that are naturally fragrant as soon as they are born.
It is undoubtedly consumed by the five great elements, as well as by the sun, the moon, living beings, and creatures such as bees. (4)
Therefore, it is called *nirmālya* (the remains of an offering). In this regard, the authority for ascetics (*yatis*) belongs to the former [the internal worship]. As Agastya said:
"The worship of one who has attained *manas* is of two kinds: external and internal; for renunciants (*nyāsins*), the internal is prescribed. As for that which—
The yogi should worship with flowers grown in the forest even while mentally engaged in worship;
for the sake of Śiva, there is no violence in the destruction of flowers, nor does he become a perpetrator of harm.
But that [liberation] belongs to the ascetic who has conquered his senses;
by mere knowledge alone, the wandering mendicant— without oblations, gifts, and the like—
becomes liberated from all the demons of suffering, and not otherwise.
Virtuous women and householders, seeking auspiciousness through auspicious rites,
should perform worship with the necessary materials and offer parched grains and respectful homage.
If forest-dwellers and ascetics were to perform these consecratory rites every day in this manner,
they would not be exempt from the fault of transgressing sacred knowledge.
For it has been said by the Pot-born Sage (Agastya): "Those who have fallen after having ascended [to a high state] shall indeed become vessels of suffering.
Thus, according to this very statement, the lack of restraint of the senses in ascetics leads only to fault;
therefore, mental worship alone is prescribed for them. Alternatively, however, everyone possesses the qualification [for worship].

As it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "In the remembrance, the worship, and likewise the mental worship of Viṣṇu, there is always the qualification for all, even for those who have committed great sins. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere, however, the qualification belongs only to householders. As it was stated by Agastya: "For others, both are likewise. For others—namely, householders—both [types of worship] exist:
the external and the internal. Here, the internal sacrifice is described as being a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of the external worship.
It is not only because prohibitions are seen regarding mental worship; for he himself has said:
"O moon-faced one, a householder does not attain auspiciousness in this world or the next through mere knowledge alone, without [the performance of] gifts, fire-offerings, and so forth. (1)
If a householder were to give gifts but not even offer oblations,
who would perform this daily according to this rite? (445.2)
O beautiful lady, those who practice celibacy have no authority to give;
nor do forest-dwellers have the power, for such things do not exist in the Kali age.
"Who indeed would even wish to give [these] to all the gurus?
Thus it is said.
Herein, the scent of the flowers and fruits is sufficient for our success; what need have we of the mind and so forth?
Therefore, because it is unavoidable and because there is no other means [to achieve it], (verse 5).
"O Beloved, because of the limited intelligence of men, [the worship] should be performed with external flowers"—
this statement from the *Tattvasāra* indicates the absolute necessity of internal worship as a constituent part of that [external ritual].
"It brings about [the fruit] for householders. Therefore, for householders, external worship alone is obligatory, and that is fivefold. And it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Worship is declared to be fivefold in the *Pañcarātra* and other Tantras."
And these consist of approaching [the deity], taking up [the materials], sacrificing, studying, and practicing yoga. || 1 ||

In that regard, what is called "approaching" (abhigamana) is described by the ministers as the purification of the temple of the deity through sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other such rites. (2)
The material offering (upādāna) would be the union that accomplishes the worship of the deity;
thereafter, there would be another [offering] consisting of perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (3)

The worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha) and the worship of the deity along with the limbs and enclosures (sāṅgāvaraṇa), preceded by the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra, as well as the recitation and the glorification of the mantra. (4)
The thorough study of that scripture is declared by the ministers to be *svādhyāya* (self-study);
the contemplation of the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Self is called *yoga*.
Sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, sārṣṭi,
and sāyujya— these they know to be the five fruits, respectively.

Thus [it is said]. Since the description of all forms of worship would first occur through the description of *ijyā* (sacrifice/worship), the primary form of *ijyā* is now described. Regarding this, the venerable *Nāradapañcarātra* states:
"At the end of the night, having remembered the Lord Nārāyaṇa from His bed..."
Having risen, one should place the left foot upon the ground with the right side [of the body].
At the end of the night, during the final watch;
or, O lord of the people, having slept through the two middle watches of the night,
they rise during the final watch and contemplate dharma and artha.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhārata*. The connection is: "having risen with the right side [of the body] and having remembered Nārāyaṇa.
The mention of "Nārāyaṇa" is illustrative; the meaning is that one should remember one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
In the *Uttaratantre*:
Having risen at the end of the night and diligently performed his necessary duties,
he discarded his night-garment and put on two [fresh] garments.
Having sipped water and purified his body, he should then cleanse and smear the temple of the deity with devotion, together with his attendants.
Having sat down on a prescribed seat in a pure place facing the east,
one should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) according to the rules.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣis* and so forth,
and having removed the remains of previous offerings (*nirmālya*), one should then offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
Having presented the water for honor (*arghya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), one should indeed give the tooth-cleansing stick (*dantadhāvana*).
Having offered water for washing the face, one should give water for sipping (ācamanīya);
then, for wiping the hands and mouth, one should give a pure and auspicious garment.
Thus, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā (Chapter 24):
"Having risen in the morning, one should visualize a radiant lotus upon the head;
there, one should remember the venerable Guru, who has the form of a deity and resembles camphor in luster. (1)

"Extremely serene, adorned with shimmering ornaments, and graced by peace"—thus [is the lotus] on the head. "One should remember the pair of the Guru’s lotus-feet upon one's own head," according to the statement in the *Uttaratantra*. In the *Bhairavatantra*:

One should meditate upon the Guru, whose divine form is seated upon a lion-throne situated in the center of the pericarp of the lotus of the sky; he shines with the luster of moonstone and holds a sacred book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons;
he is clad in white garments, adorned with white unguents, flowers, and pearls, joyful, and possesses three eyes.
[He who has] the red Śakti seated upon his left lap, possessing a gentle smile and being a treasury of intense compassion;
[and she who is] richly adorned with red unguents, ornaments, and garments, with a smiling face and full breasts, resting in the embrace of her beloved.
Seated on the left, she possesses an exceedingly red luster, holding a playful lotus in her left hand. || 3 ||
One should meditate upon her as being two-armed and three-eyed, closely embracing the Lord from behind with one arm.
One should worship him with external offerings such as perfumes and flowers, or even mentally,
by means of his names established through convention and the praises of the Guru.
If one is ignorant of that, one should worship the gurus at the end with the word "namas";
then, being pleased, one should praise the Ācārya with hymns for the sake of attaining all perfections. || 5 ||
Thus it is said. Regarding the meditation on one's own guru at times other than the morning remembrance (*prātaḥ-smaraṇa*), the Śaiva Āgama states:

"In whatever form [the guru] was seen by him during the time of initiation or during his act of bestowing grace, meditating upon him with that same disposition, one should perform the daily ritual (*āhnika*). (1)

Thus, in the *Vaikhānasa-pañcarātra*, it is stated: "In that same manner, one should perform meditation accompanied by recitation (*japa*) daily by the worshiper during the remainder of the night, until the time of sunrise; the meaning is 'until the dawn' (*aruṇodaya*), because that alone is the time for bathing. Furthermore, in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:

Having divided the night into five parts, the practitioner should daily perform the worship of the deity and other rites during the remaining portion, as well as recitation, fire-oblation, and meditation. || 1 ||
Thus, in the *Uttaratantra*:
"Having praised in this manner, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within one's own heart; and, free from agitation, one should contemplate the identity of the Guru and the Deity. (1)
Having made a prayer for one's desired object, one should then request permission from the chosen deity and the Earth, following the movement of their breath upon that ground.
Having placed his foot [on the ground] and risen, he should perform the necessary bodily functions.

The verse of supplication will be stated hereafter. Having thus uttered [the mantra] and received permission, the preceptor (deśika) should practice purification (śauca). Thus it is said in the Nāradapañcarātra.
At every step, he should recite the Astra-mantra and depart from the house to a distance;
then the preceptor should bid farewell to the deities with this mantra.
Having thrown grass and clods of earth and struck three times with the palms of his hands, he said:
"Let the sages, gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas arise! (2)
As they were leaving their places on all sides to discharge urine and feces, having voided their excrement there and wrapped it in a cloth, [they departed]. (3)
(“Kaṃ” means the head.
He should not look at the sky or the directions; then he should go to a body of water.
Having performed purification according to the scriptures, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule. || 4 ||

Then, O Nārada—where "O twice-born one" (dvija) is an address to Nārada—one should eat the tooth-stick and thereafter bathe; having gone a distance from the dwelling equal to the range of an arrow's flight, for according to the words of Viṣṇu: "Having passed a space greater than the range of an arrow's flight toward the southwest."

Regarding purification, the Nāradapañcarātra states: "Three applications of clay should be made to the penis, followed by one application of clay at intervals; five should be applied to the left hand, and three to both hands for the sake of purification. (1)
After voiding urine, purification shall be performed; likewise immediately after voiding feces.
Five applications of clay should be made to the anus, followed by one application of clay at intervals.
Ten [applications] are to be given on the left hand, and seven on both hands;
purification of the feet is by three [applications], while purification of the shanks is by five.
Then, O Brahmin, he should apply seven applications of clay to his hips;
this removes the defect of perspiration from one's own body, O Brāhmaṇa, for the sake of the success of the rite.
Thus has it been prescribed for the rainy season for the devotees and the Kṣatriyas; however, upon the conclusion of the monsoon, there shall be a single removal of mud from this place.
Those devoted to ritual action should always perform [the rite] during autumn, summer, and spring;
even from this [number], one may omit a single application of clay at each [season].
During the winter and the cool season, a self-controlled Śrotriya, remaining steadfast,
should perform purification on the path in accordance with the requirements of place and time.

"By discarding the application of perfumes, the mind becomes purified through purity. Regarding the phrase "earth [applied] with one interval between each": first, one should wash the *liṅga* once with earth and water, and then wash the left hand with earth and water.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the *liṅga*: in the *Kapila-pañcarātra* it is stated:
"The purification prescribed for the day is declared to be half that at night;
half of that is prescribed for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey. (1)
Thus, Dakṣiṇāmūrti states the mantra for the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha): "One should write *klīm* at the end, then *kāmadevāya*, and finally *sarva*; then *janāya priyāya*.
This mantra, ending with the *hṛdaya* [namas], is for the purification of the teeth. (1)
Thus [it is said]. In the *Pañcamīśvaratantra*:
"For daily use, a tooth-stick made of *plakṣa* wood is for the purpose of killing."
For the purpose of enchantment, Khadira wood is prescribed; for immobilization, the sprouts of the mango tree.
For subjugation, one should use wood from the *aśvattha* tree, and for protection, that of the *vañjula*;
indeed, O Great Goddess, this sequence is not found elsewhere in the three worlds. (2)
Thus it is said in the Uttaratantra: "One should constantly wash the mouth with the root-mantra for the sake of attaining perfection."
Now, as for bathing, it is threefold, distinguished by water, mantra, and meditation. Among these, regarding bathing with water, the *Nāradapañcarātra* states:
"I shall first describe the bath for the sake of attaining qualification."
By means of which the devotee, once consecrated, attains the fitness for sacrifice and fire-offerings.
Having taken earth from a pure place with a ritual stake over which he has recited the mantra, and having visualized it with the Astra-mantra, he should go to a body of water.
There, first of all, one should wash the edge of the water with the water of the *astra* mantra;
then, having divided the clay into two parts, one should take one portion from there.
Having carefully placed cow-dung, Darbha grass,
and consecrated sesame seeds in the middle portion, which is the single worldly and secondary part.
"Having first performed the impurity-bath (*malasnāna*), one should then perform the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).

Thus [it is said]. "Consecrated by the *astra-mantra*" [means this]. The ritual bath is the Vedic bath. In the *Smṛtisamuccaya*: "One should not perform a clay-bath in the morning, nor should one perform it at night with cow-dung. In the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
Having first performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric bath;
having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to the body.
Having drawn forth the sacred water (tīrtha) from the glorious solar orb by means of the goad mudrā,
one should then perform self-protection through the casting of water with the Astra-mantra.
Having immersed oneself there, one should meditate on the Śrīdeva and mutter the mantra according to one's ability;
then, having emerged and formed the kumbha-mudrā, one should sprinkle water upon one’s own head.

The mantras for the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) will be explained in the practical application (*prayoga*). Having thus described the bath with invocation even at this sacred ford for the sake of an excellence of fruit, the *Vahni Purāṇa* states:
"O twice-born one, whichever water it may be, if a twice-born person bathes therein according to this rite..."
He obtains the fruit of a sacred ford; at a sacred ford, the fruit is tenfold.

Thus: one should sprinkle [the deity] seven times or three times. For it is stated in the words of Kapila: "Then, having sprinkled seven times with water consecrated by the mantra... and in the *Uttaratantra*: "Having sprinkled three times with the root mantra (mūla). Likewise:
"Then, in brief, one should satisfy the gods, humans, and ancestors."
Regarding the specific procedure for bathing, the *Tripurārṇava* states:
"Having performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric one;
having taken earth with the Astra-mantra and having consecrated it with that [mantra]," (1).
Having purified [the body] with the *śikhā-mantra*, one should consecrate it with the root mantra;
then, having smeared the body from the head down to the feet with that [substance], [one should proceed].
Having bound the *sammukhīkaraṇī* mudrā and restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
he should submerge himself and then rise silently while standing in water reaching up to his navel.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, the knower of mantras,
having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), should fashion a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in front of him.
Then, the knower of mantras should pray to the Tīrtha from the Sun; thereafter, having pierced that solar orb with the Sṛṇimantra and the Aṅkuśamudrā.
O Dear One, one should invoke the sacred waters (tīrtha) with the invocation mantra (āvāhana-mantra),
having joined them to the prepared mandala of the sacred waters with the root mantra (mūla-mantra).
Having invoked the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha-śakti) right there from the solar orb,
and having meditated upon it and worshipped it with its specific mantra, one should consecrate it with the Gaṅgā-mantra.

O Śivā, O beloved, listen as I speak seven times these two mantras: [the syllable] "ja" situated in water (the letter *j*), conjoined with the sky (the vowel *u*), differentiated by the six long vowels, and accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra). (8)

"In the one consisting of all bliss, the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha-śakti) is the pair of *ehi* and *dviṭha*. Here, water is the syllable *va*, and space is the syllable *ha*; thus, *hva*. This, when differentiated by the six long vowels, becomes *hvāṃ*, *hvīṃ*, *hvūṃ*, *hvaiṃ*, *hvauṃ*, *hvaḥ*. *Dviṭha* refers to the utterance *svāhā*. Likewise:

O Dear One, the mantra of the Tīrtha-Śakti is said to consist of twenty-one syllables. Here, the word "Śakti" is a vocative term because of its divine nature. The letter *ca* indicates the absence of sandhi (visandhi), as evidenced by the statement that it consists of twenty-one syllables.
One should utter "Tāram," then "Namo Bhagavati," then "Ambe," then "Ambike," then "Ambālike," then "Mahāmālini," and then "Ehyehi Bhagavati. (9)

Then, [the mantra] consists of the syllable *dviṭhaḥ* for Gaṅgā and Ambikā, who rest upon the matted locks of Śiva at the root of the *māyā* and *śrī* seed-syllables, which serve as the basin for all holy places without exception. (10)
"This Gaṅgā-vidyā has been declared with fifty-three syllables. (p.
448) Here, *tāra* is the *praṇava* (oṃ), *māyā* is *hrīṃ*, and *dviṭha* is the utterance *svāhā*; [the word] *ambe* is included because of its divine nature.
The rest is easy to understand. Likewise:
"Having painted [the image] of Bhuvaneśī and rendered it immortal with a drop of nectar, one should then envelop it with the Kavaca mantra, protect it with the Astra mantra, and consecrate it. (11)
O Dear One, having invoked the deity there along with the limbs and the retinue by means of the root mantra,
one should meditate upon [the deity] emerging from the two feet into the water.
Having meditated and remembered the sacred ford, one should offer libations with the root mantra while reciting the mantra;
then, having emerged from the water three times, one should put on two clean garments.
"Then, having put on [the garment] and applied the *tilaka*, one should perform the *sandhyā* rites.
The meditation on the power (*śakti*) of the sacred site (*tīrtha*) will be explained in the ritual application (*prayoga*).
Now, he describes the procedure for the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*) for those who are unable to perform this water-bath (*vāruṇasnāna*):
In the Nāradapañcarātra:
"O Durgā, that which must be done in the absence of water during cold weather," (1)
O best of Brahmins, O sage, for the sake of swift success in his journey, he remained untiring in his weighty duties even when misfortune befell him during the night.
Having washed his feet and sipped water with water drawn from a vessel,
he should then purify his place and the ten directions as before and sit down.
Having placed the weapon-mantra (astra) upon the palm of the hand, one should then perform the sequential placements (nyāsa),
beginning with the root mantra (mūlamantra), using the entire collection of mantras.
Whatever fruit is obtained by a bathed student at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa through mere bathing in water, devoid of ritual consecration— [that fruit is attained here]. || 5 ||
O Nārada, it should be known that the mantra-bath is ten times superior to the [ordinary] bath;
now I shall describe the meditation-bath, which is even higher than both of those.
One should meditate upon the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who abides in the heart and whose form is the mantra;
and [one should meditate upon] the stream of water arising from his feet falling upon one's own head.
One should imagine [the breath] entering one's own body through a subtle aperture;
by means of it, one should wash away all impurity located within the body.
At that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion and clear as crystal.
This bath is superior to [ordinary] mantra; it is remembered as being a hundred times more efficacious than a mantra-bath.
Therefore, O Nārada, one who is devoted with faith should perform at least one bath, since all ritual acts performed in the assembly hall (sabhya) are preceded by bathing.
"Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should first perform the ritual bath.
Thus it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
"With the mind, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), [one should recite] the root mantra..."
One should perform the mental bath (mānasasnāna), which is prescribed for all occasions.
Thus [it is said]. The phrase "lotus-eyed" (*puṇḍarīkākṣam*) is an elliptical expression; by it, one should meditate upon one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

As for the mantra, it should be one's own preferred one. Regarding the Śaiva tradition, however, it is stated: "Then, having made the sacred water (*tīrtha*) consist of the nature of Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*mārjana*) with that water while reciting the *sahitā* mantras."

From the Śaivāgama: "The Saṃhitā states: 'The mantra Vyomavyāpin, the five Brahmans, those mantras of the Śiva-gāyatrī, and Rudra—in this sequence, these are declared to be the removers of all sins; this is the Śivasaṃhitā-vidyā. Thus, [the first is] Vyomavyāpin."
"One should recite 'ĀM ĪM ŪM MĀ' and so forth, as well as 'Vyomavyāpī.
This Vyomavyāpī is proclaimed to be enclosed by the Praṇava at its beginning and end. Thus it is stated in the Nāradapañcarātra.
Then, having put on a pair of well-washed,
unwrinkled garments— or in their absence, a lower cloth together with a meditation belt (yogapaṭṭaka)— he should proceed.
"And one must never be with only a single garment," as it is said in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"Having approached the water's edge, [one should wear] two garments that are white and washed."
Having put on the upper garment, one should not shake out one's hair.
Thus it is said in the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
"One who has bathed outside, such as in a river and so forth, should discard the bathing garment below [the waist];
when one has bathed inside the house, one should discard the bathing garment above [the waist]. (1)
For the sake of purification, one should wash the thighs and hands with clay and water;
then, having wrung out the bathing cloth, one should perform the morning twilight ritual (prātaḥsandhyā).
"At midday, after the libation (tarpaṇa), there should be the wringing out of the garment.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Yāmala*: "One should wear two pure garments and apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) according to one's caste. Vasiṣṭha says:
"Having applied either the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) or the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), one should perform the twilight devotion (sandhyā). In this regard—

The word "vā" (or), however, establishes that the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and the triple horizontal mark (*tripuṇḍra*) pertain to different castes. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "The vertical mark shall belong to the Brāhmaṇa, and the triple horizontal mark to the Kṣatriya."
The Vaiśyas' sectarian mark is a half-moon, while that of the Śūdras is circular in shape.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the characteristics of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"He who has taken refuge in the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, the remover of the distress of those who seek refuge..."
One should always apply a trident on the forehead with fragrant waters.
