That which is Pradhāna, consisting of the three guṇas and having the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—by bearing that trident, one certainly becomes [that very Pradhāna]; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said]. For the followers of Śiva and Śakti, however, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is mandatory even for those belonging to the four castes.
Without the triple mark of ashes, one should not partake of water, food, or other such things.
Because it consumes all sins, it is proclaimed as "bhasma" (ashes). || 3 ||
Even after committing thousands of improper acts, he who bathes with ashes—
everything that becomes ashes, just as a forest is consumed by the brilliance of fire.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. Furthermore, the rule for wearing the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"The ashes of the Śiva-fire should be collected, or else those produced from the *agnihotra*."
Or else, food cooked in the fire produced at the time of marriage, which is pure and fragrant. || 1 ||
The dung of a tawny cow is recommended when it is caught falling from the sky—neither stuck, nor too hard, neither foul-smelling nor dried up. (2)
If it should fall, one should discard what is above and below and pick it up;
having broken it into pieces, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the undercooked and the overcooked portions, he should take the white ashes,
stir them with his garment, and cast them into the ash-receptacle.
One should collect the ashes while the fire has not yet been extinguished;
for once the extinguishing has been performed, the ashes become *caṇḍabhasman* (fierce ashes).
Thus it is said. Regarding the specific procedure for the removal of cow dung and so forth, he states in that very same place:

"Alternatively, having brought cow dung that has not touched the ground with the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should dry it in a vessel with the *vāmadeva* mantra and burn it away with the *aghora* mantra. (6)
Having extracted it with the *puruṣa* mantra, one should purify it with the *īśāna* mantra;
thus is the ash consecrated by means of the mantras beginning with "agniriti. (7)
Therefore, one should recite the mantra "Brahman" eleven times with the Yajus formulas,
using the names of the Lords preceded by the Praṇava, in the dative case, and ending with the word "Hṛdaya."
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, and belly with the syllables beginning with the five colors, and on the head with the five-syllabled mantra.
"The practitioner of mantra should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), being like a second Śiva in person.
Thus [it is said]. By the names beginning with Sadyojāta, the word "shoulder" (aṃsa) refers to both shoulders because of the fivefold nature of the names. In this context...
Regarding the application of the *tripuṇḍra*, the rule for the fingers is stated in the Brāhmaṇa section of the Jābālopaniṣad:
"One should subsequently apply the *tripuṇḍra*, which consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, having taken [the ash] with the three middle fingers consecrated by the root mantra;
or it may be done with the ring finger, the middle finger, and the thumb."
Regarding the *tripuṇḍra*, this is the speech of Śrī Śiva to Sanatkumāra in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Having taken up [the ashes] with the five great mantras consisting of Brahman, beginning with *Sadyojāta*, one should consecrate the ashes with the mantras beginning with *agniriti*. (1)
O bull among sages, one should not smear the forehead with a mere drop [of ash] so as to obscure the *tryambaka* mark;
three lines should be made in these places.
Beginning from the middle of the eyebrows and extending as far as the ends of the eyebrows,
one should place the middle and ring fingers in reverse order between them.
The line made with the thumb is designated as the *tripuṇḍra*.
For each of the three lines, there are nine deities.
The letter *A* is the Gārhapatya fire, the element Earth, the Self, the quality of Rajas, the Ṛgveda, the power of action (Kriyā-śakti), and the morning libation (Prātaḥ-savana). || 5 ||
Mahādeva is proclaimed as the first line;
likewise, the syllable *U*, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the element ether, and Sattva constitute the Yajurveda.
The midday libation (madhyandina-savana) and the deities of the second line, Maheśvara and the others, consist of will, power, and the inner self.
The letter *ma* and the Āhavanīya fire are the Supreme Self and the sky of darkness;
likewise, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the Sāmaveda, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
And Śiva is the presiding deity of the third line;
having always offered salutations to these, one should, being pure, wear the Tripuṇḍra.
This vow of Maheśvara is proclaimed in all the Vedas;
it should be practiced by people desiring liberation, for there is no rebirth for them.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or even an ascetic, whoever applies the triple mark with ashes according to the prescribed rule— (11)
One is liberated from the multitude of great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as from the minor sins (upapātaka),
and likewise from other offenses such as the killing of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, or cows.

"One is liberated from the killing of a human and the killing of a horse; there is no doubt in this matter," and so forth. Now, the method for applying the *tilaka* in another manner: "The consecrated ash [is prepared] with the mantra beginning 'agniriti'..."
Having wiped his limbs and touched them, he should take them up again with the mantra. || 1 ||
Therefore, one should recite the mantra "Brahman" eleven times with the Yajus formula.
Brahman is to be known in the forehead, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) in the heart. (2)
Skanda is at the navel, Pūṣan at the throat, and Rudra in the right arm;
Āditya is in the middle of the arm, and Śaśin at the wrist.
Vāmadeva is on the left arm, Prabhañjana is in the middle of the arm,
the Vasus are at the wrist, and Hara is said to be in the region of the back.

"Śambhu is declared to be the crown protuberance (kakud), and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is remembered as the head. Thus it is said. Regarding the method without mantras, the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā* states: "The practitioner, having again performed the ritual placement of the hands (*nyasta-kara*), should draw the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes. This should be understood as referring to Śūdras and others. In this regard—

The specific details regarding the application of ashes shall now be stated. In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra-Ṣaṭśatikā*, within the section on the worship of Śrīvidyā for the followers of the Śākta tradition, it says:
"And one who wears the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*). This refers to the wearing of the triple mark.

It should be made with fragrant substances such as sandalwood; wearing a beautiful *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead with Nandana-sandalwood, one should meditate upon You, O Mother, for it has been said by the venerable Śrī Dūrvāsas: "I meditate upon Your auspiciousness."
Now, regarding the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*): In that regard, the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra* states:
"Having sat down in a clean place, having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in succession with the root mantra, one should perform the purification (*mārjana*) upon the body. (1)
Thus, it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should consecrate [the self] with the root mantra;
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs upon the body, preceded by the ritual placement on the hands. || 1 ||
Having rendered the water in front of him immortal with the *vaṃ* syllable and the *dhenu-mudrā*,
the practitioner should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] three times on the head with each syllable of the Mātṛkā, from 'a' to 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu, using kusa grass and the root mantra for each syllable.
Then, having meditated upon the God situated within the solar orb according to the manual, and having taken up water while consecrating it with the seed-syllables consisting of the elements; || 4 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, those [syllables] are said to be *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ maṃ*;
then [one should recite] the root mantra seven times, and again three times.
Then, having placed [the water] in the left hand, one should sprinkle it upon the head with the right hand using the root mantra, while the drops of water trickle down.
Having embraced it with the remaining portion of that [breath] in the form of fire,
it entered, purified all the internal impurity, and emerged.

Having remembered this while inhaling through the right nostril, one should visualize a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) on the left side of the [object] located in the right hand, and cast it away with the Astra-mantra. || 8 ||
Having washed his hands and sipped water, the wise knower of mantras should offer three *arghya* oblations with the root mantra, and then with the *gāyatrī* and the root mantra.
One should offer libations to Śiva, who resides within the maṇḍala, with the root mantra of the Sun;
and having recited the Gāyatrī twenty-eight times, one should do so three times.
Then, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
the practitioner of mantra, having offered that recitation and dismissed the deity from the mandala, [should proceed].
"Having placed [the deity] within one's own heart, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, the offering of the *arghya* with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) should be understood as referring to a mantra that is devoid of the *gāyatrī*. Likewise, in the Śaiva Āgama:
The omission of the Sandhyā prayers must not be committed, for such is indeed the command of Śambhu.
An initiated person who is devoid of the Sandhyā does not enjoy the fruit of initiation.
One who has missed his twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) should perform the rites of the previous saṃdhyā during another saṃdhyā time, and then,
remaining vigilant, he should perform the rites of the subsequent saṃdhyā.

Thus it is said. In this case, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must also be performed. As stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "O Śivā, in the event of the omission of bathing, the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), or worship, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred times. Likewise:
"Having meditated upon the Deity properly in the water and having worshipped Him with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*),"
One should perform the libation one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. || 1 ||
One should satisfy [the deities] ten times with half of that amount, or again with half of that;
thereafter, one should satisfy the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures in their proper order.
Then, the knower of mantras, having worshipped the Lord of Gods along with his limbs and retinue once more, offers [libations] with each handful of water while reciting the respective name-mantra.
"Having withdrawn [the deity] into one's own heart, one should meditate upon one's own self as being identical with that.
Thus it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Then, taking a vessel filled with water in one's hand..."
One should go to a solitary, uninhabited place that is pleasing and free from defects.
Meditating on Viṣṇu, who resides in the center of the heart and whose form is awakened bliss,
one should not look toward the various directions, remaining silent with eyes closed.
Thus [it is said] in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"One should go while reciting the root mantra until one reaches home."
Having reached his hands and feet, he should diligently wash them and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, one should enter after performing a circumambulation.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Having sipped water, having attained purity, and having bathed well for the worship of the deity..."
Standing outside the altar of worship at a distance of four cubits, [one should meditate] with the mind.
If he is at home, standing at the doorway, he should mentally bow to his guru,
salute his own chosen deity, and also pay homage to the guardians of the directions within his mind.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that day or on another, if it cannot be removed by expiatory rites,
then one should indeed contemplate that sin with the intellect.
For the sake of removing that sin, one should recite two mantras;
these two mantras will be stated in the application [at 20.42]. Likewise: "When this rite for the expulsion of sin has first been performed..."
Whatever sin may be most firm, it remains far away.
In the past, one returns once more to one's own station through worship;
furthermore, whatever sin may be very slight, it goes to destruction.
"For one whose sins have been abandoned through worship, the desired object shall be attained in an instant.
Thus it is said. In another Tantra:
"In the morning, having washed the feet and hands and having carefully performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)..."
One should offer the arghya to the Lord of Day; the procedure for that is stated here.
Having prepared a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung,
one should then sit upon one's own seat using vermilion.
Facing the east, the knower of mantras, intent on devotion,
should bow to his chosen deity after performing three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with the Sūrya mantra.
Having assigned the seers and other [limbs] to it and meditated upon the Sun with undistracted mind,
one should worship him with the ritual services according to the procedure prescribed in its own Kalpa.
Having fashioned a square with water in front of the mandala,
one should place there a copper vessel containing water together with its support.
One should arrange fragrant flowers, unbroken grains of rice, *darbha* grass, and *dūrvā* grass combined with mustard seeds;
likewise, one should place sesame seeds, red flowers, and *dūrvā* grass.
Touching that vessel while reciting the Sūrya mantra one hundred and eight times,
and having consecrated that vessel, he should lift it up with both hands.
The wise one should offer the arghya with the Sūrya-mantra ending in "mūrdhānta";
thereafter, he should recite the Sūrya-mantra according to his ability with undistracted mind.
The best of teachers, meditating on the Sun submerged in that arghya water, and having remembered and prostrated, should dismiss the Maker of Day within the mandala. 9.
That three-syllabled mantra of the Sun should be consulted in its specific context (Śvāsa 29).
As long as the arghya offering is not presented to the Maker of Day day after day,
one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Queen of the Gods.
This offering of the *arghya* increases the longevity and health of men;
it bestows wealth, grain, cattle, fields, sons, friends, and wives. (11)
Bestowing splendor, heroism, fame, power, knowledge, prosperity, and good fortune—
having risen from that, one should perform the worship of the door according to the rules.
Having sprinkled the door with water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should worship Vighna above it;
to its right, Mahālakṣmī, and to its left, Sarasvatī.
And in the middle of that [door], one should worship Dvāraśrī; on the right and left door-frames, one should worship Gaṇapa and Kṣetrapāla, and then Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi in sequence.
Then one should worship Māyā-śakti, Cit-śakti, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā, as well as Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, in order starting from the top (the north-east). || 15 ||
Having worshipped the threshold below, one should then honor the door-keepers;
beginning from the western door, these door-keepers are to be worshipped in sequence.
Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Vṛṣabha;
after them, Bhṛṅgiriṭi and Skanda, and then Umā and Caṇḍeśvara. (17)
These eight are proclaimed as the gatekeepers of Maheśa:
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, and the one known as Pracaṇḍabala. (18)
Prabala, Bhadra by name, and Subhadra is remembered as the eighth;
these Vaiṣṇava gatekeepers are to be worshipped in this sequence. (19)
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and thereafter Vighnarāja. (20)
And those of smoky color are declared to be the door-keepers of Vighneśa;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 21 ||
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī—
these eight goddesses are the powers (śaktis) who serve as the guardians of the gates in sequence.
p.

452) These very [goddesses] should also be known as the guardians of the solar gate (*sauradvārapālikā*). This is because of the statement in the *Vāmadevatantra*: "Victorious is the solar day, consisting of power (*śaktimaya*), the ultimate limit of beauty. [The sequence is] from the solar (*ārka*) to the equine (*āśva*) and the cool (*śiśira*).
This is because of the statement in another tantra: "The body of Viśveśikā. Here, the meditations on the deities of the doors have already been described (in the fifth chapter, page 83). Likewise:
"Having reached the western door, preceded by three *tāla* [claps]..."
Having opened the door with the Astra-mantra, [he should scatter] mustard seeds and unbroken grains consecrated by that same mantra. || 1 ||
The wise preceptor should properly scatter flowers within the pavilion using the Nārāca-mudrā while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Thus, in the *Tūrṇāyāga*:
"The wise one, regarding white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers as the Nārāca weapon, should scatter them within the pavilion while reciting the Astra mantra. (1)
Thus, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Having recited again these two mantras, 'May the beings depart' (*apakrāmantu bhūtāni*), one should then scatter unbroken grains, *sidhārtha*, and flowers. (1)
The wise knower of mantras, within the pavilion, [should act] with the Astra-mantra;
the application of these two mantras will be explained [in the twentieth chapter]. By the Astra-mantra, which is a limb (*aṅga*) of the mantra one worships oneself. As it is said in the Pārijāta:

Having uttered the syllables *ha* and *ra* accompanied by the *visarga*, followed at the end by the words *astrāya phaṭ*, one should release mustard seeds, unbroken grains, and flowers within that interval. || 1 ||
In the *Tūrṇāpaddhati*: "One should provide a path to the left of oneself for those exiting. Somaśambhu says:
"Within the pavilion, the wise [initiate] with the left foot first..."
Having entered, [he overcame] the three kinds of obstacles situated in the netherworld, the atmosphere, and the sky.

"Having cast away the weapon-mantra and having uttered [the appropriate invocation], one should dispel the obstacles by means of the three, beginning with the striking of the heels. Thus it is said. In the *Tūrṇāyāga*:
"By three heel-strikes, one should dispel the terrestrial [obstacles], and by claps of the hands, those that move in the atmosphere."
One should dispel divine obstacles by means of the fierce gaze of the [divine] weapon. || 1 ||
"By striking with the heel of the left foot—

according to the words of Somaśambhu, 'One should strike those standing on the ground three times with the left heel'— and having duly dispelled the obstacles and covered the door with a cloth, as stated in the Uttaratantra."
One should sprinkle the interior of the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (arghya).
Thus it is said in the *Śrīkulārṇava*: "Having made [the ground] like the surface of a mirror by means of sweeping, smearing, and so forth;
[it is] adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, and the like, as well as garlands of flowers. (1)
The decoration with powders of five colors is considered this purification of the site;
one should worship the Vāstu-puruṣa in the southwest with sandalwood and other offerings. (2)

Then, by the command of the Kṣetrapāla, the mantra-practitioner should seat Dīpanātha in the northeast; thus [it is said]. The mantra for the petition to the Kṣetrapāla will be explained in the application (in the 20th chapter). In the Uttaratantra:
Then, with the mantra "Aḥ Phaṭ," one should enter the altar of worship;
one should consecrate the place for the seat by means of the four [purifications], beginning with the inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Having worshipped the deities of the pedestal within the altar there with ritual offerings,
one should then place one's own seat upon it, beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).

Thus says Āpastamba: "Having brought a seat for worship covered with cloth, antelope skin, and kuśa grass, and having sat upon it according to the rule, one should joyfully remember Viṣṇu and the Guru. (1)
Thus, in the Yoginītantra: "Seated upon a seat with the earth-mantra. The mantra will be explained in the [twenty] breath-exercises (*śvāsa*). In the Bhairavītantra:
The sage is said to be Merupṛṣṭha, the meter is declared to be Sutala, the deity is said to be Pṛthivī, and the application is for one’s own seat. (1)
Thus, in the Uttaratantra: "On a quadrangular seat, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī, as well as Durgā and Kṣetrapati, in the directions beginning with the southeast. (1)
Thus it is said. In the *Gautamītantra*: "Facing either east or north, seated in the svastika posture.
In the *Uttaratantro*:
Facing either north or east, with a restrained mind, one should sit in the Svastika posture or likewise in the Padmāsana. (1)
Thus it is said. In another tantra:
"The wise one should enter with the body straight, following the sequence beginning with the svastika;
he should place his own articles of worship on the right side. (1)
On the left, one should place a beautiful pitcher filled with well-perfumed water,
and on the back, a vessel for washing the hands.
One should place auspicious lamps ignited with ghee and other substances all around,
as well as a mirror, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan, and a pair of sandals.
"Having established them each in their proper place, the self-possessed one should consecrate them.
Thus it is said in the *Uttaratantro*:
"Flowers, food offerings, scents, and so forth [should be purified] with the mantras *hāṃ hūṃ phaṭ*."
One should gaze with the Nārāca-mudrā, the [appropriate] look, and the samaya. || 1 ||
When one has not personally understood the proper defects regarding flowers and the like, or the touching of what is untouchable, or that which is acquired through unjust means; || 2 ||
Likewise, the climbing of a tree touched by the remains of offerings (nirmālya) is entirely destroyed by the mere sight of the food offering (naivedya) and other such items.
Then, with the mantra "raṃ," one should touch the crest of the lamp;
that [flame], being free from the flesh-eating portion, shall be auspicious and bestow happiness.

From the burning of moths, hair, insects, and the like, from the consumption by carnivorous creatures, and from the utilization [of substances] produced from fat, marrow, and so forth in sacrifices and other rites; || 5 ||
All that which is of unknown form is a defect; it is destroyed by touch.
One should touch [it] with the Nārasiṃha mantra at the Devatīrtha.
Then, having observed the water situated within the pitcher and the secret [mark], the officiating priest,
holding it with his left hand, stood on the left side.
Purifying the vessel with the *ādhāra-mantra*, one should touch the water, [thinking]:
"Whatever contact with undrinkable substances has occurred here through ignorance."
Whatever other defilement might arise through ignorance regarding a vessel or water—such as from touching a corpse in a reservoir, or from collyrium and bathing—it is likewise removed [by this]. (9)
Indeed, those defects perish during the worship of the deity.
The one-syllable *Nṛsiṃha* mantra is to be understood in that context (*Śvāsa* 20).
As for the *Ādhāra* mantra: "The first syllable of its own name, joined with the *bindu*, the moon, and the *argha*."
It is stated by himself: "The first syllable of the name" means the first syllable of the *saṃjñā* (the personal name). In the *Uttaratantre*:
"Having joined the palms in reverence, having bowed to the Guru on the left side, to Gaṇeśa on the right side, and to one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in front," (1)
Having taken fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste,
the practitioner who knows the mantras should thoroughly rub his hands together and make them fragrant.
Having taken it in the left hand, churned it, and smelled it again,
one should discard it at a distance toward the northeast using the mantra that will be described hereafter.

The offering is made with the *nārāca-mudrā*. "The mantra-practitioner should cast a flower to the north with the *nārāca-mudrā*," according to the statement in another tantra. In the *Kālikā-purāṇa*:
"The practitioner [should offer] a flower with the Viṣṇu-mantra using the tips of his own fingers."
One should take it for the purpose of rubbing during the rite of hand-purification. || 1 ||
Having smelled it again with the nose, using the hair-seed produced by friction,
its abandonment should be performed with a serene mind, especially toward the northeast direction.
When this is done, there shall be incomparable purification of the hands;
the tips of the fingers become pure by virtue of grasping the flowers. (3)
By massaging, the two soles become purified;
by rubbing, the backs of the hands; and by smelling, the tip of the nose becomes excellent.
The sacred sites (tīrthas) come together at the tip of the nose and the hand;
the penultimate [letter] is colored by fire and the moon and joined with the void (śūnya). (5)
This Vaiṣṇava mantra is traditionally held to be that which is touched by the end of Rudra,
or likewise joined with a letter beginning with Prānta and ending with Vāsudeva.
That which is joined with Śambhu, Cūḍā, Śikhā, and Bindu is called Prasāda.
(Agni joined with Sadya and Bindu is declared to be the seed-syllable of the body hair. || 7 ||

The penultimate letter is *ha*. Here, the status of *ha* as the penultimate is due to the fact that the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) consists of fifty letters, and thus the second *la* is not included. *Repha* is fire; *sa* is the moon;
the void is the *bindu*; and the end of Rudra is *ai*. By this [is formed] Bhairavī.
The seed-syllable of Vāgbhava has been stated. The letter *ha* is at the end of the final [group] and the beginning; the letter *au* is at the end of Vāsudeva.

Śambhu’s crest is the half-moon, which is the nasal dot (*anusvāra*). By this, the seed-syllable of Prāsāda is established as *roṃ*. The seed-syllable of Roma is *roṃ*. The mantra "Agni" will be explained in its application. In the Nṛsiṃhakalpa:
Having performed the purification of the hands, the preceptor should then perform the three *tāla* gestures;
subsequently, he should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the root mantra directed upwards. (1)
"The fire generated by that [mantra] shall provide protection on all sides by means of the weapon-mantra (astramantra). Thus,
because of its connection with the three [rites] beginning with the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), one should purify the hand with the weapon-mantra.

This is because of the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*: "Manu-vittama" [is the mantra]. Furthermore, the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) is that which constitutes each respective limb, and not merely the syllable *phaṭ*. For it is stated by the son of the Jar-born (Agastya): "Having uttered 'Raḥ astrāya phaṭ,' one should rotate the right hand. Therefore, wherever...

Wherever there is a designation by means of terms such as "weapon" (*astra*) and so forth, there the mantras for the weapons and other implements that constitute its limbs are to be inferred; however, it is not merely the syllable *phaṭ* [that is used], according to the aforementioned statement. Nor, in this way, should one offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the Lord's lotus-feet with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*).

In such cases as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including the mantras of the ancillary parts (*aṅga*), because [the primary mantra] lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*);
for if one were to extract the mantras there, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as there is no factor to restrict the inclusion to only the mantras of the ancillary parts.

This is because the extraction of the ancillary mantras occurs immediately after the extraction of the primary mantra. In some instances, this is indicated by the term "weapon" (*astra*), and in others...

And because of the extraction by means of the word *phaṭ*. The nature of the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having covered the directions with the index finger, its tip flickering from the tip of the middle finger. And in the *Uttaratantro*:
"Having performed the threefold [protection] of fire with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and one's own mudrā..."
"With one's own mudrā" means with the *agniprakāra* mudrā; this will be explained later (in the 20th chapter).
In the *Gopālakalpa* of Sanatkumāra:
"Having sat in the *sukhāsana* posture and having performed *prāṇāyāma*..."
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should immediately thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The placement of the *mātṛkā* [letters]. In the *Uttaratantra*:
"Then one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
From the feet to the knees, there is a square [mandala] together with a vajra. (1)
One should contemplate the station of the earth (Bhuḥ) as being joined with the syllable *laṃ*, yellow in color,
extending from the knees to the navel, resembling a half-moon, and marked with a lotus.
One should meditate on the region of water as white in color and joined with its own seed-syllable;
from the navel up to the throat is a triangle, red in color.
The mandala of fire has the luster of a svastika and is joined with its own seed-syllable;
the mandala of wind, extending from the throat to the middle of the eyebrows, is black.
One should contemplate a hexagon joined with six dots and the seed-syllable;
it is circular, marked by a banner, extending from the space between the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should meditate on the sky-element as smoke-colored and joined with its own seed-syllable;
having thus meditated, the most excellent of teachers [should dissolve] the elements into his own body.
The beautiful stalk of knowledge has arisen from the root-stalk of the Dharma;
it possesses the eight petals of sovereign powers and the pericarp of supreme dispassion.
One should meditate upon one's own heart-lotus, illuminated by the *praṇava* (Om),
having visualized it as situated in its pericarp and resembling the flame of a lamp.
The practitioner, through the method joined with yoga and by means of the "so 'ham" mantra, should unite the self with the Supreme Self via the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
"In that very place, one should contemplate all principles as dissolved.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "the sin resembling a man" (Śvāsa 5, p. 87) has already been stated previously.
Thereafter, one should indeed purify this [body] by means of the sequence of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth.
Having restrained the vital breath by means of the wind-seed syllable and the wind itself, || 11 ||
With that very seed-syllable of fire, the wise one should burn the entire body;
he should contemplate those ashes as having emerged through the path of the wind.
Then, one should flood the entire body with the seed-syllable *vām*;
when the body has become complete and capable of the worship of the deity, [the practice continues].
Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved within the self to return to their own respective places;
thereafter, one should lead the self into the heart-lotus of the Supreme Self.
One should contemplate that, through the *haṃsa* mantra according to the prescribed rite, the body has arisen in the form of radiant energy, fit for the worship of the deity. (15)

Thus it is said. Here, some [teachers], having joined the *jīva* (individual soul) with the extremely subtle Śiva who resides in the lotus [of the heart] via the path of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*)—according to the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "With the *haṃsa*, preceded by the city of the Lord of the Gods"—[proceed].

Thus, having meditated with the mantra upon that primordial [power] at the end of the *nāda*, which has been cultivated through spiritual attainment, one should place the particle of the individual soul (*jīvakalā*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) into the heart. || 1 ||

Furthermore, based on the statement in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*, they say that the elevation of the individual soul (*jīva*) is performed with the *Haṃsa* mantra, and its re-entry is performed with the *So'haṃ* mantra; here, one should proceed according to the instructions of one's guru. Regarding the recitation of the seed-syllable of Vāyu and others in this context, they prescribe a number such as sixty-four. In that regard:

The specific measure [of recitation] is to be considered. In reality, however, the recitation of the seed-syllables of Vāyu and others extends only as far as the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of their respective functions. As it is stated in the *Kātyāyanīsaṃhitā*:
"Then, having lifted up the air with the wind-seed-syllable (*vāyubīja*), one should dry up the deity who consists of the elements by means of that wind."

"Having known this, one should abandon it with skill. Likewise, in the *Yoginītantra*: "One should contemplate that [the body] has been previously burnt by the seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*) on the right side. Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) says: "A worship performed by one who is devoid of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is like a malevolent spell; it yields a contrary result, just as worship performed without devotion does."
Therefore, this [work] is indeed necessary. (p.
455) However, some [hold that] by the venerable feet of Śrīmacchaṅkarācārya, in the section on Yoga—
Some say that because it has been so stated, this refers to the supreme yogi; however, that is not correct, because of the mention of transgression [for failing to do so]. In the *Śrīkulārṇava*:
"O Goddess, as long as one does not perform the purification of the body—which consists of the fivefold [purification] beginning with the station of the Self—there is no worship of the Deity. (1)
O Dear One, bodily purification is said to be accomplished through thorough bathing, the complete purification of the elements, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth,
as well as by all the ritual placements (nyāsa) beginning with the six limbs.

Thus [it is said]. In the *Uttaratantro*, after performing the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in this manner, one should then establish the vital breaths (*asūn*), that is, the undiminished life-forces (*prāṇān*). The procedure for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) has already been explained previously (in the fifth chapter, page 88).
In the *Trailokyasammohanatantra*: "Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)."

"One should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. The characteristics of *prāṇāyāma*, however, have already been explained previously (see *Śvāsa*, p. 94). Hereafter, having performed the *ṛṣi*-assignment (*ṛṣinyāsa*) and the other [assignments]—namely the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*)—of the mantra one worships, one should perform the *yogapīṭha-nyāsa*. In that regard:
Since it is impossible to perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of entities such as the seers (*ṛṣi*), one must perform it using only the words that denote them.
Thus, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; I shall place myself upon my head."
O Pārvatī, one should understand that the Paṅkti meter is to be placed at the beginning. || 1 ||
"O Supreme Goddess, one should place the young goddess within the heart.

As for the method of placement (*nyāsa*), it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: "O Goddess, one should place the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, together with the fourth [the deity] and the heart," beginning with "Salutation to the Seer," "Salutation to the Metre," and so on.
In the *Prapañcasāra* (6th Paṭala, verse 2):
"The Seer (ṛṣi), because of his status as a Guru, should be borne upon the head; the Metre (chandas), because of its nature as syllables, should reside on the tongue;
and the Deity (devatā) of the Mantra, because it is to be understood by the intellect, is always established in the heart. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the meanings of the terms *ṛṣi* and so forth, it is stated in the *Uttara-tantra*: "The verbal root beginning with the letter *ṛ* has the meaning of 'going' as well as 'attaining. The one beginning with the letter *ṣi* is understood to be consciousness (*vijñāna*), and he is its pervader. (1)
Regarding the perfection of form, the seer is said to be the teacher;
the root *chād* signifies desire, while the root *dā* and its variants signify giving. (2)
The *Chandas* (meter) expresses the phonemes of Manu because it grants the desires of both [the poet and the deity];
since it gives from the root meaning "to feel shame" (*vrīḍ*), the word for the deity is thus fully established. (3)
For it is said: "Because they declare that [the deity] bestows the state of Manu upon the practitioner.
Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 2, verse 113):
"One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*)."
And the heart, O Goddess, the head, the crest-lock, and then the armor. || 1 ||
One should place the Eye-weapon ending with "ṅe" followed by "namaḥ" and "svāhā" in sequence;
one should likewise perform the placement with those ending in "vaṣaṭ," "huṃ," "vauṣaṭ," and "phaṭ."
Thus, in the *Prapañcasāra* (Chapter 6, Verse 6):

"In the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon, together with the dative case endings, and by means of *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*, is the procedure for the limbs [of the mantra]. (1)
Thus: by the word *namaḥ* through the act of bowing (*natyā*), and by the utterance *svāhā* through the oblation (*āhutyā*). As stated in the *Śāradā-tilaka* (Chapter 4, Verse 33):
"The word *namaḥ* is prescribed for the heart; for the head, the beloved of Agni (*svāhā*) is used."
"Vaṣaṭ" is said for the tuft (śikhā), and "Hum" is uttered for the armor (kavaca). || 1 ||
"Vauṣaṭ to the eyes," it is said; "Phaṭ to the weapon," it is proclaimed.

This six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) must be performed preceded by the hand assignment (karanyāsa), according to the statement in another tantra: "Having first performed the hand assignment, one should then assign [the mantras] to the six limbs. Regarding this, some [hold the following view]:

Regarding the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*), they recite the assignments such as "salutation to both thumbs" (*aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*) and so forth; however, the authority for this must be considered. In reality, based on the observation of various tantras such as the *Jñānārṇava*, it appears that [this practice] is merely a manifestation of ignorance. As stated in the *Śāradātilaka* (4.31):
One should assign [the mantras] to the fingers beginning with the thumb along with their respective *jātis*; however, one should assign the *astra* (weapon) mantra to the palms.

This is done together with their respective *jātis*, such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth. By "limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*) is meant those specified in their respective mantras; thus, for example: *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śirase svāhā*.
The meaning is "by these and others. Regarding the definition of the *jātis*, it is stated in the *Kāraṇāgama*:
"Namaḥ, svāhā, vaṣaṭ, huṃ, vauṣaṭ, and phaṭ—this is declared to be the sixfold *jāti*, associated with [the mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Weapon. (1)

Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Then one should apply the limbs; starting from the little finger and so forth, according to the sequence beginning with the Heart. Regarding the sequence beginning with the Heart: "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the Heart), "Śirase" (to the Head)... [and so on].
The meaning is that it is performed in the sequence beginning with "svāhā. In the *Yoginītantra*:
"One should first utter the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by 'Māra' joined with the Bindu (Ṃ);
then 'khaḍgāya hṛdayāya' conjoined with 'namaḥ'—this is the shortest [form]. (1)
O Goddess, one should utter the letter *ī* from the *praṇava*, conjoined with the lunar disc; thereafter, [the word] "Sukhaḍga" should be spoken, and immediately after that, "Śirase. (2)
O Goddess, one should place the syllable *svāhā* joined [with the mantra] upon the index and ring fingers;
and the syllable *huṃ*, marked at its head with a *bindu*, preceded by the *praṇava*.
Then one should utter "to Śrīvajra," and after that, "to the crest" (śikhāyai);
ending with "vaṣaṭ," one should perform the placement upon the middle phalanges of the two middle fingers.
The twelve-syllable mantra, joined with the *tāra*, the two *bindus*, and the *pāśa* [syllables], ending with "kavacāya hūm"— this should be placed on the ring finger as well as the index finger.
One should join the letters from 'a' to the visarga after the Praṇava;
then [the mantras] for the armor, protection, and illusion, followed immediately by "to the weapon" (astrāya).
"One should place [the mantra] joined with the syllable *phaṭ* upon the two palms"—
this has been clearly stated.
Thus [ends the work] by the disciple of the venerable Śrī Govindācārya, the great Mahāmahopādhyāya and worshipful teacher.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter (śvāsa) in the Tantra named Śrīvidyārṇava, composed by the venerable ascetic Vidyāraṇya, disciple of the venerable Pragalbha Ācārya, disciple of the venerable Viṣṇuśarman Ācārya, disciple of the venerable Lord Śaṅkarācārya. || 18 ||
This first half is completed.
